papers.title: Subgraph-Aware Training of Language Models for Knowledge Graph Completion Using Structure-Aware Contrastive Learning
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained language models (PLMs) has recently shown a potential to improve knowledge graph completion (KGC). However, most PLM-based methods focus solely on encoding textual information, neglecting the long-tailed nature of knowledge graphs and their various topological structures, e.g., subgraphs, shortest paths, and degrees. We claim that this is a major obstacle to achieving higher accuracy of PLMs for KGC. To this end, we propose a Subgraph-Aware Training framework for KGC (SATKGC) with two ideas: (i) subgraph-aware mini-batching to encourage hard negative sampling and to mitigate an imbalance in the frequency of entity occurrences during training, and (ii) new contrastive learning to focus more on harder in-batch negative triples and harder positive triples in terms of the structural properties of the knowledge graph. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to comprehensively incorporate the structural inductive bias of the knowledge graph into fine-tuning PLMs. Extensive experiments on three KGC benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of SATKGC. Our code is available.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning pre-trained language models (PLMs) for knowledge graph completion (KGC) usually encodes only the text of triples, ignoring the long-tailed entity distribution and topological structure such as subgraphs, shortest paths, and node degrees. The proposed Subgraph-Aware Training framework, `SATKGC`, builds mini-batches from subgraphs so that hard negatives appear together and rare entities are sampled more evenly, and adds a contrastive loss that weights in-batch negative and positive triples by their structural difficulty. The authors claim this is the first comprehensive injection of the graph's structural inductive bias into PLM fine-tuning, and **experiments on three KGC benchmarks show it outperforms prior PLM-based methods**.

papers.title: EmoXpt: Analyzing Emotional Variances in Human Comments and LLM-Generated Responses
papers.abstract: The widespread adoption of generative AI has generated diverse opinions, with individuals expressing both support and criticism of its applications. This study investigates the emotional dynamics surrounding generative AI by analyzing human tweets referencing terms such as ChatGPT, OpenAI, Copilot, and LLMs. To further understand the emotional intelligence of ChatGPT, we examine its responses to selected tweets, highlighting differences in sentiment between human comments and LLM-generated responses. We introduce EmoXpt, a sentiment analysis framework designed to assess both human perspectives on generative AI and the sentiment embedded in ChatGPT's responses. Unlike prior studies that focus exclusively on human sentiment, EmoXpt uniquely evaluates the emotional expression of ChatGPT. Experimental results demonstrate that LLM-generated responses are notably more efficient, cohesive, and consistently positive than human responses.
papers.summary: Public opinion on generative AI is mixed, and little work has examined the emotional tone of large language model replies alongside the human comments they answer. The authors collect tweets mentioning terms such as ChatGPT, OpenAI, Copilot, and LLMs, feed selected tweets to `ChatGPT`, and build `EmoXpt`, a sentiment analysis framework that scores both the human posts and the model's generated responses. They report that **LLM-generated responses are consistently more positive, cohesive, and concise than the human comments** they respond to.

papers.title: Edgewise Envelopes Between Balanced Forman and Ollivier-Ricci Curvature
papers.abstract: Evaluating Ollivier-Ricci (OR) curvature on large-scale graphs is computationally prohibitive due to the necessity of solving an optimal transport problem for every edge. We bypass this bottleneck by deriving explicit, two-sided, piecewise-affine transfer moduli between the transport-based OR curvature and the combinatorial Balanced Forman (BF) curvature. We establish deterministic bounds for $\mathfrak{c}_{\rm OR}(i,j)$ parameterized by 2-hop local graph combinatorics, reducing the edgewise evaluation complexity from an optimal transport linear program to a worst-case $\mathcal{O}\left(\max_{v \in V} \operatorname{deg}(v)^{2.5}\right)$ time, entirely eliminating the reliance on global solvers. Empirical scalability benchmarks confirm these theoretical guarantees, demonstrating that the proposed transfer moduli yield significant asymptotic and constant-factor speedups over the steep polynomial scaling of exact OR evaluation. Furthermore, the tightness of these bounds is validated via distributional analyses on canonical random graphs and empirical networks, with the derived analytical bands enclosing the empirical distributions independent of degree heterogeneity, geometry, or clustering, providing a scalable, computationally efficient framework for rigorous statistical network analysis.
papers.summary: Computing Ollivier-Ricci (OR) curvature on large graphs requires solving an optimal transport problem for every edge, which makes it impractical at scale. The authors derive explicit two-sided, piecewise-affine bounds that relate OR curvature to the purely combinatorial Balanced Forman (BF) curvature using only 2-hop neighborhood statistics, which **replaces a per-edge linear program with a worst-case cost growing as the maximum vertex degree to the 2.5 power** and removes any dependence on global solvers. Benchmarks confirm large speedups over exact OR evaluation, and distributional tests on random and real-world networks show the analytical bands enclose the empirical curvature distributions regardless of degree heterogeneity, geometry, or clustering.

papers.title: Latent Algorithmic Structure Precedes Grokking: A Mechanistic Study of ReLU MLPs on Modular Arithmetic
papers.abstract: Grokking-the phenomenon where validation accuracy of neural networks on modular addition of two integers rises long after training data has been memorized-has been characterized in previous works as producing sinusoidal input weight distributions in transformers and multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs). We find empirically that ReLU MLPs in our experimental setting instead learn near-binary square wave input weights, where intermediate-valued weights appear exclusively near sign-change boundaries, alongside output weight distributions whose dominant Fourier phases satisfy a phase-sum relation $\phi_{\mathrm{out}} = \phi_a + \phi_b$; this relation holds even when the model is trained on noisy data and fails to grok. We extract the frequency and phase of each neuron's weights via DFT and construct an idealized MLP: Input weights are replaced by perfect binary square waves and output weights by cosines, both parametrized by the frequencies, phases, and amplitudes extracted from the dominant Fourier components of the real model weights. This idealized model achieves 95.5% accuracy when the frequencies and phases are extracted from the weights of a model trained on noisy data that itself achieves only 0.23% accuracy. This suggests that grokking does not discover the correct algorithm, but rather sharpens an algorithm substantially encoded during memorization, progressively binarizing the input weights into cleaner square waves and aligning the output weights, until generalization becomes possible.
papers.summary: Grokking, where validation accuracy on modular addition jumps long after the training set is memorized, has previously been linked to sinusoidal input weights in transformers and multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs). In ReLU MLPs the authors instead find near-binary square-wave input weights, with intermediate values only near sign changes, and output weights whose dominant Fourier phases obey a phase-sum relation that holds even for models trained on noisy data that never grok. Using the DFT-extracted frequencies, phases, and amplitudes from a noisy-data model that reaches only 0.23% accuracy, they build an idealized MLP with perfect square waves and cosines that **achieves 95.5% accuracy**, suggesting grokking sharpens an algorithm already encoded during memorization rather than discovering a new one.

papers.title: Knowledge Distillation from Large Reasoning Models to Compact Student Models: A Case Study on the John O Bryan Mathematics Competition
papers.abstract: This paper investigates knowledge distillation from a large reasoning model (DeepSeek-R1) to a compact student model (Qwen2.5-7B). Using historical problems from the John O'Bryan Mathematics Competition at Northern Kentucky University (2011-2025), we build a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) training corpus through a dual-agent framework. The dataset is used to fine-tune the student model with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on Apple Silicon hardware using the MLX framework. The base Qwen2.5-7B model achieves 64.67% accuracy on competition problems, while the DeepSeek-R1 teacher achieves 91.40%. An initial 1,000-iteration training run revealed severe overfitting, with validation loss reaching a minimum at iteration 200 before rising steadily. Based on this finding, we ran five independent training runs each limited to 200 iterations with varied random seeds to assess result stability. Across these five runs, the fine-tuned student model achieves a mean accuracy of 69.43% (std dev 0.17%) on the competition dataset, a 4.76 percentage-point improvement over the base model, and generalizes to 73.1% (std dev 0.18%) on the MATH-500 benchmark. We further study how response length affects answer quality across six reasoning levels (R1-R6): accuracy declines consistently from 69.43% at R1 (mean 220 words) to 41.9% at R6 (mean 31.2 words), with the two-person speed section most sensitive to token reduction. These results demonstrate that CoT distillation improves compact student models and that response length is a critical factor in mathematical reasoning quality.
papers.summary: The study distills chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning from `DeepSeek-R1` into `Qwen2.5-7B` using problems from the John O'Bryan Mathematics Competition (2011 to 2025), with a dual-agent pipeline generating the training corpus and `LoRA` fine-tuning run on Apple Silicon through the `MLX` framework. A 1,000-iteration run overfit badly, with validation loss bottoming out at iteration 200, so the authors ran five 200-iteration seeds instead; the student rises from 64.67% to **a mean of 69.43% accuracy on the competition problems (teacher: 91.40%)** and reaches 73.1% on `MATH-500`. A response-length study across six reasoning levels shows accuracy falling steadily from 69.43% at around 220 words to 41.9% at around 31 words, with the timed two-person speed section most sensitive to shorter outputs.

papers.title: Selective Knowledge Control for Continual GUI Agent Learning over Application Streams
papers.abstract: Continual learning is a crucial capability for Graphical User Interface (GUI) agents to adapt to evolving applications while retaining knowledge acquired from previous applications. Such application streams pose a challenging knowledge modeling problem: new applications often share underlying knowledge with past ones, yet also introduce specific knowledge that must not interfere with historical knowledge. In this paper, we propose activation-conditioned selective knowledge control, a lightweight method that achieves selective knowledge retention via neuron-level gradient manipulation. Our method maintains a compact historical knowledge state to protect highly activated MLP neurons that preserve previous knowledge. When a new application arrives, it performs real-time gradient surgery conditioned on forward activation. Concretely, the protected neurons are categorized into two types: unactivated neurons holding specific knowledge, whose gradients are truncated to prevent interference; and activated neurons holding shared knowledge, whose gradients are orthogonally projected to preserve stability while enabling adaptation. After each application stage, newly identified critical neurons are merged into the historical state for future learning. Empirical evaluations on multi-app sequential benchmark demonstrate that our method effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting on prior applications while sustaining robust adaptation to new ones.
papers.summary: Graphical User Interface (GUI) agents that are trained on a stream of applications must absorb knowledge specific to each new app without overwriting what they learned on earlier ones. The proposed activation-conditioned selective knowledge control keeps a compact record of highly activated MLP neurons from past applications and performs gradient surgery during training on a new app: gradients to protected neurons that are unactivated by the new data are truncated, while gradients to protected neurons that are activated, assumed to carry shared knowledge, are orthogonally projected so they can adapt without destabilizing. After each stage, newly critical neurons are merged into the historical state, and **on a multi-app sequential benchmark the method reduces catastrophic forgetting on prior apps while still adapting to new ones**.

papers.title: Dependency, Compression, and Synergy: A Unified Information-Theoretic View of Multimodal Learning
papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have intensified the need to understand how different modalities share, preserve, and complement information. Mutual Information (MI), the Information Bottleneck (IB), and Partial Information Decomposition (PID) provide complementary perspectives, yet existing studies often treat them as isolated tools. This survey presents an information-theoretic perspective connecting these principles as progressively refined views of multimodal information processing: MI characterizes inter-modal dependency, IB explains task-oriented information preservation under compression, and PID decomposes preserved information into redundancy, uniqueness, and synergy. We review 170 recent studies (2018--2026) and 12 foundational works, organizing multimodal learning around four challenges: cross-modal alignment, information-efficient fusion, interaction-type characterization, and scaling to multimodal foundation models. Rather than using application domains as primary taxonomy axes, we interpret healthcare, robotics, recommendation systems, affective computing, and wireless communications as empirical validations of these information principles. Beyond taxonomy, we organize existing multimodal paradigms within a single information-theoretic coordinate system -- the Generalized Multimodal Information Lagrangian -- in which they occupy exact or approximate parameter corners, and whose unoccupied regions name candidate method families the literature has not yet built. We further discuss how emerging multimodal foundation models instantiate these principles at scale and identify open challenges including scalable information estimation in high-dimensional settings, standardized evaluation across information-theoretic methods, combinatorial complexity of multimodal PID, and the transition from post-hoc information analysis toward information-aware multimodal learning.
papers.summary: Mutual Information (MI), the Information Bottleneck (IB), and Partial Information Decomposition (PID) are usually applied to multimodal learning as separate tools. This survey of **170 recent studies from 2018 to 2026 plus 12 foundational works** presents them as progressively refined views: MI measures inter-modal dependency, IB explains task-driven compression, and PID splits retained information into redundancy, uniqueness, and synergy, with the literature organized around cross-modal alignment, information-efficient fusion, interaction-type characterization, and scaling to foundation models. The authors place existing paradigms within a single Generalized Multimodal Information Lagrangian whose unoccupied parameter corners point to method families not yet built, and they treat application domains such as healthcare and robotics as empirical validations of the information principles rather than as taxonomy axes.

papers.title: MRFlow: Mechanism-Structured Residual Flow Matching for Virtual Cell Perturbation Prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting cellular responses to chemical and genetic perturbations is a central test for AI virtual cells, yet many single-cell models reduce each condition to an average expression shift. This target is misaligned with perturbation biology: rare states, resistant subpopulations, and context-dependent effect sizes may coexist under the same intervention. MRFlow treats virtual-cell prediction as conditional transport between empirical single-cell measures. Control and perturbed cells are embedded in a variational latent state space, greedy low-cost supervision is constructed over detached minibatch states, and a conditional flow-matching vector field transports control populations toward perturbed populations. The field decomposes into a mechanism-structured affine dictionary, which recombines shared latent response operators with a low-rank condition-specific correction, and a spectrally controlled residual field for nonlinear cell-level variation. Genetic perturbations are encoded through a regulatory-graph GCN, chemical perturbations through Morgan fingerprints, and both enter the same conditional dynamics interface. Across eight gene and drug perturbation benchmarks, MRFlow attains the highest composite score while preserving competitive raw performance on differential-expression and distributional metrics. The results support latent distribution transport as a principled and empirically effective formulation for perturbation-aware virtual cell modeling.
papers.summary: Many single-cell perturbation models predict only the average expression shift for a condition, which misses rare states, resistant subpopulations, and context-dependent effect sizes. `MRFlow` instead treats the problem as conditional transport between empirical cell populations: control and perturbed cells are embedded in a variational latent space, and a conditional flow-matching vector field moves the control distribution toward the perturbed one, decomposed into a mechanism-structured affine dictionary of shared response operators with low-rank condition-specific corrections plus a spectrally controlled residual field for nonlinear variation. Genetic perturbations enter through a regulatory-graph GCN and chemical ones through Morgan fingerprints, and **across eight gene and drug perturbation benchmarks the model reaches the highest composite score** while staying competitive on differential-expression and distributional metrics.

papers.title: Predict Before You Modify: Learning Improvement Dynamics for Self-Evolving Agents
papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents improve through repeated cycles of modification and evaluation. However, existing methods receive feedback on modifications only after costly evaluations, and aggregate scores may obscure distinctions between failures that require different repairs. We introduce predictive self-evolution through an editable Improvement Dynamics Model (IDM). Before evaluation, the IDM predicts task-level outcomes of a proposed modification and guides an optional revision. After evaluation, past modifications and their observed outcomes are used to improve the IDM, allowing predictive knowledge to accumulate across generations. The system can thus improve how it solves tasks, proposes modifications, and predicts their effects. Building on HyperAgents, we evaluate this approach across multilingual coding, paper review, robotics reward design, and Olympiad-level mathematical grading. Our approach outperforms HyperAgents across all four domains, with up to 46% higher average performance over generations. Gains also persist under matched token budgets that include both agent evolution and task evaluation, and extend to held-out tasks. Forecast accuracy improves as the IDM evolves, and the learned predictive knowledge transfers to improve evolution in a new domain.
papers.summary: Self-evolving agents iterate by proposing a modification and then running an expensive evaluation, and aggregate scores hide which specific failures a modification would fix. The authors add an editable Improvement Dynamics Model (IDM) that forecasts task-level outcomes of a proposed change before evaluation and can trigger a revision; after evaluation, the observed results are fed back to refine the IDM so predictive knowledge accumulates across generations. Built on `HyperAgents` and tested on multilingual coding, paper review, robotics reward design, and Olympiad-level math grading, the approach **beats HyperAgents in all four domains with up to 46% higher average performance over generations**, holds under matched token budgets, generalizes to held-out tasks, and transfers its learned dynamics to a new domain.

papers.title: Posterior Flow Matching
papers.abstract: Flow matching learns how to transport noise toward data, but its mean prediction does not directly report the endpoint uncertainty remaining at an intermediate state. This paper introduces Posterior Flow Matching (PFM), a general generative modeling framework that learns conditional velocity means and componentwise variances with a Gaussian posterior model. The same model evaluation supplies both a transport prediction and endpoint uncertainty, making posterior diagnostics available throughout generation. These learned moments support a mean-driven ordinary differential equation (ODE) and a posterior-driven stochastic differential equation (SDE), whose local noise scales adapt to the predicted uncertainty. Across image, point-cloud, molecular, and action generation, PFM improves generation quality and provides endpoint-posterior readouts throughout generation.
papers.summary: Standard flow matching learns to transport noise toward data, but its mean velocity prediction says nothing about how uncertain the final endpoint still is at an intermediate state. The proposed framework fits a Gaussian posterior that outputs both conditional velocity means and componentwise variances in a single model evaluation, so every step of generation comes with an endpoint uncertainty readout. These moments drive both a mean-based ordinary differential equation (ODE) sampler and a posterior-driven stochastic differential equation (SDE) sampler whose local noise adapts to predicted uncertainty, and **across image, point-cloud, molecular, and action generation the method improves sample quality** while exposing posterior diagnostics throughout.

papers.title: GameSmith: Scaling Zero-Sum Self-Play with Synthesised Games
papers.abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) on two-player zero-sum games provides a verifiable reward, and the gains have been shown to transfer to general reasoning. Existing pipelines, however, rely on a handful of hand-written games and on advantage estimators tied to them, so both the supply of games and the advantage estimate on a large corpus limit scaling. We present GameSmith, which scales both. An LLM synthesises games inside templates whose reward, observation, and hidden-information code is fixed. Each game is verified by seed-paired replay and by an independent re-implementation of its specification, then expanded into encoding, rule, and size variants, giving 26 new games in 29 families and 336 verified variants from the three SPIRAL templates. The model is distilled from the self-play of a larger teacher (Qwen3-32B) on these games and then trained by self-play reinforcement learning with CRAB, an advantage estimator that credits each decision against a shrinkage estimate of the expected return of its position and is defined on every variant. On Qwen3-4B-Base, distillation raises the 13-benchmark mean pass@1 from 45.5 to 62.5, above the three SPIRAL games at the same budget, and self-play with CRAB reaches 64.9. The ordering holds across models, and transfer grows with the number of game families.
papers.summary: Post-training large language models (LLMs) through self-play on two-player zero-sum games gives verifiable rewards that transfer to general reasoning, but existing pipelines rely on a few hand-written games and advantage estimators tied to them. `GameSmith` has an LLM synthesize new games inside the three `SPIRAL` templates with fixed reward, observation, and hidden-information code, verifies each with seed-paired replay and an independent re-implementation, and expands them into encoding, rule, and size variants, producing 26 new games in 29 families and 336 verified variants. A student is first distilled from `Qwen3-32B` self-play on these games and then trained with self-play reinforcement learning using `CRAB`, an advantage estimator that scores each decision against a shrinkage estimate of its position's expected return; on `Qwen3-4B-Base`, **distillation lifts the 13-benchmark mean pass@1 from 45.5 to 62.5 and self-play with CRAB reaches 64.9**, with transfer growing as more game families are added.

papers.title: Splicing Hints into Reasoning Traces: Learning from Demonstrator Failures
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves mathematical reasoning when a final answer can be checked, but a correct answer does not certify the derivation behind it, and proof problems offer no answer to check. Replacing the check with a reasoning model as an in-loop verifier faces a fundamental obstacle: the policy must already produce occasional correct attempts for any reward to exist, which it may never do at olympiad level. We instead move verification and repair out of the training loop and into offline data generation with SPLICE, a workflow in which a second model, given only a reference solution, edits a reasoning model's traces as they are generated: it verifies progress, truncates a failed trace at its last verified step, and splices in an adaptively strengthened hint until progress resumes. The resulting dataset includes repaired examples whose sampled unaided trajectory failed, with failed continuations removed and progress repeatedly checked against the reference solution. A model finetuned on SPLICE traces outperforms the same model distilled from the reasoning model's unedited traces on AIME and, under a grading protocol validated against human grades, on olympiad proofs. The trained model's own traces show a corresponding behavioral signature: at difficult points it announces a branch in the style of the spliced hints and takes riskier steps, with predictive entropy rising there and just after, a pattern absent from the model trained on unedited traces.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards works when a final answer can be checked, but it cannot certify a derivation and offers nothing for proof problems, and using a reasoning model as an in-loop verifier fails when the policy never produces a correct attempt. `SPLICE` moves verification and repair into offline data generation: a second model with access to a reference solution monitors a reasoning model's trace as it is produced, truncates it at the last verified step when it fails, and splices in a progressively stronger hint until progress resumes, yielding repaired traces for problems the unaided model got wrong. A model fine-tuned on these traces **outperforms the same model distilled from unedited traces on `AIME` and on olympiad proofs** under a human-validated grading protocol, and its own outputs show the hint-like branching behavior with rising predictive entropy at hard points.

papers.title: SharedSAE: a unified sparse dictionary across u-net blocks and denoising time for diffusion models
papers.abstract: Concept representations in diffusion models drift across network depth and denoising time, yet existing sparse autoencoders offer only per-block or per-timestep dictionaries, leaving no single feature dictionary for localization and intervention in the network. We present Shared Sparse Autoencoder (SharedSAE), which learns one sparse dictionary shared across four U-Net attention blocks and all 50 denoising steps of SDXL 1.0. A block-specific low-rank input adapter aligns the residual distribution of each block before the shared encoder, and a temporal conditioning module with a shared timestep branch and a block-timestep correction branch absorbs temporal non-stationarity. Despite spanning both axes, Shared SAE preserves a coherent dictionary structure. Built on the shared dictionary, localized feature suppression reduces the number of NudeNet-positive generations in the I2P detector-positive subset from 139 to 1. Tracing sparse features across the trajectory further reveals that concept representations are redistributed across U-Net blocks during generation, shifting from the earliest downsampling block toward intermediate and later blocks as denoising proceeds. SharedSAE thus provides a unified, interpretable, and intervention-ready representation space for diffusion models, enabling concept analysis and erasure at any covered block and denoising step.
papers.summary: Concept representations in diffusion models shift across network depth and denoising time, but existing sparse autoencoders provide only per-block or per-timestep dictionaries, so there is no single feature space for localizing and intervening on concepts. The Shared Sparse Autoencoder learns one dictionary across four U-Net attention blocks and all 50 denoising steps of `SDXL 1.0`, using a block-specific low-rank input adapter to align residual distributions and a temporal conditioning module with shared and block-specific timestep branches. Suppressing features in this shared dictionary **cuts NudeNet-positive generations on the detector-positive subset of `I2P` from 139 to 1**, and tracing features along the trajectory shows concept representations migrate from the earliest downsampling block toward intermediate and later blocks as denoising proceeds.

papers.title: Enhanced Trading Systems with Intelligent Market Analysis
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a hybrid reinforcement learning trading framework integrating intraday market data with transformer-based financial sentiment signals. The system extracts sentiment dynamics and semantic event clusters from financial news and incorporates them into a PPO-based trading agent. Experiments on intraday NSE data demonstrate improved risk-adjusted returns compared to price-only baselines.
papers.summary: The system combines intraday market data with sentiment signals from financial news to drive a reinforcement learning trading agent. Transformer-based models extract sentiment dynamics and semantic event clusters from news, which are fed as features into a `PPO`-based policy, and **experiments on intraday NSE data show better risk-adjusted returns than price-only baselines**.

papers.title: SemTree: Judge-Aware Semantic Decision Trees for Inspectable and Repairable Rule Decisions
papers.abstract: Rule decisions such as content moderation, advertising compliance, and eligibility checks combine several conditions, exemptions, and missing-information cases, and an error can be fixed only once the failing condition is known. We introduce SemTree, a framework that represents a rule decision as a semantic decision tree: each node is a natural-language question with explicit Yes/No/Unknown criteria, a pluggable semantic judge answers it, and the branching structure is compiled on the answers that this judge actually gives. The executed path is the reasoning behind every decision, so errors are repaired where they occur: a reviewer corrects a single node and replays the rule, corrected nodes become training labels for the judge, and a tool-using LLM editor revises questions and subtrees while observing execution results. On all 8,276 ShARC test cases, a tree executed by a hosted judge reaches 67.70% accuracy with 2.99 questions per case, on par with asking the same judge for the final label (68.23%); an earlier tree compiled for a different judge scores 47.87% when executed by this judge, while a new tree compiled on this judge's answers to a 12-question initial pool already scores 64.39%. Node-level repair raises BANKING77 accuracy from 82.04% to 86.16%, an explicit exemption node cuts the false positives of a Chinese e-commerce moderation clause from 24 to 5, and a trained editor raises the development accuracy of edited trees from 64.47% to 73.35%.
papers.summary: Rule-based decisions such as content moderation, ad compliance, and eligibility checks combine conditions, exemptions, and missing-information cases, and a wrong outcome can only be repaired once the failing condition is identified. `SemTree` encodes a rule as a semantic decision tree whose nodes are natural-language questions with explicit Yes/No/Unknown criteria, answered by a pluggable semantic judge, with the branching structure compiled from the answers that particular judge actually gives; the executed path explains each decision, a reviewer can fix a single node and replay, corrected nodes become judge training labels, and a tool-using LLM editor revises subtrees while watching execution results. On all 8,276 `ShARC` test cases a tree run by a hosted judge reaches 67.70% accuracy with about three questions per case, matching direct labeling at 68.23%, while **a tree compiled for a different judge drops to 47.87% on this judge**, and node repair raises `BANKING77` accuracy from 82.04% to 86.16%, an exemption node cuts false positives on a Chinese e-commerce clause from 24 to 5, and a trained editor lifts development accuracy from 64.47% to 73.35%.

papers.title: VH-GPO: Verified Handoff for LLM Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Group-relative reinforcement learning methods such as GRPO train large language model (LLM) agents by comparing rollouts for the same task. When every trajectory in a group fails with the same reward, relative advantages collapse toward zero, leaving no useful learning signal. A frozen teacher can recover from a student-visited state, but letting it complete the task makes the recovered suffix entirely teacher-generated. We ask: after repairing a student failure, when should control return to the student? We propose outcome-verified teacher-student handoff, instantiated in Verified Handoff for Group Policy Optimization (VH-GPO). The teacher provides enough support to reach a state from which the student can succeed, then returns control so that successful experience is again student-generated. Given an environment-verified teacher recovery, VH-GPO selects the earliest independently confirmed handoff point found within a bounded search budget. With Qwen2.5-1.5B, VH-GPO increases success rates over GRPO from 59.38% to 94.79% on ALFWorld and from 71.62% to 77.34% on WebShop. Improvements also hold with the 7B student, for which additional teacher and student output tokens amount to 1.77% and 2.61% of regular student rollout output tokens on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively. Ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the key components. These results support using verified teacher assistance to repair failures while reinforcing the student's ability to complete tasks independently.
papers.summary: Group-relative methods such as `GRPO` train large language model (LLM) agents by comparing rollouts on the same task, so when every rollout in a group fails identically the advantages collapse to zero and no learning signal remains. Letting a frozen teacher finish the task from a failed state produces a suffix that is entirely teacher-generated, so the authors instead propose outcome-verified teacher-student handoff: the teacher repairs just enough to reach a state from which the student can succeed, and the method selects the earliest independently verified handoff point within a bounded search budget so that the successful experience is again student-generated. With a `Qwen2.5-1.5B` student the approach **raises success on `ALFWorld` from 59.38% to 94.79%** and on `WebShop` from 71.62% to 77.34%, and with a 7B student the extra teacher and student tokens amount to under 3% of regular rollout output.

papers.title: PreSO: Privileged Representation Isolation for On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses a self-teacher conditioned on privileged information to turn the sparse outcome signal of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) into dense token-level supervision. Yet the teacher's advantage may depend on information unavailable to the student at inference, raising a central question: which privileged changes are worth distilling? We use cross-problem recurrence as an empirical cue for potentially reusable guidance. Comparing the representation shifts induced by full solutions and compact hints, we find that hint-induced shifts are more concentrated and directionally consistent across problems, and yield more sustained downstream gains despite revealing less information. Motivated by this association, we propose Privileged Representation Isolation for On-Policy Self-Distillation (PreSO). At the source, PreSO uses compact hints to limit the solution-specific detail entering the privileged shift. At the target, it estimates a leading low-rank subspace from shifts pooled across related problems, projects the privilege-induced correction onto this subspace, and adds it to the student's unprivileged representation to form the representation-level distillation target. The selected subspace serves as an operational proxy for recurring structure, rather than a guaranteed separation of transferable and instance-specific information. On five competition-level mathematics benchmarks, PreSO consistently outperforms strong baselines across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B, improving average accuracy over the base model by 6.8, 9.0, and 10.0 points. Beyond peak accuracy, PreSO attains the highest final-checkpoint average at every model scale, with improvements that persist through the end of training.
papers.summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) turns the sparse rewards of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) into dense token-level supervision by using a self-teacher conditioned on privileged information, but the teacher's edge may rest on details the student never sees at inference. Comparing representation shifts induced by full solutions versus compact hints, the authors find hint-induced shifts are more concentrated and directionally consistent across problems and yield more durable gains, motivating a method that feeds compact hints at the source and, at the target, projects the privilege-induced correction onto a leading low-rank subspace estimated from shifts pooled across related problems before adding it to the student's unprivileged representation. On five competition-level math benchmarks the method consistently beats strong baselines across `Qwen3-1.7B`, `Qwen3-4B`, and `Qwen3-8B`, **improving average accuracy over the base model by 6.8, 9.0, and 10.0 points** and holding the highest final-checkpoint average at every scale.

papers.title: Showing versus Doing: Teaching by Demonstration
papers.abstract: People often learn from others' demonstrations, and inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) techniques have realized this capacity in machines. In contrast, teaching by demonstration has been less well studied computationally. Here, we develop a Bayesian model for teaching by demonstration. Stark differences arise when demonstrators are intentionally teaching (i.e. showing) a task versus simply performing (i.e. doing) a task. In two experiments, we show that human participants modify their teaching behavior consistent with the predictions of our model. Further, we show that even standard IRL algorithms benefit when learning from showing versus doing.
papers.summary: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) lets machines learn from demonstrations, but how demonstrators change their behavior when intentionally teaching rather than simply performing a task has received little computational attention. The authors develop a Bayesian model of teaching by demonstration that predicts clear differences between showing and doing, and **two human experiments confirm participants alter their demonstrations in the way the model predicts**. They further show that standard IRL algorithms learn better from demonstrations produced by showing than by doing.

papers.title: Artificiality's First Exam: An LLM-Referenced C-test for Supraintelligence
papers.abstract: Under the accelerated pace of AI development, any benchmark whose difficulty is calibrated with humans or current AI systems becomes circular, or saturates soon. How can we then evaluate machines that may become more capable than the current machines and the people who write the tests? One answer to the question hinges on inverse problems, inductive inference questions for which difficulty depends on the complexity of the underlying mechanism, given the observations and the previous knowledge. Levin's Kt, a computable variant of Kolmogorov complexity, puts a theoretical upper bound to that difficulty, balancing the simplest representation encoding for the mechanism and the logarithm of the time steps to run that mechanism. Previous tests derived from Levin's Kt, such as the original C-test, are based on minimalistic Universal Turing Machines (UTM), capable of very limited representations and no previous knowledge. Reasoning large language models (LLM) are UTMs that capture a compendium of human culture as knowledge, using prompts as natural language programs. This paper presents the first test based on Levin's Kt with LLMs as representational machines. Fresh test items can be produced at high difficulties, estimated in a ratio scale measured in bits, before any human or frontier model can solve them. We formalise the measure, devise a lightweight generation and certification pipeline, explore the effect of the power of the reference machine and the gap between examiner and examinee. We produce a first battery of certified items administered to twelve LLMs. The resulting agent characteristic curves decrease with difficulty, down to the uncharted high-difficulty region, the supra-intelligence window of items we can certify, yet beyond generations of frontier intelligence.
papers.summary: Benchmarks calibrated against humans or current AI systems saturate or become circular as models surpass them, so the authors turn to inductive inference problems whose difficulty is bounded by Levin's Kt, a computable variant of Kolmogorov complexity that trades off the shortest description of a mechanism against the log of its running time. Earlier Kt-based tests such as the original `C-test` used minimal Universal Turing Machines (UTM) with no prior knowledge, whereas here a reasoning large language model (LLM) serves as the reference machine, with prompts acting as natural-language programs that encode human cultural knowledge. The authors formalize the measure, build a lightweight generation and certification pipeline, examine how the reference machine's power and the examiner-examinee gap affect results, and administer a first battery of certified items to twelve LLMs, **yielding agent characteristic curves that fall with difficulty into a certified high-difficulty region no current frontier model solves**.

papers.title: Coding LLMs Can Be Harnessed to Learn Interpretable Models from Data
papers.abstract: Since compact, interpretable classifiers correspond to simple programs, it is natural to ask if LLM-based coding agents can be used to learn interpretable models from data. In this paper we present a simple harness that repeatedly prompts a coding LLM to produce the next rule in a rule set, given a sample of labeled examples. We show that this approach is competitive with, and often superior to, state-of-the-art rule-learning methods on tabular data, especially with small training sets, and wins by large margins on text, including against another LLM-based rule learner; that this approach outperforms standard harnesses, and that the approach immediately leads to new kinds of interpretable models, since coding agents are not restricted to search a highly restricted hypothesis space. In addition to the advances made in learning interpretable models, these results are of interest because they introduce a new class of coding benchmarks - construction of interpretable classifiers - which includes quantitative measurements of output quality (i.e., test-set error) and existing mature ``specialist coding algorithms'' (i.e., existing learning methods).
papers.summary: Compact interpretable classifiers are essentially small programs, so the authors ask whether coding agents can learn them directly from data. Their harness repeatedly prompts a coding LLM to write the next rule in a rule set given a sample of labeled examples, and **on tabular data it matches or beats state-of-the-art rule-learning methods, especially with small training sets, while winning by large margins on text**, including against another LLM-based rule learner. Because coding agents are not confined to a narrow hypothesis space, the approach also yields new kinds of interpretable models, and the authors frame interpretable-classifier construction as a new class of coding benchmark with quantitative test-set error and mature specialist algorithms to compare against.

papers.title: What Can Language Models Inherit from Solomonoff Induction? Limits, Attainable Properties, and What Served Conditionals Reveal
papers.abstract: A familiar line of reasoning runs as follows: language models are flexible approximators trained under a strictly proper loss, so scale brings them closer to Solomonoff induction, and their predictive success is evidence of that approach. We apply known results from algorithmic information theory, universal prediction and Bayesian consistency. In its uniform form the conclusion holds for no computable model: each has cheap environments it never learns, and every uniformly computable family of total predictors shares one on which each member fails beyond a horizon growing with its index, so ``closer'' can hold only pointwise, one environment at a time. Nor could the offered routes certify even that: finite evaluation cannot certify agreement on rarely reached contexts, perfect corpus fit selects the corpus law as prior, and asymptotic criteria cannot see the constants that carry Solomonoff's guarantee. Our lens is the Kraft inequality read for predictors. Every model has at most the same budget of predictive success, so Solomonoff's predictor, which leaves part of it unspent, differs from a language model not in having more of it but in where it spends it; on mutually singular families this is exact, and only full-mass Bayes mixtures reach the frontier. We then discuss what is inheritable, including in-context learning as amortised Bayesian inference; what survives within a context window; which Solomonoff-like properties a deployed system should have or avoid; and what served conditionals determine. A closing table states what common practices certify and what to report. Tests are developed in a companion paper.
papers.summary: A common argument holds that language models, as flexible approximators trained under a strictly proper loss, approach Solomonoff induction with scale, and that their predictive success is evidence of that approach. Drawing on algorithmic information theory, universal prediction, and Bayesian consistency, the analysis shows that **no computable model can approach Solomonoff induction uniformly**: each has cheap environments it never learns, so convergence can hold only pointwise, one environment at a time, and finite evaluation, perfect corpus fit, and asymptotic criteria cannot certify even that. Reading the Kraft inequality as a fixed budget of predictive success, Solomonoff's predictor differs from a language model not in having more of that budget but in where it spends it, which leads to a discussion of what is inheritable, including in-context learning as amortised Bayesian inference, what survives within a context window, which Solomonoff-like properties a deployed system should have or avoid, and what served conditionals determine.

papers.title: When Log Parsing Removes What Matters: Detecting Failures in Distributed GPU Workloads
papers.abstract: Large AI models increasingly rely on distributed GPU execution, yet it remains unclear whether established failure analysis methods transfer effectively to this setting. We introduce GF-Bench, a PyTorch-based framework and dataset for generating diverse failures in distributed GPU workloads. The framework supports extensible workload and fault-injection logic; based on this design, the current release targets failures visible in multi-GPU communication logs and provides 220 labeled two-GPU executions covering normal runs, CUDA out-of-memory fail-stop failures, and persistent straggler fail-slow failures. Using GF-Bench, we evaluate three sequence-based methods (DeepLog, LogAnomaly, and LogBERT) and the LLM-based LogPrompt on parsed logs, and additionally evaluate LogPrompt on raw logs. On parsed inputs, no method reliably detects both failure classes, and the highest overall F1 score is 0.667. Raw inputs raise the overall F1 score of in-context LogPrompt to 0.983, at 9.0x its average input-token usage and 8.7x its per-run cost. These results expose a substantial trade-off between effectiveness and efficiency: generic log parsing lowers operational cost but discards the distributed execution context required for accurate failure detection. GF-Bench provides a reproducible basis for studying cost-efficient analysis methods and can be extended to additional GPU workloads and failure types.
papers.summary: Whether established log-based failure analysis methods transfer to distributed GPU training remains unclear. `GF-Bench` is a PyTorch-based framework and dataset with extensible workload and fault-injection logic, whose first release provides 220 labeled two-GPU executions covering normal runs, CUDA out-of-memory fail-stop failures, and persistent straggler fail-slow failures. Evaluating the sequence-based `DeepLog`, `LogAnomaly`, and `LogBERT` plus the LLM-based `LogPrompt` on parsed logs, no method reliably detects both failure classes and the best overall F1 is 0.667, whereas running `LogPrompt` on raw logs **raises its overall F1 to 0.983 at 9.0x the input tokens and 8.7x the per-run cost**. The conclusion is that generic log parsing lowers operational cost but discards the distributed execution context needed for accurate failure detection.

papers.title: Physics-Informed State Space Models for Day-Ahead Photovoltaic Power Forecasting
papers.abstract: Accurate day-ahead photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting requires both strong temporal modeling and adherence to physical PV system constraints. Purely data-driven models often ignore the underlying PV conversion process and may produce predictions that are outside the operational range of a PV system. In this paper, we propose a physics-informed state space framework that combines a differentiable PV conversion model with a selective state space backbone (PowerMamba). Our approach follows a physics-residual decomposition. The physics module provides a structured baseline based on solar geometry, irradiance, temperature effects, and inverter limits, while the state space model learns residual corrections from numerical weather prediction (NWP) inputs over a 24-hour horizon. Experiments on one year of utility-scale PV data show that the proposed method significantly improves forecasting accuracy, reducing RMSE by 38.5% and MAE by 45.8% compared to a physics-only baseline, and outperforming a purely data-driven model. Results further show that incorporating system-level physics provides the largest performance gains, while additional refinements offer only marginal improvements. Beyond accuracy, the model improves robustness by constraining predictions toward physical feasibility, reducing unrealistic predictions under corrupted measurements.
papers.summary: Day-ahead photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting needs strong temporal modeling, yet purely data-driven models often ignore the PV conversion process and can predict values outside a system's operational range. The proposed framework follows a physics-residual decomposition: a differentiable PV conversion model built from solar geometry, irradiance, temperature effects, and inverter limits provides a structured baseline, while a selective state space backbone, `PowerMamba`, learns residual corrections from numerical weather prediction (NWP) inputs over a 24-hour horizon. On one year of utility-scale PV data the method **reduces RMSE by 38.5% and MAE by 45.8% relative to a physics-only baseline** and outperforms a purely data-driven model, with system-level physics providing the largest gains and further refinements adding only marginal improvements. Constraining predictions toward physical feasibility also reduces unrealistic outputs under corrupted measurements.

papers.title: Bias Robustness of Genetic Multi-Criteria Sorting versus Learned Rankers under Proxy Skew and Label Contamination
papers.abstract: Learning-to-rank (LTR) models can align rankings with undesignated signals when those signals appear as features or leak into training labels. We compare label-free genetic multi-criteria sorting (open Pikaia strategy variants), which reranks fixed candidate pools using an explicit criteria vector C, to label-trained LTR (LightGBM, XGBoost, RankSVM) under two controlled protocols on MSLR-WEB10K, Baidu-ULTR, WANDS, and Expedia. In the main proxy-skew study, labels remain clean while a calibrated proxy P is available as a feature: Genetic AI rankings show lower Spearman rank-proxy correlation than the LTR peers (e.g. about 0.15-0.16 vs. 0.59-0.87 on WANDS), with both families evaluated jointly on clean nDCG@10 on a bias-utility frontier. In a supporting label-contamination study, training labels are mixed with contaminant B: because Genetic AI methods do not use labels, their bias and utility curves stay flat, whereas LightGBM and XGBoost increase rank-B correlation as contamination rises (OLS bias_slope about 0.58-0.65 on WANDS/Baidu). The results support genetic sorting as an architectural option for optimizing declared attributes on a fixed pool when undesignated proxies or label contaminants must be refused.
papers.summary: Learning-to-rank (LTR) models can align their rankings with undesignated signals when those signals appear as features or leak into training labels. The study compares label-free genetic multi-criteria sorting, in the form of open `Pikaia` strategy variants that rerank fixed candidate pools using an explicit criteria vector, against label-trained `LightGBM`, `XGBoost`, and `RankSVM` under two controlled protocols on `MSLR-WEB10K`, `Baidu-ULTR`, `WANDS`, and `Expedia`. When labels stay clean but a calibrated proxy is available as a feature, on `WANDS` the **genetic rankings show Spearman rank-proxy correlations of about 0.15 to 0.16 versus 0.59 to 0.87 for the LTR models**, with both families evaluated jointly on clean nDCG@10 along a bias-utility frontier. Under label contamination, the label-free methods' bias and utility curves stay flat while `LightGBM` and `XGBoost` increasingly correlate with the contaminant as contamination rises, supporting genetic sorting as an architectural option when undesignated proxies or label contaminants must be refused.

papers.title: Barycentric Anchored Weight Search for Robust Model Merging
papers.abstract: We propose Barycentric Anchored Search, a post-hoc weight-space procedure for improving fine-tuned vision models under distribution shift without additional gradient training or increased inference cost. Given a pre-trained initialization and two checkpoints fine-tuned on a source dataset, the method constructs barycentric candidate weights and performs a small derivative-free search along directions connecting each candidate to the pre-trained model. Candidate weights are selected using a small validation subset of one or more out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets; the selected model is then evaluated on the held-out portions of those datasets, on additional OOD benchmarks, and on the ImageNet validation set to quantify the robustness-accuracy trade-off. The method is inspired by simplex-based derivative-free optimization, including Nelder-Mead and Torczon multidirectional search, but is specialized to the geometry of neural network weight merging. Unlike Model Soup, which typically benefits from many fine-tuned checkpoints, and unlike Model Stock, which applies a fixed geometric merge, our approach uses only two fine-tuned checkpoints and iteratively adapts the merge using validation feedback from OOD data. Experiments with CLIP ViT-B/32 show that the proposed search substantially improves performance on held-out OOD data, including ImageNet-A, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-Sketch, while keeping ImageNet accuracy competitive. The resulting weights also improve transfer to OOD datasets not used during candidate selection, outperforming the original fine-tuned checkpoints, naive model soups, and Model Stock in our evaluations. These results suggest that lightweight optimization in anchored weight space provides a practical alternative to fixed weight-averaging rules, geometric merging, or single-model selection.
papers.summary: Fine-tuned vision models often lose robustness under distribution shift, and existing weight-merging remedies either need many checkpoints, as with `Model Soup`, or apply a fixed geometric rule, as with `Model Stock`. `Barycentric Anchored Search` is a post-hoc weight-space procedure that takes a pre-trained initialization and just two checkpoints fine-tuned on a source dataset, builds barycentric candidate weights, and runs a small derivative-free search inspired by Nelder-Mead and Torczon multidirectional search along directions connecting each candidate to the pre-trained model, selecting candidates with a small validation subset of out-of-distribution (OOD) data. With `CLIP ViT-B/32`, the search **substantially improves held-out OOD accuracy while keeping in-distribution accuracy competitive**, with gains on `ImageNet-A`, `ImageNet-R`, and `ImageNet-Sketch`, and the resulting weights also transfer to OOD datasets not used during selection, beating the original checkpoints, naive soups, and `Model Stock`.

papers.title: RoboHarness: A Simple Harness Outperforms VLA and World Actions Models
papers.abstract: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has opened a path toward generalist embodied AI, raising the question of how LLMs can act in the physical world. One straightforward approach is training the model to generate actions: collect robot-action data and video demonstration, refine LLM architecture with an action head, and train a vision-language-action (VLA) model at scale. However, we argue that coding agents have the potential to realize generalist embodied manipulation. All they need is a simple yet effective robot harness. We present RoboHarness: a robotic harness that gives LLM agents a visual-geometric control panel so that they can directly understand and invoke embodied tasks. With RoboHarness, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next outperforms state-of-the-art VLA models on BEHAVIOR Challenge 2025 tasks. The implementation will be released as open source.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) raise the question of how to act in the physical world, and the standard answer is to collect robot-action data, add an action head, and train a vision-language-action (VLA) model at scale. The argument here is that coding agents can instead achieve generalist embodied manipulation given a simple harness: `RoboHarness` gives LLM agents a visual-geometric control panel through which they can directly understand and invoke embodied tasks. Using it, `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` **outperforms state-of-the-art VLA models** on `BEHAVIOR Challenge 2025` tasks, and the implementation is to be released as open source.

papers.title: LabInstruct: Benchmarking Situated Instructional Video Generation for Lab Procedures
papers.abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) aim to automate the full experimental loop, from scientific decision-making to physical execution. Ideally, AI-generated plans could be carried out directly by robotic systems, but reliable automation remains difficult in complex, open-world laboratory environments, where experiments often involve fine-grained manipulation, long-horizon procedures, and substantial variation across tasks and setups. Humans therefore remain an important execution interface between AI-generated plans and physical experiments, creating a need for clear and effective human-facing experimental guidance. Because laboratory procedures are inherently visual, spatial, and dynamic, video is particularly well suited to communicating apparatus configurations, manipulation actions, temporal dependencies, and state changes. Recent advances in video generation now make it possible to synthesize experimental demonstrations directly from an initial workspace image and a natural-language instruction. However, whether such models can reliably communicate real laboratory procedures has not been systematically studied. We introduce LabInstruct, a benchmark for situated instructional video generation in real laboratories. LabInstruct contains 204 tasks across 5 scientific disciplines, with real reference executions and structured annotations of objects, actions, contacts, and state transitions. Evaluating 8 frontier image-to-video models, we find that visually plausible generations frequently remain procedurally incorrect, revealing a substantial gap between visual realism and the reliability required for experimental instruction.
papers.summary: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) aim to automate the full experimental loop, but reliable robotic execution in open-world labs remains hard, so humans still carry out AI-generated plans and need clear guidance, which video is well suited to provide. `LabInstruct` is a benchmark for situated instructional video generation in real laboratories, with 204 tasks across 5 scientific disciplines, real reference executions, and structured annotations of objects, actions, contacts, and state transitions, where models must synthesize a demonstration from an initial workspace image and a natural-language instruction. Across 8 frontier image-to-video models, **visually plausible generations frequently remain procedurally incorrect**, exposing a substantial gap between visual realism and the reliability required for experimental instruction.

papers.title: CoEvoke: Evoking Multi-Agent Collaboration for Trajectory Collection
papers.abstract: Training multi-agent collaboration requires trajectories of checking, feedback, and repair, yet task-solving rollouts may end in immediate approval or repeat unsuccessful attempts without useful correction. We introduce CoEvoke, a cross-domain framework that evokes these interactions during trajectory collection. Controlled perturbations create recoverable difficulties, while restricted reference-based guidance directs investigation. The resulting dataset contains 4,567 reconstructable trajectories over 4,130 software-engineering and reasoning tasks, linking public interactions to evidence, decisions, and task-native outcomes. Separate experiments over 2,287 same-task pairs show feedback increases of 47.72-100 percentage points across seven perturbation groups; guidance has smaller, model-dependent effects. With identical training tasks, decision-record counts, and updates, perturbation-enriched judge training improves ACPBench-Hard success from 35.38% to 42.12% (+6.73 points). SWE verifier training gains 7.60-9.40 points over interface-matched untrained references. Workflow and post-training evaluations preserve task-solving topology with unperturbed inputs and no private-reference guidance. These results support designing collection conditions to obtain corrective supervision that improves collaborative decisions with frozen solving agents.
papers.summary: Training multi-agent collaboration needs trajectories that contain checking, feedback, and repair, yet ordinary task-solving rollouts often end in immediate approval or repeat failed attempts without useful correction. `CoEvoke` is a cross-domain collection framework that evokes these interactions by injecting controlled perturbations that create recoverable difficulties and by providing restricted reference-based guidance that directs investigation, yielding 4,567 reconstructable trajectories over 4,130 software-engineering and reasoning tasks. Across 2,287 same-task pairs, perturbation **raises feedback rates by 47.72 to 100 percentage points across seven perturbation groups**, while guidance has smaller, model-dependent effects. With identical training tasks, decision-record counts, and updates, perturbation-enriched judge training lifts `ACPBench-Hard` success from 35.38% to 42.12%, and SWE verifier training gains 7.60 to 9.40 points over interface-matched untrained references, all with frozen solving agents.

papers.title: OPMD: On-Policy Mechanism Distillation Beyond Output Supervision
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language-model by supervising a student on prefixes sampled from its own policy, but its supervision remains confined to the output space. Consequently, OPD transfers what a teacher predicts without supervising the intermediate computation that produces those predictions. Simply distilling intermediate representations like representation matching is insufficient since teacher and student representations may differ geometrically, and even well-aligned hidden states need not be usable by the student's subsequent computation. We introduce On-Policy Mechanism Distillation (OPMD), which transfers teacher-derived intermediate computation while explicitly accounting for its compatibility with the student. OPMD first constructs a student-compatible teacher that transforms teacher representations into intermediate states usable by the student's downstream computation, then it internalizes these states from on-policy trajectories. OPMD achieves the highest average accuracy among the evaluated distillation baselines in all three teacher--student settings, and generalizes to multi-teacher distillation and cross-family supervised fine-tuning. Further analyses show that mechanism supervision yields more effective reasoning and meaningfully alters the student's intermediate computation and solution strategies, supporting that it transfers information beyond output supervision alone. Together, these results establish mechanism-level supervision as an effective way to move on-policy distillation beyond output supervision, enabling students to learn inner mechanisms they can use and internalize.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on prefixes sampled from its own policy but supervises only the output space, so it transfers what a teacher predicts without the intermediate computation behind those predictions. Directly matching intermediate representations is insufficient because teacher and student representations can differ geometrically, and even well-aligned hidden states need not be usable by the student's downstream computation. On-Policy Mechanism Distillation, or `OPMD`, first builds a student-compatible teacher that transforms teacher representations into intermediate states the student can use, then internalizes those states from on-policy trajectories. `OPMD` **achieves the highest average accuracy among the evaluated distillation baselines in all three teacher-student settings**, generalizes to multi-teacher distillation and cross-family supervised fine-tuning, and measurably alters the student's intermediate computation and solution strategies.

papers.title: Contrastive Covariance Subspaces for Activation Steering
papers.abstract: Activation steering controls large language model behavior by adding a direction to hidden activations during inference. For steering to work well, that direction must be a pure signal for the target concept: any confound entangled with it, such as an incidental topic or writing style, is injected into the residual stream alongside the concept itself and degrades the generated text. We introduce Contrastive Covariance Steering (CCS), a training-free method that eliminates this confound variation. CCS projects steering vectors to a low-dimensional subspace obtained in closed form by solving a contrastive variance objective, which retains the directions along which the target concept varies while suppressing directions shared with the other classes. Across three LLMs and four steering domains, CCS consistently beats all baseline steering methods in all $12$ model-domain settings. The largest relative improvement occurs on AxBench and Emotion where we outperform the next strongest steering baseline by $48$ to $70\%$ and $13$ to $27\%$, respectively. Furthermore, CCS outperforms naive difference-of-means steering by up to $151\%$, showcasing the importance of deconfounding concepts. A toy experiment verifies our motivation on why: planting a topic nuisance into the training data reduces unprojected steering by $46\%$, whereas CCS loses only $12\%$ and recovers most of the gap to an oracle that explicitly deletes the planted direction. A human study with $23$ raters on $296$ generations reproduces the LLM judge's ranking. Our extensive ablation verifies the importance of our method's components and robustness to the number of nuisance classes. Finally, we extend our method to multi-turn conversations, where CCS sustains both concept expression and fluency, matching system prompt performance as other steering methods drift.
papers.summary: Activation steering controls large language model behavior by adding a direction to hidden activations at inference, but any confound entangled with that direction, such as an incidental topic or writing style, gets injected alongside the target concept and degrades the generated text. Contrastive Covariance Steering, or `CCS`, is a training-free method that projects steering vectors onto a low-dimensional subspace obtained in closed form from a contrastive variance objective, retaining directions along which the target concept varies while suppressing directions shared with other classes. Across three LLMs and four steering domains, `CCS` **beats all baseline steering methods in all 12 model-domain settings**, outperforming the next strongest baseline by 48 to 70% on `AxBench` and 13 to 27% on `Emotion`, and naive difference-of-means steering by up to 151%. A toy experiment with a planted topic nuisance, a human study with 23 raters on 296 generations that reproduces the LLM-judge ranking, and a multi-turn extension where `CCS` matches system-prompt performance while other methods drift all support the deconfounding motivation.

papers.title: Pick the Mixture, Not the Samples: Combinatorial Data Selection for LLMs
papers.abstract: Data selection for LLM fine-tuning faces two facts about real training: data pools draw from many distinct domains, and evaluation spans diverse tasks. As a result, the same sample helps different tasks differently, and samples interact during training so that a subset's value is not the sum of its parts. Current data-selection methods leave these realities largely unaddressed. We formalize them as Combinatorial Data Selection (CDS), a framework that separates attribution (how samples are scored) from selection (which subset to pick) and models the non-additive interactions among samples. On a real instruction-tuning data pool, we find substantial cross-domain complementarity (joint utility exceeds the sum of singletons), alongside redundancy within domains. Inspired by this, we propose Mixture-then-Select, a two-stage algorithm that first decides how many samples to take from each domain, then ranks samples within each domain by attribution score. Theoretically, the gap to the optimal subset is linear in the selection size and independent of data pool size. Empirically, Mixture-then-Select outperforms strong baselines by 20 to 54%, is robust across attribution methods, and works across different models and data pool sizes. The framework also extends to the data purchasing problem under a budget constraint when sample prices vary. Our findings suggest that allocating selection across domains offers a promising path toward more efficient and effective data selection for modern LLMs.
papers.summary: Data selection for LLM fine-tuning must cope with pools drawn from many domains and evaluation spanning diverse tasks, so the same sample helps different tasks differently and samples interact during training, making a subset's value non-additive. Combinatorial Data Selection (CDS) formalizes this by separating attribution, how samples are scored, from selection, which subset to pick, and by modeling interactions among samples, and on a real instruction-tuning pool it reveals substantial cross-domain complementarity alongside within-domain redundancy. The proposed `Mixture-then-Select` algorithm first decides how many samples to draw from each domain, then ranks samples within each domain by attribution score, with a theoretical gap to the optimal subset that is linear in selection size and independent of pool size. Empirically it **outperforms strong baselines by 20 to 54%**, is robust across attribution methods, models, and pool sizes, and extends to budgeted data purchasing when sample prices vary.

papers.title: Can We Trust This Evaluation? Instance-Level Reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge
papers.abstract: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation commonly aggregates multiple judges' decisions into a majority vote, yet this panel decision process does not guarantee that the evaluation of an individual item is reliable. We propose Structured Cross-fitted Uncertainty Risk (SCUR), a label-free approach for estimating instance-level evaluation reliability based on the judge panel's behavior. A latent measurement model serves as the backbone for measurement system analysis, from which SCUR derives three complementary signals capturing panel uncertainty, measurement cross-entropy, and perturbation sensitivity. These three sources of evidence are combined into a risk score. We evaluate the SCUR approach on five real-world benchmarks using majority-vote error ranking, selective trust, and risk stratification. Furthermore, we show our approach to be more effective at detecting high-consensus risk items, which are the blind spots for many other LLM-as-a-judge evaluation methods.
papers.summary: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation commonly aggregates several judges' decisions into a majority vote, yet that panel process does not guarantee the evaluation of any individual item is reliable. Structured Cross-fitted Uncertainty Risk, or `SCUR`, is a label-free approach that uses a latent measurement model as the backbone for measurement system analysis and derives three complementary signals, panel uncertainty, measurement cross-entropy, and perturbation sensitivity, which it combines into a per-instance risk score. On five real-world benchmarks evaluated through majority-vote error ranking, selective trust, and risk stratification, `SCUR` is **more effective at detecting high-consensus risk items**, the blind spots of many other LLM-as-a-judge evaluation methods.

papers.title: Rotate the Loop: Blockwise Conformality for Looped Transformers
papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse one shared block across many recurrent steps, so depth becomes a quantity that can be spent at runtime rather than a stack of distinct layers. Those extra steps help only if a write made on one recurrent step is still readable on later ones, and that depends on the linear map applied to the residual between recurrent steps. We show that whether the loop learns to track state is a geometric question about the form of this map, and we propose blockwise conformal injections: the residual splits into coordinate-aligned groups and rotates inside each one, so every group has its own timescale while the geometry stays exact within it. Our experiments show a performance increase on a demanding form of state tracking - last-token accuracy when the rest of the prefix is already correct - and on language modelling, where a signal written earlier has to be retrieved at the end of the sequence.
papers.summary: Looped transformers reuse one shared block across many recurrent steps, turning depth into a runtime budget, but extra steps help only if what is written to the residual on one step remains readable on later ones, which depends on the linear map applied between steps. Whether the loop learns to track state is framed as a geometric question about the form of that map, motivating blockwise conformal injections: the residual splits into coordinate-aligned groups and rotates inside each one, giving every group its own timescale while keeping the geometry exact within it. Experiments show **improved last-token accuracy on a demanding state-tracking setting where the rest of the prefix is already correct**, along with gains on language modelling where a signal written early must be retrieved at the end of the sequence.

papers.title: PLDiv: Measuring Dataset Diversity and Semantic Collapse via Persistence Landscapes
papers.abstract: Modern data pipelines increasingly combine human-created and human-curated data with AI-generated data for model training and evaluation. As datasets grow, they often add semantically redundant samples rather than expanding semantic coverage, which deteriorates the quality of the whole dataset. Existing diversity metrics primarily summarize lexical variation, entropy, or pairwise similarity, but provide limited characterization of the shape of the underlying data distribution. In this paper, we propose PLDiv, a diversity metric derived from persistence landscapes that quantifies the structural organization of a dataset from its geometric representation. PLDiv summarizes how data neighborhoods evolve as nearby samples progressively connect, producing an interpretable scalar measure of structural diversity without requiring task-specific supervision. Whether measuring intrinsic diversity in text generations or image embeddings, or detecting semantic collapse in instruction datasets and reasoning trajectories, PLDiv performs competitively against evaluated baselines and aligns strongly with diversity labels during semantic collapse. Consequently, it effectively supports applications in synthetic data monitoring, dataset construction, data augmentation, and generative model evaluation.
papers.summary: As training and evaluation pipelines mix human-created and AI-generated data, growing datasets often add semantically redundant samples rather than expanding coverage, and existing diversity metrics based on lexical variation, entropy, or pairwise similarity say little about the shape of the data distribution. `PLDiv` is a diversity metric derived from persistence landscapes that summarizes how data neighborhoods evolve as nearby samples progressively connect in embedding space, yielding an interpretable scalar measure of structural diversity without task-specific supervision.
