Across intrinsic diversity of text generations and image embeddings and detection of semantic collapse in instruction datasets and reasoning trajectories, `PLDiv` **performs competitively against evaluated baselines and aligns strongly with diversity labels during semantic collapse**, supporting uses in synthetic data monitoring, dataset construction, augmentation, and generative model evaluation.

papers.title: A Geometric Perspective on Reward Function Updates in Inverse Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) is classically solved using Lagrangian optimisation, by jointly optimising a primal-dual problem with gradient descent to obtain the optimal reward function parameters and corresponding optimal policy. While this algorithmic view of IRL has been highly influential, gradient-based reward updates only paint a partial picture, largely ignoring the geometry of the problem in occupancy space. In this paper, we present an occupancy-space view of reward updates in IRL. We leverage the insight that both the optimal solution and its geometry in occupancy space are known, and show that the geometry along the e-geodesic (straight line in occupancy space) toward the optimal occupancy directly affects the gradient of the IRL dual problem in reward parameter space. This perspective naturally suggests preconditioning the dual gradient with the average Fisher information along the occupancy trajectory. We show that this preconditioned gradient is just a convex interpolation of the old reward and a new target reward, yielding efficient natural-gradient-style updates with little additional computational overhead. We then analyse these occupancy-space reward updates from a Mirror Descent (MD) perspective, and show that policy search over the resulting rewards induces approximate entropic MD on the policy. Finally, we conclude with convergence results of such geometry-aware IRL algorithms.
papers.summary: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) is classically solved by jointly optimising a primal-dual Lagrangian problem with gradient descent, but gradient-based reward updates largely ignore the geometry of the problem in occupancy space. Exploiting the fact that both the optimal solution and its geometry in occupancy space are known, the analysis shows that the geometry along the e-geodesic, the straight line in occupancy space toward the optimal occupancy, directly shapes the gradient of the IRL dual problem in reward parameter space, which suggests preconditioning the dual gradient with the average Fisher information along the occupancy trajectory. The preconditioned gradient turns out to be **a convex interpolation of the old reward and a new target reward**, giving natural-gradient-style updates with little extra computation. Viewed through Mirror Descent (MD), policy search over the resulting rewards induces approximate entropic MD on the policy, and convergence results are given for such geometry-aware IRL algorithms.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning from Real-Robot Interaction without High-Quality State Estimates
papers.abstract: A longstanding goal for robot reinforcement learning (RL) is that robots learn from their own physical experience, as humans and animals do. A key obstacle to learning directly from physical experience, especially outside instrumented lab environments, is that the state of the world is usually unobservable to the learner and must be estimated from on-board sensing. Errors in that estimate corrupt both the policy input and potentially the reward signal. We study this challenge using the contact-rich task of a bipedal robot learning to score soccer goals. We estimate all key state variables on-board with an unscented Kalman filter (UKF) and no external instrumentation (e.g., motion capture or overhead cameras). Because the UKF may incorrectly estimate state when the ball is unobserved, we learn a new state representation with a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) that, critically, only corrects the RSSM's latent state when the ball is observed. Building on RLPD, we introduce RSSM-RLPD and apply it to the task of a NAO robot learning to dribble a soccer ball into a goal. We show that the robot learns to score from multiple starting positions after 30 minutes of real-world interaction, reaching 100% success against 0% for a feed-forward policy under the same training budget. We complement our physical robot experiments with a simulation study and show that RSSM-RLPD learns policies that achieve a higher success rate than behavior cloning, a feed-forward, and GRU baseline. Taken together, our results show that the addition of a learned state representation to existing on-robot learning methods enables RL from real-robot data even with a high degree of partial observability.
papers.summary: Robots learning from their own physical experience outside instrumented labs must cope with world state that is unobservable and has to be estimated from on-board sensing, where errors corrupt both the policy input and potentially the reward. Using the contact-rich task of a bipedal `NAO` robot learning to dribble a soccer ball into a goal, all key state variables are estimated on-board with an unscented Kalman filter (UKF) and no external instrumentation, and a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) learns a new state representation that corrects its latent state only when the ball is actually observed. Building on `RLPD`, the resulting `RSSM-RLPD` lets the robot **learn to score from multiple starting positions after 30 minutes of real-world interaction, reaching 100% success versus 0% for a feed-forward policy** under the same training budget. A simulation study further shows `RSSM-RLPD` beating behavior cloning, feed-forward, and GRU baselines, indicating that a learned state representation enables real-robot RL under heavy partial observability.

papers.title: The Future of AI-assisted Physics: Discovering, Verifying and Organizing Results via Formalization
papers.abstract: Rapid advances in AI have opened a new era for physics, enabling unprecedented capabilities in research and discovery. However, these advances also bring challenges in verifying, trusting, and reusing the results they so rapidly produce. Formalization is a necessary part of the solution to these challenges. In this paper, as well as giving an overview of the role of AI and formalization in physics, we make the case that: (1) formalization is an essential layer for AI-driven discoveries in both computational and theoretical physics; (2) AI is lowering the barrier to, and increasing the efficiency of, formalization in physics, though it remains weaker at choosing definitions and designing libraries than at writing proofs; (3) the speed AI brings to formalization in physics currently comes at the cost of trust, credit, and community; (4) shared, community-reviewed formal libraries such as Physlib should be central in making progress in this field, both as a trusted, reusable foundation for physics results and as the environment in which AI systems can reason about physics; (5) formalizing physics raises challenges beyond those in mathematics, most importantly that a checked proof does not establish that its definitions faithfully capture the intended physics. We also give our perspectives on near-term and long-term directions in these areas.
papers.summary: Rapid AI progress is producing physics results faster than they can be verified, trusted, and reused, and formalization is argued to be a necessary part of the answer. Alongside an overview of the role of AI and formalization in physics, the position is that formalization is an essential layer for AI-driven discoveries in both computational and theoretical physics, that AI is lowering the barrier to formalizing while remaining **weaker at choosing definitions and designing libraries than at writing proofs**, and that the speed it brings currently costs trust, credit, and community. Shared, community-reviewed formal libraries such as `Physlib` are proposed as the trusted foundation for physics results and the environment in which AI systems reason about physics, with the caveat that a checked proof does not establish that its definitions faithfully capture the intended physics, a challenge beyond those faced in mathematics.

papers.title: Auditing LLM Program Search for Bermudan Stopping with Primal--Dual Certificates
papers.abstract: LLM program-search agents are usually judged by the score that drives their search. We study LLM-driven search over Python exercise policies for Bermudan options, an optimal stopping problem where a trusted evaluator owns the simulation and a dual upper bound~$U$. For any policy, $0 \le V^\star - L_\pi \le U - L_\pi$; we report Monte Carlo estimates of both bounds with their sampling error. We audit 24 generation attempts from two pipelines, a six-pair feedback-representation ablation, and a holdout evaluated after selection was frozen. No selected generated program improves on Ridge LSMC consistently or by more than Monte Carlo uncertainty; holdout gap scores lie within $0.002$ of it. On six one-dimensional puts, a high-precision binomial reference places Ridge within Monte Carlo noise of optimal and attributes 99\% of the estimated gap to dual-bound looseness, so this dual audits validity but cannot certify progress at the search's scale. Structured memory showed no benefit over score-only memory in this ablation. Whether search ``worked'' depends on reporting rules: retaining the initial reference, freezing selection before holdout, and counting failures.
papers.summary: LLM program-search agents are usually judged by the very score that drives their search. The setting is LLM-driven search over Python exercise policies for Bermudan options, an optimal stopping problem where a trusted evaluator owns the simulation and a dual upper bound, so the gap between a policy's lower bound and the dual bound brackets its suboptimality, and both bounds are reported as Monte Carlo estimates with sampling error. Auditing 24 generation attempts from two pipelines, a six-pair feedback-representation ablation, and a holdout evaluated after selection was frozen, `Ridge LSMC` remains unbeaten: **no selected generated program improves on it consistently or by more than Monte Carlo uncertainty**, with holdout gap scores within 0.002 of it. On six one-dimensional puts a high-precision binomial reference places `Ridge LSMC` within Monte Carlo noise of optimal and attributes 99% of the estimated gap to dual-bound looseness, structured memory showed no benefit over score-only memory, and whether the search succeeded depends on reporting rules such as retaining the initial reference, freezing selection before holdout, and counting failures.

papers.title: Loose Lips: Understanding Privacy Leakage in Agentic Dialogue
papers.abstract: As LLM agents are increasingly deployed in high-stakes enterprise settings, understanding how they handle sensitive information in agentic dialogue has become critical. Privacy leakage in such settings requires reasoning about whether information flows respect the contextual norms under which they originated. We extend CIMemories to CIMEMORIES DIALOGUE, a benchmark of 4,410 two-agent dialogue instances grounded in Contextual Integrity theory. Using this benchmark, we systematically evaluate 7 open-weight models from the Qwen3 and Llama 3.1 families across conversation lengths of 1 and 6 turns under three prompting conditions. We find that task capability and privacy leakage are fundamentally coupled: more capable models are systematically leakier, with no model in our evaluation able to decouple the two. Thinking models consistently leak more than their non-thinking counterparts, a pattern we attribute to the extended reasoning surface created by chain-of-thought. Leakage compounds with conversation length, rising up to 3x from 1 to 6 turns. Our results suggest that the coupling between task capability and privacy leakage is not an artifact of misconfiguration but a structural feature of current agentic systems.
papers.summary: As LLM agents move into high-stakes enterprise settings, privacy leakage in agentic dialogue depends on whether information flows respect the contextual norms under which the information originated. `CIMemories` is extended into `CIMemories Dialogue`, a benchmark of 4,410 two-agent dialogue instances grounded in Contextual Integrity theory, used to evaluate 7 open-weight models from the `Qwen3` and `Llama 3.1` families across 1-turn and 6-turn conversations under three prompting conditions. **More capable models are systematically leakier, with no evaluated model able to decouple task capability from privacy leakage**, thinking models consistently leak more than their non-thinking counterparts, a pattern attributed to the extended reasoning surface of chain-of-thought, and leakage rises up to 3x from 1 to 6 turns. The coupling is argued to be a structural feature of current agentic systems rather than an artifact of misconfiguration.

papers.title: Is the Future Predictable? Modeling Future Predictability for Reliable Temporal Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain unreliable when reasoning about the future. Existing models often overlook the difference among future states, committing to specific answers even when the queried facts are inherently volatile. To capture this challenge, we introduce ChronoRegime, a future-oriented temporal reasoning task that requires models to determine whether historical temporal evidence justifies commitment to a future answer. Furthermore, we propose Confidence-Aware Temporal Reasoning (CTR), a framework that estimates future predictability from temporal dynamics and regulates answer commitment accordingly. Rather than performing unconditional forecasting, CTR commits only when the reconstructed evidence supports the target future state. Across multiple LLMs, CTR improves strict overall accuracy by 6.7 percentage points and reduces hallucination rates by 18.4 percentage points on average over the plain QA baseline. These results demonstrate that explicit predictability assessment is an effective mechanism for safer and more reliable temporal reasoning under future uncertainty.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) remain unreliable when reasoning about the future, often committing to specific answers even when the queried facts are inherently volatile. `ChronoRegime` is a future-oriented temporal reasoning task that asks whether historical temporal evidence justifies committing to a future answer, and Confidence-Aware Temporal Reasoning, or `CTR`, estimates future predictability from temporal dynamics and regulates answer commitment accordingly, answering only when the reconstructed evidence supports the target future state. Across multiple LLMs, `CTR` **improves strict overall accuracy by 6.7 percentage points and cuts hallucination rates by 18.4 percentage points on average** over a plain QA baseline.

papers.title: One Model, Multiple Compute Budgets: Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE for Flexible Compute Across Turns
papers.abstract: Large language models typically support different inference budgets through separate model sizes or fixed compute configurations. In multi-turn interactions, however, compute demand can vary substantially across turns. Using a high-compute model for every turn wastes computation, while routing among independent models may require rebuilding model-specific history states after switches. We therefore ask whether a single shared model can support multiple compute budgets that can be flexibly assigned across turns. We introduce Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE, which jointly supports token-to-concept compression ratios of 2, 4, and 8 (CR2/CR4/CR8) within a shared backbone. Lightweight full-token modules reduce compression-independent cost, ratio-specific boundary routers support distinct compression levels, and cross-ratio training enables mixed-ratio processing within the same context. Across PTBench and SFTBench, the three fixed modes outperform their compute-matched MoE baselines in all 6 comparisons while remaining competitive with independently trained fixed-ratio specialists. On CodeChat and CoSQL, mixed-ratio inference improves the accuracy--compute trade-off, outperforming the Large MoE by 5.87 and 2.68 percentage points while reducing FLOPs by 41.1% and 12.3%, respectively. Under the same turn-wise budget schedule, Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE further reduces FLOPs by 78.4% and 46.9% relative to routing among independent models. These results demonstrate that a single shared model can provide multiple compute budgets for flexible compute allocation across turns.
papers.summary: Serving several inference budgets usually means separate model sizes, which wastes compute in multi-turn conversations where demand varies by turn and forces history states to be rebuilt when switching between independent models. `Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE` supports token-to-concept compression ratios of 2, 4, and 8 inside one shared mixture-of-experts (MoE) backbone, using lightweight full-token modules, ratio-specific boundary routers, and cross-ratio training so that turns in the same context can run at different ratios. The three fixed modes beat compute-matched MoE baselines in all six comparisons on `PTBench` and `SFTBench`, and on `CodeChat` and `CoSQL` mixed-ratio inference beats a large MoE by 5.87 and 2.68 percentage points while cutting FLOPs by 41.1% and 12.3%. **Under the same turn-wise budget schedule, it uses 78.4% and 46.9% fewer FLOPs than routing among independent models.**

papers.title: Two-Stage Multi-modal Learning for Dynamic Audio-Visual Navigation: From Physical Alignment to Scene Aggregation
papers.abstract: Embodied Audio-Visual Navigation (AVN) requires an agent to locate sound targets by jointly leveraging visual and auditory cues. While prior work has achieved notable success with static sound sources, real-world scenarios often involve moving targets, giving rise to the more challenging problem of \textbf{Dynamic Audio-Visual Navigation (D-AVN)}. Existing approaches largely rely on semantic auditory features, which limits generalization to unheard sound categories and hinders fine-grained spatial reasoning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel \textbf{Two-Stage Multi-modal Learning} framework for D-AVN. In the Physical Alignment stage, the proposed \textbf{Intensity-Calibrated Geometry Encoder (ICGE)} performs physics-informed alignment of sound intensity with visual geometry to capture category-agnostic spatial correspondence. In the Scene Aggregation stage, a Transformer-based \textbf{Cross-Modal Scene Aggregator (CMSA)} dynamically integrates multi-modal features to construct a robust state representation for policy learning. Extensive experiments on Replica and Matterport3D demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art success rates, while significantly improving generalization and navigation efficiency in complex environments and under unheard sound scenarios.
papers.summary: Audio-visual navigation (AVN) asks an embodied agent to locate a sounding target using sight and hearing, and the dynamic variant (D-AVN) lets the target move; existing methods rely on semantic audio features that generalize poorly to unheard sound categories and support little fine-grained spatial reasoning. The proposed two-stage framework first applies an `Intensity-Calibrated Geometry Encoder` that aligns sound intensity with visual geometry in a physics-informed, category-agnostic way, then a Transformer-based `Cross-Modal Scene Aggregator` that fuses the multimodal features into a state representation for policy learning. **On `Replica` and `Matterport3D` the method reports state-of-the-art success rates**, with better generalization to unheard sounds and higher navigation efficiency in complex environments.

papers.title: SAGE: Efficient Protected Vision-Language Inference on Smart Glasses
papers.abstract: Smart glasses are a promising platform for vision-language assistants, but private split inference remains expensive: protecting visual representations before transmission does not remove the cost of on-device vision encoding, wide protected tokens, or hardware-unaware execution. We present SAGE (Smart-glasses-Aware Guarded Encoding), a hardware-aware framework for efficient protected VLM inference on smart glasses. SAGE keeps raw images and unprotected visual tokens on the trusted device, reduces visual input cost, executes shape-specialized INT8 graphs, and compresses protected representations into compact 256-dimensional INT8 packets before transmission. Unlike efficiency methods optimized only for nominal model size, SAGE selects its operating point using downstream answer quality together with measured latency, memory, and thermal behavior on real Mentra Live glasses. On a matched Qwen workload, SAGE reduces glasses inference latency by 39.18%, device-sensor temperature rise by 21.91%, and protected packet size by 96.56%, while retaining 85.62% of the protected reference's relaxed utility and comparable prompted containment. Direct glasses-to-phone tests deliver all 192 packets and reduce median packet-plus-acknowledgment time from 71.3 to 10.0 ms. The compact protected interface also transfers across four additional VLM families. These results show that private wearable VLM inference must be optimized jointly across representation protection, communication, and real-device execution rather than through model compression alone.
papers.summary: Private split inference for a vision-language model (VLM) assistant on smart glasses stays expensive because protecting visual features before transmission does nothing about on-device vision encoding, wide protected tokens, or hardware-unaware execution. `SAGE` (Smart-glasses-Aware Guarded Encoding) keeps raw images and unprotected visual tokens on the glasses, reduces visual input cost, runs shape-specialized INT8 graphs, and compresses protected representations into 256-dimensional INT8 packets, choosing its operating point from downstream answer quality together with latency, memory, and thermal measurements on real Mentra Live glasses. **On a matched `Qwen` workload it cuts glasses inference latency by 39.18% and protected packet size by 96.56%** while retaining 85.62% of the protected reference's relaxed utility, and glasses-to-phone tests reduce median packet-plus-acknowledgment time from 71.3 to 10.0 ms. The compact protected interface also transfers to four further VLM families.

papers.title: Embodied Zero-Shot Task Planning via Hardware-Aware LLM-VLM Integration for Grounded Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: Large language models can translate natural-language instructions into plausible manipulation plans, but robotic execution requires physically grounded decisions that respect robot embodiment, workspace geometry, reachability, collision constraints, and grasp feasibility. This paper presents a hardware-aware large language model-vision-language model (LLM-VLM) manipulation framework for a simulated Franka Research 3 robot in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. The framework separates symbolic reasoning from metric execution: an API-hosted LLM planner receives a structured scene summary and generates only symbolic task information, including the object to manipulate, target relation, approach preference, and objects to avoid. A local Qwen3-VL 8B VLM verifier supports semantic confirmation of ambiguous objects and open-container surrogates. Both the LLM planner and the VLM verifier are prohibited from generating robot coordinates, grasp poses, keepout dimensions, gripper commands, trajectory waypoints, or success labels. Instead, these decisions are handled by deterministic grounding and execution modules that use the robot model, scene geometry, MoveIt 2 collision checking, inverse kinematics, grasp validation, release verification, and final visual assessment. Execution feedback is returned only as symbolic context for replanning. The framework is evaluated through simulated digital-twin trials involving pickup, occluded-source access, keepout reasoning, relation placement, and sequential manipulation tasks.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can turn natural-language instructions into plausible manipulation plans, but a robot must also respect embodiment, workspace geometry, reachability, collisions, and grasp feasibility. For a simulated Franka Research 3 arm in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, the framework separates symbolic reasoning from metric execution: an API-hosted LLM planner receives a structured scene summary and emits only symbolic task information such as the target object, relation, approach preference, and objects to avoid, while a local `Qwen3-VL 8B` vision-language model (VLM) verifies ambiguous objects and open-container surrogates. **Neither model may produce coordinates, grasp poses, keepout dimensions, gripper commands, trajectory waypoints, or success labels**; those come from deterministic grounding and execution modules built on the robot model, scene geometry, MoveIt 2 collision checking, inverse kinematics, and grasp, release, and visual verification, with execution feedback fed back only as symbolic context. Digital-twin trials cover pickup, occluded-source access, keepout reasoning, relation placement, and sequential manipulation.

papers.title: The Silent Failures in Agentic Data Science
papers.abstract: Large language models have significantly lowered the barrier to writing code. Naturally, this has also led to the development of data science agents that promise automating the design and execution of data science from task formulation to model development. Existing evaluations of agentic data science (agentic DS) assess downstream predictive performance and code correctness, providing preliminary insight in agentic DS capabilities. We argue that these evaluations overlook the fundamental principles of data science: methodological data science- and domain knowledge. As such, only assessing downstream performance masks methodological failures such as data leakage and inappropriate validation, limiting the development of robust agentic DS systems. In this paper, we evaluate agentic DS beyond accuracy from three different angles: 1) a large-scale analysis of failure modes in common agentic DS frameworks and models across 220 data science tasks, 2) a reusable and extensible test suite with curated data science tasks that test for six specific failures in a controlled manner, and 3) a qualitative assessment of agentic DS pipelines against expert solutions on Kaggle competitions. We find that the majority of agentic solutions contain at least one failure mode despite the complexity of agentic harness or model capacity. Moreover, we identify a positive correlation between the occurrence of data leakage failures and predictive performance, confirming the necessity to evaluate agents beyond accuracy. Our qualitative analysis shows that DS agents generally lack problem solving creativity and domain knowledge, compared to competition-winning data scientists. We believe that principled failure mode analysis, as presented here, should be integral part of agentic DS evaluations, and that the insights we surface will be key in developing trustworthy agentic DS pipelines.
papers.summary: Evaluations of data science agents typically score downstream predictive performance and code correctness, which can mask methodological failures such as data leakage and inappropriate validation. The study examines agentic data science from three angles: a large-scale failure-mode analysis of common frameworks and models across 220 tasks, a reusable test suite of curated tasks that probe six specific failures under controlled conditions, and a qualitative comparison of agent pipelines against expert solutions to Kaggle competitions. **Most agentic solutions contain at least one failure mode regardless of harness complexity or model capacity**, and data leakage failures correlate positively with predictive performance, so accuracy alone rewards the wrong behavior. Against competition winners, the agents show little problem-solving creativity or domain knowledge.

papers.title: ClawLoop: Self-Improving Agents via Harness-Native Training Loop
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven their deployment toward general-purpose harness environments, where LLM-based agents operate in sandbox workspaces and interact directly with file systems and shells. While numerous post-training pipelines exist for tool-use agents, their counterparts for harness-based agents remain scarce and are predominantly one-shot and teacher-dependent: a stronger external model synthesizes tasks and collects trajectories, the target agent is trained once, and evaluation results are consumed by human researchers rather than fed back into the loop. Such pipelines are inherently bounded by the capability of the external model and the scope of human prior, leaving no room for self-improvement. To address these limitations, we propose ClawLoop, a framework that enables self-improving without any external teacher model and with minimal prior dependencies. ClawLoop composes three phases into a self-sustaining cycle: Task Synthesis, which generates a diverse pool of training tasks via two complementary construction routines, applies diagnosis-conditioned difficulty growth followed by both agent-free and agent-based task validation; Training, which updates the agent via SFT and/or RL; and Diagnosis and Feedback, which analyzes the agent's rollout behaviors to produce a capability analysis report that will be used as feedback for task synthesis in the next iteration. Using Qwen3.6-27B as the loop model, ClawLoop yields consistent improvements on SkillsBench, Claw-Eval-Live, and ClawGym-Bench. The iteratively refined tasks are further transferred to smaller-scale Qwen3.5-4B and 9B models with gains across all benchmarks, validating data quality independently of the loop model.
papers.summary: Post-training pipelines for agents that operate in sandboxed harness environments with file systems and shells are mostly one-shot and depend on a stronger teacher model to synthesize tasks and trajectories, which caps improvement at the teacher's ability. `ClawLoop` runs without an external teacher: a task-synthesis phase builds a diverse task pool through two construction routines with diagnosis-conditioned difficulty growth and both agent-free and agent-based validation, a training phase updates the agent with supervised fine-tuning and/or reinforcement learning, and a diagnosis phase turns rollout behavior into a capability report that steers the next round of synthesis. **With `Qwen3.6-27B` as the loop model, it delivers consistent gains on `SkillsBench`, `Claw-Eval-Live`, and `ClawGym-Bench`**, and the refined tasks also improve the 4B and 9B `Qwen3.5` models across all benchmarks, indicating the data quality does not depend on the loop model.

papers.title: Correction Training for Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Iterative sampling in diffusion models can lead to error accumulation due to exposure bias. The denoiser is trained on real images interpolated with noise, but at inference its inputs are constructed from its own imperfect predictions from the earlier steps, something it has never seen at training time. This might be one reason diffusion models often struggle without additional help, such as CFG. We introduce a correction step for diffusion models which attempts to reduce this training-inference gap. The corrector takes the base model's prediction as input and is trained against the same ground-truth target. This makes correction an explicit learning task, with training inputs provided by the base model. During sampling, at each denoising step, we iteratively refine the denoiser's clean-sample prediction. This allows us to correct predictions at intermediate denoising steps, preventing early artifacts from persisting into the final sample. Although the corrector is trained only on predictions from the base denoiser, it can be applied repeatedly to its own outputs at inference for better results. This simple framework leads to substantial improvement in sample quality while largely preserving diversity. We evaluate our method across DiT, SiT, and JiT. Our method substantially improves upon previously reported FID scores for unguided generation and, notably, unconditional generation, where producing high-quality samples without guidance has been particularly challenging. Our method achieves performance competitive with classifier-free guidance (CFG), and combining correction with CFG further improves diversity and reduces oversaturation typical of CFG. Finally, we show that the additional inference cost of correction can be amortized by distilling the refined predictions back into the base diffusion model, retaining the quality gains without additional inference-time overhead.
papers.summary: Iterative diffusion sampling accumulates error through exposure bias: the denoiser trains on real images mixed with noise, but at inference it sees inputs built from its own imperfect earlier predictions, which may be one reason diffusion models lean on classifier-free guidance (CFG). The proposed corrector takes the base model's clean-sample prediction as input and is trained toward the same ground-truth target, then at each denoising step iteratively refines that prediction so early artifacts do not persist; although it is trained only on base-model outputs, it can be reapplied to its own outputs. **Across `DiT`, `SiT`, and `JiT`, correction substantially improves previously reported FID for unguided and unconditional generation and reaches quality competitive with CFG**, while combining it with CFG improves diversity and reduces oversaturation. Distilling the refined predictions back into the base model keeps the quality gains with no added inference cost.

papers.title: Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench 2.0: Automating Diverse Task Construction and Measuring Sustained Agent Progress
papers.abstract: Long-horizon terminal benchmarks measure whether an agent can sustain progress through extended workflows with process rewards, not only whether its final state passes a binary check. We present Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench 2.0 (LHTB 2.0), an extension of Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench that preserves its 46 original tasks while correcting task and evaluation-infrastructure defects and extending 31 tasks. LHTB 2.0 contains 77 tasks across 13 domains and eight task types. The extended tasks are produced through a systematic reconstruction-task pipeline. We start from a working scientific or engineering artifact, then use a parameterized reference implementation to generate multiple scenarios, reveal six as behavioral evidence, hold out three for evaluation, and use dense progress ladders to reward partial progress while preventing memorization of public outputs. We also extend the evaluation horizon from 90 minutes to three hours and record verifier checkpoints every 30 minutes, enabling direct measurement of sustained progress within a run. Across 1,145 scored model-task runs from 15 frontier models, GPT-6-astra leads with dense mean reward 0.69 and 37 tasks at R at least 0.95, followed by GPT-5.6-sol with dense mean reward 0.67 and 32 tasks at the same threshold. On the 30 reconstruction tasks, binary verifier scores average 0.221, whereas dense ladder scores average 0.653, showing that outcome-only evaluation discards substantial intermediate progress. LHTB 2.0 provides a broader, hardened, and process-aware testbed for studying reliable agent execution over hours.
papers.summary: Binary pass/fail checks on an agent's final state discard the partial progress that matters in hours-long terminal workflows. `LHTB 2.0` keeps the 46 original `Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench` tasks, fixes task and evaluation-infrastructure defects, and adds 31 reconstruction tasks built from working scientific or engineering artifacts: a parameterized reference implementation generates multiple scenarios, six are revealed as behavioral evidence, three are held out, and dense progress ladders reward partial progress while blocking memorization of public outputs. The evaluation horizon grows from 90 minutes to three hours with verifier checkpoints every 30 minutes. **Across 1,145 scored runs from 15 frontier models, `GPT-6-astra` leads with a dense mean reward of 0.69**, and on the 30 reconstruction tasks binary verifier scores average 0.221 versus 0.653 for dense ladders, quantifying how much intermediate progress outcome-only evaluation throws away.

papers.title: VETNET: Assembling Benchmark Datasets for AI-Driven Veterinary Innovation
papers.abstract: VETNET represents an ecosystem of live benchmark datasets and evaluation frameworks designed to accelerate AI-driven innovation in animal science and veterinary medicine through standardized, high-quality datasets and multi-institutional collaboration across academic and non-academic sectors. This framework addresses the gap between AI advances in human medicine and the fragmented state of veterinary AI development.
papers.summary: Veterinary medicine and animal science trail human medicine in AI development, in part because the available datasets are fragmented and non-standardized. `VETNET` is proposed as an ecosystem of live benchmark datasets and evaluation frameworks assembled through multi-institutional collaboration across academic and non-academic sectors. **The stated aim is standardized, high-quality datasets that let veterinary AI progress be measured and compared**, closing the gap with human-medicine benchmarking.

papers.title: Beyond Discrimination: Evaluating Probability Calibration in Radiomics-Image Fusion for Renal Cell Carcinoma Classification
papers.abstract: Reliable probability estimates are important for the clinical interpretation of machine-learning classifiers, yet radiomics--image fusion models for renal cell carcinoma (RCC) are commonly evaluated primarily by discrimination. Using 396 patients from the KiTS23 dataset, we evaluated whether adding radiomics to four image-model families improved probabilistic performance in addition to discrimination. Seventeen individual models and four probability-average ensembles were assessed using discrimination, probability calibration, and proper scoring measures. Across 12 matched image-only versus fusion comparisons, AUC and AP improved in all 12, while Brier score and negative log likelihood (NLL) improved in 11 of 12 and expected calibration error (ECE) in eight of 12. The 3D MedVAE gated-fusion model achieved the strongest overall individual-model profile. Probability averaging across concatenation, cross-attention, and gated fusion produced favourable point estimates across all five primary metrics relative to image-only models in all four families, although paired-bootstrap support was stronger for Brier score and NLL than for ECE. These findings show that radiomics--image fusion can improve probabilistic prediction quality beyond discrimination, while calibration behaviour varies across image architectures and fusion strategies. We show that our proposed probability-average ensemble models improve discrimination and calibration simultaneously across all architectures in the study.
papers.summary: Radiomics-image fusion models for renal cell carcinoma (RCC) classification are usually judged by discrimination alone, although clinical use also needs well-calibrated probabilities. Using 396 patients from `KiTS23`, the study asks whether adding radiomics to four image-model families improves probabilistic performance, assessing seventeen individual models and four probability-average ensembles on discrimination, calibration, and proper scoring rules. **Across 12 matched image-only versus fusion comparisons, AUC and average precision improved in all 12, Brier score and negative log likelihood in 11, and expected calibration error in 8**, with the `3D MedVAE` gated-fusion model giving the strongest single-model profile. Probability averaging over concatenation, cross-attention, and gated fusion improved discrimination and calibration together in all four families, though paired-bootstrap support was stronger for Brier score and log likelihood than for calibration error.

papers.title: Beyond Gate Weights: Decision-Level Interpretation of Radiomics-Image Feature Fusion for RCC Classification
papers.abstract: Gate coefficients describe how a fusion layer weights intermediate features, but they do not necessarily reflect the magnitude of branch contributions at the classifier output. We investigate this distinction in a fixed 3D MedVAE--radiomics model for clear cell versus non-clear cell renal cell carcinoma classification from contrast-enhanced CT. Because the model uses a linear classification head, the binary decision logit can be decomposed exactly into a gated image term, a direct radiomics term, and a bias. We define effective radiomics dominance as the direct radiomics term's share of the summed absolute non-bias branch contributions and compare it with structural radiomics weighting. Internally, mean structural radiomics weighting was 0.823, whereas mean effective radiomics dominance was 0.148, with a modest case-wise association (\r{ho} = 0.290). The gated image term retained substantially stronger discriminative ranking information than the direct radiomics term. The same structural-to-effective discrepancy was observed in exploratory external evaluation. Branch-targeted permutation, integrated-gradient, and Shapley-style analyses further identified radiomics descriptors influencing the direct radiomics term. Because radiomics also generates the gate, the gated image term remains radiomics-dependent, so additive branch contribution should not be interpreted as total input influence. These findings show that structural gate weighting and decision-level branch contribution represent distinct aspects of gated feature fusion and should be interpreted separately.
papers.summary: Gate coefficients in a fusion layer describe how intermediate features are weighted, but that need not reflect how much each branch contributes at the classifier output. In a fixed `3D MedVAE`-radiomics model for clear cell versus non-clear cell renal cell carcinoma (RCC) classification from contrast-enhanced CT, the linear classification head lets the decision logit be decomposed exactly into a gated image term, a direct radiomics term, and a bias, so an effective radiomics dominance can be compared with the structural gate weighting. **Mean structural radiomics weighting was 0.823 while mean effective radiomics dominance was 0.148**, with a modest case-wise correlation of 0.290, and the gated image term carried far more discriminative ranking information; the same gap appeared in exploratory external evaluation. Because radiomics also generates the gate, additive branch contributions should not be read as total input influence.

papers.title: Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallel sampling for faster generation than autoregressive models, an increasingly important advantage as inference becomes a dominant computational workload. However, DLMs degrade quickly with fewer sampling steps, process the full sequence at every step, and require many passes over the dataset to reach good quality. We introduce Next-Concept Modeling (NCM), a two-stage, coarse-to-fine framework: a multiscale residual VQ-VAE encodes text into a hierarchy of discrete codes, and a transformer generates one level at a time, predicting all codes within a level in parallel. At matched parameter scales, NCM achieves better generative perplexity than the strongest DLM baseline on LM1B while running $21\times$ faster. On OpenWebText, NCM is competitive with the strongest DLM while running $10\times$ faster; on XSum, it matches the strongest DLM's ROUGE-L while being $31\times$ faster. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations.
papers.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) allow parallel sampling but degrade quickly with fewer steps, process the full sequence at every step, and need many passes over the data to train well. `Next-Concept Modeling` (NCM) is a two-stage coarse-to-fine scheme: a multiscale residual VQ-VAE encodes text into a hierarchy of discrete codes, and a transformer generates one level at a time, predicting all codes within a level in parallel. **At matched parameter scales NCM beats the strongest DLM baseline on `LM1B` in generative perplexity while running 21× faster**, is competitive on `OpenWebText` at 10× the speed, and matches ROUGE-L on `XSum` at 31× the speed. On `Sudoku` it outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines at every difficulty level with fewer function evaluations.

papers.title: Do you "see" what I "see"? A Multi-panel Visual Question Answer Dataset for Large Language Model Chart Analysis
papers.abstract: Digital libraries increasingly host scientific publications whose figures encode primary research findings, yet making this visual content searchable, accessible, and reusable remains an open challenge. Large language and multimodal models (LLMs/LMMs) provide the possibility to automate many figure parsing tasks such as determining data trends or extracting data from plots. In this work, we consider if these models can reliably support task-oriented visual data analysis when presented with synthetic, but realistic, scientific figures that contain multiple charts. Our Visual Question Answering (VQA) process scaffolds our tasks along a four-level description model from basic conceptual answers to interpretive and analytical understanding. Additionally, we outline our process for synthetically generating our single and multi-panel (charts in which there are multiple panels present) plots and testing the data with various LMMs using quantitative analysis. In general, we find LMMs become less accurate with increasing figure complexity as the number of panels, number of plot elements, and difficulty of questions increase. Finally, because LMM accuracy is expected to change rapidly, our analysis also considers cost relative to performance as a metric to inform future user decisions. We provide the detailed question-answer pairs used in this analysis, along with the code used to generate random plots, question-answer pairs and detailed bounding-box metadata for chart elements. The code and data are available at https://github.com/ReadingTimeMachine/LLM_VQA_MultiPanel and https://huggingface.co/datasets/ReadingTimeMachine/visual\_qa\_multipanel
papers.summary: Scientific figures in digital libraries encode primary findings, yet making that visual content searchable and reusable remains open, and large multimodal models (LMMs) might automate figure parsing. The authors synthetically generate realistic single- and multi-panel plots with bounding-box metadata for chart elements, build visual question answering (VQA) tasks along a four-level description model from basic conceptual answers to interpretive and analytical understanding, and test several LMMs quantitatively. **Accuracy falls as figure complexity rises, with more panels, more plot elements, and harder questions all degrading performance**, and cost relative to performance is reported as an extra decision metric. The question-answer pairs, plot-generation code, and metadata are released.

papers.title: Unconstrained CTI-REALM with Open-Weights
papers.abstract: Organisations that want language-model agents for security work face a choice between open-weight models, which they can run and audit themselves, and far more expensive closed frontier models. We study that choice on CTI-REALM (arXiv:2603.13517), a benchmark in which an agent turns a threat-intelligence report into a working detection by querying a live telemetry store. We evaluate twenty-six models, nineteen open-weight and seven closed, under a common harness, scorer and panel of LLM judges. Our main finding is that an open-weight model can match the strongest closed models at less than a tenth of their cost, provided it is given enough turns. The benchmark's published limit on agent messages is a confound: a task that exhausts the limit scores zero on every checkpoint, including those it had already passed, so results at that limit partly measure which models finish in time. At the published limit the leading open-weight and closed models cannot be distinguished. With the limit relaxed, the models it was truncating recover, and the highest rewards belong to open-weight models. Among the leading models, price is a poor guide to capability: models with similar rewards differ in cost by more than an order of magnitude. Because the benchmark's checkpoint scores largely record what an agent did or mentioned, we also introduce stage-level metrics that score what the agent submits, by executing its detection queries in the telemetry store and judging its outputs against the answer key. Rather than combining them into one more overall reward, we show that different models lead different stages, which suggests routing each stage of the workflow to the model that performs it best rather than choosing a single model by its overall score. We also report how many tokens each model generates, and find that the share of output spent on thinking does not track the reward.
papers.summary: Organisations wanting language-model agents for security work must choose between open-weight models they can run and audit themselves and far more expensive closed frontier models. The study compares 26 models, 19 open-weight and 7 closed, under one harness, scorer, and panel of LLM judges on `CTI-REALM`, where an agent turns a threat-intelligence report into a working detection by querying a live telemetry store. **An open-weight model can match the strongest closed models at less than a tenth of their cost, provided it gets enough turns**: the benchmark's message limit zeroes every checkpoint when exhausted, so published-limit results partly measure which models finish in time, and once the limit is relaxed the highest rewards belong to open-weight models while price proves a poor guide to capability. New stage-level metrics that execute each agent's submitted detection queries show different models lead different stages, pointing toward per-stage routing, and the share of output spent on thinking does not track reward.

papers.title: Visualizing the World Model in an Agent's Value Function
papers.abstract: Could model-free reinforcement learning algorithms actually be learning a model of the environment? In this work, we apply counterfactual interventions which hold everything about a state fixed, besides a targeted change, to explore if the value function of a Proximal Policy Optimization agent forms a world model of the Crafter environment. Despite only being trained to optimize reward, we discover that the value function learns concepts such as the rules governing when a diamond is collectible, water and food having an impact on health, heuristics regarding inventory, and more. Finally, we discuss the safety implications of our visualizations and some shortcomings of current reinforcement learning agents that will prevent us from building truly advanced machine intelligence.
papers.summary: Model-free reinforcement learning never explicitly trains an environment model, which raises the question of whether one emerges anyway. Counterfactual interventions that change one targeted aspect of a state while holding everything else fixed are used to probe the value function of a `Proximal Policy Optimization` agent trained on `Crafter`. **Although trained only to optimize reward, the value function encodes rules such as when a diamond is collectible, how water and food affect health, and inventory heuristics.** The discussion covers safety implications of the visualizations and shortcomings of current reinforcement learning agents.

papers.title: Cross-Modal Latent Influence: Patch-Level Training Sample Attribution for Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Explaining a vision--language model (VLM) prediction requires tracing training-example influence to the multimodal evidence that mediates it, yet existing attribution methods largely operate only at the sample level. Recent latent-mediated influence methods provide feature-level attribution in language models, but lack the multimodal and spatial structure needed to ground influence in VLMs. We introduce MOSAIC (Multimodal Orthogonalized Sparse Autoencoders for Influence Characterization). It learns a shared sparse image--text latent space whose concepts are 1) sparse within each modality, 2) supported on contiguous image regions, 3) aligned to the phrases that describe them, and 4) approximately decorrelated. It then applies EK-FAC to decompose training-example influence through these concepts and localize their contributions to specific text phrases and image regions. We evaluate MOSAIC on Qwen and Gemma across captioning, chest X-ray understanding, and visual question answering. The learned features are more localized and coherent without degrading task behavior, and ablating influence-ranked latents changes model outputs more than ablating latents ranked by activation or frequency. We find that visual evidence can substantially reorganize training-data attribution while preserving more of the shared latent structure. MOSAIC thus connects where model behavior comes from with what multimodal evidence carries that influence.
papers.summary: Explaining a vision-language model (VLM) prediction means tracing which training examples mattered and which multimodal evidence carried that influence, but existing attribution methods mostly stop at the sample level. `MOSAIC` (Multimodal Orthogonalized Sparse Autoencoders for Influence Characterization) learns a shared sparse image-text latent space whose concepts are sparse within each modality, supported on contiguous image regions, aligned to the phrases describing them, and approximately decorrelated, then applies `EK-FAC` to decompose training-example influence through those concepts and localize it to specific phrases and image regions. Evaluated on `Qwen` and `Gemma` across captioning, chest X-ray understanding, and visual question answering, the learned features are more localized and coherent without degrading task behavior, and **ablating influence-ranked latents changes model outputs more than ablating latents ranked by activation or frequency**. Visual evidence can substantially reorganize training-data attribution while preserving much of the shared latent structure.

papers.title: Should SLMs be in the Driver's Seat? A Study of Local Models as Interpreters in Cloud-Written Agent Programs
papers.abstract: The most accurate agents executing user-provided tasks are driven by large, cloud-hosted models, which solve them by reading the private data of the user. Agents powered by models small enough to run on edge devices keep that data local, but yield far worse results. A third option is to have cloud models write a program that devices execute: the data stays local, but as the program is written before any data is seen, it fails whenever a step depends on interpreting content that appears only at run time. We explore an intermediate architecture, in which the cloud-written program defers bounded questions over user data to a small local model through an ordinary function call. On AppWorld this improves the success rate of a code-only agent in all six combinations of backbone model and test partition we evaluate, by up to 14.9pp, recovering a substantial part of the gap to a cloud-hosted ReAct loop while keeping user data on the device.
papers.summary: Cloud-hosted models make the most accurate agents but read the user's private data, on-device small models keep data local but perform far worse, and having the cloud write a program the device runs fails whenever a step depends on content that only appears at run time. The intermediate architecture lets the cloud-written program defer bounded questions over user data to a small local model through an ordinary function call, so the local model interprets content rather than driving the agent. **On `AppWorld` this raises the success rate of a code-only agent in all six backbone-model and test-partition combinations, by up to 14.9 percentage points**, recovering a substantial part of the gap to a cloud-hosted `ReAct` loop while keeping user data on the device.

papers.title: Cortex: Measurement-Gated Evolution and Pruning of Coding-Agent Skills and Rules
papers.abstract:
Coding agents such as Claude Code also follow text files that developers write for them: a project file, skills the agent may choose to open, and rules that load automatically when the agent reads matching files. We call these files the agent's harness. Developers add to it whenever they correct the agent, but one success proves little: the same agent can pass a task once and fail it the next time.
  We present Cortex, a tool that tests changes to the harness instead of trusting them. It saves fixes from the developer's sessions as replayable tasks, finds the corrections that recur, writes one skill or rule at a time, and keeps it only if repeated runs with and without it show a net gain and no task made noticeably worse. Existing text is tested the same way before it is deleted, and Cortex neither adds nor deletes text the agent never used.
  We tested Cortex with Claude Haiku 4.5 on a repository built for the purpose, with conventions the model tends to break, one area with nothing to learn, and a script playing the developer. On held-out tasks, the harnesses it built made the agent follow the conventions far more often than no skills or rules did, left the comparison area unchanged, and added no text read on every turn. Rules, which load automatically, did most of the work; skills helped only when offered with the files a task touches, and those offered on every turn were rarely opened. Cortex kept none of the useless or harmful suggestions we planted, but the agent never opened the useless ones or the harmful skills, and it reached no verdict on the harmful rules, so the test shows that Cortex keeps no unused text, not that it detects damage. Under the stronger Claude Sonnet 5 a single run's harness added little, and on a real open-source project, where the agent was rarely corrected, Cortex found nothing to learn. We release the tool, the lab and its data.
papers.summary: Coding agents such as Claude Code follow developer-written project files, skills, and auto-loading rules, collectively the harness, and developers add to it after single corrections even though one success proves little. `Cortex` saves fixes from developer sessions as replayable tasks, finds the corrections that recur, writes one skill or rule at a time, and keeps it only if repeated runs with and without it show a net gain and no task noticeably worse; existing text is tested the same way before deletion, and text the agent never used is neither added nor removed. **On a purpose-built repository with `Claude Haiku 4.5`, the harnesses it built made the agent follow conventions far more often on held-out tasks**, with auto-loading rules doing most of the work and skills helping only when offered alongside the files a task touches. Planted harmful rules never reached a verdict, a single run added little under `Claude Sonnet 5`, and on a real open-source project where the agent was rarely corrected the tool found nothing to learn.

papers.title: Learnable Low-Rank Polynomial Sketch for Effective Linear Attention
papers.abstract: Softmax attention in Transformers suffers from quadratic complexity in sequence length, making it impractical for long-context applications. Linear attention alleviates this issue by replacing the exponential kernel with alternative functions that enable linear-time computation. Among existing linear attention approaches, recent studies have shown that polynomial kernels are particularly effective, as they exhibit sparse and spiky behavior similar to softmax attention, which emphasizes large dot products while suppressing irrelevant interactions. However, the exact computation of high-degree polynomial kernels is infeasible for high-dimensional representations. As a result, prior work relies on approximate polynomial kernels. This introduces a non-negligible approximation error. In this paper, we show that, from the perspective of polynomial kernel approximation, existing linear attention methods are still suboptimal. We propose \textbf{L}earnable \textbf{Lo}w-Rank \textbf{P}olynomial \textbf{S}ketch (LLoPS), a principled and flexible framework for approximating polynomial kernels with linear attention. Our method learns a low-rank polynomial sketch that provably achieves a strictly smaller approximation error than existing approaches. Experiment results show that LLoPS achieves the highest performance across extensive benchmarks, comparing with various linear attention baselines.
papers.summary: Softmax attention costs quadratic time in sequence length, and linear attention swaps the exponential kernel for cheaper functions; polynomial kernels work especially well because they are sparse and spiky like softmax, but exact high-degree polynomial kernels are infeasible in high dimensions, so prior work approximates them with non-negligible error. `LLoPS` (Learnable Low-Rank Polynomial Sketch) treats linear attention as polynomial kernel approximation and learns a low-rank sketch that **provably achieves strictly smaller approximation error than existing approaches**. Experiments show it reaches the highest performance across extensive benchmarks against a range of linear attention baselines.

papers.title: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World
papers.abstract: LLM agents' capabilities depend not only on their underlying models but also on their execution harnesses. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a promising approach to automatically evolve these harnesses. However, deploying RSI in open-world settings still faces two critical challenges. First, open-world tasks are typically unseen during the harness design phase and novel at test time, leaving no ground-truth verifiers to reliably guide online harness edits. Second, the RSI process remains highly task-specific and fails to generalize to novel scenarios. We introduce Harness^2, a plug-and-play, recursive agent harnessing framework that addresses these challenges through two connected levels of recursion. Task-level recursion refines the current task's harness using a contrastive Propose-Probe-Compose step that reliably guides edits without ground-truth verifiers, and can be scaled further via parallel or sequential recursion. Harnessing-level recursion then extracts experience from these edits to update a continual improvement harness, enabling the agent to better adapt to future tasks. Across three professional benchmarks and four model-harness configurations, a single step consistently improves GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash over their base harnesses, yielding gains of up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 points on JobBench, and 11.8 percentage points on LAB, with further gains as the task-level recursion budget increases.
papers.summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) could evolve an agent's execution harness automatically, but open-world tasks are unseen at design time and novel at test time, leaving no ground-truth verifiers to guide online edits, and the process tends to stay task-specific. `Harness^2` is a plug-and-play framework with two connected levels of recursion: task-level recursion refines the current task's harness with a contrastive Propose-Probe-Compose step that guides edits without verifiers and can scale through parallel or sequential recursion, and harnessing-level recursion extracts experience from those edits into a continual-improvement harness for future tasks. **A single step consistently improves `GLM-5` and `Gemini 3.5 Flash` over their base harnesses, by up to 11.5 points on `WorkBuddy-Bench`, 4.5 points on `JobBench`, and 11.8 percentage points on `LAB`**, with further gains as the task-level recursion budget increases.

papers.title: CAPTOR: a vision-language foundation model for Chest-Abdomen-Pelvis Oncologic CT
papers.abstract:
Purpose : To develop and evaluate CAPTOR, a deep-learning vision-language foundation model for oncologic chest-abdomen-pelvis (CAP) CT interpretation.
  Materials & Methods : CAPTOR (Chest-Abdomen-Pelvis foundaTion model for Oncologic Radiology) is a contrastive vision-language model, trained using a pretraining strategy for oncologic CAP CT (in single- or multiple-series acquisitions), on a multicenter retrospective dataset from North America, Europe and Asia, predominantly from tumor lesion examinations. CAPTOR was compared with state-of-the-art CT foundation models on three downstream tasks: disease detection, survival prediction using TumorImagingBench and image retrieval. Classification and retrieval were both evaluated on held-out internal and public test sets, stratified by anatomical coverage and indication. Bootstrap resampling was used to estimate confidence intervals, and pairwise comparisons were performed using permutation tests.
  Results : CAPTOR was trained and tested on 25,512 and 10,794 CT-report pairs respectively. TumorImagingBench datasets comprised between 134 and 421 studies each. CAPTOR outperformed all baseline models, on the classification task, on the CAP subset (AUC 0.767, 95%CI: 0.734-0.793, vs. 0.695, 95%CI: 0.645-0.736 for the next-best, p<0.001) and oncologic subset (AUC 0.784, 95%CI: 0.759-0.805, vs. 0.734, 95%CI: 0.703-0.767 p<0.001), ranked first on three of the four oncologic prognostic benchmarks, and achieved superior retrieval performance on CAP and oncologic subsets.
  Conclusion : A foundation model trained on oncology-enriched CAP CT data outperformed relevant state-of-the-art models in its target clinical context, underscoring the importance of clinically aligned pretraining.
  We release our preprocessing, training and inference code : https://github.com/Guerbet-AI/CAPTOR and model weights : https://huggingface.co/Guerbet-AI/CAPTOR
papers.summary: `CAPTOR` is a contrastive vision-language foundation model for oncologic chest-abdomen-pelvis (CAP) computed tomography (CT), pretrained on 25,512 CT-report pairs from centers in North America, Europe, and Asia, drawn predominantly from tumor lesion examinations and covering single- and multi-series acquisitions. It was compared with state-of-the-art CT foundation models on disease detection, survival prediction on `TumorImagingBench`, and image retrieval, using held-out internal and public test sets stratified by anatomical coverage and indication. **On the CAP classification subset it reached an AUC of 0.767 versus 0.695 for the next-best model**, ranked first on three of the four oncologic prognostic benchmarks, and gave the best retrieval results, which the authors attribute to clinically aligned pretraining; preprocessing, training, and inference code and model weights are released.

papers.title: Latent World Action Model for GUI Agents
papers.abstract: Pixel-space world models have recently emerged as a promising approach for GUI agents, predicting future screens prior to execution and subsequently re-perceiving them for action selection. However, this two-stage paradigm faces two key challenges in GUI environments: (L1) the high computational cost of pixel reconstruction and (L2) the need to reconstruct large and diverse appearance-level details beyond what is required for action selection. In practice, this screen-generation objective can induce an identity shortcut problem, where future-state prediction largely preserves the current state rather than capturing action-induced changes. In this work, we reformulate GUI world modeling by shifting the prediction target from full-screen reconstruction to action-induced future information in latent space. Concretely, we leverage a large multimodal model as the latent world model, whose shared representations support two dedicated heads for both action selection and predictive transition modeling. The action head directly translates these latent representations into action selection, while the transition head captures action-conditioned future information. To mitigate the identity shortcut, we further introduce an action-aware contrastive objective that encourages the transition representations to capture discriminative action-induced changes. Extensive experiments across offline and online GUI settings show that our method achieves up to 31.9% and 40.6% relative gains in success rate over pixel-space world models, respectively, while substantially reducing inference latency by up to 98.9%. Our code is available at https://github.com/sjyu001/latent2world.
papers.summary: Pixel-space world models for graphical user interface (GUI) agents predict the next screen before acting and then re-perceive it to choose an action, but full-screen reconstruction is costly and tends toward an identity shortcut in which the predicted future mostly copies the current state. The proposed approach shifts the prediction target to action-induced future information in latent space, using a large multimodal model as the world model with two heads on shared representations: an action head that selects the next action and a transition head that captures action-conditioned change, trained with an action-aware contrastive objective so transitions encode discriminative action effects rather than static content. Across offline and online GUI settings the method delivers **up to 31.9% and 40.6% relative gains in success rate over pixel-space world models** while cutting inference latency by up to 98.9%.

papers.title: Agentic Data Engineering for LLMs: System Design and a Controlled Empirical Study
papers.abstract: LLM data engineering requires iterative experimentation to determine how data selection, rewards, and curricula affect model learning, making it a natural setting for AI-for-AI (AI4AI) research. Can agents use experimental feedback to progressively improve strategies, and do the resulting strategies improve target-model performance on held-out data? We study how agents use experimental feedback to develop data-engineering strategies under fixed training and evaluation protocols. Our Agentic Data Engineering (ADE) framework lets agents pursue, revise, or combine research directions using cumulative findings. Strategies are selected by in-loop scores and evaluated on held-out benchmarks. Across four tasks-math and code data selection, math reward design, and math curriculum learning-selected strategies achieve absolute gains over generic baselines of up to 13.34% on AIME25 Pass@32 and 5.85% averaged across four held-out benchmarks under fixed training conditions. In-loop scores improve over successive experiments, while held-out trajectories show that later in-loop gains do not always improve generalization. Comparisons of research organization and feedback access favor combining evidence analysis with cumulative findings. Research trajectories show how earlier findings inform strategy revisions and combinations across research directions.
papers.summary: Data engineering for large language model (LLM) training, meaning which examples to select, what rewards to use, and how to order a curriculum, requires repeated experiments, which makes it a natural setting for letting AI agents run the research. The Agentic Data Engineering (`ADE`) framework has agents pursue, revise, or combine research directions using cumulative findings under fixed training and evaluation protocols, selecting strategies by in-loop scores and then measuring them on held-out benchmarks. Across math and code data selection, math reward design, and math curriculum learning, the selected strategies beat generic baselines by **up to 13.34 absolute points on `AIME25` Pass@32** and 5.85 points averaged over four held-out benchmarks. In-loop scores keep improving over successive experiments, but later in-loop gains do not always transfer to held-out generalization, and comparisons of research organization and feedback access favor combining evidence analysis with cumulative findings.

papers.title: Akule: Fast and Scalable Multi-Robot Motion Planning via Sparse Interaction Diffusion
papers.abstract: Diffusion models provide expressive trajectory priors for multi-robot motion planning (MRMP), but scaling them to large teams requires coordinating individual motions without expensive joint computation. We introduce Akule, a sparse interaction diffusion framework that augments a frozen single-robot prior with three learned modules: a reusable pairwise correction model $R_{\phi}$, a contextual selector $U_{\psi}$ that determines which corrections to evaluate, and a composer $G_{\omega}$ that combines their effects through context-dependent signed weights. This decomposition separates which interactions merit computation from how their effects should be combined into coordinated denoising updates. We train $R_{\phi}$ using matched pairwise trajectory optimizations, then learn $G_{\omega}$ and $U_{\psi}$ from physically optimized joint trajectories without requiring a prescribed ground-truth interaction graph. The resulting joint proposals are passed to a downstream search-based planner for validation and repair. Across diverse MRMP benchmarks, Akule achieves competitive planning success, complete-planner speedups of up to $25\times$, zero-shot population transfer, and successful planning with up to $256$ robots. Ablations further demonstrate that learned selection and composition reduce pre-repair conflicts and downstream repair effort relative to heuristic selection and uniform summation.
papers.summary: Diffusion models provide expressive trajectory priors for multi-robot motion planning (MRMP), but scaling them to large teams requires coordinating individual motions without expensive joint computation. `Akule` keeps a frozen single-robot prior and adds three learned modules: a reusable pairwise correction model, a contextual selector that decides which pairwise corrections are worth evaluating, and a composer that combines their effects through context-dependent signed weights, with the resulting joint proposals passed to a search-based planner for validation and repair. The pairwise model is trained on matched pairwise trajectory optimizations, and the selector and composer are learned from physically optimized joint trajectories without a prescribed ground-truth interaction graph. On MRMP benchmarks it reaches competitive success with **complete-planner speedups of up to 25x**, transfers zero-shot across team sizes, and plans for up to 256 robots, with ablations showing that learned selection and composition reduce pre-repair conflicts and repair effort compared with heuristic selection and uniform summation.

papers.title: Echo: Error-Compensated 4-Bit Tensor-Parallel Communication for LLM Training and Inference
papers.abstract: Tensor parallelism ends every layer with an all-reduce that sits between two dependent matrix multiplications, so its cost cannot be hidden and grows as compute outpaces interconnect bandwidth. Sending 4-bit instead of 16-bit values would cut this cost by nearly 4x, but the all-reduce must add the values it carries, and rounding the sum injects an error at every call. Model quality depends on how these errors accumulate over layers, yet existing methods treat each call on its own. We present Echo, a 4-bit all-reduce for training and inference that controls the accumulated error. Echo moves data in 4 bits and sums in high precision, so each value is quantized at most twice per call for any number of GPUs. The summation reveals each injected error, and Echo feeds it back into later calls, so old errors cancel instead of accumulating. We prove that the accumulated error stays bounded independently of depth. On A100 GPUs, Echo is 2.09x faster than the 16-bit NCCL all-reduce on 1 GB messages. It speeds up the time to first token by up to 1.16x and the training step by up to 1.09x on an idle interconnect, and by up to 1.44x and 1.38x as background traffic grows. It keeps the average accuracy over seven benchmarks within 0.4 points of 16-bit inference on Qwen3-8B. In 10B-token pretraining, its final loss is less than 0.9% above that of 16-bit training. Echo needs no FP8 or FP4 hardware.
papers.summary: In tensor-parallel execution every layer ends with an all-reduce sitting between two dependent matrix multiplications, so its cost cannot be hidden and grows as compute outpaces interconnect bandwidth, and although sending 4-bit instead of 16-bit values would cut that cost nearly fourfold, rounding the summed values injects an error at every call that existing methods treat in isolation. `Echo` moves data in 4 bits but sums in high precision, so each value is quantized at most twice per call for any number of GPUs, and it feeds each call's revealed quantization error back into later calls so that old errors cancel, with a proof that the accumulated error stays bounded independent of depth. On A100 GPUs it runs **2.09x faster than the 16-bit NCCL all-reduce on 1 GB messages**, improving time to first token by up to 1.16x and the training step by up to 1.09x on an idle interconnect, rising to 1.44x and 1.38x as background traffic grows. Average accuracy over seven benchmarks stays within 0.4 points of 16-bit inference on `Qwen3-8B`, final loss in 10B-token pretraining is under 0.9% above 16-bit training, and no FP8 or FP4 hardware is required.

papers.title: The RNN Homunculus: Learning to Gate Long-Term Memory
papers.abstract: Learning long-range dependencies with recurrent neural networks (RNNs) is difficult because of the vanishing gradient problem. Gated recurrent neural networks like GRUs and LSTMs address this problem and are commonly explained by their ability to create additive copy paths through time. This explanation is correct, but incomplete: useful RNN gate values must themselves be learned, which is typically done with another RNN. We study this gate-learning problem through carefully controlled sequence classification tasks. Our analysis shows that gated architectures struggle when all training samples require long-range memory and thus equally suffer from the vanishing gradient problem. We intervene by adding short-dependency samples which let gated models learn solutions that capture long-dependency samples, but also generalize across different class labels. When properly learned, gated RNNs match or even exceed the test accuracy of modern architectures like Mamba and xLSTM. Overall, our results highlight gate learning as a central part of learning long-range memory and show how training data can support this process by exposing the same task over shorter dependencies.
papers.summary: Gated recurrent neural networks (RNNs) such as `GRU` and `LSTM` are usually explained as overcoming vanishing gradients through additive copy paths through time, but the gate values that create those paths must themselves be learned, typically by another recurrent network.
