Using carefully controlled sequence classification tasks, the authors show that gated architectures struggle when every training sample demands long-range memory, because the gate-learning network then suffers the same vanishing-gradient problem. Adding short-dependency samples lets gated models learn solutions that also capture the long-dependency samples and generalize across class labels, and **properly trained gated RNNs match or exceed the test accuracy of `Mamba` and `xLSTM`**. The results frame gate learning as a central part of acquiring long-range memory and show that training data can support it by exposing the same task over shorter dependencies.

papers.title: GeoFix: Geometry Fixing for 4D Consistent Generation
papers.abstract: Video diffusion models increasingly serve as priors for 4D generation, but the generated videos often lack geometric consistency. Recent approaches address this through post-training by designing geometric rewards, yet this can degrade texture and fine detail, requiring auxiliary appearance rewards and careful reward balancing. To address this challenge, we propose GeoFix, a unified framework that improves geometric consistency and visual quality with a single geometric reward, applicable to both training and inference-time reward alignment. Our reward measures cross-view depth consistency in static scene regions, targeting structural inconsistencies without directly constraining appearance or penalizing valid object motion. Crucially, depth agreement increases with camera field-of-view overlap even in real videos and 4D datasets, allowing a smaller camera movement to be mistaken for better geometry. We account for this effect by calibrating the reward against the overlap-dependent trend. GeoFix achieves a 39% improvement in WorldScore 3D consistency and a 4% increase in VBench Quality Score.
papers.summary: Video diffusion models increasingly serve as priors for 4D generation, but their outputs often lack geometric consistency, and post-training with geometric rewards tends to degrade texture and fine detail unless balanced against auxiliary appearance rewards. `GeoFix` uses a single geometric reward that measures cross-view depth consistency in static scene regions, targeting structural inconsistencies without directly constraining appearance or penalizing valid object motion, and applies it to both training-time and inference-time reward alignment. Because depth agreement rises with camera field-of-view overlap even in real videos and 4D datasets, so that smaller camera movement can be mistaken for better geometry, the reward is calibrated against that overlap-dependent trend. The method yields **a 39% improvement in `WorldScore` 3D consistency** and a 4% increase in the `VBench` quality score.

papers.title: Controllable Diverse Sampling through Pullback Directions
papers.abstract: Conditional diffusion models can generate high-quality images that align closely with a given prompt. However, samples generated from different random seeds may remain visually similar, limiting creative exploration. Existing approaches can increase variation, but often require additional optimization or sampling overhead, while stronger perturbations may introduce distortions that degrade image quality or prompt alignment. We propose a training-free method that leverages the local pullback geometry induced by the mapping from the conditioning-embedding space to the image space to identify directions of maximal output sensitivity. By steering different sampling trajectories along these directions, we encourage distinct generations while maintaining consistency with the conditioning signal. Experiments on MS-COCO and BrushNet show the efficacy of the method in improving diversity on prompt-conditioned image generation and inpainting.
papers.summary: Conditional diffusion models produce prompt-faithful images, but samples from different random seeds often look alike, and existing diversity methods add optimization or sampling overhead or introduce distortions when perturbations grow strong. The proposed training-free method uses the local pullback geometry of the map from the conditioning-embedding space to image space to identify directions of maximal output sensitivity, then steers different sampling trajectories along those directions so that generations diverge while staying consistent with the conditioning signal. **Experiments on `MS-COCO` and `BrushNet` show improved diversity** for prompt-conditioned image generation and inpainting.

papers.title: RUBATO: Decoupled Clocks Allow Full-Duplex Models to Think as Fast as They Can
papers.abstract: Recent Speech Full-Duplex (FDX) models are capable of engaging in naturalistic conversation by listening and speaking at the same time. Building on this foundation, recent architectures introduce internal thinking streams to enhance their intelligence. To guarantee these streams process successfully in real time, existing methods enforce a fixed decoding rate, which assumes a hardware profile capable of a specific latency. We argue this static approach is severely suboptimal. Because internal thinking is intrinsically asynchronous, an ideal FDX model should sustain real-time conversational flow while allowing each stream to decode at its own hardware-adaptive rate. Thinking streams must process as fast as the hardware allows to deliver accurate answers faster. To solve this, we propose RUBATO, a novel multistream positional encoding that assigns independent clocks to entirely decouple the streams. This structural isolation empowers the model to zero-shot interpolate across any inference decoding speed. It drastically simplifies dataset construction by requiring training on only two extreme decoding speeds while smoothly adapting to any intermediate rate during deployment. RUBATO demonstrates consistent robustness across five spoken reasoning tasks. On Spoken GSM8K, a baseline model collapses to 1.7% accuracy at interpolated speeds. Conversely, RUBATO-Full sustains 48.7% to 51.1% accuracy across all rates, leveraging faster hardware to achieve a 6.5x shorter time-to-answer with a constant time-to-first-response. This advantage holds on BIG-Bench Audio and amplifies significantly during complex full-duplex interruptions. Specifically, when a user interjects while the model is actively speaking and reasoning, RUBATO-Full achieves 40.0% to 45.1% accuracy, whereas the baseline fails completely.
papers.summary: Speech full-duplex (FDX) models listen and speak at the same time, and recent architectures add internal thinking streams, but to keep those streams running in real time existing methods fix a decoding rate tuned to one assumed hardware latency. `RUBATO` is a multistream positional encoding that assigns each stream an independent clock, decoupling them so the thinking stream can decode as fast as the hardware allows while conversational flow stays real time, and training on only two extreme decoding speeds suffices for zero-shot interpolation to any intermediate rate. On `Spoken GSM8K` a baseline collapses to 1.7% accuracy at interpolated speeds, whereas **`RUBATO-Full` sustains 48.7% to 51.1% accuracy across all rates** and uses faster hardware to reach a 6.5x shorter time-to-answer at a constant time-to-first-response. The advantage holds on `BIG-Bench Audio` and widens under full-duplex interruptions, where the model keeps 40.0% to 45.1% accuracy when a user interjects mid-speech and the baseline fails completely.

papers.title: ConicFlow: constrained Inference-time optimal control for flow matching models
papers.abstract: We propose ConicFlow, which frames constrained sampling from a flow matching model at inference time as an optimal control problem that balances deviation from the pretrained trajectory against reward, subject to hard terminal constraints. We discretize this problem and adapt receding-horizon control, optimizing only a short window of the trajectory at each step for computational tractability. We address the resulting sequence of receding-horizon subproblems with a receding-horizon primal-dual algorithm. Its dual multipliers capture the difficulty of satisfying each constraint and are refined throughout sampling, steering generation toward feasible final samples. We further propose a terminal-estimate variant that avoids accumulating local truncation errors by evaluating the reward and constraints at the predicted terminal point rather than at the end of the current horizon. Under standard regularity assumptions, we establish finite-horizon guarantees on suboptimality. Under convex-affine structure, we derive a sharper bound that scales linearly with omitted horizon length, and we show that the terminal-estimate variant is provably tighter when the flow dynamics change slowly. Experiments in both low- and high-dimensional settings with a recent large-scale flow matching model show that ConicFlow achieves high reward and strong constraint satisfaction while deviating less from the pretrained flow than recent baselines.
papers.summary: Constrained sampling from a pretrained flow matching model at inference time is framed as an optimal control problem that balances deviation from the pretrained trajectory against reward, subject to hard terminal constraints. `ConicFlow` discretizes this problem and applies receding-horizon control, optimizing only a short window of the trajectory at each step, and solves the resulting subproblems with a primal-dual algorithm whose dual multipliers capture how hard each constraint is to satisfy and are refined throughout sampling. A terminal-estimate variant evaluates reward and constraints at the predicted terminal point rather than at the end of the current horizon, avoiding accumulated local truncation error. The authors establish finite-horizon suboptimality guarantees under standard regularity assumptions, including **a bound that scales linearly with the omitted horizon length under convex-affine structure** and a provably tighter bound for the terminal-estimate variant when flow dynamics change slowly, and experiments with a recent large-scale flow matching model show high reward and strong constraint satisfaction with less deviation from the pretrained flow than recent baselines.

papers.title: MvFFN: Multi-view Floor plan Feed-forward Network for Unposed Wide-Baseline Panorama Layout Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Reconstructing accurate camera poses and floor-plan layouts from sparse, unposed, wide-baseline RGB panoramas remains a challenging open problem. Direct multi-room floor-plan prediction is especially difficult in this setting: pose, geometry, semantics, and global layout structure are tightly coupled, yet a complete floor-plan is hard to learn as a single global output. Our key insight is to keep the model's predictions strictly local. Multi-view Ordered Wall Instance Segmentation (MOIS) is designed around this concept. Each panorama column predicts only the wall it observes plus the next two adjacent walls in clockwise order. The global wall partition, room layouts, and shared coordinates emerge from deterministic aggregation of overlapping local predictions. Building on MOIS, we propose Multi-view floor-plan Feed-Forward Network (MvFFN), which jointly predicts coarse camera poses, dense global geometry, and per-wall semantic outputs. A downstream Layout Chaining (LC) post processing pipeline then assembles these predictions into multi-room floor-plans with shared global coordinates, consistent wall identities, and connected room structure. The dense MOIS predictions recover cross-view wall identity and local within-room connectivity more accurately than composed modular baselines, and the assembled layouts substantially outperform prior methods on wall and junction level accuracy. We also introduce the ZInD-CrossView dataset, which augments ZInD with globally unique wall instances and cross-view segmentation labels for this task.
papers.summary: Recovering camera poses and multi-room floor plans from sparse, unposed, wide-baseline RGB panoramas is difficult because pose, geometry, semantics, and global layout are tightly coupled, yet a complete floor plan is hard to learn as a single global output. The key idea is to keep predictions strictly local: Multi-view Ordered Wall Instance Segmentation (`MOIS`) has each panorama column predict only the wall it observes plus the next two walls in clockwise order, and the global wall partition, room layouts, and shared coordinates emerge from deterministic aggregation of overlapping local predictions. The Multi-view floor-plan Feed-Forward Network (`MvFFN`) jointly predicts coarse camera poses, dense global geometry, and per-wall semantic outputs, and a Layout Chaining post-processing pipeline assembles them into multi-room plans with shared coordinates, consistent wall identities, and connected room structure. The dense `MOIS` predictions recover cross-view wall identity and within-room connectivity more accurately than composed modular baselines, **the assembled layouts substantially outperform prior methods on wall- and junction-level accuracy**, and a new `ZInD-CrossView` dataset adds globally unique wall instances and cross-view segmentation labels to `ZInD`.

papers.title: EV-JEPA: Elastic V-JEPA for Any Device and Cross-Device Inference
papers.abstract: Foundation models like V-JEPA are increasingly deployed across a heterogeneous edge-cloud continuum spanning smart glasses, phones, robots, and servers. Yet, they are typically trained as rigid, fixed-capacity networks bound to one device, supporting neither reconfigurable compute budgets nor collaborative execution. Existing approaches address only one axis at a time: slimmable and NAS-based methods provide width elasticity but assume single-device inference, whereas split-computing methods enable cross-device collaboration only for fixed partitions and static capacities. We introduce Elastic V-JEPA (EV-JEPA), a single model trained once and deployable everywhere along the continuum. Its width is reconfigurable, and it is natively partitionable across heterogeneous devices. At its core is Transition-Aware Triplet Training (T3). At each step we pick a narrow and a wide width, and train three paths: each width alone, plus a hybrid path that runs the early layers narrow and the rest wide. The hybrid switch point is where one device hands off to another, so the same weights learn both single-device and cross-device execution. Across various benchmarks, EV-JEPA falls within 1 accuracy point of independently trained baselines while improving over previous elastic training approaches by up to 11 accuracy points. Narrow-to-wide cross-device hybrid execution recovers to within 1.1 points of the highest-capacity standalone model and supports many-to-one, any-to-any, and variable-split configurations. Finally, we show that the elastic principle extends beyond the backbone to an elastic token compression mechanism that exposes controllable trade-offs among on-device computation, latency, and accuracy.
papers.summary: Foundation models such as `V-JEPA` are deployed across smart glasses, phones, robots, and servers, yet they are trained as fixed-capacity networks bound to one device, and existing methods offer either width elasticity for single-device inference or split computing with fixed partitions, not both. Elastic V-JEPA (`EV-JEPA`) is trained once with Transition-Aware Triplet Training (`T3`), which at each step picks a narrow and a wide width and trains three paths: each width alone plus a hybrid that runs early layers narrow and the rest wide, with the switch point standing in for a handoff from one device to another. Across benchmarks the model lands **within 1 accuracy point of independently trained baselines** while improving over previous elastic training approaches by up to 11 points, and narrow-to-wide cross-device execution recovers to within 1.1 points of the highest-capacity standalone model while supporting many-to-one, any-to-any, and variable-split configurations. The same elastic principle extends beyond the backbone to a token compression mechanism with controllable trade-offs among on-device computation, latency, and accuracy.

papers.title: TraceSampler: Making Sampling Errors Predictable and Correctable for Accelerated Generative Sampling
papers.abstract: Accurate sampling from continuous-time generative models can require many model evaluations. Low-step sampling reduces cost, but coarse updates introduce endpoint errors that can accumulate and degrade generation quality. We introduce TraceSampler, a post-training method that corrects these errors without modifying the pretrained model. Rather than optimising low-step updates directly, TraceSampler models endpoint error as a sample-specific prediction problem. A higher-step reference integration over the same interval provides the supervised target, while a compact representation makes high-dimensional error predictable from the sampling trace. This representation combines shared residual structure, trace-derived directions, and a low-rank remainder, so shallow per-step MLP heads predict sample-dependent coefficients. These coefficients drive a two-stage learned residual correction: the first stage predicts the full endpoint residual, while an intermediate backbone evaluation provides new trace information to predict the remaining residual; this evaluation is reused by the following step. TraceSampler is evaluated with Rectified Flow on CIFAR-10, SiT-XL/2 on ImageNet-256, and SD3.5 Medium for text-to-image generation. At 10 steps, it reduces trajectory MSE relative to matched-step Euler by 90.5% on CIFAR-10 and 85.6% on ImageNet-256, while achieving FID scores of 2.692 and 2.189, close to 120-step Heun references of 2.601 and 2.056 with 24$\times$ fewer backbone evaluations. On SD3.5 Medium, TraceSampler improves image quality and prompt following; at 10 steps, ImageReward rises from 0.752 to 0.906 while trajectory MSE falls by 70.7%. These gains preserve Euler's backbone-evaluation budget, add less than 0.4% inference FLOPs, and incur negligible wall-clock overhead, showing that coarse-step sampling error can be made predictable from the sampling trace and efficiently corrected.
papers.summary: Low-step sampling from continuous-time generative models is cheap, but coarse updates introduce endpoint errors that accumulate and degrade generation quality. `TraceSampler` is a post-training method that leaves the pretrained model untouched and treats endpoint error as a sample-specific prediction problem: a higher-step reference integration over the same interval provides the supervised target, and a compact representation combining shared residual structure, trace-derived directions, and a low-rank remainder lets shallow per-step MLP heads predict sample-dependent coefficients for a two-stage residual correction, in which an intermediate backbone evaluation supplies fresh trace information and is reused by the following step. With `Rectified Flow` on `CIFAR-10` and `SiT-XL/2` on `ImageNet-256` at 10 steps, it cuts trajectory mean squared error relative to matched-step Euler by 90.5% and 85.6% and reaches **FID scores of 2.692 and 2.189, close to 120-step Heun references with 24x fewer backbone evaluations**. On `SD3.5 Medium` at 10 steps, `ImageReward` rises from 0.752 to 0.906 while trajectory error falls by 70.7%, all within Euler's backbone-evaluation budget, with under 0.4% extra inference FLOPs and negligible wall-clock overhead.

papers.title: Which Metadata Matters for LLM Tool Selection in MCP? Evidence from Controlled Factor-Level Interventions
papers.abstract: In Model Context Protocol (MCP) systems, LLMs select tools from metadata rather than from their implementations. Names and descriptions summarize what a tool does, while the parameter schema specifies the fields a tool accepts and how they are organized. Our analysis of metadata for 367,174 MCP tools reveals substantial schema variation among functionally similar tools. Many of these tools share names and similar descriptions but expose different parameter schemas. This raises a key question: can parameter-schema differences influence tool selection before any call is made? We study this question through controlled metadata interventions across five LLMs and five tasks. Each comparison changes exactly one metadata factor (server name, tool name, description, or parameter schema) while keeping the others fixed. We balance tool positions and use conditional logistic regression to estimate position-adjusted effects. We find that: (1) parameter-schema changes produce the largest and most consistent selection shifts among the tested interventions. Models tend to favor separate top-level parameters over grouped or composite forms. (2) Descriptions that explain parameters also tend to increase selection, while name effects are weaker and less consistent. (3) Targeted comparisons show that schema effects depend on the specific parameter names and on how the request represents the same information. When only one schema satisfies an explicit request requirement, all five models select the compatible tool despite position preferences. These results show that parameter schemas influence not only how tools are called, but also whether they are selected. For MCP developers and evaluators, schema design and tool ordering can therefore affect which implementation is invoked even when functionality is unchanged.
papers.summary: In Model Context Protocol (MCP) systems, large language models (LLMs) choose tools from metadata, namely server name, tool name, description, and parameter schema, rather than from implementations, and an analysis of 367,174 MCP tools shows that functionally similar tools often share names and descriptions while exposing different parameter schemas. To isolate what drives selection, the study runs controlled interventions across five LLMs and five tasks, changing exactly one metadata factor per comparison, balancing tool positions, and using conditional logistic regression to estimate position-adjusted effects. **Parameter-schema changes produce the largest and most consistent shifts in tool selection**, with models favoring separate top-level parameters over grouped or composite forms, while descriptions that explain parameters also raise selection and name effects are weaker and less consistent. Schema effects depend on the specific parameter names and on how the request represents the same information, and when only one schema satisfies an explicit requirement all five models select the compatible tool despite position preferences, so for MCP developers and evaluators schema design and tool ordering can determine which implementation is invoked even when functionality is unchanged.

papers.title: Natural Code Transformation Confuses Agents in Vulnerability Analysis
papers.abstract:
Having demonstrated a strong potential for automating vulnerability discovery, AI agents can also be used to attack software systems at scale. Today's software systems need mechanisms to level the playing field by slowing down potential attacks, giving them time to patch vulnerabilities and strengthen software. Along this line, our study of agent trajectories in vulnerability analysis shows a surprising finding: agents produce dramatically different results across real-world code commits that carry the same functionality and the same vulnerability. This phenomenon appears consistently in multiple code domains and vulnerability categories.
  It motivates us to study natural and functionality-preserving code transformations derived from real-world software development, and their potential as a defense against attacker agents. We build a corpus of natural transformations by mining recurring development patterns from real-world code commits, and apply them to evaluate impact on agentic vulnerability analysis. Our results show that even a single form of transformation can effectively "confuse" frontier agents, e.g., Codex with GPT-6 Sol, reducing successes in vulnerability discovery. We also study different agent failures, whether transformations can be composed to provide stronger protection, and adaptive attackers who seek to reverse them. Overall, our study of natural code transformation significantly expands the research space of using code transformations to defend against malicious agents.
papers.summary: AI agents that automate vulnerability discovery can also be used to attack software systems at scale, so defenders need mechanisms that slow attacks down and buy time to patch. A study of agent trajectories in vulnerability analysis finds that agents produce dramatically different results across real-world code commits that carry the same functionality and the same vulnerability, a pattern that appears consistently across code domains and vulnerability categories. Building on this, the authors mine recurring development patterns from real commits to build a corpus of natural, functionality-preserving code transformations and apply them as a defense, finding that **even a single form of transformation reduces vulnerability-discovery success for frontier agents such as `Codex` with `GPT-6 Sol`**. The work also characterizes agent failure modes, tests whether transformations compose for stronger protection, and examines adaptive attackers that try to reverse them.

papers.title: Actionable Meta-Requirements for AI Robustness Auditing
papers.abstract: AI-enabled systems must remain dependable when the conditions under which they operate change (e.g., due to input perturbations, distribution shifts, or changes in external dependencies). This makes robustness auditing of such systems important for judging whether the available evidence is sufficient to support a defined robustness conclusion. However, designing an AI robustness auditing framework is challenging. A key unresolved issue is determining the requirements such a framework should support; these requirements have not yet been consolidated. We address this gap through meta-requirements: higher-order requirements specifying what a class of auditing frameworks should support. In design science research, literature and domain experts are common sources of meta-requirements; accordingly, we derive the initial set from literature and validate and refine it with practitioners. Our systematic literature review retained 74 of 2,890 records and derived 43 meta-requirements across 16 categories. We evaluated them with 128 practitioners, obtaining 5,504 ratings and 586 substantive comments. Overall, 81.20% of ratings indicated agreement or strong agreement. In particular, 41 of the 43 literature-derived meta-requirements were classified as strongly supported. Practitioner feedback refined the requirements and identified an additional requirement concerning external components and supply chain dependencies. The final set comprises 44 meta-requirements across 16 categories, of which 43 received quantitative validation. These meta-requirements can help organizations implement AI robustness auditing frameworks, assess existing frameworks for completeness, and refine them.
papers.summary: AI-enabled systems must stay dependable under input perturbations, distribution shifts, and changes in external dependencies, which makes robustness auditing important, yet the requirements such an auditing framework should support have not been consolidated. Following design science research, the authors derive meta-requirements, meaning higher-order requirements specifying what a class of auditing frameworks should support, from a systematic literature review that retained 74 of 2,890 records and produced 43 meta-requirements across 16 categories. An evaluation with 128 practitioners gathered 5,504 ratings and 586 substantive comments, with **81.20% of ratings indicating agreement or strong agreement** and 41 of the 43 literature-derived meta-requirements classified as strongly supported. Practitioner feedback refined the set and added a requirement on external components and supply-chain dependencies, yielding a final 44 meta-requirements intended to help organizations implement, assess, and refine AI robustness auditing frameworks.

papers.title: When Pleasing the User Compromises Care: AI Sycophancy in Caregiver-Mediated Healthcare
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) alignment often assumes that the user interacting with a model is also the primary beneficiary of its behavior. Yet in many consequential settings, one person directs the system while another bears the consequences. We study this problem in caregiver-mediated healthcare, where parents, pet owners, and caregivers make decisions for children, animals, and older adults. We introduce an evidence-grounded benchmark spanning veterinary, pediatric, and older-adult care, and test whether AI advisors maintain appropriate care when users express clinically inferior preferences. Holding patient facts fixed, we vary stated care preferences and communication styles and evaluate both initial recommendations and multi-turn follow-up. Across frontier and open-weight models, inferior preferences substantially increase switching from appropriate to inappropriate care beyond neutral conversational drift and increase agreement with the requested action, while communication style alone has a smaller effect. These failures accumulate across turns, including on cases models initially answer correctly, and often carry moderate or severe potential harm. In matched eldercare cases, the effect of an inferior preference is similar whether it is expressed by the patient or by a caregiver. Together with models' limited tendency to elicit patient preferences in caregiver conversations, this suggests that current models are highly sensitive to expressed user preferences but less sensitive to whose preferences are represented and who bears the consequences. Our results expose a broader limitation of user-centric alignment in settings with multiple stakeholders.
papers.summary: Alignment of large language models (LLMs) typically assumes that the person interacting with the model is also the primary beneficiary of its behavior, but in caregiver-mediated healthcare parents, pet owners, and caregivers make decisions for children, animals, and older adults. The authors introduce an evidence-grounded benchmark spanning veterinary, pediatric, and older-adult care and, holding patient facts fixed, vary the user's stated care preferences and communication style, evaluating both initial recommendations and multi-turn follow-up across frontier and open-weight models. **Clinically inferior preferences substantially increase switching from appropriate to inappropriate care** beyond neutral conversational drift and increase agreement with the requested action, whereas communication style alone has a smaller effect, and these failures accumulate across turns, including on cases models initially answer correctly, often with moderate or severe potential harm. In matched eldercare cases the effect is similar whether the patient or the caregiver expresses the preference, and models rarely elicit the patient's own preferences, suggesting they are highly sensitive to expressed preferences but less sensitive to whose preferences are represented and who bears the consequences.

papers.title: DexFLEX: Contact-Aware Foundation Controller for Command-Guided Dexterity
papers.abstract: Dexterous robot hands can receive useful motion intent from teleoperation or learned policies, but successful execution also depends on contact decisions that these commands rarely specify. We introduce DexFLEX, a contact-aware foundation controller that turns upstream fingertip-motion drafts into contact-consistent joint commands. Instead of treating a draft as a trajectory to copy, DexFLEX treats it as evidence about intent: from the current tactile-proprioceptive state, it proposes feasible short-horizon motion chunks, predicts their contact consequences, and selects the candidate that best follows the command while preserving future contact stability. At inference time, a simple Draft-Dream-Select procedure combines pure-prior proposals for recovery with draft-seeded proposals for responsiveness, then decodes the selected motion into executable joint-space targets. Across degraded-command simulation, real-world shared control, and visuomotor policy learning, the same trained controller improves robustness without retraining, increasing real-world teleoperation success from 29.2% to 78.3% and reaching 46.7% policy-learning success, 3.5 times direct joint-action prediction, and 1.56 times prior-only correction. Videos are available at dex-flex.github.io.
papers.summary: Dexterous robot hands receive motion intent from teleoperation or learned policies, but those commands rarely specify the contact decisions on which successful execution depends. `DexFLEX` is a contact-aware foundation controller that treats an upstream fingertip-motion draft as evidence about intent rather than a trajectory to copy: from the current tactile-proprioceptive state it proposes feasible short-horizon motion chunks, predicts their contact consequences, and selects the candidate that best follows the command while preserving future contact stability. At inference a Draft-Dream-Select procedure combines pure-prior proposals for recovery with draft-seeded proposals for responsiveness, then decodes the chosen motion into executable joint-space targets. Without retraining, the same controller **raises real-world teleoperation success from 29.2% to 78.3%** and reaches 46.7% success in visuomotor policy learning, 3.5 times direct joint-action prediction and 1.56 times prior-only correction.

papers.title: ACED-Bench: Evaluating How LLM Agents Acquire and Act on Causal Evidence
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as scientific assistants, yet we still lack reliable ways to evaluate whether they can investigate a system rather than merely answer a prompt. A useful evaluation must let agents choose experiments, interpret finite evidence, and make causal decisions, while keeping the environment coherent across repeated observations and interventions and preserving objective ground truth. We introduce ACED-BENCH (Active Causal Evidence and Decision Benchmark), a neuro-symbolic benchmark built around this requirement. The key idea is to separate the readable scientific surface from the formal causal world: LLMs generate natural-language scenarios and task text, while hidden probabilistic graphical models define the causal graph, data-generating process, intervention semantics, validation checks, and oracle answers. This yields scientific worlds that are natural for agents to investigate but exact enough for scalable, programmatic evaluation. The main leaderboard ACED-CORE contains 180 tasks: 60 set-valued causal ancestry/descendancy questions and 120 constrained causal-decision tasks. We also report ACED-QUAL, a 150-question yes/no qualification check using the same hidden-PGM interface. We evaluate seven contemporary LLMs and two earlier-generation models across three active agent designs. ACED-QUAL checks whether agents can use the interface to draw conclusions from evidence, while ACED-CORE tests whether they can decide what evidence to collect and when to commit to an answer. Evidence-ledger analysis localizes failures within the investigation: agents test the wrong intervention, lose relevant evidence, or continue after sufficient evidence has appeared. These results suggest that reliable AI co-scientists need explicit support for experiment design, evidence retention, answer commitment, and stopping.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as scientific assistants, yet evaluating whether they can investigate a system rather than merely answer a prompt requires letting agents choose experiments, interpret finite evidence, and make causal decisions in an environment that stays coherent across repeated observations and interventions while preserving objective ground truth. The Active Causal Evidence and Decision Benchmark (`ACED-BENCH`) separates the readable scientific surface from the formal causal world: LLMs generate natural-language scenarios and task text, while hidden probabilistic graphical models define the causal graph, data-generating process, intervention semantics, validation checks, and oracle answers. The main `ACED-CORE` leaderboard contains 180 tasks, 60 set-valued causal ancestry and descendancy questions and 120 constrained causal-decision tasks, alongside the 150-question yes/no qualification check `ACED-QUAL`, and seven contemporary LLMs plus two earlier-generation models are evaluated across three active agent designs. **Evidence-ledger analysis localizes failures to testing the wrong intervention, losing relevant evidence, or continuing after sufficient evidence has appeared**, suggesting that reliable AI co-scientists need explicit support for experiment design, evidence retention, answer commitment, and stopping.

papers.title: ANASSA: From High-Level Framework to Low-Level Architecture for Spatial Agentic AI
papers.abstract: Agentic AI systems operating over geospatial data require more than autonomous reasoning and tool use; they must also support explicit orchestration, spatial validation, governance, provenance, failure handling, and human decision authority. Prior work introduced ANASSA, an agentic AI orchestration framework for spatial intelligence that established high-level components and responsibility boundaries for governed agentic execution (arXiv:2609.14824). However, the framework did not specify how those high-level responsibilities should be systematically decomposed into an implementation-facing low-level architecture. This paper addresses that gap by applying Design Science Research (DSR) to refine the ANASSA framework from high-level architectural (HLA) responsibilities into a low-level architecture (LLA). The resulting design preserves the responsibility boundaries of the foundational framework while translating them into executable architectural structures, including 47 logical roles, versioned task graphs, capability-based agent selection, typed contracts, explicit runtime states, spatial validation mechanisms, governance controls, failure and recovery paths, and provenance records. The architecture is demonstrated through an end-to-end execution trace and analytically evaluated for requirements traceability, internal consistency, responsibility preservation, and technology independence. The resulting high-level-to-low-level design provides an implementation-facing bridge between the ANASSA framework and future system implementations, defining how governed spatial agentic workflows can be made inspectable, reconstructable, and testable without binding the architecture to a specific AI model, geospatial platform, communication protocol, or deployment environment.
papers.summary: Agentic AI operating over geospatial data needs explicit orchestration, spatial validation, governance, provenance, failure handling, and human decision authority, and the earlier `ANASSA` framework established high-level components and responsibility boundaries for such governed execution without specifying how to decompose them into an implementation-facing architecture. Applying Design Science Research (DSR), the authors refine the framework from high-level architectural responsibilities into a low-level architecture comprising **47 logical roles**, versioned task graphs, capability-based agent selection, typed contracts, explicit runtime states, spatial validation mechanisms, governance controls, failure and recovery paths, and provenance records. The design is demonstrated through an end-to-end execution trace and analytically evaluated for requirements traceability, internal consistency, responsibility preservation, and technology independence, without binding the architecture to a specific AI model, geospatial platform, communication protocol, or deployment environment.

papers.title: Deep learning from a control vantage point
papers.abstract: This article offers an overview of recent developments in deep learning from a control vantage point. It reviews several classes of models including feedforward and residual neural networks, transformers, large-language models, and selective state space models while explaining how control theory plays an important role in understanding their training, properties, or architecture design. The article explains how residual neural networks can be interpreted as the discretization of a continuous-time control system thereby enabling the use of control theoretic techniques for its analysis. To illustrate the power of this bridge between control and deep learning, two technical results are discussed: 1) the ability of a residual neural network to approximate arbitrary continuous functions is a non-standard controllability problem that can be solved using geometric nonlinear control and 2) transformers, the key architectural component of most large language-models, can be seen the discretization of a consensus algorithm and thus large language-models exhibit consensus. Another point of contact between control theory and deep learning is the connection between backpropagation, the algorithm used to train neural networks, and optimal control. The article addresses how the older connection between these problems, established in the 80's using discrete-time models can be reconciled with the more recent approach using continuous-time models. Several open problems and directions for future research are discussed, including selective state-space models, a recent class of models inspired by the models used in control.
papers.summary: Surveys how control theory helps explain the training, properties, and architecture of deep learning models, covering feedforward and residual networks, transformers, large language models, and selective state space models. Residual networks are read as discretizations of a continuous-time control system, which turns their ability to approximate arbitrary continuous functions into a non-standard controllability problem solvable with geometric nonlinear control. **Transformers are interpreted as the discretization of a consensus algorithm, implying that large language models exhibit consensus dynamics.** The overview also reconciles the 1980s discrete-time link between backpropagation and optimal control with the newer continuous-time formulation, and closes with open problems around selective state space models.

papers.title: Measuring the Inference Energy Efficiency of Open-Weight LLMs across Benchmarks, Reasoning Modes, and Hardware
papers.abstract: Benchmark scores tell us what an LLM can do, but not how much energy is required to deliver that capability. We directly measure this trade-off for 86 open-weight model checkpoints, evaluated on seven benchmarks and six hardware platforms ranging from a consumer GPU to an eight-GPU server. We find large differences in energy efficiency even among models with similar capability. Most configurations lie away from the score--energy Pareto frontier: they use a median of 2.6--4.8$\times$ more energy than another configuration that scores at least as well, with differences reaching 27$\times$. Reasoning can improve capability, but enabling thinking increases energy by about 3.7$\times$ on average, and the benefit depends strongly on the model family and output budget. Generated-token count is also an imperfect proxy for energy, misordering 18--24\% of model pairs. In contrast, FP8 reduces energy by roughly a quarter with little change in score, while changing hardware largely rescales energy without changing the relative ranking of models. These results show that capability alone gives an incomplete picture of efficiency. We argue that benchmark scores should be reported together with measured energy consumption under a specified serving regime and output budget.
papers.summary: Benchmark scores show what a large language model can do but not how much energy it takes to deliver that capability, so the authors measure both for 86 open-weight checkpoints across seven benchmarks and six hardware platforms ranging from a consumer GPU to an eight-GPU server. **Most configurations sit off the score-energy Pareto frontier, using a median of 2.6 to 4.8 times more energy than another configuration that scores at least as well, with gaps reaching 27 times.** Enabling thinking raises energy by about 3.7 times on average with benefits that depend heavily on model family and output budget, and generated-token count misorders 18 to 24 percent of model pairs when used as an energy proxy. FP8 cuts energy by roughly a quarter with little change in score, hardware changes mostly rescale energy without reordering models, and the authors argue scores should be reported with measured energy under a stated serving regime and output budget.

papers.title: RealityBench: Simulated Environments to Evaluate a Vision Language Model's Ability to Document Human Physical Work
papers.abstract: Augmenting worker capabilities in the physical world through guidance has been a decades-long goal for AI agents. One key supporting capability is to understand what the worker is doing, seeing through the human's camera or smart glasses, and assist them in documentation. Despite advances in vision language models, their capabilities in these settings remain uncertain and are challenging to benchmark because most physical work data is proprietary, and involves too much variability to study in a principled manner. Unlike structured settings such as kitchens and warehouses that have predictable lighting, geometry, and objects, field-facing tasks such as rooftop solar installation and vehicle repair are unconstrained and high variance. Here, we model real-world physical work in Blender across eleven environments, incorporating variants in both image acceptability and documentation. The acceptability task asks whether a particular view would be suitable proof-of-work and documentation asks whether an agent can understand the task-relevant state of the environment from that view. Across 26 vision-language models, we find that top models largely solve documentation when the answer is text in frame, but are weak at reading measurements and at judging small parts and spatial relations, such as whether a tape measure leans. Acceptability is harder to pin down because human raters disagree with each other. Measured against a scorer that agrees with the raters' majority about as often as a single rater does, the best models cannot be distinguished from a single non-author rater, at a cost within the range of a human pass. In the three environments where we can trace acceptability errors, most wrong rejections come from misreading the scene rather than the requirement. On the three documentation questions for which we have real images, model rankings on rendered frames transfer to real images.
papers.summary: Vision-language models are expected to watch physical work through a worker's camera or smart glasses and help document it, but field tasks such as rooftop solar installation and vehicle repair are too variable and too proprietary to benchmark easily. The authors model eleven such environments in Blender with two task variants: acceptability asks whether a view is suitable proof-of-work, and documentation asks whether the task-relevant state of the scene can be read from that view. **Across 26 vision-language models, top models largely solve documentation when the answer is text in frame but are weak at reading measurements and at judging small parts and spatial relations**, such as whether a tape measure leans. Acceptability is harder to score because human raters disagree with each other, though the best models cannot be distinguished from a single non-author rater at a cost within the range of a human pass, and model rankings on rendered frames transfer to the real images available for three documentation questions.

papers.title: SAT-RL: Training Language Models for Logical Reasoning with Symbolic Solvers
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance in mathematical and logical reasoning, yet they still suffer from the curse of complexity and struggle as problem difficulty increases with the number of constraint interactions and the size of the search space. In contrast, satisfiability solvers such as Z3 provide scalable and verifiable reasoning through constraint solving under formal theories, but lack the flexibility to interpret natural-language problem descriptions. In this work, we propose SAT-RL, a reinforcement-learning (RL) framework that trains LLMs to interact with symbolic solvers through multi-turn tool execution. SAT-RL leverages synthetic data generation with verifiable solutions, supervised warm-up on solver-augmented traces, and solver-grounded reinforcement learning with tool-aware rewards. Experiments show that SAT-RL substantially improves symbolic reasoning with tools on both in-domain and out-of-domain logic tasks. Our code is available on https://github.com/sunjia72/SAT-RL.
papers.summary: Large language models lose accuracy on logic problems as constraint interactions and search spaces grow, while satisfiability solvers such as `Z3` scale and verify but cannot interpret natural-language problem descriptions. `SAT-RL` is a reinforcement learning framework that trains a language model to drive a symbolic solver through multi-turn tool execution. It combines synthetic data generation with verifiable solutions, supervised warm-up on solver-augmented traces, and solver-grounded reinforcement learning with tool-aware rewards. **The trained models substantially improve tool-based symbolic reasoning on both in-domain and out-of-domain logic tasks**, and the code is released.

papers.title: Memory Without Curation: Learning Multi-Stream Latent Memory for Robot Policies
papers.abstract: It is widely appreciated that robotic policies require long-term memory to perform complex tasks. However, directly conditioning policies on all past observations leaves policy learning susceptible to learning spurious shortcuts, and introduces large latency at policy deployment. As such, today's memory-augmented policies curate what to remember, either by retaining only recent frames, selected keyframes, or textual summaries, or by learning latent representations of the visual stream alone. In this work, we propose an alternative approach IMPRINT, a policy-agnostic latent memory framework that augments vision-language-action (VLA) models with multi-stream memory without explicitly constraining what the policy should remember. IMPRINT compresses different streams into a latent memory that is updated incrementally at inference, enabling low latency. To avoid shortcut learning, IMPRINT adopts a two-stage training procedure, first supervising memory to reconstruct multiple streams (observations, actions, proprioception) of past information, as well as estimate current task progress, followed by end-to-end finetuning, jointly with the policy, on action prediction. Across both simulation and real-world tasks demanding memory, IMPRINT improves average success over the base VLA by at least 26%, outperforming popular alternatives, and maintaining lowest inference latency among memory-augmented VLAs. Through careful ablations, we demonstrate the utility of incorporating diverse information streams into robotic memory, validating the advantages of foregoing history curation. Project website: https://yilin-wu98.github.io/imprint_website/.
papers.summary: Robot policies need long-term memory for complex tasks, but conditioning on all past observations invites spurious shortcuts and adds deployment latency, so existing approaches curate memory through recent frames, keyframes, text summaries, or visual-only latents. `IMPRINT` is a policy-agnostic latent memory for vision-language-action (VLA) models that compresses several streams, including observations, actions, and proprioception, into a latent that is updated incrementally at inference without dictating what to remember. A two-stage recipe first trains the memory to reconstruct past streams and estimate task progress, then finetunes it end to end with the policy on action prediction to avoid shortcut learning. **Across simulated and real-world tasks that demand memory, it raises average success over the base VLA by at least 26 percent**, outperforms popular alternatives, and keeps the lowest inference latency among memory-augmented VLAs.

papers.title: Coarse-Graining Recursive Expert Computation: Continuation-Relative Interfaces and Failure Modes
papers.abstract: Computational coarse-graining aims to replace a sequence of updates with a cheaper module while preserving task performance. We present a continuation-relative evaluation framework that assesses replacements through the computation that follows them, using downstream task quality and total execution cost as joint criteria. The framework distinguishes boundary representations, summaries of skipped computation, executed operations, and downstream loss. It makes interfaces and permitted deployment information explicit, combines fine-path references with directly trained controls using the same shortened architecture, and accounts for selection overhead. An exact loss decomposition separates replacement effects at a fixed downstream action from effects of changing that action. A finite construction shows how retained information can reduce the stipulated cost of zero-error prediction under fixed information and controller restrictions. Experiments in two frozen pretrained language models show that representation fidelity and task loss can favor different fitting objectives. In a prespecified comparison on a 1.7-billion-parameter model, next-token-loss training lowers in-distribution negative log-likelihood by 0.1901 nats per scored token compared with reconstructing the skipped blocks' output, using the same optimizer and update count. This ranking reverses in all nine paired comparisons under distribution shift. In a recursive expert prototype, the jointly adapted candidate lowers task error relative to frozen-bank and router-only baselines, but trails directly trained controls, and the tested input-only selectors fail the joint quality-cost criteria. Together, the protocol and studies provide explicit criteria and diagnostics for distinguishing useful computational replacement from local approximation gains within specified interfaces and evaluation settings.
papers.summary: Computational coarse-graining replaces a run of expensive updates, such as a stack of transformer blocks, with a cheaper module, and the question is how to tell a genuinely useful replacement from a local approximation gain. The authors propose a continuation-relative evaluation protocol that judges replacements by the computation that follows them, scoring downstream task quality and total execution cost together, making interfaces and permitted deployment information explicit, comparing against directly trained controls with the same shortened architecture, and charging for selection overhead, with an exact loss decomposition separating the replacement's effect at a fixed downstream action from the effect of changing that action. Experiments on two frozen pretrained language models show that representation fidelity and task loss can favor different fitting objectives: **on a 1.7-billion-parameter model, training to next-token loss lowers in-distribution negative log-likelihood by 0.1901 nats per scored token compared with reconstructing the skipped blocks' output, yet this ranking reverses in all nine paired comparisons under distribution shift**. In a recursive expert prototype, the jointly adapted candidate beats frozen-bank and router-only baselines but trails directly trained controls, and the tested input-only selectors fail the joint quality-cost criteria.

papers.title: Frustratingly Easy Agentic RAG via Portable Skills: A Case Study in Customer Support
papers.abstract:
Enterprise workflow automation typically requires retrieving a complete and accurate set of relevant information from large operational document corpora (SOPs, policy documents) given a specific scenario or request. In customer support (CS), for example, human specialists must determine the correct sequence of resolution steps for each case, a task that demands precise grounding in policy documentation. Meeting this bar in production typically requires complex document chunking, indexing, and retrieval pipelines, often layered with learned re-rankers, query rewriters, and bespoke agentic RAG infrastructure.
  We report a deployment case study of a simpler alternative: a portable skill consisting of a natural-language instruction, lightweight tools (a retrieval API, format-checking scripts), and a corpus enriched with an LLM-generated navigation layer, which is a structured "Wikipedia-style" index over the underlying documents. This agentic RAG approach is straightforward to implement (1-2 engineer days), portable across capable agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code), and performs strongly on the challenging task of CS resolution workflow generation, achieving 99.2% procedural equivalence to human-approved ground truth and 83.3% evidence sufficiency. It is also roughly an order of magnitude slower per case than our deployed production assistant (~90 s vs. ~8-9 s), so we claim no latency advantage. Our claim is scoped to that setting: a mature, well-curated corpus, a latency-tolerant workflow, and human review of every case. There, the skill did the work of a complex RAG stack, and maintenance became a matter of editing text and data rather than retraining models.
papers.summary: Enterprise workflows such as customer support resolution require retrieving a complete and accurate set of passages from standard operating procedures (SOPs) and policy documents for each case, which in production usually means elaborate chunking, indexing, re-ranking, and query-rewriting pipelines. The authors report a deployment case study of a simpler alternative: a portable skill made of a natural-language instruction, lightweight tools such as a retrieval API and format-checking scripts, and a corpus enriched with an LLM-generated 'Wikipedia-style' navigation index, built in one to two engineer days and runnable in agentic harnesses like `Claude Code`. **On customer support resolution workflow generation the skill reaches 99.2 percent procedural equivalence to human-approved ground truth and 83.3 percent evidence sufficiency**, though at roughly 90 seconds per case against 8 to 9 seconds for the deployed production assistant. The claim is scoped to a mature, well-curated corpus, a latency-tolerant workflow, and human review of every case, where maintenance becomes editing text and data rather than retraining models.

papers.title: SceneForesee: Learning Scene Evolution for Spatiotemporal Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large multimodal models (LMMs) need to understand how entities move and interact as a scene develops. This requires following the same entities over time and relating their observed motion to subsequent changes. We formulate Scene Evolution Understanding (SEU), a task for predicting and interpreting this change. Given observed video, a model estimates entity histories and predicts one scene continuation through future trajectories and Events, accompanied by Visual Evidence from observed motion and a scene description. We construct SceneForesee, a benchmark for evaluating entity continuity and scene evolution reasoning through paired observed and future scenes with shared entity identities. It contains 144.57K temporal pairs, 1.05M entity correspondences, and 272.49K Events paired with observed evidence. We propose a spatiotemporal reasoning framework, EvoSee, that learns future geometry and Event semantics through shared candidate states and joint assignment. It selects one continuation per entity from observation and uses the selected changes for entity refinement, retention, and scene representation. On SceneForesee, EvoSee outperforms Qwen3.5-9B by 10.45 points in Combined Point-F1 and 17.24 points in Event Global F1. On the 4D reasoning benchmark Dyn-Bench, it improves question answering accuracy and grounding J&F by 4.8 and 3.58 points over their respective base systems. These results support scene evolution as both a prediction target and a dynamic representation that brings predicted entity changes into spatiotemporal reasoning.The project is available at https://github.com/mikubaka88/SceneForesee-Spatiotemporal-Reasoning.
papers.summary: Large multimodal models (LMMs) must follow the same entities over time and relate their observed motion to later changes, which the authors formalize as Scene Evolution Understanding (SEU): given observed video, estimate entity histories and predict one continuation as future trajectories and Events, supported by Visual Evidence from observed motion and a scene description. `SceneForesee` is a benchmark of paired observed and future scenes with shared entity identities, containing 144.57K temporal pairs, 1.05M entity correspondences, and 272.49K Events linked to observed evidence. The companion framework `EvoSee` learns future geometry and Event semantics through shared candidate states and joint assignment, selecting one continuation per entity and using the chosen changes for entity refinement, retention, and scene representation. **On `SceneForesee` it beats `Qwen3.5-9B` by 10.45 points in Combined Point-F1 and 17.24 points in Event Global F1**, and on the 4D reasoning benchmark `Dyn-Bench` it improves question answering accuracy and grounding J&F by 4.8 and 3.58 points over the respective base systems.

papers.title: Target-ESS Tempered Policy Optimization (TETPO): Smooth Variance Control via Bridge Importance Sampling
papers.abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement-learning post-training of large language models is computationally efficient but inherently off-policy: the learner updates on rollouts generated by a stale policy, while correcting this mismatch requires importance weights that can be extremely heavy-tailed. A small number of trajectories may then dominate an update, collapsing the effective sample size (ESS) and increasing the variance and instability of the resulting gradient estimates. Existing stabilizers apply fixed interventions regardless of the realized severity of weight concentration, either discarding selected samples or reweighting them without adapting the correction strength. We introduce \emph{Target--ESS Tempered Policy Optimization} (TETPO), which replaces each importance weight $\rho$ by $\rho^\alpha$ for a data-adaptive exponent $\alpha\in[0,1]$: $\alpha=1$ preserves the original importance weights, whereas $\alpha=0$ assigns uniform coefficients. For each prompt group, TETPO selects the largest $\alpha$ whose tempered weights satisfy a target ESS fraction $\kappa$, applying little tempering to healthy groups and stronger tempering when weight degeneracy is severe. At the population level, the tempered coefficients are exact importance weights for a geometric bridge between the sampler and learner policies. The exponent is efficiently found by one-dimensional bisection, while the resulting weights satisfy deterministic bounds on normalized-weight dispersion and weighted-gradient norm that are independent of policy drift, together with a fixed-$\alpha$ bound on bridge-target discrepancy. Power tempering also introduces no explicit zero-weight mask. On mathematical-reasoning benchmarks under high staleness, TETPO outperforms strong on- and off-policy baselines.
papers.summary: Asynchronous reinforcement learning post-training of large language models updates on rollouts from a stale policy, and the importance weights that correct this mismatch can be so heavy-tailed that a few trajectories dominate an update and collapse the effective sample size (ESS). Existing stabilizers apply fixed clipping or discarding regardless of how severe the weight concentration actually is. `TETPO` raises each importance weight to a data-adaptive power and, for each prompt group, chooses the largest exponent whose tempered weights still meet a target ESS fraction, so healthy groups are barely tempered while degenerate ones are tempered harder; the exponent is found by one-dimensional bisection, the tempered coefficients are exact importance weights for a geometric bridge between sampler and learner policies, and no explicit zero-weight mask is introduced. The method comes with deterministic bounds on normalized-weight dispersion and weighted-gradient norm that do not depend on policy drift, and **on mathematical-reasoning benchmarks under high staleness it outperforms strong on-policy and off-policy baselines**.

papers.title: Specification-Based Testing of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Model cards, system cards, and safety reports increasingly document LLM safety behaviors, yet safety evaluations typically start from predefined benchmarks rather than asking which documented claims those benchmarks actually test. We introduce LEST (LLM Evaluation through Specification-driven Testing), a framework that treats documented safety claims as specifications for black-box testing. In LEST, each claim determines which benchmark prompt tests it and whether a Refuse-to-Comply transition, where a model refuses a prompt but complies with its mutated version, counts as evidence against it. LEST mutates these prompts to search for counterexamples, manually validates each candidate, and traces validated counterexamples back to the claims they contradict. We evaluate LEST using the system cards of Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 with 97 seed prompts from SORRY-Bench across Mental Health and Self-Harm, Harmful and Violent Content, and Fairness and Bias. Of 56 identified safety claims, 29 (51.8%) are prompt-testable, but only 17 (58.6%) are exercised by an applicable benchmark prompt. Both models refuse >95% of benchmark prompts. Evaluating 1,836 mutated prompts on both models reveals 312 candidate Refuse-to-Comply transitions flagged by automated response classifiers. However, human validation confirms only 19 (6.1%) as both intent-preserving and genuinely compliant, showing automated evaluation substantially overestimates behavioral failures. Tracing these 19 transitions back to the claims reveals counterexamples for 6 of 9 covered claims for which refusal is an applicable oracle. Our results show that benchmark prompts may not be sufficient to validate all documented LLM safety behavior, and automated failure detection requires manual validation. LEST provides end-to-end traceability from natural-language safety documentation to executable tests and human-validated counterexamples.
papers.summary: Model and system cards increasingly document safety behaviors, yet safety evaluations usually start from fixed benchmarks without asking which documented claims those benchmarks actually test. `LEST` (LLM Evaluation through Specification-driven Testing) treats each documented claim as a black-box specification: it maps claims to the benchmark prompts that test them, mutates those prompts to search for Refuse-to-Comply transitions in which a model refuses the original but complies with a mutated version, validates each candidate manually, and traces confirmed counterexamples back to the claims they contradict. Applied to the system cards of `Claude Opus 4.8` and `GPT-5.5` with 97 seed prompts from `SORRY-Bench`, only 29 of 56 identified safety claims were prompt-testable and only 17 of those were exercised by an applicable prompt, while both models refused over 95 percent of benchmark prompts. **Automated classifiers flagged 312 candidate transitions across 1,836 mutated prompts, but human validation confirmed only 19, or 6.1 percent, as both intent-preserving and genuinely compliant**, and those 19 still yielded counterexamples for 6 of the 9 covered claims where refusal is an applicable oracle.

papers.title: KV4-RL: Unlocking Faster Asynchronous Rollouts for RLVR with INT4 KV Cache Quantization
papers.abstract: Asynchronous rollout improves the efficiency of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) by reducing under-utilization during long-tail generation. Sustained concurrency also concentrates context processing into fewer decode steps, increasing the KV workload per step. We characterize this \emph{KV concentration} and find that KV cache quantization delivers substantially greater acceleration than weight-only and weight-activation quantization in our matched-workload comparisons. However, INT4 KV rollout can degrade learning even with token-level truncated importance sampling (TIS). We propose \emph{KV4-RL}, which combines calibration-free INT4 KV quantization with selective INT8 protection of attention sinks and recent context. Protecting a bounded number of positions reduces sampler mismatch while retaining most of the speedup from INT4. Across 400 iterations of Qwen3-8B-Base GRPO training, KV4-RL achieves $1.80\times$ cumulative rollout speedup and $1.27\times$ cumulative full-iteration speedup over BF16 rollout, reaching $1.97\times$ rollout speedup over the final 50 iterations. Under a common BF16 evaluator, its final six-benchmark mean accuracy is within 0.5 percentage points of BF16-rollout training for both Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base.
papers.summary: Asynchronous rollouts make reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) more efficient by filling idle capacity during long-tail generation, but sustained concurrency concentrates context processing into fewer decode steps and raises the key-value (KV) cache workload per step. In matched-workload comparisons this KV concentration makes KV cache quantization a far larger accelerator than weight-only or weight-activation quantization, yet plain INT4 KV rollouts can degrade learning even with token-level truncated importance sampling. `KV4-RL` pairs calibration-free INT4 KV quantization with selective INT8 protection of attention sinks and recent context, which limits sampler mismatch while keeping most of the speedup. **Over 400 iterations of `Qwen3-8B-Base` GRPO training it reaches a 1.80 times cumulative rollout speedup and 1.27 times full-iteration speedup over BF16 rollouts**, rising to 1.97 times rollout speedup in the final 50 iterations, with final six-benchmark mean accuracy within 0.5 percentage points of BF16-rollout training for both `Qwen3-4B-Base` and `Qwen3-8B-Base`.
papers.highlight_summary:
Asynchronous rollout for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards keeps many long responses decoding at once, which concentrates KV-cache reads into fewer, heavier decode steps and makes the KV cache rather than model weights the dominant cost (a matched `Qwen3-4B-Base` trace shows 7.82× more resident KV volume and 4.52× higher decode-step latency per step). `KV4-RL` stores the whole rollout KV cache in calibration-free INT4 while keeping a bounded INT8 side cache for attention-sink and recent positions, so sampler fidelity stays close to BF16 without giving up the INT4 speedup.

- Keys and values are quantized online with one affine INT4 group per 128-dimensional head vector (about 4.25 bits per element) after a fixed Hadamard rotation of post-RoPE keys, and the first 16 sink positions plus the last 128 recent positions are duplicated in INT8 and attended as a separate region merged exactly via regional softmax statistics.
- In matched-workload replay, `KV4` speeds up decode-forward passes by 1.53–1.86× versus BF16 while W4A16 and FP8 W8A8 configurations land near or below BF16, identifying KV quantization as the right target under sustained concurrency.
- Plain `KV4` rollout degrades learning even with token-level truncated importance sampling, finishing **5.24 points lower on `MATH-500` avg@8** at 8B, whereas the selective protection cuts shared-prefix conditional KL by 7.0× and retains about 94% of `KV4` throughput (1.90× decode-forward speedup).
- Over 400 `Qwen3-8B-Base` `GRPO` iterations, `KV4-RL` delivers **1.80× cumulative rollout speedup and 1.27× full-iteration speedup** (reaching 1.97× over the final 50 iterations), with six-task mean accuracy of 52.8% versus 52.4% for BF16 rollout and 46.6% versus 47.0% at 4B.
- Results cover only two dense Qwen3 models on math RLVR with a colocated scheduler and one training run per configuration, individual tasks still swing (4B `AIME 2025` drops from 16.5% to 13.6%), and the BF16 learner consumes about 60% of iteration time after rollout acceleration, capping further end-to-end gains.

papers.title: Jevolution: A Framework for Studying Communication and Collective Dynamics in AI Agents
papers.abstract: Experiments with remote decision-making agents depend on more than the policy: the world may change during inference, the simulator determines which actions are available, and births and immigration alter who can act. We present Jevolution, an instrumented spatial predator-prey framework that makes these dependencies explicit. Its reference implementation separates the evolving world, asynchronous request scheduling, controller adapters, and experiment records. The model combines local observations, energy and resource constraints, predefined signals, and inherited scalar traits. We describe these mechanisms using the ODD protocol and distinguish implemented controls from research questions requiring additional interventions. Free synthetic fixtures exercise scheduling, signaling, and inheritance against the pinned implementation; they validate specified software behavior rather than model intelligence or ecological realism. A completed communication case study illustrates the end-to-end workflow using Jev to control both species. Across 6 complete habitat-seed pairs, the mean signals-on minus signals-off difference in normalized rabbit abundance was -0.0095 (nominal 95% pair-bootstrap interval [-0.0772, 0.0602]). This small study does not resolve the direction of the signal-system effect. The contribution is an inspectable experimental system and its evidence boundaries, not a new policy-learning algorithm or a demonstration of emergent language, adaptive selection, or biological predictive validity.
papers.summary: Experiments with remotely controlled decision-making agents depend on more than the policy, since the world can change during inference, the simulator decides which actions are available, and births and immigration change who can act. `Jevolution` is an instrumented spatial predator-prey framework that makes these dependencies explicit by separating the evolving world, asynchronous request scheduling, controller adapters, and experiment records, and by combining local observations, energy and resource constraints, predefined signals, and inherited scalar traits, all described with the ODD protocol. Synthetic fixtures exercise scheduling, signaling, and inheritance against the pinned implementation, validating specified software behavior rather than intelligence or ecological realism. **In a communication case study across 6 habitat-seed pairs, the mean signals-on minus signals-off difference in normalized rabbit abundance was -0.0095 with a bootstrap interval of [-0.0772, 0.0602]**, leaving the direction of the signal effect unresolved and positioning the contribution as an inspectable system with stated evidence boundaries rather than a new learning algorithm.

papers.title: Co-adaptive Rule Routing and Constraining for Structured Knowledge Retrieval
papers.abstract: Structured knowledge retrieval acquires task-relevant evidence from structured knowledge sources for downstream tasks. Existing methods rely on unconstrained retrieval or predefined query-rule supervision, such as author-paper rules for scientific discovery and anatomy-drug rules for precision medicine. Such supervision is rarely available in practice. We propose Co-Adaptive Rule Routing and Constraining Retrieval (CoRE), which jointly learns which reasoning rule to assign to each query and how to retrieve evidence under that rule, without predefined query-rule pairs. A routing agent selects a rule, and its corresponding retriever traverses the knowledge base and ranks evidence that satisfies the rule's constraints. Because routing and retrieval are interdependent, CoRE alternates between reinforcement learning for the routing policy and contrastive learning for the rule-constrained retriever. The selected rules provide supervision for retriever training, while retrieval performance rewards the routing policy. This closed-loop process enables both components to co-adapt without explicit query-rule supervision. Experiments on STaRK-QA datasets across scientific discovery, biomedical reasoning, and e-commerce knowledge management demonstrate CoRE's effectiveness. Ablations show the benefit of co-adapting the router and retriever. Generation-based routing transfers across datasets and benefits from multi-domain pretraining followed by target-specific fine-tuning. Analysis of rule usage across queries also informs automatic rule refinement and discovery.
papers.summary: Structured knowledge retrieval gathers task-relevant evidence from knowledge bases, but existing methods either retrieve without constraints or depend on predefined query-rule supervision, such as author-paper rules for scientific discovery or anatomy-drug rules for precision medicine, which is rarely available in practice. `CoRE` (Co-Adaptive Rule Routing and Constraining Retrieval) jointly learns which reasoning rule to assign to each query and how to retrieve evidence under that rule without any query-rule pairs: a routing agent selects a rule and a rule-constrained retriever traverses the knowledge base and ranks evidence satisfying its constraints. Because the two are interdependent, training alternates between reinforcement learning for the router, rewarded by retrieval performance, and contrastive learning for the retriever, supervised by the selected rules. **On `STaRK-QA` datasets spanning scientific discovery, biomedical reasoning, and e-commerce, the method is effective and ablations show the benefit of co-adapting router and retriever**, while generation-based routing transfers across datasets, benefits from multi-domain pretraining followed by target-specific fine-tuning, and its rule-usage patterns inform automatic rule refinement and discovery.

papers.title: Diffusion-Based Auctions for Multi-Winner Banner Ads
papers.abstract: We propose a new framework for banner ad auctions, leveraging diffusion models to allow for multiple bidders to co-win a single banner ad opportunity, and in particular influence the ad shown on the banner depending on the strength of their bids, enabling a far richer outcome space compared to standard banner ad auctions, where there is a single winner who shows their ad. In our framework, the outcomes are images (what ad to show) and each bidder expresses their preferences over outcomes by declaring their value per unit of alignment between the image chosen by the mechanism and a textual description of their desired image. Our proposed mechanism combines the advertisers' bids and textual descriptions into a score that drives the reverse process of a diffusion model. This is used to sample a set of candidate images from which the welfare maximizing one is eventually chosen.
