Extensive experimentation evaluates our proposed mechanism around the following axes: (1) efficiency improvements of our allocation rule relative to the single-winner allocation rule; (2) monotonicity of our allocation rule; and (3) approximate incentive compatibility when combining our allocation rule with Myerson lemma-based or Clarke rule-based payments. Improvements along all these axes are shown with the number of Monte Carlo samples. Meanwhile, these benefits are attained while preserving the image quality.
papers.summary: Standard banner ad auctions pick one winner who shows their own ad, whereas the proposed mechanism lets several bidders co-win a single slot and shape the displayed image in proportion to the strength of their bids. Each advertiser submits a textual description of the desired image and a value per unit of alignment between that description and the image finally shown; the mechanism combines bids and descriptions into a score that drives the reverse process of a diffusion model, samples a set of candidate images, and selects the welfare-maximizing one. **Experiments show efficiency gains over the single-winner allocation rule, improving monotonicity, and approximate incentive compatibility with Myerson-lemma or Clarke-rule payments, all strengthening as the number of Monte Carlo samples grows**, while image quality is preserved.

papers.title: RES-MR: Risk-Aware Reasoning for Explainable and Safe Medication Recommendation
papers.abstract: Medication recommendations seek to deliver personalized drug combinations based on patients' clinical information, where ensuring transparent decision-making and personalized safety are of paramount importance. However, existing approaches predominantly operate as ``black boxes'', offering limited interpretability and hindering clinician trust. Furthermore, they typically rely on fixed, patient-agnostic safety constraints, neglecting the heterogeneity of risk tolerance across individuals, which poses significant risks to vulnerable populations. To address these gaps, we propose \textbf{RES-MR}, a novel Risk-aware Reasoning framework for Explainable and Safe Medication Recommendation using LLMs. RES-MR follows a two-stage training paradigm: (1) an explainable clinical reasoning distillation stage to elicit diagnostic capabilities by fine-tuning on synthesized reasoning trajectories, grounded in patient-specific knowledge from graph retrieval; and (2) a risk-aware policy optimization stage to dynamically balance therapeutic efficacy with personalized safety. This stage employs disentangled drug factors to construct patient-specific reference prototypes that capture desired therapeutic drug features and risk features to avoid. These prototypes enable risk boundary calibration and guide the model toward safe recommendations via reward shaping and clipping. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that RES-MR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of accuracy, safety, and explainability. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/wangcong2001/RES-MR.
papers.summary: Medication recommendation systems propose personalized drug combinations from clinical records, but most act as black boxes and impose fixed, patient-agnostic safety constraints that ignore differences in risk tolerance across individuals. `RES-MR` trains a large language model in two stages: an explainable clinical reasoning distillation stage fine-tunes on synthesized reasoning trajectories grounded in patient-specific knowledge from graph retrieval, and a risk-aware policy optimization stage balances therapeutic efficacy against personalized safety. The second stage uses disentangled drug factors to build patient-specific prototypes of desired therapeutic features and risk features to avoid, which calibrate risk boundaries and steer the model through reward shaping and clipping. **On benchmark datasets it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on accuracy, safety, and explainability**, and code and data are released.

papers.title: Scale, Drivers, and Limits of Representational Alignment Across Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Comparing large language models can reveal shared representational structure and systematic differences between them. However, aggregate similarity measures can obscure how agreement varies across geometric scales and which linguistic properties support it. We introduce two complementary methods to resolve where models agree and what supports that agreement. Standard representational similarity analysis (RSA) summarizes similarity across all stimulus pairs, potentially obscuring differences in alignment between nearby and distant inputs. Neighborhood-Weighted RSA (NW-RSA) addresses this limitation by weighting stimulus pairs according to their proximity in representational space, placing alignment from local neighborhoods to global geometry on a common scale. Counterfactual RSA (CF-RSA) tests which linguistic properties support alignment by comparing intact representations in one model with representations under controlled linguistic perturbations in another. Across diverse language models, we find strong agreement in coarse representational geometry but substantial divergence in local neighborhoods. Alignment is observed both across broadly sampled natural text and within linguistic equivalence classes that preserve particular aspects of meaning or structure. Counterfactual analyses reveal selective sensitivity: changes to logical scope reduce alignment substantially more than the tested changes to hierarchical syntax, event roles, or discourse structure. Alignment also decreases when sentence structure or lexical meaning is disrupted in word lists and jabberwocky sentences, suggesting that the regularities of natural language support stronger convergence. These findings refine claims of representational universality by showing that strong overall similarity need not imply agreement in how models represent finer linguistic distinctions.
papers.summary: Aggregate similarity measures between large language models can hide how agreement varies across geometric scales and which linguistic properties support it. Neighborhood-Weighted Representational Similarity Analysis (`NW-RSA`) weights stimulus pairs by their proximity in representational space, placing alignment from local neighborhoods to global geometry on a common scale, while Counterfactual RSA (`CF-RSA`) compares intact representations in one model with representations under controlled linguistic perturbations in another to test which properties support alignment. **Across diverse language models, coarse representational geometry agrees strongly but local neighborhoods diverge substantially**, and counterfactual tests show that changing logical scope reduces alignment far more than the tested changes to hierarchical syntax, event roles, or discourse structure. Alignment also falls for word lists and jabberwocky sentences, suggesting that the regularities of natural language support convergence and that strong overall similarity does not imply agreement on finer linguistic distinctions.

papers.title: What Counts as the Same Task? Executable Contracts for Robustness Evaluation of Tool-Using Agents
papers.abstract: Robustness tests for tool-using agents often change the agent's environment, for example by hiding a hostile note in an invoice, and then judge the agent by what it does. The result tells us about the original task only if the changed test case is still a valid test of that task. Many evaluations decide this with weak rules, such as accepting any well-formed edit or any edit that stays close to the original in embedding space. We propose executable task contracts. A contract states which facts define a task, which edits are allowed, and what finishing the task means, and it checks each changed test case before the agent runs. We compare validity rules by scoring the same 14,336 stored agent runs under each rule. Across four encoders, embedding thresholds allowed 75-100% of edits that changed the task, such as swapping the payee, yet rejected 24-45% of valid hostile notes. With a MiniLM cosine threshold, Mistral appeared vulnerable on all 64 tasks, but only 26 had a successful valid attack. Replaying a saved solution and allowing edits to benchmark fields fail in similar ways. Evaluations should state, and check, what counts as the same task.
papers.summary: Robustness tests for tool-using agents usually alter the environment, for example by hiding a hostile note in an invoice, and then judge the agent by what it does, but the verdict only speaks to the original task if the altered case is still a valid instance of it. Many evaluations settle that with weak rules, such as accepting any well-formed edit or any edit that stays close to the original in embedding space, so the authors propose executable task contracts that state which facts define a task, which edits are allowed, and what finishing the task means, and that check every altered case before the agent runs. Rescoring the same 14,336 stored agent runs under each validity rule, **embedding thresholds across four encoders accepted 75 to 100 percent of edits that changed the task, such as swapping the payee, while rejecting 24 to 45 percent of valid hostile notes**. Under a `MiniLM` cosine threshold `Mistral` appeared vulnerable on all 64 tasks, yet only 26 had a successful valid attack, and replaying a saved solution or allowing edits to benchmark fields fail in similar ways.

papers.title: AphaVoice: Text-to-Speech Model for Aphasia Patient Simulation
papers.abstract: While language therapy is the primary treatment for post-stroke aphasia, limited clinical resources often restrict patient access to proper care. Addressing this gap requires reliable training simulations for medical professionals. However, current AI efforts focus almost exclusively on speech processing, leaving speech generation largely unexplored. This study introduces AphaVoice, a novel text-to-speech (TTS) framework explicitly engineered to synthesize highly realistic aphasic speech. Evaluated against state-of-the-art TTS systems, AphaVoice demonstrates a superior ability to capture the clinical feature of dysfluency, outperforming existing models in temporal metrics while consistently maintaining speaker identity. By leveraging latent space shifting, the model also supports multi-speaker generation without sacrificing phonetic realism. Ultimately, AphaVoice provides a scalable, high-fidelity tool for medical training and clinical simulation related to aphasia.
papers.summary: Language therapy is the primary treatment for post-stroke aphasia, but limited clinical resources restrict access, which motivates realistic training simulations for medical professionals; existing AI work on aphasia focuses almost entirely on speech processing rather than speech generation. `AphaVoice` is a text-to-speech (TTS) framework designed to synthesize realistic aphasic speech, using latent space shifting to support multiple speakers without sacrificing phonetic realism. **Against state-of-the-art TTS systems it better captures the clinical feature of dysfluency, outperforming them on temporal metrics while consistently maintaining speaker identity**, positioning it as a scalable tool for medical training and clinical simulation.

papers.title: AlignPoison: Conditional Targeted Poisoning of Generative Recommenders via Decoding-Aligned Prefixes
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation models based on autoregressive decoding have been adopted as alternatives to classical ranking-based systems. While their modeling flexibility has been widely studied, their resilience to data poisoning remains largely unexplored. In this work, we ask: how susceptible are generative recommenders to conditional targeted poisoning? Under a realistic setting where an adversary can inject limited malicious interactions and query a recommendation API as a black box, our empirical study shows that generative recommenders are vulnerable: injecting fewer than 1% synthetic interactions significantly increases the likelihood of promoting malicious targets under the trigger. To characterize this vulnerability, we analyze the synthesis of malicious interactions from two perspectives: (i) decoding alignment and (ii) prefix popularity. We observe that short, context-aligned prefixes that are both common under the model's induced transition dynamics and strongly linked to a frequent trigger consistently amplify targeted promotion. Motivated by this analysis, we develop AlignPoison, a black-box framework that discovers and samples context-aligned prefixes from API outputs. We conduct experiments on benchmarks in unimodal and multimodal generative recommendation settings. Results show that these prefixes outperform competitive baselines, improving ASR lift by up to 16.3 percentage points and highlighting a decoding-dependent, context-sensitive poisoning vulnerability in generative recommendation models.
papers.summary: Generative recommenders that produce items by autoregressive decoding are being adopted in place of ranking-based systems, but their resilience to data poisoning is largely unexplored. Under a realistic threat model in which an adversary injects a limited number of malicious interactions and queries the recommendation API as a black box, **injecting fewer than 1 percent synthetic interactions significantly raises the likelihood of promoting malicious targets when the trigger is present**. Analysis from the perspectives of decoding alignment and prefix popularity shows that short, context-aligned prefixes that are common under the model's induced transition dynamics and strongly linked to a frequent trigger consistently amplify targeted promotion, which motivates `AlignPoison`, a black-box framework that discovers and samples such prefixes from API outputs. On unimodal and multimodal generative recommendation benchmarks these prefixes beat competitive baselines, improving attack success rate (ASR) lift by up to 16.3 percentage points.

papers.title: HiPPT: Physiology-Grounded Wearable PPG Representation Learning via Multi-Scope Text Alignment
papers.abstract: Reusable wearable PPG representations should capture local pulse morphology and broader physiological regularities. Existing pretraining objectives, however, usually apply supervision at the recording or pair level, overlooking that different concepts become reliable over different scopes of waveform evidence. We propose HiPPT, a physiology-grounded framework that matches each supervision source to its appropriate evidence scope. We construct a PPG-Text corpus of over 4 million wrist-worn recordings from 202K users, pairing recordings with waveform-derived morphology and metadata-derived context descriptions. HiPPT combines record-level morphology alignment, which grounds individual recordings in pulse characteristics, with cross-recording context alignment, which aggregates recordings sharing the same metadata tuple to capture context-consistent regularities. Waveform-guided text modeling further recovers masked contextual concepts from PPG patch representations, providing fine-grained waveform-text supervision. Across six downstream tasks spanning blood pressure, vascular stiffness, physiological attributes, and cross-dataset heart-rate estimation, HiPPT achieves the best result on the primary linear-probing metrics. The aligned space also supports zero-shot profiling of age group, sex, and BMI category, individually and jointly, with performance improving as more recordings are aggregated. These results show that evidence-scope matching yields transferable and semantically accessible wearable PPG representations. Code and pretrained weights will be released.
papers.summary: Reusable representations of wearable photoplethysmography (PPG) signals should capture both local pulse morphology and broader physiological regularities, yet existing pretraining objectives supervise at the recording or pair level and overlook that different concepts become reliable over different scopes of waveform evidence. `HiPPT` builds a PPG-text corpus of over 4 million wrist-worn recordings from 202K users, pairing each recording with waveform-derived morphology descriptions and metadata-derived context descriptions. It matches each supervision source to its evidence scope: record-level morphology alignment grounds individual recordings in pulse characteristics, cross-recording context alignment aggregates recordings sharing the same metadata tuple, and waveform-guided text modeling recovers masked contextual concepts from PPG patch representations. **Across six downstream tasks spanning blood pressure, vascular stiffness, physiological attributes, and cross-dataset heart-rate estimation it achieves the best results on the primary linear-probing metrics**, and the aligned space supports zero-shot profiling of age group, sex, and BMI category that improves as more recordings are aggregated.

papers.title: Reels-RSI: Program-Level Self-Improvement for Code-Rendered Explainer Videos
papers.abstract: Explainer videos -- a worked geometry problem, why the sky is blue, how a dynasty fell -- are usually one more target for pixel video generation. We argue they are a different kind of artifact: a program (script, storyboard and per-frame animation code) that a deterministic renderer turns into frames. A program can be read, diffed, tested and audited; pixels can only be watched. Reels-RSI is an open-source reel director for any agent harness; its self-improvement happens at the program level rather than in weights or prompts. Every revision pass is logged with a code snapshot; a retrospective pairs each check finding with the diff that fixed it and proposes lessons; a lesson that a static check can catch is compiled into a rule with a must-fail and a must-pass example, so the memory is unit-tested; and a rule learned today runs over everything made before it. A bounded, benchmark-gated step lets an agent rewrite the director's playbook, kept only when blind pairwise judgments on held-out topics prefer it; nothing enters memory without a human decision. Across 111 reels -- a field study, two playbook evolutions, a 2x2 memory ablation, a weaker director, a 48-reel learning curve and a judge-reliability study -- we find that the rule learned in the field caught four latent defects in frames authored before it existed and none after; that rules are an audit for a strong director (eight unguarded reels, no violation) and a guard for a weaker one (thirty violations unguarded versus five); that lessons shorten revision loops but do not compound or move the judge; and that the first rewrite's 11--1 verdict was a position bias in our vote design (judges pick the second-shown reel 62--81% of the time), masking scripts that traded thirteen facts for craft. We document four failure modes of the preference signal, which check caught each, and the fixes. Code, rules, lessons and data are public.
papers.summary: Explainer videos are treated as programs made of a script, a storyboard, and per-frame animation code that a deterministic renderer turns into frames, so they can be read, diffed, tested, and audited rather than only watched. `Reels-RSI` is an open-source reel director for agent harnesses that improves at the program level: each revision pass is logged with a code snapshot, retrospectives pair check findings with the diffs that fixed them, lessons that a static check can catch are compiled into unit-tested rules that also run over earlier work, and a benchmark-gated step lets an agent rewrite the director's playbook only if blind pairwise judgments on held-out topics prefer it. Across 111 reels, a field-learned rule caught four latent defects in earlier frames, and rules acted as an audit for a strong director but a guard for a weaker one, **cutting its violations from thirty to five**. Lessons shortened revision loops but did not compound, and an apparent 11 to 1 win for a playbook rewrite turned out to be position bias, with judges picking the second-shown reel 62 to 81 percent of the time.

papers.title: Rethinking Activation Functions: Reducing Bias Can Improve Learning
papers.abstract: Many widely used activation functions, including ReLU, GELU, Swish, and Sigmoid, produce predominantly positive outputs, resulting in a nonzero post-activation mean that we term activation bias. Despite its ubiquity, the effect of activation bias on learning dynamics remains poorly understood. Using controlled models, we show that activation bias accelerates initial loss reduction but is accompanied by overshooting, non-smooth trajectories, and a steeper loss landscape. This early advantage also coincides with the model's use of task-relevant information encoded in the activation bias component. In contrast, reducing activation bias slows initial learning but ultimately yields a lower final loss. Experiments on larger vision and language models exhibit a similar pattern: smaller activation bias is associated with better late-stage performance. Thus, this seemingly minor property can substantially redirect learning and warrants explicit consideration in future activation function design.
papers.summary: Common activation functions such as `ReLU`, `GELU`, `Swish`, and `Sigmoid` produce mostly positive outputs, leaving a nonzero post-activation mean the authors call activation bias, whose effect on learning dynamics has been poorly understood. Using controlled models, they show that activation bias speeds up initial loss reduction but brings overshooting, non-smooth trajectories, and a steeper loss landscape, with the early gain tied to the model exploiting task-relevant information carried in the bias component. **Reducing activation bias slows early learning but yields a lower final loss**, and experiments on larger vision and language models show the same pattern, with smaller bias linked to better late-stage performance.

papers.title: MontageFlow: Physically Valid High Fidelity EEG Generation
papers.abstract: Generative modeling offers a promising solution to the scarcity of labeled clinical electroencephalography (EEG) data under strict privacy constraints. Although recent generative models report substantial improvements in generation fidelity, we show that these gains conceal a categorical failure. EEG is not an arbitrary multichannel signal: each channel records the voltage difference between two scalp electrodes. So, real recordings satisfy exact linear identities among their channels. Current generators invariably violate these identities, yet this has gone unnoticed. We therefore propose MontageFlow, a flow-matching model that enforces these identities by restricting its output to signals that satisfy them. We find that ensuring validity improves fidelity too. Furthermore, to retain the EEG characteristics that oversmoothing washes out, we also condition the model on a physiological state vector encoded from the whole EEG window. For generation, this vector is drawn from a prior fitted in latent space. Across 3 large-scale benchmarks, our model improves TS-FID by 1.6-3.6$\times$ over the closest rival while ensuring validity.
papers.summary: Generative models could ease the shortage of labeled clinical electroencephalography (EEG) data under privacy constraints, but the authors show that recent fidelity gains hide a categorical failure: each EEG channel is a voltage difference between two scalp electrodes, so real recordings satisfy exact linear identities across channels that current generators always violate. `MontageFlow` is a flow-matching model that restricts its output to signals satisfying these identities, and it additionally conditions on a physiological state vector encoded from the whole EEG window and sampled from a prior fitted in latent space, to retain characteristics that oversmoothing removes. Enforcing validity also improves fidelity, with **TS-FID improved 1.6 to 3.6 times over the closest rival** across three large-scale benchmarks.

papers.title: Compositional Concepts Erasing: Disentangling Object-Style via Domain Manifold Unlearning
papers.abstract: Diffusion models pose significant risks regarding the generation of illicit content and copyright violations. This has catalyzed the development of machine unlearning to erase harmful concepts or copyrighted styles from a model's generative repertoire without compromising its general performance. However, previous unlearning approaches on diffusion models have largely focused on either object-level or style-level removal and failed to address the challenge of object-style combination unlearning. At the same time, multiple unlearning requests often lead to catastrophic forgetting. To address these challenges, we propose Domain Manifold Unlearning (DMU), which uses an EMA-updated feature proxy extracted from intermediate diffusion features to represent the retained target-object direction. As a lightweight estimating representation of an object, DMU enables selective unlearning of domain-specific components in a specific object while preserving other semantic representations, thereby significantly enhancing robustness in multiple combination unlearning scenarios. Extensive experiments show that DMU significantly mitigates catastrophic forgetting, outperforming state-of-the-art methods of batch unlearning and sequential unlearning.
papers.summary: Unlearning methods for diffusion models have mostly removed either objects or styles, leaving object-style combinations unaddressed, and repeated unlearning requests tend to cause catastrophic forgetting. Domain Manifold Unlearning (`DMU`) uses an EMA-updated feature proxy drawn from intermediate diffusion features to represent the retained target-object direction, which lets it selectively remove domain-specific components of a particular object while preserving its other semantic representations. Experiments show that **`DMU` substantially reduces catastrophic forgetting** and outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both batch and sequential unlearning settings.

papers.title: ScienceBuddy-PV: A Verifier-Governed Recursive Improvement Protocol for Panvascular Intervention Research
papers.abstract: ScienceBuddy-PV adapts the ScienceBuddy recursive-in-recursive design to panvascular intervention research through a structured evidence ledger, device-vessel ontology, abstention contract and retained failure bank. Recursive harness optimization and outer-loop model learning, including reinforcement learning, are specified but not executed. We audit a fixed component, rather than the complete agent system, using separate ARCADE syntax and stenosis tasks (1,000 training, 200 validation and 300 test images per task). A shared task-masked convolutional model was trained once per representation setting; its parameters and the heuristic support gate were then held fixed, with the stenosis threshold selected on validation data. On the locked test sets, syntax Dice was 0.475 (95% CI 0.459-0.490) and stenosis Dice was 0.231 (95% CI 0.214-0.249). Stenosis pixel AUROC was 0.957 and AUPRC was 0.180 at prevalence 0.00975. The gate accepted 76.7% of stenosis-frame outputs versus 100% for a score-only comparator. In a constructed mask audit, it accepted 44.3% of reference candidates and rejected 55.7%, exposing the cost of abstention. Acceptance does not establish correctness or clinical safety. This public-data component audit makes support and abstention measurable and provides a reproducible protocol for future collaborative agent studies. It does not demonstrate recursive improvement, patient-level validity or clinical device recommendations.
papers.summary: `ScienceBuddy-PV` adapts the `ScienceBuddy` recursive-in-recursive design to panvascular intervention research using a structured evidence ledger, a device-vessel ontology, an abstention contract, and a retained failure bank, while recursive harness optimization and outer-loop model learning are specified but not executed. The audit covers a single fixed component rather than the full agent system: a task-masked convolutional model trained once on separate `ARCADE` syntax and stenosis tasks, with the parameters and heuristic support gate then frozen and only the stenosis threshold tuned on validation data. On locked test sets, syntax Dice was 0.475 and stenosis Dice 0.231, and **the gate accepted 76.7% of stenosis-frame outputs versus 100% for a score-only comparator**, while a constructed mask audit rejected 55.7% of reference candidates, exposing the cost of abstention. The authors state that acceptance does not establish correctness or clinical safety, and that the work does not demonstrate recursive improvement, patient-level validity, or clinical device recommendations.

papers.title: Energy Ring: Stabilizing Feature Energy for Reliable Test-Time Discovery
papers.abstract: Test-Time Discovery (TTD) aims to recognize known classes and detect novel ones while the model is already deployed, operating directly on a continual unlabeled test-time stream. Existing TTD methods are overly conservative, making known and unknown features collapse together and difficult to separate during test-time adaptation. In this paper, we revisit TTD from an energy perspective and find that the natural energy gap between known and unknown classes is unstable and easily collapses. We therefore propose Energy Ring to stabilize this gap by anchoring the two types of classes on separate energy rings. A lightweight adapter enlarges the norm-based gap while preserving known-class directions, and a perturbation consistency module forms compact clusters for unknown classes. During testing, energy-guided confidence weighting improves prediction, and a stability-based rectification mechanism corrects unreliable updates. Experimental results show that Energy Ring significantly improves TTD performance against existing TTD methods.
papers.summary: Test-Time Discovery (TTD) requires a deployed model to keep recognizing known classes while detecting novel ones from a continual unlabeled test stream, but existing methods are so conservative that known and unknown features collapse together and become hard to separate during adaptation. Revisiting the problem from an energy perspective, the authors find that the natural energy gap between known and unknown classes is unstable, and they propose `Energy Ring` to anchor the two class types on separate energy rings. A lightweight adapter widens the norm-based gap while preserving known-class directions, a perturbation consistency module forms compact clusters for unknown classes, and at test time energy-guided confidence weighting plus a stability-based rectification mechanism correct unreliable updates. **`Energy Ring` significantly outperforms existing TTD methods** in the reported experiments.

papers.title: Who to Trust in Multi-Robot Systems: Joint Robot and Object Hypothesis Trust Inference via Neural-Symbolic Cross-Validation
papers.abstract: Multi-robot systems (MRS) offer significant advantages over single-robot platforms by enabling information sharing and coordination for different tasks in complex environments. However, reliable cooperation critically depends on inferring trust over both information sources and their reported hypotheses, particularly under partial observability and potential adversarial interference. Existing approaches frequently depend on pre-established trust relationships or side-channel information, which may not be available or reliable in realistic MRS deployments. This work introduces NeST-Bayes, a neural-symbolic framework that jointly infers robot and hypothesis trust using only inter-robot observation consistency, without requiring preassigned robot trust, reputation information, or side-channel identity signals. NeST-Bayes infers instantaneous trust evidence scores for robots and object hypotheses by reasoning over ego-centric relational graphs constructed from cross-robot observation consistency. These evidence scores are accumulated over time through Bayesian updates of Beta-distributed trust beliefs to maintain temporally consistent trust estimates. Extensive evaluations show that NeST-Bayes achieves the highest mean object precision and robot recall across all benchmark settings, and the highest robot precision and object recall in most settings, compared to trust-based methods. Under aggressive optimized attacks, it achieves 98.8\% robot precision with 93.8\% recall and 98.3\% object precision with 95.4\% recall. In an occlusion-rich Webots warehouse, it maintains 92.5\% robot precision with 92.0\% recall and 97.3\% object precision with 85.0\% recall. These results demonstrate joint improvements in the reliability and coverage of retained information.
papers.summary: Multi-robot systems (MRS) depend on knowing which robots and which reported object hypotheses to trust, especially under partial observability and adversarial interference, yet existing approaches often rely on pre-established trust relationships or side-channel information that may not be available. `NeST-Bayes` is a neural-symbolic framework that infers robot and hypothesis trust jointly from inter-robot observation consistency alone, computing instantaneous evidence scores over ego-centric relational graphs and accumulating them through Bayesian updates of Beta-distributed trust beliefs. It achieves the highest mean object precision and robot recall across all benchmark settings compared with trust-based baselines, and **under aggressive optimized attacks reaches 98.8% robot precision with 93.8% recall**, while maintaining 92.5% robot precision in an occlusion-heavy `Webots` warehouse.

papers.title: FDE-Bench: Evaluating End-to-End Delivery from Underspecified Real-World Business Requests
papers.abstract: Real-world business requests often leave key requirements unstated because frontline practitioners struggle to articulate rules they know from experience. Forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) must elicit these requirements through dialogue and iteratively optimize solutions until they meet customer acceptance criteria. Existing optimization benchmarks typically start from explicit objectives, while clarification benchmarks often introduce information gaps into existing tasks. We introduce FDE-Bench, the first benchmark built from real customer projects to evaluate agents on end-to-end delivery tasks that require interactive requirement clarification and iterative optimization. Its 49 cases span combinatorial optimization and machine learning. Clarification targets are distilled from discussions between frontline practitioners and FDEs. Agents elicit missing requirements from a simulated customer, and case-specific evaluators assess final artifacts against acceptance criteria using customer-accepted FDE solutions as quality references. Across 18 agent configurations, the highest mean delivery score is only 0.5510, compared with an FDE reference of 1.0. The highest delivery success rate (DSR), defined as the fraction of planned runs reaching this reference, is only 6.12%. These results show that reliable FDE-level end-to-end delivery remains out of reach for the evaluated agents on underspecified real-world business tasks. The benchmark project page is available at https://baidubce.github.io/FM-Agent/FDE-Bench/.
papers.summary: Real-world business requests often omit requirements that frontline practitioners know from experience, so forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) must elicit them through dialogue and iterate on solutions until they meet acceptance criteria. `FDE-Bench` is built from 49 real customer projects spanning combinatorial optimization and machine learning, where agents must draw out missing requirements from a simulated customer and case-specific evaluators score the final artifacts against acceptance criteria using customer-accepted FDE solutions as references. Across 18 agent configurations, **the best mean delivery score was only 0.5510 against an FDE reference of 1.0**, and the best delivery success rate, the fraction of runs matching that reference, was just 6.12%, indicating that reliable end-to-end delivery on underspecified business tasks remains out of reach for the evaluated agents.

papers.title: GG-Nav: Goal-oriented Grounding Chain-of-Thought Elicits Reasoning in Navigation Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Emerging strong Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have advanced navigation foundation models. However, these models still have unsatisfactory performance on goal-oriented navigation settings. In this paper, we first conduct a motivating study revealing that the key issue lies in the insufficient utilization of streaming observations and imprecise target localization. To tackle these challenges, we propose GG-Nav, a simple yet effective navigation framework that learns a structured chain-of-thought (CoT) mechanism via supervised fine-tuning to explicitly localize goal-relevant instances, accumulate grounding evidence, and support more reliable decision-making. Specifically, the structured CoT is designed with two key stages: (i) Observation-to-Evidence, which reasons over all intermediate frames between adjacent decision steps to retain useful goal-related evidence; and (ii) Evidence-to-Decision, which integrates the current observation with accumulated evidence to ground the target and support the generation of navigation actions or clarification questions. Extensive experiments show that GG-Nav outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of success rates on the HM3D ObjectNav, VL-LN, and CoIN benchmarks by 3.1%, 16.6%, and 5.3%, respectively. Ablation studies further show that accumulating evidence from intermediate observations reduces evidence-missing failures by 11.6%, while explicit grounding reduces stopping errors by 49.4%. We also deploy GG-Nav on a Unitree Go2 robot, demonstrating its zero-shot generalization capability in unseen real-world environments.
papers.summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have advanced navigation foundation models, but a motivating study shows they still underperform on goal-oriented navigation because they underuse streaming observations and localize targets imprecisely. `GG-Nav` learns a structured chain-of-thought (CoT) through supervised fine-tuning with two stages: Observation-to-Evidence reasons over all intermediate frames between decision steps to retain goal-related evidence, and Evidence-to-Decision combines the current observation with accumulated evidence to ground the target and produce navigation actions or clarification questions. It improves success rates over state-of-the-art methods by **3.1%, 16.6%, and 5.3% on `HM3D ObjectNav`, `VL-LN`, and `CoIN`**, with ablations showing that evidence accumulation cuts evidence-missing failures by 11.6% and explicit grounding cuts stopping errors by 49.4%. The system is also deployed zero-shot on a Unitree Go2 robot in unseen real-world environments.

papers.title: Are Multimodal Benchmarks Really Useful? Item-Level Multimodal Benchmark Diagnosis via Structure-Response Co-Calibration
papers.abstract: Multimodal benchmarks are central to evaluating whether models can reason over information from multiple modalities. However, existing literature has revealed that some benchmarks may contain shortcut items that can be answered from a single modality or from answer-option regularities alone, thus failing to reflect models' true cross-modal inference ability. Existing methods for assessing benchmarks typically rely either on intrinsic item structure or extrinsic model response behavior, which are not adequate for a comprehensive diagnosis. To fill in this gap, we propose SRCoD, a structure-response co-calibrated diagnosis framework for item-level diagnosis of modality dependence in multimodal benchmarks. SRCoD estimates sample-wise multimodal information structure from benchmark content and target answers, and uses this signal as a soft structural anchor for modality-conditioned item response modeling. The learned model produces a calibrated item-level diagnostic profile that reflects how strongly an item depends on different forms of modality evidence, enabling fine-grained benchmark analysis beyond aggregate accuracy. SRCoD also provides interpretable attribution of the diagnosis results. Extensive experiments under two complementary protocols, i.e., benchmark-refinement oriented validation and human-labeled item validation, demonstrate that SRCoD outperforms state-of-the-art benchmark diagnosis methods.
papers.summary: Multimodal benchmarks may contain shortcut items answerable from a single modality or from answer-option regularities alone, and existing diagnosis methods rely on either intrinsic item structure or extrinsic model response behavior, neither of which suffices on its own. `SRCoD` is a structure-response co-calibrated diagnosis framework that estimates sample-wise multimodal information structure from benchmark content and target answers, then uses this signal as a soft structural anchor for modality-conditioned item response modeling. The result is a calibrated item-level profile of how strongly each item depends on different forms of modality evidence, with interpretable attribution, and **it outperforms state-of-the-art benchmark diagnosis methods** under both a benchmark-refinement protocol and a human-labeled item validation protocol.

papers.title: A Self-Defining Operator for Distributed Applications
papers.abstract: To operate distributed applications with high availability, operators must rapidly diagnose and mitigate any incident. LLM-based agents can help, but unlike experienced human operators they do not improve as they handle more incidents. Each investigation starts from scratch, re-deriving likely causes and re-testing hypotheses even when a similar fault was resolved in the past. We present a self-defining operator (SDO) that improves with time by updating its operational behavior and memory. When SDO resolves an incident, it distills that experience into playbooks, which describe reusable diagnostic instructions for future incidents with similar faults, and detectors, scripts that take application telemetry as input and output relevant playbook(s). SDO continuously runs the detectors and invokes LLMs only when one fires, so its token cost scales with incident count rather than with operational time. Across 11 open-source microservice applications, SDO cuts resolution time by 52% on recurring faults while keeping per-incident cost low. SDO is open source at https://github.com/self-defining-systems/sdo.
papers.summary: LLM-based agents can help operators diagnose and mitigate incidents in distributed applications, but unlike experienced humans they start every investigation from scratch even when a similar fault was resolved before. The self-defining operator (`SDO`) distills each resolved incident into playbooks, which hold reusable diagnostic instructions for similar faults, and detectors, scripts that take application telemetry as input and output the relevant playbooks. Because the detectors run continuously and language models are invoked only when one fires, token cost scales with incident count rather than operational time, and across 11 open-source microservice applications **`SDO` cuts resolution time by 52% on recurring faults** while keeping per-incident cost low. The system is released as open source.

papers.title: Active Neural Matter: A Finite-Window Response Framework for Physical Systems and Distributed AI Workflows
papers.abstract: Physical systems and distributed AI workflows can retain past information, receive delayed feedback and combine conflicting signals. These features pose a common modeling problem: determining what information about past interactions a state must retain to account for future responses. Active Neural Matter (ANM) addresses this problem through a finite-window response framework. Forward analysis uses each system's dynamics to predict state and output responses to perturbations, separating propagation from output sensitivity. Inverse analysis tests whether a candidate state retains enough information for these responses. With the system and future inputs or interaction rules fixed, distinguishable responses from histories assigned the same state identify distinctions the representation must preserve. Their distributional separation gives a lower bound on the worst-case error of approximating behavior from that state. Uncertainty bounds distinguish rejection, support within a fixed tolerance on tested comparisons, and unresolved cases. Delayed-consensus simulations check analytical predictions of response amplitude and phase over a narrow range of delays; flocking illustrates dependence on the chosen observable. An exact delayed-return construction establishes a sufficient state for a specified program. The AI studies identify distinctions in interaction history and evidence order that a representation must preserve to reproduce observed response distributions. Tests on new histories in a controlled feedback task provide bounded support for a state specified by the task instructions; the instructed rule predicts every observed action. ANM connects response prediction to measurable information requirements, separating behavioral fidelity from task correctness and initial-state adequacy from a closed evolution law for that state.
papers.summary: Physical systems and distributed AI workflows alike retain past information, receive delayed feedback, and combine conflicting signals, raising the shared question of what a state must retain about past interactions to account for future responses. Active Neural Matter (`ANM`) answers with a finite-window response framework: forward analysis uses a system's dynamics to predict state and output responses to perturbations, while inverse analysis tests whether a candidate state retains enough information, treating distinguishable responses from histories mapped to the same state as distinctions the representation must preserve and deriving a lower bound on worst-case approximation error from their separation. Delayed-consensus simulations check analytical predictions of response amplitude and phase over a narrow range of delays, flocking illustrates dependence on the chosen observable, and an exact delayed-return construction gives a sufficient state for a specified program. In the AI studies, **the instructed rule in a controlled feedback task predicted every observed action**, providing bounded support for a state specified by the task instructions.

papers.title: LLM-based User-Product Relevance Evaluation for Dynamic Product Advertising
papers.abstract: Dynamic Product Advertising (DPA) retrieval systems are a core component of modern e-commerce advertising; however, their evaluation remains challenging. Conventional offline engagement metrics are limited by sparse, biased feedback, while online evaluation is costly and time-consuming. In this work, we propose a user--product relevance metric for offline evaluation of DPA retrieval systems. The metric first compresses the engagement history into a compact set of intent representatives via Semantic-ID-grouped, event-stratified segmentation, then assesses the relevance of a recommended product to each individual intent and aggregates them as a user-level relevance score, yielding a stable and interpretable measure of retrieval quality. To compute this metric at scale, we leverage large language models (LLMs) as semantic relevance judges, capturing nuanced functional and semantic relationships that heuristic methods often miss. We propose an agentic, human-aligned prompting framework that generates multi-category relevance guidelines and distills teacher-model judgments into an efficient student model for scalable evaluation. The resulting metric strongly correlates with offline and online business metrics, enabling faster and more reliable DPA retrieval iteration before A/B testing.
papers.summary: Dynamic Product Advertising (DPA) retrieval systems are central to e-commerce advertising, but offline engagement metrics suffer from sparse, biased feedback and online evaluation is slow and costly. The proposed user-product relevance metric compresses a user's engagement history into a compact set of intent representatives via Semantic-ID-grouped, event-stratified segmentation, scores a recommended product against each intent, and aggregates the scores into a user-level relevance measure. Large language models (LLMs) act as semantic relevance judges through an agentic, human-aligned prompting framework that generates multi-category relevance guidelines and distills teacher judgments into an efficient student model for scale, and **the resulting metric correlates strongly with both offline and online business metrics**, allowing faster retrieval iteration before A/B testing.

papers.title: LASER: Defeasible Certificate Search for Long-Range Protocol Dependencies
papers.abstract: Protocol specifications rarely justify executable behavior in one place: a transition may inherit its source state from a remote control block, name its events only by number, and remain subject to a later correction. Recovering the nearby clause is therefore insufficient; the system must assemble a source-linked certificate and determine whether any stronger rule applies. We introduce LASER, a proof-carrying search method for sparse, defeasible protocol evidence. LASER represents missing support and unresolved corrections as explicit obligations, searches typed evidence routes, and lets an occurrence-aware symbolic checker alone decide whether a certificate warrants, refutes, or leaves a behavior unresolved. On 91 BehaviorCheck families under a matched 2K budget, LASER improves Joint Edge+Proof over the strongest local reader on two model families ($\Delta=+.132$, $p=.017$; $\Delta=+.198$, $p<.001$) while cutting false discoveries by 2--3$\times$. Controlled replays attribute the gain and its limits: neither reference routing nor deterministic citation expansion alone exceeds the local baseline; whole-document reading (29--65K tokens), two-round iterative retrieval, and even oracle minimal-certificate evidence all fail to reach LASER, localizing the bottleneck in typed obligation closure rather than evidence access. An authority-corruption replay shows source-link errors only cause abstention, while the only unsafe-warrant mechanism is mis-recording a Held erratum as Verified, confined to that erratum's family. LASER thus improves long-range dependency recovery while converting incomplete evidence and uncertain authority into explicit residual obligations rather than unsupported behavior.
papers.summary: Protocol specifications rarely justify a behavior in one place: a transition may inherit its source state from a remote control block, refer to events only by number, and be overridden by a later correction, so retrieving the nearest clause is not enough. `LASER` is a proof-carrying search method that represents missing support and unresolved corrections as explicit obligations, searches typed evidence routes, and lets an occurrence-aware symbolic checker alone decide whether an assembled certificate warrants, refutes, or leaves a behavior unresolved. On 91 `BehaviorCheck` families under a matched 2K budget, **it improves Joint Edge+Proof over the strongest local reader by 0.132 and 0.198 on two model families** while cutting false discoveries two to three times. Controlled replays show that whole-document reading, two-round iterative retrieval, and even oracle minimal-certificate evidence all fall short of `LASER`, placing the bottleneck in typed obligation closure rather than evidence access, and that source-link errors cause only abstention, with the sole unsafe-warrant path being an erratum mis-recorded as verified.

papers.title: PsyMemBehav: Psychology-Informed and Memory-Grounded Two-Level Identity-to-Action Reasoning for Social-Media Behavior Simulation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) support social simulation, but faithfully reproducing real users requires grounding both structured platform decisions and language in sparse, noisy behavioral evidence. We introduce PsyMemBehav, which maps psychology-informed profiles and retrieved memories to target-first platform behavior through two-level identity-to-action reasoning. To support this approach with comprehensive behavioral traces, we construct a dataset PsyMemBehav-bench from 5.57M observed behaviors of 5,862 real users (approximately 950 per user) across Reddit, Bluesky, and Twitter. Each recorded engagement is modeled as target selection followed by Comment, Like, or Repost and optional response generation. PsyMemBehav combines 41-dimensional user descriptors, top-5 BM25 memories, reverse-CoT supervision, and rubric-guided DPO over complete reasoning-action trajectories. Experiments show that PsyMemBehav 27B ranks first in 11 of 12 reported individual-level metrics, improving average response quality over GPT-5.4 from 54.28 to 59.68 (9.95% relative), and obtains the lowest group-level MAE (0.081) and MSE (0.009) among simulated systems. These results support evidence-grounded user modeling for observed-thread continuation; the benchmark remains conditional on recorded engagement and does not model no-action decisions.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can drive social simulation, but reproducing real users faithfully means grounding both structured platform decisions and generated language in sparse, noisy behavioral evidence. `PsyMemBehav` maps psychology-informed profiles and retrieved memories to target-first platform behavior through two-level identity-to-action reasoning, combining 41-dimensional user descriptors, top-5 `BM25` memories, reverse-CoT supervision, and rubric-guided `DPO` over full reasoning-action trajectories. It is trained and evaluated on `PsyMemBehav-bench`, built from 5.57 million observed behaviors of 5,862 real users across Reddit, Bluesky, and Twitter, where each engagement is modeled as target selection followed by a comment, like, or repost and optional response generation. The 27B model **ranks first on 11 of 12 individual-level metrics**, lifting average response quality over `GPT-5.4` from 54.28 to 59.68 and achieving the lowest group-level error among simulated systems, though the benchmark is conditional on recorded engagement and does not model no-action decisions.

papers.title: Learning after Execution with Action-Specific Credit
papers.abstract: Execution is often used as terminal feedback: it scores a generated program, but the resulting state is not used for another learning action. Learning after execution instead uses the execution result as an intermediate state that supports an additional learning interaction for the same policy. This creates a credit-assignment problem because the two actions share the same final objective but play different roles in the trajectory. Accordingly, action-specific credit assigns the initial action credit from the final trajectory outcome and the corrective action credit for improvement over the intermediate state. Image-to-TikZ serves as an executable visual testbed for this setting. On 945 held-out examples, learning after execution strengthens the shared policy under single-call inference and also produces a post-execution corrective capability. Single-call render success reaches 92.70\%, compared with 88.25\% for continued single-stage GRPO after the same number of additional training iterations. This corrective capability is not reproduced by continued single-stage training and depends on the intermediate state. Alternative credit definitions also induce different group-relative preferences over the same trajectories. Together, these results suggest that executable tasks contain useful learning structure beyond a terminal reward. Code is available at https://github.com/tianyufengcn/Learning-after-Execution.
papers.summary: Execution is usually terminal feedback that scores a generated program, whereas learning after execution treats the execution result as an intermediate state that supports a second learning interaction by the same policy. Because the initial and corrective actions share one final objective but play different roles, action-specific credit assigns the initial action credit from the final trajectory outcome and the corrective action credit for improvement over the intermediate state. On an `Image-to-TikZ` testbed with 945 held-out examples, **single-call render success reaches 92.70% versus 88.25% for continued single-stage `GRPO`** after the same number of additional training iterations, and the method also yields a post-execution corrective capability that continued single-stage training does not reproduce and that depends on the intermediate state. Alternative credit definitions induce different group-relative preferences over the same trajectories, suggesting that executable tasks carry learning structure beyond a terminal reward.

papers.title: CB-Agent: Concept-Based In-Context Learning for Sequential Action Selection
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) allows large language models to use demonstrations without updating their parameters. For interactive agents, demonstrations are trajectories of reasoning, actions, and observations that illustrate how to complete a task. Reusing demonstrations in new situations is challenging: directly inputting full trajectories consumes limited prompt space and constrains the overall effectiveness, while natural-language summaries require the agent to translate general guidance into specific action choices. Therefore, we study whether expert action choices can directly supervise a reusable scoring rule. We propose CB-Agent, which extends concept-based ICL to sequential action selection. We extract environment-action decisions from expert trajectories and fit a concept vector by maximum likelihood to model the conditional distribution over candidate actions given the context. This model combines the concept with frozen language-model features and priors. During ReAct interaction, the agent uses this distribution to select environment actions without including demonstrations in the action-scoring context. Across TextWorld, ALFWorld, and ScienceWorld, CB-Agent achieves the highest cross-benchmark average among the evaluated methods at all three tested model sizes and ranks first on TextWorld and ScienceWorld at each size. ALFWorld experiments support the learned concept's contribution beyond prior-only scoring and show further gains when combined with Reflexion. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CB-Agent-DFF9/.
papers.summary: In-context learning (ICL) lets agents reuse expert trajectories of reasoning, actions, and observations, but full trajectories consume prompt space while natural-language summaries force the agent to translate general guidance into specific action choices. `CB-Agent` extends concept-based ICL to sequential action selection by extracting environment-action decisions from expert trajectories and fitting a concept vector by maximum likelihood to model the conditional distribution over candidate actions given context, combining the concept with frozen language-model features and priors. During `ReAct` interaction the agent selects environment actions from this distribution without placing demonstrations in the action-scoring context, and **it achieves the highest cross-benchmark average across `TextWorld`, `ALFWorld`, and `ScienceWorld` at all three tested model sizes**, ranking first on `TextWorld` and `ScienceWorld` at each size. `ALFWorld` ablations show the learned concept helps beyond prior-only scoring, with further gains when combined with `Reflexion`.

papers.title: Iterate on an LLM, Serve on an SLM
papers.abstract: As frontier LLMs gain more capabilities, the cost to run them also goes up. At the same time, small language models (SLMs) also gain more capabilities but have largely been able to keep their cost stable, offering 5-40 times cheaper inference for the narrow, repetitive subtasks that agents decompose work into. However, the standing limiting factor is getting the correct behavior out of a small model in a fast, efficient, and economical way. Unfortunately, in most cases, zero-shot small models fail narrow production tasks. Furthermore, retraining one every time the behavior changes is too slow to iterate on. We propose doing both in sequence. First, develop the desired behavior in prompt space, on a frontier model, with immediate feedback from live traffic. Then, once the behavior converges, distill the recorded production behavior (not synthetic imitations of it) into an SLM through supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We show a proper use case of this method through a scheduling agent for home-care agencies that fans out a single yes/no safety decision per caregiver-shift pair on GPT-5.4-nano. A LoRA-tuned Qwen3-8B trained on 11.6k recorded production decisions reaches 0.913 agreement, while the teacher (GPT-5.4-nano), re-run on its own recorded prompts, agrees with itself only 72.7% of the time, pointing to the fact that the SLM may also be more consistent. Furthermore, when the two disagreed, a blinded professional scheduler sided with the student 48-29. Finally, we find that the SLM has approximately 2.5 times lower median latency and is a fraction of the cost. We believe this lifecycle of quick building, live feedback, and cheap inference is a blueprint for others building similar systems.
papers.summary: Small language models (SLMs) offer 5 to 40 times cheaper inference for the narrow, repetitive subtasks that agents decompose work into, but zero-shot small models usually fail narrow production tasks and retraining one after every behavior change is too slow. The proposed lifecycle first develops the desired behavior in prompt space on a frontier model with immediate feedback from live traffic, then, once behavior converges, distills the recorded production decisions rather than synthetic imitations into an SLM through supervised fine-tuning (SFT). In a home-care scheduling agent that makes one yes/no safety decision per caregiver-shift pair on `GPT-5.4-nano`, a `LoRA`-tuned `Qwen3-8B` trained on 11.6k recorded production decisions **reached 0.913 agreement with the teacher, while the teacher re-run on its own recorded prompts agreed with itself only 72.7% of the time**, and a blinded professional scheduler sided with the student 48 to 29 on disagreements. The student also had about 2.5 times lower median latency at a fraction of the cost.

papers.title: Decoupling Knowledge Forgetting and Refusal Learning in MLLM Unlearning
papers.abstract: Current evaluations of multimodal unlearning typically focus on whether a model stops outputting target information. This surface-level criterion, however, masks two critical failure modes. First, knowledge suppression techniques often induce confabulation, leading the model to hallucinate facts about the unlearned subject. Second, refusal training merely alters observable behavior without erasing the underlying knowledge; such models might decline open queries but still identify correct answers under multiple-choice probing. To overcome these limitations, we propose Forget-Aware Self-Distillation (FASD). This method is designed to achieve honest ignorance, a state where the model genuinely loses the target knowledge and learns to acknowledge its absence. FASD separates these goals into two complementary channels. The behavior channel distills appropriate refusals from an ignorance-prompted copy of the model itself. Crucially, target tokens are masked from the teacher distribution to avoid accidentally reteaching the forgotten concepts. Simultaneously, the knowledge channel directly suppresses ground-truth answer spans independently of the model's generated responses. Experiments demonstrate that FASD successfully unlearns target knowledge, prevents information leakage in open-ended tasks, and preserves performance on retained data. The resulting model not only forgets the specified information but accurately recognizes the boundaries of its own knowledge. Code and data will be released upon publication.
papers.summary: Evaluations of multimodal unlearning usually check only whether a model stops outputting target information, which hides two failure modes: knowledge suppression often induces confabulated facts about the unlearned subject, and refusal training changes behavior without erasing knowledge, so models that decline open queries still pick correct answers under multiple-choice probing. Forget-Aware Self-Distillation (`FASD`) targets honest ignorance, where the model genuinely loses the knowledge and acknowledges its absence, by splitting the goal into two channels: a behavior channel distills refusals from an ignorance-prompted copy of the model with target tokens masked from the teacher distribution to avoid reteaching the concept, and a knowledge channel directly suppresses ground-truth answer spans independently of generated responses. Experiments show that **`FASD` unlearns target knowledge without leakage in open-ended tasks while preserving retained-data performance**, yielding a model that recognizes the boundaries of its own knowledge.

papers.title: Limitations on Autoregressive Token Generation via Sequential Sampling
papers.abstract: We study autoregressive token generation through the notion of sequential samplers: A circuit that samples the next symbol only given the previous ones and possibly a small amount of state. We show that (1) a sequential sampler with $k$ bits of state can be simulated by a stateless one at a roughly $O(2^{k})$ size overhead; (2) efficient insertional sampling (Stern, Chan, Kiros, Uszkoreit, ICML 2019) is more powerful than efficient sequential sampling in any fixed order; (3) sequential samplers with small state cannot establish certain forms of covert cryptographic channels. Result (1), together with the pseudoentropy vs. sequential sampleability duality of Vadhan and Zheng (STOC 2012), characterizes efficient sequential sampleability with small state. Result (3) provides a potential safety mechanism against subliminal coordination among malicious LLM agents.
papers.summary: Autoregressive token generation is modeled as a sequential sampler, a circuit that draws the next symbol given only the previous ones and a small amount of state. Three results follow: a sequential sampler with k bits of state can be simulated by a stateless one at roughly 2^k size overhead, efficient insertional sampling in the style of Stern et al. is more powerful than efficient sequential sampling in any fixed order, and **sequential samplers with small state cannot establish certain covert cryptographic channels**. Combined with the pseudoentropy versus sequential sampleability duality of Vadhan and Zheng, the first result characterizes efficient sequential sampleability with small state, while the third suggests a potential safety mechanism against subliminal coordination among malicious LLM agents.

papers.title: EarthAlign: Learning Language-Aligned Representations of Earth System Data
papers.abstract: Interpreting Earth system conditions is central to understanding environmental risks and informing decisions across weather- and climate-sensitive sectors. Existing multimodal weather systems primarily target task-specific prediction, generation, or question answering, while general-purpose alignment between Earth system data and language remains underexplored due to the limited availability of diverse language supervision grounded in meteorological conditions. To fill this gap, we introduce EarthAlign, a large-scale dataset with broad geographic coverage spanning 2000-2024 that combines 10 expert-curated natural event and disaster data sources with climatology-derived normal-weather samples. Each sample includes temporal and geospatial information and four grounded caption styles aligned with 63-variable ERA5 meteorological data. Building on EarthAlign, we introduce MeteoLIP, a dual-encoder framework for learning aligned meteorology-language representations. MeteoLIP incorporates MetTok, which uses a geolocation- and time-conditioned query to aggregate variable-specific patch embeddings into a compact sequence of meteorology tokens. To comprehensively assess Earth system multimodal representations, we introduce three downstream tasks: cross-modal retrieval, weather-condition classification, and physical variable estimation. Our experiments show that MeteoLIP improves upon the corresponding CLIP and SigLIP baselines across these tasks. Further analyses highlight the importance of meteorological input, temporal and geospatial conditioning, and multi-style supervision for meteorology-language alignment. Thus, EarthAlign and MeteoLIP provide a foundation for learning and evaluating language-aligned representations of Earth system data. Our code, dataset, and weights are publicly available at https://github.com/mbzuai-oryx/EarthAlign.
papers.summary: Describing Earth system conditions in natural language needs paired data that barely exists, so multimodal weather models have stayed task-specific rather than learning general alignment. `EarthAlign` is a dataset spanning 2000-2024 that pairs 63-variable `ERA5` meteorological fields with four grounded caption styles, drawing on ten expert-curated natural event and disaster sources plus climatology-derived normal-weather samples, each sample carrying time and location. The companion dual-encoder model `MeteoLIP` uses a geolocation- and time-conditioned query to compress variable-specific patch embeddings into a short sequence of meteorology tokens, and **improves on `CLIP` and `SigLIP` baselines across cross-modal retrieval, weather-condition classification, and physical variable estimation**. Ablations point to meteorological input, temporal and geospatial conditioning, and multi-style captions as the ingredients that matter.

papers.title: From Existing Methods to New Research Ideas: Two Perspectives on Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a route to AI systems that participate in their own continued development. Recent methods allow language agents to retain changes to their parameters, memory, skills, and code for subsequent execution and improvement. We examine how these methods can inform new research ideas through two complementary perspectives. First, we introduce a unified taxonomy with nine design dimensions organized into four groups: update targets, update organization, update schedule and scope, feedback and selection. This taxonomy places existing methods in a shared design space, where examining individual dimensions and their interactions can inspire new research ideas. Second, we examine how existing RSI methods draw on traditional deep learning, for example through optimization, regularization, data augmentation, continual learning, and adversarial learning. We develop further ideas by examining more specific learning mechanisms and drawing on evolutionary computation. We also review how existing benchmarks assess self-improvement under online, offline, and offline-to-online settings. Together, these perspectives help researchers develop new RSI research ideas from existing designs and learning mechanisms. RSI papers and resources are available at https://prism-shadow.github.io/awesome-rsi/.
papers.summary: Language agents can now retain edits to their own parameters, memory, skills, and code, which makes recursive self-improvement (RSI) a concrete design space rather than a thought experiment. Two framings organize the literature: a taxonomy of **nine design dimensions grouped into update targets, update organization, update schedule and scope, and feedback and selection**, and a mapping of RSI techniques onto familiar deep learning machinery such as optimization, regularization, data augmentation, continual learning, and adversarial learning. The authors extend the second framing with ideas from evolutionary computation and review how current benchmarks score self-improvement in online, offline, and offline-to-online settings. The stated goal is generating new research directions from the existing design space rather than reporting new experiments.

papers.title: PEARL: Process-Experience Aware Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Agents
papers.abstract: Terminal rewards make multi-turn agents trainable without step-level annotations, but group-relative advantages provide little guidance about which intermediate decisions to adjust. Failed trajectories also contain reasonable actions, while unfavorable decision patterns can recur as training proceeds. We introduce PEARL (Process-Experience Aware Reinforcement Learning), which improves local credit assignment without an additional critic. Given two continuations from the same history with different outcomes, PEARL locates their first divergence and builds a feature representation of each branch's local decision. It clusters these decision features in recent failure and success memories to identify recurring local patterns. Using this pattern memory, PEARL selectively strengthens negative advantages at lower-reward decisions, while leaving positive advantages and the base policy optimizer unchanged. On AppWorld, PEARL improves over ARPO on Normal and Challenge tasks at both 4B and 8B scales. On ALFWorld, it achieves 97.9% mean success at 4B, 2.7 points above the strongest baseline, while remaining competitive at 8B. Ablations of shaping location, success-bank filtering, and memory window support the value of selective, recurring-pattern-based updates.
papers.summary: Agents trained on a single reward at the end of a multi-turn episode get almost no signal about which intermediate decision to change, and group-relative advantages spread blame evenly across trajectories that contain both good and bad steps. `PEARL` adds local credit assignment without training a critic: given two continuations from the same history that ended differently, it locates their first divergence, encodes each branch's decision as features, and clusters those features against recent success and failure memories to find decision patterns that keep recurring. It then amplifies only the negative advantages at the lower-reward decisions, leaving positive advantages and the base policy optimizer untouched. On `ALFWorld` it reaches **97.9% mean success at 4B parameters, 2.7 points above the strongest baseline**, and it beats `ARPO` on both Normal and Challenge splits of `AppWorld` at 4B and 8B.

papers.title: AegisVox: Factorized Privacy and Clinical Preservation for Long-Form Speech
papers.abstract: Clinical speech reveals identity through both spoken identifiers and voice, yet its pauses, delivery, and speaker roles can also carry useful clinical evidence. Protecting that speech therefore requires more than preserving its words. We present AegisVox, a factorized framework that assigns consistent surrogate voices and edits identifier-bearing turns using document-consistent replacements. Across 390 public simulated or non-patient conversations totaling 63.6 hours, a matched comparison of two speech renderers separates replacement realization from retained identifiers, speaker linkage, and clinical preservation. Text-to-speech rendering realizes 535/601 planned replacements versus 453/601 for the codec-based speech editor. However, similar aggregate clinical preservation conceals more model-labeled contradictions, and conversation-wide speaker scores conceal greater edited-speech linkage under a score-direction sensitivity analysis. Fresh transcription of original audio provides a reference for interpreting the clinical measurement chain; an independent judge tests sensitivity to model-based assessment. Better replacement realization can therefore coexist with worse clinical or speaker-linkage measurements. AegisVox supports use-specific evaluation of those tradeoffs, not a guarantee of identifier removal or clinical safety.
papers.summary: Protecting recorded clinical conversations means handling both spoken identifiers and the voice itself, while pauses, delivery, and speaker roles can carry clinical evidence worth keeping. `AegisVox` separates those concerns by assigning each speaker a consistent surrogate voice and rewriting identifier-bearing turns with document-consistent substitutes, then compares two renderers over 390 public simulated or non-patient conversations totaling 63.6 hours. Text-to-speech rendering realized **535 of 601 planned replacements versus 453 for a codec-based speech editor**, yet that better replacement rate came with more model-flagged clinical contradictions and more speaker linkage in edited audio once score direction was varied. Fresh transcription of the original audio anchors the clinical measurement chain, and the authors present the framework as a way to evaluate these tradeoffs rather than a guarantee of identifier removal.

papers.title: Shaping Latent Mixture-of-Experts: From Expert Geometry to Layerwise Capacity Allocation
papers.abstract: Fine-grained mixture-of-experts (MoE) models commonly increase expert count by narrowing each expert, treating expert shape as a by-product of routing granularity. LatentMoE moves expert computation into a lower-dimensional space, exposing the input dimension and intermediate width of each expert as explicit design choices. We show that an expert's local Jacobian rank is jointly bounded by these two dimensions, and that balancing them maximizes the rank ceiling at fixed per-expert parameters. Controlled shape sweeps across model scales and routing granularities consistently favor near-square experts. We further use layerwise intrinsic dimension (ID) to guide capacity allocation across depth, co-varying the number and shape of experts while keeping per-layer parameter count, activated FLOPs, and communication volume constant. Compared with layer-homogeneous baselines, our ID-guided allocation achieves lower validation loss and stronger downstream performance. These results establish expert shape and layerwise allocation as practical design axes for MoEs.
papers.summary: Fine-grained mixture-of-experts (MoE) models usually add experts by making each one narrower, treating expert shape as a side effect of routing granularity. `LatentMoE` moves expert computation into a lower-dimensional space so an expert's input dimension and intermediate width become explicit knobs, and the authors show its local Jacobian rank is bounded jointly by both, meaning **balancing the two maximizes the rank ceiling at a fixed per-expert parameter count**. Controlled shape sweeps across model scales and routing granularities consistently favor near-square experts. Using layerwise intrinsic dimension to decide how much capacity each depth gets, while holding per-layer parameters, activated FLOPs, and communication volume constant, lowers validation loss and improves downstream scores against layer-homogeneous baselines.

papers.title: Prospective Forcing: Learning to Look Ahead for Autoregressive Long Video Diffusion
papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generators synthesize long videos through chunk-wise rollouts, yet they are typically trained to predict only the immediate future. This limited prediction horizon makes it challenging to maintain video quality over extended rollouts.
