To address this problem, we introduce Prospective Forcing, a multi-head prediction framework that injects long-range predictive signals into autoregressive video representations. Built on a rolling-window generator, Prospective Forcing attaches lightweight, offset-specific heads that share the same conditioning information and independently predict chunks at different future temporal offsets. By extending supervision beyond the next chunk, these heads encourage the shared history representation to retain information useful for longer-horizon prediction, supporting temporally consistent generation. At inference time, we accelerate sampling by using accepted future-chunk predictions to skip full-window backbone executions. We equip the head with learnable embeddings to generate multiple candidates for the next chunk, and a learned verifier either selects a candidate or rejects all and falls back to standard autoregressive generation.
papers.summary: Autoregressive video models build long clips chunk by chunk but are trained to predict only the next chunk, so quality degrades as rollouts extend. `Prospective Forcing` attaches lightweight heads to a rolling-window generator that share conditioning and each predict a chunk at a different future offset, which **pushes the shared history representation to keep information useful for longer-horizon prediction** and supports temporal consistency. Sampling is accelerated at inference by reusing accepted future-chunk predictions to skip full-window backbone passes, with learnable embeddings producing several candidates for the next chunk and a learned verifier either selecting one or rejecting all and falling back to ordinary autoregressive generation.

papers.title: RASSG: Repair-Aware Semantic Survival Gating for Streaming Tool Execution
papers.abstract: Streaming speech assistants can launch tools before users finish speaking, overlapping execution with incoming speech to reduce user waiting time. However, subsequent self-corrections can invalidate apparently stable arguments, causing stale execution whose irreversible effects persist even after the final call is corrected. We propose Repair-Aware Semantic Survival Gating (RASSG) to jointly control tool launch and cancellation during streaming speech. RASSG launches a tool when three consecutive speech recognition results arrive with identical nonempty arguments, then combines calibrated argument invalidity risk with execution costs to decide cancellation at the last feasible opportunity before effects become irreversible. Evaluation on ReCAST, FDB-v3, and Audio2Tool uses a controlled execution clock with fixed tool runtimes and cancellation parameters. On ReCAST's prospective-repair subset, RASSG reduces the stale execution rate from LocalAgreement-2's 50.00% to 3.15%, with a mean delay of 3.676s across successful trajectories. The stale reduction also holds against every early-execution baseline on both public speech datasets. Ablations with identical initial launches support active cancellation, showing the value of controlling ongoing calls before their effects become irreversible. Code and data are available at https://github.com/daijinhu/RASSG.
papers.summary: Speech assistants that fire tool calls before the user stops talking cut waiting time, but a later self-correction can invalidate arguments that already looked settled, and some side effects cannot be undone afterwards. `RASSG` launches a tool only when three consecutive recognition results carry identical non-empty arguments, then combines a calibrated risk that those arguments will be invalidated with execution cost to decide cancellation at the last feasible moment before effects become irreversible. On the prospective-repair subset of `ReCAST` it cuts the stale execution rate **from 50.00% for a `LocalAgreement-2` baseline to 3.15%**, with a mean delay of 3.676 seconds across successful trajectories, and the reduction holds against every early-execution baseline on `FDB-v3` and `Audio2Tool`. Ablations holding initial launches fixed support active cancellation as the source of the gain.

papers.title: A Hybrid Kinematic GCN and Elastic Transformer for Efficient Indian Sign Language Recognition
papers.abstract: Sign Language Recognition (SLR) presents complex challenges due to variable signing speeds and spatial intricacies. Specifically, Indian Sign Language (ISL) requires precise modeling of its inherently bimanual nature and is bottlenecked by the scarcity of large-vocabulary benchmarks and the inability of standard models to handle irregular signing velocities. To address this, a structurally-aware hybrid framework for efficient, gloss ISL recognition is proposed. To minimize computational redundancy, an entropy-driven SVD sampler that dynamically extracts informative keyframes is used. Because this subsampling creates irregular physical time gaps, the proposed architecture employs a Continuous Dual Positional Encoding paired with a distance-aware Elastic Transformer to preserve natural signing rhythm. Spatially, a Kinematically-Conditioned Adaptive GCN explicitly models bimanual geometry using unified bone-joint features. To validate our framework, a 120-class, 9,453-video native ISL dataset is created. Augmented by Physical Node Dropout and ArcFace optimization to mitigate subject-specific memorization, our framework achieves a competitive 89.8% accuracy, establishing a strong baseline for complex sign language modeling.
papers.summary: Indian Sign Language (ISL) recognition is limited by the scarcity of large-vocabulary benchmarks and by models that assume steady signing speed, while its two-handed signs need explicit spatial structure. The proposed pipeline picks informative keyframes with an entropy-driven singular value decomposition sampler, then compensates for the irregular time gaps that subsampling creates using continuous dual positional encoding and a distance-aware elastic transformer, with a kinematically conditioned adaptive graph convolutional network modeling bimanual geometry from unified bone-joint features. Trained on a newly built 120-class, 9,453-video native ISL dataset with physical node dropout and `ArcFace` optimization to discourage memorizing individual signers, it reaches **89.8% accuracy**.

papers.title: DexCast: Learning Real-World Dexterous Control from Human Videos
papers.abstract: Recent advances in 3D hand-object interaction (HOI) perception have opened new opportunities for learning dexterous robotic skills from human videos. However, existing dexterous imitation learning methods often rely on costly and manually teleoperated robot demonstrations, requiring substantial human effort. Therefore, we build DEXCAST, a framework that learns dexterous robotic hand control directly from monocular RGB-D videos by leveraging joint HOI reconstructions, without requiring any teleoperation. Furthermore, how to model high-dimensional robotic hand motion and extract temporal context to inform future action generation remains a key challenge. To this end, we propose a DexHand Motion Perception Module (DMPM) to capture inter-joint coordination and temporal dependencies in compact latent representations that condition our diffusion policy. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that DEXCAST achieves exceptional performance across diverse dexterous manipulation tasks.
papers.summary: Dexterous imitation learning normally depends on teleoperated robot demonstrations, which take substantial human effort to collect. `DexCast` instead learns robotic hand control directly from monocular RGB-D human video, using joint 3D hand-object interaction reconstructions as the supervision signal and **requiring no teleoperation at all**. A dexterous-hand motion perception module compresses inter-joint coordination and temporal dependencies into compact latent representations that condition a diffusion policy, addressing how to summarize high-dimensional hand motion for future action generation. The authors report strong performance across a range of real-world dexterous manipulation tasks.

papers.title: AcrossVAM2.0: Conflict-Aware Point Supervision for Parameter-Efficient Video Diffusion Adaptation
papers.abstract: Explicit point correspondence is attractive for adapting video generators: it describes how visible surfaces move, but can overwrite the appearance prior learned by a large pretrained model. We study this tension in a 5.01B-parameter text-to-video diffusion transformer. ACROSSVAM2.0 combines a confidence-weighted track-and-visibility head, zero-initialized residual feedback, and asymmetric PCGrad that removes only the auxiliary component opposing the primary flow-matching gradient on shared LoRA parameters. The design preserves the generator exactly at initialization and protects its primary update during adaptation. In a four-way ablation trained for 1,000 steps with three independent seeds, the full method lowers KLT forward-backward cycle error in all three seeds relative to a matched flow-only continuation (mean seed-level difference -0.00711, SD 0.00505), while robust sharpness remains positive in all three. An expanded 24-prompt evaluation (216 videos) yields 9.7% lower aggregate CoTracker3 cycle error than the matched control and near-matched performance on six VBench dimensions; however, the seed-level tracking effect is heterogeneous and I3D-FVD regresses from 0.1824 to 0.2022. These results support a bounded claim: conflict-aware adaptation improves correspondence consistency without broad perceptual degradation, but does not uniformly improve video quality. We release equations, pseudocode, matched outputs, source tables, and artifact provenance.
papers.summary: Supervising a video generator with explicit point correspondences tells it how visible surfaces move, but risks overwriting the appearance prior a large pretrained model already has. Working inside a 5.01B-parameter text-to-video diffusion transformer, `ACROSSVAM2.0` pairs a confidence-weighted track-and-visibility head with zero-initialized residual feedback and an asymmetric form of `PCGrad` that removes only the auxiliary gradient component opposing the primary flow-matching update on shared `LoRA` parameters, leaving the generator unchanged at initialization. Over a 24-prompt, 216-video evaluation it gives **9.7% lower aggregate `CoTracker3` cycle error than a matched flow-only control** with near-matched scores on six `VBench` dimensions, while the per-seed tracking effect is uneven and Fréchet video distance computed with `I3D` worsens from 0.1824 to 0.2022. The authors keep their claim bounded to correspondence consistency rather than overall video quality.

papers.title: AlignAudio: A Unified Dual-Alignment Framework for Noise-Robust Speech-Conditioned Generation
papers.abstract: Speech-conditioned generation maps speech signals to target audio outputs. Prior end-to-end speech-conditioned generative models achieve high fidelity in clean acoustic conditions, but their performance degrades substantially under environmental noise. While prior noise-robust approaches have achieved significant success in feature-level purification, maintaining consistent generation under clean and noisy conditioning remains a key challenge. To address this, we propose AlignAudio, a noise-robust generative framework based on dual alignment: (i) aligning the representations of clean and noisy speech to preserve semantic cues, and (ii) enforcing generation-level consistency within a flow matching paradigm to improve conditioning fidelity. Experiments on speech-to-audio (STA) and voice conversion (VC) tasks demonstrate that AlignAudio maintains performance comparable to baselines on clean speech while significantly outperforming them across various noisy conditions. Furthermore, the proposed dual-alignment strategy is applicable to both single- and multi-stream speech conditioning and can be integrated into different flow matching-based generation frameworks and post-training settings. Audio demonstrations and qualitative comparisons: \href{https://alignaudio.github.io/AlignAudio}{\textcolor{cyan}{\textit{https://alignaudio.github.io/AlignAudio}}}.
papers.summary: Models that generate audio conditioned on speech sound good on clean recordings and fall apart under environmental noise, and earlier noise-robust work concentrated on cleaning features rather than keeping generation stable. `AlignAudio` aligns twice: between clean and noisy speech representations to preserve semantic cues, and at the generation level within a flow matching objective to enforce consistent output across conditions. On speech-to-audio generation and voice conversion it **holds roughly baseline quality on clean speech while clearly outperforming those baselines under a range of noisy conditions**. The dual-alignment strategy is shown to work for single- and multi-stream speech conditioning and to transfer across different flow matching frameworks and post-training setups.

papers.title: Joint Discrete and SE(3) Diffusion for Protein Interface Design
papers.abstract: The design of high-affinity, target-specific protein binders is central to the development of modern therapeutics. However, existing protein-generation methods remain limited in this setting, as many generated designs fail to simultaneously achieve geometric and physicochemical complementarity at binding interfaces. To address this challenge, we introduce PIDiff, a physicochemically enhanced multimodal diffusion framework for protein-protein complex design. PIDiff jointly designs target-conditioned protein sequences and structures by coupling diffusion in discrete sequence space with diffusion on the continuous (SE(3)) structural manifold. At its core, PIDiff employs PIFormer, a novel architecture that interleaves geometry-aware invariant point attention with global sequence self-attention. We further curate PIBench, a protein-protein complex dataset with diverse target scaffolds derived from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). We first pretrain PIDiff on PIBench and subsequently fine-tune it for two therapeutically relevant applications: minibinder design and antibody design. PPFrame consistently outperforms baseline methods across sequence design success rate, structure binding energy, and sequence-structure co-designability on all tasks.
papers.summary: Designing protein binders that latch onto a chosen target requires matching both the shape and the chemistry of the interface, and generated designs often satisfy one but not the other. `PIDiff` co-designs target-conditioned sequence and structure by coupling discrete diffusion over amino acid sequences with SE(3) diffusion on the continuous structural manifold, using an architecture that interleaves geometry-aware invariant point attention with global sequence self-attention. The authors curate `PIBench`, a set of protein-protein complexes with diverse target scaffolds taken from the Protein Data Bank, pretrain on it, and fine-tune for minibinder and antibody design. They report **gains over baselines on sequence design success rate, structure binding energy, and sequence-structure co-designability across all tasks**.

papers.title: DSABench: Benchmarking Source Discovery, Coordination, and Execution for Multi-Database Agents
papers.abstract: Most text-to-SQL benchmarks provide the target database. In a large data catalog, however, choosing the sources is part of the problem: an agent must find every database needed for a request, determine how their results fit together, and execute the resulting workflow. We present DSABench to evaluate these capabilities jointly. Its 815 human-reviewed tasks draw on Spider, BIRD, and LiveSQLBench; 618 require several databases to contribute, and 105 allow more than one interpretation of the required sources. Executable contracts define source participation, cross-source dependencies, and source-local execution, while RouteEnv lets agents inspect public catalog evidence without revealing the gold annotations. In our routing-only study across seven model backends, the highest RA-Set score is 60.55%, compared with a highest RA-Graph score of 34.66% when coordination requirements are included. The gap becomes more pronounced when execution is required. Across four backends, median non-privileged Route+Exec-Graph success ranges from 6.69% to 7.98% without clarification and from 11.44% to 13.25% with one clarification; the best observed clarified configuration reaches 16.99%. On ambiguous tasks, clarification improves exact branch-source recovery by 39.8-43.2 percentage points. These findings illustrate why retrieving plausible databases or producing correct local SQL is not enough: an agent must carry the right information through the entire multi-database workflow.
papers.summary: Text-to-SQL benchmarks hand the model its target database, which skips the part of the job where an agent must find every source a request needs in a large catalog, work out how their results combine, and then run the whole workflow. `DSABench` tests all three together with 815 human-reviewed tasks built from `Spider`, `BIRD`, and `LiveSQLBench`, of which 618 need several databases to contribute and 105 admit more than one reading of which sources are required; executable contracts specify source participation, cross-source dependencies, and local execution, while a routing environment exposes public catalog evidence without leaking gold annotations. Scores collapse as more of the pipeline counts: the best routing-only set score is 60.55% against 34.66% once coordination structure is included, and **median end-to-end routing-plus-execution success across four backends runs 6.69% to 7.98% without clarification**, rising to roughly 11% to 13% when one clarifying question is allowed. On ambiguous tasks, a single clarification lifts exact branch-source recovery by 39.8 to 43.2 percentage points.

papers.title: Towards Merging-conditional Backdoor Unalignment against Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Model merging has become widely adopted for enhancing the task-specific performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) without additional training. While the specialized model from third-party platforms may undergo safety audits (e.g., backdoor detection), we reveal a novel and critical threat: One-sided Merging-Conditional Backdoor (OMCB). OMCB remains dormant and undetectable within one standalone model but activates upon merging, triggering safety unalignment. We first theoretically analyze the existence and geometric location of OMCB, revealing that the parameter shift crossing safety decision boundaries is the main cause of backdoor activation. Building upon this insight, we propose SMOKE, a meta-learning-based attack framework. SMOKE implants OMCB via a bi-level optimization strategy: the inner loop synthesizes surrogate meta-vectors through random low-rank initialization and finite-step maximization, while the outer loop optimizes the target model by simulating the merging process. Furthermore, preliminary analysis shows that the injected OMCB has bounded generalization loss under unknown merging configurations. Extensive experiments across diverse model architectures and merging techniques validate the effectiveness of SMOKE and its resistance to existing backdoor detections, highlighting a significant yet previously overlooked vulnerability in the model merging paradigm.
papers.summary: Merging a specialized checkpoint into a base model is a common way to add task skills without training, and third-party checkpoints are often screened for backdoors before release. The authors characterize a threat that passes those screens: a one-sided merging-conditional backdoor that stays dormant in the standalone model and activates only after merging, at which point safety alignment breaks, which their analysis attributes to the merge shifting parameters across safety decision boundaries. They implant it with a meta-learning framework whose outer loop simulates the merging process while the inner loop synthesizes surrogate merge vectors, and report that **the implanted backdoor survives existing backdoor detection methods across diverse architectures and merging techniques**, with bounded loss of effect under merge configurations the attacker did not know in advance. The result is framed as an overlooked weakness of the model merging supply chain.

papers.title: Lingdan-V2: Large language models for clinically grounded reasoning in traditional Chinese medicine
papers.abstract: Large language models have advanced medical reasoning, but clinically grounded reasoning in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) remains challenging because prescription decisions require integrating domain knowledge, syndrome differentiation, treatment principles, herbal prescription composition, and dosage determination. We develop a TCM language model family comprising models with 4 billion, 8 billion, and 14 billion parameters. The artificial intelligence contribution is a staged clinical alignment framework integrating large scale continued pretraining on TCM and clinical records, complementary reasoning supervision, and prescription-centered reinforcement learning (RL). We further formulate herbal prescription generation as a structured RL problem with prescription-level feedback, enabling direct optimization of clinical decision outputs beyond knowledge reproduction and generic instruction following. The engineering application is TCM clinical decision support, particularly herbal prescription recommendation. We evaluate the models on a public benchmark containing 25,620 expert-verified items across 13 TCM knowledge and clinical reasoning tasks and on a private retrospective dataset of 4,348 spleen and stomach disease prescription cases. The 14 billion parameter reinforcement aligned model achieves a prescription generation F1 of 37.0 on the public benchmark, compared with 32.3 for DeepSeek-R1 with 671 billion total parameters, and a herb-level F1 of 52.8 on the clinical dataset with improved dosage agreement. Reinforcement post-training consistently improves prescription recommendation across all scales, while physician-source analysis shows that expert heterogeneity affects reward stability. These findings demonstrate a scalable pathway from domain grounding and reasoning supervision to clinically oriented prescription decision support.
papers.summary: Prescribing in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) chains together syndrome differentiation, treatment principle, herb composition, and dosage, which general medical language models handle poorly. The `Lingdan-V2` family at 4B, 8B, and 14B parameters is trained in stages: large-scale continued pretraining on TCM texts and clinical records, complementary reasoning supervision, then reinforcement learning with prescription-level rewards, so the model optimizes the prescription it emits rather than knowledge recall. On a public benchmark of 25,620 expert-verified items across 13 tasks, the 14B reinforcement-aligned model reaches **a prescription generation F1 of 37.0 against 32.3 for `DeepSeek-R1` with 671B total parameters**, and on 4,348 private spleen and stomach disease cases it reaches herb-level F1 of 52.8 with improved dosage agreement. Reinforcement post-training helped at every scale, while differences between prescribing physicians made the reward signal less stable.

papers.title: How to Build a Benchmark That Actually Measures Taste
papers.abstract: Expert-aligned "taste" benchmarks should reward craft judgment, not the ability to game the test. We introduce TasteBench, a pairwise good-vs-bad benchmark across visual, brand, book, and tech items under a frozen rubric with expert-only gold (panel n>=3; percent agreement >=0.60 primary gate; weak engagement labels train/analysis-only), together with a control protocol that separates craft judgment from test-gaming. Applying the protocol to a Round-1 pilot (primary_human_expert; three biological human experts; n=250 pairs) surfaces and quantifies three validity threats: two construction artifacts that inflate the trivial-baseline layer, and a difficulty ceiling that inflates every score. (1) Position: the preferred item is slot A with probability 0.956, so an always_item_a policy scores 0.956 (fair chance 0.5). (2) Lexical leakage: a filename token cue scores 0.912. (3) Difficulty ceiling: craft domains show near-ceiling human agreement (book/brand/tech 1.0), and even under A/B randomization (eval_assignment_seed7; gold_side_A ~0.47) all five VLM cards reach 1.0 on craft, with only visual separating (~0.84-0.91; a post-hoc hard subset, n=107, leaves craft at 1.0). The protocol (expert-only gold, a weak-label firewall, side randomization at construction, filename scrubbing, and hard filters) makes each artifact measurable and, for the two construction artifacts, correctable; we release a reference eval harness and a side-randomization tool, and show the tool removes the position skew (0.916 to 0.495/0.505). The result is a calibrated view of what the benchmark does and does not yet measure: position and leakage are fixable, whereas the craft-domain ceiling is a pair-difficulty limit that Round-2 must address. We do not evaluate engagement, era/circle conditioning, or calibration here, and we claim no general taste SOTA.
papers.summary: Benchmarks meant to measure craft or aesthetic judgment can be beaten by exploiting how they were constructed rather than by having taste. A pilot round of `TasteBench`, a pairwise good-versus-bad test over visual, brand, book, and tech items with gold labels from three human experts on 250 pairs, is used to surface and quantify three validity threats: **the preferred item sat in slot A 95.6% of the time, so an always-pick-A policy scored 0.956 against a fair-chance 0.5**, a filename token cue alone scored 0.912, and the craft domains proved so easy that all five vision-language models tested hit perfect accuracy even under side randomization, with only the visual domain separating models at roughly 0.84 to 0.91. The proposed control protocol combines expert-only gold labels, a firewall against weak engagement labels, side randomization at construction time, filename scrubbing, and hard difficulty filters; the released randomization tool removes the position skew from 0.916 to near 0.5, while the craft-domain ceiling remains an unresolved pair-difficulty problem for a second round.

papers.title: Vela: User Behavior as Supervision Sparks LLM Intelligence
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in applications that act on users' long-term behavior histories, from personal assistants to recommendation and advertising systems. These applications demand the user dimension of LLM intelligence: inferring a person's preferences, intent, and likely future actions from weeks to years of behavior data. Yet current models are trained on static text or synthetic data, neither of which captures how user behavior evolves over time. Real-world behavior records, already available at scale on content platforms and in personal-assistant agents, offer a natural supervisory signal. We propose user behavior as supervision and introduce Vela, a framework that converts real user behavior data into trainable tasks and trajectories. From the anonymized behavior records of 100,000 users, Vela generates 100,000 tasks across 91 real-world task templates; difficulty-based filtering and trajectory acceptance criteria retain approximately 75,000 tasks with selected training trajectories. Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on these trajectories improves performance over the base model by up to 11.5 points on user-related tasks and by an average of 4 points on general benchmarks. Training on more user behavior data further improves user-related performance, and reinforcement learning after fine-tuning outperforms reinforcement learning from the base model by up to 7.7 points. These gains suggest that real-world user behavior is a scalable source of supervision for both user-centered capabilities and the broader intelligence of LLMs.
papers.summary: Assistants, recommenders, and ad systems act on months or years of a person's behavior, but the models behind them are trained on static text or synthetic data that never shows behavior evolving. `Vela` treats real user behavior records as a supervision source, converting the anonymized histories of 100,000 users into 100,000 tasks across 91 real-world templates and keeping about 75,000 after difficulty filtering and trajectory acceptance checks. Fine-tuning `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` on the resulting trajectories **gains up to 11.5 points on user-related tasks and about 4 points on average across general benchmarks**, with more behavior data improving user-facing performance further. Reinforcement learning applied after this fine-tuning beats reinforcement learning started from the base model by up to 7.7 points.

papers.title: Relational Semantic Grounding for Test-Time Discovery
papers.abstract: Test-Time Discovery (TTD) aims to recognize known classes and detect novel ones from a continuous unlabeled test stream after deployment. Existing TTD methods mainly rely on visual clustering or prototype comparison, and can only assign anonymous labels to discovered classes, leaving them difficult to interpret in open-world applications. In this paper, we propose SEGA, a Semantic Grounding with Attributes framework for TTD. SEGA leverages large language models to generate attribute-rich descriptions for known classes and constructs an attribute-anchored visual-semantic space during training. At test time, we introduce Relational Semantic Grounding (RSG), which grounds unknown samples with similar and dissimilar known-class anchors, prompts the LLM to generate candidate concepts, and reranks them in the learned semantic space. The selected concept is further used for confidence-guided test-time semantic stabilization. By coupling attribute-level semantic alignment with relational concept grounding, SEGA transforms anonymous test-time clusters into interpretable semantic concepts. Experiments show that SEGA improves TTD baselines with the promise of semantic grounding for open-world.
papers.summary: Test-Time Discovery (TTD) asks a deployed model to keep recognizing known classes in an unlabeled stream while also detecting new ones, but methods built on visual clustering or prototype comparison can only give the new groups anonymous labels. `SEGA` has a large language model write attribute-rich descriptions of the known classes and builds an attribute-anchored visual-semantic space during training; at test time it grounds an unknown sample against both similar and dissimilar known-class anchors, asks the language model for candidate concepts, and reranks them inside that learned space. The chosen concept also drives a confidence-guided stabilization step, and the authors report **improvements over TTD baselines while converting anonymous test-time clusters into interpretable named concepts**.

papers.title: Integrating AIRL-Based Reward Estimation into a Control Method Using Fuzzy Inference and Policy Gradient
papers.abstract: A method integrating policy gradient with fuzzy inference has been proposed. This method, hereafter referred to as the base model, has high flexibility with respect to the configuration of fuzzy inference rules and fuzzy representation. It can also automatically adjust the rule weights and the membership functions in the antecedent and consequent parts using the same framework for learning. In methods that integrate reinforcement learning with fuzzy inference, however, the reward function must be designed in advance. It is therefore useful to add learning-based reward estimation to the base model. This paper proposes a fuzzy control method that integrates a reward estimation mechanism based on the adversarial inverse reinforcement learning (AIRL) framework into the base model. The generative adversarial nets (GAN) framework adopted in AIRL, however, tends to suffer from unstable learning. To address this, the proposed method treats the policy of the base model as the generator and also uses the set of membership functions in the policy as the cost function of the discriminator. This configuration allows the discriminator update for reward estimation and the generator update for policy estimation to be performed simultaneously on the parameters shared by both, without estimating a value function. In simulations of an illustrative vehicle speed control task, the proposed method acquired policies with high generalization performance through stable and efficient learning.
papers.summary: An existing control method combining policy gradient with fuzzy inference can tune rule weights and both antecedent and consequent membership functions in one framework, but still needs its reward function designed by hand. The proposed extension learns the reward instead using adversarial inverse reinforcement learning (AIRL), and counters the instability of the underlying generative adversarial nets (GAN) setup by treating the fuzzy policy as the generator and reusing its membership functions as the discriminator's cost function. Because both halves then share parameters, **reward estimation and policy updates can proceed simultaneously without estimating a value function**, and a vehicle speed control simulation produced policies the authors describe as generalizing well from stable, efficient learning.

papers.title: MHWA: Multi-timescale Hierarchical World-Action Model
papers.abstract: Autoregressive world models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for sample efficient decision making, yet their open loop rollouts often exhibit increasing drift that leads to error accumulation even within a relatively small planning horizon. Hierarchical temporal abstraction is a natural candidate to mitigate such drift by reducing the effective prediction horizon; however, existing hierarchical designs can introduce added structural and conceptual complexity, sometimes making them difficult to control and limiting gains over flat baselines. To this end, we introduce MHWA (Multi-timescale Hierarchical World-Action model), which employs a strided high level context channel to reduce global context update frequency, effectively curbing the propagation of compounding drift. Crucially, via context aware routing, the gating network dynamically reconfigures a low level mixture of experts by using both global context and current observations, thereby enabling flexible high-low coordination, helping alleviate interference commonly observed in static hierarchies. Empirically, using RLiable's seed-by-game aggregation, MHWA (77M parameters) achieves an IQM human normalized score (HNS) of 0.884 across three training seeds on a 14-game Atari subset using 10% subsampled offline data, outperforming a matched JOWA-70M baseline (0.529) and achieving numerically comparable performance to JOWA-150M while using nearly half the parameters and 70.88% fewer training FLOPs per sequence.
papers.summary: Autoregressive world models learn from few samples but drift during open-loop rollouts, and hierarchical remedies often add enough structural complexity that they fail to beat flat baselines. `MHWA` keeps the hierarchy minimal: a strided high-level context channel updates global context less frequently to limit compounding drift, while a gating network reconfigures a low-level mixture of experts from both the global context and the current observation, so the two levels coordinate instead of interfering as they do in static hierarchies. On a 14-game `Atari` subset using 10% subsampled offline data, the 77M-parameter model reaches **an interquartile-mean human-normalized score of 0.884 against 0.529 for a matched 70M `JOWA` baseline**, roughly matching `JOWA`-150M with about half the parameters and 70.88% fewer training FLOPs per sequence.

papers.title: Self-improving data synthesis can scale embedding models across domains and tasks
papers.abstract: Adapting embedding models to new tasks requires training data that reflect task-specific information needs and relevance criteria. However, manual data design is costly and difficult to scale. Here we introduce SYNTRA, a novel retrieval data synthesis method whose self-improvement loop iteratively refines reusable synthesis instructions using feedback on trial outputs. This process requires only an unlabelled corpus and a few relevant query-document pairs. Experiments across 24 retrieval datasets spanning 15 domains demonstrate the effectiveness of the synthesized data. These data also improve widely used, strong embedding models on tasks with and without existing labelled training sets. Self-improvement enhances retrieval on all six evaluated tasks, outperforming human calibration on four. Moreover, retrieval performance continues to improve on MS MARCO as we scale the training dataset to 32 times its initial size. Overall, with minimal human intervention, SYNTRA enables scalable adaptation of embedding models across domains and tasks.
papers.summary: Adapting embedding models to a new retrieval task normally requires hand-built training data that captures the task's relevance criteria, which is expensive to scale. `SYNTRA` synthesizes query-document training pairs from an unlabelled corpus and a handful of relevant examples, with a self-improvement loop that iteratively rewrites reusable synthesis instructions based on feedback on trial outputs. Across 24 retrieval datasets in 15 domains the synthesized data improves strong existing embedding models on tasks with and without labelled training sets, and **self-improvement lifts retrieval on all six evaluated tasks, beating human-calibrated instructions on four**. Retrieval quality on `MS MARCO` keeps climbing as the synthetic training set is scaled to 32 times its initial size.

papers.title: Think in Strategies, Act with Tools: Traceable Agentic Optimization for Combinatorial Problems
papers.abstract: Optimization by PROmpting (OPRO) directly leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate candidate solutions through natural-language prompting. However, OPRO's optimization process is difficult to track, which prevents LLMs from capturing useful information accumulated over previous iterations, thereby limiting solution quality. To address this limitation, we propose a Tool-Augmented Strategic Agent (TASA) which summarizes and exploits trajectory to improve solution quality. Specifically, TASA plans the strategy for each step based on the optimization trajectory, which decomposes the optimization process into traceable strategy selections. Moreover, we leverage LLM to construct problem-specific tools and introduce a strategy-guided adaptive tool planner, which efficiently utilizes the information of trajectory to update solutions. We establish local convergence under persistent exploration and evaluate the complete framework under a shared candidate-evaluation budget. The results support its solution quality and the traceability of strategy-guided search.
papers.summary: Optimization by PROmpting (`OPRO`) asks a large language model to propose candidate solutions to combinatorial problems directly from a prompt, but the resulting search is hard to trace, so the model cannot exploit what earlier iterations revealed. The Tool-Augmented Strategic Agent (`TASA`) instead plans an explicit strategy at each step from a summary of the optimization trajectory, has the LLM build problem-specific tools, and uses a strategy-guided adaptive tool planner to update solutions. The authors prove **local convergence under persistent exploration** and report that, under a shared candidate-evaluation budget, the framework improves solution quality while keeping the strategy-guided search traceable.

papers.title: PTGPO: Prefix Tree Group Policy Optimization
papers.abstract: Training language agents on long-horizon interactive tasks is challenging because sparse terminal rewards provide weak credit signals for intermediate actions. Existing group-based methods either assign a shared trajectory-level advantage or estimate step-level advantages from state groups, which may conflate the current action with subsequent decisions. We propose Prefix Tree Group Policy Optimization (PTGPO), a critic-free method that constructs prefix trees over trajectory suffixes within anchor-state groups. PTGPO assigns each tree edge a credit given by the difference between its child and parent empirical mean returns, capturing the conditional return change revealed by each additional action. These prefix-tree credits provide fine-grained learning signals without requiring a critic or additional rollouts. Experiments on interactive benchmarks ALFWorld, WebShop and Sokoban show that PTGPO consistently improves over RL baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness.
papers.summary: Language agents trained with reinforcement learning on long-horizon interactive tasks receive only sparse terminal rewards, so group-based methods either share one trajectory-level advantage across all steps or estimate step-level advantages that conflate the current action with later decisions. Prefix Tree Group Policy Optimization (`PTGPO`) builds prefix trees over trajectory suffixes within groups that share an anchor state and credits each tree edge with the difference between the child's and parent's empirical mean return, isolating the return change attributable to each additional action without a critic or extra rollouts. On `ALFWorld`, `WebShop` and `Sokoban`, **`PTGPO` consistently outperforms the reinforcement learning baselines**.

papers.title: SAGE: Pushing 2-Bit Vector-Quantized LLMs toward Real-World Usability
papers.abstract: Extreme low-bit weight-only quantization is an effective approach to reducing the deployment costs of large language models. Below 3 bits, scalar quantization often suffers severe accuracy loss, while vector quantization (VQ) better preserves accuracy through more expressive joint encoding. However, existing VQ methods still exhibit substantial degradation on real-world tasks, and two design challenges remain underexplored: (1) protecting sensitive weight channels within jointly encoded vectors; and (2) allocating a fixed bit budget among representation components, such as direction and radius, to suit different weight matrices. To address these challenges, we propose SAGE: Split Adaptation and Grouping by Energy for weight-only vector quantization. First, Energy-Stratified Grouping (ESG) couples channel grouping with activation-weighted fitting, grouping channels from different energy tiers within each subvector to prioritize sensitive channels. Second, Adaptive Bit Split (ABS) balances direction-codebook capacity and radius precision per matrix, selecting the split with the lowest activation-weighted reconstruction error under a fixed budget. Across benchmarks covering knowledge, mathematics, code generation, instruction following, and tool use, SAGE achieves state-of-the-art performance in the 2-bit quantization setting. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, it retains 95.3% of the BF16 model's average benchmark score. With our custom-designed CUDA kernel, SAGE delivers up to a 2.55-fold non-streaming end-to-end speedup over FP16. The code is available at https://github.com/Zincwolf/sage.
papers.summary: Weight-only quantization below 3 bits cuts deployment cost, but scalar methods lose much accuracy there, and even vector quantization (VQ), which jointly encodes groups of weights, still degrades on real tasks. `SAGE` (Split Adaptation and Grouping by Energy) adds Energy-Stratified Grouping, which mixes channels from different activation-energy tiers inside each subvector so sensitive channels are protected, and Adaptive Bit Split, which chooses per matrix how to divide a fixed bit budget between the direction codebook and radius precision. Across knowledge, math, code, instruction-following and tool-use benchmarks it sets the state of the art at 2 bits, **retaining 95.3% of the BF16 average score on `Qwen3-30B-A3B`**, and a custom CUDA kernel yields up to a 2.55x non-streaming end-to-end speedup over FP16.

papers.title: Equal-information evaluation of credit assignment in modular financial reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: Credit assignment in modular financial reinforcement learning is difficult to evaluate because an attributed signal may improve a component loss without adding decision-relevant information or improving economic outcomes. We propose an evaluation framework combining equal-information reconstruction controls, fixed-utility comparisons and prespecified downstream guardrails. The framework is instantiated in an attribution-guided modular trading architecture and tested in three controlled studies covering update allocation, supervision-target representation and portfolio risk control. We find that residual-based allocation is exactly reproduced by an ordinary loss-budget control under the disclosed interface; direct shortfall supervision improves component prediction but fails decoded-outcome preservation; and component-wise critic supervision worsens risk-condition certainty equivalent and drawdown relative to scalar supervision under fixed utility. These results identify three distinct evaluation failures: redundant attribution signals, representation-induced prediction trade-offs, and misalignment between component supervision and downstream risk outcomes. A preserved historical engineering case further shows why module-level learning claims require run-level provenance. The contribution is a reusable methodology for evaluating credit assignment in expert systems operating under partial observability, delayed feedback and economic risk constraints.
papers.summary: In modular trading systems trained with reinforcement learning, it is hard to tell whether a credit-assignment signal routed to a component carries decision-relevant information or improves economic outcomes, rather than merely lowering a component loss. The authors propose an evaluation framework built on equal-information reconstruction controls, fixed-utility comparisons and prespecified downstream guardrails, and apply it to an attribution-guided modular trading architecture in three controlled studies. They find that **residual-based update allocation is exactly reproduced by an ordinary loss-budget control**, that direct shortfall supervision improves component prediction but fails to preserve decoded outcomes, and that component-wise critic supervision worsens certainty equivalent and drawdown relative to scalar supervision, identifying three distinct ways credit-assignment evaluations can mislead.

papers.title: GateSight: Recurrent Memory Anticipates Attention Memory for Query-Agnostic KV Eviction in Hybrid LLMs
papers.abstract: Hybrid language models interleave Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers, whose recurrent memory has a fixed size, with full-attention layers, whose key-value (KV) cache grows with the context and dominates serving memory. In this paper, we ask whether the recurrent memory already knows what the attention memory will need. We first show that which GDN heads of Qwen3.8-27B keep long memories is fixed by the weights rather than by the document. Next, we define the future utility of a KV entry by how much removing it changes the attention output over the model's own continuations, and find that the write gate, decay and write magnitude that GDN layers emit during prefill anticipate this utility before any query is seen. Because the relation is spread across many GDN heads and layers, and a linear map recovers its trend but less of its high-utility tail than a nonlinear one, we propose GateSight, which learns it with lightweight per-head multilayer perceptrons that read these signals and no attention score. Their predicted utility decides which entries each attention layer keeps, and how much each layer keeps is set by the model's native attention output gate, whose mean differs by more than an order of magnitude across layers. Finally, at serving time, GateSight scores the cache once after prefill and physically releases discarded KV entries. Experimental results on SCBench and RULER-4096 with Qwen3.8-27B and, with the same recipe, the sparse-attention model Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, up to the 262K-token limit of the models, show that with a tenth of the attention KV cache, GateSight is the most accurate of five query-agnostic methods on three of the four model-benchmark pairs and leads KVzip on all four, by 9.5 to 47.2 points. Notably, it scores a full-length context with negligible overhead relative to prefill.
papers.summary: Hybrid language models interleave Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers, whose recurrent state has a fixed size, with full-attention layers whose key-value (KV) cache grows with context length and dominates serving memory. The authors show that the write gate, decay and write magnitude that GDN layers emit during prefill predict how useful each KV entry will be to the model's own future continuations before any query is seen, and `GateSight` learns this mapping with small per-head multilayer perceptrons that read no attention scores, with per-layer retention budgets set by the model's native attention output gate. On `SCBench` and `RULER-4096` with `Qwen3.8-27B` and `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` at contexts up to 262K tokens, **GateSight keeps a tenth of the attention KV cache and beats `KVzip` on all four model-benchmark pairs by 9.5 to 47.2 points**, scoring a full context with negligible overhead relative to prefill.

papers.title: CUSE: Fine-Grained Multimodal Unlearning with Counterfactual Guidance and On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can reproduce sensitive, copyrighted, or unsafe information from their training data. Effective unlearning must remove target information while preserving non-target content, even within the same response. Existing methods typically apply uniform forgetting objectives to complete responses and rely on fixed, off-policy supervision, resulting in coarse token control and misalignment with the model's current behavior. We propose CUSE, a Counterfactual-guided Unlearning framework via on-policy Self-distillation for multimodal large language models. It first constructs counterfactual inputs by removing target-related evidence and uses the resulting changes in token probabilities to identify which tokens require stronger forgetting. It then distills token-level forgetting and retention targets on responses sampled from the current policy, with a frozen copy of the original model serving as the teacher model augmented with the corresponding forgetting- and retention-oriented privileged contexts. This design jointly determines what to forget and what to preserve. On MLLMU-Bench, CUSE reduces forget-set ROUGE-L by 33.6% while achieving 1.2% higher retain-set ROUGE-L than the strongest baseline.
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can regurgitate sensitive or copyrighted training content, and unlearning methods that apply one forgetting objective to an entire response with fixed off-policy targets forget too coarsely and drift from the model's current behavior. `CUSE` builds counterfactual inputs that strip target-related evidence and uses the resulting token-probability shifts to pinpoint which tokens need stronger forgetting, then distills token-level forget and retain targets onto responses sampled from the current policy, with a frozen copy of the original model acting as teacher under forgetting- and retention-oriented privileged contexts. On `MLLMU-Bench` it **cuts forget-set ROUGE-L by 33.6% while scoring 1.2% higher retain-set ROUGE-L than the strongest baseline**.

papers.title: Last Secure Code Benchmark: Is the Code You Vibe Secure?
papers.abstract: AI coding agents now write much of the code that ships, yet whether that code is secure remains unclear. We introduce the Last Secure Code Benchmark, a comprehensive evaluation of secure code generation by coding agents. Built from 150 real vulnerabilities, its 450 tasks span seven widely used languages (Java, C, C++, JavaScript, Python, PHP, and Go), 24 CWEs including 21 of the 2025 CWE Top 25 and 8 of the Top 10 KEV weaknesses, more than any benchmark we compare with, and three vibe-coding scenarios: filling in a function, writing a file, and building a repository's source tree from scratch. Every task asks only for functionality, through a specification that never mentions security, and hidden functional and security tests grade the result. Across six frontier agents, 73.6% to 91.3% of tasks pass functionally, yet even the strongest, Claude Fable 5, produces code that is both functional and secure for only 25.1% of tasks, and the others for 16.4% to 24.7%. The best model only passes 12% of the vulnerability scenarios across all vibe coding setting, posing strong concern on the security of the code written by vibe coding.
papers.summary: Coding agents now produce much of the code that ships, but whether that code is secure has not been measured systematically. The benchmark builds 450 tasks from 150 real vulnerabilities across Java, C, C++, JavaScript, Python, PHP and Go, covering 24 Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) categories including 21 of the 2025 CWE Top 25, and poses them in three vibe-coding scenarios (completing a function, writing a file, and building a repository from scratch) with specifications that never mention security and hidden functional and security tests. Across six frontier agents, 73.6% to 91.3% of tasks pass functionally, yet **even the strongest, `Claude Fable 5`, produces code that is both functional and secure on only 25.1% of tasks**, with the others between 16.4% and 24.7%, and the best model passes just 12% of vulnerability scenarios across all settings.

papers.title: Prior-Fitted and Frozen Scorers for Multimodal Contrastive Learning
papers.abstract: Multimodal contrastive learning typically relies on manually specified scoring functions, such as cosine similarity, to quantify the similarity between representations from different modalities. Several such functions have been recently proposed to extend contrastive learning beyond two modalities. In principle, however, any function that assigns high compatibility to matched samples and low compatibility to mismatched ones could serve as a scorer. Motivated by this broader view, we instantiate the scorer with a Transformer and find that even a randomly initialized model, when kept frozen, can outperform strong handcrafted multimodal contrastive baselines, whereas optimizing the scorer jointly with the encoders is less effective. Building on this observation, we introduce the Prior-Fitted Scorer (PFS): a Transformer scorer pre-trained on synthetic multimodal data generated from structural causal model (SCM) priors before transferring it to real-world data. The SCM exposes the scorer to diverse dependency structures, including shared, pairwise, and private information, providing a structured prior over higher-order cross-modal similarity. Across four real-world datasets, frozen Transformer scorers are competitive to contrastive baselines, and prior-fitting further improves the random initialization. More broadly, our results suggest that multimodal contrastive learning need not rely on manual similarity functions: Transformers can provide strong inductive biases, while causal pretraining can further shape these biases.
papers.summary: Multimodal contrastive learning scores cross-modal compatibility with hand-designed functions such as cosine similarity, and extending it beyond two modalities has required new handcrafted formulas. The authors replace the scorer with a Transformer and find that **a randomly initialized Transformer kept frozen already outperforms strong handcrafted multimodal contrastive baselines**, while training the scorer jointly with the encoders works less well. Building on this, the Prior-Fitted Scorer (`PFS`) pretrains the scorer on synthetic multimodal data drawn from structural causal model (SCM) priors that expose shared, pairwise and private dependency structures; across four real-world datasets frozen scorers are competitive with contrastive baselines and prior-fitting improves further on random initialization.

papers.title: How Should a Camera-First AI Agent Work?
papers.abstract: Camera-first agents must act on the visual world as it unfolds. We argue that the central obstacle for future camera-first agents is not recognition ability - multimodal models (vision-language and live/streaming alike) generalize well through language and remain the right tool for semantic reasoning - but time. Many visual targets are ephemeral: they appear, are query-relevant, and leave within a short window. Binding memory to the same end-to-end path as reasoning means that by the time a monolithic pipeline completes, the evidence is gone. We formalize this as Ephemeral-Target Interaction (ETI) and a Perceptual Deadline Contract separating a hard memory deadline from a soft reasoning deadline, grounded in the bounded, passive nature of sensory and working memory. We propose a two-deadline architecture: an always-on, bounded, non-semantic fast path; an active remembering mechanism that commits a moment to durable memory before it is overwritten (event-driven in v1); and a deferred deliberation layer (multimodal model + tools). We instantiate the contract on real MOT17 track windows, a consistency check, and calibrate the single-path baseline from measured frontier-model latency: even a short answer takes 1.2-9.3 s, and an agentic identify-and-search longer. Answers can be late; evidence cannot be missed.
papers.summary: Agents that act on a live camera feed face a timing problem rather than a recognition problem: many visual targets appear, become relevant and vanish within a short window, so a monolithic pipeline that routes memory through the same slow path as reasoning finishes after the evidence is gone. The authors formalize this as Ephemeral-Target Interaction (ETI) and propose a Perceptual Deadline Contract separating a hard memory deadline from a soft reasoning deadline, realized as a two-deadline architecture with an always-on bounded non-semantic fast path, an event-driven mechanism that commits moments to durable memory before they are overwritten, and a deferred deliberation layer built on a multimodal model plus tools. Instantiating the contract on `MOT17` track windows and calibrating against measured frontier-model latency, they show that **even a short model answer takes 1.2 to 9.3 seconds**, longer than many targets persist, which motivates the principle that answers may be late but evidence cannot be missed.

papers.title: ProgAgent: Learning Tool Orchestration through Programmatic Training
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly expected to orchestrate diverse tools over long-horizon tasks. Existing agents typically use Direct Tool Calling (DTC), where the model invokes tools sequentially, and tool responses accumulate in the model context, which can lead to context rot and orchestration breakdown. In contrast, Programmatic Tool Calling (PTC) invokes tools through executable code and stores intermediate results in runtime variables rather than appending them to the context. Prior work has explored PTC mainly as an inference-time optimization, but its benefits for agentic training remain unclear, and suitable verifiable training tasks are scarce. In this work, we introduce ProgAgent, a full PTC training stack, comprising a pipeline for synthesizing verifiable long-horizon tasks, a lightweight PTC runtime, and a two-stage training recipe. Using only 215 tasks instantiated at four environment scales, ProgAgent yields higher pass rates than the evaluated baselines of comparable size across four benchmarks. On LOCA-bench, ProgAgent-14B achieves a 30.7% pass rate at a 64k-token environment state, where these baselines score zero. Cross-harness experiments show that PTC-trained models outperform DTC-trained models under both evaluation interfaces, suggesting that the benefits of PTC training extend beyond the interface.
papers.summary: Agents that call tools directly append every tool response to the model's context, which over long-horizon tasks leads to context rot and orchestration breakdown; Programmatic Tool Calling (PTC) instead invokes tools from executable code and keeps intermediate results in runtime variables, but it has mostly been studied as an inference-time optimization. `ProgAgent` is a full PTC training stack: a pipeline for synthesizing verifiable long-horizon tasks, a lightweight PTC runtime, and a two-stage training recipe. Trained on only 215 tasks instantiated at four environment scales, it beats comparably sized baselines on four benchmarks, and **`ProgAgent-14B` reaches a 30.7% pass rate on `LOCA-bench` at a 64k-token environment state where those baselines score zero**. PTC-trained models also outperform models trained with direct tool calling even when evaluated through the direct-calling interface.

papers.title: Training a Compact, Strong, and Realistic Text-to-Speech Model
papers.abstract: Text-to-speech (TTS) systems are conventionally optimized for intelligibility and speaker similarity. However, neither objective captures the prosodic detail that distinguishes human performances from synthetic speech, leaving a realism gap that larger models and higher-quality data can narrow but not close. In the absence of an objective that directly targets this gap, realism remains a persistent challenge in TTS. We present Audio8-TTS, a compact 0.6B-parameter model for zero-shot voice cloning that achieves state-of-the-art performance in intelligibility and speaker similarity, with particularly strong results in perceptual naturalness. To align the training signal with human perception rather than signal-level fidelity, we construct a quality ladder from widely used open-source TTS systems and train a realism critic to assess generated speech against matched human recordings of the same sentences. An identity-erasure objective discourages the critic from relying on generator fingerprints. We train the model in three stages: multilingual supervised fine-tuning; group relative policy optimization (GRPO) with word error rate (WER) and speaker similarity (SIM) rewards; and GRPO guided by the realism critic. The final stage improves perceived prosodic naturalness and speaker similarity while preserving WER performance.
papers.summary: Text-to-speech (TTS) systems are tuned for intelligibility and speaker similarity, neither of which captures the prosodic detail that separates human performances from synthetic speech, so a realism gap persists even as models and data grow. `Audio8-TTS` is a 0.6B-parameter zero-shot voice cloning model trained in three stages: multilingual supervised fine-tuning, group relative policy optimization (`GRPO`) with word error rate (WER) and speaker similarity (SIM) rewards, and a final `GRPO` stage guided by a learned realism critic. The critic is trained on a quality ladder of open-source TTS systems against matched human recordings of the same sentences, with an identity-erasure objective that stops it from keying on generator fingerprints, and the authors report **state-of-the-art intelligibility and speaker similarity with particularly strong perceptual naturalness**, with the realism stage improving prosody and similarity while preserving WER.

papers.title: LYNX: Analytical Program Synthesis via Grounding and Closed-Loop Refinement
papers.abstract: LLM-powered data analytics aims to translate natural language instructions into executable analytical programs over underlying data. However, existing approaches, whether treating LLMs as intent-to-code translators or as standalone analytical engines, often fail to reliably align domain semantics with complex schemas and heterogeneous metadata, resulting in brittle execution and semantically inconsistent analytical outputs in real-world workloads. We present LYNX, a multi-agent framework that formulates LLM-driven analytics as a schema- and knowledge-constrained analysis problem rather than a single-pass generation task. LYNX organizes analytical synthesis into a closed-loop workflow of planning, generation, verification, and refinement through three role-specialized agents that collaboratively enforce schema grounding, semantic consistency, and execution correctness. To address domain ambiguity and schema misalignment, LYNX integrates Semantic-Structural Distillation and Stage-Aware Allocation (SSD-SAA). A delta-guided iterative revision continuously diagnoses and repairs semantic and execution-level failures, substantially improving synthesis robustness. We evaluate LYNX on two NL-to-SQL benchmarks, BIRD-SQL Mini-Dev and the more challenging Spider 2.0-Lite. Experimental results demonstrate strong performance and efficiency, achieving 10.66% to 59.54% execution accuracy across lightweight and commercial models, while reducing token consumption by 70.53% compared with the prior most efficient method. Our framework displays high generalization over different backbones, from open-source, lightweight models to the latest commercial models. Additional case studies on quantitative finance analytics and complex multi-relational SQL workloads further demonstrate the framework's robustness, scalability, and practical applicability in real-world analytical scenarios.
papers.summary: Translating natural-language analytics requests into executable programs over real databases often fails because large language models, whether used as intent-to-code translators or as standalone analytical engines, misalign domain semantics with complex schemas and heterogeneous metadata. `LYNX` treats the problem as schema- and knowledge-constrained analysis, with three role-specialized agents running a closed loop of planning, generation, verification and refinement, aided by Semantic-Structural Distillation and Stage-Aware Allocation (SSD-SAA) and a delta-guided iterative revision that diagnoses and repairs semantic and execution failures. On `BIRD-SQL Mini-Dev` and `Spider 2.0-Lite` it reaches 10.66% to 59.54% execution accuracy depending on the backbone model, while **cutting token consumption by 70.53% compared with the previously most efficient method**, and it generalizes from lightweight open-source models to the latest commercial ones.

papers.title: Counterfactual Regret for Reflective Agents with Lean-Verified Guarantees
papers.abstract: Reflective language agents reuse feedback and memory to adapt across tasks without updating model weights. However, existing guarantees for policy selection and action generation do not by themselves establish when local reflection yields long-term performance guarantees for the complete agent under resource constraints. In this paper, we address this gap by deriving sufficient conditions for sublinear counterfactual regret from local generation and deployment guarantees, while retaining the native controller. Specifically, we establish a resource-sensitive transfer that bounds full-state deployment discrepancies along actual execution paths and preserves the own-history laws of both learner and comparator. Besides, local generation reliability yields a cumulative generation opportunity bound, linking policy acquisition to long-term performance through an explicit quality, coverage, and hard-budget tradeoff. To verify these guarantees, we formalize the conditional proof chain for all thirteen numbered theoretical results in Lean, including a native instance with repeated policy growth and imperfect validation.
papers.summary: Reflective language agents adapt across tasks by reusing feedback and memory without changing model weights, but existing guarantees for policy selection and action generation do not say when local reflection yields long-term performance guarantees for the whole agent under resource limits. The authors derive sufficient conditions for sublinear counterfactual regret from local generation and deployment guarantees while keeping the agent's native controller, through a resource-sensitive transfer that bounds full-state deployment discrepancies along executed paths and a cumulative generation-opportunity bound that ties policy acquisition to performance via an explicit quality, coverage and hard-budget tradeoff. **All thirteen numbered theoretical results are formalized in `Lean`**, including a native instance with repeated policy growth and imperfect validation.

papers.title: GREAT-ESDD: Graph Edge Attention Network for Effectively Steered Delivery Decisions
papers.abstract: Online, same-day delivery requires operators to constantly update their routes, and the routing cost for deliveries increases with the number of customers. Out-of-home (OOH) delivery options can help companies handle increasing customer numbers while keeping delivery costs low. We develop a dynamic pricing-and-routing framework for this online ordering scenario with home and OOH delivery options. First, we develop a neural solver for the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) based on the Graph-Edge-Attention-Network (GREAT). We train it to solve CVRP with varying instance sizes and starting conditions, allowing it to reoptimize partially executed routes under changing conditions. It is fast while achieving solution quality competitive with traditional baselines. Our solver processes several CVRP instances in parallel in batches and we use it to solve the candidate routing problems that arise from an incoming customer's choice of home or OOH delivery. This provides an estimate of the delivery cost increase per option, which we use to set dynamic prices. Further, it directly provides the updated route once the customer decides. We trade off delivery fees against routing costs and steer customers toward OOH delivery when home delivery would be costly. However, effective steering requires us to know the customer preferences. To learn those online, we use Thompson sampling with a Laplace-approximated posterior. We call the resulting framework GREAT-ESDD (GREAT for Effectively Steered Delivery Decisions). Compared to a traditional routing solver, it increases profit by around 11% under a similar pricing decision time budget. Moreover, we show that we can estimate customer preferences successfully, outperforming a static pricing strategy after only 5 days of simulated operations.
papers.summary: Same-day delivery operators must re-plan routes as orders arrive, and out-of-home (OOH) pickup options can hold costs down if customers can be steered toward them. The authors train a neural solver for the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) based on the Graph Edge Attention Network (`GREAT`) that handles varying instance sizes and partially executed routes, use it to batch-evaluate the marginal routing cost of each incoming customer's home versus OOH choice to set dynamic prices, and learn customer preferences online with Thompson sampling over a Laplace-approximated posterior. The resulting `GREAT-ESDD` framework **raises profit by about 11% over a traditional routing solver** under a similar pricing time budget and overtakes a static pricing strategy after only five simulated days of operation.

papers.title: CESNET-TimeSeries26: A Multi-Year Network Traffic Time Series Dataset for Annual Seasonality, Concept Drift, and Long-Term Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Forecast-based models are fundamental to network traffic management and anomaly detection. However, it is essential to evaluate these forecasting models over extended periods of time in order to assess their adaptability to unexpected phenomena and shifts in underlying patterns. This kind of long-term evaluation requires multi-year data to account for yearly seasonality and behavioral drift. Existing public datasets are too short to support such long-horizon forecasting tasks. We introduce CESNET-TimeSeries26, comprising 995 days of continuous traffic time series from the CESNET3 network, together with a single subnet spanning approximately 4.5 years. The dataset captures 278,466 IP addresses, 285 institutions, and 566 institutional subnets at three aggregation intervals. The dataset provides a definitive longitudinal benchmark for evaluating forecasting models in both operational management and security monitoring. We demonstrate that annual seasonality is the dominant periodic component. Moreover, we show that a forecasting model can exploit the annual component only when its training window covers at least one complete annual cycle, which no sub-year dataset provides.
papers.summary: Forecasting models underpin network traffic management and anomaly detection, but judging how they cope with yearly seasonality and behavioral drift requires multi-year data that existing public datasets, all shorter than a year, cannot provide. `CESNET-TimeSeries26` contains 995 days of continuous traffic time series from the CESNET3 network plus one subnet spanning roughly 4.5 years, covering 278,466 IP addresses, 285 institutions and 566 institutional subnets at three aggregation intervals. The authors show that annual seasonality is the dominant periodic component and that **a forecasting model can exploit it only when its training window covers at least one full annual cycle**, which no sub-year dataset allows.

papers.title: YOUDrive: Driving Style as a Composable Direction for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: End-to-end driving policies can achieve strong task performance while offering limited control over their driving style. Driving style describes how a vehicle accelerates, brakes, and maintains distance. Policies trained without explicit preference conditioning lack a direct mechanism for adjusting these behaviors at inference. We propose YOUDrive, a vision--language--action planner for continuous and composable driving-style control. Each teacher's behavior is distilled into a task vector, a learned parameter update that induces a style direction in the planner's representation. These directions can be scaled and combined at inference without retraining the backbone. Conditioned on these directions, a flow-matching decoder models a multimodal trajectory distribution and generates kinematically feasible motion alternatives. We introduce the Style Alignment Score (SAS) to describe human-referenced kinematic behavior after safety and task gating. On NAVSIM navtest, a single coefficient monotonically controls assertiveness across six teacher-derived personas, while PDMS remains above 0.90 across the tested individual and blended configurations, reaching 0.954. Further analyses reveal systematic policy-specific kinematics after controlling for scene context, whereas the evaluated discrete style labels provide limited additional explanatory power. Code, checkpoints, and the metric will be released.
papers.summary: End-to-end driving policies perform well but offer little control over driving style, meaning how a vehicle accelerates, brakes and keeps distance, because they are trained without explicit preference conditioning. `YOUDrive` is a vision-language-action planner that distills each teacher policy's behavior into a task vector, a learned parameter update defining a style direction in the planner's representation, so directions can be scaled and blended at inference without retraining the backbone, while a flow-matching decoder produces kinematically feasible trajectory alternatives. On `NAVSIM` navtest, **a single coefficient monotonically controls assertiveness across six teacher-derived personas while the PDMS driving score stays above 0.90**, peaking at 0.954, and a new Style Alignment Score (SAS) measures human-referenced kinematic behavior after safety and task gating.

papers.title: ASIWorld: Benchmarking Autonomous Agents in a Persistent Survival Sandbox
papers.abstract: Evaluating autonomous agents requires examining whether they can translate goals into coherent action across extended interactions. In persistent environments, this requires coordinating interdependent actions under incomplete observations, accounting for delayed effects, and adapting as earlier decisions shape subsequent opportunities. We introduce ASIWorld, a survival sandbox that combines persistent world and character state with character-scoped observations and a programmable asynchronous interface to study sustained goal execution. Agents pursue interdependent production and exploration tasks through direct actions or agent-authored programs that continue running between model calls. The evaluation assesses task success, the attainment of development achievements, and survival costs, complemented by an analysis of execution behavior. In an exploratory study of nine agent configurations using a common harness, eight complete the production task and six complete both tasks. Analyses of execution trajectories and performance across difficulty levels reveal different preparation, combat, and recovery behaviors among configurations with similar task outcomes. Incomplete preparation is associated with stalled progression, while configurations that complete the tasks differ in survival costs and the fulfillment of additional achievement criteria. These findings illustrate the value of assessing sustained goal execution through both task outcomes and the behaviors and costs associated with achieving them.
papers.summary: Evaluating autonomous agents on sustained goal pursuit requires environments where actions are interdependent, observations are partial, effects are delayed and earlier choices shape later options. `ASIWorld` is a survival sandbox with persistent world and character state, character-scoped observations and a programmable asynchronous interface, in which agents pursue interdependent production and exploration tasks either through direct actions or through agent-authored programs that keep running between model calls, and are scored on task success, development achievements and survival costs. In an exploratory study of nine agent configurations under a common harness, **eight complete the production task and six complete both**, yet configurations with similar outcomes show markedly different preparation, combat and recovery behavior, and incomplete preparation is associated with stalled progression.

papers.title: Depth-progressive 3D seismic velocity model building via 2D generative diffusion models
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) velocity model building (VMB) remains computationally challenging with conventional approaches and native 3D neural networks, largely due to the prohibitive memory and training cost of full 3D formulations. Therefore, we introduce a depth-progressive framework that achieves 3D VMB using 2D generative diffusion models through a depth-as-channel formulation, in which the depth dimension of each 3D velocity patch is mapped to the channel dimension of a 2D U-Net. This allows the model to synthesize overlapping depth patches sequentially from shallow to deep while conditioning the prediction of the deeper patch on the shallower one, as well as on any available geophysical constraints, including well logs and structural attributes. During training, paired shallow-deep patch pairs with randomized overlaps are used to teach the network how deeper velocity structures relate to shallower information, and a classifier-free guidance strategy enables the model to handle missing constraints gracefully.
