At inference, starting from a shallow velocity prior, the model recursively generates deeper patches in a top-down manner, and a depth-attenuated Gaussian blending scheme merges overlapping predictions into spatially coherent 3D volumes while accounting for the progressive accumulation of uncertainty at greater depths. Numerical experiments on both in-distribution benchmark models, including Overthrust, SEAM Arid, and SEG/EAGE, and the out-of-distribution Marmousi model demonstrate that the method effectively propagates shallow velocity priors downward and produces high-quality 3D velocity volumes across a range of geological settings and conditioning scenarios. Compared to a 3D benchmark of equivalent architecture, the proposed method significantly reduces parameter count, training cost, and inference cost, while maintaining superior VMB accuracy.
papers.summary: Three-dimensional (3D) seismic velocity model building (VMB) is expensive both for conventional methods and for native 3D neural networks because of the memory and training cost of full 3D formulations. The proposed depth-progressive framework maps the depth axis of each 3D velocity patch onto the channel dimension of a 2D U-Net diffusion model and generates overlapping depth patches sequentially from shallow to deep, conditioning each on the patch above and on any available constraints such as well logs or structural attributes, with classifier-free guidance to handle missing constraints and a depth-attenuated Gaussian blending scheme to merge patches into coherent volumes. On `Overthrust`, `SEAM Arid`, `SEG/EAGE` and the out-of-distribution `Marmousi` model, the method propagates shallow priors downward to produce high-quality 3D volumes and **cuts parameter count, training cost and inference cost relative to an equivalent 3D architecture while achieving higher accuracy**.

papers.title: Seamless Deployment of Machine Learning Inference at the Far Edge: An Empirical AWS IoT Greengrass Architecture for Industrial Predictive Maintenance
papers.abstract: Industrial IoT sensors produce continuous, high-volume data streams that predictive maintenance needs to analyse in real time. Cloud-centric architectures send all raw telemetry to central servers, which costs latency, bandwidth and resilience. This paper presents a hybrid cloud-edge architecture for manufacturing predictive maintenance built on AWS IoT Core and AWS IoT Greengrass v2, with local machine learning inference at the edge and selective cloud synchronization. We deploy two configurations on real AWS infrastructure and compare them: a cloud-only baseline (Configuration A) and the proposed hybrid edge architecture (Configuration B). We measure end-to-end inference latency, bandwidth consumption and inference accuracy. Configuration B cuts cloud-bound bandwidth by 86.8% (63.6 KB to 7.2 KB per 200-reading window) and decision latency by 256x (23.1 ms cloud round trip to 0.09 ms local inference). At the edge, with no cloud involvement, it keeps an anomaly-class F1 score of 0.84 and 91% recall. The evaluation also instruments system uptime and Stream Manager queuing under cloud disconnection; the quantitative disconnection experiment is left as planned work. Our review of the literature points to four gaps that this work addresses: the lack of empirically validated Greengrass v2 deployments for predictive maintenance, unquantified bandwidth savings from selective edge synchronization, unmeasured resilience under cloud disconnection, and the open MLOps feedback loop at the edge.
papers.summary: Industrial sensors stream high volumes of telemetry that predictive maintenance must analyze in real time, and cloud-centric designs that ship all raw data to central servers pay in latency, bandwidth and resilience. The authors build a hybrid cloud-edge architecture on `AWS IoT Core` and `AWS IoT Greengrass v2` that runs machine learning inference locally and synchronizes selectively to the cloud, and compare it against a cloud-only baseline deployed on real AWS infrastructure. The hybrid configuration **cuts cloud-bound bandwidth by 86.8% and decision latency by 256x**, from a 23.1 ms cloud round trip to 0.09 ms local inference, while keeping an anomaly-class F1 of 0.84 and 91% recall at the edge. The quantitative cloud-disconnection experiment is instrumented but left as planned work.

papers.title: A Reference Architecture for Integrating Agentic AI into Enterprise Software: Responsibilities, Interactions, and Variability
papers.abstract: Agentic AI moves generative AI applications toward systems that coordinate reasoning, enterprise context, model inference, and external actions. Integrating these capabilities into enterprise software introduces diverse architectural concerns, from orchestration, knowledge and memory, and model access to tools and actions, security, runtime infrastructure, and evaluation. Existing research and industry architectures address many of these concerns but differ in scope, abstraction, responsibility organization, interaction representation, and assumptions about which capabilities are required. This paper presents a technology-neutral reference architecture for enterprise agentic AI integration. We synthesize architectural capabilities from research publications, industry architecture guidance, and interoperability specifications by architectural purpose, organize them into ten responsibilities, and define boundary invariants, typed cross-responsibility interactions, and variation points that distinguish responsibilities from condition-dependent capabilities and replaceable realization mechanisms. We instantiate the architecture as an ESG portfolio-analysis and pre-trade compliance agent over an existing service-oriented ESG metric computation and reporting system, and complement the case with a mapping of an independently published agentic architecture. The case realizes seven of the ten responsibilities; different questions take different interaction paths, controls activate only under their conditions, and the probed boundary invariants hold. The independent architecture maps onto the proposed responsibilities without requiring an additional one. These results provide initial evidence for the architecture's organization and applicability rather than its completeness. The deployment and recorded results are available as a replication package.
papers.summary: Integrating agentic AI into enterprise software raises architectural concerns spanning orchestration, knowledge and memory, model access, tools and actions, security, runtime infrastructure, and evaluation, and existing research and industry architectures address these with inconsistent scope and assumptions. The authors synthesize capabilities from research publications, industry guidance, and interoperability specifications into a technology-neutral reference architecture organized around **ten responsibilities**, with boundary invariants, typed cross-responsibility interactions, and variation points that separate required responsibilities from condition-dependent capabilities and replaceable realization mechanisms. Instantiated as an ESG portfolio-analysis and pre-trade compliance agent over an existing service-oriented metric system, the case realizes seven of the ten responsibilities, the probed invariants hold, and an independently published agentic architecture maps onto the responsibilities without needing an additional one. The authors present this as initial evidence for the organization and applicability of the architecture rather than its completeness, and release a replication package.

papers.title: AI-Native Product Management: A Vision
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to support product management tasks. At the same time, AI-native research and development (R&D) may increase software realization capacity. Organizations may realize software faster than they can identify, qualify, and reconsider what should be realized. This paper asks how product management should be re-envisioned under these conditions. We synthesize research on software product management, product learning, human-AI collaboration, and the Product Management and R&D boundary. We propose a vision in which AI becomes a persistent participant in product work. The vision covers sensing, exploration, decision-making, realization, and learning. We propose six principles and make the vision tangible through an operating model grounded in human professionals, AI personas, agents, skills, and a shared product context. We further argue that AI-native Product Management and AI-native R&D can form a continuous product-learning process. Finally, we identify four AI-specific research directions that require empirical investigation.
papers.summary: As AI-native research and development (R&D) raises software realization capacity, organizations may ship faster than they can identify, qualify, and reconsider what should be built, which prompts the question of how product management should be re-envisioned. Drawing on research in software product management, product learning, human-AI collaboration, and the boundary between product management and R&D, the authors propose a vision in which **AI becomes a persistent participant in product work** across sensing, exploration, decision-making, realization, and learning. The vision is expressed through six principles and an operating model built from human professionals, AI personas, agents, skills, and a shared product context, with the argument that AI-native product management and AI-native R&D can form a continuous product-learning process. Four AI-specific research directions requiring empirical investigation close the proposal.

papers.title: Cross-Lingual TTS for Indian Languages: A Benchmark and Inference-Time Duration Estimation Strategies
papers.abstract: Recent alignment-free Text-to-Speech (TTS) models achieve high synthesis quality by removing explicit alignment modules and simplifying training. However, they often struggle in cross-lingual scenarios due to differences in character durations across languages, leading to duration mismatch and degraded speech quality. Existing approaches typically address this issue using explicit duration predictors, increasing model complexity. Systematic evaluation of TTS performance for Indian languages in cross-lingual settings remains under-explored due to the lack of standardized evaluation benchmarks. In this work, we construct a cross-lingual evaluation benchmark covering English and nine Indian languages and propose a language-aware inference-time duration estimation strategy for alignment-free TTS that incorporates language-specific duration-per character statistics without retraining or architectural modifications. We further develop heuristic formulations that refine duration estimation based on language-dependent duration variations. Experiments on bilingual and multilingual A-DMA models demonstrate improved speech naturalness, intelligibility, and speaker similarity while reducing duration mismatch.
papers.summary: Alignment-free Text-to-Speech (TTS) models synthesize high-quality speech without explicit alignment modules, but in cross-lingual settings differences in per-character duration across languages cause duration mismatch and degraded output, and Indian languages lack a standardized benchmark for evaluating this. The authors build a cross-lingual evaluation benchmark covering English and nine Indian languages and propose a language-aware inference-time duration estimation strategy that plugs language-specific duration-per-character statistics into alignment-free TTS **without retraining or architectural changes**, along with heuristic refinements for language-dependent duration variation. Experiments on bilingual and multilingual `A-DMA` models show improved naturalness, intelligibility, and speaker similarity alongside reduced duration mismatch.

papers.title: EvoCowork: A Benchmark for Real-World Office Tasks
papers.abstract: Office workflows are a demanding testbed for self-improving agents because their deliverables must be correct, natively editable, and mutually consistent. A central question is whether gains on feedback tasks reflect reusable procedures rather than task-specific fixes. We introduce EvoCowork, a 240-task benchmark for evaluating harness-level recursive self-improvement across four office modalities, with model weights held fixed. The benchmark covers presentations, documents, spreadsheets, and cross-office workflows, and scores submitted artifacts for content, native structure, formulas, cross-file consistency, and visual quality where needed. Its protocol separates feedback, revision selection, and final testing: methods learn from single-modality tasks, then are evaluated on unseen single-modality tasks and cross-office workflows under a shared initial harness and explicit budgets. In static evaluations of two models and four harnesses, the best configuration scores 42.25 overall and 30.62 on cross-office tasks. Starting from the same MSA harness with GLM 5.3, ACE and AHE improve in-domain scores by 4.90 and 2.64 points, respectively, but change cross-office scores by only +0.03 and -1.72. Thus, gains on the file types that provide feedback do not necessarily transfer to coordinated workflows. EvoCowork makes this distinction explicit while recording the capability, transfer, and cost of harness evolution. Code and task packages: https://github.com/DeepThinkingZhouLiu/cowork-evolution-benchmark.
papers.summary: Office workflows are a demanding test of self-improving agents because deliverables must be correct, natively editable, and consistent with each other, and it is unclear whether gains from feedback reflect reusable procedures or task-specific patches. `EvoCowork` is a 240-task benchmark for harness-level recursive self-improvement with model weights held fixed, spanning presentations, documents, spreadsheets, and cross-office workflows, and scoring artifacts on content, native structure, formulas, cross-file consistency, and visual quality; its protocol lets methods learn from single-modality tasks before testing on unseen single-modality tasks and cross-office workflows under a shared starting harness and explicit budgets. Across two models and four harnesses the best static configuration scores 42.25 overall and 30.62 on cross-office tasks, and starting from the `MSA` harness with `GLM 5.3`, the `ACE` and `AHE` methods raise in-domain scores by 4.90 and 2.64 points but **shift cross-office scores by only +0.03 and -1.72**, showing that improvements on the file types that supply feedback do not necessarily transfer to coordinated workflows.

papers.title: Pre-Registered Genesis Accounting for Recursive Self-Improvement: First Audited Operator-Genesis Events in a Physics-Discovery Runtime
papers.abstract: Claims of recursive self-improvement are easy to make and hard to falsify: did improvement come from re-using designer-provided mechanisms, or from mechanisms the system authored itself? We introduce a pre-registered, two-tier accounting: M1 counts machine-generated content instances within a designer-provided vocabulary, while M2 counts machine-authored mechanism types (new operators registered into the runtime's own vocabulary, with a held-out-validation certificate). We report the first audited M2 genesis events. In the primary event, depth-limited compositional search over elementary operators, judged by held-out R^2 on real NIST hydrogen Balmer measurements, produced the operator sq(inv(n)) = 1/n^2 -- the Rydberg-level form -- which no standard-library transform could express (held-out R^2: -0.546 best standard transform vs. 1.0000000 composed). A protocol flaw (independent variable built by inverting the very law under test) was caught in audit and repaired via an independent-label protocol; extrapolation to unseen levels (n=8,9 trained on n<=7) attains relative error ~10^-6, four to six orders beyond the best standard operator. A second event independently recovered sqrt(inv(a)) -- Kepler's velocity law -- from JPL ephemeris vectors. Also incorporated: an audited compounding channel (first domain-level measurement: 1.109x accuracy ratio on a real held-out domain) and blind, decurated genesis exams whose honest tally is zero. The Kepler event passes line audit; the hydrogen gap reproduces on He II; the certificate is threshold-stable. Against eleven prior systems, the contribution is the measurement and governance of machine-authored mechanisms, not the search algorithm or rediscovered physics. Limitations: exams were curated by agents who knew the textbook answer, triggers manual, grammar observer-injected; both events demonstrate capability to author, not yet autonomous genesis.
papers.summary: Claims of recursive self-improvement are hard to falsify because gains may come from reusing designer-provided mechanisms rather than mechanisms the system authored itself. The authors introduce a pre-registered two-tier accounting in which M1 counts machine-generated content within a designer-provided vocabulary and M2 counts machine-authored mechanism types, meaning new operators registered into the runtime vocabulary with a held-out-validation certificate, and report the first audited M2 events in a physics-discovery runtime. In the primary event, depth-limited compositional search over elementary operators judged by held-out R^2 on `NIST` hydrogen Balmer measurements produced the operator 1/n^2, the Rydberg-level form, which no standard-library transform could express, and after an audit caught and repaired a protocol flaw, **extrapolation to unseen levels reached relative error of about 10^-6**, four to six orders beyond the best standard operator; a second event recovered the Kepler velocity law from `JPL` ephemeris vectors. The authors position the contribution as measurement and governance of machine-authored mechanisms rather than the search algorithm or the rediscovered physics, noting that exams were curated by agents who knew the textbook answer, triggers were manual, and the events show capability to author rather than autonomous genesis.

papers.title: Getting Space Right: Agentic Rewards for Image Generation
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is promising for spatial text-to-image generation, but existing work largely focuses on policy optimization, assuming accurate rewards and effective online rollouts. We observe in-domain gains with out-of-domain degradation, exposing two limitations: unreliable spatial rewards in open-world settings and rollouts lacking basic-to-complex progression. We propose a curriculum-guided RL framework. First, we introduce SpatialCritic, an agentic reward model equipped with a spatial perception harness that combines reusable verification guidance with specialized vision tools. We then construct spatial preference datasets through targeted counterfactual perturbations and perform agent-harness alignment to improve tool selection and evidence integration efficiently. Second, curriculum learning organizes shared foundational capabilities and their compositional dependencies in a capability graph for mastery-guided rollouts, periodic review, and targeted remediation. On SpaRW-Eval, SpatialCritic achieves 95.1% verification accuracy, outperforming 320B GLM-5.3-Flash with a 40x smaller 8B backbone and raising average baseline scores from 78.4 to 83.9 on SD3.5-Medium and 83.2 to 86.5 on BAGEL. Project page: https://xiaofeng-tan.github.io/projects/spatialcritic/
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning for spatial text-to-image generation has focused on policy optimization while assuming accurate rewards and useful rollouts, yet the authors observe in-domain gains with out-of-domain degradation, which they trace to unreliable spatial rewards in open-world settings and rollouts that lack basic-to-complex progression. They propose a curriculum-guided RL framework built on `SpatialCritic`, an agentic reward model with a spatial perception harness that pairs reusable verification guidance with specialized vision tools, trained via spatial preference datasets from targeted counterfactual perturbations and an agent-harness alignment step to improve tool selection and evidence integration. A curriculum organizes foundational capabilities and their compositional dependencies in a capability graph to drive mastery-guided rollouts, periodic review, and targeted remediation. On `SpaRW-Eval`, `SpatialCritic` reaches **95.1% verification accuracy with an 8B backbone**, outperforming the 40x larger 320B `GLM-5.3-Flash`, and raises average baseline scores from 78.4 to 83.9 on `SD3.5-Medium` and from 83.2 to 86.5 on `BAGEL`.

papers.title: PEAM: On-device Communication Agent for Personalized, Efficient and Autonomous Mobile Network Configuration
papers.abstract: The growing deployment of compact large language models on smartphones is enabling autonomous on-device decision-making, such as emerging mobile GUI agents. However, many mobile decisions, such as network configuration when users switch apps or connectivity conditions change, must satisfy stringent latency constraints to preserve user experience. In this paper, we propose PEAM, an on-device LLM-based communication agent that autonomously generates personalized network-configuration rules executable within milliseconds. Specifically, PEAM first fine-tune the on-device LLM with a dataset constructed from manually annotated real-user data to integrate the communication knowledge into the local model. PEAM then operates in two phases. In the rule-generation phase, which is performed when the device is idle, such as overnight, PEAM analyzes historical network-configuration records in batches and reflects across batches to consolidate consistent evidence, reduce local bias, and derive robust configuration rules. To enable more accurate and stable rule generation over time, PEAM further constructs a user profile from high-confidence rules to capture the user's network preferences and incorporates this profile into each rule-generation cycle. In the rule-execution phase, PEAM is invoked when the communication context changes, such as when users switch apps or connectivity conditions change, and searches the rule library to identify and execute the appropriate rule. Experiments demonstrate that PEAM, based on a fine-tuned 4B model, achieves 99.13% correct network configuration decisions, while 92.50% of the rules generated by PEAM are valid, outperforming the traditional expert-rule based method by 4.41% and 84.50%, respectively.
papers.summary: Compact language models on smartphones can make autonomous decisions, but choices such as network configuration when a user switches apps or connectivity changes must complete within strict latency limits. `PEAM` is an on-device LLM-based communication agent that first fine-tunes a local model on a dataset built from manually annotated real-user data, then during idle periods such as overnight analyzes historical network-configuration records in batches, reflects across batches to consolidate evidence and reduce local bias, and maintains a user profile from high-confidence rules that feeds back into each generation cycle. When the communication context changes, the agent searches its rule library and executes the matching rule within milliseconds. Built on a fine-tuned 4B model, `PEAM` makes **99.13% correct network configuration decisions** and 92.50% of its generated rules are valid, beating a traditional expert-rule method by 4.41% and 84.50% respectively.

papers.title: WeatherBridge: Forecast-Aware Multi-Source Input Adaptation for Pretrained Weather Forecasting Models
papers.abstract: Data-driven weather forecasting models are commonly trained on ERA5, yet operational deployment must use timely initial states from physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems whose distributions differ substantially from ERA5. Direct initialization with these states can degrade autoregressive forecasts, motivating input adaptation that keeps the pretrained forecasting model unchanged. Here, we introduce WeatherBridge, a unified, source-conditioned adapter that maps heterogeneous operational NWP initial states to ERA5 reference states without updating the pretrained forecasting model. WeatherBridge predicts the structured residual corrections with a Swin-UNet and injects source embeddings across multiple spatial scales, allowing the model to capture shared atmospheric structure and source-specific discrepancies. Its training objective combines latitude-weighted ERA5 reconstruction with One-step Rollout Alignment (ORA), which backpropagates one-step forecast error through a frozen FuXi model to optimize the adapted states for both initial state fidelity and downstream forecast compatibility. We evaluate WeatherBridge using daily GFS, HRES, and CMA initializations from 1 January to 22 November 2025 across six variables and lead times up to 240 hours. Relative to raw source initialization of FuXi, WeatherBridge reduces the mean RMSE of FuXi over the 6- 240-hour rollout for 17 of 18 source-variable combinations, with a median reduction of 10.2% and a maximum reduction of 46.3%. The adapter trained with frozen FuXi also improves FengWu forecasts on GFS inputs without retraining either the adapter or FengWu. These results demonstrate that forecast-aware input adaptation can improve forecasts from heterogeneous operational NWP inputs and transfer across pretrained ERA5-based forecasting models.
papers.summary: Data-driven weather models are usually trained on `ERA5` reanalysis, but operational use must initialize from physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) states whose distributions differ substantially, and feeding those states directly can degrade autoregressive forecasts. `WeatherBridge` is a source-conditioned adapter that maps heterogeneous operational NWP initial states to `ERA5`-like reference states while leaving the pretrained forecaster untouched, predicting structured residual corrections with a `Swin-UNet` that injects source embeddings at multiple spatial scales. Its objective combines latitude-weighted `ERA5` reconstruction with One-step Rollout Alignment (ORA), which backpropagates one-step forecast error through a frozen `FuXi` model so adapted states are both faithful and compatible with downstream forecasting. Evaluated on daily `GFS`, `HRES`, and `CMA` initializations across six variables and lead times up to 240 hours, the adapter reduces mean `FuXi` RMSE over the 6-to-240-hour rollout for 17 of 18 source-variable combinations, with a **median reduction of 10.2%** and a maximum of 46.3%, and the same adapter also improves `FengWu` forecasts on `GFS` inputs without retraining either model.

papers.title: Beyond Outcome Feedback: Trajectory-Quality-Guided Experience-based Learning
papers.abstract: Experience-based learning enables large language model (LLM) agents to improve over time by reusing knowledge from past executions. However, existing methods typically rely on final task outcomes as feedback for experience learning, overlooking the execution process and limiting their ability to evaluate and optimize experience based on trajectory quality. To address this limitation, we propose TQG-Exp, a trajectory-quality-guided experience-based learning framework that introduces process feedback. Specifically, we introduce Trajectory Quality Loss (TQL), which jointly considers task completion and process quality to provide a learning signal beyond final task outcomes. Based on this signal, we employ paired rollouts with and without retrieved experience to guide experience optimization. Representative trajectories are selected based on their outcomes and trajectory quality to extract task-level and task-type-level experiences. Meanwhile, differences in trajectory quality between the paired groups are used to estimate the contribution of retrieved experience and update its utility. The learned utility is then combined with semantic relevance to guide subsequent experience retrieval. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld with two backbone LLMs show that TQG-Exp outperforms existing experience-based methods, improving Avg.@3 over the strongest baseline by 4.50 and 8.55 percentage points on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3.5-Flash, respectively.
papers.summary: Experience-based learning lets large language model (LLM) agents improve by reusing knowledge from past executions, but existing methods judge experiences only by final task outcomes and ignore the quality of the execution process. `TQG-Exp` introduces a Trajectory Quality Loss (TQL) that scores both task completion and process quality, then runs paired rollouts with and without retrieved experience: representative trajectories chosen by outcome and quality are distilled into task-level and task-type-level experiences, while quality differences between the paired groups estimate how much each retrieved experience contributed and update a utility score that is combined with semantic relevance at retrieval time. On `ALFWorld`, `WebShop`, and `ScienceWorld` with two backbone models, `TQG-Exp` **improves Avg.@3 over the strongest baseline by 4.50 and 8.55 percentage points** on `DeepSeek-V4-Flash` and `Qwen3.5-Flash` respectively.

papers.title: MARL-BattleGrounds: A Novel JAX-native Benchmark for Heterogeneous and Competitive Multi-agent RL
papers.abstract: We present MARL-BattleGrounds (MARL-BGs), an easy-to-use JAX-native benchmark for heterogeneous and competitive multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), designed to be sample-efficient, computationally efficient, and researcher-centric. MARL benchmarks are typically simple and efficient, like SMAX, where winning reduces to unit micromanagement, or rich and costly, like Dota 2. MARL-BGs fills this missing middle. Its first mode, Team Deathmatch, is a simultaneous turn-based game between two teams of five heterogeneous agents. The five classes have distinct basic, passive, and ultimate abilities designed to synergize with allies and counter enemies. Our 52 hand-designed maps with diverse obstacles include a 12-map curriculum and ten held-out validation and test maps. MARL-BGs provides two canonical evaluation modes. First, eight endgame scenarios form a hard generalization challenge: each asks a team to win an unseen, nearly lost position against a strong reactive controller within 5-10 ticks. Second, a monthly round-robin tournament retrains each submission on equal compute, plays it against every member of the current "Big Nine" field, and publishes the Elo results on the official leaderboard. All entrants are publicly released as downloadable opponents. MARL-BGs records 11,192 metrics per game in 28 topics. We also include three strong scripted opponents, an analytical replay viewer, and off-the-shelf tools for self-play, cross-play, curriculum learning, and zero-shot coordination evaluation. We even provide an API for LLM-based agents and use it to evaluate Qwen3.5-9B against our strongest policy. In our BattleClient, humans can play alongside or against any mix of policies, enabling human-AI evaluation. We benchmark MARL-BGs with six additional deep MARL baselines, which we release. On one RTX 5090 with 1,024 parallel games, the simulator runs 50,000 5v5 game steps per second.
papers.summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) benchmarks tend to be either simple and cheap, like `SMAX` where winning reduces to unit micromanagement, or rich and expensive, like Dota 2. `MARL-BattleGrounds` targets the missing middle with a JAX-native Team Deathmatch mode in which two teams of five heterogeneous agents with distinct basic, passive, and ultimate abilities fight across 52 hand-designed maps, including a 12-map curriculum and ten held-out validation and test maps. Evaluation comes in two forms: eight endgame scenarios that ask a team to win a nearly lost position against a strong reactive controller within 5-10 ticks, and a monthly round-robin tournament that retrains each submission on equal compute, plays it against the current Big Nine field, and publishes Elo results on a public leaderboard with all entrants released as downloadable opponents. The package also includes three scripted opponents, six additional deep MARL baselines, a replay viewer, tools for self-play, cross-play, curriculum learning, and zero-shot coordination, an API for LLM-based agents used to evaluate `Qwen3.5-9B` against the strongest policy, a human-playable client, and a simulator that **runs 50,000 5v5 game steps per second on one RTX 5090** with 1,024 parallel games.

papers.title: Probable but Not Valid: A Psychometric Audit of Decision Models as Synthetic Survey Respondents
papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly used to create synthetic survey samples, also called silicon samples. Decision models are a new class of language models that return a probability for each point of a rating scale instead of text. We ask whether these models, or the newest generative LLMs, can stand in for human respondents on a psychometric survey. We test fourteen decision models from eleven providers and 47 generative LLMs on an open Lithuanian organisational-psychology survey (n=263, 68 items), with 100 real respondent profiles, the Psychometric Similarity Score (PSS) and statistical baselines. The best generative model, MiniMax M3, reaches PSS 0.813. This is level with a Gaussian copula fit only on other respondents (0.824) and below a copula fit in sample (0.927). A second sample of 100 real people scores below the best models, so at this size PSS cannot rank them against real respondents. In 5 of 10 product lines the newest generative release scores below an earlier release of the same line beyond resampling noise, and none gains beyond it. With the default rounded readout, 13 of 14 decision models score below the generative reference gpt-5.4-mini. Of the 47 generative models, 33 reproduce the pattern of item correlations better than any decision model. Averaged over respondents, the probability vectors are much closer to the human item marginals than rounded answers. They also rank respondents about as well as a profile regression fit on 163 real people. As forecasts of each person's own answers, however, every decision model is worse than the answer frequencies of other respondents, mainly because its average vector differs from them. The profile regression improves on these frequencies by only 1.0%, so the profile fields say little about how a person answers. Synthetic respondents built on such profiles should therefore aim at sample-level fidelity.
papers.summary: Language models are increasingly used to generate synthetic survey samples, and a new class of decision models returns a probability over each point of a rating scale rather than text, raising the question of whether either can stand in for human respondents. The authors test fourteen decision models from eleven providers and 47 generative LLMs on an open Lithuanian organisational-psychology survey with 263 respondents and 68 items, using 100 real respondent profiles, a Psychometric Similarity Score (PSS), and statistical baselines. The best generative model, `MiniMax M3`, reaches PSS 0.813, level with a Gaussian copula fit on other respondents (0.824) and below an in-sample copula (0.927), while in 5 of 10 product lines the newest release scores below an earlier one and 13 of 14 decision models fall below the generative reference `gpt-5.4-mini` under rounded readout. Decision-model probability vectors match human item marginals and rank respondents about as well as a profile regression, but **as forecasts of each individual person's answers every decision model is worse than simply using other respondents' answer frequencies**, and since profile fields explain little of individual answers the authors conclude synthetic respondents should aim at sample-level fidelity.

papers.title: Bridging Risk Approximation Gaps in Model Predictive Task Sampling via In-Context Modeling
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is essential for adaptive decision-making, e.g., robust Meta-RL and domain randomization (DR), and efficient post-training of large language models (LLMs), where tasks are commonly structured as Markov decision processes or prompts. A central bottleneck in all these settings is the cost of agent-environment interactions required for task selection and policy optimization. Model predictive task sampling (MPTS) has emerged as a promising approach to improve sample efficiency by querying informative tasks via a risk predictive model (RPM) trained on optimization history. However, existing RPMs suffer from two failure modes: (i) sparse optimization histories, which limit RPMs' generalization across the task space, and (ii) a one-step lag in risk approximation, which causes biased difficulty estimation as the policy evolves. This work formalizes these failure modes, derives lagged-risk decompositions that expose the resulting temporal bias, and recasts risk prediction as an in-context sequence modeling problem. The developed RPM integrates a one-step look-ahead mechanism with a temporal-weighted sliding window to mitigate data non-stationarity and scarcity, without requiring additional rollouts. Empirically, our approach yields more reliable difficulty estimates and consistent performance gains across robust Meta-RL, DR, and prompt curriculum RL post-training of LLMs.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning settings such as robust meta-RL, domain randomization (DR), and prompt-curriculum post-training of large language models all pay heavily for agent-environment interactions during task selection, and model predictive task sampling (MPTS) reduces that cost by querying informative tasks via a risk predictive model (RPM) trained on optimization history. Existing RPMs fail in two ways: sparse optimization histories limit generalization across the task space, and a one-step lag in risk approximation biases difficulty estimates as the policy evolves. The authors formalize both failure modes, derive lagged-risk decompositions that expose the temporal bias, and **recast risk prediction as in-context sequence modeling** with a one-step look-ahead and a temporal-weighted sliding window that handle non-stationarity and scarcity without extra rollouts. Empirically the approach gives more reliable difficulty estimates and consistent gains across robust meta-RL, DR, and prompt-curriculum RL post-training of LLMs.

papers.title: WorkBorne: Discovering Agentic Tasks from Real-World Artifact Transitions
papers.abstract: Developing terminal-based agents for long-horizon execution demands synthetic tasks that tightly couple complex instructions with authentic, interactive environments. However, current automated synthesis suffers from a fundamental asymmetry: instruction-oriented methods fabricate low-fidelity, synthetic environments, whereas resource-oriented methods treat real artifacts merely as static inputs, degrading task instructions into shallow, trivial operations. To address this limitation, we introduce WorkBorne, a synthesis framework that uses artifact transitions as the central primitive for modeling the full life-cycle of agentic tasks. In WorkBorne, each transition specifies who performs the task, which artifacts anchor the initial state and intended outcome, and the corresponding relationship between them. Specifically, WorkBorne first constructs coherent and diverse artifact corpora from iterative web retrieval, then discovers non-trivial transitions by identifying meaningful input-output artifact assemblies and the relations that connect them. Each discovered transition is finally instantiated into grounded agentic tasks. We construct 1,061 artifact corpora and 7,882 task environments, yielding 15,485 high-quality trajectories, with 53.6% exceeding 30 assistant turns. Experiments on Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B show that WorkBorne substantially improves over base models (i.e., improving Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 43.1% to 61.8% and ClawEval General score from 75.0 to 80.2) and achieves the strongest overall performance among other synthesis baselines (e.g., TMax (Ivison et al., 2026), RST (Li et al., 2026a), Terminal-Universe (Wu et al., 2026a)). Further analysis shows that transition is strongly associated with execution depth, while corpus breadth and transition depth provide complementary scaling gains.
papers.summary: Training terminal-based agents for long-horizon work needs synthetic tasks that pair complex instructions with authentic interactive environments, but instruction-oriented synthesis fabricates low-fidelity environments while resource-oriented synthesis treats real artifacts as static inputs and yields shallow tasks. `WorkBorne` makes artifact transitions the central primitive: each transition specifies who performs the task, which artifacts anchor the initial state and intended outcome, and the relationship between them, and the framework builds artifact corpora through iterative web retrieval, discovers non-trivial input-output transitions, and instantiates them as grounded tasks. This produces 1,061 corpora, 7,882 task environments, and 15,485 trajectories, over half exceeding 30 assistant turns. Training `Qwen3.5-27B` and `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B` on the data lifts the `Terminal-Bench 2.1` score **from 43.1% to 61.8%** and `ClawEval` General from 75.0 to 80.2, outperforming synthesis baselines such as `TMax`, `RST`, and `Terminal-Universe`, with analysis tying transitions to execution depth and showing complementary scaling from corpus breadth and transition depth.

papers.title: SkillForgeBench: Evaluating Agent Reliability Grounded in Agent Skill Specifications
papers.abstract: Evaluating an agent's ability to strictly satisfy diverse and procedurally complex requirements is essential to determining its practical reliability. Conducting such an evaluation demands agentic tasks that reconcile broad domain coverage with deep procedural complexity. Existing paradigms face a fundamental trade-off: expert-curated benchmarks achieve procedural depth but suffer from domain diversity bottlenecks, whereas crowdsourced benchmarks span diverse scenarios but lack execution rigor. To resolve this tension, we present SkillForgeBench, which leverages agent skills as unifying execution blueprints across three co-designed stages: (1) Resource Preparation uses domain-balanced skills to guide artifact retrieval, establishing broad workflow coverage; (2) Skill-driven Task Synthesis employs skills as procedural anchors to partition artifact roles, synthesize naturalistic task instructions, and package sandboxed scenarios for deep procedural execution; and (3) Holistic Evaluation Design translates skill-embedded requirements into fine-grained completion and process rubrics to enable strict requirement-level scoring. Comprising 842 sandboxed tasks across five major professional domains, SkillForgeBench reveals a steep capability hierarchy among eight mainstream agents, led by Opus 4.8 ($40.9\%$ strict completion). Requiring all constrains satisfaction uncovers severe capability bottlenecks across all model tiers that remain masked under individual rubric pass rates ($70.0\%$ to $85.7\%$ vs. $12.6\%$ to $40.9\%$). Crucially, under the external guidance from skills, top-tier agents obtain larger gains than low-tier agents (i.e., $\Delta 19.2\%$ for Opus 4.8 vs. $\Delta 5.8\%$ for Haiku 4.5). Finally, agents satisfy process rubrics far less frequently than completion rubrics (under $3\%$ for Haiku 4.5), proving that completion-only checks overestimate real-world agent reliability.
papers.summary: Judging whether an agent can strictly satisfy diverse, procedurally complex requirements is central to its practical reliability, yet expert-curated benchmarks offer procedural depth with narrow domain coverage while crowdsourced ones cover many scenarios without execution rigor. `SkillForgeBench` uses agent skills as execution blueprints in three stages: domain-balanced skills guide artifact retrieval, skills anchor the synthesis of naturalistic task instructions and sandboxed scenarios, and skill-embedded requirements become fine-grained completion and process rubrics for requirement-level scoring. Across 842 sandboxed tasks in five professional domains, eight mainstream agents show a steep hierarchy led by `Opus 4.8` at 40.9% strict completion, and **requiring all constraints to be satisfied collapses pass rates from 70.0-85.7% on individual rubrics to 12.6-40.9%**. Skill guidance helps top-tier agents more than weaker ones, with gains of 19.2% for `Opus 4.8` versus 5.8% for `Haiku 4.5`, and agents satisfy process rubrics far less often than completion rubrics, under 3% for `Haiku 4.5`, indicating that completion-only checks overestimate reliability.

papers.title: Predicting how model propensities generalize out of distribution
papers.abstract:
How do language models generalize from their training data? This is a central challenge for alignment: models reliably learn their training distribution given enough samples, but we want models that behave well when deployed in new contexts. We study out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization of propensities. Our central experiment uses a range of elicitation techniques -- system prompting, few-shot learning, SFT on reference answers, and GRPO -- to increase a target propensity in a model, then measures how it spills over onto others across the resulting cross-elicitation matrices. We find that spillover is highly correlated between models when the same elicitation technique is used, but our SFT and GRPO runs induce different spillover profiles.
  Elicitation of benign traits can sometimes generalize towards undesired traits, for example a model trained to claim that it is sentient often becomes more power-seeking. We further find that spillover partially resembles trait correlations found in humans and identify three clusters of traits that account for about half of the variance using exploratory factor analysis (EFA). Across many elicitation runs, we observe that models change in characteristic ways that don't depend on the targeted trait, a phenomenon we refer to as drift. Drift moves Qwen3.5-9B towards its base model.
  When investigating if LLMs are able to predict spillover, we find that Claude Opus 5.5 predicts spillover slightly better than the models themselves, but worse than data-driven approaches using alternative elicitation methods or models. Overall, no single dominant predictor emerges, and generalization remains hard to predict. Code and data are available at https://github.com/nielsrolf/propensity-spillover.
papers.summary: How language models generalize from their training data is central to alignment, since models learn their training distribution but must behave well in new contexts. The authors study out-of-distribution generalization of propensities by using system prompting, few-shot learning, SFT on reference answers, and GRPO to raise a target propensity and then measuring how it spills over onto other traits in cross-elicitation matrices. Spillover is highly correlated between models when the same elicitation technique is used, but SFT and GRPO produce different profiles, and **elicitation of benign traits can generalize to undesired ones, with a model trained to claim it is sentient often becoming more power-seeking**; spillover partly mirrors human trait correlations, three clusters found by exploratory factor analysis (EFA) explain about half the variance, and a trait-independent drift moves `Qwen3.5-9B` toward its base model. `Claude Opus 5.5` predicts spillover slightly better than the models themselves but worse than data-driven approaches, and no single dominant predictor emerges, so generalization remains hard to predict; code and data are released.

papers.title: VC-OPD: Visual Counterfactual On-Policy Distillation for Grounded Vision-Language Reasoning
papers.abstract: GRPO-style reinforcement learning has advanced vision-language reasoning, but its sequence-level rewards provide limited credit assignment for individual reasoning tokens. On-policy distillation (OPD) addresses this issue by providing dense supervision on student-generated trajectories, yet standard OPD assigns similar importance to all teacher-preferred tokens, including template phrases and visually irrelevant continuations. We introduce Visual Counterfactual On-Policy Distillation (VC-OPD), a grounding-aware distillation method that prioritizes tokens whose correctness depends on image-specific evidence. After a teacher-supervised warm start that stabilizes response formats and reduces noisy rollouts, VC-OPD performs on-policy distillation with two teacher evaluations for each student trajectory: one under the original image and one under a counterfactual image with corrupted instance-specific evidence. The original-image teacher distribution determines the distillation target, while the original--counterfactual teacher gap estimates token-level visual dependence and softly reweights the loss. To avoid unstable response-level update scales, VC-OPD further applies mass-preserving normalization to the token weights. This design preserves the dense supervision of OPD while shifting learning capacity toward visually grounded reasoning tokens. Experiments on multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that VC-OPD improves visual reasoning performance and produces more effective token-level distillation.
papers.summary: GRPO-style reinforcement learning has improved vision-language reasoning, but its sequence-level rewards give weak credit assignment to individual tokens, and on-policy distillation (OPD), which supplies dense supervision on student-generated trajectories, treats every teacher-preferred token alike, including template phrases and visually irrelevant continuations. Visual Counterfactual On-Policy Distillation (`VC-OPD`) is a grounding-aware variant that, after a teacher-supervised warm start to stabilize response formats, evaluates each student trajectory with the teacher twice, once under the original image and once under a counterfactual image with corrupted instance-specific evidence. The original-image teacher distribution serves as the distillation target while the gap between the two teacher evaluations estimates each token's visual dependence and **softly reweights the loss toward visually grounded reasoning tokens**, with mass-preserving normalization of the weights to avoid unstable response-level update scales. Experiments on multimodal reasoning benchmarks show improved visual reasoning performance and more effective token-level distillation.

papers.title: Probabilistic Multi-Source Data Selection via Learnable Categorical Priors: Variance Reduction and Guaranteed Derandomization
papers.abstract: Bilevel data selection is a fundamental task with numerous applications in machine learning and statistics. A common strategy for tackling this problem is to relax the original bilevel combinatorial optimization into a continuous one. However, existing methods, including 0-1 relaxation and probabilistic relaxation, still suffer from several limitations, such as unstable gradient estimation and infeasible rounding. To address these issues, this paper proposes a new probabilistic relaxation for the multi-source bilevel data selection problem. Our key idea is to introduce multiple learnable categorical priors to parameterize a probability distribution supported only on feasible data subsets, thus naturally yielding a lossless rounding scheme. We further show that our proposed relaxation admits an effective two-point gradient estimator, which can simultaneously avoid the inverse-Hessian computation required by existing 0-1 relaxation and the unbounded score term appearing in prior probabilistic relaxation. Furthermore, we develop a reducible representation of this estimator, which substantially reduces the number of lower-level retrainings required for gradient computation. Built upon this reducible two-point estimator, we then design a novel stochastic gradient algorithm, termed ReSGD, for multi-source bilevel data selection problem, and establish a rigorous approximation guarantee for the subset returned by ReSGD under weak submodularity. Finally, extensive experiments are conducted to validate the effectiveness of our proposed ReSGD.
papers.summary: Bilevel data selection is usually made tractable by relaxing the combinatorial problem into a continuous one, but existing 0-1 and probabilistic relaxations suffer from unstable gradient estimation and infeasible rounding. The authors propose a new probabilistic relaxation for multi-source bilevel data selection that uses multiple learnable categorical priors to define a distribution supported only on feasible subsets, which **makes rounding lossless by construction**, and show it admits a two-point gradient estimator that avoids both the inverse-Hessian computation of 0-1 relaxation and the unbounded score term of prior probabilistic relaxations. A reducible representation of that estimator cuts the number of lower-level retrainings needed per gradient, and the resulting stochastic algorithm `ReSGD` comes with an approximation guarantee for the returned subset under weak submodularity. Experiments validate the effectiveness of `ReSGD`.

papers.title: Counterfactual Rollouts for Offline Contrastive Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Contrastive reinforcement learning (CRL) learns goal-conditioned values by associating state--action pairs with the states subsequently reached, assuming that no unobserved variable jointly affects the recorded action and its outcome. When offline demonstrations come from a demonstrator with information hidden from the learner, this assumption fails and the critic absorbs spurious action--outcome associations. We formalize this setting with confounded Markov decision processes and introduce counterfactual transitions that separate what the data identify from what they do not; minimizing over all compatible transitions yields a worst-case occupancy that lower-bounds the true one. Causal Contrastive Reinforcement Learning (CauCRL) learns a pessimistic counterfactual transition from positive and negative offline demonstrations and trains the critic on counterfactual rollouts, substantially improving success rates over standard CRL on confounded goal-reaching tasks.
papers.summary: Contrastive reinforcement learning (CRL) learns goal-conditioned values by associating state-action pairs with the states later reached, which assumes no unobserved variable jointly influences the recorded action and its outcome; when offline demonstrations come from a demonstrator with information hidden from the learner, that assumption fails and the critic absorbs spurious action-outcome associations. The authors formalize the setting with confounded Markov decision processes and introduce counterfactual transitions that separate what the data identify from what they do not, showing that minimizing over all compatible transitions yields a worst-case occupancy that lower-bounds the true one. Causal Contrastive Reinforcement Learning (`CauCRL`) learns a pessimistic counterfactual transition from positive and negative offline demonstrations and trains the critic on counterfactual rollouts, **substantially improving success rates over standard CRL** on confounded goal-reaching tasks.

papers.title: MCPDisCo: Seesaw-Mitigated Tuning for MCP-Native Agents
papers.abstract: The Model Context Protocol provides a shared interaction substrate for the agentic web, allowing heterogeneous services to expose capabilities through a standardized interface. Learning to use this ecosystem entails a hierarchy of capabilities: tool-format skills, server-level transfer, and cross-server composition. We present MCPDisCo, an ecosystem-scale reinforcement learning framework for MCP-native agents. Using a Thought-Markov Decision Process (Thought-MDP), the framework explicitly represents internal reasoning alongside routing, execution, and termination and trains on real-server, long-horizon interactions spanning 70 MCP servers and 527 tools across six domains. We study the reasoning--tool seesaw, a joint-learning failure mode in which improvement in one objective can accompany deterioration in the other. To mitigate potential interference, MCPDisCo combines token-masked reward attribution with bidirectional gradient surgery: the former separates direct supervision for reasoning and action spans, while the latter removes conflicting components from both objective gradients in shared parameters. MCPDisCo achieves higher success with fewer chain-of-thought tokens. On the out-of-distribution MCP-Atlas and the GAIA benchmark, MCPDisCo maintains monotone gains, confirming that the learned behavior generalizes beyond the training server distribution and broader agentic tasks. Model weight and implementation are available.
papers.summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) gives heterogeneous services a standardized interface on the agentic web, and learning to use it spans tool-format skills, server-level transfer, and cross-server composition. `MCPDisCo` is an ecosystem-scale reinforcement learning framework for MCP-native agents that models internal reasoning alongside routing, execution, and termination as a Thought-Markov Decision Process (Thought-MDP) and trains on real-server, long-horizon interactions across 70 MCP servers and 527 tools in six domains. The authors study the reasoning-tool seesaw, a joint-learning failure where improving one objective degrades the other, and counter it with token-masked reward attribution that separately supervises reasoning and action spans plus bidirectional gradient surgery that removes conflicting components from both objectives in shared parameters. The result is **higher success with fewer chain-of-thought tokens**, and gains hold monotonically on the out-of-distribution `MCP-Atlas` and `GAIA` benchmarks, with weights and code released.

papers.title: What Survives When Activation Steering Is Used as Memory
papers.abstract: Activation steering has recently been used as a memory for skills: past experiences of an agent are stored as steering vectors and retrieved later. Facts and preferences about the user are assumed to need text instead. We test that assumption with a training-free activation memory beside a frozen LLM. The change an experience causes in late-layer states is stored as a shift, filed under a whitened key for the conversation's gist, and added back in a later session only when the gist matches. We argue that such a shift is a fixed average of an effect that attention, in context, recomputes for every question, so only question-independent content can survive. In a pre-registered study on Qwen3.5-2B and 9B, with judges from four model families, the memory is selective (about 98% of unrelated replies are unchanged), but facts are stored as the word to say, in the last layers only, and are almost never used (at most 15% clean use, against 96-98% in context). Leanings transfer only in a narrow strength window. Most strikingly, the reference subtracted when writing a preference decides whether its concept or its direction survives: unless the opposite is subtracted, a stored dislike is recalled as a like.
papers.summary: Activation steering has been used as a memory for agent skills, storing past experiences as steering vectors, while facts and preferences about the user are assumed to require text. The authors test that assumption with a training-free activation memory beside a frozen LLM: the shift an experience causes in late-layer states is stored under a whitened key for the conversation gist and added back in a later session only when the gist matches, and they argue such a shift is a fixed average of an effect that attention normally recomputes per question, so only question-independent content can survive. In a pre-registered study on `Qwen3.5-2B` and `Qwen3.5-9B` with judges from four model families, the memory is selective, leaving about 98% of unrelated replies unchanged, but facts are stored as the word to say in the last layers only and are almost never used, **at most 15% clean use versus 96-98% when the fact is in context**. Leanings transfer only within a narrow strength window, and the reference subtracted when writing a preference decides whether its concept or its direction survives: unless the opposite is subtracted, a stored dislike is recalled as a like.

papers.title: AlphaRLM: Aligning Language Models for Literature-Grounded Symbolic Factor Discovery
papers.abstract: Formulaic alpha mining seeks to discover executable expressions that capture predictive market signals in a vast, noisy search space. Recent LLM-based approaches use prompting, iterative search, or seed-factor evolution, leaving direct factor construction through policy learning less explored. To address this, we introduce AlphaRLM, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains LLMs to construct executable symbolic factors from financial literature without input factor expressions. AlphaRLM incorporates Literature-Guided Operator Assembly (LEGO), which conditions factor construction on literature-derived ideas and executable operators, providing semantic priors for exploration. It further aligns the generation policy with market feedback through executable-validity and grouped-return-separation rewards that capture non-monotonic structures across factor quantiles. Extensive experiments on CSI 300, CSI 1000, and S&P 500 show that AlphaRLM outperforms strong factor-mining and LLM-based baselines in annualized excess return. Notably, the 8B model achieves strong cross-market performance, highlighting the promise of literature-conditioned, market-aligned factor generation.
papers.summary: Formulaic alpha mining searches a vast, noisy space for executable expressions that capture predictive market signals, and prior large language model (LLM) approaches rely on prompting, iterative search, or evolving seed factors rather than learning a construction policy directly. `AlphaRLM` trains an LLM with reinforcement learning to build symbolic factors from financial literature without any input factor expressions, using Literature-Guided Operator Assembly (LEGO) to condition generation on literature-derived ideas and executable operators, plus rewards for executable validity and grouped-return separation across factor quantiles. On `CSI 300`, `CSI 1000`, and `S&P 500`, it reports higher annualized excess return than factor-mining and LLM-based baselines, and **an 8B model achieves strong cross-market performance**.

papers.title: Humans vs. Machines: A Comparison With AI Agents in Software Reverse Engineering
papers.abstract: Can an autonomous AI agent reverse engineer a binary as well as a skilled human analyst? Do they adopt the same strategy, and can agents scale to real-world programs? We compare human and LLM-based software reverse engineering (SRE): nine models tackle two compact static-analysis challenges previously solved by human analysts, scored with a common understanding rubric, and we record their complete interactions with IDA Pro. This lets us compare not only what humans and agents recover, but also how they investigate a binary. The best agents (GPT-5.5 Pro, Claude Opus 4.8, and Kimi K3) achieve statistically human-competitive understanding on both tasks, while weaker models remain far behind. Ablations show that the gap depends on code representation and workflow demands, not on model capability alone: open-weight models improve substantially with richer code representations, whereas frontier models show no significant change. Similar success rates hide different workflows. Humans repeatedly revisit functions and follow local program structure; strong agents jump across the binary, retrieve information broadly, and rarely return to inspected code, a behavior we call greedy fetching. This strategy is not fixed: given semantically richer code, agents fetch less without losing understanding. Because greedy fetching aggregates large amounts of code in the agent's context, we measure context-window saturation across 4,000 real-world binaries: large windows accommodate many programs, but larger applications and lower-level representations quickly exhaust them. Autonomous reverse engineering is becoming competitive, with a large speed advantage, but scaling it will require better navigation, selective retrieval, and persistent analysis state, not merely larger context windows.
papers.summary: The question is whether autonomous LLM agents can reverse engineer a binary as well as a skilled human analyst, and whether they investigate it the same way. Nine models tackle two compact static-analysis challenges previously solved by human analysts, scored with a shared understanding rubric, with every interaction with `IDA Pro` recorded. **The best agents, `GPT-5.5 Pro`, `Claude Opus 4.8`, and `Kimi K3`, reach statistically human-competitive understanding on both tasks**, and ablations show open-weight models gain substantially from richer code representations while frontier models do not. Humans revisit functions and follow local program structure, whereas strong agents jump across the binary, retrieve broadly, and rarely return to inspected code, a behavior called greedy fetching, and a context-saturation study over 4,000 real-world binaries shows that larger applications and lower-level representations quickly exhaust even large context windows.

papers.title: SkillHorizon: Constructing Long-Horizon Agent Tasks through Skill Composition
papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents must complete workflows in which later activities depend on earlier outputs and changes to shared state. A key challenge for evaluation is to expand task requirements and their dependencies while keeping tasks executable and outcomes verifiable. We introduce SkillHorizon, a benchmark that constructs long-horizon tasks through skill composition in seven business environments. Its generators use domain-specific rules to turn reusable skill procedures into concrete business activities. These activities are connected through input-output dependencies, shared resources, and state updates, allowing workload and coordination demands to grow together. Successful reference executions validate task feasibility and measure interaction workload, while programmatic evaluators assess local completion and whole-task success. We evaluate five language models on 1,050 tasks with reference interaction workloads ranging from 64K to 1M tokens. Across these scales, mean local-goal completion falls from 90.4% to 46.8%, as completed work fails to keep pace with growing requirements. At larger workloads, agents more often submit unsuccessful final answers with substantial work unfinished and tool-call allowance remaining. Trace analysis also identifies cases where scripts execute successfully but their outputs fail downstream business checks. SkillHorizon provides a configurable testbed for studying sustained progress, dependency coordination, and complete task delivery in growing workflows. Our code is available at https://github.com/KnowComp/SkillHorizon.
papers.summary: Evaluating long-horizon agents requires tasks whose requirements and dependencies can grow while the tasks stay executable and their outcomes verifiable. `SkillHorizon` builds such tasks by composing reusable skill procedures into concrete business activities across seven business environments, linking them through input-output dependencies, shared resources, and state updates, with successful reference executions validating feasibility and programmatic evaluators scoring both local completion and whole-task success. Across 1,050 tasks with reference workloads from 64K to 1M tokens, **mean local-goal completion for five language models falls from 90.4% to 46.8%** as requirements grow, and at larger workloads agents more often submit final answers with substantial work unfinished and tool-call allowance remaining. Trace analysis also surfaces scripts that execute successfully but produce outputs that fail downstream business checks.

papers.title: FleetPilot: Fine-Grained Steering Empowers Real-World LLM Personalization
papers.abstract: With the rapid evolution of large language models (LLMs), there is an increasing demand for effective personalization techniques that can adapt model behavior to individual user preferences. Personalized LLMs must infer a user's query-dependent preferences from limited, heterogeneous, and evolving interaction histories. Existing approaches rely primarily on in-context personalization, parametric adaptation, or personalized reward modeling, but respectively incur recurring costs in context management, model optimization and deployment, or multi-candidate generation and scoring. These limitations become particularly restrictive when user observations are sparse and the preference evidence relevant to each query varies across contexts and over time. To address these challenges, we propose \modelname, a fine-grained and instance-tailored steering framework that dynamically generates sample-level interference vectors from user data and injects them into the model's forward pass for personalized adaptation. Our approach introduces: match contrast that produces user-relevant signals, fine-grained steering component that captures nuanced signals by hooking activations from attention and MLP layers, and query-conditioned aggregation module that synthesizes these signals into contextually relevant enhancements. Extensive experiments across diverse scenarios, including short-to-long text generation, and web function calling, validate the effectiveness and compatibility of \modelname. Results show that our method consistently brings significant performance gains, and show extreme superiority in fast-shifting and data-sparse environments. Additionally, \modelname rids us of training cycles and incurs light overhead of storage or inference latency. These make \modelname a strong and real-world deployable method. Implementation is available \footnote{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FleetPilot}.
papers.summary: Personalized large language models (LLMs) must infer query-dependent user preferences from sparse, heterogeneous, and evolving interaction histories, and existing in-context, parametric, and reward-model approaches each carry recurring costs in context management, model training and deployment, or multi-candidate generation and scoring. `FleetPilot` instead generates sample-level steering vectors from user data and injects them into the model's forward pass, combining a match-contrast step that extracts user-relevant signals, a fine-grained component that hooks activations from attention and MLP layers, and a query-conditioned aggregation module that synthesizes them for the current query. Across short-to-long text generation and web function calling, the method reports consistent gains, **with its largest advantages in fast-shifting and data-sparse settings**, and it requires no training cycles while adding only light storage and inference-latency overhead.

papers.title: Single-Sample Decoding of a Two-Layer Sound-Word Canvas Model for Thai Klon Pad
papers.abstract: We present a generator of Thai klon pad verse, one stanza from a short topic, and evaluate it against human verse on held-out topics. The generator is a masked language model initialised from WangchanBERTa over a fixed canvas with two layers: a sound layer of pronounced syllables, where rhyme, tone and syllable count are enforced as hard masks, and a word layer of whole words, so that no word is cut into written pieces. Decoding commits one cell at a time and samples at temperature 0.4; one sample is drawn per topic, with no selection, reranking or repair. On 78 held-out topics never used in development, judged by three independent runs of a frozen LLM judge in the same pools as the human stanzas from which the topics were written, 70.5% of the generated stanzas pass form, lexical cleanness of all four lines and topic alignment together, against 76.9% for the human stanzas (difference -6.4 points, 95% CI [-19.2, +6.4]). Cleanness is level with human (85.9% vs. 87.2%), and the stanzas pass form and cleanness together slightly more often than the human ones (+3.8 points, [-6.4, +14.1]); the difference lies in alignment (84.6% vs. 91.0%), on topics that were written from the human stanzas. The low temperature matters: at higher temperatures the same model passes clearly fewer of the same topics, because lexical errors lie in the model's lower-probability choices; sharpening the sampling distribution removes most of them, at a cost in vocabulary (7.5% rare words against 16.5% in the human stanzas) and diversity. The pre-registered target, all-three within 5 points of human, is missed by 1.4 points. KlonSuphap-LM, the only public klon pad generator we know of, passes none of the 78 held-out topics when judged in separate pools together with the method's and the human stanzas (form 19.2%, cleanness 3.8%).
papers.summary: Generating Thai klon pad verse requires meeting strict rhyme, tone, and syllable-count rules while staying on a given topic. The generator is a masked language model initialized from `WangchanBERTa` over a fixed two-layer canvas, a sound layer of pronounced syllables where those rules are enforced as hard masks and a word layer of whole words so no word is split, decoded one cell at a time at temperature 0.4 with a single sample per topic and no reranking or repair. On 78 held-out topics judged by three runs of a frozen LLM judge, **70.5% of generated stanzas pass form, lexical cleanness, and topic alignment together versus 76.9% for human stanzas**, with the gap lying in topic alignment, the pre-registered target of within 5 points missed by 1.4 points, and the only prior public generator `KlonSuphap-LM` passing none of the topics. The low temperature matters because lexical errors sit in low-probability choices, so sharpening the sampling distribution removes most of them at a cost in rare-word usage and diversity.

papers.title: Fitting Every Hint Is Not Enough: Premature Floods in Recurrent Algorithmic Reasoners
papers.abstract: Recurrent algorithmic reasoners are trained with per-step hints on small graphs and run for many more steps on large ones. On breadth-first search in SALSA-CLRS, we find that a reasoner can reproduce every training hint and still fail on deep graphs: after some exact steps, it declares nodes reached before the search gets there. We call this a premature flood and trace two routes to it. In our GRU processor with a degree input, the flood is carried in the hidden state and set off when that input is in the tail of the training distribution. Setting the input higher at inference brings the flood sooner, and none of the six flooding models counts steps. Without the input, summing the neighbors' states instead of averaging them also breaks the processor. In the benchmark's own GIN and PGN, trained with its code, some seeds instead flood from a fixed step, on sparse and dense graphs alike. Clamping the degree input or adding 200 dense training graphs removes every failure of the GRU processor. Detaching the state between steps avoids the flood in that processor (0 of 23 seeds, against 6 under full backpropagation) but not with sums or a residual update, and two published remedies leave floods. None of the benchmark's test sets is both deep and dense, but its deepest one shows the second route: on its Delaunay graphs at 1,600 nodes, one GIN seed floods from step 18. We therefore recommend auditing the range of every input and aggregate, which catches the first route, and testing on deep graphs, which catches both.
papers.summary: Recurrent algorithmic reasoners are trained with per-step hints on small graphs and then run for many more steps on larger ones. On breadth-first search in `SALSA-CLRS`, a reasoner can reproduce every training hint yet still fail on deep graphs by declaring nodes reached before the search arrives, a failure the authors call a premature flood. Two routes are traced: in a `GRU` processor with a degree input, the flood is carried in the hidden state and triggered when that input falls in the tail of the training distribution, while the benchmark's own `GIN` and `PGN` processors sometimes flood from a fixed step on sparse and dense graphs alike. **Clamping the degree input or adding 200 dense training graphs removes every failure of the `GRU` processor**, detaching the state between steps also avoids the flood there, and the recommended practice is to audit the range of every input and aggregate and to test on deep graphs, which catches both routes.

papers.title: Too Late to Prune: Generative AI, the Screen, and Team Creative Decisions
papers.abstract: Generative AI makes options cheap and shifts the bottleneck of creative work from generating options to screening them. We argue that AI's value depends on whether its options arrive before or after the team's screen. In our model, early options compete for a place in the portfolio; late options arrive after that competition and are kept unscreened. In a preregistered experiment, we randomly assigned 148 three-person teams to five schedules of access to the same language model during a product-design task with timed search and selection stages. Moving the same 15 minutes of access from search to selection lowered expert-rated creativity by 0.62 standard deviations, although teams used the model at similar rates. Platform logs locate the difference at the screen. Early access enlarged the pool of ideas fivefold, and teams pruned it. Late-access teams reached the screen with the same small pool as teams without AI and then searched again, devoting 29% of their selection-stage queries to generating new options, compared with 11% for teams with access throughout. Late access added breadth, not quality: these teams submitted 73% more proposals than did teams without AI. Language-model judges detected the benefit of access but not the cost of late timing.
papers.summary: Generative AI makes options cheap, shifting the bottleneck of creative work from generating ideas to screening them, so the value of AI may hinge on whether its options arrive before or after a team's screen. A preregistered experiment randomly assigned 148 three-person teams to five schedules of access to the same language model during a product-design task with timed search and selection stages. **Moving the same 15 minutes of access from the search stage to the selection stage lowered expert-rated creativity by 0.62 standard deviations**, even though teams used the model at similar rates. Early access enlarged the idea pool fivefold and teams pruned it, whereas late-access teams reached the screen with a small pool, spent 29% of selection-stage queries generating new options, and submitted 73% more proposals without higher quality, while language-model judges detected the benefit of access but not the cost of late timing.

papers.title: Mixing Regularization for Average-Reward $Q$-Learning and $Q$-Planning
papers.abstract: The average-reward setting for reinforcement learning is challenging because its Bellman operator is known to contract in span only when the underlying Markov chain is mixing.
