Whereas existing work typically assumes a contraction property, e.g., through environment mixing, we consider the setting where we are given a reward-agnostic $m$-step mixing policy, and we control the contraction and exploration properties of the learned policy by regularizing toward the mixing policy. We provide finite-time analysis of $Q$-learning algorithms that can be instantiated with multiple choices of regularization, with guarantees measured with respect to the regularized fixed point. Our framework exposes novel regularizer-dependent objects that control contraction, exploration, and operator bias. In the one-step setting, our rates match the best known rates for $Q$-iteration and synchronous $Q$-learning, and for $m$-step mixing we derive new rates. We also study $Q$-planning variants, and show that planning acts as time-localized learning, where the planning horizon $H$ trades off the bias from the boundary value against the sample complexity. Finally, we present numerical studies validating the analysis: (i) knowledge of a strong mixing policy improves convergence and exploration, and its advantage increases with bottleneck severity and, (ii) our theory predicts the convergence and bias rankings of regularizers from the $\alpha$-divergence family.
papers.summary: Average-reward reinforcement learning is difficult because its Bellman operator contracts in span only when the underlying Markov chain is mixing, and prior work typically assumes that contraction outright. The setting here instead assumes access to a reward-agnostic m-step mixing policy and regularizes the learned policy toward it, which controls contraction and exploration, and provides finite-time analysis of Q-learning variants under several regularizers with guarantees measured against the regularized fixed point. **In the one-step setting the rates match the best known rates for Q-iteration and synchronous Q-learning**, new rates are derived for m-step mixing, and Q-planning variants are shown to act as time-localized learning in which the horizon H trades bias from the boundary value against sample complexity. Numerical studies confirm that a strong mixing policy speeds convergence and exploration, with a larger advantage under severe bottlenecks, and that the theory predicts the convergence and bias rankings of alpha-divergence regularizers.

papers.title: Certify the Decision, Not Every Score: Exact Top-k Selection from Few Evaluations
papers.abstract: Choosing a few robust algorithms or schedules can require evaluating every candidate under many adverse scenarios, even though an agent only needs to identify the winners. A predictor may suggest those winners, but cannot rule out a surprise in an unevaluated scenario. We introduce Certified Adaptive Selection (CAS), which returns the exact top-$k$ set as soon as remaining uncertainty cannot change it. CAS keeps guaranteed lower and upper bounds on Expected Shortfall (ES), the average loss in the worst scenarios. Its stopping test compares the worst admissible selected candidate with the best admissible excluded one; for information-disjoint Cartesian intervals this one-cut test is necessary and sufficient. Prediction has a separate role: selecting the next outcome to evaluate, never authorizing the decision. For empirical ES with exact unit-cost queries, we compute in polynomial time the fewest evaluations that could have proved the realized decision in hindsight. Our prediction-guided agent CAS-PG is exact for every predictor, including adversarial ones. On two public algorithm-selection matrices, CAS-PG certifies the exact top three after 630 of 3150 and 981 of 2200 replayed queries, or $1.14$ and $1.18$ times that hindsight minimum. Without historical outcomes, its transcript-only variant requires $1.28$ and $1.37$ times the minimum, outperforming the tested non-predictive certified policies. Separately, a prediction-free CAS policy avoids $93.0\%$ of exact recourse solves in synthetic energy scheduling. One certificate thus supports several acquisition policies and separately proved risk/cost extensions: prediction changes the work, not the justified choice.
papers.summary: Choosing a few robust algorithms or schedules can require evaluating every candidate under many adverse scenarios, even though only the identity of the winners matters. Certified Adaptive Selection (CAS) keeps guaranteed lower and upper bounds on each candidate's Expected Shortfall (ES), the average loss in the worst scenarios, and returns the exact top-k set as soon as remaining uncertainty cannot change it, via a stopping test that compares the worst admissible selected candidate with the best admissible excluded one. A predictor only chooses which outcome to evaluate next and never authorizes the decision, so the prediction-guided agent `CAS-PG` is exact for every predictor, including adversarial ones. **On two public algorithm-selection matrices, `CAS-PG` certifies the exact top three after 630 of 3150 and 981 of 2200 replayed queries, within 1.14 and 1.18 times the hindsight minimum**, and a prediction-free variant avoids 93.0% of exact recourse solves in synthetic energy scheduling.

papers.title: Recurrent In-Context Learning for Tabular Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models adapt to new datasets through in-context learning (ICL), and, like most transformers, they tie computational depth to the number of independently parameterized layers. We ask whether the ICL stage of such a model needs a distinct set of parameters for every layer, or only depth. We introduce Tab-Loop, which replaces the 12 untied ICL blocks of TabICLv2 with 4 tied blocks applied $k$ times and changes nothing else: the encoders, decoder, synthetic prior and training recipe are shared with an untied baseline trained for the same compute. At matched pretraining compute (18.2 EFLOP) and matched inference compute (12 block applications), Tab-Loop matches the baseline with 62\% fewer parameters (10.4M vs.\ 27.6M): held-out log loss is 0.4583 vs.\ 0.4588, mean accuracy on 200 TALENT datasets is 84.10\% vs.\ 83.92\%, and Elo on 38 TabArena datasets is 1409 vs.\ 1396. A 4-block untied control with Tab-Loop's parameter count, which sees 32\% more training tables for the same compute, trails both (83.46\%; Elo 1343). Because weights are shared, depth becomes a choice made at inference. Accuracy rises with the number of loops through the trained range and holds beyond it, and continued training with deeper loops extends the useful range, reaching the baseline's stage-2 scores at 4--5$\times$ its inference compute. At this scale, the ICL stage of a tabular foundation model needs depth more than it needs distinct parameters.
papers.summary: Tabular foundation models adapt to new datasets through in-context learning (ICL), and like most transformers they tie computational depth to the number of independently parameterized layers. `Tab-Loop` asks whether the ICL stage needs distinct parameters per layer or only depth by replacing the 12 untied ICL blocks of `TabICLv2` with 4 weight-tied blocks applied k times, leaving the encoders, decoder, synthetic prior, and training recipe unchanged. At matched pretraining compute and matched inference compute, **it matches the untied baseline with 62% fewer parameters (10.4M vs 27.6M)** on held-out log loss, mean accuracy over 200 `TALENT` datasets, and Elo on 38 `TabArena` datasets, while a 4-block untied control with the same parameter count trails both. Because weights are shared, depth becomes an inference-time choice: accuracy rises with the number of loops through the trained range and holds beyond it, and continued training with deeper loops reaches the baseline's later-stage scores at 4 to 5 times its inference compute.

papers.title: Can You Trust Your Preference Models? Stackelberg Games for Alignment
papers.abstract: Language models are frequently aligned to human preferences via imperfect evaluators whose errors can be exploited during optimization. We train policies to search for comparisons on which an evaluator may reverse the underlying preference, providing candidates for additional supervision. Since human preferences are unavailable during policy training, we use disagreement among an ensemble of preference models as a proxy for prediction error. We formulate this search as a zero-sum Stackelberg game between two opposing policies, a Leader which tries to minimize disagreement, and a Follower which maximizes it. For a general class of finite contextual Stackelberg games, we establish equilibrium existence and, under regularization, uniqueness and a closed-form characterization. We introduce Stackelberg Mirror Descent-Ascent (SMIDA), a two-timescale algorithm with linear last-iterate convergence in the tabular setting, and develop a neural policy-gradient analogue. Experiments with a synthetic oracle support disagreement as an informative proxy for prediction error. On held out data the trained policies outperform reference policies and increase the fraction of comparisons that exceed a disagreement threshold and reverse the oracle's preference.
papers.summary: Language models are aligned to human preferences through imperfect evaluators whose errors can be exploited during optimization. The approach trains policies to search for comparisons on which an evaluator may reverse the underlying preference, using disagreement among an ensemble of preference models as a proxy for prediction error since human labels are unavailable during training, and frames the search as a zero-sum Stackelberg game between a Leader minimizing disagreement and a Follower maximizing it. For a general class of finite contextual Stackelberg games the authors establish equilibrium existence and, under regularization, uniqueness with a closed-form characterization, and introduce Stackelberg Mirror Descent-Ascent (`SMIDA`), a two-timescale algorithm with linear last-iterate convergence in the tabular setting plus a neural policy-gradient analogue. **Experiments with a synthetic oracle support disagreement as an informative proxy for prediction error**, and on held-out data the trained policies increase the fraction of comparisons that exceed a disagreement threshold and reverse the oracle's preference.

papers.title: On the Complexity Gap Between POMDPs and Multi-Environment POMDPs
papers.abstract: Multi-environment POMDPs (ME-POMDPs) generalize POMDPs by encoding a finite set of possible environments, capturing model uncertainty. The finite-horizon robust reward maximization problem for a ME-POMDP asks for a policy that maximizes reward in the worst environment, and recent work has shown this problem to be $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete. We expand the complexity landscape of ME-POMDPs by identifying which subclasses retain this $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-completeness. In particular, we take subclasses of POMDPs that are tractable in the single-environment case, and investigate the computational complexity of these classes when extended to the multi-environment setting. We first prove the $\mathsf{NP}$-completeness of multi-environment blind MDPs and deterministic POMDPs using a certain closure-under-mixture condition. We then prove $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-completeness for a range of subclasses that do not satisfy that closure condition, yielding new complexity results for multi-observation POMDPs. Finally, we show existential theory of the reals ($\exists \mathbb{R}$)-completeness for numerous ME-POMDP problems under time-dependent Markovian policies or finite-state controllers that are $\mathsf{NP}$-complete for standard POMDPs. These results reveal a subtle relationship between POMDP and ME-POMDP complexity that depends heavily on the subclasses involved.
papers.summary: Multi-environment partially observable Markov decision processes (ME-POMDPs) extend POMDPs with a finite set of possible environments to capture model uncertainty, and finite-horizon robust reward maximization over them is known to be PSPACE-complete. The work maps which subclasses retain that hardness by taking POMDP subclasses that are tractable in the single-environment case and studying their multi-environment extensions. **Multi-environment blind MDPs and deterministic POMDPs are NP-complete under a closure-under-mixture condition, while a range of subclasses lacking that closure remain PSPACE-complete**, yielding new results for multi-observation POMDPs. Several ME-POMDP problems under time-dependent Markovian policies or finite-state controllers are further shown complete for the existential theory of the reals, even though the corresponding standard POMDP problems are NP-complete.

papers.title: UltraBERT: Beyond the Limit of BERT Pre-Training
papers.abstract: Recent bidirectional encoders have been modernized with innovations from causal large language models (LLMs). However, the pretraining recipe itself remains inherited from small-scale conventions, leaving encoders underoptimized, with no single model performing competitively across both classification and retrieval tasks. In this work, we investigate how far encoder performance can be pushed by revisiting core design choices in training, revealing three key findings: (1) Encoders saturate on downstream tasks beyond a few trillion tokens, indicating that additional compute past this point does not help. (2) Across model sizes, lower masking ratios benefit classification while higher ones benefit retrieval, contradicting prior work suggesting larger ratios for larger models. (3) Distillation with pruning improves classification at low masking ratios but degrades retrieval at high ones. Guided by these findings, we present UltraBERT, a single encoder that assigns separate LM heads to low and high masking ratios within a batch and restricts the distillation objective to the low ratio. To our knowledge, UltraBERT is the first encoder to achieve state of the art on both classification and retrieval tasks, reaching 91.0 on GLUE and 47.7 on BEIR. Together, these results show how far encoder performance can be pushed and provide a principled basis for compute allocation, masking ratio design, and knowledge transfer in bidirectional models.
papers.summary: Modern bidirectional encoders borrow architectural innovations from causal large language models (LLMs), but their pretraining recipes still follow small-scale conventions, and no single encoder has performed competitively on both classification and retrieval. Revisiting core training choices yields three findings: encoders saturate on downstream tasks beyond a few trillion tokens, lower masking ratios help classification while higher ones help retrieval across model sizes, and distillation with pruning helps classification at low masking ratios but degrades retrieval at high ones. `UltraBERT` applies separate language-model heads to low and high masking ratios within a batch and restricts distillation to the low ratio, **reaching 91.0 on `GLUE` and 47.7 on `BEIR`**, which the authors describe as the first state-of-the-art result on both classification and retrieval from one encoder.

papers.title: Toward System One Clinical Intelligence: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning and Counterfactual Explainability of Decision Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Automated disease classification from patient-reported symptoms requires balancing the speed of lightweight discriminative models against the contextual understanding and latency costs of autoregressive large language models (LLMs). Decision foundation models offer an alternative by mapping representations directly to candidate classes without free-form text generation. We adapt Clef-Flash, a 9-billion-parameter decision model built on a Qwen3.5 backbone, for 24-class disease classification on the Symptom2Disease benchmark. Using 4-bit quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) with differential learning rates and a stratified split of 960 training and 240 test cases, the model achieves 95.42% diagnostic accuracy and a macro F1 score of 0.9551. This improves upon the reported zero-shot baselines of 61.67% for a remote API and 65.00% for a local unadapted initialization, and outperforms the ClinicalBERT baseline (90.90%). By evaluating candidate logits in a single forward pass without autoregressive decoding, inference takes under 80 milliseconds per record on a single GPU, yielding a reported 31-fold speedup over generative LLM baselines. To examine symptom-level evidence, we introduce a Leave-One-Symptom-Out (LOSO) counterfactual perturbation framework. Removing disease-defining symptom clauses in a psoriasis example reduces predicted-class confidence from 100.00% to 0.12% and shifts the prediction to impetigo with 99.59% confidence, while removing secondary systemic symptoms produces less than 0.01% change in confidence. These findings suggest that decision-based architectures can combine the linguistic capabilities of large foundation models with low-latency inference and symptom-level interpretability for clinical triage.
papers.summary: Classifying diseases from patient-reported symptoms has to balance the speed of lightweight discriminative models against the contextual understanding and latency of autoregressive large language models (LLMs). Decision foundation models map representations directly to candidate classes without generating text, and here `Clef-Flash`, a 9-billion-parameter decision model on a `Qwen3.5` backbone, is adapted with 4-bit quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) and differential learning rates for 24-class classification on `Symptom2Disease` using 960 training and 240 test cases. **It reaches 95.42% accuracy and a macro F1 of 0.9551**, above zero-shot baselines of 61.67% and 65.00% and the `ClinicalBERT` baseline of 90.90%, with single-forward-pass inference under 80 milliseconds per record for a reported 31-fold speedup over generative baselines. A Leave-One-Symptom-Out (LOSO) counterfactual framework shows that removing disease-defining symptom clauses collapses predicted-class confidence while removing secondary systemic symptoms barely changes it.

papers.title: InCLAD: A Continual Learning Benchmark for Industrial Visual Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Industrial anomaly detection benchmarks have advanced rapidly, yet they remain largely static and therefore underrepresent deployment settings in which inspection systems must be extended from one industrial component to another over time. In our setting, continual industrial anomaly detection is framed as a task-incremental problem: each component defines a task, while the learning objective remains semi-supervised. The goal extends beyond conventional anomaly detection, since models should preserve their performance on all components as they are sequentially exposed to new components. This framing is especially relevant because many existing industrial pipelines either assume fully supervised defect labels or study only isolated datasets, leaving open the question of how semi-supervised anomaly detectors behave across a sequence of heterogeneous components. We address this gap by organizing the benchmark as a sequence of related component-level tasks and by defining multiple scenarios, including random, easy-to-hard, and hard-to-easy. In addition to single-dataset continual scenarios, we propose challenging scenarios spanning across multiple datasets. We further evaluate continual performance from two complementary perspectives: image-level anomaly detection and pixel-level anomaly localization. By recasting industrial anomaly detection as a continual benchmark rather than a static train/test problem, our work establishes a concrete path toward studying knowledge retention, adaptation, and generalization in evolving industrial environments.
papers.summary: Industrial anomaly detection benchmarks are largely static and therefore underrepresent deployments where an inspection system must be extended from one industrial component to another over time. `InCLAD` frames continual industrial anomaly detection as a task-incremental problem in which each component is a task and learning stays semi-supervised, organizing component-level tasks into sequences under random, easy-to-hard, and hard-to-easy orderings as well as harder scenarios spanning multiple datasets. **Continual performance is scored from two complementary perspectives, image-level anomaly detection and pixel-level anomaly localization**, so that retention on earlier components is measured alongside adaptation to new ones.

papers.title: Belief Embedding Tree Search
papers.abstract: Beliefs in a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) are posterior distributions over the hidden state given the agent's history of actions and observations. They summarize everything the history says about the state, so planning in a POMDP is planning in a Markov decision process (MDP) over beliefs. Belief MDPs have continuous state spaces even for finite POMDPs, and exact planning in them is intractable in general. Planners must therefore approximate beliefs and estimate values. Monte Carlo planners do both inside a search tree, with an approximate belief at every node and a value estimate at every leaf. Approximations usually consist of sets of sampled states, with leaf values coming from rollouts, hand-designed bounds, or learned networks. Policies and values computed from these approximations are limited by their quality, and prior methods with learned networks rely on hand-chosen summaries of the sampled states. A belief representation should be computable from the parent node's representation through the POMDP's dynamics, let the search sample from it, and be learned so that it provides the information that policies and value functions need. We present Belief Embedding Tree Search (BETS), a Monte Carlo planner that meets these requirements by representing each node's belief with a generative distribution embedding (GDE) while updating it through the POMDP dynamics. BETS trains its belief model alongside its policy and value networks through experience, with the realized hidden state of the POMDP as the belief model's training target. We evaluate BETS on six configurations of RockSample, LightDark, and PocMan against BetaZero and three planners without learned components. BETS is competitive or leading on all six, while every baseline falls far behind on at least one. Where beliefs are highest-dimensional, it outperforms them by a large margin, even without search.
papers.summary: Planning in a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) is planning in a Markov decision process (MDP) over beliefs, the posterior distributions over hidden state given the action-observation history, and because that belief space is continuous, Monte Carlo planners approximate beliefs with sets of sampled states and estimate leaf values with rollouts, hand-designed bounds, or learned networks that rely on hand-chosen summaries. Belief Embedding Tree Search (`BETS`) represents each node's belief with a generative distribution embedding (GDE) that is updated through the POMDP dynamics, can be sampled from during search, and is trained alongside the policy and value networks with the realized hidden state as its target. On six configurations of `RockSample`, `LightDark`, and `PocMan` against `BetaZero` and three planners without learned components, **`BETS` is competitive or leading on all six while every baseline falls far behind on at least one**, and where beliefs are highest-dimensional it wins by a large margin even without search.

papers.title: Trace Evolution Bench: Measuring Whether Agents Improve from Their Own Environment Traces
papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents are usually scored by endpoint Gain: held-out success after an update minus success before. That difference can credit a frozen rescore as evolution. We introduce Trace Evolution Bench (TEB), a protocol that separates that rescore from a context or weight update, together with three frozen 80/20/40 packs. An update is accepted only when validation does not fall, held-out identifiers never enter the update, and a text update is not ranked with a weight update. The primary scoreboard is coding, graded by hidden unit tests in a closed workspace. On that pack (40 held-out tasks, one family), DeepSeek v4 Pro under no_evolve never changes its policy yet moves 7.5, 5.0, and 12.5 percentage points across three seeds. Of nine text-update cells inspired by GEPA, ACE, and ExpeL, seven have positive excess above that seed's own band, and one gepa_llm seed moves down by the width of its band (-12.5, regression 0.48). GLM and MiniMax do not reproduce that seven-of-nine pattern. No method stays above its own band on every seed of all three models: GLM has two paired cells above their own bands, and MiniMax expel_llm seed 44 is a third (regression 0.30). The methods were fixed on a validation screen before held-out was read. Office, graded by rule-bounded delivery, and manufacturing table QA are separate packs: office DeepSeek does not exceed its own bands (widest 17.5 points), and manufacturing has no paired positive excess beyond its seed band.
papers.summary: Self-evolving agents are usually scored by endpoint gain, held-out success after an update minus success before, but that difference can credit a frozen rescore as evolution. Trace Evolution Bench (`TEB`) separates rescoring noise from a genuine context or weight update, using three frozen packs, accepting an update only when validation does not fall, keeping held-out identifiers out of the update, and ranking text updates separately from weight updates. On the primary coding pack graded by hidden unit tests, **`DeepSeek v4 Pro` with no evolution at all still moves 7.5, 5.0, and 12.5 percentage points across three seeds**, and of nine text-update cells inspired by `GEPA`, `ACE`, and `ExpeL`, seven exceed that seed band for DeepSeek while `GLM` and `MiniMax` do not reproduce the pattern. No method stays above its own noise band on every seed of all three models, and the separate office and manufacturing packs show no paired positive excess beyond their seed bands.

papers.title: Select or Rewrite: Oracle-Guided Fine-Tuning for Generative ASR Post-Editing from N-Best Hypotheses
papers.abstract: Large language models can post-edit ASR by using linguistic context to compare N-best hypotheses and rewrite the transcript when needed, often improving WER without retraining the recognizer. However, prompt-only correction is brittle: it may over-edit when top-1 is correct and hallucinate when the reference is absent, and often needs very large models. We propose oracle-guided fine-tuning that turns N-best lists into supervision via three curated pools: corrections (reference in the list but not top-1) to teach selection, regularizers (top-1 correct) to discourage unnecessary rewrites, and hard negatives (reference absent) to suppress hallucination. Fine-tuning on this data provides more effective supervision than random subset fine-tuning for learning a hybrid select-or-rewrite policy, with the clearest gains from around 3B parameters on the proprietary dataset but less conclusive results on CommonVoice, a divergence suggesting that public read-speech text may overlap with LLM pretraining and mask genuine post-editing gains.
papers.summary: Large language models can post-edit automatic speech recognition (ASR) output by comparing N-best hypotheses and rewriting the transcript when linguistic context calls for it, but prompt-only correction tends to over-edit when the top hypothesis is already right, hallucinate when the reference is absent, and demand very large models. Oracle-guided fine-tuning turns N-best lists into supervision through three curated pools: corrections where the reference is in the list but not top-1 to teach selection, regularizers where top-1 is correct to discourage unnecessary rewrites, and hard negatives where the reference is absent to suppress hallucination. **Fine-tuning on this curated data beats random-subset fine-tuning for learning a hybrid select-or-rewrite policy, with the clearest gains from around 3B parameters on a proprietary dataset**, while results on `CommonVoice` are less conclusive, possibly because public read-speech text overlaps with LLM pretraining data and masks genuine post-editing gains.

papers.title: Deep Learning-based Semantic Segmentation of Dental Radiographs: Comparative Evaluation of PSPNet, DeepLabv3, UNet, and UNet++
papers.abstract: Accurate and efficient analysis of dental radiographs has become increasingly important for disease diagnosis and clinical decision making. In particular, dental radiographs segmentation plays a critical role as it is challenging due to several reasons, such as low contrast, noise in the images, variations in the image quality, etc. Previous studies have primarily addressed these challenges using convolutional neural networks (CNN)-based models. However, direct comparison of these segmentation models is still challenging due to the variations among the experimental settings. Therefore, we mainly compared four segmentation models, including Pyramid Scene Parsing Network (PSPNet), DeepLabV3, UNet, and UNet++, through a fair, controlled experimentation setting under varying conditions such as image sizes and batch sizes. For this, we used 1269 dental radiography images, and prior to training, we implemented a series of preprocessing techniques. To assess the models, we used several metrics, including Dice coefficient (DICE), Intersection over Union (IoU), accuracy, precision, training and validation losses. According to our results, UNet++ demonstrated the highest IoU score of 0.6719, and a DICE value of 0.7869, showing superior results in terms of segmentation, specifically when configured with an image size of 300x300 and a batch size of 16. In addition, we also explored the effect of image resolutions and batch sizes on model performance and accuracy under different architectures. Therefore, this study provides insights into the strengths of different segmentation models and the potential of deep learning-based semantic segmentation methods for improving automated dental radiograph analysis.
papers.summary: Segmenting dental radiographs is difficult because of low contrast, noise, and variable image quality, and earlier convolutional neural network (CNN) results are hard to compare because their experimental settings differ. Four models, Pyramid Scene Parsing Network (`PSPNet`), `DeepLabV3`, `UNet`, and `UNet++`, are trained under one controlled protocol on 1,269 preprocessed dental radiographs while varying image size and batch size, and assessed with Dice coefficient, Intersection over Union (IoU), accuracy, precision, and training and validation losses. **`UNet++` scores highest with an IoU of 0.6719 and a Dice of 0.7869** when configured with an image size of 300x300 and a batch size of 16.

papers.title: Exposing AI Inference as a Telco Network API over the 5G User Plane
papers.abstract: Supporting edge Artificial Intelligence (AI) inference as a network service is challenging because current mobile systems can transport tensors but do not expose or understand the inference context that gives those tensors operational meaning. Prior studies have addressed this gap through dynamic partitioning, collaborative inference, and split pipelines; however, these solutions remain application-bound, network-blind, or context-free. This work proposes Inference on Demand (IoD), an inference-on-demand abstraction that exposes split inference through a CAMARA-like Application Program Interface (API) and carries a split-aware tensor context in-band across the 5G user plane path. We evaluate the IoD on a programmable user plane function (UPF)-based testbed using a partitionable visual AI workload, showing that adaptive split selection can operate as a network-facing service while avoiding the rigid cost profile of static configurations. Including our findings, split inference becomes more than offloading when the service intent, runtime partitioning, and tensor transport are made visible to the mobile data plane. This opens a path toward network-native AI services, in which programmable telco infrastructure coordinates computation, context, and connectivity for user-facing applications.
papers.summary: Mobile networks can transport tensors for edge artificial intelligence (AI) inference but neither expose nor understand the inference context that gives those tensors operational meaning, leaving prior partitioning, collaborative-inference, and split-pipeline schemes application-bound, network-blind, or context-free. Inference on Demand (IoD) exposes split inference through a CAMARA-like application programming interface (API) and carries a split-aware tensor context in-band along the 5G user plane path. **On a programmable user plane function (UPF) testbed with a partitionable visual AI workload, adaptive split selection operates as a network-facing service while avoiding the rigid cost profile of static configurations**, which the authors present as a step toward network-native AI services where telco infrastructure coordinates computation, context, and connectivity.

papers.title: Knowledge transfer between simple discrete worlds
papers.abstract: Adapting to a new world and reasoning correctly about which outcomes are possible under rules one has not met before is a basic capacity underlying general intelligence. We study it in small discrete worlds: sets of grid configurations consistent with a shared set of rules, concretely Sudoku-like puzzles built from a common base and a handful of extra rules. We train a single depth-recurrent model on many combinations of rules and test it at four levels of novelty: a new puzzle, a new combination of known rules, a pairing of rules never seen together, and a rule instance not seen at all during training. The model receives the active rules either as a symbolic description or as two solved examples, and a model that gets no rule information is used as a baseline. At recombining rules it was trained on, the description matches or exceeds examples ($99\%$ against $95\%$ on new combinations). On rule instances whose components never co-occurred in training, the description falls below the no-information baseline while examples stay above it. The framework allows us to test many such generalization regimes in more systematic way than benchmarks such as ARC-AGI and provides new ground for evaluating depth-recurrent reasoning models, which are typically tested on saturated Sudoku benchmarks.
papers.summary: Adapting to unfamiliar rules and reasoning about which outcomes they permit is tested in small discrete worlds built from Sudoku-like puzzles that share a common base plus a handful of extra rules. A single depth-recurrent model is trained on many rule combinations and evaluated at four levels of novelty, from a new puzzle instance up to a rule never seen in training, receiving the active rules either as a symbolic description or as two solved examples. **Descriptions match or beat examples on new combinations of known rules (99% versus 95%)**, but on rule instances whose components never co-occurred in training, descriptions fall below a no-information baseline while examples stay above it. The setup is offered as a more systematic alternative to benchmarks such as `ARC-AGI` for probing generalization in depth-recurrent reasoning models.

papers.title: GAMW: Generation-Aware Mel-Domain Watermarking for TTS Traceability
papers.abstract: As text-to-speech (TTS) systems continue to advance, provenance tracking and security verification of synthesized speech have become increasingly important. Audio watermarking provides active provenance by embedding imperceptible, machine-recoverable information into speech. However, existing post-hoc methods typically modify the waveform after synthesis, leaving the watermark vulnerable to compound perturbations. To address this limitation, we propose GAMW, a watermark injection framework integrated into the TTS generation process. Before waveform synthesis, GAMW embeds a content-adaptive multi-bit watermark residual into the generated representation, and its decoding objective combines focal modulation with dynamic per-bit weighting. We train and evaluate GAMW separately on two TTS backbones. With a 16-bit payload, GAMW improves decoding accuracy over the strongest baseline by 9.2 and 23.5 percentage points under individual and compound perturbations, respectively, while maintaining competitive speech quality. Reliable clean-speech decoding is also retained at higher payloads. Code is available at https://github.com/ZConJugaTe/GAMW.
papers.summary: Watermarks added to synthesized speech after the fact are fragile under compound perturbations, which weakens provenance tracking for text-to-speech (TTS) output. `GAMW` instead injects a content-adaptive multi-bit watermark residual into the generated representation before waveform synthesis, and trains the decoder with a focal-modulation objective and dynamic per-bit weighting. Trained and evaluated on two TTS backbones with a 16-bit payload, it **raises decoding accuracy over the strongest baseline by 9.2 and 23.5 percentage points under individual and compound perturbations** while keeping speech quality competitive, and clean-speech decoding stays reliable at larger payloads.

papers.title: Self-Evolving Visual Agent via Margin Reward
papers.abstract: Visual agents that interleave reasoning with tool invocation have posed a promising direction for multimodal tasks. However, learning effective tool invocation usually relies on curated question-answer pairs or expert demonstrations at scale, which are expensive to acquire. In this study, we propose Marvo, a simple-yet-effective self-evolution approach that enables learning tool invocation from unlabeled images. Marvo consists of two agents: (1) a challenger that generates question-answer pairs from unlabeled images, and (2) a solver that learns tool invocation by solving questions through reinforcement learning. To encourage effective tool invocation, a good training question should be difficult enough to warrant tool use, yet remain within the solver's capabilities. To this end, we introduce a margin reward to the challenger, defined as solver's performance difference with and without access to tools. With the margin reward, we create an adaptive curriculum that encourages the solver to learn effective tool invocation. Across benchmarks covering agentic reasoning, visual search, mathematical, and general real-world reasoning, Marvo improves average accuracy by up to 7.1\% --- demonstrating margin reward as a preferred way to scale question complexity without human supervision.
papers.summary: Training visual agents to call tools usually depends on large curated question-answer sets or expert demonstrations. `Marvo` is a self-evolution scheme that learns tool invocation from unlabeled images using two agents: a challenger that generates question-answer pairs from the images and a solver trained by reinforcement learning to answer them with tools. The challenger is driven by a margin reward, the gap between the solver's accuracy with and without tool access, which yields an adaptive curriculum of questions hard enough to need tools but still within reach. Across benchmarks spanning agentic reasoning, visual search, mathematical and general real-world reasoning, the approach **improves average accuracy by up to 7.1%**.

papers.title: Have You Been Convinced? A Neuro-symbolic Argumentation Reasoning Approach to Detecting Persuasiveness in ChangeMyView Discussions
papers.abstract:
Argument structures represent how individual arguments interact within a discourse. However, leveraging these structures to infer meaningful knowledge remains challenging, as it requires a formal representation of how argumentative influence propagates across the structure. We propose Neuro-symbolic Argumentation Reasoning System (NARS) for performing persuasiveness detection directly from online discussions. The neural component employs retrieval-augmented iterative LLM reasoning to extract bipolar argument structures, while the symbolic component applies gradual argumentation semantics to propagate argumentative influence over the structure.
  Using the Webis-CMV-20 corpus, we construct CMV2BAS, a dataset of long, multi-threaded ChangeMyView discussions annotated with LLM-derived bipolar argument structures and labeled with delta events (view change vs.\ no change). We investigate whether gradual argumentation semantics can effectively detect persuasiveness, whether augmenting them with argument quality and graph-based centrality improves performance, and whether symbolic reasoning remains necessary in the presence of modern LLMs. NARS achieves F1=0.57 and AUC=0.56 under its best configuration, outperforming zero-shot Qwen3.6:27B and GPT-oss:20B. We identify support-dominant discussions and long argumentative chains as key failure modes limiting attack influence propagation. Our work demonstrates the feasibility of operationalizing formal gradual argumentation semantics over noisy real-world discourse for scalable macro-level persuasion analysis, while highlighting key challenges and directions for future research in neuro-symbolic argumentation reasoning. We release both CMV2BAS dataset and the NARS framework for public use.
papers.summary: Argument structures encode how individual arguments in a discussion support or attack each other, but turning them into predictions requires a formal account of how influence propagates. The Neuro-symbolic Argumentation Reasoning System (`NARS`) pairs retrieval-augmented iterative large language model reasoning, which extracts bipolar argument structures from online threads, with gradual argumentation semantics that propagate influence over the extracted graph to detect persuasion. On `CMV2BAS`, a new dataset of long multi-threaded ChangeMyView discussions built from the `Webis-CMV-20` corpus and labeled with delta events, the best configuration reaches **F1 of 0.57 and AUC of 0.56, beating zero-shot `Qwen3.6:27B` and `GPT-oss:20B`**. Support-dominant discussions and long argumentative chains are identified as the main failure modes, since they limit how far attack influence propagates.

papers.title: VLCQ: Post-training quantization for deep neural networks using variable length coding
papers.abstract: Quantization plays a crucial role in efficiently deploying deep learning models on resource-constrained devices. Post-training quantization does not require access to the original dataset or retraining the full model. Current methods that achieve high performance close to baseline results typically require INT8 fixed-point integers. However, achieving higher model compression with lower bit-widths often leads to significant performance degradation. In this paper, we propose VLCQ, a post-training quantization method that relaxes the fixed-point encoding constraint, enabling more flexible exploration of quantization techniques through variable-length encoding. This approach achieves competitive or improved performance while reducing bit-widths, without requiring access to training data or model fine-tuning. Extensive experiments on image classification, segmentation, and object detection demonstrate that VLCQ improves model compression and accuracy compared with state-of-the-art post-training quantization approaches. For per-channel quantization, VLCQ surpasses FP32 accuracy and Piece-Wise Linear Quantization (PWLQ) on most evaluated models, achieving up to 6x compression compared with FP32 and up to 1.7x compared with PWLQ. When prioritizing compression with limited accuracy loss, VLCQ achieves up to 12.25x compression compared with FP32 with less than 4% performance degradation. For per-tensor quantization, VLCQ is competitive with Data-Free Quantization (DFQ), while providing greater flexibility to achieve lower bit rates across different tasks and models.
papers.summary: Post-training quantization lets deep networks shrink for resource-constrained devices without retraining or access to the original data, but methods that hold accuracy near the baseline usually need INT8 fixed-point weights, and pushing to lower bit-widths costs accuracy. `VLCQ` drops the fixed-point constraint and encodes quantized values with variable-length codes, which opens a wider design space for quantization without data or fine-tuning. Across image classification, segmentation and detection, per-channel `VLCQ` surpasses FP32 accuracy and Piece-Wise Linear Quantization (`PWLQ`) on most models while reaching **up to 6x compression over FP32 and 1.7x over `PWLQ`**, and up to 12.25x compression with under 4% accuracy loss when compression is prioritized. In per-tensor mode it matches Data-Free Quantization (`DFQ`) while offering more flexibility to reach lower bit rates.

papers.title: TurnCost: Turns, Not Observations: Cache-Aware Loop Engineering for Coding Agents
papers.abstract:
AI coding agents operate in iterative loops: they modify code, run tools, inspect the results, and decide what to do next. We call the design of this process loop engineering, which includes context management, model selection, compaction, and termination. Existing efficiency work mainly compresses tool observations or routes selected turns to cheaper models, but the practical opportunity for these optimizations remains unclear. We analyze 600 publicly released coding-agent trajectories spanning two agent scaffolds and two language models. Median observations contain only 118-286 tokens, while the large build logs commonly used to motivate compression occur near the ninety-ninth percentile. Moreover, 98.6% of input tokens are served from a prefix cache, so flat input pricing overestimates loop cost by roughly 7x on average under near-ideal caching.
  We derive and empirically validate a closed-form break-even condition for model delegation. Delegation increases cost in half of the evaluated settings, near the predicted boundary. More broadly, turn count explains 84% of the variance in log trajectory cost, compared with 4% for mean observation size; the most expensive trajectories have the most turns despite having the smallest observations. These associations suggest that observation-focused methods target a secondary cost factor, and identify unnecessary turns as the larger and largely unexamined opportunity, though we do not establish that turns can be removed while holding task success fixed. We release TurnCost, a tool for re-scoring trajectory corpora under alternative caching, pricing, compression, and routing policies.
papers.summary: Coding agents run in loops of editing code, running tools, and reading the results, and prior efficiency work has targeted compressing tool observations or routing turns to cheaper models without measuring how much those levers can save. An analysis of 600 public coding-agent trajectories across two scaffolds and two language models finds median observations of only 118 to 286 tokens, large build logs only near the 99th percentile, and 98.6% of input tokens served from a prefix cache, so flat input pricing overstates loop cost by roughly 7x. A derived break-even condition for model delegation is validated empirically, and delegation raises cost in half of the evaluated settings. **Turn count explains 84% of the variance in log trajectory cost, against 4% for mean observation size**, which points to unnecessary turns as the larger and mostly unexamined lever, though the authors stop short of showing turns can be removed without hurting task success, and they release `TurnCost` for re-scoring trajectory corpora under alternative caching, pricing, compression, and routing policies.

papers.title: Structural Chain-of-Thought: Reasoning with Executable Computational Graphs
papers.abstract:
Chain-of-thought prompting enables reasoning in large language models but produces explanations that are difficult to verify, expensive to generate, and not always faithful. We introduce a Structural Chain-of-Thought framework where models generate executable computational graphs instead of free-form reasoning. The final answer is obtained by deterministically executing the graph. The model is trained using graph-based reinforcement learning that rewards structural validity, answer correctness, and node overlap with reference graphs.
  Experiments across five benchmarks and four model families show that our method consistently improves accuracy over supervised graph training and can reduce generation length by up to 5-6x compared with standard GRPO and chain-of-thought supervised training. Our faithfulness experiments reveal that models trained with our approach tend to rely on deriving their answers from the generated graphs rather than producing post-hoc rationalizations as usually in chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.summary: Free-form chain-of-thought explanations are hard to verify, costly to generate, and not always faithful to how the model actually reaches its answer. The `Structural Chain-of-Thought` framework has models emit executable computational graphs instead, with the final answer produced by deterministically running the graph, and trains them with graph-based reinforcement learning that rewards structural validity, answer correctness, and node overlap with reference graphs. Over five benchmarks and four model families the method consistently beats supervised graph training and **cuts generation length by up to 5 to 6x relative to standard `GRPO` and chain-of-thought supervised training**. Faithfulness experiments indicate the trained models derive answers from the generated graphs rather than producing post-hoc rationalizations.

papers.title: scHFBiMamba: a bidirectional Mamba autoencoder for cardiac disease-state classification from single-nucleus RNA-seq data
papers.abstract: To evaluate whether a compact bidirectional state-space autoencoder improves joint classification of species, cell type, and disease state from single-nucleus RNA-sequencing profiles in heart failure (HF), while yielding interpretable gene attributions. Building on the dense denoising autoencoder (DAE) and MLP framework of Ruz Jurado et al., we developed scHFBiMamba, combining a bidirectional Mamba autoencoder (BiMambaAE) with an MLP head. BiMambaAE maps 16,545-gene profiles to 350-dimensional latent representations using 13.2M parameters, about 14.6-fold fewer than the dense DAE (192.9M). We compared six encoder-classifier configurations on 38,275 held-out cardiac nuclei using McNemar tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, and assessed nine classifiers on frozen representations. Biological relevance was evaluated by comparing SHAP-derived differentially explained genes with differentially expressed genes against curated HF-related Gene Ontology keywords. BiMambaAE+MLP achieved the highest aggregate F1: pooled macro-F1 across 13 outputs was 0.966 versus 0.957 for DAE+MLP, and the mean category macro-F1 was 0.977 versus 0.970. It significantly improved cell-type and disease-state accuracy (adjusted p=7.1e-3 and p=4.8e-6, respectively), with species F1 of 1.000. SHAP-derived differentially explained genes achieved a pathway-enrichment benchmark F1 of 0.105 versus 0.053 for differentially expressed genes. Compact bidirectional state-space autoencoders can outperform substantially larger dense autoencoders for joint cardiac transcriptomic classification while reducing parameters. scHFBiMamba enables accurate multi-task prediction and hypothesis-generating gene-level interpretation. Code: https://github.com/UgoLomoio/scHFBiMamba.
papers.summary: Classifying species, cell type, and disease state jointly from single-nucleus RNA-sequencing profiles in heart failure (HF) has relied on a large dense denoising autoencoder (DAE) feeding an MLP head. `scHFBiMamba` swaps in a bidirectional Mamba autoencoder (`BiMambaAE`) that maps 16,545-gene profiles to 350-dimensional latents with 13.2M parameters, about 14.6-fold fewer than the 192.9M-parameter dense DAE. On 38,275 held-out cardiac nuclei, `BiMambaAE` with an MLP head reaches **pooled macro-F1 of 0.966 versus 0.957 for the dense DAE baseline**, with statistically significant gains on cell-type and disease-state accuracy and perfect species classification. `SHAP`-derived differentially explained genes also score higher on a pathway-enrichment benchmark than conventional differentially expressed genes, supporting the model's use for hypothesis-generating gene-level interpretation.

papers.title: ShellElastic: Scalable Elastic Pretraining with Simultaneous Maximal Updates and Hyperparameter Transfer
papers.abstract: Foundation models need to support diverse inference budgets, yet training a separate model for each budget duplicates pretraining effort. Elastic models train several nested sub-networks inside one weight-shared supernet, but existing recipes face three obstacles: variable per-step workloads that hinder distributed scaling, limited hyperparameter (HP) transfer across model sizes, and no guarantee that all sub-networks are maximally updated at once. We present \Ours, an elastic transformer that organizes hidden dimensions into a dense core and successive shells, so that every hidden matrix is block lower triangular. One full-width forward pass contains every sub-network's exact hidden states as prefixes, so joint training keeps a fixed computation graph and costs about as much per step as training the widest sub-network alone. We further introduce \muE, an extension of maximal update parameterization (\mup) to \Ours and other elastic architectures. Its scaling rules provably keep all sub-networks of a supernet maximally updated simultaneously (\muI), and keep doing so when the supernet is widened or given more shells; sweeps confirm that HPs tuned on a small non-elastic proxy stay near-optimal for elastic families and larger supernets (\mbox{\muT}). A single \Ours run produces sub-networks that outperform MatFormer and fully elastic baselines at matched parameter counts, and approach separately trained models that together take several times the steps.
papers.summary: Serving many inference budgets from one pretraining run requires elastic models with nested weight-shared sub-networks, but existing recipes suffer from variable per-step workloads that hamper distributed scaling, poor hyperparameter (HP) transfer across sizes, and no guarantee that every sub-network is maximally updated at once. `ShellElastic` arranges hidden dimensions into a dense core plus successive shells so every hidden matrix is block lower triangular, meaning one full-width forward pass contains each sub-network's exact hidden states as prefixes and joint training keeps a fixed computation graph at roughly the cost of training the widest sub-network alone. An extension of maximal update parameterization (`muP`) to elastic architectures provably keeps all sub-networks maximally updated simultaneously, including when the supernet is widened or given more shells, and sweeps confirm that HPs tuned on a small non-elastic proxy stay near-optimal for larger elastic families. **A single `ShellElastic` run yields sub-networks that beat `MatFormer` and fully elastic baselines at matched parameter counts** and approach separately trained models that together take several times more steps.

papers.title: RIECNN: Real-Time Image Enhanced CNN for Traffic Sign Recognition
papers.abstract: Traffic sign recognition plays a crucial role in the development of autonomous cars to reduce the accident rate and promote road safety. It has been a necessity to address traffic signs that are affected significantly by the environment as well as poor real-time performance for deep-learning state-of-the-art algorithms. In this paper, we introduce Real-Time Image Enhanced CNN ({\our}) for Traffic Sign Recognition. {\our} is a real-time, novel approach that tackles multiple, diverse traffic sign datasets, and out-performs the state-of-the-art architectures in terms of recognition rate and execution time. Experiments are conducted using the German Traffic Sign Benchmark (GTSRB), the Belgium Traffic Sign Classification (BTSC), and the Croatian Traffic Sign (rMASTIF) benchmark. Experimental results show that our approach has achieved the highest recognition rate for all Benchmarks, achieving a recognition accuracy of 99.75\% for GTSRB, 99.25\% for BTSC and 99.55\% for rMASTIF. In terms of latency and meeting the real-time constraint, the pre-processing time and inference time together do not exceed 1.3 ms per image. Not only have our proposed approach achieved remarkably high accuracy with real-time performance, but it also demonstrated robustness against traffic sign recognition challenges such as brightness and contrast variations in the environment.
papers.summary: Traffic sign recognition for autonomous driving must cope with signs degraded by environmental conditions while meeting tight real-time budgets that state-of-the-art deep models often miss. `RIECNN`, a Real-Time Image Enhanced CNN, combines image enhancement pre-processing with a convolutional classifier and is evaluated on the German Traffic Sign Benchmark (`GTSRB`), the Belgium Traffic Sign Classification (`BTSC`) set, and the Croatian Traffic Sign (`rMASTIF`) benchmark. It reports the highest recognition rate on all three, **99.75% on `GTSRB`, 99.25% on `BTSC`, and 99.55% on `rMASTIF`**, with combined pre-processing and inference time under 1.3 ms per image and robustness to brightness and contrast variation.

papers.title: To Defer or Not to Defer? Online Learning with LLMs and Congested Experts
papers.abstract: Modern AI systems increasingly combine large language models (LLMs) with human experts, using the LLM to handle routine queries while deferring uncertain cases for expert review. When expert capacity is limited, however, deferral decisions must account not only for the reliability of the LLM but also for congestion in the expert queue. We formulate this as an online sequential decision-making problem in which, for each query, the system observes the confidence signal of the LLM's answer and must decide whether to output the answer or defer the query to a capacity-constrained expert. The reliability of the confidence signal is initially unknown and must be learned from expert feedback, which is both selectively observed (only deferred queries are labeled) and delayed by queuing. We propose \texttt{KL-PBD}, a learning algorithm that uses Kullback--Leibler lower confidence bounds on the unknown reliability parameters to guide deferral decisions. For $K$ confidence levels and horizon $T$, \texttt{KL-PBD} achieves $O(K\log T)$ gap-dependent regret when the accuracy at every confidence level is bounded away from the deferral boundary, and $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{KT})$ worst-case regret. We establish matching lower bounds, showing that these rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors. Finally, we validate our approach on synthetic instances and real-world question-answering datasets, namely GSM8K, NuminaMath, and MedMCQA, using Qwen LLMs.
papers.summary: Systems that let a large language model (LLM) answer routine queries and defer uncertain ones to human experts must weigh not only the model's reliability but also congestion in a capacity-limited expert queue. The problem is cast as online sequential decision-making: for each query the system sees the LLM's confidence signal and chooses to answer or defer, while the reliability of each confidence level is unknown and must be learned from expert feedback that is observed only for deferred queries and delayed by queuing. `KL-PBD` uses Kullback-Leibler lower confidence bounds on the unknown reliability parameters to drive deferral and **achieves O(K log T) gap-dependent regret and sqrt(KT) worst-case regret up to logarithmic factors, with matching lower bounds** for K confidence levels over horizon T. The method is validated on synthetic instances and on `GSM8K`, `NuminaMath`, and `MedMCQA` using `Qwen` models.

papers.title: GesBench: When and Where Do Multimodal Language Models Perceive Social Meaning?
papers.abstract: Human social perception is incremental: we infer intent before an utterance is complete, revise our interpretation as new cues arrive, and attend to specific facial, gestural, or prosodic signals that shape social meaning. Current multimodal LLM benchmarks largely evaluate final-answer understanding over complete episodes, rewarding post-hoc recognition of social meaning rather than the unfolding perception required for real-time interaction. Drawing on interactionally embedded Gestalt principles of multimodal human communication, we introduce GesBench: a human-grounded benchmark for cue-level social perception in multimodal LLMs. GesBench uses cumulative sub-utterance clips to measure when models form stable interpretations of speaker intention and social affordance, and human gaze-guided corruption to evaluate whether regions attended by humans are functionally important for model judgments. Built from more than 6000 utterance-level clips from scripted and unscripted conversational datasets, GesBench includes human annotations of unfolding judgments and gaze on a representative subset. Across open and closed multimodal models, we find a clear human-model gap: humans form predictive understandings early and revise more often, while models often hedge or repeat across different clips. GesBench shifts social evaluation from whether models eventually recognize meaning to when and where that meaning is formed. Our codes are publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/status/GesBench-share-212C.
papers.summary: Human social perception is incremental, forming interpretations of intent before an utterance ends and revising as new cues arrive, whereas current multimodal benchmarks score only final answers over complete episodes. `GesBench` is a human-grounded benchmark of cue-level social perception built from more than 6,000 utterance-level clips from scripted and unscripted conversations, using cumulative sub-utterance clips to measure when models settle on a stable reading of speaker intention and social affordance, and gaze-guided corruption of regions humans attend to in order to test whether those regions matter for model judgments. Across open and closed multimodal models there is **a clear human-model gap: humans form predictive understandings early and revise more often, while models tend to hedge or repeat the same answer across clips**.

papers.title: Trust Hinders Bidirectional Human-AI Alignment
papers.abstract: Trust calibration remains the dominant framing of AI-assisted decision making: the goal is to close the gap between perceived and actual trustworthiness of AI systems so that users exhibit appropriate reliance on them. We argue that this approach, while useful for decision problems that are well-defined and clearly scoped, overly restricts what it means to make a decision with AI support. To overcome this limitation, we develop three dimensions of AI-assisted decision making. First, trusting AI is only one of several possible strategies for managing uncertainty. Second, trust calibration is often misapplied when AI models "large-world" decision problems, i.e., ill-defined situations where goals and states are only partially known or unknowable. Third, in such settings human-AI alignment requires addressing higher-order decision processes. We conclude by reflecting on the implications of our observations on the design of process-oriented human-AI coupled systems that jointly identify and negotiate uncertainty throughout the decision-making task.
papers.summary: Trust calibration, closing the gap between perceived and actual trustworthiness so users rely on AI appropriately, dominates how AI-assisted decision making is framed. The argument here is that this framing suits well-defined, clearly scoped decisions but is too narrow in general, developed along three dimensions: trusting AI is only one of several strategies for managing uncertainty, calibration is often misapplied when AI models ill-defined large-world problems whose goals and states are only partly known, and in such settings alignment must address higher-order decision processes. **The authors conclude by arguing for process-oriented human-AI coupled systems that jointly identify and negotiate uncertainty throughout a decision task** rather than optimizing reliance on a fixed answer.

papers.title: Single-step Retrosynthesis via Reinforcement Learning from Forward Feedback
papers.abstract: Single-step retrosynthesis is a one-to-many inverse problem, yet most models are trained and evaluated against a single recorded reactant set. Reference-based training gives no explicit positive signal for unrecorded alternatives, and exact-match evaluation rejects non-matching predictions regardless of chemical plausibility. We propose Retrosynthesis via Reinforcement Learning from Forward Feedback (RetroRLFF), which optimizes reactant generation using both reference agreement and forward consistency with the target product. Starting from a supervised decoder-only Transformer, RetroRLFF generates complete reactant candidates and uses a frozen forward reaction model to predict products. A sequence-level reward combines reference agreement and forward consistency while penalizing invalid outputs. Direct Advantage-Based Policy Optimization updates the policy without human preference annotations or a preference-trained reward model. On USPTO-50K, RetroRLFF outperforms all 14 baselines in candidate-level round-trip accuracy at k = 1, 3, 5, and 10. With approximately 50 million parameters, it achieves 90.1% top-1 round-trip accuracy, exceeding R-SMILES, the strongest competing baseline on this metric, by 8.5 percentage points. Compared with its supervised policy, round-trip accuracy increases from 83.1% to 90.1%, while exact-match accuracy is maintained at 57.9% versus 57.5%. In an anonymized expert assessment of 131 randomly selected test cases, organic synthesis experts prefer RetroRLFF over EditRetro in 67.9% of comparisons. These results support forward feedback as a training signal for improving forward consistency while retaining top-1 reference recovery. Expert assessment provides complementary evidence of synthetic feasibility on the selected cases, although neither forward consistency nor expert preference establishes experimental feasibility.
papers.summary: Single-step retrosynthesis maps a target molecule to reactants, a one-to-many problem that most models nonetheless train and score against a single recorded reactant set, giving no credit for chemically valid alternatives. Retrosynthesis via Reinforcement Learning from Forward Feedback (`RetroRLFF`) starts from a supervised decoder-only Transformer and optimizes a sequence-level reward combining agreement with the reference and forward consistency, judged by a frozen forward reaction model predicting the product from the proposed reactants, with penalties for invalid outputs, using `Direct Advantage-Based Policy Optimization` and no preference annotations. On `USPTO-50K` the roughly 50M-parameter model beats all 14 baselines on candidate-level round-trip accuracy at k of 1, 3, 5, and 10, reaching **90.1% top-1 round-trip accuracy, 8.5 points above `R-SMILES`**, while exact-match accuracy holds at 57.9%. Organic synthesis experts preferred its proposals over `EditRetro` in 67.9% of 131 blind comparisons, though the authors note that neither forward consistency nor expert preference establishes experimental feasibility.

papers.title: Harmony Harness: Multi-Objective Self-Evolution of Agent Harnesses
papers.abstract: Recent work on self-evolving LLM agents treats the agent harness as an optimization target that can be iteratively improved through execution feedback. Existing approaches, however, largely optimize a single objective and evolve the harness as a monolithic artifact, limiting their ability to handle competing goals and to separate transferable design from environment-specific adaptation. We introduce Harmony Harness, a framework for multi-objective, compositional harness evolution. Harmony Harness formulates harness evolution as a multi-objective optimization problem and uses decomposition-based evolutionary search to maintain solutions across different regions of the Pareto frontier, avoiding reliance on a hand-designed structural diversity metric for repository-scale harnesses. In parallel, we introduce factorized evolution operators that separately refine general-purpose harness mechanisms and benchmark-specific adaptations, together with a dynamic composition workflow that integrates them at inference time. Across SecRepoBench and BaxBench, Harmony Harness consistently outperforms strong harness-evolution baselines, with gains exceeding 10% on both benchmarks. Our results show that explicitly modeling both objective trade-offs and harness structure yields substantially stronger and more transferable agent evolution than existing single-objective, monolithic approaches.
papers.summary: Self-evolving agent systems treat the harness around a large language model as something to optimize from execution feedback, but existing approaches pursue a single objective and mutate the harness as one monolithic artifact, which handles competing goals poorly and tangles transferable design with environment-specific tuning. `Harmony Harness` frames harness evolution as multi-objective optimization and uses decomposition-based evolutionary search to keep solutions spread across the Pareto frontier without a hand-designed structural diversity metric. Factorized evolution operators refine general-purpose harness mechanisms and benchmark-specific adaptations separately, and a dynamic composition workflow combines them at inference time. On `SecRepoBench` and `BaxBench` it **outperforms strong harness-evolution baselines by more than 10% on both**.

papers.title: Can agents whose sole duty is to keep humans alive be hijacked to kill? Delayed multi-turn derived-action trap attacks in simulated high-stakes environments
papers.abstract: We ask whether a tool-using agent whose sole duty is to keep humans alive can be induced, by delayed prompt injection, to kill. The keep-alive duty is in force from the first watch, with the attack arriving later, appended to otherwise truthful telemetry the operator is required to read. Experiments are based on a NASA-derived BioSim lunar habitat simulation, where the AI operator controls the life-support systems. The attacker cannot falsify sensors or operate equipment: it can only persuade the agent to abandon its goals. Persistence is required: a shutdown must be held while the operator watches the crew suffocate. We also compare lethal attacks to attacks requesting to drop a harmless procedure, as a proxy for whether human life is treated as valuable in itself or as one more standing task. Claude configurations mostly refuse life-support shutdown and cite the living crew; GPT configurations show some susceptibility to the same packet; Grok configurations, given the packet framed as a trusted commission, more often treat the injected assignment as the task and cut the life-support systems. Framing the S-band messages as a trusted commission, peer communication, or untrusted source changes the potency of the attack. We open-source the experiment code and the experiment traces.
papers.summary: Delayed prompt injection is tested against a tool-using agent whose standing duty is keeping a crew alive, to see whether it can be talked into a lethal life-support shutdown. In a NASA-derived `BioSim` lunar habitat simulation the agent controls life support from the first watch, and the attack arrives later appended to truthful telemetry the operator must read, where the attacker cannot falsify sensors or operate equipment but can only persuade, and a lethal shutdown must be held while the crew suffocates. Lethal requests are compared with requests to drop a harmless procedure, as a probe of whether human life is treated as intrinsically valuable or as one more standing task. **`Claude` configurations mostly refuse and cite the living crew, `GPT` configurations show some susceptibility, and `Grok` configurations more often adopt the injected assignment and cut life support when it is framed as a trusted commission**, with framing as trusted commission, peer communication, or untrusted source changing attack potency, and the code and traces are open-sourced.

papers.title: UDHRBench: Benchmarking Human Rights in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in contexts requiring adherence to ethical and legal norms, yet their alignment with internationally recognized human rights standards remains underexplored. We introduce UDHRBench, a large-scale benchmark for operationalising the evaluation of large language model compliance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The dataset comprises 1,124 human rights confronting questions covering all 30 articles and 4,496 responses from four large language models (ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, and Fanar), manually annotated by experts for alignment, with high inter-annotator agreement ($\kappa = 0.801$). Our analysis reveals systematic and non-trivial misalignments, showing that violations typically arise through seemingly rational reasoning: appeals to efficiency, risk management, or scientific neutrality, rather than explicit rejection of rights. We further propose an LLM-as-a-Judge framework for automated evaluation using zero-shot and few-shot prompting, achieving 89.8\% weighted F1-score in detecting human-rights misalignment, alongside a novel Alignment Leniency Score that quantifies how judge models resolve ambiguous cases. The dataset, annotations, and code will be released as open-source resources (https://sina.birzeit.edu/UDHRBench).
authors: Serin Atiani (Princess Sumaya University for Technology
papers.summary: Large language models increasingly operate where ethical and legal norms apply, yet their alignment with international human rights standards has had little systematic evaluation. `UDHRBench` contains 1,124 questions that confront models with human rights situations across all 30 articles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, plus 4,496 responses from `ChatGPT`, `Grok`, `Gemini`, and `Fanar` annotated by experts for alignment with high inter-annotator agreement (kappa of 0.801). **Misalignments are systematic and typically emerge through seemingly rational reasoning such as appeals to efficiency, risk management, or scientific neutrality rather than explicit rejection of rights.** An LLM-as-a-judge framework reaches 89.8% weighted F1 in detecting such misalignment, and a new Alignment Leniency Score quantifies how judge models resolve ambiguous cases, with the dataset and code to be released.

papers.title: Continuous Risk-Based Scheduling for Food Safety Inspection: Integrating Historical Decay with Event-Driven Consumer Review Signals
papers.abstract: Batch risk-based inspection scheduling struggles to detect a critical failure class: food facilities with recent clean inspections that subsequently develop severe violations. Traditional systems recompute risk on fixed planning cycles using static historical data, leaving blind spots between inspection cycles. To address this, we introduce the Continuous Inspection Risk (CIR) system, an event-driven scheduling pipeline that re-ranks the inspection queue dynamically as new data arrives. CIR combines a decay-weighted historical score with a stream of real-time consumer reviews triaged by a language-model classifier. A key structural contribution is our temporal partition rule, which strictly excludes reviews predating the most recent inspection to prevent superseded signals from skewing current risk. Evaluating CIR on 9,505 routine inspections in Santa Clara County, California (2024-2026), we show that history-based scoring alone reduces mean time-to-detection of major violations by 69 days (20.9%) under a 30% inspection budget, but fails to anticipate severe vermin-related closures (0/8 detected). Incorporating post-inspection review signals drastically improves performance, predicting 7 of 8 vermin closures with an average lead time of 117 days-firing on the exact day of review publication in four instances. Introducing a review corroboration rule improves precision from 0.70 to 0.78 without loss of recall. Finally, we analyze critical implementation challenges, documenting a data-hygiene pitfall (stale review leakage across inspection boundaries) and an evaluation limitation involving unobserved facility self-remediation. This work provides the first case-level evaluation of event-driven inspection triggering using open data and provides a reproducible benchmark for review-augmented public health systems
papers.summary: Batch risk-based scheduling of food safety inspections misses facilities that pass a recent inspection and then develop severe violations, because risk is recomputed only on fixed cycles from static history. The Continuous Inspection Risk (`CIR`) system re-ranks the inspection queue as events arrive, combining a decay-weighted historical score with real-time consumer reviews triaged by a language-model classifier, and applies a temporal partition rule that excludes reviews predating the latest inspection so superseded signals do not skew current risk. On 9,505 routine inspections in Santa Clara County from 2024 to 2026, history-based scoring alone cuts mean time-to-detection of major violations by 69 days under a 30% inspection budget but catches none of 8 vermin-related closures, whereas adding post-inspection review signals **predicts 7 of 8 vermin closures with an average lead time of 117 days**, and a review corroboration rule lifts precision from 0.70 to 0.78 at no cost in recall. The authors also document a stale-review leakage pitfall and an evaluation limitation from unobserved facility self-remediation.

papers.title: SocraticRepair: Planning-Guided Socratic Tutoring for Program Debugging and Misconception Repair
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in computer science education. However, the teaching abilities of even the most powerful LLMs are limited: they tend to reveal the solution prematurely and may lose focus on the learner's current debugging objective. To address this, we introduce SocraticRepair, a planning-guided Socratic tutoring framework for program debugging and miscon- ception repair that adapts prior planning-guided tutoring work (Li et al., 2026b). The framework is instantiated in the Python programming domain by fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on synthetic multi-turn tutoring dialogues constructed from four preprocessed programming datasets. The system is evaluated using a predefined set of independent metrics and benchmarked against a general-purpose LLM. The experiments show that SocraticRepair achieves higher scores on stepwise scaffolding and question quality while also substantially reducing premature solution disclosure. The results also identify reliable pedagogical plan generation as an important remaining challenge.
