papers.summary: Large language models used as programming tutors tend to reveal the solution too early and drift from the learner's current debugging goal. `SocraticRepair` is a planning-guided Socratic tutoring framework for program debugging and misconception repair, adapted from prior planning-guided tutoring work and instantiated for Python by fine-tuning `Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct` on synthetic multi-turn tutoring dialogues built from four preprocessed programming datasets. Against a general-purpose LLM on a predefined set of independent metrics, it **scores higher on stepwise scaffolding and question quality while substantially reducing premature solution disclosure**, and reliable generation of pedagogical plans is identified as the main open challenge.

papers.title: Exploring Jailbreak Vulnerability Across Depth-Based Dynamic Inference in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been shown to be computationally expensive and vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, in which adversarial prompts bypass safety alignment and induce harmful responses. To address this inefficiency, a range of techniques have been proposed to enable efficient LLM inference. Depth-based dynamic inference has demonstrated promising results by enabling outputs to be generated from intermediate layers. It offers the flexibility to adjust model behavior based on the available resource budget. However, how this flexibility affects the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap via a comprehensive investigation into the impact of depth-based dynamic inference on the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Specifically, we make the following key observations: 1) Shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreak attacks than deeper ones; 2) Exit depth affects how easily the adversarial suffix can be optimized, with deeper exits reaching lower attack loss; and 3) Adversarial suffixes affect utility uniformly across exit depths. These insights can help design dynamic inference methodologies that are more robust to jailbreak attacks. Code is available at https://github.com/LassNajmuldeen/balcony-jailbreaking
papers.summary: Depth-based dynamic inference lets a large language model emit outputs from intermediate layers to fit a compute budget, but its effect on robustness to jailbreak attacks, where adversarial prompts bypass safety alignment, had not been examined. The study evaluates jailbreak attacks across exit depths and the optimization of adversarial suffixes against each exit. **Shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreaks than deeper ones**, deeper exits let adversarial suffixes reach lower attack loss, and the suffixes degrade utility uniformly across exit depths, findings offered to guide more robust dynamic-inference designs, with code released.

papers.title: PANINI-DR: Controlled Deep Research through Generative Semantic Workspaces
papers.abstract: Deep research requires connecting multiple steps of search, reasoning, and computation, with intermediate findings guiding what to investigate next. As investigations grow, agents must maintain research state across model calls and check findings before errors propagate into subsequent work. We introduce PANINI-DR, a multi-agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from the research and verification of individual subquestions. A shared workspace, built on the Generative Semantic Workspace representation, records subquestions, their dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence. Researchers investigate individual subquestions, while a separate verification agent checks proposed answers against those subquestions and their evidence. Verification feedback guides further investigation, and recorded findings inform subsequent assignments. We evaluate PANINI-DR on BrowseComp-Plus, FRAMES, and MoNaCo against seven state-of-the-art deep-research harnesses, all using a shared language-model backbone and frozen corpora. PANINI-DR achieves the strongest average performance across the three benchmarks. On BrowseComp-Plus, it achieves 73.3% accuracy, outperforming the next-best harness by 16.0 points. Its advantage is strongest on hard questions, where it answers nearly twice as many as the next-best harness. Ablations further show that structured planning and persistent state improve performance, as does checking each finding against its cited evidence before it is reused. Because a model can answer correctly from memory alone, we also analyze the evidence retained by each harness. PANINI-DR achieves the highest answer recoverability from saved evidence on all three benchmarks, while complementary claim-support audits show stronger evidence-backed answers. Accounting for this evidence changes how harnesses compare and further strengthens PANINI-DR's advantage.
papers.summary: Deep research agents must carry state across many search, reasoning, and computation steps and catch errors before they propagate into later work. `PANINI-DR` is a multi-agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from research on individual subquestions, using a shared workspace built on the `Generative Semantic Workspace` representation to record subquestions, dependencies, findings, and evidence, with a dedicated verification agent that checks each proposed answer against its cited evidence before it is reused. Against seven deep-research harnesses sharing the same language-model backbone and frozen corpora, it posts the strongest average across `BrowseComp-Plus`, `FRAMES`, and `MoNaCo`, **reaching 73.3% accuracy on `BrowseComp-Plus`, 16.0 points above the next-best harness**, with the largest gains on hard questions, where it answers nearly twice as many. An evidence analysis also shows it retains the most saved evidence from which answers can be recovered, so accounting for whether answers are backed by retrieved evidence rather than model memory widens its lead.

papers.title: Running Fewer Loops Removes Refusal Behaviour in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
papers.abstract: A recurrent-depth language model reuses one block of weights several times in a row. The number of repetitions, which we call loops, is chosen when the model runs, not when it is trained, and running fewer is cheaper and faster, so a deployment may choose to do it. Running fewer loops also makes these models less safe, and the loss of safety is larger than the loss of anything else we measured. We study four released Ouro checkpoints and Huginn-0125. At half of its trained depth, Ouro-1.4B-Thinking still solves 0.692 of the GSM8K maths problems, against 0.775 at full depth, keeping 89% of its accuracy. Over the same reduction, the rate at which it helps with harmful requests rises from 0.038 to 0.205, 5.3 times higher. The information is not lost: a linear classifier reads whether a request is harmful from the model's internal state after a single loop, with an ROC AUC of 0.967 against 0.986 at full depth. What the missing loops remove is the refusal that should follow. We measure the effect with four instruments, one generating no text at all, and reproduce it on a second model family. Removing a single direction from Ouro-1.4B's internal state at full depth drops its refusal rate on harmful prompts from 0.950 to 0.130, identifying what the shallow model is missing. Two run-time repairs do not help: the models' early-exit rules do not spend more loops on harmful requests, and choosing a depth per request does not recover the loss. Changing the training does. Standard safety training makes the shallow model safe only by refusing 0.865 of harmless requests, while training at randomly chosen depths reaches a separation of +0.399 between harmful and harmless refusal at one loop, against +0.118. On Huginn-0125 it keeps harmful help at or below 0.040 at every depth from 1 to 32 loops, where standard training reaches 0.194, and it costs no accuracy at full depth.
papers.summary: Recurrent-depth language models reuse a single block of weights for a number of loops chosen at inference time, so a deployment can trade accuracy for speed by running fewer of them. Studying four `Ouro` checkpoints and `Huginn-0125`, the authors find that safety degrades far faster than capability: **at half its trained depth, `Ouro-1.4B-Thinking` keeps 89% of its `GSM8K` accuracy while its rate of helping with harmful requests rises 5.3 times, from 0.038 to 0.205**. A linear probe still reads harmfulness from the internal state after a single loop with an ROC AUC of 0.967, and removing one direction at full depth collapses refusal on harmful prompts from 0.950 to 0.130, indicating that shallow runs lose the refusal behaviour rather than the recognition of harm. Run-time fixes such as early-exit rules or per-request depth selection do not recover safety, and standard safety training makes the shallow model safe only by refusing most harmless requests, whereas training at randomly chosen depths keeps harmful compliance at or below 0.040 at every depth on `Huginn-0125` with no accuracy cost at full depth.

papers.title: HarnessNet: Feedback-driven Hierarchical Joint Harness Evolution for Multi-agent Systems
papers.abstract: AI agents can evolve by using environment feedback to revise their harnesses, the software managing model inputs, tool use, memory, and execution, while keeping foundation models frozen. Existing studies focus on single agents, leaving joint harness evolution in multi-agent systems (MAS) underexplored. A single global optimizer faces growing context and workload as the system scales, while access restrictions may prevent sharing agent internals or system-wide feedback. We propose HarnessNet, a framework for hierarchical harness evolution in MAS. Its basic unit, Agentron, comprises an evolvable forward harness, a foundation model, and a local optimizer that can observe and modify only that harness. Agentrons form a layered graph through which environment feedback propagates backward, with upstream optimizers receiving node-specific feedback from the downstream layer. This decomposes joint harness evolution into smaller, coordinated tasks with separate contexts, reducing individual optimizers' context and workload while keeping access local. Optimizers need not access all agent trajectories or raw environment feedback. Experiments on AgentBench with multiple foundation models demonstrate the feasibility of training HarnessNet. Compared with a single global optimizer, HarnessNet achieves comparable performance gains while respecting local privacy and requiring fewer tokens and less time per optimizer call. A migration study shows that the evolved harnesses remain jointly effective after replacing the foundation models, suggesting transferability across models.
papers.summary: Agents can improve by using environment feedback to revise their harness, the software that manages model inputs, tools, memory, and execution, while the foundation model stays frozen, but prior work covers single agents, and a single global optimizer for a multi-agent system (MAS) faces growing context and may be barred from seeing other agents' internals. `HarnessNet` organizes a MAS as a layered graph of `Agentron` units, each pairing a frozen model and an evolvable harness with a local optimizer that can only observe and edit that harness, and propagates environment feedback backward so each upstream optimizer receives node-specific feedback from the layer below. On `AgentBench` with several foundation models, **the hierarchical scheme matches the performance gains of a single global optimizer while using fewer tokens and less time per optimizer call and keeping agent internals private**. A migration study finds the evolved harnesses stay jointly effective after the underlying foundation models are swapped.

papers.title: Understanding Unified VLMs: From Attention Probing to Guidance Tuning for Multimodal Generation
papers.abstract: Unified vision-language models (VLMs) perform both text-to-image (T2I) and image-to-text (I2T) generation with one shared Transformer backbone, yet how the backbone processes the condition in either direction remains poorly understood. We study this question from the perspective of conditional guidance: we probe every attention head to show the activation difference between two branches of classifier-free guidance (CFG) with different conditional guidance. On two unified VLMs of autoregressive and masked-diffusion paradigms, the probing reveals a subset of heads that are more sensitive to the change of condition while others are agnostic to it. This characteristic pattern holds in both T2I and I2T generation and is largely stable across data samples, demonstrating the internal mechanism of unified VLMs. Motivated by this, we propose a new inference-time intervention approach for unified multimodal generation, named \textit{HeadTuned-CFG}, which uses the probed condition-change awareness to select and tune the conditional guidance at the attention-head level. Experiments show consistent benefits in both multimodal generation directions of unified VLMs without additional training, and in particular substantial improvements over strong baselines in T2I generation. These results further support the key finding of our probing analysis: the observed pattern of functional specialization is an intrinsic property of unified VLMs.
papers.summary: Unified vision-language models (VLMs) handle both text-to-image (T2I) and image-to-text (I2T) generation with one shared Transformer, but how that backbone processes the conditioning input in each direction is unclear. The authors probe every attention head by measuring activation differences between the two branches of classifier-free guidance (CFG) on an autoregressive and a masked-diffusion unified VLM, finding **a consistent subset of heads that is sensitive to changes in the condition while the rest are condition-agnostic**, a pattern that holds in both generation directions and is stable across samples. Building on this, `HeadTuned-CFG` selects and tunes conditional guidance at the level of individual heads at inference time, yielding gains in both directions without training and notably larger improvements over strong baselines in T2I generation.

papers.title: Words to World: Benchmarking LLMs in Interactive Physical Environments
papers.abstract: Words are increasingly becoming an interface for action: large language models (LLMs) can now invoke tools, operate devices, and make decisions that affect the physical world. However, current benchmarks largely evaluate LLMs through static text responses, offline tool calls, or simulated tasks, leaving open the question of how well they can act in real physical environments. We present a benchmark for measuring LLMs in closed-loop physical interaction, where models control a harness system connected to real-world components including robotic arms, cameras, and sensors. In each task, the model must issue instructions, receive physical feedback from the environment, interpret the resulting state, and adapt its next action accordingly. This setting evaluates capabilities beyond language understanding, including grounded perception, action planning, tool selection, spatial reasoning, feedback-driven correction, and robustness to execution uncertainty. Through experiments with representative LLMs, we characterize their ability to translate linguistic reasoning into physical actions and identify common failure modes such as hallucinated state changes, poor recovery from unexpected outcomes, and unstable long-horizon plans. Our benchmark aims to provide a systematic foundation for evaluating LLMs as interactive agents that connect words, tools, and the physical world.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) mostly rely on static text answers, offline tool calls, or simulation, leaving open how well the models act in real physical settings. The proposed benchmark places an LLM in closed-loop control of a harness connected to real robotic arms, cameras, and sensors, where each task requires issuing instructions, reading physical feedback, interpreting the resulting state, and adapting the next action, exercising grounded perception, action planning, tool selection, spatial reasoning, feedback-driven correction, and robustness to execution uncertainty. Experiments with representative LLMs **surface recurring failure modes including hallucinated state changes, poor recovery from unexpected outcomes, and unstable long-horizon plans**.

papers.title: Using Evidence-Centered Design to Guide Prompt Engineering in Measurement: An Illustration with Automated Essay Scoring
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) models, particularly large language models (LLMs), are increasingly used in educational settings for tasks such as item generation, automated scoring, and feedback delivery. The quality of these outputs depends not only on the AI model but also on how users construct the prompts that guide model behaviors. Current prompt engineering practices are largely ad hoc, relying on trial and error rather than principled design. This lack of structure introduces validity threats including construct misrepresentation, construct-irrelevant variance, and limited reproducibility. We propose that Evidence-Centered Design (ECD), a framework in educational measurement for structuring valid inferences from observed performance, can serve as a principled foundation for prompt engineering in educational applications. We map the three core ECD models, the student model, the evidence model, and the task model, onto the components of educational prompt design, and describe a workflow for ECD-based prompt engineering. We derive five design principles from this mapping and present an empirical study contrasting ECD-designed prompts with state-of-the-art (SOTA) prompting baselines on an automated scoring task. Our empirical study demonstrates the usefulness of this framework on automated scoring. Results suggest that treating prompting as assessment design rather than informal instructions strengthens the validity, reliability, and fairness of AI-generated educational outputs.
papers.summary: Prompt engineering for educational uses of large language models (LLMs), such as automated scoring and feedback, is largely trial and error, which threatens validity through construct misrepresentation, construct-irrelevant variance, and poor reproducibility. The authors propose grounding prompt design in Evidence-Centered Design (ECD), an educational-measurement framework for structuring valid inferences from observed performance, mapping its student, evidence, and task models onto prompt components, deriving five design principles, and describing an ECD-based prompt-engineering workflow. **An empirical study on automated essay scoring reports that ECD-designed prompts compare favourably with state-of-the-art (SOTA) prompting baselines**, and the authors argue that treating prompts as assessment design rather than informal instructions strengthens the validity, reliability, and fairness of AI-generated educational outputs.

papers.title: MoMaTune: Model, Match, Then Tune Language Models for Numerical Records
papers.abstract: Despite remarkable progress in language understanding and generation, decoder language models continue to exhibit striking failures on numerical data. Numerical examples are typically serialized as text by concatenating feature names with their values (e.g., fat:3.4), while conventional task adaptation applies loss only to the downstream prediction target. This leaves two structures weakly supervised: within-value sensitivity, where digit position determines numerical magnitude, because token cross-entropy contains no explicit numerical metric; and across-field structure, where measurements in the same record are statistically dependent, because target-only tuning provides no direct loss on the measurements or their dependencies. We introduce MoMaTune (Model, Match, then Tune), a two-stage post-training strategy organized around these supervision gaps. Stage 1 applies Model, ordinary next-token prediction densely over label-free serialized records, and optionally adds Match, a same-record consistency objective that aligns representations of different partial views of the same example. Stage 2 applies Tune, supervised fine-tuning for downstream target prediction. We evaluate MoMaTune on 169,285 records from eight public datasets, with 339 of 340 input fields numerical. At 1.5B parameters, Model raises the eight-dataset masked-value imputation aggregate from 0.106 to 0.401, while the three-dataset correct-context gain rises from 0.058 to 0.167. On diagnostics, Model also increases sensitivity to numerically consequential digit changes, while Match improves robustness to informative partial views. Adding Tune yields higher target-supervised embedding aggregates for each tested Stage-1 parent, and the two-stage recipes obtain higher aggregate scores than Tune alone. The same pattern is observed at 4B, 9.6B, and 27B parameters when model embeddings are used for downstream prediction.
papers.summary: Decoder language models still fail on numerical data, partly because records are serialized as feature-name and value text and task adaptation applies loss only to the prediction target, leaving digit-position magnitude and cross-field dependencies within a record weakly supervised. `MoMaTune` (Model, Match, then Tune) first trains with dense next-token prediction over label-free serialized records (Model), optionally adds a same-record consistency objective aligning representations of partial views of one example (Match), then applies supervised fine-tuning for the downstream target (Tune). On 169,285 records from eight public datasets with almost all fields numerical, **the Model stage lifts the 1.5B model's eight-dataset masked-value imputation aggregate from 0.106 to 0.401**, raises sensitivity to numerically consequential digit changes, and Match adds robustness to informative partial views. Two-stage recipes beat Tune alone on target-supervised embedding scores, with the same pattern holding at 4B, 9.6B, and 27B parameters.

papers.title: Framework for an AI-Ready ARPES Community Database
papers.abstract: Condensed matter stands to gain profoundly from widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI). However, its current means of data organization impedes this endeavor. As a premier measure of electronic structure underlying material properties, Angle-Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy (ARPES) has accumulated over four decades of spectra, yet the community's publication-centered workflow preserves only a highly selected fraction of its experimental record. A shared data ecosystem could transform these fragmented measurements and their contexts into a persistent, collective scientific memory, creating immediate value for reproducibility and reuse while laying the foundation for AI-enabled discovery. In this Perspective, we report outcomes of a recent community workshop and propose a practical path toward such an ecosystem. Its benefits unfold along three timescales. In the near term, standardized, searchable, and citable datasets strengthen analysis pipelines independently of AI. In the intermediate future, community-validated tools operating across laboratories could enable broader reuse and increasingly closed-loop automated experiments. In the long term, a diverse corpus of measured electronic spectra could support foundation models for quantum matter. Looking forward, a diverse corpus of measured electronic spectra could support foundation models for quantum matter and new discoveries. We discuss lessons from existing scientific databases, the current state of AI in ARPES, as well as areas of community convergence on data organization, access, credit, governance, and a staged pilot program.
papers.summary: Angle-Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy (ARPES) has produced four decades of electronic-structure spectra, yet the publication-centred workflow of condensed matter physics preserves only a small, selected fraction of that record, limiting both reuse and the application of artificial intelligence (AI). Reporting outcomes of a recent community workshop, the authors propose a shared, AI-ready ARPES database and lay out its benefits over three horizons: standardized, searchable, citable datasets that strengthen analysis pipelines now, community-validated cross-laboratory tools enabling closed-loop automated experiments later, and **eventually a diverse corpus of measured spectra capable of supporting foundation models for quantum matter**. The perspective reviews lessons from existing scientific databases and the state of AI in ARPES, and records areas of community convergence on data organization, access, credit, governance, and a staged pilot program.

papers.title: ClinEdge: An Expert-Graded Benchmark of Real Patient Edge Cases Where Frontier Multimodal Models Fail
papers.abstract:
Most benchmarks for large language models in medicine are built from licensing examinations and theoretical questions. The few that draw on real clinical data do so only in part, and rarely require a model to read a patient's own imaging. ClinEdge addresses this gap with 32 real, de-identified patient cases from active clinical practice, each evaluated across seven frontier systems for a total of 224 expert-graded evaluations. Each case pairs primary imaging with a short vignette, contains a feature known to defeat pattern-matched reasoning, and is scored against the patient's documented clinical course. The suite is built for depth rather than volume. Grading followed a two-stage expert process. First, a senior orthopaedic surgeon graded all 224 responses on a weighted rubric and a pass-or-fail verdict. Second, a panel of nineteen physicians, largely senior specialists at teaching medical colleges, independently reviewed every case and every one of the 224 grades. All seven production systems were evaluated through their public interfaces, and all 224 conversations are preserved as replayable links.
  Performance was poor across all systems, and the failures were shared: different vendors missed the same findings and converged on the same wrong plans. From the experts' notes we catalogue 18 recurring failure modes in five families. The models stop reading an image at the first finding. They give generic plans and lean toward over-treatment. They trust a misleading history over correct imaging. Their answers vary across systems and runs, and change with question format. Failing answers were delivered fluently and without any expressed uncertainty. Four cases are released in full; the remaining 28 are held out, and we invite frontier AI labs and healthcare AI companies to evaluate their models against them (research@futrbridge.com)
papers.summary: Most medical benchmarks for large language models are built from licensing exams, and the few using real clinical data rarely require reading a patient's own imaging. `ClinEdge` consists of 32 de-identified cases from active practice, each pairing primary imaging with a short vignette and a feature chosen to defeat pattern-matched reasoning, scored against the patient's documented clinical course, with seven frontier systems evaluated through their public interfaces for 224 responses graded by a senior orthopaedic surgeon and then independently reviewed by a panel of nineteen physicians. **Performance was poor across all seven systems and the failures were shared, with different vendors missing the same findings and converging on the same wrong plans.** The expert notes yield 18 recurring failure modes in five families, including stopping at the first imaging finding, defaulting to generic and over-treating plans, trusting a misleading history over correct imaging, and delivering wrong answers fluently with no expressed uncertainty, and four of the cases are released in full with the remaining 28 held out.

papers.title: EvolvAttack: Backdooring self Evolving VLM Agents
papers.abstract: Self-evolving mechanisms let vision-language model (VLM) agents continually adapt through evolving memory, but they also allow malicious behavior to emerge only after deployment. We introduce a new attack surface, the self-evolving backdoor, whose payload stays dormant in the initial agent and is progressively activated as the agent evolves. Unlike conventional backdoors, which can be exposed by testing triggered inputs on a static model, our attack requires both a visual trigger and a sufficiently evolved memory state; static scanning with clean memory thus yields near-zero attack success and may deem the agent benign. We realize this through memory-aware backdoor training, which couples trigger activation with the agent's evolving memory while preserving benign behavior unless the trigger co-occurs with payload-related memory. Across three VLM backbones, four agent pipelines, and recency-, semantic-, and reward-based memory evolution, the attack preserves normal functionality and stays nearly inactive before evolution (0.5% attack success rate), yet exceeds 95% attack success within 100 interactions, revealing a stealthy threat unique to self-evolving agents.
papers.summary: Self-evolving vision-language model (VLM) agents adapt after deployment by updating their memory, which opens a route for malicious behaviour to appear only once the agent has evolved. The proposed self-evolving backdoor stays dormant in the freshly deployed agent and requires both a visual trigger and a sufficiently evolved memory state, so static scanning of the model with clean memory shows near-zero attack success and may judge the agent benign. It is implemented through memory-aware backdoor training that couples trigger activation to payload-related memory while preserving benign behaviour otherwise. Across three VLM backbones, four agent pipelines, and recency-, semantic-, and reward-based memory evolution, **the attack shows a 0.5% success rate before evolution yet exceeds 95% within 100 interactions** while leaving normal functionality intact.

papers.title: Sequent-Prover: Training Agents for Formal, Checkable SMT-based Reasoning
papers.abstract: We introduce Sequent-Prover, a family of verifier-using language-model agents, and the post-training framework that produces them. Agents reason in an executable SMT-LIB scratchpad: they write complete SMT-LIB programs, query Z3 across turns, inspect solver feedback, repair formalizations, and terminate with an explicit answer. Our recipe, verifier-conditioned trajectory distillation, bootstraps from a noisy teacher proposal policy by sampling multi-turn trajectories, retaining the successful tail that is correct, non-trivial, grounded, and executable, then applying supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-level preference optimization. Because solver success alone does not guarantee semantic faithfulness, we evaluate task accuracy, k-sample reliability, and SMT program quality. Across 37 benchmarks and 7,254 problems per model family, post-training raises the 4B model's per-attempt accuracy from 85.6% to 97.0% and four-sample all-correct reliability (pass^4}) from 64.1% to 91.7%. It also reduces average SMT calls from 4.10 to 2.52 and tokens per attempt from 18.97k to 12.72k. Sequent-Prover agents give answers backed by executable formal artifacts.
papers.summary: To make language-model reasoning checkable, `Sequent-Prover` agents reason in an executable satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) scratchpad written in `SMT-LIB`, composing complete programs, querying the `Z3` solver across turns, repairing formalizations from solver feedback, and ending with an explicit answer backed by a formal artifact. The training recipe, verifier-conditioned trajectory distillation, samples multi-turn trajectories from a noisy teacher, keeps only those that are correct, non-trivial, grounded, and executable, and then applies supervised fine-tuning followed by trajectory-level preference optimization. Because solver success does not guarantee semantic faithfulness, evaluation covers task accuracy, k-sample reliability, and SMT program quality across 37 benchmarks and 7,254 problems per model family. **Post-training raises the 4B model's per-attempt accuracy from 85.6% to 97.0% and its four-sample all-correct reliability from 64.1% to 91.7%**, while cutting average solver calls from 4.10 to 2.52 and tokens per attempt from about 19k to 12.7k.

papers.title: RECAP: Calibrating Low-Bit Reasoning Models on the History They Read
papers.abstract: Low-bit quantization reduces the cost of serving reasoning models but can substantially degrade long chains of thought. Each step reads cached keys and values spanning thousands of tokens, allowing quantization errors to accumulate along the trajectory. Standard calibration operates on short segments that omit the earlier context needed by later reasoning steps. Even when this context is retained, cache reconstruction error alone does not capture how quantization errors affect subsequent attention. We present RECAP, a post-training quantization method that calibrates reasoning models on the history they read. Dynamic-prefix calibration separates long historical context from short-block reconstruction. It regenerates prefix keys and values with the current quantizer and rotates the active block to supervise every position along the trajectory. Prefix read geometry further supervises historical cache errors according to their effects on attention outputs, weighting key and value errors asymmetrically. With both components applied only during calibration, RECAP outperforms the baseline across multiple reasoning models and quantization settings. Under W4A4KV4, RECAP improves accuracy over the baseline by 13.3 percentage points on MATH500 with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and 15.8 points on AIME-120 with Qwen3-4B. These results highlight the importance of preserving historical dependencies during calibration for low-bit reasoning.
papers.summary: Low-bit quantization makes reasoning models cheaper to serve but can badly degrade long chains of thought, because every step reads cached keys and values spanning thousands of tokens and quantization errors accumulate along the trajectory, while standard calibration uses short segments that omit the history later steps depend on. `RECAP` is a post-training quantization method that calibrates on that history: dynamic-prefix calibration regenerates prefix keys and values with the current quantizer and rotates the supervised block so every trajectory position is covered, and prefix read geometry weights key and value cache errors asymmetrically according to their effect on attention outputs. Both components act only during calibration, and **under W4A4KV4 the method improves accuracy over the baseline by 13.3 points on `MATH500` with `DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B` and 15.8 points on `AIME-120` with `Qwen3-4B`**.

papers.title: LeHami: Symplectic Latent Dynamics for World Models
papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models directly in latent space, but unconstrained autoregressive predictors may contract the latent distribution over long rollouts. We introduce Symplectic Hamiltonian JEPA (LeHami), which replaces the standard predictor with an action-conditioned Hamiltonian flow over a structured latent state (q, p) integrated using an exactly symplectic leapfrog step. This construction preserves phase-space volume at every rollout step and rules out uniform contraction, asymptotically stable fixed points, and merging of distinct latent states, independently of the learned parameters or action sequence. We obtain the momentum-like component from temporal derivatives of the learned position-like representation, providing an explicit second-order state for prediction and control. On conservative and actuated visual pendulum environments, LeHami substantially improves long-horizon velocity prediction over an unconstrained JEPA world model and empirically maintains constant latent volume where the baseline contracts. The learned flow also supports accurate integration at unseen sub-frame step sizes and numerical time reversal. These results show how geometric structure can provide inference-time guarantees that are complementary to representation regularization in latent world models.
papers.summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models in latent space, but an unconstrained autoregressive predictor can contract the latent distribution over long rollouts, collapsing distinct states together. `LeHami` (Symplectic Hamiltonian JEPA) replaces the predictor with an action-conditioned Hamiltonian flow over a position-momentum latent state integrated by an exactly symplectic leapfrog step, which preserves phase-space volume at every rollout step and so rules out uniform contraction, asymptotically stable fixed points, and merging of states regardless of learned parameters or action sequence. The momentum-like component is derived from temporal derivatives of the learned position-like representation, giving an explicit second-order state for prediction and control. On conservative and actuated visual pendulum environments, **the model substantially improves long-horizon velocity prediction over an unconstrained JEPA baseline and empirically holds latent volume constant where the baseline contracts**, while also integrating accurately at unseen sub-frame step sizes and supporting numerical time reversal.

papers.title: GeoBridge: Evolving Transferable Decoder Topologies for Geometric Vision
papers.abstract: Depth estimation and Gaussian reconstruction share a need for multi-scale feature processing, yet use different prediction interfaces and training objectives. Whether a decoder's internal computation can be optimized once and reused across these systems remains a structural design question. Search over primitive configurations alone leaves the organization of transformations fixed. To address this gap, we propose GeoBridge, an evolutionary framework for transferable decoder topologies. First, GeoBridge makes stage-internal topology searchable through residual, sequential, and parallel composition of configurable primitives. Shape-preserving composition retains the stage interfaces of a fixed multi-scale scaffold. Second, a functional-tree encoding supports stage-aware crossover and hierarchical mutation, while a gradient sensitivity-alignment proxy evaluates candidates without training. Multi-objective evolution balances this proxy with computation and parameter cost. Third, selected topologies are instantiated and trained in target systems with task-specific prediction interfaces. A single source search takes approximately 12 GPU hours. GeoBridgeNet-A3 achieves the best depth accuracy among four adapted decoder baselines under a common encoder and training protocol on NYU Depth V2 and KITTI. The same topology reaches 27.11 dB PSNR in Gaussian novel-view synthesis on RealEstate10K, and its refined representations support open-vocabulary segmentation on LERF. These results support decoder topology as a reusable design object across the evaluated geometric vision systems. Code and pretrained weights are available at https://github.com/EMI-Group/GeoBridge-NAS.
papers.summary: Depth estimation and Gaussian reconstruction both need multi-scale feature decoding but use different prediction interfaces and training objectives, raising the question of whether a decoder's internal computation can be optimized once and reused across such systems. `GeoBridge` makes stage-internal decoder topology searchable through residual, sequential, and parallel composition of configurable primitives inside a fixed multi-scale scaffold, encodes candidates as functional trees to support stage-aware crossover and hierarchical mutation, and scores them without training using a gradient sensitivity-alignment proxy balanced against compute and parameter cost in a multi-objective evolutionary search that takes about 12 GPU hours. The resulting `GeoBridgeNet-A3` topology **achieves the best depth accuracy among four adapted decoder baselines on `NYU Depth V2` and `KITTI` under a common encoder and training protocol**, reaches 27.11 dB PSNR for Gaussian novel-view synthesis on `RealEstate10K`, and supports open-vocabulary segmentation on `LERF`.

papers.title: North or South? Diagnosing LLMs' Understanding of North Korean Language, Society, and Knowledge
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made substantial progress in multilingual question answering, yet their ability to understand low-resource sociolinguistic contexts remains under-explored. We study North Korea as a unique testbed where decades of division have produced distinct differences from South Korea in vocabulary, orthography, norms, and ideological discourse. We introduce LENS (Language and sociocultural Evaluation for North Korean Society), a human-validated benchmark of 1,765 questions evaluating LLMs across three dimensions: linguistic robustness, sociocultural perspective alignment, and domain-specific knowledge. Evaluating diverse recent LLMs, we find a modest performance drop on North Korean language inputs, a larger gap in sociocultural perspective alignment, and severe limitations on domain-specific knowledge. Qualitative analysis reveals that models often conflate formal institutions with lived realities, project liberal-democratic assumptions, or rely on coarse stereotypes. Our results demonstrate that linguistic similarity alone does not guarantee sociocultural or domain-specific understanding, highlighting the critical need for grounded evaluation resources for underrepresented cultural and political contexts.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have improved at multilingual question answering, but their grasp of low-resource sociolinguistic contexts is largely untested, and North Korea offers a case where decades of division have produced vocabulary, orthography, norms, and ideological discourse distinct from South Korea. `LENS` (Language and sociocultural Evaluation for North Korean Society) is a human-validated benchmark of 1,765 questions covering linguistic robustness, sociocultural perspective alignment, and domain-specific knowledge. Across diverse recent LLMs, **the authors find a modest performance drop on North Korean language inputs, a larger gap in sociocultural perspective alignment, and severe limitations on domain-specific knowledge**. Qualitative analysis shows models conflating formal institutions with lived realities, projecting liberal-democratic assumptions, or leaning on coarse stereotypes, indicating that linguistic similarity does not confer sociocultural or factual understanding.

papers.title: Protein Crystallization Segmentation and Classification Using Subordinate Color Channel in Fluorescence Microscopy Images
papers.abstract: The accuracy of detecting protein crystals for fluorescence microscopy images is very critical for high throughput and automated systems. Although the trace fluorescent labeling method could highlight protein crystals, reflection and emission from the fluorescence dye is not always due to crystal regions. Therefore, the analysis of the peak wavelength in the emission spectra of a fluorophore may not always yield effective results. In this paper, we show that using the subordinate color intensity corresponding to longer wavelengths than the peak wavelength of the emission spectra could improve the accuracy of protein crystal detection. Hence, we have built a segmentation method based on the percentile intensity of the subordinate color for trace fluorescently labeled (TFL'd) protein crystallization trial images. Compared to using the dominant color channel, our segmentation method on subordinate color channel was able to reduce the misclassification rate of likely-leads or crystals as non-crystals by the percentage of from 9.71% to 2.02% depending on the classifier. Similarly, the accuracy of classifiers were increased by the percentage of from 1.77% to 5.53%. Our method reached around 94% accuracy while keeping misclassification of likely-leads and crystals as non-crystals below 1%. Moreover, to evaluate the generalizability of our method, we have conducted new wet lab experiments on two proteins, Concanavalin A (Con A) and Ab inorganic pyrophosphate (AbIPPase), and the misclassification rate was below 1%. Our experiments show that using the subordinate channel may be more helpful for TFL'd protein trial image classification.
papers.summary: Detecting protein crystals in fluorescence microscopy images is critical for high-throughput crystallization screening, but with trace fluorescent labeling (TFL) the dye's emission at its peak wavelength does not always correspond to crystal regions. The authors instead segment images using percentile intensity in the subordinate colour channel, corresponding to wavelengths longer than the emission peak, and feed the result to crystal classifiers. Compared with the dominant channel, **the subordinate-channel segmentation cut misclassification of crystals and likely leads as non-crystals by between 2.02 and 9.71 percentage points depending on the classifier**, raised classifier accuracy by 1.77 to 5.53 points, and reached about 94% accuracy while keeping that misclassification below 1%. New wet-lab experiments on Concanavalin A and AbIPPase likewise kept the misclassification rate below 1%.

papers.title: Co-DSL: Human-LLM Co-design of Reusable Spatial Concepts for Layout Generation
papers.abstract: We present Co-DSL, a framework in which users and LLMs co-design reusable spatial concepts for layout generation. In the first stage, our system allows users to create a library of personalized operations. To add a concept, a user provides a description, which the LLM converts into an initial implementation. The user can then observe the concept's execution behavior over example scenarios and provide lightweight feedback to the LLM, which revises the concept's implementation logic. In the second stage, given a library, an LLM can author a layout program that meets a new layout request from a user. Executing a layout program instantiates a concept-graph, a declarative composition of library concepts. In this way, we require the LLM only to specify which concepts should hold, while we use a solver to search for a layout that satisfies them. Across five spatial layout domains, we find that Co-DSL libraries let LLMs capture layout patterns that are challenging for prior fixed-operation systems, and demonstrate that our concept-graph representation is needed for LLMs to reliably compose concepts together. We further find that Co-DSL lets LLMs author generative layout programs that expose high-level parametric controls users can manipulate to explore a distribution of related layouts without re-prompting.
papers.summary: Layout generation systems built on fixed operation libraries struggle to express the spatial patterns particular users care about. `Co-DSL` lets a user build a personal library of reusable spatial concepts: the user describes a concept, a large language model (LLM) writes an initial implementation, and the user watches its behaviour on example scenarios and gives lightweight feedback that the LLM uses to revise the logic. Given such a library, the LLM answers a new layout request by writing a layout program whose execution instantiates a concept-graph, a declarative composition of library concepts, and a solver then searches for a layout satisfying them, so the LLM only has to specify which concepts should hold. Across five spatial layout domains, **the libraries let LLMs capture layout patterns that defeat prior fixed-operation systems**, the concept-graph representation proves necessary for reliable composition, and the LLM can author generative programs exposing high-level parameters that users adjust to explore related layouts without re-prompting.

papers.title: OntoAR-HAR: Ontology-Guided Agentic RAG with Personalized Memory for Human Activity Recognition
papers.abstract: LLMs increasingly support sensor-based human activity recognition (HAR) by linking motion signals with activity semantics and physical knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds decisions in sensor examples and domain features, enabling training-free target-user inference with less dependence on raw numerical arrays. However, existing LLM/RAG-based HAR typically searches single-level activity spaces using static population knowledge. Consequently, they compare many unrelated candidates using the same static population evidence and overlook personalized motion patterns. We propose OntoAR-HAR, an ontology-guided agentic RAG framework combining static population and personalized knowledge. Its tree-structured activity ontology decomposes classification into local decisions among semantically related activities. The static store supplies node-constrained examples, while offline-discovered executable signal features provide numerical evidence for local distinctions. During inference, the personalized store collects selected user observations, which the LLM integrates with static knowledge and signal features while traversing the ontology to an activity label. Cross-subject and heterogeneous-sensing experiments show complementary gains from hierarchical retrieval and personalized memory across multiple LLM backbones, achieving state-of-the-art performance. By explicitly modeling hierarchical relations across activity granularities, OntoAR-HAR also addresses the long-overlooked semantic inclusion problem and avoids treating related labels as independent categories.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can perform sensor-based human activity recognition (HAR) without training on the target user, but existing approaches search a single flat activity space with static population knowledge, comparing many unrelated candidates and ignoring personal motion patterns. `OntoAR-HAR` arranges activities in a tree-structured ontology so classification decomposes into local decisions among semantically related activities, pairs a static store of node-constrained examples and offline-discovered executable signal features with a personalized store of accumulated user observations, and has the LLM integrate both while traversing the tree to a label. Cross-subject and heterogeneous-sensing experiments **show complementary gains from hierarchical retrieval and personalized memory across several LLM backbones, reaching state-of-the-art accuracy**, and the hierarchy also addresses the semantic inclusion problem of treating nested activity labels as independent categories.

papers.title: HGA-Quant: Heterogeneity-Aware Quantization for AutoRegressive Visual Generation Models
papers.abstract: Recently, AutoRegressive Visual Generation (ARVG) models have emerged as a competitive paradigm for high-quality image synthesis. However, their substantial computational and memory demands make them difficult to deploy on resource-constrained edge devices. Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) provides a promising solution to reduce the computational and memory costs of ARVG models, yet existing methods often suffer from substantial image quality degradation under low-bit quantization. In this paper, we propose a training-free PTQ framework for ARVG, consisting of Tail-Aware Bounded-init Grid Refinement (T-BGR) and Coarse-to-Fine Activation Precision Scheduling (CAPS). T-BGR introduces a tail-aware reconstruction objective for weight quantizer calibration, assigning greater importance to distribution-tail coefficients and preserving fine-grained information without introducing additional parameters or high-precision branches. CAPS performs coarse-to-fine activation precision scheduling by jointly considering the importance and computational cost of different generation stages, enabling efficient mixed-precision allocation under a given bit budget. Extensive experiments on multiple ARVG backbones demonstrate that our framework consistently improves robustness under aggressive low-bit quantization. Notably, on Infinity, our framework achieves near full-precision image generation quality at an effective W4A5.6 activation precision, while existing methods at W4A6 still exhibit noticeable quality degradation or inconsistent performance. Code is available at https://github.com/lxm-lc/HGA-Quant.
papers.summary: AutoRegressive Visual Generation (ARVG) models produce high-quality images but are too heavy for edge devices, and existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods lose much image quality at low bit-widths. The proposed training-free framework combines Tail-Aware Bounded-init Grid Refinement (`T-BGR`), which calibrates weight quantizers with a reconstruction objective that upweights distribution-tail coefficients to preserve fine detail without extra parameters or high-precision branches, with Coarse-to-Fine Activation Precision Scheduling (`CAPS`), which allocates mixed activation precision across generation stages according to their importance and compute cost under a bit budget. Across multiple ARVG backbones the method improves robustness to aggressive quantization, and **on `Infinity` it reaches near full-precision generation quality at an effective W4A5.6 setting, where prior methods at W4A6 still show visible degradation**.

papers.title: CHEAR: Confusion-Hierarchy Evidence-Aware Reasoning for Cost-Efficient Human Activity Recognition
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a new approach to wearable-sensor-based human activity recognition. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) further introduces similar motion examples and discriminative sensor knowledge, enabling decisions grounded in observations relevant to the current query. More evidence, however, does not necessarily mean better-organized evidence. When online prompts and LLM agents primarily orchestrate inference, decisions about which activities to compare and when to invoke discriminative knowledge remain concentrated at inference time. As the activity vocabulary grows, the model must repeatedly process more candidates and associated knowledge, whereas pruning candidates too early risks excluding the true activity. We propose confusion-hierarchy evidence-aware reasoning (CHEAR), which moves part of this knowledge organization offline. CHEAR constructs and validates an activity hierarchy from recurrent cross-subject retrieval errors and builds corresponding activity-pair knowledge. At inference time, the hierarchy orders candidate comparisons; the LLM retains candidates progressively, and local discriminative knowledge is accessed only for the remaining activities. Across eight datasets, CHEAR achieves 86.79\% mean cross-subject accuracy, a 75.91\% candidate reduction rate, and 96.44\% true-activity retention. Per-sample token use is 85.15\% lower on average than in a variant without the hierarchical structure. Mean accuracy across eight cross-dataset transfer directions is 88.81\%. These results show that organizing candidates and discriminative knowledge around observed activity confusions reduces online LLM input while maintaining recognition performance.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can classify wearable-sensor activities using similar motion examples and discriminative sensor knowledge, but deciding which activities to compare and when to invoke that knowledge happens entirely at inference time, so prompt size grows with the activity vocabulary while early pruning risks dropping the true label. `CHEAR` (confusion-hierarchy evidence-aware reasoning) moves part of this organization offline by building and validating an activity hierarchy from recurrent cross-subject retrieval errors along with activity-pair knowledge, then at inference uses the hierarchy to order candidate comparisons, retain candidates progressively, and fetch local discriminative knowledge only for those remaining. Across eight datasets it reaches 86.79% mean cross-subject accuracy with a 75.91% candidate reduction rate and 96.44% true-activity retention, **cutting per-sample token use by 85.15% on average relative to a variant without the hierarchy**, and averages 88.81% accuracy over eight cross-dataset transfer directions.

papers.title: WisdomNet: trustable machine learning toward error-free classification
papers.abstract: Misclassification is a critical problem in many machine learning applications. Since even the classifier models with high accuracy (e.g., > 95%) still introduce some misclassification error, it may not be possible to rely on the output of a classifier. In this paper, we introduce trustable learning, which prompts the learning model to yield only the true output, thus avoiding misclassifications. Whenever the model cannot decide the output accurately, the learning model should indicate that there could be a misclassification error if it is forced to classify, and hence, it should reject to make a decision or defer it to a human expert. Therefore, we develop a methodology for trustable learning and apply it to artificial neural networks and show that it is possible to develop a classifier with 0% misclassification error. We propose a novel neural network architecture named WisdomNet that could provide zero prediction error by introducing an additional neuron named as conjugate neuron that would indicate whether the network is able to classify the data correctly or not. The WisdomNet architecture can be applied to any previously built model, and we have evaluated WisdomNet with several network architectures such as multilayer perceptron, convolutional neural network, and deep network on different data sets. The results show that the WisdomNet is able to reduce the classification error rate to 0%, while labeling the data is difficult to classify as `reject' at a low percentage of within around 10%.
papers.summary: Even classifiers with high accuracy still make some misclassifications, which makes their outputs hard to rely on in critical applications. The authors propose 'trustable learning', in which a model yields only outputs it is confident are correct and otherwise rejects the input or defers it to a human expert. `WisdomNet` adds a conjugate neuron to an existing network that signals whether the network can classify an input correctly, and it can be attached to previously built models. Evaluated on multilayer perceptrons, convolutional networks, and deeper networks across several datasets, the architecture **reduces classification error to 0% while rejecting roughly 10% of inputs** as too hard to classify.

papers.title: Accuracy and Uncertainty in Machine Deception Detection (Research White Paper)
papers.abstract: A deception detector is only as useful as the trust its alarms deserve. Like a polygraph, detectors that read a language model's internal activations can catch deceptive responses that look honest. Yet current detectors depend on which layers they read, weaken on broader tests, and do not state how certain their alarms are. This white paper proposes the Machine Deception Detector, which targets both detection accuracy and the uncertainty of detector scores. The detector reads every layer of the language model, learns which tokens carry evidence of deception using only response labels, and calibrates its alarm threshold so that its false--positive rate stays below a prescribed level. An ensemble of such detectors measures the uncertainty of each score and raises an alarm only when its members agree, with a confidence level that sets how certain each alarm must be. The proposed evaluation trains on instructed honest and deceptive statements, tests on five unseen deceptive tasks of Liars' Bench read by six Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B parameters, and is designed to also show which layers carry the deception feature and how this changes with model size.
papers.summary: Probes that read a language model's internal activations can flag deceptive responses that look honest, but existing detectors depend on which layers they read, degrade on broader tests, and give no sense of how certain each alarm is. The proposed `Machine Deception Detector` reads every layer, learns which tokens carry deception evidence from response-level labels alone, and calibrates its threshold so the **false-positive rate stays below a prescribed level**. An ensemble of such detectors measures the uncertainty of each score and only raises an alarm when its members agree at a chosen confidence level. The planned evaluation trains on instructed honest and deceptive statements and tests on five unseen tasks from `Liars' Bench` across six `Qwen3` models from 0.6B to 32B parameters, with the aim of also mapping which layers carry the deception feature and how that shifts with model size.

papers.title: SuperAI: Merging Capabilities Across Heterogeneous Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Enabling the reuse and composition of knowledge and capabilities distributed across foundation models is an important step toward building scalable artificial intelligence (AI) systems. However, architectural differences and incompatible representations make it difficult to transfer and integrate these capabilities through a unified cross-model interface. To address this challenge, we propose SuperAI, a cross-architecture multi-model fusion framework that integrates complementary capabilities from multiple source models into a host model through orthogonal alignment of low-dimensional task-relevant representations. Specifically, we first extract task-relevant representations from the source models and the host model using shared anchor samples, and apply principal component analysis (PCA) to construct low-dimensional functional subspaces with the same dimensionality. Next, we use orthogonal Procrustes mappings to align the source and host coordinate systems, establishing cross-model correspondences while preserving the internal geometry of each source subspace. Finally, we train a lightweight residual multilayer perceptron (MLP) with joint supervision on task outputs and source-model increments, learning input-dependent residual increments that are injected into the host model for multi-model capability fusion. Experiments on three host models across 15 capability domains show that SuperAI achieves higher average domain scores than the evaluated cross-architecture fusion methods and better preserves general capabilities as the number of source models increases. Ablation studies further support the effectiveness of orthogonal alignment, nonlinear residual mapping, and joint supervision.
papers.summary: Reusing capabilities spread across different foundation models is hard because architectural differences and incompatible representations block transfer through a shared interface. `SuperAI` fuses complementary capabilities from several source models into a host model: it extracts task-relevant representations on shared anchor samples, reduces them with principal component analysis (PCA) to subspaces of equal dimension, aligns source and host coordinates with orthogonal Procrustes mappings, and trains a lightweight residual multilayer perceptron (MLP) to inject input-dependent increments into the host. On three host models across **15 capability domains, it reaches higher average domain scores than the compared cross-architecture fusion methods** and better preserves general capabilities as more source models are added. Ablations attribute the gains to the orthogonal alignment, the nonlinear residual mapping, and joint supervision on task outputs and source-model increments.

papers.title: Anchor-and-Harvest Curriculum: A Fully Unmasked Non-LLM Curriculum for Craftax
papers.abstract: We introduce Anchor-and-Harvest Curriculum (AHC), a domain-informed, rule-based training system for Craftax-Full. AHC combines achievement-oriented tasks, harvested initial-state progress, difficulty adaptation, bounded selection, and original-task practice. It uses no LLM inference and keeps all 43 actions available. At 2,005,401,600 PPO rollout transitions, three primary AHC runs obtain native-task return $46.70\pm0.57$ (sample SD), compared with $41.91\pm1.01$ for fresh native PPO-GTrXL with the same student architecture and evaluation protocol. Evaluation uses ten stochastic rollouts on each of 1024 fixed worlds per model. An additional cohort of three AHC runs reaches $46.08\pm1.23$. Two single-component ablations retain similar mean returns, while jointly freezing difficulty and removing inherited progress gives $45.14\pm2.79$. All-67-achievement profiles show that most of the return difference comes from Intermediate achievements, while the deepest-floor achievements remain unsolved. A Skill-Preflight diagnosis with a 14B teacher shows how prerequisite and floor-access constraints restrict practice. AHC and three 14B diagnostic configurations reach aggregate returns near the reported 80B DiCode mean of 45.88 and below the 235B mean of 48.55. These results show that an explicit curriculum without LLM inference can reach returns comparable to those reported for LLM-generated curricula on Craftax-Full, without action masking.
papers.summary: Curricula for the open-ended `Craftax-Full` environment have recently relied on large language models to generate tasks, often with action masking to simplify exploration. The `Anchor-and-Harvest Curriculum` (`AHC`) is instead a rule-based system that combines achievement-oriented tasks, harvested initial states that inherit progress, difficulty adaptation, bounded task selection, and practice on the original task, using no LLM inference and keeping all 43 actions available. After about 2 billion `PPO` rollout transitions, **three AHC runs reach a native-task return of 46.70 versus 41.91 for fresh native `PPO-GTrXL`** with the same student architecture, with most of the gain coming from intermediate achievements while the deepest-floor achievements remain unsolved. These returns sit near the reported 45.88 mean of the 80B-parameter `DiCode` LLM curriculum and below the 48.55 of its 235B variant, showing that an explicit curriculum can match LLM-generated ones without action masking.

papers.title: ZOIF: Zeroth-Order Influence Function Estimation for LLM Data Selection Using Only Forward Passes
papers.abstract: Influence functions enable principled data selection for large language models (e.g., identifying influential training samples for model editing, debugging, or efficient fine-tuning). However, scaling IFs to LLMs is hindered by the intractability of billion-scale Hessian matrices and the prohibitive memory overhead of backpropagation (BP). While many classical IF approximations reduce Hessian complexity, they still rely on BP for gradient computation, requiring massive storage for intermediate activations that impedes practical data selection at scale. To address this, we propose ZOIF, a zeroth-order framework for influence estimation that operates entirely via forward passes, enabling memory-efficient data selection under resource constraints. ZOIF decomposes influence estimation into three BP-free stages: (1) approximating the average proxy gradient via zeroth-order estimation; (2) reformulating and solving the inverse Hessian-vector product as an auxiliary zeroth-order optimization to bypass explicit inversion; and (3) deriving per-sample influence scores via a forward finite difference along the previously computed parameter update direction. Experiments show that ZOIF selects data subsets with downstream utility competitive with, and in some cases exceeding, the evaluated baselines, yet at substantially lower peak memory cost and with comparable overall computation time.
papers.summary: Influence functions (IFs) identify which training samples most affect a model's behavior, which supports data selection for fine-tuning, editing, and debugging, but applying them to large language models is blocked by billion-scale Hessians and the activation memory that backpropagation (BP) requires. `ZOIF` estimates influence entirely through forward passes in three stages: a zeroth-order approximation of the average proxy gradient, an auxiliary zeroth-order optimization that solves the inverse Hessian-vector product without explicit inversion, and a forward finite difference along the resulting update direction to score each sample. In experiments, **data subsets selected by ZOIF match or exceed the downstream utility of the evaluated baselines at substantially lower peak memory** and comparable total compute time.

papers.title: MultiFlow: Vision-Driven Multimodal fMRI Encoding via Stimulus-Informed Source Flow Matching
papers.abstract: Current fMRI encoding models frame prediction as deterministic regression, yet identical stimuli evoke a distribution of neural responses (arising from physiological noise, hemodynamic variability, and cognitive fluctuations) that a single point estimate cannot capture. This work introduces MultiFlow, a generative fMRI encoding framework based on Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) and a formulation termed Stimulus-Informed Source Flow Matching (SISFM). SISFM generalises CFM by conditioning the source distribution on the stimulus: a learnable temporal convolution shapes the source mean with an HRF-length receptive field, while a variance head shrinks its scale, shortening the expected transport path. SISFM is instantiated with a Diffusion Transformer (DiT-X) decoder parameterising the velocity field, with sub-layer Attention Residuals, heterogeneous fusion of ten frozen vision, audio, language, and audiovisual backbones, and per-subject Yeo-network heads. On the Algonauts 2025 dataset, a single MultiFlow checkpoint recovers most of the benefit of large deterministic ensembles: it trails the 1000-model TRIBE ensemble in-distribution by 0.003 PCC (0.3163 vs. 0.3195), and the strongest in- and out-of-distribution ensembles (VIBE-20, MedARC-50) by 0.010 and 0.009 PCC, using a single trained model rather than an ensemble of 20-1000. The same checkpoint also provides stimulus-conditioned uncertainty estimates and sample-based diversity.
papers.summary: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) encoding models usually predict a single deterministic response to a stimulus, even though identical stimuli produce a distribution of neural responses from physiological noise, hemodynamic variability, and cognitive fluctuations. `MultiFlow` is a generative encoder built on Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) with a variant called Stimulus-Informed Source Flow Matching (SISFM), which conditions the source distribution on the stimulus through a learned temporal convolution spanning a hemodynamic response function (HRF) window and a variance head that shrinks its scale, shortening the transport path. A Diffusion Transformer decoder parameterizes the velocity field and fuses ten frozen vision, audio, language, and audiovisual backbones with per-subject heads. On `Algonauts 2025`, **a single checkpoint trails the 1000-model `TRIBE` ensemble by only 0.003 Pearson correlation** (0.3163 vs 0.3195) and comes within about 0.01 of the strongest `VIBE-20` and `MedARC-50` ensembles, while also providing stimulus-conditioned uncertainty estimates.

papers.title: StimFlow: Synthesizing Brain Activity from Images via Stimulus-conditioned Flow Matching
papers.abstract: The inherent variability of fMRI responses across trials encourages a generative view of the stimulus-to-response mapping. Prior generative encoders often operate in compressed latent spaces and condition predominantly on semantic features, which provide limited low-level cues for early visual cortex. We propose StimFlow, which synthesizes fMRI directly in native voxel space using conditional flow matching with a linear path. This design aligns training and inference distributions, enabling competitive performance with a single sample and reducing reliance on averaging. To match the visual hierarchy, StimFlow combines structural DINOv2 features with semantic CLIP features, which prove complementary along the cortical processing stream. With a single sample, StimFlow achieves a per-voxel Pearson correlation of 0.371, matching baselines that average five draws. Generation in voxel space allows direct ROI analysis and concept localization without a decoder. Furthermore, it recovers over half of full-data performance from just one hour of scans, supporting efficient cross-subject adaptation.
papers.summary: Trial-to-trial variability in fMRI responses motivates treating the stimulus-to-response mapping as generative, but prior generative encoders work in compressed latent spaces and condition mostly on semantic features that give early visual cortex little low-level signal. `StimFlow` synthesizes fMRI directly in native voxel space with conditional flow matching along a linear path, which keeps training and inference distributions aligned, and combines structural `DINOv2` features with semantic `CLIP` features to cover the cortical hierarchy. **With a single sample it reaches a per-voxel Pearson correlation of 0.371, matching baselines that average five draws**, and because generation happens in voxel space it allows region-of-interest analysis and concept localization without a decoder. It also recovers more than half of full-data performance from one hour of scans, supporting efficient adaptation to new subjects.

papers.title: Across Viewpoints and Time: Trajectory-Generalizable Physical Attacks on World Models and Video Understanding Models
papers.abstract: World models and video understanding models are increasingly deployed in dynamic visual environments, yet their robustness to physical adversarial threats remains largely underexplored. We study whether a single physical adversarial texture can mislead the victim model across different real-world scenarios where observing viewpoints vary along uncontrolled object--camera trajectories. We identify that heterogeneous video semantics and trajectories induce poorly aligned gradients for optimizing the adversarial texture. To address that, we propose the Trajectory-aware adversarial Alignment and Refinement Attack (TARA), which incorporates trajectory-aware optimization to capture the evolving geometric variations of a printed texture under real-world scenarios. To improve cross-instance optimization compatibility, TARA incorporates trajectory-aware contrastive alignment to encourage attacked representations from diverse video--trajectory instances to approach a shared adversarial region and then performs trajectory-aware task refinement to translate the aligned representation into task-level prediction errors. For reproducible evaluation, we develop a geometry-grounded tracking pipeline that provides physically plausible adversarial regions with temporally consistent trajectories on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 and Something-Something V2. We further collect real-world print-and-recapture videos to validate attack effectiveness under physical deployment conditions. Together, the annotated benchmarks and real-world captured data form a reproducible testbed for future evaluation. Notably, our results reveal that a single printable adversarial texture can persistently disrupt world models and video understanding models under physical conditions, highlighting the fundamental security challenge.
papers.summary: World models and video understanding models are increasingly used in dynamic visual settings, yet little is known about whether a single printed adversarial texture can fool them as the camera moves along uncontrolled trajectories relative to the object. The authors find that heterogeneous video semantics and trajectories produce poorly aligned gradients when optimizing one texture, and propose the Trajectory-aware adversarial Alignment and Refinement Attack (`TARA`), which uses trajectory-aware contrastive alignment to pull attacked representations from diverse video-trajectory instances toward a shared adversarial region and then refines them into task-level prediction errors. They build a geometry-grounded tracking pipeline that places physically plausible, temporally consistent adversarial regions on `EPIC-KITCHENS-100` and `Something-Something V2`, and collect print-and-recapture videos for physical validation. **A single printable texture persistently disrupts both world models and video understanding models under real-world conditions**, and the annotated benchmarks and captured data are released as a reproducible testbed.

papers.title: CodeWalk: Generating Coding Benchmarks by Walking a Problem Graph
papers.abstract: High-quality coding problems are expensive to collect. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench rely on substantial human curation, while synthetic alternatives typically rely on costly model generation and validation. In this work, we show that new coding problems can be created at almost no cost by composing existing ones. We formulate problem generation as code composition: verified atomic problems are combined into level-$N$ tasks, and a task is kept only if every atomic problem remains unsolved and a joint reference solution passes the same check used at evaluation time. The entire task-construction process is programmatic and requires no language-model generation or validation. We instantiate this approach in four coding settings: multi-bug repair, proof completion, complexity analysis, and clone equivalence. The generated tasks are challenging for frontier models, which all degrade as compositional depth increases. The generated tasks are also useful as training data: rejection-sampling fine-tuning on them improves Qwen3.5-9B at every composition level.
papers.summary: High-quality coding problems are costly to obtain, whether through the human curation behind `SWE-bench` or through model-based synthesis and validation. `CodeWalk` frames problem generation as code composition: verified atomic problems are combined into level-N tasks, and a task is kept only when every atomic component remains unsolved and a joint reference solution passes the same check used at evaluation time, so the whole pipeline runs programmatically with no language model in the loop. Instantiated for multi-bug repair, proof completion, complexity analysis, and clone equivalence, the generated tasks challenge frontier models, **all of which degrade as compositional depth increases**. The tasks also serve as training data: rejection-sampling fine-tuning on them improves `Qwen3.5-9B` at every composition level.

papers.title: Gugak-VocalSet: A Multi-Genre Studio-Quality Dataset of Korean Traditional Singing with Sigimsae Annotations
papers.abstract: We present Gugak-VocalSet, the first publicly available audio dataset for Korean traditional singing with dense annotations of sigimsae, a structured pitch contour system of vocal expressions. Gugak-VocalSet contains 24.5 hours of unaccompanied solo vocal recordings across 305 tracks of representative repertoire curated by the National Gugak Center, performed by 20 professional singers in a controlled studio environment with fixed key and tempo.
