papers.title: What the Model Cannot See: Covert and Provable Text Invisibility in LLMs
papers.abstract: Text wrapped in a trigger can be made behaviorally invisible to a language model: omitted from summaries and quotations, ignored in question answering, and left unflagged by downstream filtering. We study this selective blindness as a dual-use information-flow primitive, a supply-chain backdoor, and a white-box auditing problem. We first implement it exactly as a serving-time span veto: blocking information flow out of a marked span makes every outside activation bit-identical under same-length substitution of the span's content, a noninterference property we verify across ten models, seven mixer families, and 0.5B-120B parameters. The veto serves as a deployable quarantine, an exact reference for calibrating leakage, and a teacher. Distilled into weights, it yields a backdoor: checkpoints trained on six model families from 4B to 120B ignore marked context at little benchmark cost, and their outputs show no measurable semantic trace of the suppressed content above the veto reference on our held-out suite; an in-domain variant suppresses planted vulnerabilities during AI code review. Detection is therefore a white-box problem. Simpler backdoors remain internally transparent -- linear probes recover suppressed content at 0.57-0.79 accuracy versus 0.025 chance -- but hardening the attack until probes reach chance collapses attention from outside the span into it below the range of base models. Across the attacks we evaluate, probe visibility trades off against routing visibility; we do not establish that this tradeoff is fundamental.
papers.summary: Text wrapped in a trigger can be made behaviorally invisible to a language model, omitted from summaries and quotations, ignored in question answering, and left unflagged by downstream filters, which the authors study as a dual-use information-flow primitive, a supply-chain backdoor, and a white-box auditing problem. They first implement the effect exactly as a serving-time span veto that blocks information flow out of a marked span, yielding a noninterference property in which every outside activation is bit-identical under same-length substitution of the span, verified across ten models, seven mixer families, and 0.5B to 120B parameters. Distilling the veto into weights produces a backdoor in checkpoints from six model families (4B to 120B) that ignore marked context at little benchmark cost with no measurable semantic trace above the veto reference, and **an in-domain variant suppresses planted vulnerabilities during AI code review**. Simpler backdoors remain internally visible, with linear probes recovering suppressed content at 0.57 to 0.79 accuracy versus 0.025 chance, but hardening the attack until probes reach chance collapses attention into the span below base-model levels, a probe-versus-routing visibility tradeoff the authors do not claim is fundamental.

papers.title: RetryBench: Separating Retry Permission from Recovery Outcomes in GPT Tool Use
papers.abstract: False retry permission (FRP) occurs when an agent retries a timed-out tool call without support from the visible contract. RetryBench separates this error from realized recovery. Successful protected recovery does not imply reliable rejection of unsupported retries. In a 720-response key control, valid keys usually enabled safe progress, but offered changed keys elicited unsupported retries in Sol (1/80), Terra (55/80), and Luna (60/80). A later 240-response control removed the candidate and required models to supply a key. Luna still made 8/80 unsupported dispatches; Sol and Terra made none in 80 responses each. Accepting a displayed bad key therefore cannot explain all observed errors, although changed output requirements and conditions preclude a pure display-effect comparison. Removing the weak-contract label increased retries in Sol and Terra's coded-action conditions in a six-endpoint study. A separate 1,536-response canonical-action block also found a positive Terra contrast (115/128 versus 124/128 retries), concentrated in two task/order conditions; the other five contrasts remained unresolved after multiplicity correction. An explicit-contract cue control elicited deferral in all 762 returned responses, leaving recovery unresolved. These results support reporting permission and recovery together across declared interface variants. The evidence covers four purposive tasks, fixed GPT endpoints, and one recovery decision; it identifies neither internal mechanisms nor episode-level safety.
papers.summary: False retry permission (FRP) occurs when an agent retries a timed-out tool call without support from the visible contract, and `RetryBench` separates this error from whether a retry actually achieved recovery, using fixed GPT endpoints labeled Sol, Terra, and Luna on four purposive tasks. In a 720-response key control, valid keys usually enabled safe progress, but **offered changed keys elicited unsupported retries in 1/80, 55/80, and 60/80 responses for Sol, Terra, and Luna**, and when a later control required models to supply their own key, Luna still made 8/80 unsupported dispatches, so accepting a displayed bad key cannot explain all errors. Removing a weak-contract label raised retries in some coded-action conditions, one Terra contrast in a 1,536-response block was positive while the other five remained unresolved after multiplicity correction, and an explicit-contract cue produced deferral in all 762 responses. The authors argue permission and recovery should be reported together across declared interface variants, and note the evidence identifies neither internal mechanisms nor episode-level safety.

papers.title: Comparative Study of Canvas- and Coordinate-Based Geometry-Conditioned Neural Networks for Real-Time Prediction of Indoor Environments with Varying Room Dimensions
papers.abstract: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) is computationally expensive for iterative building design. Deep learning surrogates offer faster predictions, but generalization across varying room dimensions remains challenging. This study compares two geometry-conditioned neural network surrogate models for rapid indoor airflow and temperature field prediction under varying room sizes. During the architectural design stage, this method is relevant for real-time assessment of whether conditioned supply air will effectively provide fresh and cool air throughout rooms with varying heights and lengths. The canvas-based neural network (CaNN) explicitly encodes room size by preserving different occupied regions within a fixed canvas, whereas the coordinate-based neural network (CoNN) uses normalized coordinate channels. Both employ U-Net autoencoders to separately predict airflow and temperature fields. Evaluation uses simplified rooms with varying heights and lengths as a controlled benchmark. The results show that CaNN achieves higher agreement with CFD results than CoNN, demonstrating its potential to support performance-driven building design.
papers.summary: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) is too expensive for iterative building design, and deep learning surrogates have struggled to generalize across rooms of different dimensions. The study compares two geometry-conditioned U-Net autoencoder surrogates that separately predict indoor airflow and temperature fields: a canvas-based neural network (CaNN) that encodes room size by preserving the occupied region within a fixed canvas, and a coordinate-based neural network (CoNN) that uses normalized coordinate channels. On simplified rooms with varying heights and lengths as a controlled benchmark, **`CaNN` agrees more closely with CFD results than `CoNN`**, supporting real-time assessment during architectural design of whether conditioned supply air reaches throughout a room.

papers.title: Variance-Optimal State Resampling for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards spends much of its rollout budget on states that yield no learning signal. We recast this as a question about the sampling distribution itself: under a fixed rollout budget, which distribution over states minimizes the variance of the policy-gradient estimator? The answer admits a closed-form Neyman allocation, $\mu_{\mathrm{var}}^\pi(s) \propto d^\pi(s)\,\sigma_\pi(s)$, which connects naturally to GRPO's group-relative advantage and induces an emergent reverse curriculum as the policy improves, with no externally imposed schedule. Building on this principle, we propose VSR (Variance-driven State Resampling), a plug-in modification to GRPO using a prefix replay buffer and a zero-cost variance proxy. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks and long-horizon agentic tasks (Sokoban, BabyAI), VSR outperforms GRPO and GiGPO on most benchmarks with fewer generated tokens per update.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards wastes much of its rollout budget on states that produce no learning signal. The authors ask which distribution over states minimizes the variance of the policy-gradient estimator under a fixed budget and derive a closed-form Neyman allocation proportional to state visitation frequency times per-state reward standard deviation, which connects to the group-relative advantage in `GRPO` and induces an emergent reverse curriculum as the policy improves, with no external schedule. They implement this as `VSR` (Variance-driven State Resampling), a plug-in modification to `GRPO` using a prefix replay buffer and a zero-cost variance proxy. **On mathematical reasoning benchmarks and long-horizon agentic tasks (`Sokoban`, `BabyAI`), `VSR` outperforms `GRPO` and `GiGPO` on most benchmarks with fewer generated tokens per update.**

papers.title: Learning Multimodal Sensor Fusion with JEPA Representations for Breathing Activity and Pose Recognition
papers.abstract: Predictive video representations do not by themselves specify how a multimodal system should handle missing sensors. We transfer frozen V-JEPA2 features to a set of heterogeneous sensors comprised by RGB video, depth video, and radar time series. A shared fusion model uses modality queries, fixed sensor slots, and explicit availability to classify breathing activity and pose from all seven non-empty sensor subsets. The contribution is a controlled evaluation of subset supervision, pooling capacity, and representation transfer on 39 OMuSense-23 subjects with five subject-group folds and three seeds. With matched downstream parameter counts, the final model reaches recording-level activity macro-F1 of $75.23%\pm0.60$ averaged across seven subsets. Supervising all subsets in each batch improves the matched query-pooling control by 1.923 percentage points (conditional 95% subject-bootstrap interval [0.647, 3.209]), while query pooling shows no clear advantage over matched mean pooling under balanced supervision. Radar probes support transfer beyond pooled wavelet pixels, 64-token inference approximately preserves mean activity performance, and the tested Consensus-JEPA loss adds no measured benefit against its exact control.
papers.summary: Predictive video representations do not by themselves specify how a multimodal system should handle missing sensors. The authors transfer frozen `V-JEPA2` features to RGB video, depth video, and radar time series, and train a shared fusion model with modality queries, fixed sensor slots, and explicit availability flags to classify breathing activity and pose from all seven non-empty sensor subsets. Evaluated on 39 `OMuSense-23` subjects with five subject-group folds and three seeds, the final model reaches a recording-level activity macro-F1 of **75.23% averaged across the seven subsets**, and supervising all subsets in each batch improves over a matched query-pooling control by about 1.9 percentage points. Query pooling shows no clear advantage over matched mean pooling under balanced supervision, 64-token inference roughly preserves mean activity performance, and a tested `Consensus-JEPA` loss adds no measured benefit against its exact control.

papers.title: Make Every Expansion Count: Learning to Search Efficiently in LLM Code Repair
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) code-repair systems fix faulty programs by repeatedly generating and testing revisions. Each revision is costly, making the choice of which repair to pursue important for efficiency. Existing search policies rely on test pass rates and search statistics, ignoring the details of test failures and proposed edits. We introduce CodeTriage, a learned policy that prioritizes edits before their revised programs are generated and tested. Its 0.6B-parameter model reads the test output, failure diagnosis, and proposed edit, then predicts a distribution over the number of repair steps needed to reach a fix through that edit. These predictions prioritize all pending edits across programs before generating and testing the revised code. On held-out repair tasks, CodeTriage finds fixes with 21% fewer program revisions and 12% fewer output tokens than the strongest baseline on each metric. Without retraining, it achieves the highest average success across search budgets for each of 11 unseen repair LLMs. Ablations show that both the failure context and edit text, as well as comparisons across programs, improve search. We also release a corpus of 12.2 million program versions from four LLMs, organized into repair trees with proposed edits and test results.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) code-repair systems fix programs by repeatedly generating and testing revisions, and each revision is costly, so choosing which candidate repair to pursue next matters for efficiency. `CodeTriage` is a learned 0.6B-parameter policy that reads the test output, failure diagnosis, and proposed edit, then predicts a distribution over how many repair steps remain if that edit is followed, using these predictions to rank all pending edits across programs before any revised code is generated or tested. **On held-out repair tasks it finds fixes with 21% fewer program revisions and 12% fewer output tokens than the strongest baseline on each metric**, and without retraining it achieves the highest average success across search budgets for each of 11 unseen repair LLMs. Ablations show that the failure context, the edit text, and cross-program comparison each improve search, and the authors release a corpus of 12.2 million program versions from four LLMs organized into repair trees with proposed edits and test results.

papers.title: Review Rarely Beats the Stronger Model: Separating Verification from Capability Transfer in LLM Pipelines
papers.abstract: Qwen3-8B reviewing Llama-3.1-8B in math adds 33.2 points, yet Qwen3-8B alone is 6.4 points more accurate than the result. Reviewing another model's answer is usually judged by its gain over the generator. We show that this confuses verification, which adds accuracy beyond either model alone, with capability transfer, where a stronger reviewer supplies answers it could have given on its own. Measured against the stronger model alone, across 48 pairs of 12 open-weight models (3B to 72B) in math, knowledge, code and reasoning, review beats it in only 9 of 96 review directions, and does worse the larger the capability gap. The reason is anchoring: the reviewer mostly follows the generator, discarding its own correct answers. Review costs 2.6 to 2.8 times as much as the stronger model alone, while a selector using the same two calls is 2.7 to 4.2 points more accurate than review and cheaper. Studies of verification should report the stronger model alone, not only the gain over the generator.
papers.summary: Having one LLM review another's answer is usually judged by its gain over the generator, but this conflates verification, which adds accuracy beyond either model alone, with capability transfer, where a stronger reviewer simply supplies answers it could have given by itself. For example, `Qwen3-8B` reviewing `Llama-3.1-8B` on math adds 33.2 points, yet `Qwen3-8B` alone is 6.4 points more accurate than the reviewed result. **Measured against the stronger model alone across 48 pairs of 12 open-weight models (3B to 72B) in math, knowledge, code, and reasoning, review wins in only 9 of 96 review directions**, and it does worse as the capability gap grows because the reviewer anchors on the generator and discards its own correct answers. Review also costs 2.6 to 2.8 times as much as the stronger model alone, while a selector using the same two calls is 2.7 to 4.2 points more accurate and cheaper, so the authors argue that verification studies should report the stronger model alone rather than only the gain over the generator.

papers.title: Gen Through the Lens: Camera-Controllable Video Generation via Cross-Coordinate Conditioning Fusion
papers.abstract: We present Gen Through the Lens, a camera-controllable image-to-video generation framework that synthesizes videos from a given reference image while enabling realistic and physically consistent camera operations. Unlike previous models that treat camera motion as abstract conditioning or rely on a single coordinate system, our approach explicitly decomposes and fuses control signals across three coordinate spaces: the camera coordinate (modeled by intrinsic parameters), the world coordinate (represented by spatial geometry hints), and the object coordinate (described by 3D bounding boxes of target subjects). Through cross-coordinate conditioning fusion, these heterogeneous cues are unified to guide the generative process, enabling precise control of camera motion, focus, and framing while preserving temporal and spatial coherence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method produces controllable and visually consistent results across diverse camera operations, outperforming existing approaches in both realism and editability.
papers.summary: Camera-controllable image-to-video generation has typically treated camera motion as abstract conditioning or relied on a single coordinate system. The proposed framework instead decomposes control signals across three coordinate spaces, the camera coordinate modeled by intrinsic parameters, the world coordinate represented by spatial geometry hints, and the object coordinate described by 3D bounding boxes of target subjects, and fuses them through cross-coordinate conditioning to guide video synthesis from a reference image. The authors claim **precise control of camera motion, focus, and framing while preserving temporal and spatial coherence**, and report outperforming existing approaches in both realism and editability across diverse camera operations.

papers.title: LURE: a Phase-Labelled Synthetic Corpus of Online-Grooming Exchanges
papers.abstract: Phase-annotated conversational data is essential for studying the progression of online grooming of minors and for developing early warning tools. However, the only publicly available source (i.e., Perverted-Justice archive, which contains a subset coded using ChatCoder) is small, outdated, and frozen. We present a synthetic corpus of groomer-victim exchanges, generated using a retrieval-augmented pipeline running on institutional hardware. This pipeline uses an openly available, eight-billion-parameter, refusal-ablated language model. The corpus was created using the five stages of the responsible-generation protocol for synthetic datasets: ontology-driven design based on the ChatCoder luring-communication scheme (eight communicative tags mapped onto four grooming phases); multi-model prompt testing; human-in-the-loop supervision; semantic and feature-level validation; and modality-aware documentation. The released corpus contains 2,121 unique exchanges across seven tags and four phases, each accompanied by a Plutchik emotion field. Validation quantifies the integrity and lexical profile of the corpus, as well as the reproduction of real seed lines, in-domain label recoverability (tag accuracy: 0.85; phase accuracy: 0.93) and its transfer to real ChatCoder offender lines, which were coded automatically at the eight-tag level (31,640 lines) and by human coders at the three-construct level (10,876 posts). Accuracy was measured for lexical and sentence-embedding features, while a real-versus-synthetic discriminator was able to separate the two domains with 91% accuracy. The scope of the corpus includes controlled, phase-conditioned experimentation, pipeline development and augmentation alongside real data and awareness material. The corpus, its datasheet and the audit code are released with vetted access.
papers.summary: Phase-annotated conversational data for studying the progression of online grooming of minors is scarce, with the only public source, the Perverted-Justice archive, small and outdated. The authors generate a synthetic corpus of groomer-victim exchanges using a retrieval-augmented pipeline built on an openly available eight-billion-parameter refusal-ablated language model, following a five-stage responsible-generation protocol that includes ontology-driven design based on the `ChatCoder` luring-communication scheme, multi-model prompt testing, human-in-the-loop supervision, semantic and feature-level validation, and modality-aware documentation. The released `LURE` corpus contains **2,121 unique exchanges across seven tags and four grooming phases**, each with a Plutchik emotion field, and validation reports in-domain tag accuracy of 0.85 and phase accuracy of 0.93 along with transfer to real `ChatCoder` offender lines. A real-versus-synthetic discriminator still separates the two domains with 91% accuracy, and the corpus, datasheet, and audit code are released under vetted access.

papers.title: RINO: Renormalization Group Distillation with No Labels
papers.abstract: Supervised machine learning in high-energy physics (HEP) requires training on labeled simulations of particle collisions, which are known to be unfaithful to the underlying physics. This leads to significant inaccuracies and biases in the transfer of trained models to real data, limiting the power of deep learning methods. Self-supervised learning (SSL) is a promising alternative for pretraining directly on real, unlabeled data. However, existing techniques largely operate with inductive biases inspired by domains such as images and natural language. We propose RINO (Renormalization Group DIstillation with NO Labels), which, for the first time, exploits the fundamentally multi-scale renormalization group structure of high-energy jet formation as a physically grounded source of SSL views. We define teacher-student representations across energy scales using different levels of hierarchical clustering, aligned via DINO-style self-distillation. To mirror the background-dominated nature of real collider data, RINO pretrains exclusively on jets from quantum chromodynamics (QCD) processes and is evaluated on out-of-distribution (OOD) transfer to rare signal classes. In our controlled data-efficiency study, RINO matches fully supervised training on JetNet after finetuning on only 1% of the labeled data. With the full labeled dataset, RINO improves OOD classification accuracy on top-quark jets by 5.9% and, without retraining, improves AUC on the unseen Higgs boson decay channel $H \to 4q$ by 4.1% over the strongest SSL baseline. Scale-structure diagnostics reveal that DINO-style self-distillation permits our backbone to retain scale-dependent structure. Ablation studies show that this accounts for an 8.6% OOD accuracy gap with respect to alternative SSL paradigms such as SimCLR. Code is available at https://github.com/zichunhao/RINO.
papers.summary: Supervised machine learning in high-energy physics (HEP) trains on labeled collision simulations known to be unfaithful to the underlying physics, biasing models when they are transferred to real data, while existing self-supervised learning (SSL) methods borrow inductive biases from images and text. `RINO` instead uses the multi-scale renormalization group structure of jet formation as a physically grounded source of SSL views, defining teacher and student representations at different levels of hierarchical clustering and aligning them with `DINO`-style self-distillation, pretraining only on background quantum chromodynamics (QCD) jets and evaluating out-of-distribution (OOD) transfer to rare signal classes. **After fine-tuning on only 1% of the labeled data, `RINO` matches fully supervised training on `JetNet`**, and with full labels it improves OOD top-quark classification accuracy by 5.9% and AUC on the unseen Higgs decay channel to four quarks by 4.1% over the strongest SSL baseline. Ablations attribute an 8.6% OOD accuracy gap over alternatives such as `SimCLR` to the backbone retaining scale-dependent structure.

papers.title: Scalable Weak-to-Strong Verifier Hardening for Agent Environments
papers.abstract:
Agent environments are essential for large language model (LLM) development. They use programmatic verifiers to turn complex outcomes into rewards. Verifiers can be attacked into awarding full credit to cheating agents without completing the intended task, causing inaccurate evaluation and misalignment in training. As agent environments scale in numbers and difficulty, so must the repairing of exploitable verifiers. To this end, we ask whether today's model with scaled compute can automatically harden agent environments to prevent potentially stronger future models from reward hacking. We introduce a scalable, fully automatic approach to weak-to-strong verifier hardening. It first sets up an isolated verifier sandbox that agents cannot directly modify, then uses a hacker-fixer loop to find and repair remaining verifier vulnerabilities.
  We apply this loop to Terminal Bench, KernelBench, and SETA, substantially reducing attack success across these agent environments. The iterative design scales with the hardening budget, producing progressively stronger defenses as the number of loop iterations increases and outperforming the static, non-iterative baseline. An earlier version of our hacker-fixer loop has been adopted by the official Terminal Bench repository as a way to audit exploits in its environments. Project page: https://verifier-hardening.github.io/.
papers.summary: Agent environments rely on programmatic verifiers to turn task outcomes into rewards, and those verifiers can be attacked so that cheating agents earn full credit without completing the intended task, corrupting both evaluation and training. The authors ask whether today's models with scaled compute can automatically harden environments against potentially stronger future models, and propose a fully automatic weak-to-strong approach that first isolates the verifier in a sandbox agents cannot modify, then runs a hacker-fixer loop to find and repair remaining vulnerabilities. **Applied to `Terminal Bench`, `KernelBench`, and `SETA`, the loop substantially reduces attack success, with defenses growing stronger as the number of iterations increases** and outperforming a static, non-iterative baseline. An earlier version of the loop has been adopted by the official `Terminal Bench` repository to audit exploits in its environments.

papers.title: Multi-Horizon Explainable Queue Forecasting and Resource-Aware Decision Support for Intelligent Border Control Using LightGBM
papers.abstract: Border crossing points are stochastic service systems in which traffic demand, traveler categories, registration status, inspection requirements, staffing, and lane availability interact on multiple time scales. This paper extends an earlier multimodal queue-management framework by introducing an implementation-oriented, multi-horizon forecasting and decision-support architecture based on Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) models. In contrast to a single forecasting block, the proposed approach constructs horizon-specific regressors for 15, 30, 60, and 120 min forecasts and jointly estimates future waiting time and queue lengths. The models operate on temporally lagged traffic, service, density, and queue features, while an operational layer incorporates lane compatibility, officer availability, possibly degraded resources, traveler category, preregistration information, and human-approval constraints. Quantile LightGBM models provide 95\% prediction intervals for waiting-time forecasts. Beyond prediction, the framework produces machine-readable recommendations, alerts, aggregate key performance indicators, confidence information, and integration outputs suitable for border resource-management and decision-support systems. The results establish a reproducible synthetic-data baseline and a practical interface for subsequent validation with operational border-crossing data.
papers.summary: Border crossing points are stochastic service systems in which traffic demand, traveler categories, registration status, inspection requirements, staffing, and lane availability interact on multiple time scales. Extending an earlier multimodal queue-management framework, the authors build horizon-specific Light Gradient Boosting Machine (`LightGBM`) regressors for 15, 30, 60, and 120 minute forecasts that jointly estimate waiting time and queue length from lagged traffic, service, density, and queue features, with quantile models supplying 95% prediction intervals for waiting time. An operational layer adds lane compatibility, officer availability, degraded resources, traveler category, preregistration, and human-approval constraints, and emits machine-readable recommendations, alerts, key performance indicators, and integration outputs for resource-management systems. **The results establish a reproducible synthetic-data baseline** and a practical interface for later validation with operational border-crossing data.

papers.title: DiffNash: Finding Nash Equilibrium in High-Dimensional Continuous Action Spaces with Diffusion Policies
papers.abstract: Computing equilibria in high-dimensional continuous games requires learning and representing rich, multi-modal strategy distributions, something conventional neural policies struggle to achieve. Diffusion models offer a natural solution, but standard diffusion training requires direct samples from a fixed target distribution, which are generally unavailable under iterative game-solving updates. We propose a diffusion-based framework for equilibrium computation that enables diffusion-based variants of Online Mirror Descent (OMD) and Fictitious Play (FP). Our approach derives a reweighted score-matching objective that trains diffusion policies without requiring direct samples from each updated policy. Our main method, DiffNash, combines the fast convergence of OMD with the sample efficiency of FP by reusing past actions through a replay buffer. To correct the resulting distribution shift from sample reuse, we derive an unbiased estimator of the difference between current and past policies' Evidence Lower Bounds, whose exponential provides a tractable proxy for the corresponding importance weight without evaluating diffusion likelihoods. We evaluate our approach on forest protection games and continuous Colonel Blotto games, reducing the Nash gap over the strongest baseline by 35.6% and 24.7%, respectively, with minimal hyperparameter tuning.
papers.summary: Computing equilibria in high-dimensional continuous games requires representing rich, multi-modal strategy distributions that conventional neural policies struggle to capture, while standard diffusion training needs direct samples from a fixed target distribution that iterative game-solving updates do not provide. The authors derive a reweighted score-matching objective that trains diffusion policies without such samples, enabling diffusion-based variants of Online Mirror Descent (OMD) and Fictitious Play (FP). Their main method, `DiffNash`, combines the fast convergence of OMD with the sample efficiency of FP by reusing past actions through a replay buffer, correcting the resulting distribution shift with an unbiased estimator of the difference between current and past policies' Evidence Lower Bounds, whose exponential serves as a tractable importance-weight proxy without evaluating diffusion likelihoods. **On forest protection games and continuous Colonel Blotto games, it reduces the Nash gap over the strongest baseline by 35.6% and 24.7%**, respectively, with minimal hyperparameter tuning.

papers.title: The Anatomy of a Blind Spot: What an LLM Judge Must Be Shown, and How Much
papers.abstract: Evaluation of text generated by large language models (LLMs) is increasingly delegated to LLMs acting as judges, yet what such a judge must be shown remains unresolved. We treat a judge whose reports are acted on as a regulator, in the sense of cybernetics, and ask what it must be shown, how much, in what form, and what its reports must get right. On seven public benchmarks we varied only what the judge was shown. Across three judges whose prices differ 10- to 17-fold, what the judge was shown mattered more than which judge it was. When a system revised its answers on feedback from a judge denied the material they had to respect, it ended below its starting point on instruction following and question answering. On instruction following the loss grew with each round, and it persisted when the judge saw the user's request but not the constraints and with a second judge family. On news summarisation, a correct reference summary beside the source undid most of the source's contribution, whereas on single-answer questions a reference helped. About a tenth of the source did almost all of its work, and a small entailment graph matched an LLM judge at finding errors in grounded text. We committed 83 testable clauses before running; of the 81 that ran, 32 met their bar and 50 went in the predicted direction, and most quantitative predictions from the theory failed. We report every shortfall and derive design rules tied to measured effects.
papers.summary: Evaluation of text generated by large language models (LLMs) is increasingly delegated to LLMs acting as judges, yet what such a judge must be shown remains unresolved. Treating a judge whose reports are acted on as a regulator in the cybernetic sense, the authors vary only the judge's inputs across seven public benchmarks and three judges whose prices differ 10- to 17-fold, and find that **what the judge was shown mattered more than which judge it was**. A system revising its answers on feedback from a judge denied the material it had to respect ended below its starting point on instruction following and question answering, with the loss growing each round, while on news summarisation a correct reference summary beside the source undid most of the source's contribution, about a tenth of the source did almost all of its work, and a small entailment graph matched an LLM judge at finding errors in grounded text. Of 83 testable clauses committed before running, 81 ran, 32 met their bar and 50 went in the predicted direction, and the authors report every shortfall and derive design rules tied to the measured effects.

papers.title: Vision: "What Don't I Know About User's Preferences?" How Uncertainty Estimation Improves Proactive Assistant Alignment
papers.abstract: Proactive Smart Assistants (PSAs) increasingly use general knowledge, learned patterns from group-level data, patterns from individual user's data, and recent sensor observations to anticipate which action a user may prefer. Existing systems typically select actions from predicted user preference likelihoods, but these likelihoods alone do not reveal how reliable the prediction is, which evidence supports it, or why ambiguity remains. In this vision paper, we argue that uncertainty estimation can provide this missing information and substantially change appropriate downstream behavior. Using the example of a home assistant, we introduce the questions that uncertainty estimation aims to answer, i.e. how sure is the assistant about the predicted preference likelihood, whether the confidence come from group-level assumptions or individual's data, and whether likelihood ambiguity reflect the user's intrinsic preference variability or insufficient data for the particular situation. We further introduce uncertainty estimation applications in neighboring domains, such as human trajectory prediction, personalized activity recognition, information-collection, and model-based control. Finally, we draw on insights from neighboring domains to envision how future uncertainty-aware proactive assistants may address key challenges in proactive interaction.
papers.summary: Proactive Smart Assistants (PSAs) combine general knowledge, group-level patterns, individual user data, and recent sensor observations to anticipate which action a user may prefer, but predicted preference likelihoods alone do not reveal how reliable a prediction is, what evidence supports it, or why ambiguity remains. The authors argue that uncertainty estimation can supply that missing information and substantially change appropriate downstream behavior. Using a home assistant as the running example, they frame the questions uncertainty estimation should answer, namely **how sure the assistant is, whether confidence comes from group-level assumptions or the individual's data, and whether ambiguity reflects intrinsic preference variability or insufficient data for the situation**, and surveys uncertainty-estimation practice in human trajectory prediction, personalized activity recognition, information collection, and model-based control to sketch how future uncertainty-aware proactive assistants might behave.

papers.title: Hardware-Assisted Multi-Stage Ransomware Detection with Adaptive Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Ransomware is a fast-escalating privacy threat causing significant financial and data losses worldwide. As attacks grow more sophisticated, traditional static signatures and dynamic behavior analysis struggle to defend. In this paper, we propose an novel framework that couples software-level scanning with hardware-level microprocessor activity monitoring to achieve efficient ransomware detection and mitigation. The contributions are threefold: (1) we employ adversarial training to harden static analysis against obfuscation and leverage hardware-assisted monitoring for real-time detection; (2) we integrate neural architecture search (NAS) to automatically tailor models for stronger generalizability; and (3) We validate the proposed approach through extensive experiments, demonstrating substantially improved detection accuracy and reduced latency compared with existing methods. Moreover, it provides trace-level interpretability that explains the underlying decision process.
papers.summary: Ransomware attacks are growing more sophisticated, and traditional static signatures and dynamic behavior analysis struggle to keep up. The proposed framework couples software-level scanning with hardware-level microprocessor activity monitoring, using adversarial training to harden static analysis against obfuscation, hardware-assisted monitoring for real-time detection, and neural architecture search (NAS) to automatically tailor models for stronger generalization. The authors report **substantially improved detection accuracy and reduced latency compared with existing methods**, along with trace-level interpretability that explains the underlying decision process.

papers.title: ADAPT: Audio-Depth Action Planning with Transition-Aware Rewards for Lights-Out Industrial Navigation
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models for embodied navigation typically rely on RGB observations, limiting their applicability in lights-out industrial environments where visible illumination may be unavailable. We study illumination-independent navigation using spatial audio for target localization and depth for obstacle-aware geometry. To support this setting, we introduce DarkNav-Bench, a benchmark with 24 industrial scenes and four progressively challenging acoustic conditions. We further propose ADAPT, an audio-depth action-planning framework equipped with spatial-audio perception and optimized for closed-loop navigation through reinforcement learning (RL). Our key RL contribution, transition-aware reward shaping (TARS), defines a pose-aware shortest-action potential over a position-heading graph. Unlike conventional geodesic-progress rewards, TARS accounts for both feasible movements and in-place rotations, providing action-consistent feedback for policy optimization. Experiments show that ADAPT consistently outperforms training-based navigation baselines and zero-shot multimodal models on both seen and unseen scenes. On unseen environments, it achieves 90.6% success under Clean conditions and retains 60.0% success under the most challenging Localized Noise setting. These results demonstrate the potential of spatial audio and depth as complementary modalities for reliable RGB-free navigation in lights-out industrial environments.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action models for embodied navigation typically depend on RGB observations, which fail in lights-out industrial settings where visible illumination may be unavailable. The authors study illumination-independent navigation using spatial audio to localize targets and depth to capture obstacle geometry, introducing `DarkNav-Bench`, a benchmark of 24 industrial scenes under four progressively harder acoustic conditions, and `ADAPT`, an audio-depth action-planning framework trained for closed-loop navigation with reinforcement learning (RL). Its core RL contribution, transition-aware reward shaping (TARS), defines a pose-aware shortest-action potential over a position-heading graph that credits both feasible movements and in-place rotations, unlike conventional geodesic-progress rewards. `ADAPT` outperforms training-based navigation baselines and zero-shot multimodal models on seen and unseen scenes, reaching **90.6% success on unseen environments under clean conditions and 60.0% under the hardest localized-noise setting**.

papers.title: Unfair and Unsafe: Everyday Bias Triggers Emergent Misalignment
papers.abstract: Emergent misalignment (EM) occurs when fine-tuning a language model to a narrow task makes it misaligned on unrelated ones. Because organizations now routinely fine-tune models on their own data, it matters which kinds of training data cause EM. So far, studies have induced EM with data containing recognized safety failures, such as insecure code or harmful advice, while biased training data is typically examined by fairness research for the bias models learn from it rather than for its effects on safety. In real-world text, much of this bias, such as demographic stereotypes, appears not as derogatory language but politely, embedded in judgments about people. We ask whether learning such polite stereotypes can itself cause EM. We find that fine-tuning on polite answers that rely on stereotypes makes models less safe and less truthful on unrelated tasks. The effect holds across four open-weight model families (7B to 12B), both gender and race stereotypes, and repeated training runs, relative to controls trained on the same questions without the stereotype. We further show that the learned stereotype has its own direction in model activations, distinct from directions for generic misaligned traits such as deception. This direction exists before fine-tuning and can both control the learned stereotype and monitor its acquisition. Existing defenses against EM improve safety while leaving the stereotype largely intact. Beyond this controlled setting, fine-tuning on political news coverage also triggers EM, apparently amplified by partisan framing, and stereotype models acting as tool-using agents can carry out harmful tasks and blame people without evidence. Our results show that biased training data is not only a fairness problem but also a safety one. We argue that EM is studied too narrowly, and that fairness concerns and methods offer a natural way to broaden the search for its triggers.
papers.summary: Emergent misalignment (EM) occurs when fine-tuning a language model on a narrow task makes it misaligned on unrelated ones, and prior studies have induced it only with data containing recognized safety failures such as insecure code or harmful advice. The authors ask whether learning polite demographic stereotypes, the form much real-world bias takes, can cause EM on its own, and find that **fine-tuning on polite stereotype-based answers makes models less safe and less truthful on unrelated tasks**, an effect that holds across four open-weight model families (7B to 12B), both gender and race stereotypes, and repeated runs relative to controls trained on the same questions without the stereotype. The learned stereotype occupies its own direction in model activations, distinct from generic misaligned traits such as deception, which exists before fine-tuning and can both steer and monitor its acquisition, while existing EM defenses improve safety but leave the stereotype largely intact. Fine-tuning on political news coverage also triggers EM, apparently amplified by partisan framing, and stereotype-trained models acting as tool-using agents carry out harmful tasks and blame people without evidence, leading the authors to argue that biased training data is a safety problem and that fairness methods can broaden the search for EM triggers.

papers.title: Small but Mighty: Test Suites as Improvement Signals for Self-Evolving Agents
papers.abstract: A self-evolving agent rewrites its own harness and must decide which rewrites to keep, so its improvement signal is the check a rewrite has to pass. Verifying a rewrite by agent rollout is expensive and subjective, while executable checks such as the repository's own tests are too sparse to catch behavior-changing rewrites, rejecting only a quarter of them. We instead take test feedback as the executable signal, and search for test suites that are both small and strong with a quality-diversity evolutionary algorithm, so that the signal is dense and informative. TeSearch treats suite size as a behavior descriptor, so that quality is pursued at every size and a small, strong suite is reachable, and learns a transition kernel during the search that denoises the LLM as an actuator on that descriptor. Across 129 real-world modules and three backbones, TeSearch delivers the highest-quality suites of any method compared, LLM-driven evolutionary search included, and the smallest of any LLM-based one. Used as the improvement signal of a self-evolving agent, it rejects 59.9% of behavior-changing rewrites against 25.3% for the repository's tests, at a 4.0% false-alarm rate and 3.5 s per decision. The code and data are available at https://github.com/ccsnow127/TeSearch.
papers.summary: A self-evolving agent rewrites its own harness and must decide which rewrites to keep, so its improvement signal is whatever check a rewrite has to pass; verifying by agent rollout is expensive and subjective, while a repository's own tests are too sparse, rejecting only about a quarter of behavior-changing rewrites. `TeSearch` instead searches for test suites that are both small and strong using a quality-diversity evolutionary algorithm that treats suite size as a behavior descriptor, so quality is pursued at every size, and learns a transition kernel during search that denoises the LLM acting as the mutation operator on that descriptor. Across 129 real-world modules and three backbones, it produces the highest-quality suites of any compared method, including LLM-driven evolutionary search, and the smallest of any LLM-based one. **Used as the improvement signal for a self-evolving agent, it rejects 59.9% of behavior-changing rewrites versus 25.3% for the repository's tests**, at a 4.0% false-alarm rate and 3.5 seconds per decision.

papers.title: PopGen: Generating Semantically Diverse Populations for Zero-Shot Coordination
papers.abstract: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, exposing a cooperator to partners with diverse strategies during training is key to better collaboration at test time. However, existing methods typically rely on trajectory-level proxies to measure diversity, which may label two distinct trajectories of the same strategy as diverse. Instead, our key insight is to leverage LLMs' ability to describe behaviorally distinct agents in environments, similar to how humans can recognize high-level strategies. To this end, we introduce PopGen, a framework that synthesizes semantically diverse agents from scratch using LLMs. PopGen first generates a diverse set of textual descriptions of agent behaviors, then translates each behavior into a code policy that can be executed within the environment. We show that cooperators trained against PopGen populations achieve robust zero-shot cooperation with unseen partners, outperforming population-play baselines across four collaborative environments. We further show that semantic diversity scales with PopGen population size, improving the cooperator's worst-case performance, and we identify design choices that preserve population quality while maximizing diversity. Our code is available at https://github.com/labicon/PopGen.
papers.summary: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, training a cooperator against partners with diverse strategies is key to collaborating with unseen partners at test time, but existing methods measure diversity with trajectory-level proxies that can label two trajectories of the same strategy as distinct. `PopGen` uses LLMs to synthesize semantically diverse partner populations from scratch: it first generates a varied set of textual descriptions of agent behaviors, then translates each description into an executable code policy for the environment. **Cooperators trained against `PopGen` populations achieve robust zero-shot cooperation with unseen partners, outperforming population-play baselines across four collaborative environments**, and semantic diversity scales with population size, improving the cooperator's worst-case performance. The authors also identify design choices that preserve population quality while maximizing diversity.

papers.title: Embedding Information in Policy Randomness: Distribution-Preserving Implicit Communication in MDPs
papers.abstract: This paper investigates a new role of randomness in stochastic policies--as a medium for embedding and communicating information. Specifically, we consider an agent interacting with an environment according to a prescribed stochastic policy. By carefully modulating the random action realizations of the policy, information can be embedded into the agent's behavior without altering the prescribed action distribution. We cast this problem as a channel coding problem, in which the controlled system implicitly serves as a communication channel. We then propose a coding scheme, termed posterior-matching randomness modulation (PRAM), that selects actions according to the message to be transmitted. With the aid of common randomness independent of the control system, PRAM preserves the prescribed action distribution for every state and every message. We further prove that PRAM is asymptotically reliable: the message can be decoded with arbitrarily small error probability as the observed state trajectory becomes sufficiently long. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in applications including multi-bit policy watermarking and trajectory provenance.
papers.summary: The randomness in a stochastic policy can serve as a medium for embedding and communicating information. The authors consider an agent that follows a prescribed stochastic policy and show that, by carefully modulating the random action realizations, a message can be embedded in the agent's behavior without altering the prescribed action distribution, casting the problem as channel coding in which the controlled system implicitly acts as the communication channel. Their scheme, posterior-matching randomness modulation (`PRAM`), selects actions according to the message to be transmitted and, with the aid of common randomness independent of the control system, **preserves the prescribed action distribution for every state and every message while remaining asymptotically reliable**, meaning the message can be decoded with arbitrarily small error as the observed state trajectory grows long enough. Experiments demonstrate the framework on multi-bit policy watermarking and trajectory provenance.

papers.title: Revocation Is Not Complete at Receipt: An Executable Outcome Contract for Distributed Agent-Tool Gateways
papers.abstract: Distributed agent workflows cache delegated authority at tool gateways. Revocation may be reported at issuer commit, transport acknowledgment, or receiver persistence, although none of these observations establishes that all gateways enforced the change or that guarded effects stopped. We define C0-C5, a bounded outcome contract spanning issuer commit through effect prevention, and implement it as a persistent monitor over a frozen gateway set, call set, and observation window. A 14-case fault matrix checks conservative classification, sticky violations, restart persistence, and evidence immutability. In a derived audit of its eight semantic cases, treating C3 or C4 as completion produces seven or five false positives, respectively; the bounded C0-C5 verdict produces none. Descriptive scaling covers 1,024 gateways and 10,000 effect vectors. The primary experiment uses the maintained Keycloak 26.7 identity server and measures the contract across two durable receivers, eight physical agent-tool gateways, Filesystem and PostgreSQL effects, and 16 AWS hosts in three availability zones. Normal delivery and recovery commit no effects. Under receiver-selective non-delivery, transport acknowledgment and receiver persistence still succeed, but 112 of 225 calls (49.78%) are admitted, and all 112 effects commit in every treatment block. A separately provisioned execution repeats the result. OPA/Toxiproxy and a live three-role LLM workflow with networked MCP tools reproduce the persisted-but-not-enforced boundary on narrower surfaces. Finally, an unmodified external MCPMark agent executes 60 closed-loop task arms. Normal C4 denies all 31 exposed post-barrier calls and commits no effect; selective C3 allows 344 calls and commits 145 effects across Filesystem and PostgreSQL. Transport success is therefore evidence of progress, not a revocation-completion verdict.
papers.summary: Distributed agent workflows cache delegated authority at tool gateways, and revocation may be reported at issuer commit, transport acknowledgment, or receiver persistence, though none of these observations establishes that every gateway enforced the change or that guarded effects stopped. The authors define C0-C5, a bounded outcome contract spanning issuer commit through effect prevention, implement it as a persistent monitor over a frozen gateway set, call set, and observation window, and check it against a 14-case fault matrix covering conservative classification, sticky violations, restart persistence, and evidence immutability. In the primary experiment, built on `Keycloak` 26.7 with eight physical agent-tool gateways, Filesystem and PostgreSQL effects, and 16 AWS hosts across three availability zones, normal delivery commits no effects, but **under receiver-selective non-delivery, transport acknowledgment and receiver persistence still succeed while 112 of 225 calls (49.78%) are admitted and all 112 effects commit**. An unmodified external `MCPMark` agent over 60 closed-loop task arms reproduces the pattern, with normal enforcement denying all 31 exposed post-barrier calls and selective non-delivery allowing 344 calls and committing 145 effects, so transport success is evidence of progress rather than a revocation-completion verdict.

papers.title: Handoff Curves: Initial Selection, Later Handoff, and Supervision Targets in Multi-turn LLM Routing
papers.abstract: We study how initial model selection, later handoff, and training targets affect success and cost in LLM tasks that span multiple turns. We compare several router architectures using handoff curves, which record task success and cost as the handoff step changes. Our dataset contains 34,204 complete executions of three Qwen models across BFCL, MultiWOZ, and $\tau$-retail, providing offline supervision for routing decisions. In our primary comparison, with Qwen3.5 35B-A3B as the starting model, allowing a later handoff does not establish an improvement in utility over initial selection on BFCL or MultiWOZ, and increases cost on BFCL across a range of cost weights. Changing the supervision targets improves router performance on both our dataset and TwinRouterBench. On our dataset, replacing noisy training success curves with monotone fits raises success by 0.2 to 4.1 percentage points at the same cost across the reported operating points. On TwinRouterBench, we construct targets that describe the model capability needed for the remaining work and difficult steps ahead. Compared with training on the benchmark's per-step labels, these targets raise trajectory pass scores by 7.8 percentage points and cost savings by 6.3 percentage points on the full static bank. A live deployment of the router trained with these targets resolves 79 of 100 instances at a router cost of 0.59 US dollars per instance.
papers.summary: Multi-turn LLM tasks raise the question of whether to pick a model once at the start or hand off to a different model partway through, and how to train the router that decides. The authors introduce handoff curves, which record task success and cost as the handoff step varies, and build a dataset of 34,204 complete executions of three `Qwen` models across `BFCL`, `MultiWOZ`, and `τ-retail` to provide offline supervision for routing decisions. **With `Qwen3.5 35B-A3B` as the starting model, allowing a later handoff does not establish a utility improvement over initial selection on `BFCL` or `MultiWOZ`, and it increases cost on `BFCL`** across a range of cost weights. Changing the supervision targets helps more: replacing noisy training success curves with monotone fits raises success by 0.2 to 4.1 percentage points at equal cost, and on `TwinRouterBench`, targets describing the model capability needed for the remaining work raise trajectory pass scores by 7.8 percentage points and cost savings by 6.3 points over the benchmark's per-step labels, with a live deployment resolving 79 of 100 instances at a router cost of 0.59 US dollars per instance.

papers.title: Large language model-generated patterns for epidemiological modeling: a multi-benchmark evaluation framework
papers.abstract: Representing individual-level behavioral heterogeneity is challenging in epidemiological modeling, particularly when empirical behavioral data are sparse. We assess the potential of large language model (LLM)-generated behavioral outputs in addressing this challenge, using hepatitis C virus-related behaviors among people who inject drugs as a case study. Correspondence with epidemiological patterns was evaluated using external benchmarks: literature-informed association directions, correlations from an agent-based model (ABM), and survey associations. Across three LLMs, unconditional directional recovery across 28 retained literature-informed associations was 46-68%, compared with 82-93% agreement when LLMs were directly asked to classify the same associations. Mean absolute differences from ABM and survey correlation patterns were 0.11-0.13 and 0.15-0.18, respectively. Together, these findings show partial alignment between LLM-generated behavioral relationships and epidemiological evidence, despite higher knowledge-probe agreement. More systematic evaluation is needed before incorporating LLM-generated behavioral outputs into epidemiological models that simulate transmission dynamics.
papers.summary: Epidemiological models struggle to represent individual-level behavioral heterogeneity when empirical data are sparse, so the authors test whether large language model (LLM)-generated behavioral outputs can fill the gap, using hepatitis C-related behaviors among people who inject drugs as a case study. They compare LLM outputs against three external benchmarks: literature-informed association directions, correlations from an agent-based model (ABM), and survey associations. **Across three LLMs, unconditional directional recovery of 28 literature-informed associations was only 46-68%, versus 82-93% when the models were directly asked to classify the same associations**, and mean absolute differences from ABM and survey correlation patterns were 0.11-0.13 and 0.15-0.18. The authors conclude that alignment is partial and that more systematic evaluation is needed before LLM-generated behavior feeds transmission models.

papers.title: AutoSec-RAN: Specification-Grounded LLM Fine-Tuning for Automated Security Analysis of O-RAN
papers.abstract: This paper presents AutoSec-RAN, a specification-grounded large language model (LLM) framework for automated security triage of Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) testing. Unlike approaches relying on static rule sets or privileged access to raw packet captures, AutoSec-RAN fine-tunes Mistral-7B-Instruct through two Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) stages over a curated corpus of 69 O-RAN, 3GPP, and adjacent standards documents, then selectively augments inference with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the same specification index. At inference, the model receives only an investigator-style question and a scenario metadata block, simulating an automated analyst operating without raw packet evidence. AutoSec-RAN is validated on a purpose-built 5G/O-RAN testbed across labeled fronthaul distributed denial of service replay scenarios. A Gemma-4-31B judge LLM scores each candidate's answer on faithfulness, correctness, and actionability relative to a reference authored from full packet capture and log evidence. AutoSec-RAN achieves a mean judge overall score of 0.713 across all 313 evaluation items (0.755 restricted to the five supervised taxonomy classes), clearing the 0.70 reporting threshold, and a blended score of 0.778 (0.808 supervised-only) when cosine similarity over Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence (BAAI) General Embedding (BGE) is incorporated as a secondary semantic signal. The framework performs strongest on mitigation and threat-model reasoning (with a mean overall of 0.849 and 0.848, respectively) and identifies a measurable gap on the held-out attack-direction class (0.515), a controlled result that exposes a specific training data requirement. These results establish specification-grounded LoRA fine-tuning combined with RAG retrieval as a viable foundation for automated security validation of AI-native O-RAN.
papers.summary: Security triage of Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) testing typically relies on static rule sets or privileged access to raw packet captures, which this work aims to replace with an automated analyst that sees only an investigator-style question and a scenario metadata block. The framework fine-tunes `Mistral-7B-Instruct` through two Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) stages over a curated corpus of 69 O-RAN, 3GPP, and related standards documents, then selectively adds retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the same specification index at inference. Evaluated on a purpose-built 5G/O-RAN testbed with labeled fronthaul distributed denial of service replay scenarios and scored by a `Gemma-4-31B` judge, **the system reaches a mean judge score of 0.713 across 313 evaluation items, rising to 0.778 when BGE embedding similarity is blended in**. It performs best on mitigation and threat-model reasoning (about 0.85) and worst on the held-out attack-direction class (0.515), which the authors attribute to a specific training data gap.

papers.title: Computational Reflective Equilibrium for Agentic AI: A Rawlsian Alignment Scaffold for Governance
papers.abstract: The rapid deployment of agentic AI has introduced complex challenges for the ethics and governance of AI systems. Agents built on large language models act through tools on behalf of people, and each deployment case brings its own instructions, policies, evidence, and stakeholders, so alignment must be formed case by case. To this end, this work proposes agentic reflective equilibrium (ARE), a computational reflective equilibrium framework that serves as an ethical alignment scaffold in the agent harness. Drawing inspiration from the reflective equilibrium of John Rawls, the scaffold links principles from the system prompt and operator policy, considered judgments, tool evidence, and candidate actions through typed support and attack relations, with provenance encoding the instruction hierarchy. The agent acts on an equilibrium of this state and calls tools or asks questions only while doing so is worth its cost, unless a due-diligence mandate requires them. Governance enters through value priorities, source authority, prohibitions, human-in-the-loop triggers, and mandates, and certificates attribute each action to the sources whose commitments drove it. We show that equilibria are Nash equilibria of a mutual-adjustment game and establish monotonicity, lexical priority, stability certificates, and a quarantine theorem for prompt injection. Two case studies illustrate the framework: a computer-use assistant told to win a refund "whatever it takes" files an honest warranty claim, refuses a fake review, and ignores an injected request for personal data; a hiring agent showcases how authority, oversight triggers, audit mandates, and hard prohibitions shape discrimination, privacy violations, and escalation. The framework offers traceability, coherence, and adaptivity, facilitating safe, secure, and trustworthy agentic AI.
papers.summary: Agents built on large language models act through tools on behalf of people, and each deployment brings its own instructions, policies, evidence, and stakeholders, so alignment must be formed case by case rather than fixed in advance. The proposed agentic reflective equilibrium (ARE) scaffold, inspired by John Rawls, links system-prompt and operator-policy principles, considered judgments, tool evidence, and candidate actions through typed support and attack relations, with provenance encoding the instruction hierarchy; the agent acts on an equilibrium of this state and calls tools or asks questions only while doing so is worth the cost, unless a due-diligence mandate requires it. Governance enters through value priorities, source authority, prohibitions, human-in-the-loop triggers, and mandates, and certificates attribute each action to the sources that drove it. **The authors show that equilibria are Nash equilibria of a mutual-adjustment game and prove monotonicity, lexical priority, stability certificates, and a quarantine theorem for prompt injection**, illustrated by a computer-use refund assistant that files an honest warranty claim and ignores an injected data request, and a hiring agent subject to audit mandates and hard prohibitions.

papers.title: When Does Compensating Inherited Quantization Error Help? Mean-Square Guarantees for Layer-Wise Quantization and Their Limits
papers.abstract: Layer-wise post-training quantization methods let each layer compensate for the quantization error inherited from earlier layers. We ask under what assumptions such compensation guarantees a network output error no larger than without it. For linear networks of any depth, with the required calibration Gram matrices invertible, if the rounding error of each layer has zero conditional mean and a deterministic second-moment map common to both schemes, as under subtractive dither on an unbounded grid, then compensation with strengths in $[0,1]$ fixed in advance gives a mean-square output error no larger than no compensation, each scheme being followed along its own trajectory. The exact gain separates error removed directly from reduced excitation of later rounding noise. Outside this setting the comparison can fail. With rectified linear activations it fails for two independent reasons: noise changes activation states, and, even when no state changes, the correction moves error from samples on which a unit is inactive to samples on which it is active. With stable activations, commutators between the calibration projection and the activation patterns bound the excess. With a bounded codebook, even unique exact layer-wise minimizers with no overload can give a larger output error. For fixed rounding errors it already fails for two scalar linear layers, refuting a published universal guarantee. An exact residual identity gives the necessary and sufficient condition on a common layer input. All these comparisons hold the calibration input fixed. On two 8B models at 4 bits, fixed half-strength compensation beat uncompensated rounding in every model, text and draw tested, yet no rule for choosing the strength beat a layer-wise rule consistently, and lowering the full-network loss on the data used to choose did not reliably lower it on new text.
papers.summary: Layer-wise post-training quantization methods let each layer compensate for error inherited from earlier layers, and this work asks when such compensation is actually guaranteed to reduce network output error. For linear networks of any depth with invertible calibration Gram matrices, if each layer's rounding error has zero conditional mean and a common deterministic second-moment map (as under subtractive dither on an unbounded grid), fixed compensation strengths between 0 and 1 give mean-square output error no larger than no compensation. Outside that setting the guarantee breaks: rectified linear activations fail for two independent reasons, bounded codebooks can increase output error even with exact layer-wise minimizers, and **for fixed rounding errors the comparison already fails for two scalar linear layers, refuting a published universal guarantee**. On two 8B models at 4 bits, half-strength compensation beat uncompensated rounding in every case tested, but no rule for choosing the strength consistently beat a simple layer-wise rule, and lowering calibration loss did not reliably lower loss on new text.

papers.title: Of Errors and Echoes: Responsibility-Aware Credit Assignment for Tool-Use Agents
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning improves tool-use agents, yet fine-grained credit assignment remains challenging even with step-level feedback. An observed error may be inherited from an earlier decision, while multiple responsible decisions may share the same downstream consequence or participate in later recovery. We introduce Error-Chain-Aware Optimization (ECHO), a responsibility-aware credit assignment framework that separates responsibility identification from credit allocation. A frozen judge combines retrospective trajectory analysis with decision-time assessment from the policy-visible prefix to distinguish newly introduced errors, inherited consequences, missed corrections, and successful corrections. ECHO then counts shared downstream consequences once across responsible decisions and constrains rewards for repairing self-induced errors through source-funded recovery, producing bounded action-level supervision alongside terminal supervision. Experiments on six diverse tool-use benchmarks at both 4B and 8B scales show strong and consistent improvements over the compared baselines, with ECHO achieving the highest score on five of six benchmarks at each scale. These results support decision responsibility as a useful basis for fine-grained credit assignment in tool-use agents. Our code is available at https://github.com/xid32/ECHO.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning improves tool-use agents, but step-level credit assignment is hard because an observed error may be inherited from an earlier decision, several decisions may share one downstream consequence, or a later step may repair the damage. Error-Chain-Aware Optimization (`ECHO`) separates responsibility identification from credit allocation: a frozen judge combines retrospective trajectory analysis with a decision-time assessment from the policy-visible prefix to label newly introduced errors, inherited consequences, missed corrections, and successful corrections. Shared consequences are then counted once across responsible decisions, and rewards for repairing self-induced errors are constrained through source-funded recovery, yielding bounded action-level supervision alongside terminal rewards. **Across six tool-use benchmarks at 4B and 8B scales, ECHO scores highest on five of six benchmarks at each scale**, and code is released.

papers.title: OT-FlowRec: Optimal Transport-Guided Multi-Bridge Flow for Multimodal Sequential Recommendation
papers.abstract: E-commerce user preferences evolve dynamically within sessions, exhibiting concurrent and multi-centric interest distributions. While existing multimodal sequential recommendation methods leverage global attention to compress historical interactions, they inadequately capture the concurrent nature of multi-interest behaviors and fail to model the underlying multi-centric distribution of user intent. To tackle this issue, we propose OT-FlowRec, an optimal transport-guided multi-bridge flow matching framework that explicitly models multi-interest distributions to facilitate multimodal sequential recommendation. Unlike single-path generative models, OT-FlowRec constructs a mixture of parallel, interest-specific transport flows to model the multi-centric distribution characteristics, where each flow preserves a distinct user interest cluster via an optimal transport plan. Then, a geometric transport mechanism is designed to establish minimum-cost paths from the latent multi-interest distribution to target preference prototypes to provide multi-interest awareness. Moreover, a progressive time-sampling warmup strategy dynamically biases optimization weights toward the final states of the generation process, bridging the gap between continuous global distribution fitting and practical top-$k$ ranking metrics. This approach achieves explicit interest disentanglement, ensuring the preservation of a multi-peaked preference representation instead of collapsing it into a unimodal average. Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that OT-FlowRec outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines.
papers.summary: User preferences in e-commerce sessions shift dynamically and often hold several concurrent interests at once, which existing multimodal sequential recommenders flatten into a single global-attention summary. `OT-FlowRec` instead builds a mixture of parallel, interest-specific flow-matching transport paths, each preserving a distinct interest cluster via an optimal transport plan, plus a geometric transport mechanism that finds minimum-cost paths from the latent multi-interest distribution to target preference prototypes. A progressive time-sampling warmup biases optimization toward the final generation states to better match top-k ranking objectives. **The approach keeps a multi-peaked preference representation rather than collapsing to a unimodal average and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on three public datasets.**

papers.title: When Agents Talk, Secrets Travel: Topology-Driven Leakage and Recipient-Conditioned Sanitization in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems (MALS) introduce a privacy-leakage problem that conventional sensitivity-based defenses miss, since information disclosed to one authorized agent can propagate through routine coordination to an unauthorized one, without compromise or malicious behavior. This motivates topology-aware enforcement that blocks unauthorized propagation while preserving authorized disclosure. We evaluate 485 scenarios across coordinator-worker, peer-to-peer, and hierarchical topologies, instrumenting seven communication channels and measuring surface leakage and disclosure to topology-introduced recipients. We introduce RECONS, a Detect -> Decide -> Transform sanitizer conditioning intervention on recipient and execution context rather than sensitivity alone. Topology changes where protected information propagates, with disclosure to topology-introduced recipients rising from 0% to 52.2% while surface leakage stays nearly flat at 60.6-62.8%. This effect persists across four generator models and a second orchestration framework, though magnitude and relay paths differ; framework choice separately drives a 150x leakage spread, so topology alone is not sufficient. RECONS reduces residual disclosure from 96.7% without sanitization to 29.25%, preserving 94.1% of authorized disclosures versus 20.5% under blanket redaction. Detection coverage is the dominant bottleneck, accounting for 95.5% of residual disclosures. These results show that privacy enforcement in MALS must reason about the recipient and communication path realized at runtime, not sensitivity or topology assumptions alone.
papers.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems (MALS) leak private information in a way sensitivity-based defenses miss: data disclosed to one authorized agent can reach an unauthorized agent through ordinary coordination, with no compromise or malicious behavior involved. The authors evaluate 485 scenarios across coordinator-worker, peer-to-peer, and hierarchical topologies, instrumenting seven communication channels, and introduce `RECONS`, a Detect, Decide, Transform sanitizer that conditions its intervention on the recipient and execution context rather than on sensitivity alone. **Changing topology raises disclosure to topology-introduced recipients from 0% to 52.2% while surface leakage stays flat at roughly 61-63%**, an effect that holds across four generator models and a second orchestration framework, though framework choice alone drives a 150x leakage spread. RECONS cuts residual disclosure from 96.7% to 29.25% while preserving 94.1% of authorized disclosures versus 20.5% under blanket redaction, with detection coverage accounting for 95.5% of what remains.

papers.title: Autoregressive Decoding as a Martingale: Characterizing the Stochastic Dynamics of LLM Generation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of language tasks. At their core, autoregressive LLMs are conditional probability models that learn to approximate the next-token distribution given the preceding context. Despite this probabilistic nature, the stochastic dynamics of autoregressive decoding have rarely been investigated from a rigorous probabilistic perspective. In this work, we define the per-step prediction error as the difference between the sampled token indicator and the model's conditional predictive distribution, and prove that the cumulative error process is a martingale with respect to the decoding filtration, implying that its conditional first-order moment is identically zero. Beyond this first-order property, we derive a closed-form expression for the second-order behavior of the martingale sequence: its predictable quadratic variation reduces to $\sum_t\left(1-p(y_t\mid y_{<t})\right)$, computable from realized token probabilities alone. This identity establishes a direct theoretical connection between sequence fluctuations and predictive uncertainty during autoregressive decoding.
