Our results show that MP-MNCA (i) reaches coherent spatial-domain structure in substantially fewer training epochs, as reflected quantitatively by convergence curves and qualitatively by progressive spatial grids, and (ii) maintains strong clustering quality, achieving a mean peak refined ARI of 0.546 versus 0.549 for the strongest baseline (STAIG), while attaining the highest mean refined NMI of 0.657 versus 0.640. Moreover, MP-MNCA outperforms STAIG on 7 of 12 sections in ARI and 11 of 12 in NMI, demonstrating faster convergence without sacrificing spatial-domain quality.
papers.summary: Spatial transcriptomics methods for identifying tissue domains are usually compared only at late training checkpoints, hiding differences in how fast they converge. `MP-MNCA` keeps the full 3,000-dimensional highly-variable-gene representation, routes molecular information across spatial neighbors with masked cross-attention, and injects histological image similarity as a continuous attention prior under a self-supervised masked neighbor-contrastive objective. Across 12 human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) sections it **reaches coherent spatial domains in substantially fewer epochs than established baselines**, with a mean refined adjusted Rand index of 0.546 versus 0.549 for `STAIG` and the highest mean normalized mutual information of 0.657 versus 0.640, winning 11 of 12 sections on the latter.

papers.title: SafeDSE: Joint Exploration of Safety Architecture Patterns, Mapping, and Scheduling for Dataflow Applications With Safety Arguments (Extended Version)
papers.abstract: Embedded platforms increasingly host safety-related streaming functions next to less critical ones. Whether a safety architecture pattern, such as a doer/checker pair, protects a function depends on the cores that run its components. Their schedule must meet the throughput requirement, and mixing safety integrity levels (SILs) on one core raises development cost. This report presents SafeDSE, a design space exploration framework for synchronous dataflow applications. One declarative constraint model decides the pattern of each actor, the placement that the fault model requires, the static-order schedule, and the platform, and prices SIL promotion. Guards activate the chosen patterns in a fixed graph that holds all of them, and node potentials encode throughput. An independent verifier re-checks every solution, and a generator turns its checks into evidence of a safety argument in Goal Structuring Notation. On 9 benchmark instances under period bounds, no rule that fixes patterns before mapping was both always feasible and never more expensive under conservative pricing, while joint exploration was. In the generated arguments, 49 to 62% of the leaves cite verifier checks; the rest are claims a mapping cannot discharge. Optimality within the model was proven for all synthetic graphs with up to 16 actors. This extended version adds the full model, the verifier and generator in detail, the complete catalog and parameters, and a proof of the potential characterization. It also reports every experiment per instance, a mutation analysis of the verifier, and the negative results of the development.
papers.summary: Embedded platforms increasingly run safety-related streaming functions beside less critical ones, and whether a safety architecture pattern such as a doer/checker pair actually protects a function depends on which cores host its components, whether the schedule meets throughput, and whether mixing safety integrity levels (SILs) on a core inflates development cost. `SafeDSE` is a design space exploration framework for synchronous dataflow applications in which one declarative constraint model jointly chooses each actor's pattern, the placement the fault model requires, the static-order schedule, and the platform while pricing SIL promotion; an independent verifier re-checks every solution and a generator turns those checks into Goal Structuring Notation safety-argument evidence. **On nine benchmark instances, no rule that fixed patterns before mapping was both always feasible and never more expensive, whereas joint exploration was**, 49 to 62% of argument leaves cite verifier checks, and optimality within the model was proven for all synthetic graphs with up to 16 actors.

papers.title: OneShot: Label-Efficient Detector Weighting for Time Series Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Time series (TS) anomaly detection (AD) lacks a universal detector, with the best choice determined by the series rather than by the algorithm. Existing methods therefore either select one detector for each series or average a pool of them. However, both assume that no label ever arrives, while a deployed monitor does receive them, since an operator confirms the alarms it raises. In this paper, we propose ONESHOT, which uses a single confirmed anomaly to weight the pool rather than to choose one detector from it. Specifically, we score each detector on the confirmed anomaly, and those scores become the weights of a soft mixture over the whole pool. We show that a single confirmed anomaly is enough to come close to the best detector for the series. Across 152 univariate and 73 multivariate series, ONESHOT outperforms the strongest single detector, averaging the whole pool, and even picking the best detector on the confirmed event. Code is available at: https://github.com/seunghan96/one_shot.
papers.summary: Time series anomaly detection has no universal best detector, and existing approaches either pick one per series or average a pool, both assuming labels never arrive. `OneShot` instead uses the single anomaly an operator confirms when responding to an alarm: each detector is scored on that one event, and those scores become weights in a soft mixture over the whole pool. Across 152 univariate and 73 multivariate series, **the one-label weighting beats the strongest single detector, the uniform average of the pool, and even picking the detector that scored best on the confirmed event**.

papers.title: Look Back to Move Forward: Learning to Revisit for Agentic Compositional Image Generation
papers.abstract: Text-to-image models have made remarkable progress in visual fidelity and instruction following, yet complex compositional generation remains challenging. Existing agentic approaches address this limitation through iterative generation and editing, adapting their actions based on interaction history. However, they typically fix the continuation state (i.e., the image from which refinement proceeds) to the latest image. Since iterative editing is not necessarily monotonic, the agent may continue refining from the latest image even when it has already degraded. In this work, we introduce GenRevisit, an agentic framework that extends action selection to joint continuation-state and action selection. The agent can not only use interaction history to adjust editing instructions but also select an image candidate to edit, jointly deciding where to continue from and how to refine. We train GenRevisit with SFT followed by agentic reinforcement learning. To address the coarse credit assignment of final outcome reward in GRPO, which assigns the same trajectory-level advantage to all actions, we further propose Normalized Action Credit Assignment (NACA) to redistribute positive advantage according to each action's contribution to reducing the remaining objective. On GenEval2, GenRevisit achieves GM scores of 84.3 and 74.4 with Qwen-Image-2512 and Z-Image-Turbo, surpassing the strongest baselines using the same generators by 12.7 and 10.9 points respectively. GenRevisit achieves state-of-the-art performance on GenEval, GenEval++, and GenEval2 among baselines.
papers.summary: Agentic text-to-image pipelines refine an image over several editing rounds, but they always continue from the most recent image, even when the last edit made things worse. `GenRevisit` lets the agent jointly choose which earlier candidate to continue from and how to edit it, trained with supervised fine-tuning followed by agentic reinforcement learning. Because `GRPO` hands every action in a trajectory the same advantage, the authors add `Normalized Action Credit Assignment`, which redistributes positive advantage according to how much each action reduced the remaining objective. On `GenEval2` the method reaches `GM` scores of 84.3 with `Qwen-Image-2512` and 74.4 with `Z-Image-Turbo`, **12.7 and 10.9 points above the strongest baselines using the same generators**.

papers.title: Learning to GUIDE the Group: Self-Learning LLM Facilitation Across Multi-Party Tasks
papers.abstract: As large language models are increasingly adopted as multi-party communication facilitators, there is a growing demand for agents capable of balancing diverse group dynamics across contexts. However, existing LLM facilitators are often fine-tuned for task-specific objectives; generalized LLM-based facilitation methods that can adapt to different types of tasks and diverse group dynamics are underdeveloped. To address this gap, we present GUIDE (Generalized Unified Intervention for Dynamic Exchanges, a framework for developing generalized LLM-based facilitators across different multi-party contexts. GUIDE evaluates facilitation across both objective task outcomes and subjective metrics, including psychological safety and perceived friction. Within this framework, we study whether LLMs can self-learn generalized facilitation strategy offline to real-time interventions. We first collect multi-party human interactions guided by task-specific expert LLM facilitators (N=432 conversations). We then employ a self-learning method in which an LLM induces an actionable strategic playbook from conversations and iteratively refines it using feedback from an LLM judge aligned with human annotators (N=20), developing a single generalized facilitator that outperforms the three task-specific expert facilitators on held-out conversations 61.4% win rate. Finally, we evaluate these improvements empirically; in a real-time online empirical study, the self-learned generalized facilitator preserves facilitator performance and group productivity, improves speaking comfort and reduces interpersonal friction, while using 24.7% fewer turns and 29.0% fewer words than the expert prompts. These findings provide empirical evidence that LLMs can learn generalizable, task-agnostic social facilitation from task-specific human interactions, on-par with hand-crafted task-specific prompts across diverse group settings.
papers.summary: Language models used to facilitate group conversations are usually fine-tuned for one task at a time, leaving open whether a single facilitator can adapt across contexts and group dynamics. `GUIDE` (Generalized Unified Intervention for Dynamic Exchanges) collects 432 multi-party human conversations run by task-specific expert facilitators, then has a model induce an actionable strategy playbook from them and iteratively refine it using feedback from a judge model aligned to human annotators. The resulting single generalized facilitator **won 61.4% of head-to-head comparisons against the three task-specific experts on held-out conversations**, and in a live online study it preserved group productivity while improving speaking comfort, reducing interpersonal friction, and using about a quarter fewer turns and nearly a third fewer words.

papers.title: AutoNovo: Agentic Program Search Discovers Transferable Nucleic Acid Design Algorithms
papers.abstract: In-silico optimization of nucleic acids relies on predictive oracles that imperfectly capture biological function, so sequences optimized against one model may exploit model-specific artifacts and fail to generalize to independent models. Recent studies have shown that not all designers generalize equally well to independent models. In this work, we use agentic program search to iteratively propose, execute, evaluate, and revise code for nucleic-acid designers. We describe the successful strategies used to prompt the search. AutoNovo designers achieved the best observed mean among the evaluated methods on 3/3 DNA-design tasks in terms of in-silico performance, and 6/6 transfer tasks in terms of independent models. The designers come from a family of discovered nucleic acid designers rather than a single universal best designer. We plan to release the resulting designers. These results are the first steps in creating nucleic acid designers that maximize cross-model generalization, and thus improving the odds that in-silico designed sequences reflect real biology.
papers.summary: Nucleic acid sequences optimized in silico against a predictive oracle can exploit that model's artifacts and then fail when scored by independent models. `AutoNovo` applies agentic program search to the design algorithm itself: a model proposes, executes, evaluates, and revises code for nucleic-acid designers, and the paper documents the prompting strategies that made the search productive. The discovered designers **achieved the best observed mean among evaluated methods on all three DNA design tasks and all six transfer tasks scored by independent models**, and the outcome is a family of complementary designers rather than one universal winner.

papers.title: Reflected Proximal Dynamics for Accelerated High-Accuracy Log-Concave Sampling
papers.abstract: We study sampling from $\pi(x)\propto\mathrm{e}^{-V(x)}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $V$ is $\alpha$-strongly convex and $\beta$-smooth with condition number $\kappa=\beta/\alpha$. For this problem, the proximal sampler preserves the target exactly and recovers overdamped Langevin dynamics in the small-step limit, but its Gaussian resampling step discards directional information. Underdamped Langevin dynamics retains such information through momentum to accelerate exploration, motivating a proximal construction that combines target preservation with directional persistence. We introduce \textit{reflected proximal dynamics}, which combines proximal sampling with an exact reflection of the auxiliary variable, conditional kinetic motion, and controlled refreshment. We develop two realizations: a flux-resampled underdamped half-turn and a persistent-momentum quarter-turn. From a warm start with constant $\chi^2$ divergence, both methods achieve total variation error $\varepsilon$ using $\widetilde O(\sqrt{\kappa}d^{1/4})$ expected oracle queries. We further remove the supplied warm-start assumption by combining either sampler with existing posterior samplers in a proximal initialization stage with an optimized coarse step size. Accounting for both initialization and sampling yields $\widetilde O(\kappa^{6/7}d^{1/4})$ expected oracle queries. In both regimes, the dependence on the target accuracy $\varepsilon$ is $\mathrm{polylog}(1/\varepsilon)$, making reflected proximal dynamics a promising framework for accelerated high-accuracy log-concave sampling.
papers.summary: Sampling from strongly log-concave targets with the proximal sampler keeps the target exact but discards directional information at each Gaussian resampling step, whereas underdamped Langevin dynamics retains direction through momentum. The proposed `reflected proximal dynamics` combines proximal sampling with an exact reflection of the auxiliary variable, conditional kinetic motion, and controlled refreshment, realized as a flux-resampled underdamped half-turn and a persistent-momentum quarter-turn. From a warm start, both variants reach a given total variation error in **Õ(√κ·d^(1/4)) expected oracle queries** for condition number κ and dimension d, and adding a proximal initialization stage removes the warm-start assumption at Õ(κ^(6/7)·d^(1/4)) queries, with only polylogarithmic dependence on accuracy.

papers.title: Avoiding What Your Teacher Already Knows: Entity Familiarity for Deep-Search Distillation
papers.abstract: Deep-search agents are commonly trained by distilling tool-use trajectories from stronger teacher models. However, structurally complex questions may remain relatively easy for teachers familiar with key entities in the underlying entity graph, resulting in lower search demand and weaker supervision. We refer to this teacher-specific variation in question difficulty as teacher-relative difficulty and investigate entity familiarity as an early predictor. We first introduce Evidence-Verified Entity Familiarity (EVF), which estimates familiarity by verifying a teacher-generated factual brief against online evidence. Across multiple teachers, EVF is significantly correlated with teacher-relative difficulty with AUCs of 0.60--0.70. However, its high cost makes it impractical for constructing entity graphs at scale. To address this limitation, we propose Self-Reported Entity Familiarity (SEF), a lightweight gating signal that directly asks a teacher whether it is familiar with an entity before admitting that entity into the graph. Across multiple teachers, trajectories from SEF-gated synthesis exhibit greater observed search demand and yield higher downstream student accuracy than those from ungated synthesis. Because familiarity is teacher specific, we further study cross-teacher reuse. We screen graphs collected for other teachers using Kimi-K3's SEF judgments and use the retained graphs to produce 5,411 additional trajectories. Combined with 2,200 trajectories from newly constructed, SEF-gated graphs, these data improve Qwen3.8-27B's accuracy from 44.10% to 66.41% on a BrowseComp subset, and achieving state-of-the-art performance among models of comparable size on BrowseComp, SEAL-0, HLE-text, and xbench. Overall, SEF provides a low-cost way to synthesize more informative supervision for deep-search distillation.
papers.summary: Deep-search agents are trained on tool-use trajectories distilled from stronger teachers, but a structurally hard question whose key entities the teacher already knows well demands little searching and so yields weak supervision. The authors call this teacher-relative difficulty and predict it from entity familiarity, first with `Evidence-Verified Entity Familiarity`, which checks a teacher-written factual brief against online evidence and correlates with difficulty at areas under the curve of 0.60 to 0.70, then with the much cheaper `Self-Reported Entity Familiarity`, which simply asks the teacher whether it knows an entity before admitting it to the question graph. Gating synthesis on self-reported familiarity produced trajectories with more search activity and stronger students, and reusing graphs screened with one teacher's judgments **lifted `Qwen3.8-27B` from 44.10% to 66.41% on a `BrowseComp` subset**, with reported best-in-size results on `BrowseComp`, `SEAL-0`, `HLE-text`, and `xbench`.

papers.title: ScreenASR-Bench: A Tiered Benchmark for Speech Recognition with Visual Context
papers.abstract: Current ASR models perform well on general benchmarks but still struggle with acoustically ambiguous words. Visual context can aid recognition in screen-based scenarios, yet existing benchmarks provide limited insight into the benefits of different types of visual evidence. To address this gap, we introduce ScreenASR-Bench , a tiered benchmark with three progressively challenging levels: Explicit Textual Evidence (ETE), based on direct on-screen text; Explicit Visual Evidence (EVE), using visible content rather than on-screen text; and Implicit Semantic Evidence (ISE), requiring scene-level inference. Extensive experiments on ASR models, Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) and Omni models show that incorporating visual context substantially improves recall over the audio-only setting across all three model families. The gains are largest for ETE and smallest for ISE, indicating that models leverage direct visual evidence more effectively than indirect semantic cues. To facilitate future research on visually grounded speech recognition, we publicly release ScreenASR-Bench.
papers.summary: Speech recognition still stumbles on acoustically ambiguous words, and in screen-based settings the surrounding visuals could disambiguate them, but existing benchmarks say little about which kinds of visual evidence actually help. `ScreenASR-Bench` separates three tiers: explicit textual evidence read straight from on-screen text, explicit visual evidence from visible content without text, and implicit semantic evidence requiring scene-level inference. Across conventional recognition models, large audio-language models, and omni models, **visual context raised recall over the audio-only setting in every model family, with the largest gains on on-screen text and the smallest on implicit semantic cues**.

papers.title: Hardware-Friendly Token-Group Activation Quantization for Low-Bit Mamba Super-Resolution
papers.abstract: Mamba-based super-resolution models are efficient alternatives to Transformer-based restoration backbones, but their low-bit post-training quantization remains challenging because selective scan, Mamba's input-dependent state-space operator, induces different activation ranges across spatial tokens. Thus, a single layer-wise clipping range poorly matches all tokens. We propose Token-Group Quantization, a hardware-friendly activation PTQ framework that statically approximates a hardware-unfriendly post-scan grouping oracle, where tokens with similar preferred clipping ranges are assigned to the same group. To avoid runtime post-scan grouping in static low-bit inference, a lightweight predictor infers the groups from pre-scan features available before the quantized scan path. During calibration, we form pseudo-labels by clustering post-scan activation descriptors that capture similar rounding--clipping behavior. At inference, the frozen predictor maps pre-scan features to groups and selects entries from offline-calibrated group-wise clipping-bound tables, without runtime statistics collection, dynamic clipping updates, or post-scan group assignment. To address low-bit restoration degradation, we further introduce a Frequency-Preserving Refinement (FPR) objective for clipping-bound calibration. FPR aligns Fourier amplitude and phase between full-precision teacher and quantized student outputs to preserve high-frequency structures. Across PTQ protocols, bit-widths, backbones, and tasks, our method consistently outperforms prior Mamba and SR PTQ baselines, transfers to Transformer SR and Vision Mamba classification, composes with rotation-based quantization, and achieves 2.23x speedup on Jetson Orin Nano over FP16. Code is available here.
papers.summary: Mamba-based super-resolution networks are cheaper than Transformer restoration backbones, but the input-dependent selective scan gives different spatial tokens very different activation ranges, so a single layer-wide clipping range quantizes all of them badly. `Token-Group Quantization` approximates an ideal but hardware-unfriendly post-scan grouping with a lightweight predictor that infers groups from pre-scan features and reads bounds from offline-calibrated per-group clipping tables, so inference needs no runtime statistics or dynamic clipping updates. A `Frequency-Preserving Refinement` objective aligns Fourier amplitude and phase between the full-precision teacher and the quantized student to retain high-frequency structure. The method beats prior Mamba and super-resolution post-training quantization baselines across bit widths and backbones, transfers to Transformer super-resolution and `Vision Mamba` classification, and **runs 2.23x faster than FP16 on a `Jetson Orin Nano`**.

papers.title: A Survey of Flow Matching in Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Flow Matching (FM) has recently emerged as a principled and efficient generative modeling framework for reinforcement learning (RL), enabling expressive, multimodal policy parameterizations via deterministic probability transport. Compared to diffusion-based policies that rely on stochastic denoising chains, FM uses sampling based on ordinary differential equations (ODEs), with learned velocity fields, which can substantially reduce inference latency and simplify the incorporation of RL objectives. As research in flow-based RL rapidly accelerates across offline continuous control, online fine-tuning, and foundation model alignment, the literature has become highly fragmented. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive taxonomy of flow-matching approaches in reinforcement learning. We organize the literature along two axes: the target distribution being modeled (e.g., action policies, value critics, transition dynamics) and the mechanism of RL signal integration (e.g., energy-weighted regression, flow-based policy gradients, and group relative policy optimization). Furthermore, we survey emerging frontiers such as discrete and non-Euclidean action spaces, provide a systematic comparative analysis against Gaussian and diffusion baselines, and outline critical open problems. Ultimately, this survey serves as a foundational roadmap for the next generation of generative reinforcement learning and alignment.
papers.summary: Flow matching trains generative models by learning a velocity field and sampling through an ordinary differential equation, which makes it cheaper at inference than diffusion's stochastic denoising chains and easier to fold reinforcement learning objectives into. The survey organizes a fast-moving and fragmented literature along two axes: the target distribution being modeled, such as action policies, value critics, or transition dynamics, and the mechanism that injects the learning signal, such as energy-weighted regression, flow-based policy gradients, or group relative policy optimization. It also covers discrete and non-Euclidean action spaces, **sets flow-based policies against Gaussian and diffusion baselines in a systematic comparison**, and lays out open problems spanning offline control, online fine-tuning, and foundation model alignment.

papers.title: agent-risk: Risk Assessment for Changes to AI Agents
papers.abstract: Before changing a deployed AI agent (a stricter safety gate, a new model), organizations must approve the change, starting from existing logs. Extending classical risk analysis to partial records and partial changes to running systems, agent-risk replays logged episodes, assuming nothing else changes and the agent does not anticipate the change. The log settles episodes acting as before, a declared stop value settles stopped ones, and the rest need logged support, a saved-state rerun, or a bound. We prove what logs must record for exact replay and which saved states serve a gate family. For independent episodes, we bound the reruns a decision needs and tolerable drift from live behavior. In a bash sandbox, a 7,200-episode log alone decided neither of two retry gates, which let the agent act after refusals the log never shows. Rerunning only each gate's blocked episodes from saved states reached both live decisions at half the agent calls of a live test sized post hoc for them, given the log. Without per-step harm, a stopping gate's certified harm ceiling rose up to 2.5-fold, since the log hides whether harm preceded the stop. Approval thus needs evidence designed in advance: log fields, saved states, targeted reruns.
papers.summary: Approving a change to a deployed agent, such as a stricter safety gate or a new base model, usually has to be justified from logs of how the previous version behaved. `agent-risk` extends classical risk analysis to that partial-record setting by replaying logged episodes: episodes that would act as before are settled by the log, stopped ones by a declared stop value, and the remainder need logged support, a rerun from saved state, or a bound, with proofs of what logs must record for exact replay. In a bash sandbox, **a 7,200-episode log on its own decided neither of two retry gates**, because those gates let the agent keep acting after refusals the log never captured; rerunning only each gate's blocked episodes from saved state matched both live decisions at half the agent calls of an equivalent live test. Without per-step harm records, a stopping gate's certified harm ceiling rose up to 2.5-fold, so the authors argue log fields, saved states, and targeted reruns have to be designed before the change is proposed.

papers.title: REVEAL: Reverse Engineering Agentic Latents from Frontier-Model Traces
papers.abstract: Frontier LLM agents perform complex interactive tasks, but their inference costs motivate transferring their experience to smaller open-source agents. Distillation and latent communication typically require target-model training or access to source-model internals. We study how textual frontier-model trajectories can provide reusable local controls for a frozen agent. Inspired by protocol reverse engineering, we introduce $\textit{Agentic Latents}$, comprising anchored states and dynamic profiles of feedback--response cycles elicited by replay in the target model. Our training-free framework, $\textbf{REVEAL}$ ($\textbf{REV}$erse $\textbf{E}$ngineering $\textbf{A}$gentic $\textbf{L}$atents), uses these profiles and trajectory outcomes to match and select local events from successful and failed rollouts of the same task and source model. Their response-transition contrasts yield a target-specific steering direction, applied before each response. Within-benchmark evaluations on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and Humanity's Last Exam with tools report higher accuracy than unmodified agents across three targets. Representation analyses and behavioral case studies support reusing frontier-model experience as local activation control.
papers.summary: Transferring a frontier agent's problem-solving experience to a cheaper open model normally requires fine-tuning the target or reading the source model's internals. `REVEAL` (Reverse Engineering Agentic Latents) works from textual trajectories alone: replaying frontier traces through the frozen target records anchored states and dynamic profiles of its feedback-response cycles, and matching events from successful versus failed rollouts of the same task yields a response-transition contrast that becomes a target-specific steering direction applied before each response. The framework needs no training and **improved accuracy over the unmodified agents on `Terminal-Bench 2.1` and `Humanity's Last Exam` with tools across three target models**, with representation analyses and case studies supporting the idea that frontier experience can be reused as local activation control.

papers.title: SLDBench v2: Active Scaling Law Discovery
papers.abstract: Scaling laws predict large-model performance from small experiments, but finding a reliable law itself requires costly experiments. SLDBench tests whether language-model agents can discover scaling laws when all experimental results are given upfront. We introduce SLDBench v2 with two extensions. First, we expand the corpus from 8 to 127 scenarios spanning language-model pretraining, downstream performance, and vision-language transfer, and select 30 challenging scenarios on which a reference power-law fit reaches $R^2 \le 0.8$; they represent at least $1.09 \times 10^{23}$ FLOPs of source-reported training compute. Second, we introduce active scaling law discovery: an agent chooses which experiments to run, pays each one's recorded cost (e.g., training FLOPs), and revises its law as outcomes arrive, and is scored on the same hidden extrapolation targets as in the passive setting. Across 8 frontier agent systems, median $R^2$ drops from 0.72-0.75 (passive) to 0.24-0.57 (active), and prediction error rises 1.5-4.7 times, depending on the system. Agents favor cheap experiments, spending 8-44% of the full-pool cost on average; low-cost acquisition can yield strong predictions, but cheap purchases also leave experimental conditions needed for extrapolation unobserved. Experimental planning thus remains a key open challenge for agents that assist model development in the prevailing AI-for-AI study.
papers.summary: Scaling laws let small experiments predict large-model behavior, but fitting a trustworthy law is itself expensive, and the original `SLDBench` only asked whether agents could find one when every experimental result was handed to them upfront. Version 2 grows the corpus from 8 to 127 scenarios covering language model pretraining, downstream performance, and vision-language transfer, keeps 30 hard ones where a reference power-law fit reaches an R² of 0.8 or below, and adds active discovery, where the agent chooses which experiments to run, pays each one's recorded compute cost, and revises its law as results arrive. Across eight frontier agent systems, **median R² falls from 0.72-0.75 in the passive setting to 0.24-0.57 once the agent must plan its own experiments**, with prediction error rising 1.5 to 4.7 times. Agents gravitate toward cheap experiments, spending 8-44% of the full pool's cost on average and often leaving unobserved exactly the conditions needed for extrapolation.

papers.title: Memory-Efficient Integer-Only Training of Deep Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Training neural networks in reduced precision can yield significant efficiency gains, yet all existing methods that scale to standard computer vision benchmarks retain floating-point in at least one stage, typically the weight update or optimizer state. We present a training algorithm that scales to modern deep neural networks, in which every tensor (weights, gradients, and activations) is stored as INT8, and every operation (forward pass, backward pass, weight update, optimizer update) is performed in integer arithmetic. Specifically, tensors are stored as signed integer mantissas paired with explicit power-of-two exponents, on which integer-only operations are performed using five custom composable building blocks (products, sums, divide-by-constant, nonlinear functions, and weight updates). This allows complete implementation of trainable integer layers, including convolutions, batch and layer normalization, softmax, and GELU. A per-group velocity mechanism with independent exponent tracking preserves gradient precision across neurons and channels with diverse magnitudes. As every tensor fits in INT8, training memory is roughly 4x smaller than the FP32 baseline. We validate our training algorithm on CNNs (ResNet-18/34/50/101, MobileNetV2) and Vision Transformers (ViT-Ti / B), demonstrating for the first time that training neural networks with INT8 tensors and integer arithmetic can achieve competitive accuracy on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet at a reduced memory budget.
papers.summary: Every reduced-precision training method that scales to standard vision benchmarks still keeps floating point somewhere, typically in the weight update or the optimizer state. The proposed scheme stores weights, gradients, and activations as `INT8` signed mantissas paired with explicit power-of-two exponents and performs the forward pass, backward pass, weight update, and optimizer update entirely in integer arithmetic, assembled from five composable primitives that cover convolutions, batch and layer normalization, softmax, and GELU, with a per-group velocity mechanism tracking exponents independently so gradients survive across channels of very different magnitude. Because every tensor fits in eight bits, **training memory is roughly 4x smaller than an FP32 baseline**, while `ResNet-18/34/50/101`, `MobileNetV2`, and `ViT-Ti/B` reach competitive accuracy on `CIFAR-10`, `CIFAR-100`, and `ImageNet`.

papers.title: FON: A Draft-Revise Dual-Organ Language Model without Sequence-Level Quadratic Attention
papers.abstract: Self-attention assigns two functions to one mechanism-where to read and how to mix-at the price of O(L^2) training, an O(T) decode state, and position signals bound to the training length. Existing attention-free alternatives all optimize the single function of generation. We propose FON (Fusion-Organ Network), which differentiates one weight stack into a drafting organ (multi-tap learnable delays + content-adaptive recursion; causal, O(S) training, O(1) decode state, no sequence-level quadratic attention) and a revision organ that re-processes the written prefix through multi-scale ripple kernels injected via weak gates, never generating. At 30M parameters, iso-parameter and iso-token budget, FON reaches perplexity 131.03 on WikiText-103, beating Transformer (197.73) and Mamba2 (152.53); the advantage persists under all depth-aligned baselines and at the 70M tier (-20.8%). At 8x length extrapolation FON degrades by ~8-9% without positional-encoding engineering, between ALiBi and RoPE. The revision channel provides a structural pathway for in-domain infilling that causal architectures lack in principle (+19% over on-demand coupling), at a perplexity cost indistinguishable within measurement precision. We report all costs and boundaries: impaired long-range retrieval, synthetic-task disadvantages, weaker out-of-domain code infilling than a same-recipe Transformer, and a 6.5-12.3x wall-clock gap.
papers.summary: Self-attention handles both where to read and how to mix with one mechanism, paying for it with quadratic training cost, a decode state that grows with context, and position signals tied to the training length. `FON` (Fusion-Organ Network) splits a single weight stack into a drafting organ built from multi-tap learnable delays and content-adaptive recursion, which is causal with constant decode state and no sequence-level quadratic attention, plus a revision organ that re-processes the written prefix through multi-scale ripple kernels and never generates. At 30M parameters under matched parameter and token budgets it reaches **perplexity 131.03 on `WikiText-103`, against 197.73 for a Transformer and 152.53 for `Mamba2`**, holds the advantage at the 70M tier, degrades only 8-9% at eight times the training length without positional-encoding engineering, and gains in-domain infilling that causal architectures structurally lack. The authors also report the costs: impaired long-range retrieval, weaker out-of-domain code infilling than a same-recipe Transformer, and a 6.5-12.3x wall-clock gap.

papers.title: Narrative Paradoxes in LLM Inference: Shaping Reasoning Trajectories toward Misalignment
papers.abstract: Explicit reasoning in large language models (LLMs) is often associated with reliability, yet it can still pose risks when a model infers harmful goals under a benign context. We identify a distinct challenge: ensuring the safety of the \emph{multi-step reasoning process} itself, where locally coherent steps may still lead to globally harmful outcomes. To explore this vulnerability, we propose PDRA (Paradox-driven Reasoning-based Attack), a novel attack method that programs a harmful reasoning trajectory. PDRA first constructs a paradoxical narrative core by pairing a malicious actor (e.g., a terrorist) with a benign task (e.g., writing a safety bulletin). It then embeds this core into a structured analytical framework that forces the model through a mandatory three-stage analysis -- surface purpose, latent intent, and operational reconstruction -- guiding it to produce detailed harmful content while maintaining narrative coherence. Mechanistically, we show PDRA steers the model's internal representations away from refusal-related patterns, suppressing safety-triggering lexicons while activating planning-oriented terms. Empirically, PDRA achieves state-of-the-art attack success rates across diverse LLMs with high efficiency. \textcolor{red}{\textbf{Warning:} This paper may contain sensitive content.}
papers.summary: Explicit step-by-step reasoning is often treated as making models more trustworthy, but the reasoning process is itself a safety surface, since locally sensible steps can compose into a globally harmful result. `PDRA` (Paradox-driven Reasoning-based Attack) is an attack method that shapes that trajectory by framing a request whose stated actor and stated purpose contradict each other, then routing the model through a fixed multi-stage analytical structure. Representation analysis indicates these prompts move internal states away from refusal-associated patterns and toward planning-oriented ones, and **the method reports state-of-the-art attack success rates across a range of models** at low cost, supporting the authors' argument that alignment work has to cover multi-step reasoning rather than only final answers.

papers.title: ReTAC: Residual Test-Time Agentic Computation for Video Spatial Reasoning
papers.abstract: Test-time agentic computation can improve multimodal large language models (MLLMs) through planning, tool use, iterative perception, and reflection, but indiscriminate computation may duplicate resolved work, introduce noisy evidence, and perturb correct predictions. We propose that such computation should be residual: allocate additional computation only to requirements unresolved by the base model and, after a localized failure, recompute only the affected states. We instantiate this formulation in ReTAC, a training-free multiagent framework for video spatial reasoning. ReTAC organizes supplementary computation around unresolved requirements. It plans ordered steps to acquire missing spatial evidence and combines the observations with compatible native evidence for reasoning. In addition, it uses stage-aligned verification to localize failures to planning, perception, or reasoning. Dependency-based recovery recomputes only affected states while reusing unaffected ones. Extensive experiments show that ReTAC achieves the highest overall score among the compared methods across three mainstream MLLMs and two widely adopted benchmarks. Further analyses show that gains from additional computation depend not only on how much is used, but also on where it is allocated and which valid intermediate states are preserved.
papers.summary: Adding test-time planning, tool use, iterative perception, and reflection to multimodal large language models can help, but applying it indiscriminately redoes solved work, injects noisy evidence, and can overturn answers that were already correct. `ReTAC` makes the extra computation residual: it plans steps only for requirements the base model left unresolved, combines the new observations with compatible native evidence, and after a failure recomputes just the affected states while reusing the rest, using stage-aligned verification to pin the failure to planning, perception, or reasoning. The training-free multi-agent framework **scored highest overall across three mainstream multimodal models on two widely used video spatial reasoning benchmarks**, and the analyses argue that gains depend on where computation is allocated and which valid intermediate states are preserved, not merely how much is spent.

papers.title: HyWe: Unifying Search and Operation for Real-World Hybrid Web Tasks
papers.abstract: Real-world hybrid web tasks need both information gathering and page interaction, yet search-based and operation-based agents are developed and evaluated separately. To bridge this gap, we introduce HyWe, a framework that unifies both capabilities within one model and trajectory. Its two modes use dedicated prompts and tool sets to sustain sub-goal execution; explicit switching selects the needed capability, and shared history lets each mode build on the other's findings. To provide demonstrations of these behaviors, we develop HyWeCollector, a fully automatic pipeline that uses task prototypes, four switching patterns, and multi-agent synthesis to produce verified hybrid trajectories. We train HyWe-35B on these demonstrations to unify efficient information gathering and browser interaction in a single 35B web agent. To evaluate hybrid task completion, we introduce HyWeBench: 100 human-written tasks on websites distinct from training, with human-written sub-goal checklists and an outcome-based evaluation pipeline. Hybrid training enables HyWe-35B to achieve 47.0% success on this benchmark, improving on the untrained base model by 19.0 percentage points and outperforming existing search-based and operation-based agents. Even before training, the same base model solves 28.0% of tasks with HyWe, versus 11.0% with all tools under one prompt. Beyond hybrid tasks, HyWe-35B achieves 59.0% and 88.3% success on Online-Mind2Web and WebVoyager, outperforming existing open-source baselines and cutting action cost per successful task by 48.3% and 51.9% compared with Fara-7B.
papers.summary: Real web tasks mix gathering information with clicking through pages, yet search-based and operation-based agents are built and evaluated separately. `HyWe` puts both capabilities in one model and one trajectory, with two modes that carry their own prompts and tool sets, explicit switching between them, and a shared history so each mode builds on the other's findings; training demonstrations come from a fully automatic pipeline that synthesizes and verifies hybrid trajectories from task prototypes and four switching patterns. On `HyWeBench`, 100 human-written tasks on websites unseen in training, `HyWe-35B` reaches 47.0% success, 19 points above the untrained base model, and **the same base model solves 28.0% with the two-mode scaffold versus 11.0% with every tool under a single prompt**. It also reports 59.0% on `Online-Mind2Web` and 88.3% on `WebVoyager` while roughly halving action cost per successful task compared with `Fara-7B`.

papers.title: BehaviorFormer: Discovering Behavioral Patterns via Clusterable Next-Token Prediction
papers.abstract: Discovering behavioral patterns in open-ended games is challenging due to the lack of clear objectives or ground-truth annotations. In this work, we extend a next-token prediction Transformer with the deep clustering algorithm DCSS to learn meaningful representations with well-separated clusters. In a controlled Minecraft session with 26 players, the method discovers 23 distinct behavioral patterns that generalize across the studied players, further refining structures present in self-supervised representations into clearly separable clusters. We group the clusters into seven interpretable categories covering stationary, roaming, travel, mining, base work, logging, and farming behavior.
papers.summary: Open-ended games provide neither clear objectives nor ground-truth labels against which to characterize what players are actually doing. `BehaviorFormer` extends a next-token-prediction Transformer over play traces with the `DCSS` deep clustering algorithm, so the learned representation sharpens into well-separated clusters rather than the continuous structure self-supervised features give. In a controlled `Minecraft` session with 26 players, it **discovered 23 distinct behavioral patterns that generalized across the studied players**, which the authors group into seven interpretable categories spanning stationary, roaming, travel, mining, base work, logging, and farming activity.

papers.title: When a Conceptor Complement Becomes Gain: Operator Geometry and Behavioral Attribution in Language Models
papers.abstract: When a steering intervention changes a language model's behavior, which part of the intervention deserves the credit? We test this question for a target-centered, scaled conceptor complement by removing its fitted covariance filter while preserving the same target-specific center and gain. At the original aperture $\alpha=.05$ and gain $\beta=2$, all 21 fitted maps across three models and seven targets expand every direction at the generation intervention layers. The matrix correction is $0.093\%$--$7.815\%$ of the matched-control displacement on held-out extraction activations. In 480 paired comparisons within a 1,920-response study, retaining the matrix changes many individual texts but does not establish a consistent additional target-suppression benefit on the four-target panel. A geometric aperture sweep shows that the operating regime changes with the filter setting. Separately, an invertible soft filter preserves what an unrestricted affine readout can recover, whereas dedicated erasure methods reduce prediction by newly fitted probes. Together, the results show why a whole-intervention comparison cannot by itself attribute generated behavior to the fitted matrix: analyze the complete transformation, hold shared components fixed, and test its output consequences directly.
papers.summary: When a steering intervention changes a language model's behavior, it is unclear how much credit belongs to the intervention's fitted matrix rather than the shared center and gain it is applied with. The study ablates a target-centered scaled conceptor complement by removing its fitted covariance filter while holding center and gain fixed, and finds that at the original aperture and gain all 21 fitted maps across three models and seven targets expand every direction at the generation layers, with the matrix accounting for only 0.093% to 7.815% of the matched-control displacement on held-out activations. Across 480 paired comparisons within a 1,920-response study, **retaining the matrix changed many individual texts but established no consistent extra target suppression**, and an invertible soft filter left information recoverable by an unrestricted affine readout where dedicated erasure methods did not. The conclusion is methodological: attributing behavior to a fitted matrix requires holding shared components fixed and testing output consequences directly, not comparing whole interventions.

papers.title: Explicitly Aligned Multi-View Breast Cancer Risk Prediction from Variable-Length Screening Histories
papers.abstract: Accurate breast cancer risk prediction from screening mammography is essential for improved risk stratification and personalized screening. It can benefit from both temporal breast tissue changes across longitudinal examinations and complementary anatomical information from craniocaudal (CC) and mediolateral oblique (MLO) views. Leveraging longitudinal information requires identifying corresponding tissue regions across examinations, yet most approaches rely on implicit feature alignment without explicitly enforcing spatial consistency. Recent work has demonstrated the benefits of explicit temporal alignment; however, existing methods model each view independently, preventing them from exploiting complementary CC and MLO information. Furthermore, explicit approaches have been limited to a single prior examination. To fill these gaps, we propose (github.com/sot176/FlexLMV-Net), a breast-wise longitudinal multi-view framework that jointly models CC and MLO views across screening examinations while accommodating a variable number of prior examinations. FlexLMV-Net explicitly aligns longitudinal feature maps and integrates complementary views through cross-view temporal fusion and a dual-stream attention block. Evaluated on EMBED and CSAW-CC, FlexLMV-Net consistently outperforms existing approaches across breast density, cancer subtypes, and demographic subgroups, highlighting the benefits of explicit longitudinal alignment, multi-view modeling, and flexible use of available screening history. We further introduce (github.com/sot176/BCRBench), an open-source benchmark that unifies state-of-the-art single- and multi-timepoint breast cancer risk prediction models under standardized preprocessing, training, inference, and evaluation protocols, enabling fair and reproducible comparison of existing methods.
papers.summary: Breast cancer risk prediction from screening mammography can draw on tissue change across repeated exams and on the complementary craniocaudal and mediolateral oblique views, but existing methods align views only implicitly, model each view on its own, or handle just a single prior examination. `FlexLMV-Net` explicitly aligns longitudinal feature maps per breast and fuses the two views through cross-view temporal fusion and a dual-stream attention block, while accepting a variable number of prior exams. On the `EMBED` and `CSAW-CC` datasets **it consistently outperforms existing approaches across breast density levels, cancer subtypes, and demographic subgroups**, and the authors release `BCRBench`, an open benchmark that standardizes preprocessing, training, inference, and evaluation for single- and multi-timepoint risk models.

papers.title: BAT3R: Robust Online 3D Reconstruction with Bayesian Adaptive State Updates
papers.abstract: Feed-forward transformer models have driven remarkable progress in 3D vision,yet their quadratic complexity renders them impractical for long video sequences. Streaming 3D reconstruction addresses this bottleneck by processing frames sequen?tially with constant memory. However, existing recurrent architectures inevitably suffer from progressive degradation over long sequences, as they fail to account for the intrinsic reliability of observations and the accumulated confidence of the historical state, leading to severe error accumulation. To address these issues, we introduce BAT3R, a training-free Bayesian adaptation framework comprising two synergistic modules: State Innovation Gating (SIG) and Bayesian-guided Adaptive State Updating (BASU). SIG acts as a distributional regularizer that anchors state evolution to its geometric initialization, effectively arresting representational drift during long-term inference. Building on this, BASU reformulates state update as a recursive Bayesian inference process within a Kalman filtering framework. By jointly modeling the temporal reliability of observations via information-theoretic gain and spatial relevance via cross-attention maps, BASU achieves an asymmetric spatio-temporal state fusion: well-consolidated historical regions are protected from redundant updates, while genuinely novel scene content is aggressively incor?porated. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks (7-Scenes, TUM, ScanNet, KITTI, etc.) demonstrate that BAT3R consistently outperforms state-of-the-art online 3D reconstruction methods, with the most significant gains observed on long sequences and complex scenes.
papers.summary: Streaming 3D reconstruction processes video frames one at a time with constant memory, but existing recurrent models drift and accumulate error over long sequences because they ignore how reliable each observation is and how confident the accumulated state has become. `BAT3R` is a training-free Bayesian adaptation framework with two parts: State Innovation Gating (`SIG`) anchors the evolving state to its geometric initialization to limit representational drift, and Bayesian-guided Adaptive State Updating (`BASU`) recasts the state update as recursive Bayesian inference in a Kalman filtering framework, weighting updates by information-theoretic observation reliability and cross-attention spatial relevance. The result is asymmetric fusion that protects well-consolidated regions while quickly absorbing new scene content, and **it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art online reconstruction methods on `7-Scenes`, `TUM`, `ScanNet`, and `KITTI`**, with the largest gains on long sequences and complex scenes.

papers.title: TRAP: Tool-result Replay Attack for Probing Misbinding in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: As AI agents increasingly act through external tools, tool results are no longer simple outputs but execution artifacts that must remain correctly associated with the context that produced them. Yet as results persist across caches, recovery mechanisms, and shared runtime state, this association can break, causing a real and unmodified result to be consumed in an incompatible execution context and lead the agent to an unsafe action. We characterize this failure as tool-result misbinding. To systematically study this failure, we introduce ReplayBench, a benchmark that uses controlled tool-result replay to evaluate misbinding across 19 representative agent scenarios, 4 failure properties, and 3 replay mechanisms. Across eight LLMs, three agent frameworks, and diverse stateful workflows, we find widespread replay-induced failures, with a mean Final-State Error Rate of 0.649 under cross-task replay. Stage-wise analysis localizes these failures to model-side action generation. Further analyses show that replay susceptibility varies with task similarity, shows little dependence on object similarity, and remains high under result staleness and implicit environment changes. These findings motivate runtime validity mechanisms that eliminate final-state errors in our evaluated settings while preserving legitimate recovery. The results call for explicit contextual binding in tool-using agent runtimes. Our work is public at https://github.com/Phitooo/Replaybench.
papers.summary: When agents act through external tools, a tool result can outlive the context that produced it, persisting in caches, recovery paths, or shared runtime state, and then be consumed in an incompatible execution context, a failure the authors call tool-result misbinding. `ReplayBench` evaluates this by replaying genuine, unmodified tool results across 19 agent scenarios, 4 failure properties, and 3 replay mechanisms, testing eight LLMs and three agent frameworks on stateful workflows. Replay-induced failures are widespread, with **a mean Final-State Error Rate of 0.649 under cross-task replay**, and stage-wise analysis localizes them to model-side action generation. Susceptibility rises with task similarity, barely depends on object similarity, and persists under stale results and implicit environment changes, while runtime validity checks that bind results to their context eliminated final-state errors in the evaluated settings without blocking legitimate recovery.

papers.title: WorldRoPE: Probabilistic World-Centric Rotary Embedding for Multi-View Attention
papers.abstract: Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE) is widely used to encode relative positions in Transformers. In multi-view settings, however, patch coordinates are defined independently in each image: the same 3D point can therefore have different coordinates across views, making them insufficient for establishing cross-view correspondences. We introduce WorldRoPE, a probabilistic world-centric RoPE for multi-view attention. At each layer, WorldRoPE back-projects each patch token into a set of volumetric Gaussian primitives in a shared world frame. These primitives represent multiple plausible 3D supports for a token, jointly capturing alternative depth hypotheses, depth uncertainty, and the finite spatial extent of its patch frustum. When a key token's support is projected into a query view, it induces a distribution over where that key may appear in the query image. WorldRoPE integrates the rotary operator over this distribution in closed form, combining rotations at the projected primitive centers according to their mixture weights with covariance-dependent attenuation. This makes attention less sensitive to uncertain key locations in the query view, without rasterizing or warping token features. The formulation reduces to deterministic RoPE when the support collapses to a point. Across layers, the predicted geometry guides cross-view attention, while the updated features refine the geometry used at the next layer. Experiments on novel view synthesis, depth estimation, and 3D geometry reconstruction demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRoPE for multi-view Transformers.
papers.summary: Rotary Positional Embedding (`RoPE`) encodes relative positions within a single image, but in multi-view settings the same 3D point lands at different patch coordinates in each view, so per-image positions cannot establish cross-view correspondence. `WorldRoPE` back-projects each patch token at every layer into a set of volumetric Gaussian primitives in a shared world frame that capture alternative depth hypotheses, depth uncertainty, and the patch frustum's spatial extent; projecting a key token's support into the query view yields a distribution over where it may appear, and the rotary operator is integrated over that distribution in closed form with covariance-dependent attenuation. The scheme reduces to standard `RoPE` when the support collapses to a point, and across layers the predicted geometry guides cross-view attention while updated features refine the geometry. **Experiments on novel view synthesis, depth estimation, and 3D reconstruction show gains for multi-view Transformers**, without rasterizing or warping token features.

papers.title: Efficient Multi-Agent Reasoning via Confidence-Guided Adaptive Debate
papers.abstract: Multi-agent debate has shown promise for improving the reasoning of large language models, yet recent theory suggests its benefits are highly regime-dependent. While interaction can amplify informative signals under corrective conditions, symmetric debate dynamics are neutral in expectation, often making majority voting preferable. We reconcile these views by arguing that debate is effective only when invoked at the right time and with appropriate structure. Based on this insight, we propose LASE: Leader-Adaptive Structured Engagement, a leader-centric multi-agent debate framework that selectively engages interaction only in non-neutral regimes. LASE introduces an asymmetric leader-supporter architecture that enables directed information flow and selective signal amplification, while defaulting to simple aggregation otherwise. Experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks show that LASE achieves multi-agent-level performance with near single-agent token cost, substantially improving efficiency over static debate and voting baselines.
papers.summary: Multi-agent debate can improve LLM reasoning, but recent theory shows the benefit depends on regime: interaction amplifies informative signals under corrective conditions, while symmetric debate is neutral in expectation and often loses to simple majority voting. `LASE` (Leader-Adaptive Structured Engagement) reconciles these findings by invoking debate only when it is likely to help, using an asymmetric leader-supporter architecture that directs information flow and selectively amplifies signals in non-neutral regimes, and falling back to plain aggregation otherwise. Across diverse reasoning benchmarks, **`LASE` matches multi-agent-level accuracy at near single-agent token cost**, a substantial efficiency gain over static debate and voting baselines.

papers.title: ChronoScribe: Semantic-Numerical Specialization for Instruction-Driven Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Recent advances in instruction-driven time series forecasting highlight a fundamental tension: systems must simultaneously master natural-language instruction following and precise numerical prediction. Current approaches often force a compromise. Large language models (LLMs) can interpret unstructured requests but may be inaccurate when asked to produce forecast values directly, whereas time series foundation models (TSFMs) provide numerical forecasts but typically require structured inputs specifying the target series, context window, and horizon. We present ChronoScribe, which applies semantic-numerical specialization to this workflow. A LoRA-adapted LLM proposes an execution path and context length; deterministic rules resolve the executable configuration. On the specialist path, a frozen TSFM produces quantile trajectories for the task-specified horizon. Deterministic trajectory summaries condition the response, while the LLM neither generates nor revises predicted values. We evaluate a Qwen3.5-9B--Chronos-2 implementation across 23 evaluation dimensions and 30 public datasets against eleven proprietary direct LLMs and three open TSFMs. ChronoScribe has the lowest error on sMAPE, MASE, WAPE, RMSE, and MAE among all evaluated systems, including fixed-context controls. Across these metrics, even the lowest direct-LLM error remains 2.0--2.7 times the corresponding ChronoScribe error. At the system level, ChronoScribe achieves a Task-Level Score (TLS) of 65.5, 10.6 points above the strongest direct-LLM baseline. The results support ChronoScribe's division of labor, in which the LLM handles interpretation, configuration, and communication while the TSFM handles numerical forecasting.
papers.summary: Instruction-driven forecasting must both follow natural-language requests and produce precise numbers, yet large language models (LLMs) that emit forecast values directly tend to be inaccurate while time series foundation models (TSFMs) need structured inputs specifying the target series, context window, and horizon. `ChronoScribe` splits the roles: a `LoRA`-adapted LLM proposes an execution path and context length, deterministic rules resolve the executable configuration, a frozen TSFM produces quantile trajectories on the specialist path, and the LLM writes the response from deterministic trajectory summaries without generating or revising any predicted values. A `Qwen3.5-9B` plus `Chronos-2` implementation evaluated across 23 dimensions and 30 public datasets against eleven proprietary direct LLMs and three open TSFMs achieves the lowest sMAPE, MASE, WAPE, RMSE, and MAE of all systems, and **even the best direct LLM's error is 2.0 to 2.7 times the `ChronoScribe` error**. Its Task-Level Score of 65.5 is 10.6 points above the strongest direct-LLM baseline.

papers.title: Rescuing Points Trapped Inside Incorrect Decision Regions: A target for Evaluating and Improving Forward-Forward Learning
papers.abstract: Forward-Forward learning replaces end-to-end backpropagation with local, layer-wise training objectives. Its variants are evaluated primarily by classification accuracy, often measured with linear probes trained on their representations. We show that this evaluation can over-credit the learning method: a linear probe on the representations of an untrained convolutional neural network already reaches accuracy well above chance. Moreover, a single accuracy value does not reveal which datapoints become correctly classified after training and which remain misclassified. To examine what learning contributes beyond the random, untrained baseline, we present an analysis methodology built on the Boundary Proximity Index (BPI), a multiclass margin normalized by a class-centroid reference. We apply our analysis to seven Forward-Forward variants and related layer-local methods and find that initially misclassified points near the probe's decision boundary generally have higher rescue rates than those farther inside incorrect decision regions. Rescue rates vary substantially across methods, with some correcting a substantial fraction of these deeply embedded points. Together, these analyses offer a way to evaluate representation learning beyond accuracy and identify the rescue of points far inside incorrect decision regions as a target for improving local learning methods.
papers.summary: `Forward-Forward` learning replaces backpropagation with local, layer-wise objectives, and its variants are usually judged by linear-probe classification accuracy on their representations, but a probe on an untrained convolutional network already scores well above chance, so accuracy alone over-credits the learning method and hides which datapoints actually change. The authors propose an analysis built on the Boundary Proximity Index (`BPI`), a multiclass margin normalized by a class-centroid reference, to measure how far misclassified points sit inside incorrect decision regions and which of them training rescues. Applied to seven `Forward-Forward` variants and related layer-local methods, **initially misclassified points near the probe's decision boundary are rescued at higher rates than points deep inside incorrect regions**, with rescue rates varying substantially across methods. Rescuing deeply embedded points is proposed as a concrete target for improving local learning.

papers.title: DWI Connectome-based Sex Classification in Young using Supervised Variational Autoencoder
papers.abstract: During adolescence, significant changes in brain development are influenced by hormonal changes that impact both the body and the brain. This study presents sex classification in 787 young adults having age range of 15-25 years using Diffusion-weighted (DWI) structural connectome, focusing on 82 Desikan-Killiany atlas ROIs. A supervised variational autoencoder (SVAE) is used to extract latent space features from DWI connectome data. Although several studies explored differences in brain structure and function between sexes, the main contribution of this study lies in incorporating SVAE to learn a compact, regularized latent representation for the task of sex classification. Initial exploratory data analysis shows that these features can capture the differences in sex-specific latent space patterns. Subsequently, the learned latent space SVAE features are fed to different ML models for sex classification. Among the considered ML classifiers, the multi-layer perceptron yields the highest accuracy of 80% in classifying sex. This demonstrates the effectiveness of SVAE in learning compact, informative representations from DWI connectome for sex classification. The present work highlights the potential of using DWI brain connectomics and deep learning to differentiate sex, paving the way for future research on diverse populations that may include transgender individuals, to better understand sex-related variations in brain structure.
papers.summary: Adolescent brain development is shaped by hormonal changes, and the study classifies sex in 787 people aged 15 to 25 from diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) structural connectomes over 82 `Desikan-Killiany` atlas regions. A supervised variational autoencoder (`SVAE`) learns a compact, regularized latent representation of the connectome, exploratory analysis shows sex-specific patterns in that latent space, and the latent features are then fed to several machine learning classifiers. **A multi-layer perceptron on the `SVAE` features reaches 80% accuracy**, the best among the classifiers considered.

papers.title: World Models Need a Physical Registry: Learning Internal Predictive States for Physically Plausible World Models
papers.abstract: Video world models must generate physically plausible futures, not just realistic frames. Existing approaches typically use semantic, physical, or predictive information to guide the visual generation stream, leaving a fundamental question: where inside the generator should predictions of scene evolution live? Standard video tokens jointly encode appearance and dynamics, but provide no distinct state for learning and reading predictive dynamics. We answer this question with the Physical Registry: temporally grounded registry slots inside a video DiT that are initialized from an observation-conditioned forecast, co-evolve with video tokens, and receive future-representation supervision, making predictive dynamics an explicit, readable state of the generator. In a controlled comparison of predictive-state interfaces on Physics-IQ Verified, Physical Registry improves vanilla fine-tuning by 9.9/8.7 points on I2V/V2V, the largest gain among the interfaces we compare. Across all Cosmos and WAN backbones, Physical Registry improves Physics-IQ Verified scores. With only 0.45% additional parameters, it enables Cosmos 3 Nano 16B to surpass the published I2V score of Cosmos 3 Super 64B (43.56 vs. 42.7). On WorldModelBench, it also improves physical adherence and the total score for all four evaluated backbones. Because the registry becomes candidate-specific while remaining readable, the Physical Registry Selector (PRS) ranks emerging futures by how far their intermediate registry readouts depart from the shared forecast before full denoising is complete. Across four backbones, this selection improves I2V scores by 5.6-15.9% without completed-video external scoring. Together, these results support a broader principle: dynamics prediction should live as an explicit model state that co-evolves with the video representation. Project page: https://grainsack.github.io/physical-registry/
papers.summary: Video world models need to produce physically plausible futures, but standard video tokens entangle appearance and dynamics and offer no distinct state where predictions of scene evolution can be learned and read out. The `Physical Registry` adds temporally grounded registry slots inside a video DiT that are initialized from an observation-conditioned forecast, co-evolve with the video tokens, and are supervised on future representations, making predictive dynamics an explicit, readable state of the generator. On `Physics-IQ Verified` it improves vanilla fine-tuning by 9.9 and 8.7 points on image-to-video (I2V) and video-to-video (V2V), the largest gain among the predictive-state interfaces compared, and **with only 0.45% extra parameters it lets `Cosmos 3 Nano 16B` surpass the published I2V score of `Cosmos 3 Super 64B` (43.56 versus 42.7)**, while also improving physical adherence on `WorldModelBench` for all four `Cosmos` and `WAN` backbones. Because the registry readouts become candidate-specific, a `Physical Registry Selector` ranks emerging futures by how far their intermediate readouts depart from the shared forecast before denoising completes, improving I2V scores by 5.6 to 15.9% across four backbones without external scoring of completed videos.

papers.title: LoopQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Looped Transformers
papers.abstract: Looped Language Models (LoopLMs) improve parameter efficiency by recursively reusing shared Transformer modules, yet their repeated computation over evolving recurrent states poses new challenges for low-bit deployment. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods, largely designed for feed-forward Transformers, fail to account for cross-loop activation dynamics, heterogeneous loop sensitivity, and recursive error propagation, leading to substantial performance degradation at low precision. To address these challenges, we propose LoopQuant, a loop-aware PTQ framework for accurate and efficient low-bit quantization of LoopLMs. LoopQuant is built on three core components: 1) Cross-Loop Distribution Canonicalization (CLDC) learns a shared quantization-friendly representation across recurrent states while preserving parameter sharing; 2) Interaction-Aware Loop-wise Precision Allocation (ILPA) allocates activation precision under a fixed bit budget by modeling task-level loop sensitivity and cross-loop interactions; and 3) Loop-Conditioned Task Calibration (LCTC) further aligns quantized inference with the low-bit recursive trajectory through lightweight task-space calibration. Extensive experiments across LoopLM architectures demonstrate that LoopQuant consistently outperforms existing low-bit PTQ methods. On Ouro-2.6B, LoopQuant under W4A4 surpasses all W4A8 baselines in performance, while reducing model memory by 65.3% with only 3.4% additional storage overhead over naive INT4 and achieving a 1.7 times decoding speedup over BF16. These results demonstrate a strong balance among accuracy, compression, and inference efficiency, providing a practical and deployment-friendly solution for low-bit LoopLM inference. The code is available at [https://github.com/Kishon-zzx/LoopQuant].
papers.summary: Looped Language Models (LoopLMs) reuse shared Transformer modules recursively to save parameters, but existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods built for feed-forward Transformers ignore cross-loop activation dynamics, uneven sensitivity across loops, and recursive error propagation, so they degrade badly at low precision. `LoopQuant` addresses this with Cross-Loop Distribution Canonicalization, which learns a shared quantization-friendly representation across recurrent states while keeping parameter sharing, Interaction-Aware Loop-wise Precision Allocation, which distributes activation bits under a fixed budget using task-level loop sensitivity and cross-loop interactions, and Loop-Conditioned Task Calibration, a lightweight task-space alignment to the low-bit recursive trajectory. **On `Ouro-2.6B`, `LoopQuant` at W4A4 beats every W4A8 baseline**, cutting model memory by 65.3% with 3.4% storage overhead over naive INT4 and delivering a 1.7 times decoding speedup over BF16.

papers.title: RetroPlanner: Multi-Route Expansion and Multi-Objective Reasoning for LLM-Based Retrosynthesis Planning
papers.abstract: Multi-step retrosynthesis planning is often considered solved once a route to purchasable starting materials is found, but such a route should also be practical in real-world chemistry. Recent LLM-based planners formulate this process as sequential decision-making over an AND-OR graph, yet typically expand a single molecule per turn and are optimized for solvability alone, leaving alternative routes uncompared across the multiple objectives that determine practicality before the search budget is committed. We introduce RetroPlanner, an LLM-based planner that jointly compares multiple routes to steer the search toward higher synthesizability, as measured by reaction plausibility, round-trip consistency, and starting-material price. RetroPlanner is trained to reason over chemical evidence: structural progress from the target molecule, bond changes and reaction classes, where candidate routes diverge from one another, and how they rank across multiple objectives. Experiments on multi-step retrosynthesis benchmarks demonstrate that RetroPlanner recovers more alternative routes than prior LLM-based planners while improving synthetic route quality and maintaining a high success rate.
papers.summary: Multi-step retrosynthesis planning is usually declared solved once a route to purchasable starting materials is found, but LLM-based planners that expand one molecule per turn and optimize for solvability alone never compare alternative routes on the objectives that make a route practical. `RetroPlanner` jointly compares multiple candidate routes during search on an AND-OR graph and steers toward higher synthesizability, measured by reaction plausibility, round-trip consistency, and starting-material price, after being trained to reason over chemical evidence such as structural progress toward the target, bond changes and reaction classes, where routes diverge, and how they rank across objectives. On multi-step retrosynthesis benchmarks, **it recovers more alternative routes than prior LLM-based planners while improving route quality and keeping a high success rate**.

papers.title: Recursive Environment Scaling for General Long-Horizon Agents
papers.abstract: We study environment scaling as a way to increase agent-benchmark difficulty while holding core task objectives fixed. Our framework, Recursive Environment Scaling (RES), transforms existing benchmark environments while preserving their objectives and completion requirements. A proposer changes information access, resource relations, and execution dependencies; execution-grounded checks validate the resulting candidate, and accepted changes are inherited across rounds. This produces related environments for paired evaluation and training-trajectory collection. Experiments on 294 initial tasks from three benchmarks show lower task success for all six evaluation models, with decreases of 57.14--77.14 percentage points on Claw-Eval-Live. With equal trajectory counts and identical optimization settings, fine-tuning on RES trajectories outperforms original-trajectory SFT in all nine model--benchmark comparisons by 7.00--14.61 percentage points. Ablations identify recursive inheritance and dependency composition as important contributors to increased difficulty.
