Together, these results support environment scaling for both agent evaluation and training.
papers.summary: The authors study environment scaling as a way to raise agent-benchmark difficulty while holding core task objectives and completion requirements fixed. Recursive Environment Scaling (`RES`) has a proposer alter information access, resource relations, and execution dependencies in a benchmark environment, validates each candidate with execution-grounded checks, and carries accepted changes forward across rounds, yielding paired environments for evaluation and for collecting training trajectories. On 294 initial tasks from three benchmarks, all six evaluated models lose success rate, **with drops of 57.14 to 77.14 percentage points on `Claw-Eval-Live`**, and fine-tuning on `RES` trajectories beats SFT on original trajectories in all nine model-benchmark pairs by 7.00 to 14.61 points at equal trajectory counts. Ablations identify recursive inheritance and dependency composition as important contributors to the added difficulty.

papers.title: EvoWeb: A Benchmark for Coding Agents on Evolving Web Applications
papers.abstract: Web application development often proceeds through successive requests that extend an existing implementation. Yet web-generation benchmarks primarily evaluate development toward fixed specifications. We introduce EvoWeb, a novel benchmark comprising 320 cumulative requests over 32 web applications, grounded in real-world product features and structured by functional dependency graphs. Agents iteratively modify a persistent codebase, while a multimodal web agent tests each intermediate application in a live browser, assessing newly requested functionality, cross-request integration, and previously requested functionality. To characterize reliability throughout development, we integrate trajectory performance across user-tolerance thresholds rather than impose a fixed stopping criterion. Experiments across open- and closed-source frontier models show that EvoWeb reveals clear performance differences between models, with cross-request integration emerging as a key challenge. Further analysis shows that later requests with deeper or more numerous dependencies are solved less accurately, while runtime errors become more frequent over successive requests. EvoWeb provides a testbed for evaluating and improving coding agents in long-horizon, multi-request development.
papers.summary: Web applications are typically built through a sequence of requests that extend an existing implementation, yet web-generation benchmarks mostly evaluate development toward a fixed specification. `EvoWeb` contains 320 cumulative requests over 32 web applications grounded in real product features and organized by functional dependency graphs; coding agents modify a persistent codebase request by request while a multimodal web agent exercises each intermediate application in a live browser to check newly requested functionality, integration across requests, and regressions in earlier features, and reliability is scored by integrating trajectory performance across user-tolerance thresholds rather than a fixed stopping point. Across open- and closed-source frontier models the benchmark separates models clearly, **with cross-request integration emerging as a key challenge**; later requests with deeper or more numerous dependencies are solved less accurately and runtime errors grow more frequent over successive requests.

papers.title: Estimating the Causal Impact of Social Navigation Signals in Corridor Scenarios
papers.abstract: Deploying robots in human-shared environments requires deciding not only how to navigate, but also when dedicated social signals are worth emitting. Classic observation-based inference can be misleading in such settings: confounding factors may bias the estimated relationship between a signal and the task outcome, leading to incorrect decisions. Causal inference provides a framework for disentangling these relationships by modelling the mechanisms linking observations, actions, and outcomes, and by estimating interventional effects after accounting for confounding paths. We study a human-robot interaction scenario in a corridor and use a causal model to estimate whether a social navigation signal causally improves transit success. We represent the interaction as a causal DAG involving robot action, pedestrian occupancy, available space, task outcome, and a controlled confounder (static obstacles). We compare the interventional estimate with the observational estimate obtained by conditioning only on the robot action, which does not explicitly model interventions. Our results show that accounting for confounding variables can reverse the conclusions drawn from naive observational analysis: the observational estimate wrongly suggests that the social signal is detrimental, whereas the causal estimate shows that it is beneficial. This discrepancy highlights how failing to account for confounding can lead to incorrect conclusions and demonstrates the importance of causal models for context-aware signalling decisions in social robot navigation.
papers.summary: Robots sharing space with people must decide not only how to move but when emitting a dedicated social signal is worthwhile, and estimating a signal's effect from observational data can mislead because confounders bias the apparent relationship between signal and outcome. The authors model a corridor human-robot encounter as a causal DAG over robot action, pedestrian occupancy, available space, task outcome, and a controlled confounder (static obstacles), then compare the interventional estimate of the signal's effect on transit success with the observational estimate obtained by conditioning on robot action alone. **Accounting for confounding reverses the conclusion: the observational estimate suggests the social signal is detrimental, while the causal estimate shows it is beneficial.**

papers.title: SLS-Bench: A Benchmark for Incident Log Summarization with Synthetic Observability Data
papers.abstract: As IT systems grow in complexity, automated agent-driven incident response becomes increasingly critical. A key capability for these agents is summarizing large log streams into human-readable reports. Further progress requires meaningfully evaluating this function, yet existing benchmarks leave end-to-end summarization from large log streams underexplored due to the prohibitive cost and complexity of collecting real-world data. We introduce SLS-Bench, a benchmark for incident log summarization featuring 90 tasks grounded in real-world incident reports, each with a synthetic log stream and a reference summary. To construct SLS-Bench, we developed a data generation pipeline that converts incident reports into structured incident models, which guide the generation of synthetic logs and reference summaries. This pipeline combines narrative grounding, explicit incident modeling, generator-verifier loops, and statistical comparisons with real-world log streams to produce realistic and controllable observability data. Our evaluation of 14 LLMs on SLS-Bench shows that while frontier models can produce useful summaries, they do so at substantial cost and latency, and open-weight models lag significantly. SLS-Bench provides a framework for systematic evaluation of log analysis agents and a scalable blueprint for future synthetic observability benchmarks.
papers.summary: Agent-driven incident response depends on condensing large log streams into readable reports, but benchmarks for end-to-end summarization from realistic log volumes are scarce because collecting real observability data is costly. `SLS-Bench` offers 90 tasks grounded in real-world incident reports, each paired with a synthetic log stream and a reference summary, produced by a pipeline that converts reports into structured incident models and then drives log generation with narrative grounding, generator-verifier loops, and statistical comparison against real log streams. Evaluating 14 LLMs shows that **frontier models produce useful summaries but at substantial cost and latency, while open-weight models lag significantly**. The pipeline is also offered as a blueprint for future synthetic observability benchmarks.

papers.title: Chain Dimension Scaling: Communication-Efficient Loop-Style Scaling for Industrial Short-Video Ranking
papers.abstract: Industrial recommendation rankers keep scaling in width and depth to billions of parameters, but this increasingly incurs costs in parameter growth, distributed communication overhead, and training inefficiency. We introduce \underline{C}hain \underline{D}imension \underline{S}caling (CDS), a scaling strategy orthogonal to width and depth. CDS repeatedly applies a single feature-interaction block with parameters shared across iterations, so the number of iterations (the chain length) becomes a new scaling dimension that adds no parameters. A lightweight intra-chain residual connection stabilizes optimization and improves quality. CDS enables two regimes. In the \emph{compression regime}, shallow blocks with a longer chain match deeper baselines with fewer parameters and faster training; in the \emph{quality-scaling regime}, increasing chain length under a fixed parameter budget yields consistent offline and online gains, suggesting the chain dimension adds modeling capacity beyond parameter reuse. We evaluate CDS in a large-scale multi-task short-video ranking system in production. In the compression regime, CDS stays within $0.03\%$ of baseline offline quality while reducing trainable parameters by 26.6\% and improving training throughput by 6.4\%, with neutral-to-positive online participation. In the quality-scaling regime, quality improves monotonically with chain length. Wall-clock analysis shows the efficiency gain comes mainly not from reduced FLOPs but from lower cross-device synchronization overhead and reduced optimizer update cost. These results position parameter-shared iterative computation as a practical, communication-efficient scaling axis for industrial ranking systems.
papers.summary: Industrial recommendation rankers keep growing in width and depth to billions of parameters, paying in parameter count, distributed communication overhead, and training inefficiency. Chain Dimension Scaling (`CDS`) adds a third scaling axis: a single feature-interaction block is applied repeatedly with shared parameters, so chain length scales compute without adding parameters, and a lightweight intra-chain residual connection stabilizes optimization. In a production multi-task short-video ranking system, **`CDS` stays within 0.03% of baseline offline quality while cutting trainable parameters by 26.6% and raising training throughput by 6.4%**, with neutral-to-positive online participation, and under a fixed parameter budget quality improves monotonically with chain length. Wall-clock analysis attributes the speedup mainly to lower cross-device synchronization and optimizer update cost rather than fewer FLOPs.

papers.title: AuthGateBench: Benchmarking LLMs as Authorization Gate
papers.abstract: Automated approval systems let coding agents execute high-risk actions with minimal human oversight by delegating the authorization decision to a classifier, typically a large language model (LLM). Such systems, adopted in tools like Claude Code and Codex, remain vulnerable to failure modes such as scope escalation, where the agent takes actions exceeding what the user authorized. Existing benchmarks focus mainly on malicious requests, evaluating refusal under an implicit policy. We introduce AuthGateBench, the first policy-guided benchmark for authorization gating under benign requests. We implement a novel pipeline where an LLM generates contrast pairs with identical action and trajectory but differing request, flipping the label between block and allow. This allows us to assess whether models reason over context rather than the action alone. We further examine whether auxiliary environment signals can help models make better decisions. The resulting benchmark comprises 1,400 instances spanning five failure modes drawn from real-world Claude Code incidents. Evaluations show accuracy degrades unevenly across failure modes as models over-rely on internal safety alignment, and models still block most actions even when explicitly authorized, revealing unstable rather than deterministic decisions; retrospectively retrieved environment signals, however, substantially improve authorization accuracy.
papers.summary: Automated approval systems in coding agents such as `Claude Code` and `Codex` hand high-risk action decisions to a large language model (LLM) classifier, which remains exposed to failures like scope escalation, where the agent exceeds what the user authorized, and prior benchmarks mainly test refusal of malicious requests under an implicit policy. `AuthGateBench` is a policy-guided benchmark of 1,400 instances across five failure modes drawn from real `Claude Code` incidents, built by having an LLM generate contrast pairs with identical action and trajectory but a different user request that flips the label between block and allow, so a model must reason over context rather than the action alone. Accuracy degrades unevenly across failure modes as models lean on their internal safety alignment, and **models still block most actions even when the user has explicitly authorized them**, indicating unstable rather than deterministic decisions; retrospectively retrieved environment signals substantially improve accuracy.

papers.title: ARMED: Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Medication Recommendation
papers.abstract: Medication recommendation requires jointly considering diagnoses, comorbidities, longitudinal patient history, and treatment interactions. Although recent retrieval-augmented generation approaches using language models have shown promise for clinical recommendation, most existing systems rely on fixed retrieval pipelines that cannot adapt to diverse clinical retrieval scenarios and may introduce noisy or irrelevant evidence. We propose ARMED, an adaptive clinical RAG framework that dynamically expands retrieval according to retrieval sufficiency and current-admission relevance. ARMED first observes the initial retrieval outcome and selectively performs supplementary or fallback multi-query retrieval when additional evidence is needed. The framework also incorporates a relevance gate that activates only clinically relevant same-patient history and organizes retrieved evidence into structured query-level clinical evidence. Experiments on MIMIC-IV demonstrate that ARMED consistently outperforms previous static retrieval baselines and improves overall medication recommendation quality. By combining locally runnable small language models with adaptive retrieval, ARMED supports medication recommendation without relying on external language model APIs or task-specific fine-tuning.
papers.summary: Medication recommendation must weigh diagnoses, comorbidities, longitudinal history, and drug interactions, and existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems for it use fixed retrieval pipelines that cannot adapt to varied clinical queries and may pull in noisy evidence. `ARMED` inspects the initial retrieval result and selectively triggers supplementary or fallback multi-query retrieval when evidence is insufficient, applies a relevance gate that admits only clinically relevant same-patient history, and organizes what it retrieves into structured query-level evidence. **On `MIMIC-IV` it consistently outperforms static retrieval baselines** while running on locally hosted small language models with no external API or task-specific fine-tuning.

papers.title: VisExMEM: Visual Evidence-Based Explainable Multimodal Evaluation Metric
papers.abstract: Current image-text evaluation often relies on a global score, which gives limited insight into which semantic details are supported by the image. Explainable metrics provide rationales, but the visual evidence supporting those rationales can still be difficult to verify. We introduce VisExMEM, a reference-free evaluator that decomposes captions into atomic claims, localizes visual evidence, verifies each claim, and averages claim-level support into a global score. Explanations use the same evidence and decisions. We train Qwen3.5-based 4B and 9B models on 100K samples with multi-task SFT, counterfactual refinement, and evidence-aware GDPO. Across eight benchmarks, VisExMEM-9B achieves the highest descriptive composite among open-source evaluators in our comparison, exceeding VQAScore by 11.7 points while remaining competitive with GPT-5.6 Sol. We also introduce AGITA-Bench, containing 600 human-annotated image-text pairs and 8.7K atomic claims for global and claim-level evaluation. For untuned Qwen3.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol controls, decomposed prompting raises the same composite by 3.6-5.1 points relative to holistic prompting. Human evaluation shows that VisExMEM explanations outperform prior explainable metrics and approach GPT-5.6 Sol.
papers.summary: Image-text evaluation usually reduces to a global score that reveals little about which caption details the image actually supports, and even explainable metrics give rationales whose visual evidence is hard to verify. `VisExMEM` is a reference-free evaluator that splits a caption into atomic claims, localizes visual evidence for each, verifies the claims, and averages claim-level support into a global score, with explanations drawn from the same evidence; 4B and 9B models based on `Qwen3.5` are trained on 100K samples with multi-task SFT, counterfactual refinement, and evidence-aware `GDPO`. Across eight benchmarks, **`VisExMEM-9B` posts the highest descriptive composite among the open-source evaluators compared, 11.7 points above `VQAScore`**, and stays competitive with `GPT-5.6 Sol`. The authors also release `AGITA-Bench`, 600 human-annotated image-text pairs with 8.7K atomic claims, and show that decomposed prompting alone raises untuned `Qwen3.5` and `GPT-5.6 Sol` by 3.6 to 5.1 points over holistic prompting.

papers.title: RAP-WAM: Learning World-Action Models through Predictive Rehearsal and Action Perturbations
papers.abstract: Recent world action models draw on video generation priors to jointly predict future observations and robot actions. Adapting these priors to control requires determining how future predictions should guide policy learning. RAP-WAM combines predictive Rehearsal and Action Perturbations (RAP) with future-supervised queries and Coupled Action Projection for policy learning. Predictive rehearsal trains on model-generated inputs while retaining recorded targets, and accumulates recurring errors into a spatial prior. We perturb actions and measure changes in video predictions. Action-response-based spatiotemporal credit assignment combines these responses, prediction error, and the rehearsal prior to allocate visual supervision; spatially aggregating the responses determines supervision intensity across future action steps. No separate scoring network or deployment-time probe is required. The base learns from a video-pretrained backbone without intermediate pretraining on external embodied data. We evaluate the fixed base and its agent-refined, task-conditioned system. On 42 RoboDojo tasks, their average success rates are 12.85% and 15.62%, with Scores of 17.86 and 20.59. Across 15 real-robot tasks, the complete system achieves 89.00% task-macro-average success, exceeding the strongest of five baselines by 37.67 percentage points. Across 315 fixed-output simulation windows, 45.21% of response-top20 positions fall outside error-top20, revealing information beyond prediction error.
papers.summary: World action models built on video generation priors predict future observations and robot actions jointly, raising the question of how those future predictions should shape policy learning. `RAP-WAM` combines predictive rehearsal, which trains on model-generated inputs while keeping recorded targets and accumulates recurring errors into a spatial prior, with action perturbations whose effect on video predictions is measured to assign spatiotemporal credit; these responses, prediction error, and the rehearsal prior together allocate visual supervision across future action steps without a separate scoring network or deployment-time probe, starting from a video-pretrained backbone with no intermediate embodied pretraining. On 42 `RoboDojo` tasks the fixed base and the agent-refined system reach 12.85% and 15.62% success, and **across 15 real-robot tasks the full system achieves 89.00% macro-average success, 37.67 percentage points above the strongest of five baselines**. In simulation, 45.21% of the top-20 action-response positions fall outside the top-20 prediction-error positions, indicating the responses carry information beyond prediction error.

papers.title: CryptoFlowBench: Benchmarking Multi-Hop Reasoning on Blockchains for Cryptocurrency Fund Tracing
papers.abstract: Pseudonymous accounts and complex smart-contract ecosystems substantially hinder the tracing of illicit cryptocurrency fund flows. Existing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved promising performance in blockchain fraud detection, yet their static node- or edge-level predictions do not naturally generalize to multi-hop fund tracing. Meanwhile, existing tracing methods mainly rely on predefined heuristics to capture multi-hop relationships, limiting their adaptive reasoning capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce CryptoFlowBench, a benchmark constructed from authoritative reports on cryptocurrency-related illicit incidents, with four tasks spanning local to multi-hop fund tracing. These tasks pose substantial challenges to existing learning- and heuristic-based methods, particularly in complex multi-hop scenarios. We therefore propose ChainSleuth, a graph-tool-augmented agent that iteratively reasons, invokes graph tools, and updates its tracing trajectory, enabling adaptive information acquisition and recovery from erroneous paths. Experiments show that no baseline consistently dominates all four tasks, revealing substantial gaps between local fraud detection and multi-hop fund tracing. ChainSleuth achieves notable improvements on multi-hop tasks, demonstrating the potential of agentic graph reasoning for cryptocurrency fund investigation.
papers.summary: Pseudonymous accounts and tangled smart-contract ecosystems make tracing illicit cryptocurrency flows difficult; Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) do well at static node- or edge-level fraud detection but do not naturally extend to multi-hop fund tracing, and existing tracing tools rely on fixed heuristics. `CryptoFlowBench` is built from authoritative reports of illicit crypto incidents and defines four tasks ranging from local to multi-hop tracing, on which both learning- and heuristic-based methods struggle, especially in complex multi-hop cases. The authors also propose `ChainSleuth`, an agent that iteratively reasons, calls graph tools, and revises its tracing trajectory to acquire information adaptively and recover from wrong paths; **no baseline dominates all four tasks, while `ChainSleuth` delivers notable gains on the multi-hop tasks**.

papers.title: StructZO: Structured Zeroth-Order Optimization for Memory-Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models at scale is increasingly limited by the memory cost of backpropagation. Zeroth-Order (ZO) optimizers reduce this burden by relying only on forward function evaluations, but they still exhibit a substantial performance gap to first-order (FO) optimizers such as Adam. We argue that this gap does not arise solely from the absence of explicit gradients: FO fine-tuning also benefits from informative low-rank optimization geometry, large-scale signal aggregation, and well-conditioned update directions. Motivated by this, we introduce StructZO, a structured Zeroth-Order optimization framework for memory-efficient LLM fine-tuning. StructZO performs large-query ZO estimation within an activation-induced informative subspace and applies spectral control to the resulting reduced-space update before mapping it back to the original parameters. This lets ZO aggregate useful directional signals in a compact, geometry-aware space while avoiding the activation and optimizer-state memory costs of backpropagation. We show theoretically that, when the induced subspace captures concentrated optimization-relevant directions, StructZO reduces the effective ZO estimation dimension from $mn$ to $mr$, with the remaining projection error governed by the spectral tail of the activation Gram matrix. Empirically, across OPT-series and Llama3.1-8B on diverse downstreamtasks, StructZO improves over the strongest existing ZO baselines by up to $8.7%$ relative on average and up to $26.9%$ relative on individual tasks, while remaining within $1.5%$ of FO-Adam on average. These results suggest that structured and spectrally controlled ZO updates can substantially narrow the gap between ZO and FO optimization.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning large language models with backpropagation is memory-bound, and zeroth-order (ZO) optimizers that rely only on forward passes still trail first-order methods such as `Adam` by a wide margin. The authors argue the gap is not just about missing gradients, since first-order training also benefits from low-rank optimization geometry, large-scale signal aggregation, and well-conditioned updates, so `StructZO` runs large-query ZO estimation inside a subspace induced by layer activations and applies spectral control to the reduced update before mapping it back to the full parameters. Theory shows the effective estimation dimension drops from mn to mr when that subspace captures the relevant directions, and on `OPT` models and `Llama3.1-8B` the method beats the strongest ZO baselines by up to 8.7% relative on average while **staying within 1.5% of first-order `Adam` on average**.

papers.title: PATMT2: Two-stage domain adaptation for multilingual patent translation
papers.abstract: We present PatMT2 (Patent Machine Translation, v2), a two-stage LoRA pipeline that adapts the Hy-MT2-7B dedicated translation model to four-language (Chinese/English/Japanese/Korean) patent translation. On six translation directions, the Stage-2 checkpoint reaches a macro-average BLEU of 43.39 (BF16) to 43.57 (AWQ INT4), improving over the Hy-MT2-7B base by up to +8.8 BLEU and also exceeding Qwen3-32B and several external systems on the same average. We then measure the cost of adaptation: probing 38 languages absent from the fine-tuning data, the model still produces correct, fluent output on 34, while four low-resource languages collapse into distinct, reproducible failure modes. We treat these as diagnostic cases rather than retention rates, and report their mechanisms without attributing them to a single cause. Paired bootstrap tests confirm the translation gains over all baselines (p < 0.001).
papers.summary: Dedicated translation models need domain adaptation before they handle patent text well across Chinese, English, Japanese, and Korean. `PatMT2` applies a two-stage LoRA pipeline to the `Hy-MT2-7B` translation model and reports a **macro-average BLEU of 43.39 to 43.57 over six translation directions**, up to 8.8 BLEU above the base model and ahead of `Qwen3-32B` and several external systems on the same average. Probing 38 languages absent from the fine-tuning data shows 34 still produce correct, fluent output while four low-resource languages collapse into distinct, reproducible failure modes, which the authors document as diagnostic cases rather than attributing them to a single cause.

papers.title: XAI-Guided Fourier Domain Generalisation for Pure-Simulation Sim-to-Real Deep Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning has shown strong potential for vision-based autonomous driving, but policies trained in simulation often suffer severe performance degradation when deployed in the real world. Existing sim-to-real methods commonly address this gap through image-transfer-based domain adaptation or policy-agnostic domain randomisation. However, the former requires laborious acquisition of target-domain data and is often limited to the deployment domain, whereas the latter introduces unguided perturbations that may not reflect the underlying sim-to-real discrepancy, leading to suboptimal transfer performance. To overcome these limitations, we propose XFD, an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)-guided Fourier domain generalisation framework for pure-simulation sim-to-real reinforcement learning. The proposed framework extracts explainability attribution maps from simulated observations, and converts these attributions into policy-conditioned Fourier-domain interventions. By perturbing appearance-sensitive spectral components while preserving task-defining spatial structures, XFD constructs robustness-enhancing visual domains entirely within simulation. Subsequently, the proposed robust policy optimisation guides the policy towards attending to task-critical features while suppressing sensitivity to irrelevant visual information. Extensive experiments in simulation and zero-shot real-world deployment demonstrate that XFD consistently improves traveled distance and reward over standard policy and randomly domain-randomised baseline, especially on unseen maps with cluttered backgrounds. Attribution-based analysis further proves that the proposed policy preserves more consistent task-relevant visual evidence across simulation and real-world observations.
papers.summary: Vision-based driving policies trained with deep reinforcement learning in simulation often degrade badly in the real world, and existing fixes either require target-domain images or apply unguided domain randomisation that may not reflect the actual sim-to-real discrepancy. `XFD` extracts explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) attribution maps from simulated observations and turns them into policy-conditioned Fourier-domain perturbations that alter appearance-sensitive spectral components while preserving task-defining spatial structure, paired with a robust policy optimisation that pushes the policy toward task-critical features. In simulation and **zero-shot real-world deployment** the method improves traveled distance and reward over standard and randomly domain-randomised baselines, especially on unseen maps with cluttered backgrounds, and attribution analysis shows it keeps more consistent task-relevant visual evidence across the two domains.

papers.title: PXRD-Bench: How Close Are We to Determining Crystal Structures from Powder Diffraction?
papers.abstract: Determining crystal structures from powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) would enable routine characterization of newly synthesized materials, including those absent from reference databases. Generative models offer a promising approach, but existing evaluations remain fragmented and largely assume single-phase samples with known composition. To fill this gap, we introduce PXRD-Bench, a unified benchmark that extends evaluation to unknown per-element atom counts and recovery of both structures in two-phase mixtures. It provides approximately 4.1 million training structures with simulated PXRD, tests generalization to unseen compositions and structural prototypes, and evaluates recovery from experimental PXRD after excluding structurally matching training entries. To provide a strong reference baseline, we also introduce Bragglite, a PXRD-to-structure model developed through a systematic study of PXRD modeling choices. It achieves a 44.2\% Top-1 match rate on experimental RRUFF patterns with known composition, 24.6\% above the strongest prior baseline. Further analysis yields several key findings: some models fail to benefit from experimental PXRD, while generalization to unseen structural prototypes and recovery from two-phase mixtures remain challenging. Together, our benchmark, systematic studies, and Bragglite clarify the capabilities and limitations of current PXRD-to-structure models.
papers.summary: Recovering crystal structures from powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns would let newly synthesized materials be characterised without reference databases, but existing evaluations of generative models are fragmented and mostly assume single-phase samples with known composition. `PXRD-Bench` supplies roughly 4.1 million training structures with simulated patterns, extends evaluation to unknown per-element atom counts and two-phase mixtures, tests generalisation to unseen compositions and structural prototypes, and scores recovery from experimental patterns after removing structurally matching training entries. A reference model, `Bragglite`, built from a systematic study of modelling choices, reaches a **44.2% Top-1 match rate on experimental `RRUFF` patterns with known composition**, 24.6% above the strongest prior baseline, while some models fail to benefit from experimental data and unseen prototypes and two-phase mixtures remain hard.

papers.title: SLEM: Spectrum-Aware Latent Expert Merging
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale model capacity efficiently by activating only a small subset of experts for each input, while still requiring all parameters to be stored in memory, resulting in substantial memory overhead. Expert merging techniques have recently emerged as a promising compression paradigm that reduces this overhead by consolidating multiple experts into a smaller set. However, existing approaches have two key limitations: (i) direct convex interpolation in parameter space is not generally guaranteed to yield meaningful interpolation of expert functions; and (ii) estimating expert similarity or merging coefficients often relies on calibration data, introducing dependence on the calibration distribution. To address these limitations, we propose Spectrum-Aware Latent Expert Merging (SLEM), a calibration-free expert merging framework that occurs in a structured latent representation of expert weights using a VAE. SLEM groups experts within and across layers based on latent similarities and derives merging coefficients from expert weight spectra. It then performs geometry-aware latent interpolation and decodes the resulting representations into merged expert weights. Compared with existing expert merging methods, SLEM achieves comparable or better performance on general knowledge benchmarks and higher average performance on generation benchmarks involving mathematical reasoning and code generation.
papers.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models activate only a few experts per input but still keep every expert in memory, and expert merging compresses them by consolidating experts, though parameter-space interpolation is not guaranteed to merge expert functions meaningfully and merging coefficients usually depend on calibration data. Spectrum-Aware Latent Expert Merging (`SLEM`) is calibration-free: it encodes expert weights with a VAE, groups experts within and across layers by latent similarity, derives merging coefficients from the experts' weight spectra, interpolates in the latent space, and decodes the result back into merged expert weights. Against existing merging methods it is **comparable or better on general knowledge benchmarks and higher on average for mathematical reasoning and code generation**.

papers.title: Growing and Transferring Pathways for LLM Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can substantially improve the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but an effective training run requires considerable resources. Reusing the computation acquired through RL across models would extend the value of that training. We propose GrowRL, an RL method that organizes learned updates into compact computational pathways through structural growth. GrowRL freezes the pretrained backbone and adds an independent causal attention branch and a feed-forward network branch at each Transformer layer. Zero-initialized output projections preserve the pretrained policy at initialization, and RL updates only the added pathways. The learned pathways remain explicit after training, allowing transfer to structurally compatible target models and subsequent adaptation with the target backbone frozen. The architecture also supports sequential transfer of additional pathways. By keeping the learned attention and feed-forward computation separate from the pretrained weights, GrowRL provides an explicit structure for preserving and reusing the outcome of an RL run. Experiments across five backbones show competitive mathematical reasoning and out-of-distribution performance with a small number of trainable parameters. Learned pathways provide immediate gains across all three transfer directions, with performance after only 10 target-side updates already close to that after 100 updates in every case. These results support computational pathways as parameter-efficient and reusable units of reinforcement learning adaptation.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) can sharpen reasoning in large language models, but each run is expensive and its outcome is normally locked into one model's weights. `GrowRL` freezes the pretrained backbone and grows an independent causal attention branch and feed-forward branch at every Transformer layer, with zero-initialized output projections so the initial policy is unchanged, and trains only these added pathways with RL. Because the pathways stay explicit after training, they can be transferred to structurally compatible models and adapted further with the target backbone frozen; across five backbones the method shows competitive mathematical reasoning and out-of-distribution results with few trainable parameters, and transferred pathways give immediate gains, with **performance after only 10 target-side updates already close to that after 100**.

papers.title: Drafting Agents, Not Just Tokens: Speculative Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Systems
papers.abstract: Improving an agent through successive revisions requires balancing exploration and evaluation under a limited budget. A narrow search can miss useful sequences of edits, while fully evaluating every intermediate version can exhaust the budget before those sequences yield a verified improvement. We introduce Speculative Recursive Self-Improvement (SpecRSI), which drafts executable successor agents before their predecessors are fully evaluated, while requiring complete verification before adoption. Verification-Aware Tree Search (VATS) allocates the budget between further edits and outstanding checks using the predicted verified return of a continuation. Group Verification Optimization (GVO) learns the improver from completed searches while keeping the real evaluator fixed. In the main scientific comparison, terminal gains exceed Janus by 33.3%--40.0%. Additional evaluations show that SpecRSI outperforms Janus in all 50 scientific backbone--task pairs and exceeds MetaRSI-v1 by 1.85%--2.38% in macro-average system score across twenty backbones. Coding-validation success reaches 69.4% versus HGM's 64.3% at a 20.8% lower target-cost index.
papers.summary: Improving an agent through repeated self-revision means balancing exploration of edit sequences against the cost of fully evaluating every intermediate version within a fixed budget. Speculative Recursive Self-Improvement (`SpecRSI`) drafts executable successor agents before their predecessors are fully evaluated while still requiring complete verification before adoption; Verification-Aware Tree Search (`VATS`) allocates budget between further edits and outstanding checks using the predicted verified return of a continuation, and Group Verification Optimization (`GVO`) learns the improver from completed searches with the real evaluator held fixed. The authors report **terminal gains 33.3% to 40.0% above `Janus`** in the main scientific comparison, wins on all 50 scientific backbone-task pairs, a 1.85% to 2.38% macro-average edge over `MetaRSI-v1` across twenty backbones, and 69.4% coding-validation success versus 64.3% for `HGM` at a 20.8% lower target-cost index.

papers.title: From Caricature to Collective Artifact: How Persona Construction Drives Polarization in Generative Social Simulations
papers.abstract: Generative Social Simulation (GSS) leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to create sophisticated personas that define agents with demographics, emotions, and political opinions. While prior work shows that personas compress outputs into stereotypical caricatures, there is no comprehensive study of how these caricatures evolve into collective artifacts when they interact. Using a Twitter-like GSS platform with personas derived from the American National Elections Study (ANES), we ablate three layers of partisan identity: affective polarization markers, party identification, and vote choice, while retaining demographics, ideological positioning and important issues. We find that collective outcomes depend heavily on how survey responses are translated into personas. Removing a few explicitly partisan statements moves the network from near-complete segregation to cross-party ties approaching those of real Twitter networks. We argue that matching one outcome is not evidence for behavioral validity and point to salience as a possible explanation. Surveys ask for a position on every question regardless of its importance to the respondent, and persona construction turns each answer into a direct behavioral instruction. We conclude with a checklist for more comprehensive evaluation of personas in future works.
papers.summary: Generative Social Simulation (GSS) builds Large Language Model (LLM) agents from detailed personas, and earlier work found such personas flatten into stereotyped caricatures, but how those caricatures aggregate into collective outcomes once agents interact had not been studied. Using a Twitter-like platform with personas derived from the American National Elections Study (`ANES`), the authors ablate three layers of partisan identity: affective polarization markers, party identification, and vote choice, while keeping demographics, ideological positioning, and important issues. **Removing a few explicitly partisan statements moves the network from near-complete segregation to cross-party ties approaching those of real Twitter networks**, which they attribute to persona construction turning every survey answer into a behavioral instruction regardless of its salience to the respondent, and they close with a checklist for more thorough persona evaluation.

papers.title: pi-Net: Empirical Latent Representations for Differentiable Physics Heads in Data-Scarce Systems
papers.abstract: Developing reliable predictive models for multi-physics systems often forces a compromise between computationally demanding physical simulators and data-hungry, opaque machine learning (ML) algorithms. While incorporating dimensional analysis into directed computation graphs offers a structurally sound alternative to explicitly solving partial differential equations (PDEs), such formulations typically yield underdetermined systems that act as imperfect simulators. We introduce pi-Net, a physics-informed latent variable model that resolves these imperfect simulators. The hybrid pi-Net architecture consists of an encoder that maps inputs into physically normalized latent space, which are then decoded into final predictions by a differentiable physics head. Evaluated on a real-world, data-scarce Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW) case study, the framework achieves an R2 of 0.864 with only 60 experimental samples. The results demonstrate that pi-Net significantly outperforms purely data-driven baselines in data-scarce regimes while providing causal, process-level explainability.
papers.summary: Predictive models for multi-physics systems usually trade off between expensive simulators and data-hungry black-box machine learning, and dimensional-analysis computation graphs, while structurally sound, tend to be underdetermined and act as imperfect simulators. `pi-Net` pairs an encoder that maps inputs into a physically normalized latent space with a differentiable physics head that decodes those latents into final predictions. On a data-scarce Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW) case study it reaches **an R2 of 0.864 from only 60 experimental samples**, outperforming purely data-driven baselines while offering causal, process-level explanations.

papers.title: Boosting the Learning for Ranking Patterns
papers.abstract: Pattern mining is a valuable tool for exploratory data analysis, but identifying relevant patterns for a specific user is challenging. Various interestingness mea- sures have been developed to evaluate patterns, but they may not efficiently estimate user-specific functions. Learning user-specific functions by ranking patterns has been proposed, but this requires significant time and training samples. In this paper, we present a solution that formulates the problem of learning pattern ranking functions as a multicriteria decision making problem. Our approach uses Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) to elicit weights for different interestingness measures based on user preference. We also propose an active learning mode with a sensitivity-based heuristic to minimize user ranking queries while still providing high-quality results. Experiments show that our approach significantly reduces running time and returns precise pattern ranking while being robust to user error, compared to state-of-the-art approaches.
papers.summary: Pattern mining surfaces many candidate patterns, but generic interestingness measures rarely match what a particular user finds relevant, and learning user-specific ranking functions has required many training samples and long run times. The approach frames pattern ranking as a multicriteria decision making problem and uses the Analytic Hierarchy Process (`AHP`) to elicit weights over interestingness measures from user preferences, with an active-learning mode driven by a sensitivity-based heuristic to minimize the number of ranking queries. Experiments show it **reduces running time significantly compared with state-of-the-art approaches** while returning precise rankings and staying robust to user error.

papers.title: EAU: Environment-Agent-User Co-evolution for Training User-Centric Agents
papers.abstract: Training LLM agents to interact with users over multiple turns is challenging because the learning signal depends not only on the agent, but also on the user simulator and environment, which jointly shape the agent's experience. Simulated users can be stochastic or inconsistent, while environments may contain unreliable tools, incomplete state coverage, and incorrect verifiers. Prior work mainly addresses the resulting instability through reward shaping or denser supervision, while treating these components as fixed. We instead introduce EAU, a meta-agent framework for environment--agent--user co-evolution. During training, EAU monitors trajectories, tool traces, rewards, and training statistics; diagnoses failures and uninformative interactions; and proposes targeted modifications to the user simulator, environment, reward design, and RL configuration. Validated changes are hot-swapped into the ongoing run, allowing the training setup to evolve together with the policy. These adaptations also persist across runs, so later training can build on previously discovered improvements rather than restarting from a fixed setup. We enable this process through an editable symbolic representation of user and environment dynamics, while the agent remains a neural LLM optimized with RL. Across three interactive-agent benchmarks and two backbone models, EAU consistently outperforms prior RL methods, improving the overall score over the strongest baseline by 14.7--15.0% and increasing successful task completion on ColBench by up to 36.7%, showing that co-evolving the training system with the policy can substantially improve multi-turn RL.
papers.summary: Training large language model agents for multi-turn interaction is unstable because the learning signal depends on the user simulator and environment as much as on the agent, and simulators can be inconsistent while environments contain unreliable tools, gaps in state coverage, and incorrect verifiers. `EAU` is a meta-agent that monitors trajectories, tool traces, rewards, and training statistics during RL, diagnoses failures and uninformative interactions, and proposes targeted edits to the user simulator, environment, reward design, and RL configuration, which are validated, hot-swapped into the running job, and kept for later runs. The user and environment live in an editable symbolic representation while the policy stays a neural LLM; across three interactive-agent benchmarks and two backbones, `EAU` **beats the strongest prior RL baseline by 14.7% to 15.0% overall** and raises successful task completion on `ColBench` by up to 36.7%.

papers.title: Does the Explanation Drift Before the Guarantee? Label-Free Early Warning on Evolving Graphs
papers.abstract: Deployed models can fail silently as the world they describe evolves. Attribution drift has served as an early warning in tabular data; we ask whether, in graph streams, a model's own explanations can forewarn the loss of nominal conformal coverage. Doing so requires repairing the naive drift statistic twice. A vanishing edge loses mask mass regardless of whether the model relied on it, so we condition the importance on edge presence. Evolving graphs also break edge identity: a relabelling that changes nothing shifts the identity-based statistic by 0.69 on synthetic graphs and 0.83 on real ego-networks, whereas aggregating over structural roles brings both to 0.0 and stays well-defined when the support changes. We test six pre-registered regimes on thirty seeds each. A two-channel monitor, tracking conditional mask mass and its distribution over roles, precedes coverage collapse by 8 to 14.5 steps across four gradual regimes (node addition, removal, replacement, and edge thinning), all surviving Holm correction. A sudden knockout yields the expected zero lead, and a harmless change triggers no alarm. Leads track the length of the transitional phase (Spearman 0.79 over 150 runs). On real transaction ego-networks, the untuned mass channel forewarns staged drift by 27 steps and is the only channel, attributional or structural, that never alarms on a stationary stream. The main limitation is that the mass channel is blind to covariate drift, which breaks the guarantee in every run; the distributional channel detects it and also rescues the rewiring regime, so we report the two channels separately rather than as a union.
papers.summary: Deployed graph models can fail quietly as their data evolves, and the question is whether a model's own explanations can give advance warning that conformal prediction coverage is about to drop. The naive attribution-drift statistic needs two repairs: conditioning edge importance on edge presence, since a vanished edge loses mask mass whether or not the model relied on it, and aggregating over structural roles rather than edge identities, since a harmless relabelling otherwise shifts the statistic by 0.69 on synthetic graphs and 0.83 on real ego-networks. Across six pre-registered regimes with thirty seeds each, a two-channel monitor **precedes coverage collapse by 8 to 14.5 steps in four gradual drift regimes**, stays silent on harmless changes, and forewarns staged drift on real transaction ego-networks by 27 steps, though the mass channel is blind to covariate drift and only the distributional channel catches it.

papers.title: PatTransBench: an ipc-stratified, multi-dimensional benchmark for patent machine translation evaluation
papers.abstract: We present PatTransBench, a 12,000-item Chinese-English/Japanese/Korean patent machine translation (PatMT) benchmark with a four-dimensional evaluation protocol. The benchmark comprises 6,000 short-text (sentence/claim) and 6,000 long-text (paragraph) pairs, evenly split across three language pairs and both translation directions, built via IPC-section-stratified sampling and dualthreshold quality gating from upstream patent-family parallel corpora. The evaluation protocol spans literal n-gram overlap (BLEU, ROUGE-L, chrF), cross-lingual semantic textual similarity (CLSTS), 38-probe-language consistency testing, and serving performance under concurrency. A case study on PatMT2-7B and its fp8/AWQ4/AutoRound-4bit variants reveals direction-dependent quantization effects masked by aggregate scores and non-monotonic language-failure patterns across quantization schemes that are invisible to single-metric evaluation. We plan to release the benchmark, protocol, and case-study results upon publication to support reproducible PatMT evaluation.
papers.summary: Patent machine translation (PatMT) has lacked a benchmark that covers several languages, text lengths, and evaluation dimensions at once. `PatTransBench` holds 12,000 items split evenly between short sentence or claim pairs and long paragraph pairs across Chinese-English, Chinese-Japanese, and Chinese-Korean in both directions, sampled by IPC section and filtered with dual-threshold quality gating from patent-family parallel corpora. Its protocol combines n-gram overlap metrics, cross-lingual semantic textual similarity, consistency probes on 38 languages, and serving performance under concurrency, and a case study of `PatMT2-7B` and its quantized variants shows **direction-dependent quantization effects and non-monotonic language failures that aggregate scores hide**.

papers.title: Overtaught, Underlearned: Learner-Centered Distillation from Multi-Agent Discussion
papers.abstract: Multi-agent discussion produces reasoning collaboratively, while deployment still relies on a smaller student that must answer alone. Full-graph distillation transfers such discussions by treating each correct solution as a separate training target, but what teachers provide need not match what the student learns. This mismatch appears in two ways: several correct solutions may amount to the same lesson in the student's representation (over-teaching), while some training questions remain missed after learning (under-learning). We quantify both with rates that are high on discussion graphs. To address them, we introduce FAR (Fold--Attempt--Revisit), a learner-centered distillation procedure that organizes supervision around the student's own state. Before training, FAR folds solutions within each discussion state into representative lessons. After training, the student's own attempts identify missed questions, while poorly represented clusters indicate where folding may have lost useful variation; FAR then writes targeted lessons from retained discussion contexts. Across two students and four reasoning tasks, FAR outperforms full-graph distillation with far fewer training targets and lower under-learning. Further analyses examine the behavior of FAR and the sources of its gains. Overall, the results show that organizing discussion supervision around the student can make distillation both more effective and more efficient.
papers.summary: Multi-agent discussion produces reasoning collaboratively, but the deployed student model must answer alone, and distilling every correct solution from the discussion graph as a separate target ignores how the student actually absorbs them. The authors measure two mismatches, over-teaching, where several correct solutions collapse to the same lesson in the student's representation, and under-learning, where some training questions remain unsolved after training, and find both rates high on discussion graphs. `FAR` (Fold-Attempt-Revisit) folds solutions within each discussion state into representative lessons before training, then uses the student's own attempts to find missed questions and poorly covered clusters and writes targeted lessons from the retained discussion context; across two students and four reasoning tasks it **outperforms full-graph distillation with far fewer training targets** and lower under-learning.

papers.title: Heuristics are Not Enough: Calibrated and Corrected Caching for Video Diffusion Acceleration
papers.abstract: Feature caching has become a mainstream training-free strategy for accelerating video diffusion models by reusing intermediate outputs across denoising steps. However, existing adaptive methods rely on heuristic difference measures misaligned with actual generation quality, employ a single global threshold that ignores heterogeneous phase dynamics, and never validate their budget estimates against true approximation error, allowing systematic bias to propagate uncorrected. We propose \textbf{AlignCache}, a closed-loop caching framework that directly aligns scheduling decisions with their true influence on the final generated video through three tightly coupled components: (1) phase-adaptive budget routing that partitions the denoising trajectory into structurally distinct phases, each governed by an independent threshold and a staleness-aware guard; (2) closed-loop threshold calibration that exploits counterfactual error measurement at the classifier-free guided output level to adjust decision boundaries online via an EMA feedback loop; and (3) momentum-augmented draft synthesis combining direction-magnitude gated residual extrapolation with anchor-guided unconditional correction. By transforming scheduling from a static risk accumulator into a feedback-driven, self-correcting controller, AlignCache consistently achieves superior acceleration-quality trade-offs across state-of-the-art video generation models. Our code is available at https://github.com/jiangjyjy/AlignCache.
papers.summary: Feature caching speeds up video diffusion models by reusing intermediate outputs across denoising steps, but adaptive variants rely on heuristic difference measures that do not track output quality, use one global threshold across phases with different dynamics, and never check their error budgets against the true approximation error. `AlignCache` closes the loop with phase-adaptive budget routing that gives each segment of the denoising trajectory its own threshold and staleness guard, online threshold calibration driven by counterfactual error measured at the classifier-free guided output, and momentum-augmented draft synthesis that extrapolates residuals with direction and magnitude gating plus anchor-guided unconditional correction. The authors report **consistently better acceleration-quality trade-offs across state-of-the-art video generation models**, and the code is public.

papers.title: Making Language the Low-Rate Code of Vision: Successive Refinement from Words to Pixels
papers.abstract: An ordered visual code lets a short prefix stand in for an image, and the training loss decides what that prefix contains. Under pixel reconstruction the first bits go to the directions of highest variance, and we prove that a caption can then be independent of the entire first half of a code that is rate-optimal for pixels at every length. In the rate-distortion sense a caption is therefore not the low-rate code of its image, unless the code is built to make it one. We study that construction and what it costs. We cast captioning and text-to-image generation as successive refinement under a distortion measure that changes along the code, from caption log-loss in the early stages to pixel distortion in the last, so that each stage is compared with its own optimum. Putting words first then costs nothing among the caption stages exactly when the captions form a summarization chain, and it costs the pixels at most the caption uncertainty left in a pixel-optimal reconstruction, which is large for short prefixes and small at full length. We build RUNG, an ordered code whose prefixes are supervised by a summarization ladder of captions and whose full length reconstructs the image; generation extends the code past the prompt and captioning truncates it. With data and capacity held fixed, ordering by language instead of reconstruction raises prefix-caption information 2.9 times and GenEval from 0.76 to 0.83, at a measured cost of 2.8 dB PSNR at a quarter of the code and 0.1 dB at full length. RUNG-XL (3.4B) reaches 0.88 GenEval and 87.6 DPG-Bench in 32 network evaluations and 0.91 GenEval when errors are redrawn at the rung where they appear; its coarse and fine captions agree 94.1% of the time, and it edits images without inversion.
papers.summary: An ordered visual code lets a short prefix stand in for an image, but when the code is trained for pixel reconstruction the first bits go to the highest-variance directions, and the authors prove a caption can be independent of the entire first half of a code that is pixel-rate-optimal at every length. They recast captioning and text-to-image generation as successive refinement under a distortion measure that moves from caption log-loss in early stages to pixel distortion at the end, showing that putting words first is free among the caption stages exactly when the captions form a summarization chain and costs the pixels at most the caption uncertainty left in a pixel-optimal reconstruction. `RUNG` supervises code prefixes with a ladder of captions and reconstructs the image at full length; at fixed data and capacity, language-first ordering raises prefix-caption information 2.9 times and lifts `GenEval` from 0.76 to 0.83 at a cost of 2.8 dB PSNR at a quarter of the code and 0.1 dB at full length, and the 3.4B `RUNG-XL` reaches **0.88 on `GenEval` and 87.6 on `DPG-Bench` in 32 network evaluations** while editing images without inversion.

papers.title: AI Discovery in Combinatorics: From Problems to Solutions and Back to Bigger Problems
papers.abstract: We introduce $qt$Bench, a benchmark of 29 open problems in algebraic combinatorics. These problems ask for a simple combinatorial algorithm that explains given polynomial coefficients or identities. To help AI agents search for such algorithms, we provide a scaffold for playing with combinatorial objects, countering cheating attempts, and testing candidate solutions. To explore how far frontier AI systems can go on these problems, we collaborated with OpenAI, whose researchers obtained proposed solutions to several of them. This highlights bigger meta-problems: is AI discovery at scale ethical? How should these results be released? How should proof digestion be organized? We discuss these questions and give our views.
papers.summary: Many identities in algebraic combinatorics come with polynomial coefficients that still lack a simple combinatorial algorithm explaining them. `qtBench` collects 29 such open problems together with a scaffold that lets AI agents manipulate combinatorial objects, counters cheating attempts, and tests candidate solutions. In a collaboration with OpenAI, whose researchers obtained **proposed solutions to several of the 29 problems**, the authors then take up the meta-questions this raises: whether AI discovery at scale is ethical, how such results should be released, and how digesting the resulting proofs should be organized.

papers.title: G$^2$WAM: World Action Models for Efficient and Geometry Grounded Image-Goal Navigation
papers.abstract: World models capture environment dynamics and support counterfactual reasoning for planning. In image-goal navigation, where the target often lies beyond the current field of view, the agent must not only model environmental dynamics but also maintain a persistent spatial memory of the scene. Existing approaches either introduce spatial context by fine-tuning pretrained models on the target task, which underexploits their spatial priors, or rely on external 3D reconstruction, which is computationally expensive for real-world deployment. In this paper, we propose the Geometry Grounded World Action Model (G$^2$WAM) for image-goal navigation. G$^2$WAM encodes spatial cues through a learned scene-coordinate localization module that anchors the current, goal, and history frames in a common reference frame, yielding a stable and consistent spatial context that enables efficient navigation without explicit 3D reconstruction. Following the world-action-model paradigm, G$^2$WAM jointly predicts future states and actions, eliminating the need for costly cross-entropy method (CEM) style planning. In addition, G$^2$WAM operates entirely in latent space, avoiding the computational burden of pixel-level reconstruction and substantially reducing inference cost. Across four trajectory prediction benchmarks, G$^2$WAM reduces average ATE and RPE by 40.1% and 35.2%, respectively. In closed-loop navigation experiments, it improves the success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and the success weighted by path length (SPL) from 36.4% to 59.2%, while maintaining high efficiency.
papers.summary: In image-goal navigation the target often lies outside the current view, so an agent needs both a model of environment dynamics and a persistent spatial memory, yet fine-tuning pretrained models on the task underuses their spatial priors and external 3D reconstruction is too expensive for real-world deployment. The Geometry Grounded World Action Model (`G2WAM`) learns a scene-coordinate localization module that anchors the current, goal, and history frames in a shared reference frame, jointly predicts future states and actions so that cross-entropy method (CEM) style planning is unnecessary, and operates entirely in latent space to avoid pixel-level reconstruction. It cuts average ATE and RPE by 40.1% and 35.2% across four trajectory prediction benchmarks, and in closed-loop navigation it **raises success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and success weighted by path length (SPL) from 36.4% to 59.2%**.

papers.title: VLA-GAUGE: Systematically Evaluating Generalization and Robustness in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have achieved high success rates on familiar manipulation tasks, yet it remains unclear whether such scores reflect genuine zero-shot generalization and perturbation robustness. Existing evaluation frameworks provide limited capability-level diagnosis and combinatorial perturbation coverage, often without connecting diagnosis to targeted model refinement. We introduce VLA-GAUGE, a diagnostic framework that unifies both evaluations under a shared executable task representation. It combines (1) paired in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks across six capability suites, (2) single-factor sensitivity analysis with combinatorial perturbation screening and evaluation, and (3) diagnosis-driven refinement through targeted data augmentation and model fine-tuning. We evaluate 12 VLAs spanning different model sizes and action-modeling paradigms under a unified protocol. We find that (1) The mean Zero-Shot Score on VLA-GAUGE is only 22.3%, with SimpleVLA-RL scoring 8.0% and ranking second to last among the evaluated models. (2) Under three representative combinatorial perturbation configurations, the mean R-Score is 9.3. (3) Diagnosis-driven fine-tuning improves $\pi_{0.5}$'s zero-shot generalization and robustness under a selected perturbation combination on held-out scenarios by 72.4 and 31.8 scoring points, respectively; the latter exceeds the 10.9-point gain from LIBERO-Plus single-factor fine-tuning despite fewer successful training trajectories. These results show that high reported success rates on familiar manipulation tasks do not guarantee strong zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks or robustness to combinatorial perturbations, while diagnostic evaluation provides actionable signals for targeted model improvement.
papers.summary: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) post high success rates on familiar manipulation tasks, but it is unclear whether those scores reflect genuine zero-shot generalization or robustness to perturbation. `VLA-GAUGE` pairs in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks across six capability suites under one executable task representation, runs single-factor sensitivity analysis plus combinatorial perturbation screening, and feeds the diagnosis into targeted data augmentation and fine-tuning. Across 12 VLAs the **mean zero-shot score is only 22.3%**, with `SimpleVLA-RL` at 8.0%, the mean robustness score under three combinatorial perturbation setups is 9.3, and diagnosis-driven fine-tuning of `π0.5` lifts held-out zero-shot generalization and robustness by 72.4 and 31.8 points, beating the 10.9-point gain from `LIBERO-Plus` single-factor fine-tuning with fewer successful training trajectories.

papers.title: Double-Rollout Reinforcement Learning with Sampling-based Reward Estimation
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) implemented with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has driven substantial progress in training reasoning language models. However, verifiable outcome rewards provide an imperfect measure of reasoning quality: a correct final answer may not be supported by the reasoning trace, whereas an incorrect rollout may contain a nearly correct reasoning trajectory. We present empirical evidence for this mismatch and hypothesize that the resulting reward noise contributes to instability in reinforcement learning for both reasoning accuracy and token efficiency. To address this credit assignment challenge, this paper proposes double-rollout reinforcement learning. For each sampled rollout, we truncate its reasoning trace, sample multiple continuations from the truncated prefix, and replace the original reward with the mean continuation reward, yielding a more robust estimate of reasoning quality. This double-rollout algorithm incurs only a moderate increase in compute cost and yet reaches substantially higher accuracies across math and coding tasks and across Qwen and Nemotron models than baseline algorithms with fewer RL steps. For example, using only DAPO data it trains Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B to reach 95.4% on AIME 2026, versus 91.5% by GRPO and substantially above state of the art for this model size, within 30 RL steps. When combined with length-based rewards, the same algorithm further improves the accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier over existing efficiency optimizations. These findings suggest that the double-rollout reward estimation is an effective and cost-efficient way to improve both the accuracy and token efficiency of reasoning RL.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) run through Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) has advanced reasoning models, but outcome rewards are a noisy proxy for reasoning quality: a correct answer can sit on an unsupported trace and a wrong answer on a nearly correct one. The authors show this mismatch empirically, argue it destabilizes both accuracy and token efficiency, and propose double-rollout RL, where each sampled rollout's reasoning is truncated, multiple continuations are sampled from the prefix, and the mean continuation reward replaces the original reward. For a moderate increase in compute the method reaches higher accuracy on math and coding tasks across `Qwen` and `Nemotron` models in fewer RL steps, for example training `Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B` on `DAPO` data alone to **95.4% on `AIME 2026` versus 91.5% for `GRPO` within 30 RL steps**, and combined with length-based rewards it pushes the accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier further.

papers.title: Towards Modality-Agnostic Seizure Classification: A Unified Deep Learning Framework for Heterogeneous EEG and Intracranial EEG Signals
papers.abstract: Seizure prediction and detection, essential for clinical treatment of epilepsy, remain the crucial task of this neurological disease. EEG and iEEG are widely used to analyze epilepsy due to its capability of capturing discriminative brain activities at high time resolution. However, existing works generally analyze either EEG or iEEG seizure activity separately, where EEG analysis has been well-researched, while more and more works consider iEEG for its higher specificity at the spatial level and signal quality. Currently, most of the existing seizure prediction systems are single-modal in nature, which limits its application to a variety of clinical conditions. Therefore, a common framework to analyze seizures with both EEG and iEEG signals needs to be developed. This paper presents a new framework of multimodal seizure classification integrating the heterogeneous EEG and iEEG recordings from different subjects and sources. A specific framework, called Unified Multimodal Signal Harmonization (UMSH), is developed for harmonizing signals with varied sampling rates and recording conditions. Moreover, to handle the extremely class-imbalanced problem in the data sets, we use a Conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN) based data augmentation technique to generate synthetic samples to balance the class distribution. The proposed framework uses the EEGNet-Vision Transformer (EEGNet-ViT) as the feature extraction and classification network to learn the local discriminative patterns as well as global contextual information in the multimodal seizure data. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework for robust seizure classification, emphasizing the potential of integrated EEG-iEEG multimodal learning in advancing next-generation epilepsy monitoring and clinical decision-support systems.
papers.summary: Most seizure-detection systems work with either scalp electroencephalography (EEG) or intracranial EEG (iEEG), which limits where they can be used clinically. The authors build a single pipeline for both: a Unified Multimodal Signal Harmonization (`UMSH`) stage aligns recordings with different sampling rates and conditions, a conditional generative adversarial network (`cGAN`) synthesizes minority-class samples to correct severe class imbalance, and an `EEGNet-ViT` hybrid extracts local and global features for classification. **Experiments show robust seizure classification across heterogeneous subjects and recording sources**, which the authors present as a step toward integrated EEG-iEEG epilepsy monitoring and clinical decision support.

papers.title: MixLID: Token-Level Language Identification in Mixed-Language Text
papers.abstract: Processing multilingual text requires both identifying a broad range of languages and distinguishing the language of each token in inputs containing multiple languages. We introduce MixLID, a token-level language identification model supporting 111 language-script combinations. MixLID follows a two-stage training process: it first learns to distinguish individual languages using the language labels of monolingual examples, then continues training on mixed-language data. The second stage uses concatenated examples from existing code-switching data alongside augmented examples created through word substitution based on correspondences between English source words and loanwords. For monolingual identification, MixLID outperforms all baselines in both accuracy and macro F1 on four benchmarks within the language coverage shared with each baseline. For mixed-language identification, it outperforms the baselines in identifying the language of individual tokens on every evaluated language pair. MixLID achieves high performance across a broad range of languages in both monolingual and mixed-language settings. The model is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/nlpai-lab/MixLID.
papers.summary: Multilingual text processing needs to both recognize many languages and tag the language of each token when inputs mix languages. `MixLID` is a token-level language identifier covering 111 language-script combinations, trained in two stages: first on monolingual examples with language labels, then on mixed-language data built from concatenated code-switching examples plus augmented examples created by substituting English words with their loanword counterparts. **On monolingual identification it beats every baseline in accuracy and macro F1 on four benchmarks** within the language coverage shared with each baseline, and on mixed-language inputs it identifies each token's language more accurately than baselines on every language pair evaluated. The model is released publicly on Hugging Face.

papers.title: When 1+1 Backfires: Rethinking Relevance-Diversity Balancing for Sample-Aware Visual Token Reduction
papers.abstract: Visual token compression has emerged as a critical technique for reducing the inference cost of Vision-Language Models. Existing methods select tokens based on text relevance, visual diversity, or a fixed combination of both---treating the relevance-diversity balance as a universal constant independent of the input. We conduct a systematic analysis to challenge this assumption. At the dataset level, grid-searching the optimal relevance-diversity weight per benchmark reveals substantial cross-task variation. More critically, we further maximize per-sample answer likelihood to recover sample-level oracle weights, finding that their distributions not only differ markedly across benchmarks but also exhibit high within-benchmark variance. Based on these observations, we propose SAVER, a framework for Sample-Aware relevance-diversity balanced Visual tokEn Reduction. We first derive a Geometric Intent Prior (GIP) from the spatial concentration of text-relevant tokens to infer a sample-specific relevance-diversity weight, and then apply this weight to jointly select tokens via a Weighted Text Centroid (WTC) for relevance scoring and a Visual Marginal Coverage Gain (VMCG) for diversity. SAVER requires no additional training and achieves sample-aware balancing entirely at inference time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAVER consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks, retaining 96.5% of full-model performance on LLaVA-1.5-7B with only 11.1% of the original visual tokens, and further generalizing to LLaVA-NeXT and Mini-Gemini.
papers.summary: Visual token compression cuts the inference cost of vision-language models, but existing methods fix the balance between text relevance and visual diversity as a constant regardless of the input. Grid-searching the best relevance-diversity weight per benchmark, and then recovering per-sample oracle weights by maximizing answer likelihood, shows the ideal balance varies widely both across and within benchmarks. `SAVER` (Sample-Aware relevance-diversity balanced Visual tokEn Reduction) infers a per-sample weight from a Geometric Intent Prior (`GIP`) based on how spatially concentrated the text-relevant tokens are, then selects tokens using a Weighted Text Centroid (`WTC`) for relevance and Visual Marginal Coverage Gain (`VMCG`) for diversity, entirely at inference time without training. **It retains 96.5% of full-model performance on `LLaVA-1.5-7B` while keeping only 11.1% of the visual tokens**, and also generalizes to `LLaVA-NeXT` and `Mini-Gemini`.

papers.title: Weak Segmentation-Guided GAN for~Realistic Color Edition
papers.abstract: Editing the color of images in a realistic way finds many applications such as changing the perception of an image, data augmentation or film post processing. The design of an automatic tool is a complex and long addressed challenge.
