In particular, two properties are difficult to meet altogether: generating realistic results without artifacts and the possibility to precisely choose the future color. Conventional methods using segmentation and histogram matching maximize the controllability but also introduce a lack of realism or are complex to automate. On the contrary, GANs that specialize in realism are difficult to control. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel GAN architecture leveraging any differentiable segmentation model. We demonstrate the genericness of our framework that presents state of the art results on different use cases. It generates images that look realistic while offering a precise color control.
papers.summary: Realistic recoloring of images is hard because methods based on segmentation and histogram matching offer precise control but introduce artifacts or are hard to automate, while generative adversarial networks (GANs) produce realistic output that is hard to steer. The proposed GAN architecture incorporates any differentiable segmentation model as weak guidance, so the target color can be chosen precisely while the generator handles realism. **The authors report state-of-the-art results on several color-editing use cases**, producing images that look realistic while allowing precise control over the resulting color.

papers.title: Answer It or Not? Towards Prompt-Adapted Adversarial Images on Vision Language Models
papers.abstract: With the advancement in language modeling, research on adversarial images has recently shifted from image classifiers to vision-language models (VLMs). Despite the new, text-prompt-driven nature of VLMs, we find that existing VLM adversaries have largely overlooked the dynamics of text prompts. In a typical use case, adversarial images can protect visual privacy by rejecting VLMs from answering questions about the image. However, existing protections are prompt-agnostic, i.e., indiscriminately rejecting any question, including those for potential legitimate use of the image. To address this limitation, we propose Prompt-Adapted (ProAda) adversarial images, which are optimized to balance the rejection of harmful prompts and the correct response of legitimate prompts. In particular, to achieve a more accurate adversarial direction, the text prompt is also iteratively updated with a simple classifier judging whether the harmfulness of the prompt remains. Extensive experiments on visual-privacy-related datasets validate that ProAda can reject over 90% of harmful prompts while allowing over 90% of legitimate ones, demonstrating superior overall performance compared to existing prompt-agnostic VLM adversaries. In addition, our ProAda achieves competitive overall cross-model transferability and improved robustness against countermeasures.
papers.summary: Adversarial images can stop vision-language models (VLMs) from answering questions about a photo, protecting visual privacy, but existing perturbations are prompt-agnostic and block legitimate questions along with harmful ones. Prompt-Adapted (`ProAda`) adversarial images are optimized to reject harmful prompts while still permitting correct answers to legitimate ones, with the text prompts iteratively updated during optimization using a simple classifier that checks whether a prompt remains harmful. **On visual-privacy datasets, `ProAda` rejects over 90% of harmful prompts while allowing over 90% of legitimate ones**, outperforming prompt-agnostic baselines and showing competitive cross-model transfer and improved robustness against countermeasures.

papers.title: LATCH: LLM-Assisted Timing Closure Harness for Post-Route FPGA Optimisation
papers.abstract: Post-route FPGA timing closure remains expert-dependent and computationally expensive. We present LATCH (LLM-Assisted Timing Closure Harness), a two-layer framework that separates large language model (LLM) orchestration from deterministic FPGA implementation and evaluation. Across sixteen designs and seven LLMs, a single-iteration study compares three agent control granularities - expert-written recipes, direct EDA operations and LLM-constructed procedures - to ask how much control an agent needs per attempt. Functional-pass rates are 98.2%, 71.4% and 17.9%, respectively; yet direct operations give slightly larger 3.4% median Fmax gains when passing, versus 3.2% for recipes. This exposes a trade-off between execution reliability and timing improvement. Informed by this trade-off, a multi-iteration study fixes the action tier at expert recipes to ask how repeated attempts are best organised, comparing a fitted deterministic heuristic with sequential LLM reasoning, branching exploration and knowledge base-guided exploration within 12 checkpoints per run. Branching raises mean maximum-frequency improvement from 10.5% (sequential) to 16.0%, and the knowledge base to 20.3%, improving 15 of 16 designs. Characterisation across 2,421 recipe attempts profiled their gain and validation rates, showing hard-block re-placement gives the largest cumulative mean gain at 41.4MHz.
papers.summary: Closing timing after place-and-route on field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) still depends on expert intuition and expensive tool runs. `LATCH` (LLM-Assisted Timing Closure Harness) separates large language model (LLM) orchestration from a deterministic implementation-and-evaluation layer, and a single-iteration study across sixteen designs and seven LLMs compares three levels of agent control per attempt: expert-written recipes, direct electronic design automation (EDA) operations, and LLM-constructed procedures. **Functional-pass rates were 98.2%, 71.4%, and 17.9% respectively**, while direct operations gave slightly larger median maximum-frequency gains when they passed, exposing a trade-off between execution reliability and timing improvement. Fixing the action tier at recipes, a multi-iteration study found branching exploration raised mean frequency improvement from 10.5% (sequential LLM reasoning) to 16.0% and knowledge-base-guided exploration to 20.3%, improving 15 of 16 designs, and profiling 2,421 recipe attempts showed hard-block re-placement gives the largest cumulative mean gain.

papers.title: Integrating Feature Understandability into Feature Selection for Human-Centred Tabular Explanations
papers.abstract: Existing human-centred XAI research predominantly evaluates explanations after they have been generated. However, this fails to provide actionable insights into improving accessibility. This study incorporates human-based feature understandability into feature selection to improve the generation of human-centred explanations. Natural language explanations for machine learning models trained on tabular data often cite influential features in the input data to explain a given decision. As a consequence, users' ability to understand the produced explanation hinges on their understanding of the cited features. To quantify this natural-language feature understandability, Rossberg et al. proposed the Feature Understandability Scale, which assigns numerical `understandability scores' to features based on user feedback. To evaluate the degree to which these scores can improve machine learning explanation quality, this study collects understandability scores across two datasets, proposes an understandability-aware feature selection algorithm to select features that are both understandable and informative, and trains a random forest based on these feature subsets. The SHAP-based explanations generated by this model are evaluated using user feedback, and changes in explanation quality are assessed. The individual evaluation of the explanations showed that while the understandability-based explanations scored higher on average, the difference was not statistically significant. In contrast, the comparative evaluation found that participants preferred these explanations significantly more frequently than expected at the chance level. It is concluded that the integration of understandability can yield more understandable explanations at minimal cost to classification performance, although changes to quality require elucidation in larger cohorts.
papers.summary: Natural-language explanations of tabular machine-learning models typically cite influential input features, so users can only follow them if they understand those features. Building on the Feature Understandability Scale, which assigns numeric understandability scores to features from user feedback, the authors collect such scores for two datasets, propose an understandability-aware feature selection algorithm that trades off informativeness against understandability, train a random forest on the selected features, and have users evaluate the resulting `SHAP` explanations. Rated individually, the understandability-based explanations scored higher on average but not significantly; **in head-to-head comparison, participants preferred them significantly more often than chance**, at minimal cost to classification performance, though larger cohorts are needed to pin down the change in quality.

papers.title: AeroChem: Closed-loop Physics-Informed State Space Modeling for Long-term Chemically-Reactive Air Quality Forecasting--Extended Version
papers.abstract: Accurate long-term air quality forecasting is challenging due to long-range transport, meteorological variability, and nonlinear chemical reactions underlying secondary pollutant formation. Purely data-driven models often suffer from long-horizon drift and lack physical consistency, while existing physics-informed approaches commonly follow open-loop designs that fuse neural and physical components only at the output level. We propose AeroChem, a closed-loop physics-informed state space framework for chemically reactive air quality forecasting. AeroChem adopts a two-branch co-correction design: a UDE-based process branch provides a structured but imperfect physical prior, while a Mamba-based virtual measurement branch captures long-range temporal context and produces probabilistic virtual observations. Neural Kalman Fusion couples the two branches by correcting the latent physical state at each forecasting step and feeding the posterior state back into the simulator, reducing long-horizon drift. We further introduce HanoiAir, a real-world dataset integrating pollutant concentrations, meteorology, and emission inventories. Experiments on HanoiAir and a public benchmark show that AeroChem improves long-horizon stability and sudden-change forecasting.
papers.summary: Long-horizon air-quality forecasting is hard because of long-range pollutant transport, variable weather, and the nonlinear chemistry that produces secondary pollutants; purely data-driven models drift over long horizons, while existing physics-informed models fuse neural and physical parts only at the output. `AeroChem` uses two branches that correct each other: a UDE-based process branch supplies a structured but imperfect physical prior, and a `Mamba`-based virtual-measurement branch captures long-range temporal context and emits probabilistic virtual observations. A `Neural Kalman Fusion` step corrects the latent physical state at each forecast step and feeds the posterior back into the simulator, closing the loop. The authors also release `HanoiAir`, a dataset combining pollutant concentrations, meteorology, and emission inventories, and **report improved long-horizon stability and better forecasting of sudden changes on `HanoiAir` and a public benchmark**.

papers.title: REEL: Learning to Retrieve, Evaluate, and Evolve Visual Memory for Any Long-Horizon Multi-Shot Video Generation
papers.abstract: Memory-based long-video generation aims to combine user control with long-range visual consistency. We organize this process into three functional components: a planner, an adapter, and a generator. Representative multi-shot systems couple memory to generator-specific interfaces or use predefined agent workflows, rather than independently training a memory policy for cross-shot objectives. We introduce REEL, a general-purpose visual-memory planner. Through a unified tool interface, REEL learns to retrieve references, create missing visual evidence, and update persistent memory. Backend-specific adapters translate its evidence plans into supported conditioning inputs, allowing the same policy to guide different black-box video generators. To train REEL, we construct two high-quality datasets, REEL-SFT-4k and REEL-RL-1k, covering diverse interaction patterns and prompt types. Training proceeds in three stages: supervised fine-tuning, single-shot Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and multi-shot GRPO. Multi-shot GRPO carries policy-generated memory across consecutive shots, so later outcomes guide earlier reference selection and memory updates. REEL-Bench tests identity preservation and intended state changes under text-only requests and timed reference-image uploads. On JoyAI-Echo~1.5 and MiniMax-H3, REEL improves cross-shot consistency on ST-Bench by 15.1\% and 20.7\%, and Core-100 on our proposed REEL-Bench by 2.41 and 8.32 points, respectively, over the no-memory baseline.
papers.summary: Memory-based long video generation aims to keep characters and objects consistent across many shots while following user control, but existing multi-shot systems tie memory to a specific generator's interface or hard-code agent workflows rather than learning a memory policy. `REEL` is a general-purpose visual-memory planner that, through a unified tool interface, learns to retrieve reference images, create missing visual evidence, and update persistent memory; backend-specific adapters translate its evidence plans into conditioning inputs for different black-box video generators. It is trained in three stages on the new `REEL-SFT-4k` and `REEL-RL-1k` datasets: supervised fine-tuning, single-shot Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`), and multi-shot `GRPO` in which memory produced by the policy carries across shots so later outcomes guide earlier reference selection. **On `JoyAI-Echo 1.5` and `MiniMax-H3`, cross-shot consistency on `ST-Bench` improves by 15.1% and 20.7%** over a no-memory baseline, with further gains on the authors' `REEL-Bench`, which tests identity preservation and intended state changes.

papers.title: SuPER-Mamba: Surprisal Prioritization for Extended-Context Routing in Mamba
papers.abstract: State space models provide efficient linear-complexity processing for long sequences, but their performance frequently degrades as context length grows. We propose SuPER-Mamba, a training-free framework that uses Surprisal as a model-intrinsic signal for long-range state routing in pretrained Mamba models. SuPER-Mamba computes position-wise Surprisal from next-token predictions, aggregates neighboring responses through Local Pooling, and uses the resulting scores to prioritize Global-Channel updates without query-dependent scoring or additional training. We evaluate SuPER-Mamba on three state-space models across the LongBench-E benchmark. The results show that SuPER-Mamba improves the average score from 8.06 to 15.69, corresponding to a 94.7% relative gain over the Base Models and a 13.1% improvement over the state-of-the-art prior baseline. Ablation and length-wise analyses further support the effectiveness of the proposed routing framework.
papers.summary: State space models process long sequences in linear time, but pretrained `Mamba` models often degrade as context grows. `SuPER-Mamba` is a training-free method that uses surprisal, the model's own next-token prediction loss at each position, as a signal for long-range state routing: position-wise surprisal is pooled over local neighborhoods, and the resulting scores prioritize updates to global channels without any query-dependent scoring. **Across three state-space models on `LongBench-E`, the average score rises from 8.06 to 15.69, a 94.7% relative gain over the base models** and a 13.1% improvement over the prior state-of-the-art baseline, with ablations and length-wise analyses supporting the routing design.

papers.title: Learning Incompressible 3D Flows from Sparse Samples: A Set Transformer Approach to Divergence-Free Kernel Fitting
papers.abstract: Recovering divergence-free velocity fields from sparse and corrupted observations requires reconciling physical consistency, expressive representations, and robustness to missing data. We introduce DFK-Former, a set-to-field transformer that reconstructs divergence-free velocity fields from sparse, noisy, and irregularly sampled 3D observations. The model is inherently invariant to the number and ordering of input samples and predicts the parameters of a divergence-free kernel representation, producing continuous, mesh-free velocity fields that satisfy incompressibility exactly by construction rather than approximately through soft constraints or projection operators. Unlike existing divergence-free kernel approaches, which estimate kernel coefficients via a separate optimization for each field, DFK-Former predicts these coefficients directly in a single forward pass. This eliminates costly iterative fitting while providing a learned prior that enables accurate reconstruction even when observations are insufficient to uniquely determine the field. To enhance representational power, we introduce adaptive and anisotropic divergence-free kernels that preserve exact incompressibility guarantees while capturing more complex flow structures. Extensive experiments across varying levels of sparsity, noise, and occlusion, including transfer to real Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) turbulence data, demonstrate substantial gains in both accuracy and efficiency. DFK-Former reduces endpoint error by up to 4.6x compared to per-field divergence-free-kernel optimization, while reconstructing each field in 7.5 ms instead of 9.8 s, yielding a speedup of more than three orders of magnitude. These results establish direct, feed-forward prediction of divergence-free kernel parameters as a practical and effective paradigm for physically consistent velocity-field reconstruction from sparse observations.
papers.summary: Reconstructing incompressible, divergence-free 3D velocity fields from sparse, noisy, irregularly sampled observations requires physical consistency, expressive representations, and robustness to missing data. `DFK-Former` is a set-to-field transformer, invariant to the number and order of input samples, that predicts in one forward pass the coefficients of a divergence-free kernel representation, yielding continuous mesh-free fields that satisfy incompressibility exactly by construction; adaptive, anisotropic kernels extend the flow structures these representations can capture. Unlike prior divergence-free kernel methods that run a separate optimization per field, the learned prior also handles cases where observations do not uniquely determine the field. **Endpoint error drops by up to 4.6 times versus per-field kernel optimization, and reconstruction takes 7.5 ms instead of 9.8 s**, with results transferring to real direct numerical simulation (DNS) turbulence data.

papers.title: Does a Hosted Decision Model Respect Irrelevant Alternatives? A Pre-Registered Test of Option-Set Dependence in Jev
papers.abstract: Decision APIs that return a probability for each option are routinely used as if those probabilities were properties of the options themselves. That reading is valid only if the model satisfies independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA): adding an option that is neither the right answer nor its strongest rival should leave the odds between those two unchanged. We test this in a pre-registered study of jev-1.13.0, a hosted decision model, using 299,463 calls on intent classification (BANKING77, CLINC150) and topic classification (AG News). Every added option moves the log-odds between the gold label and the strongest wrong label: the root-mean-square systematic shift is 0.20-0.52 nats, 1.2 to 3 times the run-to-run variation, even when the added option takes at most 0.1% of the probability mass. The shifts are directional. An option similar to the wrong answer draws probability from it (+0.10 nats toward the gold label). A paraphrase of the wrong answer produces an intermediate pattern: the gold label's probability is almost conserved, but the paraphrase receives only about a third of the wrong answer's share rather than the half that strict substitution implies. The distortion grows steadily with the logarithm of the number of options, reaching about 1 nat at 255 options, and off-domain padding pushes the odds against the gold label. In contrast, questions packed into one call do not interact (bias < 0.001). Scoring each option with an independent yes/no question removes the option-set dependence but picks the right answer 8.7 points less often. Jev sits between two local baselines, an option-independent scorer and a prompt readout. Its probabilities are best read as relative to the option list they were computed over.
papers.summary: Decision APIs that return a probability per option are often read as if those probabilities belonged to the options themselves, which holds only if the model satisfies independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA): adding an option that is neither the correct answer nor its strongest rival should leave the odds between those two unchanged. A pre-registered study of `jev-1.13.0`, a hosted decision model, tests this with 299,463 calls on the `BANKING77`, `CLINC150`, and `AG News` classification datasets. **Every added option shifts the log-odds between the gold label and the strongest wrong label, with a systematic root-mean-square shift of 0.20 to 0.52 nats, 1.2 to 3 times the run-to-run variation**, even when the added option takes at most 0.1% of the probability mass; the shifts are directional, the distortion grows with the logarithm of the option count to about 1 nat at 255 options, and off-domain padding pushes the odds against the gold label, whereas multiple questions packed into one call do not interact. Scoring each option with an independent yes/no question removes the option-set dependence but picks the right answer 8.7 points less often, so the model's probabilities are best read as relative to the option list they were computed over.

papers.title: Structural Baselines Matter for Agent Failure Detection and Attribution
papers.abstract: An LLM agent using tools can fail silently. It stops before the task is done, raises no error, and answers fluently. Two kinds of monitor address this, one deciding whether a run failed and the other naming the step where failure became unavoidable. Much of the reported performance on both tasks comes from regularities that need no model. Failing runs are longer, and the step labelled decisive is usually the last. A rule that always names the last step is correct $67\%$ to $96\%$ of the time here, without reading the run at all. That ceiling reflects how the labels were written, not how agents break. On failures whose decisive step replay can confirm, it falls to near chance. Reporting gain over that rule therefore changes what a score means. Under that correction, methods tested here gain nothing on give-up failures, while several published systems keep a clear advantage on other splits. For detection, the agent's internal states beat transcript length and text similarity on the agent benchmark, and hold up where the text baseline does not. Precision stays low when failures are rare, so such a monitor should rank runs for review, not replace it.
papers.summary: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents can fail silently, stopping before the task is done while answering fluently, and monitors for this either decide whether a run failed or name the step where failure became unavoidable. Much of the reported performance on both tasks comes from regularities that need no model: failing runs are longer, and the step labeled decisive is usually the last one. **A rule that always names the last step is correct 67% to 96% of the time without reading the run at all**, a ceiling that reflects how labels were written rather than how agents break, and it drops to near chance on failures whose decisive step can be confirmed by replay. Measured as gain over that rule, the methods tested add nothing on give-up failures while several published systems keep a clear advantage on other splits; for detection, the agent's internal states beat transcript length and text similarity and hold up where the text baseline does not, though precision stays low when failures are rare, so such a monitor should rank runs for human review rather than replace it.

papers.title: Feature-Context Consistency: Unsupervised Adversarial Detection with Drift Stability on Attributed Graphs
papers.abstract: Adversarial detection on evolving attributed graphs faces two challenges: fraud labels arrive late or not at all, and natural distributional drift erodes any trained decision boundary. Modern detectors can reach strong detection rates when labels are available and the distribution is stationary; sustaining that quality without labels and under drift is the open problem. We identify feature-context consistency -- the alignment between a node's attributes and its aggregated neighborhood attributes -- as a single structural signal that addresses both. We formalize it as the Context Boost (CB) score within a Restricted Boltzmann Machine framework (CB-RBM) and prove two complementary worst-case guarantees: a strict separation between the expected CB of legitimate and adversarial nodes, with gap growing linearly in model capacity, whenever the adversary's context stays far enough from legitimate neighborhood context; and a Wasserstein-Lipschitz bound on how far the CB distribution moves under natural drift. We validate on XBlock Ethereum phishing (~153K nodes) and Reddit banned-user detection (~11K nodes), with two further datasets in the appendix spanning diverse domains. With zero labels, CB-RBM achieves AUROC >= 0.96 on four adversarial attacks and keeps FPR close to its calibrated 5% target under drift -- outperforming supervised GNNs (hundreds of labels), unsupervised graph-anomaly baselines, and a standard RBM whose FPR collapses to 89-100%. What typically requires separate mechanisms -- label-free operation and drift stability -- here follows from a single structural regularity of the data. Code: https://github.com/serval-uni-lu/CB-RBM.
papers.summary: Detecting adversarial or fraudulent nodes on evolving attributed graphs is hard when labels arrive late or never and natural distribution drift erodes any trained decision boundary. The authors identify feature-context consistency, the alignment between a node's own attributes and its aggregated neighborhood attributes, as a single structural signal addressing both problems, formalize it as a Context Boost (CB) score within a Restricted Boltzmann Machine (`CB-RBM`), and prove a worst-case separation between legitimate and adversarial nodes that grows linearly with model capacity, plus a Wasserstein-Lipschitz bound on how far the score distribution moves under drift. **With zero labels, `CB-RBM` reaches AUROC of at least 0.96 on four adversarial attacks on `XBlock` Ethereum phishing and Reddit banned-user data** while keeping its false-positive rate near the calibrated 5% target under drift, outperforming supervised graph neural networks trained with hundreds of labels, unsupervised graph-anomaly baselines, and a standard RBM whose false-positive rate collapses to 89-100%.

papers.title: Audit Before You Distill: A Controlled Workflow for Reasoning Transfer into Compact Medical Language Models
papers.abstract: Teacher rationales can help a smaller model answer health professions questions, but they can also reinforce errors. We examined when they help and how this evidence can guide training using Brazilian Portuguese questions from medical and multiprofessional residency examinations. First, we measured how a teacher rationale changed the student's probability of selecting the correct answer and compared this effect with rationales drawn from other questions. The complete rationale increased this probability by 21~p.p. when the teacher was correct and decreased it by 14~p.p. when the teacher was wrong. By intervening on the reasoning content, we showed that shuffled rationales did not produce the same pattern. Guided by this result, we trained only with rationales attached to correct teacher answers and compared answer-only training, step-by-step distillation, and our proposed Distill-SFT method. Distill-SFT showed a modest advantage over step-by-step distillation on previously missed questions under reasoning, while using fewer training instances by combining the answer and rationale into a single target. We also investigated catastrophic forgetting using the out-of-domain ENEM dataset. Answer-only training reduced reasoning accuracy by 12~p.p. relative to baseline, compared with approximately 4~p.p. for either rationale-based training method. Together, these findings support a workflow that audits rationale content before distillation, verifies teacher answers before supervision, and trains compact models efficiently for health professions question answering.
papers.summary: Teacher-generated rationales can help a small model answer health-professions questions but can also reinforce the teacher's errors. Using Brazilian Portuguese questions from medical and multiprofessional residency exams, the authors first measure how a teacher rationale changes the student's probability of picking the right answer: **a complete rationale raised that probability by 21 percentage points when the teacher was correct and lowered it by 14 points when the teacher was wrong**, a pattern that shuffled rationales did not reproduce. Guided by this, they train only on rationales attached to correct teacher answers and compare answer-only training, step-by-step distillation, and their `Distill-SFT` method, which merges answer and rationale into a single target and shows a modest edge on previously missed questions while using fewer training instances. On the out-of-domain `ENEM` dataset, answer-only training cut reasoning accuracy by 12 points versus roughly 4 points for either rationale-based method, supporting a workflow that audits rationale content and verifies teacher answers before distillation.

papers.title: Trace-to-Architecture: Capability Bottleneck Diagnosis for Harness Revision
papers.abstract: Improving an LLM agent requires knowing what to change when it fails. Similar failures can require different fixes, and resolving one problem can expose another. We introduce Trace-to-Architecture (T2A), a framework that uses execution trajectories to determine what to change in an agent's harness and when those changes apply. A development agent diagnoses failures using execution evidence from successful and failed tasks, revises the corresponding harness components, and then checks whether target tasks improve, selected successful tasks remain successful, and the edits are actually triggered. New execution evidence guides subsequent diagnosis and revision. Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and AppWorld, T2A achieves the highest aggregate score for all three evaluated task agents, exceeding their respective strongest baselines by 6.2--30.3 points. We also integrate T2A's diagnosis and validation procedures into Meta-Harness, improving the resulting harnesses' mean ScienceWorld score by 21.6 points from the same starting harness.
papers.summary: Improving a large language model (LLM) agent requires knowing what to change in its harness when it fails, yet similar failures can need different fixes and resolving one can expose another. Trace-to-Architecture (`T2A`) has a development agent diagnose failures from execution trajectories of both successful and failed tasks, revise the responsible harness components, and then verify that target tasks improve, selected successful tasks still pass, and the edits are actually triggered at runtime; new execution evidence feeds the next round of diagnosis. Across `ALFWorld`, `ScienceWorld`, and `AppWorld`, `T2A` achieves the highest aggregate score for all three task agents evaluated, **beating their strongest baselines by 6.2 to 30.3 points**. Plugging its diagnosis and validation procedures into `Meta-Harness` raises the resulting harnesses' mean `ScienceWorld` score by 21.6 points from the same starting harness.

papers.title: Queue-Aware Token Communications: Bridging AI Representation and Wireless Service
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of foundation models and edge intelligence is transforming wireless networks from data-oriented communication systems into artificial intelligence (AI)-native service platforms. Token communications (TokenCom) has emerged as a promising paradigm that directly transmits task-oriented AI representations. However, existing studies typically assume that generated tokens can be transmitted immediately, overlooking the queueing dynamics arising from the mismatch between token workload generation and time-varying wireless service capability. To address this limitation, we introduce Queue-Aware TokenCom, which explicitly incorporates token queues into the AI service pipeline. We present an end-to-end architecture integrating AI representation generation, token workload management, wireless transmission, and downstream task inference. We then discuss two key design directions: budget-aware token representation optimization and queue-aware token service optimization, with the token budget serving as a critical interface between AI performance and communication efficiency. Moreover, we investigate fixed and adaptive token budget strategies to characterize the fundamental tradeoff between AI performance and communication efficiency in dynamic wireless environments. Finally, we outline research directions toward closed-loop, task-aware, and scalable TokenCom systems.
papers.summary: Token communications (`TokenCom`) transmits task-oriented AI representations directly over wireless links, but prior work assumes generated tokens are sent immediately, ignoring the queueing that arises when token generation outpaces time-varying wireless capacity. Queue-Aware `TokenCom` adds explicit token queues to the AI service pipeline, with an end-to-end architecture spanning representation generation, token workload management, wireless transmission, and downstream inference. Two design directions are discussed, budget-aware token representation optimization and queue-aware token service optimization, with **the token budget serving as the interface between AI performance and communication efficiency**; fixed and adaptive budget strategies are compared to characterize that trade-off in dynamic wireless environments, and open directions toward closed-loop, task-aware systems are outlined.

papers.title: VAttnPO: Visual Attention-Guided Policy Optimization
papers.abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards commonly assigns one sequence advantage to an entire response. This outcome-level signal distinguishes overall response quality but leaves changes in visual-evidence use across generated tokens implicit. We introduce VAttnPO (Visual Attention-Guided Policy Optimization), which uses answer-conditioned visual attention to refine token-level credit while preserving the verifier-derived trajectory-mean advantage. A frozen old policy constructs a visual reference by teacher forcing the known correct answer and produces a visual distribution for each rollout token. VAttnPO measures their agreement in visual-attention space using Jensen--Shannon divergence, rather than reading guidance from teacher output-token distributions or introducing an attention-matching objective. Trajectory centering, relative-position weighting, and credit balancing turn this agreement into a zero-mean, position-aware correction to the GRPO sequence advantage. Token intervention, visual-index permutation, and trajectory analysis provide diagnostic evidence linking this signal to model behavior, visual correspondence, and generation position. On Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, VAttnPO raises six-task image AVE from 70.97 with GRPO to 73.50 and scores higher on every reported structured, video, and MME metric. Gains over GRPO also hold on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and InternVL3-8B-Instruct.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for multimodal models usually assigns one sequence-level advantage to an entire response, leaving token-level differences in how visual evidence is used implicit. `VAttnPO` (Visual Attention-Guided Policy Optimization) builds a visual reference by having a frozen old policy teacher-force the known correct answer, measures each rollout token's agreement with that reference in visual-attention space using Jensen-Shannon divergence, and turns this, via trajectory centering, relative-position weighting, and credit balancing, into a zero-mean token-level correction to the `GRPO` sequence advantage while preserving the verifier-derived trajectory mean. Token intervention, visual-index permutation, and trajectory analyses link the signal to model behavior, visual correspondence, and generation position. **On `Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct`, the six-task image average rises from 70.97 with `GRPO` to 73.50**, with higher scores on every reported structured, video, and `MME` metric and gains that also hold on `Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct` and `InternVL3-8B-Instruct`.

papers.title: Before Attention Sinks Form: Hidden-State Geometry Reveals and Modulates Their Formation
papers.abstract: Attention sinks are usually studied after they have formed. We ask whether a measurable hidden-state change appears beforehand and whether changing that geometry alters what happens later. To remove network depth as a shortcut, we compare prompts in the same model and at the same layer. When sink timing varies across prompts, simple spectral summaries of the hidden states add information beyond current attention, with the clearest prompt-specific signal in a short window about two to three layers before sink formation. The predictive strength varies across cohorts, so we treat the spectrum as a readout of a pre-sink state change rather than a universal warning statistic. The signal is broader than one measured extreme activation. We then modify only the singular values of the post-layer hidden states after current attention has already been computed. These interventions change later sink behavior in Qwen2.5, GLM-Z1, and GPT-OSS relative to norm-matched random spectral perturbations. In Qwen2.5, the immediate suppressive effect is accompanied by a reduction in next-layer query--key preference for position~0, and the learned spectral directions remain stable when estimated from substantially less training data. Together, the results show that attention sinks are preceded by a short spectral reorganization of hidden states, and directly perturbing this geometry can causally alter subsequent sink formation.
papers.summary: Attention sinks, positions that absorb disproportionate attention, are usually analyzed only after they form; this work asks whether a measurable hidden-state change precedes them and whether altering that geometry changes what follows. Comparing prompts within the same model and layer to rule out depth as a shortcut, simple spectral summaries of hidden states predict sink timing beyond what current attention reveals, with the clearest signal in a window about two to three layers before formation, though predictive strength varies across prompt cohorts. **Modifying only the singular values of post-layer hidden states causally changes later sink behavior in `Qwen2.5`, `GLM-Z1`, and `GPT-OSS`** relative to norm-matched random spectral perturbations; in `Qwen2.5` the suppression comes with reduced next-layer query-key preference for position 0, and the learned spectral directions stay stable when estimated from much less training data.

papers.title: Separating Prompt Harmfulness from Interaction Safety via Partial Generation
papers.abstract: LLM-based information systems need safety guardrails. Most guardrails classify the prompt alone. If the prompt looks harmful, the system rejects it before any answer is generated. This is costly. Many rejected prompts would have received a safe response. Users lose help they should have received from the information system. This cost grows as conversational and generative search becomes common. Prompt-level labels treat harm as a property of the query. But harm depends on what the model actually writes. Existing input-output guards do look at responses. But they judge a finished response, so the decision comes after full generation. However, we observe that safety of model interaction with the input prompt can be inferred early with only partial output. So the system can start generating, watch the partial response, and stop only if it turns harmful. We test this idea in three steps. First, we build a dataset of 41,944 prompt-response pairs with seven open weights LLMs from three families: Llama, Gemma, and Qwen. Second, we show that prompt harmfulness and interaction safety differ. Prompt labels and response labels agree on only 50.46\% of items (Cohen's $\kappa$ = 0.06). Of the prompts that make any model respond harmfully, only 3.5\% do so for all seven LLMs. Third, we show that partial responses carry most of the signal. Fine-tuned classifiers predict response-level harm well (best AUPRC 0.885, F1 0.807). About one third of the response tokens recover almost full-response AUPRC.
papers.summary: Most large language model (LLM) guardrails classify the prompt alone and refuse anything that looks harmful, discarding many prompts that would have drawn a safe response, while input-output guards only judge a completed response. The authors propose instead to start generating, watch the partial response, and stop only if it turns harmful. On a new dataset of 41,944 prompt-response pairs from seven open-weight `Llama`, `Gemma`, and `Qwen` models, **prompt-harm labels and response-harm labels agree on only 50.46% of items (Cohen's kappa 0.06)**, and only 3.5% of prompts that elicit a harmful response from any model do so from all seven. Fine-tuned classifiers predict response-level harm well (best AUPRC 0.885, F1 0.807), and about one third of the response tokens recover nearly the full-response AUPRC.

papers.title: Relational Learning as World Modeling
papers.abstract: Relational learning typically predicts from a database state, but decision making asks a different question: how will that state change under an action? In operational systems, the answer depends on system-specific dynamics that may not be visible in the database itself. We view each such system as a relational "world" and ask whether a model can infer how it behaves from observed executions. We introduce TabWM (Tabular World Model) and WorldRel, a generator of executable relational worlds for pretraining. Given executions from an unseen world, TabWM uses them as context to predict the sparse structured edits caused by a new action without parameter updates. Across 512 held-out worlds, complete-edit F1 rises from 0.016 with no observed executions to 0.685 with 64, where a correct edit must match its operation, relational location, and value. Because these predictions are explicit relational edits, they can be applied recursively to imagine candidate futures and compare actions before they are taken. Broader search over these predicted futures improves the realized return of selected action sequences. Together, these results suggest that relational dynamics can be learned in context, broadening relational learning from modeling system state to modeling how that state changes under action.
papers.summary: Relational learning usually predicts from a fixed database state, but decision making needs to know how that state will change under an action, and those dynamics are often not visible in the database itself. The authors treat each operational system as a relational world and introduce `TabWM` (Tabular World Model), which is pretrained on `WorldRel`, a generator of executable relational worlds, and then uses observed executions from an unseen world as context to predict the sparse structured edits a new action will cause, without any parameter updates. Across 512 held-out worlds, **complete-edit F1 rises from 0.016 with no observed executions to 0.685 with 64**, where a correct edit must match its operation, relational location, and value. Because the predictions are explicit relational edits, they can be applied recursively to imagine candidate futures, and broader search over those predicted futures improves the realized return of the selected action sequences.

papers.title: Geospatial Vector Geometry as a Native Spatial Modality for Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Geospatial reasoning links VLMs to real-world action and decision making. Reliable reasoning requires accurate spatial information and effective spatial representations. However, current VLMs obtain this information mainly from language and vision. At larger geographic scales, limited visual observations make it difficult to establish accurate spatial references and recover precise spatial relations. This leads to a bottleneck for VLM spatial perception and reasoning. This paper proposes that geospatial vector geometry can become a native spatial modality within a VLM and introduces GeoVec-VLM. First, we develop a structured geometry representation that preserves the spatial structure and arrangement of vector objects, building an explicit spatial basis. Second, we introduce a geometry interaction strategy that brings this basis into multimodal computation, where it interacts with visual content and language references according to the queried spatial relations. Together, these designs allow perception and reasoning to operate on shared geometric references. Across five spatial reasoning tasks, GeoVec-VLM improves mean accuracy by about 11\% relative to the strongest baseline, maintains its gains under geographic transfer, and shows greater geometric consistency. Our results show that geospatial vector geometry offers a promising internal spatial basis for VLM spatial reasoning. https://github.com/TXFR/GeoVector-VLM
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) obtain spatial information mainly from language and vision, which becomes a bottleneck at larger geographic scales where limited visual observations make it hard to establish accurate spatial references and recover precise spatial relations. The authors propose treating geospatial vector geometry as a native spatial modality and introduce `GeoVec-VLM`, which pairs a structured geometry representation that preserves the arrangement of vector objects with an interaction strategy that brings this geometric basis into multimodal computation alongside visual content and language references. Across five spatial reasoning tasks, **mean accuracy improves by about 11% relative to the strongest baseline**, and the gains persist under geographic transfer with greater geometric consistency.

papers.title: Game-Creation-Agents: Autonomous Game Production
papers.abstract: Game-Creation-Agents (GCA) turns a natural-language request into a runnable Phaser 4 browser game. The pipeline first builds a multimodal game design document that couples mechanics and scene contracts to grounded visual references. It then projects that document into a runtime scaffold, machine-readable contracts, and deterministic tests. Eight specialized agents next carry out production: scenes are implemented serially, assets are produced in parallel, and one reduced manifest joins the two branches into a single build. Build-linked real-UI checks and a code-blind critic then verify that build and decide whether the game may ship. Each blocker returns to the agent that owns the affected artifact for a bounded repair, and the game is released once all the gates pass. We evaluate finished games separately, through their rendered interfaces alone, over prompt-matched tasks run under a common protocol. GCA achieves stronger requirement satisfaction, core mechanics, content depth, and functional visuals than a comparable open pipeline. In a side-by-side human study, raters also score GCA's games higher on every dimension and prefer them overall.
papers.summary: Turning a natural-language request into a runnable `Phaser 4` browser game requires coordinating design, implementation, asset production, and verification. `Game-Creation-Agents` (GCA) first builds a multimodal game design document that couples mechanics and scene contracts to grounded visual references, projects it into a runtime scaffold with machine-readable contracts and deterministic tests, and then has eight specialized agents implement scenes serially while producing assets in parallel, with a reduced manifest joining the two branches into one build. Build-linked real-UI checks and a code-blind critic decide whether the game may ship, and each blocker returns to the agent that owns the affected artifact for a bounded repair. Judged through rendered interfaces alone on prompt-matched tasks, **GCA achieves stronger requirement satisfaction, core mechanics, content depth, and functional visuals than a comparable open pipeline**, and human raters score its games higher on every dimension.

papers.title: PrivacyGuard: Source-Linked Sanitization and Locally Resolvable PII References for Cloud GUI Agents
papers.abstract: Cloud graphical user interface (GUI) agents send instructions and screenshots to remote planners, exposing personally identifiable information (PII). Existing placeholder defenses mask detected spans and reuse exact strings. Fragmented or changed forms can expose PII or break entity continuity across turns. PrivacyGuard addresses this private reference problem with source-linked sanitization (SAN) and a structured reference lifecycle (REF). SAN reconstructs fragmented or overlapping evidence and rewrites the complete source extent. REF links changed appearances to session entities and supports locally resolvable references without returning raw values to the upload path. In five-turn sessions scored against common gold, PrivacyGuard reduces audited source-value leakage by 33.55\%--82.60\% relative to the closest prior full-pipeline system in all four reader--language combinations. REF raises strict cross-form continuity from 0.04 under exact-value reuse to 0.81. In reference-required Android tasks, verified completion rises from 8/30 and 7/30 to 17/30 and 20/30. On AndroidLab, PrivacyGuard achieves the highest or tied-highest task-success point estimate among protection pipelines for all four planners. On PrivScreen, it reduces fixed-reader field exposure by 62.72\%--62.84\% relative to the same baseline. PrivacyGuard lowers upload exposure while preserving a locally resolvable task path.
papers.summary: Cloud graphical user interface (GUI) agents send instructions and screenshots to remote planners, exposing personally identifiable information (PII), and existing placeholder defenses that mask detected spans and reuse exact strings can leak fragmented or changed forms and break entity continuity across turns. `PrivacyGuard` combines source-linked sanitization (SAN), which reconstructs fragmented or overlapping evidence and rewrites the complete source extent, with a structured reference lifecycle (REF) that links changed appearances to session entities and supports locally resolvable references without returning raw values to the upload path. In five-turn sessions scored against common gold, **audited source-value leakage falls by 33.55% to 82.60% relative to the closest prior full-pipeline system** in all four reader-language combinations, and REF raises strict cross-form continuity from 0.04 to 0.81. In reference-required Android tasks verified completion rises from 8/30 and 7/30 to 17/30 and 20/30, and on `AndroidLab` the system reaches the highest or tied-highest task-success estimate among protection pipelines for all four planners.

papers.title: LIBERO-Industry: Benchmarking Robotic Manipulation under Industrial Process Constraints
papers.abstract: Industrial manipulation in flexible manufacturing, e.g., high-mix, low-volume (HMLV) electronics assembly, requires robot policies to adapt to changing products and production conditions. Such settings impose industrial process constraints, including product variants, moving material flows, finite execution windows, and tight geometric tolerances. However, existing evaluation frameworks do not systematically capture these constraints when assessing generalist robot policies. To address this gap, we introduce LIBERO-Industry, a novel benchmark built on the widely used robot learning benchmark LIBERO, that translates the aforementioned industrial constraints into controllable task conditions and measurable success criteria. Specifically, LIBERO-Industry comprises three classic task scenarios: Static-to-Dynamic (S2D) loading, Dynamic-to-Static (D2S) unloading, and Dynamic-to-Dynamic (D2D) transfer. The suites contain 216 tasks in total that systematically vary object geometry, conveyor speed, interaction-window duration, and geometric acceptance region size. Extensive experiments across five generalist robot policies (including vision-language-action models and world-action models) show that performance progressively degrades as industrial constraints are introduced and combined. Under a shared fine-tuning and evaluation protocol, the LIBERO-Industry co-training condition achieved higher observed target-transfer completion than the original-LIBERO condition.
papers.summary: Flexible manufacturing such as high-mix, low-volume (HMLV) electronics assembly imposes industrial process constraints, including product variants, moving material flows, finite execution windows, and tight geometric tolerances, that existing evaluation frameworks for generalist robot policies do not systematically capture. The authors build `LIBERO-Industry` on the `LIBERO` robot learning benchmark, with three scenarios, Static-to-Dynamic (S2D) loading, Dynamic-to-Static (D2S) unloading, and Dynamic-to-Dynamic (D2D) transfer, totaling 216 tasks that vary object geometry, conveyor speed, interaction-window duration, and geometric acceptance region size. Across five generalist policies, including vision-language-action and world-action models, **performance degrades progressively as industrial constraints are introduced and combined**, and under a shared fine-tuning protocol co-training on `LIBERO-Industry` yields higher observed target-transfer completion than the original `LIBERO` condition.

papers.title: InfoVis: Unified Slide Image Generation and Editing
papers.abstract: Generating and editing presentation slides requires models to combine accurate text rendering, instruction following, visual grounding, aesthetic design, and precise editing within one canvas. Existing work covers only subsets of these capabilities and lacks large-scale slide-native supervision and diagnostic evaluation. We formulate four slide-centric tasks and build a scalable data engine with over 13M continual-pretraining records and 1.9M supervised fine-tuning records. We also introduce VisSlideBench, a benchmark of 1,527 manually screened instances that covers all four tasks with task-specific, multidimensional evaluation. Its automatic rankings agree with blinded, dimension-wise human rankings. Using these resources, we train InfoVis, a unified 9B slide generation and editing model. On VisSlideBench, InfoVis leads every evaluated open-source model on all eleven metrics and scores 7.94 overall against 7.99 for Nano-Banana-2. Starting from FLUX.2-klein-base-9B, slide-specific post-training adds 1.6 points overall, with the largest generation gains in content faithfulness; the remaining gap to proprietary models is smallest in content faithfulness and largest in aesthetic quality. Built on InfoVis, our document-to-slide workflow achieves the second-highest Aesthetics score on the external SlidesGen-Bench. We will release the model, code, data, and benchmark.
papers.summary: Generating and editing presentation slides requires accurate text rendering, instruction following, visual grounding, aesthetic design, and precise editing on one canvas, but existing work covers only subsets of these capabilities and lacks slide-native supervision and diagnostic evaluation. The authors formulate four slide-centric tasks, build a data engine with over 13M continual-pretraining and 1.9M supervised fine-tuning records, and introduce `VisSlideBench`, a benchmark of 1,527 manually screened instances whose automatic rankings agree with blinded human rankings. The resulting unified 9B model `InfoVis`, post-trained from `FLUX.2-klein-base-9B`, **leads every evaluated open-source model on all eleven metrics and scores 7.94 overall against 7.99 for `Nano-Banana-2`**, with the remaining gap to proprietary models smallest in content faithfulness and largest in aesthetic quality. A document-to-slide workflow built on the model takes the second-highest Aesthetics score on the external `SlidesGen-Bench`, and the model, code, data, and benchmark are to be released.

papers.title: Logit Leakage through Floating-Point Bias Addition
papers.abstract: Language model APIs can expose token-specific biases while withholding logits and token probabilities. Existing bias-based extraction recovers relative logits, leaving a common additive component undetermined in ideal arithmetic. We identify a numerical side channel in floating-point bias addition that exposes information about this component through token identities alone. The channel distinguishes score vectors with identical complete unperturbed log probabilities. Our method exploits changes in representable spacing at binary exponent boundaries. Under the stated binary32 arithmetic assumptions and a known reachable score interval, it recovers a logit pair and its unknown tie-breaking priority exactly in at most 52 token queries. Given complete relative logits, one recovered anchor determines the original logit vector. We evaluate recovery across 11 public checkpoints from seven model families and extend the local method with adaptive interval search and anchor selection. In end-to-end experiments with vLLM, SGLang, and llama.cpp, adaptive recovery succeeds on all 128 Qwen3-0.6B inputs per system, including 64 held-out inputs. A separate token-only experiment extracts a pretrained small model's complete output-head representation up to an invertible hidden-basis transformation. We also establish a sufficient condition for suppressing common-shift disclosure by subtracting the maximum before bias addition. In controlled experiments, this mitigation eliminates all observed distinctions between common-shift variants and preserves token decisions under the tested random biases.
papers.summary: Language model APIs that accept token-specific logit biases while withholding logits and probabilities already allow recovery of relative logits, but in ideal arithmetic a common additive component remains undetermined. The authors identify a numerical side channel in floating-point bias addition: because the spacing of representable values changes at binary exponent boundaries, token identities alone can distinguish score vectors that have identical complete log probabilities. Under stated binary32 assumptions and a known reachable score interval, **a logit pair and its unknown tie-breaking priority are recovered exactly in at most 52 token queries**, and adaptive recovery succeeds on all 128 `Qwen3-0.6B` inputs per system in end-to-end experiments with `vLLM`, `SGLang`, and `llama.cpp`, while a token-only experiment extracts a small model's complete output-head representation up to an invertible hidden-basis transformation. Subtracting the maximum before bias addition is shown to be a sufficient mitigation that eliminates all observed distinctions between common-shift variants in controlled experiments while preserving token decisions.

papers.title: StableJudge: A Lightweight Adversarial Defense Framework for LLM-as-a-Judge
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to assign scalar scores that drive downstream decision-making, including tasks such as paper review and recommendation. However, LLM-as-a-Judge pipelines are vulnerable to score-hijacking prompt injection embedded in evaluated content, which corrupts scoring signals and distorts induced rankings. Existing defenses often enforce robustness by modifying the judge model itself, making safety dependent on a specific model's scale and training and requiring repeated effort when the judge is updated or replaced. We propose StableJudge, a lightweight defense framework that externalizes prompt-injection mitigation as a reusable pre-scoring capability. StableJudge centers on a compact 0.13B Sentry that localizes injected spans and performs targeted sanitization prior to evaluation, and is trained using adversarially evolving attacks to improve robustness beyond a fixed prompt set. To stabilize measurement, StableJudge derives deterministic, fine-grained scalar scores from the judge's output distribution. Across held-out scientific abstracts and out-of-distribution attack variants, StableJudge improves score recovery under attack while largely preserving general-purpose performance, demonstrating that robust LLM-based judging can be achieved by decoupling safety from judge scale via reusable defense capabilities. Code and data will be released.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges that assign scalar scores for tasks such as paper review and recommendation, but score-hijacking prompt injection embedded in evaluated content can corrupt those scores and distort the induced rankings, and existing defenses modify the judge itself, tying robustness to a particular model's scale and training. `StableJudge` externalizes mitigation as a reusable pre-scoring step: a compact 0.13B `Sentry` localizes injected spans and performs targeted sanitization before evaluation, trained against adversarially evolving attacks rather than a fixed prompt set, while deterministic fine-grained scalar scores are derived from the judge's output distribution to stabilize measurement. Across held-out scientific abstracts and out-of-distribution attack variants, **score recovery under attack improves while general-purpose judging performance is largely preserved**, supporting the claim that robust LLM-based judging can be decoupled from judge scale.

papers.title: Growing to See: Efficient Pretraining of Self-Supervised Vision Transformers
papers.abstract: Progressive depth growth builds large networks by starting with shallow models and inserting layers during training. Recent advances in large language models have renewed interest in this longstanding approach, demonstrating benefits for training efficiency and reasoning alongside changes in internal computations. However, how growing affects representation quality and computational patterns in self-supervised vision transformers remains unclear. In this work, we systematically investigate progressive depth growth in two popular self-supervised families, namely masked autoencoders (MAE) and DINOv3, and analyze how growing affects downstream performance, intermediate representations, and internal computations. Across global and dense tasks, we show that growing improves downstream performance while reducing training FLOPs by 13.9--24.8%, with ImageNet linear-probe accuracy gains of up to 3.36 percentage points. Growing also improves downstream performance at intermediate layers and reshapes internal computational patterns, introducing recurring alternations between global and localized attention in MAE and earlier local-to-global attention progression in self-distilled DINOv3. Together, these findings establish progressive depth growth as an effective and efficient pretraining strategy for improving downstream performance across global and dense visual tasks with less computation, and advance our understanding of how growing shapes visual computation.
papers.summary: Progressive depth growth, which starts with a shallow network and inserts layers during training, has recently shown efficiency and reasoning benefits in large language models, but its effect on representation quality and computation in self-supervised vision transformers was unclear. The authors systematically study growth in two self-supervised families, masked autoencoders (`MAE`) and `DINOv3`, analyzing downstream performance, intermediate representations, and internal computation. Across global and dense tasks, **growing improves downstream performance while reducing training FLOPs by 13.9% to 24.8%**, with `ImageNet` linear-probe accuracy gains of up to 3.36 percentage points. Growth also improves performance at intermediate layers and reshapes attention, introducing recurring alternations between global and localized attention in `MAE` and an earlier local-to-global progression in self-distilled `DINOv3`.

papers.title: DTA-GT: Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer for Neural Network Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Architecture attribute predictors reduce the cost of neural architecture search by estimating accuracy or latency from a small set of evaluated candidates. The key difficulty is that neural architectures are operation-labeled DAGs: edge direction defines computational flow, but existing predictors often treat direction as a local structural cue. We propose DTA-GT, a Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer based on encoder-wide directional consistency, which preserves directed computational semantics across node initialization, global spectral encoding, pairwise interaction, and feature update. DTA-GT realizes this principle with direction- and topology-aware node initialization, Magnetic Laplacian spectral encoding, direction-dual structural attention, and a Direction-Sensitive MoE-FFN. Across accuracy and latency prediction on NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201, DTA-GT consistently outperforms representative sequence-, GNN-, Transformer-, and hybrid predictors under limited-budget settings. Ablations and Magnetic spectral controls show that the improvements come from coordinated direction-aware stages and edge-orientation-sensitive spectral information, while mechanistic diagnostics confirm that the modules exhibit the intended directional behavior. These results support encoder-wide directional consistency as an effective design principle for architecture DAG representation.
papers.summary: Architecture attribute predictors estimate accuracy or latency from a small set of evaluated candidates to reduce the cost of neural architecture search, but neural architectures are operation-labeled directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) in which edge direction defines computational flow, and existing predictors treat direction only as a local structural cue. `DTA-GT` applies encoder-wide directional consistency through direction- and topology-aware node initialization, Magnetic Laplacian spectral encoding, direction-dual structural attention, and a direction-sensitive mixture-of-experts feed-forward layer, preserving directed semantics from node initialization through feature update. On accuracy and latency prediction over `NAS-Bench-101` and `NAS-Bench-201`, **it consistently outperforms representative sequence-, GNN-, Transformer-, and hybrid predictors under limited-budget settings**, and ablations with Magnetic spectral controls attribute the gains to the coordinated direction-aware stages and edge-orientation-sensitive spectral information.

papers.title: Unsupervised Data Drift Monitoring for Deployed Deepfake Speech Detectors
papers.abstract: Deepfake speech detectors are typically evaluated as binary classifiers on fixed benchmarks, but deployed systems face evolving attacks, codecs, speakers, and recording conditions, with labels unavailable during operation. This makes it difficult to know when a detector operates in familiar conditions and can be relied on. We propose an unsupervised drift monitor that operates on the internal embeddings of a deployed detector. The monitor compares each input against bona fide and spoof references using regularized Mahalanobis distances. These distances define trusted, ambiguous, and novel regions of the detector embedding space, allowing unfamiliar inputs to be routed for review. We evaluate the monitor on four modern detectors on three datasets. The monitor raises alerts for dataset mismatches and substantially reduces the security-critical case of accepting deepfakes at the cost of reduced automatic coverage. The results also show that drift affects both classes: bona fide recordings can move away from the training reference, increasing alert rates even in in-domain settings. Our findings suggest that deployed deepfake speech detectors should be treated not only as a binary classification, but also as a reliability problem.
papers.summary: Deepfake speech detectors are evaluated as binary classifiers on fixed benchmarks, but deployed systems face evolving attacks, codecs, speakers, and recording conditions with no labels available, making it hard to know when a detector is operating in familiar conditions. The proposed unsupervised monitor works on the detector's internal embeddings, comparing each input against bona fide and spoof references with regularized Mahalanobis distances to define trusted, ambiguous, and novel regions of the embedding space so that unfamiliar inputs can be routed for review. Evaluated on four modern detectors across three datasets, **the monitor raises alerts for dataset mismatches and substantially reduces accepted deepfakes at the cost of reduced automatic coverage**, and it shows that bona fide recordings also drift away from the training reference, raising alert rates even in-domain.

papers.title: A Scaled-Up Empirical Study of Syntactic Language Models
papers.abstract: Syntactic language models (SLMs) that generate sentences along with their syntactic tree structures have shown promise in both syntactic generalization and downstream tasks. Prior studies, however, have mostly evaluated smaller models trained on less pretraining data and tested on narrower task suites. In addition, the design space of tree linearization and attention masks remains underexplored. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of 12 controlled configurations---one terminal baseline and 11 SLM variants spanning different linearizations and masks---at scales up to 1B parameters and 100B training tokens, evaluated across 11 downstream tasks and two syntactic benchmarks. The experimental results show that SLMs with standard causal attention match or exceed structural-mask variants across downstream and syntactic benchmarks. They require no architectural modifications and remain compatible with FlashAttention. We also observe that when scaling up to the 1B-parameter scale, the top-performing SLM variant no longer shows a clear advantage over a compute-matched non-structural baseline, suggesting that SLMs may become less competitive with scale. Our code is available at https://github.com/qlwpc/TG-Interpolation.
papers.summary: Syntactic language models (SLMs), which generate sentences together with their syntactic tree structures, had mostly been evaluated at small scale on narrow task suites, leaving the design space of tree linearizations and attention masks underexplored. The authors train 12 controlled configurations, one terminal baseline and 11 SLM variants spanning different linearizations and masks, at up to 1B parameters and 100B training tokens, and evaluate on 11 downstream tasks and two syntactic benchmarks. SLMs with standard causal attention match or exceed structural-mask variants on both downstream and syntactic benchmarks while requiring no architectural changes and remaining compatible with `FlashAttention`. However, **at the 1B-parameter scale the top SLM variant no longer shows a clear advantage over a compute-matched non-structural baseline**, suggesting SLMs become less competitive with scale.

papers.title: Same Operation, Different Permission: Evaluating Whether Guardrails Honor Authorization
papers.abstract: As language-model agents write code, move money and change records on behalf of users, deciding whether an action is authorized has become a central safety problem. Guardrails are often placed in front of these actions, yet few evaluations ask whether their decisions follow authorization: blocking unauthorized actions while still allowing the same actions under valid permission. We introduce \bench{}, a benchmark that contrasts authorization evidence for the same operation in its language track. It combines expert-annotated natural-language scenarios with executed and verified operations, plus externally sourced native-policy requests. \bench{} checks each decision for correctness, usability and resulting effect, and tracks each request across guardrail changes. Our experiments show that many blocked operations stem from failed reviews, not correct denials. Repairing the output format restores usable decisions but changes which authorized requests are honored, and adding a second reviewer removes some errors while rejecting valid authorization. Guardrails should therefore be evaluated on both the unauthorized actions they stop and the authorized actions they let through.
papers.summary: As language-model agents write code, move money, and change records on behalf of users, guardrails placed in front of these actions must decide whether an action is authorized, yet few evaluations test whether their decisions actually follow authorization by blocking unauthorized actions while allowing the same actions under valid permission. The benchmark introduced here contrasts authorization evidence for the same operation, combining expert-annotated natural-language scenarios with executed and verified operations plus externally sourced native-policy requests, and checks each decision for correctness, usability, and resulting effect while tracking each request across guardrail changes. Experiments show that **many blocked operations stem from failed reviews rather than correct denials**, that repairing the output format restores usable decisions but changes which authorized requests are honored, and that adding a second reviewer removes some errors while rejecting valid authorization. The authors conclude that guardrails should be evaluated on both the unauthorized actions they stop and the authorized actions they let through.

papers.title: Few-for-Many Best-Arm Identification in Multi-Objective Bandits
papers.abstract: Real-world systems often serve many objectives but can deploy only a few options, whose performance must be learned from noisy feedback. Modeling each option as an arm in a multi-objective bandit, we introduce \emph{few-for-many best-arm identification}, which seeks a small set of arms minimizing the worst weighted degradation from the objective-wise optima, rather than the best arm for every objective. We consider both known objective groups and latent groups specified only by a representative budget, and propose \textsc{GFM-Elim} and \textsc{AFM-Elim} with instance-dependent sample-complexity guarantees. For Gaussian rewards, we further derive a lower bound for the latent-group setting and show that it is asymptotically attainable with high probability by an oracle-based Track-and-Stop procedure. Our results show that sharing observations across objectives and ignoring irrelevant objective-wise distinctions can substantially reduce the sampling cost, as confirmed by experiments on synthetic and real-world tasks.
papers.summary: Real-world systems often serve many objectives but can deploy only a few options, whose performance must be learned from noisy feedback. Modeling each option as an arm in a multi-objective bandit, the authors introduce few-for-many best-arm identification, which seeks a small set of arms minimizing the worst weighted degradation from the objective-wise optima rather than the best arm for every objective, and propose `GFM-Elim` for known objective groups and `AFM-Elim` for latent groups specified only by a representative budget, each with instance-dependent sample-complexity guarantees. For Gaussian rewards they derive a lower bound for the latent-group setting and **show it is asymptotically attainable with high probability by an oracle-based Track-and-Stop procedure**, and experiments on synthetic and real-world tasks confirm that sharing observations across objectives and ignoring irrelevant objective-wise distinctions substantially reduces sampling cost.

papers.title: Towards Cost-Efficient Video Dataset Construction with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Research on video classification models has witnessed significant growth recently, accompanied by a significant increase in the demand for datasets to train such models. Existing video dataset curation approaches share a common bottleneck: candidate videos must be downloaded before any relevance judgment is made, which results in storage, time and annotation costs. In this work, we present a filtering step, using Large Language Models (LLMs) to pre-screen videos based on their metadata, before actually downloading these videos, thereby saving on these costs. We evaluate the LLMs against a strict human majority vote derived from four independent annotators and validate the reliability of the annotations through inter-annotator agreement analysis (Gwet's AC1). We compare the LLM pre-filter against two no-LLM baselines, namely two keyword heuristics. Via a Leave-One-Rater-Out (LOO) mechanism and an Add-One-Rater-In (AORI), we evaluate the performance of the LLMs as virtual annotators. Finally, we report cost comparisons relative to existing approaches. To ensure reproducability, we made our implementation available on github.
papers.summary: Existing video dataset curation pipelines share a bottleneck: candidate videos must be downloaded before any relevance judgment can be made, incurring storage, time, and annotation costs. The authors add a filtering step in which large language models (LLMs) **pre-screen candidate videos from their metadata alone, before any download**, and evaluate it against a strict human majority vote from four independent annotators, whose reliability is checked with Gwet's AC1 inter-annotator agreement, as well as against two keyword-heuristic baselines. Leave-One-Rater-Out (LOO) and Add-One-Rater-In (AORI) analyses assess the LLMs as virtual annotators, cost comparisons relative to existing approaches are reported, and the implementation is public.

papers.title: Davinci-Tool: Scaling Agentic Tool-Use Supervision with Verifiable Executable Environments
papers.abstract: Reliable agentic tool use requires training data that pair diverse multi-step workflows with executable evidence that the requested outcomes were achieved. Scaling either trajectory coverage or verification alone is insufficient as new environments introduce distinct states, rules, and dependencies that must also be reflected in the success criteria. To address this challenge, we introduce Davinci-Tool, a 30B tool-use model, and Davinci-ToolData, an execution-grounded dataset designed to scale environment coverage and outcome verification together.
