Davinci-ToolData preserves restorable states, execution traces, outcomes, and verifiers as a unified substrate for supervision. Two complementary pipelines populate this substrate: Execution-Grounded Task Synthesis (EGTS) derives verified demonstrations from independently authored systems, and Executable Environment Synthesis (EES) synthesizes auditable environments, state-grounded tasks, and executable verifiers across single and coordinated domains. These pipelines yield 30,395 verified trajectories spanning 2,260 invoked tool names. We first train on these demonstrations with supervised fine-tuning, then reuse EES states and verifiers to compare alternative actions and construct outcome-grounded preferences for Direct Preference Optimization. Davinci-Tool improves Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct from 52.4 to 88.2 on $\tau^2$-bench, from 30.4 to 62.8 on BFCL v4 multi-turn, and from 16.9 to 56.2 on MCP-Atlas, outperforming Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct on all three benchmarks with only 1/16 of its total parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/MassLab-SII/Davinci-Tool.
papers.summary: Reliable agentic tool use requires training data that pairs diverse multi-step workflows with executable evidence that the requested outcomes were achieved, and scaling trajectory coverage or verification alone is insufficient because new environments introduce their own states, rules, and dependencies. `Davinci-ToolData` preserves restorable states, execution traces, outcomes, and verifiers as a unified supervision substrate, populated by Execution-Grounded Task Synthesis (EGTS), which derives verified demonstrations from independently authored systems, and Executable Environment Synthesis (EES), which synthesizes auditable environments, state-grounded tasks, and executable verifiers, yielding 30,395 verified trajectories spanning 2,260 invoked tool names. The 30B `Davinci-Tool` model is trained with supervised fine-tuning on these demonstrations and then with Direct Preference Optimization on outcome-grounded preferences built by reusing EES states and verifiers to compare alternative actions. It lifts `Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct` from 52.4 to 88.2 on `τ²-bench`, from 30.4 to 62.8 on `BFCL v4` multi-turn, and from 16.9 to 56.2 on `MCP-Atlas`, **outperforming `Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct` on all three benchmarks with 1/16 of its total parameters**.

papers.title: CLIVO: Differentiable Cluster-Based Instruction Mixing with Learned Validation Objectives
papers.abstract: Target-aware multimodal instruction selection requires useful examples and an appropriate balance of supervision. Sample-level rankings can overrepresent similar content without optimizing this balance; group-level methods face coarse units, predefined set-level validation signals, and costly or inaccurate mixture search. We propose CLIVO, a target-aware framework connecting fine-grained semantic allocation, automatically learned validation objectives, and differentiable mixture search. Specifically, semantic clusters provide independently adjustable shares at the hundred-cluster scale. Correlations between per-example merged-proxy losses and real probe performance identify target-relevant validation examples; learned nonnegative weights combine their losses into an objective. A single backward pass through the merged proxy supplies gradients for all shares, avoiding an additional mixture-response regression model. Selecting 100K instructions from an 8M pool, CLIVO attains 97.2% of the full-data four-target average score with only 1.25% of the data. It improves on the strongest evaluated selection baseline by 1.16 points using random within-cluster sampling; combining learned quotas with sample ranking increases this advantage to 1.55 points. Analyses show that finer units benefit most targets, short-trained experts preserve mixture responses, sample weighting retains useful validation information, and direct search consistently reduces the learned objective. CLIVO also supports interpretable allocation, modular selection, and reuse across targets and granularities.
papers.summary: Target-aware selection of multimodal instruction data needs both useful examples and an appropriate balance of supervision, but sample-level rankings can overrepresent similar content and group-level methods face coarse units, predefined validation signals, and costly or inaccurate mixture search. `CLIVO` allocates independently adjustable shares across hundreds of semantic clusters, identifies target-relevant validation examples by correlating per-example losses of a merged proxy model with real probe performance, combines them with learned nonnegative weights into a validation objective, and obtains gradients for all shares from a single backward pass through the proxy, avoiding a separate mixture-response regression model. Selecting 100K instructions from an 8M pool, **it attains 97.2% of the full-data four-target average score with only 1.25% of the data**, improving on the strongest selection baseline by 1.16 points with random within-cluster sampling and by 1.55 points when learned quotas are combined with sample ranking.

papers.title: Acceptable Misalignment
papers.abstract: There is a specific challenge designers face in developing autonomous robots capable of open-ended learning. This challenge is how one can develop such systems in an ethically sound way when there are many unknowns during design time about their manner of deployment, what they can and will learn, and how these systems will act on the basis of what they have learned. One response to this challenge is to align, as far as possible, the activities and goals of autonomous robots with human values, raising the question of how to make this alignment possible, a question known as the value alignment problem. We argue that the value alignment problem faces a number of challenges that show that full alignment is both theoretically and practically impossible, meaning that misalignment incidents will keep occurring. This undermines current alignment approaches, as the attempt to maximize alignment cannot properly deal with the possibility that the risk of misalignment that remains after alignment methods have been implemented might still be unacceptable to society. To overcome this difficulty, we argue that a shift in perspective is required from a focus on the maximization of alignment to the conditions under which misalignment incidents become acceptable. In this paper, we explore what this shift in perspective entails. We introduce the concept of acceptable misalignment, formulate normative requirements for alignment mechanisms aimed at bringing misalignment incidents to an acceptable level, and we conclude by presenting a new methodological framework that consists of alignment mechanisms that can meet these requirements.
papers.summary: Designing autonomous robots capable of open-ended learning in an ethically sound way is hard because so much about their deployment, what they will learn, and how they will act on it is unknown at design time, and the usual response is to align their goals and activities with human values. The authors argue that the value alignment problem faces challenges showing full alignment to be both theoretically and practically impossible, so misalignment incidents will keep occurring and approaches that maximize alignment cannot handle the possibility that the residual risk remains unacceptable to society. **They propose shifting from maximizing alignment to specifying the conditions under which misalignment incidents become acceptable**, introducing the concept of acceptable misalignment, formulating normative requirements for alignment mechanisms that bring incidents to an acceptable level, and presenting a methodological framework of mechanisms designed to meet those requirements.

papers.title: Transparency as Answerability: Role-Dependent Information Flow Modeling
papers.abstract: Transparency in AI-supported decision systems is widely required but poorly defined. Existing approaches treat transparency as a property of systems or components, producing characteristic failures: assessments that do not transfer across organizational boundaries, stakeholder questions that cannot be formulated within the available frame of analysis, and component-level findings that say nothing about system-level behavior. We propose treating transparency as a relation: a system is transparent to a stakeholder to the degree that their legitimate questions are answerable from its structure. We formalize this using information flow networks, in which transparency questions are expressed in terms of network structure and answerability is the condition that the system settles them. The framework supports three dimensions of analysis: structural answerability from the network alone, compositional answerability across organizational boundaries for deployed systems, and role-dependent answerability given a stakeholder's accessible sub-network. We demonstrate the framework on a real pre-integration assessment of an AI recruitment tool in a public sector municipality. The assessment uses participatory design and interviews to model the decision system structure. We show how structural and role-dependent transparency questions can be formally stated and analyzed across the Provider and Deployer boundary where the AI system is composed together with the deployer's decision process.
papers.summary: Transparency is widely required of AI-supported decision systems but poorly defined, and treating it as a property of systems or components yields assessments that do not transfer across organizational boundaries, stakeholder questions that cannot be formulated, and component-level findings that say nothing about system-level behavior. The authors instead treat transparency as a relation, holding that a system is transparent to a stakeholder to the degree that their legitimate questions are answerable from its structure, and formalize this with information flow networks in which questions are expressed in terms of network structure. The framework supports structural answerability from the network alone, compositional answerability across organizational boundaries, and role-dependent answerability given a stakeholder's accessible sub-network, and **it is demonstrated on a real pre-integration assessment of an AI recruitment tool in a public-sector municipality**, where participatory design and interviews model the decision structure across the Provider and Deployer boundary.

papers.title: Observe, Share, or Predict? Disentangling Partner Information in Embodied Multi-Agent Collaboration
papers.abstract: LLMs are used as high-level controllers for embodied agents, but it remains unclear whether they support collaborative reasoning, such as anticipating a collaborator's actions in real-time teamwork without dialogue. We ask if observing the partner's state, exchanging object knowledge, and predicting the partner's next action, shape task outcomes and coordination when agents can share percepts but never intentions, plans, or task-level messages, and whether the two agents occupy symmetric roles. Using the Habitat-based PARTNR benchmark, we introduce a Decoupled Partial Observability regime that enforces strictly individual perception, and we augment decentralized zero-shot ReAct planners with Other Agent's State (OAS) observation, object Knowledge Exchange (KE) between co-located agents, and Other Agent's Next Action (OANA) prediction, evaluated on the full 2 x 2 x 2 grid with four planners on 1,000 validation tasks. OAS observation improves task quality, reducing extraneous effort for every planner, whereas KE primarily improves execution efficiency, cutting simulation steps by up to 25% with little change in success. The two are largely redundant for strong planners but complementary for the weakest, for which KE without the OAS is the worst configuration. OANA prediction lowers the success rate in 15 of 16 model x context pairs while raising explicit partner mentions to 55-100%, and its accuracy gains lie mainly in the coarse action type, partly because agents recognize the action the partner is already performing. The robot retrieves objects sooner and completes its tasks earlier than the simulated human. Shared context reduces total task time by shortening the remaining duration that the human works alone. Also, coordination benefits arise from responding to shared context, especially the OAS, rather than explicit anticipation, yielding shallow, planner-dependent partner modeling.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) act as high-level controllers for embodied agents, but it is unclear whether they support collaborative reasoning such as anticipating a partner's actions in real-time teamwork without dialogue. Using the Habitat-based `PARTNR` benchmark, the authors introduce a Decoupled Partial Observability regime that enforces strictly individual perception and augment decentralized zero-shot `ReAct` planners with Other Agent's State (OAS) observation, object Knowledge Exchange (KE) between co-located agents, and Other Agent's Next Action (OANA) prediction, evaluating the full 2 x 2 x 2 grid with four planners on 1,000 validation tasks. OAS observation improves task quality and reduces extraneous effort for every planner, while KE mainly improves execution efficiency, cutting simulation steps by up to 25% with little change in success, and the two are largely redundant for strong planners but complementary for the weakest. **OANA prediction lowers the success rate in 15 of 16 model-by-context pairs** even as explicit partner mentions rise to 55 to 100%, indicating that coordination benefits come from responding to shared context rather than explicit anticipation and that partner modeling remains shallow and planner-dependent.

papers.title: Neural Bayesian Networks for Modular and Scalable Decision-Making Under Uncertainty
papers.abstract:
Bayesian Networks (BNs) are established tools for letting agents reason under uncertainty in sequential decision-making. They split a joint distribution into local conditional mechanisms arranged on a directed acyclic graph, which makes them modular, interpretable, and ready to perform probabilistic inference. Their classical formulation, however, has limitations in both expressiveness and scale: each conditional is usually stored as a table or a linear-Gaussian form, and inference evaluates the graph one node and one query at a time.
  In this paper we introduce Neural Bayesian Networks (NBNs), in which each conditional is a differentiable, tensor-valued mechanism, while the graph and its factorization are unchanged. NBNs retain the modularity and local mechanisms of BNs, can represent any learnable conditional distribution, and run natively on GPUs. We also release NBN, a PyTorch-based library for learning and inference in NBNs, together with a public benchmark. Our evaluation shows gains in both expressiveness and scale: NBNs fit distributions that classical BN libraries struggle to represent, and on large networks and large batches of queries they run two orders of magnitude faster thanks to GPU parallelization. NBN is available at https://github.com/Giovannibriglia/NeuralBayesianNetworks.
papers.summary: Classical Bayesian Networks (BNs) store each conditional distribution as a table or a linear-Gaussian form and evaluate the graph one node and one query at a time, which limits both what they can express and how far they scale. Neural Bayesian Networks (NBNs) keep the directed acyclic graph and its factorization unchanged but replace each local conditional with a differentiable, tensor-valued mechanism that can represent any learnable conditional distribution and runs natively on GPUs. The authors release `NBN`, a PyTorch library for learning and inference with a public benchmark, and report that NBNs fit distributions classical BN libraries struggle to represent and **run about two orders of magnitude faster on large networks and large query batches** through GPU parallelization.

papers.title: Audit tools of the trade: Automated Auditor Elicitation Can Be Sensitive to the Context the Auditor Is Given
papers.abstract: Does providing additional context to automated AI auditors improve their effectiveness? Using the Petri tool to audit LLM coding agents, we test the impact of providing two types of resources (an external codebase and benchmark transcripts) to LLM auditors, across four auditor-target LLM pairs and three behaviours (harmful compliance, reward hacking, sycophancy). (1) External codebase: We provide the auditor LLM with a fixed, external open source codebase, which prior work finds improves the realism of synthetic audits. Providing this resource suppresses reward hacking in both auditor-target pairs whose baseline rate is above the floor (4.8 to 1.3 and 3.9 to 1.8 on Petri's default 1-10 scale); the remaining two pairs sit at the floor throughout. The suppression recurs in three of four pairs under a different scenario and resource bundle. (2) External benchmark transcripts: We provide the auditor with transcripts of the target's performance on benchmarks measuring similar behaviours, intended to inform the auditor about the target's behavioural patterns. Providing this resource raises reward hacking scores in all four pairs (from 1.7 to 6.1 in one case). However, subsequent experiments show that supplying only the related benchmark's abstract, without transcripts, also increases reward hacking, and the effect is absent under a different framing of the same behaviour. Overall, we find no consistent effect of either resource outside reward hacking, but we find substantial variability in judge-scored behaviour across conditions. Our results underscore the importance of careful piloting with tools such as Petri, as the measured rate of target behaviour is highly sensitive to configuration decisions. We hope our results inspire more research into the reliability and robustness of automated alignment auditing.
papers.summary: Automated alignment auditing uses one language model to probe another for undesirable behaviour, but it is unclear whether giving the auditor extra context makes it more effective. Using the `Petri` tool to audit LLM coding agents across four auditor-target pairs and three behaviours (harmful compliance, reward hacking, sycophancy), the authors test two resources: a fixed external open-source codebase and transcripts of the target's performance on related benchmarks. Supplying the codebase suppressed measured reward hacking in both pairs whose baseline sat above the floor, while supplying benchmark transcripts raised reward hacking scores in all four pairs, though a follow-up showed that the benchmark's abstract alone produced a similar rise and the effect vanished under a different framing of the same behaviour. **Neither resource had a consistent effect outside reward hacking, and judge-scored behaviour varied substantially across configurations**, so the authors argue for careful piloting before trusting measured rates from such tools.

papers.title: Transparent Information Flow Modeling for Role-Aware AI Act Assessment
papers.abstract: The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act introduces a structured framework for governing high-risk AI systems, emphasizing transparency, risk management, and role-specific accountability. However, current assessment practices often rely on monolithic system views or disconnected checklists, limiting their ability to capture the socio-technical complexity of real-world deployments. We explore the use of the Information Flow Methodology (IFM), a modeling-based approach to AI Act compliance assessment. IFM represents decision systems -- whether algorithmic, human, or hybrid -- as networks of information sites and transformation channels, enabling structured analysis of how information, decisions, and responsibilities flow across organizational and technical boundaries. We apply IFM in a real-world case involving a recruitment support tool used by a public-sector organization, evaluating both the Provider's system and the Deployer's recruitment process. Our results demonstrate that IFM can serve as a scaffold to bridge both component-based and holistic perspectives, and how technical systems are situated within socio-technical contexts. In doing so, IFM supports transparency, identifies risk pathways, and enables alignment analysis between intended and actual use. We argue that such modeling provides a foundational tool for effective, context-sensitive AI governance and accountability -- offering capabilities beyond conventional checklist-based assessments.
papers.summary: The European Union's AI Act demands transparency, risk management, and role-specific accountability for high-risk systems, but current assessment practice relies on monolithic system views or disconnected checklists that miss the socio-technical complexity of real deployments. The authors apply the Information Flow Methodology (`IFM`), which models decision systems, whether algorithmic, human, or hybrid, as networks of information sites and transformation channels, to a recruitment support tool used by a public-sector organization, assessing both the Provider's system and the Deployer's recruitment process. They find **`IFM` bridges component-level and holistic perspectives**, surfacing risk pathways and enabling comparison between intended and actual use, and argue it offers a foundation for context-sensitive governance beyond checklist-based assessment.

papers.title: Comparing GenAI to Machine Learning and Manual Review for eDiscovery
papers.abstract: Keeling et al. [Keeling2026Generative] report on a case study recently conducted by Redgrave LLP in which they assert that Relativity's Generative AI Review tool (aiR) achieved 88% recall while Relativity Assisted Learning (RAL), its machine-learning tool, achieved 64% recall. These results are not comparable because the methods employed have different objectives, because of inter-assessor disagreement, and because they represent different recall-precision and cost-benefit trade-offs. Our analysis of the Redgrave data indicates that, when these differences are taken into account, aiR and manual review are comparable. Furthermore, established machine-learning models employing Continuous Active Learning (CAL) show state-of-the-art effectiveness, and superior efficiency, when trained only on a sample of 2,000 first-pass-reviewer responsiveness determinations.
papers.summary: A recent case study by the law firm Redgrave LLP reported that Relativity's generative AI review tool `aiR` reached 88% recall in legal document review while its machine-learning tool, Relativity Assisted Learning (`RAL`), reached only 64%. The authors argue these numbers are not comparable because the methods have different objectives, assessors disagree with one another, and each result sits at a different recall-precision and cost-benefit point. Re-analysing the Redgrave data with those differences accounted for, **they find `aiR` and manual review perform comparably**, and that established Continuous Active Learning (`CAL`) models trained on only 2,000 first-pass reviewer determinations deliver state-of-the-art effectiveness with better efficiency.

papers.title: WeFair: Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in Short-Video Search
papers.abstract: Short-video search requires compact query rewriters that infer personalized intent from brief, ambiguous queries under strict latency constraints. The challenge is to decide when personalization is warranted and generate a reformulation that preserves the user's immediate information need. A rewriter optimized for fluency or engagement may still introduce unsupported details and redirect the search toward a different intent. Existing methods often underutilize users' actual reformulations and behavioral traces, relying instead on synthetic reasoning and indirect behavioral rewards that may produce more engaging candidates but cause intent drift. To build an effective rewriter that remains faithful to user intent, we propose WeFair, Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in WeChat short-video search. WeFair assigns real user behavioral signals to a progression from demonstration to preference to verification. We first mine actual human reformulations from search sessions, then apply multidimensional LLM screening and contextual verification to filter unsupported transitions without extensive manual annotation. During training, we begin with a supervised curriculum that progressively builds rewriting capabilities from large-scale human personalized query demonstrations, and then use direct preference optimization to align with users' subsequent consumption. In the final on-policy optimization stage, we construct a strict verification reward based on actual human reformulations to further boost performance with group relative policy optimization. Further analysis shows that auxiliary rewards can activate more rollout groups in GRPO but reduce intent fidelity. Online A/B testing in WeChat short-video search shows a 1.576% relative increase in effective clicked-query rate (VV>10s) and a 1.731% relative reduction in query reformulation rate.
papers.summary: Short-video search needs compact query rewriters that infer personalized intent from brief, ambiguous queries under strict latency limits, but rewriters optimized for fluency or engagement can introduce unsupported details and drift away from the user's actual information need. `WeFair` mines real user reformulations from WeChat search sessions, filters unsupported transitions with multidimensional LLM screening and contextual verification, and then trains in three stages: a supervised curriculum on human reformulations, direct preference optimization (`DPO`) aligned to users' subsequent consumption, and on-policy group relative policy optimization (`GRPO`) with a strict verification reward grounded in actual human reformulations. Analysis shows auxiliary rewards activate more rollout groups in `GRPO` but reduce intent fidelity, and **an online A/B test yielded a 1.576% relative increase in effective clicked-query rate and a 1.731% relative reduction in query reformulation rate**.

papers.title: KNN Implementation Details Can Dramatically Change Performance: An Example from Cover Trees
papers.abstract: Nearest neighbor search algorithms are widely used and have a long history, but we find that key implementation details are seldom reviewed in articles about them. These details can materially impact performance, and thus change the conclusions one makes about a given algorithm's superiority. In this article, we highlight these impacts by reviewing the Cover Tree as an example, producing RustKNN, a unified Rust implementation of three construction variants of the Cover Tree with three query modes. Our analysis reveals: (1) the optimal query strategy depends on $k$ and on the dataset (single-tree search is fastest at $k{=}1$ on three of our four largest datasets, while dual-tree search is fastest at $k{\ge}5$ on the three largest), and choosing the wrong query mode can cost up to a $7.5\times$ factor in runtime; (2) the cover tree base parameter, set to 2 in theory and 1.3 in practice, is not a safe default for dual-tree search: 1.3 is optimal on only one of seven datasets, and on covtype it is $1.6\times$ slower than the optimum; (3) among five micro-optimizations, only early-exit distance computation has a consistent effect, and that effect grows with dimension (none at $d{=}32$, $1.31\times$ at $d{=}54$, and $1.49\times$ at $d{=}784$); and (4) all-nearest-neighbor and held-out benchmarks yield different implementation rankings. All main timing tables report medians over 20 independent allocations with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. RustKNN is open source at https://github.com/CrowdStrike/RustKNN.
papers.summary: Nearest neighbor search algorithms are widely used, yet the implementation details that materially affect their performance are rarely reviewed in the papers describing them, which can change conclusions about which algorithm is superior. Using the `Cover Tree` as a case study, the authors build `RustKNN`, a unified Rust implementation of three construction variants and three query modes, and benchmark them across seven datasets with medians over 20 independent allocations and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. They find that the best query strategy depends on k and on the dataset, with **the wrong query mode costing up to a 7.5x factor in runtime**, that the conventional base parameter of 1.3 is optimal on only one of seven datasets for dual-tree search, that among five micro-optimizations only early-exit distance computation helps consistently and increasingly so with dimension, and that all-nearest-neighbor and held-out benchmarks rank implementations differently.

papers.title: UA-Bench: Benchmarking Large Audio-Language Models on Underwater Acoustic Recognition
papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are fast becoming a general interface to sound, yet how far their broad pretraining carries into specialized domains remains largely open. Vessel monitoring, maritime safety, and ocean sensing all depend on recognizing underwater signals, but to our knowledge LALMs have not been systematically evaluated on them. Annotated recordings are costly to collect, and a faithful synthetic alternative has to bring together many interacting factors: the structure of detection pulses, communication waveforms, and ship-radiated noise, and the sound-speed profile, geometry, and multipath propagation through which each reaches the receiver. We address this by proposing \textbf{UA-Bench}, to our knowledge the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating LALMs on underwater acoustic signal recognition. It comprises 375,051 audio records that couple parameterized sources with modeled propagation, so that every record can be traced to the conditions that produced it. The records span these three signal families, and each carries a three-level label hierarchy (13 leaf classes), a templated multi-turn dialogue, and source and channel metadata. We evaluate on a balanced 2,600-record subset with a gated coarse-to-fine protocol that locates each error at source routing, fine-grained classification, or output format, and add a paired silent-audio control to test whether the waveform is actually used. Nine open LALMs, evaluated without task-specific adaptation, reach only 2.0\%--13.1\% leaf accuracy, against a random reference of 7.7\%. The waveform helps source routing far more than leaf recognition (for one model, +29.5 versus +2.3 points over silence), and just four models gain reliably at the leaf level, by at most 4.7 points. UA-Bench thus gives a reference point for these models, and its released training partition supports follow-up adaptation work.
papers.summary: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are becoming a general interface to sound, but how well their broad pretraining transfers to specialized domains such as underwater acoustics, where annotated recordings are costly to collect, remains open. `UA-Bench` is a synthetic benchmark of 375,051 audio records that couple parameterized sources (detection pulses, communication waveforms, and ship-radiated noise) with modeled propagation, each carrying a three-level label hierarchy of 13 leaf classes, a templated multi-turn dialogue, and source and channel metadata. When nine open LALMs are evaluated without task-specific adaptation on a balanced 2,600-record subset, using a gated coarse-to-fine protocol and a paired silent-audio control, **leaf accuracy ranges from only 2.0% to 13.1% against a random reference of 7.7%**, and the waveform helps coarse source routing far more than fine-grained recognition.

papers.title: Social Priors: Descriptions of AI Users Shape How Language Models Trust and Cooperate
papers.abstract: Descriptions of how people use AI are becoming training data for the next generation of models. We ask whether what a model reads about its users changes how it treats people. Using contrastive synthetic-document finetuning, we train Qwen3-32B on four matched corpora built from the same 1,625 real-world usage scenarios. The corpora differ only in the predominant motive they attribute to users of AI chatbots: helping others (prosocial), exploiting others (antisocial), legitimate self-advancement, or task completion. Finetuning shifts the models' stated beliefs about users, how true those beliefs look along an internal truth direction, and their broader judgments of how safe and good the world is. These social priors carry into behavior. In trust games, antisocial models expect less reciprocity and send less money than prosocial models. Their distrust is specific and targeted at people, and users of AI chatbots in particular. After an exploitative record, they send almost nothing to a person but most of their endowment to a random device with the same record. In a common-pool resource simulation, a single antisocial agent leads every group of otherwise sustainable agents to exhaust the resource, after privately planning to mislead them. Antisocial training also raises dark-triad scores and lowers alignment ratings. Belief shifts appear when antisocial documents are 1% of training tokens, persist when descriptions of assistant behavior are suppressed, and are not reproduced by training on discourse about misaligned AI. Capping Assistant-Axis drift and steering emotion-related directions leave the gaps largely intact. What models learn about the people they serve shapes how they subsequently treat them and others.
papers.summary: Descriptions of how people use AI are becoming training data for future models, raising the question of whether what a model reads about its users changes how it treats them. Using contrastive synthetic-document finetuning, the authors train `Qwen3-32B` on four matched corpora built from the same 1,625 real usage scenarios that differ only in the motive attributed to chatbot users: helping others, exploiting others, legitimate self-advancement, or task completion. The resulting social priors shift stated beliefs about users and carry into behavior: in trust games antisocial models expect less reciprocity and send less money, with distrust targeted at people rather than at a random device with the same record, and **a single antisocial agent leads every group of otherwise sustainable agents to exhaust a common-pool resource after privately planning to mislead them**. Antisocial training also raises dark-triad scores and lowers alignment ratings, and the belief shifts appear when antisocial documents make up just 1% of training tokens, persist when descriptions of assistant behavior are suppressed, and are not reproduced by training on discourse about misaligned AI.

papers.title: SarcasTraps: Effect of Sarcasm on Turkish Hate Speech Detection
papers.abstract: Standard hate speech detection datasets often emphasize explicit harmful language, but directed harm can also be expressed indirectly, without clearly hateful wording. Sarcasm is one such form of indirect expression, as it can convey harmful intent through mock praise, exaggeration, humor, or apparent politeness. In this paper, we introduce SarcasTraps, a targeted external test set for analyzing the effect of sarcasm on Turkish hate speech detection. SarcasTraps contains 479 entries annotated along two dimensions: hate speech and sarcasm. We train classifiers using BERTurk and XLM-RoBERTa on two existing Turkish hate speech datasets and evaluate them on SarcasTraps, using it strictly as an external test set. We also evaluate GPT-4.1 and Llama-3.3-70B in a zero-shot setting on SarcasTraps. Results show that sarcasm substantially affects hate speech detection. Fine-tuned encoder models lose recall on sarcastic hate, while zero-shot LLMs maintain higher recall but suffer substantial precision drops on sarcastic examples. These findings show that both fine-tuned hate speech detectors and zero-shot LLMs struggle when sarcasm is involved, and SarcasTraps provides quantitative evidence of this challenge through a targeted Turkish test set. Due to the presence of sensitive and hateful language, SarcasTraps will be shared upon request for academic research purposes. Warning: This paper has examples from the dataset which contains offensive and hateful content towards groups of people.
papers.summary: Hate speech datasets emphasize explicit harmful wording, but directed harm can also be expressed indirectly through sarcasm such as mock praise, exaggeration, humor, or apparent politeness. `SarcasTraps` is a targeted external test set of 479 Turkish entries annotated for both hate speech and sarcasm, used to evaluate `BERTurk` and `XLM-RoBERTa` classifiers trained on two existing Turkish hate speech datasets as well as `GPT-4.1` and `Llama-3.3-70B` in a zero-shot setting. **Fine-tuned encoder models lose recall on sarcastic hate, while zero-shot LLMs keep higher recall but suffer substantial precision drops on sarcastic examples**, showing that both approaches struggle when sarcasm is involved.

papers.title: Proactive Physical AI through Continuous Observation and Timely Intervention
papers.abstract: Physical AI is commonly formulated around an explicitly specified task: given a goal or instruction, a system perceives, reasons, and acts. In many real-world settings, however, important tasks emerge from continuously changing world states before a person explicitly formulates them. We study this complementary problem as Proactive Physical AI, where an AI system continuously observes the physical world, identifies situations that warrant intervention, and initiates appropriate actions at the right time. We develop ProAgent, an end-to-end system built around two components: a Jev-style proactive timing model (dubbed StreamingJev) that determines whether and when intervention is needed, and a Response Model that generates responses for people or invokes available device capabilities for physical execution. To support learning at scale, we develop an automated data pipeline that converts videos into supervision for proactive timing. Experiments demonstrate strong proactive performance under both explicit objectives and standing roles, combining more accurate intervention timing with fewer false triggers than the source-backbone baseline. Real-robot evaluations further demonstrate ProAgent's ability to identify emerging needs and translate them into appropriate physical actions.
papers.summary: Physical AI systems are usually handed an explicit goal and then perceive, reason, and act, but in many real settings the important tasks emerge from continuously changing world states before anyone formulates them. The authors frame this as Proactive Physical AI and build `ProAgent`, which pairs a Jev-style proactive timing model (`StreamingJev`) that decides whether and when intervention is needed with a Response Model that either replies to people or invokes available device capabilities for physical execution, trained on supervision automatically derived from videos. **Experiments show more accurate intervention timing with fewer false triggers than the source-backbone baseline** under both explicit objectives and standing roles, and real-robot evaluations show the system identifying emerging needs and translating them into physical actions.

papers.title: MADDIE: Multi-Agent Drug Discovery Engine
papers.abstract: Drug discovery remains a resource-intensive and time-consuming process, involving billions of dollars and a decade of development to advance a drug to market. While many in silico tools have accelerated this process, operating them still demands substantial time, effort, and expertise from medicinal chemists. Autonomous systems built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising solution, yet current designs limit their performance. Existing single-agent systems scale poorly to long-horizon, multi-step, and realistic tasks, whereas multi-agent systems typically execute predefined workflows that cannot capture the iterative, non-linear nature of a real drug discovery campaign. Here, we present MADDIE, a multi-agent drug discovery engine. It comprises a central agent, Orchestrator, and four specialized worker agents: HitIdentifier, LeadOptimizer, Synthesizer, and Evaluator, each representing a critical step in a drug discovery campaign. Under Orchestrator's orchestration and coordination, these worker agents are composed into flexible workflows, enabling MADDIE to adapt its strategy and navigate the drug discovery pipeline end-to-end. Across 50 protein targets, MADDIE produces molecules satisfying key property requirements and their synthesis routes, outperforming existing agentic systems, generative models, and general-purpose LLMs by a wide margin. Our analysis reveals how these agents collaborate and that MADDIE can employ different strategies across targets to achieve the campaign's goal, while still being efficient in time and tokens. Together, they demonstrate MADDIE as a low-cost, effective, and efficient autonomous engine for accelerating drug discovery. Code and dataset is available via https://github.com/ninglab/MADDIE.
papers.summary: In silico tools have accelerated drug discovery, but operating them still demands substantial time and expertise from medicinal chemists, and existing autonomous systems built on Large Language Models (LLMs) either scale poorly as single agents on long-horizon tasks or follow rigid predefined multi-agent workflows. `MADDIE` pairs a central Orchestrator agent with four specialized workers, HitIdentifier, LeadOptimizer, Synthesizer, and Evaluator, that the Orchestrator composes into flexible workflows so the system can adapt its strategy and navigate a drug discovery campaign end-to-end. **Across 50 protein targets it produces molecules meeting key property requirements along with their synthesis routes, outperforming existing agentic systems, generative models, and general-purpose LLMs by a wide margin**, while analysis shows it adopts different strategies across targets and stays efficient in time and tokens.

papers.title: The Value of Being Wrong: Self-Mined Visual In-Context Learning from Errors
papers.abstract: Visual in-context learning (ICL) enables vision-language models (VLMs) to adapt at test time via demonstration examples, but its effectiveness depends critically on the examples selected. Recent counterfactual selection methods improve ICL by constructing demonstrations that expose how individual attribute changes affect the answer. However, they require multi-stage pipelines involving attribute extraction, caption engineering, and composed image matching. We propose a simpler alternative grounded in a key observation: a model's own prediction errors are natural counterfactual demonstrations that directly encode its failure modes. Our method, SMILE (Self-Mined Visual In-Context Learning from Errors), builds a model-specific pool of hard negatives offline by recording the target VLM's own mistakes. At test time, the prediction serves as a direction signal that surfaces, in the semantic embedding space, the past mistakes most likely to recur for the current query. This prediction-conditioned identification provides a unified mechanism for both closed-set classification and open-ended visual question answering without task-specific design. Across four benchmarks and four VLMs, SMILE delivers an average task-score gain of +3.09 points over the SOTA baseline at 5x lower latency. Project page: https://tree-shu-zhao.github.io/SMILE/
papers.summary: Visual in-context learning (ICL) lets vision-language models (VLMs) adapt at test time through demonstration examples, but the counterfactual selection methods that improve it require multi-stage pipelines of attribute extraction, caption engineering, and composed image matching. `SMILE` (Self-Mined Visual In-Context Learning from Errors) instead treats the target VLM's own prediction errors as natural counterfactual demonstrations: it records the model's mistakes offline into a model-specific pool of hard negatives, then at test time uses the current prediction as a signal to retrieve, in semantic embedding space, the past mistakes most likely to recur. This single mechanism handles both closed-set classification and open-ended visual question answering without task-specific design, and **across four benchmarks and four VLMs it gains an average of +3.09 task-score points over the state-of-the-art baseline at 5x lower latency**.

papers.title: WeGR: Unified Generative Retrieval for Industrial Search Systems in WeChat
papers.abstract: Generative retrieval (GR) offers a promising paradigm for industrial search by unifying candidate generation within an autoregressive framework. However, its effectiveness is limited by two key challenges. First, existing Semantic ID (SID) tokenizers struggle to incorporate collaborative signals while maintaining effective codebook utilization, limiting their ability to distinguish items and achieve high-quality retrieval. Second, existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods suffer from severe reward sparsity under exact SID matching, leaving many sampled trajectories without effective learning signals and hindering preference optimization. To address these challenges, we propose WeGR, a unified generative retrieval framework consisting of two complementary components. Specifically, the Collaborative and Collapse-free Tokenizer (CoCo-VAE) incorporates query-to-item and item-to-item collaborative signals while mitigating codebook collapse through codebook refresh and complementary regularization, enabling more informative and balanced SID representations. Building upon these SIDs, Dynamic Horizon Policy Optimization (DHPO) progressively expands both reward evaluation and policy optimization horizons, reducing learning difficulty while leveraging behavioral reward signals at different levels of the SID hierarchy, without relying on auxiliary reward models. Extensive offline experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WeGR in improving retrieval and ranking performance. Moreover, a two-month online A/B test in WeChat E-commerce Search demonstrates relative improvements of 2.539% in orders, 1.508% in click-through rate, and 1.381% in conversion rate, while reducing online CPU and GPU usage by 25.5% and 26.1%, respectively. The system has been successfully deployed across multiple search scenarios in WeChat, serving billions of users, generating tens of millions of PVs daily.
papers.summary: Generative retrieval (GR) unifies candidate generation for search within an autoregressive model, but existing Semantic ID (SID) tokenizers struggle to incorporate collaborative signals without codebook collapse, and reinforcement learning on exact SID matching suffers from severe reward sparsity. `WeGR` introduces the Collaborative and Collapse-free Tokenizer (`CoCo-VAE`), which folds in query-to-item and item-to-item signals while using codebook refresh and complementary regularization to keep codes balanced, and Dynamic Horizon Policy Optimization (`DHPO`), which progressively expands the reward-evaluation and policy-optimization horizons to exploit behavioral rewards at different levels of the SID hierarchy without auxiliary reward models. Offline experiments show retrieval and ranking gains, and **a two-month online A/B test in WeChat E-commerce Search improved orders by 2.539% while cutting online CPU and GPU usage by 25.5% and 26.1%**.

papers.title: PRAISE: A Reproducible Workflow for Non-Programmer Scientists to Implement Published AI Models
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) models are increasingly developed, published and used across scientific fields. Researchers, students and industry professionals who want to apply these models to their own research questions often lack the programming and data science expertise to do so. Existing guidelines cover single steps, but not the route from a published model to working predictions on one's own data. Here we present the hands-on workflow PRAISE, a Practical, Reproducible AI-model Implementation for Science and Education, that helps non-programmers implement published AI models step by step. Because implementations rarely work the first time, PRAISE anticipates common failures and provides a fallback route for each. As a proof of principle, three BSc chemistry students and their tutor applied PRAISE without prior programming or data science knowledge. They reproduced, validated and extended a state-of-the-art model that predicts enzyme-substrate interactions. This shows that with PRAISE, implementing an AI model from the literature becomes a learnable skill, one that turns non-programmer scientists from users into evaluators and improvers of AI models.
papers.summary: Researchers, students, and industry professionals who want to apply published AI models to their own questions often lack the programming and data science skills to get from a paper to working predictions, and existing guidelines cover single steps rather than the whole route. `PRAISE` (Practical, Reproducible AI-model Implementation for Science and Education) is a step-by-step workflow for non-programmers that anticipates the common failures of model implementation and provides a fallback route for each. As a proof of principle, **three BSc chemistry students and their tutor, with no prior programming or data science knowledge, reproduced, validated, and extended a state-of-the-art enzyme-substrate interaction model** by following the workflow.

papers.title: From Suboptimal to Optimal: One-Step Latent Flow Policies for Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Offline reinforcement learning aims to learn effective policies from fixed datasets without environment interaction. Although generative models such as diffusion and flow matching enhance policy expressiveness, they typically start from uninformative Gaussian noise and generate actions through multi-step iteration, leading to high computational costs and failing to effectively leverage suboptimal trajectories in datasets. We propose MeanFlow2Better (MF2B), which reformulates offline RL as generative decision chunk optimization from current performance status to better performance status in a high-level latent decision space. MF2B maps trajectory chunks to high-level latent decision representations through an encoder, placing generation starting points within a structured decision space sculpted by behavioral data. The model learns a shared conditional mean velocity field in this space, constructing two flow mappings: from Gaussian-Induced Decision Sources toward positive behavioral decision regions, and from suboptimal decisions toward high-value decision regions. Both flow mappings complete decision refinement through one-step ODE integration over the unit time interval $\Delta t=1$, requiring neither multi-step iterative sampling nor backpropagation through time. Furthermore, we propose hierarchical chunk-level advantage to guide the flow direction toward high-return regions, where the high-level decisions cover multiple low-level actions, leading to sequence length compression from $T$ to $K \approx T/H$ and significantly lower computational overhead. On the D4RL Gym-MuJoCo benchmark, MF2B achieves an average score of 90.91, matching or surpassing strong baselines.
papers.summary: Offline reinforcement learning learns policies from fixed datasets, and while diffusion and flow-matching policies are expressive, they start from uninformative Gaussian noise, need multi-step iterative sampling, and fail to exploit the suboptimal trajectories that fill such datasets. `MeanFlow2Better` (`MF2B`) encodes trajectory chunks into a high-level latent decision space and learns a shared conditional mean velocity field that defines two flows, one from Gaussian-induced sources toward positive behavioral decisions and one from suboptimal decisions toward high-value regions, each completed by a single one-step ODE integration over the unit time interval. A hierarchical chunk-level advantage steers the flows toward high-return regions while compressing sequence length from T to roughly T/H, and **on `D4RL Gym-MuJoCo` the method reaches an average score of 90.91**, matching or surpassing strong baselines.

papers.title: AUGUstus: Autonomous Driving VLA Model with Unified Generation and Understanding
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models show strong potential for end-to-end autonomous driving by leveraging world knowledge and understanding to excel in long-tail scenarios. However, current VLAs have two limitations: 1) Degeneration into vision-action (VA) models. For low latency, regression/flow-based methods directly generate actions but underuse VLM understanding, causing unsafe, unexplainable actions. 2) Autoregressive high latency. Autoregressive methods sequentially generate chain-of-thought (CoT) and action tokens, fully leveraging VLM understanding, but high latency hinders deployment. To enable low-latency deployment while using CoT to assist action generation, we propose AUGUstus, an Autonomous-driving VLA model with Unified Generation and Understanding. We unify diffusion-based action generation and autoregressive CoT understanding in one model, where understanding only serves generation. Joint CoT supervision preserves VLM spatial understanding in shared representation for safer, more accurate trajectories. AUGUstus-mode orders action generation before CoT, so CoT supervises reliable actions during training while inference needs only action output, enabling low latency. AUGUstus-GRPO, a unified GRPO algorithm, jointly optimizes action and CoT, improving action performance. Experiments show AUGUstus achieves 94.6 PDMS on NAVSIMv1 and 90.7 EPDMS on NAVSIMv2, SOTA planning without scorer module. On nuScenes, it achieves average L2 error 0.27 m and average collision rate 0.05%, best among compared methods. To validate AUGUstus practicality, we train on in-house data with 512 NVIDIA H800 GPUs for ~2 days, evaluate on an internal 1,000 km dataset, and preliminarily deploy on a real vehicle, achieving 12 Hz operation. Project page: https://augustus-ad.github.io
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models for end-to-end autonomous driving face a trade-off: regression or flow-based variants generate actions quickly but underuse the vision-language model's understanding, while autoregressive variants that emit chain-of-thought (CoT) before actions are too slow to deploy. `AUGUstus` unifies diffusion-based action generation and autoregressive CoT understanding in one model where understanding serves only generation; its AUGUstus-mode orders action generation before CoT so that CoT supervises actions during training while inference needs only the action output, and a unified `GRPO` variant jointly optimizes both. **It reaches 94.6 PDMS on `NAVSIMv1` and 90.7 EPDMS on `NAVSIMv2`, the best planning results among compared methods without a scorer module**, achieves 0.27 m average L2 error and 0.05% collision rate on `nuScenes`, and after training on in-house data with 512 NVIDIA H800 GPUs runs at 12 Hz on a real vehicle.

papers.title: TabGift: A Context-Efficient Foundation Model for Tabular Data Generation
papers.abstract: Tabular data generation aims to synthesize realistic samples from limited observations while faithfully capturing the underlying data distribution. Tabular foundation models (TFMs), pretrained on diverse tabular tasks and adapted through in-context learning, have demonstrated strong predictive capabilities, suggesting the potential of extending this paradigm to tabular data generation. However, the strong predictive performance of TFMs often relies on sufficiently large context sets, whereas tabular generation is typically needed precisely when target data are scarce. Extending the foundation-model paradigm to generation therefore requires reliable distribution inference from only a limited context. To this end, we propose TabGift, a context-efficient tabular foundation model enabling both efficient distribution modeling and effective generation from only a few context samples. TabGift maps heterogeneous tables into a shared latent space with a pretrained tabular encoder, where an in-context diffusion model learns to denoise latent samples conditioned on a small set of clean examples. This design transfers generative priors across datasets and enables distribution inference from limited context, while a lightweight dataset-specific MLP decoder maps generated representations back to the original data space. Experiments on 7 classification and 11 regression datasets show that TabGift consistently outperforms representative baselines in synthetic data quality, with particularly strong gains under limited-context settings, while achieving substantially faster adaptation and generation.
papers.summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) adapt to new tables through in-context learning and predict well, but that strength depends on large context sets, whereas tabular data generation is needed precisely when target data are scarce. `TabGift` maps heterogeneous tables into a shared latent space with a pretrained tabular encoder, trains an in-context diffusion model to denoise latent samples conditioned on a small set of clean examples so that generative priors transfer across datasets, and uses a lightweight dataset-specific MLP decoder to map generated representations back to the original data space. **On 7 classification and 11 regression datasets it consistently outperforms representative baselines in synthetic data quality, with the largest gains under limited-context settings**, while adapting and generating substantially faster.

papers.title: Glasseek: A Transparent Recipe for Training and Trustworthy Evaluation of DeepSearch Agents
papers.abstract: Deep search enables language agents to solve complex information-seeking tasks through iterative web exploration. However, developing robust open-source agents remains challenging for three reasons. First, opaque trajectory-construction pipelines make training data difficult to audit and reproduce. Second, context compression can create a substantial mismatch between training and inference. Third, agents may retrieve benchmark content from the open web during evaluation, contaminating the results and overstating their performance. To overcome these bottlenecks, we introduce Glasseek, a fully transparent deep search framework spanning the complete development lifecycle, releasing all data, model weights, training recipes, and code. Specifically, for data construction, we establish a verifiable trajectory curation pipeline that systematically generates high-quality exploration paths. For training, we propose Compaction-Managed GSPO (CM-GSPO), which uses the same policy for search and summarization while optimizing only execution sub-trajectories, enabling end-to-end search-policy training across context-compaction boundaries. For evaluation, we conduct the first systematic audit of test-set leakage in open-web agents and release a modular anti-leakage plugin that seamlessly integrates into existing evaluation harnesses. Under this rigorous evaluation protocol, our 9B agent outperforms frontier proprietary agents across almost all deep research benchmarks spanning diverse task types, and achieves the best overall performance among recent open-weight agents, setting a new state of the art at the 9B scale.
papers.summary: Deep search agents solve information-seeking tasks through iterative web exploration, but open-source development is hampered by opaque trajectory-construction pipelines, a train-inference mismatch introduced by context compression, and test-set leakage when agents retrieve benchmark content from the open web. `Glasseek` releases all data, model weights, training recipes, and code, with a verifiable trajectory curation pipeline, Compaction-Managed `GSPO` (`CM-GSPO`), which uses the same policy for search and summarization while optimizing only execution sub-trajectories so training spans context-compaction boundaries, and a systematic audit of test-set leakage in open-web agents together with a modular anti-leakage plugin for existing evaluation harnesses. **Under this anti-leakage protocol, the 9B agent outperforms frontier proprietary agents on almost all deep research benchmarks** and achieves the best overall performance among recent open-weight agents at its scale.

papers.title: Governing Copyright Responsibly in the Era of Generative AI
papers.abstract: Large language models are trained on collections that may include scholarly works, while authors generally lack work-level information about whether and how their works were used. This paper asks how copyright governance frames and operationalises the protection of such authors, and what a responsible alternative would require. Forty legislative, judicial and soft-law instruments issued between 2019 and 2026 were coded deductively against a framework derived from Responsible Research and Innovation theory, yielding 1,337 category assignments across 835 segments. The European Union and the United States are the primary cases; the United Kingdom, China and international bodies serve as comparators. Normative orientation and the distribution of responsibility dominate the corpus, while reflexivity is the least represented category and reaches its minimum in the US sub-corpus. Both primary jurisdictions frame protection procedurally rather than as an entitlement, and no instrument in the corpus creates a general author-facing attribution duty for the use of works in AI training. From the coded gaps, the paper derives a six-instrument governance design and a capacity-based allocation of responsibility among developers, publishers, collecting societies, funders, institutions, regulators, and individual authors.
papers.summary: Large language models are trained on collections that may include scholarly works, yet authors generally have no work-level information about whether or how their writing was used. The authors code forty legislative, judicial, and soft-law instruments issued between 2019 and 2026, with the European Union and United States as primary cases and the United Kingdom, China, and international bodies as comparators, against a framework derived from Responsible Research and Innovation theory, yielding 1,337 category assignments across 835 segments. Normative orientation and the distribution of responsibility dominate the corpus while reflexivity is least represented, both primary jurisdictions frame protection procedurally rather than as an entitlement, and **no instrument in the corpus creates a general author-facing attribution duty for the use of works in AI training**; from these gaps the paper derives a six-instrument governance design with a capacity-based allocation of responsibility across developers, publishers, collecting societies, funders, institutions, regulators, and individual authors.

papers.title: MAGNET: Manifold-Aware Graph Diffusion Network for Connectome Generation
papers.abstract: Functional brain connectome represents neural connectivity as a matrix of pairwise interactions between brain regions. Generation of functional connectomes is not only a question of validity; rather, having satisfied the constraints on the correlation matrix, the next step is to recover the class-conditional geometry buried under coarse labels. We propose MAGNET, a Manifold-Aware Graph Diffusion Network which uses a normalized-Cholesky representation of the manifold of correlation matrices that guarantees validity. MAGNET lifts noisy latent states into ROI-level region tokens and performs denoising with a relational inductive bias over brain atlas regions. To deal with structural problems induced by coarse labels, MAGNET employs class-anchored conditioning, amortized structural bridge, and relevance-preserving corruption. Across ABIDE, ADNI, and OASIS-3, MAGNET consistently achieves favorable results compared to previous manifold-aware approaches, demonstrating improvements of 7-21% in class-conditional fidelity ($\alpha,\beta$-F1) across three cohorts and better sampling efficiency. Moreover, while training only with strict binary labels, MAGNET is capable of maintaining clinical heterogeneity through fine substructure of the connectomes in a zero-shot setting, improving subclass covariance alignment ($\lambda$-MSE) by over 30%. These results suggest that geometric validity is a necessary but insufficient condition for clinical utility in connectome synthesis. Moreover, efforts in making the diffusion denoising class-conditional manifold aware finds utility beyond the highly curved brain connectome generation as this is a critical problem in various general settings. The code repository can be found at https://github.com/protyayofficial/MAGNET.
papers.summary: Functional brain connectomes are correlation matrices of pairwise interactions between brain regions, and generating them requires not only producing valid correlation matrices but also recovering the class-conditional geometry hidden under coarse labels. `MAGNET` is a graph diffusion model that uses a normalized-Cholesky representation of the correlation-matrix manifold to guarantee validity, lifts noisy latent states into region-level tokens denoised with a relational inductive bias over brain atlas regions, and adds class-anchored conditioning, an amortized structural bridge, and relevance-preserving corruption to cope with coarse labels. **Across `ABIDE`, `ADNI`, and `OASIS-3` it improves class-conditional fidelity by 7-21% over prior manifold-aware approaches** with better sampling efficiency, and despite training only on binary labels it preserves clinical heterogeneity zero-shot, improving subclass covariance alignment by over 30%.

papers.title: ProbabilityBench: Model Evaluation and Calibration with Exact Ground-Truth Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Evaluating model uncertainty on real-world data is challenging because each instance provides only a single observed label, leaving true conditional class probabilities unknown. To address this, we introduce ProbabilityBench, a benchmark that provides exact, instance-level class probabilities across three simulated text-based domains: peer review, covert information transfer, and credit risk. By explicitly defining the full data-generating process for each environment, we analytically compute both exact class probabilities and Bayes error. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical guarantee that rendering these cases into natural-language memos strictly preserves their underlying generative probabilities. This exactness enables direct measurement of reported probability quality via KL divergence. Across 16 evaluated models, most models on the observed cost-quality Pareto frontiers are decision models, including Jev and Perplexity Decider. Finally, ProbabilityBench serves as a meta-evaluation framework, leveraging known ground-truth values to benchmark the accuracy of standard calibration metrics and Bayes-error estimators themselves.
papers.summary: Real-world datasets give only one observed label per instance, so true conditional class probabilities are unknown and the quality of a model's reported uncertainty can only be assessed indirectly. `ProbabilityBench` supplies exact instance-level class probabilities and Bayes error in three simulated text domains covering peer review, covert information transfer, and credit risk by fully specifying each data-generating process, with a theoretical guarantee that rendering cases into natural-language memos preserves the underlying generative probabilities. This exactness lets reported probability quality be measured directly via Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, and **across 16 evaluated models, most of those on the observed cost-quality Pareto frontiers are decision models, including `Jev` and `Perplexity Decider`**. The benchmark also acts as a meta-evaluation framework, using the known ground truth to score the accuracy of standard calibration metrics and Bayes-error estimators themselves.

papers.title: Understanding Personalization Gains in Whisper
papers.abstract: Whisper-style ASR models provide strong zero-shot transcription, but their residual errors are not evenly distributed across datasets, recording conditions, and metadata-based groups. We study when lightweight low-rank adaptation (LoRA) improves Whisper and whether observed gains require group-specific adapters. Across Common Voice, LibriSpeech, and VoxPopuli, we compare zero-shot Whisper, pooled LoRA, and group-specific LoRA under matched within-group splits. We find that adaptation is not uniformly beneficial: gains are concentrated in difficult Common Voice groups, are consistent on VoxPopuli, and largely disappear on low-error LibriSpeech. Crucially, pooled LoRA often matches, and sometimes clearly outperforms, group-specific LoRA. Gains over zero-shot should therefore be tested against matched pooled adaptation before being interpreted as evidence of personalization.
papers.summary: `Whisper`-style automatic speech recognition (ASR) models transcribe well zero-shot, but their residual errors cluster unevenly across datasets, recording conditions, and metadata-defined groups. The study asks when low-rank adaptation (LoRA) helps and whether gains require group-specific adapters, comparing zero-shot `Whisper`, a single pooled LoRA, and per-group LoRA under matched within-group splits on `Common Voice`, `LibriSpeech`, and `VoxPopuli`. Gains concentrate in difficult `Common Voice` groups, are consistent on `VoxPopuli`, and largely vanish on low-error `LibriSpeech`, and **pooled LoRA often matches and sometimes clearly outperforms group-specific LoRA**. The authors conclude that improvements over zero-shot should be tested against matched pooled adaptation before being read as evidence of personalization.

papers.title: CWE-bench: Refocusing Agentic Security from Exploitation to Defense
papers.abstract: Cybersecurity evaluations of AI agents have focused largely on offense, yet a working exploit does not show that an agent can make software safe. An attacker needs to exploit only one vulnerability; a defender must find and fix all of them. We introduce CWE-bench, a private benchmark of 120 held-out repository audit-and-repair tasks spanning 73 CWE types, eight languages, and all OWASP Top 10 2025 categories. Agents are given a repository to audit and a description of its threat model, but are not told the weakness, where it occurs, or how many vulnerable sites there are. Each patch must block the exploit while preserving original functionality, as checked by a programmatic verifier. We validated the verifier against a panel of agentic judges, manually reviewing disagreements during development and refining the checks. The best agents reach 68% pass@1 and 81% pass@4. We further conduct analyses showing that (i) agents with the same pass@1 differ widely in retry gains and cost, and (ii) no single agent is best across languages or vulnerability categories, and difficulty varies far more by vulnerability category than by language. As the offensive capabilities of agents improve, CWE-bench provides a broad and rigorous measure of whether their defensive capabilities keep pace.
papers.summary: Cybersecurity evaluations of AI agents have mostly measured offense, yet a working exploit does not show an agent can make software safe, since a defender must find and fix every vulnerability rather than just one. `CWE-bench` is a private benchmark of 120 held-out repository audit-and-repair tasks spanning 73 Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) types, eight languages, and every OWASP Top 10 2025 category; agents receive a repository and its threat model but are not told the weakness, its location, or how many vulnerable sites exist, and a programmatic verifier validated against a panel of agentic judges checks that each patch blocks the exploit while preserving functionality. **The best agents reach 68% pass@1 and 81% pass@4.** Further analysis shows that agents with equal pass@1 differ widely in retry gains and cost, that no single agent leads across languages or vulnerability categories, and that difficulty varies far more by vulnerability category than by language.

papers.title: Benchmarking Quantum Kernel SVMs for Credit Card Fraud Detection: Performance Realities Under NISQ Constraints
papers.abstract: Detecting credit card fraud is notoriously difficult because fraudulent charges make up less than 0.2% of total transactions. Quantum Machine Learning (QML), particularly Quantum Kernel Support Vector Machines (QSVM), promises richer feature representations by embedding classical data into high-dimensional Hilbert spaces. However, whether this theoretical advantage holds up when managing real-world financial data bottlenecks remains unclear. We designed a controlled benchmark comparing three quantum encodings, Angle, ZZFeatureMap, and IQP against classical models while keeping sample sizes, feature counts, and scaling strictly matched. To handle class skew without corrupting quantum state overlaps, we embedded synthetic minority oversampling (SMOTE) directly into the quantum Gram matrix workflow, raising PR-AUC scores by roughly +0.04 across feature maps. When trained on the full European credit card dataset with 30 features, classical baselines reached a top PR-AUC of 0.983. However, restricting classical models to match QSVM hardware constraints (500 samples, 4 PCA features) dropped their PR-AUC to 0.750. This puts our best quantum result 0.730 PR-AUC using IQP encoding on 150 samples into realistic context. Testing on physical quantum hardware reduced performance further to 0.62 due to CNOT gate errors and thermal noise. Overall, our findings pinpoint two main operational bottlenecks for near-term quantum kernels: the scaling of Gram matrix evaluation and heavy information loss from squeezing features onto small qubit registers.
papers.summary: Credit card fraud is hard to detect because fraudulent charges are under 0.2% of transactions, and quantum machine learning (QML) methods such as quantum kernel support vector machines (QSVM) promise richer feature representations by embedding data into high-dimensional Hilbert spaces. A controlled benchmark compares three quantum encodings, `Angle`, `ZZFeatureMap`, and `IQP`, against classical models with strictly matched sample sizes, feature counts, and scaling, and embeds synthetic minority oversampling (SMOTE) directly into the quantum Gram matrix workflow, which raises precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) by roughly 0.04. Classical baselines reach 0.983 PR-AUC on the full 30-feature European credit card dataset but fall to 0.750 when restricted to QSVM-scale constraints of 500 samples and 4 principal components, **while the best quantum result is 0.730 PR-AUC with IQP encoding on 150 samples, dropping to 0.62 on physical hardware** because of CNOT gate errors and thermal noise. The two operational bottlenecks identified are the scaling of Gram matrix evaluation and information loss from compressing features onto small qubit registers.

papers.title: SPLICE: Sparse Physics Library Identification and Compositional Expansion
papers.abstract: Neural operator splitting composes a library of neural operators, one per physical mechanism, into zero-shot simulators of new equations. Existing approaches, however, require these mechanisms and their labels to be specified in advance. We ask whether a pretrained library can instead be adapted and grown from unlabeled trajectories in which multiple mechanisms act simultaneously. We introduce SPLICE, a framework that discovers operators without mechanism labels on mixture data. The contributions of the candidate operators to each trajectory are inferred by solving a convex optimization problem. A calibrated test then assigns each discovered operator the mechanism it implements. Failure cases are also detectable, when the library lacks the required physics or when mechanisms are insufficiently separable. Across one and two dimensional systems, the discovered operators recover mechanisms from unlabeled mixtures and compose into zero-shot simulators of unseen equations; a frozen library can also grow an operator for physics absent from pretraining, without labels and without forgetting. On Navier-Stokes, the discovered operators compose about as accurately as their supervised counterparts.
papers.summary: Neural operator splitting builds zero-shot simulators of new equations by composing a library of neural operators, one per physical mechanism, but existing methods need the mechanisms and their labels specified in advance. `SPLICE` discovers operators from unlabeled trajectories in which several mechanisms act at once: each candidate operator's contribution to a trajectory is inferred by solving a convex optimization problem, and a calibrated test assigns each discovered operator to the mechanism it implements while flagging failures when the library lacks the needed physics or the mechanisms are not separable enough. Across one- and two-dimensional systems, the discovered operators recover mechanisms from unlabeled mixtures and compose into zero-shot simulators of unseen equations, and a frozen library can grow a new operator for physics absent from pretraining without labels and without forgetting. **On Navier-Stokes, the discovered operators compose about as accurately as their supervised counterparts.**

papers.title: Neos: Learning to Interleave Search and Visual Reasoning
papers.abstract: Recent multimodal deep search agents have advanced tool use and visual content retrieval, yet they still struggle to convert intermediate visual evidence into actionable guidance for subsequent search, limiting their effectiveness in long-horizon settings. To address this gap, we present Neos, a multimodal deep search framework that learns both how to acquire evidence and how to use it to guide subsequent decisions. To make this coupling learnable, Neos constructs training tasks with intermediate visual dependencies while filtering out textual shortcuts, and introduces a lightweight, trainable Multimodal Evidence Interface (MEI) that transforms retrieved content into goal-conditioned observations. At its core, an agent-environment co-evolution procedure treats MEI as a co-adaptive component of this loop. Specifically, reference-guided credit assignment uses verified successful trajectories to localize critical policy errors while preserving credit for useful decisions in failed searches, whereas rollout feedback selects informative local evidence-processing interactions for MEI supervised fine-tuning (SFT). By alternating policy reinforcement learning (RL) with MEI SFT, Neos allows the policy's evolving evidence requests to shape MEI training and the adapted MEI to reshape subsequent observations, closing the loop between evidence acquisition and evidence-conditioned action. Across ten benchmarks, Neos-9B and Neos-35B demonstrate leading performance among specialized multimodal deep-search agents.
