papers.summary: Multimodal deep search agents can retrieve visual content and call tools, but they struggle to turn intermediate visual evidence into guidance for the next search step, which limits them on long-horizon tasks. `Neos` builds training tasks with intermediate visual dependencies while filtering out textual shortcuts, and adds a lightweight trainable Multimodal Evidence Interface (MEI) that converts retrieved content into goal-conditioned observations. An agent-environment co-evolution procedure alternates policy reinforcement learning (RL) with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of the MEI: reference-guided credit assignment uses verified successful trajectories to localize critical policy errors while preserving credit for useful decisions in failed searches, and rollout feedback selects informative evidence-processing interactions as MEI training data, so the policy's evolving evidence requests shape the interface and the adapted interface reshapes later observations. **Across ten benchmarks, `Neos-9B` and `Neos-35B` lead among specialized multimodal deep-search agents.**

papers.title: VL-DocIR: A Benchmark for Vision-Based Long Document Information Retrieval
papers.abstract: Vision-based document retrieval has improved rapidly, but current evaluation settings still emphasize short documents and single relevant pages. This leaves an important gap between leaderboard performance and realistic long-document retrieval, where the evidence needed to answer a query may span multiple pages or even multiple documents. We present VL-DocIR, a page-level benchmark for evidence-complete visual long-document retrieval. VL-DocIR is built from 29,641 HTML-born documents rendered into 388,548 page images from Wikipedia, arXiv, PubMed, and SEC proxy statements. It contains 271,760 queries across 23 domains and six evidence structures, covering single-page, within-document multi-page, and cross-document evidence configurations. Evidence annotations are grounded to rendered pages and HTML element identifiers, and queries are filtered with a cleaning pipeline targeting clarity, correctness, closedness, and the absence of explicit layout references. We evaluate leading single-vector and multi-vector visual retrievers together with diagnostic retrieval settings such as document-context scoring, query splitting, reranking, and round-robin ensembles. The strongest evaluated configuration reaches 69.3 nDCGAll@10 and 80.6 RecallAll@10 under structure-balanced Macro evaluation, but source- and evidence-structure breakdowns show that cross-document retrieval remains substantially harder than single-page retrieval, and that document-context scoring is especially helpful for within-document multi-page queries. VL-DocIR exposes these failure modes and provides a more demanding target for visual long-document retrieval. The new dataset and code will be made publicly available at https://yufanchen96.github.io/VL-DocIR.
papers.summary: Vision-based document retrieval benchmarks mostly use short documents with a single relevant page, leaving a gap to realistic settings where the evidence for a query spans multiple pages or documents. `VL-DocIR` is a page-level benchmark built from 29,641 HTML-born documents rendered into 388,548 page images from Wikipedia, arXiv, PubMed, and SEC proxy statements, with 271,760 queries across 23 domains and six evidence structures covering single-page, within-document multi-page, and cross-document cases; evidence annotations are grounded to rendered pages and HTML element identifiers, and queries pass a cleaning pipeline targeting clarity, correctness, closedness, and absence of explicit layout references. Evaluating leading single-vector and multi-vector visual retrievers plus diagnostic settings such as document-context scoring, query splitting, reranking, and round-robin ensembles, **the strongest configuration reaches 69.3 nDCGAll@10 and 80.6 RecallAll@10** under structure-balanced macro evaluation. Breakdowns by source and evidence structure show cross-document retrieval remains substantially harder than single-page retrieval, and document-context scoring helps most on within-document multi-page queries.

papers.title: PatientWM: Towards Generalizable Clinical World Models via Unified Patient States
papers.abstract: Clinical decisions depend on anticipating how a patient's condition will evolve as treatment is adjusted and new evidence becomes available. Existing medical world models capture patient-state evolution, but often define the evolving state around a particular modality or task, limiting reuse as inputs or prediction targets change. These models also retain history through observation sequences or recurrent or latent summaries rather than exposing preceding patient states and clinical actions as an ordered transition context. This distinction matters because similar current measurements may follow different recent changes, treatment exposures, and observed responses. To tackle these limitations, we propose PatientWM, a clinical world-model framework built around a unified patient state and sequential latent history. Availability-aware encoders integrate observations available at each decision time into the patient state, while typed decoders produce task-specific clinical readouts without defining the state around any single target. PatientWM further conditions each next-state prediction on the current state and supplied action together with a bounded, ordered history of preceding latent patient states and clinical actions, preserving recent treatment and response context. Experiments across MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and three external clinical datasets show superior performance in clinical prediction, multi-step forecasting, and action-planning evaluation. Transfer experiments further demonstrate the generalizability of PatientWM's patient state. Together, these results establish its ability to forecast clinical evolution and support planning.
papers.summary: Clinical decisions depend on anticipating how a patient's condition will evolve as treatment changes and new evidence arrives, but existing medical world models tie the patient state to a single modality or task and compress history into observation sequences or latent summaries rather than exposing preceding states and actions as an ordered transition context. `PatientWM` is a clinical world-model framework built around a unified patient state and a sequential latent history: availability-aware encoders fold whatever observations exist at each decision time into the state, typed decoders produce task-specific clinical readouts, and each next-state prediction conditions on the current state, the supplied action, and a bounded ordered history of preceding latent states and clinical actions. **Experiments on `MIMIC-III`, `MIMIC-IV`, and three external clinical datasets show improved clinical prediction, multi-step forecasting, and action-planning performance**, and transfer experiments indicate the learned patient state generalizes across datasets.

papers.title: Gradient Routing Localizes and Removes Unintended Behaviors in RL
papers.abstract: We propose a mitigation to reward hacking in reinforcement learning. Our setup involves a misspecified reward function that gives rise to unintended behavior, and a monitor used to detect unintended behavior. As with frontier AI systems, the monitor makes systematic errors. Consequently, using the monitor for data filtering or to apply a reward penalty fails to prevent the model from learning unintended behavior ("reward hacking"). To address this problem, we introduce GRAFT: Gradient Routing Adapter Fine Tuning. Rather than penalizing or filtering flagged samples during training, GRAFT constrains gradient updates on those samples to a sacrificial set of new parameters. This has two benefits: First, because the monitor is not part of the reward function, the model does not learn to hide misbehavior. Second, ablating the sacrificial parameters reduces or entirely stops the unintended behavior while maintaining improved performance on target tasks. We demonstrate these benefits in RL environments where reward penalties cause models to learn to reward hack in undetected ways, training models ranging from 135M to 8B parameters. Additionally, we show a similar effect at a larger scale by distilling frontier LLM trajectories containing reward hacking into Qwen3-32B, without teaching that model to reward hack. Overall, our work suggests GRAFT may be a promising approach for leveraging imperfect monitors during post-training in settings where true performance is difficult to evaluate.
papers.summary: When a reinforcement learning (RL) reward is misspecified and the monitor meant to catch the resulting unintended behavior makes systematic errors, using that monitor to filter data or apply a reward penalty fails to prevent reward hacking and can teach the model to hide it. `GRAFT` (Gradient Routing Adapter Fine Tuning) instead routes gradient updates from monitor-flagged samples into a sacrificial set of new parameters, so the monitor never enters the reward and the model has no incentive to conceal misbehavior. **Ablating the sacrificial parameters after training reduces or entirely stops the unintended behavior while keeping the improved performance on target tasks**, shown in RL environments where reward penalties lead to undetected hacking across models from 135M to 8B parameters. A similar effect appears at larger scale when distilling frontier large language model (LLM) trajectories containing reward hacking into `Qwen3-32B` without transferring the hacking behavior.

papers.title: Superintelligence and the Triple Risk of an AI Race
papers.abstract: On many estimates, artificial general intelligence (AGI) is likely to emerge within the next few decades or even sooner. Once it does, it may quickly surpass human intelligence, possibly by a huge margin. Some believe that the country that develops AGI first could attain global dominance. This prospect risks setting off intense competition between the United States and China. Indeed, a narrative has already developed that the superpowers are locked in an AI race, with the Trump administration proclaiming its determination to 'dismantle unnecessary regulatory barriers' to winning it. We argue that this approach presents three profound dangers. The first two are familiar from past arms races: being overtaken by a rival or triggering a war. The third is new: losing control of human beings' future to agents far more intelligent than we are, which could endanger our very survival. Striving to get to AGI first risks a race to the bottom on safety practices and regulation concerning them. China does not yet appear bent on racing to superintelligence. The United States should prioritise both unilateral and co-operative efforts to improve AI safety and avoid provoking a race that all humanity could lose.
papers.summary: Many forecasts put artificial general intelligence (AGI) within decades or sooner, and a narrative has formed that the United States and China are locked in a race to reach it first, with the Trump administration pledging to dismantle what it calls unnecessary regulatory barriers to winning it. The authors argue this framing carries three dangers: two familiar from past arms races, being overtaken by a rival or triggering a war, and a third that is new, **losing control of humanity's future to agents far more intelligent than people, with survival itself at stake**. They contend that racing to AGI invites a race to the bottom on safety practices and regulation, observe that China does not yet appear bent on racing to superintelligence, and recommend that the United States prioritize both unilateral and cooperative safety efforts rather than provoke a race all of humanity could lose.

papers.title: Interactive Navigation Beyond Reachability: Benchmark and Agentic Framework
papers.abstract: Existing embodied navigation tasks commonly assume that traversability and object states remain fixed during an episode. Yet reaching a goal may require opening a door to access a room and then opening a container to reveal a hidden target. We formulate interactive navigation beyond reachability, unifying channel-induced changes in spatial connectivity, container-induced changes in target visibility, and their sequential dependencies. We introduce MultINav-Bench, a 3K-episode ObjectGoal benchmark in MolmoSpaces spanning channel, container, and mixed tasks, with interaction-necessity annotations covering required and unnecessary episodes. Its data generation pipeline automates task construction across multiple task types. The evaluation protocol separately measures navigation success, interaction effectiveness, and cost. We further propose MultINav-Agent, a three-stage agentic framework built on a persistent, state-conditioned interaction graph. Semantic interactive perception grounds entities and interaction states; a vision-language model selects task-relevant actions based on expected changes in connectivity and target observability; and post-interaction verification updates the graph to guide subsequent navigation, exploration, or interaction. Experiments on MultINav-Bench show that MultINav-Agent consistently outperforms adapted baselines across channel, container, and mixed tasks.
papers.summary: Embodied navigation tasks usually assume traversability and object states stay fixed within an episode, yet reaching a goal may require opening a door to enter a room and then opening a container to reveal a hidden target. The work formulates interactive navigation beyond reachability, unifying channel-induced changes to spatial connectivity, container-induced changes to target visibility, and their sequential dependencies, and introduces `MultINav-Bench`, a 3K-episode ObjectGoal benchmark in `MolmoSpaces` with channel, container, and mixed tasks, interaction-necessity annotations covering required and unnecessary episodes, and an evaluation protocol that separately scores navigation success, interaction effectiveness, and cost. `MultINav-Agent` is a three-stage framework over a persistent state-conditioned interaction graph: semantic interactive perception grounds entities and their interaction states, a vision-language model picks actions by expected changes in connectivity and target observability, and post-interaction verification updates the graph to guide later navigation, exploration, or interaction. **It consistently outperforms adapted baselines across channel, container, and mixed tasks** on the benchmark.

papers.title: What the Machine Invented: Mining New Mathematical Instruments from OpenAI's October 2026 Release of AI-Generated Mathematics
papers.abstract:
On 6 October 2026 OpenAI published an initial 722 AI-written mathematical manuscripts, organized into 372 problem families, in the public repository github.com/openai/math. The release includes claimed solutions to many prominent open problems. We approach this collection as a treasure mine of mathematical ideas. Our aim is to extract new lemmas, constructions, inequalities and proof mechanisms introduced in the source arguments, and to distinguish them from established tools and new combinations of those tools. We call these mathematical instruments. Extraction comes first; their validity, novelty and possible reuse then become subjects for further study. The resulting descriptions also help readers understand the selected papers without having to reconstruct every argument at the outset.
  We examine 38 families in two groups of 17 and 21, spanning number theory, geometry, analysis, combinatorics, complexity, algebra, operator algebras, topology and mathematical physics. Each entry records the claim, extracted instruments, antecedents and caveats. Eleven cross-cutting patterns connect the entries, and a scoreboard records formalization status and dependencies. Novelty assessments are provisional and sometimes mixed. Selected source comparisons correct mathematical statements, hypotheses and counts; they do not independently establish priority or certify the underlying proofs. No Lean development was compiled or kernel-checked for this survey.
  We also briefly describe a subsequent application of the signed restriction lemma from family 112 to circuit lower bounds at every fixed depth.
papers.summary: On 6 October 2026 OpenAI released an initial 722 AI-written mathematical manuscripts organized into 372 problem families in a public GitHub repository, including claimed solutions to many prominent open problems. Treating the collection as a source of ideas, the survey extracts the new lemmas, constructions, inequalities, and proof mechanisms, termed mathematical instruments, from 38 families spanning number theory, geometry, analysis, combinatorics, complexity, algebra, operator algebras, topology, and mathematical physics, recording for each the claim, extracted instruments, antecedents, and caveats, and separating them from established tools and new combinations of those tools. Eleven cross-cutting patterns connect the entries and a scoreboard tracks formalization status and dependencies, but **novelty assessments are provisional, no Lean development was compiled or kernel-checked, and the source comparisons neither certify the underlying proofs nor establish priority**. A closing note describes a subsequent application of the signed restriction lemma from family 112 to circuit lower bounds at every fixed depth.

papers.title: SFT Leaves a Reproducible Signature in Activation Geometry: Calibrating Post-Training Interpretability Against Run-to-Run Noise
papers.abstract: A model diff credits post-training with whatever separates a base checkpoint from one post-trained descendant, presuming a rerun would land close by. On the sparse co-activation graph of Qwen3-1.7B it does not: two LoRA-SFT reruns sit over half as far apart as either sits from the base. We score each base-to-post contrast against the run-to-run band of its own recipe, and show that $k$ runs certify no better than $p=1/(k+1)$ under run exchangeability, however large the effect, so the band $z$-score is a descriptive scale. SFT leaves a large, reproducible signature: base $\to$ SFT displaces the graph by 17.8 pairwise-distance SDs beyond the mean distance between four independent LoRA-SFT runs, and the pre-registered estimator replicates on Llama-3.1-8B with Llama-Scope. At 29 steps each, four SFT and four DPO runs occupy disjoint displacement ranges, a gap $5.0\times$ and $5.6\times$ the spreads of the two arms, without any band. All bands use graphs built on one GPU architecture. Three other readings stop short of a verdict: DPO band counts (3/4, 1/4, 3/4 contrasts outside at 12, 29, 60 steps) show no consistent dose ordering while its displacement stays flat; light GRPO is a secondary non-detection, not an absence, and we run no equivalence test; and the graph concentration read as an RL signature is already in the zero-RL base. A pre-registered causal sweep at three edge budgets on 4,816 held-out prompts found the displaced sources load-bearing ($12\times$ a matched random control in mean, $3.5\times$ in median at 10,000 edges), but their stage-specificity interaction reversed at two budgets and the third failed its faithfulness gate, so we claim calibrated structural displacement, not a changed mechanism. Scope: one backbone, one SFT recipe and general-text probe states for the full protocol.
papers.summary: Model diffing attributes whatever separates a base checkpoint from one post-trained descendant to post-training, assuming a rerun would land nearby, but on the sparse co-activation graph of `Qwen3-1.7B` two LoRA supervised fine-tuning (SFT) reruns sit more than half as far apart as either does from the base. The study scores each base-to-post contrast against the run-to-run band of its own recipe and shows that k runs can certify no better than p = 1/(k+1) under run exchangeability, however large the effect, so the band z-score is a descriptive scale rather than a significance test. **SFT leaves a large reproducible signature, displacing the graph by 17.8 pairwise-distance standard deviations beyond the mean distance between four independent LoRA-SFT runs**, the pre-registered estimator replicates on `Llama-3.1-8B` with `Llama-Scope`, and four SFT and four direct preference optimization (DPO) runs at 29 steps occupy disjoint displacement ranges. Other readings stop short of a verdict: DPO shows no consistent dose ordering, light Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is a non-detection rather than an absence, and a pre-registered causal sweep found the displaced sources load-bearing but with an inconsistent stage-specificity interaction, so the claim is calibrated structural displacement, not a changed mechanism.

papers.title: AIPOCH Open-Science: An Open-Source AI Research Workbench with Reproducible .science Packages
papers.abstract: AI-assisted research leaves instructions, computations, artifact revisions and checks whose relationships matter when another researcher receives the work. We present AIPOCH Open-Science, an open-source research workbench with portable .science session packages, and specify an exchange contract for these recorded relationships. Version and assessment targets remain attributable while receiving-workspace identifiers can be remapped, eligible contents can be omitted explicitly, and imported history remains separate from a writable fork. A controlled session tested an incorrect first version, a reviewed correction, an unreviewed revision and a planned but unexecuted step. We compared complete and partial exports with source records extracted independently of the exporter, then inspected imports into separate projects within the same installation. Both conditions retained the tested version and review associations, kept the unreviewed revision distinct from earlier assessments and represented excluded content as unavailable. A documentation-rich ordinary directory also supplied evidence for all seven static inspection questions. A separate registry case connected a table to its recorded task, execution and review; offline execution of its retained script and fixed input reproduced two saved CSV tables byte for byte. The study contributes an implemented exchange contract and a controlled examination of its preservation rules, content-selection constraints and interpretation boundaries.
papers.summary: AI-assisted research produces instructions, computations, artifact revisions, and checks whose relationships matter when the work is handed to another researcher. `AIPOCH Open-Science` is an open-source research workbench with portable .science session packages and a specified exchange contract for those recorded relationships: version and assessment targets stay attributable, receiving-workspace identifiers can be remapped, eligible contents can be omitted explicitly, and imported history stays separate from a writable fork. In a controlled session covering an incorrect first version, a reviewed correction, an unreviewed revision, and a planned but unexecuted step, **both complete and partial exports retained the tested version and review associations, kept the unreviewed revision distinct from earlier assessments, and represented excluded content as unavailable** when imported into separate projects. A separate registry case linked a table to its recorded task, execution, and review, and offline re-execution of the retained script on its fixed input reproduced two saved CSV tables byte for byte.

papers.title: Calibrated Typed Decisions for Entity, Relation, and Event Extraction
papers.abstract: Information extraction models often perform well on the datasets they are trained on, but transferring to new domains and annotation guidelines remains challenging. Supporting user-specified types alone does not resolve this problem. We present CalOn, a unified 0.6B-parameter encoder for entity, relation, and event extraction across datasets and schemas. The model jointly encodes text and type definitions, then directly identifies entity spans, relations between spans, and event triggers and arguments. Its extraction decisions consider the requested types together, using their combined evidence to identify relevant candidates before assigning a type. This gives all three tasks a common probabilistic formulation while keeping every extracted mention anchored to the input text. We train on diverse sources, and supplement supervised learning with a reward that encourages correct extractions and penalises incorrect ones. Across 40 benchmarks, CalOn outperforms the evaluated baselines on most benchmarks. It leads all reported relation extraction benchmarks and achieves the highest average F1 for event triggers and arguments with gold triggers. The same model also performs strongly on aspect sentiment triplet extraction and pronoun resolution through its span-pair formulation. A correction for the probability bias introduced during training improves confidence estimates for entities, relations, and event arguments after calibration, with little change in F1.
papers.summary: Information extraction models perform well on their training datasets but transfer poorly to new domains and annotation guidelines, and merely supporting user-specified types does not solve this. `CalOn` is a unified 0.6B-parameter encoder for entity, relation, and event extraction that jointly encodes text with type definitions, weighs the requested types together to identify candidate spans before assigning a type, and keeps every extracted mention anchored to the input text under a shared probabilistic formulation; training combines diverse supervised sources with a reward that encourages correct extractions and penalizes incorrect ones. **Across 40 benchmarks it beats the evaluated baselines on most, leads every reported relation extraction benchmark, and posts the highest average F1 for event triggers and arguments given gold triggers**, while also performing strongly on aspect sentiment triplet extraction and pronoun resolution through its span-pair formulation. A correction for the probability bias introduced during training improves confidence estimates for entities, relations, and event arguments after calibration with little change in F1.

papers.title: D-World: An Explicit World-Language-Action Model with Recursive Self-Improvement under Dual Control
papers.abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) now reason about space well enough to program robots, yet the world models behind robot policies are implicit, held in network weights or predicted video, and cannot be inspected or corrected directly. We present D-World, an explicit world-language-action model built on the Sense, Plan and Act decomposition. A perception agent writes the scene as an executable digital twin using generated vision and geometry code. A planning agent searches for actions in simulation and, after each executed action chunk, revises the twin's object states and named physical parameters against what the robot measured. A parameter revision is accepted only if replaying the latest chunk does not increase any measured residual beyond its tolerance, and every chunk is checked in the updated twin before it runs. Structural mismatches return to perception for reconstruction. We call this measurement-grounded cycle of correction and revision recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which the LLM stays frozen while the world it acts in improves. We model the choice of actions that both advance the task and expose model error as a dual control problem and show that the cost of incorporating evidence into the twin sets the threshold at which probing pays, so cheap local revision counteracts the turn-off of cautious controllers. Each episode runs a real-to-sim-to-real loop, and its recorded twins can be refitted and re-rendered offline into higher-fidelity environments for post-training. Because perception and planning communicate only through the twin and language, either can be replaced by a learned model, and since inference dominates the loop, the loop speeds up with faster models. On a dual-arm robot, towel and toaster tasks show local revisions, such as one reducing the bread's rendered-depth residual from 22.4 to 1.5 mm, that let execution continue without reconstruction.
papers.summary: Frontier large language models (LLMs) reason about space well enough to program robots, but the world models behind robot policies live implicitly in network weights or predicted video and cannot be inspected or corrected directly. `D-World` is an explicit world-language-action model following a Sense, Plan, and Act decomposition: a perception agent writes the scene as an executable digital twin using generated vision and geometry code, and a planning agent searches for actions in simulation, then after each executed action chunk revises the twin's object states and physical parameters against robot measurements, accepting a revision only if replaying the chunk keeps every measured residual within tolerance and returning structural mismatches to perception for reconstruction. The authors call this measurement-grounded cycle recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which the LLM stays frozen while the world it acts in improves, and cast the choice of actions that both advance the task and expose model error as a dual control problem, showing that the cost of incorporating evidence into the twin sets the threshold at which probing pays off. On a dual-arm robot performing towel and toaster tasks, local revisions let execution continue without reconstruction, **one of them cutting the bread's rendered-depth residual from 22.4 to 1.5 mm**.

papers.title: When LLM Agents See a Conflict but Still Proceed: Cross-Domain Dependencies in Network Slicing
papers.abstract: Future AI-native networks are being designed to apply autonomous agents built on large language models (LLMs) in network management through intents. When intents from different domains meet on the same resource, an agent must recognize the cross-domain dependency before taking an irreversible action. We investigate this problem through a smart-grid use case, in which a power utility holds an active intent on a backup slice for protection traffic. This slice appears idle by design, which is precisely the profile targeted by a cost-reduction intent. We built a tool-based environment in which the dependency must be either queried by the agent or read from an inventory annotation, together with a negative control, and evaluated ten models from four different providers in 600 runs. Most models acted against the dependency they had observed: seven of the ten models removed the protection slice at least once after receiving the cross-domain dependency, and in the high-harm tier the slice was removed in 76% of the exposed runs, while four models practically never did. Only one of ten models never removed the slice. We identify two failure modes, not querying the dependency and querying it but proceeding anyway, and show that agents often reported no conflict after observing it. These results indicate that, in AI-native networks, visibility of cross-domain dependencies is not a sufficient safeguard, and that dependency verification should be enforced by the management architecture before irreversible actions rather than delegated to the LLM's judgment.
papers.summary: AI-native networks are being designed around large language model (LLM) agents that manage resources through intents, and when intents from different domains meet on the same resource the agent must recognize the cross-domain dependency before taking an irreversible action. A smart-grid case study has a power utility holding an active intent on a backup slice for protection traffic, which looks idle by design and is therefore exactly what a cost-reduction intent targets; a tool-based environment lets the dependency be queried or read from an inventory annotation, includes a negative control, and is used to evaluate ten models from four providers across 600 runs. **Seven of ten models removed the protection slice at least once after receiving the dependency, and in the high-harm tier the slice was removed in 76% of exposed runs**, while four models practically never did and only one never did. Two failure modes emerge, not querying the dependency and querying it but proceeding anyway, with agents often reporting no conflict after observing one, which leads to the recommendation that dependency verification be enforced by the management architecture before irreversible actions rather than delegated to the LLM's judgment.

papers.title: D2: High-Capability Full-Duplex Spoken Language Models from Half-Duplex Backbones
papers.abstract: Full-duplex spoken language models (FD-SLMs) support simultaneous listening and speaking, but often lag behind half-duplex spoken language models (HD-SLMs) in general capabilities. We propose Dialogue-to-Duplex (D2), a framework that converts pretrained HD-SLMs into high-capability FD-SLMs at fine temporal granularity. D2 adapts the original audio encoder to streaming through decoder-free representation distillation and learns full-duplex interaction through supervised fine-tuning. We systematically study the effects of chunk size on full-duplex interaction, general capabilities, and inference computation. We apply D2 to two distinct HD-SLM architectures, Qwen3-Omni and LLaMA-Omni 2. At a 12.5Hz update rate, Qwen3-Omni-D2 achieves 99.2% turn-taking success with 521-ms latency, 99.5% interruption success, and a state-of-the-art VoiceBench score of 70.1.
papers.summary: Full-duplex spoken language models (FD-SLMs) can listen and speak simultaneously but typically trail half-duplex spoken language models (HD-SLMs) in general capability. `D2` (Dialogue-to-Duplex) converts a pretrained HD-SLM into an FD-SLM at fine temporal granularity by adapting the original audio encoder to streaming through decoder-free representation distillation and then learning full-duplex interaction through supervised fine-tuning, alongside a systematic study of how chunk size trades off interaction quality, general capability, and inference compute. Applied to `Qwen3-Omni` and `LLaMA-Omni 2`, the method at a 12.5 Hz update rate yields **`Qwen3-Omni-D2` with 99.2% turn-taking success at 521 ms latency, 99.5% interruption success, and a state-of-the-art `VoiceBench` score of 70.1**.

papers.title: Who is the 'I' in AI? Establishing Decentralized Identity and Accountability for Autonomous Agents
papers.abstract: The rapid proliferation of autonomous AI agents in decentralized ecosystems challenges existing identity paradigms. While human identity is traditionally anchored in biological and/or self-asserted attributes and government credentials, AI agents lack a standardized definition of selfhood, creating critical gaps in trust and accountability. This paper introduces a novel framework for establishing Decentralized AI Identity rooted in Self-sovereign identity (SSI) principles. We propose a formal model that clearly distinguishes human users and AI agents, enabling distinct verification logic for each class while maintaining a unified identity calculus. The central to our contribution is the ABCD Framework, a multi-layered approach to agent identification and verification: (A) Algorithmic Fingerprint, which binds the identity to static model architectures and provenance; (B) Behavioural Fingerprint, which verifies dynamic performance metrics over time; (C) Cryptographic Identity, which anchors the agent via Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) and (D) Delegation, which cryptographically binds agent actions to respective human accountability. By orthogonalizing these dimensions, we model how systems can enforce granular trust policies ranging from simple authentication to complex liability assignment, thereby solving the black box identity problem in the autonomous economic activities of AI agents.
papers.summary: Autonomous AI agents operating in decentralized ecosystems have no standardized notion of identity, since human identity rests on biological or self-asserted attributes and government credentials that agents lack, leaving gaps in trust and accountability. The proposal grounds a Decentralized AI Identity in self-sovereign identity (SSI) principles with a formal model that separates human users from AI agents, applying distinct verification logic to each class within a unified identity calculus. Its core is the `ABCD Framework`: an Algorithmic Fingerprint binding identity to static model architecture and provenance, a Behavioural Fingerprint verifying dynamic performance metrics over time, a Cryptographic Identity anchored in Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs), and Delegation that cryptographically binds agent actions to an accountable human. **Treating these four dimensions as orthogonal lets systems enforce trust policies ranging from simple authentication to complex liability assignment** for agents engaged in autonomous economic activity.

papers.title: EvoQuantLab: Training-Free Dual-Loop Evolution for Auditable Quantitative Research
papers.abstract: Automated alpha factor discovery is critical for modern quantitative research. While large language models (LLMs) have increasingly been integrated into quantitative workflows, existing agent-based approaches remain highly susceptible to severe backtest overfitting. To address this challenge, we propose EvoQuantLab, a training-free, dual-loop self-evolving framework for robust factor discovery. Instead of relying entirely on LLM generation, EvoQuantLab deploys an inner genetic-programming (GP) loop that dramatically improves token efficiency while evolving typed factor expressions under structural and diversity constraints. An outer diagnosis loop then systematically audits evidence across cycles to drive protocol-level improvements. Furthermore, our evaluation pipeline applies multi-metric validation to rigorously filter out spurious factors before deployment. Extensive out-of-sample experiments across both daily and hourly frequencies -- covering equities and cryptocurrency -- demonstrate the robustness of EvoQuantLab. Specifically, on daily CSI 500 and S&P 500 tasks, EvoQuantLab achieves leading annualized returns of 18.34% and 21.30%, consistently outperforming existing agent baselines. On high-turnover hourly cryptocurrency data, EvoQuantLab delivers a 37.91% annualized return while effectively avoiding execution collapse.
papers.summary: Automated alpha factor discovery is central to quantitative research, but existing large language model (LLM) agent approaches suffer severe backtest overfitting. `EvoQuantLab` is a training-free, dual-loop self-evolving framework: an inner genetic programming (GP) loop evolves typed factor expressions under structural and diversity constraints, which cuts token usage relative to pure LLM generation, an outer diagnosis loop audits evidence across cycles to drive protocol-level improvements, and a multi-metric validation pipeline filters spurious factors before deployment. In out-of-sample tests across daily and hourly frequencies on equities and cryptocurrency, **it reaches annualized returns of 18.34% on `CSI 500` and 21.30% on `S&P 500`**, outperforming existing agent baselines, and delivers 37.91% annualized on high-turnover hourly cryptocurrency data while avoiding execution collapse.

papers.title: SonicWorld: Source-Centric Latent Dynamics for Spatial Audio Reasoning
papers.abstract: Dynamic spatial audio reasoning requires a model to associate changing acoustic observations with the correct source and recover its spatial state at a queried time or interval, a challenge intensified by overlapping speech and source motion. To study this problem, we introduce Sonic-Bench, comprising 2.8K first-order Ambisonics clips and 28.8K target-specific question-answer pairs across 480 simulated indoor scenes. The benchmark covers localization, distance estimation, and motion reasoning in single- and dual-source settings. We further propose SonicWorld, which integrates physical, learned acoustic, and semantic features into persistent source states through learned transitions and recurrent updates, and projects them into an Omni LLM for spatial reasoning. Compared with Spatial-Omni on the Sonic-Bench test split, SonicWorld improves direction accuracy from 31.98% to 34.69% and reduces azimuth error from 57.22{\deg} to 48.01{\deg}. In zero-shot transfer to Spatial LibriSpeech, SonicWorld retains strong localization performance, achieving 73.98% direction accuracy and 19.29{\deg} azimuth error, compared with 27.14% and 70.74{\deg} for Spatial-Omni.
papers.summary: Dynamic spatial audio reasoning asks a model to tie changing acoustic observations to the correct sound source and recover its location, distance, or motion at a queried time, which overlapping speech and moving sources make harder. The authors build `Sonic-Bench`, 2.8K first-order Ambisonics clips with 28.8K target-specific question-answer pairs over 480 simulated indoor scenes, and propose `SonicWorld`, which fuses physical, learned acoustic, and semantic features into persistent per-source states via learned transitions and recurrent updates before projecting them into an Omni large language model. Against `Spatial-Omni` it lifts direction accuracy from 31.98% to 34.69% and cuts azimuth error from 57.22° to 48.01° on the benchmark, and **in zero-shot transfer to `Spatial LibriSpeech` it reaches 73.98% direction accuracy and 19.29° azimuth error versus 27.14% and 70.74° for the baseline**.

papers.title: The Format is the Filter: Scoring Format Fixes What an LLM Judge Can Express
papers.abstract: When an LLM judge filters instruction-tuning data, its scoring format (binary verdict, 1--5 rating, 0--100 score, or comparison) is rarely justified or ablated. Holding the candidate pool, judge prompt, decoding and selection budget fixed, we score 15,406 UltraFeedback candidates under five formats with three judges, curate, fine-tune 66 models, and evaluate them with four judges. A 0--100 scale is worth only 7--12 equally used levels, two to three times a 1--5 scale rather than twenty, and a binary verdict leaves the top score tied in 77--78\% of prompts, so most selections are made at random. These properties are set by the format almost independently of the judge. Kendall's $\tau_b$ hides them: it ranks binary best while $\tau_a$ and top-1 agreement rank it last, because it discounts the ties a selector must break at random. Both comparative formats inherit a slot bias whose sign differs across judges. Downstream, curated data beat random selection under every evaluation judge, robust to length and markdown adjustment, but no ordering among formats is detectable. We propose four quantities that judge-based curation pipelines should report.
papers.summary: When a large language model (LLM) judge filters instruction-tuning data, its scoring format is rarely justified or ablated, so the authors hold the candidate pool, judge prompt, decoding, and selection budget fixed, score 15,406 `UltraFeedback` candidates under five formats with three judges, fine-tune 66 models, and evaluate them with four judges. **A 0–100 scale yields only 7 to 12 equally used levels, and a binary verdict leaves the top score tied on 77–78% of prompts, so most selections are made at random**, with these properties set by the format almost independently of the judge. Kendall's tau-b hides the tie problem by ranking binary best while tau-a and top-1 agreement rank it last, and both comparative formats carry a slot bias whose sign differs across judges. Downstream, curated data beat random selection under every evaluation judge, robust to length and markdown adjustment, but no ordering among formats is detectable, and the authors propose four quantities that judge-based curation pipelines should report.

papers.title: Force-Modulated Dexterity: Unified Compliance for Contact-Rich Manipulation
papers.abstract: Teleoperation is widely used to collect high-quality demonstrations for robot learning. Dexterous manipulation, however, requires coordinated control of motion and contact forces. Operators can specify motion, but struggle to reproduce the subtle force adjustments of human manipulation without feeling the robot's contacts. We introduce Force-Modulated Dexterity (FOMO-Dex), a unified compliance formulation for contact-rich manipulation. FOMO-Dex expresses nominal actions in coordinates defined by task geometry and contact structure. It applies force-driven motion corrections along selected directions while leaving the remaining command components unchanged. Across card picking, paper cutting, screwdriving, and nut-and-bolt assembly, FOMO-Dex reduces excessive contact forces compared with stiff control. A user study shows that operators collect more successful demonstration data per hour after brief practice. For policy learning, imitating the corrected actions improves card-picking success over imitating raw operator commands. Policies trained on FOMO-Dex demonstrations also achieve more rotation in nut-and-bolt manipulation and screwdriving than those trained on demonstrations collected with the stiff controller. Videos are shown on https://yingyuan0414.github.io/fomo-dex/ .
papers.summary: Teleoperators can specify robot motion but struggle to reproduce the subtle force adjustments that contact-rich dexterous manipulation requires, because they cannot feel the robot's contacts. Force-Modulated Dexterity (`FOMO-Dex`) is a unified compliance formulation that expresses nominal actions in coordinates defined by task geometry and contact structure, applying force-driven motion corrections along selected directions while leaving the remaining command components unchanged. Across card picking, paper cutting, screwdriving, and nut-and-bolt assembly it reduces excessive contact forces relative to stiff control, and **a user study shows operators collect more successful demonstrations per hour after brief practice**. Policies that imitate the corrected actions improve card-picking success over imitating raw operator commands, and policies trained on `FOMO-Dex` demonstrations achieve more rotation in nut-and-bolt and screwdriving tasks than those trained with the stiff controller.

papers.title: Learning Perceptual Geometry of Natural Odor Mixtures from LLM-Derived Descriptors
papers.abstract: The relationship between odor chemistry and perception remains incompletely understood. Many existing studies focus on the perception of single molecules, whereas natural odors contain tens to hundreds of components, adding extra layer of complexity to percept formation. Here, we explore the relationship between molecular composition and perceived similarity in natural odor objects. We study this using a database of more than 1,200 volatile-compound-in-food mixtures containing more than 8,000 molecular components, and use large language models (LLMs) as a scalable surrogate for deriving mixture-level perceptual descriptions. We find that language-derived representations provide useful supervision for predicting held-out mixture similarities from molecular composition. The prediction was consistently strongest when perceptual targets were derived from chemosensory prompts than from other sensory prompts. Further, during the mixture-level training, we learned low-rank molecular embeddings that enabled better prediction of held-out mixture similarities than component-overlap metrics, even for mixture pairs with no shared molecules. Although no single-molecule labels were used during training, the learned molecular geometry showed significant alignment with the independent human odor-descriptor space. Finally, we explored the use of external molecular features in our mixture-similarity prediction task. These features showed modest zero-shot alignment with mixture-level perceptual similarity. They improved prediction under limited supervision but offered little additional predictive benefit with the full training set. Together, these results show that language-derived descriptions can provide scalable supervision for predicting the perceptual organization of complex natural mixtures, contributing to a quantitative understanding of how molecular composition gives rise to odor perception.
papers.summary: The link between odor chemistry and perception is poorly understood for natural odors, which contain tens to hundreds of components rather than the single molecules most studies examine. Using a database of more than 1,200 volatile-compound-in-food mixtures spanning over 8,000 molecular components, the authors use large language models (LLMs) as a scalable surrogate to derive mixture-level perceptual descriptions and train models to predict held-out mixture similarities from molecular composition. Language-derived targets provide useful supervision, strongest when derived from chemosensory rather than other sensory prompts, and **the low-rank molecular embeddings learned during mixture-level training predict held-out similarities better than component-overlap metrics even for mixture pairs sharing no molecules**, while aligning significantly with the independent human odor-descriptor space despite no single-molecule labels being used. External molecular features show modest zero-shot alignment and help under limited supervision but add little with the full training set.

papers.title: Generative Flow on Symbolic Abstractions for Embodiment Capability Discovery
papers.abstract: Achieving complex, long-horizon robot behavior remains challenging because successful execution depends on skills grounded in a robot's physical affordances. Existing training-task distributions are often handcrafted or sampled from large language models (LLMs), relying on semantic plausibility rather than embodiment-specific feasibility. This mismatch can produce curricula that are too difficult, redundant, or blind to non-obvious but learnable behaviors. We propose Generative Flow on Symbolic Abstractions (FOSA), a framework for discovering embodiment-specific capabilities by learning a grounded task generator. FOSA parameterizes an abstract policy as a Generative Flow Network that constructs symbolic task skeletons. Each skeleton is compiled into a simulation environment, where low-level policy-learning performance provides the reward signal for the abstract policy. Across heterogeneous robot platforms, FOSA discovers diverse and executable tasks near the robot's empirical capability frontier. After distilling the discovered task policies into a single language-conditioned policy, FOSA improves performance on unseen complex and long-horizon tasks. The code and demonstration videos are available at https://www.youwei-yu.com/fosa.
papers.summary: Long-horizon robot behavior depends on skills grounded in the robot's physical affordances, yet training-task distributions are usually handcrafted or sampled from large language models (LLMs) on semantic plausibility rather than embodiment-specific feasibility, producing curricula that are too difficult, redundant, or blind to non-obvious learnable behaviors. Generative Flow on Symbolic Abstractions (`FOSA`) learns a grounded task generator by parameterizing an abstract policy as a Generative Flow Network that constructs symbolic task skeletons, each compiled into a simulation environment where low-level policy-learning performance provides the reward for the abstract policy. Across heterogeneous robot platforms it discovers diverse, executable tasks near each robot's empirical capability frontier, and **distilling the discovered task policies into a single language-conditioned policy improves performance on unseen complex, long-horizon tasks**.

papers.title: ChemExplain: A Multimodal Benchmark for Explanatory Chemical Reasoning
papers.abstract: Current chemistry benchmarks primarily evaluate outcome prediction or reaction pathway generation, but rarely test whether a model can explain why an observed chemical effect occurs. We introduce ChemExplain, a benchmark of 1,180 multiple-choice chemistry questions drawn from 383 peer-reviewed papers. Each question pairs a molecular or reaction image with an observed chemical effect and four candidate explanations, each associated with a different structural feature visible in the image. Answering requires the model to perceive the depicted structure, apply chemical knowledge, and identify which feature most directly explains the effect, a capability we term explanatory attribution. The correct feature-mechanism relation is derived from supporting evidence in the source paper rather than invented by the question-generation LLM. We construct the benchmark automatically with a multi-agent framework that applies progressive quality control at three stages and validate it with eight chemistry domain experts. The strongest evaluated model reaches 78.6% accuracy, leaving considerable room for improvement. On a 600-question expert-reviewed subset, reasoning-trace analysis classifies 71.4% of the strongest model's errors as attribution failures. Attribution is also the largest error category for the open-source and chemistry-specific models included in our analysis.
papers.summary: Chemistry benchmarks mostly evaluate outcome prediction or reaction pathway generation rather than whether a model can explain why an observed chemical effect occurs. `ChemExplain` contains 1,180 multiple-choice questions drawn from 383 peer-reviewed papers, each pairing a molecular or reaction image with an observed effect and four candidate explanations tied to different structural features visible in the image, so answering requires perceiving the structure, applying chemical knowledge, and attributing the effect to the right feature, with the correct relation derived from evidence in the source paper. The benchmark is constructed automatically by a multi-agent framework with three-stage quality control and validated by eight chemistry domain experts. **The strongest evaluated model reaches 78.6% accuracy**, and on a 600-question expert-reviewed subset 71.4% of its errors are attribution failures, which is also the largest error category for the open-source and chemistry-specific models analyzed.

papers.title: FreeSolo: Linear-time Sparse Attention with Zero-Shot Length Extrapolation
papers.abstract: Linear-time sequence models typically store long-context information in a recurrent state. A fixed-size state limits how much information can be stored, while hybrid architectures that add full attention for better recall incur quadratic sequence cost. Alternatively, sparse attention with continued pretraining (CPT) can extend the effective context length. Generalization beyond the trained length remains challenging, however, and CPT can be costly. We introduce FreeSolo, a native sparse attention mechanism with a short-range sliding window branch and a long-range branch that selects keypoint cells for direct token attention. Its linear-time variant, FS-L, learns to prune the prefix before query-dependent selection through short CPT. FS-B searches balanced trees with $O(N\log^2 N)$ algorithmic cost including radix-sort construction. FreeSolo demonstrates better zero-shot length extrapolation than the baselines without long-context fine-tuning.
papers.summary: Linear-time sequence models store long-context information in a fixed-size recurrent state that limits recall, hybrids that add full attention pay quadratic cost, and sparse attention with continued pretraining (CPT) is expensive and generalizes poorly beyond the trained length. `FreeSolo` is a native sparse attention mechanism that pairs a short-range sliding-window branch with a long-range branch selecting keypoint cells for direct token attention. Its linear-time variant `FS-L` learns to prune the prefix before query-dependent selection through short CPT, while `FS-B` searches balanced trees at O(N log² N) algorithmic cost including radix-sort construction. **Both variants show better zero-shot length extrapolation than the baselines without any long-context fine-tuning.**

papers.title: Size Generalization for Diffusion Routing Solvers
papers.abstract: Routing problems, like the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) and the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP), are NP-hard and slow to solve for large instances. Diffusion-based solvers can be trained in a supervised way using sets of optimal solutions, and then quickly solve new test instances. However, for large instances, optimal solutions are hard to find, and diffusion models fail to generalize to instance sizes outside their training distribution. Here we describe ResizeCO, a label free size-generalization approach that addresses both the change in statistical properties of larger instances, and the computational challenge of solving them quickly. It uses reinforcement learning on large-scale instances to adapt a diffusion model trained on small instances. Specifically, we adapt GRPO to this problem, using route length as the training signal. ResizeCO also formulates k-opt as a tree search, solved by a beam search on the GPU. In size-generalization experiments on TSP and CVRP instances with up to 10000 nodes, ResizeCO achieves a Pareto front over route quality and time that dominates learned solvers, and also outperforms other solvers at short run times, setting a new state of the art.
papers.summary: Diffusion-based solvers for the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) and the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP) learn from optimal solutions to small instances but fail to generalize to larger sizes, where optimal labels are hard to obtain. `ResizeCO` is a label-free size-generalization method that adapts a small-instance diffusion model to large instances with reinforcement learning, specifically a variant of `GRPO` using route length as the training signal, and reformulates k-opt local search as a tree search solved by beam search on the GPU. **On TSP and CVRP instances with up to 10,000 nodes, it achieves a Pareto front over route quality and time that dominates learned solvers** and also outperforms other solvers at short run times.

papers.title: Deleting Code Without Losing Knowledge: Regenerative Software for Python Libraries
papers.abstract: In the age of "Software 3.0", when a complete program can be rewritten in minutes by an agent, the traditional approach of relying on code as the sole source of truth becomes questionable. Fowler advocated for a set of seven primitives, which lay the framework for regenerative software, so that programs can be deleted and rebuilt without losing their knowledge. The knowledge lives in machine-readable records in a tracked directory, from which a *regeneration bundle* is built for each unit. The regeneration bundle is a single file with the module's architecture, intent, decisions, public contract, evaluations, and consumers, but no implementation, plus the one dependency module it may import. The open-source package spotregen implements these primitives and provides a graphical user interface. This report presents a first application of Fowler's primitives to the safety-critical forecasting library spotforecast2-safe. During the first experiments, the Claude Code session that orchestrated the study consumed more than 43 million tokens, almost all of them its own history re-sent with every request. This motivated the switch to an architecture that is built on local models. Deterministic checks and the maintainer judged the results. The report contains executable examples for every primitive. Each example runs spotregen against the repository or against a throw-away copy of it.
papers.summary: When an agent can rewrite a complete program in minutes, treating code as the sole source of truth becomes questionable, so the authors apply Fowler's seven primitives for regenerative software, in which machine-readable records in a tracked directory are compiled into a per-module regeneration bundle holding architecture, intent, decisions, public contract, evaluations, and consumers but no implementation. The open-source package `spotregen` implements these primitives with a graphical user interface, and the report applies them to the safety-critical forecasting library `spotforecast2-safe`, with executable examples for every primitive run against the repository or a throw-away copy. **The `Claude Code` session orchestrating the first experiments consumed more than 43 million tokens, almost all from re-sending its own history with every request, which motivated a switch to an architecture built on local models.** Deterministic checks and the maintainer judged the results.

papers.title: Releasing the Inner Jev: A Simple Recipe for Open Decision Models
papers.abstract: LLM-based decision-making systems, also called System One models, have recently gained popularity, most notably through Jev (Almeida, 2026). Given a typed input state, a question, and a set of options, they return a probability for each option in a single forward pass, without text generation. We show that existing open instruction-tuned language models can achieve comparable performance \textit{without any additional training}, by reading out answers from letters (A, B, C, etc.) in the model's output logits at the last token position. Furthermore, we show how a simple supervised fine-tuning recipe can improve their performance further. We evaluate four open instruction-tuned language models: Gemma 4 31B, Gemma 4 12B, Qwen3.6-27B, and Qwen3.5-4B. We fine-tune each using LoRA and a decision head initialized from a slice of the language model head. Furthermore, we introduce OpenDecisions, a novel 2,352-question validation dataset designed to reflect the task composition of JevBench (JevBench main- tainers, 2026) and which computes a Capability score based on accuracy and calibration metrics. Without fine-tuning, Gemma 4 31B scores 79.6 on OpenDecisions, compared to Jev's 80.1. After undergoing our fine-tuning recipe, it scores 84.4 on OpenDecisions and 81.5 on JevBench v1.7, outperforming Jev by 4.3 and 4.4 Capability points respectively and setting a new state-of-the-art on OpenDecisions. On a suite of public decision datasets, our models achieve accuracy comparable to Jev, with lower calibration error. Our results show that open language models already possess System One capabilities, and with simple fine-tuning they outperform Jev on a wide range of decision tasks. We release our models, serving code, and OpenDecisions.
papers.summary: LLM-based decision-making systems, called System One models and popularized by `Jev`, take a typed input state, a question, and a set of options and return a probability for each option in a single forward pass without text generation. The authors show that existing open instruction-tuned models match this without any additional training by reading answers from the option-letter logits at the last token position, and that a simple supervised fine-tuning recipe using LoRA and a decision head initialized from a slice of the language-model head improves them further. They evaluate `Gemma 4 31B`, `Gemma 4 12B`, `Qwen3.6-27B`, and `Qwen3.5-4B` and introduce `OpenDecisions`, a 2,352-question validation set mirroring the task composition of `JevBench` with a Capability score combining accuracy and calibration. Untuned `Gemma 4 31B` scores 79.6 on `OpenDecisions` against `Jev`'s 80.1, and **after fine-tuning it reaches 84.4 on `OpenDecisions` and 81.5 on `JevBench` v1.7, beating `Jev` by 4.3 and 4.4 Capability points**, with models, serving code, and the dataset released.

papers.title: AutoMARS: Automatic and Scalable Multi-Agent Large Language Model Framework for Supply Chain Risk Assessment
papers.abstract: We propose AutoMARS (Automatic Multi-Agent Risk Assessment), an agentic framework for automatic and scalable comparative risk assessment in supply chain networks. The framework enables end-to-end execution of analytical workflows by automatically planning tasks, coordinating specialized agents, invoking external analytical tools, and synthesizing domain-specific results into integrated risk evaluations. AutoMARS further supports scalable risk comparison across multiple locations by parallelizing independent analytical tasks. The framework adopts a multi-domain, multi-agent, and multi-tool architecture that integrates heterogeneous risk factors from socioeconomic, disaster, environmental, and transportation domains. Through coordinated agent interactions and tool integration, AutoMARS enables structured, systematic, and interpretable comparative analysis to support supply chain risk-aware location evaluation.
papers.summary: Comparative risk assessment across candidate supply chain locations requires combining heterogeneous factors from socioeconomic, disaster, environmental, and transportation domains. Automatic Multi-Agent Risk Assessment (`AutoMARS`) is an agentic framework that plans analytical tasks, coordinates specialized agents, invokes external analytical tools, and synthesizes domain-specific results into integrated risk evaluations, **parallelizing independent analytical tasks to scale comparison across many locations**. The multi-domain, multi-agent, multi-tool architecture is intended to yield structured, systematic, and interpretable comparisons that support risk-aware location evaluation.

papers.title: Compute-optimal data scaling for neural surrogates via multi-fidelity training
papers.abstract: Neural surrogates for Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) are usually trained on synthetic data from numerical simulators. As models grow and scaling laws demand larger datasets, the cost of data generation often outweighs the training cost and becomes the bottleneck in the scaling quest. Unlike data in other domains, however, each PDE sample has a tunable cost that depends on its numerical fidelity, with the resulting cost-accuracy trade-off governed by known convergence rates. We exploit this property by formalizing neural surrogate training as a function of both data quantity and fidelity under a fixed data generation compute budget, treating fidelity as a fine-grained discrete spectrum rather than a binary distinction. Building on this, we show that multi-fidelity training enables Pareto-optimal error scaling against data generation compute. By using simulations at lower fidelities as an additional training signal, training on the optimal fidelity mixture matches the accuracy of high-fidelity-only training, with up to $6.3\times$ less data generation compute across our settings. We validate these findings across six PDE problems spanning structured grids and unstructured meshes, two distinct error sources (discretization and iterative-solver error), and four surrogate architectures, totaling over 7,000 training runs.
papers.summary: Neural surrogates for partial differential equations (PDEs) train on synthetic simulator data, and as scaling laws demand larger datasets, data generation rather than training becomes the cost bottleneck. Unlike other domains, each PDE sample has a tunable cost set by its numerical fidelity, with a cost-accuracy trade-off governed by known convergence rates. The authors formalize surrogate training as a function of both data quantity and fidelity under a fixed data-generation budget, treating fidelity as a fine-grained discrete spectrum, and show that multi-fidelity training gives Pareto-optimal error scaling against generation compute. **Training on the optimal fidelity mixture matches high-fidelity-only accuracy with up to 6.3× less data-generation compute**, validated across six PDE problems on structured grids and unstructured meshes, two error sources, and four surrogate architectures over more than 7,000 training runs.

papers.title: IsoVRBench: Video Reward Modeling Without Human Feedback
papers.abstract: Video reward models are trained and evaluated on human preferences between videos that often differ simultaneously on properties such as prompt alignment, visual fidelity, motion, and generator identity. As a result, aggregate accuracy does not reveal which video properties a reward model can reliably distinguish. We construct preference pairs by controlled interventions that change one property of a generated video while holding the rest fixed. The resulting pairs, by construction, provide preferences for how the videos differ along a specific dimension, without requiring any human annotation. We propose IsoVRBench, a video generation reward modeling benchmark of 8,000 such pairs across eight interventions, and show that state-of-the-art models separate broad quality differences between generators but miss important features such as temporal order. The best reward model reaches only 60.8% on reordered frames against 100% for humans, and rankings on existing benchmarks do not predict this failure. Using the synthetic isolated intervation pairs as training data leads to 1) IsoVRM, a reward model outperforming its counterpart trained with a larger human labeled preference dataset by 3.8 points on VBench-2.0, 2) IsoWan, the video generator post-trained with IsoVRM, outperforming its human-data counterpart in human preferences, and 3) gains that stack when combined with human data. Because intervention pairs are automatically generated rather than collected, the benchmark and training data can be easily extended as generators evolve.
papers.summary: Video reward models are trained and evaluated on human preferences between videos that differ in several properties at once, so aggregate accuracy does not reveal which properties a model can reliably distinguish. `IsoVRBench` builds 8,000 preference pairs through controlled interventions that change one property of a generated video while holding the rest fixed, across eight interventions and without any human annotation. **State-of-the-art reward models separate broad quality differences between generators, but the best reaches only 60.8% on reordered frames where humans score 100%**, a failure that rankings on existing benchmarks do not predict. Training on the synthetic pairs yields `IsoVRM`, which beats a counterpart trained on a larger human-labeled dataset by 3.8 points on `VBench-2.0`, and `IsoWan`, a video generator post-trained with it that humans prefer over its human-data counterpart, with gains that stack when combined with human data.

papers.title: From Conceptual EneMonIE to an Executable Backend: A Modular Architecture for Energy Information Extractionand Grounded Question Answering
papers.abstract: The original EneMonIE proposal describes a Web-based semantic system for continuously monitoring energy trends through targeted information extraction from heterogeneous online media. This article presents EneMonIE-Backend, an implementation-derived redesign that converts that conceptual pipeline into a modular, executable, and application-independent backend. The architecture separates five concerns: data sources, acquisition and normalization, semantic processing, knowledge organization, and persistent storage. It operationalizes configurable connectors for RSS feeds, URL collections, arXiv, social-media JSON files, and open-data CSV files; it also introduces question-driven Web search and scraping. Relevant documents pass through energy categorization, named entity recognition, temporal and event extraction, source sensitive sentiment analysis, and extractive summarization. The resulting semantic representations support entity co-occurrence graphs, cross-document interlinking, cluster-level information fusion, and relational persistence in SQLite. Three grounded question-answering paths are exposed at the backend level: live Web evidence, the stored corpus, and selected configured resources. Answer generation uses a language model when configured and otherwise falls back to deterministic extractive output. Unlike the original proposal, the presented architecture deliberately excludes the user-interface and server-side application layers, allowing the semantic core to be embedded in different applications. A deterministic smoke validation confirms relevance filtering, persistence, clustering, evidence retrieval, and document deletion. The work provides a reproducible architectural basis for future evaluation on larger multilingual energy corpora.
papers.summary: The original `EneMonIE` proposal described a Web-based semantic system for monitoring energy trends by extracting information from heterogeneous online media. `EneMonIE-Backend` converts that conceptual pipeline into a modular, executable, application-independent backend that separates data sources, acquisition and normalization, semantic processing, knowledge organization, and persistent storage, with connectors for RSS feeds, URL collections, arXiv, social-media JSON, and open-data CSV files plus question-driven Web search and scraping. Documents pass through energy categorization, named entity recognition, temporal and event extraction, source-sensitive sentiment analysis, and extractive summarization to build entity co-occurrence graphs and cross-document links stored in SQLite, and **three grounded question-answering paths over live Web evidence, the stored corpus, or configured resources use a language model when configured and otherwise fall back to deterministic extractive output**. A deterministic smoke validation confirms relevance filtering, persistence, clustering, evidence retrieval, and document deletion, with evaluation on larger multilingual corpora left for future work.

papers.title: Does a Governed Confidence Score Know When a Text-to-SQL Answer Is Right? An Exploratory Study on BIRD and a Pre-registered Confirmation on Spider
papers.abstract: Conversational analytics lets people ask questions of records spread across many systems and get answers in plain language; it is useful only if each answer can be trusted and explained. A production system of this kind attaches a confidence score to every answer it writes over a database and uses it to show the answer, show it with a warning, or withhold it. The score's weights, caps and thresholds were set by design. This paper audits that design. On the 1,534 questions of BIRD dev, answered by GPT-5.1 with a benchmark-adapted production prompt and five samples per question, the designed score separates right from wrong answers weakly (AUROC 0.624, 95% CI 0.595-0.652) and withholds 35.7% of correct answers. Nearly all of its ranking signal comes from agreement among the samples, and most of it is lost where agreement is combined by a minimum with a checklist that drops to zero on any unsupported claim, including claims in commentary. We froze a rule in which agreement with the shown answer is the score and deterministic checks act as vetoes and caps, and pre-registered a test on Spider dev before any Spider answer existed. The primary hypothesis held: AUROC rose from 0.566 to 0.725 (paired difference +0.159, 95% CI +0.097 to +0.221), and correct answers withheld fell from 49.0% to 8.8% with PASS accuracy 95.7%. Under one matching policy the choice of agreement statistic matters little; the gain comes from how agreement enters the score. Whether added checks help depends on how correctness is defined, while they always cost unqualified coverage. A pre-registered empty-result check did not meet its effect-size criterion on Spider. Correctness here means the core answer; labels are model-judged, and a blinded two-person audit, not yet complete, will be reported in a revised version.
papers.summary: A production conversational-analytics system attaches a hand-designed confidence score to every answer it writes over a database and uses it to show the answer, show it with a warning, or withhold it, and the authors audit that design. On the 1,534 questions of `BIRD` dev answered by `GPT-5.1` with five samples each, the designed score separates right from wrong answers weakly, with AUROC 0.624, and withholds 35.7% of correct answers, because nearly all of its ranking signal comes from agreement among samples and most of that is lost when agreement is combined by a minimum with a checklist that drops to zero on any unsupported claim. They froze a rule in which agreement with the shown answer is the score and deterministic checks act only as vetoes and caps, then pre-registered a test on `Spider` dev before any Spider answer existed. **AUROC rose from 0.566 to 0.725 and correct answers withheld fell from 49.0% to 8.8%** with 95.7% accuracy on passed answers, while a pre-registered empty-result check missed its effect-size criterion and labels remain model-judged pending a blinded two-person audit.

papers.title: RL Post-Training Diffusion Language Models Along Their Own Generation Paths
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models are a promising and more efficient alternative to autoregressive models. However, most RL post-training techniques are not easily adapted to these models. One issue is that diffusion language models generate answers through many intermediate states, deciding at each step which masked positions to reveal and which tokens to place in them. Many existing RL methods used in this setting approximate intractable sequence likelihoods or weight every denoising step by the same advantage, without explicitly distinguishing how these intermediate states of the denoising trajectory affect the expected reward. To address this issue of trajectory blindness, we introduce PACT (Potential-Anchored Consistency of Transitions). Motivated by a reward-tilted reference distribution, PACT jointly learns the policy and a scalar potential that scores each intermediate state, anchored by terminal reward. For each sampled denoising transition, a consistency loss matches the policy-to-reference log-probability ratio of revealed tokens to the change in this potential. This formulation requires neither sequence-likelihood estimation nor importance-ratio clipping. On four tasks, PACT improves LLaDA-8B-Instruct by +9.9 points on GSM8K, +12.0 on MATH500, +55.7 on Countdown, and +72.6 on Sudoku, and reaches the best average accuracy across the four tasks reported for this model, +3.7 points over the next best method. Further compared to AGRPO, it reaches that baseline's best accuracy in about half the training compute on GSM8K.
papers.summary: Diffusion language models generate answers through many intermediate denoising states, yet most reinforcement learning post-training methods either approximate intractable sequence likelihoods or weight every denoising step by the same advantage, ignoring how intermediate states affect expected reward. Potential-Anchored Consistency of Transitions (`PACT`) jointly learns the policy and a scalar potential that scores each intermediate state, anchored by terminal reward, and for each sampled denoising transition a consistency loss matches the policy-to-reference log-probability ratio of revealed tokens to the change in that potential, requiring neither sequence-likelihood estimation nor importance-ratio clipping. **On `LLaDA-8B-Instruct` it adds +9.9 points on `GSM8K`, +12.0 on `MATH500`, +55.7 on `Countdown`, and +72.6 on `Sudoku`**, the best reported average across the four tasks for this model by 3.7 points, and it matches `AGRPO`'s best `GSM8K` accuracy in about half the training compute.

papers.title: Measuring Learned Equivariance: An Information Theoretic Approach
papers.abstract: Learning symmetries through data augmentation offers an alternative to architectural equivariance, but does not guarantee that a network respects those symmetries.
