Experiments show **competitive or improved accuracy compared to state-of-the-art equivariant methods at significantly lower computational cost**, and the paper analyzes how equivariance and invariance differ in their effects on robustness and flexibility.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning In Partially Verifiable Environments for Colon Cancer Treatment Planning
papers.abstract: Clinical decision-making is a sequential process of information collection, clinical inference, and forecasting under partial observability, often without a uniquely correct treatment decision. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong medical question-answering capabilities but extending these advances to clinical reasoning remains challenging because many clinical tasks are only partially verifiable. Recent clinical reinforcement learning (RL) work has therefore largely focused on diagnostic endpoints, where correctness can be more directly verified. Oncology treatment decision making is a particularly challenging instance of this problem that extends beyond medical question-answering in which multiple decision trajectories can be clinically defensible for the same partially observed patient state. We formulate oncology treatment planning as an interactive RL problem under partial observability and construct patient-specific, process-aware rewards from decision processes observed in real world clinical records. The agent must learn to sequentially acquire information from a structured patient representation before committing to a first-line treatment recommendation, and is evaluated on information gathering, treatment selection, and reasoning alignment. Using GRPO and GDPO to optimize Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct within this environment, RL substantially improves the base policy beyond frontier model capabilities. The GDPO-trained policy increases Mean@3 scalar clinical reward by $79.60\%$ over base Llama and exceeds GPT-5.2 by $18.82\%$ under the same interactive environment, while reducing query count during training. Overall, our results show that patient-specific, partially verifiable rewards can provide an effective learning signal for interactive clinical RL when both the patient state and the underlying clinical decision process are only partially observed.
papers.summary: Oncology treatment planning is a sequential decision process under partial observability in which several treatment trajectories can be clinically defensible, so correctness cannot be fully verified and recent clinical reinforcement learning (RL) work has mostly targeted diagnostic endpoints. The authors formulate first-line colon cancer treatment planning as an interactive RL environment in which an agent must query a structured patient representation to gather information before recommending treatment, with patient-specific, process-aware rewards derived from real clinical records that score information gathering, treatment selection, and reasoning alignment. Training `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct` with `GRPO` and `GDPO`, the `GDPO` policy **raises Mean@3 clinical reward by 79.60% over the base model and exceeds `GPT-5.2` by 18.82%** in the same environment while reducing query count during training.

papers.title: World-T3: Test-Time Training as Persistent Memory for Real-Time Video World Models
papers.abstract: Recent advances in video world models have enabled plausible interactive environments, yet long-horizon generation places a fundamental demand on visual memory: the previously observed world must remain consistent as the model continues to generate. Existing autoregressive approaches often implicitly rely on the generative model itself to retain such information, leading to spatial memory decay beyond the active context. We introduce World-T3, a camera-controlled video world model with a test-time training memory that consolidates past observations into dedicated model parameters. To robustly update this memory, we propose a recursive least-squares rule that incrementally absorbs novel visual features via online pose-keyed memory updates. Our TTT memory reads out previously observed scene features from the fast-weight state by camera pose, enabling consistent generation with constant storage and per-step computation regardless of rollout length. To facilitate real-time interactive generation with this robust memory, we further distill the autoregressive model into a few-step generator via dual-teacher distribution matching. On a long-horizon revisit benchmark, World-T3 raises revisit PSNR from 13.52 to 18.31 dB and reduces absolute rotation error from 3.344 to 1.075 relative to the strongest baseline on both metrics, while sustaining 20.6 FPS at 1280 x 704 on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU.
papers.summary: Autoregressive video world models lose track of previously observed scenes once those observations fall outside the active context, so revisited locations drift during long rollouts. `World-T3` is a camera-controlled video world model with a test-time training (TTT) memory that consolidates past observations into fast-weight parameters through a recursive least-squares update keyed by camera pose, so previously seen scene features can be read back with constant storage and per-step compute regardless of rollout length. The autoregressive model is also distilled into a few-step generator via dual-teacher distribution matching, and on a long-horizon revisit benchmark it **raises revisit PSNR from 13.52 to 18.31 dB and cuts absolute rotation error from 3.344 to 1.075** versus the strongest baseline while sustaining 20.6 FPS at 1280 x 704 on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU.

papers.title: SchemaWeaver: Accelerating On-Device Mobile Agentic AI via Schema-Guided Parallel LLM Decoding
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) on mobile devices can act as agents that call external software tools to complete complex tasks, but the major challenge of supporting on-device mobile agentic AI with LLMs is the long latency of LLM tool calling on mobile devices. In particular, the decode phase is the main contributor of such long latency, but is hard to speed up on mobile processors as it is bound by memory bandwidth rather than compute power. To address this limitation, in this paper we present SchemaWeaver, a new on-device mobile agentic AI technique that enforces schema-guided parallel decoding in the decode phase of LLM tool calling, to reduce its latency by producing multiple tokens in each decode pass. SchemaWeaver can be generically applied to the LLM inference engine on mobile devices without involving any training efforts or changes on LLMs, and our experiment results on major mobile SoCs and LLM families show that SchemaWeaver can reduce the LLM tool calling latency by up to 3.9 times, compared to the competitive baselines.
papers.summary: On-device large language model (LLM) agents on phones suffer long tool-calling latency, dominated by the decode phase, which is bound by memory bandwidth rather than compute on mobile processors. The technique applies schema-guided parallel decoding to tool calls: because the structure of a call is constrained by its tool schema, the inference engine can emit multiple tokens per decode pass, with no training and no changes to the model, so it plugs into existing mobile inference engines. Experiments across major mobile systems-on-chip and several LLM families show it **reduces tool-calling latency by up to 3.9 times** over competitive baselines.

papers.title: Large Language Models Extend Known Research But Do Not Create New Research Directions
papers.abstract: The success of autonomous research systems relies on the quality of the scientific hypotheses they generate. Recent studies report that human reviewers often rate LLM-generated ideas as more novel than those from human experts, raising hope that AI can accelerate scientific discovery. Yet it is unclear whether these models can do more than extend existing knowledge. Can LLMs drive genuine innovation by revealing new research directions, or are they limited to repeating and recombining what science already knows? This unresolved question lies at the heart of discussions about AI and the future of science. To address this, we distinguish two types of novelty: distance, which measures how far a hypothesis lies from existing work, and direction, which captures whether the hypothesis pursues new lines of inquiry beyond those already present. These two measures diverge sharply for LLM-generated work. We represent scientific papers in a shared conceptual space using a pretrained scientific-paper embedding model. Within this space, we embed 26.9 million human-authored papers across 1,325 research topics in six natural-science fields and 524,308 LLM-generated hypotheses from eight models. Distance is measured using existing metrics. To quantify direction, we introduce the orthogonal novelty score (ONS). LLMs consistently generate ideas more distant from existing work than human-authored papers, up to 16\% further when the LLM is given the papers farthest from the centre of the topic. However, LLM hypotheses have a 15--23\% lower median ONS than published papers from the same topic. Thus, LLMs move further from what is already known, but remain within established directions. This pattern persists across changes in various configurations. As a result, LLMs excel at extending the frontier but the creation of new directions is still led by human scientists.
papers.summary: Human reviewers often rate LLM-generated research ideas as more novel than expert-written ones, but it is unclear whether the models go beyond recombining existing knowledge. The authors separate two kinds of novelty, distance from existing work and direction toward lines of inquiry not already present, and introduce the orthogonal novelty score (ONS) to measure the latter, embedding 26.9 million human-authored papers across 1,325 topics in six natural-science fields alongside 524,308 hypotheses from eight LLMs in a shared scientific-paper embedding space. LLM hypotheses land up to 16% farther from existing work than human papers, yet **have a 15-23% lower median ONS than published papers on the same topic**, a pattern that persists across configurations, suggesting LLMs extend the frontier while new directions still come from human scientists.

papers.title: Know-Thy-Not: Training-Free Targeted Negation in Dual-Encoder Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Dual-encoder vision-language models systematically fail at negation, scoring ''a cat without a dog'' nearly identically to ''a cat with a dog.'' We show that this failure is inherent to the single-embedding framework. Under contrastive training, single-embedding methods can at best ignore the negated concept (dilution) but never penalize its presence (rejection). We propose Know-Thy-Not (KTN), a training-free method that introduces an image-side rejection dimension to penalize the negated concept directly in the visual representation. We also introduce COCO-Confusion, the first benchmark requiring genuine rejection to succeed. Across 9 backbones, KTN improves COCO-Confusion mAP by up to +25.6 over vanilla VLMs and +9.6 over the strongest existing method.
papers.summary: Dual-encoder vision-language models score a caption like 'a cat without a dog' almost identically to 'a cat with a dog', and the authors show this is inherent to single-embedding contrastive training, which can at best ignore a negated concept (dilution) but never penalize its presence (rejection). `Know-Thy-Not` (`KTN`) is a training-free method that adds an image-side rejection dimension so the negated concept is penalized directly in the visual representation, and the paper introduces `COCO-Confusion`, a benchmark that requires genuine rejection to succeed. Across nine backbones, `KTN` improves `COCO-Confusion` mean average precision by **up to 25.6 points over vanilla models and 9.6 points over the strongest existing method**.

papers.title: The belief-action gap in language model agents
papers.abstract: Language model (LM) agents can fail for different reasons, requiring different explanations and interventions. We study how state beliefs, action values, and action preferences interact as LM agents reason and commit to decisions in text-rendered grid worlds. We estimate task-relevant beliefs using report-based and representation-based probes, and action values using inverse reinforcement learning. We find that task-relevant state and value information is often represented more reliably than it is reflected in behaviour. Tracking action preferences throughout reasoning further shows that decisions sharpen around a commitment point and reported belief uncertainty decreases near commitment, although individual belief changes do not consistently explain shifts in action preference. Finally, forced actions follow reasoning prefixes from other decisions when transplanted, whereas the tested reasoning-window activation edits provide limited control over the action. Together, these results suggest that some failures arise not from missing task-relevant information, but from how available information is translated into action. Our measurements distinguish information availability from belief-action consistency without by themselves identifying the cause of each failure. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/belief-action-gap-F745/
papers.summary: Language model agents fail for different reasons that call for different interventions, and the authors study how state beliefs, action values, and action preferences interact as agents reason and commit to decisions in text-rendered grid worlds. They estimate task-relevant beliefs with report-based and representation-based probes, infer action values with inverse reinforcement learning, and track action preferences throughout the reasoning trace. **Task-relevant state and value information is often represented more reliably than it is reflected in behaviour**, decisions sharpen around a commitment point where reported uncertainty drops, and transplanted reasoning prefixes from other decisions steer forced actions while activation edits in the reasoning window provide limited control, suggesting that some failures stem from how available information is translated into action rather than from missing information.

papers.title: Compositional RL: Evaluating and Training LLMs for Collaborative Reasoning
papers.abstract: Language models are often evaluated alone but increasingly deployed together, routed between, made to debate, ensembled, or collaboratively trained. For a model inside a system, what matters most is not how well it performs on its own, but how much the system gains from its presence. We call this a model's compositional strength and formalize it using the Shapley value of a cooperative game over coalitions of a model pool, and use a model's leave-one-out contribution to the full coalition as a tractable proxy, requiring n+1 rather than 2^n system evaluations. Evaluating individual vs. compositional strengths across five model pools, twelve collaboration methods, and twelve datasets, we find them largely uncorrelated: in 12 of 15 (pool, method-family) settings, individual strength does not translate into compositional advantages, and the coupling is weakest among general-purpose models that practitioners are most likely to deploy. Standalone benchmarks are therefore often poor proxies for models' value in collaborative systems. We then propose compositional reinforcement learning (C-RL), which trains a policy inside a live multi-model system and rewards the outcome produced by the system as a whole, rather than the policy's correctness in isolation. The leave-one-out baseline in Shapley values cancels under a group policy gradient, so this needs no additional rollout cost beyond RL on the collaborative system's outcome and never requires running a coalition without the policy. Across three collaboration protocols and eight tasks spanning reasoning, coding, and scientific discovery, C-RL produces the strongest collaborator in 21 of 24 settings, lifting collaborative performance by +4.0 to +5.4 pts on average (~3x the gain of baselines), up to +13.1 pts.
papers.summary: Language models are evaluated alone but deployed in routed, debating, ensembled, or collaboratively trained systems, where what matters is how much the system gains from a model's presence. The authors formalize this compositional strength as a Shapley value over coalitions of a model pool, approximate it with each model's leave-one-out contribution, and find across five pools, twelve collaboration methods, and twelve datasets that **individual and compositional strength are largely uncorrelated, with standalone benchmarks failing to predict collaborative value in 12 of 15 settings**. They then propose compositional reinforcement learning (`C-RL`), which trains a policy inside a live multi-model system and rewards the outcome of the system as a whole, at no extra rollout cost because the leave-one-out baseline cancels under a group policy gradient; across three collaboration protocols and eight tasks spanning reasoning, coding, and scientific discovery, `C-RL` produces the strongest collaborator in 21 of 24 settings with average gains of 4.0 to 5.4 points.

papers.title: An FPGA-Based Spiking Neural Network for Spatiotemporal Pattern Learning and Classification
papers.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are promising for energy-efficient spatiotemporal pattern recognition at the edge, but efficient deployment and on-device adaptation require specialized hardware. In this work, we present an FPGA implementation of multilayer SNNs for spatiotemporal pattern classification, in which both inference and training take place on the same hardware. Our design adopts a temporal-forward-only training algorithm that avoids the memory and latency overhead associated with traditional Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT). A mixed-precision scheme balances training stability with resource efficiency, and architectural optimization maximizes hardware and memory utilization. We further identify and resolve hazards that arise when inference and learning share the same memory, including port conflicts between the forward and backward access patterns and read-after-write dependencies in floating-point potential accumulation. Experimental evaluations on MNIST and five multivariate time-series classification datasets demonstrate that, with fully on-chip training, our SNN model achieves accuracy comparable to SNN or LSTM trained with BPTT. Compared to CPU and GPU based implementations, our FPGA design delivers 2.5 to 6 times higher throughput while consuming an order of magnitude less energy per sample.
papers.summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient spatiotemporal pattern recognition at the edge, but on-device adaptation usually relies on Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT), whose memory and latency overheads suit specialized hardware poorly. The authors implement multilayer SNNs on an FPGA with inference and training on the same chip, using a temporal-forward-only training algorithm, a mixed-precision scheme, and architectural optimizations, and they resolve memory hazards such as port conflicts between forward and backward access patterns and read-after-write dependencies in floating-point potential accumulation. On `MNIST` and five multivariate time-series datasets, fully on-chip training reaches accuracy comparable to SNNs or LSTMs trained with BPTT, while delivering **2.5 to 6 times higher throughput than CPU and GPU implementations at an order of magnitude less energy per sample**.

papers.title: Assessing the Performance of AI Models in Misinformation Detection Using Predefined Social Noise Constructs
papers.abstract: Social media platforms generate vast volumes of user-generated content that often obscure meaningful discourse, a phenomenon conceptualized as social noise. While existing misinformation detection methods primarily focus on factual verification, they largely overlook the role of social noise in amplifying misinformation. This study assesses the performance of six text-based models and a graph neural network (GNN) in mitigating the effects of misinformation using predefined social noise constructs. The dataset consists of 500,000 tweets collected from the X platform using the Ukraine hashtag during the Russia-Ukraine conflict from March 2024 to March 2025. Advanced machine learning models achieve strong performance, with accuracies ranging from 79.94% to 97.17%. RoBERTa demonstrates the highest performance, with an accuracy of 97.17%, Cohen's kappa of 0.9660, MCC of 0.9660, and AUC of 0.9977. The GNN achieves an accuracy of 64.52% and an AUC of 0.899, demonstrating performance above random-chance classification by exploiting the relational structure between tweets. All text-based models achieve kappa values greater than 0.75, indicating substantial overall agreement. Explainable AI analysis using LIME reveals that 89.6% of predictive weight is attributed to contextual features rather than isolated keywords. The findings highlight that integrating social noise into AI pipelines enhances misinformation detection and supports more effective mitigation strategies in large-scale social media environments.
papers.summary: Misinformation detectors usually focus on factual verification and overlook social noise, the flood of user-generated content that obscures meaningful discourse and amplifies false claims. The study evaluates six text-based models and a graph neural network (GNN) on 500,000 tweets collected under the Ukraine hashtag between March 2024 and March 2025, labeled using predefined social noise constructs. `RoBERTa` performs best with **97.17% accuracy and an AUC of 0.9977**, all text-based models reach Cohen's kappa above 0.75, the GNN reaches 64.52% accuracy by exploiting relational structure between tweets, and LIME-based analysis attributes 89.6% of predictive weight to contextual features rather than isolated keywords.

papers.title: REA: From Correct LLM Judgments to Safe Decision Delivery
papers.abstract: Generative safety guards must classify requests correctly and return outputs that applications can parse. Reasoning guards can improve classification accuracy while producing outputs that applications cannot parse. When applications cannot extract a correct prediction, fallback handling can allow harmful requests or block safe ones. We introduce Resolve--Express--Act (REA), a framework that traces judgments through parsing and fallback to application actions. Experiments on classifiers and safety guards show that correct predictions can appear in incorrectly formatted outputs. Parsing the safety verdict preserves the reasoning guard's accuracy advantage, while stricter explanation requirements reject additional correct predictions. Accepting formatting variations recovers most rejected correct predictions. Held-out tests confirm that output requirements and generation limits affect whether correct predictions can be parsed. In our fail-open replay, matching the parser to the output and fixing formatting reduced the fraction of harmful requests allowed despite correct guard judgments from 95.5% to 0%. A fixed-output comparison shows that model-based extraction can preserve guard verdicts, but is not automatically reliable; deterministic normalization already repairs the observed native-format failures. Fallback replay shows that the same correct prediction can lead to different safety actions depending on the parser and fallback policy, including allowing requests the guard correctly identifies as harmful.
papers.summary: Generative safety guards must both classify requests correctly and emit outputs the calling application can parse, and reasoning-based guards that improve accuracy often produce verdicts in formats that break parsers, triggering fallback behavior that can let harmful requests through or block safe ones. The Resolve-Express-Act (`REA`) framework traces a guard's judgment through parsing and fallback to the final application action, and experiments on classifiers and safety guards show that correct predictions frequently hide inside incorrectly formatted outputs, that strict explanation requirements reject additional correct predictions, and that accepting formatting variations recovers most of them. In a fail-open replay, **matching the parser to the guard's output and fixing formatting reduced the share of harmful requests allowed despite correct guard judgments from 95.5% to 0%**, and deterministic normalization alone repairs the observed native-format failures, whereas model-based extraction preserves verdicts but is not automatically reliable.

papers.title: VeriPIE: Checkable Query Plans and Evidence-Guided Selection for Text-to-SQL
papers.abstract: Financial Artificial Intelligence (AI) governance and model risk management (MRM) emphasize independent validation, transparency, and effective challenge of AI-generated computations. Text-to-SQL translates natural-language questions into Structured Query Language (SQL), but queries that agree on one database can still express different computations. We present VeriPIE, a neurosymbolic framework combining language-model generation with symbolic checks. It ensembles direct SQL generation with QuerySketch, a structured plan language checked by a backend implemented in Lean, a theorem prover and programming language. Plan diagnostics guide repair before SQL generation, while execution agreement and bounded searches for distinguishing databases inform candidate selection. These checks expose malformed plans and hidden disagreement without proving agreement with the user's intent. In single-run experiments on the complete Spider development set, VeriPIE achieves 72.05% test-suite accuracy (745/1,034), compared with DeepEye's 65.67% (679/1,034). Its two-query shortlist covers 78.43% (811 questions), compared with 74.66% for DIN-SQL (772) and 69.05% for DeepEye (714). On BIRD, VeriPIE reaches 68.90% execution accuracy and 73.73% two-query coverage. The central benefit is reviewable evidence about the generated computation: explicit plan checks, repair diagnostics, and concrete disagreements that support safer financial analysis.
papers.summary: Financial model risk management (MRM) demands independent validation and effective challenge of AI-generated computations, yet text-to-SQL systems can produce queries that agree on one database while expressing different computations. The neurosymbolic framework ensembles direct Structured Query Language (SQL) generation with `QuerySketch`, a structured plan language whose checker is implemented in the `Lean` theorem prover, using plan diagnostics to guide repair before SQL generation and execution agreement plus bounded searches for distinguishing databases to select among candidates. On the full `Spider` development set it reaches **72.05% test-suite accuracy** compared with 65.67% for `DeepEye`, its two-query shortlist covers 78.43% of questions versus 74.66% for `DIN-SQL`, and on `BIRD` it achieves 68.90% execution accuracy and 73.73% two-query coverage, while the checks expose malformed plans and hidden disagreement without proving agreement with user intent.

papers.title: Foundation Models for Event Prediction Across Heterogeneous Event Logs
papers.abstract: Event logs are ubiquitous across real-world domains, including business processes, manufacturing workflows, healthcare, and many other operational systems. Yet event logs can differ substantially in their event semantics, label spaces, interaction patterns, and temporal scales, making it difficult to build a single foundation model that generalizes directly to previously unseen systems. We address this challenge with the Foundation Event Predictor (FEP), a simple and scalable in-context architecture that performs next-event prediction through learned, event-level nonparametric inference. Causal self-attention encodes context and target histories into key and query representations, respectively, while the observed next context events are encoded as values. Cross-attention then performs learned, relevance-weighted aggregation of next-event outcomes over all context transitions, allowing the entire nonparametric prediction procedure to be expressed as standard attention operations and efficiently parallelized with modern kernels such as FlashAttention. To promote cross-system generalization, we introduce permutation-robust embedding learning and random fixed embeddings to decouple event IDs from persistent semantics, together with empirical quantile transforms and robust normalization to handle diverse temporal scales. We pretrain FEP on 696 real-world event datasets spanning heterogeneous event systems and evaluate it on 50 held-out datasets unseen during pretraining. Across these datasets, FEP generalizes effectively to new event systems without parameter adaptation, frequently approaching the performance of strong models trained separately on each target dataset while substantially outperforming existing foundation-model baselines, particularly on challenging prediction tasks.
papers.summary: Event logs from business processes, manufacturing, healthcare and other operational systems differ widely in event semantics, label spaces and temporal scales, which makes it hard to build one model that transfers to unseen systems. The Foundation Event Predictor (`FEP`) is an in-context architecture that frames next-event prediction as learned nonparametric inference: causal self-attention encodes context and target histories as keys and queries, observed next events become values, and cross-attention performs relevance-weighted aggregation, so the whole procedure runs as standard attention compatible with kernels like `FlashAttention`. Permutation-robust embedding learning, random fixed embeddings, and quantile-based normalization decouple event IDs and time scales from any one system. Pretrained on 696 real-world event datasets and tested on 50 held-out ones, **`FEP` generalizes to new event systems with no parameter adaptation**, often approaching models trained separately per dataset and substantially outperforming existing foundation-model baselines.

papers.title: YUBI-Real2Sim: 3DGS Scene Verification for Reliable Policy Evaluation
papers.abstract: Evaluating VLA policies on real robots is costly, time-consuming, and difficult to reproduce, making real-to-sim simulation essential for scalable evaluation. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables rapid real-to-sim scene generation, the reconstruction quality required for reliable policy evaluation remains unquantified. In particular, policies relying on wrist-mounted fisheye cameras (e.g., YUBI handheld gripper data) are heavily exposed to visual artifacts (holes, floaters) in wide-angle views, directly degrading task performance. To address this, we present YUBI-Real2Sim, a unified framework for 3DGS-based scene reconstruction and real-to-sim policy evaluation under dual fisheye wrist views. We develop an integrated pipeline combining 200-degree fisheye camera capture, 3DGS training, 3D foundation models for object modeling, and MuJoCo-based physical simulation, reproducing the observed real-world policy ordering in eight of nine scene-task comparisons. Using this framework, we construct a benchmark across two bimanual robot platforms, three scenes, three tasks, and dual pi0.5-based policies. This systematically measures real-to-sim rank agreement and evaluates policy sensitivity against counterfactual 3DGS artifacts (ceiling holes, floaters, warping) and capture disturbances. We further analyze whether novel-view quality scores can indicate policy-ranking reliability under a scene-held-out evaluation protocol. The results show task-dependent performance and limitations of quality-based reliability prediction, highlighting the need to assess reconstruction quality when using Real2Sim for policy evaluation. These results do not yet establish a generally reliable scene-acceptance rule. Project Page: https://yubi-real2sim.airoa.io.
papers.summary: Evaluating vision-language-action (VLA) policies on physical robots is expensive and hard to reproduce, and although 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) can quickly build real-to-sim scenes, the reconstruction quality needed for trustworthy policy evaluation has not been quantified, especially for policies that see through wide-angle wrist cameras exposed to holes and floaters. `YUBI-Real2Sim` is a pipeline combining 200-degree fisheye capture, 3DGS training, 3D foundation models for object modeling, and `MuJoCo` physics, used to build a benchmark spanning two bimanual platforms, three scenes, three tasks and two `pi0.5`-based policies. **The simulation reproduced the real-world policy ordering in eight of nine scene-task comparisons**, but policy sensitivity to counterfactual artifacts such as ceiling holes, floaters and warping was task-dependent, and novel-view quality scores did not reliably predict ranking reliability under a scene-held-out protocol. The authors state that these results do not yet establish a general scene-acceptance rule.

papers.title: Enhanced Detective: A Dual-Stage Proactive Defense Against Internal Poisoning Attacks in Financial Fraud Detection Using Federated Learning
papers.abstract: With recent developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI), the adoption of distributed learning paradigms such as Federated Learning (FL) has emerged. In simple terms, FL enables multiple entities to collaboratively train AI models without sharing local data. The FL paradigm is particularly valuable in privacy-sensitive settings, such as financial services, because it enables institutions to collaboratively improve fraud-detection models while keeping sensitive transaction data local. However, FL schemes are prone to security vulnerabilities, where malicious clients can poison local data or model updates and degrade the global model, and hence the performance of the resulting model might be affected. Therefore, in this work, we propose Enhanced Detective, a dual-stage robust aggregation strategy that combines Median Absolute Deviation (MAD), distance-based update filtering, and FedMedian aggregation. Experiments on an imbalanced credit card dataset evaluate targeted label-flipping and weight-scaling attacks over 50 communication rounds. With 40% malicious clients, Enhanced Detective achieves an AUPRC of 0.796 and a Recall of 0.847.
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) lets financial institutions jointly train fraud-detection models without sharing transaction data, but malicious clients can poison their local data or model updates to degrade the shared global model. `Enhanced Detective` is a dual-stage robust aggregation strategy that combines Median Absolute Deviation (MAD) screening with distance-based update filtering and `FedMedian` aggregation. Evaluated on an imbalanced credit card dataset under targeted label-flipping and weight-scaling attacks over 50 communication rounds, **it reaches an area under the precision-recall curve of 0.796 and recall of 0.847 with 40% malicious clients**.

papers.title: Box-WAM: Box Trajectories as Compact State Representations for World Action Models
papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) are a category of policy models that ex- plicitly predict both actions and future world states. They have been shown to outperform action-only models across various robotic manipulation tasks. How- ever, representing the future with full-frame video prediction can be computation- ally expensive during both training and inference. This raises a central question: what compact state representation preserves the planning and supervision bene- fits of future prediction? In this paper, we propose BoxWAM, which replaces dense future frames with oriented bounding box trajectories of task-relevant ob- jects. By explicitly imagining object-centric future motion, our method provides a lightweight prediction target that captures the key physical changes induced by robot actions. We show that box trajectory prediction substantially reduces com- putational cost while improving action prediction performance, suggesting that object-centric compact states can serve as an efficient alternative to video-based world action modeling for robotic manipulation. Result videos can be found on https://box-wam.github.io
papers.summary: World action models (WAMs), policies that predict both actions and future world states, outperform action-only models on manipulation tasks, but predicting full future video frames is expensive at both training and inference time. `BoxWAM` replaces dense future frames with oriented bounding box trajectories of task-relevant objects, so the model imagines object-centric future motion rather than pixels. **Box trajectory prediction substantially cuts computational cost while improving action prediction performance**, suggesting that compact object-centric states can stand in for video-based world action modeling in robotic manipulation.

papers.title: Towards Green AI: Evaluating Energy Efficiency for Quantized LLM Inference
papers.abstract: While it is known that quantization of large language models (LLMs) reduces memory usage via lower-bit weights, studies quantifying the resulting impact on energy usage and carbon intensity are scarce. We present the first unified evaluation of weight-only quantization strategies for LLM inference across varying input/output lengths and GPUs, highlighting differences in energy efficiency in addition to accuracy degradation and runtime. We study quantized inference on Llama 2 7B, Phi 3.5 Mini Instruct, OLMo 1B, Qwen 2.5 7B, and Qwen 2.5 14B across GLUE MNLI, MMLU, HumanEval, and GSM8K datasets, evaluating 10 post-training quantization (PTQ) strategies on NVIDIA H100, A6000, A100, and L4 GPUs. We identify a novel trend showing that quantization techniques tend to exhibit peak energy efficiency relative to full-precision baselines when inputs are sufficiently long and outputs are short. Furthermore, we show that quantization strategies become marginally more energy-efficient relative to full-precision models as batch sizes increase, though gains are modest. Notably, fused-kernel implementations such as EETQ int8 and Bitsandbytes int8 offer the highest energy savings, up to 4x compared to FP32 on short text generation, with negligible accuracy loss. Finally, we observe that energy usage closely tracks runtime on our evaluated benchmarks, indicating that, in practice, latency optimization can serve as a reliable proxy for reducing the environmental footprint of LLM services. We conclude with suggested directions for strategically selecting low-carbon quantization strategies based on specific inference requirements.
papers.summary: Quantizing large language models (LLMs) is known to cut memory use, but its effect on inference energy and carbon footprint has rarely been measured. The authors run a unified evaluation of 10 post-training quantization (PTQ) strategies on `Llama 2 7B`, `Phi 3.5 Mini Instruct`, `OLMo 1B`, `Qwen 2.5 7B` and `Qwen 2.5 14B` across `GLUE MNLI`, `MMLU`, `HumanEval` and `GSM8K`, on NVIDIA H100, A100, A6000 and L4 GPUs, varying input/output lengths and batch sizes. Quantization is most energy-efficient relative to full precision when inputs are long and outputs short, gains grow only modestly with batch size, and **fused-kernel int8 implementations such as `EETQ` and `Bitsandbytes` save up to 4x energy versus FP32 on short generation with negligible accuracy loss**. Energy closely tracks runtime, so latency optimization serves as a practical proxy for reducing an LLM service's environmental footprint.

papers.title: TacitVLA: Reasoning Vision-Language-Action Models Without Reasoning Latency
papers.abstract: Textual reasoning before acting has improved vision-language-action (VLA) models, but at the cost of latency: every action conditioned on the reasoning text must wait for autoregressive decoding. We show that actions do not need to wait for or condition on the generated reasoning to benefit from it, because the reasoning supervision already improves the backbone representation. We introduce TacitVLA, a reasoning VLA whose action expert never attends to the reasoning it generates for the current call. On long-horizon tasks where the reasoning text also serves as episodic memory, it can generate each entry during action execution rather than before acting. We evaluate it in a controlled study on four benchmarks spanning manipulation and autonomous driving, memory and non-memory tasks: RoboMME, RMBench, LIBERO, and PhysicalAI-AV. On all four, TacitVLA matches the performance of its explicit-reasoning counterpart at up to 3.4x lower latency, and matches the latency of the same architecture trained without reasoning at up to +17.1% success. In absolute terms, it surpasses the best previously published results on the RoboMME Counting suite (82.7% vs. 66.8%) and RMBench (77.5% vs. 56.5%), and reaches 72.9% on LIBERO-Plus and a 52.5% scene score on the public split of the PhysicalAI-AV closed-loop driving challenge. Project page: https://tacitvla.github.io.
papers.summary: Adding textual reasoning before acting improves vision-language-action (VLA) models, but every action that conditions on that text must wait for autoregressive decoding. `TacitVLA` keeps reasoning as a training signal while its action expert never attends to the reasoning generated for the current call, on the premise that reasoning supervision already improves the backbone representation; on long-horizon tasks where the text serves as episodic memory, it is generated during action execution rather than before. Across `RoboMME`, `RMBench`, `LIBERO` and `PhysicalAI-AV`, **it matches its explicit-reasoning counterpart at up to 3.4x lower latency** and matches the latency of a no-reasoning model with up to 17.1% higher success, including 82.7% on the `RoboMME` Counting suite versus a prior best of 66.8%.

papers.title: Convex-Analytic View of Query Selection for Safety Verification of Markov Decision Processes
papers.abstract: Safety verification of a Markov decision process (MDP) asks whether the probabilities of reaching several failure states jointly lie in a convex safe region under every scheduler. Watanabe and Unno (2026) prove safety by refining an outer approximation of the failure probabilities, where each query bounds a nonnegative weighted sum of the probabilities. Their rule selects weights by the largest Euclidean violation. We present a unified framework to measure violation in an explicitly chosen error unit: directions are scored by the support-function gap between the outer approximation and the safe region, normalized by the support function of the unit. We show that the maximal score, when positive, equals the smallest enlargement of the safe region in multiples of that unit that contains the outer approximation. The Euclidean unit recovers the earlier rule; two new rules are generated by the unit cube and the safe region itself. We experimentally evaluate how the choice of measurement rule affects the performance of safety verification for MDPs.
papers.summary: Safety verification of a Markov decision process (MDP) asks whether the probabilities of reaching several failure states jointly stay inside a convex safe region under every scheduler, and a recent method proves this by iteratively refining an outer approximation with queries that bound weighted sums of those probabilities, picking weights by the largest Euclidean violation. The authors recast weight selection in a unified framework that scores directions by the support-function gap between the outer approximation and the safe region, normalized by a chosen error unit, and show the maximal score equals the smallest enlargement of the safe region in multiples of that unit that contains the approximation. **The Euclidean unit recovers the existing rule, while the unit cube and the safe region itself yield two new rules**, whose effect on verification performance is compared experimentally.

papers.title: Many Steps into One: Reasoning Contraction and the Limits of Safe Memory Reuse for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Thought templates, skill libraries, agent memories and caches turn many reasoning steps into one. We call this reasoning contraction. A contracted memory saves reasoning steps and errors until its facts change, then quietly answers wrong. Most systems trust memories by counting successes and failures. We prove that such counters are badly tuned change detectors: a symmetric counter notices a partial change only after a power of its false-alarm horizon, and an unclipped one may never notice it. On five LLMs answering multi-hop questions over edited facts, ExpeL- and ACE-style counters serve 7.0-13.5x more stale answers than certified memories given the same information, and on code tasks with an exact verifier 35-73x more. Safety also has a price. When facts change and each memory is judged only by its own verified outcomes, one number, the certification load, sets how much reasoning any safe memory can skip, and under Zipf demand it yields a scaling law. Our recipe weighs each memory's failures by its own likelihood ratio, certifies its utility against live reasoning, and restarts the certificate when facts change, with the likelihood-ratio detector as the safety net for unannounced changes; for large edits it also invalidates the memory.
papers.summary: Thought templates, skill libraries, agent memories and caches collapse many reasoning steps into one reused answer, which the authors call reasoning contraction; such memories keep paying off until the underlying facts change and then silently answer wrong. Most systems gauge trust in a memory by counting successes and failures, and the paper proves these counters are poorly tuned change detectors: a symmetric counter notices a partial change only after a power of its false-alarm horizon, and an unclipped one may never notice. On five LLMs answering multi-hop questions over edited facts, **`ExpeL`- and `ACE`-style counters served 7.0-13.5x more stale answers than certified memories given the same information**, and 35-73x more on code tasks with an exact verifier. The proposed recipe weighs each memory's failures by its own likelihood ratio, certifies its utility against live reasoning, and restarts the certificate when facts change, with a certification load quantity bounding how much reasoning a safe memory can skip and yielding a scaling law under Zipf demand.

papers.title: Reference Wording Shapes Retrieval of Robot Task Instructions
papers.abstract: Identifying a robot task from a short instruction is sensitive to which descriptions are available for retrieval. We investigate this effect in the natural-language instructions included with the RLBench manipulation benchmark. We extract 296 fixed descriptions from 62 publicly available task files and compare five training-free lexical rankers over 80 random choices of one indexed description per task. Exact strings assigned to conflicting task labels are excluded from the primary score. Character n-gram TF-IDF achieves 61.3% mean top-1 accuracy on the resulting held-out instructions, compared with 55.6% for BM25 and 54.9% for word TF-IDF. Across gallery choices, character TF-IDF ranges from 55.2% to 66.8%; its 5th-95th percentile range is 56.9%-64.8%. Adding a second indexed description improves character TF-IDF by 7.0 percentage points on matched queries. These results quantify the influence of reference wording and representation choice on instruction-to-task retrieval under a consistent evaluation protocol.
papers.summary: Matching a short natural-language instruction to the robot task it names depends on which reference descriptions are indexed for retrieval. Using 296 fixed descriptions extracted from 62 publicly available `RLBench` task files, the study compares five training-free lexical rankers over 80 random choices of one indexed description per task, excluding exact strings assigned to conflicting labels. **Character n-gram `TF-IDF` reaches 61.3% mean top-1 accuracy**, against 55.6% for `BM25` and 54.9% for word `TF-IDF`, with its accuracy ranging from 55.2% to 66.8% depending on the gallery choice, and indexing a second description per task adds 7.0 percentage points on matched queries.

papers.title: FlashVSR+: Efficient Video Super-Resolution via Hybrid Attention and Reward-Yield Distribution Matching
papers.abstract: Recent video super-resolution (VSR) models achieve efficient one-step generation through diffusion distillation. However, high-resolution inference remains costly, and distilled models are difficult to align with human preferences. These challenges call for improvements in both model architecture and training strategy. We present \textbf{FlashVSR+} to address both limitations. On the architecture side, we introduce hybrid attention based on the strong locality observed in pretrained VSR models, while retaining sparse global interaction for long-range consistency. It achieves up to $2\times$ DiT speedup and 45\% lower peak memory, enabling spatially untiled 4K VSR on a single 24GB RTX 4090. On the training side, we propose Reward-Yield Distribution Matching Distillation (Ry-DMD) for preference-aligned one-step generation. Ry-DMD uses reward-weighted teacher rollouts to incorporate black-box rewards into distribution matching, without backpropagating through the reward model. We further show that Ry-DMD generalizes beyond VSR to T2I generation. Together, FlashVSR+ delivers stronger restoration quality and substantially improves high-resolution efficiency, with consistent gains in user preference. We release our code, models, and training data at \href{https://www.flashvsr.tech}{\textcolor{FlashBlue}{\textbf{www.flashvsr.tech}}}.
papers.summary: One-step video super-resolution (VSR) models obtained by diffusion distillation are fast, but high-resolution inference stays costly and distilled models are hard to align with human preferences. `FlashVSR+` addresses both: a hybrid attention design exploits the strong locality found in pretrained VSR models while keeping sparse global interaction for long-range consistency, and Reward-Yield Distribution Matching Distillation (`Ry-DMD`) folds black-box rewards into distribution matching via reward-weighted teacher rollouts without backpropagating through the reward model. **The architecture gives up to 2x DiT speedup and 45% lower peak memory, enabling untiled 4K VSR on a single 24GB RTX 4090**, and `Ry-DMD` also transfers to text-to-image generation. Code, models and training data are released.

papers.title: Benchmarking Self-Supervised 3D Medical Vision Foundation Models and Transferability Estimation
papers.abstract: Self-supervised pretraining has expanded the pool of 3D medical foundation models, but published evaluations use different datasets, endpoints and fine-tuning protocols. Models also differ in architecture, pretraining objective and data, while downstream targets range from voxel-level masks to patient-level diagnoses and outcomes. As a result, published findings provide little directly comparable evidence for choosing a model for a new task. Direct comparison of adaptation performance requires fine-tuning candidates on labelled target data, at substantial computational cost. We benchmark 23 candidates across the same 14 segmentation, classification and regression tasks spanning multiple anatomies and modalities. No candidate ranked among the top three across all segmentation tasks or across all classification and regression tasks; a convolutional encoder could outperform a transformer trained with the same objective on one task but underperform it on another. We benchmark transferability estimators against the fine-tuned rankings and find that their agreement varies across dense segmentation, classification and regression. InsightRank uses task-appropriate frozen-feature statistics and architecture-aware pairwise comparisons to rank candidates before fine-tuning. Across the 23-model pool, mean Kendall tau-b was 0.431 for segmentation and 0.352 for classification and regression. The segmentation Top 3 contained a task winner on four of nine tasks; the image-level Top 3 contained none on the five tasks, despite better full-ranking agreement than the matched conventional estimators. A three-model shortlist reduced recorded extraction-plus-training job time by 85.8% across seven segmentation tasks. Together, the benchmark provides a common reference for model selection and InsightRank offers a lower-cost way to prioritize fine-tuning, with shortlist performance that differs by target type.
papers.summary: Self-supervised pretraining has produced many 3D medical foundation models, but published evaluations use different datasets, endpoints and fine-tuning protocols, leaving little comparable evidence for picking a model for a new task. The authors fine-tune 23 candidates on the same 14 segmentation, classification and regression tasks across anatomies and modalities, and find that no model ranks in the top three across all segmentation tasks or across all classification and regression tasks; a convolutional encoder can beat a transformer with the same objective on one task and lose on another. They also propose `InsightRank`, which ranks candidates before fine-tuning using task-appropriate frozen-feature statistics and architecture-aware pairwise comparisons, reaching mean Kendall tau-b of 0.431 for segmentation and 0.352 for image-level tasks. **A three-model shortlist cut recorded extraction-plus-training time by 85.8% across seven segmentation tasks**, though the top-3 shortlist contained the task winner on four of nine segmentation tasks and none of the five image-level ones.

papers.title: Dissociating Answerability from Extraction in LLM Question Answering over Radiology Reports
papers.abstract: Answering questions from radiology reports involves two decisions: whether the report contains an answer and which span gives it. A false answer presents an unsupported claim as fact; an over-abstention hides what the report says. Yet RadQA results are reported as a single F1 that merges both. We propose an evaluation method that separates them, reporting false-answer and over-abstention rates beside F1 and splitting F1 changes into extraction and answerability terms. We apply it to 13 LLMs on the RadQA test set, zero-shot and with three cumulative demonstration sets, the last adding an unanswerable example. Models with similar F1 differed more than twofold in false-answer rate. The unanswerable example changed when models answered, not how well they extracted: 12 of 13 models abstained more often, and three-quarters of the answers they withdrew had F1 $\geq$ 0.5. Within models, false answers showed no clear association with extraction quality, but acting on the decision itself helped: keeping an answer only when enough other models also answered lowered the zero-shot false-answer rate by 4 points without a detectable F1 change. Because the two decisions can change independently, we suggest radiology QA evaluations report them separately, not through F1 alone.
papers.summary: Answering a question from a radiology report involves two decisions, whether the report contains an answer at all and which span gives it, yet `RadQA` results are usually reported as a single F1 score that merges them. The authors propose reporting false-answer and over-abstention rates alongside F1 and decomposing F1 changes into extraction and answerability terms, then apply this to 13 LLMs on the `RadQA` test set zero-shot and with three cumulative demonstration sets, the last adding an unanswerable example. **Models with similar F1 differed more than twofold in false-answer rate**, and the unanswerable demonstration changed when models answered rather than how well they extracted: 12 of 13 models abstained more, and three-quarters of withdrawn answers had F1 of at least 0.5. Keeping an answer only when enough other models also answered lowered the zero-shot false-answer rate by 4 points with no detectable F1 change.

papers.title: Chasing Label Shifters: A Change-Aware Framework for Dynamic Graph Node Classification
papers.abstract: Entities in real-world systems often evolve over time: users shift between information consumption patterns, researchers migrate between fields, and firms transition between financial risk states. When such systems are modeled as dynamic graphs, these transitions correspond to nodes whose class labels change between consecutive snapshots, which we call shifters. Correctly classifying shifters is often more consequential than classifying stable nodes with persistent labels, as detecting such transitions enables timely intervention in high-stakes settings. Yet, we identify a systematic failure mode across all major dynamic graph neural network architectures: shifter performance consistently lags behind stable nodes, with errors concentrated on the old label. Our structural analysis traces this failure to embedding inertia: neighborhood aggregation keeps shifter representations anchored to the old-class centroid, and this effect is strongest precisely where it is hardest to correct, namely for shifters whose neighborhoods remain aligned with the old class. Guided by this finding, we propose CHASE, a model-agnostic CHange-Aware framework for Shifting nodEs that wraps any dynamic GNN with targeted components for detecting label shifts and overriding stale neighborhood signals. CHASE consistently improves shifter performance across all tested models and datasets (up to 114.9% and 202.5% improvement on accuracy and F1 score, respectively) while preserving stable-node performance. We additionally contribute three dynamic graph benchmarks with naturally shifting labels, filling a gap in existing resources. The source code is available at https://github.com/jhkim611/CHASE
papers.summary: In dynamic graphs, some nodes change class between consecutive snapshots, such as users shifting consumption patterns or firms moving between risk states, and these shifters are often the nodes that matter most to classify correctly. The authors show that every major dynamic graph neural network (GNN) architecture performs consistently worse on shifters than on stable nodes, with errors concentrated on the old label, and trace this to embedding inertia: neighborhood aggregation anchors a shifter's representation to its old-class centroid, most strongly when its neighborhood still aligns with the old class. `CHASE` is a model-agnostic wrapper that adds components for detecting label shifts and overriding stale neighborhood signals, and **it improves shifter accuracy by up to 114.9% and F1 by up to 202.5%** across all tested models and datasets while preserving stable-node performance. Three new dynamic graph benchmarks with naturally shifting labels are also released.

papers.title: RAN-JEPA: An Action-Conditioned World Model for Energy-efficient Mobile Network Control
papers.abstract: Operational mobile networks are rich in observations but poor in interventions: they continuously generate large volumes of passive telemetry, while controlled action--response trajectories remain comparatively scarce and costly to collect. This observation--intervention asymmetry is a central obstacle to building practical world models for RAN control. We address this problem with RAN-JEPA, an action-conditioned world model that separates representation learning from intervention learning. The model first learns a predictive latent representation from observation-only network data, adapts that representation to the target deployment domain, and then learns action-conditioned latent dynamics from controlled sleep/wake trajectories while keeping the encoder fixed. We evaluate RAN-JEPA using public operator performance data for pretraining and a real-equipment four-cell 5G testbed for domain adaptation, post-training, and control. Across four future 15-minute intervals, RAN-JEPA achieves lower action-conditioned prediction error than a GPT-2 world-model baseline and a mechanistic rule, while remaining close to a strong persistence reference. What-if evaluation further shows that the model produces distinct and coherent future trajectories under matched SLEEP and KEEP plans. In closed-loop control, RAN-JEPA consistently supports higher sleep ratios than the two baselines at comparable congestion cost. These results show that observation-first, action-conditioned learning can turn abundant passive telemetry and limited intervention data into a practical predictive model for energy-aware RAN control.
papers.summary: Operational mobile networks generate abundant passive telemetry but few controlled action-response trajectories, which makes it hard to learn world models for radio access network (RAN) control. `RAN-JEPA` is an action-conditioned world model that first learns a predictive latent representation from observation-only data, adapts it to the target deployment, and then learns action-conditioned latent dynamics from controlled sleep/wake trajectories with the encoder frozen. Pretrained on public operator data and evaluated on a real four-cell 5G testbed, **it achieves lower action-conditioned prediction error over four future 15-minute intervals than a `GPT-2` world-model baseline and a mechanistic rule**, produces distinct and coherent what-if trajectories under matched SLEEP and KEEP plans, and in closed-loop control supports higher cell sleep ratios than both baselines at comparable congestion cost.

papers.title: Taming Softmax at the Limits of Muon: A Unified Approach through Hilbert Geometry
papers.abstract: Muon controls weight updates through the RMS movement of a linear layer's output. This implicitly treats the linear output as a proxy for the full module, including the nonlinearity that follows. This proxy can be misleading for softmax, where the RMS shift in activations does not faithfully measure the change in the output distribution. We propose Hilbert distance as a natural metric for bounding changes in these output distributions. Hilbert distance bounds changes in cross-entropy loss and limits probability redistribution. For softmax, it takes the form of the variation seminorm of the preactivation perturbation, allowing probability constraints to be expressed as parameter constraints. Formulating the steepest descent problem with a Hilbert distance constraint brings two recently proposed methods under a unified mathematical framework. For the LM head, solving a row-wise approximation to the resulting diameter-constrained problem leads us to RowNorm \citep{pethick2025trainingdeeplearningmodels}. For scaled dot-product attention, the same principle yields the first-order query--key steepest descent problem underlying Compositional Muon \citep{keigwin2026compositional}. These connections motivate using Hilbert distance as a guiding principle for optimizer design in softmax modules.
papers.summary: `Muon` bounds weight updates by the root-mean-square (RMS) movement of a linear layer's output, treating that output as a proxy for the whole module including its nonlinearity, but for softmax the RMS shift in activations does not faithfully reflect the change in the output distribution. The authors propose Hilbert distance as the metric for bounding changes in softmax outputs: it bounds changes in cross-entropy loss and probability redistribution, and for softmax it reduces to the variation seminorm of the preactivation perturbation, turning probability constraints into parameter constraints. **Formulating steepest descent under a Hilbert distance constraint recovers both `RowNorm` for the language-model head and the query-key steepest descent problem behind `Compositional Muon` for attention**, unifying two recently proposed methods under one framework.

papers.title: Revisiting the 16x Pretraining Compute Gap between Diffusion and Autoregressive Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) have attracted wide attention for their fast, parallel decoding, but they are believed to be far less efficient to train than autoregressive language models (ARMs): a widely cited study reports that a DLM needs roughly 16x the training compute of an ARM to match its likelihood, a figure that has made pretraining DLMs from scratch look prohibitive at scale. We find that the methodology behind this figure has fallen out of step with current DLM practice: it scores the model with its evidence lower bound (ELBO) and trains a full-sequence, decoder-only model. We therefore revisit the scaling laws of DLMs, adopting the exact likelihood under the model's own decoding order, block diffusion training, an encoder-decoder architecture, and a sweep over the block sizes used in practice. Under this new protocol, we study across ten model variants, about 1,700 models in total, and find that pretraining DLMs is far cheaper than previously thought. Concretely, scoring with the exact likelihood reduces the compute multiple to 12.8x; block diffusion training and an encoder-decoder architecture further reduce it to 7.8x at block size 32, and smaller block sizes narrow it to 4.6x at block size 8 and 3.0x at block size 4. We complement these scaling analyses with an empirical rule for the optimal decoder depth of encoder-decoder block diffusion, a held-out compute budget beyond the fitting range at which the gap between variants persists, and downstream benchmark results where likelihood improvements carry over to accuracy. Overall, the 16x figure substantially overstates the pretraining cost gap between DLMs and ARMs, and pretraining DLMs from scratch is far more viable than previously assumed.
papers.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) decode in parallel but are widely believed to need about 16x the pretraining compute of autoregressive language models (ARMs) to match likelihood, a figure that has made training them from scratch look prohibitive. The authors argue that the methodology behind that figure is out of step with current practice, since it scores with the evidence lower bound (ELBO) and trains a full-sequence decoder-only model, and they refit DLM scaling laws using exact likelihood under the model's own decoding order, block diffusion training, an encoder-decoder architecture, and a sweep over practical block sizes, across about 1,700 models. **Exact-likelihood scoring alone lowers the compute multiple to 12.8x, block diffusion with an encoder-decoder cuts it to 7.8x at block size 32, and smaller blocks bring it to 4.6x at block size 8 and 3.0x at block size 4.** They also give an empirical rule for optimal decoder depth, confirm the gap persists at a held-out compute budget beyond the fitting range, and show likelihood gains carry over to downstream benchmark accuracy.

papers.title: Tanawpamana: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models on Philippine Cultural Heritage Sites
papers.abstract: Vision-language models are increasingly used to identify and describe places, yet their recognition and knowledge of specific cultures remain poorly understood, particularly in underrepresented regions such as the Philippines. This study introduces the Tanawpamana Dataset, a repository of Philippine heritage site images with metadata based on the Talapamana registry of the National Commission for Culture and the Arts of the Philippines. We also introduce the Tanawpamana Benchmark, comprising 4,046 tasks designed to evaluate models' recognition and knowledge of heritage sites. Evaluating seven vision-language models, we find that they struggle more with fine-grained visual discrimination among similar heritage sites than with coarse recognition, and that their geographic knowledge is weaker when inferred from image inputs than from text.
papers.summary: Vision-language models are increasingly used to identify and describe places, but how well they recognize and know sites from underrepresented regions such as the Philippines is poorly understood. The `Tanawpamana Dataset` collects Philippine heritage site images with metadata drawn from the Talapamana registry of the National Commission for Culture and the Arts, and the accompanying `Tanawpamana Benchmark` comprises 4,046 tasks probing recognition and knowledge of those sites. Evaluating seven vision-language models, **the authors find they struggle more with fine-grained discrimination among similar heritage sites than with coarse recognition**, and that their geographic knowledge is weaker when it must be inferred from images than from text.

papers.title: Morphology-aware deep learning predicts colorectal cancer survival from whole-slide images
papers.abstract:
Background: Five-year survival prediction from hematoxylin-and-eosin whole-slide images could support risk stratification, but the task is weakly supervised, and the tissue morphologies carrying prognostic information remain incompletely characterized.
  Methods: We conducted a retrospective secondary analysis using TCGA-COAD/READ (n=562) for morphology-specific analysis, Alliance/ CALGB 89803 (n=424) for model development, and SurGen (n=218) for external evaluation. We propose MorphContrast, a morphology-aware contrastive multiple-instance learning framework that uses tissue labels as structural supervision for five-year survival prediction. MorphContrast combines gated-attention pooling with three auxiliary objectives: patch-level morphology labels define within-patient contrasts, outcome concordance or discordance defines cross-patient contrasts within matched morphologies, and diversity regularization discourages representational collapse. Morphology-matched patches from patients with discordant outcomes serve as hard negatives, encouraging prognostic discrimination within comparable histologic contexts.
  Results: Morphology-specific models show weak but distributed prognostic discrimination: adipose tissue achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.622, stroma achieves 0.604, and both perform comparably to tumor epithelium (0.601-0.605). On Alliance/CALGB 89803, the single model achieves an AUC of 0.642, while the post hoc ensemble reaches a pooled out-of-fold AUC of 0.70 and a risk-group hazard ratio of 3.79 (95% confidence interval: 2.55-5.63). On the external SurGen colon cancer cohort (n=218), the single model and ensemble achieve AUCs of 0.669 and 0.678, respectively.
  Conclusions: These findings support tissue morphology as structural supervision for outcome-aware representation learning in colorectal cancer prognosis.
papers.summary: Predicting five-year survival from hematoxylin-and-eosin whole-slide images could aid risk stratification in colorectal cancer, but the task is weakly supervised and the tissue morphologies that carry prognostic signal are not well characterized. `MorphContrast` is a morphology-aware contrastive multiple-instance learning framework that uses tissue-type labels as structural supervision, combining gated-attention pooling with within-patient contrasts defined by patch-level morphology labels, cross-patient contrasts within matched morphologies defined by outcome concordance, and a diversity regularizer. Morphology-specific analysis on `TCGA-COAD/READ` shows weak but distributed prognostic signal, with adipose tissue reaching an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.622 and stroma 0.604, comparable to tumor epithelium. On the `Alliance/CALGB 89803` development cohort the ensemble reaches **a pooled out-of-fold AUC of 0.70 and a risk-group hazard ratio of 3.79**, and on the external `SurGen` cohort the single model and ensemble reach AUCs of 0.669 and 0.678.

papers.title: Verifier-Harness Co-Evolution for Training-Free Self-Improvement on Open-Ended Tasks
papers.abstract: Training-free self-improvement lets an agent use feedback to revise the response it is about to return and to update the harness state that shapes how it handles later tasks. On open-ended tasks that feedback rarely comes from reference answers or executable tests, so the agent has to rely on a model-based verifier. When the verifier is wrong, the current response can get worse, and misleading experience can persist across the task stream. A verifier that never changes also grows stale as the agent's responses improve and task demands shift. We introduce Unified Co-Evolution (UCoE), a training-free method that evolves an executable verifier program together with the agent's harness state while all model parameters stay fixed. UCoE synthesizes candidate verifier programs and tests them on response contrasts, pairs of responses that differ in one declared property and have a known preferred side. It selects the candidate whose discrimination on its weakest contrast family is highest, a quantity we call driving capacity. The selected verifier diagnoses one weakness in each draft, guides a single repair, decides which response is served, and determines whether the accepted repair may enter the harness state. As tasks complete, their diagnostics seed new candidate verifiers, which must beat the current verifier on the same contrasts before adoption. Across six open-ended benchmarks, UCoE averages 59.00% preference against matched direct generation with Qwen3-8B and 57.19% with Qwen3.8-27B, margins of 9.00 and 7.19 percentage points. On three verifiable benchmarks, the same method raises the mean from 36.06% for direct generation to 38.48%. Code is available at https://github.com/tianyi0216/Unified-Co-Evolution.
papers.summary: Training-free self-improvement lets an agent use feedback to revise the response it is about to return and to update the harness state that shapes later tasks, but on open-ended tasks that feedback must come from a model-based verifier, which can be wrong and grows stale as responses improve. Unified Co-Evolution (`UCoE`) evolves an executable verifier program together with the harness state while all model parameters stay fixed: candidate verifiers are synthesized and tested on response contrasts, pairs differing in one declared property with a known preferred side, and the candidate with the highest discrimination on its weakest contrast family, called driving capacity, is selected. That verifier diagnoses one weakness per draft, guides a single repair, decides which response is served, and gates what enters the harness state, while completed tasks seed new candidate verifiers that must beat the incumbent on the same contrasts. **Across six open-ended benchmarks, `UCoE` wins 59.00% of preference judgments against matched direct generation with `Qwen3-8B`** and 57.19% with `Qwen3.8-27B`, and raises the mean on three verifiable benchmarks from 36.06% to 38.48%.

papers.title: OpenDepth: Repurposing Image Editing Priors for Robust Open-World Monocular Depth Estimation
papers.abstract: Recently, the integration of generative priors has revolutionized Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE), achieving state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance with remarkably high data efficiency. However, although methods based on Text-to-Image (T2I) models excel in general scenes, their efficacy degrades sharply when confronted with open-world environmental perturbations, such as illumination variations and adverse weather. Since T2I priors are optimized for semantic synthesis rather than preserving pixel-level structure, they struggle to decouple geometry from appearance under severe visual shifts, easily triggering structural hallucinations. Therefore, our core insight is to model open-world depth estimation as consistent geometric inference across multi-style images, fully leveraging the powerful structure-preserving editing priors of Image-to-Image (I2I) models. Based on this, we propose OpenDepth, a robust open-world MDE framework that introduces "Intra-Domain Awareness" -- the capability to map diverse stylistic inputs sharing identical geometry into a unified latent space. To achieve this, we first align shallow features within the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) to anchor degraded observations to unified geometric representations. Additionally, we introduce a joint RGB latent reconstruction task, requiring the model to recover clean RGB information from degraded inputs. This multi-stage strategy effectively decouples environmental style interference, compelling the model to focus strictly on underlying geometric recovery. Extensive evaluations show that OpenDepth sets new SOTA records for robust zero-shot depth estimation across standard and extreme weather benchmarks, demonstrating exceptional structural integrity and adaptability.
papers.summary: Generative priors have made monocular depth estimation (MDE) highly data-efficient, but methods built on text-to-image (T2I) models degrade sharply under open-world perturbations such as illumination changes and adverse weather, because T2I priors optimize for semantic synthesis rather than pixel-level structure and can hallucinate geometry. `OpenDepth` instead treats open-world depth estimation as consistent geometric inference across multi-style images, drawing on the structure-preserving editing priors of image-to-image (I2I) models, and introduces intra-domain awareness, the ability to map stylistically diverse inputs with identical geometry into one latent space. It aligns shallow features inside the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) to anchor degraded observations to shared geometric representations and adds a joint RGB latent reconstruction task that recovers clean RGB from degraded inputs. **It sets new state-of-the-art results for robust zero-shot depth estimation across standard and extreme-weather benchmarks.**

papers.title: MAS-Gate: Unlocking Multi-Agent System Lifecycle via Node-Centric Quantification
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) can solve complex problems beyond the reach of a single agent by decomposing tasks and coordinating complementary capabilities. Despite extensive research on MAS, existing work largely focuses on specific aspects or individual phases of their development and operation, resulting in fragmented perspectives with objectives and signals that are difficult to reconcile across these different settings. To bridge these disconnected perspectives, we conceptualize MAS development and operation as a three-phase lifecycle spanning design-time orchestration before execution, runtime intervention during execution, and post-hoc attribution after execution, and introduce MAS-Gate, a unified node-centric quantification applicable across these phases. Modeling each execution as a directed acyclic graph, MAS-Gate combines within-node utility, which estimates a node's contribution through changes in reference-answer likelihood, with inter-node strength, which approximates semantic uptake and potential downstream reach. We adapt this shared quantification to three objectives: providing a structure-aware dense reward for Orchestrator training, training an Editor to act on execution prefixes using paired rewards from completed edited and unedited trajectories, and supplying risk-ranked nodes as auxiliary evidence for LLM-based post-hoc attribution. Experiments spanning interaction environments, knowledge-intensive multi-hop question answering, general reasoning, and post-hoc attribution demonstrate that MAS-Gate improves workflow construction, targeted runtime editing, and LLM-assisted error localization over corresponding phase-specific baselines.
