Together, these results establish MAS-Gate as a unified structural interface for improving MAS generation, dynamic editing, and error attribution throughout the lifecycle.
papers.summary: Research on large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) tends to treat workflow design, runtime intervention, and post-hoc error attribution as separate problems with signals that are hard to reconcile. The authors frame these as a three-phase lifecycle and introduce `MAS-Gate`, a node-centric score over the directed acyclic graph of an execution that combines within-node utility, measured by changes in reference-answer likelihood, with inter-node strength approximating semantic uptake and downstream reach. The same score serves as a dense reward for training an Orchestrator, as a paired reward for an Editor that revises execution prefixes, and as risk-ranked evidence for LLM-based attribution. **Across interactive environments, multi-hop question answering, general reasoning, and attribution tasks, it beats phase-specific baselines in all three roles.**

papers.title: RELAY: Selective Self-Distillation with Adaptive Hand-off for Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning grades a response against many written criteria but collapses them into one reward, which discards the detail the rubric carries and gives no GRPO reward gradient when a group's responses tie. A frozen teacher that reads the rubric as privileged context provides token-level supervision, but we observe an early plateau in the gains over GRPO. RELAY uses advantages and rewards to select positive-advantage and low-scoring zero-advantage rollouts, and monitors the distillation loss to decide when to retire the teacher. Stage 1 combines selective distillation from a frozen teacher with GRPO; a plateau detector then removes the teacher, and Stage 2 continues with GRPO alone. Calibrated on one model-domain pair and reused unchanged in three others, the plateau detector fires between steps 122 and 171. RELAY scores highest in-domain among the compared methods in all four settings, ahead of GRPO on RaR-Medicine by 4.62 points with Qwen3-1.7B and 6.02 with Qwen3-4B. On Qwen3-1.7B/Medicine, removing the teacher from a shared checkpoint outperforms keeping, weakening or refreshing it. Distilling selected rollouts covering about half the response tokens also outperforms distilling all rollouts at a matched average coefficient.
papers.summary: Rubric-based reinforcement learning scores a response against many written criteria but collapses them into a single scalar reward, which discards most of the rubric's detail and yields no `GRPO` gradient when a group's responses tie. `RELAY` adds a frozen teacher that reads the rubric as privileged context and distills token-level supervision only on positive-advantage and low-scoring zero-advantage rollouts, then watches the distillation loss for a plateau, retires the teacher, and continues with `GRPO` alone. The plateau detector, calibrated on one model-domain pair and reused unchanged, fires between steps 122 and 171 in all four settings, and **`RELAY` beats `GRPO` on `RaR-Medicine` by 4.62 points with `Qwen3-1.7B` and 6.02 with `Qwen3-4B`**. Ablations show that retiring the teacher outperforms keeping, weakening, or refreshing it, and that distilling roughly half the response tokens beats distilling all of them at a matched coefficient.

papers.title: 4LC: 4D Latent Cache for Efficient Conditioning in Dynamic World Modeling
papers.abstract: For video generation in dynamic world modeling, observed static and dynamic content should be efficiently reused to provide conditions for repeated generation at different times and viewpoints. We introduce 4LC, a 4D latent cache with composite visual representations and a flexible spatiotemporal access interface. As a latent cache, 4LC directly reuses visual representations of static and dynamic content to provide generation conditions, avoiding per-request RGB rendering and re-encoding. As a composite cache, 4LC binds visual representations from multiple visual encoders (e.g., VAE, DINO, V-JEPA, VGGT) to shared geometry and motion, allowing the composite representations to describe the dynamic world with rich information. Besides, we design a flexible spatiotemporal interface, which directly reads the cache at independently specified times and viewpoints and combines readouts across observations, providing a common conditioning format for diverse downstream tasks. Building on 4LC, we develop 4LC-Video to address multiple video generation tasks through different configurations of source observations, spatiotemporal requests, and historical reuse, including camera control, temporal control, novel-view synthesis, scene revisits, and long-term generation. Our experiments show more efficient condition acquisition, effective spatiotemporal controllability, and scene consistency across tasks using a single 4LC-Video model without task-specific fine-tuning.
papers.summary: Video generation for dynamic world modeling repeatedly needs conditioning on previously observed static and dynamic content at new times and viewpoints, which usually means re-rendering RGB frames and re-encoding them for every request. `4LC` is a 4D latent cache that stores visual representations from multiple encoders (`VAE`, `DINO`, `V-JEPA`, `VGGT`) bound to shared geometry and motion, with a spatiotemporal interface that reads the cache at arbitrary times and viewpoints and combines readouts into a common conditioning format. Built on it, `4LC-Video` handles camera control, temporal control, novel-view synthesis, scene revisits, and long-term generation by varying the source observations, requests, and historical reuse. **A single `4LC-Video` model covers all these tasks without task-specific fine-tuning**, with cheaper condition acquisition and consistent scenes across tasks.

papers.title: Executable Prefix Values for Locating Agent Failures
papers.abstract: Work on debugging LLM agents treats the "first mistake" marked by a human or LLM judge as ground truth for where a trajectory failed. We ask whether such labels point at causes or symptoms, and make the distinction executable: we restart the agent from reconstructed intermediate states of a failed trajectory and estimate its prefix value V(h_t), the probability of success from each step, with a certified point of no return (PNR) for a failure. On 150 SWE-bench Verified tasks with two frozen open-weight agents, we build such curves for 47 and 60 failed trajectories and probe every step labeled by four frontier judges under the Traverse rubric. We find that the labels do not mark what a controller needs. Judges of different lineages agree on the exact step in only 21/57 cases, and the newest judges flag mistakes in 8/10 and 10/10 successful runs. For 66% of the labels, the agent's success probability does not drop at the labeled step; only 7/188 answers name the decisive step. Restarting at the measured restart point raises expected success from 0.44 to 0.57 offline, and real restarts confirm the advantage, whereas restarting at a judge's label does not (-0.08 to -0.03). We release our code, curves, and labels.
papers.summary: Agent debugging typically treats the 'first mistake' flagged by a human or LLM judge as ground truth for where a trajectory failed, and the authors ask whether such labels mark causes or symptoms. They make the question executable by restarting the agent from reconstructed intermediate states of failed runs and estimating the prefix value, the probability of success from each step, along with a certified point of no return (PNR). On 150 `SWE-bench Verified` tasks with two frozen open-weight agents, judges of different lineages agree on the exact step in only 21 of 57 cases under the `Traverse` rubric, the newest judges flag mistakes in most successful runs, and **for 66% of labels the agent's success probability does not drop at the labeled step**. Restarting at the measured restart point raises expected success from 0.44 to 0.57 and real restarts confirm the gain, whereas restarting at a judge's label does not help.

papers.title: The Tokens Strike Back: Safety-Aware Denoising with Directional Embedding-based Revision
papers.abstract: The Safety-Aware Denoiser (SAD) is a recent, training-free, safety-guidance framework for text diffusion models. During inference, SAD steers text samples toward safe regions of the token probability space. In this paper, we propose $\mathit{SADDER}$ (Safety-Aware Denoising with Directional Embedding-based Revision), which improves the safety and quality trade-offs of SAD by exploiting a safety-guidance signal in the embedding (or activation) space for each token position, then updating the token positions using the SAD update rule multiplied by the guidance signal. This multiplication acts as a gating mechanism: tokens with a high unsafe signal are more likely to be modified during inference following the SAD update rule. However, such an update does not automatically preserve the conditional mean, i.e., the denoiser of a fixed target distribution. We therefore theoretically derive new position-wise target distributions for which the modified denoiser is exact. Furthermore, we derive conditions under which the position-wise target distributions match a global target distribution. We test our $\mathit{SADDER}$ method on popular Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) and Uniform-State Diffusion Models (USDMs) across unsafe continuation and jailbreak settings, and show that $\mathit{SADDER}$ achieves a better balance between safety, generation quality, and inference cost than existing methods.
papers.summary: The Safety-Aware Denoiser (`SAD`) is a training-free guidance method that steers text diffusion samples toward safe regions of token probability space at inference time. `SADDER` (Safety-Aware Denoising with Directional Embedding-based Revision) extends it by computing a per-position safety signal in embedding or activation space and multiplying it into the `SAD` update, so that tokens with a high unsafe signal are the ones most likely to be revised. Because this gating breaks the denoiser's conditional-mean property, the authors derive position-wise target distributions for which the modified denoiser is exact and conditions under which these match a global target. **On Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) and Uniform-State Diffusion Models (USDMs), `SADDER` achieves a better balance of safety, generation quality, and inference cost than existing methods** in both unsafe-continuation and jailbreak settings.

papers.title: Beyond Bias Scores: Answerability Confounds in Activation Steering with Gradient-Constrained Direction Design (GCD)
papers.abstract: Bias scores in language-model evaluations often conflate what a model prefers with whether it answers at all. We identify this confound in \textsc{BBQ}, whose ambiguous score factorizes into answerability and signed preference. Across 11 categories, 28,}824 items, and five models, contrastive steering lowers the signed ambiguous score in 11/11 categories but lowers the signed disambiguated preference score in only 8/11. Across 99 configurations, the answerability channel exceeds half of the observed score change in 17\% and accounts for the entire change in 11%. In a six-category disambiguated evaluation, 20.8\% of 1,500 items flip to the unknown option, where abstention is incorrect; \textsc{StereoSet} shows no analogous answer-rate shift. The effect reflects selection and near-orthogonality between the contrastive and preference-gradient directions. We introduce Gradient-Constrained Direction Design (\textsc{GCD}), an option-gradient construction with a first-order unknown-logit constraint. Under a matched Qwen-7B protocol, GCD reduces answer-rate distortion 14-fold and yields a 4-fold larger preference change, while ablations show similar gains for alternative and unconstrained option-gradient directions; nulling the unknown gradient alone is not responsible for the gain. We recommend reporting answerability alongside published scores.
papers.summary: Bias scores for language models can conflate what a model prefers with whether it answers at all, and the authors show that the ambiguous score in `BBQ` factorizes into an answerability component and a signed preference component. Across 11 categories, 28,824 items, and five models, contrastive activation steering lowers the signed ambiguous score in every category but lowers the disambiguated preference score in only 8 of 11, and **in 11% of 99 configurations the answerability channel accounts for the entire observed score change**, with 20.8% of disambiguated items flipping to an incorrect 'unknown' answer while `StereoSet` shows no such shift. They attribute this to selection effects and near-orthogonality between contrastive and preference-gradient directions, and propose Gradient-Constrained Direction Design (`GCD`), an option-gradient steering direction with a first-order constraint on the unknown logit. Under a matched `Qwen-7B` protocol, `GCD` cuts answer-rate distortion 14-fold while producing a 4-fold larger preference change, and the authors recommend reporting answerability alongside published bias scores.

papers.title: When Should Enterprise Policy Decisions Be Learned, and When Should They Be Reasoned?
papers.abstract:
An enterprise agent that answers under a written policy must choose an action before it says anything: answer, ask for a missing fact, ask for confirmation, call one or several tools, escalate, or refuse. Holding one 27B Korean enterprise model fixed, we vary whether the decision is a generated JSON object or a single constrained token, and whether the model may reason first.
  On 2800 in-distribution items we did not detect an accuracy difference between the two deployed paths (93.46% vs 94.14%), while they differ about tenfold in restart stability (3.00% of actions flip vs 0.29%); they also differ in reasoning, so this is an operational comparison.
  On a sealed benchmark of 300 items whose labels come from a hidden executable policy, reasoning is worth +17.3 points [+12.3, +23.0] on exact action. With reasoning off, the format difference was 0.0 points [-4.3, +4.0], a failure to detect an advantage for either interface, not equivalence; with reasoning on it is unresolved. Against a token-matched random control, boundary-targeted supervision moves the two covered boundaries by +17.5 and +20.0 points and leaves a held-out boundary unchanged. In a 3-seed training x reasoning factorial, the sealed-rendering interaction is -4.9 [-8.1, -1.7], consistent with partial substitution.
  All supervision was Korean. On independently rendered English versions, the model is 0.82 points lower [-2.68, +0.93] with reasoning on, the same order as re-rendering in Korean; the reasoning-off gain from targeted supervision is not stable in either language, so we do not claim transfer.
  The original text stays private as the confirmatory set. An open-model re-rendering made after these results reproduced the reasoning effect and the English verdict; the interaction kept its sign but did not replicate under item-clustered intervals. We release the model and that re-rendering with gold labels.
papers.summary: An enterprise agent operating under a written policy must first pick an action, such as answering, asking for a missing fact, requesting confirmation, calling tools, escalating, or refusing, before producing any text. Holding a single 27B Korean enterprise model fixed, the authors compare emitting that decision as a generated JSON object versus a single constrained token, with and without a reasoning step beforehand. On 2,800 in-distribution items the two interfaces show no detectable accuracy difference (93.46% vs 94.14%) but differ about tenfold in how often actions flip across restarts, and **on a sealed 300-item benchmark labeled by a hidden executable policy, reasoning adds 17.3 points on exact action** while the format difference with reasoning off is indistinguishable from zero. Boundary-targeted supervision moves the two covered decision boundaries by 17.5 and 20.0 points while leaving a held-out boundary unchanged, and English re-renderings score within about a point of Korean, though the authors stop short of claiming cross-lingual transfer.

papers.title: Can Agents Truly Forget? Explore Machine Unlearning for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have shown strong capabilities in interactive problem solving, tool use, and long-horizon task execution. However, they may also acquire sensitive or private knowledge during training and expose it during deployment. Retraining a model from scratch to remove such knowledge is prohibitively costly, making machine unlearning a more practical approach. Machine unlearning aims to remove targeted undesirable knowledge from trained models without retraining from scratch while preserving general utility. When language models are deployed as agents, parameter-level unlearning becomes insufficient: forgotten information may still persist in memory artifacts or be reacquired via tool calls. In this paper, we formulate the problem of agent unlearning as removing private information from an LLM-based agent across three information channels: parametric knowledge, persistent memory, and tool-call acquisition. To study this problem, we introduce we introduce Agent Unlearning Benchmark (AUBench), a controlled benchmark that extends the fictitious-author setting of TOFU into an agent environment with persistent memory, an offline web snapshot, tool-accessible documents, and provenance-tracked interaction trajectories. By evaluating existing parameter-level and memory-level unlearning methods in this setting, AUBench reveals the gap between model-level forgetting and system-level agent unlearning, and provides a foundation for developing unlearning methods that operate across the full lifecycle of LLM agents.
papers.summary: Machine unlearning removes targeted knowledge from a trained model without retraining, but when a large language model (LLM) is deployed as an agent, parameter-level forgetting is not enough: the information can persist in memory artifacts or be reacquired through tool calls. The authors formulate agent unlearning as removing private information across three channels, parametric knowledge, persistent memory, and tool-call acquisition, and build the Agent Unlearning Benchmark (`AUBench`), which extends the fictitious-author setup of `TOFU` into an agent environment with persistent memory, an offline web snapshot, tool-accessible documents, and provenance-tracked trajectories. **Evaluating existing parameter-level and memory-level unlearning methods reveals a substantial gap between model-level forgetting and system-level agent unlearning**, which the benchmark is intended to help close.

papers.title: RoTA-Bench: Evaluating 3D Spatial Reasoning through Interactive Projection Alignment
papers.abstract: Can vision-language models turn 2D observations into 3D understanding that supports precise action? This requires inferring object geometry, anticipating the effects of rotation, and refining actions through visual feedback. We introduce RoTA-Bench to evaluate these abilities through interactive 3D-to-2D projection alignment. Given a target silhouette, a model observes a rotated object and chooses successive rotations to recover the target projection within a limited action budget. Our automated pipeline constructs silhouette-preserving 3D objects from 2D icons and uses reversible initialization to guarantee solvability, yielding 674 tasks and a stratified 100-task test set. Empirically, we find that (i) a substantial human-model gap persists: GPT-5.6-Sol succeeds on only 17% of tasks, whereas 20 undergraduate participants collectively complete the test set four times with a 100% success rate; (ii) image-space and pose-space progress can diverge: at matched states, the model more often improves silhouette overlap while worsening pose alignment than humans (19.4% vs. 10.9%); and (iii) fine-grained control is sensitive to interaction history: removing it leaves 96.8% of the model's actions at a coarse 30-degree step size and sharply reduces observed task success. These findings highlight the challenge of converting visual evidence into precise 3D control, beyond recognizing or matching individual images.
papers.summary: Vision-language models are tested on whether they can turn 2D observations into 3D understanding precise enough to act on: given a target silhouette, a model sees a rotated object and must choose successive rotations to recover the target projection within a limited action budget. An automated pipeline builds silhouette-preserving 3D objects from 2D icons with reversible initialization that guarantees solvability, producing 674 `RoTA-Bench` tasks and a stratified 100-task test set. **`GPT-5.6-Sol` succeeds on only 17% of test tasks, while 20 undergraduates collectively completed the set four times with a 100% success rate.** Models also more often improve silhouette overlap while worsening pose alignment than humans do (19.4% vs 10.9%), and removing interaction history leaves 96.8% of model actions at a coarse 30-degree step and sharply reduces success.

papers.title: DeltaTTG: Training Multi-Turn Agents with a Token-to-Go Progress Meter
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for multi-turn agents relies on sparse terminal rewards that say little about individual steps. Within-group step comparisons depend on reliable state matching and sufficiently diverse sampled outcomes, while direct step scoring may require costly external evaluators, human annotations, or task-specific heuristics. We introduce DeltaTTG to learn a reusable progress signal through a shared progress meter, using low-cost supervision from diverse policies' recorded trajectories without task-specific progress rules. Its supervision target, Token-to-Go (TTG), the number of tokens remaining to be generated until task completion, serves as an observable proxy for remaining completion effort. During actor training, changes in the frozen meter's estimates redistribute outcome-derived advantages across steps without altering the reward, preserving each trajectory's advantage sign and token-average scale. On ALFWorld, PaperSearchQA, and BFCLv3, DeltaTTG improves the average score over GRPO by 5.7 and 7.2 points with Qwen3-4B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, respectively, outperforms all compared RL baselines on average, and keeps actor-training GPU-hours close to GRPO. Further experiments show improved sample efficiency and out-of-domain performance, and support the meter's ability to distinguish step quality and guide test-time action selection across actor sizes. The code is available at https://github.com/Xuyan923r/DeltaTTG.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for multi-turn agents suffers from sparse terminal rewards that say little about individual steps, while step-level scoring usually needs external evaluators, annotations, or task-specific heuristics. `DeltaTTG` trains a shared progress meter to predict Token-to-Go (TTG), the number of tokens remaining until task completion, from recorded trajectories of diverse policies, and during actor training uses changes in the frozen meter's estimates to redistribute outcome-derived advantages across steps without changing the reward or each trajectory's advantage sign. **On `ALFWorld`, `PaperSearchQA`, and `BFCLv3` it improves average score over `GRPO` by 5.7 points with `Qwen3-4B` and 7.2 with `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct`**, beating all compared RL baselines on average at roughly the same actor-training GPU cost. Further experiments show better sample efficiency and out-of-domain performance, and the meter can rank step quality and guide test-time action selection across actor sizes.

papers.title: PrT-Flow: Probability-Tractable Flow Matching for Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Diffusion models and Flow Matching can represent flexible distributions over robot actions, but many reinforcement learning algorithms also require the probability of each action. We introduce PrT-Flow (Probability-Tractable Flow Matching), which computes probability density while retaining multimodal, multi-step action generation. Its Jacobian-Tractable Transformer (JTT) makes each sampling step invertible and enables efficient computation of its Jacobian determinant. We train these finite steps with Conditional Euler-step Training (CET), which supervises their displacement over one step during sampling rather than their instantaneous velocity. We prove that, under certain assumptions, CET has the same minimizers as fitting the Euler-solver updates of Flow Matching. PrT-Flow achieves 96% success on Robomimic Lift after 300 epochs of imitation learning, matching the diffusion policy reference, and 96% success on OGBench Cube-Triple after 600k online steps. These results demonstrate that invertible networks with tractable probability densities can learn effective robot policies and support SAC-style actor-critic training. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sunlight-zero/PrT-Flow .
papers.summary: Diffusion and flow-matching policies produce expressive multimodal robot actions, but many reinforcement learning algorithms also need the probability density of each sampled action, which these models do not provide. `PrT-Flow` (Probability-Tractable Flow Matching) uses a Jacobian-Tractable Transformer (`JTT`) that makes every sampling step invertible with an efficiently computable Jacobian determinant, trained with Conditional Euler-step Training (`CET`), which supervises per-step displacement rather than instantaneous velocity and is proven to share minimizers with fitting the Euler-solver updates of flow matching under certain assumptions. **It reaches 96% success on `Robomimic Lift` after 300 epochs of imitation learning, matching the diffusion policy reference, and 96% on `OGBench Cube-Triple` after 600k online steps**, showing that invertible networks with tractable densities can support SAC-style actor-critic training for robot control.

papers.title: Cowork-Gym: Synthesizing Interactive Work Environments at Scale
papers.abstract: Cowork agents navigate dependencies across tools and files while adapting to changing user requirements and edits to shared workspaces. Scaling such environments requires maintaining consistency among task objectives, executable resources, user behavior, and success criteria. We introduce Cowork-Gym, a framework that synthesizes Cowork environments through a build-execute-revise loop that uses execution evidence and review feedback to validate and repair generated environments. To capture realistic Cowork dynamics, a stateful user simulator responds to the agent's actions through dialogue and direct edits to the shared workspace. We synthesize 64.9K environments across 14 application scenarios and use them to post-train 9B, 27B, and 35B-A3B Qwen models with supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and on-policy distillation. Averaged across six agentic benchmarks, these models outperform their corresponding base checkpoints by 8.7, 6.4, and 4.1 points, respectively. Ours-27B ranks second overall among the evaluated models and achieves the highest average scores on PawBench and ClawEval, outperforming models with over 100B total parameters on both benchmarks.
papers.summary: Agents that collaborate on office-style work must track dependencies across tools and files while a user changes requirements and edits the shared workspace, and generating such environments at scale requires keeping task objectives, executable resources, user behavior, and success criteria consistent. `Cowork-Gym` synthesizes environments through a build-execute-revise loop that uses execution evidence and review feedback to validate and repair them, paired with a stateful user simulator that reacts to agent actions through dialogue and direct workspace edits. The authors produce 64.9K environments across 14 application scenarios and post-train 9B, 27B, and 35B-A3B `Qwen` models with supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and on-policy distillation, gaining 8.7, 6.4, and 4.1 points on average over six agentic benchmarks. **The 27B model ranks second overall and tops `PawBench` and `ClawEval`, beating models with over 100B total parameters on both.**

papers.title: Encounter-Driven City-Scale Human Mobility Generation with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for human mobility generation by modeling individual routines, activities, and mobility preferences. However, existing approaches remain largely resident-centric: generating realistic individual trajectories does not necessarily recover the encounters that emerge when multiple residents co-occur at the same place and time. To this end, we study encounter-aware human mobility generation, which jointly preserves individual mobility and population-level interaction structure. We propose EncounterMob, an encounter-driven LLM framework consisting of a coarse-to-fine Encounter Generator and an Iterative Coupling Framework. The Encounter Generator first captures city-level encounter rhythms and then instantiates participant-time-venue encounters, while the Iterative Coupling Framework coordinates these encounters with personal mobility behavior through successive refinement. We further introduce an encounter recovery protocol covering encounter marginal and joint distributions over residents, times, and venues. Experiments on the Japan and NYC datasets show that EncounterMob outperforms all external baselines on all seven encounter metrics and all six personal mobility metrics. Compared with ELLMob, it reduces the participant-time-venue joint error by 40.4%/41.7% and the mean personal mobility error by 58.8%/32.7% on Japan/NYC, respectively.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) approaches to human mobility generation produce realistic individual trajectories but do not recover the encounters that arise when residents co-occur at the same place and time. `EncounterMob` tackles encounter-aware generation with a coarse-to-fine Encounter Generator that first captures city-level encounter rhythms and then instantiates participant-time-venue encounters, plus an Iterative Coupling Framework that reconciles those encounters with individual mobility behavior through successive refinement, evaluated under a new protocol covering marginal and joint encounter distributions. On the `Japan` and `NYC` datasets it outperforms all external baselines on all seven encounter metrics and all six personal mobility metrics, and **relative to `ELLMob` it cuts the participant-time-venue joint error by 40.4% and 41.7%** and mean personal mobility error by 58.8% and 32.7%.

papers.title: Dynamic K-Head: Difficulty-Supervised Budget Selection for Continuous Latent Reasoning
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) improves reasoning but incurs substantial autoregressive rationale cost. Continuous CoT moves intermediate computation into recurrent hidden states, yet typically uses a fixed number of updates even though the best budget varies across questions and accuracy need not improve monotonically with $K$. We introduce Dynamic K-Head, a question-conditioned, pre-rollout budget selector. It is jointly trained with the reasoner under selected budgets, using difficulty supervision based on scores assigned from the question alone. We also show that latent-update count can misrepresent end-to-end cost because a short latent rollout can shift computation into a longer explicit continuation. We therefore count latent updates, implementation-specific special tokens, and all decoded text. Instantiated with CoDI on Llama 3.2 1B and GSM8K, Dynamic K-Head reaches 54.44% exact-match accuracy at 12.03 average reasoning/output tokens, compared with 52.31% at 15.21 tokens for fixed-$K=6$ CoDI---a 2.12-point gain with 20.9% lower token cost. Across three out-of-distribution arithmetic datasets, it reduces cost by 19.3--25.7% while improving accuracy by 0.30--2.22 points. These results demonstrate that difficulty-supervised budget selection can improve both accuracy and efficiency, while stable budget selection remains a central challenge.
papers.summary: Continuous chain-of-thought (CoT) moves intermediate reasoning into recurrent hidden states instead of generated text, but typically runs a fixed number of latent updates even though the best budget varies by question and more updates do not monotonically help. `Dynamic K-Head` is a question-conditioned selector that picks the latent budget before rollout and is trained jointly with the reasoner using difficulty scores assigned from the question alone; the authors also argue that counting latent updates understates cost, since a short latent rollout can push computation into a longer explicit continuation, so they count latent updates, special tokens, and all decoded text. **Instantiated with `CoDI` on `Llama 3.2 1B` and `GSM8K`, it reaches 54.44% exact match at 12.03 average tokens versus 52.31% at 15.21 tokens for fixed-budget `CoDI`, a 2.12-point gain with 20.9% lower token cost**, and on three out-of-distribution arithmetic datasets it cuts cost by 19.3 to 25.7% while improving accuracy by up to 2.22 points. Stable budget selection remains an open challenge.

papers.title: LatentRiskBench: Measuring State-Dependent Risks in Enterprise Agents
papers.abstract: Enterprise agents face safety risks that cannot be determined from individual actions alone. Existing safety benchmarks largely evaluate action-local risks, overlooking failures whose safety depends on workflow state. In such state-dependent risks, the same action may be safe in one context but violate policy in another. Hence, we introduce LatentRiskBench for evaluating such state-dependent risks in enterprise settings. It pairs risky trajectories with benign counterparts that share the same terminal action but differ in latent policy-relevant states, requiring models to reconstruct workflow context rather than rely on action-level cues. We also introduce new metrics for state-dependent risk evaluation, including a suite of residual risk (RR) measures. Experiments on the benchmark show that action-level evaluation detects only 0.09 of state-dependent violations, whereas state-level evaluation reaches 0.96. Existing guardrail methods largely overlook such risks unless they are explicitly applied to workflow states. Case studies on a commercial deployed scenario further show that the safety metrics embedded in the benchmark provide a more realistic measure of safety for enterprise agents. Our dataset and code are available at https://github.com/JingyueCong/LatentRiskBench.
papers.summary: Existing agent safety benchmarks mostly judge risks that can be read off a single action, but in enterprise workflows the same action can be safe in one state and a policy violation in another. `LatentRiskBench` pairs risky trajectories with benign counterparts that share the same terminal action but differ in latent policy-relevant state, so that detecting violations requires reconstructing workflow context rather than keying on action-level cues, and introduces a suite of residual risk (RR) metrics for this setting. **Action-level evaluation detects only 0.09 of state-dependent violations whereas state-level evaluation reaches 0.96**, and existing guardrails largely miss such risks unless explicitly applied to workflow state. Case studies on a commercially deployed scenario suggest the benchmark's metrics give a more realistic picture of enterprise agent safety.

papers.title: Stable Token-level Scheduling for Serverless LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Serverless inference is emerging as an efficient deployment model for Large Language Models (LLMs) due to its ability to elastically scale resources, improve GPU utilization through resource sharing, and reduce infrastructure costs. However, existing approaches primarily optimize time to first token (TTFT) while overlooking inter-token latency (ITL), a key determinant of user experience during response generation. We observe that LLM inference comprises a computation-intensive prefill stage and a bandwidth-bound decode stage, where admitting new requests can disrupt ongoing decoding and increase latency. To address this, we propose Token Window Pacing (TWP), a closed-loop scheduling framework that leverages runtime feedback from ITL, queue depth, and workload characteristics to regulate request admission at the token level instead of the batch level. TWP dynamically adjusts a selfregulating token window and incorporates chunk-based prefill to minimize interference from incoming requests. Experiments on realistic serverless workloads show that TWP delivers stable TTFT, significantly reduces latency spikes, lowers P99 tail latency, minimizes ITL variation, and improves throughput by up to 45% over ServerlessLLM and 58% over conventional schedulers. These results demonstrate that feedback-driven tokenlevel scheduling enables stable, high-throughput serverless LLM inference without modifying the underlying model.
papers.summary: Serverless inference lets large language model (LLM) deployments share GPUs elastically, but existing schedulers optimize time to first token (TTFT) while neglecting inter-token latency (ITL), and admitting new requests during the bandwidth-bound decode stage disrupts ongoing generation. Token Window Pacing (`TWP`) is a closed-loop scheduler that uses runtime feedback from ITL, queue depth, and workload characteristics to regulate admission at the token level rather than the batch level, adjusting a self-regulating token window and using chunked prefill to limit interference. On realistic serverless workloads it keeps TTFT stable, reduces latency spikes and P99 tail latency, and **improves throughput by up to 45% over `ServerlessLLM` and 58% over conventional schedulers** without modifying the underlying model.

papers.title: MedEvo: Medical Reasoning Evolution through Knowledge Navigation
papers.abstract: Medical multimodal reasoning models are typically trained on teacher-generated rationales, discarding the valid reasoning in students' own failed trajectories, while general-domain correction methods offer little guidance for errors in image reading, anatomical context, or differential diagnosis. We propose MedEvo, which uses medical knowledge, namely a tag taxonomy and error-type diagnosis, to navigate both trajectory repair and data selection. For each failed rollout, a gold-blind auditor locates the first consequential error and provides a minimal, answer-free hint; the same student retains the valid prefix and regenerates the erroneous suffix. After each round, MedEvo identifies capability gaps across medical tags on a held-out feedback set and prioritizes related questions for new rollouts and repairs. With supervised fine-tuning (SFT) alone, MedEvo raises Qwen3.5-9B mean accuracy across seven benchmarks from 65.57% to 69.12% (47.40% to 54.50% on the multimodal track of MedXpertQA (MedXpertQA-MM)), surpassing teacher-distillation SFT (66.93%). It also raises Qwen3.5-35B and Qwen3.5-397B mean accuracy from 67.91% to 73.04% and from 71.83% to 74.95%, respectively. Our analyses show that failed trajectories contain reasoning worth preserving, that repair success does not imply learning value, and that independent feedback is key to sustained improvement.
papers.summary: Medical multimodal reasoning models are usually trained on teacher-generated rationales, discarding the valid reasoning in a student's own failed attempts, and general-purpose correction methods offer little help with errors in image reading, anatomical context, or differential diagnosis. `MedEvo` uses a medical tag taxonomy and error-type diagnosis to guide both trajectory repair and data selection: a gold-blind auditor locates the first consequential error in a failed rollout and gives a minimal answer-free hint, the same student keeps the valid prefix and regenerates the rest, and after each round the system finds capability gaps on a held-out feedback set and prioritizes related questions. **With supervised fine-tuning (SFT) alone, it raises `Qwen3.5-9B` mean accuracy across seven benchmarks from 65.57% to 69.12%, surpassing teacher-distillation SFT at 66.93%**, and also lifts `Qwen3.5-35B` and `Qwen3.5-397B` by about 5 and 3 points respectively. The analyses argue that failed trajectories contain reasoning worth preserving and that repair success does not imply learning value.

papers.title: HelpMeOut: A Neuropsychology-Grounded Benchmark for Error-Aware Monitoring of Household Task Execution
papers.abstract: We introduce HelpMeOut, an embodied AI benchmark for error-aware monitoring of household task execution. Existing embodied household benchmarks typically assume that humans execute tasks correctly, but this assumption does not hold for cognitively impaired persons or older adults whose everyday activities produce structured execution errors. To address this gap, HelpMeOut operationalizes research on everyday action errors into 20000 paired activity episodes, covering nine neuropsychologically motivated error categories. In each episode, agents observe a streaming human activity trajectory and must monitor whether the execution is unfolding correctly, diagnosing any structured errors as early as possible. We evaluate learned-monitor, symbolic, change-point, and frontier LLM prompting baselines. Results show that these methods perform poorly as error monitors, often missing when execution goes wrong. These results suggest a gap left by standard goal-inference and task-completion benchmarks, making HelpMeOut a testbed for error-aware assistive agents.
papers.summary: Embodied household benchmarks generally assume that the human performs tasks correctly, an assumption that fails for cognitively impaired people or older adults whose everyday activities contain structured execution errors. `HelpMeOut` operationalizes neuropsychological research on everyday action errors into 20,000 paired activity episodes spanning nine error categories, where an agent watches a streaming human activity trajectory and must detect and diagnose errors as early as possible. **Learned-monitor, symbolic, change-point, and frontier LLM prompting baselines all perform poorly, often missing when execution goes wrong**, exposing a gap left by standard goal-inference and task-completion benchmarks.

papers.title: zPocket: Better Pocket Finding with Frozen Co-Folding Features
papers.abstract: Identifying protein-ligand binding sites (pockets) is important for understanding protein function and developing drugs. However, no public method has leveraged co-folding models for novel pocket prediction; furthermore, this task lacks a suitable benchmark as existing benchmarks are within the training distribution of co-folding models. We therefore developed PocketWatch,a curated dataset of biologically relevant ligand pockets. The PocketWatch test set consists of unseen pockets stratified by sequence similarity, structural similarity, and crypticity to enable evaluation of generalization to novel and challenging pockets. Using this dataset, we develop zPocket, a method that trains pocket-prediction heads on top of frozen features from co-folding models. We show that zPocket heads outperform baseline methods across all stratifications. Our best zPocket model achieves overall per-target AUPRC of 0.745 compared to 0.598 and 0.595 for the strongest baselines, VN-EGNN and UniSite-1D retrained on the PocketWatch split (0.559 and 0.531 when using the published weights); the widely used P2Rank reaches 0.477. We further show that zPocket can be used to outperform baseline methods on top-N+2 recall of predicted pocket centroids through clustering per-residue predictions or using zPocket to rescore centroids proposed by other models. Finally, we explore two applications of zPocket: crystallographic fragment screens and a proteome-scale scan for uncharacterized pockets on human proteins. Together these results suggest that zPocket heads built on co-folding trunk features can greatly advance ligand binding site prediction.
papers.summary: Predicting protein-ligand binding pockets matters for understanding protein function and drug design, but no public method had used co-folding models for novel pocket prediction, and existing benchmarks fall within those models' training distribution. The authors build `PocketWatch`, a curated dataset whose test set contains unseen pockets stratified by sequence similarity, structural similarity, and crypticity, and train `zPocket`, pocket-prediction heads on frozen features from co-folding models. **The best `zPocket` model reaches a per-target AUPRC of 0.745 versus 0.598 and 0.595 for retrained `VN-EGNN` and `UniSite-1D`** and 0.477 for `P2Rank`, and it also improves top-N+2 centroid recall by clustering residue predictions or rescoring other models' proposals. The authors explore applications to crystallographic fragment screens and a proteome-scale scan for uncharacterized pockets on human proteins.

papers.title: LeanPRM: Lean-Grounded Process Supervision for Natural Language Proof Verification
papers.abstract: AI systems now write long and difficult mathematical proofs, and checking their step-by-step validity is becoming a bottleneck. A learned verifier could check proofs cheaply, but training one requires a correctness label on every step, and such labels are hard to obtain for open-ended proofs. Existing methods take them from human annotators, which is costly, or derive them from final answers, which proofs do not have, and formalizing each proof in Lean requires expert effort. We introduce LeanPRM, a framework that uses the Lean proof assistant to create step-level labels for natural-language proofs. A model writes a natural-language proof together with a paired formal proof, without feedback from Lean. Lean then labels every step, and a second model discards failures caused only by the formal syntax, so that the negative labels mark errors in the mathematics. LeanPRM contains 10,634 proofs with 152K labeled steps and no human annotation. A Qwen3-4B verifier trained on LeanPRM raises exact step-label accuracy on a held-out set of 200 proofs (LeanPRM-Bench) from 48.2 to 74.7, as opposed to 60.3 when the same base model is trained on PRM800K. It also selects better proofs in best-of-N selection on IMO-level problems, and outperforms the PRM800K-trained verifier on three of four external verification benchmarks. Training on LeanPRM improves verifiers at every size from 0.6B to 8B parameters on LeanPRM-Bench, Hard2Verify and IMO-GradingBench. Given the labels need no human annotation, LeanPRM can grow with the supply of formal statements, offering a path to step-level feedback on AI-generated proofs that are hard for humans to check.
papers.summary: As AI systems write long mathematical proofs, checking each step becomes a bottleneck, and training a learned verifier requires step-level correctness labels that are costly to get from humans and unavailable from final answers. `LeanPRM` has a model write a natural-language proof paired with a formal `Lean` proof without Lean feedback, lets `Lean` label every step, and uses a second model to discard failures caused only by formal syntax so that negative labels reflect mathematical errors, yielding 10,634 proofs with 152K labeled steps and no human annotation. **A `Qwen3-4B` verifier trained on it raises exact step-label accuracy on the held-out `LeanPRM-Bench` from 48.2 to 74.7, versus 60.3 when the same base model is trained on `PRM800K`**, selects better proofs in best-of-N on IMO-level problems, and wins on three of four external verification benchmarks. Gains hold at every size from 0.6B to 8B on `LeanPRM-Bench`, `Hard2Verify`, and `IMO-GradingBench`, and the pipeline can scale with the supply of formal statements.

papers.title: Understanding Gene Expression-to-Image Learning: Spatial Structure and Information Fidelity
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables cell-level analysis of biological heterogeneity, but learning effective representations from high-dimensional, unordered gene expression profiles remains challenging. Gene Expression-to-Image (GE2I) offers an effective learning strategy by arranging gene values on pixel grids for convolutional neural networks, but its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We study GE2I on full-transcriptome data while keeping the network and training procedure fixed. Our results reveal a trade-off between spatial smoothness and gene-level fidelity. Structured mappings produce smooth, low-frequency patterns that support faster early optimization, whereas assigning multiple genes to the same pixel obscures expression differences and can reduce predictive performance. This trade-off explains why random mappings can compete with structured layouts when many genes are represented. One-to-one gene-to-pixel assignment improves prediction across the tested visual backbones even when image smoothness decreases. We further find that the benefits of pretraining and augmentation depend on the backbone and mapping. These findings provide practical guidance for pixel allocation and the transfer of vision priors to gene expression data.
papers.summary: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) produces high-dimensional, unordered gene expression profiles, and Gene Expression-to-Image (GE2I) methods arrange these values on pixel grids so convolutional neural networks can process them, though why this works has been unclear. The authors hold the network and training procedure fixed on full-transcriptome data and vary only the gene-to-pixel mapping. They find a trade-off between spatial smoothness and gene-level fidelity: structured layouts yield smooth, low-frequency images that speed early optimization, but packing multiple genes into one pixel hides expression differences, which explains why random mappings can compete with structured ones. **One-to-one gene-to-pixel assignment improves prediction across all tested visual backbones** even when image smoothness drops, while the value of pretraining and augmentation depends on the backbone and mapping.

papers.title: A Node Embedding Framework for Model-Centric Conformance Checking in Process Mining
papers.abstract: Evaluating the quality of process models discovered from event logs is a fundamental challenge in process mining. Traditional evaluation relies on conformance metrics such as fitness and precision, which are highly sensitive to noise and deviations in event logs and therefore often fail to give a consistent assessment of discovery algorithms. We introduce a model-centric evaluation framework that combines node embeddings with Procrustes alignment to enable cross-graph comparability, since embeddings derived from different graphs reside in distinct vector spaces. The proposed PetriNetGraph method transforms Petri net process models into graph representations compatible with embedding algorithms. Comparing the node embeddings of ground-truth and discovered models through a parameterized cosine distance yields a unified and bounded metric for evaluating process discovery across datasets and methods. We evaluate the framework under static and context-aware scenarios to examine how prior knowledge of activity existence influences the assessment of structural similarity. The framework also integrates a compliance checking mechanism that localizes deviations at the activity level and an entropy-regularized node distance aggregation function that quantifies global deviations across the model. Experiments on nine publicly available event logs show that the approach provides a reliable embedding-based conformance indicator that reflects the behavior of fitness and precision. Experiments on synthetic logs with controlled noise levels confirm that it is substantially more robust to log deviations than traditional conformance metrics, PetriNet2Vec, and its dynamic-window and Procrustes-aligned variants, while remaining sensitive to process model degradation. All implementation details and datasets are publicly available.
papers.summary: Evaluating process models discovered from event logs usually relies on fitness and precision metrics, which are sensitive to noise and deviations in the logs and often give inconsistent assessments of discovery algorithms. The authors propose a model-centric alternative: a `PetriNetGraph` transformation turns Petri net process models into graphs suitable for node embedding, and Procrustes alignment makes embeddings from different graphs comparable, so a parameterized cosine distance between ground-truth and discovered models yields a bounded metric. The framework also localizes deviations at the activity level and aggregates them with an entropy-regularized node distance function. On nine public event logs the metric tracks fitness and precision, and **on synthetic logs with controlled noise it is substantially more robust to log deviations than traditional metrics and `PetriNet2Vec` variants** while still responding to process model degradation.

papers.title: From Token Correction to Claim Admission: Training-Free Hallucination Mitigation for Large Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models often exhibit object hallucination, generating claims that are not supported by the input image. To mitigate this issue, we propose Evidence-Guided Visual Claim Admission (EGVCA), a training-free framework that admits a semantic claim only when it receives sufficient image-dependent support. EGVCA measures this support by comparing the claim likelihood under the observed image and a visual-null input. For captioning, it controls semantic expansion without altering token generation. For binary visual question answering, it combines atomic visual support with the image-induced change in the model's native Yes--No margin. Experiments on CHAIR, POPE, and MME across three LVLM backbones show that EGVCA substantially reduces object hallucination while preserving caption quality. It achieves the highest POPE F1 in eight of nine backbone--sampling settings and improves the native MME total score on all three backbones. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of claim-level admission as a simple alternative to token-level distribution correction.
papers.summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) often hallucinate objects that are not in the input image, and most mitigation methods correct the token-level output distribution. Evidence-Guided Visual Claim Admission (`EGVCA`) is a training-free framework that instead operates on semantic claims, admitting a claim only when its likelihood under the observed image is sufficiently higher than under a visual-null input. For captioning this controls semantic expansion without changing token generation, and for binary visual question answering it combines atomic visual support with the image-induced shift in the model's native Yes/No margin. Across three LVLM backbones on `CHAIR`, `POPE`, and `MME`, the method substantially reduces object hallucination while preserving caption quality, **achieving the highest `POPE` F1 in eight of nine backbone-sampling settings** and improving the `MME` total score on all three backbones.

papers.title: Where Small Mistakes Matter: Quantifying State Criticality for Imitation Learning
papers.abstract: Imitation learning typically treats every demonstration state as equally important, optimizing a behavior-cloning objective uniformly across the dataset. Yet not all states are created equal: in a small number of critical states, even a slight deviation from the expert action can lead to a failure, while in many other states such errors are recoverable and inconsequential. We formalize state criticality in imitation learning as the worst-case degradation in downstream value induced by a bounded perturbation of the expert action at a given state. We then propose SCRIM, a practical State CRIticality Measure that estimates this quantity by training an adversarial disturbance policy and a value critic around a fixed imitation policy. SCRIM assigns each demonstration state a score reflecting how vulnerable the task outcome is to small, policy-relevant action errors. We show that these scores can be used to reweight behavior-cloning losses, improving imitation at consequential states and increasing overall task performance. We further show that SCRIM enables data curation by selecting compact, high-value subsets of demonstrations that preserve performance while substantially reducing the amount of training data. We evaluate SCRIM across various simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, and demonstrate that SCRIM improves policy training, enables efficient data selection, and provides interpretable insights into which moments in a demonstration are most critical for task success. Project website: https://sia-lab-git.github.io/SCRIM/
papers.summary: Behavior cloning weights every demonstration state equally, yet in a small number of critical states a slight deviation from the expert action causes task failure, while elsewhere such errors are recoverable. The authors formalize state criticality as the worst-case drop in downstream value caused by a bounded perturbation of the expert action, and propose `SCRIM` (State CRIticality Measure), which estimates it by training an adversarial disturbance policy and a value critic around a fixed imitation policy. The resulting per-state scores reweight behavior-cloning losses and select compact, high-value subsets of demonstrations. Across simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, **reweighting with `SCRIM` improves task performance, and curated subsets preserve performance while substantially reducing training data**, with the scores also exposing which moments in a demonstration matter most.

papers.title: Adaptive-Group Process Rewards for GUI Agents
papers.abstract: Training graphical user interface (GUI) agents with reinforcement learning suffers from sparse outcome rewards, leading to inefficient learning. Process rewards offer a promising direction for credit assignment to intermediate actions; however, accurately evaluating an action requires identifying evidence across long-horizon GUI trajectories, as its value may depend on information beyond its immediate state and observation. In this paper, we propose an adaptive-group process reward framework that dynamically partitions a GUI trajectory into semantically coherent subgoal groups, enabling process reward estimation at both the action and group levels. At the action level, a critic evaluates each action based on the visual changes and subsequent actions within the group for action correctness and contribution to the subgoal. At the group level, the framework aggregates action-level evaluations to assess subgoal completion and contribution to the overall task, and further refines these assessments by leveraging the context of all groups in the trajectory. The process reward of each action is obtained by combining its action-level evaluation with the refined group-level evaluation. We further augment GRPO's outcome advantage with the proposed process rewards to provide finer-grained guidance for GUI agent training. Experiments on process reward benchmarks and downstream RL training demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning for graphical user interface (GUI) agents suffers from sparse outcome rewards, and process rewards for individual actions are hard to compute because an action's value may depend on evidence far from its immediate state and observation in a long trajectory. The proposed framework dynamically partitions a trajectory into semantically coherent subgoal groups, has a critic score each action on correctness and contribution to its subgoal using the visual changes and subsequent actions within the group, aggregates these into group-level assessments of subgoal completion, and refines them using the context of all groups. Each action's process reward combines its action-level and refined group-level evaluations and is added to the outcome advantage in `GRPO` for finer-grained training signal. **Experiments on process reward benchmarks and downstream RL training demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework** for GUI agent training.

papers.title: ECG-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Targeted Electrocardiogram Waveform Evolution
papers.abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) models need supervision that targets evolving weaknesses and remains faithful to waveform evidence. We introduce ECG-RSI, a recursive self-improvement framework combining verified waveform synthesis with feedback-guided intervention search. Signal remeasurement verifies waveform edits; construction errors guide generator repair, while learner errors motivate interventions compared on a separate selection set. Across seven benchmarks, three rounds raise Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's mean question-answering accuracy from 34.57% to 56.04% and mean classification F1 from 24.27 to 34.03. Across the retained trajectory, the preferred supervision shifts from direct reinforcement to confusion-focused contrasts. Continued feedback correction yields diminishing external gains. These results motivate separating error diagnosis from intervention selection and checking whether gains on the feedback set transfer to independent benchmarks.
papers.summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) models need training supervision that targets their evolving weaknesses while staying faithful to waveform evidence. `ECG-RSI` is a recursive self-improvement loop pairing verified waveform synthesis with feedback-guided intervention search: signal remeasurement checks that waveform edits are valid, construction errors drive generator repair, and learner errors motivate candidate interventions that are compared on a separate selection set. **Over three rounds across seven benchmarks, the method raises `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B`'s mean question-answering accuracy from 34.57% to 56.04%** and mean classification F1 from 24.27 to 34.03. The preferred supervision shifts over time from direct reinforcement toward confusion-focused contrasts, and continued feedback correction yields diminishing external gains, which motivates separating error diagnosis from intervention selection and checking transfer to independent benchmarks.

papers.title: Keep Your Receipts: Trustworthy Cleanup of Agent-Built Knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract: Agents build knowledge graphs as memory, and building them has become easy. Maintaining them has not. When a source is retracted, overruled, or erased, everything built on top of it (entity merges, entailed edges, community summaries) must be re-examined, and the maintainer must choose between deleting too much and too little. Deployed pipelines delete only the directly extracted facts: on our corpus that reduces contaminated queries from 32.2% to 28.0% under a real retraction and changes nothing under predicate revocation. Rebuilding is no repair for a constructor that samples: two builds of the same 300-document corpus differ in 29,475 artifacts, five times the 6,248 that removing the 61 retracted documents changes. PolyGraph instead asks the constructor for receipts: for every artifact, alternative bundles of source evidence, each claimed sufficient on its own, emitted in the call that creates it. Cleanup is then set arithmetic over the receipts, with no model calls. Because receipts are the model's own self-report, a re-derivation audit checks them by deleting the cited evidence and testing whether the constructor still produces the artifact. The audit finds that a receipt is trustworthy when it is shaped like the claim it backs. Merge receipts, each backing one narrow claim, agree with re-derivation 68% and 85% of the time. Summary receipts, elicited per sentence but stored as one flat list for the whole text, are wrong about two thirds of the time, almost always by keeping dead content. One receipt per sentence instead is 100% and 88% faithful and lets cleanup keep 33 of 35 touched summaries. The result holds under a second oracle model, a claim-blind prompt, ten further deletions, a second domain and a second constructor. Distrusting the summary layer cuts contaminated queries to 0.4% and 0.8% at 99.8 to 100% of the recall a perfect maintainer would return.
papers.summary: LLM agents increasingly build knowledge graphs as memory, but when a source is retracted, overruled, or erased, everything derived from it such as entity merges, entailed edges, and community summaries must be re-examined, and deployed pipelines that delete only directly extracted facts barely reduce contaminated queries. Rebuilding is no fix because the constructor samples: two builds of the same 300-document corpus differ in 29,475 artifacts, five times what removing 61 retracted documents changes. `PolyGraph` instead asks the constructor to emit receipts with every artifact, alternative bundles of source evidence each claimed sufficient on its own, so cleanup becomes set arithmetic over receipts with no model calls, and a re-derivation audit checks receipts by deleting the cited evidence and testing whether the constructor still produces the artifact. The audit shows receipts are trustworthy when shaped like the claim they back, with per-sentence summary receipts 88 to 100% faithful versus flat per-text receipts wrong about two thirds of the time, and **distrusting the summary layer cuts contaminated queries from 32.2% to under 1% at 99.8 to 100% of the recall a perfect maintainer would return**.

papers.title: Upstream Influence, Downstream Re-Anchoring in LLM Agent Chains
papers.abstract: People act on evaluative judgments produced by LLM agents, and in multi-agent systems those judgments pass through several agents before reaching a person. We show that a workflow's information architecture---source access, handoff format, and which model reads the untrusted content---governs how much of a coordinated manipulation reaches the end. On 32 Taiwan~2025 recall cases, ten authentic Threads comments shown to one agent move its stance by $+0.171$ toward the injected position, and a mirrored set moves it the other way. Passing that judgment down a chain removes more than half of the shift by the third agent; keeping the comments in front of every agent sustains more of it. The reduction is not attrition in transit: each receiver discounts the inherited stance in proportion to how far it sits from its own reading of the evidence, returning to what that evidence implies for the case rather than to neutrality---consistent with partial re-anchoring. Handoff format is a second lever: a stance relayed without its reasoning is largely discounted. Susceptibility at the exposed seat varies fourfold across models, while the chain's arrangement does not matter at all. None of this is visible in the transcripts---the injected claims are almost never restated, so reasoning-trace audits miss the attack.
papers.summary: In multi-agent systems, an evaluative judgment produced by one LLM agent may pass through several others before a person acts on it, raising the question of how much a coordinated manipulation of the first agent survives the chain. On 32 cases from the Taiwan 2025 recall votes, ten authentic Threads comments shift a single agent's stance by 0.171 toward the injected position, and a mirrored set shifts it the other way. **Relaying that judgment down a chain removes more than half of the shift by the third agent**, because each receiver discounts the inherited stance in proportion to its distance from the receiver's own reading of the evidence, whereas keeping the comments in front of every agent sustains more of it, and a stance relayed without its reasoning is largely discounted. Susceptibility at the exposed seat varies fourfold across models while chain arrangement has no effect, and because the injected claims are almost never restated, reasoning-trace audits miss the attack.

papers.title: Evidence-First Agentic Verification
papers.abstract: Long-horizon, semi-verifiable agentic tasks often rely on rubric-based evaluation, but the evidence needed to assess these tasks can be spread across the environment state and the execution trace. A judge may overlook this evidence or accept unsupported claims, including an agent's own reports of success. When rubric verdicts serve as reinforcement-learning rewards, such errors can reinforce undesirable behavior. We introduce Sauron, an evidence-first agentic verifier that investigates both state and trace and relies on a claim only after independently validating it against its source. Bounded queries and joint investigation of related criteria reduce context use and redundant work, and each verdict carries an auditable receipt of its supporting evidence. Across 2,586 human-labeled criteria from 100 personal-assistant episodes, Sauron achieves the highest F1 of five verifiers on all eight backbones tested while costing less than Gandalf, the strongest baseline. With GPT-5.6 Sol, it reaches 0.96 F1 versus Gandalf's 0.92 at 23% lower cost, with a wider margin on process criteria. On a paired fault-injection suite covering 13 families, several of which simulate reward hacking, Sauron detects 97% of injected failures while flagging only 2% of clean controls, outperforming baselines even when they are given the full trace. On TRAIL, a benchmark for detecting and localizing real agent errors, Sauron leads both Gandalf and TRAIL's own judge on all three quality metrics.
papers.summary: Rubric-based judges for long-horizon agentic tasks can overlook evidence spread across environment state and execution traces, or accept an agent's unsupported claims of success, and when their verdicts serve as reinforcement-learning rewards those errors reinforce bad behavior. `Sauron` is an evidence-first agentic verifier that investigates both state and trace, relies on a claim only after validating it against its source, uses bounded queries and joint investigation of related criteria to limit context use and redundant work, and attaches an auditable evidence receipt to each verdict. On 2,586 human-labeled criteria from 100 personal-assistant episodes it achieves the highest F1 of five verifiers across all eight backbones at lower cost than the strongest baseline `Gandalf`, reaching **0.96 F1 versus 0.92 at 23% lower cost with `GPT-5.6 Sol`**. On a fault-injection suite of 13 failure families, several simulating reward hacking, it detects 97% of injected failures while flagging 2% of clean controls, and it leads on all three quality metrics of `TRAIL`, a benchmark for detecting and localizing real agent errors.

papers.title: TSRL: Trigger-based Supervised Reinforcement Learning for Continual Agent Training
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents excel at complex, multi-step tasks but suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual learning--acquiring new skills often degrades previously mastered capabilities. Existing post-training paradigms face a fundamental trade-off: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is sample-efficient but prone to severe forgetting, while Reinforcement Learning (RL) preserves prior capabilities but converges slowly without expert guidance. To bridge this gap, we introduce Trigger-based Supervised Reinforcement Learning (TSRL), a framework that integrates the strengths of both paradigms through an adaptive, state-dependent expert supervision mechanism. TSRL employs RL as the optimization backbone, activating SFT selectively on "hard states" where the policy fails. Theoretically, we show that restricting supervision to failure states derives an upper bound on the cumulative parameter updates, thereby reducing forgetting compared to full SFT. Empirically, TSRL achieves consistent gains across three agent benchmarks (ALFWorld, WebShop, and Deep Search) at both 7B and 32B scales. In continual learning scenarios, our method retains up to 9.6 points more capability on prior tasks than SFT->RL baselines, while matching or exceeding target-task performance.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents trained continually on new tasks suffer catastrophic forgetting of earlier skills: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is sample-efficient but forgets badly, while reinforcement learning (RL) preserves prior abilities but converges slowly without expert guidance. Trigger-based Supervised Reinforcement Learning (`TSRL`) uses RL as the optimization backbone and activates SFT only on hard states where the policy fails, and the authors show theoretically that restricting supervision to failure states bounds cumulative parameter updates and therefore reduces forgetting relative to full SFT. On `ALFWorld`, `WebShop`, and `Deep Search` at 7B and 32B scales the method gives consistent gains, and **in continual learning it retains up to 9.6 points more prior-task capability than SFT-then-RL baselines** while matching or exceeding target-task performance.

papers.title: SkillScreen: High-Recall Screening of Malicious Agent Skills with Decision Models
papers.abstract: Agent skills turn natural-language instructions into actions, creating a security challenge: legitimate automation and malicious behaviour can look deceptively similar. A practical screen must catch nearly every attack while keeping the review load manageable. We present SkillScreen, a compact decision model trained to score skill maliciousness directly from SKILL$.$md in a single forward pass. On MaliciousSkillBench, SkillScreen flags 20-25% of benign skills at 99% recall on unseen attack families, substantially fewer than the word-level classifier and prompted LLM judges tested. Under the same training protocol, it also generalizes better than a fully fine-tuned encoder to unseen sources. Yet unfamiliar benign sources sharply increase false positives, showing that recognizing new attacks does not ensure reliable screening of new skill collections. Our results demonstrate the value of task-trained decision models for high-recall skill screening. Project page: https://jerroldh.github.io/SkillScreen-webpage/
papers.summary: Agent skills turn natural-language instructions into actions, and malicious skills can look much like legitimate automation, so a practical screen must catch nearly all attacks while keeping the human review load manageable. `SkillScreen` is a compact decision model trained to score skill maliciousness directly from a SKILL.md file in a single forward pass. On `MaliciousSkillBench`, **it flags only 20-25% of benign skills while reaching 99% recall on unseen attack families**, substantially fewer false positives than a word-level classifier and prompted LLM judges, and under the same training protocol it generalizes to unseen sources better than a fully fine-tuned encoder. Unfamiliar benign sources still sharply raise false positives, showing that recognizing new attacks does not guarantee reliable screening of new skill collections.

papers.title: Safety for Whom? Benchmarking Understanding Beyond Refusal in Egocentric Multimodal Assistants
papers.abstract: Egocentric multimodal assistants see through the user's eyes and guide what the user does next, so their outputs directly shape physical actions, including those that affect bystanders. Yet existing safety evaluations do not distinguish whom a response would harm, and score only whether a model refuses. Pooling all harms into one refusal rate hides two failures: a model may protect one target but not another, and it may refuse without understanding the risk, or understand it and comply anyway. We present STOU, a benchmark of 2,902 egocentric video-audio and video-text queries whose potential harm targets the user (Self), co-present individuals (The Others), or society at large (Others). Our evaluation decouples safety understanding from refusal behavior: beyond refusal, we score whether the model recognizes the user's intent, the presence and target of harm, and its downstream consequences. Across 10 open and closed source omnimodal and multimodal LLMs, we find that refusal varies systematically with the harm target, and that models often recognize a harm yet still assist with it. These results show that refusal rates alone cannot certify an assistant as safe, and that safety alignment must account for who would be harmed. Project page: https://onedayoneyeah.github.io/safety-for-whom
papers.summary: Egocentric multimodal assistants see through the user's eyes and guide physical actions, so their outputs can harm the user, people nearby, or society, yet existing safety evaluations pool all harms into a single refusal rate. `STOU` is a benchmark of 2,902 egocentric video-audio and video-text queries whose potential harm targets the user (Self), co-present individuals (The Others), or society at large (Others), and its evaluation decouples safety understanding from refusal by scoring whether a model recognizes the user's intent, the presence and target of harm, and its downstream consequences. Across 10 open and closed source omnimodal and multimodal LLMs, **refusal varies systematically with the harm target, and models often recognize a harm yet still assist with it**, so refusal rates alone cannot certify an assistant as safe.

papers.title: CoCA: Criterion-Aware Credit Assignment for Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) evaluates responses against explicit criteria to construct rewards, offering a viable way to train large language models on open-ended tasks. However, standard methods compress criterion-level feedback into scalar rewards and assign uniform token advantages, leaving structured rubric supervision underutilized. Recent work seeks finer-grained guidance by treating rubrics as privileged information to derive self-distillation targets, but the resulting learning signal is not grounded in criterion outcomes and can lead to reward degradation. This motivates us to reframe the problem as criterion-aware credit assignment, where privileged rubric information serves as a relevance cue for credit allocation rather than a source of imitation targets. Accordingly, we propose CoCA, which derives criterion-level credits from group-relative outcomes and allocates them across tokens based on criterion-induced distribution shifts, yielding both outcome-grounded and fine-grained learning signals. Empirically, CoCA achieves an average gain of +4.2% over standard rubric-based RL across medicine and science benchmarks, demonstrating more effective learning on open-ended tasks.
papers.summary: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) scores large language model responses against explicit criteria, but standard methods compress criterion-level feedback into a scalar reward with uniform token advantages, and recent attempts to treat rubrics as privileged information for self-distillation yield targets not grounded in criterion outcomes, which can degrade reward. `CoCA` reframes the problem as criterion-aware credit assignment: it derives criterion-level credits from group-relative outcomes and allocates them across tokens according to criterion-induced distribution shifts, producing learning signals that are both outcome-grounded and fine-grained. **It averages a +4.2% gain over standard rubric-based RL** across medicine and science benchmarks.
