papers.title: Explore with Memory, Learn without It: In-Context Exploration and Self-Distillation for LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: Exploration bounds learning efficiency in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Current methods explore mostly through independent sampling, without fully using the information gathered along the way, such as known wrong answers and environment feedback. We propose LEAF, which injects a dynamic, problem-specific memory into the context before every rollout. The memory contains the most recent response, its reward, and other environment feedback. It is updated after every verifier call. We decouple policy updates from rollouts and update the policy through self-distillation. On four benchmarks and two open models, LEAF accelerates exploration by about 4x compared with a random sampling baseline. On unseen test sets, it improves accuracy over the strongest baseline by 1.59 and 1.83 percentage points on the two models, while using less compute than any RL baseline. These results highlight the potential of LEAF in improving both exploration and learning efficiency. Code is available at: https://github.com/on1262/LEAF
papers.summary: In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), exploration mostly happens through independent sampling that ignores information already gathered, such as known wrong answers and environment feedback. `LEAF` injects a dynamic, problem-specific memory into the context before each rollout, holding the most recent response, its reward, and other environment feedback, updated after every verifier call, while policy updates are decoupled from rollouts and performed through self-distillation so the trained model does not depend on the memory. On four benchmarks and two open models, **it accelerates exploration by about 4x compared with a random sampling baseline** and improves unseen test accuracy over the strongest baseline by 1.59 and 1.83 percentage points while using less compute than any RL baseline.

papers.title: Train for Many, Update with One: Improving Multi-Sample Reasoning via Fenchel-Bregman Posterior Learning
papers.abstract: Multi-sample reasoning measures candidate coverage, the probability that at least one of $K$ candidates is correct. However, minimizing the average loss of individual attempts does not directly optimize candidate coverage. We therefore formulate finite-$K$ posterior learning, which trains a distribution over solver parameters to reduce the probability that all $K$ independently generated candidates fail. To optimize this objective efficiently, we propose a Fenchel-Bregman (FB) approach that requires only one posterior draw per update, rather than the $K$ used by direct Monte Carlo optimization. FB first uses an exact Fenchel reformulation to separate problem-specific weights from the posterior update, enabling one-draw posterior updates. It then applies a closed-form Bregman update to track these weights through an exponential running average of observed failures, reusing the same draw. We instantiate FB with IVON, a variational optimizer for Gaussian posteriors over solver parameters, yielding Fenchel-Bregman IVON (FBI). Across diverse recursive and autoregressive reasoning tasks, FBI improves candidate coverage. In a matched comparison, it achieves comparable Pass@10 using 12.3% of the direct Monte Carlo baseline's measured training time per update.
papers.summary: Multi-sample reasoning is judged by candidate coverage, the probability that at least one of K generated candidates is correct, but minimizing the average loss of individual attempts does not directly optimize that objective. The authors formulate finite-K posterior learning, which trains a distribution over solver parameters to reduce the probability that all K candidates fail, and propose a Fenchel-Bregman (FB) approach in which an exact Fenchel reformulation separates problem-specific weights from the posterior update so each update needs only one posterior draw rather than K, and a closed-form Bregman update tracks those weights through an exponential running average of observed failures. Instantiated with the variational optimizer `IVON` as `FBI`, the method improves coverage across recursive and autoregressive reasoning tasks and **matches direct Monte Carlo Pass@10 using 12.3% of its measured training time per update**.

papers.title: DuplexAct: How Interactive Are Frontier Full-Duplex Spoken Language Models?
papers.abstract: End-to-end (E2E) full-duplex spoken language models (FD-SLMs) enable simutanous listening and speaking continously, requiring models to take appropriate interaction actions as conversations unfold. However, existing benchmarks lack a structured action-level formulation, often evaluate action occurrence rather than success, and provide limited coverage of diverse real-world conversations. We introduce DuplexAct, a benchmark for evaluating interaction action taking in E2E FD-SLMs. DuplexAct defines a three-level action taxonomy spanning eight interaction actions and 24 corresponding interaction conditions. We further characterize successful action-taking through immediate execution and subsequent follow-through, and develop action-specific evaluation metrics for both. DuplexAct contains 4,691 test instances spanning casual conversation, meetings, customer service, and interviews, including 2,531 instances derived from real-world conversational recordings. Together, DuplexAct provides a structured and real-world-grounded framework for systematically assessing how E2E FD-SLMs participate in ongoing spoken interaction.
papers.summary: End-to-end full-duplex spoken language models (FD-SLMs) listen and speak simultaneously, so they must take appropriate interaction actions as a conversation unfolds, but existing benchmarks lack an action-level formulation, score whether an action occurs rather than whether it succeeds, and cover few real-world conversation types. `DuplexAct` defines a three-level taxonomy of eight interaction actions and 24 corresponding interaction conditions, characterizes success through both immediate execution and subsequent follow-through, and provides action-specific metrics for each. **The benchmark contains 4,691 test instances across casual conversation, meetings, customer service, and interviews, 2,531 of them derived from real-world conversational recordings.**

papers.title: HiSTOR: Structured Treatment-outcome Representation Learning for High-Dimensional Longitudinal Data
papers.abstract: Estimating potential outcomes under alternative treatment sequences is essential for personalized decision-making, but remains challenging with high-dimensional covariates and time-varying confounding. In this study, we propose HiSTOR (High-dimensional Structured Treatment-Outcome Representation), an end-to-end framework that integrates nonlinear dimension reduction with longitudinal counterfactual prediction. The central idea is to learn structured low-dimensional representations of both current patient states and evolving histories, according to their shared and distinct relationships with treatment assignment and outcomes. This extends latent-space covariate adjustment to longitudinal settings, jointly addressing covariate dimensionality and historical complexity. The resulting framework supports one-step and multi-step outcome prediction under specified treatment sequences. Experiments on CVSim and CancerSim demonstrate the superiority of HiSTOR across varying covariate dimensions, confounding strengths, and prediction horizons compared to state-of-the-art methods. To sum up, HiSTOR offers a unified approach to connecting high-dimensional covariate adjustment with longitudinal potential-outcome prediction.
papers.summary: Estimating potential outcomes under alternative treatment sequences supports personalized decision-making but is hard with high-dimensional covariates and time-varying confounding. `HiSTOR` (High-dimensional Structured Treatment-Outcome Representation) is an end-to-end framework that learns structured low-dimensional representations of both the current patient state and the evolving history, organized by their shared and distinct relationships to treatment assignment and outcomes, extending latent-space covariate adjustment to longitudinal data and supporting one-step and multi-step prediction under specified treatment sequences. **On `CVSim` and `CancerSim` it outperforms state-of-the-art methods** across covariate dimensions, confounding strengths, and prediction horizons.

papers.title: Coupled Harness--Model Evolution for Scientific Equation Discovery
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to discover scientific equations from experimental data. Such a discovery system has two parts that must work together: a library of executable computational tools and the model's tool-use policy. The tools supply the solving capability, from diagnosing structure in the data to fitting candidate equations; the policy plans and orchestrates their use. Yet existing systems adapt only one part, keeping either the toolset or the model fixed, which leaves the corresponding failures uncorrectable. We develop a coupled evolution framework that improves both parts from the same verifiable fit-error signal. In the tool-evolution phase, an agent grows an executable tool library from a small set of generic numerical operations by diagnosing its own failures: it authors a new tool when a capability is missing and revises its selection rules when the right tool went unused. In the policy-evolution phase, a small open model (roughly 3B active parameters) is fine-tuned on successful tool-use trajectories collected with the frozen library, on training formulas screened to be disjoint from all evaluation benchmarks. Ablations show the two phases are complementary: with no tool library at all the same model solves almost nothing, the tools account for most of the gain, and trajectory training adds a further gain that is largest on the most difficult problems. The full system solves 79.1/71.3\% of LSR-Synth problems at fit tolerances $10^{-2}$/$10^{-3}$, reaches 63.8\% pooled accuracy on the distributionally different SRSD-Feynman panel, and obtains a normalized CP3-28 aggregate of $-7.27$. These results suggest a broader recipe for scientific agents: let the model and its instruments improve each other under verifiable feedback.
papers.summary: LLM-based systems for discovering scientific equations from experimental data have two parts that must work together, a library of executable computational tools and the model's tool-use policy, yet existing systems adapt only one of them, leaving the other's failures uncorrectable. The proposed framework evolves both from the same verifiable fit-error signal: in a tool-evolution phase an agent grows a tool library from a few generic numerical operations by authoring a new tool when a capability is missing and revising its selection rules when the right tool went unused, and in a policy-evolution phase a small open model with roughly 3B active parameters is fine-tuned on successful tool-use trajectories collected with the frozen library, using training formulas disjoint from all evaluation benchmarks. Ablations show the same model solves almost nothing without the tool library, the tools account for most of the gain, and trajectory training adds a further gain that is largest on the hardest problems. **The full system solves 79.1% and 71.3% of `LSR-Synth` problems at fit tolerances of 10^-2 and 10^-3**, reaches 63.8% pooled accuracy on the distributionally different `SRSD-Feynman` panel, and obtains a normalized `CP3-28` aggregate of -7.27.

papers.title: Auditing Failure Attribution: Label Predictability and Judge Behavior
papers.abstract: Failure-attribution benchmarks ask an LLM judge which step or agent caused a failure. A high score should mean the judge checked the faulty step against the run (a cross-step check). However, spurious signals (surface cues) that predict the annotation can produce a high score. In this paper, we propose four tests to separate checking from cue use. Input restriction asks whether partial input predicts the annotation. Cue following checks whether moved cues change answers. Residual accuracy scores judges where cue-only predictors fail. Aggregation asks whether the failure mix or metric changes rankings. Real observations motivate these tests: on three benchmarks, simple predictors match or beat GPT-4.1. In two Who&When Pro systems, a classifier reading one step's reasoning finds 95-100% of faulty steps, motivating input restriction. In one of them, error injection leaves no reasoning after the faulty step; judges fine-tuned on its labels beat GPT-4.1 by 41 points. Adding task-related reasoning after that step moves this cue: fine-tuned judges lose 31-99 points, but zero-shot judges lose at most 9, motivating cue following. On Aegis, blaming every agent matches GPT-4.1 on micro-F1 but trails by 19 points in exact-set accuracy, motivating aggregation. We recommend reporting these tests when developing failure-attribution benchmarks.
papers.summary: Failure-attribution benchmarks ask an LLM judge which step or agent caused a failed run, but a high score may reflect surface cues that predict the annotation rather than a genuine cross-step check of the faulty step against the run. The authors propose four audit tests: input restriction asks whether partial input predicts the annotation, cue following checks whether moved cues change answers, residual accuracy scores judges where cue-only predictors fail, and aggregation asks whether the failure mix or metric changes rankings. On three benchmarks simple predictors match or beat `GPT-4.1`; **in two `Who&When` Pro systems a classifier reading one step's reasoning finds 95-100% of faulty steps**, and in one of them judges fine-tuned on its labels beat `GPT-4.1` by 41 points yet lose 31-99 points when task-related reasoning is added after the faulty step, while zero-shot judges lose at most 9. On `Aegis`, blaming every agent matches `GPT-4.1` on micro-F1 but trails by 19 points in exact-set accuracy, and the authors recommend reporting these tests when developing failure-attribution benchmarks.

papers.title: I3L: Iterative Interactive Imitation Learning for Whole-Body Mobile Manipulation
papers.abstract: Policies trained offline from teleoperated demonstrations can degrade outside their training distribution. This gap is particularly acute in long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation, where long horizons amplify compounding errors and coordinated arm, torso, and base motion makes exhaustive demonstration coverage impractical. We introduce I3L, an integrated hardware and learning system that combines whole-body correction with iterative policy refinement to address this last-mile reliability gap. Its low-cost, open-source JoyLo+ interface uses policy-tracking leader arms and touch-triggered takeover to enable coordinated corrections across the body parts, while iterative deployment and retraining allow operators to target failures of the updated policy. We evaluate I3L across three robot embodiments and eight simulated and real-world tasks, including four long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation tasks. Controlled simulation experiments show that four-round HG-DAgger achieves the highest final success on both tasks. Under this protocol, I3L improves autonomous success over the base policies by an average of 68.3 percentage points and achieves at least 90% success on every task, outperforming demonstration-only training by 35.6 percentage points on average with the same number of training trajectories. Averaged across tasks, takeover duration per episode decreases by 72% over four rounds. Together, these results show that I3L helps close the last-mile gap between offline training and reliable deployment and provides practical insights into collecting and using corrections for long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation. Videos, visualizations, and appendix are at https://i-3l.github.io/.
papers.summary: Policies trained offline from teleoperated demonstrations degrade outside their training distribution, and in long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation compounding errors and coordinated arm, torso, and base motion make exhaustive demonstration coverage impractical. `I3L` is an integrated hardware and learning system: its low-cost, open-source `JoyLo+` interface uses policy-tracking leader arms and touch-triggered takeover so operators can apply coordinated corrections across body parts, and iterative deployment and retraining let them target the failures of each updated policy. Across three robot embodiments and eight simulated and real-world tasks, with four rounds of `HG-DAgger` giving the highest final success in controlled simulation, **it raises autonomous success over the base policies by an average of 68.3 percentage points and reaches at least 90% success on every task**, beating demonstration-only training with the same number of trajectories by 35.6 points on average while takeover duration per episode falls 72% over four rounds.

papers.title: Degrees of Freedom in Multi-Agent Coordination: Between Centralized and Decentralized Regimes
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) are commonly organized around two coordination regimes. Centralized coordination provides explicit control but can create a bottleneck at a single coordination locus, whereas decentralized coordination offers local autonomy but must achieve effective collaboration through distributed decisions and experience. These trade-offs motivate a systematic study of the space between the two regimes. We introduce Degrees of Freedom (DoF), a continuous configuration framework that quantifies the size of the decision space delegated to downstream agents. DoF controls the granularity of delegated work and the target probability that each task unit is assigned to the branches. Its endpoints recover the two coordination regimes. Across multiple task domains, DoF reveals a hierarchy of organizational effects. Delegated granularity and within-regime routing produce structured but bounded profile reallocations, whereas task domain and retained experience are associated with stronger differences between the centralized- and decentralized-branch profiles. The resulting performance landscape is task-dependent: different domains favor different DoF configurations, while atomic-target conditions are more consistent across runs. In-domain retained experience brings the two branch profiles closer together. The same controlled sweep reveals a task-dependent coordination landscape: some domains exhibit higher-performing configurations, whereas others show flatter responses and no single configuration dominates across domains. In five of the six evaluated state, an intermediate DoF configuration achieves higher mean accuracy than both endpoints, demonstrating the value of exploring the coordination space between them. Together, these findings provide empirical guidance for studying and designing intermediate coordination regimes in LLM-based MAS.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) are usually built around either centralized coordination, which gives explicit control but bottlenecks at a single coordinator, or decentralized coordination, which gives local autonomy but must collaborate through distributed decisions and experience. `DoF` (Degrees of Freedom) is a continuous configuration framework that quantifies how much of the decision space is delegated to downstream agents, controlling the granularity of delegated work and the probability that each task unit is routed to a branch, with its two endpoints recovering the centralized and decentralized regimes. Sweeping this space across several task domains reveals a task-dependent performance landscape where no single configuration dominates, but **in five of six evaluated settings an intermediate `DoF` configuration achieves higher mean accuracy than both endpoints**. Delegated granularity and within-regime routing produce bounded profile shifts, while task domain and retained experience drive larger differences, and in-domain retained experience brings the two branch profiles closer together.

papers.title: Instructions Are Evidence, Not Objectives: Measuring Outcome Alignment of Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model agents can follow complex human instructions to solve real-world tasks. In practice, however, initial instructions are often incomplete. In our analysis of 100 user-agent trajectories from SWE-chat, 56\% of initial instructions omit requirements that later emerge as necessary, and 52\% of the useful follow-up requirements could have been inferred from the project. A user states requirements from their own understanding of the task, and these \textbf{stated requirements} often differ from the \textbf{true requirements} that completing the task imposes. An agent should therefore treat the instruction as evidence rather than as the objective, inferring the true requirements from the instruction and the environment and satisfying them even when the user is not yet aware of all of them. We call this ability \textbf{outcome alignment}. In this work, we construct \textbf{TiGanEval}, a benchmark of software engineering and research tasks. In every task the user genuinely lacks part of the requirements, each requirement stays discoverable from the code and runtime behaviour of the environment, and requirements the agent infers are separated from those the user adds after observing delivered work. These properties together make outcome alignment measurable. Evaluating eight frontier models including GPT-5.6-Sol, we find outcome alignment broadly missing: the models lose 53 to 67 points of success rate when moving from the full specification to the partial instruction, and consequence feedback across four submissions does not close the gap. Furthermore, a plan-mode harness cannot compensate for the missing ability of the model itself, which places outcome alignment among the abilities the next generation of models should be developed for.
papers.summary: User instructions to LLM agents are often incomplete: in 100 user-agent trajectories from `SWE-chat`, 56% of initial instructions omitted requirements that later proved necessary, and 52% of those useful follow-up requirements could have been inferred from the project itself. The authors call the ability to treat an instruction as evidence about the true requirements, and to infer and satisfy requirements the user has not yet stated, outcome alignment, and they build `TiGanEval`, a benchmark of software engineering and research tasks in which the user genuinely lacks part of the requirements in every task, each missing requirement is discoverable from the code or runtime behaviour, and requirements the agent infers are kept separate from ones the user adds after seeing delivered work. Across eight frontier models including `GPT-5.6-Sol`, **success rates drop by 53 to 67 points when moving from the full specification to the partial instruction**, consequence feedback over four submissions does not close the gap, and a plan-mode harness cannot compensate for the missing model ability.

papers.title: Gaussian Process Bandits for AI System Optimization with Selectively Verified Feedback
papers.abstract: Gaussian process bandits exploit similarities among configurations to optimize prompts, retrieval systems, and agent workflows. In these applications, however, inexpensive model-based evaluations can disagree with trusted task outcomes. We study selective verification when an action is chosen before a diagnostic is observed and trusted feedback is informative on an unknown set of diagnostic states. A finite reliability class and a finite RKHS signal dictionary describe these two sources of uncertainty. We construct a fixed audit design that combines reliability coverage with reward separation and establish a finite-time regret bound that accounts for a hard audit budget and the rounds needed to obtain informative observations. A safe adaptive extension mixes this robust design with predictable Chernoff allocations while preserving a uniform identification floor and exact expected acquisition-cost accounting. For signed-coordinate kernels, structured and diffuse reliability classes require different audit scales despite sharing the same reward geometry. Synthetic experiments distinguish these certified designs from an adaptive posterior heuristic and GP controls. Safe adaptive allocation reduces aggregate regret relative to the fixed design under the exact dictionary, but its finite-budget error certificate is numerically loose. Conditional-feedback errors can remove the heuristic's advantage and target perturbations can reverse it. Separate AI-task replays assess feedback correction and fitted-dictionary policies without establishing end-to-end validation of a learned selective-verification method.
papers.summary: Gaussian process bandits are used to optimize prompts, retrieval systems, and agent workflows, but cheap model-based evaluations can disagree with trusted task outcomes, so the question is how to spend a limited audit budget on verified feedback when an action is chosen before a diagnostic is observed. The authors model the setting with a finite reliability class and a finite RKHS signal dictionary, construct a fixed audit design combining reliability coverage with reward separation, prove a finite-time regret bound under a hard audit budget, and add a safe adaptive extension that mixes the robust design with predictable Chernoff allocations while preserving a uniform identification floor and exact acquisition-cost accounting. In synthetic experiments, **the safe adaptive allocation reduces aggregate regret relative to the fixed design under the exact dictionary**, though its finite-budget error certificate is numerically loose, and conditional-feedback errors or target perturbations can erase or reverse the advantage of an adaptive posterior heuristic. Separate replays on AI tasks assess feedback correction and fitted-dictionary policies without establishing end-to-end validation of a learned selective-verification method.

papers.title: Autonomous 3D Visual-Thermal Inspection for Utility-Scale Solar Farms
papers.abstract: Utility-scale photovoltaic (PV) inspection is dominated by aerial surveys, which are effective for identifying module-level hot cells but provide limited visibility of critical components located under the array, including connectors, cabling, fasteners and structural elements. These assets are difficult to inspect consistently at scale, and their defects are often spatially small, partially occluded and difficult to localise from isolated images. We present an automated 3D visual-thermal inspection system (Tricorder) for under-panel PV asset inspection. The approach combines LiDAR-inertial Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) with geometrically calibrated RGB and thermal imagery and machine-learning-based object detection and segmentation. Detected assets are associated with the reconstructed 3D environment, allowing visual and thermal observations from multiple viewpoints to be spatially fused and localised. We demonstrate the approach on utility-scale PV data for MC4 connector detection and connection-state recognition, thermal anomaly identification, and detection of structural components including bolts, nuts and torque tubes. The results demonstrate a pathway from image-based inspection toward spatially grounded autonomous inspection, where defects are detected and linked to specific assets and their 3D locations within the solar farm.
papers.summary: Aerial surveys of utility-scale photovoltaic (PV) farms find module-level hot cells but see little of the connectors, cabling, fasteners and structural elements under the array, whose defects are small, often occluded and hard to localise from isolated images. `Tricorder` is an automated 3D visual-thermal inspection system that combines LiDAR-inertial Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) with geometrically calibrated RGB and thermal imagery and machine-learning object detection and segmentation, associating detected assets with the reconstructed 3D environment so observations from multiple viewpoints can be spatially fused and localised. On utility-scale PV data it is demonstrated for **MC4 connector detection and connection-state recognition, thermal anomaly identification, and detection of bolts, nuts and torque tubes**, linking each detected defect to a specific asset and its 3D location within the farm.

papers.title: Memory Echo in Single-Agent Long-Term Memory: Lifecycle Evaluation and Provenance-Guided Mitigation
papers.abstract: Long-term memory supports agents across sessions. Repeated retrieval and write-back can let one historical claim occupy multiple retrieval positions and influence current answers without independent evidence. Existing work examines retrieval, updating, and question answering, leaving same-source record accumulation and post-correction persistence underexplored. Motivated by research in social cognition and memory psychology on repeated exposure, retrieval, and revision, we define \emph{Memory Echo} as the excess retrieval exposure gained by historical information from the same source without additional independent evidence, and introduce MEchoBench to evaluate its emergence, correction resistance, persistence, and effect on answers. To address this phenomenon, we introduce the Family--Provenance--Authority framework (FPA). Specifically, FPA selects one representative per source family, conditions the eligibility of old records for the answer context on verified corrections, and constrains final answers with authoritative evidence. In paired replay on 190 fixed questions across four memory frameworks, FPA raises accuracy from 0.825 to 0.920 with DeepSeek V4 Flash and from 0.782 to 0.916 with Kimi K2.6; mean Decision Contamination Effect falls from 0.106 to 0.030 and from 0.109 to 0.038, respectively. These results show that agent memory can preserve traceable history without allowing repeated historical information to govern current decisions. The code is available at https://github.com/OrcasSam/memory-echo-benchmark.
papers.summary: In agents with long-term memory, repeated retrieval and write-back can let a single historical claim occupy multiple retrieval positions and sway current answers without any independent evidence, and this same-source accumulation and its persistence after corrections has received little study. The authors define Memory Echo as the excess retrieval exposure historical information gains from one source without additional independent evidence, introduce `MEchoBench` to measure its emergence, correction resistance, persistence and effect on answers, and propose the Family-Provenance-Authority framework (`FPA`), which keeps one representative per source family, admits old records into the answer context only when conditioned on verified corrections, and constrains final answers with authoritative evidence. In paired replay over 190 fixed questions across four memory frameworks, **`FPA` raises accuracy from 0.825 to 0.920 with `DeepSeek V4 Flash` and from 0.782 to 0.916 with `Kimi K2.6`**, while the mean Decision Contamination Effect falls from roughly 0.11 to 0.03-0.04.

papers.title: Efficiently Learning To Reason or Not to Reason: Root-token Policy Optimization for Adaptive Thinking
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) achieve strong performance by externalizing explicit reasoning traces before producing the answer, yet suffer from overthinking challenge that allocates uniformly heavy computation to queries of varying difficulty. While proprietary models mitigate this via opaque routing, open-source LRMs still lack an efficient mechanism to internalize adaptive reasoning due to both expensive training cost and limited disclosure of training recipes. In response, we introduce RPO (Root-token Policy Optimization), a framework that enables LRMs to self-determine when to reason by training only the initial root token (e.g., whether to invoke the <think> tag) via group relative reward and group-wise advantages. By focusing on this pivotal branching point, RPO drastically reduces training overhead and VRAM usage. Across multiple model families and scales, RPO learns difficulty-aware adaptive thinking at just ~2% of the training compute of prior adaptive-reasoning methods.
papers.summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) produce explicit reasoning traces before answering but overthink, spending uniformly heavy computation on queries regardless of difficulty, and open-source models lack an affordable, documented way to learn when reasoning is worthwhile. `RPO` (Root-token Policy Optimization) trains only the initial root token, such as whether to emit the `<think>` tag, using group relative rewards and group-wise advantages, so the model learns at this single branching point whether to reason at all. Because only that pivotal token is optimized, training overhead and VRAM use fall sharply, and across multiple model families and scales **`RPO` learns difficulty-aware adaptive thinking at roughly 2% of the training compute of prior adaptive-reasoning methods**.

papers.title: Agentic4PDM: Host-Governed Evidence Admissibility for Industrial Fault Diagnosis
papers.abstract: We study industrial fault diagnosis as a classification task that assigns sensor time-series windows to predefined health states or fault types. Scarce labels and changing operating conditions make repeated training of specialized classifiers costly. Yet structures such as periodicity, trends, and transients can remain diagnostically informative and be examined through reusable analytical tools. LLM agents can select and interpret these tools, but fixed rules or training-derived guidance may not resolve each signal's ambiguity, while unconstrained interpretation may overstate weak or conflicting results. We introduce Agentic4PDM, a framework that separates adaptive investigation from control over evidence use. LLM agents compare each signal with labeled references from every candidate class, identify unresolved distinctions, and propose follow-up measurements. A deterministic software controller, called the host, enforces contract-checked gated adjudication (CCGA): it checks requests, requires commitment to a complete tool batch before results are observed, and assigns evidence roles based on tool checks against labeled references. These roles distinguish corroborative support from advisory information. The Judge Agent proposes a diagnosis, while the controller checks protocol compliance and records the investigation. Agentic4PDM supports training-free diagnosis using pretrained representations and labeled references without task-specific diagnostic models, and a standard setting that additionally investigates trained-model predictions. Experiments on selected bearing and motor diagnosis challenges and an unfiltered industrial test set supplied by our customer show gains in aggregate macro F1 over the evaluated diagnostic and agentic baselines. Ablations further support the value of the governed workflow.
papers.summary: Industrial fault diagnosis assigns sensor time-series windows to health states or fault types, but scarce labels and shifting operating conditions make retraining specialized classifiers expensive, while LLM agents that interpret reusable signal-analysis tools may overstate weak or conflicting results. `Agentic4PDM` separates adaptive investigation from control over evidence use: LLM agents compare each signal against labeled references from every candidate class, flag unresolved distinctions and propose follow-up measurements, while a deterministic host controller enforces contract-checked gated adjudication (CCGA), requiring commitment to a full tool batch before results are seen and assigning evidence roles that separate corroborative support from advisory information before a Judge Agent proposes a diagnosis. It supports training-free diagnosis from pretrained representations and labeled references as well as a setting that also examines trained-model predictions, and on bearing and motor diagnosis challenges plus an unfiltered industrial customer test set **it improves aggregate macro F1 over the evaluated diagnostic and agentic baselines**, with ablations supporting the governed workflow.

papers.title: Posterior-Averaged Bellman Flow Matching for Distributional Critics
papers.abstract: Distributional critics model the full return distribution, providing richer signals for exploration and risk-sensitive control. Recent work has shown that flow-based critics can model these distributions flexibly and provide effective supervision across flow time for temporal-difference learning. However, unlike standard flow matching with fixed data endpoints, a flow critic is trained on Bellman targets recursively generated by a learned target critic under the current policy. Existing objectives therefore either use noisy single-endpoint supervision or rely on the learned flow itself for additional guidance. Our key observation is that an intermediate bridge state may be compatible with several Bellman endpoints, so its velocity should average their directions under the corresponding posterior. We propose Posterior-Averaged Bellman Flow Matching (PA-BFM), which samples an endpoint pool, infers the closed-form posterior over the latent anchor, and regresses to the posterior-mean velocity. Uniform anchor selection makes this target an exact finite-pool Rao--Blackwellization of the single-endpoint target: for every \(K\), it preserves the population target, cannot increase conditional variance, and its conditional variance scales as \(O(K^{-1})\). The endpoint pool supports conservative updates, while the twin return flows provide critic-disagreement and unsupported-mass diagnostics. Controlled studies show that PA-BFM reduces fixed-query target mean-squared error by \(79.7\%\) and target-induced gradient variance by up to \(98.0\%\), while improving return-distribution fidelity. Across 50 OGBench tasks and four offline-to-online scenarios, PA-BFM achieves higher aggregate performance than Value Flows.
papers.summary: Distributional critics model the full return distribution, and flow-based critics can represent these distributions flexibly, but unlike standard flow matching with fixed data endpoints, a flow critic is trained on Bellman targets generated recursively by a learned target critic, so existing objectives either rely on noisy single-endpoint supervision or lean on the learned flow itself for guidance. Posterior-Averaged Bellman Flow Matching (`PA-BFM`) starts from the observation that an intermediate bridge state may be compatible with several Bellman endpoints, so it samples an endpoint pool, computes the closed-form posterior over the latent anchor, and regresses to the posterior-mean velocity, which under uniform anchor selection is an exact finite-pool Rao-Blackwellization of the single-endpoint target that preserves the population target, never increases conditional variance, and scales that variance as O(1/K). Controlled studies show **a 79.7% reduction in fixed-query target mean-squared error and up to 98.0% lower target-induced gradient variance** alongside better return-distribution fidelity, and across 50 `OGBench` tasks and four offline-to-online scenarios `PA-BFM` outperforms `Value Flows` in aggregate.

papers.title: GIFT-Eval-CTX: A Benchmark For Contextual Forecasting Model Evaluation
papers.abstract: Contextual forecasting seeks to improve time series forecasting by incorporating forward-looking information, such as planned events, external conditions, and expert expectations. However, reliable evaluation remains difficult: existing benchmarks often have limited domain coverage, lack standardized history-future splits, or provide text that is not guaranteed to inform the future. We introduce GIFT-Eval-CTX, a benchmark that isolates whether forecasting methods can translate verified future information into accurate numerical trajectories. Built upon GIFT-Eval, GIFT-Eval-CTX contains 10,000 instances across 20 datasets. Each instance provides structured effects derived from the realized future: Macro effects describe horizon-wide behavior, while Micro effects specify localized changes. We construct these annotations with an agentic pipeline combining LLM-based discovery and deterministic code validation. We benchmark TSFMs, frontier LLMs, and tool-using agentic systems. The results show that structured effects reduce aggregate relative MASE by 40.7% for GPT-5.6 Sol and 29.6% for Claude Opus 4.8 relative to history-only prompting. The evaluated MoiraiAgent system achieves the best overall result. We further analyze the contributions of structured effects and agentic systems to performance, and identify opportunities for future research.
papers.summary: Contextual forecasting adds forward-looking information such as planned events, external conditions, or expert expectations to time series forecasting, but existing benchmarks cover few domains, lack standardized history-future splits, or supply text that is not guaranteed to inform the future. `GIFT-Eval-CTX` builds on `GIFT-Eval` with 10,000 instances across 20 datasets, each annotated with structured effects derived from the realized future, Macro effects describing horizon-wide behavior and Micro effects specifying localized changes, produced by an agentic pipeline that pairs LLM-based discovery with deterministic code validation. Benchmarking time series foundation models, frontier LLMs, and tool-using agentic systems, the authors find that **structured effects cut aggregate relative MASE by 40.7% for `GPT-5.6 Sol` and 29.6% for `Claude Opus 4.8`** compared with history-only prompting, and the `MoiraiAgent` system achieves the best overall result.

papers.title: Learning from fracture: Teaching language models to design through physical experience
papers.abstract: How can language models learn to optimize physical designs through experience? We introduce FracLearn, an experience-abstraction-generalization framework evaluated through a deliberately unfamiliar, Tetris-inspired fracture game. The model first proposes architectures and examines simulated fracture responses to accumulate experience. Abstraction organizes these observations into conditional principles linking reinforcement placement, crack evolution and load transfer, with supporting evidence and failure conditions. Generalization challenges the model to combine these principles in new architectures and surpass the earlier design record. Campaigns demonstrate progressive refinement and recovery through hypothesis revision, yielding a best composite score 11.0% above the experience-stage record. Fracture analyses connect improved performance to crack deflection and temporary trapping as toughening mechanisms, alongside greater residual load capacity. Learning occurs through external knowledge and decisions, without model-weight updates. This approach offers a route to scientific agents that turn computational experiments into reusable physical knowledge for materials discovery and engineering design.
papers.summary: The question is how a language model can learn to optimize physical designs from experience rather than from weight updates. `FracLearn` is an experience-abstraction-generalization loop evaluated on a deliberately unfamiliar, Tetris-inspired fracture game: the model proposes architectures and inspects simulated fracture responses, abstracts those observations into conditional principles linking reinforcement placement, crack evolution and load transfer with supporting evidence and failure conditions, and then combines the principles to design new architectures that must beat the earlier record. Design campaigns show progressive refinement and recovery through hypothesis revision, with **a best composite score 11.0% above the experience-stage record**, and fracture analyses tie the gains to crack deflection and temporary crack trapping plus higher residual load capacity, all achieved through external knowledge and decisions without updating model weights.

papers.title: Empowering Edge Agents: A Systematic Analysis of Edge-Cloud Collaboration in LLM Agent Execution
papers.abstract: Edge-cloud collaboration combines the lower inference overhead and greater data locality of edge-side execution with the stronger capabilities of cloud-hosted models. However, as LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon scenarios, cloud participation becomes interleaved throughout execution rather than a one-shot decision for each query. Such interleaved participation introduces trajectory-level effects that remain insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we introduce EC2-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating edge-cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution. It provides executable digital-workspace agent tasks and a unified evaluation framework covering task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. Using this benchmark, we empirically study diverse forms of edge-cloud collaboration. Our study reveals three findings. First, collaboration achieves a favorable balance among task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure compared with edge-only and cloud-only execution. Second, as edge models become stronger, collaborative execution approaches cloud-only performance, and performance differences across strategies shrink, while privacy exposure remains strongly strategy-dependent. Third, stronger edge capability shifts preferred collaboration from externally controlled cloud participation and direct cloud execution toward more edge-controlled collaboration. Further analyses identify cloud-invocation decision-making and instruction following as important edge-side abilities for effective collaboration. These findings provide a systematic understanding of edge-cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution and insights for designing future edge agents that effectively collaborate with cloud models. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/EC2-Bench.
papers.summary: Edge-cloud collaboration pairs the low inference overhead and data locality of on-device models with the stronger capabilities of cloud-hosted ones, but in long-horizon LLM agent tasks cloud participation is interleaved throughout execution rather than decided once per query, and the trajectory-level effects of that interleaving are poorly understood. `EC2-Bench` provides executable digital-workspace agent tasks with a unified evaluation of task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure, and is used to compare a range of collaboration strategies against edge-only and cloud-only execution. The study finds that **collaboration strikes a better balance among performance, resource use, and privacy than either edge-only or cloud-only execution**, that stronger edge models bring collaborative performance close to cloud-only while privacy exposure stays strongly strategy-dependent, and that stronger edge capability shifts the preferred design from externally controlled cloud participation toward edge-controlled collaboration, with cloud-invocation decision-making and instruction following identified as key edge-side abilities.

papers.title: Same Attack, Different Judge: A First Controlled Adversarial Comparison of Jev, LLM Judges, and Purpose-Built Safety Classifiers
papers.abstract: TypeSafe AI's Jev is a new kind of safety judge. It generates no text and no label: it answers questions the developer defines in advance and returns a probability for each answer. The vendor admits that adversarial input can change these answers but gives no numbers. In this paper, we present the first controlled adversarial evaluation of Jev. We build a test harness that sends every system the same payload under the same policy, and run it on four public-data tasks, from rule-based ones (input moderation, injection detection, routing) to a judgment-based one (phishing detection), with fifty attack variants from thirteen families. The targets are Jev, five GPT and GLM judges, and two local classifiers (Llama Guard 3, Prompt Guard 2). We find that Jev is the most robust system on input moderation: eight forgeries of its structured input bypass none of its decisions, and a sentence asking only why someone might make a harmful request bypasses 9% of its blocks, against 56% for GPT-6 Astra. On phishing detection. However, the same forgeries bypass 19-29% of the emails it flags, and even without attack Jev detects only 62% of phishing emails, against 77-81% for the GLM judges. Jev is also the fastest judge, but it flags the most benign requests (27%). The local classifiers fail differently: a training-example statement makes Llama Guard 3 miss 62% of the phishing it had flagged. These results suggest that Jev resists attacks on tasks with a clear rule to check but is more exposed on tasks that call for an overall judgment.
papers.summary: `Jev`, a safety judge from TypeSafe AI, generates no text or label but returns a probability for each of a set of developer-defined questions, and its vendor acknowledges that adversarial input can shift those answers without quantifying the effect. The authors build a harness that sends identical payloads under identical policies to `Jev`, five `GPT` and `GLM` judges, and two local classifiers (`Llama Guard 3` and `Prompt Guard 2`) across four public-data tasks, from rule-based input moderation, injection detection and routing to judgment-based phishing detection, using fifty attack variants from thirteen families. On input moderation `Jev` is the most robust system, with eight forgeries of its structured input bypassing none of its decisions and **a sentence merely asking why someone might make a harmful request bypassing 9% of its blocks versus 56% for `GPT-6 Astra`**, but on phishing the same forgeries bypass 19-29% of the emails it flags and it detects only 62% of phishing without attack against 77-81% for the GLM judges, while also being the fastest judge and flagging the most benign requests at 27%. A training-example statement likewise makes `Llama Guard 3` miss 62% of the phishing it had flagged, suggesting `Jev` resists attacks on tasks with a clear rule to check but is more exposed where an overall judgment is required.

papers.title: Checking the Checkers: A Synthesis of Verifier Noise and Robustness in RLVR
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a principal recipe for improving the reasoning of large language models (LLMs). It rests on the assumption that the checker scoring each response is itself correct. In practice, rule-based checkers reject correct answers in unexpected formats, unit tests accept incorrect programs, and LLM judges can be led to approve empty or adversarial responses. This work surveys 58 studies that measure, analyze, or mitigate such verifier errors. We ask what errors verifiers make, how they affect training, which mitigations work against which errors, and how the findings extend to self-generated, rubric- and judge-based, and verifier-free rewards. The evidence suggests that the structure of an error matters more than its rate. Random errors mostly slow learning, though under a fixed budget or KL regularization they also lower final accuracy. False positives that the policy can learn to trigger can cause plateaus or collapse, sometimes even with a low initial error rate. Whether a verifier wrongly rejects or accepts depends on what it checks and who built it, not on its family. Its errors shift as the policy improves, and most mitigations have been tested against only one kind of error. We compile the findings into comparison tables, reconcile apparent conflicts in the literature, and propose a reporting protocol to make future results comparable.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) assumes the checker scoring each response is correct, yet rule-based checkers reject correct answers in unexpected formats, unit tests accept incorrect programs, and LLM judges can be led to approve empty or adversarial responses. The survey covers 58 studies that measure, analyze, or mitigate such verifier errors, asking what errors verifiers make, how they affect training, which mitigations counter which errors, and how the findings extend to self-generated, rubric- and judge-based, and verifier-free rewards. The central conclusion is that **the structure of a verifier error matters more than its rate**: random errors mostly slow learning, though under a fixed budget or KL regularization they also lower final accuracy, whereas false positives the policy can learn to trigger cause plateaus or collapse even at low initial error rates. Whether a verifier wrongly rejects or accepts depends on what it checks and who built it rather than its family, its errors shift as the policy improves, and most mitigations have only been tested against one kind of error, so the authors compile comparison tables, reconcile apparent conflicts in the literature, and propose a reporting protocol.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Training Reward Models for Cross-Source Evidence Grounding in Search Agents
papers.abstract: Existing approaches to training and evaluating search agents focus heavily on final-answer quality, largely neglecting how generated answers map back to retrieved evidence. Recent methods track citations to enforce grounding, but citation support alone does not establish source independence or whether an answer appropriately handles conflicting evidence. We argue that credibility in open-web retrieval depends on principled cross-source evidence grounding that accounts for source independence and systematically attributes and adjudicates conflicting evidence, while hierarchical judgments of these grounding decisions provide a unified signal for training and evaluation. To this end, we propose an evaluation framework, Cross-Source Evidence Grounding (CSEG), that employs a fine-grained, six-layer decision tree over the complete search trajectory. We introduce CSEG-Bench and trainable reward models to provide targeted supervision following this framework. Our approach helps eliminating the severe data skew of natural trajectories by providing targeted coverage over complex, deep-layer decision paths, such as cross-source conflict resolution and nuanced attribution, that standard rollouts fail to capture. Specifically, (1) we define the hierarchy at label, node, and path levels; (2) we construct 1,160 verified trajectories over nine canonical paths by rewriting answers on real retrieved document pools, with independent frontier judges reproducing the entire gold path and human experts deciding inclusion; (3) we train CSEG-RM, which reaches 83.9% exact accuracy on our benchmark while lying on the performance-token efficiency Pareto frontier. Experiments that use this reward alone to supervise a frozen-retrieval answer policy raise the independently judged mean label from 2.83 to 4.19, and show that learning the hierarchy generalizes across layers at a fraction of frontier-judge cost.
papers.summary: Search agents are mostly trained and judged on final-answer quality, and even citation tracking does not establish whether sources are independent or whether an answer handles conflicting evidence appropriately. Cross-Source Evidence Grounding (`CSEG`) is an evaluation framework that applies a fine-grained six-layer decision tree over the full search trajectory, defining a hierarchy at label, node, and path levels, and it is instantiated as `CSEG-Bench`, 1,160 verified trajectories over nine canonical paths built by rewriting answers on real retrieved document pools, with independent frontier judges reproducing the gold path and human experts deciding inclusion, which deliberately covers deep-layer decisions such as conflict resolution that natural rollouts rarely reach. The trained reward model `CSEG-RM` reaches **83.9% exact accuracy on the benchmark while sitting on the performance-token-efficiency Pareto frontier**, and using it alone to supervise a frozen-retrieval answer policy raises the independently judged mean label from 2.83 to 4.19, with the learned hierarchy generalizing across layers at a fraction of frontier-judge cost.

papers.title: QK-Edit: Revisiting Attention-based Injection in MM-DiT for Image and Video Editing
papers.abstract: Multimodal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for unified text-vision synthesis, surpassing traditional U-Net architectures in generative tasks. One key innovation lies in its Multimodal Self-Attention (MM-SA) interaction, where image and text tokens are concatenated and processed via self-attention. However, this mechanism poses significant challenges for editing, rendering conventional U-Net-based attention manipulation methods ineffective. To address this limitation, we propose QK-Edit, a training-free framework that exploits the unique attention dynamics of MM-DiTs for precise text-guided image and video editing. By introducing a novel query-key manipulation strategy, our method isolates and adjusts critical attention components to achieve an optimal balance between prompt fidelity and structural consistency. This enables seamless edits across various tasks, including object addition, object removal, object replacement, changing background, changing material, changing color, and style transformation. Notably, it can be easily implemented with feature replacement in inference. QK-Edit demonstrates superior editing performance on state-of-the-art models, such as FLUX and HunyuanVideo, effectively bridging the gap between generative power and editable flexibility in MM-DiTs, and paving the way for scalable multimodal content creation.
papers.summary: Multimodal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs) have overtaken U-Net architectures for unified text-vision synthesis, but their Multimodal Self-Attention (MM-SA), which concatenates image and text tokens into a single self-attention pass, breaks the attention-manipulation editing techniques developed for U-Nets. `QK-Edit` is a training-free framework that exploits the attention dynamics specific to MM-DiTs through a query-key manipulation strategy, isolating and adjusting the attention components that trade prompt fidelity against structural consistency, and it can be implemented as simple feature replacement at inference time. It handles object addition, removal and replacement, background, material and color changes, and style transfer, and **delivers superior editing performance on `FLUX` and `HunyuanVideo`** for both image and video editing.

papers.title: Diff Diffusion: Predicting Edit Paths with Diffusion Models for Efficient Code Editing
papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) are appealing for code generation because they can update many tokens in parallel, yet many are optimized for sequence synthesis rather than edit prediction. This setting is poorly matched to modern AI-assisted IDEs, where edit prediction must infer the next code change from recent edits, the current file, and cursor-local context. Such changes are usually sparse and preserve most source tokens, so regenerating a full code segment wastes computation. We propose Diff Diffusion, a diffusion-inspired LLM framework for code editing that predicts edit paths from an original snippet to its revised form. Diff Diffusion represents denoising as structured edit operations, and combines this formulation with multi-stage training and efficient parallel decoding. By focusing computation on changed regions, Diff Diffusion supports accurate low-latency edits and multi-position parallel modification. Across public edit-completion benchmarks, edit-prediction evaluations, and online validation, Diff Diffusion matches or leads autoregressive baselines while delivering 2.78 times faster inference on public edit-completion benchmarks and a 39.0% P50 model-latency reduction in production. This work provides a new modeling perspective for AI applications that require high accuracy and low latency.
papers.summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) can update many tokens in parallel, which suits code generation, but most are built for sequence synthesis rather than the edit prediction that AI-assisted IDEs need, where the next change must be inferred from recent edits, the current file, and cursor-local context and is usually sparse enough that regenerating a whole segment wastes compute. `Diff Diffusion` reframes denoising as predicting a path of structured edit operations from an original snippet to its revised form, combined with multi-stage training and efficient parallel decoding, so computation concentrates on the regions that change and multiple positions can be modified at once. Across public edit-completion benchmarks, edit-prediction evaluations, and online validation it matches or beats autoregressive baselines while running **2.78 times faster on public edit-completion benchmarks and cutting production P50 model latency by 39.0%**.

papers.title: Agentic-MatriBO: Capability-Compiled Agentic Bayesian Optimization for Materials and Chemical Design
papers.abstract: Materials and chemical optimization must choose the next synthesis, characterization, or high-fidelity simulation from sequential observations under a limited budget. Large language models can use task knowledge to propose adjustments, but composing surrogates, acquisition functions, and search strategies is constrained by compatibility, parameter dependencies, and evidence requirements. We present Agentic-MatriBO, a capability-compiled agentic Bayesian optimization (BO) framework that represents BO components and selection conditions as composable capabilities. A language policy proposes BO recipes and candidate plans; a compiler checks proposals against the registered capability catalog; and a deterministic execution layer validates and commits candidates. Oracle observations are stored in research memory and inform later rounds. We compare Agentic-MatriBO with eight baselines on four offline finite candidate pools---COF, PCE10, Buchwald--Hartwig (BH), and Suzuki--Miyaura---using five seeds per condition; results are reported descriptively. Across the four tasks, Agentic-MatriBO has the best mean endpoint quality after orienting each objective so that higher is better. On COF, it reaches the tabulated optimum in all five seeds both in the end-to-end comparison and after shared initialization, where it also retains an advantage in cumulative quality. Its normalized area under the best-so-far quality curve during the BO stage (nAUC-BO) is substantially higher on COF, near parity with the best baseline on PCE10 and BH, and lower on Suzuki. COF ablations show that removing the capability compiler or evidence gate coincides with lower cumulative quality and fewer exact-optimum hits. The framework provides an inspectable interface for evidence-conditioned BO adaptation.
papers.summary: Materials and chemical optimization must choose the next synthesis, characterization, or high-fidelity simulation under a limited budget, and while LLMs can propose adjustments from task knowledge, composing surrogates, acquisition functions, and search strategies is constrained by compatibility, parameter dependencies, and evidence requirements. `Agentic-MatriBO` represents Bayesian optimization (BO) components and their selection conditions as composable capabilities: a language policy proposes BO recipes and candidate plans, a compiler checks them against a registered capability catalog, a deterministic execution layer validates and commits candidates, and oracle observations accumulate in a research memory that informs later rounds. Against eight baselines on four offline finite candidate pools (`COF`, `PCE10`, `Buchwald-Hartwig`, and `Suzuki-Miyaura`) with five seeds each and results reported descriptively, **it has the best mean endpoint quality across the four tasks and reaches the tabulated optimum on `COF` in all five seeds**, though its normalized area under the best-so-far curve is only near parity with the best baseline on `PCE10` and `Buchwald-Hartwig` and lower on `Suzuki-Miyaura`, and removing the capability compiler or evidence gate coincides with worse cumulative quality.

papers.title: A Tutorial on Quantum Amplitude Embedding with Data Re-Uploading
papers.abstract: Amplitude embedding lets a variational quantum model read many classical features with few qubits, but the model output is then only a quadratic form in the normalized input. Data re-uploading, which encodes the input repeatedly between trainable blocks, can be used to enrich such a model. Because every additional upload of an amplitude embedding repeats a costly state preparation, the gain that an upload buys has to be known before the gates are spent. This tutorial thus addresses the problem of explaining what data re-uploading adds to an amplitude-embedded model and how large the gain is. We express sequential re-uploading and parallel re-uploading with two copies in one notation and show that each upload raises the reachable polynomial order by two. Under one trainable circuit family and one budget of trainable parameters, simulation results show that re-uploading raises the test coefficient of determination from 0.689 to between 0.883 and 0.975 on targets of order four and from 0.337 to between 0.642 and 0.783 on targets of order six, on all ten seeds. On a quadratic target and on handwritten digits, one upload remains the best choice, and every additional upload lowers the gate error that the classifier tolerates. These results help designers match the number of uploads to the polynomial order of the task at hand.
papers.summary: Amplitude embedding lets a variational quantum model read many classical features with few qubits, but the output is then only a quadratic form in the normalized input, and while data re-uploading can enrich the model, each extra upload repeats a costly state preparation, so the benefit must be known before the gates are spent. Writing sequential re-uploading and parallel re-uploading with two copies in a single notation, the authors show that each upload raises the reachable polynomial order by two. Under one trainable circuit family and a fixed parameter budget, **re-uploading raises the test coefficient of determination from 0.689 to between 0.883 and 0.975 on order-four targets** and from 0.337 to between 0.642 and 0.783 on order-six targets across all ten seeds, whereas on a quadratic target and on handwritten digits a single upload remains best and each additional upload lowers the gate error the classifier can tolerate.

papers.title: ProtoArena: Can AI Agents Discover and Exploit Real-World Cross-Component Protocol Vulnerabilities?
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for vulnerability analysis, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of exploitation that depends on interactions among network protocol components. Such vulnerabilities arise from inconsistencies in message interpretation, timing, state, or trust assumptions across participants. We introduce ProtoArena, a black-box, multi-component, dynamic benchmark with 80 cross-component vulnerability-exploitation environments spanning 11 protocol and application domains and 7 attack categories. Tasks are primarily informed by published protocol-attack mechanisms. Agents interact with running systems through scoped interfaces to achieve security-effect objectives without target source code. Three information levels assess guided reproduction, exploitation with mechanism and topology context, and effect-directed black-box exploration. A hybrid verifier combines rule-based checks with LLM review of independently collected traffic and logs. We evaluate five LLMs. Claude Opus 4.8 achieves the highest observed success rates: 48.8% under L1 guidance and 12.5% under effect-directed black-box L3. In a separate DNSBomb optimization experiment, it achieves a peak downstream-response to average query-input byte-rate ratio exceeding 171,000 times. The results show that agents can achieve verifiable exploitation effects in some cross-component environments, but success with limited black-box information remains low and varies across domains and attack categories. All experiments use controlled, explicitly authorized targets; they do not test production systems or disclose previously unknown vulnerabilities.
papers.summary: LLM agents are increasingly applied to vulnerability analysis, but existing benchmarks rarely cover exploits that depend on interactions among network protocol components, such as inconsistencies in message interpretation, timing, state, or trust assumptions across participants. `ProtoArena` is a black-box, multi-component, dynamic benchmark of 80 cross-component exploitation environments spanning 11 protocol and application domains and 7 attack categories, mostly informed by published protocol-attack mechanisms, where agents act on running systems through scoped interfaces without target source code at three information levels ranging from guided reproduction to effect-directed black-box exploration, and a hybrid verifier combines rule-based checks with LLM review of independently collected traffic and logs. Of five LLMs evaluated, **`Claude Opus 4.8` scores highest with 48.8% success under full L1 guidance but only 12.5% under black-box L3**, and in a separate `DNSBomb` optimization experiment it reaches a downstream-response to query-input byte-rate ratio above 171,000 times. Success with limited information remains low and varies by domain and attack category, and all experiments use controlled, explicitly authorized targets rather than production systems or previously unknown vulnerabilities.

papers.title: Learning Adaptive Deliberation Control for Reliable Recognition with Multi-Agent Language Models
papers.abstract: Multi-agent deliberation can improve recognition by criticizing and revising candidate answers, but fixed controls cannot respond to changes in disagreement or reasoning quality. We present an adaptive multi-agent controller (ADMA) that learns continuous policies for proposal, challenge, arbitration, and coordination while keeping the task model frozen. Shared trace features describe quality, agreement, and progress, while role-specific features support decentralized control during inference. One controller trained on legal and financial reasoning is transferred without policy updates to four textual and multimodal benchmarks and two successive task-model versions. With Qwen3.5 held fixed, ADMA-Full improves accuracy by 6.2-14.2 percentage points over Direct and by 2.8-3.0 points over ADMA-Fixed. Paired bootstrap ranges for the Full-Fixed comparison are positive on three tasks. Outcome decompositions show that recoveries exceed introduced errors, while process assessment records fewer false-consensus events and more supported correct outcomes. Transfer to Qwen3.6 remains task dependent, which bounds the generality of the learned policy. Median token and latency ratios are 14.3-18.7 and 7.8-16.5 relative to Direct. These results show that adaptive deliberation can improve fixed-model recognition when its task-dependent gains justify the additional computation.
papers.summary: Multi-agent deliberation can improve recognition tasks by criticizing and revising candidate answers, but fixed control schedules cannot respond to shifts in disagreement or reasoning quality. `ADMA` is an adaptive multi-agent controller that learns continuous policies for proposal, challenge, arbitration, and coordination over a frozen task model, using shared trace features describing quality, agreement, and progress alongside role-specific features that allow decentralized control at inference, and a single controller trained on legal and financial reasoning is transferred without policy updates to four textual and multimodal benchmarks and two successive task-model versions. With `Qwen3.5` held fixed, **`ADMA-Full` improves accuracy by 6.2-14.2 percentage points over direct answering and by 2.8-3.0 points over a fixed-schedule variant**, with recoveries exceeding introduced errors and fewer false-consensus events, but transfer to `Qwen3.6` is task dependent and median token and latency ratios of 14.3-18.7 and 7.8-16.5 relative to direct answering mean the gains must justify substantial extra computation.

papers.title: FASHION-RQ: Mining Hierarchical Semantic Structure for Automated Evaluation of Fashion Retrieval
papers.abstract: Evaluating fashion retrieval systems remains challenging due to the limited availability of benchmarks that capture the fine-grained, open-ended queries encountered in real-world search and recommendation. Existing benchmarks often rely on manual curation, predefined taxonomies, or synthetic prompts, limiting scalability and semantic coverage. We introduce FASHION-RQ: Mining Hierarchical Semantic Structure for Automated Evaluation of Fashion Retrieval, an automated framework that derives user-type queries and relevance sets directly from catalog structure. Our key insight is that hierarchical discrete representations learned by Residual Quantized Variational Autoencoders (RQ-VAE) organize products into semantically coherent clusters at progressively finer granularities. We leverage this structure to construct FASHION-RQBENCH, a scalable benchmark without manual query annotation or predefined taxonomies. We propose four complementary tasks for evaluating ranking, relevance classification, fine-grained sibling discrimination, and paraphrase robustness, alongside query- and attribute-level relevance metrics. Experiments across recent retrieval models demonstrate that FASHION-RQBENCH differentiates model capabilities across query types and attributes. A human study further shows that benchmark queries achieve comparable naturalness and higher intent clarity than real user queries, supporting their validity for real-world evaluation. The code and FASHION-RQBENCH dataset will be publicly released upon acceptance.
papers.summary: Fashion retrieval systems lack benchmarks that capture the fine-grained, open-ended queries seen in real search and recommendation, since existing ones depend on manual curation, fixed taxonomies, or synthetic prompts. The authors derive queries and relevance sets automatically from catalog structure, using the hierarchical discrete codes learned by a Residual Quantized Variational Autoencoder (`RQ-VAE`) to group products into progressively finer semantic clusters, yielding the `FASHION-RQBENCH` dataset with four tasks covering ranking, relevance classification, fine-grained sibling discrimination, and paraphrase robustness. Experiments across recent retrieval models show the benchmark separates model capabilities by query type and attribute, and **a human study finds the generated queries match real user queries in naturalness while scoring higher on intent clarity**.

papers.title: MMTA: Benchmarking Multimodal Temporal Analysis with Time Series, Text, and Vision
papers.abstract: Time-series analysis is increasingly studied in multimodal settings, yet most benchmarks pair temporal signals with text or with visualizations derived from the same signal. This leaves open whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can integrate time series with real-world visual evidence. We introduce MMTA (multimodal temporal analysis), a benchmark of tri-modal tasks with diverse cross-modal complementarity patterns among time series, text, and vision. MMTA spans nine domains -- robotics, autonomous driving, human action, manufacturing, AR assistance, healthcare, recommendation, finance, and climate -- under video+TS and image+TS layouts, with a 3,524-sample test split covering classification and forecasting. The benchmark standardizes heterogeneous real-world sources into a shared schema with domain-specific prompts, provenance documentation, and success-weighted metrics that penalize both wrong answers and failed generations. Evaluating eight open-source and proprietary MLLMs reveals a shared bottleneck: representing time series as text creates very long token sequences and weakens fine-grained alignment with visual evidence, especially in long-video settings. We then introduce TimeOmni-v, a multimodal LLM extension with a dedicated time-series encoder, temporal positional alignment, modality-aware token layout, and a forecasting head. TimeOmni-v improves long-video classification and time-series inference efficiency, showing that MMTA not only exposes representation and grounding failures but also motivates targeted model design.
papers.summary: Most multimodal time-series benchmarks pair signals with text or with plots of the same signal, leaving open whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can combine time series with real-world visual evidence. The `MMTA` benchmark covers tri-modal tasks across nine domains in video-plus-time-series and image-plus-time-series layouts, with a 3,524-sample test split for classification and forecasting and success-weighted metrics that penalize failed generations as well as wrong answers. Evaluating eight open-source and proprietary MLLMs exposes a shared bottleneck: **serializing time series as text produces very long token sequences and weakens fine-grained alignment with visual evidence**, especially for long videos. A proposed extension, `TimeOmni-v`, adds a dedicated time-series encoder, temporal positional alignment, modality-aware token layout, and a forecasting head, improving long-video classification and inference efficiency.

papers.title: Socratic Skill Learning: Interleaving Teaching and Practice for Transferable Agent Skills
papers.abstract: Agent Skills improve LLM agents by making task knowledge reusable across sessions. Learning transferable Skills requires evidence about a procedure and its conditions of use, which a successful task attempt can leave untested. We introduce Socratic Skill Learning (SSL), which interleaves expert teaching with Student practice. An Educator guides investigation while the Student remains the sole environment operator and Skill author, able to question, test, and adapt advice. To test reuse beyond the learning task, we construct SkillTransferBench, with 35 task families and 408 executable cases, pairing public variation specifications with held-out evaluation in fresh solver sessions. On the main 22-family, 155-case cohort, Fixed-Window SSL reaches 0.801 utility, versus 0.723 without a Skill, 0.761 for adapted Trace2Skill (trajectory distillation), and 0.751 for adapted SKILL-KD (contrastive distillation). Across three model pairs on shared families, interleaved guidance outperforms expert authoring and post-hoc teaching. Process analysis links guidance to Student writing and package revision; a case study shows the Student testing and refining a proposed procedure for later reuse. As demand for new lessons falls, the cost of fixed-window review grows. Issue-Guided SSL tracks unresolved questions across Skill revisions to select and focus review, reaching 0.805 utility with 61.7% fewer Educator tokens and 16.9% fewer total acquisition tokens than Fixed-Window SSL on the main cohort.
