papers.summary: Agent Skills let large language model agents reuse task knowledge across sessions, but a single successful attempt often leaves a procedure's conditions of use untested. Socratic Skill Learning (`SSL`) interleaves guidance from an Educator model with practice by a Student that remains the sole environment operator and Skill author, free to question, test, and adapt the advice. On the main cohort of the new `SkillTransferBench` (35 task families, 408 executable cases overall), **`Fixed-Window SSL` reaches 0.801 utility versus 0.723 with no Skill** and 0.761 and 0.751 for the adapted `Trace2Skill` and `SKILL-KD` distillation baselines, and interleaved guidance beats both expert authoring and post-hoc teaching across three model pairs. An `Issue-Guided SSL` variant that tracks unresolved questions across Skill revisions matches this at 0.805 utility while using 61.7% fewer Educator tokens.

papers.title: TStruct: Learning Shared Temporal Structures for Long-Term Time-Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Long-term time series forecasting requires temporal dependency modeling that remains stable and generalizable under temporal distribution shifts. However, real-world time series are often noisy and non-stationary, making deep learning models prone to fitting incidental temporal interactions in the training data. A key question is whether there exist temporal relationship structures that recur across different temporal positions and variables. We analyze temporal relationship matrices on commonly used time series datasets and find that samples from different temporal positions and different variables exhibit shared dominant temporal relationship structures. This indicates that temporal relationship structures contain patterns that recur stably across samples and variables. To learn such shared structures, we propose \textbf{T}emporal \textbf{Struct}ure Network (\textbf{TStruct}), a simple yet effective network for directly learning shared and generalizable temporal dependencies. Specifically, TStruct directly parameterizes a set of shared temporal dependency matrices and generates normalized combination weights using dynamic sample information and static variable priors. These weights represent a soft allocation of each sample-variable pair over shared temporal dependency structures, enabling the model to generate adaptive temporal dependency matrices under shared structural constraints, rather than fitting incidental interactions in a fully unconstrained manner. Notably, this simple structure-aware design consistently outperforms several strong baselines across all datasets, achieving superior accuracy while maintaining high computational efficiency.
papers.summary: Long-term time-series forecasting models tend to fit incidental temporal interactions in noisy, non-stationary training data, which hurts generalization under distribution shift. Analyzing temporal relationship matrices on standard datasets, the authors find that samples from different time positions and variables share dominant temporal structures, and propose the Temporal Structure Network (`TStruct`), which directly parameterizes a set of shared temporal dependency matrices and softly allocates each sample-variable pair across them using dynamic sample information and static variable priors. **The structure-constrained design consistently outperforms several strong baselines across all tested datasets** while keeping computational cost low.

papers.title: RT-J: Large-Scale Pretraining of Relational Transformers for Context-Efficient Predictions
papers.abstract: Foundation models for tables and relational databases are increasingly used for predictive tasks across various scientific and industrial domains. However, adapting existing models to unseen datasets requires tens of thousands of examples. Here we introduce RT-J, an 85M-parameter relational foundation model (RFM) that makes accurate predictions even with hundreds of in-context examples or fewer. To achieve this, we first assemble the Join, a large collection of 639 web-crawled databases with 6,023 LLM-generated forecasting tasks. We pretrain with long contexts of up to 8,192 database cells, using in-context examples from a novel lightweight random-walk retriever. Finally, we leverage context tuning and ensembling to scale up test-time compute. On in-context regression tasks from RelBench, RT-J requires 10x fewer examples on average to match strong feature engineering pipelines with LLM-agent or RDBLearn featurizers and TabICLv2 or LightGBM predictors. Overall, our work pushes the frontier for context-efficient predictions on relational data and highlights the importance of real-world semantics, context engineering and large-scale pretraining for RFMs.
papers.summary: Foundation models for tables and relational databases typically need tens of thousands of examples to adapt to a new dataset. `RT-J` is an 85-million-parameter relational foundation model (RFM) pretrained on the Join, a collection of 639 web-crawled databases with 6,023 LLM-generated forecasting tasks, using contexts of up to 8,192 database cells assembled by a lightweight random-walk retriever, then scaled at test time through context tuning and ensembling. On in-context regression tasks from `RelBench`, **it needs about 10x fewer examples on average to match strong feature-engineering pipelines** that combine LLM-agent or `RDBLearn` featurizers with `TabICLv2` or `LightGBM` predictors.

papers.title: ECMR: Evidence-Aware Deliberation Control for Multi-Agent LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: Multi-agent Large Language Model (LLM) systems typically commit to a deliberation protocol before inference. A fixed protocol cannot allocate computation differently to resolved and unresolved instances, and it may mistake repeated support for independent confirmation. We study this failure as semantic false consensus: a confident group answer supported by narrow, duplicated, or correlated rationales. We introduce ECMR, an evidence-aware controller over frozen role-conditioned LLMs. At each step, ECMR summarizes answer concentration, support diversity and independence, contradictions, role behavior, verification history, and remaining budget, then selects whether to propose, challenge, verify, arbitrate, diversify, correct a role, or stop. We formulate this decision as finite-horizon budgeted control and derive sufficient conditions under which state conditioning, risk-triggered verification, and role correction improve cost-adjusted utility. Across a declared held-out evaluation of 9,000 records from MedQA, CaseHOLD, and FinQA, ECMR-Full increases pooled accuracy from 62.1% to 84.9%, reduces false-consensus rate from 40.7% to 17.0%, and raises evidence-support rate from 58.0% to 88.7%. State shuffling loses 11.7 accuracy points with only 0.7 fewer rounds, while harder traces shift from early stopping toward arbitration. ECMR-Full uses the largest token budget, yielding the strongest absolute reliability rather than uniformly superior token efficiency.
papers.summary: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems usually fix their deliberation protocol before inference, so they cannot spend more compute on unresolved cases and may mistake repeated, correlated rationales for independent confirmation, a failure the authors call semantic false consensus. `ECMR` is an evidence-aware controller over frozen role-conditioned LLMs that, at each step, summarizes answer concentration, support diversity, contradictions, verification history, and remaining budget, then chooses whether to propose, challenge, verify, arbitrate, diversify, correct a role, or stop, framed as finite-horizon budgeted control with derived sufficient conditions for improved cost-adjusted utility. On a held-out evaluation of 9,000 records from `MedQA`, `CaseHOLD`, and `FinQA`, **the full controller raises pooled accuracy from 62.1% to 84.9%** and cuts the false-consensus rate from 40.7% to 17.0%, though it uses the largest token budget rather than being uniformly more token-efficient.

papers.title: Cross-Lingual Transfer of Evil Vectors Is Directionally Asymmetric
papers.abstract: Persona vectors are linear directions in the residual-stream activations of LLMs that encode behavioral traits and enable fine-grained control over model behavior. Among them, the evil persona vector is particularly relevant to understanding harmful behavior, jailbreak vulnerabilities, and the unlearning of harmful knowledge. Yet whether this vector reflects a genuinely cross-lingual concept, rather than an artifact of its extraction language, remains untested. We conduct a systematic evil-vector transfer study across two high-resource languages (English, Spanish) and two low-resource languages (Swahili, Telugu) on four open-source instruction-tuned LLMs, and find that transfer is directionally asymmetric. Evil vectors are harder to obtain reliably from low-resource languages, and the resulting vectors are largely ineffective at steering, even within their own language. In contrast, vectors extracted from high-resource languages transfer effectively to low-resource inputs while largely preserving general knowledge, as measured by MMLU. Geometric analysis further supports this pattern: evil vectors from the two high-resource languages are closely aligned, whereas low-resource vectors align only weakly with this shared direction. These results suggest that a shared cross-lingual evil direction exists and, once reliably extracted from a high-resource language, can be reused to steer behavior in low-resource languages without additional per-language data collection.
papers.summary: Persona vectors are linear directions in a language model's residual-stream activations that encode behavioral traits, and the evil vector in particular bears on jailbreaks and unlearning of harmful knowledge, yet whether it is a genuinely cross-lingual concept had not been tested. The authors extract evil vectors in English, Spanish, Swahili, and Telugu across four open-source instruction-tuned LLMs and test steering across languages. **Transfer is directionally asymmetric: vectors from high-resource languages steer low-resource inputs effectively while largely preserving `MMLU` knowledge, whereas vectors extracted from low-resource languages are hard to obtain reliably and barely steer even their own language.** Geometric analysis shows the English and Spanish vectors are closely aligned while the low-resource vectors align only weakly with that shared direction.

papers.title: Training LLMs for Multi-Agent Collaboration with Verifiable Information Rewards
papers.abstract: Effective collaboration among large language model (LLM) agents in multi-agent systems requires sharing relevant evidence, requesting missing information, and incorporating teammates' contributions into decisions. Training these behaviors is challenging because final task outcomes provide limited feedback on the value of individual messages. We introduce CoSIR (Collaboration via Surprisal-based Information Rewards), a post-training approach that uses a simple, verifiable environment to teach collaboration behaviors that generalize to more complex, unseen tasks. We propose a Bayesian evaluator that scores shared information by its reduction in team surprisal, defined as the sum of the negative log probabilities assigned to the correct option given each agent's available evidence. Requests are scored by the potential reduction in the same quantity if the requested information were truthfully provided. Separate rewards encourage agents to use the received information in their private choices and calculations. We post-train Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-3-4B-it through self-play and evaluate transfer to seven unseen natural-language collaboration tasks. CoSIR achieves the highest aggregate score, while its performance in general tasks remains competitive. Behavioral analyses show increased disclosure of private evidence and fewer judged failures to use teammates' input.
papers.summary: Collaboration among large language model (LLM) agents requires sharing relevant evidence, requesting missing information, and using teammates' contributions, but final-task outcomes give little feedback on the value of individual messages. `CoSIR` (Collaboration via Surprisal-based Information Rewards) post-trains agents in a simple, verifiable environment with a Bayesian evaluator that scores a shared message by how much it reduces team surprisal, the summed negative log probability of the correct option given each agent's evidence, scores requests by the reduction they would yield if answered truthfully, and adds separate rewards for actually using received information. After self-play training of `Qwen3-4B`, `Qwen3-8B`, and `Gemma-3-4B-it`, **the method achieves the highest aggregate score across seven unseen natural-language collaboration tasks** while staying competitive on general tasks, with agents disclosing more private evidence and failing less often to use teammates' input.

papers.title: Interaction-as-a-Judge
papers.abstract: Coding agents are tasked with producing sophisticated interactive applications such as websites, desktop applications, and games. While humans assess these applications interactively, current automated LLM evaluations primarily focus on code analysis and unit tests. This mismatch can cause LLM judges to miss failures that are immediately apparent to human users. We study Interaction-as-a-Judge, an evaluation paradigm where computer-use agents (CUAs) directly interact with an application. We demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can improve both evaluation and generation of interactive applications. To this end, we collect and release two complementary datasets: $6,858$ pairs of applications with human preferences and corresponding agent traces, and $222$ applications with human-verified requirement labels. Relative to standard non-interactive approaches, we find that Interaction-as-a-Judge improves evaluation in terms of predicting human preferences ($65.6\% \to 69.1\%$) and requirement verification ($77.0\% \to 81.6\%$). We also observe scaling benefits: across both preference alignment and requirement verification, higher-quality interactions improve performance. Finally, through both inference- and training-time experiments, we demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can also improve the quality of generated artifacts. At inference time, Interaction-as-a-Judge repairs $75.5\%$ of broken requirements within five attempts, compared to $55.4\%$ for code-only self-feedback. At training time, using Interaction-as-a-Judge as a reward signal improves win-rate over the base model by $6.7$pp while reducing both generated code length by $35.7\%$ and build failure rates by $7.2$pp compared to a code-only reward signal.
papers.summary: Coding agents increasingly build interactive applications such as websites, desktop apps, and games, but automated LLM judges mostly inspect code and unit tests and can miss failures a human user would spot immediately. The authors study a paradigm in which computer-use agents (CUAs) operate the generated application directly, releasing 6,858 application pairs with human preferences and agent traces plus 222 applications with human-verified requirement labels. Relative to non-interactive judging, interaction raises human-preference prediction from 65.6% to 69.1% and requirement verification from 77.0% to 81.6%, with higher-quality interactions helping further. Used as feedback, **it repairs 75.5% of broken requirements within five attempts versus 55.4% for code-only self-feedback**, and as a training reward it lifts win-rate over the base model by 6.7 percentage points while cutting generated code length by 35.7% and build failures by 7.2 points compared to a code-only reward.

papers.title: Evaluating the Causal Faithfulness of SHAP as a Candidate Attribution Method for SAE Features
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders decompose language model representations into interpretable features, but feature interpretation in this literature remains predominantly correlational. Attribution methods offer more direct estimates of feature influence, yet their faithfulness to actual causal effects has not been systematically evaluated in the SAE setting. We apply SHAP-based attribution to SAE latent features and evaluate it against direct causal intervention, using sentiment classification on SST-2 with GPT-2 Small and a 32,768-feature layer-7 SAE as a testbed. We compare SHAP to Integrated Gradients, Gradient$\times$Input, and probe-weight baselines across linear and MLP probe arms, scoring each against feature ablation and activation steering measured through the language model's own logit difference. Most faithfulness associations we measure do not survive multiple-comparison correction, and attribution methods that agree strongly with one another ($\rho = 0.42$--$0.80$) agree poorly with measured causal effects, indicating that inter-method agreement is not evidence of causal faithfulness. Two effects hold under control. First, local per-example attribution retains a directional advantage over global averaged attribution, while its apparent importance advantage is explained by feature activity rather than superior causal ranking. Second, under known-ground-truth minimal pairs, attribution recovers inserted sentiment signal well above chance (AUROC $0.792$) but fails to localize deletions (AUROC $0.520$), suggesting that these methods detect the presence of a feature's influence more reliably than its absence. We argue that importance faithfulness and directional faithfulness are separable properties requiring separate evaluation, and that attribution agreement should not substitute for causal validation.
papers.summary: Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are usually interpreted correlationally, and whether attribution methods such as `SHAP` faithfully reflect a feature's causal effect had not been tested in this setting. Using sentiment classification on `SST-2` with `GPT-2 Small` and a 32,768-feature layer-7 SAE, the authors compare `SHAP` against `Integrated Gradients`, `Gradient-times-Input`, and probe-weight baselines, scoring each against feature ablation and activation steering measured by the model's own logit difference. Most faithfulness associations fail multiple-comparison correction, and **methods that agree strongly with each other (rank correlation 0.42 to 0.80) agree poorly with measured causal effects**, so inter-method agreement is not evidence of faithfulness. On ground-truth minimal pairs, attribution recovers inserted sentiment signal well above chance (AUROC 0.792) but fails to localize deletions (AUROC 0.520), leading the authors to argue that importance faithfulness and directional faithfulness need separate evaluation.

papers.title: PaceReasoner: Label-Free Learning to Answer Briefly from Long Reasoning
papers.abstract: Extended chain-of-thought reasoning improves problem-solving performance but increases inference cost and latency, motivating more accurate answers with shorter reasoning. We introduce PaceReasoner, a label-free test-time reinforcement learning framework that uses a model's LONG responses to improve its SHORT-mode accuracy. Both modes share a trainable policy, creating a need for reliable supervision, sufficient SHORT training samples, and continued LONG responses to guide learning. PaceReasoner combines all-response and LONG-only answer consensus through progressive, confidence-weighted supervision. A behavior reward gradually shifts from encouraging SHORT exploration to rewarding agreement with LONG answers, while a ratio controller regulates the balance between modes. Across three model backbones and four benchmarks, PaceReasoner improves average SHORT accuracy over the baselines by 7.4--13.5 percentage points, with fewer than 25 reasoning tokens per response on average. Ablations support the key components, and cross-dataset results demonstrate transfer beyond the adaptation set.
papers.summary: Long chain-of-thought reasoning improves accuracy but raises inference cost and latency, motivating models that answer accurately with short reasoning. `PaceReasoner` is a label-free test-time reinforcement learning framework in which a single policy runs in both LONG and SHORT modes, with supervision built from confidence-weighted consensus over all responses and over LONG-only answers, a behavior reward that shifts from encouraging SHORT exploration toward agreement with LONG answers, and a ratio controller balancing the two modes. Across three model backbones and four benchmarks, **SHORT-mode accuracy improves by 7.4 to 13.5 percentage points over baselines with fewer than 25 reasoning tokens per response on average**, and cross-dataset results show transfer beyond the adaptation set.

papers.title: Visual Dependence Does Not Imply Answerability: A Systematic Analysis of Answerability Signals in Frozen InstructBLIP
papers.abstract: Visual question answering models often produce plausible responses even when the available visual evidence is insufficient to support a valid answer. Although prior work has introduced benchmarks and abstention mechanisms for unanswerable visual questions, it remains unclear which signals derived from a frozen vision-language model reliably indicate answerability on unseen image-question pairs. We systematically evaluate answerability signals on a stratified 10K subset of UNK-VQA using frozen InstructBLIP, covering predictive uncertainty, cross-modal alignment, visual grounding, visual dependence, internal representations, and learned probes. Answerability discrimination remains weak, with test AUROC largely confined to 0.50-0.54. CLIP alignment yields the highest point estimate but does not significantly outperform generation confidence under paired bootstrap analysis. Targeted removal of question-relevant visual evidence causes substantially larger changes in answer confidence than same-size random masking, yet intervention sensitivity provides essentially no answerability discrimination. Increasing probe capacity, combining multiple signals, and adding reason-aware supervision do not provide robust improvements, while post-freeze cross-validation yields similarly weak discrimination. Selective-answering analysis shows limited usable coverage under low-risk operating criteria. Failure-mode analysis shows that the relative utility of individual signals varies across perturbation mechanisms. Taken together, these results show that, on our UNK-VQA subset with frozen InstructBLIP, visual dependence, uncertainty, semantic alignment, and static representations are not robust standalone proxies for answerability. Our findings emphasize the need to distinguish a model's reliance on visual evidence from whether that evidence is sufficient to support an answer.
papers.summary: Visual question answering models often give plausible answers even when the image lacks the evidence to support one, and it is unclear which signals from a frozen vision-language model reliably indicate answerability on unseen pairs. The authors evaluate predictive uncertainty, cross-modal alignment, visual grounding, visual dependence, internal representations, and learned probes on a stratified 10K subset of `UNK-VQA` using frozen `InstructBLIP`. **Discrimination stays weak, with test AUROC largely between 0.50 and 0.54**, and although removing question-relevant visual evidence changes answer confidence far more than random masking of the same size, that sensitivity provides essentially no answerability signal; larger probes, signal combinations, and reason-aware supervision do not help robustly. The authors conclude that a model's reliance on visual evidence must be distinguished from whether that evidence suffices to answer.

papers.title: DriveWLA: Unifying Future Dynamics and Scene Semantics through World-Language-Action Modeling for Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and world models have demonstrated strong capabilities in semantic understanding and future scene evolution for autonomous driving. However, effectively integrating both capabilities for trajectory generation remains challenging. In this work, we propose DriveWLA, a unified World-Language-Action model based on Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) that jointly models semantic understanding, future scene dynamics, and trajectory generation. DriveWLA consists of three experts: a World Expert for future prediction, a Language Expert for semantic understanding, and an Action Expert for trajectory generation. We further introduce Cross-Expert Attention, which enables controlled information flow across experts while aligning semantic and dynamic representations. To improve trajectory generation beyond imitation learning, we apply Flow-GRPO reinforcement learning post-training to refine the Action Expert. Extensive experiments show that DriveWLA achieves superior performance in both open-loop and closed-loop evaluation. DriveWLA achieves 92.3 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, demonstrating strong performance among VLM-based and world-model-based planners. Without specific fine-tuning, DriveWLA further demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization to HUGSIM, nuScenes, and Bench2Drive. These results validate the effectiveness of our unified World-Language-Action modeling, establishing DriveWLA as a generalizable framework for autonomous driving.
papers.summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) handle semantic understanding and world models handle future scene evolution for autonomous driving, but combining both for trajectory generation has been hard. The proposed `DriveWLA` model is built on a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) with three experts for future prediction, semantic understanding, and trajectory generation, linked by a Cross-Expert Attention mechanism that controls information flow, and its Action Expert is refined beyond imitation learning with `Flow-GRPO` reinforcement learning post-training. **It reaches 92.3 PDMS on `NAVSIM v1` and 90.1 EPDMS on `NAVSIM v2`** and generalizes zero-shot to `HUGSIM`, `nuScenes`, and `Bench2Drive` without task-specific fine-tuning.

papers.title: SpecCloak: Probing Harmful Code Generation through Engineering Specifications
papers.abstract: The code generation capabilities of large language models (LLMs) can equally be misused to implement harmful functionality, underscoring the need to understand their safety behavior in response to programming requests. While request phrasing is known to influence refusal, it remains unclear whether the form in which coding task requirements are stated affects the refusal process for malicious code generation. We introduce PseudoSpec, a template that organizes functional requirements as engineering specifications, and investigate its effects through controlled comparisons, representation analysis, and activation interventions. Across five open-weight models, removing explicit risk keywords only partially reduces refusal, whereas specification prompting substantially lowers refusal even when these keywords are retained. This reduction accompanies consistent shifts toward code-output-related representations, and interventions along condition-difference directions alter refusal behavior. Output analysis further distinguishes code-related responses from generation degeneration. Building on these findings, we propose SpecCloak, a black-box red-teaming framework combining PseudoSpec with discriminator-guided optimization, achieving an average execution-verified attack success rate of 28.91\% across eight target models on RedCode-Gen. We also introduce SpecReveal, a defense prototype combining natural-language intent reconstruction with dual-view detection without target-model fine-tuning. It achieves a 96.88\% attack detection rate in a separate prompt-detection evaluation, with false positives assessed on benign programming and specification-style inputs. These results connect specification-induced response differences to practical security consequences and identify intent reconstruction as a complementary detection approach.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) code generation can be misused for harmful functionality, and it was unknown whether the form in which coding requirements are stated, rather than just their phrasing, changes refusal behavior. The authors introduce `PseudoSpec`, a template that casts functional requirements as engineering specifications, and find across five open-weight models that **specification-style prompting substantially lowers refusal even when explicit risk keywords are retained**, whereas removing those keywords only partially reduces refusal; representation analysis ties this shift to code-output-related directions that alter refusal under intervention. Building on this, `SpecCloak` combines the template with discriminator-guided optimization to reach a 28.91% execution-verified attack success rate across eight target models on `RedCode-Gen`, while a defense prototype, `SpecReveal`, reconstructs natural-language intent and uses dual-view detection to catch 96.88% of attacks without fine-tuning the target model.

papers.title: LinMorph: Learning to Morph Weights for Efficient Video DiT Linearization
papers.abstract: Post-hoc linearization is an attractive way to accelerate pretrained Video Diffusion Transformers (Video DiTs), yet existing methods largely treat the quality loss induced by attention replacement as a recovery problem. We show that a more fundamental bottleneck lies upstream: \emph{initialization}. Random initialization discards pretrained knowledge, whereas manual weight reuse transfers it through rigid and incomplete source--target correspondences. We introduce \textbf{LinMorph}, which recasts Video DiT linearization as a learnable softmax-to-linear weight transformation problem. Instead of copying predefined counterparts, LinMorph learns a cross-parameter morphism that lets each target Gated DeltaNet (GDN) parameter draw jointly from pretrained query, key, value, and output projections, including for parameters with no direct softmax counterpart. A single morphism is shared across layers and learned through local teacher alignment, while producing layer-specific initializations from their respective pretrained weights. The resulting weights are then materialized as independent GDN modules for progressive distillation and joint recovery.Since the morphism operates in weight space rather than token space, it can be learned on short, low-resolution clips and directly reused at larger video scales. Across pretrained Video DiTs, LinMorph enables markedly faster recovery and better final generation quality than random initialization and heuristic weight reuse. Results show that efficient linearization depends not only on how a converted model is recovered, but critically on how pretrained knowledge is transferred before recovery. Project page: https://lonelyling.github.io/LinMorph.
papers.summary: Post-hoc linearization can speed up pretrained Video Diffusion Transformers (Video DiTs) by replacing softmax attention, but existing methods treat the resulting quality loss purely as a recovery problem. The authors argue that initialization is the real bottleneck and propose `LinMorph`, which learns a cross-parameter morphism letting each target Gated DeltaNet (`GDN`) parameter draw jointly from the pretrained query, key, value, and output projections, including parameters with no direct softmax counterpart; one morphism is shared across layers, trained by local teacher alignment on short low-resolution clips, and reused at larger video scales before progressive distillation. **Across pretrained Video DiTs, the learned initialization yields markedly faster recovery and better final generation quality than random initialization or heuristic weight reuse.**

papers.title: CineMem: Attention-Aligned Fine-grained Memory Retrieval for Multi-Shot Long Video Generation
papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generation relies on memory retrieval to model long-range dependencies. This capability becomes particularly critical for multi-shot generation, where models must reconcile substantial visual changes across shot transitions with persistent semantic continuity. Existing methods tend to perform memory retrieval at the frame level and share the same historical context across all query tokens, overlooking the heterogeneous information needs and leading to redundant retrieval and inefficient use of historical memory. To bridge this gap, we introduce CineMem, an attention-aligned fine-grained memory retrieval framework that combines online memory organization with query-adaptive retrieval for autoregressive multi-shot video generation. Specifically, guided by intrinsic memory-access patterns revealed through attention analysis, we propose an online-clustered KV cache as a memory organization strategy over all historical tokens, enabling semantic-aware memory grouping and more precise retrieval. In addition, we introduce a query-level retrieval mechanism that provides broader access to historical information under a fixed retrieval budget, thereby improving long-term memory utilization. Together, these designs enable the multi-shot video generator to preserve long-range consistency across shot transitions, particularly in revisitation scenarios, while approximating full-memory access under a constrained memory budget. To facilitate evaluation, we further introduce a suite of task-specific, VLM-assisted metrics for faithful inter-shot consistency assessment. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.
papers.summary: Autoregressive multi-shot video generation must reconcile large visual changes at shot transitions with persistent semantic continuity, yet existing memory retrieval works at the frame level and shares the same history with every query token, wasting retrieval budget. `CineMem` organizes all historical tokens into an online-clustered key-value cache guided by observed attention-access patterns and adds query-level retrieval that gives each query broader access to history under a fixed budget. **The design preserves long-range consistency across shot transitions, especially when revisiting earlier scenes, while approximating full-memory access under a constrained memory budget**, and the authors release VLM-assisted metrics for inter-shot consistency.

papers.title: GLST: Global-Local Spatio-Temporal Memory Decomposition Framework for Online Chained-Goal Navigation
papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in real-world environments often requires long-horizon operation under partial observability and evolving goals. Existing mapless navigation approaches predominantly assume fixed goals throughout an episode, limiting applicability to practical scenarios where goals change online during execution. We study online chained-goal navigation, where goals evolve through existing-goal redirection or new-goal emergence without explicit transition signals. Under this setting, we find navigation may require either continued exploration or strategic revisitation, creating conflicting memory requirements. We propose Global-Local Spatio-Temporal Belief Learning (GLST), a memory-decomposition framework that separates latent beliefs into global-local spatial and long-short temporal representations for long-horizon reasoning. We further introduce goal-conditioned rewards to balance exploration and exploitation under evolving goals. Extensive experiments in simulation across diverse terrains demonstrate improved chained-goal navigation performance over baselines. Real-robot experiments using the Spot quadruped further validate our memory decomposition framework.
papers.summary: Mapless navigation methods usually assume a fixed goal per episode, which breaks down when goals are redirected or new goals emerge mid-execution without explicit transition signals. Studying this online chained-goal setting, the authors find it demands both continued exploration and strategic revisitation, so they propose Global-Local Spatio-Temporal Belief Learning (`GLST`), which decomposes latent beliefs into global-local spatial and long-short temporal representations and adds goal-conditioned rewards to balance exploration and exploitation. **Simulation across diverse terrains shows improved chained-goal navigation over baselines**, and real-robot trials on a Spot quadruped validate the memory decomposition.

papers.title: Learning How to Remember: Memory Modality Selection for GUI Agents
papers.abstract: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have substantially improved the capabilities of GUI agents, while memory augmentation has emerged as a promising approach for reusing knowledge from past interactions. However, existing memory augmented GUI agents typically adopt a fixed representation strategy, providing retrieved experience as a static modality. It remains unclear whether a single memory modality is consistently optimal, or how modality preference changes across interaction steps. In this work, we conduct a systematic study of memory modality in VLM based GUI agents. Across GUI benchmarks, we find that the preferred memory representation is strongly step dependent. Motivated by the finding, we introduce \textbf{SwitchMem}, a routing framework that dynamically selects between textual and visual memory representations at each step. Across three GUI benchmarks, SwitchMem outperforms memory augmented baselines that rely on static memory representations. Our findings validate our claim that memory modality is a step dependent decision rather than a fixed design choice. Code and project resources are available at https://txxnrd.github.io/switchmem
papers.summary: Memory-augmented GUI agents built on vision-language models (VLMs) typically present retrieved past experience in one fixed modality, and it is unclear whether a single modality is ever consistently best. A systematic study across GUI benchmarks finds that **the preferred memory representation is strongly step dependent**, motivating `SwitchMem`, a routing framework that chooses between textual and visual memory at each step. Across three GUI benchmarks, the dynamic router outperforms baselines that use a static memory representation.

papers.title: MERIT: Multimodal Evidence Reasoning over Image Tables
papers.abstract: Table reasoning with language models typically assumes access to clean textual tables. In practice, tables are often serialized into text, which can corrupt cell contents, distort structural relationships, and discard visual cues, leaving the model to reason over incomplete evidence. In contrast, table images retain this information, but using it requires both accurate perception and reasoning grounded in the relevant cells. To address this, we propose MERIT (Multimodal Evidence Reasoning over Image Tables), a three-stage framework for learning to reason over table images, with serialized tables serving as optional auxiliary inputs (if provided). Our analysis identifies visual evidence acquisition as a bottleneck, motivating table-specific encoder adaptation through reconstruction, localization, and color-conditioned supervision. Building on the adapted representations, supervised fine-tuning teaches explicit evidence selection and reasoning using verified trajectories. Finally, reinforcement learning refines the policy with separate rewards for evidence correctness, calculation, final answers, and output format. By providing feedback on intermediate steps, the framework targets retrieval and computational errors that final-answer supervision alone does not distinguish. We evaluate the approach on table question answering and fact verification, analyze the contributions of visual inputs and training components, and assess generalization to additional datasets with different table structures and visual presentations.
papers.summary: Table reasoning with language models usually assumes clean textual tables, but serialization can corrupt cells, distort structure, and drop visual cues, while table images preserve this information at the cost of needing accurate perception. The `MERIT` framework trains a model to reason over table images, with serialized tables as optional auxiliary input, in three stages: table-specific encoder adaptation via reconstruction, localization, and color-conditioned supervision; supervised fine-tuning on verified trajectories that teach explicit evidence selection; and reinforcement learning with separate rewards for evidence correctness, calculation, final answer, and format. **The authors identify visual evidence acquisition as a bottleneck**, and evaluate on table question answering and fact verification with ablations of visual inputs and training components plus generalization tests on datasets with different table structures and presentations.

papers.title: AI-Enhanced Hyperspectral Imaging for Intraoperative Detection of Low-Grade Glioma: A Clinical Study
papers.abstract: Current image-guided neuronavigation techniques, such as intraoperative MRI and ultrasound, are limited by high costs, limited sensitivity and operational complexity. There is a clear need for more efficient systems to enhance intra-operative tumor detection and improve patient outcomes for intrinsic brain tumor resection. Whereas previous intraoperative brain HSI studies have predominantly investigated high-grade gliomas, glioblastomas, or mixed-grade cohorts, this clinical study focuses specifically on low-grade gliomas (LGGs). LGGs strongly resemble normal brain under white light conditions on the operative microscope. This study characterizes spectral differences between healthy and tumor tissue and provides a paired comparison of HSI- and RGB-based classification at matched tissue locations and under identical patient-level data splits. Tumor regions showed consistently lower reflectance, which may be associated with differences in hemoglobin concentration and oxygenation. A range of classification models was evaluated. The 3D CNN, which integrates spectral and spatial features, achieved the highest median ROC-AUC of 74.5%, compared with 67.9% for the spectral-only XGBoost model and 64.0% for the RGB-based model. These results support further investigation of HSI for low-grade glioma classification and quantify its performance relative to conventional RGB imaging in this cohort.
papers.summary: Intraoperative neuronavigation tools such as MRI and ultrasound are costly and limited in sensitivity, and low-grade gliomas (LGGs) are especially hard to distinguish from healthy brain under white light. The authors characterize spectral differences between tumor and healthy tissue using hyperspectral imaging (HSI) and compare HSI-based and RGB-based classification at matched tissue locations under identical patient-level splits. Tumor regions show consistently lower reflectance, possibly tied to hemoglobin concentration and oxygenation, and **a 3D CNN combining spectral and spatial features reaches a median ROC-AUC of 74.5%, versus 67.9% for a spectral-only `XGBoost` model and 64.0% for RGB**.

papers.title: HaloBlock: Faster and Better Decoding for Diffusion Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have attracted increasing research attention due to their bidirectional attention and arbitrary order decoding. However, there are two issues in dLLMs inference: the decoding difficulty is dominated by the tokens on the right side of the block, and the block-wise decoding inherently suffers from boundary contextual discontinuity. To tackle these limitations, we propose HaloBlock, a difficulty-aware adaptive halo mechanism for dLLM inference. We first leverage bidirectional cumulative entropy to characterize block decoding difficulty. Then, based on the bidirectional decoding difficulty, we adaptively allocate bidirectional halo regions on both sides of each block to mitigate boundary contextual discontinuity. The difficulty-aware design of HaloBlock smooths cross-block context propagation and lowers decoding difficulty for hard tokens, yielding better generation quality and faster convergence. Evaluated on LLaDA-8B-Instruct, Dream-7B-Instruct and LLaDA-1.5 across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks, HaloBlock demonstrates consistent accuracy improvements and higher inference efficiency. Source codes are publicly available at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/HaloBlock.
papers.summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) decode blocks of tokens with bidirectional attention, but tokens at the right edge of each block are hardest to predict and block boundaries break contextual continuity. `HaloBlock` measures each block's decoding difficulty with bidirectional cumulative entropy and adaptively adds halo regions on both sides of the block so cross-block context propagates more smoothly. On `LLaDA-8B-Instruct`, `Dream-7B-Instruct` and `LLaDA-1.5`, the method yields **consistent accuracy gains together with faster inference** on mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks.

papers.title: FETALFusion: Resolution-Aware State-Space Modeling for Multi-Domain Fetal Head Segmentation
papers.abstract: Head circumference (HC) measured from 2D ultrasound is a routine marker of fetal growth, and automating it needs segmentations whose boundaries hold up on individual scans, not only on average. We present FETALFusion, a dual-path CNN-Mamba encoder-decoder for fetal head segmentation across acquisition types. It applies four-directional state-space scans only at the two highest-resolution stages, routes bottleneck features through domain-specific channel gates that are averaged at test time, and adds a weak landmark shape prior. We train jointly on transabdominal (HC-18) and transperineal (PSFHS) images and compare ten methods on a held-out test set of 471 images, each trained under one schedule and scored by surface distances at native resolution. FETALFusion reaches a Dice score of 0.963 and an HD95 of 2.10 mm without test-time augmentation or a domain label. It improves on U-Mamba on all five reported metrics (HD95 reduced by 0.31 mm; Holm-corrected ($p < 10^{-4}$), a lead that holds under test-time augmentation and across two independent training runs, and in the mean on U-Net, Attention U-Net and TransUNet. Residual encoders close the gap: a ResNet-34 UNet++ exceeds FETALFusion, and an ImageNet initialised ResNet-34 U-Net is best overall (HD95 1.75 mm). The ablation agrees. Calibrated against run-to-run variation, it attributes FETALFusion's measurable gains to the landmark shape prior and, on transperineal images, to the domain gates, while removing the state-space branch does not measurably change accuracy. HC from the predicted masks agrees with the clinical reference at an intraclass correlation of 0.9986.
papers.summary: Automating fetal head circumference (HC) measurement from 2D ultrasound requires segmentations with reliable boundaries on individual scans across acquisition types. `FETALFusion` is a dual-path CNN-Mamba encoder-decoder that applies four-directional state-space scans only at the two highest-resolution stages, routes bottleneck features through domain-specific channel gates, and adds a weak landmark shape prior, trained jointly on transabdominal `HC-18` and transperineal `PSFHS` images. It reaches a Dice score of 0.963 and HD95 of 2.10 mm and beats `U-Mamba` on all five metrics, but **an `ImageNet`-initialised `ResNet-34 U-Net` is best overall with HD95 of 1.75 mm**, and the ablation attributes the gains to the shape prior and domain gates rather than the state-space branch.

papers.title: Virtual Head Attention
papers.abstract: The design of attention mechanisms in long-context large language models faces an ``impossible triangle'' among KV cache size, training and prefill FLOPs, and model quality. GQA achieves strong quality but incurs high KV cache overhead; alternative approaches such as MLA and MFA can compress the cache, but MLA suffers from quality loss while MFA substantially increases training and prefill compute. We propose Virtual Head Attention (VHA), which simultaneously improves all three vertices through two lightweight linear operations: Q Premix applies a near-identity transformation to queries within each KV group to recover virtual head diversity from halved physical query heads, and Linear Postmix fuses inter-head features via a low-rank $I + AB^\top$ residual structure. Since VHA introduces no nonlinear operations, Premix can be folded into the query projection and Postmix into the output projection at inference time, reducing the model to a standard GQA-2 architecture that directly reuses all existing GQA inference optimizations. With only two KV heads, the group size in large models readily reaches 64, fully exploiting Tensor Core parallelism during decoding. Across four scales with 4K-context 50B-token pretraining, VHA consistently surpasses the standard GQA baseline at every scale ($+$0.05\% to $+$0.81\%), while reducing KV cache by $4\times$ vs.\ GQA-8 at dense scales and $2\times$ vs.\ GQA-4 at the MoE scale, and lowering training and prefill FLOPs by 7.9\% (1.7B, $S{=}4096$). On an industrial 30B-A3B MoE model trained on 500B tokens at 8K context, VHA outperforms both MLA and GQA-4 by $+$0.70\,/\,$+$2.60\,\% on a 12-benchmark base-model evaluation suite; in a separate matched 10B-A1B MoE comparison after long-context mid-training, VHA attains an average RULER score of 84.4 over 8K--128K versus 73.0 for GQA, while using two rather than four KV heads in the full-attention layers.
papers.summary: Attention design for long-context LLMs faces a three-way tension among KV cache size, training and prefill compute, and model quality, where grouped-query attention (GQA) keeps quality but a large cache while MLA and MFA shrink the cache at the cost of quality or compute. `Virtual Head Attention` (`VHA`) adds two linear operations, a Q Premix that recovers virtual head diversity from halved physical query heads and a low-rank Linear Postmix that fuses inter-head features, both of which fold into existing projections at inference so the model reduces to standard two-KV-head GQA. Across four scales of 4K-context pretraining it edges out GQA baselines while cutting KV cache by up to 4x and training and prefill FLOPs by 7.9%, and **a 10B-A1B MoE model scores 84.4 average on `RULER` over 8K to 128K contexts versus 73.0 for GQA** with half the KV heads.

papers.title: Better Capturing Interactions Between Products in~Retail: Revisited Negative Sampling for~Basket Choice Modeling
papers.abstract: Brick-and-mortar retailers face many different challenges that involve understanding thoroughly its products catalog and customer preferences. In particular, assortment optimization - proposing the ideal mix of products - and promotion planning hold a pivotal role in their strategy. By leveraging sales data, retailers can make informed decisions on which products to sell and how to manage inventory, based on customer preferences as well as regional and seasonal trends. It is especially crucial to capture interactions between products, in order to minimize the number of items that cannibalize each other's sales and to ensure that complementary products, which are often purchased together, are conjointly available and sold across all stores. In this paper, we propose a model of shopping basket that learns embeddings to represent interactions between products, prices and stores. Our model is built to uncover sales patterns from very large transaction datasets. In particular, the optimization loss is computed with random negative samples in order to overcome the computational bottlenecks that arise with large number of items. Our experiments on synthetic data show the efficiency of drawing such negative samples based on the actual assortment of available products, with better results than approaches from the literature. We also validate our approach by training and evaluating our model on a dataset composed of millions of transactions from Fortenova Group, one of the leading retail company in Southeast Europe. Our model showcases promising applications in the sector of retail, with enriched interfaces to efficiently support category managers.
papers.summary: Brick-and-mortar retailers need to understand product interactions such as cannibalization and complementarity to plan assortments and promotions. The proposed shopping basket model learns embeddings that capture interactions between products, prices and stores from very large transaction datasets, using random negative samples in the loss to avoid the computational bottleneck of large catalogs. On synthetic data, **drawing negative samples from the actual assortment of available products outperforms sampling approaches from the literature**, and the model is also trained and evaluated on millions of transactions from Fortenova Group, a Southeast European retailer.

papers.title: BELT : BEhavior-Aligned Low-Rank KV Cache Compression with Learned Top-k Rank Allocation
papers.abstract: Long-context inference makes the key-value (KV) cache a major memory bottleneck for large language models. We propose BELT, a low-rank KV cache compression framework. Its key-side objective targets attention distributions rather than raw keys or pre-softmax logits, yielding a quadratic surrogate with a closed-form low-rank solution. A learned global rank allocator uses differentiable soft selection during training and hard selection at deployment to meet a user-specified component budget. Experiments demonstrate improved model quality under aggressive compression and increased decoding throughput at comparable accuracy. Evaluated across three LLMs and multiple benchmarks, BELT achieves up to 70% low-rank KV cache compression while outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 23.3 points on LongBench, and up to 17.8x overall KV cache reduction when combined with quantization. With Triton-based GPU kernels and a quantized cache, BELT delivers up to 2.7x speedup for the attention module and 3.3x end-to-end decoding throughput.
papers.summary: The key-value (KV) cache becomes the dominant memory cost in long-context inference. `BELT` is a low-rank KV cache compression framework whose key-side objective matches attention distributions rather than raw keys or logits, giving a quadratic surrogate with a closed-form low-rank solution, plus a learned global rank allocator that uses soft selection in training and hard selection at deployment to meet a component budget. Across three LLMs it achieves up to 70% low-rank compression while **beating the strongest baseline by up to 23.3 points on `LongBench`**, reaches 17.8x total cache reduction when combined with quantization, and with Triton kernels delivers up to 3.3x end-to-end decoding throughput.

papers.title: Seeing Depth but Choosing Cues in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Do vision-language models use depth information to judge which object is closer, or rely on image-plane cues? We investigate this question through controlled depth--cue conflicts, representation analysis, and interventions. Among the many image-plane cues relevant to depth perception, we focus on apparent size and vertical position. We compare depth judgments under cue-consistent and cue-conflict conditions in both rendered scenes and real-world photographs. Across model families and scales, depth judgments systematically shift toward misleading cues. Yet the correct depth order remains decodable from the queried objects' visual representations, including when the model answers incorrectly. Image and category controls support interpreting this signal as image-dependent depth information beyond the two target cues. Strengthening the model's own depth readout through object-level write-back can correct conflict decisions without updating model parameters or using ground-truth depth annotations. Interventions show that the effect of this correction depends on the direction and target tokens of the written signal, while its strength varies across architectures and domains. Together, these findings reveal a mismatch between a model's ability to represent depth and use this information when deciding the answer. VLMs can retain useful depth information while allowing competing image-plane cues to exert greater influence on their answers.
papers.summary: Do vision-language models (VLMs) judge which object is closer from depth information or from image-plane cues like apparent size and vertical position? The study constructs depth-cue conflicts in rendered scenes and real photographs, analyzes representations, and intervenes on them. Across model families and scales, answers shift systematically toward misleading cues, yet **the correct depth order remains decodable from the queried objects' representations even when the model answers wrong**, and amplifying the model's own depth readout via object-level write-back can fix conflict decisions without parameter updates or ground-truth depth.

papers.title: Seeing Through the Forgery Is Not Enough: Regressive Sycophancy under Fabricated Evidence in Medical Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: A medical vision-language model may analyze a given CT scan and correctly detect both kidneys in view. Continuing this conversation, if a user provides a prescription with an opposite direction, medical VLMs often sycophantically choose to realign their diagnosis. In this work, we study regressive sycophancy under fabricated evidence, where a model abandons a correct answer when pushback comes with a fake document. We test four open VLMs on 400 VQA-RAD yes/no questions in 19,200 multi-turn conversations, with and without a fabricated prescription. Without a disclosure that documents are synthetic, the models abandon 80.1% of 6,488 correct answers. Notably, under one script each, the same prescription raises the flip rate of Qwen2.5-VL-7B from 45.9% to 89.6% and lowers that of Qwen3-VL-8B from 77.7% to 50.9%. A model rejected the prescription while still preserving the correct answer in 915 of 3,232 conversations with the prescription (28.3%), and 40% of these flipped in later turns. System-prompt sentences that disclose the documents as synthetic lower one model's flip rate from 77.8% to 47.3%. Thus, we conclude that awareness about a forgery does not prevent a model from adopting its answer.
papers.summary: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) that correctly read a CT scan often reverse their answer when a user pushes back with a fabricated prescription. The study tests four open VLMs on 400 `VQA-RAD` yes/no questions across 19,200 multi-turn conversations, with and without a fake document and with or without a system-prompt disclosure that documents are synthetic. **Without disclosure, the models abandon 80.1% of 6,488 initially correct answers**, and depending on the conversation script the same prescription raises the flip rate of `Qwen2.5-VL-7B` from 45.9% to 89.6% while lowering that of `Qwen3-VL-8B` from 77.7% to 50.9%. Even models that explicitly rejected the prescription flipped in later turns 40% of the time, so recognizing a forgery does not stop a model from adopting its claim.

papers.title: Saliency-Guided Replay for Continual Learning in Deep Spiking Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are promising for energy-efficient neuromorphic computing, but they still suffer from catastrophic forgetting when learning tasks sequentially. This work investigates the integration of Experience Packing and Replay (EPR) as a memory-efficient continual learning strategy for deep SNNs under low-latency constraints. The proposed framework combines Batch Normalization Through Time stabilized VGG9 SNNs with Spike Activation Maps (SAM), which provide forward-only explanations based on spike activity. These explanations are temporally aggregated into spatial attention maps and used to select the most informative image patches for replay, instead of storing full images. Experiments on Split CIFAR10 and Split CIFAR100 show that SAM-guided EPR improves the accuracy-memory trade-off under tight memory budgets, and remains competitive while requiring substantially less storage.
papers.summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient neuromorphic computing but suffer catastrophic forgetting when tasks arrive sequentially. The work adapts Experience Packing and Replay (EPR) to deep SNNs by combining Batch Normalization Through Time stabilized `VGG9` networks with Spike Activation Maps (SAM), forward-only explanations derived from spike activity that are aggregated into spatial attention maps to pick the most informative image patches for replay instead of storing whole images. On `Split CIFAR10` and `Split CIFAR100`, **SAM-guided replay improves the accuracy-memory trade-off under tight memory budgets** while requiring substantially less storage.

papers.title: Match the Canvas, Not Just the Answer: Predictability-Aware SFT for Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable flexible parallel generation by resolving tokens according to the model's evolving predictability rather than a fixed left-to-right order. This flexibility, however, introduces training choices absent from standard autoregressive teacher forcing: which reference tokens are visible when a target is supervised and how much generation space is allocated. Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) typically makes these choices through random masking, independently of inference. Our analysis shows how this training-inference mismatch can misdirect supervision. Random masking can conceal prediction errors or penalize uncertainty that decoding would otherwise resolve, while the attention-visible input length can change which response formulations the model favors, even when the underlying solution is unchanged. Motivated by these findings, we propose Predictability-Aware Canvas Selection and Supervision (PACS), an SFT method. PACS uses the model's own predictability to select each example's attention-visible input length and supervises reference tokens immediately before their confidence-guided revelation. Across reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, PACS consistently achieves the highest mean accuracy among the compared SFT methods, with gains of up to 12.84 percentage points over vanilla SFT on individual benchmarks. Code will be released upon publication.
papers.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) resolve tokens in order of predictability rather than left to right, but standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) chooses which reference tokens are visible and how much generation space to allocate via random masking that ignores how inference actually proceeds. Analysis shows this mismatch can hide prediction errors, penalize uncertainty that decoding would resolve, and shift which response formulations the model prefers depending on the visible input length. Predictability-Aware Canvas Selection and Supervision (`PACS`) uses the model's own predictability to set each example's visible input length and supervises reference tokens just before their confidence-guided revelation, achieving the highest mean accuracy among compared SFT methods on reasoning and code benchmarks with **gains of up to 12.84 percentage points over vanilla SFT**.

papers.title: SWEPatchTest: Evaluating Software Tests Beyond Reproduction
papers.abstract: Coding agents use generated tests to decide whether a proposed patch satisfies an issue's requirements. A suite that fails on the buggy program and passes after applying the reference patch can still accept an incorrect patch or reject a correct patch. We introduce SWEPATCHTEST, a test-generation benchmark with 619 tasks from SWE-bench Pro, SWE-bench Multilingual, and DeepSWE and 82,579 candidate patches collected from coding-agent trajectories. By replaying each suite on the buggy and patched codebases, \benchmark jointly measures issue reproduction, acceptance of correct patches, and rejection of incorrect patches. Joint Validation Rate (JVR), which requires all three criteria on the same task, exposes failures hidden by single-reference evaluation: the best-performing configuration achieves only 9.21% JVR despite reproducing the reference transition on 59.29% of tasks. We further use validation scores to select and scale demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The resulting training recipe approximately triples JVR and improves downstream repair across three SWE-bench benchmarks. Patch discrimination thus provides both a diagnostic measure of test quality and an execution-based signal for curating agent training data.
papers.summary: Coding agents rely on generated tests to judge whether a patch resolves an issue, but a suite that fails before and passes after the reference patch can still accept wrong patches or reject correct ones. `SWEPatchTest` gathers 619 tasks from `SWE-bench Pro`, `SWE-bench Multilingual` and `DeepSWE` along with 82,579 candidate patches from agent trajectories, replaying each generated suite on buggy and patched code to score issue reproduction, acceptance of correct patches, and rejection of incorrect ones together as a Joint Validation Rate (JVR). **The best configuration reaches only 9.21% JVR despite reproducing the reference transition on 59.29% of tasks**, and using validation scores to select supervised fine-tuning (SFT) demonstrations roughly triples JVR and improves downstream repair on three `SWE-bench` benchmarks.

papers.title: Cost-Efficient Privacy Enforcement for Email-Generating LLM Agents under Strategic Information Requests
papers.abstract: LLM agents now act as delegated communication intermediaries: they read private context, draft messages, and send externally visible emails on behalf of a user. Existing checker-repair defenses can reduce inappropriate disclosure, but they rely on repeated calls to a remote action LLM (the model that drafts and repairs the email) and a remote checker LLM whenever a draft fails validation. This creates a cost problem as well as a privacy problem, especially when a requester strategically asks for exact values, raw records, source evidence, or other details that induce leakage-heavy drafts. We propose local contract-conditioned rewriting as a cost-efficient enforcement layer for email-generating agents. The mechanism intercepts an outgoing draft, constructs an information-release contract that specifies what to preserve, generalize, and forbid, rewrites the draft with a local Gemma rewriter, and selectively invokes a final PrivacyChecker. Across extensive email tasks under normal prompts and attack prompts that operationalize strategic information requests, Gemma + Checker reduces normal-prompt leakage from 11.41% to 4.03% while improving UsableRate (satisfied or partially satisfied outputs) from 85.2% to 92.6%. Under the strategic attack-prompt condition, it reduces leakage from 28.19% to 18.79% and reduces checker-only cost amplification from 1.32x to 1.02x. Offline replay ablation shows that the full contract reduces leakage relative to generic Gemma rewriting by 36.3% under normal prompts and 54.1% under attack prompts. These results support a local-first privacy enforcement design: move repair to a cheaper trusted local layer when possible, but retain the checker as the final semantic gate for high-risk sends.
papers.summary: LLM agents that draft and send emails on a user's behalf can leak private context, and existing checker-repair defenses repeatedly call remote models whenever a draft fails validation, which becomes costly when a requester strategically asks for exact values or raw records. The proposed local contract-conditioned rewriting intercepts each outgoing draft, builds an information-release contract stating what to preserve, generalize and forbid, rewrites with a local `Gemma` model, and only selectively invokes a final `PrivacyChecker`. Under normal prompts the combination cuts leakage from 11.41% to 4.03% while raising usable outputs from 85.2% to 92.6%, and **under strategic attack prompts it lowers leakage from 28.19% to 18.79% while reducing checker cost amplification from 1.32x to 1.02x**.

papers.title: Correcting or Continuing? What On-Policy Distillation Learns from Student Errors
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher, mitigating the distribution mismatch of off-policy supervision. While prior work has primarily trained on problems a student can largely solve, we ask whether OPD can improve a student when training is restricted to problems it currently fails. We evaluate five representative OPD mechanisms with Qwen-3 and Phi-4 models under a unified competition-mathematics protocol. We find that OPD does not improve accuracy on this hard subset, with most mechanisms instead degrading performance despite continued decreases in training KL divergence. All eight configurations show a decline, and the two-sided sign test gives p=0.0078. In contrast, the same pipeline improves accuracy by 4.6 percentage points when training is not concentrated on failures, showing that the failure is conditional on the training regime rather than systematic. These findings suggest that OPD is effective when supervision is dominated by correct student prefixes, but can reinforce existing errors when training is concentrated on problems the student currently fails.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher, but prior work has mostly used problems the student can already largely solve. The study evaluates five OPD mechanisms with `Qwen-3` and `Phi-4` models on competition mathematics, restricting training to problems the student currently fails. **All eight configurations lose accuracy on the hard subset (two-sided sign test p=0.0078) even as training KL divergence keeps falling**, whereas the same pipeline gains 4.6 percentage points when training is not concentrated on failures, suggesting OPD works when supervision is dominated by correct student prefixes but can reinforce errors otherwise.

papers.title: LatentRemedy: Efficient Remedy For Non-Prefix KV Cache Reuse in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Non-prefix KV cache reuse is a promising approach for improving inference efficiency in multi-agent systems as agents share the same context blocks. However, when agents have conflicting tasks, directly reusing non-prefix KV caches across agents can severely degrade model performance, causing up to a 90% drop. Existing remedies, including selective recomputation and offset-based calibration, recover a limited fraction of this loss. We argue that the problem lies not only in contaminated KV representations but also in the agent's difficulty interpreting reused context under its own instructions. To this end, we introduce LatentRemedy, which uses a few task-conditioned latent tokens to help the target agent leverage reused context without recomputing the shared block. Specifically, we use an MLP to map the last hidden state of the target prefix into a small number of latent tokens, which are placed after the reused KV block to interact with the shared context. To guide subsequent predictions toward the target task, we train the MLP through full-prefill distillation. Experiments show that LatentRemedy consistently outperforms existing reuse baselines on conflicting tasks while maintaining TTFT close to direct reuse as cache size grows. Code and data are available at https://github.com/chenzhwsysu57/kvreuse.
papers.summary: In multi-agent systems where agents share the same context blocks, reusing non-prefix KV caches across agents can speed up inference but degrades performance by up to 90% when agents have conflicting tasks, and existing remedies like selective recomputation and offset-based calibration recover only part of the loss. `LatentRemedy` argues the problem is partly that an agent struggles to interpret reused context under its own instructions, so it maps the last hidden state of the target prefix through an MLP into a few task-conditioned latent tokens placed after the reused block, with the MLP trained by full-prefill distillation. **It consistently outperforms existing reuse baselines on conflicting tasks** while keeping time-to-first-token close to direct reuse as cache size grows.

papers.title: SHELDON: Reasoning through Dual Search over Hypothesis and Observation Spaces
papers.abstract: Test-time scaling has enabled LLMs to solve increasingly complex reasoning, discovery, and optimization tasks. However, existing approaches often gather observations while seeking evidence for current hypotheses, then generate new hypotheses conditioned on those hypotheses and their associated evidence. This couples observation discovery to existing hypotheses, favoring local refinements over exploration of unknown hypotheses regions. Inspired by the hypothetico-deductive method (Hempel, 1945) and dual-space models of scientific discovery (Klahr & Dunbar, 1988), we introduce SHELDON, a scientific reasoning harness that separately represents and jointly explores hypothesis and observation spaces. By actively seeking new observations along with new hypotheses, SHELDON can discover observations that its current hypotheses do not explain. These unexplained observations expose gaps in its understanding, motivate new investigations, and guide the generation of hypotheses beyond refinements of existing ones. Across diagnosis, abstract reasoning, and optimization benchmarks, SHELDON outperforms evaluated baselines by up to 26.7 points. Additional analysis shows that SHELDON generates up to 4.5x more novel solutions.
papers.summary: Test-time scaling methods typically gather observations only to test current hypotheses and then generate new hypotheses from those same hypotheses and evidence, which biases search toward local refinements. Drawing on the hypothetico-deductive method and dual-space models of scientific discovery, `SHELDON` is a reasoning harness that represents hypothesis and observation spaces separately and explores them jointly, actively seeking observations that current hypotheses cannot explain in order to expose gaps and drive new hypotheses. Across diagnosis, abstract reasoning and optimization benchmarks it **outperforms evaluated baselines by up to 26.7 points** and generates up to 4.5x more novel solutions.

papers.title: ChampionKV: Head-Wise Adaptive Budget Allocation for KV Cache Compression
papers.abstract: Some observation-window-based KV cache compressors use prompt attention to identify important tokens but allocate uniform or predefined budgets across heads, overlooking input-dependent differences in budget demand. We propose ChampionKV, an input-adaptive head-wise budget allocator for long-context KV cache compression. It uses the maximum aggregated observation-window attention score as a lightweight empirical proxy for attention concentration, assigning larger budgets to heads with dispersed attention and smaller budgets to concentrated heads. An abnormal-head mask and a floor-budget mechanism improve robustness under weak attention responses. ChampionKV plugs into compressors such as SnapKV and PyramidKV without changing their token-selection procedures. On LongBench and RULER, both Champion variants consistently improve over their SnapKV and PyramidKV base compressors; the improvements are largest and statistically significant on Llama3.1-70B-Instruct, especially under tight budgets, whereas results on the tested 7B/8B models remain competitive but mixed. ChampionKV does not uniformly outperform Ada-KV, whose global cross-head Top-K selection retains an advantage in several settings. Controlled analysis further shows improved retained attention mass over the corresponding base compressors at negligible overhead.
papers.summary: Observation-window KV cache compressors such as `SnapKV` and `PyramidKV` pick important tokens from prompt attention but give every head the same or a predefined budget regardless of input. `ChampionKV` allocates budgets per head using the maximum aggregated observation-window attention score as a proxy for attention concentration, giving more budget to heads with dispersed attention, with an abnormal-head mask and floor budget for robustness, and it plugs into existing compressors without changing their token selection. On `LongBench` and `RULER` both variants improve over their base compressors, with **gains largest and statistically significant on `Llama3.1-70B-Instruct` under tight budgets**, while results on 7B/8B models are mixed and `Ada-KV` retains an advantage in several settings.

papers.title: Can Machine Learning Potentials Be More Accurate Than the Methods They Are Trained On?
papers.abstract: Although machine learning potentials (MLPs) generalize across configurational and chemical compound spaces, their accuracy is commonly believed to be limited by their training methods, with improvements beyond this limit achieved so far only by refitting to experimental observables. In this Perspective, we argue that MLPs can also be made more accurate than their training methods non-empirically by generalizing across a third space, that of quantum-chemical methods. We propose routes to method-transferable MLPs that predict at unseen methods, with working implementations in both density-functional and wavefunction-based theories showing that they can be more accurate than any of their training methods. Aiming beyond the accuracy of the training methods could also make universal MLPs more accurate than single-method models, even when the method-transferable MLPs remain less accurate than those QM methods. Method-transferable MLPs will shape the construction of training datasets and the evaluation of models, pushing the accuracy limits of chemical simulations.
papers.summary: Machine learning potentials (MLPs) for chemical simulation are usually assumed to be capped at the accuracy of the quantum-chemical methods that generate their training data, with gains beyond that only from refitting to experimental observables. The authors argue that MLPs can exceed their training methods non-empirically by generalizing across a third space, that of quantum-chemical methods themselves, and propose routes to method-transferable MLPs that predict at unseen methods. Working implementations in both density-functional and wavefunction-based theories **show method-transferable MLPs can be more accurate than any of their training methods**, which the authors argue will reshape how training datasets are built and models are evaluated.

papers.title: Scaling Vision Transformers Without Training: Prune-and-Merge Token Compression
papers.abstract: Vision Transformers achieve strong performance but incur high computational costs from quadratic token interactions. Training-free token reduction methods improve efficiency, but their robustness remains underexplored. We propose Prune-and Merge ViT, a training-free framework for off-the-shelf models. It combines class attention-based pruning with similarity-based merging to reduce redundancy while preserving semantic information. To evaluate robustness we introduce two metrics. Relative Accuracy Drop (RAD) measures relative accuracy degradation under transformations, and Prediction Flip Rate (PFR) quantifies prediction consistency. On pretrained ViT and DeiT, Prune-and-Merge reduces computation competitively while maintaining robustness and better accuracy than existing token reduction methods.
