Drawing on the Condorcet principle from social choice theory, `Pairwise-Guided Logit Adjustment (PGLA)` introduces pairwise confidence comparisons between paths that support different answers and combines this comparative evidence with voting support through a KL-regularized objective, which the authors show is equivalent to an adjustment of the traditional voting logits, so that comparative evidence can compensate for weaker voting support and correct voting-based ranking errors. **Experiments on 10 challenging benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, knowledge reasoning, and code generation with 7 models from 1.7B to 32B parameters support the effectiveness of the plug-and-play term**, and further evaluations with external reward scores and online sampling show it applies in those settings too.

papers.title: GeoMER: A Joint Euclidean-Hyperbolic Geometry Framework for Multimodal Emotion Recognition
papers.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) aims to understand human emotions by integrating information from multiple modalities such as speech and text. Psychological studies suggest that emotions exhibit latent hierarchical structured relationships in their semantic representations. However, most MER approaches rely on Euclidean representations, which capture fine-grained cross-modal interactions but do not explicitly provide a geometric prior for organizing hierarchical emotional structures. To mitigate this gap, we propose GeoMER, a joint Euclidean-Hyperbolic modeling framework that introduces hyperbolic emotion-core routing to capture higher-level, abstract emotional representations for MER. The proposed framework jointly models token-level cross-modal semantic interactions and latent emotion representations in two complementary geometric spaces. Specifically, GeoMER consists of a Euclidean Multimodal Fusion Module (EuclFusion) for multimodal representation fusion and a Hyperbolic Geometric Core Routing (HypGeoRoute) module that performs geometry-aware core assignment and aggregation in a hyperbolic manifold to capture more abstract feature representations. The HypGeoRoute module complements the Euclidean token-level modeling. We experiment on the IEMOCAP multimodal MER benchmark and demonstrate that the proposed method achieves the best performance, with 83.54% weighted accuracy and 83.35% unweighted accuracy, outperforming Euclidean baselines, including MemoCMT.
papers.summary: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) fuses signals such as speech and text to infer emotion, but most methods rely on Euclidean representations that capture fine-grained cross-modal interactions without a geometric prior for the hierarchical structure that psychology attributes to emotions. `GeoMER` models both: a Euclidean Multimodal Fusion Module (`EuclFusion`) handles token-level cross-modal fusion, while a Hyperbolic Geometric Core Routing module (`HypGeoRoute`) performs geometry-aware assignment and aggregation around emotion cores in a hyperbolic manifold to capture more abstract representations. On the `IEMOCAP` benchmark the method reaches **83.54% weighted accuracy and 83.35% unweighted accuracy**, outperforming Euclidean baselines including `MemoCMT`.

papers.title: ACCRUE: Continual Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Robot Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves robot foundation models (RFMs) beyond their demonstrations, but real-world deployment demands more: learning new tasks efficiently while retaining previously acquired behaviors. Existing continual RL methods on top of VLAs mitigate forgetting but rely on on-policy updates with limited forward transfer, whereas off-policy methods improve single-task sample efficiency without addressing learner persistence across tasks. We propose ACCRUE, a continual off-policy RL framework that carries lightweight actor and critic networks across tasks, allowing each stage to reuse behavioral and value knowledge acquired through prior RL. The inherited critic adapts only on current-task transitions and guides current-task actor learning, while prior behavior is preserved by distilling the actor toward cached targets on a small number of retained episodes. Fixed visual features keep the inherited learner and its replay compatible with base-policy updates. Across contact-rich assembly sequences in simulation and on real-robot hardware, ACCRUE accelerates subsequent-task learning with near-zero forgetting and significantly reduces real-robot training time by 31.0\% to 68.5\%.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training pushes robot foundation models (RFMs) beyond their demonstrations, but deployment also demands learning new tasks efficiently without forgetting old ones, and existing continual RL on vision-language-action (VLA) models relies on on-policy updates with limited forward transfer while off-policy methods improve single-task efficiency without carrying a learner across tasks. `ACCRUE` is a continual off-policy RL framework that passes lightweight actor and critic networks from task to task: the inherited critic adapts only on current-task transitions and guides actor learning, prior behavior is preserved by distilling the actor toward cached targets on a small number of retained episodes, and fixed visual features keep the inherited learner and its replay compatible with base-policy updates. On contact-rich assembly sequences in simulation and on real-robot hardware it accelerates subsequent-task learning with near-zero forgetting and **reduces real-robot training time by 31.0% to 68.5%**.

papers.title: PhysicsSliders: Learning Physical Controls for Audio Foley Generation
papers.abstract: Physical properties provide intuitive controls for sounds made by interacting objects. The challenge is to make a generative model respond predictably to these controls, both individually and in combination. We present \method\ (PXS), trained on simulated contact sounds with 15 material, geometry and contact parameters. Two separately trained variants accept direct parameter inputs or numerical captions. PXS controls hardness, size, speed and damping, supports room descriptions and produces spectrally distinct outputs at fixed targets. When controlling damping and size together, specifying thickness improves frequency accuracy and joint target delivery. Measurements from real recordings define effective-damping targets, which simulator inversion maps to generation inputs without real-audio fine-tuning. Across 18 impact classes from five real-audio datasets, PXS-Physical follows these targets with mean grouped Spearman correlation $\rho=0.976$ and class-median error 0.094 dex (a factor of 1.24).
papers.summary: Physical properties such as hardness, size, and damping are natural controls for the sounds of interacting objects, but getting a generative audio model to respond predictably to them, alone and in combination, is difficult. `PhysicsSliders (PXS)` is trained on simulated contact sounds labeled with 15 material, geometry, and contact parameters, in two separately trained variants that accept either direct parameter inputs or numerical captions, and it controls hardness, size, speed, and damping, supports room descriptions, and produces spectrally distinct outputs at fixed targets, with thickness specification improving frequency accuracy when damping and size are controlled jointly. Effective-damping targets measured from real recordings are mapped to generation inputs by simulator inversion without real-audio fine-tuning, and across 18 impact classes from five real-audio datasets `PXS-Physical` follows these targets with **a mean grouped Spearman correlation of 0.976** and a class-median error of 0.094 dex, a factor of 1.24.

papers.title: Rethinking Projector Training in Multimodal LLMs
papers.abstract: Multimodal LLMs are typically trained by first aligning a vision encoder with a language model via projector training on large image-caption datasets, followed by joint training of the full multimodal model. Despite its widespread use, the role of the projector training stage remains poorly understood. We find that (i) using only $10$ to $20\%$ of the data for training the projector already recovers most downstream performance gains, and (ii) projectors trained on different datasets can be linearly interpolated while largely preserving performance. These results suggest that projector training mainly performs a coarse alignment, which many different projectors achieve equally well. Motivated by these findings, we propose PORTAL, a training-free projector initialization that requires neither paired image-caption data nor gradient-based optimization, but only per-modality summary statistics. PORTAL computes an optimal-transport-based map between Gaussian approximations of the vision and language feature distributions on a shared principal subspace, so that the projector training stage can be skipped entirely. Without any paired data, PORTAL matches the standard pipeline trained on 558k image-caption pairs across six LLM backbones, two vision encoders, and 16 benchmarks. It outperforms that pipeline in $3$ of $7$ (vision encoder, LLM) settings and reaches an average $98\%$ of its score across the other four.
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) are usually built by first training a projector to align a vision encoder with a language model on large image-caption datasets and then jointly training the full model, yet what the projector stage actually contributes has been poorly understood. The authors find that training the projector on only 10 to 20% of the data already recovers most downstream gains and that projectors trained on different datasets can be linearly interpolated with little loss, suggesting the stage performs a coarse alignment that many different projectors achieve equally well. Building on this, `PORTAL` initializes the projector with no paired data and no gradient-based optimization, computing an optimal-transport map between Gaussian approximations of the vision and language feature distributions on a shared principal subspace from per-modality summary statistics alone. **Without any paired data it matches the standard pipeline trained on 558k image-caption pairs across six LLM backbones, two vision encoders, and 16 benchmarks**, outperforming that pipeline in 3 of 7 vision-encoder and LLM settings and reaching an average 98% of its score across the other four.

papers.title: Auditing Future-Memory Use in Point-in-Time Language Agents
papers.abstract: Point-in-time (PIT) agents can recall post-cutoff facts even when their external evidence respects a historical cutoff. We examine whether this access predicts evidence gathering in 48 historical company-comparison tasks. Independent closed-book revenue probes identify the better-remembered company for each model on tasks with unequal recall, fixing the predicted direction before agent runs. We then compare paired runs with real or anonymized company identities while keeping external evidence PIT-valid. Both Qwen and DeepSeek recalled future facts, but neither supported the prespecified shift toward the better-remembered company. Qwen's four allocation estimates on 28 unequal-recall tasks were negative, with descriptive intervals spanning zero. A prospective DeepSeek replication showed an inverse pattern across all four metrics on 20 such tasks, with intervals below zero. These estimates remained negative after each company, pair, and future-fact omission, and all four post-hoc max-T-adjusted sign-flip p-values were below .05. In a prospectively specified follow-up, explicit future facts produced small estimated shifts away from the supplied-fact company, with intervals spanning zero, while final choices shifted toward it. The mechanism behind the natural inverse pattern remains unresolved. These findings support separate assessments of memory accessibility, search allocation, and final outputs alongside cutoff checks on external evidence.
papers.summary: Point-in-time (PIT) agents receive external evidence restricted to a historical cutoff, yet the underlying model may still recall facts from after that date, raising the question of whether such memory steers evidence gathering. Across 48 historical company-comparison tasks, the authors first run independent closed-book revenue probes to fix which company each model remembers better, then compare paired agent runs using real versus anonymized company identities while keeping the external evidence PIT-valid. Both `Qwen` and `DeepSeek` recalled future facts, but **neither shifted its search toward the better-remembered company**: Qwen's allocation estimates were negative with intervals spanning zero, and a prospective DeepSeek replication showed an inverse pattern on all four metrics with intervals below zero that held up under the authors' robustness checks. A prespecified follow-up that supplied explicit future facts produced small search shifts away from the supplied-fact company while final choices shifted toward it, and the authors conclude that memory accessibility, search allocation, and final outputs should be assessed separately alongside cutoff checks on external evidence.

papers.title: AgentStripes: An Evidence-Graded Maturity Model for AI Agents
papers.abstract: Benchmarks report what an Artificial Intelligence (AI) agent can do on a task suite, but not whether one released version has been engineered with the controls that make it reliable, safe and observable, or how strongly that is shown. This paper proposes AgentStripes, an evidence-graded maturity model for AI agents. It defines levels (0 to 7 stripes), process areas (12 areas holding 40 capabilities), three gates (basic, safety, proof) that hold an agent at a level however high its score, and evidence grades E0 to E5. Each applicable capability receives a rating from 0 to 3 and a separate evidence level; these are combined into a credit, aggregated into a severity-weighted score and converted into stripes that the gates limit. Instruments gather evidence, language-model judges interpret it under explicit criteria, and the arithmetic is deterministic. The model is compared with standards at topic level without a claim of conformance, and an unexecuted validation protocol is specified. An empirical evaluation (exploratory, non-confirmatory) of 30 public Python agent repositories, with static evidence only, is a demonstration and not a validation: static evidence caps every final stripe at 2, 26 repositories end at one stripe and 4 at two, and this distinction is unreliable, since re-judging changed the final stripe of 4 of 22 repositories (engine, dossier and panel changed), whereas none of 8 panel-only repeats, all at stripe 1, changed. The parameters are expert conventions without outcome based calibration, and the stripes have not been shown to predict reliability or safety.
papers.summary: Benchmarks report what an Artificial Intelligence (AI) agent can do on a task suite but not whether a released version was engineered with the controls that make it reliable, safe, and observable, or how strongly that has been shown. `AgentStripes` is an evidence-graded maturity model with levels from 0 to 7 stripes, 12 process areas holding 40 capabilities, three gates (basic, safety, proof) that hold an agent at a level however high its score, and evidence grades E0 to E5, where per-capability ratings and evidence levels are combined into a severity-weighted score and converted into gated stripes, with instruments gathering evidence, language-model judges interpreting it, and deterministic arithmetic. An exploratory evaluation of 30 public Python agent repositories using static evidence only is presented as a demonstration rather than a validation: **static evidence caps every final stripe at 2, with 26 repositories ending at one stripe and 4 at two**, and re-judging changed the final stripe of 4 of 22 repositories. The authors state that the parameters are expert conventions without outcome-based calibration and that the stripes have not been shown to predict reliability or safety.

papers.title: LLM2R: From Large Language Models to 3D Reassemblers
papers.abstract: 3D part assembly aims to reconstruct a complete shape from a set of unassembled parts by predicting a rigid SE(3) transformation for each part. Because the placement of a part is rarely determined by its own geometry, the task demands reasoning over the entire part set, and existing methods, which rely on pairwise relations or iterative generation and verification, scale poorly to objects with many parts. We present LLM2R, which casts part assembly as sequence modeling with a pretrained decoder-only large language model (LLM): a Point-BERT encoder and a Q-Former compress each part into a block of geometric tokens, the blocks of all parts are concatenated, and a causal LLM adapted with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) processes the sequence in one forward pass. Causal attention, however, lets the hidden states of a part observe only the parts that precede it. LLM2R therefore appends a block of learnable summary tokens after the last part: these tokens follow every part, so their states aggregate the whole assembly at a constant token cost, and a part-aware pose head fuses each part's states with them before predicting its rotation and translation. One architecture thus handles semantic and geometric assembly and predicts all poses in a single non-autoregressive pass. LLM2R achieves the highest part accuracy and success rate on all three PartNet categories, the best rotation error, translation error, and part accuracy on PartNeXt, and the lowest translation error and fastest inference on Breaking Bad, where only a fracture-specialized method is more accurate. Its advantage grows with the number of parts: at 100 parts it exceeds GARF by 33.5 points in part accuracy on Breaking Bad and Assembler by 29.1 points on PartNet, and it transfers zero-shot to unseen categories with more than 16 points higher part accuracy than the strongest of three baselines.
papers.summary: 3D part assembly predicts a rigid SE(3) transformation for each of a set of unassembled parts to reconstruct a complete shape, and because a part's placement depends on the whole set, methods built on pairwise relations or iterative generate-and-verify loops scale poorly as part counts grow. `LLM2R` casts assembly as sequence modeling: a `Point-BERT` encoder and a `Q-Former` compress each part into a block of geometric tokens, a causal decoder-only large language model (LLM) adapted with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) processes the concatenated blocks in one forward pass, and learnable summary tokens appended after the last part aggregate the whole assembly at constant token cost so a part-aware pose head can predict every rotation and translation in a single non-autoregressive pass. It achieves the highest part accuracy and success rate on all three `PartNet` categories, the best rotation error, translation error, and part accuracy on `PartNeXt`, and the lowest translation error and fastest inference on `Breaking Bad`, where only a fracture-specialized method is more accurate. Its advantage grows with the number of parts: at 100 parts it beats `GARF` by **33.5 points in part accuracy** on `Breaking Bad` and `Assembler` by 29.1 points on `PartNet`, and it transfers zero-shot to unseen categories with more than 16 points higher part accuracy than the strongest of three baselines.

papers.title: Beyond Answer Voting: Fine-Grained Correction of LLM Reasoning through Graph Alignment across Sampled Traces
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly tackle tasks that require multi-step reasoning, where errors in intermediate claims can affect the final answer. Self-consistency (SC) improves reasoning by voting over sampled final answers, but its vote leaves intermediate disagreements unresolved. To address this problem, we introduce DDRG (Disagreement-Driven Verification Guided by Reasoning Graphs), a framework for selective correction from a frozen bank of reasoning traces. Our insight is that graph alignment can expose claim-level disagreements and provide correction evidence without expanding the sampled trace bank. DDRG builds source-grounded claim graphs and sends localized conflicts to an answer-blind verifier. A verifier-supported refutation that reaches the majority answer's supporting path triggers one focused repair; otherwise, DDRG returns the exact SC vote. Experimental results across five benchmarks show that native zero-shot DDRG improves macro-average accuracy over direct answering by 8.65 and 15.83 percentage points for Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B. It also exceeds CoT, the evaluated GoT and GoV question-answering adaptations, and SC on this macro metric. DDRG links local verification to selective correction without enlarging the initial candidate bank.
papers.summary: Self-consistency improves multi-step reasoning by voting over sampled final answers, but the vote leaves disagreements between intermediate claims unresolved. Disagreement-Driven Verification Guided by Reasoning Graphs (`DDRG`) builds source-grounded claim graphs from a frozen bank of sampled traces, aligns them to expose claim-level conflicts, and sends each localized conflict to an answer-blind verifier. A verifier-supported refutation that reaches the majority answer's supporting path triggers one focused repair, and otherwise the plain self-consistency vote is returned unchanged. Across five benchmarks, zero-shot `DDRG` **improves macro-average accuracy over direct answering by 8.65 points on `Qwen2.5-7B` and 15.83 points on `Llama3.1-8B`**, and it also exceeds chain-of-thought, the evaluated `GoT` and `GoV` adaptations, and self-consistency without enlarging the candidate bank.

papers.title: DPOison-VL: Clean Preference Poisoning in Vision-Language Direct Preference Optimization
papers.abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has become a widely adopted approach for aligning vision-language models (VLMs), yet the security of multimodal preference data remains largely unexplored. Existing preference poisoning attacks either corrupt explicit supervision signals or require visible triggers, making them detectable under human inspection. We introduce DPOison-VL, the first clean preference poisoning attack against VLM-DPO, which manipulates model alignment solely through imperceptible perturbations on a small fraction of training images, while leaving all prompts, responses, and preference annotations semantically intact. We formulate poison construction as a bilevel optimization and derive a gradient alignment surrogate that efficiently steers image perturbations toward the attacker-specified preference. We further introduce a preference displacement score for principled poison selection with provable first-order optimality under a fixed poison budget, and derive a sufficient condition for preference inversion. Extensive experiments across diverse attack tasks, different VLM architectures and scales, and baseline comparisons demonstrate that DPOison-VL achieves up to 98\% ASR with only 2\% poisoned data and exhibits cross-model transferability, while largely preserving clean accuracy and general utility. Our findings reveal a critical vulnerability in VLM-DPO, where imperceptible image perturbations in preference training data can silently redirect alignment.
papers.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is widely used to align vision-language models (VLMs), but existing preference poisoning attacks either corrupt the explicit supervision signal or need visible triggers that human inspection can catch. `DPOison-VL` instead applies imperceptible perturbations to a small fraction of training images while leaving every prompt, response, and preference annotation semantically intact. Poison construction is cast as a bilevel optimization solved through a gradient alignment surrogate, with a preference displacement score for choosing which samples to poison under a fixed budget and a derived sufficient condition for preference inversion. Across attack tasks, VLM architectures, and scales, the attack **reaches up to 98% attack success rate with only 2% poisoned data**, transfers across models, and largely preserves clean accuracy and general utility.

papers.title: Jev-ToM: Evaluating Theory of Mind in Typed Decision Models
papers.abstract: Dialogue and collaborative assistants repeatedly judge what a partner knows, believes, or intends. Typed decision models offer a potential alternative to generative large language models for bounded Theory of Mind (ToM) selection. We present Jev-ToM, comparing five typed decision models and seven generative baselines on 11,117 English text questions from nine ToM benchmarks across six capability groups. TypeSafe Jev reaches 73.2% source-balanced accuracy including native controls and ranks first or second across all six capabilities, leading beliefs, goals/desires/intentions, and emotions. Other typed models show distinct strengths across tasks. Separate resource comparisons suggest that Jev could reduce the cost and waiting time of repeated ToM selection. Confidence-based selection remains benchmark-dependent, and supplied reasons can repair errors or overturn correct answers depending on their attachment. Candidate expansion reveals distinct selection and output-validity problems. Related-question cues account for most of Jev's downstream gains, with task-dependent effects from predicted states. The findings motivate testing Jev as a ToM selection component in assistants, with task-specific confidence calibration, candidate design, and output validation as integration priorities.
papers.summary: Dialogue and collaborative assistants repeatedly judge what a partner knows, believes, or intends, and typed decision models are examined as an alternative to generative large language models for bounded Theory of Mind (ToM) selection. The evaluation compares five typed decision models with seven generative baselines on 11,117 English text questions from nine ToM benchmarks covering six capability groups. **`TypeSafe Jev` reaches 73.2% source-balanced accuracy and ranks first or second on all six capabilities**, leading on beliefs, goals and intentions, and emotions, while separate resource comparisons suggest it could cut the cost and latency of repeated ToM selection. Confidence-based selection remains benchmark-dependent, supplied reasons can both repair and overturn answers, and most of the downstream gains trace to related-question cues rather than predicted mental states.

papers.title: Nudge the Judge: Uncovering Program Decision Hijacking in Real-World Jev Applications
papers.abstract:
System One models such as Jev change how software makes decisions by mapping open-ended semantic contexts into structured judgments that directly drive program execution. However, this paradigm introduces a new security risk, which we term Jev Program Decision Hijacking (JPDH): attacker-controlled contexts can redirect program decisions through schema-valid Jev judgments. Existing evaluations focus primarily on model-level attacks or predefined injection channels, leaving attack reachability and downstream security consequences in real-world Jev applications underexplored.
  In this paper, we present JevProbe, the first automated framework to evaluate JPDH by tracing adversarial influence from reachable context surfaces through program-consumed decisions to downstream security consequences in real-world Jev applications. Our key insight is that application logic maps diverse Jev judgments to observable decisions, enabling systematic, program-grounded attack evaluation. Across 228 popular real-world Jev applications and 2,273 test cases, 81.5% exhibit decision flips, of which 98.6% lead to potential downstream security impacts. Compared with the strongest adapted baseline, JevProbe improves macro-average Decision Flip Rate (DFR) by 50.4 percentage points, while existing defenses offer limited protection. We further construct JevProbeBench to support systematic evaluation of JPDH in real-world Jev applications. We have responsibly disclosed our findings to Jev application maintainers, pending their responses. The source code of JevProbe and the JevProbeBench dataset are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/xiaoxiaohg8d/JevProbe-).
papers.summary: System One models such as `Jev` map open-ended semantic context into structured judgments that programs consume directly, which creates a risk the authors call Jev Program Decision Hijacking (JPDH), where attacker-controlled context redirects program decisions through schema-valid judgments. `JevProbe` is an automated framework that traces adversarial influence from reachable context surfaces through program-consumed decisions to downstream security consequences in real-world Jev applications, and the accompanying `JevProbeBench` dataset supports systematic evaluation. Across 228 popular applications and 2,273 test cases, **81.5% of applications exhibit decision flips, and 98.6% of those lead to potential downstream security impact**. The framework raises macro-average Decision Flip Rate by 50.4 percentage points over the strongest adapted baseline, existing defenses offer limited protection, and the findings were responsibly disclosed to maintainers.

papers.title: Does self-distillation improve reasoning?
papers.abstract: Self-distillation is an emerging approach that trains a model to imitate its own predictions when conditioned on privileged information, such as correct answers or environmental feedback. Recent methods have reported better sample efficiency and generalization than reinforcement learning (RL), but it remains unclear whether these gains extend beyond in-distribution evaluations and whether they stem from privileged distillation. In this paper, we revisit two representative methods, Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) and On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), across code, science, tool use, and math reasoning tasks. We find that their reported gains do not consistently generalize to unseen problems and are largely explained by overfitting or transferring existing reasoning behavior, rather than effectively using privileged information. Moreover, self-distillation gradients show weak alignment with policy gradients that directly optimize expected reward, questioning whether they provide an effective direction for policy improvement. Our experiments across Qwen3 models (1.7B-14B) and OLMo-3-7B suggest that effectively leveraging privileged information to improve reasoning remains an open challenge. Our code is available at https://github.com/sleepypandu/does-sd-improve-reasoning
papers.summary: Self-distillation trains a model to imitate its own predictions when conditioned on privileged information such as correct answers or environment feedback, and recent methods report better sample efficiency and generalization than reinforcement learning (RL). Revisiting Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (`SDPO`) and On-Policy Self-Distillation (`OPSD`) across code, science, tool-use, and math tasks on `Qwen3` models from 1.7B to 14B and `OLMo-3-7B`, the study finds that **the reported gains do not consistently generalize to unseen problems and are largely explained by overfitting or by transferring existing reasoning behavior** rather than by using the privileged information. Self-distillation gradients also align weakly with policy gradients that directly optimize expected reward, which questions whether they offer a useful direction for policy improvement and leaves effective use of privileged information an open problem.

papers.title: Can an Agent Learn to Predict Its Own Failure? Outcome-Grounded Confidence Calibration in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Controlling an acting LLM agent means deciding, at each step of a long-horizon task, whether to trust its next action, abstain, or hand off to a human. That decision needs a per-step confidence signal predicting whether the current rollout will eventually succeed. The agent's own self-reported verbalized confidence is the natural candidate, but existing reinforcement learning methods calibrate it against the correctness of a decision at the current step. We propose a method to calibrate it against the eventual outcome of a multi-step episode: under GRPO, the group of rollouts for a task supplies success labels, and a proper scoring rule scores each step's confidence against the realized outcome. In offline RL on recorded trajectories of a Qwen2.5-7B agent in ALFWorld, TextWorld, and WebShop environments, the AUROC of step confidence against episode outcome rises from near chance to 0.68-0.85, and the top-10% of steps the agent is most confident about succeed ~4.3x more often than average. In online RL on the live ALFWorld agent, four calibration rewards improve early-step AUROC, expected calibration error goes from 0.42 to below 0.12, and selective execution improves over both the untrained agent and a format-only RL control, without degrading task success. We also introduce an evaluation protocol that separates episode depth, task difficulty, and attempt-level foresight, which shows where the gain lies: the trained agent recognizes from its first step which tasks it will fail, while telling a succeeding attempt from a failing one at the same task is harder, with some early-window signal emerging on TextWorld.
papers.summary: Controlling an acting LLM agent means deciding at each step whether to trust its next action, abstain, or hand off to a human, which calls for a per-step confidence signal that predicts whether the rollout will eventually succeed, yet existing reinforcement learning methods calibrate verbalized confidence only against the correctness of the current step. The proposed method calibrates against episode outcome instead: under `GRPO`, the group of rollouts for a task supplies success labels, and a proper scoring rule grades each step's stated confidence against the realized result. In offline RL on recorded `Qwen2.5-7B` trajectories in `ALFWorld`, `TextWorld`, and `WebShop`, **AUROC of step confidence against episode outcome rises from near chance to 0.68-0.85**, and the top 10% most confident steps succeed about 4.3 times more often than average. Online RL on the live `ALFWorld` agent cuts expected calibration error from 0.42 to below 0.12 and improves selective execution without hurting task success, and a new evaluation protocol shows the gain comes mostly from recognizing at the first step which tasks will fail rather than from telling a succeeding attempt from a failing one on the same task.

papers.title: Knowledge Graphs as Files: An Agent Harness Where Tool Creation and Tool Use Co-Evolve
papers.abstract: Searching text-rich knowledge graphs requires following relations while examining textual evidence. Predefined graph interfaces constrain what evidence agents can access, even when they write code to combine tool calls or process retrieved subgraphs. We propose direct knowledge graph interaction (DKGI), a harness in which language model agents create graph access tools directly over complete node and edge files. The agent writes Python code to follow relations, combine node sets, and select textual evidence, interleaving execution with shell search and file inspection. This lets agents process large node sets in bulk while returning selected text for the model to assess. Execution feedback guides tool creation and revision, while the evolving tools determine what evidence the agent gathers next. On benchmark datasets spanning three domains, training-free DKGI exceeds the strongest published baseline by at least 6.7 Hit@1 points on every graph, even with a minimal harness. Controlled ablations show the benefits of multi-turn programming over shell-only access and predefined graph tools, while trajectories show agents revising code to extend searches or address errors. These findings highlight the value of allowing tool creation and tool use to co-evolve during graph search. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/leopoldwhite/DKGI.
papers.summary: Searching text-rich knowledge graphs means following relations while reading textual evidence, and predefined graph interfaces limit what evidence an agent can reach even when it composes tool calls in code. Direct knowledge graph interaction (`DKGI`) is an agent harness that exposes the complete node and edge files directly, letting a language model agent write Python to traverse relations, combine node sets, and select text, interleaved with shell search and file inspection, so that execution feedback drives tool revision and the evolving tools shape what evidence is gathered next. Without any training, **`DKGI` beats the strongest published baseline by at least 6.7 Hit@1 points on every graph** across three domains, and ablations show multi-turn programming outperforms both shell-only access and predefined graph tools.

papers.title: Two Routes to Interoceptive Prioritisation: Dissociating Likelihood Precision and Preference Reweighting in Active Inference
papers.abstract: An embodied agent must prioritise among competing bodily needs. In active inference, it can respond to an urgent need by increasing the precision of information about that need or by increasing its preference for outcomes that relieve it. We compare these two interventions, separately and together, in a foraging gridworld with three lethal needs, and ask how each changes survival, perception and the body model the agent learns. Precision sharpens interoceptive posteriors and improves survival. Preference reweighting keeps bodily states further from their lethal boundaries and changes the states from which the agent learns, so its learned model covers fewer need levels, with lower quality across all levels but slightly higher quality on the levels it visits. An experiment on 72 further layouts does not establish the predicted preference benefit on difficult layouts, but both interventions improve average survival there and their interaction is positive. Survival alone therefore gives an incomplete account of how a model prioritises needs and learns about its body.
papers.summary: An embodied agent must prioritise among competing bodily needs, and within active inference it can respond to an urgent need either by sharpening the precision of information about that need or by increasing its preference for outcomes that relieve it. The two interventions are compared separately and together in a foraging gridworld with three lethal needs, measuring survival, perception, and the body model the agent learns. **Precision sharpening improves interoceptive posteriors and survival, while preference reweighting keeps bodily states further from lethal boundaries but narrows the range of need levels the agent learns about**, lowering model quality overall. On 72 additional layouts the predicted preference advantage on hard layouts does not appear, though both interventions raise average survival and interact positively.

papers.title: Falsification-proof non-market allocation mechanisms
papers.abstract: Relying on manipulable characteristics to target the allocation of resources is fraught with difficulties. Naively optimal rules lead to falsification and allocative inefficiency. Optimizing the rule for allocative efficiency while accounting for falsification typically induces falsification, at a heavy cost to the agents. Moreover, falsification generates negative externalities. We characterize optimal falsification-proof rules under a broad range of falsification technologies. We also provide an honesty condition under which they solve the unconstrained problem of a planner who maximizes a weighted sum of allocative surplus and agents' welfare.
papers.summary: Allocating resources based on characteristics that agents can falsify creates a dilemma: naively optimal rules invite falsification and lose allocative efficiency, while rules optimized for efficiency under falsification still induce costly misreporting and negative externalities. The work characterizes optimal falsification-proof allocation rules under a broad range of falsification technologies. **It also gives an honesty condition under which these falsification-proof rules solve the unconstrained problem** of a planner maximizing a weighted sum of allocative surplus and agents' welfare.

papers.title: Geometric Calibration of Supervised Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Recent studies investigate the weight geometry through its spectral structure, which characterizes how the weights transform different input directions. Within this view, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is shown to induce dense updates that perturb the spectral geometry of pre-SFT weights along their principal directions, potentially disrupting the model's prior knowledge. These observations motivate using the geometry of pre-SFT weights as a reference for refining learned SFT updates. We study this perspective as Geometric Calibration and develop SPACE Subspace Projection for Adapted Checkpoint Enhancement), a lightweight post-hoc method that selectively reverts SFT update components within the principal subspace of the pre-SFT weights while preserving those in its orthogonal complement. SPACE is a data-free, training-free method that requires only the pre- and post-SFT checkpoints. We evaluate SPACE on Qwen2.5, Qwen3, Qwen3.5, Llama-3.1, and Olmo-3 models ranging from 2B to 14B, across mathematical, coding, and medical SFT, as well as several SFT variants. Overall, SPACE mitigates out-of-domain (OOD) capability regression while further improving in-domain (ID) performance over the uncalibrated SFT checkpoints. For math SFT, SPACE yields average ID/OOD gains of 2.85/2.26 points on Qwen2.5-7B, and 2.41/1.52 points on Qwen3-14B-Base, respectively. These results highlight how the geometric relationship between SFT updates and pre-SFT weights shapes the adapted model's capabilities and, more broadly, motivate geometry-aware parameter updates for continual model improvement.
papers.summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) produces dense weight updates that perturb the spectral geometry of the pre-SFT weights along their principal directions, which can erode prior knowledge. `SPACE` (Subspace Projection for Adapted Checkpoint Enhancement) is a data-free, training-free post-hoc method that needs only the pre- and post-SFT checkpoints: it selectively reverts update components lying in the principal subspace of the original weights while keeping those in the orthogonal complement. Evaluated on `Qwen2.5`, `Qwen3`, `Qwen3.5`, `Llama-3.1`, and `Olmo-3` models from 2B to 14B across math, coding, and medical SFT, **`SPACE` reduces out-of-domain regression while also improving in-domain scores**, for example average in-domain and out-of-domain gains of 2.85 and 2.26 points on `Qwen2.5-7B` after math SFT.

papers.title: DTScribe: Generating Models for Digital Twin Reporting using Local Large Language Models
papers.abstract:
The development of a digital twin brings together many stakeholders and technical components. We have previously investigated the reporting of the conceptual architecture for these digital twins as an artifact for discussion. However, we find that the activity of modeling the digital twin for visualization and consensus-building can be quite tedious and time-consuming.
  In this article, we explore the automation of model generation using large language models, targeting the model required for digital twin reporting. Our approach is designed to ingest digital twin documents and output both the conceptual architecture visualization and a reporting page for that digital twin. We first extract from the input the key details aligning with our twenty-one-characteristic Digital Twin Description Framework described in previous work. Then, we generate a description model in the Ontological Modeling Language, representing the digital twin as a constellation of models, data, enablers, and services. We utilize refinement loops with large language models acting as judges and ontological reasoning to increase artifact quality as measured by our metrics.
  We investigate how architectural and parameter choices affect artifact quality, such as how refinement loops enable local large language models to produce sufficiently high-quality results comparable to larger models. We also detail insights and lessons learned useful for practitioners, such that they can integrate our techniques to accelerate their digital twin reporting or for other model generation tasks. These insights include the use of medium-sized local models (around 20 billion parameters), the avoidance of large language models as judges and clustering for characteristic extraction, and the recommendation of at least two reasoner loops for Ontological Modeling Language refinement.
papers.summary: Modeling a digital twin's conceptual architecture for reporting and consensus-building among stakeholders is tedious, so `DTScribe` automates it with large language models. The pipeline ingests digital twin documents, extracts details matching a twenty-one-characteristic Digital Twin Description Framework, generates a description model in the Ontological Modeling Language (OML) that represents the twin as models, data, enablers, and services, and improves quality through refinement loops using LLM judges and ontological reasoning. The study examines how architecture and parameter choices affect artifact quality and reports that **refinement loops let medium-sized local models of around 20 billion parameters match larger models**, alongside practitioner lessons such as avoiding LLM judges and clustering for characteristic extraction and running at least two reasoner loops for OML refinement.

papers.title: To Align or Not To Align: Check Your COMPASS Before You Train
papers.abstract: Combining pretrained models is a common strategy for building AI systems, whether by aligning a vision encoder with a language model or merging fine-tuned checkpoints. However, finding compatible pairs typically requires costly empirical search, as compatibility is known only after alignment or merging. We propose COMPASS (COMPatibility ASsessment Score), a theoretically motivated diagnostic that estimates whether a model pair will be compatible prior to alignment or merging. Building on the observation that representational convergence is most robust at the level of local neighborhoods, COMPASS decomposes model compatibility into two cheap-to-compute axes: a pair-specific ease, defined as the $k$-NN overlap between the two encoders, and a paradigm-level ceiling, capturing the maximum overlap their training paradigms allow. Together, these two axes provide a ranking of candidate model pairs and prescribe how to act on each pair: (i) prioritize pairs that already agree and whose paradigms are compatible, (ii) invest additional compute on pairs with compatible paradigms but low initial agreement, (iii) switch the pretraining paradigm when it cannot support sufficient agreement, or (iv) deprioritize pairs that score poorly on both axes. We apply COMPASS to $72$ cross-modal alignment experiments and $392$ task-arithmetic model merges and show that compatibility estimates by COMPASS strongly correlate with downstream success, achieving average Pearson correlation of $0.91$ on cross-modal alignment tasks and $0.70$ on model merging.
papers.summary: Building systems from pretrained components, whether aligning a vision encoder to a language model or merging fine-tuned checkpoints, usually requires expensive trial and error because compatibility is only known after the fact. `COMPASS` (COMPatibility ASsessment Score) estimates compatibility beforehand by decomposing it into two cheap axes: a pair-specific ease measured as k-nearest-neighbor overlap between the two encoders, and a paradigm-level ceiling capturing the maximum overlap their training paradigms allow, which together rank candidate pairs and prescribe whether to proceed, invest more compute, switch pretraining paradigm, or deprioritize. Across 72 cross-modal alignment experiments and 392 task-arithmetic merges, **`COMPASS` estimates correlate with downstream success at an average Pearson of 0.91 for alignment and 0.70 for merging**.

papers.title: ST-GRU PredRNN-V2: A GRU-Based Reformulation of PredRNN-V2 for Video Prediction
papers.abstract: Video prediction requires models to capture complex spatiotemporal dependencies and to retain relevant information over long sequences. PredRNN and its successor PredRNN-V2 address this challenge with spatiotemporal Long Short-Term Memory (ST-LSTM) units that maintain two separate memory states, at the cost of a relatively complex recurrent building block. In this work, we investigate whether the simpler gating of Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) can be transferred to spatiotemporal predictive learning. To this end, we develop a spatiotemporal GRU (ST-GRU) unit as a GRU-based alternative to the ST-LSTM. The ST-GRU replaces the ST-LSTM's three gates per memory state with two GRU-style gates (update and reset), and merges the temporal memory state into the hidden state, which reduces the number of parameters by about 5%. We incorporate the ST-GRU into PredRNN-V2 and evaluate the resulting model on the Moving MNIST video prediction benchmark, following the original experimental protocol. Averaged over ten predicted frames, the ST-GRU-based PredRNN-V2 achieves an MSE of 55.1, an SSIM of 0.883, an LPIPS of 0.065 and a PSNR of 19.53dB. It does not surpass the original ST-LSTM-based PredRNN-V2 on MSE, SSIM or PSNR, but it achieves a lower LPIPS and performs on par with the earlier ST-LSTM-based PredRNN, while using a simpler recurrent cell. These results suggest that ST-GRUs are a promising building block for spatiotemporal predictive learning and motivate further work on their design and integration.
papers.summary: Video prediction models such as `PredRNN` and `PredRNN-V2` rely on spatiotemporal Long Short-Term Memory (ST-LSTM) units that maintain two memory states at the cost of a complex recurrent cell. The work asks whether the simpler gating of Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) transfers to this setting and builds a spatiotemporal GRU unit that replaces three gates per memory state with update and reset gates and merges the temporal memory into the hidden state, cutting parameters by about 5%. Plugged into `PredRNN-V2` and evaluated on `Moving MNIST`, **the GRU-based variant does not beat the original on MSE, SSIM, or PSNR but achieves a lower LPIPS** and matches the earlier `PredRNN` with a simpler cell.

papers.title: Tiny Recursive Message Passing
papers.abstract: Message passing neural networks have shown remarkable performance in algorithmic and constraint reasoning, due to their ability to encode the structure of the task directly in the architecture. Recent work has shown that better results can be achieved using recursive transformers trained with deep supervision and truncated recursions, which make extremely deep loops stable to train, and equipped with test-time procedures such as discrete deduction lattices. In this work, we apply the same procedures to message passing networks, and show that the two ingredients are complementary, and lead to parameter efficient models: we obtain about $99\%$ test accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme with a model of $16$k parameters that trains in about $10$ minutes on an H100, or in $9$ hours on a CPU. We further show that the cost of truncating gradients grows with the number of rounds information needs to cross the graph, making the choice of wiring a trade-off between robustness to truncation and transfer across problem sizes. We conclude by showing that our models transfer zero-shot to larger instances than those seen during training, outperforming popular neural baselines on N-queens and Boolean satisfiability with a fraction of their parameters.
papers.summary: Message passing neural networks encode task structure directly in their architecture for algorithmic and constraint reasoning, while recent recursive transformers gain from deep supervision, truncated recursion, and test-time deduction lattices. Applying those same procedures to message passing networks turns out to be complementary and highly parameter efficient: **a 16k-parameter model reaches about 99% test accuracy on `Sudoku-Extreme`, training in roughly 10 minutes on an H100 or 9 hours on a CPU**. The analysis shows the cost of truncating gradients grows with the number of rounds information must travel across the graph, making wiring a trade-off between truncation robustness and size transfer, and the models generalize zero-shot to larger `N-queens` and Boolean satisfiability instances than seen in training, beating popular neural baselines with a fraction of the parameters.

papers.title: AMemOps: Evaluating Memory Updates in Long Audio Streams
papers.abstract: Audio memory must recognise recurring sources across acoustic changes while keeping their attributes up to date. Overall accuracy does not reveal how these demands interact. We introduce Audio Memory Operations (AMemOps), a benchmark for latest-attribute retrieval, preservation of unchanged attributes and absent-source rejection in long audio streams. Paired controls vary recordings, training identities and earlier events to examine their effects on updating. Training on other recordings of the test instruments increases a reference delta-rule memory's update advantage over matched attention by 13.4 percentage points. At retrieval delays of 120\,s, matched histories separate benefits of consistent repetition from costs of conflicting earlier values, while additive-memory controls identify benefits of erasure.
papers.summary: Audio memory must recognise recurring sound sources across acoustic changes while keeping their attributes current, and aggregate accuracy hides how these demands interact. Audio Memory Operations (`AMemOps`) is a benchmark for latest-attribute retrieval, preservation of unchanged attributes, and rejection of absent sources in long audio streams, with paired controls that vary recordings, training identities, and earlier events to isolate their effect on updating. **Training on other recordings of the test instruments widens a reference delta-rule memory's update advantage over matched attention by 13.4 percentage points**, and at 120-second retrieval delays matched histories separate the benefit of consistent repetition from the cost of conflicting earlier values, while additive-memory controls isolate the benefit of erasure.

papers.title: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report
papers.abstract: Summary-token architectures such as Kwai Summary Attention (KSA) compress distant context into learnable Summary token per chunk, and hybrid variants interleave these layers with full attention to retain exact access to the original text. In such hybrid KSA-Full architecture, the interleaving inserted summary tokens are served as a streaming flow role across different layers. Although effective, however, it also introduce some bottlenecks: (1) the different layers summary compression chunk must be same, therefore hard to reach a flexible KV Cache compression, e.g., different layer set different summary compression chunk window. (2) in the full-attention layers, the summary token introduced additional computation cost, but such layer ignore them and still pay quadratic prefilling, therefore unfriendly to the computation side. Motivated by them, we developed the KSA V2, which not only achieves a more flexible KV cache memory compression but also reduces the computation cost in Full attention layer. Specifically, we found that the summary tokens can serve two roles: the KV memory and sparse indexer.
papers.summary: Summary-token architectures such as Kwai Summary Attention (`KSA`) compress distant context into a learnable summary token per chunk and interleave these layers with full attention to keep exact access to the original text, but streaming summary tokens across layers forces every layer to share the same compression chunk size and makes full-attention layers pay quadratic prefill cost on summary tokens they ignore. `KSA V2` addresses both issues by letting summary tokens play two roles, as key-value memory and as a sparse indexer. The report claims this yields **more flexible per-layer KV cache compression together with lower computation in the full-attention layers**.

papers.title: Known-Voice Cloning and the Limits of Personality Transfer for Character Design
papers.abstract: Recent advances in zero-shot voice cloning systems make it possible to reproduce a recognizable voice from a short recording and attach it to arbitrary virtual characters. Prior work suggests that familiar vocal identity can carry over associated personality impressions to new targets such as robots or virtual characters. However, these works have mainly examined familiarity and personalization effects rather than directly testing whether a cloned familiar voice systematically transfers personality impressions to an embodied virtual character. Such transference raises the concern that cloned voices could be used to manipulate people into engaging with virtual characters as capable social actors. Across two studies, we investigated whether personality impressions transfer when a virtual character speaks with the cloned voice of a familiar person. Study 1 examined this question in a real-world university setting using the cloned voice of a lecturer familiar to the participating students. Study 2 examined the same question online using voices of social media content creators and members of their communities. Drawing on the concepts of identity activation, trait transfer, and person reconstruction, we show that evidence of personality transfer was limited in both studies. Observed effects were selective and did not generalize across traits or study contexts. In the online study in particular, recognizable voice identity cues activated expectations about the speaker but did not reconstruct the broader person impression. Qualitative responses further indicated that judgments were frequently shaped by perceived artificiality and by whether voice and appearance fit together. Our findings moderate common concerns that cloned voices straightforwardly manipulate people into perceiving artificial characters as capable social actors.
papers.summary: Zero-shot voice cloning can attach a recognizable familiar voice to any virtual character, raising the worry that the original speaker's personality impressions carry over and make the character seem a capable social actor. Two studies test this directly: one in a university setting using the cloned voice of a lecturer the student participants knew, and one online using the voices of social media creators judged by members of their communities, analyzed through identity activation, trait transfer, and person reconstruction. **Evidence of personality transfer was limited in both studies**, with effects that were selective and did not generalize across traits or contexts. Recognizable voice cues activated expectations about the speaker without rebuilding the broader person impression, and open responses showed judgments were often driven by perceived artificiality and by whether voice and appearance fit together.

papers.title: SMI: Ontology-Grounded Semantic IDs for Hierarchy-Aware Medical Concept Representation
papers.abstract: Biomedical language models (LMs) provide strong representations for clinical tasks, but they often fail to capture the hierarchical structure among medical concepts. This limitation is especially pronounced for rare and fine-grained clinical codes in long-tailed vocabularies, where hierarchy-agnostic LM representations become less informative as concept frequency decreases. We introduce Semantic Medical Identifier (SMI), a training-free framework for constructing ontology-grounded Semantic IDs and hierarchy-aware medical concept representations. For each diagnosis, procedure, or medication concept, SMI defines its Semantic ID as the coarse-to-fine path through an expert-defined medical ontology. SMI then aggregates frozen biomedical LM embeddings across the corresponding ontology levels to form hierarchy-aware medical concept representations that preserve coarse-to-fine clinical semantics. The base SMI uses uniform aggregation across ontology levels, while a level-weighted variant selects global level weights on validation data. Our theoretical analysis shows that SMI yields more informative medical concept representations than hierarchy-agnostic LM embeddings, particularly for rare and fine-grained clinical concepts. Experiments show that SMI captures meaningful hierarchical structure and improves clinical relation prediction. On MIMIC-IV, SMI improves mortality prediction, readmission prediction, drug recommendation, and rare drug prediction. On eICU, SMI yields more robust patient representations under cross-hospital distribution shift.
papers.summary: Biomedical language models give strong clinical representations but miss the hierarchical structure among medical concepts, which hurts most for rare, fine-grained codes in long-tailed vocabularies. Semantic Medical Identifier (`SMI`) is a training-free framework that defines each diagnosis, procedure, or medication concept's Semantic ID as its coarse-to-fine path through an expert medical ontology, then aggregates frozen biomedical LM embeddings across the ontology levels, either uniformly or with validation-tuned level weights, to form hierarchy-aware representations. Theory shows these are more informative than hierarchy-agnostic embeddings especially for rare concepts, and experiments show **improved mortality, readmission, drug recommendation, and rare drug prediction on `MIMIC-IV`**, plus more robust patient representations under cross-hospital shift on `eICU`.

papers.title: From Relation-Specific Heads to Shared Interventions: Contextual Entrainment in Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models rely on prompt context to perform in-context learning, follow formats, and adapt to local evidence. This ability, however, also raises a robustness concern: models may reuse irrelevant tokens from earlier context when answering a later query. Prior work identifies this behavior as contextual entrainment and finds attention heads whose ablation reduces it, arguing that these heads are largely task- or relation-specific. But are the mechanisms behind contextual entrainment truly isolated by relation, or do relation-conditioned searches recover reusable components shared across relations? Using factual-distractor relation-completion prompts across 19 lexical-semantic subtypes, we identify attention heads whose ablation reduces entrainment and test how the resulting head sets transfer recovery ability across exact relations, semantic families, and mixed relation distributions. Same-family transfer exceeds different-family transfer, family residuals weaken once globally shared heads are removed, and subtype-specific searches repeatedly rediscover many global heads. Clean-completion and context-use probes further suggest that this shared intervention can reduce harmful copying while preserving ordinary relation completion and simple in-context abilities. Our findings provide a more precise perspective on contextual entrainment and its mitigation: harmful context following is not best addressed by searching for isolated relation-specific circuits, but by using heterogeneous attack prompts to reveal reusable intervention targets whose effects are shaped by semantic relation structure.
papers.summary: Language models can wrongly reuse irrelevant tokens from earlier context when answering a later query, a behavior called contextual entrainment, and prior work found attention heads whose ablation reduces it but argued those heads are largely relation-specific. Using factual-distractor relation-completion prompts across 19 lexical-semantic subtypes, the study identifies entrainment heads and tests how well head sets found on one relation transfer to exact relations, semantic families, and mixed distributions. **Same-family transfer exceeds different-family transfer, yet family-specific residuals shrink once globally shared heads are removed, and subtype-specific searches repeatedly rediscover the same global heads**, pointing to a shared intervention target. Probes indicate this shared ablation reduces harmful copying while preserving ordinary relation completion and simple in-context abilities.

papers.title: Model-Based Online Decision Making via Generative Trajectory Planning
papers.abstract: Online decision-making faces a tension between efficient inference and long-horizon reasoning. Value-based methods rely on short-horizon bootstrapping that limits the propagation of long-term information, while trajectory optimization methods plan explicitly but must solve a high-dimensional optimization problem at every decision step. We propose Generative Trajectory Planning (GTP), a model-based framework that addresses this tension by learning a generative model as a proposal distribution over action sequences. Instead of optimizing sequences from scratch, GTP samples candidate sequences from a diffusion prior and refines them using learned dynamics, reward, and value models, enabling efficient trajectory-level reasoning. Across continuous control and long-horizon manipulation tasks, GTP matches or exceeds state-of-the-art model-free, diffusion-policy, and model-based baselines, and remains stable in regimes where strong baselines degrade. Our results suggest that generative models are best understood not as policies, but as structured proposal distributions for planning, offering a new perspective on how to integrate generative modeling with model-based decision-making.
papers.summary: Online decision-making pits efficient inference against long-horizon reasoning: value-based methods bootstrap over short horizons and propagate long-term information poorly, while trajectory optimization plans explicitly but must solve a high-dimensional problem at every step. Generative Trajectory Planning (`GTP`) learns a diffusion model as a proposal distribution over action sequences, sampling candidates from it and refining them with learned dynamics, reward, and value models rather than optimizing from scratch. **Across continuous control and long-horizon manipulation tasks, `GTP` matches or exceeds state-of-the-art model-free, diffusion-policy, and model-based baselines** and stays stable in regimes where strong baselines degrade, supporting the view of generative models as structured proposal distributions for planning rather than as policies.

papers.title: ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for optimizing Large Language Model (LLM) agents, yet efficient critic-free algorithms (e.g., GRPO) suffer from a fundamental uniform credit assignment dilemma that broadcasts trajectory-level advantages equally to all actions. Our analysis reveals that this uniformity inherently reinforces structurally invalid actions in preferred trajectories and ignores the downstream cascading influence of early pivotal deviations in unpreferred ones. To resolve this without introducing critic overhead, we propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), a plug-and-play framework that leverages a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG) to achieve fine-grained credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). Extensive experiments across Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct demonstrate that ProAS universally elevates mainstream group-based baselines to new state-of-the-art performance, achieving peak success rates of 91.9\% and 94.3\% on ALFWorld, alongside 66.7\% and 70.8\% on WebShop, respectively. Furthermore, it accelerates training convergence by up to $2.44\times$ while maintaining strong robustness against imperfect or distilled ARGs. Codes: https://github.com/LINs-lab/ProAS.
papers.summary: Critic-free reinforcement learning methods such as `GRPO` assign one trajectory-level advantage to every action in a multi-turn agent episode, which rewards structurally invalid actions in good trajectories and ignores how early mistakes cascade in bad ones. Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (`ProAS`) builds a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph that tracks task progress, then reshapes per-step credit with Masking Unreasonable Incentives and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution, without adding a critic. On `Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct` and `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct` it lifts group-based baselines to **success rates of 91.9% and 94.3% on `ALFWorld`** and 66.7% and 70.8% on `WebShop`, while converging up to 2.44x faster and tolerating imperfect or distilled reference graphs.

papers.title: Knowing the User Is Not Knowing What We Established: Grounding Awareness in Personal Agents
papers.abstract: Personal-agent memory has largely focused on learning what users know, prefer, and want. However, knowing the user does not necessarily mean knowing what the user and the agent have established together. An assistant's proposal should not become an authorized instruction merely because it is remembered. We introduce Grounding Awareness, the ability to distinguish accepted, unacknowledged, revised, and scoped arrangements when selecting actions. We develop a controlled benchmark to test whether agents can tell the difference between proposals users have accepted and those they have not, and whether they apply accepted arrangements only where appropriate. Across multiple agents and memory systems, we find that strong memory performance does not ensure Grounding Awareness. More surprisingly, providing more complete user information can increase execution of unacknowledged proposals, while persistent memory can cause agents to treat these proposals as if they were user instructions. We trace these failures through memory writing, retrieval, and action selection. Finally, we introduce Grounding Layer, a lightweight, training-free extension that explicitly tracks grounding status and checks consequential actions, substantially improving agent behavior without modifying models or memory systems.
papers.summary: Personal-agent memory research has focused on learning what users know and prefer, but an assistant's own remembered proposal should not count as an authorized instruction unless the user actually accepted it. The authors define Grounding Awareness as the ability to tell accepted, unacknowledged, revised, and scoped arrangements apart when choosing actions, and build a controlled benchmark to test it across several agents and memory systems. They find that **strong memory performance does not ensure grounding awareness, and richer user information can actually increase execution of unacknowledged proposals**, with persistent memory causing agents to treat such proposals as user instructions. A training-free `Grounding Layer` that tracks grounding status and checks consequential actions substantially improves behavior without changing models or memory systems.

papers.title: RadarGSOcc: Doppler-Aware 3D Semantic Occupancy Prediction Using 4D Radar Tensor with Geometric-Semantic Feature Extraction
papers.abstract: 3D semantic occupancy prediction is crucial for autonomous driving, but camera-based methods degrade in low-light conditions and LiDAR-based methods are sensitive to adverse weather. 4D radar is more robust, yet its sparsity and the high cost of radar tensor processing limit its use. We propose Radar Geometric-Semantic Occupancy Prediction (RadarGSOcc), an efficient framework that directly processes 4D radar tensors by separately extracting geometric and semantic features, including Doppler information, with a deformable attention-based geometric refinement module as its key component. We also introduce the K-Radar 3DSemOcc benchmark, the first large-scale benchmark for 3D semantic occupancy prediction using 4D radar tensors, built on the K-Radar dataset with refined LiDAR-based annotations. RadarGSOcc predicts 15 classes within a 51.2m range and achieves 38.2% IoU, 7.6% mIoU, and 25.5% weighted mIoU, outperforming RadarOcc by 17% relative (25.5 vs. 21.9) in weighted mIoU while using fewer parameters and lower computation. It substantially improves truck prediction while trading off car accuracy, outperforms camera-based approaches, and narrows the gap with LiDAR-based methods. To assess robustness without per-frame ground truth in adverse weather, we further propose a novel proxy metric, Environment-Based KL Divergence (EBKL), under which 4D radar proves a reliable and efficient modality for 3D semantic occupancy prediction. The dataset and code will be publicly available.
papers.summary: Image-token compression for vision-language models must cut compute without destroying the meaning of the image. `Varest` follows the principle of semantic fungibility: tokens inside a coherent region can be merged coarsely, while object boundaries and literal text need finer resolution, so object and text localizers guide variable-resolution merging before the language model, and learned relevance registers prune visual tokens after early decoder layers. Training across budgets yields a single checkpoint per backbone, and across three backbones and 13 benchmarks it beats 15 baselines in mean performance retention at every budget, **retaining 86.10 to 92.33% of full-token performance with only 5.56% of the original image tokens**.

papers.title: Just Respect the Semantics: Image-Token Compression via Pre-LLM Semantic Variable-Resolution Tokenization and In-LLM Relevance Pruning
papers.abstract: Image-token compression must reduce computation without hurting the semantics. We introduce Varest, guided by semantic fungibility: tokens within a coherent semantic region can be summarized coarsely, while object boundaries and literal text require finer distinctions. Object and text localizers guide variable-resolution merging, preserving spatial coverage and finer detail at boundaries and text. Learned [REL] registers then prune visual tokens after early decoder processing. Training across budgets enables one checkpoint per backbone. Across three backbones and 13 benchmarks, Varest outperforms 15 baselines in mean performance retention at every evaluated budget, retaining 86.10-92.33% of full-token performance with only 5.56% of the original layer-averaged image-token count.
papers.summary: Camera-based 3D semantic occupancy prediction degrades in low light and LiDAR degrades in bad weather, while 4D radar is robust but sparse and costly to process as a raw tensor. Radar Geometric-Semantic Occupancy Prediction (`RadarGSOcc`) processes 4D radar tensors directly, extracting geometric and semantic features including Doppler information and refining geometry with deformable attention, and the authors release `K-Radar 3DSemOcc`, a large-scale benchmark built on `K-Radar` with refined LiDAR-based labels. Predicting 15 classes within a 51.2 m range, it reaches **25.5% weighted mIoU, a 17% relative gain over `RadarOcc`** with fewer parameters and less compute, beating camera-based methods and narrowing the gap to LiDAR. A proxy metric, Environment-Based KL Divergence, is proposed to assess robustness in adverse weather where per-frame ground truth is unavailable.

papers.title: GeoReader: Learning Latent Geometry for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with metric and multi-view relationships that remain implicit in RGB observations. Geometry foundation models recover this structure from RGB, but existing methods either fuse the estimated features with visual tokens and learn to use them from question answering alone, or align VLM latents with geometry features. Capturing geometry, however, does not ensure its use: zeroing the aligned latents of a released feature-alignment model leaves its accuracy unchanged. We introduce GeoReader, a framework that learns geometric representations for the VLM that reads them. First, we train lightweight Geometric Readers to produce continuous input tokens, supervising them with geometry descriptions decoded by a frozen VLM, so that the Readers express geometry in a form the target model can already read. We then freeze the Readers to preserve this interface while fine-tuning the VLM on spatial QA, with geometry injection conditioned on the question. Geometry descriptions serve only as training targets: at inference, the VLM answers directly from the continuous geometric tokens without generating a geometry chain of thought. With geometry predicted from RGB images, our approach reaches 94.3 on MindCube-Tiny with Qwen3-VL-4B and, with a multi-source QA mixture, an average of 72.5 across six additional spatial benchmarks with Qwen3.5-9B. These results suggest that a useful geometric representation is one the receiving model can use, not merely one from which geometry can be reconstructed.
papers.summary: Vision-language models struggle with metric and multi-view spatial relationships that stay implicit in RGB images, and existing attempts to inject geometry foundation model features either fuse them and hope question answering teaches their use or align latents that the model never actually reads, as shown by zeroing aligned latents in a released model with no accuracy change. `GeoReader` trains lightweight Geometric Readers to emit continuous input tokens supervised by geometry descriptions decoded from a frozen vision-language model, then freezes the Readers and fine-tunes the model on spatial question answering with question-conditioned geometry injection. At inference the model answers directly from the geometric tokens with no geometry chain of thought, reaching **94.3 on `MindCube-Tiny` with `Qwen3-VL-4B`** and an average of 72.5 across six further spatial benchmarks with `Qwen3.5-9B`. The authors argue a useful geometric representation is one the receiving model can use, not merely one from which geometry can be reconstructed.

papers.title: UniW(A)M: A Unified Mixture-of-Experts Framework for World and World-Action Models
papers.abstract:
World models (WMs) and world-action models (WAMs) focus on future world prediction and executable action generation, respectively. Although these models learn shared physical dynamics and interaction semantics from embodied trajectories, they are typically trained in isolation, which restricts knowledge reuse between prediction and control. The central challenge is therefore to develop a unified learning framework that shares these dynamics while preserving the distinct modeling capabilities required by each paradigm.
  We propose UniW(A)M, a mixture-of-experts world-(action) model built upon diffusion Transformers that unifies action-conditioned world modeling and diverse WAM variants. Shared experts capture common dynamics, while atomic capability experts are reused across interfaces so that each interface keeps its own conditional pathway. At deployment, a plug-in adaptive interface router (PAIR) learns from a small subset of target-task chunk scenarios to select a suitable WAM interface for each execution chunk, balancing task success and execution efficiency while keeping the backbone frozen.
