  We evaluate UniW(A)M on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and three real-world manipulation tasks, where it achieves 88.3% average real-world success versus 76.7% for the strongest baseline. On WorldArena, it leads action-conditioned world modeling on all three tasks. AC-WM co-training contributes to action generation on every action interface and PAIR raises OOD success from 63.3% to 76.7%.
papers.summary: World models predict future states while world-action models generate executable actions, yet the two are usually trained separately despite learning the same physical dynamics from embodied trajectories. `UniW(A)M` is a mixture-of-experts diffusion Transformer in which shared experts capture common dynamics and reusable atomic capability experts give each interface its own conditional pathway, plus a plug-in adaptive interface router that learns from a small set of target-task chunks to pick a suitable action interface per execution chunk with the backbone frozen. On `LIBERO`, `RoboTwin 2.0`, and three real-world manipulation tasks it reaches **88.3% average real-world success versus 76.7% for the strongest baseline**, leads action-conditioned world modeling on all three `WorldArena` tasks, and the router raises out-of-distribution success from 63.3% to 76.7%.

papers.title: Unlocking Token Rewards via Training-Free Reward Attribution
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose an extremely efficient, training-free method to extract token-level reward signals directly from an existing deep reward model. Our core idea is to attribute the overall process reward to individual tokens by estimating each token's influence. This influence is defined as the change in the final macroscopic reward (e.g., the process reward) when a token is replaced with a semantically null token. Naively calculating this influence is computationally infeasible, requiring N forward passes through the PRM for an N-token sequence. We overcome this bottleneck by proposing a highly efficient gradient-based estimator. Specifically, we use a first-order Taylor approximation, which simplifies the influence calculation to the inner product of the difference between the token embedding and the null token embedding, and the gradient of the reward with respect to the token embedding. This requires only a single forward and backward pass. The resulting token-level rewards enable standard RL algorithms to perform precise credit assignment without requiring additional reward model training. Experiments on challenging reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our method substantially improves policy optimization efficiency and enhances the generalization of LLM reasoning capabilities. Our P2T outperforms the outcome reward by +4.9% on MathVista for Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, and +11.5% on AIME24 for Qwen2.5-Math-7B. The code will be released via https://github.com/stonewst/P2T.
papers.summary: Process reward models score whole reasoning steps, which leaves standard reinforcement learning without precise token-level credit assignment. The proposed method, `P2T`, attributes a reward model's output to individual tokens by estimating how the reward would change if each token were replaced with a semantically null token, and makes this tractable with a first-order Taylor approximation: the influence becomes the inner product of the embedding difference and the reward gradient, costing one forward and one backward pass instead of N forward passes. The resulting token rewards plug into existing RL algorithms without extra reward model training, giving **+11.5% on `AIME24` for `Qwen2.5-Math-7B`** and +4.9% on `MathVista` for `Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct` over outcome rewards.

papers.title: Steertuning Policies from a Few Human Videos
papers.abstract:
Current recipes for robot learning require massive amounts of robot demonstrations to obtain robust and adaptive policies. In this work, we introduce Steertuning, a system that enables robots to learn new tasks in new environments from 5 human demonstrations in under 5
  Steertuning consists of two parts. (1) We pretrain a 400M-parameter diffusion policy on our egocentric human dataset, which consists of 100 hours of densely annotated random interactions. This pretraining makes Steertuning robust to background differences and enables spatial and object generalization when deployed on new tasks. (2) Given 5 demonstrations of a new task, we finetune our model for only 2 minutes (2000 training updates) and steer the policy's actions during reverse sampling using the demonstration whose observation is closest to that of the deployment environment. Together with a carefully designed data processing pipeline for embodiment transfer, this enables Steertuning to achieve a 71% success rate across 12 tasks in 12 new environments, ranging from lab settings to kitchens in new homes. The entire process, from data collection for a new task to robot policy deployment, takes less than 5 minutes. Our full dataset, model weights, codebase, and robot videos will be made available at our website: https://steertuning.github.io.
papers.summary: Current robot learning recipes need large numbers of robot demonstrations to produce robust policies. `Steertuning` pretrains a 400M-parameter diffusion policy on 100 hours of densely annotated egocentric human interaction data, then adapts to a new task from 5 human demonstrations with 2 minutes of fine-tuning and steers actions during reverse sampling toward the demonstration whose observation best matches the deployment scene, using a data pipeline designed for embodiment transfer. The system achieves **71% success across 12 tasks in 12 new environments**, from lab settings to kitchens in unfamiliar homes, with the full process from data collection to deployment taking under 5 minutes. The dataset, weights, and code are to be released.

papers.title: A Rate Transfer Method: Convergence Rates in Stochastic Gradient Descent via Stochastic Calculus
papers.abstract: We develop a rate-transfer method that converts finite-time Lyapunov estimates for an associated stochastic differential equation (SDE) into finite-time convergence bounds for stochastic gradient algorithms. Under generic moment and smoothness conditions, the convergence analysis of the stochastic gradient method reduces to a calculus argument verifying a Lyapunov generator inequality for the SDE. The method recovers established rates for classical stochastic gradient methods and provides a way to establish convergence rates for new optimization algorithms through calculus arguments applied to their associated SDEs.
papers.summary: Convergence proofs for stochastic gradient algorithms are typically built case by case. The authors develop a rate-transfer method that converts finite-time Lyapunov estimates for an associated stochastic differential equation into finite-time convergence bounds for the discrete algorithm, so that under generic moment and smoothness conditions the analysis reduces to verifying a Lyapunov generator inequality by calculus. **The method recovers established rates for classical stochastic gradient methods** and offers a route to deriving rates for new optimizers through calculus on their associated stochastic differential equations.

papers.title: SolBehave: Evaluating the Behavioural Correctness of LLM-Generated Smart Contracts
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly generate Solidity smart contracts that, once deployed, can never be patched, making a single latent fault permanent and exploitable. Yet current evaluations mostly ask only whether generated code compiles. We introduce SolBehave, a benchmark for evaluating the correctness of model-generated contracts at scale, moving beyond ad hoc unit tests. Across 250 real, reproducible Ethereum contracts, we apply three complementary tests of behavioural fidelity: differential fuzzing, historical-transaction replay, and, as our core contribution, synthetic-transaction replay guided by a Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graph that enumerates the space of legitimate function-call sequences. Differential fuzzing compares each generated function with the original on automatically generated inputs; historical replay compares the whole contract on the transactions it actually received on-chain; DCR-guided replay compares it on sequences of calls that follow its intended usage, including orderings that never occurred on-chain. We evaluate seven state-of-the-art open-weight models after one round of automated repair. Compilation success ranges from 26.4% to 92.7%, but under differential fuzzing only 31.4% of all generated function bodies that compile, pooled over models and samples, are equivalent to the original. Divergence at the contract level is the norm rather than the exception: for six of the seven models, between 13% and 31% of the generated contracts that compile diverge from the original under historical replay, and between 13% and 44% under DCR-guided replay; only Gemma-4-31B stays below 3% on both. Compilation is therefore a necessary condition for correctness and far from a sufficient one.
papers.summary: Solidity contracts generated by large language models cannot be patched after deployment, yet evaluations mostly check only whether the code compiles. `SolBehave` tests behavioural correctness on 250 real, reproducible Ethereum contracts using differential fuzzing of individual functions, replay of the historical transactions each contract actually received, and, as the core contribution, synthetic-transaction replay guided by a Dynamic Condition Response graph that enumerates legitimate call sequences including orderings never seen on-chain. Across seven open-weight models after one automated repair round, compilation success ranges from 26.4% to 92.7%, but **only 31.4% of compiling generated function bodies are equivalent to the original under differential fuzzing**, and for six of seven models 13% to 44% of compiling contracts diverge under replay, with only `Gemma-4-31B` staying below 3%.

papers.title: PreciseCoder: Faithful and Generalizable Debugging Beyond Unit-Test Rewards
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) from unit tests is the common recipe for post-training code models, but a unit test only asks whether the final program passes. We analyze what this unit-test-only reward teaches a model during debugging and find that, while it raises pass rates, it also teaches the model to edit more and to hallucinate bugs in code that is already correct. We introduce PreciseCoder, a training algorithm that augments the unit-test reward with a signal for semantically verified, localized edits, which correlates with smaller edits and higher pass rates. On 4B, 9B, and 27B models, PreciseCoder reduces the average number of edit lines from 7-15to 3 at a pass rate on par with unit-test-only training. Trained only on single-line bugs, PreciseCoder can generalize to repository-level program repair, where it resolves more issues with smaller patches. Its precision also transfers from weaker to stronger models: given the reasoning trace of a 9B PreciseCoder model, frontier models such as GPT-5.6 Sol and Qwen3.8-Max gain 4.6-12.4 points in edit precision with no additional training. Linguistic analysis of the thinking traces shows that our reward encourages the model to reason about individual lines, name the buggy ones, and form consistent bug hypotheses.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning from unit tests is the standard post-training recipe for code models, but a unit test only checks whether the final program passes, and the authors show this reward teaches models to edit more and hallucinate bugs in already-correct code. `PreciseCoder` adds a reward for semantically verified, localized edits, which correlates with smaller patches and higher pass rates. On 4B, 9B, and 27B models it **cuts average edited lines from 7 to 15 down to 3 at pass rates matching unit-test-only training**, generalizes from single-line bugs to repository-level program repair, and its reasoning traces from a 9B model raise the edit precision of frontier models such as `GPT-5.6 Sol` and `Qwen3.8-Max` by 4.6 to 12.4 points with no extra training. Analysis of thinking traces shows the reward pushes the model to reason line by line, name buggy lines, and form consistent bug hypotheses.

papers.title: Beyond the Verdict: Agentic Code Judging with Verifiable Feedback
papers.abstract: Test-time scaling for large language models (LLMs) can involve generating multiple candidate solutions for selection or revising an earlier attempt. To guide selection and revision, we need a verifier that can estimate candidate correctness and provide evidence of failure. In competitive programming, however, official judging systems provide authoritative verdicts under finite submission budgets, without revealing failure explanations or failing inputs. To provide informative feedback without consuming official submissions, we formulate a task in which a model judges and diagnoses a candidate program using only the problem statement and source code, with generated counterexamples serving as checkable evidence. To evaluate this task, we build USACO-JUDGE from the USACO 2026 contests, using accepted and unaccepted programs written by human experts and multiple LLMs. We then train ARBITER, a 35B mixture-of-experts (MoE) agentic verifier, with reinforcement learning in a generic execution sandbox. Training raises counterexample success on incorrect programs from 40.61% to 62.67% and mean binary verdict accuracy on USACO-JUDGE from 71.41% to 87.41%, approaching frontier verification performance. Beyond verification, ARBITER outperforms baselines in both code selection and refinement. In an IOI 2026 case study, ARBITER-guided refinement raises GPT-OSS-120B's expected score above the gold-medal threshold under the official submission limit.
papers.summary: Test-time scaling for code needs a verifier that can judge candidate programs and explain failures, but competitive programming judges give only verdicts under limited submission budgets. The authors formulate a task where a model judges a program from the problem statement and source alone, producing counterexamples as checkable evidence, and build `USACO-JUDGE` from the 2026 USACO contests using accepted and rejected programs by humans and several LLMs. `ARBITER`, a 35B mixture-of-experts agentic verifier trained with reinforcement learning in a generic execution sandbox, **raises counterexample success on incorrect programs from 40.61% to 62.67% and verdict accuracy from 71.41% to 87.41%**, approaching frontier verifiers. It also outperforms baselines in code selection and refinement, and in an IOI 2026 case study lifts `GPT-OSS-120B` above the gold-medal threshold within the official submission limit.

papers.title: Jeva: System One Models from First Principles
papers.abstract: System one models enable direct, low-latency decision-making. Yet recent practice of predicting an answer from serialized text does not, by itself, respect the structure of a decision problem. We argue that current designs underemphasize four important structural requirements. (i) null-aware: Models should distinguish answer absence from uncertainty among candidates; (ii) permutation-invariant: Reordering alternatives should not change the decision; (iii) option-scalable: Growing candidate sets should not require redefining the output space; (iv) cacheable: Request-independent computation over recurring alternatives should be reusable across requests. We introduce Jeva, a decision-native architecture that addresses these requirements jointly. A shared encoder independently represents the request and each option, while a compact decision stack refines only the request state against immutable option memory. Symmetric aggregation yields permutation-equivariant probabilities; shared scoring accommodates variable-size candidate sets. A separate coverage estimate distinguishes answer absence from candidate competition, enabling explicit null outcomes. Request-independent option representations and layer projections support reuse across newly assembled sets. These mechanisms unify Choice, Noul, and Score outputs. Across evaluations, Jeva combines strong typed-decision performance with near-perfect null detection and no decision flips under any tested permutations. It scales to thousands of candidates and substantially reduces latency through cross-request reuse without changing decisions.
papers.summary: Fast, low-latency decision models built by predicting an answer from serialized text ignore the structure of a decision problem, which the authors argue should be null-aware, permutation-invariant, option-scalable, and cacheable. `Jeva` is a decision-native architecture in which a shared encoder represents the request and each option independently, a compact decision stack refines only the request state against immutable option memory, symmetric aggregation yields permutation-equivariant probabilities, and a separate coverage estimate distinguishes answer absence from competition among candidates. Across evaluations it combines strong typed-decision performance with **near-perfect null detection and no decision flips under any tested permutation**, scales to thousands of candidates, and cuts latency through cross-request reuse of option representations.

papers.title: BLADE: Auditing Information Use for Failure Attribution in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Large language model multi-agent systems extend individual agents' capabilities through collaboration across specialized roles, tools, and workflows. Yet collaboration makes failures harder to diagnose: one agent may misinterpret a correct result while others carry the mistake forward. Failure attribution therefore seeks to identify the responsible agent and decisive error step. Recent methods trace dependencies, but knowing where information came from is not the same as knowing where it went wrong. We introduce BLADE (Blame Localization via Audited Dependency Evidence), a training-free framework that moves beyond tracing information to auditing its use. Using Jev for structured probabilistic judgments, BLADE uses dependency probabilities to select relevant source-decision handoffs for auditing. At these handoffs, it examines whether receiving decisions use their sources faithfully and within task requirements, distinguishing error introduction, propagation, and repair. These findings inform a global diagnosis that considers all execution steps. Without reference answers, BLADE achieves the best or tied-best step accuracy among eight strategies under a shared Jev decision interface on 1,228 failed runs across five Who&When and Who&When Pro subsets, outperforming All-at-once by 2.2-11.1 percentage points. Making responsibility evidence explicit offers a path toward more interpretable and reliable agentic systems.
papers.summary: In LLM multi-agent systems, one agent can misinterpret a correct result and others carry the error forward, so failure attribution must find the responsible agent and the decisive error step. `BLADE` (Blame Localization via Audited Dependency Evidence) is a training-free framework that goes beyond tracing where information came from to auditing how it was used: it uses dependency probabilities from the `Jev` structured-judgment interface to select source-decision handoffs, checks whether each receiving decision uses its sources faithfully and within task requirements, distinguishes error introduction, propagation, and repair, and folds the findings into a global diagnosis over all steps. Without reference answers, it achieves **best or tied-best step accuracy among eight strategies on 1,228 failed runs** across five `Who&When` and `Who&When Pro` subsets, beating an all-at-once baseline by 2.2 to 11.1 percentage points.

papers.title: Pack Light, CarryOn: Building Object-Oriented Context for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents accumulate progress in persistent task state, yet repeatedly process interaction histories describing how that progress was achieved. This raises a natural question: can long-horizon context instead be organized around reusable progress rather than the history that produced it? In this paper, we introduce CarryOn, an object-oriented context runtime that organizes continuation around reusable task objects. Rather than treating compressed histories or reconstructed accounts of progress as the primary basis for continuation, CarryOn builds a context view from continuation carriers, complementary execution context, and a live tail of recent interactions. A core challenge is keeping this reusable basis valid after its surrounding history is retired: how can CarryOn update the basis without reconstructing the full representation at every fold? CarryOn maintains carrier records across folds, revising affected records against bound evidence and applicable environment checks while carrying forward unaffected records and jointly updating execution context. Experiments on OSWorld 2.0 and BrowseComp-Plus show improved gains of 5.8% and 7.0% while reducing total token usage by 51.9% and 22.9%, respectively. Project page: https://ethannju.github.io/carryon
papers.summary: Long-horizon agents keep their real progress in persistent task state yet repeatedly reprocess the interaction history that produced it. `CarryOn` is an object-oriented context runtime that organizes continuation around reusable task objects, building a context view from continuation carriers, complementary execution context, and a live tail of recent interactions rather than from compressed histories. When old history is retired, it revises only the carrier records affected, checking them against bound evidence and environment state, and carries the rest forward. On `OSWorld 2.0` and `BrowseComp-Plus` it **improves results by 5.8% and 7.0% while cutting total token usage by 51.9% and 22.9%**.

papers.title: Where Do LLM Ensemble Gains Come From? Decomposing Candidate Value, Diversity, and Aggregation
papers.abstract: LLM ensemble gains are often measured against a single baseline, but the value attributed to additional candidates can change with the comparison used. We study an LLM aggregator under four matched conditions: Direct (no candidates), Single-slot (one candidate in a multi-slot interface), Duplicate (one candidate repeated), and Multi-candidate (separately generated candidates). Under either non-diverse control, overall candidate gain (CIV) splits algebraically into an additional-candidate contrast (DSV) and a candidate-context contrast (CCV); the split, but not CIV, depends on the chosen control. On MultiHopRAG model diversity (k=2), the repetition gap Rep=-8.33 pp [-13.25, -3.75] quantifies the difference between gains measured against Duplicate and Single-slot. On a matched FRAMES stronger-panel extension (n=200, k=3, aggregator output limit 4096), paired Delta Rep=+9.67 pp [+6.00, +13.50]; within panels, Rep changes sign (original -6.33; stronger +3.33). In FRAMES evidence aggregation, candidate-context contrasts remain strongly negative under both non-diverse controls. Our results show why ensemble evaluations should state the reference control before attributing gains to additional candidates.
papers.summary: Gains from LLM ensembles are usually measured against a single baseline, but the value credited to extra candidates depends on which control is used. The authors evaluate an LLM aggregator under four matched conditions, direct answering with no candidates, a single candidate in a multi-slot interface, one candidate duplicated, and separately generated candidates, and show that total candidate gain splits algebraically into an additional-candidate contrast and a candidate-context contrast whose split depends on the control. On `MultiHopRAG` with two diverse models the repetition gap is **-8.33 percentage points**, while on a stronger-panel `FRAMES` extension with three candidates it flips sign to +3.33, and candidate-context contrasts stay strongly negative in `FRAMES` evidence aggregation under both controls. The conclusion is that ensemble evaluations should state their reference control before attributing gains to extra candidates.

papers.title: Bytes to Threats: Byte-Sequence Transformer For Malware Detection
papers.abstract: Existing malware detection approaches heavily rely on handcrafted features derived from static or dynamic analysis of the executable files. These methods require specialized domain expertise, dedicated analysis tools, and time-consuming analysis, which limits their scalability and robustness in the face of the increasing complexity and diversity of modern malware. Consequently, there is a growing interest in approaches that operate directly on raw bytes, which contain rich semantic and structural information. However, capturing long-range dependencies within executable files remains challenging for conventional static and CNN-based methods. This paper presents MalwareFormer, a transformer-based, byte-level malware detection framework that operates directly on raw bytes, without requiring domain knowledge or feature extraction. MalwareFormer achieves an accuracy of 98.35%, a balanced accuracy of 98.32%, a macro-F1 of 98.32%, and a false positive rate of 1.94%, outperforming both baselines across all threshold-dependent classification metrics and demonstrating that transformers provide a powerful and scalable approach for byte-level malware detection.
papers.summary: Most malware detectors depend on handcrafted features from static or dynamic analysis, which demands expertise and tooling and scales poorly, and raw-byte approaches based on convolutional networks struggle with long-range dependencies in executables. `MalwareFormer` is a transformer that classifies executables directly from raw bytes with no feature extraction or domain knowledge. It reports **98.35% accuracy, 98.32% macro-F1, and a 1.94% false positive rate**, outperforming both baselines on all threshold-dependent metrics.

papers.title: SEAR: Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics
papers.abstract: Frontier language-model agents can now improve robots on their own: they write control code, test it, and keep what works as skills and memories for the next task. We introduce SEAR (Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics), a framework and benchmark built around two questions. Is the agent really learning, or just trying more often? And does what it learns still help on new tasks, in a new simulator, and on a real robot? The framework runs an agent in three modes: it writes code that becomes the policy (code-as-policy), acts live in the control loop (agent-as-policy), or works as a researcher that fine-tunes a vision-language-action model (auto-research). The benchmark adds controls that separate retained experience from repeated attempts, familiar tasks, privileged simulator state, larger budgets, and luck. Across seven frontier language models, 330 simulated and five physical tasks, and over four years of agent runtime, we highlight three findings. First, the learning curve of a robotic agent depends both on the overall time budget and the task difficulty relative to model capability. Harder tasks make longer sessions worthwhile; on easier tasks, re-rolling short attempts does just as well. Second, control code and shared routines transfer across tasks and simulators, while task-specific solutions do not. On a real robot, we observe a performance gap between agent-designed practice and novel human-designed scenes. Third, different models evolve more effectively in different ways. Some do best acting live, others writing code first. And a text-only model keeps pace with a comparable multimodal one: perception helps with error assessment, but agentic reasoning and tool use can matter more. We release the benchmark and codebase to support future research.
papers.summary: Frontier language-model agents can improve robots by writing control code, testing it, and keeping what works as skills and memories, but it is unclear whether they truly learn or merely retry more often, and whether gains transfer to new tasks, simulators, and real robots. `SEAR` (Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics) runs an agent as code-as-policy, agent-as-policy in the live control loop, or auto-research that fine-tunes a vision-language-action model, with benchmark controls that separate retained experience from repeated attempts, familiar tasks, privileged simulator state, larger budgets, and luck. Across seven frontier models, 330 simulated and five physical tasks, and over four years of agent runtime, **longer sessions pay off only when task difficulty is high relative to model capability, while re-rolling short attempts does just as well on easy tasks**; control code and shared routines transfer across tasks and simulators but task-specific solutions do not, and a text-only model keeps pace with a comparable multimodal one. The benchmark and codebase are released.

papers.title: Optimizing Team Behavior via Extremum-seeking Control in Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: In cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), agents must learn to coordinate their actions to achieve shared objectives. A key indicator of effective coordination is behavioral diversity, i.e., the agents' potential to enact distinct yet complementary control policies given the same set of observations. Although behavioral diversity can enable role specialization and richer joint behaviors, its appropriate level is highly context- and task-dependent and often costly to tune. We propose Adaptive Diversity Control (ADiCo), a two-timescale framework that adapts behavioral diversity online during training. On a fast timescale, Diversity Control (DiCo) regulates system diversity toward a target value. On a slower timescale, an Extremum Seeking Controller (ESC) adjusts this target using only mean episodic returns, without requiring an explicit model or analytical gradient of the diversity-performance landscape. We evaluate ADiCo on six configurations across two cooperative MARL tasks, where it maintains task-appropriate diversity levels: low diversity when homogeneous policies are beneficial and higher diversity when heterogeneous policies are required. Through this adaptation, ADiCo matches or exceeds the mean performance of DiCo (best grid-searched diversity target) and Unconstrained DiCo (diversity allowed to emerge without target regulation). These results demonstrate that incorporating classical feedback control into MARL training enables effective coordination by providing a systematic alternative to task-specific manual selection of the diversity target.
papers.summary: In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, the right level of behavioral diversity, meaning how differently agents act on the same observations, is task-dependent and costly to tune by hand. Adaptive Diversity Control (`ADiCo`) runs two timescales: a fast `DiCo` loop regulates diversity toward a target value, while a slower Extremum Seeking Controller adjusts that target using only mean episodic returns, with no model or analytic gradient of the diversity-performance landscape. On six configurations across two cooperative tasks it settles on low diversity where homogeneous policies work and higher diversity where heterogeneous ones are needed, and **matches or exceeds `DiCo` with the best grid-searched target** as well as unconstrained diversity.

papers.title: Self-Evolving Agent Harness
papers.abstract: Harness self-evolution revises an agent's software scaffolding, including prompts, memory, workflows, and executable components, while keeping model weights fixed. We formalize a feedback-driven process in which accepted revisions persist across runs. The framework separates update targets from proposal and admission mechanisms. It distinguishes changes to interpreted state from revisions to tools and code, repository-level control logic, and plugin composition. We characterize search through evolutionary optimization and examine its reliability through continual PAC-learning. Under explicit assumptions, the analysis yields an expected generalization bound, a retention bound conditional on historical regression budgets, and a high-probability admission rule using fresh, independent validation data. We examine how persistent harness revisions affect knowledge sharing and organizational workflows, with implications for scientific reliability, physical safety, and institutional accountability. Cases from prior work illustrate model--harness co-design, distributed execution, and plugin reuse. Reliable deployment requires continual validation as task distributions and evaluators change, with independent safeguards for learning, runtime privileges, and consequential actions. We provide a comprehensive 66-page discussion of related work, theory, algorithms, evaluation, applications, and the broader impact of Harness RSI, together with continuously updated code and supplementary materials, at https://github.com/zgcagi/Harness-RSI.
papers.summary: Harness self-evolution revises an agent's scaffolding, including prompts, memory, workflows, and executable components, while model weights stay fixed, with accepted revisions persisting across runs. The authors formalize this feedback-driven process by separating update targets from proposal and admission mechanisms, distinguishing changes to interpreted state from revisions to tools and code, repository-level control logic, and plugin composition, and analyze search as evolutionary optimization with reliability examined through continual PAC-learning. Under explicit assumptions they derive **an expected generalization bound, a retention bound conditional on historical regression budgets, and a high-probability admission rule based on fresh independent validation data**, and discuss implications for knowledge sharing, scientific reliability, physical safety, and accountability. A 66-page discussion of related work, theory, algorithms, evaluation, and applications accompanies the code at the project repository.

papers.title: Back-Translation Still Matters: Leveraging Monolingual Data for Low-Resource Machine Translation with LLMs
papers.abstract: Pre-trained Large Language Model (LLMs) are effective on many tasks in zero-shot and few-shot settings. For machine translation of low-resource languages, the obvious options are few-shot prompting and fine-tuning on a small parallel set. We ask: what if moderate amounts of low-resource monolingual data are also available? We argue that, rather than continued pretraining, a more effective use of this data is the pre-LLM era technique of back-translation (BT). The current fine-tuned LLM translates monolingual sentences in each language, and the resulting pairs train it in the reverse direction. Updates on the parallel set are interleaved for stable learning. With 1K parallel pairs on Odia and Swahili, BT beats continued pretraining into the low-resource language by 7.7 to 16.4 XCOMET-XXL points in domain. With beam-decoded intermediate translations, it also beats a model with 10 time more parallel data. In-context examples retrieved from the parallel data further improve BT. We also analyze the source, quality and amount of monolingual text. Across five low-resource languages, with Hindi as a high-resource control, and two 3B backbones, BT improves translation into the low-resource language by 16 to 173% XCOMET-XXL over parallel-only fine-tuning. Blind human evaluation on Odia and Sanskrit agrees with the automatic metrics.
papers.summary: Machine translation into low-resource languages with large language models (LLMs) usually relies on few-shot prompting or fine-tuning on a small parallel set, leaving moderate amounts of monolingual text unused. The authors argue that back-translation (BT), where the current fine-tuned model translates monolingual sentences in each language and the synthetic pairs train it in the reverse direction, uses that text better than continued pretraining, with updates on the parallel set interleaved for stable learning. With 1K parallel pairs on Odia and Swahili, BT beats continued pretraining by 7.7 to 16.4 `XCOMET-XXL` points in domain, and with beam-decoded intermediate translations it beats a model trained on ten times more parallel data. **Across five low-resource languages and two 3B backbones, BT improves translation into the low-resource language by 16 to 173% `XCOMET-XXL` over parallel-only fine-tuning**, and blind human evaluation on Odia and Sanskrit agrees with the automatic metrics.

papers.title: Read the Room Before Your Model Generates
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generally rely on sampling temperature to regulate the amount of randomness in their outputs. Mainstream methods for selecting temperature typically involve fixed, heuristic global settings and context or token-level calibration, rather than a geometrically interpretable representation of the communicative scenario. In this work, we introduce a simple and interpretable temperature selection framework, the Scenario-Actor, which adapts decoding to the inferred situational characteristics. Scenario-Actor extracts scenario-relevant structures from Transformer hidden states and determines the temperature from scenario embedding, a structured geometric representation of the communicative setting. Empirical results show that on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Scenario-Actor achieves strong goal-completion performance in interactive social scenarios, significant gains on open-ended instruction following, and competitive performance on multi-turn conversation compared to multiple baselines.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) regulate output randomness through a sampling temperature that is usually a fixed global heuristic or a context- or token-level calibration, with no interpretable representation of the communicative situation. The authors propose `Scenario-Actor`, which extracts scenario-relevant structure from Transformer hidden states, builds a geometric scenario embedding of the communicative setting, and derives the decoding temperature from it. On `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct`, the method **achieves strong goal completion in interactive social scenarios and significant gains on open-ended instruction following**, with competitive multi-turn conversation performance against multiple baselines.

papers.title: RoboSimStudio: An Interactive Toolkit for Human and Agent Rapid Real2Sim of Robot Manipulation Tasks
papers.abstract: It has been difficult to accurately model the physics of the interaction between a robot and the objects it manipulates, including contact mechanics, coupled contact dynamics, deformations, stiffness and friction. We present RoboSimStudio (RSS), an interactive toolkit that makes choices of solver, contact model, and physical parameters explicit and editable, allowing both humans and coding agents to quickly create and iteratively refine simulations based on observed physical behavior. We implement RSS with the open Newton physics simulation system and describe experiments with human-guided real2sim using (1) visual evaluation, (2) force-feedback and (3) agentic Real2Sim2Real. Code, video and additional information can be found on the project website: https://robosimstudio.github.io
papers.summary: Accurately simulating the physics of robot manipulation, including contact mechanics, coupled contact dynamics, deformation, stiffness, and friction, remains difficult, which slows real-to-sim workflows. `RoboSimStudio` (RSS) is an interactive toolkit built on the open `Newton` physics simulator that exposes the choice of solver, contact model, and physical parameters as explicit, editable settings so that both humans and coding agents can create simulations and iteratively refine them against observed physical behavior. The authors describe human-guided real2sim experiments using visual evaluation and force feedback, and **an agentic Real2Sim2Real loop in which a coding agent tunes the simulation itself**.

papers.title: Fast Rates for Offline Q-Learning with KL Regularization
papers.abstract: This paper investigates offline Q-learning for finite-horizon Markov decision processes with Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. Recent studies have shown that KL regularization can yield fast rates in offline decision-making problems. However, it remains unclear whether Q-learning, which adopts incremental stochastic approximation updates, can achieve such fast rates in the offline setting. We first propose KL-regularized Q-Learning (KLQ), a simple variant of classical Q-learning. By exploiting KL regularization, we prove that KLQ achieves a sample complexity of $\widetilde{O}(1/\epsilon)$ without explicit pessimism. This guarantee, however, has an exponential dependence on the KL regularization parameter and the horizon. To address this limitation, we further propose KL-regularized Pessimistic Q-Learning (KLPQ), which incorporates pessimism into KLQ. We prove that KLPQ retains the same \(\widetilde O(1/\epsilon)\) rate while removing the explicit exponential dependence, thereby further improving the sample complexity. To the best of our knowledge, these results establish the first fast-rate guarantees for offline Q-learning in tabular finite-horizon KL-regularized MDPs.
papers.summary: Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization has recently been shown to yield fast rates in offline decision-making, but it was unknown whether Q-learning, with its incremental stochastic-approximation updates, could achieve such rates offline. The authors propose `KLQ`, a simple KL-regularized variant of classical Q-learning for finite-horizon Markov decision processes, and prove it reaches a sample complexity of order 1/epsilon (up to log factors) without explicit pessimism, though with exponential dependence on the regularization parameter and the horizon. A pessimistic variant, `KLPQ`, **keeps the same order-1/epsilon rate while removing the explicit exponential dependence**, which the authors state is the first fast-rate guarantee for offline Q-learning in tabular finite-horizon KL-regularized MDPs.

papers.title: Who Improves the Robot? Toward Physical Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.abstract: Robots are increasingly autonomous in task execution, yet their improvement remains largely human-driven. This study investigates Physical Recursive Self-Improvement (Physical RSI), in which physical experience guides lasting updates to both a robot's capabilities and its improvement procedure, making subsequent improvement more effective across tasks. Physical RSI faces challenges from noisy observations, continuous dynamics, costly trials, and irreversible consequences. We present an L0-L5 framework that differentiates capability-level from meta-level updates and within-task from across-task gains, reserving L5 for independently verified recursive gain. We study existing methods around harness adaptation and model training, alongside safety and control mechanisms that govern execution and successive updates. Our analysis reveals that, despite substantial progress in self-improvement, the surveyed literature does not yet demonstrate Physical RSI as defined by our framework. We identify research priorities in reliable feedback, causal attribution, safety preservation, and benchmarking, outlining a path toward robots that autonomously improve how they learn while ensuring safety. The GitHub repository for Physical RSI is available at https://github.com/SAIL-Research-Lab/Physical-RSI.
papers.summary: Robots execute tasks autonomously, yet their improvement is still driven by humans, so the authors define Physical Recursive Self-Improvement (Physical RSI) as the case where physical experience produces lasting updates to both a robot's capabilities and its improvement procedure, making later improvement more effective across tasks despite noisy observations, continuous dynamics, costly trials, and irreversible consequences. They introduce an L0-L5 framework that separates capability-level from meta-level updates and within-task from across-task gains, reserving L5 for independently verified recursive gain, and survey existing work on harness adaptation, model training, and the safety and control mechanisms that govern execution and successive updates. **The surveyed literature does not yet demonstrate Physical RSI as defined by the framework**, and the authors name reliable feedback, causal attribution, safety preservation, and benchmarking as research priorities.

papers.title: LIBERO-RIG: A Hardware-Setup Robustness Benchmark for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Robot policies are expected to generalize across deployment environments, including variations in the robot itself: cameras are bumped and remounted, calibrations drift, controllers run at different rates, and end-effector pads wear down. We present LIBERO-RIG, a benchmark that perturbs only the robot's hardware and setup while holding every LIBERO task fixed. The benchmark spans eleven perturbation axes, including camera mounting and optics, camera-to-arm calibration, actuation gain, control rate, proprioceptive noise, base pose, table height, and gripper pads. Each axis has five severity levels, yielding 210 conditions across the four LIBERO suites. We evaluate nine recent vision-language-action models using 500 episodes per condition and substantiate each finding with rigorous statistical tests. Pooled success falls from 0.932 to 0.767 at the middle severity and 0.509 at the highest severity. Performance degradation varies substantially across perturbation axes and action interfaces, and training on visual perturbations does not mitigate faults that leave camera images unchanged. We release the benchmark together with manifests specifying the fixed perturbation parameters for each episode.
papers.summary: Robot policies are expected to tolerate variation in the robot itself, such as bumped cameras, drifting calibration, different controller rates, and worn end-effector pads, but existing benchmarks vary the scene rather than the rig. `LIBERO-RIG` perturbs only the robot hardware and setup while holding every `LIBERO` task fixed, spanning eleven perturbation axes at five severity levels for 210 conditions across the four `LIBERO` suites. Evaluating nine recent vision-language-action (VLA) models with 500 episodes per condition and rigorous statistical tests, **pooled success falls from 0.932 to 0.767 at middle severity and 0.509 at the highest severity**, degradation varies substantially across axes and action interfaces, and training on visual perturbations does not mitigate faults that leave camera images unchanged.

papers.title: MFG: Multi-turn Feedback Guided Molecular Optimization
papers.abstract: Multi-objective molecular optimization is a critical process in drug discovery that aims to modify a given molecule to simultaneously improve multiple properties while maintaining a similar overall structure. This process often requires iterative modifications guided by computational or experimental feedback. Recent large language model (LLM)-based methods have begun to explore this iterative approach; however, these methods are not explicitly trained to leverage such feedback, while existing approaches primarily focus on single-turn molecular optimization. To address this gap, we introduce Multi-turn Feedback Guided (MFG) molecular optimization, a reinforcement learning framework that trains an LLM to progressively optimize molecules using feedback from previous turns. MFG introduces a feedback vector capturing both property improvements and source molecule similarity, alongside a feedback-aligned reward function that promotes progressive improvement across turns. We apply MFG over $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O}$, a state-of-the-art LLM model for multi-objective molecular optimization, evaluate $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O-MFG}$ on ten multi-objective molecular optimization tasks. The results demonstrate that $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O-MFG}$ achieves the highest average similarity-constrained success rate ($81.50%$), outperforming the base model $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O}$ ($70.81%$).
papers.summary: Multi-objective molecular optimization in drug discovery modifies a molecule to improve several properties at once while keeping its overall structure similar, usually through iterative rounds guided by feedback, but existing large language model (LLM) methods are single-turn and not trained to use that feedback. Multi-turn Feedback Guided (`MFG`) optimization is a reinforcement learning framework that trains an LLM to refine molecules across turns using a feedback vector capturing property improvements and similarity to the source molecule, together with a feedback-aligned reward that promotes progressive improvement. Applied to `GeLLM3O`, a state-of-the-art model for this task, the resulting `GeLLM3O-MFG` **reaches an average similarity-constrained success rate of 81.50% versus 70.81% for the base model** across ten multi-objective optimization tasks.

papers.title: Two Clocks: Why Larger Rollout Batches Learn Slower but Fail on Schedule in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) relies on costly model-generated responses, motivating larger rollout batches and square-root learning-rate scaling. Reported to approximately preserve progress per sample with one optimizer step per rollout, this rule is less understood in practical multi-step training. We develop a two-clock framework that separates the samples needed to make progress from those consumed before collapse. Under a local quadratic model, the square-root rule preserves first-order drift per sample but not progress: larger batches take fewer, longer updates and lose more to curvature, yielding a learning-rate-dependent critical batch beyond which sample efficiency degrades. A drift-threshold hypothesis predicts a complementary failure clock whose sample count remains approximately invariant along the square-root rule. Controlled GRPO experiments on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B across a $16\times$ batch range support both predictions. Ratio clipping delays failure, especially for larger batches, but the progress gap persists without it. Widening the clip trades stability for a transient speed gain. The progress gap reappears on another dataset, a general-purpose checkpoint, and a 7B model. Finally, we use the two-clock framework to derive a simple multi-step RLVR schedule: start below the critical batch and switch to a larger batch before failure. Our code is available at: https://github.com/WinstonLiyt/two-clocks-rlvr.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) depends on costly model-generated rollouts, which pushes practitioners toward larger rollout batches with square-root learning-rate scaling, a rule whose behavior in practical multi-step training is poorly understood. The authors build a two-clock framework separating the samples needed to make progress from those consumed before collapse: under a local quadratic model the square-root rule preserves first-order drift per sample but not progress, since larger batches take fewer, longer updates that lose more to curvature, giving a learning-rate-dependent critical batch beyond which sample efficiency degrades, while a drift-threshold hypothesis predicts a failure clock whose sample count stays roughly invariant along the rule. **Controlled `GRPO` experiments on `Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B` across a 16x batch range support both predictions**, ratio clipping delays failure but the progress gap persists without it, the gap reappears on another dataset, a general-purpose checkpoint, and a 7B model, and the framework yields a simple schedule: start below the critical batch and switch to a larger batch before failure.

papers.title: AesCode: Aesthetic Code Generation with Decoupled Cross-Modal Rewards
papers.abstract: Generating information-rich visual artifacts such as slides, posters, and dashboards as code is appealing because the outputs are structured, editable, and verifiable. Yet code models cannot see how their choices of layout and color come together on the canvas, often limiting spatial planning and aesthetic quality. Image generators excel at visual design but can misrender requested content, making their outputs unreliable targets for direct reproduction. We therefore introduce AesCode, which generates code grounded in the content prompt while using an image generated from the same prompt as an aesthetic guidance. To do so, AesCode represents the target as a design graph that describes the whole canvas and makes each property attributable. From this graph, we derive complementary cross-modal rewards: deterministic verifiers score properties parsable from code and rendering, while a VLM judge assesses the non-parsable ones with a sample-specific Visual Graph Rubric (VGR) tied to graph elements and relations. We optimize these decoupled rewards through reinforcement learning with per-channel normalization to jointly improve spatial planning, aesthetic quality, and verifiable correctness. To evaluate this setting, we build a benchmark that scores verifiable correctness and visual quality separately, with visual scores highly consistent with human judgments. We find that reference images substantially improve the visual quality of code generated by existing models, and ablations show that AesCode benefits from references both as model input and as a source of visual rewards. Relative to same-scale Qwen3-VL baselines given the same references, AesCode-8B and AesCode-32B improve visual quality by 31.1 and 22.4 percentage points, reaching scores comparable to those of closed-source frontier models such as GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8.
papers.summary: Generating slides, posters, and dashboards as code yields structured, editable, verifiable outputs, but code models cannot see how their layout and color choices render, while image generators design well yet misrender requested content. `AesCode` generates code grounded in the content prompt while using an image generated from the same prompt as aesthetic guidance, representing the target as a design graph over the whole canvas; from that graph it derives decoupled cross-modal rewards, with deterministic verifiers scoring properties parsable from code and rendering and a vision-language model (VLM) judge scoring the rest against a sample-specific Visual Graph Rubric (VGR), optimized through reinforcement learning with per-channel normalization. On a new benchmark that scores verifiable correctness and visual quality separately, reference images substantially improve the visual quality of existing models, and **`AesCode-8B` and `AesCode-32B` improve visual quality by 31.1 and 22.4 percentage points over same-scale `Qwen3-VL` baselines given the same references**, reaching scores comparable to `GPT-5.5` and `Claude Opus 4.8`.

papers.title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents
papers.abstract: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. Code and data are available at https://github.com/togethercomputer/HybridAgent.
papers.summary: Modern large language model (LLM) agents reason and act entirely in text, while latent reasoning offers a more efficient internal medium that lacks native tool access and transparency. `HybridAgent` moves dynamically between latent reasoning and text-based interaction within one generation process: a lightweight `HybridLink` module handles transitions between modes and a continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across turns, keeping tool use intact while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Post-training runs in two stages, `HybridSFT` to stabilize tool-integrated hybrid generation and `HybridRL` to learn when to think in latent space and when to act through text; across 3 model scales and 11 benchmarks covering math, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning, **it improves performance by 10.4% over frontier text-based and latent agent baselines while cutting tokens by 35.5% to 54.7%**, with 1.8x to 2.6x faster inference and 2.7x to 3.7x lower cost.
papers.highlight_summary:
LLM agents reason and act entirely through decoded text, while latent reasoning in continuous hidden space is faster but has no native tool access and no inspectable trace. `HybridAgent` switches between the two modes inside a single generation, thinking in latent space and dropping back to text only for tool calls, key decisions, and the final answer.

- A roughly **10M-parameter** residual adapter, `HybridLink`, maps last-layer hidden states back into the input embedding space, with a `<latent>` token entering the mode, exit firing when the nearest token embedding is `</latent>`, the KV cache carrying the mixed text-latent-tool context across turns, and every latent step readable as pseudo-text via nearest-token lookup.
- Training runs `HybridSFT`, which activates the format and adapter and then does two-pass self-conditioned training on 54K auto-annotated hybrid trajectories so the backbone learns to reason over its own adapter outputs, followed by `HybridRL`, a GRPO-style update that computes importance ratios only at sampled text positions, replays recorded latents exactly, freezes the adapter, and rewards correctness, format, and multi-tool use with no reward on mode choice.
- At 14B the agent scores **52.4 on `GAIA` and 49.5 on `WebWalker`** against 43.7 and 40.5 for the strongest matched text-RL baseline `ARPO`, and it uses **35.5–54.7% fewer tokens, runs 1.8–2.6× faster, and costs 2.7–3.7× less** than text-only agents.
- Latent thoughts are load-bearing and auditable: swapping in latents from a different problem drops `MATH500` accuracy from 84.6 to 44.8 at 8B, while visible text shrinks 43–49% yet a monitor's AUROC for predicting rollout correctness stays within 0.022 of matched text agents.
- Limits: math margins over text-RL baselines are only 1–2 points (39.2 vs 37.1 on `AIME25` at 8B, 88.2 vs 87.4 on `MATH500` at 14B), `HLE` stays far below frontier agents (16.0 vs 31.4 for `Kimi-K3`), all results use `Qwen3-Base` backbones with 4B relegated to the appendix, and multi-turn hybrid generation needed a custom serving stack since no existing engine supports it.

papers.title: DoubtLess: Training-Free Contrastive Decoding for Efficient Reasoning
papers.abstract: Reasoning models achieve strong performance through long chains of thought (CoT), but often spend more tokens than needed to solve a problem. Existing ways to shorten the CoT require additional training for each model, add a fixed steering vector to the model's hidden states, or use decoding heuristics such as stopping early or banning words like "wait", which can reduce accuracy. We propose DoubtLess, a training-free decoding method in which a much smaller reasoning model steers the large one towards brevity. The small model reads the large model's CoT so far twice, once prompted to be brief (the brief thinker) and once prompted to be verbose (the verbose thinker), and the difference between its two logit vectors, scaled by a strength, is added to the large model's logits at every step of the CoT. On seven benchmarks of competition mathematics, graduate-level science and competitive programming, DoubtLess shortens the CoT of Qwen3-32B by 31% with unchanged accuracy, outperforming five inference-time baselines. We also show that DoubtLess reduces thinking tokens per turn by 20% in a self-debugging coding agent with unchanged task performance. It also generalizes to two other model families with unchanged accuracy. When combined with training-based compression, it further shortens the CoT of a model already trained for brevity. Ablations and behavioral analysis show that DoubtLess reduces repeated checking, with most token savings coming after the correct answer first appears in the CoT. Our code is available at https://github.com/leoluolol/DoubtLess.
papers.summary: Reasoning models earn their accuracy through long chains of thought (CoT) but often spend far more tokens than a problem needs, and existing remedies require per-model training, add a fixed steering vector, or use decoding heuristics such as early stopping or banning words like "wait" that can cost accuracy. `DoubtLess` is a training-free decoding method in which a much smaller reasoning model reads the large model's CoT so far twice, once prompted to be brief and once to be verbose, and the scaled difference between its two logit vectors is added to the large model's logits at every step. On seven benchmarks of competition mathematics, graduate-level science, and competitive programming, **it shortens the CoT of `Qwen3-32B` by 31% with unchanged accuracy**, outperforming five inference-time baselines, and it also cuts thinking tokens per turn by 20% in a self-debugging coding agent without hurting task performance, generalizes to two other model families, and stacks with training-based compression; analysis shows most savings come from less repeated checking after the correct answer first appears.

papers.title: Tev: Scaling Long-Horizon Agentic Environments with Dense Progress Rewards
papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents have drawn growing attention for their ability to work autonomously -- from hours to days -- on economically valuable tasks, a capability essential to automated discovery and recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet open-source models still struggle on long-horizon tasks, largely for lack of both training data and a working recipe, and scaling both is hard: long, complex tasks are difficult to curate and verify, and their rewards are sparse. We address both. First, we introduce Tev-Gym, the first long-horizon agent training dataset with verifiable, dense, progressive rewards -- 1,170 verified task environments across 7 domains. It is built on a latent-world-first approach that first constructs a latent world: a complete and correct hidden specification of the task domain, workflow, and expected state after each step. Each task is then progressively rendered from this specification into an agent-facing environment, enabling controllable complexity and a natural progress metric. Second, we turn this metric into a training recipe: via progress-potential reward shaping (PPRS), we convert progress into a dense per-step reward that improves training efficiency and makes otherwise-intractable tasks trainable. Training with this recipe yields Tev-27B, which achieves substantial gains on the Agents' Last Exam computing and math sciences domains (ALE-CM), matching GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 at Pass@5. Despite training only on ALE-related data, it generalizes to the Terminal-Bench (TB) 3.0 and 4.0 subsets, surpassing GLM 5.2 and Gemini 3.7 Flash, and reaches Claude Opus 4.8-level performance on middle-horizon tasks such as TB 2.1.
papers.summary: Open-source models lag on long-horizon agentic tasks largely because such tasks are hard to curate and verify and their rewards are sparse. `Tev-Gym` is a training set of 1,170 verified task environments across 7 domains with dense, progressive, verifiable rewards, built by first constructing a latent world, a complete hidden specification of each task's domain, workflow, and expected state after every step, and then rendering it into an agent-facing environment with controllable complexity and a natural progress metric. Progress-potential reward shaping (PPRS) turns that metric into a dense per-step reward, and the resulting `Tev-27B` **matches `GPT-6 Astra` and `Claude Opus 5` at Pass@5 on the computing and math sciences domains of `Agents' Last Exam`**, while generalizing to the `Terminal-Bench` 3.0 and 4.0 subsets, surpassing `GLM 5.2` and `Gemini 3.7 Flash`, and reaching `Claude Opus 4.8`-level performance on middle-horizon tasks such as `Terminal-Bench 2.1`.

papers.title: What Matters in Quality-Aware VLA Pretraining: A Benchmark and Empirical Study
papers.abstract: How should demonstration quality be used during vision-language-action (VLA) pretraining to improve performance after target-task fine-tuning? We compare weighting, filtering, and conditioning across reward definitions and label granularities using 5,000 naturally suboptimal human demonstrations and 24 target tasks. Within each VLA, we match demonstrations and training budgets. Additional comparisons examine pretraining data size and the roles of quality tags during fine-tuning and inference. Across three VLAs, we find that approach-aware episode conditioning improves mean success over plain behavioral cloning; conditioning and filtering favor episode and chunk labels, respectively, on average, with model-dependent reversals; and constant-tag fine-tuning improves mean success after conditioned pretraining with either tagged or untagged inference. We introduce AXIS-Bench to support these controlled comparisons. Built on crowdsourced simulation demonstrations, it provides recorded object and contact states for recomputing quality labels on shared trajectories. Replayable trajectories support workspace-aligned rendering and user-defined real-world target tasks. In our real-world experiment, simulation pretraining raises success from 9.6\% to 31.7\%. Project page: https://axis-bench.github.io/.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) pretraining draws on human demonstrations of uneven quality, and it is unclear whether that quality is best used by weighting, filtering, or conditioning. The authors compare these strategies across reward definitions and label granularities using 5,000 naturally suboptimal demonstrations and 24 target tasks, matching demonstrations and training budgets within each of three VLAs, and introduce `AXIS-Bench`, built on crowdsourced simulation demonstrations with recorded object and contact states so quality labels can be recomputed on shared, replayable trajectories. Approach-aware episode conditioning improves mean success over plain behavioral cloning, conditioning and filtering favor episode and chunk labels respectively with model-dependent reversals, constant-tag fine-tuning helps after conditioned pretraining, and **in a real-world experiment simulation pretraining raises success from 9.6% to 31.7%**.

papers.title: ChunkAct: Action Chunking for Agentic Robotics
papers.abstract: Agentic robotics places a large language model (LLM) agent in the robot control loop, where it composes perception, motion, and vision-language-action (VLA) tools under the guidance of a memory and thereby generalizes to new tasks without retraining. This generality comes at a steep price in efficiency. Every primitive requires a round of LLM reasoning over the full interaction history, so the cost of an episode grows with the number of primitives. We find this reasoning largely redundant: once a sub-goal is chosen, its primitives follow a routine already prescribed by memory. We present ChunkAct, which introduces action chunking to agentic robotics. Online, a single call launches a chunk of chained primitives, which executes autonomously and returns control only upon failure. Offline, ChunkAct compiles the memory into these chunks, so execution is memory-free at test time and the planner is reserved for decisions that require reasoning. LLM computation therefore scales with the number of decisions rather than the number of primitives. On LIBERO-Pro, ChunkAct improves task success by 5.0 points over the state of the art in agentic robotics while requiring 2.9x fewer LLM calls, 4.4x fewer input tokens, and 2.3x fewer output tokens.
papers.summary: Agentic robotics puts a large language model (LLM) agent in the control loop to compose perception, motion, and vision-language-action (VLA) tools guided by a memory, which generalizes to new tasks without retraining but demands a round of LLM reasoning over the full interaction history for every primitive. Observing that this reasoning is largely redundant once a sub-goal is chosen, `ChunkAct` compiles the memory offline into chunks of chained primitives; online, a single call launches a chunk that executes autonomously and returns control only on failure, so LLM computation scales with the number of decisions rather than the number of primitives. On `LIBERO-Pro`, **it improves task success by 5.0 points over the prior state of the art in agentic robotics while using 2.9x fewer LLM calls**, 4.4x fewer input tokens, and 2.3x fewer output tokens.

papers.title: Lotus: Learning to Understand Time-series by Learning to Forecast
papers.abstract: Time-series language models typically align numerical signals with language using labels, captions, or question-answer pairs. Although such supervision encourages linguistic representations, it does not explicitly require them to preserve information about how the underlying time-series signal evolves. We introduce forecast grounding, a pretraining principle that requires language-aligned time-series representations to remain predictive of the future evolution before they are adapted to downstream tasks. We instantiate this principle in LOTUS, which divides each time-series channel into non-overlapping patches and maps them into the LLM embedding space. It then predicts the next patch from the LLM hidden states of the time-series tokens, encouraging the learned representation to retain temporal information. To capture both temporal changes and periodic patterns, we also propose a temporal-spectral patch representation that combines each raw time-series patch with its spectral representation before mapping it into the LLM embedding space. Across three language model backbones and six downstream evaluation datasets, LOTUS achieves the best average performance with minimal trainable parameters, reaching 59.91% accuracy and outperforming the strongest matched baseline by 3.36%. Our representation analyses further show that LOTUS uses the numerical input and preserves temporal structure in its learned patch representations. These results establish forecast grounding as a promising pretraining principle, enabling compact time-series language models to outperform models 25 to 50 times their size on TSRBench.
papers.summary: Time-series language models typically align numerical signals with language through labels, captions, or question-answer pairs, which does not require the representation to preserve how the underlying signal evolves. Forecast grounding is a pretraining principle requiring language-aligned time-series representations to remain predictive of the future before downstream adaptation; `LOTUS` instantiates it by splitting each channel into non-overlapping patches, combining each raw patch with its spectral representation, mapping them into the LLM embedding space, and predicting the next patch from the LLM hidden states of the time-series tokens. Across three language model backbones and six downstream datasets, `LOTUS` achieves the best average performance with minimal trainable parameters, **reaching 59.91% accuracy and beating the strongest matched baseline by 3.36%**, and on `TSRBench` compact models trained this way outperform models 25 to 50 times larger.

papers.title: Inverse Reasoning Models for Efficient Post-Training and Verification from Answer-Only Data
papers.abstract: Post-training reasoning LLMs often requires making a tradeoff between costly supervision and compute inefficiency: supervised finetuning typically requires reasoning traces, which is data inefficient since in many applications one only has prompt-answer tuples and lacks the groundtruth chain-of-thought (CoT) sequence. On the other hand, reinforcement learning (with verifiable rewards, for example) can operate without CoT data but it is much more compute-inefficient since it requires multiple autoregressive completions per optimization step, none of which are guaranteed to give a non-zero policy gradient. In this work we explore a middleground, a self-distillation technique that uses answer-only data, treating CoT as latent variables. This relies on training a partner ``inverse reasoning LLM" that generates the original's reasoning traces conditioned on the answer. The inverse model is trained once and reused across incoming batches of answer-only data, with all generation happening offline and up front, making the approach particularly suited to continual post-training. Using Qwen3-0.6B on the Countdown and GSM8K tasks, we show that after GRPO training has saturated, a single offline distillation round from the inverse model roughly doubles pass@1 on hard prompts and, on Countdown, outperforms rejection-sampling self-distillation on every hard-tail metric at every mix ratio (with smaller gains on GSM8K); rejection sampling by construction has no signal on problems the model never solves on its own. Continued GRPO on the fresh data retains an edge at hard pass@1 but trails distillation at pass@8 and pass@32 while regenerating rollouts at every step. As an added bonus we see that the inverse model has a second application as an accurate verifier of correctness. When used for best-of-$n$ selection at test time, it raises selection accuracy on Countdown from 0.753 (majority voting) to 0.969.
papers.summary: Post-training reasoning LLMs forces a tradeoff: supervised fine-tuning needs reasoning traces that most prompt-answer datasets lack, while reinforcement learning works from answers alone but spends compute on many rollouts per step that may yield no gradient at all. The authors propose a self-distillation middle ground that treats chain-of-thought (CoT) as a latent variable and trains a partner inverse reasoning LLM to generate the original model's reasoning traces conditioned on the answer; the inverse model is trained once, reused across incoming batches of answer-only data, and generates everything offline up front, which suits continual post-training. With `Qwen3-0.6B` on `Countdown` and `GSM8K`, a single offline distillation round after `GRPO` has saturated **roughly doubles pass@1 on hard prompts** and beats rejection-sampling self-distillation on every hard-tail metric on `Countdown`, and the inverse model doubles as a verifier that raises best-of-n selection accuracy on `Countdown` from 0.753 with majority voting to 0.969.

papers.title: Do Vision CIL Methods Transfer to Protein? A Diagnostic Benchmark of Frozen Protein Encoders
papers.abstract: Protein function annotation operates over an expanding label space, making class-incremental learning (CIL) a natural framework for incorporating newly discovered functions without full retraining. Yet existing CIL methods have been developed largely in vision and have not been systematically evaluated over frozen protein representations. We conduct a controlled benchmark of nine representative CIL methods across five sequence-, structure-, and sequence--structure-based protein encoders and two enzyme function datasets at different scales, while keeping the encoders frozen and evaluation settings consistent across representations. We find that no method transfers reliably across encoders, and that these failures persist across alternative phase constructions. Diagnostic analyses reveal that this instability arises from weak gradient-based stability signals, substantial heterogeneity in embedding geometry, and covariance assumptions whose appropriate capacity changes with both dataset scale and encoder. These findings suggest that the representation itself should be treated as a central component of continual-learning design rather than a passive feature extractor. More generally, reliable protein CIL will require encoder-aware methods that adapt their statistical assumptions and capacity to the geometry of the representation on which they operate. Code is available at https://github.com/zygao930/ProteinCIL.
papers.summary: Protein function annotation faces a continually expanding label space, making class-incremental learning (CIL) a natural fit, but CIL methods were developed for vision and have not been evaluated systematically over frozen protein representations. The authors benchmark nine representative CIL methods across five sequence-, structure-, and sequence-structure-based protein encoders and two enzyme function datasets of different scales, keeping encoders frozen and evaluation settings consistent. **No method transfers reliably across encoders**, the failures persist under alternative phase constructions, and diagnostics trace the instability to weak gradient-based stability signals, heterogeneous embedding geometry, and covariance assumptions whose appropriate capacity shifts with dataset scale and encoder, leading the authors to argue that the representation must be treated as a central component of continual-learning design rather than a passive feature extractor.

papers.title: Do Perturbation Predictors Learn Gene Interactions? Diagnosing Extrapolation in Agentic Screening
papers.abstract: High-throughput perturbation screens increasingly use machine-learning models to predict the effects of gene combinations that were never measured. A difficult case arises when both genes in a test pair were seen individually during training, but their combination was not. In this setting, standard OOD methods often fail because neither gene appears unfamiliar on its own. We therefore compare each model prediction with a simple additive prediction obtained by summing the two observed single-gene effects. The difference between them, which we call additive disagreement (AD), measures how much extra interaction effect the model introduces for an unseen combination. Across eight prediction methods and three Perturb-seq datasets, specialised neural predictors do not consistently outperform this simple additive baseline. More importantly, predictions with larger deviations from the additive baseline tend to have larger errors. Conventional output-based and embedding-based confidence signals are inconsistent across datasets and models, whereas AD remains informative across all evaluated compositional settings. We further study how this signal can guide decisions in an agentic perturbation-screening workflow. The code is available at https://github.com/zygao930/OOD.
