papers.summary: Machine-learning models in high-throughput perturbation screens predict the effects of gene combinations never measured, and the hard case is a pair whose genes were each seen alone in training but never together, where standard out-of-distribution (OOD) detection fails because neither gene looks unfamiliar. The authors compare each model prediction with a simple additive baseline that sums the two observed single-gene effects and call the gap additive disagreement (AD), a measure of how much extra interaction effect the model introduces for an unseen pair. Across eight prediction methods and three `Perturb-seq` datasets, **specialised neural predictors do not consistently outperform the additive baseline**, larger deviations from it tend to carry larger errors, and AD stays informative where output- and embedding-based confidence signals are inconsistent, so the authors show how it can guide decisions in an agentic perturbation-screening workflow.

papers.title: Following the Flow the Law Requires: Training Voice Agents to Transfer to Unseen Regulated Procedures in Debt Collection
papers.abstract: Voice agents built on large language models (LLMs) now handle customer calls, but in regulated applications completing the task is not enough: the agent must follow a conversational flow set by law. In debt collection, it must confirm it is speaking to the debtor before mentioning the debt, identify itself and the creditor, state the amount, and avoid prohibited language. Every creditor turns these rules into its own procedure and revises it. We ask whether a small, self-hosted policy can be trained once and then follow regulated procedures it has never seen. One machine-readable specification per deployment, FlowSpec, generates the policy instruction, gates the tools, supplies the supervision and defines the tests; the agent speaks only approved catalogue sentences. We fine-tune a 9-billion-parameter model on 2,506 conversations from 297 randomized procedures and evaluate a Thai outbound-call agent on four unseen deployment procedures (three debt collection, one non-debt), one from a wholly withheld lineage. Documented checks, fixed by the procedure, rise from 67--71 percents to 93--100 percents, while grounded checks, fixed by the conversation, already pass at 97--100 percents before training; scenario pass rate rises from 15/43 to 40/43. An audit of the shared specification finds 11 defects, 3 of which its own metric did not expose.
papers.summary: Voice agents built on large language models (LLMs) that handle regulated calls must follow a conversational flow set by law; in debt collection that means confirming the debtor before mentioning the debt, identifying the agent and the creditor, stating the amount, and avoiding prohibited language, with every creditor encoding and revising its own procedure. The authors ask whether a small self-hosted policy can be trained once and then follow unseen procedures: a per-deployment machine-readable specification, `FlowSpec`, generates the policy instruction, gates the tools, supplies supervision, and defines the tests, and the agent speaks only approved catalogue sentences. Fine-tuning a 9-billion-parameter model on 2,506 conversations from 297 randomized procedures and evaluating a Thai outbound-call agent on four unseen deployment procedures, **procedure-fixed documented checks rise from 67-71 percent to 93-100 percent and scenario pass rate rises from 15/43 to 40/43**, while conversation-grounded checks already passed at 97-100 percent before training; an audit of the shared specification also found 11 defects, 3 of which its own metric did not expose.

papers.title: Token Utility for On-Policy Distillation via Local Trust-Region Optimization
papers.abstract: Token-selection methods for on-policy distillation (OPD) prioritize student-visited positions using diverse signals, including uncertainty, teacher-student disagreement, and mismatch direction. We instead derive token importance from the distillation objective itself: how much can each position's loss decrease under an equal local KL budget on the student's predictive distribution? The answer is the utility $s_t=g_t^\top F_t^\dagger g_t$, where $g_t$ is the logit gradient and $F_t$ is the categorical Fisher matrix. For reverse-KL it equals the student-weighted variance of the student-teacher log-probability ratio, and for forward-KL it equals the Pearson $\chi^2$ divergence, so the appropriate utility follows from the choice of objective. On shared training checkpoints, several independently motivated criteria, including student entropy, KL disagreement, and TIP, concentrate their importance on nearly the same positions as the derived utility at a 50\% selection fraction, while diverging at stricter fractions and for direction-specific criteria. We instantiate the utility as Fisher Utility Weighting (FUW), a continuous, mean-normalized token weighting. Across seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three Qwen3 student-teacher pairs, FUW improves over matched uniform OPD under both reverse-KL (1.35-4.0 macro points) and forward-KL (1.08-2.71 macro points), and is competitive with existing selective methods using a single closed-form score derived from the training objective.
papers.summary: Token-selection methods for on-policy distillation (OPD) prioritize positions in the student's own samples using heuristics such as uncertainty, teacher-student disagreement, or mismatch direction. The authors instead derive token importance from the distillation objective itself, asking how much each position's loss can decrease under an equal local Kullback-Leibler (KL) budget on the student's predictive distribution; the answer is a quadratic form of the logit gradient under the pseudo-inverse categorical Fisher matrix, which for reverse KL equals the student-weighted variance of the student-teacher log-probability ratio and for forward KL equals the Pearson chi-squared divergence. On shared checkpoints, independently motivated criteria including student entropy, KL disagreement, and `TIP` concentrate on nearly the same positions as this utility at a 50% selection fraction but diverge at stricter fractions, and the resulting continuous, mean-normalized `Fisher Utility Weighting` (`FUW`) **improves over matched uniform OPD by 1.35 to 4.0 macro points under reverse KL and 1.08 to 2.71 under forward KL** across seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three `Qwen3` student-teacher pairs.

papers.title: Physics-Guided Multi-Fidelity Surrogate Modeling for Natural Supercavity Geometry of an Axisymmetric Conical Cavitator
papers.abstract: Natural supercavitation behind conical cavitators generates a vapor-filled envelope that, when sustained over the full body of a high-speed underwater vehicles, reduces hydrodynamic skin-friction drag and enables performance levels unattainable in fully wetted flow. Accurate prediction of maximum cavity length and maximum cavity radius and local cavity profile as functions of cavitation number and cone half-angle is essential for both the static design and the real-time shape management of super-cavitating torpedo cavitators. Classical analytical models provide computationally inexpensive predictions but exhibit systematic disagreements in the practically important regime of moderate cavitation number and large angle, where slender-body assumptions begin to break down. Existing data-driven machine learning approaches offer higher accuracy but are constrained by the prohibitive cost of multiphase computational fluid dynamics (CFD) sweeps over the full design space. This study proposes a physics-guided multi-fidelity surrogate framework based on Extended Hierarchical Kriging (PG-EHK) that addresses this challenge by fusing the multiple competing analytical cavity formulas as non-level low-fidelity (LF) trend functions corrected by a sparse set of high-fidelity (HF) CFD data. It simultaneously incorporates the analytical models regardless of their local fidelity ordering, using Bayesian-estimated scaling factors to construct the trend function as physical baseline. The resulting surrogate maps operational condition inputs to cavity geometry responses using fewer than 20 high-fidelity CFD evaluations. Cross-validation on five independent hold-out CFD cases demonstrates that the proposed PG-EHK surrogate achieves 61% reduction in prediction error compared to the best-performing individual analytical approach.
papers.summary: Predicting the vapor cavity that forms behind a conical cavitator on a high-speed underwater vehicle matters for drag reduction, but analytical formulas break down at moderate cavitation numbers and large cone angles, while multiphase computational fluid dynamics (CFD) sweeps over the design space are too costly. The proposed physics-guided Extended Hierarchical Kriging surrogate (`PG-EHK`) treats several competing analytical cavity formulas as low-fidelity trend functions, weights them with Bayesian-estimated scaling factors regardless of which is locally more accurate, and corrects the result with fewer than 20 high-fidelity CFD evaluations. On five held-out CFD cases the surrogate cuts prediction error by **61%** relative to the best single analytical model.

papers.title: Bayesian Causal Forests for Zero-Inflated Continuous Outcomes
papers.abstract: Estimating (heterogeneous) treatment effects is still challenging when the outcome is semicontinuous (i.e., exhibiting both a discrete point mass at zero and a skewed continuous distribution for positive values), despite the strong presence of this data type in real world settings. Existing methods either ignore the zero mass, impose fragile parametric assumptions, or suffer from extreme computational costs and data augmentation noise. This paper proposes Zero-Inflated Continuous Bayesian Causal Forests with Duan's Smearing (ZIC-BCF-Smear), a decoupled two-part nonparametric estimator that fits a Probit BCF on the full sample to model participation and a Gaussian BCF strictly on the active subpopulation to model positive intensity. Subpopulation Propensity Adjustment (SPA) mitigates regularization-induced confounding within the active subpopulation, and Duan's non-parametric smearing estimator re-transforms predictions to the response scale, bypassing the fragile scale multipliers of parametric models. A comprehensive simulation benchmark shows that ZIC-BCF-Smear matches well-specified parametric models without their assumptions and remains stable and calibrated where competitors either diverge or pathologically over-cover for nonlinear data. The method is then applied to individual-participant data from the SPECTRUM randomized phase III head-and-neck cancer trial, estimating the causal effect of assignment to panitumumab plus chemotherapy on the number of days patients spend with severe toxicity, an outcome for which a quarter of patients contribute an exact zero. Panitumumab assignment raises that burden by about ten days per patient under the trial's own differential treatment duration, and the decoupled structure localizes the effect mainly in the positive-intensity part rather than in whether the reconstructed severe-AE burden is positive.
papers.summary: Treatment-effect estimation struggles with semicontinuous outcomes that pile up at exactly zero and spread out skewedly above it, since existing options either ignore the zero mass, lean on fragile parametric forms, or cost too much to run. `ZIC-BCF-Smear` splits the problem in two: a Probit Bayesian Causal Forest models whether the outcome is positive, a Gaussian one models its magnitude among active cases only, a subpopulation propensity adjustment counters regularization-induced confounding, and Duan's nonparametric smearing estimator maps predictions back to the response scale. Simulations show it matches well-specified parametric models without their assumptions and stays calibrated where competitors diverge or over-cover on nonlinear data. Applied to the `SPECTRUM` phase III head-and-neck cancer trial, assignment to panitumumab plus chemotherapy raises severe-toxicity burden by **about ten days per patient**, with the effect localized in the positive-intensity part rather than in whether any burden occurs.

papers.title: AI-Driven, Timing-Aware Power Optimization
papers.abstract: Post-route power recovery changes cell choices under tightly coupled timing, electrical and physical constraints, and the value of each change depends on what it costs to repair its side effects. We propose an AI-driven framework in which a learned model drives both phases of the optimization: it ranks the powerrecovery edits to try and the repair actions that follow, while deterministic electronic design automation (EDA) analyses govern every acceptance. The framework records baseline constraint margins, identifies the damage a recovery transaction introduces in each analysis view, holds pre-existing violations at their baseline rather than working them inside the power step, and caps repair spending at a fraction of the measured saving. An ensemble of gradient-boosted models predicts power change, normalized damage reduction and constraint-regression risk from action and timing-context features available before each trial; calibrated, conservative estimates feed separate acquisition scores for recovery and repair, with a deterministic fallback when the model is uncertain. Recovery and repair remain speculative until physical implementation and fresh analysis establish baseline preservation and positive net saving. We specify the contract, the learned policy, the transactional flow and a pre-registered public evaluation protocol on open designs. Evidence from a companion study on public designs supports the contract; the learned policy is proposed, and no trained-model results or proprietary design measurements are reported.
papers.summary: Post-route power recovery in chip design swaps cell choices under tightly coupled timing, electrical, and physical constraints, where each edit's value depends on what it costs to repair the side effects it introduces. The proposed framework has an ensemble of gradient-boosted models rank both the recovery edits to try and the repair actions that follow, while deterministic electronic design automation (EDA) analyses retain authority over every acceptance, pre-existing violations are held at baseline, and repair spending is capped at a fraction of the measured saving. The authors specify the contract, the transactional flow, and a pre-registered public evaluation protocol on open designs, but **report no trained-model results or proprietary design measurements**, leaving the learned policy proposed rather than demonstrated.

papers.title: Distinguishing Process Change, Instrument Fault and Data-Path Corruption in Streaming Telemetry: A Reference Implementation and Benchmark
papers.abstract: A reading departs from what a monitoring system expects for one of three reasons: the physical process changed, the instrument is failing, or the value was corrupted between the instrument and the software. The three call for different responses and look alike in a single sample. We state the three-cause problem, prove which pairs of causes one channel cannot separate, and propose a bank of online detectors - a Kalman tracker with CUSUM and EWMA charts on its innovation, a Hampel median with generalized-ESD confirmation, a robust noise statistic with ADWIN, exact-value checks and an optional two-channel complementary filter - combined by a deterministic, inspectable attribution rule. The detectors were merged into a public algorithm library. On 2,942 injected events of thirteen fault types the method detects 96.3% (95% interval 95.7-97.0) at 0.22 false alarms per hour and attributes 91.2% (90.6-91.8) of detected events correctly from one channel and 99.0% (98.6-99.4) with a second, rate channel; from one channel only 2 of 207 detected sensor drifts are attributed to the instrument, as the problem statement predicts. Injected into recorded industrial signals, the same catalogue is detected at 80.8% and attributed correctly at 84.5%, at 3.6 false alarms per hour. On the Skoltech Anomaly Benchmark the method detects 32 of 33 experiments with a median delay of 15 s, at 46 false alarms per hour against 11 for a rolling z-score.
papers.summary: A monitoring reading can deviate for three reasons, namely the physical process changed, the instrument is failing, or the value was corrupted between instrument and software, and the three demand different responses while looking identical in a single sample. The work proves which pairs of causes one channel cannot separate, then combines a bank of online detectors, including a Kalman tracker with CUSUM and EWMA charts on its innovation, a Hampel median with generalized-ESD confirmation, and a robust noise statistic with ADWIN, under a deterministic attribution rule released in a public library. Across 2,942 injected events of thirteen fault types it detects 96.3% at 0.22 false alarms per hour and attributes **91.2% of detected events correctly from one channel, rising to 99.0% with a second rate channel**. On recorded industrial signals detection falls to 80.8% with attribution at 84.5%, and on the `Skoltech Anomaly Benchmark` it catches 32 of 33 experiments with a 15-second median delay but at 46 false alarms per hour against 11 for a rolling z-score.

papers.title: Popularity Trajectories and Mixing Patterns of Urban Venues in Two European Cities
papers.abstract: Urban venues such as restaurants, shops, bars and parks host the daily life of a city, and their collective rise and fall signals how vibrant a neighbourhood is. The usual assumption is that a venue's fortunes follow its neighbourhood's, so that how wealthy an area is and how many people live there will decide a venue's performance. Yet whether there is a common performance trajectory shared by venues over time is underexplored. In this study, we use 5.5 years of Foursquare data for about 10^4 venues in London and Barcelona. We found six distinguishable shapes recur in both cities, that are (1) Fall, (2) Rise, (3) Rise & Fall, (4) Steady, (5) Ephemeral (an early hit that loses popularity fast) and (6) Underdogs (a slow starter that gains popularity late). However, no recovery shape appears, that is neither city yields a U-shaped fall-and-rise group. Additionally, we found that deprivation and population density are not indicative which shape a venue follows. We also discovered that how early a shape can be recognized depends on when its distinctive segment occurs, not a shape's complexity. Proximity between venues, however, does predict how well-performing a venue is. We uncovered a mixing pattern where venues of the same shape tend to locate together more often than chance within roughly 200 to 600 metres. Finally, our qualitative reading of two contrasting districts, one rising in London and one falling in Barcelona, show that comparable socioeconomic conditions but divergent gentrification histories can generate vastly different popularity trajectories. All in all, our results altogether point at that urban vibrancy emerges at the block- and street- level, and social and historical contexts matter in terms of the characteristics of such patterns.
papers.summary: Conventional wisdom holds that a venue's fortunes track its neighbourhood's wealth and population density, but whether venues share common performance trajectories over time is largely untested. Using 5.5 years of `Foursquare` data on roughly 10,000 venues in London and Barcelona, the study finds six recurring popularity shapes in both cities, namely fall, rise, rise-and-fall, steady, ephemeral early hits, and late-blooming underdogs, with **no U-shaped recovery trajectory appearing in either city**. Deprivation and density do not predict which shape a venue follows, but spatial proximity does, as venues sharing a shape cluster together more often than chance within roughly 200 to 600 metres. Readings of a rising London district and a falling Barcelona one suggest gentrification history rather than socioeconomic level drives divergent trajectories, pointing to vibrancy that emerges at block and street level.

papers.title: TorchSpin: Differentiable Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Simulation in PyTorch
papers.abstract: Interpreting electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectra commonly requires repeated forward simulation and optimization of spin Hamiltonian parameters. Established software provides mature simulation and fitting methods, but these calculations are not generally available as differentiable components within machine-learning workflows. We present TorchSpin, an open-source PyTorch framework that ports the organization and numerical conventions of EasySpin into a tensor-based computational environment. Representative calculations spanning continuous-wave EPR, ENDOR, pulse EPR, spin dynamics, trajectory simulation, and magnetometry closely reproduced corresponding EasySpin results. In matched benchmarks, TorchSpin CPU execution was faster than EasySpin for six of nine workloads although performance depended strongly on the calculation. We therefore focused on the capabilities enabled by automatic differentiation in PyTorch. In a Cu(II) powder-spectrum demonstration, feedback propagated through TorchSpin improved the quality of a supervised convolutional neural network (CNN) without using parameter labels during refinement. Models trained from randomly initialized CNNs using only noisy spectra and TorchSpin reconstruction loss achieved median similarities of $\geq$ 0.99. CNNs trained on TorchSpin-generated libraries also transferred without adaptation to independently generated EasySpin spectra with performance comparable to EasySpin-trained controls. Once trained, the CNN produced initial parameter estimates in approximately 1 ms per spectrum while a batch of 512 was processed in approximately 1.3 ms with GPU acceleration. TorchSpin therefore provides both a tested Python implementation of established EPR calculations and a differentiable physical layer for rapid learned inference, spectral refinement, and parameter-label-free training.
papers.summary: Fitting electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectra means repeatedly simulating spin Hamiltonians, and the established tools are not differentiable components that machine-learning pipelines can train through. `TorchSpin` ports `EasySpin`'s organization and numerical conventions into PyTorch tensors, closely reproducing continuous-wave EPR, ENDOR, pulse EPR, spin dynamics, trajectory, and magnetometry calculations and running faster on CPU in six of nine matched benchmarks. Because gradients flow through the simulator, convolutional networks trained on noisy spectra and a reconstruction loss alone, with no parameter labels, reached **median similarities of at least 0.99**, and networks trained on `TorchSpin`-generated libraries transferred unchanged to independently generated `EasySpin` spectra. A trained network produces initial parameter estimates in about 1 ms per spectrum, or 1.3 ms for a batch of 512 with GPU acceleration.

papers.title: The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery
papers.abstract: Modern coding agents are fundamentally reshaping the role of human input for computational research: they write code, launch in silico experiments, analyze their results, and autonomously operate with ever-increasing time horizons. Despite these developments, fully autonomous research agents suffer from a limited ideation radius and myopic hill-climbing search dynamics. To bridge this gap, we introduce The Agentic Scientist, an end-to-end distributed pipeline for human researchers to conduct computational research alongside modern coding agents. Building on its predecessor, our system decomposes research into task drafting, idea generation, planning, sandboxed experimentation, result aggregation, baseline and ablation construction, post-hoc analysis, and report writing. Importantly, each step in the pipeline is powered by the next generation of coding agents and leverages agentic self-verification. The overall research process is driven by a meta-controller that manages parallel research agents and enforces rubric verification at each stage. This design enables the same orchestration layer to be reused across heterogeneous domains with different execution environments, agentic coding harnesses, and evaluation metrics. Our system can be used across a spectrum of autonomy: either as a co-scientist tool or to perform end-to-end scientific investigation. Within the co-scientist setting, we leveraged a development version of our system to submit a single research paper, which got accepted for publication at ALIFE 2026. We further apply The Agentic Scientist fully autonomously to open problem-solving tasks in machine learning, and demonstrate the system's capability of scientific discovery across different domains of computational research. Our ablations suggest that reliable scientific autonomy depends not only on base model capabilities, but also on the cross-agent orchestration layer.
papers.summary: Fully autonomous research agents tend to have a narrow ideation radius and to hill-climb myopically toward local improvements. `The Agentic Scientist` is a distributed pipeline that decomposes computational research into task drafting, idea generation, planning, sandboxed experimentation, result aggregation, baseline and ablation construction, post-hoc analysis, and report writing, with each stage run by coding agents that self-verify and a meta-controller that manages parallel research agents and enforces rubric checks. The same orchestration layer is reused across domains with different execution environments, coding harnesses, and metrics, and the system can act either as a co-scientist tool or end to end. **A paper produced with a development version in co-scientist mode was accepted for publication at ALIFE 2026**, and ablations indicate reliable autonomy depends on the cross-agent orchestration layer, not base model capability alone.

papers.title: An Initial Study of Physiological Markers for Deepfake Speech Detection
papers.abstract: Conventional deepfake speech detectors primarily target synthesis artifacts and often degrade under unseen attacks or recording conditions. Human speech, however, contains physiological markers associated with respiration, phonation, and temporal coordination arising from the speech-production system that synthesizers may not reproduce faithfully. This motivates the hypothesis that deepfake speech can be detected by identifying inconsistencies in these patterns, which we test using 36 handcrafted physiological markers organized into respiratory, vocal, and temporal categories. We evaluate the marker vectors with logistic regression and SVM classifiers on pooled English recordings. The best in-domain system achieves a 21.40% equal error rate (EER), while logistic regression achieves 32.77% on the out-of-domain dataset pair. Since the markers describe specific speech-production properties, the logistic-regression coefficients indicate whether higher marker values push the classifier toward bona fide or deepfake speech. These results provide initial evidence that physiological markers offer a useful, interpretable signal for deepfake speech detection.
papers.summary: Deepfake speech detectors keyed to synthesis artifacts degrade on unseen attacks and recording conditions, so this work tests whether genuine speech instead carries physiological signatures of respiration, phonation, and temporal coordination that synthesizers fail to reproduce. Thirty-six handcrafted markers grouped into respiratory, vocal, and temporal categories feed logistic regression and support vector machine classifiers on pooled English recordings. The best in-domain system reaches a **21.40% equal error rate (EER)**, while logistic regression reaches 32.77% on an out-of-domain dataset pair, and because each marker describes a specific production property, its regression coefficient shows which direction pushes toward genuine or synthetic speech.

papers.title: Delay Complexity Dimension: Learning with Delayed and Censored Labels
papers.abstract: We study PAC learning of binary classifiers when labels arrive after random delays and are censored beyond an observation window $W$. How many samples does this observation model require? We propose a distribution-dependent answer, the Delay Complexity Dimension (DCD). The DCD combines the VC dimension with the exact label-information rate of the observation channel. Every learner needs $\Omega(\mathrm{DCD}/\varepsilon^2)$ samples. An oracle pseudo-label ERM matches this rate on the instance family of the lower bound, up to constants and logarithmic factors. On that family the DCD is within a constant factor of the classical censored-ERM complexity, and whether the DCD rate is achievable where the two separate remains open. The theory also yields a quantization scheme under which delay information lowers the residual label variance, an expedition policy with a $(1-1/e)$ guarantee for its version-space objective, and a phenomenon with no analogue in the no-delay setting. Under a fixed collection horizon, a moderate window can strictly beat immediate labels. Experiments on synthetic data and the Criteo conversion logs support these predictions. A budget-matched test of a companion labeler-diversity prediction is reported as a negative result.
papers.summary: In settings like ad conversion tracking, labels arrive after random delays and are censored past an observation window, so standard sample-complexity theory does not say how much data a learner needs. The proposed Delay Complexity Dimension (DCD) combines the VC dimension with the exact label-information rate of the observation channel, giving a lower bound that an oracle pseudo-label empirical risk minimizer matches on the instance family used to prove it. The theory also predicts an effect with no analogue in the undelayed setting: under a fixed collection horizon, **a moderate observation window can strictly beat immediate labels**. Synthetic experiments and `Criteo` conversion logs support the predictions, while a budget-matched test of a companion labeler-diversity prediction is reported as a negative result and achievability where DCD separates from censored-ERM complexity is left open.

papers.title: Beyond Equation Search: Conjecture-Guided Discovery with SCOPE and ClosureBench
papers.abstract: Most symbolic regression methods optimize candidate equations, but improving an equation's fit does not establish whether its underlying scientific conjecture should be retained, revised, or rejected. A conjecture may admit multiple mathematical realizations, and similarly accurate equations may imply different explanations. This motivates a shift from refining individual expressions to developing and testing the conjectures that guide them. We introduce SCOPE, a framework that sustains multiple conjecture-driven research trajectories. Multiple scientist agents independently pursue conjectures through equation modeling, question formulation, and active experimentation, then exchange evidence to revise their conjectures and research directions. Their findings are consolidated into a scientific report linking models, conclusions, and evidence. Existing equation-discovery benchmarks primarily assess recovered expressions, leaving the evidence and scientific conclusions established through the investigation underexamined. We therefore introduce ClosureBench, an interactive benchmark of 60 closure-discovery tasks across five scientific domains. ClosureBench focuses on closure-discovery tasks to give equation discovery a concrete scientific purpose. Each task embeds an unknown algebraic relation in a known PDE system, where agents control experimental conditions in OpenFOAM to acquire new data for equation discovery. Beyond equation accuracy, ClosureBench proposes three metrics to evaluate the discovery process: evidence faithfulness, mechanism insight, and experimental effectiveness. Compared with diverse baselines, SCOPE achieves higher equation accuracy on both ClosureBench and a real-world scientific discovery case, while producing more accurate, reliable, and effective scientific discoveries.
papers.summary: Symbolic regression optimizes candidate equations, but a better fit says nothing about whether the scientific conjecture behind the equation should be kept, revised, or rejected, since similarly accurate expressions can imply different explanations. `SCOPE` runs multiple scientist agents that each pursue a conjecture through equation modeling, question formulation, and active experimentation, then exchange evidence to revise conjectures and consolidate findings into a report linking models, conclusions, and evidence. Its companion benchmark `ClosureBench` provides 60 closure-discovery tasks across five domains, each embedding an unknown algebraic relation in a known partial differential equation system where agents control `OpenFOAM` experiments to gather data, and scores evidence faithfulness, mechanism insight, and experimental effectiveness alongside equation accuracy. **`SCOPE` reaches higher equation accuracy than diverse baselines on both `ClosureBench` and a real-world discovery case** while producing better-supported scientific conclusions.

papers.title: Wong--Zakai Convergence and FNO Learning for Stochastic Volterra Equations
papers.abstract: This paper studies Wong--Zakai convergence and Fourier neural operator learning for stochastic Volterra integral equations (SVIEs) describing random systems with memory. A Wong--Zakai theorem establishes convergence of pathwise solutions driven by piecewise linear approximations of Brownian motion to the corresponding SVIE solution. This convergence provides a foundation for using mirror-padded Fourier neural operators to learn the solution operator mapping initial conditions and driving noise to entire solution trajectories. Numerical experiments demonstrate competitive prediction accuracy and generalization to temporal grids finer than those used for training, while assessing the influence of padding and computational cost. As a follow-up to \citet{LKP:26}, this study extends their operator-learning framework to SVIEs through separate convergence and approximation analyses tailored to convolutional memory.
papers.summary: Stochastic Volterra integral equations describe random systems whose evolution depends on their whole history, and repeatedly solving them is expensive. A Wong-Zakai theorem is proved showing that pathwise solutions driven by piecewise linear approximations of Brownian motion converge to the true solution, which justifies training mirror-padded Fourier neural operators to learn the operator mapping initial conditions and driving noise to entire solution trajectories. Numerical experiments report competitive accuracy and **generalization to temporal grids finer than those used in training**, together with an assessment of padding choices and computational cost.

papers.title: Semi-Amortized Bayesian Inference with Reusable Local Posteriors
papers.abstract: Amortized Bayesian inference uses simulations to perform Bayesian estimation when likelihoods are expensive or analytically unavailable. However, learning the full joint posterior is challenging in high-dimensional models with complex dependencies. We introduce a semi-amortized method that divides parameters into smaller blocks, and uses conditional independence to identify the information needed to infer each block. We train neural estimators for blocks whose posterior updates are computationally expensive or frequently repeated. Each estimator learns from simulations of the relevant model components to approximate the block's full conditional posterior, given the relevant observations and the values of the variables on which it depends. A Markov chain then alternates direct draws from these estimators with conventional updates of the remaining variables. Each neural update uses the current conditioning values and requires neither likelihood evaluation nor an acceptance-rejection step. Where the same conditional structure recurs, one estimator can be reused across blocks and datasets, with an output dimension determined by the block rather than the full model. We illustrate the approach in high-dimensional and computationally expensive hierarchical and spatiotemporal models.
papers.summary: Amortized Bayesian inference trains networks on simulations to replace expensive or unavailable likelihoods, but learning a full joint posterior is hard in high-dimensional models with complex dependencies. The proposed semi-amortized scheme divides parameters into blocks, uses conditional independence to identify what information each block's posterior actually needs, and trains neural estimators only for blocks whose updates are costly or frequently repeated, after which a Markov chain alternates direct draws from those estimators with conventional updates of the remaining variables. Each neural update requires **neither likelihood evaluation nor an acceptance-rejection step**, and a single estimator can be reused across blocks and datasets wherever the same conditional structure recurs, with output dimension set by the block rather than the whole model. The approach is illustrated on high-dimensional and computationally expensive hierarchical and spatiotemporal models.

papers.title: Physical Layer Anomaly Detection via Adaptive Gaussian Mixture Model
papers.abstract: Physical-layer spoofing attacks pose a critical threat to wireless localization systems by manipulating channel state information (CSI). Detecting such attacks becomes particularly challenging when the attacker and the legitimate node are spatially proximate, as their CSI characteristics become increasingly similar. To address this challenge in indoor scenarios, we propose an adaptive Gaussian mixture model (GMM)-based detection framework that learns legitimate CSI patterns and detects spatial inconsistency through statistical anomaly detection. Using a massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) experimental dataset with 64 uniform linear array (ULA) antenna and 5 mm spatial resolution, we evaluated our detector against CSI spoofing attacks with spatial displacements ranging from 50 mm to 450 mm. The adaptive GMM achieves 95-98% detection rate for displacements above 150 mm while maintaining 1% false alarm rate. We benchmark our approach against conventional GMM, local outlier factor (LOF), one-class support vector machine (SVM) and k-nearest neighbors (k-NN) classifiers, demonstrating overall superior detection performance of our proposed classifier.
papers.summary: Spoofing attacks on wireless localization forge channel state information (CSI), and they are hardest to catch when attacker and legitimate node sit close together so their channel signatures nearly coincide. The detector learns legitimate indoor CSI patterns with an adaptive Gaussian mixture model (GMM) and flags spatial inconsistency as a statistical anomaly, evaluated on a massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) measurement dataset with a 64-element uniform linear array (ULA) and 5 mm spatial resolution against displacements from 50 mm to 450 mm. For displacements above 150 mm it reaches **95-98% detection at a 1% false alarm rate**, ahead of a conventional GMM, local outlier factor (LOF), one-class support vector machine (SVM), and k-nearest neighbors baselines.

papers.title: Limits of Statistical Assurance for Embodied and Agentic AI under Adaptive Adversaries
papers.abstract: Finite safety assessments cannot exclude an adversary that preserves unattacked behavior until certification and activates afterward. We characterize this limitation for embodied and tool-use AI. An adversary that matches the complete observation law until observable, irrevocable certification and retains intervention access afterward attains $v\mathbb{E}[(n-S_0)_+]$ expected post-certification events over $n$ trials, where $v$ is the active event probability and $S_0$ the unattacked certification time. The result covers adaptive and privately randomized evaluators. Switching at certification is exactly optimal for a fixed likelihood-ratio test under memoryless, event-increasing interventions without a binding intervention budget. A positive clean-certification requirement forces linear worst-case expected excess when intervention raises event rates over an authorized deployment horizon, even if certification is deferred to the deadline. In simulated RoCo collaboration, switching yields commanded-separation violations in 34 of 36 post-certification episodes. Preregistered randomized AgentDojo trials estimate 1.98 additional security violations per four-task continuation (95% interval [1.67, 2.29]). An adversarial language-model controller infers hidden certification from noisy evaluation receipts and times intervention accordingly. With permanent revocation, a mixture likelihood-ratio monitor bounds cumulative excess above a prespecified reference rate at square-root order, up to logarithmic factors, on every sample path. A single fixed alternative can permit linear expected excess under stationary attacks. Against a controller observing the monitor's rule and statistic, live mixture monitoring reduces violations from 12.00 to 3.81 per 24 assigned task opportunities. Revocation also reduces tasks executed.
papers.summary: No finite safety assessment can rule out an adversary that behaves normally until certification is observable and irrevocable, then activates afterward. The analysis formalizes this for embodied and tool-using AI, showing such an adversary attains expected post-certification events proportional to the active event probability times the shortfall of the unattacked certification time, that switching exactly at certification is optimal for a fixed likelihood-ratio test under memoryless unbudgeted interventions, and that requiring clean certification forces linear worst-case excess over an authorized deployment horizon. Demonstrations include commanded-separation violations in 34 of 36 post-certification episodes in simulated `RoCo` collaboration, an estimated 1.98 extra security violations per four-task continuation in preregistered `AgentDojo` trials, and a language-model controller that infers hidden certification from noisy evaluation receipts to time its switch. Adding permanent revocation with a mixture likelihood-ratio monitor bounds cumulative excess at square-root order on every sample path and **reduces violations from 12.00 to 3.81 per 24 assigned task opportunities**, at the cost of fewer tasks executed.

papers.title: Virtual-Alloy Physics-Aware Semantic System for extrapolative prediction of perovskite solar cells
papers.abstract: Existing machine-learning models for perovskite solar cells struggle to predict devices made from new materials. Most treat device layers as arbitrary categorical labels and represent perovskite absorbers either through featureless composition vectors or through rigid crystal graphs that require a pre-solved unit cell. As a result, they cannot generalize to unrecorded alloys or unfamiliar cell architectures. We present the Virtual-Alloy Physics-Aware Semantic System (V-PaSS), an architecture built around the physical continuity of perovskite solid solutions. V-PaSS represents arbitrary mixed-cation, mixed-halide absorbers by interpolating relaxed crystal graphs of 23 pure $ABX_3$ endpoint compounds via Vegard's law with learned bandgap bowing. For the device stack, it couples layer sequence and cell polarity (n-i-p or p-i-n) with interfacial band offsets and encodes chemical descriptions with a scientific language model. Evaluated under an institution-grouped protocol where test devices come exclusively from unseen laboratories, an untuned default configuration of V-PaSS achieves the lowest error among fourteen tested models (2.861% MAE, a 5.2% relative reduction over a gradient-boosted baseline at 3.017%, and outperforming the best tuned benchmark at 2.912%). V-PaSS pulls furthest ahead where test devices differ most from training: reducing error by 15.7-19.0% on unseen absorber alloys, by 16.1% on mixed absorbers from new laboratories, and widening its lead over the baseline by 3.6$\times$ on devices with unobserved transport layers. Combined with tree ensembles, V-PaSS sets a new state of the art across all five benchmark splits.
papers.summary: Machine-learning models for perovskite solar cells fail on devices built from unfamiliar materials because they encode device layers as arbitrary categorical labels and absorbers as featureless composition vectors or rigid crystal graphs that need a pre-solved unit cell. `V-PaSS` instead represents arbitrary mixed-cation, mixed-halide absorbers by interpolating relaxed crystal graphs of 23 pure ABX3 endpoint compounds via Vegard's law with learned bandgap bowing, and couples layer sequence and cell polarity with interfacial band offsets plus chemical descriptions encoded by a scientific language model. Under an institution-grouped protocol where test devices come only from unseen laboratories, an untuned default configuration posts the lowest error among fourteen models at 2.861% mean absolute error, beating a gradient-boosted baseline at 3.017%. Its advantage grows with distribution shift, **cutting error by 15.7-19.0% on unseen absorber alloys** and widening its lead over the baseline 3.6 times on devices with unobserved transport layers.

papers.title: Discovering Undisclosed Concepts in LoRA Adapters for Diffusion-Based AIGC Models
papers.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has made diffusion model personalization affordable and widely shareable, but it also creates moderation risks when harmful or problematic content is not faithfully disclosed. Hence, it is desired to develop a mechanism that, given a LoRA adapter, discovers the concept it was trained to generate, so as to support downstream investigation. We characterize the target concept through the conditioning input that most clearly exposes what the LoRA has learned. Such an input should induce coherent LoRA outputs that are distinctive from those of the base model and strongly align with the learned LoRA subspace. We therefore formulate concept discovery as searching for the conditioning input that jointly maximizes output coherence, LoRA-induced distinctiveness, and subspace alignment. Even with a clear objective, however, optimizing it over an open-ended input space is prohibitively expensive, since reliable evaluation of coherence and distinctiveness requires repeated diffusion rendering. Crucially, we observe that an input need not be rendered to determine whether it is promising. Its alignment with the learned LoRA subspace provides a lightweight signal for localizing promising candidates before visual verification. Based on this insight, we develop a two-stage framework for text-to-image LoRAs. Subspace-Guided Evolutionary Search (SGES) uses render-free subspace alignment to explore candidate prompts and retain a compact shortlist, while Paired Visual Identification (PVI) renders only these candidates and compares the LoRA and base-model outputs to identify those exhibiting coherent and distinctive generation behavior. This design enables efficient and reliable discovery of previously unknown concepts encoded in LoRA adapters.
papers.summary: Shared Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters make diffusion-model personalization cheap and widely distributable, but authors need not disclose what an adapter was trained to generate, creating a moderation gap. Concept discovery is framed as searching for the conditioning input that jointly maximizes output coherence, distinctiveness from the base model, and alignment with the LoRA's learned subspace, an objective otherwise prohibitive because judging coherence requires repeated diffusion rendering. The key observation is that **subspace alignment scores a candidate prompt without rendering it**, so Subspace-Guided Evolutionary Search explores prompts render-free down to a compact shortlist and Paired Visual Identification renders only those, comparing adapter against base-model outputs to pick the coherent and distinctive ones.

papers.title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Multilingual Abstractive Summarization: A Comprehensive Study of English and Bengali
papers.abstract: Abstractive summarization remains challenging across languages, where linguistic quality and factual consistency may diverge, particularly in low-resource settings. We present a standardized zero-shot benchmark of eight closed-source and open-weight LLMs on size-matched English and Bengali XL-Sum test sets. Our evaluation combines lexical and semantic metrics with reference-free factuality verification and multidimensional LLM-as-a-Judge assessment, providing a comprehensive analysis of both surface-level quality and factual reliability in multilingual summarization. Results reveal substantial cross-lingual variation: GPT-5.6 Luna leads several English lexical metrics but does not maintain the same advantage in Bengali, where LLaMA 3.3 70B achieves the highest ROUGE and BLEU scores. Gemini 2.5 Flash obtains the highest observed Bengali factuality score. Furthermore, evaluation methods produce different model rankings, highlighting the limitations of relying on a single metric for multilingual summarization assessment. These findings demonstrate that strong English summarization performance does not necessarily transfer to Bengali and emphasize the need for comprehensive evaluation frameworks for low-resource languages.
papers.summary: Linguistic quality and factual consistency can diverge in abstractive summarization, especially for low-resource languages. A standardized zero-shot benchmark evaluates eight closed-source and open-weight large language models on size-matched English and Bengali `XL-Sum` test sets, combining lexical and semantic metrics with reference-free factuality verification and multidimensional LLM-as-a-Judge assessment. `GPT-5.6 Luna` leads several English lexical metrics but loses that edge in Bengali, where `LLaMA 3.3 70B` takes the top ROUGE and BLEU scores and `Gemini 2.5 Flash` the highest factuality score. **Different evaluation methods yield different model rankings**, which argues against trusting any single metric when assessing multilingual summarization.

papers.title: PMO-Dock: Benchmarking Docking, Specificity, and Generalization in Molecular Optimization
papers.abstract: The Practical Molecular Optimization (PMO) benchmark standardized evaluation in molecular optimization, but it is built on simple property-based oracles that do not capture structure-based drug design. As the field has moved to docking-based objectives, evaluation practice has become unstandardized, and different methods report results on different docking tasks, often without a shared protocol for fair comparison or sample-efficiency constraints. To address this, we introduce Practical Molecular Optimization for Docking (PMO-Dock), a benchmark and protocol for docking-based optimization consisting of 25 tasks covering hit generation, lead optimization, and a new specificity task requiring strong on-target binding while penalizing off-target interactions. The protocol separates model development from final evaluation: validation tasks are used for hyperparameter tuning, and test tasks are held out for final evaluation and are not used during development. Evaluation on the test tasks is done under a strict oracle budget to reflect realistic drug-discovery settings. We benchmark four diverse high-performing methods spanning different optimization paradigms, Saturn (reinforcement learning), GenMol (discrete diffusion), Genetic-guided GFlowNet, and ChemLlama (LLM-based evolutionary search). Our results show no universally best method across tasks, additional analyses of hyperparameter transfer (cross-task and cross-category) and sensitivity show that transfer is often limited and varies by method, motivating method-dependent selection strategies. This benchmark provides a concrete standard for evaluating generalization to unseen tasks and sample efficiency under a limited test-time oracle budget.
papers.summary: The Practical Molecular Optimization benchmark standardized evaluation using simple property oracles, but the field has moved to docking-based objectives where methods report on different tasks with no shared protocol or sample-efficiency constraint. `PMO-Dock` supplies 25 docking tasks covering hit generation, lead optimization, and a new specificity task that rewards strong on-target binding while penalizing off-target interactions, separating validation tasks for tuning from held-out test tasks scored under a strict oracle budget. Benchmarking `Saturn` (reinforcement learning), `GenMol` (discrete diffusion), Genetic-guided `GFlowNet`, and `ChemLlama` (language-model evolutionary search) finds **no universally best method across tasks**, and hyperparameter transfer across tasks and categories is often limited and varies by method, favoring method-specific selection strategies.

papers.title: Data Density Scaling Laws for Image Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: Current scaling law formulations suggest that increasing the number of unique samples in a dataset improves model performance, while repeated exposure to the same samples provides diminishing value. In this work, we examine this assumption for image self-distillation models. Through systematic experiments across diverse datasets, namely Maxar, SATLAS, Waymo, nuPlan, Ego4D, ImageNet, and YFCC15M, we demonstrate that the effects of sample repetition on downstream performance are non-trivial and dataset-dependent. We identify settings where repeatedly training on a smaller random subset can outperform training on a larger set of unique samples. This finding highlights a limitation of existing scaling laws. To address this gap, we propose a modified version of a Chinchilla-style scaling law that explicitly accounts for two factors: the number of unique samples and repetition per sample. This formulation provides a framework for understanding data-compute trade-offs and improves prediction in some regimes where repetition plays a central role, although its benefits are not consistent across datasets. Finally, we examine how subset selection and augmentation affect downstream performance.
papers.summary: Scaling laws assume more unique samples help while repeated exposure to the same samples yields diminishing value, an assumption tested here for image self-distillation across `Maxar`, `SATLAS`, `Waymo`, `nuPlan`, `Ego4D`, `ImageNet`, and `YFCC15M`. Repetition effects turn out to be dataset-dependent, and in some settings **repeatedly training on a smaller random subset outperforms training on a larger set of unique samples**. The authors propose a modified `Chinchilla`-style scaling law with explicit terms for unique sample count and repeats per sample, which improves prediction in repetition-dominated regimes, though they note the benefits are not consistent across datasets. Effects of subset selection and augmentation are examined as well.

papers.title: Scaling Cheap Synthetic Pretraining Improves Indoor Radio-Map Prediction
papers.abstract: Real measurements are too limited to train an accurate indoor pathloss predictor that works across a wide range of buildings. Large-scale synthetic pretraining offers a way forward, but real building layouts are also scarce, and accurate ray-tracing simulators are slow, expensive, and often proprietary. We address both problems by introducing a generator that automatically creates diverse indoor layouts and a fast, open-source approximate ray tracer that computes radio maps for them. Using this pipeline, we generate 128M synthetic samples, pretrain ResNet-101 and Swin-T encoder-decoders, and fine-tune them on high-quality benchmark data. Despite simulator mismatch, our ResNet-101 model reduces error by 15% on average relative to the best known methods across five indoor radio-map prediction tasks and improves transfer on a small real-measurement dataset. Both architectures show predictable data-scaling trends: power laws fitted on 2M-16M samples predict the mean normalized downstream RMSE at 32M-128M with 3.33% mean absolute percentage error for ResNet-101 and 7.10% for Swin-T. These results show that pretraining on large amounts of cheap simulated data can improve indoor radio-map prediction, even when real measurements and high-quality simulations are limited.
papers.summary: Indoor pathloss prediction is short of data twice over, since real measurements are scarce and so are real building layouts, while accurate ray tracers are slow, costly, and often proprietary. The pipeline generates diverse indoor layouts automatically and computes their radio maps with a fast open-source approximate ray tracer, yielding 128M synthetic samples used to pretrain `ResNet-101` and `Swin-T` encoder-decoders before fine-tuning on high-quality benchmark data. Despite simulator mismatch the `ResNet-101` model **reduces error by 15% on average across five indoor radio-map prediction tasks** relative to the best known methods and transfers better to a small real-measurement dataset. Power laws fitted on 2M-16M samples predicted mean normalized downstream error at 32M-128M to within 3.33% mean absolute percentage error for `ResNet-101` and 7.10% for `Swin-T`.

papers.title: IR-PRM+ with Previous-Utility Prediction: Constant Regret and Best-Iterate Convergence
papers.abstract: Regret matching (and its variants) and counterfactual regret minimization are central algorithms in practice for normal-form and extensive-form game solving. Yet these have historically lacked the stronger theoretical convergence guarantees available to optimistic and extra-gradient methods. Recent work introduced IREG-PRM+, a regret matching variant which does have strong theoretical convergence guarantees. However, it relies on a simultaneous, extra-gradient update. IREG-PRM+ is an instance of the more general IR-PRM framework, where empirically optimistic and alternating updates often have better performance. However, the prior extra-gradient analysis does not extend to these cases. We introduce a new approach that covers both settings. For simultaneous and alternating IR-PRM+ in finite two-player zero-sum matrix games, previous-utility prediction recovers the constant-regret and convergence-rate guarantees previously obtained with extra-gradient prediction: external regret bounded independently of T, an O(T^{-1}) average duality gap, and an O(T^{-1/2}) best-current-iterate gap. Moreover, the current duality gap vanishes and the current profile converges to the Nash equilibrium set. The key step bounds the component of consecutive strategy movement not controlled by the existing IR-PRM+ regret inequality using the relative growth of the nondecreasing regret-vector norm rho_t. Coupling this bound across the two players yields recurrences whose effective coefficient scales as 1/(rho_t^X rho_t^Y), preventing unbounded norm growth. We extend the analysis to finitely many simplex learners under a weighted Minty condition and, through the corresponding CFR variant IR-PCFR+, recover analogous guarantees for finite two-player zero-sum perfect-recall extensive-form games under the same full-reach condition as prior work.
papers.summary: Regret matching and counterfactual regret minimization (CFR) are the workhorse algorithms for solving games in practice, but their convergence guarantees have trailed those of optimistic and extra-gradient methods, and the recent `IREG-PRM+` closed that gap only for a simultaneous extra-gradient update. The authors analyze the broader `IR-PRM+` family with previous-utility prediction, covering both simultaneous and alternating updates in finite two-player zero-sum matrix games. They show **external regret bounded independently of T, an O(1/T) average duality gap, and an O(T^-1/2) best-iterate gap**, along with convergence of the current iterate to the Nash equilibrium set. The key step bounds strategy movement using the relative growth of the nondecreasing regret-vector norm, and the results extend to extensive-form games through the CFR variant `IR-PCFR+`.

papers.title: Discrete Diffusion Models are Minimax Optimal Under Sparsity
papers.abstract: Discrete diffusion models have emerged as a leading alternative to autoregressive models for generating text and other categorical data, yet their theoretical foundations remain less developed than those of their continuous counterparts. For continuous diffusion models, a prominent line of theory suggests that these models can adapt to low-dimensional structure in the data, thereby improving statistical efficiency and generalization. In this work, we investigate the discrete analogue of this phenomenon by studying the statistical rates of discrete diffusion models under sparsity assumptions. By analyzing a nonparametric estimator derived from a regularized score-entropy objective, we establish minimax-optimal rates in the sparse regime. The proposed regularization can be viewed as an adaptation of label smoothing techniques introduced for classification, and does not require the knowledge of the sparsity parameter. This shows that discrete diffusion models can adapt intrinsically to sparsity.
papers.summary: Discrete diffusion models are a leading alternative to autoregressive models for text and categorical data, but their statistical theory lags that of continuous diffusion, where adaptation to low-dimensional structure is known to improve efficiency and generalization. The authors study the discrete analogue by analyzing a nonparametric estimator derived from a regularized score-entropy objective under sparsity assumptions. They prove that **the estimator attains minimax-optimal rates in the sparse regime without knowing the sparsity parameter**, with the regularization acting like the label smoothing used in classification. The result shows discrete diffusion models adapt intrinsically to sparsity.

papers.title: Can LLMs Access their World Knowledge for Event Prediction?
papers.abstract: Recent work has questioned whether large language models (LLMs) can be useful for temporal event prediction. Despite vast pretrained world knowledge, LLMs often underperform simpler specialized models. We ask whether this knowledge is truly inaccessible, or whether current methods fail to present event prediction in a form LLMs can use. We argue for the latter and show that LLMs become effective event forecasters when the interface is designed around two choices. The first grounds each event in a natural-language description, and the second separates event semantics from the prediction space to prevent semantic bias from label associations. To test this, we introduce DescribeEvent, a benchmark of ~150K events across seven datasets and six domains with event-level descriptions. We find that capable LLMs substantially benefit from descriptions and symbolic labels, outperforming description-free variants and non-LLM baselines, while weaker models gain little. These results suggest that accessing LLM world knowledge for event prediction is an interface problem, and that event descriptions offer a practical way to elicit the knowledge LLMs already encode.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) often underperform simple specialized models on temporal event prediction despite broad world knowledge, raising the question of whether that knowledge is inaccessible or just poorly interfaced. The authors argue for the interface explanation and propose two design choices: ground each event in a natural-language description, and separate event semantics from the prediction space with symbolic labels so label associations do not bias predictions. They introduce `DescribeEvent`, a benchmark of about 150K events across seven datasets and six domains with event-level descriptions. **Capable LLMs given descriptions and symbolic labels outperform both description-free variants and non-LLM baselines**, while weaker models gain little.

papers.title: How Far Can Coding Agents Go in Visual Generation?
papers.abstract: Modern image generation largely relies on specialized generative models that leave the process of image construction implicit in learned parameters. We explore an alternative: general-purpose coding agents that construct images through executable programs. Our study of zero-shot drawing on AgentDrawBench, a 200-prompt benchmark, reveals a distinctive capability profile. Agents excel at preserving structure and satisfying precise visual constraints, achieving competitive results in domains where compositional accuracy matters more than photorealistic appearance, while remaining limited in perceptual richness. Their visual expressiveness varies with the drawing interface, and a qualitative study on reconstruction shows how procedural skills extracted from human demonstrations support different artistic media. We then examine code as an external visual language of thought: a structured, executable representation that agents can construct and inspect. We test it in visual question answering task and find reconstructed visual code retains substantial information for question answering and, in some domains, supports higher accuracy than the original image. These abilities raise a further question: do agents draw on a shared internal representation of scene content beyond a particular drawing program? We explore an internal visual language-of-thought hypothesis, in which a shared, compositionally structured representation supports visual operations across drawing languages. Cross-harness drawings and images assembled from independent single-pixel queries exhibit related layouts and tones. Agents also maintain self-generated room arrangements across viewpoints after visible drawings are removed. These results demonstrate that the coding agent would maintain a consistent and coherent world inside its imagine even before the harness gets involved and the generation starts.
papers.summary: Instead of specialized generative models that leave image construction implicit in learned weights, the authors study general-purpose coding agents that produce images by writing executable drawing programs. On `AgentDrawBench`, a 200-prompt zero-shot benchmark, **agents excel at preserving structure and satisfying precise visual constraints, competing where compositional accuracy matters more than photorealism, but remain limited in perceptual richness**, with expressiveness varying by drawing interface. Treating code as an external visual language of thought, they find that visual code reconstructed from an image retains enough information for visual question answering and in some domains yields higher accuracy than the original image. Further experiments with cross-harness drawings, images assembled from independent single-pixel queries, and room arrangements maintained across viewpoints after drawings are removed suggest agents hold a shared internal scene representation independent of any particular drawing program.

papers.title: Joint Subspace Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Decoding
papers.abstract: Sparse attention reduces the KV-cache traffic that dominates long-context LLM decoding, but practical methods largely operate at coarse granularity. Token-level selection offers finer control, yet presents two challenges: low-dimensional scoring may lose query--key structure needed for accurate ranking, while gathering scattered selected tokens can offset the resulting latency benefit. We introduce Joint Subspace Sparse Attention (JSSA) to address both challenges. For selection quality, JSSA learns a shared low-dimensional query--key subspace by minimizing token-score preservation error. We upper-bound the resulting non-convex objective with a tractable marginal objective that admits a closed-form spectral solution; direct refinement of the exact objective provides no measurable improvement in the tested settings. For execution efficiency, we develop a gather-free token-level indexed-attention kernel that supports distinct per-KV-head selections under the standard grouped-query attention (GQA) KV-cache layout. Across standard GQA, hybrid sliding-window/global attention, and Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) models, JSSA consistently remains close to full-KV accuracy while avoiding the substantial generation-length inflation and architecture-dependent failures observed with competing methods. On an NVIDIA B200 GPU, JSSA achieves up to $6.43\times$ the decoding throughput of full-KV attention at 128K context. JSSA achieves reasoning accuracy comparable to model-native DSA without model training and reaches 96--99\% of its decoding throughput even at 700B scale large models.
papers.summary: Sparse attention cuts the KV-cache traffic that dominates long-context decoding, but token-level selection faces two obstacles: low-dimensional scoring can lose the query-key structure needed for accurate ranking, and gathering scattered tokens can erase the latency gain. Joint Subspace Sparse Attention (`JSSA`) learns a shared low-dimensional query-key subspace by minimizing token-score preservation error, using a tractable upper bound with a closed-form spectral solution, and pairs it with a gather-free indexed-attention kernel that supports distinct per-head selections under the grouped-query attention (GQA) cache layout. Across GQA, hybrid sliding-window/global, and Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) models, `JSSA` stays close to full-KV accuracy while avoiding the generation-length inflation and architecture-dependent failures seen with competing methods. **On an NVIDIA B200 it reaches up to 6.43 times the decoding throughput of full-KV attention at 128K context**, and without any training it matches the reasoning accuracy of model-native `DSA` at 96 to 99 percent of its throughput even at 700B scale.

papers.title: Optimization for One, Feasibility for Most: Decoupling Optimization from Feasibility in Chance-Constrained Programs
papers.abstract: Chance-constrained stochastic programs (CCSPs) require solutions that satisfy uncertain constraints with high probability. Standard approaches either embed scenarios directly into optimization by considering sample average approximation (SAA)-based reformulations, growing prohibitively expensive and often failing to find feasible solutions; or employ conservative reformulations that guarantee feasibility but sacrifice objective quality by design. We propose ACCESS (Adaptive Chance-Constrained Exploration via Structured Sampling), a structured sampling framework that decouples optimization from feasibility evaluation. First, high-quality candidate solutions are generated by solving many inexpensive single-scenario subproblems, avoiding sampling directly in the constrained high-dimensional solution space. Second, feasibility is assessed separately via large-scale batched simulation over a massive number of scenarios, which is naturally amenable to GPU parallelism. That reduces the search from a high-dimensional solution space to a two-dimensional parameter space controlling conservatism and scenario diversity; while concentrating on candidates near the feasibility boundary, where high-quality feasible solutions lie. We also introduce a variant, ACCESS($\delta$), which provides certified feasibility guarantees with probability $1-\delta$. Experiments across three benchmark classes and five scenario distributions show that ACCESS matches or exceeds the best objective found by any method in nearly every setting, while ACCESS($\delta$) is empirically feasible on every instance. The conservative reformulations remain several percent worse in objective, and SAA is frequently infeasible while taking an order of magnitude longer on the harder benchmarks.
papers.summary: Chance-constrained stochastic programs (CCSPs) require solutions that satisfy uncertain constraints with high probability, but sample average approximation (SAA) reformulations scale poorly and often fail to find feasible points, while conservative reformulations guarantee feasibility at the cost of objective quality. `ACCESS` (Adaptive Chance-Constrained Exploration via Structured Sampling) decouples the two steps: it generates candidates by solving many cheap single-scenario subproblems, then checks feasibility with large batched GPU simulation over a massive number of scenarios, reducing the search to a two-dimensional space of conservatism and scenario diversity concentrated near the feasibility boundary. A variant, `ACCESS(δ)`, certifies feasibility with probability 1 minus δ. Across three benchmark classes and five scenario distributions, **the method matches or exceeds the best objective found by any method in nearly every setting**, while conservative reformulations stay several percent worse and SAA is frequently infeasible and an order of magnitude slower on harder instances.

papers.title: Crossing the Gender Binary: Modelling Gendered Reference in Science Fiction and General Fiction
papers.abstract: Science fiction is widely credited with unsettling gender. This article asks whether that holds at the linguistic level, in how readily gendered reference gives way to its counterpart, a neutral term, or other social category, and whether it separates the genre from general fiction. It does so by masking man/men, woman/women, and person/people across same-period science fiction and general fiction corpora and classifying RoBERTa's five likeliest substitutes by gender. Retention and displacement are permutation-tested over five resampling rounds, and the underlying sentences are read closely. Both corpora cross the gender binary in both directions, but unequally: where woman is masked, the model predicts a masculine term about twice as often as it predicts a feminine term where man is masked. Each mismatch marks a statistical surprise, a word the corpus did not expect there. Against this shared pattern, science fiction shows greater gender permeability than the general fiction corpus, placing man in feminine contexts more often than general fiction while the reverse rate holds steady. Its degendering tendency is stronger too, drawing both gendered terms toward the neutral. Beyond the binary, a masked woman also draws substitutes naming a social category and no gender far more often than a masked man does. In measuring the gender permeability of man, woman, and person in linguistic distribution and testing whether genre changes it, the study gives science fiction studies linguistic evidence for thematic claims and computational literary studies a pipeline applicable to other category vocabularies, such as race and class.
papers.summary: Science fiction is often credited with unsettling gender, and this study tests whether that shows up linguistically in how readily gendered reference gives way to its counterpart, a neutral term, or another social category. The method masks man/men, woman/women, and person/people in same-period science fiction and general fiction corpora, classifies the five likeliest `RoBERTa` substitutes by gender, and permutation-tests retention and displacement over five resampling rounds alongside close reading of the sentences. Both corpora cross the binary in both directions but unequally: **where woman is masked the model predicts a masculine term about twice as often as it predicts a feminine term where man is masked**. Science fiction shows greater permeability, placing man in feminine contexts more often and drawing both gendered terms toward the neutral, and the pipeline is offered for other category vocabularies such as race and class.

papers.title: How Many Ranks Does a Token Need? A Noise-Floor Squelch for Rank-One LoRA Experts
papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) applies every rank-one component of its update to every token, and mixture-of-experts variants replace this with a learned router that activates a fixed number of components. We argue that the number of components a token needs is a detection question with a classical answer. A token's responses to the rank-one components of a trained LoRA consist of a few large values on a Gaussian noise floor whose width matches that of an untrained adapter, and the floor carries cross-talk rather than adaptation. We introduce SQUELCH, a router-free mixture of rank-one experts that (i) soft-thresholds each token's responses at a multiple of its own robust noise level, so the active rank varies per token; (ii) chooses that multiple for each module by Stein's unbiased risk estimate, so no rank budget is specified; and (iii) replaces the resulting marginal keep-or-drop decisions by one explaining-away step on the value Gram matrix, which suppresses redundant co-active components and recruits complementary ones. SQUELCH adds no trainable parameters to LoRA. We prove that the squelch is within a logarithmic factor of the oracle input-dependent allocation, that the selected threshold is risk-consistent, and that explaining away is a descent step toward the joint sparse code whose error is controlled by the coherence of co-active components. On commonsense reasoning, knowledge, math, code, and GLUE with LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen3, and DeBERTaV3, SQUELCH improves over LoRA by 2.2--3.2 points and over the strongest mixture baseline by 0.8--1.2 points while activating 8.6 of 32 components per token on average.
papers.summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) applies every rank-one component of its update to every token, and mixture-of-experts variants instead train a router that activates a fixed number of components. The authors reframe how many components a token needs as a signal-detection problem: a token's responses to a trained LoRA's rank-one components consist of a few large values over a Gaussian noise floor whose width matches that of an untrained adapter. `SQUELCH` is a router-free mixture of rank-one experts that soft-thresholds each token's responses at a multiple of its own robust noise level, picks that multiple per module via Stein's unbiased risk estimate so no rank budget is specified, and applies one explaining-away step on the value Gram matrix to suppress redundant components, all without adding trainable parameters. On commonsense reasoning, knowledge, math, code, and `GLUE` with `LLaMA-3.1-8B`, `Qwen3`, and `DeBERTaV3`, **it improves over LoRA by 2.2 to 3.2 points and over the strongest mixture baseline by 0.8 to 1.2 points while activating 8.6 of 32 components per token on average**.

papers.title: Who Should We Listen to More? Welfare-Aware Preference Acquisition for Pluralistic Alignment
papers.abstract: Pluralistic alignment needs to accommodate diverse preferences under limited human feedback. Using AI simulators to label preference comparisons reduces annotation costs, but variation in simulation accuracy across individuals can leave some people's preferences poorly represented in training. We study how to allocate human feedback across people to construct training data for pluralistic alignment, and how this allocation affects the trained policy. To make this allocation explicit and controllable, we define a social welfare objective over individual supervision utilities that measure label quality.
