Each query's marginal welfare gain depends on its expected supervision improvement, the recipient's current utility, and application-designated priority. Welfare-Aware Preference Acquisition (WAPA) uses auxiliary reference models to estimate query gains and individual utilities, then selects queries by estimated marginal welfare gain while updating recipient utilities. We prove exact optimality of the acquisition algorithm for the estimated welfare objective under a fixed query budget and model predictions. Experiments on six Roleplay collections and four OpinionQA regions demonstrate improved supervision and controllable allocation tradeoffs. Policy training on four Roleplay collections improves preference prediction for both seen and unseen individuals. When prioritizing a designated group and poorly represented individuals, acquiring human labels for 20% of comparisons recovers 75-86% of the average predictive utility gap between policies trained entirely on AI-generated labels and entirely on ground-truth labels.
papers.summary: Pluralistic alignment must represent diverse preferences under a limited human-feedback budget, and using AI simulators to label comparisons can leave people whose preferences are simulated poorly underrepresented in training. The authors define a social welfare objective over per-person supervision utilities measuring label quality, where each query's marginal gain depends on its expected supervision improvement, the recipient's current utility, and an application-set priority. Welfare-Aware Preference Acquisition (`WAPA`) uses auxiliary reference models to estimate these quantities and greedily selects queries by estimated marginal welfare gain, with a proof of exact optimality for the estimated objective under a fixed budget. On six `Roleplay` collections and four `OpinionQA` regions it improves supervision with controllable allocation tradeoffs, and **when prioritizing a designated group and poorly represented individuals, human labels for 20 percent of comparisons recover 75 to 86 percent of the predictive-utility gap between fully AI-labeled and fully ground-truth-labeled policies**.

papers.title: Lag: A Mean-Field Optimal Policy for Online Assignment with Reusable Resources
papers.abstract:
We study online task assignment with reusable resources. This problem arises in peer reviewer assignment, skill-based call routing, rideshare matching, emergency dispatch, and crowdsourcing: Tasks arrive according to a geometric process and must be immediately assigned to servers that become temporarily busy, yielding rewards that depend on the task-server pair. The goal is to maximize long-run average reward.
  We cast the problem as a contextual restless multi-armed bandit (CRMAB). We derive an occupancy-measure LP (OCC-LP) that upper-bounds the reward of any work-conserving policy. From its dual we obtain Lag, a closed-form index policy. We introduce a scaling regime in which the number of copies of each server and the number of arrivals per step grow together. This regime yields the first deterministic fluid limit for a contextual bandit. In it, Lag is asymptotically optimal.
  Finally, we evaluate our algorithms on peer review datasets and call center routing. The Lagrangian index achieves 83-99% of the LP upper bound across all load levels. Moreover, the Lagrangian index policy significantly outperforms the natural greedy assignment scheme, improving reward by up to 12.3% on journal data and 36% on structured synthetic instances.
papers.summary: Online task assignment with reusable resources, as in peer-reviewer assignment, call routing, rideshare matching, and emergency dispatch, requires immediately assigning arriving tasks to servers that then become temporarily busy, with the goal of maximizing long-run average reward. The authors cast this as a contextual restless multi-armed bandit (CRMAB), derive an occupancy-measure linear program (`OCC-LP`) that upper-bounds any work-conserving policy, and obtain from its dual a closed-form index policy called `Lag`. In a scaling regime where server copies and arrivals per step grow together, they establish the first deterministic fluid limit for a contextual bandit and show `Lag` is asymptotically optimal. On peer review datasets and call center routing, **the index policy achieves 83 to 99 percent of the LP upper bound across all load levels** and beats greedy assignment by up to 12.3 percent on journal data and 36 percent on structured synthetic instances.

papers.title: Tracing Morphology, Semantics, and Divergence in Language Acquisition
papers.abstract: Understanding the dynamics of language acquisition in Large Language Models (LLMs) is crucial for uncovering how statistical representations evolve into structured linguistic capabilities. However, most existing studies focus primarily on fully trained models, leaving the developmental trajectory across intermediate training stages largely underexplored. In this work, we leverage intermediate checkpoints from open-source models (e.g., Pythia and OLMo) under teacher-forcing evaluation to systematically investigate language acquisition across training steps and model scales. We focus on four core characteristics: morphological structure acquisition, embedding drift, repetition dominance, and co-occurrence effects. Our findings reveal that models acquire morphological structures well before semantic embeddings stabilize. Furthermore, we show that training dataset size has a positive impact on divergence recognition, while co-occurrence during pre-training and repetition during inference have a negative impact on divergence recognition and associative link generation.
papers.summary: Most studies of how large language models (LLMs) acquire linguistic structure examine only fully trained models, leaving the developmental trajectory across training largely unexplored. The authors use intermediate checkpoints from open-source models such as `Pythia` and `OLMo` under teacher-forcing evaluation to track four characteristics across training steps and model scales: morphological structure acquisition, embedding drift, repetition dominance, and co-occurrence effects. They find that **models acquire morphological structure well before semantic embeddings stabilize**. Larger training datasets improve divergence recognition, while co-occurrence during pretraining and repetition at inference hurt both divergence recognition and associative link generation.

papers.title: Loss Curvature as a Sampling-Free Proxy for Memorization in Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Understanding the mechanism behind why diffusion models memorize their training data remains an open question in generative modeling. In this paper, we examine this question from two perspectives: (a) the model-level perspective concerning the onset of memorization in a model during training, and (b) the sample-level perspective concerning the proclivity of an individual sample to be memorized by a given model. We show that the so-called input loss curvature, or the Frobenius norm of the Hessian of the diffusion model's training loss, is an effective metric for quantifying both perspectives on memorization. In particular, we empirically demonstrate that input curvatures averaged across training and validation samples can identify when a model is likely to start regurgitating its training data when tracked over training time. However, this metric is not sufficient for measuring an individual sample's likelihood of being memorized. To address this perspective, we introduce a counterfactual definition of memorization in diffusion models, extending the analogous notion from supervised learning proposed by [Feldman, 2019]. We prove that this counterfactual memorization is controlled by the input curvature of the leave-one-out model, thus establishing a direct theoretical link between a sample's local loss landscape and its generation likelihood. We validate our derived bounds through several empirical experiments and show that input-dependent curvature provides a proxy for memorization.
papers.summary: Why diffusion models memorize training data remains open, both at the model level (when memorization begins during training) and at the sample level (which individual samples are prone to being memorized). The authors propose input loss curvature, the Frobenius norm of the Hessian of the training loss with respect to the input, as a sampling-free metric for both perspectives. Empirically, **curvature averaged over training and validation samples and tracked over training identifies when a model is about to start regurgitating its data**, though it does not by itself predict per-sample memorization. For the sample level they define counterfactual memorization for diffusion models, extending Feldman's supervised-learning notion, and prove it is controlled by the input curvature of the leave-one-out model, validating the bounds empirically.

papers.title: Graph Coarsening Enables Escaping Local Optima in Compute-Constrained Nonconvex MAX-CUT
papers.abstract: Because its binary optimization landscape contains exponentially many local optima, MAX-CUT is highly sensitive to initialization. We study Particle Polynomial Relaxation (PPR), a moment-based nonconvex continuous reformulation possessing an advantageous optimization landscape. We warm-start PPR with Combinatorial Multigrid (CMG), a spectral graph-coarsening method that produces structure-aware initial solutions in near-linear time without training data. On \texttt{t2g20} ($n=400$), benchmark instance with known exact optimum, the combined CMG+PPR pipeline reaches $97.5\%$ of optimum on average and $98.4\%$ on the best run. An extended variant with discrete local-search refinement reaches the published optimum on all sixty Biq Mac instances evaluated by a recent neural branch-and-bound method. Using a sparse CSR representation, the same approach scales to G-set instances with up to $20{,}000$ vertices reducing memory requirements by up to $3333\times$ while maintaining a consistent improvement over the CMG warm start. Gains are largest on sparse weighted graphs; on dense graphs we complement the pipeline with spectral sparsification.
papers.summary: The binary landscape of MAX-CUT has exponentially many local optima, making solvers highly sensitive to initialization. The authors warm-start Particle Polynomial Relaxation (`PPR`), a moment-based nonconvex continuous reformulation with a favorable landscape, using Combinatorial Multigrid (`CMG`), a spectral graph-coarsening method that yields structure-aware initial solutions in near-linear time with no training data. On the `t2g20` instance with a known optimum the pipeline averages 97.5 percent of optimal, and on the `Biq Mac` benchmark a variant with discrete local-search refinement **reaches the published optimum on all sixty instances** evaluated by a recent neural branch-and-bound method. With a sparse CSR representation the approach scales to `G-set` graphs of up to 20,000 vertices while cutting memory by up to 3333 times, with the largest gains on sparse weighted graphs and spectral sparsification added for dense ones.

papers.title: What Information Buys in Active Inference
papers.abstract: Information-theoretic exploration is of primary interest in methodological studies of reinforcement learning (RL) and computational cognitive neuroscience, while the established RL theory builds regret guarantees on confidence sets. This situation leaves open the conditions under which the information-driven exploration found in nature is more advantageous than the exploration of the established RL theory. We put the state-of-the-art methods of these two paradigms, Active Inference (AIF) and Bayes-UCBVI, on an equal footing: both act through the same state abstraction of a tabular MDP with $S$ states, and their greedy forms differ only in the exploration term. We find that AIF's information gain decays too fast to serve as a confidence width, locking greedy agents that explore by it out of the optimal action. Calibrating the information gain by a square root yields calibrated AIF, which attains regret of order $\sqrt T$ for an exact abstraction, but no better guarantee than Bayes-UCBVI for a fixed reward. When an adversary chooses rewards from the agent's data, Bayes-UCBVI's value-specific widths lock out, whereas calibrated AIF pays a factor $\sqrt S$, which no goal-memoryless agent avoids on some MDP whose start states the adversary also chooses. Calibrated information gain thus acts as a reward-agnostic $\ell_1$ confidence set, preferable to value-specific widths when rewards are chosen from the agent's data, not when they are fixed.
papers.summary: Information-theoretic exploration drives active inference in computational neuroscience, while reinforcement learning (RL) theory builds regret guarantees on confidence sets, and it has been unclear when the former is advantageous. The authors put Active Inference (`AIF`) and `Bayes-UCBVI` on equal footing in a tabular MDP with S states, with greedy forms differing only in their exploration term. They find that the AIF information gain decays too fast to serve as a confidence width, locking greedy agents out of the optimal action, but **calibrating it by a square root yields regret of order square root of T for an exact abstraction**, matching but not beating `Bayes-UCBVI` for fixed rewards. When an adversary chooses rewards from the agent's data, the value-specific widths of `Bayes-UCBVI` lock out while calibrated AIF pays only a factor of square root of S, so calibrated information gain acts as a reward-agnostic L1 confidence set.

papers.title: Pre-Trained Language Models as Zero-Shot Tools for Social Science Research
papers.abstract: Record linkage and demographic inference from names are routine demands in social science. Most approaches to these problems require labeled training data that are difficult or costly to acquire. I show that pre-trained language models perform both tasks accurately without requiring task-specific training. For record linkage, I introduce EnsembleLink, an algorithm that uses pre-trained embeddings alongside string-based scorers to retrieve a short list of candidates and then identify the likeliest matches. EnsembleLink matches or exceeds the performance of most prior approaches while generalizing across scripts and formats that those methods are unable to handle. For ethnicity inference from names, I show that large language models (LLMs) achieve up to 83.8% accuracy on U.S. voter files, compared to 78.0% for name-supplemented BISG. Open-weight models offer reproducible implementations that approach these models in accuracy. Moreover, LLMs are able to infer group membership for religious, caste-based, and other ethnic group categories outside of the United States, and reduce bias in downstream estimates of geographic racial gaps. Where pre-training encodes the world knowledge required by each task, task-specific labels add less information.
papers.summary: Record linkage and demographic inference from names are routine social-science tasks that usually require costly labeled training data. The author shows pre-trained language models handle both without task-specific training: `EnsembleLink` combines pre-trained embeddings with string-based scorers to retrieve a candidate shortlist and pick the likeliest matches, matching or exceeding most prior approaches while generalizing across scripts and formats they cannot handle. For ethnicity inference from names, **large language models (LLMs) reach up to 83.8 percent accuracy on US voter files**, compared with 78.0 percent for name-supplemented `BISG`, and open-weight models approach that accuracy with reproducible implementations. LLMs also infer religious, caste-based, and other group memberships outside the United States and reduce bias in downstream estimates of geographic racial gaps.

papers.title: Smart Alone, Blind Together: Why Accuracy Fails to CertifyTheory of Mind in Multi-Agent Teams
papers.abstract: Coordinators that act on what they infer about teammates are usually certified by the accuracy of those inferences. We argue that accuracy is the wrong certificate, for two reasons. First, the accuracy needed to act depends on what a wrong action costs, so the bar belongs to the deployment, not the module. Second, a module's errors are rarely independent, and dependence has a sign: positively associated errors help where their damage overlaps and hurt where it compounds, so an accuracy threshold fails in a predictable direction, and once wrong beliefs interact and can do harm, no rule based on accuracy is right for every module. We test these predictions in task assignment, Level-Based Foraging and Hanabi, with injected errors, trained and Bayesian modules and five language models, and in human judgments. Accuracy fails in both directions, approving harmful language-model deployments in Hanabi, where shared errors compound, and rejecting beneficial ones in task assignment, where costly errors are rare. In our tasks it also buys far less redundancy than independence predicts: from GPT-5.4-mini to Claude Opus 5.5, error on teammates the models have evidence about falls from 32% to 11%, but the chance that all three observers misread one falls only from 16% to 9% (independence: 3.4% to 0.15%). We propose certifying the deployment, with a Blind-Spot Gate that prices error costs, pairwise interactions and measured dependence without deploying the module. On held-out data from the cells it was developed on, it makes no significant false approval in 20 splits (accuracy: 3.2 per split), and in preregistered tests on modules it was not developed on, it recovers what accuracy rejects (seven classifiers: regret 0.004 against 0.479) and catches what accuracy approves (a Bayesian module: significant false approvals in 17 of 20 splits for accuracy, 1 for the gate).
papers.summary: Coordinators that act on inferences about teammates are usually certified by the accuracy of those inferences, but the authors argue accuracy is the wrong certificate: the accuracy needed depends on what a wrong action costs in deployment, and correlated errors help where their damage overlaps and hurt where it compounds. They test this in task assignment, `Level-Based Foraging`, and `Hanabi` with injected errors, trained and Bayesian modules, five language models, and human judgments, finding that accuracy fails in both directions by approving harmful language-model deployments in `Hanabi` and rejecting beneficial ones in task assignment. Stronger models also buy less redundancy than independence predicts: moving from `GPT-5.4-mini` to `Claude Opus 5.5` cuts per-observer error on evidenced teammates from 32 to 11 percent, **yet the chance that all three observers misread the same teammate falls only from 16 to 9 percent**, against 3.4 to 0.15 percent under independence. The proposed `Blind-Spot Gate` prices error costs, pairwise interactions, and measured dependence without deploying the module, makes no significant false approvals on held-out splits, and in preregistered tests recovers what accuracy rejects and catches what accuracy approves.

papers.title: Deep Generative Models for Phylogenetic Inference with Complex Evolutionary Processes
papers.abstract: Inference of phylogenetic trees from sequences plays a central role in understanding evolutionary relationships, with applications ranging from tracking pathogen spread to reconstructing the history of life. Conventionally, practitioners obtain posteriors over trees using likelihood-based methods like MCMC. However, likelihoods are only available for simple evolutionary models with restrictive assumptions. For realistic evolutionary models, inference using conventional methods is prohibitively expensive, inaccurate, or even impossible. In practice, practitioners settle for using as flexible a conventional method as possible, even though they expect it is misspecified. In principle, we could use simulation-based inference: simulate tree and sequence data from an evolutionary model and train a neural network to predict the posterior over trees given sequences. However it is a mathematical challenge to represent and train complex posterior distributions over trees. Here we present a flexible family of conditional generative models over trees. Our models iteratively build trees using three natural paradigms -- top-down, middle-out, or bottom-up -- and are trained using a discrete diffusion framework. For real and synthetic datasets of up to $65$ taxa and $>10^5$ tokens, our models recover MCMC posteriors much more accurately than the previous state-of-the-art simulation-based method Phyloformer 2. Finally, we compare to IQ-Tree, a popular flexible-but-misspecified conventional method. Our models match its tree estimates on simple data, but on more realistic data, our method is reliably more accurate.
papers.summary: Phylogenetic tree inference from sequences usually relies on likelihood-based MCMC, but likelihoods exist only for simple evolutionary models, so practitioners settle for flexible but misspecified conventional methods on realistic data. Simulation-based inference could sidestep this by training a neural network on simulated trees and sequences, but representing and training complex posteriors over trees is mathematically difficult. The authors present a family of conditional generative models that build trees iteratively in top-down, middle-out, or bottom-up order and are trained with a discrete diffusion framework. On real and synthetic datasets of up to 65 taxa and over 100,000 tokens, **the models recover MCMC posteriors far more accurately than the previous simulation-based state of the art**, `Phyloformer 2`, and they match `IQ-Tree` on simple data while being reliably more accurate on realistic data.

papers.title: Conformalized Physics-Informed Weak Regression for Parameter Estimation in Epidemic Models
papers.abstract: Compartment models of infectious diseases are often linear in coefficients that are physical parameters or products or ratios of them. We exploit this with closed-form least squares and equip the estimates with distribution-free uncertainty. Physics-informed regression (PIR) fits the parameters to finite-difference derivatives of the data; we introduce physics-informed weak regression (PIWR), which integrates the model in time instead, needs no derivatives of the data, estimates the initial state jointly and is high-order accurate. To quantify uncertainty we wrap both estimators in split conformal prediction, with a calibration population generated by the physics-based model itself, giving simultaneous intervals for all parameters with a finite-sample coverage guarantee. A residual-adaptive factor, computed without ground truth, scales the intervals to each data set (PIWR-RACC). On the eleven benchmark models of disease-informed neural networks (DINNs), PIWR or PIR-FD6 is one to four orders of magnitude more accurate than the reported DINN results wherever the sampling resolves the dynamics, in about a millisecond per fit instead of minutes to hours of training, and the 90% intervals achieve 87-92% coverage in all 88 settings. On the S3I3R model of the original PIR study, PIWR lowers the reported PIR errors by about three orders of magnitude. On real data from the 1978 boarding-school influenza outbreak, a variable-projection variant gives calibrated 95% intervals that overlap those of a Bayesian analysis. On a time-varying transmission benchmark, a B-spline expansion of beta(t) keeps PIR and PIWR linear; they are more accurate than physics-informed neural networks in three of four cases and comparable in the noisiest, with simultaneous bands for beta(t). The complete conformal calibration takes less than two minutes for every benchmark.
papers.summary: Compartment models of infectious disease are often linear in coefficients that are physical parameters or their products and ratios, which allows closed-form least-squares estimation. Physics-informed regression (PIR) fits parameters to finite-difference derivatives of the data, whereas the proposed physics-informed weak regression (PIWR) integrates the model in time instead, needs no data derivatives, jointly estimates the initial state, and is high-order accurate. Both estimators are wrapped in split conformal prediction with a calibration population generated by the physics model itself, giving simultaneous parameter intervals with a finite-sample coverage guarantee, plus a residual-adaptive scaling factor (`PIWR-RACC`) computed without ground truth. On the eleven benchmark models of disease-informed neural networks (DINNs), `PIWR` or `PIR-FD6` is **one to four orders of magnitude more accurate than the reported DINN results, in about a millisecond per fit rather than minutes to hours of training**, with 90 percent intervals achieving 87 to 92 percent coverage across all 88 settings.

papers.title: How Inner Optimizers Shape Replica Scaling
papers.abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) across geographically distributed and poorly interconnected compute pools or data centers has become a topic of significant interest. This has led to increased study of local optimization methods such as DiLoco for LLMs, especially those that use local (or inner) adaptive or preconditioned optimizers, which are critical for high-performance LLM training. However, a central challenge remains: it is well known that increasing the number of model replicas (replica scaling) while fixing the total training budget leads to monotonically decreasing performance. Existing work has empirically demonstrated that the choice of inner optimizer (Muon v.s. AdamW) can significantly improve this trend, but offers only limited explanation of the performance difference. In this work, we consider a range of inner-optimizers and identify two important factors that impact replica scaling: (1) the covariance structure of the pseudo-gradients and (2) the impact of batch size on the pseudogradient's noise scale. Based on these insights, we theoretically and empirically demonstrate that whitening-based pre-conditioning is a powerful inner-optimizer desideratum. Our empirical evaluation extends the results to reveal that whitening-based inner-optimizers achieve strong replica scaling (for 8-96 replicas), with performance relative to DP improving as parameters and data are scaled.
papers.summary: Training large language models (LLMs) across poorly connected compute pools has driven interest in local optimization methods such as `DiLoco`, but increasing the number of model replicas at a fixed training budget monotonically degrades performance, and prior work only showed empirically that the inner optimizer (`Muon` versus `AdamW`) changes this trend. The authors study a range of inner optimizers and identify two factors governing replica scaling: the covariance structure of the pseudo-gradients and how batch size affects the pseudo-gradient noise scale. They argue theoretically and empirically that **whitening-based preconditioning is a key inner-optimizer property for strong replica scaling**, with whitening-based optimizers scaling well from 8 to 96 replicas and their performance relative to the `DP` baseline improving as parameters and data grow.

papers.title: Revisiting Generative vs. Dense Retrieval: A Static Value Prior Reverses the Gap
papers.abstract: Generative retrieval (GR) has emerged as a strong candidate generator for sequential recommendation as language models and semantic-item identifiers have improved. However, GR is not a uniformly stronger replacement of dense retrieval (DR) in online retail candidate generation. We examine their differences on two Amazon Toys datasets under different metrics. GR leads on best relevant item value among users both methods cover, while DR leads on exact-target recall and relevant value across the ranked list. With deep analysis, we find that popularity contributes the most to GR's measured value lead. Adding the same static item value to DR in one reranking step reverses this lead and keeps recall above GR. Finally, on an industrial-scale internal e-commerce dataset with LLM-judged relevance, we show that a 14B SID-LLM still underperforms a $47\times$ smaller dense encoder.
papers.summary: Generative retrieval (GR) with semantic item identifiers has become a strong candidate generator for sequential recommendation, but it is not uniformly better than dense retrieval (DR) for online retail. On two `Amazon Toys` datasets, GR leads on the best relevant item value among users both methods cover, while DR leads on exact-target recall and relevant value across the ranked list. Analysis attributes most of GR's value lead to popularity, and **adding the same static item value to DR in a single reranking step reverses that lead while keeping recall above GR**. On an industrial-scale internal e-commerce dataset with LLM-judged relevance, a 14B `SID-LLM` still underperforms a dense encoder 47 times smaller.

papers.title: Theoretical and Practical Advances in Hierarchical Bayesian Deep Learning Methodology
papers.abstract: Reliable uncertainty quantification remains an important challenge in AI. Hierarchical Bayesian methods provide a principled framework for this by representing unknown quantities through posterior distributions. Joint inference of neural-network parameters and prior hyperparameters is challenging for conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods due to strong dependencies. In this work, we introduce the multilevel particle marginal Metropolis-Hastings (MLPMMH) method, which combines pseudo-marginal inference for the hyperparameters with coupled sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) across hierarchy of network-width truncations for conditional parameter inference. The hierarchy is induced by a trace-class neural network (TNN) prior with width-dependent decay, motivated empirically by the compressible structure observed in trained neural-network parameters. Under standard multilevel coupling assumptions, we establish that MLPMMH achieves mean-square error (MSE) $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^2)$ at expected computational cost $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$, and verify the predicted rate on a Bayesian regression problem. To address larger-scale applications, we further introduce S-MLPMMH, a practical approximation that replaces the exact sampling components with a PCA-based hierarchy and scalable Bayesian Monte Carlo. Experiments on MNIST demonstrate competitive predictive performance and uncertainty quantification while exploiting the parallel structure of the approximation. Software has been made publicly available at https://github.com/submission-code-anon/mlpmmh-anon.
papers.summary: Jointly inferring neural-network parameters and prior hyperparameters with Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) is hard because the two are strongly dependent, which limits reliable uncertainty quantification. The multilevel particle marginal Metropolis-Hastings (`MLPMMH`) method combines pseudo-marginal inference for the hyperparameters with coupled sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) across a hierarchy of network-width truncations, where the hierarchy is induced by a trace-class neural network (`TNN`) prior whose weights decay with width, motivated by the compressible structure seen in trained networks. Under standard multilevel coupling assumptions, the method achieves **mean-square error of O(ε²) at expected computational cost O(ε⁻²)**, a rate verified on a Bayesian regression problem. A practical approximation, `S-MLPMMH`, replaces the exact sampling components with a PCA-based hierarchy and scalable Bayesian Monte Carlo, and delivers competitive predictive performance and uncertainty quantification on `MNIST` while exploiting the parallel structure of the approximation.

papers.title: Backpropagating Verifier Rewards Through Continuous Flow Language Models
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has substantially improved the reasoning of autoregressive and discrete-diffusion language models. Language models that generate continuous token embeddings are emerging as a strong alternative, but RL post-training for them remains understudied. We propose \method{}, a post-training framework for continuous flow language models. Such a model denoises token embeddings over multiple steps and decodes them into discrete tokens only at the last step. To obtain pathwise gradients, which backpropagate through continuous actions and have much lower variance than REINFORCE, we introduce a critic that estimates the value of intermediate token embeddings, bypassing the non-differentiable decoding step. The critic must also keep track of the value function as the policy changes; to this end, we design a critic that predicts a value from every token representation and improves policy optimization. Across four reasoning tasks, \method{} reliably improves a continuous flow language model through RL post-training and outperforms baseline methods of the same type.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has improved reasoning in autoregressive and discrete-diffusion language models, but it remains understudied for models that generate continuous token embeddings and decode them into discrete tokens only at the final denoising step. The proposed post-training framework obtains pathwise gradients, which backpropagate through continuous actions with far lower variance than REINFORCE, by introducing a critic that estimates the value of intermediate token embeddings and thereby bypasses the non-differentiable decoding step. Because the critic must track the value function as the policy changes, it is designed to predict a value from every token representation, which also improves policy optimization. **Across four reasoning tasks, the method reliably improves a continuous flow language model through RL post-training and outperforms baseline methods of the same type.**

papers.title: Beyond Aggregate Accuracy: Item-Level Transitions in Prompt Optimization
papers.abstract: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) uses feedback from model responses to improve prompts automatically. However, its effectiveness is usually measured through overall scores, which do not reveal which questions become correct, which previously correct answers become wrong, or whether improvements extend to unseen questions. We introduce Reflective Feedback-Driven Prompt Optimization (RFDPO), a tool that tracks recoveries (incorrect to correct), regressions (correct to incorrect), and churn (all changed outcomes). RFDPO uses this feedback to guide subsequent revisions and records prompt changes throughout optimization. We evaluate RFDPO across five benchmarks covering law, knowledge, instruction following, mathematics, and privacy, using GPT-5 as the optimizer and GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4.1 Mini as solvers. Our results show that overall accuracy can hide substantial changes: in five of nine configurations, churn was at least five times the absolute net change, and a single-item net change concealed up to 17 changed outcomes. Average validation gains were 7.9 percentage points, compared with 5.2 points on held-out tests. In a controlled ablation on LegalBench-Hearsay, item-level feedback reduced churn by 40% ($p=0.024$) while maintaining similar net gains. These findings motivate reporting recovery, regression, churn, and performance on unseen data alongside overall accuracy.
papers.summary: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) is usually judged by overall accuracy, which does not reveal which questions become correct, which previously correct answers break, or whether gains carry over to unseen questions. Reflective Feedback-Driven Prompt Optimization (`RFDPO`) tracks recoveries from incorrect to correct, regressions from correct to incorrect, and churn across all changed outcomes, uses that item-level feedback to guide subsequent revisions, and records every prompt change. Evaluated on five benchmarks covering law, knowledge, instruction following, mathematics, and privacy with `GPT-5` as the optimizer and `GPT-4o-mini` and `GPT-4.1 Mini` as solvers, **churn was at least five times the absolute net change in five of nine configurations**, a single-item net change concealed up to 17 changed outcomes, and average validation gains of 7.9 percentage points fell to 5.2 points on held-out tests. A controlled ablation on `LegalBench-Hearsay` showed item-level feedback reduced churn by 40% at similar net gain, motivating reporting of recovery, regression, churn, and held-out performance alongside overall accuracy.

papers.title: Similar Models, Broken Odds: Where Luce's Axiom Fails in Chatbot Arena
papers.abstract: Chatbot Arena ranks language models with the Bradley-Terry model, which gives each model one score and so assumes Luce's choice axiom. Choice theory predicts where this fails: near-copies are told apart more decisively than their scores imply. On 1.8 million Arena votes, votes between versions of one model are 1.37 times as decisive as Bradley-Terry predicts, between sizes of one generation 1.26 times and between models of one lab 1.12 times; a release a year later gives consistent multipliers, and the effect survives alternative tie treatments, prompt subsets and topics, and timing checks. How alike two models' answers are worded and formatted tracks the effect. A correction with four to six parameters predicts held-out votes better than Bradley-Terry and than models with hundreds of parameters, mostly by modelling ties; frozen and carried to new releases in a test fixed in advance, its gains are concentrated in ties, and better head-to-head odds are not established. The leaderboard order barely moves. With language-model judges and three-answer menus, a near-copy takes votes mostly from its twin when choices are pooled over prompts (log-odds shift +0.10, 95% interval 0.05 to 0.16); within a prompt the shift is smaller and clear for two of four judges.
papers.summary: `Chatbot Arena` ranks language models with the `Bradley-Terry` model, which gives each model a single score and therefore assumes Luce's choice axiom, and choice theory predicts that axiom should fail for near-copies, which voters tell apart more decisively than their scores imply. On 1.8 million Arena votes, **matchups between versions of one model are 1.37 times as decisive as Bradley-Terry predicts**, with multipliers of 1.26 between sizes of one generation and 1.12 between models from one lab, and the effect holds across tie treatments, prompt subsets, topics, timing checks, and a data release a year later. Similarity in how two models word and format their answers tracks the effect, and a correction with four to six parameters predicts held-out votes better than Bradley-Terry and than models with hundreds of parameters, mostly by modelling ties, while the leaderboard order barely moves. With language-model judges and three-answer menus, a near-copy takes votes mostly from its twin when choices are pooled over prompts, with a smaller within-prompt shift that is clear for two of four judges.

papers.title: GroundGUI: GUI Grounding by High-Quality Data and Distillation-to-Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Constructing robust GUI agents relies on multimodal visual grounding: the ability to precisely map natural language intents to actionable on-screen components. Despite abundant desktop, web, and mobile benchmarks, high-fidelity resources tailored for diverse environments are surprisingly scarce. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Screen Referring Grounding Dataset (ScreenRef), a comprehensive GUI grounding dataset consisting of GUI screenshots paired with natural language referring expressions and box or point annotations. Spanning desktop, web, and mobile domains, ScreenRef comprises 586K screenshots and over 633K referring expression instances, covering tasks such as text recognition, visual matching, spatial understanding, and refusal scenarios. To boost the model's grounding performance, we propose the Distillation-to-Reinforcement Learning (D2RL) method to address the limited generalization of supervised fine-tuning and the sparse reward problem in reinforcement learning. Utilizing ScreenRef, we train Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct via sequential SFT and D2RL training, yielding GroundGUI-8B. GroundGUI-8B achieves 95.2% on ScreenSpot-V2, 63.9% on ScreenSpot-Pro, 65.4% on OSWorld-G, 86.8% on MMBench-GUI L2, and 38.3% on UI-Vision. Among 8B-scale models, it produces substantial gains over models trained on open-source datasets, with performance comparable or even superior to models trained on closed-source data. Code, models, and datasets are available at https://github.com/PrentisAI/GroundGUI.
papers.summary: Robust GUI agents depend on visual grounding, the ability to map natural-language intents to actionable on-screen components, yet high-fidelity grounding data spanning desktop, web, and mobile environments is scarce. The Screen Referring Grounding Dataset (`ScreenRef`) supplies 586K screenshots and over 633K referring-expression instances with box or point annotations, covering text recognition, visual matching, spatial understanding, and refusal scenarios. A Distillation-to-Reinforcement Learning (`D2RL`) method addresses the limited generalization of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and the sparse-reward problem in reinforcement learning, and training `Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct` with SFT followed by D2RL on ScreenRef yields `GroundGUI-8B`. The model reaches **95.2% on `ScreenSpot-V2`**, 63.9% on `ScreenSpot-Pro`, 65.4% on `OSWorld-G`, 86.8% on `MMBench-GUI` L2, and 38.3% on `UI-Vision`, substantially outperforming 8B-scale models trained on open-source data and matching or exceeding those trained on closed-source data.

papers.title: Contextual Credit Policy Optimization
papers.abstract: Group-based reinforcement learning enables large language model agents to learn from sparse outcome rewards in long-horizon tasks. Recent methods derive step-level credit by comparing observation-matched experiences across trajectories. However, identical observations can occur in different contexts, and matched peers are not equally informative for a given decision. Moreover, favorable terminal outcomes can obscure redundant actions or detours within successful trajectories. To address these two challenges, we propose Contextual Credit Policy Optimization (CCPO). For the first, CCPO weights observation-matched peers from other trajectories by contextual similarity, computed from frozen LLM representations and accumulated trajectory statistics, allowing peers from similar contexts to contribute more to a step's baseline. For the second, CCPO pairs historical credit, which compares the realized return against the weighted peer baseline, with future credit, which measures the change in contextual outcome value over a short realized continuation. A step is thus credited for the progress it makes, not only for its trajectory's eventual outcome. Both credits are computed in hindsight from rollouts already collected for training, enabling CCPO to address these challenges without an auxiliary value critic. Across two Qwen2.5-Instruct backbones (1.5B and 7B), CCPO achieves up to 97.4% success on ALFWorld and 79.4% on WebShop and outperforms GRPO by up to 21.6 and 18.5 points. Ablations show that contextual weighting outperforms uniform weighting, and that historical and future credit serve as complementary learning signals.
papers.summary: Group-based reinforcement learning lets large language model (LLM) agents learn from sparse outcome rewards on long-horizon tasks, and recent methods derive step-level credit by comparing experiences that share an observation across trajectories, but identical observations can occur in different contexts, and a favorable final outcome can hide redundant actions or detours inside a successful trajectory. Contextual Credit Policy Optimization (`CCPO`) weights observation-matched peers from other trajectories by contextual similarity computed from frozen LLM representations and accumulated trajectory statistics, and pairs a historical credit, which compares the realized return against that weighted peer baseline, with a future credit that measures the change in contextual outcome value over a short realized continuation, so a step is credited for the progress it makes. Both credits are computed in hindsight from rollouts already collected for training, avoiding an auxiliary value critic. On `Qwen2.5-Instruct` backbones at 1.5B and 7B, CCPO reaches **97.4% success on `ALFWorld` and 79.4% on `WebShop`, outperforming `GRPO` by up to 21.6 and 18.5 points**, with ablations showing contextual weighting beats uniform weighting and that historical and future credit are complementary signals.

papers.title: Neural Supervised Clustering for Learning Individualized Treatment Rules with Many Treatments
papers.abstract: Learning an individualized treatment rule (ITR) with many treatments requires estimating treatment-specific effects from limited observations per arm. Treatments with similar conditional responses can share information, but linear contrast models may miss nonlinear heterogeneity. We propose nonlinear supervised clustering fusion (NSCF), a neural Q-learning framework with a shared nonlinear covariate representation and low-dimensional treatment embeddings. Pairwise fusion groups treatments with similar learned contrasts, yielding an ITR and an interpretable partition. An alternating algorithm combines neural training, embedding fusion, validation-based partition selection, and unpenalized grouped refitting. NSCF lowers regret relative to a strong neural reference in nonlinear exact-sharing simulations; perturbations characterize the limits of hard sharing. In a melanoma xenograft application, NSCF improves average policy value over the neural reference. These results support nonlinear representation learning with supervised treatment fusion when treatment effects exhibit shared structure.
papers.summary: Learning an individualized treatment rule (ITR) with many treatments requires estimating treatment-specific effects from few observations per arm, and while similar treatments could share information, linear contrast models can miss nonlinear heterogeneity. Nonlinear supervised clustering fusion (`NSCF`) is a neural Q-learning framework with a shared nonlinear covariate representation and low-dimensional treatment embeddings, in which pairwise fusion groups treatments with similar learned contrasts to yield both a treatment rule and an interpretable partition. An alternating algorithm combines neural training, embedding fusion, validation-based partition selection, and unpenalized grouped refitting. **NSCF lowers regret relative to a strong neural reference in nonlinear exact-sharing simulations** and improves average policy value in a melanoma xenograft application, while perturbation experiments characterize the limits of hard sharing.

papers.title: Towards a Data-Centric Understanding of Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have been widely applied in embodied agents and robotics for vision tasks. However, MLLMs suffer from limitations in spatial reasoning and perception. Post-training techniques have shown promise for improving these capabilities; yet, there are limited data-driven surveys of such approaches. In this survey, we consider approaches to fine-tuning pretrained MLLMs for spatial reasoning tasks, ranging from supervised to reinforcement learning, with an emphasis on the datasets used. We investigate themes of dataset construction, data modality and annotation, and evaluation of the resulting models. Based on these themes, we categorize research into three groups: dataset design, dataset construction and evaluation. We find four main methods for constructing fixed spatial annotations: rules and templates, LLM prompting, procedural generation, and human-in-the-loop. We also observe substantial variation in evaluation approaches, including different scoring methods, tolerance metrics, and benchmark types. Finally, we identify opportunities for future research in unified dynamic annotation, efficient spatial reasoning, standardization of evaluation, expanded spatial range, and human-centered spatial interactions.
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are widely deployed in embodied agents and robotics but remain limited in spatial reasoning and perception, and post-training approaches to fix this have not been surveyed from a data-centric perspective. The survey covers supervised and reinforcement-learning fine-tuning of pretrained MLLMs for spatial reasoning tasks with an emphasis on the datasets used, organizing the literature into dataset design, dataset construction, and evaluation. **It identifies four main methods for constructing fixed spatial annotations: rules and templates, LLM prompting, procedural generation, and human-in-the-loop**, and documents substantial variation in evaluation, including different scoring methods, tolerance metrics, and benchmark types. Open opportunities include unified dynamic annotation, efficient spatial reasoning, standardized evaluation, expanded spatial range, and human-centered spatial interactions.

papers.title: From Copying to Composition: How Language Models Develop In-Context Learning
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) allows language models to adapt their behavior from instructions and demonstrations in a prompt, but accuracy alone does not reveal how contextual information controls their predictions. We study the acquisition and trainability of ICL with a controlled diagnostic that separates copying a nearby demonstration from integrating information across the prompt. Across 17 models, about a third prefer the copied answer, a few are undecided, and the rest prefer the rule-consistent answer, which goes with higher accuracy and with control by the requested value rather than the closest conflicting example. Checkpoint analyses show that models begin prioritizing task-relevant prompt tokens over conflicting examples long before their accuracy improves beyond chance level. In matched training experiments, synthetic documents that define endings and then query them shift models toward compositional responses on the controlled diagnostic, whereas fine-tuning on definition exercises built from rewritten real documents improves accuracy when prompts reassign label meanings. The results suggest that ICL is not acquired as a single, uniform capability. Instead, prompt control, answer preference, construction without candidates, and transfer can develop along distinct trajectories.
papers.summary: In-context learning (ICL) lets language models adapt their behavior from instructions and demonstrations in a prompt, but accuracy alone does not reveal how contextual information actually controls predictions. A controlled diagnostic separates copying a nearby demonstration from integrating information across the prompt, and **across 17 models about a third prefer the copied answer**, a few are undecided, and the rest prefer the rule-consistent answer, which goes with higher accuracy and with control by the requested value rather than the closest conflicting example. Checkpoint analyses show models begin prioritizing task-relevant prompt tokens over conflicting examples long before their accuracy rises above chance. In matched training experiments, synthetic documents that define endings and then query them shift models toward compositional responses on the diagnostic, while fine-tuning on definition exercises built from rewritten real documents improves accuracy when prompts reassign label meanings, suggesting that prompt control, answer preference, construction without candidates, and transfer develop along distinct trajectories rather than as one uniform capability.

papers.title: Genesis Steering: Better Activation Steering Through Training Data
papers.abstract: Activation steering controls large language models at inference time, but its effectiveness depends on the choice of reference data. We introduce genesis steering, which derives a genesis vector from contrastive examples in the model's own fine-tuning data. When these data are unavailable, we draw on the membership inference literature to identify likely training examples and construct a proxy dataset. We establish two theoretical results on optimal displacement to the decision boundary and reduced proxy-estimation bias. We evaluate genesis steering and membership-based proxy construction on T\"ulu-3-8B, whose fine-tuning data are publicly available, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as a control. We find that safety data from T\"ulu-3-8B's training mixture yield stronger steering than external datasets on both models. On T\"ulu-3-8B, membership scores largely agree in identifying training examples, and vectors built from top-ranked examples achieve competitive performance against random subsets of the same size. In contrast, the results on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct hint that a MIA method will only have a positive effect if the mean direction shift with MIA-filtered in-distribution data is much less severe than the direction shift with OoD data.
papers.summary: Activation steering controls large language models at inference time, but its effectiveness depends heavily on the reference data used to build the steering vector. Genesis steering derives a genesis vector from contrastive examples in the model's own fine-tuning data, and when that data is unavailable it borrows from the membership inference attack (MIA) literature to identify likely training examples and construct a proxy dataset, supported by two theoretical results on optimal displacement to the decision boundary and reduced proxy-estimation bias. On `Tülu-3-8B`, whose fine-tuning data are public, and `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct` as a control, **safety data from Tülu-3's own training mixture yields stronger steering than external datasets on both models**. Membership scores largely agree in identifying training examples, and vectors built from top-ranked examples are competitive with random subsets of the same size, though the Llama results suggest membership filtering only helps when the mean direction shift from filtered in-distribution data is much smaller than the shift from out-of-distribution data.

papers.title: DecisionRobust: Benchmarking Robustness for JEV Style Decision Models Across Text and Vision
papers.abstract: Emerging decision models such as JEV provide typed interfaces that map task instructions and observations directly to choices, judgments, and scores. As these models are increasingly used for automated decision-making, understanding their reliability under adversarial manipulation becomes critical. We introduce DecisionRobust, a benchmark for systematically evaluating the robustness of decision models across textual and visual inputs. Our benchmark covers practical decision-making scenarios and a diverse suite of attacks, including semantics-preserving text perturbations, image perturbations, and prompt injection in both modalities. We curate evaluation sets through external validity checks and cross-model candidate selection. We evaluate 30 model configurations on text tasks and 17 on vision tasks, including 24 and 12 held-out models, respectively, that are excluded from candidate selection. Our experiments reveal several key findings. First, attacks expose vulnerabilities beyond the models used for construction and selection, although optimized image perturbations transfer weakly to many targets even with multiple surrogates. Second, relative model robustness varies across tasks and attack types, and resistance to input perturbations does not necessarily imply resistance to prompt injection. Third, label-consistency checks substantially reduce measured attack success across text and image settings, highlighting the importance of validating apparent failures. The benchmark is available at https://yifan-lan.github.io/DecisionRobust/.
papers.summary: Decision models such as `JEV` expose typed interfaces that map task instructions and observations directly to choices, judgments, and scores, so their reliability under adversarial manipulation matters as they are used for automated decision-making. `DecisionRobust` benchmarks these models across textual and visual inputs with semantics-preserving text perturbations, image perturbations, and prompt injection in both modalities, with evaluation sets curated through external validity checks and cross-model candidate selection. Evaluating 30 model configurations on text tasks and 17 on vision tasks, including 24 and 12 held-out models excluded from candidate selection, shows that attacks expose vulnerabilities beyond the models used for construction, although optimized image perturbations transfer weakly to many targets even with multiple surrogates. **Resistance to input perturbations does not imply resistance to prompt injection**, relative robustness varies across tasks and attack types, and label-consistency checks substantially reduce measured attack success, showing that apparent failures need validation.

papers.title: Unlocking Structured Pruning for Reasoning Language Models via Attention-Preserving MLP Trimming
papers.abstract: Structured pruning reduces LLM inference costs by removing model components to produce smaller dense models. However, existing methods can cause reasoning performance to collapse on long-form reasoning tasks such as AIME. We propose \textit{LayerTrim}, a training-free structured pruning method that identifies redundant decoder layers and selectively trims their MLP features while preserving attention and decoder depth. LayerTrim is the first training-free structured pruning method designed to preserve long-form reasoning without gradients or recovery training. Across three reasoning language models and five benchmarks, LayerTrim outperforms existing structured pruning methods in most evaluated settings, improving average accuracy by up to 21.4 percentage points over RESP. On \texttt{Qwen3-14B}, LayerTrim achieves 1.24$\times$ faster prefill and 19.7\% lower peak GPU memory than the dense model, while better preserving reasoning ability. It also achieves the shortest average generation length among evaluated pruned models, while retaining the highest average accuracy. These results demonstrate that LayerTrim improves reasoning efficiency through both structural compression and reduced token generation.
papers.summary: Structured pruning lowers LLM inference cost by removing components to produce smaller dense models, but existing methods can cause reasoning performance to collapse on long-form tasks such as `AIME`. `LayerTrim` is a training-free structured pruning method that identifies redundant decoder layers and selectively trims their MLP features while preserving attention and decoder depth, requiring no gradients or recovery training. Across three reasoning language models and five benchmarks it outperforms existing structured pruning methods in most settings, **improving average accuracy by up to 21.4 percentage points over `RESP`**. On `Qwen3-14B` it achieves 1.24× faster prefill and 19.7% lower peak GPU memory than the dense model while better preserving reasoning, and it produces the shortest average generation length among evaluated pruned models while retaining the highest average accuracy.

papers.title: PairIT: Autoregressive Transformers for Low-Data Molecule Optimization
papers.abstract: Generating novel molecules with desired properties is a central challenge in drug discovery. Although foundational work focused on de novo generation, practical use cases require a more complex setting: conditioning on an initial seed molecule, optimizing multiple properties, and operating in data-sparse regimes. We introduce PairIT, a flexible training framework for autoregressive transformers over SMILES sequences that enables seeded generation by learning from pairs of structurally similar molecules. By leveraging matched pairs, the model learns to generate local, chemically meaningful edits that improve a property of the seed molecule. Prompt tokens extend this framework by specifying the target property, desired direction, and approximate magnitude of change. Multiple prompt tokens can be concatenated to enable multi-property optimization at inference time. For properties where pair supervision alone is insufficient, reinforcement learning post-training can further improve optimization, providing a tunable trade-off between proximity to the seed and the optimization objective. PairIT naturally supports pretraining on a large dataset and fine-tuning on a smaller dataset, which is critical for performance in data-sparse regimes. Surprisingly, we observe diminishing returns to the scale of the pretraining dataset. We demonstrate empirically on MoleculeNet and Therapeutics Data Commons datasets that, with appropriate paired-data curation, a standard transformer model of modest size (68M parameters) can achieve robust seeded molecular optimization in low-data regimes.
papers.summary: Practical molecule generation for drug discovery must condition on a seed molecule, optimize several properties at once, and operate in data-sparse regimes, unlike the de novo generation emphasized by earlier work. `PairIT` is a training framework for autoregressive transformers over SMILES sequences that learns from pairs of structurally similar molecules, so the model produces local, chemically meaningful edits that improve a property of the seed, with prompt tokens specifying the target property, direction, and approximate magnitude of change and multiple tokens concatenated for multi-property optimization at inference time. Reinforcement learning post-training can further improve properties where pair supervision alone is insufficient, offering a tunable trade-off between proximity to the seed and the objective, and the framework supports large-scale pretraining followed by fine-tuning on a small dataset. On `MoleculeNet` and `Therapeutics Data Commons` datasets, **a standard 68M-parameter transformer achieves robust seeded molecular optimization in low-data regimes** given appropriate paired-data curation, with surprisingly diminishing returns from larger pretraining sets.

papers.title: Imagining Goals with Geometric Horizon Models for Policy Generalization
papers.abstract: Training from offline data has allowed for substantial progress in domains such as robotics, leading to general-purpose policies that can be easily applied zero-shot or efficiently finetuned for downstream tasks. However, these policies can still have poor generalization, both due to the choice of modeling objective and from learning from a static dataset. In this work, we focus on the challenging task of zero-shot goal generalization, where a policy is evaluated on unseen tasks that require combining its existing knowledge (compositional generalization). An avenue for improving a policy's generalization is by generating new experience with world models; however, such generation has proven difficult for longer horizons. Thus, to alleviate this issue, we propose TD-Aug, which samples from a geometric horizon model and allows for directly imagining novel outcomes that can be achieved by composing existing knowledge. We demonstrate that training on these future outcomes as goals for goal-conditioned BC policies significantly improves generalization in stitching-based OGBench tasks.
papers.summary: General-purpose policies trained from offline data can generalize poorly to unseen goals that require composing existing knowledge, both because of the modeling objective and because the dataset is static, and generating new experience with world models has proven difficult over longer horizons. `TD-Aug` samples from a geometric horizon model to directly imagine novel outcomes achievable by composing existing knowledge, then uses those imagined future outcomes as goals when training goal-conditioned behavior cloning (BC) policies. **Training on these imagined goals significantly improves zero-shot goal generalization on stitching-based `OGBench` tasks.**

papers.title: Plant Memory: Technical Language Processing and a Verified Maintenance Ontology for Agent-Accessible Failure Knowledge from SAP PM Work Orders
papers.abstract: Maintenance work orders are the largest written record of how industrial equipment fails, yet in most plants they are close to unusable for analysis. Short texts are abbreviated and misspelt, asset identity is buried in free text, work-type labels contradict the work described, and the fields that matter most for reliability (symptom, root cause, action taken) are usually empty. As a result, diagnostic knowledge stays with senior technicians and leaves when they do. We present Plant Memory, a system that applies technical language processing (TLP) to SAP Plant Maintenance (PM) exports and builds an ISO 14224-aligned maintenance ontology in which every extracted statement is a reified fact carrying a confidence score, the evidence it was read from, and a verification state. Extraction is rule-first, with an optional large language model (LLM) acting as a second reader whose disagreements raise a fact's review priority rather than overwrite it. Technicians verify facts through a review queue, answer targeted knowledge-gap questions where failures repeat without a recorded cause, and approve or reject ontology drift proposals when new terms appear. The resulting graph is served to people through a web application and to AI agents through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, so both query the same verified knowledge and every answer cites the work orders behind it. On a synthetic 12-month export of 400 work orders from a parboiled-rice plant, rule-based extraction reaches 96.2% component accuracy, 88.9% failure-mode accuracy and 100% root-cause precision at 62% coverage; on 28 diagnostic questions, ranked root causes from the ontology are correct at top-1 in 82.1% of cases against 53.6% for the raw SAP root-cause column.
papers.summary: Maintenance work orders are the largest written record of how industrial equipment fails, but abbreviated and misspelt free text, buried asset identities, contradictory work-type labels, and empty symptom, cause, and action fields make them nearly unusable for analysis, so diagnostic knowledge stays with senior technicians. `Plant Memory` applies technical language processing (TLP) to SAP Plant Maintenance (PM) exports and builds an ISO 14224-aligned ontology in which every extracted statement is a reified fact carrying a confidence score, its source evidence, and a verification state, using rule-first extraction, an optional large language model (LLM) second reader whose disagreements raise a fact's review priority rather than overwrite it, and a technician review queue for verification, knowledge-gap questions, and ontology drift proposals. The verified graph is served to people through a web application and to AI agents through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, so both query the same knowledge and every answer cites the work orders behind it. On a synthetic 12-month export of 400 work orders from a parboiled-rice plant, rule-based extraction reaches 96.2% component accuracy, 88.9% failure-mode accuracy, and 100% root-cause precision at 62% coverage, and **ranked root causes from the ontology are correct at top-1 in 82.1% of 28 diagnostic questions, versus 53.6% for the raw SAP root-cause column**.

papers.title: TRACER: Trace-Regularized Training Against Indirect Prompt Injection
papers.abstract: Indirect prompt injection uses untrusted retrieved content, tool outputs, or agent messages to override an LLM's intended behavior. We show that defense robustness is channel-conditioned: the same attack succeeds 18% of the time as a follow-up message but 53% when placed in retrieved context. We propose TRACER (Trace-Regularized Adversarial Channel Exposure with Reward-shaping), a channel-aware adversarial training method that samples presentation wrappers and combines an answer-anchored, evidence-gated reward with ATRC, which aligns attacked reasoning with clean evidence when an injection is invalid. On GSM8K with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, TRACER reduces RAG-framed ASR from 65.5% to 6.1% while preserving 78-82% clean accuracy. Joint RAG+tool training achieves 13.9% average ASR across framings at 3B scale, while a single epoch at 7B reaches 9.4%. These results demonstrate that robust defenses must explicitly train and evaluate across deployment channels.
papers.summary: Indirect prompt injection uses untrusted retrieved content, tool outputs, or agent messages to override an LLM's intended behavior, and defense robustness turns out to be channel-conditioned: **the same attack succeeds 18% of the time as a follow-up message but 53% when placed in retrieved context**. `TRACER` (Trace-Regularized Adversarial Channel Exposure with Reward-shaping) is a channel-aware adversarial training method that samples presentation wrappers and combines an answer-anchored, evidence-gated reward with `ATRC`, which aligns attacked reasoning with the clean evidence when an injection is invalid. On `GSM8K` with `Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct`, it reduces retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-framed attack success rate (ASR) from 65.5% to 6.1% while preserving 78-82% clean accuracy, and joint RAG-plus-tool training reaches 13.9% average ASR across framings at 3B scale and 9.4% after a single epoch at 7B. The results argue that robust defenses must be explicitly trained and evaluated across deployment channels rather than a single one.

papers.title: CAFE: Confining Feature Distillation to Language-Routed Adapters for Compact Multilingual Automatic Speech Recognition
papers.abstract: Feature distillation is usually expected to add to logit distillation. We find that this expectation does not hold for two common feature losses in compact multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR), and analyze why through their gradients. The gradient of a projection-based loss is orthogonal to the task gradient, while that of Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), a similarity-based loss, is weakly aligned with it. CKA lowers the word error rate (WER) on non-English languages, but at the expense of data-rich English. Three loss-level remedies (one trained, two probed) all fall short, and the CKA gradient overlaps with the subspace English uses in the shared encoder by 97.5% to 99.5% (about 81% by chance). Guided by this diagnosis, we propose CAFE (Confined-Adapter Feature distillation), which confines the CKA gradient to adapters that English bypasses, addressing the trade-off in the parameters rather than in the loss. On the Open ASR Leaderboard, CAFE lowers the average WER from 8.55% to 8.02%, beats an adapter-only capacity control at 8.51%, and makes English more stable across checkpoints. At 254M parameters, it trails the 0.6B teacher by 2 WER points and is competitive with much larger models across 48 test sets in 24 languages. We use 564k hours of training data and state-of-the-art models to keep the findings relevant to practice.
papers.summary: Feature distillation is usually expected to add to logit distillation, but for compact multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR) two common feature losses do not: the gradient of a projection-based loss is orthogonal to the task gradient, and Centered Kernel Alignment (`CKA`), a similarity-based loss, is only weakly aligned with it and lowers word error rate (WER) on non-English languages at the expense of data-rich English. Three loss-level remedies all fall short, and the CKA gradient overlaps 97.5% to 99.5% with the subspace English uses in the shared encoder, against about 81% by chance. `CAFE` (Confined-Adapter Feature distillation) confines the CKA gradient to language-routed adapters that English bypasses, resolving the trade-off in the parameters rather than in the loss. On the `Open ASR Leaderboard`, **CAFE lowers average WER from 8.55% to 8.02%**, beats an adapter-only capacity control at 8.51%, makes English more stable across checkpoints, and at 254M parameters trails its 0.6B teacher by 2 WER points while staying competitive with much larger models across 48 test sets in 24 languages, using 564k hours of training data.

papers.title: Student Copula Markov Networks
papers.abstract: This paper extends the applicability of probabilistic graphical models to non Gaussian data. It establishes a characterization of the pairwise Markov property in undirected probabilistic graphical models in terms of copula densities. Building on this characterization, we derive a necessary condition for the pairwise Markov property in Student copula Markov networks. An Expectation-Conditional Maximization algorithm (ECM) is provided to facilitate the penalized maximum likelihood estimation and graph selection. The performance of the proposed algorithm is evaluated through simulation studies, which demonstrate its effectiveness in estimating model parameters and recovering the underlying graph structure.
papers.summary: Undirected probabilistic graphical models are typically built for Gaussian data, and this work extends them to non-Gaussian settings by characterizing the pairwise Markov property in terms of copula densities. Building on that characterization, it derives **a necessary condition for the pairwise Markov property in Student copula Markov networks**. An Expectation-Conditional Maximization (`ECM`) algorithm supports penalized maximum likelihood estimation and graph selection, and simulation studies show it estimates model parameters and recovers the underlying graph structure effectively.

papers.title: MA-Bench: Measuring Operational Planning in Language Models
papers.abstract: How well can a language model turn a large, incomplete and partly contradictory body of documents into a plan when no single correct answer exists? We introduce Mission Analysis (MA)-Bench, built on mission analysis, the first step of military operational planning, in which a staff reads the full situation and states the problem before anyone proposes a solution. Its 10 expert-built scenarios pair synthetic packets of ten to twelve documents with 1,257 expert-written pass/fail requirements, each containing information on their source, question type, and importance level. A reasoning-model judge grades each brief against the requirements without seeing the documents; it grades like a fifth credentialed planner, leaving a four-planner panel's agreement unchanged (Fleiss $\kappa$ 0.42 to 0.41), and a judge from a second provider reproduces the model ranking (Spearman 0.94). Across twenty frontier and open-weights models the best gets 62% of the rubric items right. Models are strongest on facts stated in the documents (58%) and weakest on judgments that must be inferred (33%), and six failures in ten are omissions rather than errors. MA-Bench grades the determinations, not the prose. We release the packets, rubrics, prompts, scorer and every graded brief with item-level verdicts.
papers.summary: How well can a language model turn a large, incomplete, and partly contradictory body of documents into a plan when no single correct answer exists? `MA-Bench` builds on mission analysis, the first step of military operational planning in which a staff reads the full situation and states the problem before proposing a solution, pairing 10 expert-built scenarios of ten to twelve synthetic documents with 1,257 expert-written pass/fail requirements, each annotated with source, question type, and importance level. A reasoning-model judge grades each brief against the requirements without seeing the documents and behaves like a fifth credentialed planner, leaving a four-planner panel's Fleiss κ essentially unchanged at 0.42 to 0.41, while a judge from a second provider reproduces the model ranking with Spearman 0.94. **Across twenty frontier and open-weights models, the best gets 62% of rubric items right**, with models strongest on facts stated in the documents at 58% and weakest on judgments that must be inferred at 33%, and six failures in ten are omissions rather than errors.

papers.title: Online Tokenization with Optimal Delay in Linear Time
papers.abstract:
Tokenization is an essential preprocessing step in almost all large language models (LLMs). One of the most popular frameworks is BPE tokenization, which consists of special token segmentation, pretokenization, and byte-pair encoding (BPE). However, existing algorithms are sequential, with each stage only processing complete output from the previous stage. In order to reduce latency and memory footprints, recent works (Jiang and Gong, ICML 2026) (Li, Yang and Mamouras, ASPLOS 2026) (Mamouras, Li and Yang, PLDI 2026) have initiated the study of online algorithms for subroutines such as pretokenization and BPE with a goal of streaming input to output as the input arrives online. However, the search for efficient online tokenization remains open.
  In this work, we formalize and resolve online tokenization. We introduce the notion of delay for online tokenization which characterizes the extent to which the algorithm output lags behind the (possibly computationally intractable) optimum. We give a near-linear time algorithm with optimal delay (up to constant factors). We complement this algorithm with a conditional lower bound: unless $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{NP}$, there is no polynomial time algorithm that beats the delay of our algorithm by more than a constant factor.
  We implement a practical variant for tokenizers from OpenAI's tiktoken and HuggingFace's tokenizers. We obtain a $7.9\times$-$34.8\times$ latency advantage (measured as time to first token) over tiktoken (as well as the recent gigatoken tokenizer) and our implementation maintains approximately constant memory usage independent of input size. Our implementation also achieves a $2.4\times$-$7.0\times$ improvement in throughput over tiktoken and $15.8\times$-$38.1\times$ over tokenizers.
papers.summary: Byte-pair encoding (BPE) tokenization pipelines, consisting of special-token segmentation, pretokenization, and BPE merging, run sequentially with each stage waiting for complete output from the previous one, which adds latency and memory before a model sees its first token, and efficient online tokenization has remained an open problem. This work formalizes online tokenization through a notion of delay, the extent to which streaming output lags behind the possibly intractable optimum, and gives a near-linear-time algorithm with optimal delay up to constant factors, complemented by a conditional lower bound that no polynomial-time algorithm beats its delay by more than a constant factor unless P equals NP. A practical implementation for OpenAI's `tiktoken` and HuggingFace's `tokenizers` achieves **a 7.9× to 34.8× latency advantage in time to first token over tiktoken** and the recent `gigatoken` tokenizer, keeps memory roughly constant regardless of input size, and improves throughput 2.4× to 7.0× over tiktoken and 15.8× to 38.1× over tokenizers.

papers.title: Towards Training and Inference of Graph Neural Networks in Graph Databases
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks on large graphs commonly rely on in-memory graph storage with ad hoc data processing pipelines for both training and inference. Graph databases provide scalable storage and efficient traversal for graphs that can evolve over time, but their applicability in GNN training and inference are rarely studied.
