We show that graph DBs can be used in GNN training and inference directly, executing sampling, feature retrieval, and even the full forward pass. We show different GNN training pipelines can perform on-the-fly sampling and retrieval in graph DBs using Cypher. We further provide optimisations that speed up the training process by \~2.5x while maintaining the same accuracy. We illustrate that fully in-DB inference is possible, independent of how the GNNs are trained. Our inference setup can be >10x faster than cold loading the graph into RAM with no extra memory overhead on real-world graphs. Our work lays the foundation for in-graph-DB GNN training and inference.
papers.summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) on large graphs usually depend on in-memory storage and bespoke data pipelines, even though graph databases already offer scalable storage and efficient traversal for graphs that evolve over time. The authors show that sampling, feature retrieval, and even the full forward pass can run directly inside a graph database through Cypher queries, and they add optimisations that make training **about 2.5x faster at the same accuracy**. Fully in-database inference works regardless of how the model was trained and runs more than 10x faster than cold-loading the graph into RAM, with no extra memory overhead on real-world graphs.

papers.title: Demystifying On-Policy Distillation: Where Does the Teacher's Advantage Live?
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is increasingly studied as a cheaper alternative to reinforcement learning, yet it remains a form of knowledge distillation (KD) that relies on teacher supervision. We revisit OPD from the KD perspective by asking where the teacher's advantage lies along student-generated trajectories. Controlled token flips at teacher-student disagreements directly measure the accuracy gained from teacher corrections. Single-token flips yield a modest average gain on selected failed trajectories, whereas repeated flips raise accuracy from 28.4% to 74.5%, close to the teacher's 76.9%. Gains continue to accumulate with more flips, but mass- and KL-based selection outperform random flips by 15-18 percentage points at counts of similar magnitude. Selective intervention remains useful after OPD, but greater argmax agreement does not consistently improve accuracy across model pairs. We advocate training schedules that learn more valuable teacher corrections while maintaining distributional stability. Controlled flips and fork-resolution analysis evaluate OPD beyond accuracy by measuring which teacher preferences the student acquires and what further correction can recover.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) is pitched as a cheaper alternative to reinforcement learning, but it is still knowledge distillation (KD) that depends on teacher supervision, so the authors ask where along a student's own trajectories the teacher's advantage actually lives. They flip individual tokens at points where teacher and student disagree, measuring the accuracy gained directly from teacher corrections. Single flips give modest gains on failed trajectories, but **repeated flips raise accuracy from 28.4% to 74.5%**, close to the teacher's 76.9%, and selecting flips by probability mass or KL divergence beats random selection by 15 to 18 percentage points at similar flip counts. Greater argmax agreement after OPD does not consistently translate into higher accuracy across model pairs, so the authors argue for training schedules that prioritise the most valuable teacher corrections while keeping the student's distribution stable.

papers.title: DivAlgo: A systematic evaluation of algorithmic diversity for code generation models
papers.abstract: Code generation models are actively being used in professional and educational settings. However, the competence of large language models (LLMs) to generate algorithmically diverse code remains largely unknown. We propose the DivAlgo benchmark, a large-scale dataset constituting algorithmically diverse solutions to programming problems. We also introduce a lightweight similarity metric to enable large-scale evaluation. Our experiments across 24 modern code generation models found that uncontrolled model-generated code is significantly less diverse than human solutions (capturing ~31% of human diversity), and even the best diverse code generation strategy could achieve only ~70% of human diversity. Moreover, while it was possible to steer the models to generate solutions based on human strategies, they were unable to reproduce the diversity of the human solutions. These findings indicate the limitations of code generation models in capturing the algorithmic diversity humans exhibit, and that overexposure to model-generated code can narrow programmers' algorithmic vocabulary.
papers.summary: Code generation models are in daily professional and educational use, but how well large language models (LLMs) can produce algorithmically diverse solutions to the same problem is largely unknown. The `DivAlgo` benchmark pairs a large dataset of algorithmically diverse human solutions with a lightweight similarity metric that makes large-scale evaluation feasible across 24 modern code models. Uncontrolled model output captures **only about 31% of human algorithmic diversity**, the best diversity-promoting generation strategy reaches about 70%, and while models can be steered toward specific human strategies they cannot reproduce the overall spread. The authors warn that heavy exposure to model-generated code could narrow programmers' algorithmic vocabulary.

papers.title: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems
papers.abstract: Can AI agents carry out research on open scientific problems? We introduce Into the Unknown, a benchmark that provides an agent with a science paper along with a research direction to pursue and tasks it to write a follow-up paper. We work with scientists at US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories, who each contribute an unpublished follow-up direction from their own work together with the necessary conditions a submission must meet. While assessing the quality of a follow-up paper is challenging in general, using these conditions to form a rubric makes evaluation more tractable for research problems that have no reference answer. We have nine frontier agents write 15 follow-ups each, spanning quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning domains. None of the 135 submissions satisfies all the conditions, and 114 fail our integrity check, most often because the paper claims work that was never done or reports numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. Overall, agents readily produce papers that look like follow-ups, but none meets the standard of the domain scientist, leaving substantial headroom. Our code and data are publicly available.
papers.summary: Whether AI agents can do research on open scientific problems is the question behind `Into the Unknown`, in which each task hands an agent a published paper plus an unpublished follow-up direction contributed by a scientist at a US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratory, and asks it to write the follow-up paper. Because such papers have no reference answer, each contributor also supplies the conditions a submission must meet, which become a rubric that makes evaluation tractable. Nine frontier agents each wrote 15 follow-ups across quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning; **none of the 135 submissions met all conditions, and 114 failed an integrity check**, most often by claiming work that was never done or reporting numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. Code and data are public.

papers.title: From Qualitative Text to Integrated Evidence: The Parallel-Then-Integrated (PTI) Procedure
papers.abstract: Mixed methods research offers established strategies for integrating qualitative and quantitative evidence, but less guidance for integrating two computational representations of the same qualitative corpus. This methodological study introduces Parallel-Then-Integrated (PTI), a four-step procedure for explicit and traceable integration. We present PTI using 1,203 interview paragraphs from 29 mothers in Nepal. The two representations were ontology-guided Patient Voice (PV) coding with PVminer and data-driven themes generated through non-negative matrix factorization (NMF). A theme-complete crosswalk documented convergence, divergence, and preprocessing-sensitive differences. Depression status, based on Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) scores, served as a secondary external anchor for exploratory association checks. PTI provides a structured approach for integrating computational representations of qualitative text within mixed methods research.
papers.summary: Mixed methods research has established ways to integrate qualitative and quantitative evidence but offers little guidance for integrating two computational representations of the same qualitative corpus. The Parallel-Then-Integrated (`PTI`) procedure is a four-step method for explicit, traceable integration, demonstrated on 1,203 interview paragraphs from 29 mothers in Nepal. One representation came from ontology-guided Patient Voice (PV) coding with `PVminer` and the other from data-driven themes produced by non-negative matrix factorization (NMF); **a theme-complete crosswalk documented where the two converged, diverged, or differed because of preprocessing**, with depression status from Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) scores serving as an external anchor for exploratory association checks.

papers.title: ListQA: A Benchmark for Evaluating List-Formatted Factual Knowledge Retrieval in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Many real-world questions demand not a single fact but an organized collection of them, yet existing factual knowledge benchmarks almost exclusively target single answer retrieval. We introduce ListQA, a benchmark of 9,045 human-curated, cross-validated questions (audited error rate of 1.7%) that require LLMs to recall multiple facts and compose them into structured lists of 3-10 elements. Questions range from flat lists ("Which NCAA teams went undefeated between 2000 and 2024?") to hierarchical lists with sub-attributes ("...and what was their record and result?"), spanning eight categories across 60+ countries. An evergreen design (explicit temporal constraints or historically immutable facts) keeps ground truth valid without periodic updates. For evaluation, we frame element matching as a linear sum assignment problem: optimal bipartite matching paired with LLM-based semantic grading jointly captures factual accuracy, hallucination, and format compliance. We benchmark 34 models (8 families, 42 configurations across standard and thinking enabled inference) and find: the best standard-inference model scores below 37% LLM-Judge-F1, multi-faceted questions are harder across the board, and providing the source Wikipedia page lifts scores dramatically, confirming that models can organize facts but struggle to retrieve them from parameters alone. Extended analyses cover base vs. instruction-tuned checkpoints and token efficiency. We release the dataset and evaluation code.
papers.summary: Most factual knowledge benchmarks test single-answer retrieval, yet many real questions require assembling an organized collection of facts. `ListQA` contains 9,045 human-curated, cross-validated questions with an audited error rate of 1.7%, whose answers are structured lists of 3 to 10 elements ranging from flat lists (which NCAA teams went undefeated in a given span) to hierarchical lists with sub-attributes, spanning eight categories and more than 60 countries, with an evergreen design so ground truth needs no periodic updates. Scoring treats element matching as a linear sum assignment problem, combining optimal bipartite matching with LLM-based semantic grading to capture factual accuracy, hallucination, and format compliance together. Across 34 models in 42 configurations, **the best standard-inference model scores below 37% LLM-judge F1**, multi-faceted questions are harder for every model, and supplying the source Wikipedia page lifts scores dramatically, indicating that models can organize facts but struggle to retrieve them from their parameters alone.

papers.title: Fantastic Metrics and How to Find Them: Meta-Evaluating Metrics for Multi-lingual Style-Personalized Generation
papers.abstract: Meta-evaluation of text generation metrics and LLM-judges is primarily conducted using metric-human correlations. However, prior work has shown that correlation is not an appropriate estimate of a metric's evaluation capability and can be unstable across evaluation settings, such as different datasets or languages. Therefore, we propose a regression-based meta-evaluation of metrics that learns on calibrated metric outputs to predict human ratings. We ground this measurement relative to a trivial constant-mean baseline and human agreements to provide a comparable measure of metric capability across evaluation settings. To test our meta-evaluation framework, we developed a large-scale multi-lingual style-personalized text generation (SPTG) benchmark, collecting multiple annotations across 10 topologically diverse languages and four evaluation dimensions, each with varying degrees of subjectivity. We meta-evaluated 32 metrics from three style evaluation paradigms (string-based, embedding-based, and LLM-judges) and their ensembles over these 40 evaluation settings. Our analysis revealed that even simple string- and embedding-based measurements can match strong LLM-judges when calibrated to human ratings. We also identified characteristics of human annotations that determine metric performance, as well as conditions under which a metric ensemble outperforms its individual constituents.
papers.summary: Meta-evaluation of text generation metrics and LLM judges usually relies on correlation with human ratings, which prior work has shown to be an unreliable gauge that shifts across datasets and languages. The authors instead propose a regression-based meta-evaluation that learns from calibrated metric outputs to predict human ratings, grounded against a constant-mean baseline and human agreement so results are comparable across settings. To exercise it they built a multilingual style-personalized text generation (SPTG) benchmark with annotations in 10 typologically diverse languages and four evaluation dimensions of varying subjectivity, then meta-evaluated 32 metrics from string-based, embedding-based, and LLM-judge paradigms, plus their ensembles, over 40 settings. **Simple string- and embedding-based metrics can match strong LLM judges once calibrated to human ratings**, and the analysis identifies which annotation characteristics drive metric performance and when an ensemble beats its components.

papers.title: Diagnosing Low-Confidence Patient Profiles via Localized Harmful Covariate Shift Detection
papers.abstract: Before deploying clinical prediction models, their reliability must be assessed to ensure safe use. Errors may arise from distribution shifts between training and deployment or from heterogeneous performance where the model systematically underperforms for certain patient subgroups. Yet most post-hoc diagnostic methods evaluate reliability only at the population level, checking whether the deployment data resemble the training data and whether the model performs well on average, without accounting for heterogeneity that may cause some patients to be disproportionately affected. We propose a unified diagnostic pipeline that combines both perspectives. MED3pa first discovers interpretable low-confidence patient profiles, and Detectron is then applied within each profile to test whether its degradation is associated with a detectable harmful covariate shift. Across three clinical prediction tasks and three injected subgroup shifts in MIMIC-IV, we find that shift detectability itself is informative. An injected age shift, undetectable at the population level, was nonetheless localized to specific degraded profiles, whereas sex- and race-related shifts were detected broadly and therefore offered little guidance for identifying the most affected patients.
authors: Centre for Outcomes Research and Evaluation)
papers.summary: Clinical prediction models can fail after deployment because of distribution shift or because they systematically underperform for particular patient subgroups, yet most post-hoc diagnostics check only population-level resemblance to training data and average performance. The proposed pipeline first uses `MED3pa` to discover interpretable low-confidence patient profiles, then applies `Detectron` within each profile to test whether its degradation coincides with a detectable harmful covariate shift. Across three clinical prediction tasks and three injected subgroup shifts in `MIMIC-IV`, **an injected age shift that was undetectable at the population level was localized to specific degraded profiles**, whereas sex- and race-related shifts were detected broadly and so gave little guidance on which patients were most affected.

papers.title: Learning in Strategic Queuing with Geometric Recharge: From Bandits to Systems
papers.abstract:
We study packet routing in queuing systems where queues act as selfish, myopic agents that use no-regret learning algorithms to select servers with unknown service rates. To model the small buffers used in data centers, we assume that each server has a single-packet buffer. Even such a tiny buffer already captures the features of buffering: routers can exploit multiple servers while accepted packets remain in service, but packets can occupy servers for multiple rounds, complicating future service and learning.
  We first analyze a single queue routing packets to $m$ buffered servers with service rates $\mu_1, \dots, \mu_m$. This setting is equivalent to an instance of the recharging bandits problem with geometric recharge. We prove that any no-regret learner achieves a long-run average throughput of at least the Hamacher sum of the server rates, and that this bound is tight. Consequently, a single no-regret queue is stable if and only if its arrival rate is below the Hamacher sum of the server rates. Moreover, comparing against an optimal policy, we show that any no-regret learner is at least $0.77$-competitive, which is also tight.
  We then study multi-queue systems where $n$ queues with arrival rates $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n$, each at most $\lambda_{\max}$, compete for service from $m$ buffered servers. We show that the smallest overprovisioning factor that guarantees the system to be stable under high-probability no-regret learning is $\frac{1}{1-\lambda_{\max}}$. Equivalently, in terms of the total arrival and service rates, the condition $\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i < (1-\lambda_{\max})\sum_{j=1}^m \mu_j$ is sufficient, and sometimes necessary, for stability under no-regret learning. In particular, for $\lambda_{\max} = 1/2$, this improves the upper bound of Abel et al. (EC 2026) from $3$ to $2$, matching their lower bound and resolving their open question.
papers.summary: Packet routing is modelled as a game in which queues are selfish, myopic agents running no-regret learning to choose among servers with unknown service rates, and each server holds a single-packet buffer to mimic the small buffers in data centres. For one queue facing many buffered servers the setting is equivalent to recharging bandits with geometric recharge; the authors prove that any no-regret learner achieves long-run throughput of at least the Hamacher sum of the server rates, that this bound is tight, and that such a learner is **at least 0.77-competitive against the optimal policy**, which is also tight. For many competing queues, the smallest overprovisioning factor that guarantees stability under high-probability no-regret learning is one over one minus the largest per-queue arrival rate; when that maximum is one half this tightens the previous upper bound from 3 to 2, matching the known lower bound and resolving an open question from Abel et al.

papers.title: HERO: Harnessing Evidence for Test-time Refinement and Prompt Optimization in Program Generation
papers.abstract: Harness optimization improves LLMs by refining reusable prompts and scaffolding, yet requires further adaptation for program generation tasks such as text-to-SQL and text-to-Python. Existing methods often rely on LLM reflectors to propose harness updates, which can fix observed failures but also disrupt previously correct behavior. Text-to-code tasks offer a natural way to mitigate this issue: we can execute generated outputs, allowing us to evaluate and verify the effects of proposed updates directly. Building on this signal, we introduce \textsc{HERO} (\textbf{H}arnessing \textbf{E}vidence for \textbf{R}efinement and \textbf{O}ptimization), which combines offline and test-time harness optimization. At the first stage, \method{} learns reusable prompt updates from execution-verified successes and failures and validates candidate revisions before adoption. At test time, we treat the generated code as an instance-specific harness and refine it using execution feedback. Across four SQL, Cypher, and Python benchmarks, \method{} achieves the best offline performance, improving pass@1 by \(7.6\) points over the initial prompt, while test-time refinement adds another \(2.0\) points and improves execution efficiency.
papers.summary: Harness optimization refines the reusable prompts and scaffolding around a large language model, but existing approaches rely on LLM reflectors whose proposed updates can fix observed failures while breaking behaviour that previously worked. For program generation tasks such as text-to-SQL and text-to-Python the generated code can simply be executed, so `HERO` (Harnessing Evidence for Refinement and Optimization) learns reusable prompt updates offline from execution-verified successes and failures, validates candidate revisions before adopting them, and at test time treats each generated program as an instance-specific harness refined with execution feedback. Across four SQL, Cypher, and Python benchmarks, **the offline stage improves pass@1 by 7.6 points over the initial prompt**, and test-time refinement adds another 2.0 points while also improving execution efficiency.

papers.title: How to Evaluate When You Don't Know How to Evaluate? Choosing Reliable Setups for Base Language Model Benchmarking
papers.abstract: Evaluation of large language models (LLMs) remains largely pre-scientific: it involves many design decisions, with little guidance on how to make them. These choices can substantially affect measured performance and, consequently, decisions about subsequent pretraining. To identify effective evaluation setups, we investigate 8 aspects, such as task formulation or the number of in-context examples. We compare the setups using three widely-used signal criteria, repurposed as normative meta-measures: monotonicity, non-randomness, and ranking consistency of the evaluation scores across intermediate checkpoints. In an early pretraining scenario, we evaluate these setups on 26 monolingual 2B-parameter models trained on different types of data, using 80 tasks in four languages. We also examine the setups on three larger LLMs ($\geq$7B) in the same four languages and explore how the preferred setups change with model scale. Our results yield concrete recommendations: some choices, such as the use of multiple prompts, are consistently useful, whereas others, such as task formulation, depend on model scale. More generally, our framework serves as a recipe for the choice of evaluation setups in new scenarios.
papers.summary: Benchmarking base language models involves many design decisions with little guidance, and those decisions can change measured performance and therefore pretraining choices. The authors examine eight aspects of evaluation setup, such as task formulation and the number of in-context examples, and compare setups with three signal criteria repurposed as normative meta-measures: monotonicity, non-randomness, and ranking consistency of scores across intermediate checkpoints. Experiments cover 26 monolingual 2B-parameter models trained on different kinds of data over 80 tasks in four languages, plus three larger models of at least 7B parameters to see how preferred setups change with scale. **Using multiple prompts is consistently useful, whereas choices such as task formulation depend on model scale**, and the framework is offered as a recipe for choosing evaluation setups in new scenarios.

papers.title: Structure-aware Bayesian full waveform inversion via diffusion-regularized Stein variational gradient descent
papers.abstract: Full waveform inversion (FWI) is a powerful tool for high-resolution subsurface model reconstruction, but it remains highly nonlinear and ill-posed, especially when the initial model is inaccurate or the acquired data are noisy and incomplete. Annealed Stein variational gradient descent (ASVGD) provides a particle-based Bayesian framework for FWI by approximating the posterior distribution with an ensemble of velocity models, thereby enabling uncertainty quantification beyond a single deterministic solution. However, conventional ASVGD-FWI commonly relies on simple handcrafted priors, such as Gaussian or smoothing assumptions, which are often insufficient to represent complex geological structures. To address this limitation, we introduce a learned diffusion model (DM) as an implicit regularization mechanism within the ASVGD-FWI framework. Instead of explicitly evaluating the diffusion prior density, the trained diffusion model acts as a learned geological projection operator that guides updated particles toward the distribution of plausible velocity models. In this way, the proposed method combines data consistency from FWI, posterior diversity from ASVGD, and structural realism from the diffusion prior. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the diffusion-regularized ASVGD-FWI produces more geologically consistent mean models, suppresses nonphysical artifacts, and yields uncertainty estimates that are more concentrated around structurally complex and poorly constrained regions. These results suggest that learned diffusion priors can effectively enhance Bayesian FWI by improving both inversion stability and the interpretability of posterior uncertainty.
papers.summary: Full waveform inversion (FWI) reconstructs high-resolution subsurface velocity models from seismic data but is strongly nonlinear and ill-posed, especially with an inaccurate starting model or noisy, incomplete data. Annealed Stein variational gradient descent (ASVGD) gives a particle-based Bayesian treatment that approximates the posterior with an ensemble of velocity models, but it normally leans on simple handcrafted priors such as Gaussian or smoothness assumptions that cannot capture complex geology. The authors insert a trained diffusion model as an implicit regularizer that acts as a learned geological projection operator, steering updated particles toward plausible velocity models without evaluating the prior density explicitly. Numerical experiments show more geologically consistent mean models, fewer nonphysical artifacts, and **uncertainty estimates that concentrate in structurally complex, poorly constrained regions**.

papers.title: Adaptive Computation with Conformal Certification
papers.abstract: Scientific imaging data involving medical (e.g., 3D radiographic, microscopic images) and astronomical sensors pose different challenges from natural images. One key challenge is that these datasets are often orders of magnitude larger than natural images. Efficient training and inference on such data is challenging due to the increased hardware requirements, often needing bespoke solutions. Moreover, the relevant objects such as tumors and astronomical phenomena are sparsely distributed with respect to the background information. Standard efficiency techniques like quantization and pruning apply uniform scaling of all regions, potentially compromising the precision/fidelity of predictions. Thus, efficient methods that reduce computational requirements without losing resolution for relevant parts of the data and with uncertainty estimates on predictions are essential. We present \textit{Conformal Adaptation} with risk guarantees for uncertainty-aware sparse computations. Our formalism is general, spanning dense pixel-level classification and regression tasks where hierarchical models predict at low resolution, certify the signal using conformal risk control, and refine the certified predictions. We benchmark our method on multiple tasks such as 3D medical image segmentation, 2D galaxy flux prediction, and 1D calcium spike rate prediction, achieving $2.5$--$72\times$ wall-clock speedup across the various tasks, including on commodity CPUs.
papers.summary: Scientific imaging data from medical and astronomical sensors can be orders of magnitude larger than natural images, with the relevant signal such as tumours sparsely scattered against background, so uniform efficiency techniques like quantization and pruning risk losing precision exactly where it matters. `Conformal Adaptation` is a general framework for dense pixel-level classification and regression in which hierarchical models predict at low resolution, certify where the signal is using conformal risk control, and then refine only the certified regions, carrying a formal risk guarantee. Benchmarks on 3D medical image segmentation, 2D galaxy flux prediction, and 1D calcium spike rate prediction show **wall-clock speedups of 2.5x to 72x**, including on commodity CPUs.

papers.title: NEPSEE: A Double-Annotated Benchmark for Nepali Sentiment Analysis
papers.abstract: Many sentiment datasets use one annotator for each item, so the test labels show the conventions of that person. We build a Nepali benchmark from two annotators who labelled the same sentences blind. They labelled 5,614 sentences from tweets of Nepali public figures on a five-point scale. We keep only the 3,189 sentences where both give the same polarity. On the three-class benchmark, NepBERTa with a fixed tokenizer gets a macro-F1 of 0.877 and IndicBERTv2 0.867. Three commercial large language models (LLMs) get 0.882 to 0.896 zero-shot, and these differences are not significant. On the five-point scale, 766 sentences have two adjacent labels, for example Pos and SPos. We accept both labels and train on both. On this task, Claude Opus 5.5 beats the best encoders by 0.10 to 0.12 macro-F1. A tokenizer audit adds a second result. The default tokenizers of three Nepali BERT models delete the non-spacing Devanagari vowel signs and the virama. When we restore the marks, macro-F1 increases by 0.084 for NepBERTa but decreases by 0.095 for a model pretrained on stripped text.
papers.summary: Most sentiment datasets use a single annotator per item, so test labels encode one person's conventions. `NEPSEE` is a Nepali benchmark built from 5,614 tweet sentences by public figures, each labelled blind by two annotators on a five-point scale, keeping the 3,189 sentences where both agree on polarity. On the three-class task, `NepBERTa` with a fixed tokenizer reaches macro-F1 0.877 and `IndicBERTv2` 0.867, three commercial large language models (LLMs) score 0.882 to 0.896 zero-shot with no significant differences, and on a five-point task that accepts adjacent labels `Claude Opus 5.5` beats the best encoders by **0.10 to 0.12 macro-F1**. A tokenizer audit finds that the default tokenizers of three Nepali BERT models drop non-spacing Devanagari vowel signs and the virama; restoring them raises macro-F1 by 0.084 for `NepBERTa` but lowers it by 0.095 for a model pretrained on stripped text.

papers.title: FireGraphNet: Sub-daily wildfire spread prediction with directed graph neural networks
papers.abstract: Wildfire decisions are made in hours, yet most learned spread models predict daily on targets including burned area. We propose FireGraphNet which formulates 12-hour growth as node classification on directed H3 graphs, with candidates ahead of the front and wind alignment, terrain, fuel continuity and barriers on edges. On satellite perimeters it achieves average precision 1.7-1.9x the strongest distance baseline on test California fires and 1.62x out of state. We show this skill comes from message passing rather than cell features or the aggregator, is highest on young fires in state, is carried deep along the wind by its edges, and is hidden by pooling. A convolutional network matches this ranking once trained on new growth, at worse calibration, so candidate construction, target definition, and aggregation shape conclusions about model skill. Editing fuel and barrier attributes reduces predicted spread more under guided than random placement, extending FireGraphNet to operational intervention analysis.
papers.summary: Wildfire response decisions are made within hours, but most learned spread models predict daily targets such as burned area. `FireGraphNet` casts 12-hour fire growth as node classification on directed graphs over H3 hexagonal cells, with candidate cells placed ahead of the front and edges carrying wind alignment, terrain, fuel continuity, and barriers. On satellite-derived perimeters it reaches **average precision 1.7 to 1.9x the strongest distance baseline** on held-out California fires and 1.62x out of state, with the skill traced to message passing rather than cell features or the aggregator, strongest on young in-state fires, carried deep along the wind by the edges, and hidden by pooling. A convolutional network matches the ranking once trained on new growth but with worse calibration, and editing fuel and barrier attributes reduces predicted spread more under guided than random placement, pointing to use in intervention analysis.

papers.title: Embedding Geometry Shapes LLM Routing: Tracing Failure Modes and Improving Generalization
papers.abstract: With the growing number of LLMs available, selecting which one to use for a prompt has become a key question. A large part of the routing literature relies on semantically embedding prompts into a vector space and then applying a lightweight classifier to the embedded representations. These methods perform robustly in-distribution but they struggle to generalize to unseen tasks. By studying the geometry of semantic embeddings, we trace a clear failure mode: features that determine the neighbors of unseen prompts are an unreliable proxy for LLM selection. We therefore replace the semantic embedding with the following map: we run a partial forward pass of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on the prompt and use the hidden state of its last token at a deep layer as the representation. When applying kNN and other simple classifiers to this new representation, we obtain a clear result in generalization: on average across cost penalties, their performance improves. Moreover, kNN and another simple classifier that we propose outperform every evaluated semantic-embedding baseline. Our two simple methods also beat a recent SoTA hidden-states based router on RouterBench.
papers.summary: With many LLMs available, routing each prompt to the right one has become a practical question, and most routers embed prompts semantically and train a lightweight classifier on top, which works in-distribution but generalizes poorly to unseen tasks. By studying the geometry of semantic embeddings, the authors trace the failure to the fact that the features determining a prompt's nearest neighbours are an unreliable proxy for which model will answer it well. They replace the semantic embedding with the hidden state of the last token at a deep layer from a partial forward pass of `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct`, after which k-nearest-neighbours and a second simple classifier generalize better on average across cost penalties, **beat every evaluated semantic-embedding baseline, and outperform a recent state-of-the-art hidden-state router on `RouterBench`**.

papers.title: Weighted Ensemble Sampling for Rare-Event Estimation in Language Models
papers.abstract: Rare but severe failures of large language models can become practically significant at deployment scale. Estimating their probabilities with direct Monte Carlo sampling is highly inefficient, while proposal-based methods typically require auxiliary learning of an additional proposal distribution. We introduce \textbf{Weighted Ensemble (WE)}, a training-free framework for rare-event estimation in language models. WE samples exclusively from the original language model and improves upon direct Monte Carlo by periodically reallocating the sampling budget toward prefixes that appear more likely to reach the target rare event. To guide this reallocation without learning a separate proposal distribution, we exploit internal LLM representations as prefix-level signals and empirically validate their effectiveness. We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed algorithm. Experiments on safety-related tasks spanning both small-scale and modern large-scale LLMs demonstrate that WE improves the efficiency and reliability of rare-event probability estimation.
papers.summary: Rare but severe failures of large language models matter at deployment scale, yet estimating their probabilities by direct Monte Carlo sampling is wasteful and proposal-based alternatives need an auxiliary proposal distribution to be learned. `Weighted Ensemble` is a training-free method that samples only from the original model and periodically reallocates the sampling budget toward prefixes that look more likely to reach the target rare event, using the model's internal representations as the prefix-level steering signal. The authors give a theoretical analysis of the algorithm and show on safety-related tasks with both small and modern large LLMs that **the method improves the efficiency and reliability of rare-event probability estimates over direct Monte Carlo**.

papers.title: DUALVIEW: Leveraging Broad and Output-Specific Evidence for LLM-based Multi-Output Text Regression
papers.abstract: While work on LLM-based regression has largely focused on scalar prediction, multi-output text regression remains less explored. We present DualView, a parameter-efficient approach to leverage LLMs for multi-output text regression. \method{} first extracts broad and output-specific representations from a frozen LLM, then uses a dual-branch architecture to produce the full score vector. Across five heterogeneous regression tasks and eight LLMs (up to 122B), DualView outperforms seven supervised regression baselines while requiring 82--1842 times fewer fitted parameters than the three strongest baselines. These improvements extend across individual output dimensions and persist even with limited training data. Notably, DualView using a smaller open-weight LLM can outperform unsupervised prediction with Gemini 3.1 Pro. Controlled ablations show that broad and output-specific evidence provide complementary predictive benefits, while lightweight shared predictors achieve strong performance with fewer trainable parameters.
papers.summary: LLM-based regression work has mostly targeted scalar prediction, leaving multi-output text regression, where one text maps to a vector of scores, less explored. `DualView` extracts both broad and output-specific representations from a frozen LLM and feeds them through a dual-branch architecture that produces the full score vector with few trainable parameters. Across five heterogeneous regression tasks and eight LLMs up to 122B parameters, it **outperforms seven supervised baselines while fitting 82 to 1,842 times fewer parameters than the three strongest of them**, holds up with limited training data, and with a smaller open-weight LLM can beat unsupervised prediction by `Gemini 3.1 Pro`; ablations show that the broad and output-specific evidence are complementary.

papers.title: Titan-Llama: Retrofitting Pre-trained LLMs with External Neural Memory Modules
papers.abstract: Transformers are efficient to pre-train at scale because attention permits parallel computation across sequence positions, but long-context inference requires increasingly large KV caches. Efficient recurrent alternatives reduce the asymptotic complexity of inference, but their sequential dependence limits token-wise parallelism during training, making them harder to scale. Further, the current paradigm of extending long context tasks creates competing notions of retaining information precisely and keeping long-context inference efficient. To address this gap, we introduce Titan-Llama, a post-training method for retrofitting attention-based language models with a hierarchical memory architecture that updates parameters at test-time. Titan-Llama applies a blockwise attention mask and preserves full-fidelity attention over recent tokens while compressing historical context into recurrent, fixed-size neural memory modules (NMMs). Our formulation allows pre-trained attention layers to be replaced without training a new language model from scratch. On Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, Titan-Llama raises accuracy over segmented attention windows from 23.87\% to 40.51\% on QuALITY and from 14.50\% to 40.75\% on LongHealth. Inference benchmarks show more than 20\% faster prefill, 37\% faster decode at medium context lengths, and 24\% lower steady-state decode memory usage in the evaluated configurations. Together, these results demonstrate that incorporating memory architecture mechanisms that utilize test-time training effectively modulates long-context behavior of pre-trained models, offering a practical route to adapting pre-trained transformers for efficient long-context inference. Our code is released on Github \href{https://github.com/sarahpannn/titans-pytorch/tree/main}{GitHub}
papers.summary: Attention-based transformers train efficiently in parallel but need ever-larger key-value caches for long-context inference, while recurrent alternatives are cheaper at inference yet hard to train at scale. `Titan-Llama` is a post-training method that retrofits a pre-trained attention model with a hierarchical memory architecture: a blockwise mask keeps full-fidelity attention over recent tokens while historical context is compressed into fixed-size neural memory modules (NMMs) whose parameters update at test time, so existing attention layers are swapped out without training a new model from scratch. On `Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct`, **accuracy over segmented attention windows rises from 23.87% to 40.51% on `QuALITY` and from 14.50% to 40.75% on `LongHealth`**, with more than 20% faster prefill, 37% faster decode at medium context lengths, and 24% lower steady-state decode memory in the evaluated configurations. Code is released.

papers.title: Generalizing Identifiability Results in Causal Discovery from Complete Data to Missing Data Settings
papers.abstract: While causal discovery methods have matured for complete data, such algorithms for handling missing values remain limited. We establish general sufficient conditions under which causal graphs remain identifiable (i.e., uniquely determined from the available data distribution) under various missingness categories, including Missing Not At Random, and provide a framework to extend correctness guarantees from causal discovery algorithms for complete data to missing data settings. Our results show that identifiability of causal graphs with no unobserved confounders is preserved when (1) missingness mechanisms do not causally interact, (2) no variable directly causes its own missingness, and (3) either faithfulness holds for missingness mechanisms, or they follow generalized linear models. Guided by these theoretical results, we introduce two asymptotically correct algorithms for Additive Noise Models (ANMs) that recover the underlying causal graph and provide consistent parameter estimates.
papers.summary: Causal discovery algorithms are mature for complete data but limited when values are missing, especially under Missing Not At Random mechanisms. The authors give general sufficient conditions under which a causal graph remains identifiable from the observed data distribution and a framework for transferring correctness guarantees from complete-data algorithms to missing-data settings. With no unobserved confounders, identifiability is preserved when **missingness mechanisms do not causally interact, no variable directly causes its own missingness, and either faithfulness holds for the missingness mechanisms or they follow generalized linear models**. Guided by these results, they propose two asymptotically correct algorithms for Additive Noise Models (ANMs) that recover the graph and give consistent parameter estimates.

papers.title: Narrowing the Collaboration Gap, Probably
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as teams of agents that hold different private information about a shared task. How should such agents concisely communicate in a way that promotes aggregation of decision-relevant information? Communicating only proposed actions can discard decision-relevant uncertainty: two agents may prefer the same action for different reasons. We study an alternative interface in which agents communicate calibrated beliefs over actions. We first analyze a simple synthetic setting that captures the structure of multi-round reasoning under partial information. In this setting, we show theoretically and empirically that communicating unbiased probabilities can be strictly more powerful than communicating actions. We then test the same principle in a collaborative maze-solving task with trained transformers and pretrained LLM agents. Our results demonstrate that probability communication outperforms action communication when the exchanged predictions preserve calibrated uncertainty. When communicated probabilities are biased, we show that the benefits of probability communication can disappear. We give a post-hoc conversational calibration intervention that consistently improves decision-making by correcting these biases both in a toy transformer setting and when pretrained LLMs use the corrections in context. These results suggest that probabilistic communication is useful for multi-agent collaboration not merely because it transmits more information, but because calibrated uncertainty gives other agents a reliable object to update on.
papers.summary: Teams of language-model agents that each hold private information must decide what to communicate, and sharing only a proposed action discards the uncertainty behind it, since two agents may prefer the same action for different reasons. The authors compare action communication against an interface where agents exchange calibrated probability distributions over actions, first in a synthetic multi-round setting analyzed theoretically and empirically, then in a collaborative maze-solving task with trained transformers and pretrained LLM agents. **Probability communication outperforms action communication whenever the exchanged predictions preserve calibrated uncertainty**, but the advantage disappears when the communicated probabilities are biased. A post-hoc conversational calibration intervention that corrects these biases consistently improves decision-making, both in the toy transformer setting and when pretrained LLMs apply the corrections in context.

papers.title: Riding the Fixed-Point Curve: Image Classification in the Continuous Thought Machine
papers.abstract: The Continuous Thought Machine (CTM) is a recurrent network that attends to inputs and makes predictions based on the synchronization between its neurons. On tasks spanning many domains, it displays emergent thought processes that have not been explained. We report a number of findings about how the CTM classifies images, focusing on ImageNet. Each thinking step is an attracting but strongly non-normal map exhibiting balanced amplification (Murphy and Miller, 2009); while attraction is already present at CTM initialization, training highly promotes non-normality. By Banach's theorem, the neural state has a locally unique attracting fixed point, which moves at every step, and the thought trajectory is the curve these fixed points trace, followed one tick behind. Most of that curve's motion is shared across images, and visible as a previously reported traveling wave of activity across neurons. The attention schedule along the thought is largely generic: shuffling queries across images at every tick costs only 7 percent of classification accuracy, while image-independent increments predict the next query with R^2 = 0.98 (held out). Our results suggest that the CTM has found a single strategy to process all ImageNet images.
papers.summary: The Continuous Thought Machine (`CTM`) is a recurrent network that makes predictions from the synchronization between its neurons, and its emergent thinking process had not previously been explained. Analyzing `ImageNet` classification, the authors show that each thinking step is an attracting but strongly non-normal map exhibiting balanced amplification, so the neural state has a locally unique fixed point that moves every tick and the thought trajectory follows the curve those fixed points trace, one step behind. Most of that motion is shared across images and shows up as a previously reported traveling wave of activity across neurons. **Shuffling attention queries across images at every tick costs only 7 percent of classification accuracy**, and image-independent increments predict the next query with a held-out R-squared of 0.98, suggesting the network applies a single generic strategy to all images.

papers.title: Do Syntax Heads Influence Model Behavior?
papers.abstract: Transformer language models develop attention heads that specialize in syntactic relations, for example, attending from verbs to their subjects. Do these heads play a causal role in the model's syntactic predictions? Evidence for such a role is mixed to negative: even when we force these heads to attend to a distractor noun other than the subject, the model's syntactic predictions are still more consistent with the subject than with the distractor. Interventions on specialized syntax heads had a significantly stronger effect on syntactic predictions than interventions on random heads, but only in one of the two measures we propose.
papers.summary: Transformer language models develop attention heads that specialize in syntactic relations such as attending from a verb to its subject, which raises the question of whether these heads causally drive the model's syntactic predictions. The authors intervene on these heads, forcing them to attend to a distractor noun instead of the true subject, and measure the effect on syntactic predictions with two proposed measures, comparing against the same interventions on random heads. **Even when forced to attend to the distractor, the model's syntactic predictions remain more consistent with the subject than with the distractor**, and interventions on syntax heads beat interventions on random heads under only one of the two measures, leaving the evidence for a causal role mixed to negative.

papers.title: Spectral-MoE: Heterogeneous Per-Layer Expert Utilization in Dense-to-MoE Conversion
papers.abstract: Large language models impose substantial memory demands and arithmetic costs during inference. Dense-to-mixture-of-experts (MoE) conversion is a model optimization technique that aims to reduce these arithmetic costs. Dense-to-MoE conversion partitions pretrained feed-forward network (FFN) neurons into experts and selects a subset for each token. Leading methods fall into two categories: analytic methods produce a converted model quickly using heuristics, while learning methods produce a model much more slowly by optimizing via gradients. Both approaches, however, fix the same active expert count, or "utilization," at every layer. We introduce Spectral-MoE, which learns to allocate a utilization budget heterogeneously across layers. Its name draws a metaphor between separating a dense FFN into experts and separating a light beam into its spectrum. Spectral-MoE consists of two distinct approaches: a static approach that uses a single per-layer scalar which is shared across tokens, and a dynamic approach which emits a per-token schedule. We demonstrate that both allocators improve performance over uniform on both the analytic-based and learning-based SOTA dense-to-MoE methods. At 25% FFN utilization, dynamic allocation reduces WikiText-2 perplexity relative to uniform by 1.04, 2.96, and 2.71 points on the learned base for Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, respectively. The corresponding reductions on the analytic base are 2.45, 6.26, and 2.17 points. On the learned base, dynamic allocation improves six-task mean accuracy over uniform by an average of 1.5, 4.2, and 3.6 percentage points across the three models at FFN utilizations of 12.5%, 25%, and 50%, respectively. These results establish per-layer expert utilization as a novel optimization axis in dense-to-MoE conversion.
papers.summary: Dense-to-mixture-of-experts (MoE) conversion partitions the feed-forward network (FFN) neurons of a pretrained model into experts and activates only a subset per token to cut inference cost, but both the fast analytic and the slower gradient-based conversion methods fix the same number of active experts at every layer. `Spectral-MoE` instead learns to distribute a utilization budget heterogeneously across layers, either through a static per-layer scalar shared across tokens or a dynamic per-token schedule. Both allocators improve on uniform allocation for state-of-the-art analytic and learned conversion methods; **at 25 percent FFN utilization, dynamic allocation lowers `WikiText-2` perplexity by 1.04, 2.96, and 2.71 points on `Llama-2-7B`, `Llama-3-8B`, and `Qwen2.5-7B`** on the learned base, with reductions of 2.45, 6.26, and 2.17 points on the analytic base. Six-task mean accuracy on the learned base also rises over uniform by an average of 1.5, 4.2, and 3.6 percentage points at utilizations of 12.5, 25, and 50 percent.

papers.title: From Detection To Anticipation: Continuous Onset Forecasting For Stuttered Speech
papers.abstract: Automatic stuttering systems primarily detect dysfluencies after they have occurred, limiting their use for anticipatory intervention. We address this gap by formulating stuttering prediction as continuous causal time-to-event forecasting, where a model estimates the risk of an upcoming stuttering onset every 100 ms using only preceding speech. To support this task, we augment FluencyBank Timestamped for 36 speakers with manually reviewed repetitions, prolongations, and blocks, yielding 2,872 forecasting events. We then model the temporal evolution of frozen Whisper-large-v3 speech representations using a compact causal Conformer with 3.67M trainable parameters. The proposed approach achieves an AUROC of 0.63. Temporal analysis further shows that explicitly modeling preceding speech states outperforms simply increasing the static acoustic window, while a discrete-time survival formulation provides coherent forecasts from 300 ms to 1.5 s using a single model. These results provide initial evidence that stuttering onset is preceded by measurable temporal information in speech and establish a framework for future anticipatory stuttering systems.
papers.summary: Automatic stuttering systems mostly detect dysfluencies after they have occurred, which is too late for anticipatory intervention. The authors reframe the task as continuous causal time-to-event forecasting, estimating the risk of an upcoming stuttering onset every 100 milliseconds from preceding speech alone, and augment `FluencyBank Timestamped` for 36 speakers with manually reviewed repetitions, prolongations, and blocks to obtain 2,872 forecasting events. A compact causal `Conformer` with 3.67 million trainable parameters models the temporal evolution of frozen `Whisper-large-v3` representations and **reaches an AUROC of 0.63**. Explicitly modeling preceding speech states beats simply widening the static acoustic window, and a discrete-time survival formulation yields coherent forecasts from 300 milliseconds to 1.5 seconds with a single model.

papers.title: LLMs program using Reusable and Composable Abstract Representations
papers.abstract: When writing code, the same computation can be expressed in different programming languages and through different implementation strategies. We show that the activations of LLMs capture this shared structure in reusable and composable abstract representations when they generate code. These representations emerge in the middle layers, are reusable across programming languages, and afford the model an impressive amount of generalization ability when generating code under various interventions. Using activation steering, we show that function, programming language, and implementation strategy can be independently manipulated. The independent interventions on language and function can be flexibly composed to control code generation, even in cases when the prompt contains no information about language and function. We additionally find that finetuning on examples of arbitrarily defined functions in one programming language transfers to other languages, consistent with the models reusing abstract features of code generation that are shared across different examples. Finally, to study how such abstract representations come to be, we implement a minimal model of shared, reusable, and composable structure in a synthetic setting, and show that transformers trained on such data learn representations that reuse these parts flexibly across contexts.
papers.summary: The same computation can be written in different programming languages and with different implementation strategies, and the question is whether LLMs internally represent this shared structure when they generate code. Using activation steering, the authors find that middle-layer representations capture function, programming language, and implementation strategy as independently manipulable factors that are reusable across languages, and that **steering interventions on language and function can be composed to control code generation even when the prompt contains no information about either**. Finetuning on examples of arbitrarily defined functions in one language transfers to other languages, consistent with reuse of shared abstract features, and a minimal synthetic setting shows that transformers trained on data with shared, composable structure learn representations that reuse those parts flexibly across contexts.

papers.title: FinGREAT: Evaluating LLMs on Financial Graph-guided Retrieval And Typing
papers.abstract: Financial disclosures express the underlying relationships of double-entry accounting through unstructured text. While financial LLM benchmarks predominantly emphasize question answering and classification, schema-guided evidence discovery remains relatively under-explored. We investigate whether open-weight LLMs can extract and classify evidence corresponding to predefined double-entry accounting relationships underlying the text. Using a financial accounting graph comprising 11 nodes (accounts) and 11 edges (transaction types), we evaluate mid-sized models from 5 open-weight families across 1,300 SEC 10-K Item 7 filings spanning 26 years, comparing their extraction performance against three proprietary models. Results reveal substantial differences in extraction volume, edge distributions, and cross-model agreement. Building on this study, we introduce a human-annotated relation classification benchmark comprising 483 passages across three financial accounting categories, evaluating 34 open-weight and 10 proprietary models. The strongest open-weight and proprietary models achieve 84.1\% and 92.8\% accuracy, respectively, with considerable variation across accounting categories. Our findings highlight the importance of evaluating evidence discovery and relation understanding separately, while investigating locally deployable models for scalable, privacy-sensitive financial analysis.
papers.summary: Financial disclosures express double-entry accounting relationships in unstructured text, yet financial LLM benchmarks focus on question answering and classification rather than schema-guided evidence discovery. Using an accounting graph of 11 account nodes and 11 transaction-type edges, the authors evaluate mid-sized open-weight models from five families against three proprietary models on extracting and classifying evidence from 1,300 SEC 10-K Item 7 filings spanning 26 years, finding substantial differences in extraction volume, edge distributions, and cross-model agreement. They also introduce a human-annotated relation classification benchmark of 483 passages across three accounting categories, evaluated on 34 open-weight and 10 proprietary models, where **the strongest open-weight and proprietary models reach 84.1 percent and 92.8 percent accuracy** with considerable variation across categories. The results argue for evaluating evidence discovery and relation understanding separately and for examining locally deployable models for privacy-sensitive financial analysis.

papers.title: Refined Topology-Pass Scheduling: Damped Trust-Region Compensation for Dynamic k-NN Graphs in SE(3)-Equivariant Structure Prediction
papers.abstract: Equivariant structure-prediction pipelines alternate coordinate updates with the construction of a k-nearest-neighbour (kNN) graph whose membership is a discrete, piecewise-constant function of the coordinates. Rebuilding that graph at every block boundary (PB) is the expensive part of an epoch, whereas reusing one frozen graph (F) is fast but leaves a topology gap. We study a two-pass design in which the cheap pass records a small amount of state (margins, kNN radii, measured per-boundary displacements) and a second pass compensates conservatively. We formulate the choice of the graph-construction basis as a damped fixed-point iteration whose unique fixed point is exactly PB, and derive (i) exact non-flip certificates with the two-sided constant $m_i/4$ and one-sided constant $m_i/2$, (ii) the minimum-variance (BLUE) replay gain $\gamma^*$ and the resulting feasibility crossover, (iii) an $\ell_\infty$ trust-region projection that preserves convergence, and (iv) an analytic near-tie spacing law $E[m] \approx r_k/(3k)$ that matches measurements to 1\%. Three compensation levels are implemented in C++ (L1: frozen set with live geometry; L2: margin-gated local repair; L3: damped, projected basis) and validated under a matched-conditions protocol (identical seed, MSA depth and trajectory family, only the topology mode differs). L2 reproduces the PB edge set exactly ($D = 0.0000$ at every boundary), L1 stays within 0.6% and L3 interpolates monotonically: L2 reproduces the PB edge set exactly when the trust region is removed, and L3 interpolates between the frozen and the PB topology. The recorded trajectory itself yields a measured $1.5\times$ Pass-1 and $1.76\times$ epoch speed-up with no measurable loss gap. An open-source implementation of the runtime and of all the experiments reported here is available at https://github.com/AlbertHuang96/ProteinPredictMachineLearning.
papers.summary: SE(3)-equivariant structure-prediction pipelines alternate coordinate updates with rebuilding a k-nearest-neighbour (kNN) graph, and rebuilding at every block boundary is the expensive part of an epoch while reusing one frozen graph is fast but leaves a topology gap. The authors propose a two-pass scheme in which a cheap pass records margins, kNN radii, and per-boundary displacements and a second pass compensates conservatively, framed as a damped fixed-point iteration whose unique fixed point is the full per-boundary rebuild. They derive exact non-flip certificates, a minimum-variance replay gain, a trust-region projection that preserves convergence, and a near-tie spacing law matching measurements to 1 percent, and implement three compensation levels in C++ validated under a matched-conditions protocol. The margin-gated repair level reproduces the full-rebuild edge set exactly, and **the recorded trajectory yields a 1.5x pass-one and 1.76x epoch speed-up with no measurable loss gap**.

papers.title: Copy-Paste Language Models
papers.abstract: Transformers are intuitively considered to be efficient at copying from their inputs. We actually show that the ability of LLMs to copy in context can be improved through explicit modeling. We propose Copy-Paste Language Models (CPLMs), which add a lightweight Copy-Paste head to the conventional language modeling (LM) head. CPLMs improve training efficiency, downstream performance, and offer new operating points in long-context and retrieval setups. We validate our approach by pretraining models from 135M to 1.7B parameters, showing improvements across all scales and backbones with negligible training and inference overheads. We explain the success of CPLMs by showing that they partially mitigate the LM head gradient bottleneck through an alternative gradient path.
papers.summary: Transformers are assumed to copy from their inputs easily, but the authors show that in-context copying can be improved through explicit modeling. Copy-Paste Language Models (`CPLMs`) add a lightweight copy-paste head alongside the standard language modeling (LM) head, and the authors validate the idea by pretraining models from 135M to 1.7B parameters. **`CPLMs` improve training efficiency and downstream performance across all scales and backbones with negligible training and inference overhead**, and they open new operating points in long-context and retrieval settings. The gains are attributed to the extra head partially bypassing the gradient bottleneck of the LM head through an alternative gradient path.

papers.title: Multi-Sensitive Distributional Fairness: Joint Wasserstein Audits and Shapley Allocation
papers.abstract: Fairness audits with several sensitive attributes are often performed one coordinate at a time. This can miss purely intersectional disparities: a score may be independent of each sensitive coordinate while depending on their joint profile. We study distributional demographic parity for a real-valued score using one-dimensional Wasserstein geometry. We distinguish two complementary constructions. Conditional and sequential audits characterize joint parity through their zero sets, but their positive values do not generally decompose a fixed joint Wasserstein disparity. By contrast, full-cell conditional quantile functions define a Hilbert-valued random variable whose variance is the joint disparity. Conditional expectations of this quantile process induce a monotone information game: every reveal order yields an exact martingale decomposition of the same joint disparity, while Shapley values provide an order-free attribution across sensitive attributes. Under independent sensitive attributes, the game reduces to a Hoeffding-ANOVA decomposition and Shapley splits each interaction energy equally among its members; under dependence, orthogonality is lost and explicit formulas reveal suppression and redundancy effects that marginal audits can hide. We give fixed-grid estimators and permutation calibration, and illustrate the framework on synthetic examples and ACSIncome. The resulting framework separates three questions that are often conflated: whether joint distributional parity holds, how a fixed joint disparity decomposes along an information path, and how that disparity can be attributed across sensitive coordinates without privileging an ordering.
papers.summary: Fairness audits with several sensitive attributes are usually run one attribute at a time, which can miss disparities that appear only in the joint profile. Working with distributional demographic parity for a real-valued score under one-dimensional Wasserstein geometry, the authors show that conditional and sequential audits identify joint parity through their zero sets but do not decompose a fixed joint disparity, whereas full-cell conditional quantile functions define a Hilbert-valued random variable whose variance equals the joint disparity. Conditional expectations of this quantile process induce a monotone information game in which **every reveal order gives an exact martingale decomposition of the same joint disparity, and Shapley values provide an order-free attribution across sensitive attributes**. Under independent attributes the game reduces to a Hoeffding-ANOVA decomposition, under dependence explicit formulas expose suppression and redundancy effects that marginal audits hide, and fixed-grid estimators with permutation calibration are illustrated on synthetic examples and `ACSIncome`.

papers.title: Beyond Time Induction: Structured Conditional Neural Solvers for Parametric Stochastic-Volatility Pricing
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks provide a flexible framework for learning parametric PDE solution families without labeled data, yet preserving accurate derivatives across heterogeneous regimes remains challenging. Structured neural solvers offer compact representations, but restrictive conditional parameterizations can limit adaptation across the solution family. We introduce BeTINN, a structured conditional architecture extending time-induced modulation through multi-directional time-parameter conditioning and a joint residual pathway. We evaluate BeTINN on the Heston stochastic-volatility PDE, a demanding parametric problem with mixed derivatives and economically relevant first- and second-order sensitivities. BeTINN improves joint accuracy across normalized option value and key sensitivity metrics relative to our baselines. Controlled ablations characterize the roles of its architectural components. We further find that validation physics loss is informative but does not fully determine differential fidelity, and that accurate solution values can coexist with localized derivative errors. These results support structured conditional adaptation and motivate derivative-aware evaluation when sensitivities are downstream quantities of interest.
papers.summary: Physics-informed neural networks can learn families of parametric partial differential equation (PDE) solutions without labeled data, but keeping derivatives accurate across heterogeneous regimes is hard, and restrictive conditional parameterizations in structured solvers can limit adaptation across the solution family. `BeTINN` is a structured conditional architecture that extends time-induced modulation with multi-directional time-parameter conditioning and a joint residual pathway, evaluated on the `Heston` stochastic-volatility PDE, where mixed derivatives and first- and second-order sensitivities carry economic meaning. **It improves joint accuracy across normalized option value and key sensitivity metrics relative to the baselines**, and controlled ablations isolate the role of each architectural component. The authors also find that validation physics loss does not fully determine derivative fidelity, since accurate solution values can coexist with localized derivative errors, which motivates derivative-aware evaluation when sensitivities are the quantities of interest.

papers.title: MemeTrace: A Multimodal LLM-Based Agent for Safety-Aware Meme Provenance Analysis
papers.abstract: Online memes are often carriers of unsafe content such as disinformation and propaganda. Their rapid evolution in response to news events and strong dependence on contextual information make it difficult for platforms and moderators to detect and moderate them effectively. Moreover, existing moderation studies typically classify memes as safe or unsafe based on individual images, lacking the ability to perform broader provenance analysis, i.e., where a meme originates, how it spreads, what cultural symbolism it represents, whether it poses potential risks to society, etc. To bridge this gap, we introduce MemeTrace, a multimodal LLM-based agent that automatically traces the provenance and potential risks of emerging memes. We evaluate MemeTrace on Meme100, a dataset of 100 real-world memes, using both human annotation and automatic metrics. The results demonstrate that MemeTrace substantially outperforms the VLM baseline. More importantly, MemeTrace achieves higher accuracy in detecting unsafe memes, especially those involving disinformation and sensitive content, and remains robust under visual perturbations.
papers.summary: Memes often carry disinformation and propaganda, evolve rapidly with news events, and depend heavily on context, which makes them hard to moderate, and existing work classifies individual images as safe or unsafe without tracing where a meme originated or how it spread. `MemeTrace` is a multimodal LLM-based agent that automatically investigates the provenance, cultural symbolism, and potential societal risks of emerging memes. Evaluated on `Meme100`, a set of 100 real-world memes, with both human annotation and automatic metrics, **it substantially outperforms a vision-language model baseline** and achieves higher accuracy at detecting unsafe memes, particularly those involving disinformation and sensitive content, while remaining robust under visual perturbations.

papers.title: Whose Data, Whose Benchmark? A User-Centric Framework for Auditing Evaluation Resources
papers.abstract: Benchmarks shape how model capabilities are measured and interpreted, yet their scores can obscure whose conventions, contexts, and judgments define successful performance. We introduce a user-centric audit framework that distinguishes users who contribute benchmark content from those whose needs evaluation results are intended to represent. The framework operationalizes seven dimensions across benchmark content, metadata, documentation, and scoring procedures. Across 16 resources, we find that American-centered conventions account for 62.4-94.4% of matched signals in 11 text benchmarks, while geographic visibility in five image-text resources is concentrated and strongly associated with national GDP share (mean Pearson r = 0.780; Spearman p = 0.778). Documentation reveals a systematic source-target gap: all 16 resources operationalize source-user context, but none operationalize target-user context. Paired scoring experiments further show that meaning-preserving answer variants reduce DROP exact-match accuracy from 100.0% to 33.3%, while TruthfulQA exhibits metric-dependent reductions in reference similarity. Our framework and documentation checklist make user assumptions auditable, clarifying what benchmark scores represent and where evaluation claims are supported.
papers.summary: Benchmark scores can obscure whose conventions and judgments define success, so the authors propose a user-centric audit framework that separates the users who contribute benchmark content from the target users whose needs the results are meant to represent, operationalized through seven dimensions spanning content, metadata, documentation, and scoring procedures. Applied to 16 resources, the audit finds that American-centered conventions account for 62.4 to 94.4 percent of matched signals in 11 text benchmarks, that geographic visibility in five image-text resources is concentrated and strongly correlated with national GDP share, and that **all 16 resources operationalize source-user context while none operationalize target-user context**. Paired scoring experiments show that meaning-preserving answer variants cut `DROP` exact-match accuracy from 100 percent to 33.3 percent, with metric-dependent reductions on `TruthfulQA`, and an accompanying documentation checklist is intended to make these user assumptions auditable.

papers.title: Exploring Interpretability in Deep Learning-Based Forest Classification - Separating Similar Forest Classes using Sentinel-2 Time Series
papers.abstract: The ecological insurance theory posits that diverse forests are more resilient and better able to adapt to changing environmental conditions. Increasing drought and heat stress in Central Europe promotes mixed forests for maintaining ecosystem services. However, a diverse species distribution complicates remote sensing-based species mapping, as distinguishing pure from mixed species compositions at the pixel level remains challenging. We evaluated the potential of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for tree-species classification from Sentinel-2 time series and investigated the spectral-temporal features underlying class discrimination, with particular emphasis on separating pure from mixed Norway spruce pixels. We compared RNN classification models with Random Forest (RF) and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) and used Integrated Gradients (IG) to quantify feature attributions across spectral bands and time. The best-performing RNN achieved a Macro-F1 score of 0.851 on the test data, outperforming XGBoost by 0.012 and Random Forest by 0.103. Beyond classification performance, the attribution analysis revealed distinct spectral-temporal patterns associated with the separation of pure and mixed Norway spruce pixels. Attribution values increased particularly after approximately day of year (DOY) 125, while B11 showed the strongest contribution during periods of increasing spectral divergence between the two classes. These findings show that recurrent models can provide competitive classification performance while also revealing the phenological periods and spectral regions that are most relevant for distinguishing closely related forest compositions. Combining time-series classification with explainability therefore provides additional insight into the spectral-temporal mechanisms underlying tree-species discrimination and may support more detailed mapping of mixed forest structures.
papers.summary: Mixed-species forests are more resilient under the rising drought and heat stress in Central Europe, but distinguishing pure from mixed species compositions at the pixel level in satellite imagery remains difficult. The authors train recurrent neural networks (RNNs) on `Sentinel-2` time series for tree-species classification, compare them with `Random Forest` and `XGBoost`, and apply Integrated Gradients (`IG`) to attribute predictions across spectral bands and time, focusing on separating pure from mixed Norway spruce pixels. **The best RNN reaches a macro-F1 of 0.851 on test data**, ahead of `XGBoost` by 0.012 and `Random Forest` by 0.103. Attribution values rise notably after roughly day of year 125, and band B11 contributes most during periods of growing spectral divergence between the two classes, pointing to the phenological windows and spectral regions that matter for the distinction.

papers.title: Outcome-Routed Distillation and Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract:
On-policy distillation provides dense supervision on the student's own samples, but its targets still come from the teacher. Verifier reinforcement learning (RL) instead uses an outcome signal, but it provides no direct constraint on capabilities outside the verifier. Combining the two is difficult for diffusion language models (dLLMs), because bidirectional denoising makes the policy likelihoods required by ratio-based RL unreliable.
