  We develop a likelihood-free pipeline for a mixture-of-experts dLLM. Each rollout group is routed by verifier outcome. Mixed groups use ratio-free, group-centred REINFORCE. If every student rollout fails but a teacher succeeds, the model receives dense KL supervision on the student's denoising canvases. All other groups are skipped. A KL term anchored to the distilled checkpoint limits changes outside the verifier reward.
  The tool-calling teacher succeeds on only 18.6% of the training prompts. At 24 denoising steps, distillation exceeds the teacher by 6.77 percentage points, and routing improves the distilled checkpoint by a further 18.31 points. Routing lowers reasoning-trace accuracy by 0.71 points but raises direct-answer accuracy on the same items by 13.21 points. The anchored arm restores trace accuracy. Its tool-calling score differs by -0.16 points, with a confidence interval that includes zero, although this comparison also removes a small fallback distillation route. A domain-conditional recipe retains a 16.37-point tool-calling gain; a second seed gives 18.23 points and reproduces both preservation results, but the math result is seed-dependent. We pre-registered every arm and evaluated each comparison on paired items in a single sweep on one machine.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation gives dense supervision on a student's own samples but its targets come from the teacher, while verifier reinforcement learning (RL) uses outcome rewards but leaves capabilities outside the verifier unconstrained, and combining the two is hard for diffusion language models (dLLMs) because bidirectional denoising makes the policy likelihoods needed by ratio-based RL unreliable. The authors build a likelihood-free pipeline for a mixture-of-experts dLLM that routes each rollout group by verifier outcome: mixed groups get ratio-free, group-centred `REINFORCE`, groups where every student rollout fails but the teacher succeeds get dense KL supervision on the student's denoising canvases, other groups are skipped, and a KL term anchored to the distilled checkpoint limits drift outside the reward. With a tool-calling teacher that succeeds on only 18.6 percent of training prompts, **distillation at 24 denoising steps exceeds the teacher by 6.77 points and routing adds a further 18.31 points**, while the anchored variant restores the reasoning-trace accuracy that routing had lowered. A domain-conditional recipe retains a 16.37-point tool-calling gain and a second seed reproduces the preservation results, though the math result is seed-dependent; every arm was pre-registered and evaluated on paired items in a single sweep.

papers.title: Dimension-Free Scaling Laws for Size Generalization: An Exponential Separation
papers.abstract: Modern machine learning models increasingly operate on variable-size structured data, such as sets and graphs. A central requirement is \emph{size generalization}: the ability of a model trained on inputs of one size to generalize to inputs of a different, potentially much larger, size. Classical statistical learning theory, however, primarily considers fixed input domains, and its guarantees often deteriorate with input dimension. Although extensive work has established when models on sets and graphs can be transferred across input sizes, such results do not characterize the statistical cost of doing so: the sample complexity of size generalization, and its relationship to classical in-domain learning, remain largely unknown. We develop a statistical learning theory of size generalization and establish a sharp exponential separation in sample complexity. Letting $n$ denote the number of training samples, we show that polynomial source decay is insufficient for efficient size generalization: while it yields error $n^{-\Theta(1)}$ and hence polynomial sample complexity for in-domain learning, size-generalization error decays only as $(\log n)^{-\Theta(1)}$, yielding an exponential separation. Thus, polynomial in-domain sample complexity can become exponential across sizes. We then identify an exponential source condition under which size generalization achieves error $n^{-\Theta(1)}$, recovering polynomial sample complexity. These guarantees are independent of input dimension and depend only on the number of training samples, yielding dimension-free scaling laws. We also provide matching minimax lower bounds, establishing optimality. To our knowledge, this work provides the first dimension-free minimax theory of size generalization and a rigorous characterization of when, and at what statistical cost, learning can transfer across input sizes.
papers.summary: Models on sets and graphs must often generalize from training inputs of one size to much larger ones, but classical statistical learning theory assumes fixed input domains and says little about the sample complexity of such size generalization. The authors develop a statistical learning theory of size generalization and prove a sharp exponential separation: **under polynomial source decay, in-domain error falls polynomially in the number of samples n while size-generalization error decays only as an inverse power of log n**, so polynomial in-domain sample complexity can become exponential across sizes. An exponential source condition restores polynomial rates, the resulting guarantees depend only on the number of training samples rather than input dimension, and matching minimax lower bounds establish optimality.

papers.title: Exact Scaling Laws for a Random-Features Bigram Model
papers.abstract: Understanding neural scaling laws is increasingly important for theory and practice, yet first-principles explanations remain limited even in simple settings. In this work, we study capacity-limited scaling in a bottlenecked bigram model with power-law (Zipf) token statistics, viewed as an analytically tractable toy model of a large language model. Fixed random embeddings serve as a proxy for representational capacity and induce an explicit bottleneck of width, allowing us to derive scaling laws for prediction regret as a function of model width, vocabulary size, and the Zipf exponent. Our results complement recent theoretical accounts based on optimization dynamics by isolating scaling due purely to representational constraints. In the appropriate regime, the theory recovers the functional form of classical neural scaling laws and suggests that heavy-tailed language statistics may underlie both optimization- and capacity-driven scaling. Experiments natural language datasets (WikiText2, OpenWebText) closely match the predicted curves.
papers.summary: First-principles explanations of neural scaling laws remain limited even in simple settings. The authors study a bottlenecked bigram model with Zipf-distributed token statistics as a tractable toy model of a language model, using fixed random embeddings as a proxy for representational capacity, and derive scaling laws for prediction regret as a function of model width, vocabulary size, and the Zipf exponent. The analysis isolates scaling driven purely by representational constraints rather than optimization dynamics, and **in the appropriate regime it recovers the functional form of classical neural scaling laws**, suggesting that heavy-tailed language statistics may underlie both capacity-driven and optimization-driven scaling. Experiments on `WikiText2` and `OpenWebText` closely match the predicted curves.

papers.title: From Efficiency to Sufficiency: The Cost-Aware Measurement Design Framework for Automated Essay Scoring
papers.abstract: Compute cost in automated essay scoring (AES) is usually treated as a technical efficiency issue rather than a measurement design concern. Yet deployment decisions require more than reporting latency, model size, or inference expense. In high-stakes settings, total burden includes validation, monitoring, adjudication, compliance, and governance; in instructional settings, pricing, licensing, and integration may dominate cost. This paper reframes AES as a cost-constrained measurement system and introduces the Cost-Aware Measurement Design (CAMD) Framework, a four-layer structure consisting of metering, allocation, unit economics, and decision, for translating computational and workflow resource records into decision-relevant cost constructs. Direct cost is specified as monetary outlay plus attributable labor and time, and two criteria, design attribution and auditability, determine what the cost boundary excludes. Burdens that satisfy neither criterion, such as institutional capability and governance posture, are represented as constraints on which designs are admissible rather than priced. The paper defines cost per defensible score (CPDS) and argues that AES systems should be compared by quality-cost sufficiency: minimizing cost among defensible scoring designs that satisfy measurement requirements. Scoring volume conditions all four layers, so cost per defensible score is treated as a function of scale rather than as a single transferable number. CAMD provides a portable basis for representing, comparing, and evaluating cost across AES studies and deployment contexts.
papers.summary: Compute cost in automated essay scoring (AES) is usually treated as a technical efficiency matter, yet deployment decisions in high-stakes settings also carry validation, monitoring, adjudication, compliance, and governance burdens, and in instructional settings pricing, licensing, and integration may dominate. The Cost-Aware Measurement Design (`CAMD`) framework reframes AES as a cost-constrained measurement system with four layers covering metering, allocation, unit economics, and decision, which translate computational and workflow records into decision-relevant cost constructs. Direct cost is defined as monetary outlay plus attributable labor and time, two criteria of design attribution and auditability fix the cost boundary, and burdens that meet neither, such as institutional capability, are treated as admissibility constraints rather than priced. **The framework proposes cost per defensible score (`CPDS`), treated as a function of scoring volume rather than a single transferable number, as the basis for comparing AES systems by quality-cost sufficiency**, meaning minimizing cost among designs that satisfy measurement requirements.

papers.title: Can LLM Agents Efficiently Identify Appliance Faults? Insights From Diagnosing a Simulated Appliance
papers.abstract: In so-called "Industry 4.0," integrated sensors, analytics tools, and other digital technologies supplement industrial workflows, potentiating enhanced visibility and automation. Prognostics and health management (PHM) and natural language processing (NLP) practitioners alike have explored the application of large language models (LLMs) to industrial asset management, but many prior works' focus on exam-like benchmarks has limited their assessment of LLMs' ability to automate practical operations. Herein, we introduce CoffeeBench, a fault diagnostics task for LLM agents, using a simulated appliance. The LLMs we evaluate struggle to consistently identify faults from the sensor information alone, but the best-performing ones can iteratively refine the fault-option space to eventually obtain a successful diagnosis. Our subsequent analyses, therefore, focus on: differentiating models by diagnostic efficiency (RQ1); examining the lagging performance of the three worst models (RQ2); and identifying viable heuristics for selective prediction (RQ3), including that initial diagnostic uncertainty and LLM-judged soundness of reasoning are high-signal predictors of diagnostic success. In addition to our benchmark results (Section 3.1), we provide practical insights for improving the performance of the open-weight models on CoffeeBench, such as by explicitly tracking episode state on their behalf to reduce timeouts (Section 3.2) or applying a deliberation loop to refine diagnostic hypotheses (Section 3.3).
papers.summary: Prior work applying large language models (LLMs) to industrial asset management has leaned on exam-style benchmarks, leaving open how well they automate practical prognostics and health management (PHM) operations. `CoffeeBench` is a fault diagnostics task in which LLM agents must identify faults in a simulated appliance from sensor information. **The evaluated models struggle to identify faults consistently from sensor data alone, though the best ones iteratively narrow the fault-option space until they reach a correct diagnosis**. Follow-up analyses rank models by diagnostic efficiency, examine why the three weakest models lag, and find that initial diagnostic uncertainty and LLM-judged soundness of reasoning are strong predictors of success for selective prediction, alongside practical fixes for open-weight models such as tracking episode state on the model's behalf to reduce timeouts and adding a deliberation loop to refine hypotheses.

papers.title: Qwenfant: Train Big Character-level BabyLMs on Concise Parallel Text
papers.abstract: This work concerns our submission for the Multilingual track of the 2026 BabyLM Challenge. We improve on our baseline using data that has been summarized and translated by an LLM, showing that higher-quality data can come from synthetic sources. We further improve with 2 simple changes: using a larger model, and using a character-level vocabulary. Both of these changes require LoRA-style fine-tuning for realizing their full potential. We dub our final Qwen3-based model Qwenfant, which, at the time of submission, ranks 1st in the Multilingual track.
papers.summary: For the Multilingual track of the 2026 `BabyLM Challenge`, the authors improve on their baseline by training on text that an LLM has summarized and translated, showing that higher-quality data can come from synthetic sources. Two further simple changes, a larger model and a character-level vocabulary, add gains, and both require LoRA-style fine-tuning to realize their full potential. The resulting `Qwen3`-based model, `Qwenfant`, **ranked first in the Multilingual track at the time of submission**.

papers.title: Verifier-Grounded Agentic RL for Provably Correct Code
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning for code usually rewards passing tests, which a model can do while remaining wrong on the inputs the tests do not cover. A program verifier instead decides whether a program satisfies a formal specification for all inputs. Language models are almost always paired with verifiers at inference time only, and turning a verifier into a reward raises two difficulties. It reports only acceptance or rejection, which gives no gradient when every attempt fails, and a policy can cheat it, most simply by telling it to assume what the proof was supposed to establish. We build an agentic environment and reward that address both. The reward reads the verifier's diagnostics rather than its verdict, scoring a candidate by the weighted fraction of proof obligations it discharges, extended with hidden probes from a reference proof's annotations. An integrity audit outranks the verifier, rejecting any candidate that alters the specification or assumes what it was meant to prove. The model works as an agent against a live verifier over many turns, with a separately trained proof specialist as a frozen collaborator. Across Qwen3 models from 1.7B to 14B and a 35B Qwen3.6 mixture-of-experts model, held-out verification on code generation rises from 66.1% to 93.5% on DafnyBench and from 56.3% to 100% on SWE-Proof. This reward leads every other training signal we compare, including a binary pass-or-fail reward trained under otherwise identical settings, with the widest margin on code generation. When the agent must also deliver the repository patch, graded by each project's withheld tests, the fraction of held-out issues it resolves rises from 59.6% to 72.5%. Evaluated unchanged on three verification suites withheld from training, the checkpoints improve on all of them, including one whose language and verifier are absent from training.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning for code usually rewards passing tests, which a program can do while remaining wrong on inputs the tests miss, whereas a formal verifier checks a specification for all inputs but reports only accept or reject and can be cheated by a policy that assumes what it was meant to prove. The authors build an agentic environment whose reward reads the verifier's diagnostics, scoring a candidate by the weighted fraction of proof obligations it discharges plus hidden probes from a reference proof, with an integrity audit that outranks the verifier and rejects any candidate that alters the specification or assumes its own goal, and the model works over many turns against a live verifier alongside a separately trained, frozen proof specialist. Across `Qwen3` models from 1.7B to 14B and a 35B `Qwen3.6` mixture-of-experts model, **held-out verification on code generation rises from 66.1% to 93.5% on `DafnyBench` and from 56.3% to 100% on `SWE-Proof`**, beating every other training signal compared, including a binary pass-or-fail reward trained under identical settings. When the agent must also deliver a repository patch graded by each project's withheld tests, the share of held-out issues resolved rises from 59.6% to 72.5%, and the checkpoints also improve on three verification suites withheld from training, including one whose language and verifier are absent from training.

papers.title: DTDD: Divergence-Triggered Dynamic Distillation for Reliable On-Policy Supervision
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision on student rollouts, but this supervision can become unreliable when the student and teacher diverge, either because of a large initial policy gap or compounding errors in long-horizon reasoning and tool use. We introduce Divergence-Triggered Dynamic Distillation (DTDD), an adaptive OPD framework that uses segment-level student-teacher divergence to trigger teacher takeover during training. When divergence triggers an intervention during reasoning, the student prefix continues to receive standard OPD supervision. The teacher then generates a recovery suffix, which the student learns through behavior cloning, using cross-entropy on the teacher-generated tokens. We evaluate DTDD in three regimes: long-horizon reasoning, distillation from a base initialization without offline supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and multi-turn agents. We also compare alternative trigger designs and teacher-intervention rates. DTDD reduces the post-warmup peak gradient norm by $8.6\times$ and, from a base initialization, reaches $21.3\%$ held-out math accuracy in $2.6\times$ fewer optimizer updates than OPD; both methods finish near $22\%$. It improves best-observed performance by $4.8$ and $4.1$ percentage points on ALFWorld with LoRA and agentic code, respectively. Ablations show that segment-averaged triggers outperform token-spike triggers. Behavior cloning is also more effective than the tested OPD surrogate for training teacher-generated recoveries. Across 23 experimental arms, takeover tends to help when the teacher substantially outperforms the OPD-trained student, provided that the teacher can recover from student-visited states, the student can learn those recoveries, and teacher intervention is neither excessive nor insufficient.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation, which gives a student dense token-level supervision from a teacher on the student's own rollouts, becomes unreliable when the two policies diverge, whether from a large initial gap or from compounding errors in long reasoning and tool use. `DTDD` (Divergence-Triggered Dynamic Distillation) monitors segment-level student-teacher divergence and, when it triggers, has the teacher take over: the student prefix still receives standard on-policy distillation supervision while the teacher generates a recovery suffix that the student learns by behavior cloning with cross-entropy. Evaluated on long-horizon reasoning, distillation from a base model without supervised fine-tuning, and multi-turn agents, the method **cuts the post-warmup peak gradient norm by 8.6 times** and reaches 21.3% held-out math accuracy in 2.6 times fewer optimizer updates than plain on-policy distillation, with both finishing near 22%, and improves best-observed performance by 4.8 and 4.1 points on `ALFWorld` with `LoRA` and on agentic code. Ablations across 23 experimental arms show that segment-averaged triggers beat token-spike triggers, that behavior cloning beats the tested on-policy surrogate for learning recoveries, and that takeover helps mainly when the teacher substantially outperforms the student, can recover from student-visited states, and intervenes neither too much nor too little.

papers.title: Did the LLM Answer the Question? A Semantic Reconstruction Game for Jailbreak Evaluation
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attacks against large language models (LLMs) are evaluated using attack success rate (ASR), which depends on correctly identifying responses that fulfill prohibited requests. Existing evaluators can mistake refusals or topically related responses for successful attacks. We show that changing only the judge LLM can alter reported ASR by up to $82$ percentage points. We introduce the semantic reconstruction game, a training-free evaluator that decomposes compliance judgments into constrained semantic comparisons. Given only a response, an LLM reconstructs the request answered by its substantive content, excluding information merely repeated or refused. The game compares this reconstruction against similar decoy requests to determine whether it matches the original request, allowing abstention when neither candidate matches. Across three off-the-shelf LLM judges, the game achieves the lowest mean error against human labels among evaluated methods and reduces variation in reported ASR. It prioritizes avoiding false positives, even at the cost of missing some successful jailbreaks.
papers.summary: Jailbreak attacks on large language models (LLMs) are scored by attack success rate (ASR), which hinges on correctly deciding whether a response actually fulfilled the prohibited request, and existing judges often mistake refusals or merely topical responses for successes. The authors show that **swapping only the judge LLM can shift reported ASR by up to 82 percentage points**. Their training-free evaluator, the semantic reconstruction game, has an LLM reconstruct from the response alone which request its substantive content answers, excluding repeated or refused material, then compares that reconstruction against the original request and similar decoys, abstaining when neither matches. Across three off-the-shelf judges the game gives the lowest mean error against human labels among the methods tested and reduces variation in reported ASR, while deliberately favoring fewer false positives at the cost of missing some successful jailbreaks.

papers.title: PersEvalBench: Can LLM Evaluators Judge Contextually Appropriate Use of Persona Information?
papers.abstract:
Large language model (LLM) evaluators are increasingly used to assess personalized assistants, yet whether they can reliably judge personalization has rarely been tested. We introduce PersEvalBench, a benchmark testing whether an evaluator can recognize appropriate and inappropriate uses of user history. It contains 403 multi-episode scenarios where user information should persist, transfer, or cease to apply. The benchmark covers nine controlled error subtypes across three families: under-personalization, over-personalization, and misapplied-state errors. Human audits confirm that generated errors match their intended types and that the prescribed uses of user information are reasonable.
  Across five LLM evaluators, recognition of controlled personalization errors remains limited even with the full dialogue history. On the human-evaluated subset, under-personalization shows the largest gap: humans recognize 94.4% of these errors, compared with 63.9% for the strongest reported evaluator. Evaluators often recognize that a response is problematic but reverse the error direction, mistaking failure to follow an applicable preference (UNDER) for use of an inapplicable preference (OVER). Easier evidence access offers little help: highlighting the relevant history turns raises error recognition only slightly, suggesting that the remaining difficulty lies in judging what role that information should play in the response.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) evaluators are increasingly used to grade personalized assistants, but whether they can reliably judge personalization itself has rarely been tested. `PersEvalBench` contains 403 multi-episode scenarios in which user information should persist, transfer, or stop applying, with nine controlled error subtypes spanning under-personalization, over-personalization, and misapplied-state errors, validated by human audits. Across five LLM evaluators, recognition of these errors stays limited even with the full dialogue history: **humans catch 94.4% of under-personalization errors versus 63.9% for the strongest evaluator**, and evaluators often sense that a response is problematic but reverse the error direction, confusing a missed applicable preference with an applied inapplicable one. Highlighting the relevant history turns helps only slightly, suggesting the difficulty lies in judging what role the information should play rather than in finding it.

papers.title: Historical-Feature Residual Adaptation for Sequential Screening
papers.abstract: Sequential screening policies must use acquired feedback effectively under a fixed experiment budget. We study acquisition-time residual adaptation: a small ranking correction built from fixed historical features and anchored to base scores recorded before feedback is revealed. The interface accepts a history-conditioned scorer and a candidate feature table; its primary instantiation augments AssayFormer's ten-dimensional representation with 64 historical directions while retaining the pretrained model. In retrospective evaluation on 20 official-test screens from 15 recorded sources, a comparison fixed before target-outcome access increased source-macro fraction of hits recovered from 22.58% to 28.61%, exceeding all six prespecified comparators. A same-feature ordinary ranking head achieved 25.73%. Supplementary strong logistic, rank-fusion, and unprojected controls achieved 26.42%, 26.02%, and 26.78%, respectively. A separate model-independent pilot on 13 reused development screens reconstructs the features without AssayFormer assets. Across three seeds, residual adaptation improves random-forest hit recovery from 28.87% to 31.27%, while logistic recovery changes from 30.22% to 29.78%. The results show effective pretrained-policy adaptation and useful transfer to an independent nonlinear base, with gains that depend on the base model.
papers.summary: Sequential screening policies, which choose what to test next in experimental campaigns, must exploit feedback acquired during the campaign under a fixed budget. The authors propose acquisition-time residual adaptation: a small ranking correction built from fixed historical features and anchored to base scores recorded before feedback is revealed, instantiated by augmenting `AssayFormer`'s ten-dimensional representation with 64 historical directions while keeping the pretrained model intact. In a retrospective evaluation on 20 official-test screens from 15 sources, with the comparison fixed before outcomes were accessed, the method **raised the source-macro fraction of hits recovered from 22.58% to 28.61%**, beating all six prespecified comparators, while a same-feature ordinary ranking head reached 25.73%. A model-independent pilot on 13 development screens that rebuilds the features without `AssayFormer` assets shows gains for a random-forest base but not for a logistic one, so the benefit depends on the base model.

papers.title: Truthful and Expected-Payment-Optimal Model Routing in Graph-Based Agentic Workflows
papers.abstract: Assigning routine tasks to cheaper large language model (LLM) providers can reduce generation cost, but switching providers may require processing accumulated context again. Keeping dependent tasks with the same provider can instead reuse eligible context. Graph-based workflows therefore couple routing decisions across tasks. Independent providers may also privately know their real-time unit costs and strategically misreport them. We formulate this routing problem as a single-parameter procurement auction and propose STAR (Strategy-proof Topology-aware Agent Routing), which minimizes virtual-cost-weighted graph workloads. Its allocation rule and payments, computed by integrating workload over possible cost reports, make truthful reporting utility-maximizing regardless of other providers' reports and cover each truthful provider's execution cost. With independent cost distributions and non-decreasing virtual costs, STAR additionally minimizes the user's expected total payment to providers. Controlled synthetic experiments separate the execution-cost benefit of topology awareness from the payment benefit of virtual-cost optimization: the former grows with fan-out and transferred payload, while the latter increases gradually along the tested prior-shape heterogeneity path. A paired sensitivity study quantifies how payment savings vary with prior misspecification while strategy-proofness is preserved.
papers.summary: Routing routine tasks in a large language model (LLM) workflow to cheaper providers saves generation cost, but switching providers can force accumulated context to be reprocessed, so routing decisions across a task graph are coupled, and providers may privately know and strategically misreport their real-time unit costs. The authors cast the problem as a single-parameter procurement auction and propose `STAR` (Strategy-proof Topology-aware Agent Routing), which minimizes virtual-cost-weighted graph workloads and computes payments by integrating workload over possible cost reports. They prove that **truthful cost reporting is utility-maximizing for every provider regardless of what others report**, that payments cover each truthful provider's execution cost, and that under independent cost distributions with non-decreasing virtual costs the mechanism also minimizes the user's expected total payment. Controlled synthetic experiments separate the execution-cost benefit of topology awareness, which grows with fan-out and transferred payload, from the payment benefit of virtual-cost optimization, and a paired sensitivity study quantifies how savings vary under prior misspecification while strategy-proofness is preserved.

papers.title: TopicMerge: A Divide and Conquer Approach to Topic Modeling
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in topic modeling have split into two main paths: efficient embedding-based methods that offer scalability but are often outperformed on standard clustering metrics, and Large Language Model (LLM) approaches that achieve state-of-the-art clustering performance but at the cost of prohibitive computational expense and poor scalability. This paper introduces TopicMerge, a novel multi-stage pipeline that bridges these approaches to achieve both state-of-the-art clustering performance and computational efficiency. TopicMerge first employs an efficient clustering pipeline to deliberately over-segment a document corpus into a large set of fine-grained, semantically pure micro-clusters, which are then given initial semantic labels. It then introduces a novel, iterative merging algorithm where an LLM, guided by local neighborhood context, arbitrates on consolidating candidate pairs. These approved merges are then selectively executed and semantically relabeled by the LLM, hierarchically building broader, more coherent topics. Extensive experiments on the Bills and Wiki datasets show that TopicMerge achieves state-of-the-art clustering performance while reducing required LLM calls by over 92% compared to document-level methods, offering a practical and scalable solution.
papers.summary: Topic modeling has split between efficient embedding-based clustering, which scales but trails on standard clustering metrics, and large language model (LLM) approaches that cluster best but are too expensive to scale. `TopicMerge` first over-segments a corpus into many fine-grained, semantically pure micro-clusters using an efficient clustering pipeline and gives them initial labels, then runs an iterative merging algorithm in which an LLM, guided by local neighborhood context, decides whether candidate cluster pairs should be consolidated, executing approved merges and relabeling them to build broader topics hierarchically. On the `Bills` and `Wiki` datasets the authors report state-of-the-art clustering performance while **cutting required LLM calls by over 92%** compared with document-level methods.

papers.title: Why don't Graph Transformers attend to the same token?
papers.abstract: In large language models (LLMs), attention concentrates heavily on the first token. This 'attention sink' is believed to protect deep models against over-mixing. Even though graph transformers face a related pressure, we find that a SoTA graph transformer, GRIT, rarely forms sinks on molecules, and that it sinks less when trained on larger graphs, the opposite of the trend in LLMs. In principle, a graph can prevent sinks: we prove and show empirically that its symmetry and locality limit the attention any node can receive. On molecules, however, with distinguishable atoms and global attention, neither limit prevents sinks; what stops them lies in the model. We find that the attention scoring function is the main cause. Replacing GRIT's gated logit with a dot product raises its sink rate from 0.09 to 0.68 on identical graphs. In Graph Transformers using dot-product attention, removing the sink gives about the same error as removing a random node, while GRIT's most-attended nodes matter to its predictions. Attention sinks are therefore a property of dot-product attention rather than of Transformers. In our experiments, they form when dot-product scoring has a distinguishable node to concentrate on.
papers.summary: In large language models (LLMs), attention concentrates heavily on the first token, forming an 'attention sink' thought to protect deep models against over-mixing, yet the state-of-the-art graph transformer `GRIT` rarely forms sinks on molecules and sinks less when trained on larger graphs, the reverse of the LLM trend. The authors prove and confirm empirically that a graph's symmetry and locality bound how much attention any node can receive, but on molecules with distinguishable atoms and global attention neither bound applies, so the cause must lie in the model. They trace it to the attention scoring function: **replacing `GRIT`'s gated logit with a dot product raises its sink rate from 0.09 to 0.68 on identical graphs**. In dot-product graph transformers, removing the sink node hurts about as much as removing a random node, whereas `GRIT`'s most-attended nodes matter to its predictions, leading to the conclusion that sinks are a property of dot-product attention that, in their experiments, forms when a distinguishable node is available to concentrate on.

papers.title: LLM-jp-4 Technical Report
papers.abstract: This paper presents LLM-jp-4, a family of Japanese sovereign large language models (LLMs) developed with an emphasis on transparency, reproducibility, and practical usability. LLM-jp-4 comprises an 8B dense model and a 32B-A3B mixture-of-experts model, both trained from scratch on approximately 12 trillion tokens. To support independent verification and reproduction, we establish explicit criteria for selecting training data, external models, and software, and make the development process publicly available. Evaluation results demonstrate substantial improvements over previous LLM-jp models and competitive performance against open-weight models of similar scale. By documenting the development principles, training procedures, and empirical findings of LLM-jp-4, we aim to provide a reference for future sovereign AI development.
papers.summary: `LLM-jp-4` is a family of Japanese sovereign large language models (LLMs) built with an emphasis on transparency, reproducibility, and practical usability. It comprises an 8B dense model and a 32B-A3B mixture-of-experts model, both trained from scratch on roughly 12 trillion tokens, with explicit published criteria for choosing training data, external models, and software so that others can verify and reproduce the process. The authors report **substantial improvements over earlier `LLM-jp` models and competitive performance against open-weight models of similar scale**, and position the documented development principles, training procedures, and empirical findings as a reference for future sovereign AI efforts.

papers.title: Counterfactual Gate-Support Decomposition: Separating Selection from Redistribution in Training-Data Filtering
papers.abstract: A training-data quality gate changes both which examples survive within regions of the input space and how training mass is distributed across those regions, so a gate-versus-random comparison does not isolate these mechanisms. We introduce Counterfactual Gate-Support Decomposition (CGSD), a four-arm, budget-matched design that crosses gate eligibility with support distribution and decomposes the observed gate effect into within-support selection, between-support redistribution, and their interaction. The practical constraint is finite-pool realizability: we characterize mass and token-assembly conditions under which the required arms can be constructed, together with a support-extinction case in which the ordinary design is undefined. On Korean-English and Korean-Japanese retrieval, the mean within-support selection component is the only one that exceeds its calibrated null band (+29.7 and +5.6 holdout items; 30/30 positive replicates), decisively in Korean-English and marginally in Korean-Japanese; redistribution and interaction remain unresolved at the available power. The same pattern holds for a second, unrelated gate family -- a model-confidence threshold rather than a deterministic verifier -- judged against its own null (+27.3 items, 9/9 positive), so the result is not a property of one gate's mechanism. On a mathematics gate, zero-eligibility supports leave the ordinary design undefined at every budget, while the extended design is constructible only inside narrow budget bands that an exhaustive scan locates and that the natural operating point misses -- the assembly condition separating a property of the pool from a limitation of the packer. CGSD therefore returns a decomposition, a constructible-but-underpowered design, or an explicit non-constructibility result, and says which; it prevents support redistribution from being silently interpreted as sample-level gate quality.
papers.summary: A training-data quality gate changes both which examples survive within regions of the input space and how much training mass each region receives, so comparing a gated set against a random one cannot tell selection quality apart from redistribution. `CGSD` (Counterfactual Gate-Support Decomposition) is a four-arm, budget-matched design that crosses gate eligibility with support distribution to split the observed gate effect into within-support selection, between-support redistribution, and their interaction, together with conditions on pool mass and token assembly under which the arms can actually be built from a finite pool. On Korean-English and Korean-Japanese retrieval, **only the within-support selection component exceeds its calibrated null band**, with gains of 29.7 and 5.6 holdout items and 30 of 30 positive replicates, and the same pattern holds for an unrelated model-confidence gate judged against its own null. On a mathematics gate, zero-eligibility supports leave the ordinary design undefined at every budget and the extended design constructible only inside narrow budget bands, and the method reports such cases explicitly rather than letting support redistribution pass as sample-level gate quality.

papers.title: Target-Token Asymmetry Can Masquerade As Depth Specialization
papers.abstract: Layer-ablation studies often perturb early or late layers of a language model, compare the damage to prediction on two corpora, and read a larger early-layer effect on one corpus as early-layer specialization for its task. Such a comparison averages over the tokens that each corpus asks the model to predict, and these target tokens differ: math solutions, for example, ask for far more whitespace and numbers than encyclopedia prose. We show that this difference can create the appearance of depth specialization. We split a cross-corpus early--late damage interaction by target-token type and recompute it under a target mixture shared by both corpora. Between GSM8K and Wikitext, a positive interaction replicates across five model instances. In the three fully decomposed models, only whitespace has a positive interaction. Removing whitespace reverses the pooled effect in all three, and matching the full target mixture reverses it in two. The diagnosis holds under position matching, adversarial reassignment of token types, and a continuous readout. The risk can also be anticipated from the tokenizer alone. A screen computed before any model runs places every held-out pair it scored in the region its label predicts, and on the pairs it rates at high or medium risk, removing whitespace reverses every positive pooled estimate. A smaller content-word effect one token ahead follows the share of content targets that the unablated model already predicts. A cross-corpus depth effect therefore supports an interpretation of task specialization only after the target-token mixture is reported, the effect is decomposed by token type, and a mixture-matched summary keeps its sign.
papers.summary: Layer-ablation studies that damage early or late layers and compare the harm across two corpora often read a larger early-layer effect on one corpus as early-layer specialization for that task, but such comparisons average over target tokens that differ by corpus, since math solutions demand far more whitespace and numbers than encyclopedia prose. The authors split the cross-corpus early-versus-late damage interaction between `GSM8K` and `Wikitext` by target-token type and recompute it under a target mixture shared by both corpora. A positive interaction replicates across five model instances, yet in the three fully decomposed models **only whitespace tokens carry a positive interaction, and removing whitespace reverses the pooled effect in all three**, a diagnosis that survives position matching, adversarial reassignment of token types, and a continuous readout. A screen computed from the tokenizer alone, before any model runs, correctly flags the risky corpus pairs, and the authors argue a cross-corpus depth effect supports a specialization claim only once the target-token mixture is reported, the effect is decomposed by token type, and a mixture-matched summary keeps its sign.

papers.title: Integrated Novelty Detection Systems: From Sensor Networks to Multi-Novelty Computer Vision
papers.abstract:
Novelty detection is crucial in various technological and scientific domains. Its importance spans from ensuring the reliability of sensor networks to enhancing the adaptability of computer vision systems. As AI systems become increasingly sophisticated and complex, effective anomaly detection is essential for maintaining reliability and accuracy. This work addresses novelty detection in weather sensor networks and computer vision. In weather sensor networks, particularly for monitoring rainfall, detecting blocked rain gauges can significantly impact data reliability, food security, and disaster management. This work evaluates four existing quality control methods for detecting blocked rain gauges and demonstrates their limitations, particularly in detecting clusters of faulty sensors. By comparing methods such as the Conditional Mixture Model (CMM), PSWQ (Fz-filter), Kernel Regression, and Gaussian Method, we identify their shortcomings and propose three novel quality control techniques that integrate probabilistic fault detection and consistency-based diagnosis framework to improve timely detection of blocked sensors, while reducing false alarms.
  In the realm of computer vision, current systems often fail to handle multiple types of novelty due to their focus on single-novelty scenarios. We highlight the need for integrated systems capable of handling multiple types of novelty. To support this, we introduce the Novel Snapshot Serengeti (NOVEL-SS) dataset, derived from the Snapshot Serengeti camera trap data, which includes various forms of novelty. We also present the DCA (Detect, Characterize, and Accommodate) baseline system, designed to handle multiple novelty by detecting, characterizing, and accommodating them. This work aims to advance the robustness and adaptability of novelty detection systems across both weather sensor networks and computer vision applications.
papers.summary: Novelty detection is examined in two settings: blocked rain gauges in weather sensor networks, where undetected faults degrade data used for food security and disaster management, and computer vision systems that handle only one type of novelty at a time. For the sensor setting, the authors evaluate four existing quality control methods, the Conditional Mixture Model, the `PSWQ` Fz-filter, kernel regression, and a Gaussian method, show that **all four fail to reliably detect clusters of faulty sensors**, and propose three new techniques combining probabilistic fault detection with consistency-based diagnosis to detect blocked gauges sooner with fewer false alarms. For vision, they introduce the `NOVEL-SS` dataset derived from `Snapshot Serengeti` camera-trap data, which contains multiple forms of novelty, and a Detect, Characterize, and Accommodate (`DCA`) baseline system for handling them.

papers.title: Where to Start, How to Move: Analyzing Curricula under GRPO for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) provides no reward-relative learning signal when all rollouts receive identical rewards. In long-horizon tasks that require multiple interactions, rewards are given only upon successful task completion, making all-fail groups common early in training and limiting opportunities to practice later steps. Guide Assisted GRPO replays a successful reference prefix before the learner continues. We study how initial positions, handoff units, and movement rules affect unassisted task completion. Across three model sizes on BFCL, starting near completion is more effective under a fixed turn-level threshold rule. Finer handoffs alone do not consistently help, but outcome-informed tool-call selection outperforms GRPO on trained and untrained task categories. Guided starts also improve AppWorld success on both evaluation splits. These findings highlight where learning starts and how starting positions move as key curriculum choices.
papers.summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) yields no learning signal when every rollout in a group earns the same reward, which is common early in long-horizon agent tasks where reward arrives only on successful completion. Guide Assisted `GRPO` replays a successful reference prefix before the learner takes over, and the authors study how the initial handoff position, the handoff unit, and the rule for moving the handoff affect unassisted task completion. Across three model sizes on `BFCL`, **starting the learner near task completion is more effective under a fixed turn-level threshold rule**, finer handoffs alone do not consistently help, but outcome-informed selection of the tool call at which to hand off outperforms plain `GRPO` on both trained and untrained task categories. Guided starts also raise success on both `AppWorld` evaluation splits, pointing to where learning starts and how the start moves as key curriculum choices.

papers.title: BFHD: Bidirectional Feature Harmonization Decomposition for Heterogeneous Clinical Assessments
papers.abstract: Clinical assessments are often collected using heterogeneous assessment systems across centers and time, leading to records that mix different but related sets of measurements. This motivates harmonization beyond total-score linking. We formulate clinical harmonization at the measurement level as a bidirectional recoverability problem: given paired observations from two assessment systems, the goal is to identify which measurements can be reliably translated in both directions within an application-defined tolerance, while separating non-translatable components. We propose Bidirectional Feature Harmonization Decomposition (BFHD), a feasibility-driven framework that enforces bidirectionally coupled translation and uses feature-wise output gating to produce an explicit decomposition in the original measurement space. Experiments on synthetic data and real clinical assessment pairs show that BFHD achieves broader feasible harmonization coverage and improved subset stability compared to baselines.
papers.summary: Clinical assessments are collected with different but related measurement systems across centers and over time, producing records that need harmonization at the level of individual measurements rather than total scores. The authors frame this as a bidirectional recoverability problem: given paired observations from two assessment systems, identify which measurements can be reliably translated in both directions within an application-defined tolerance and separate out the non-translatable components. `BFHD` (Bidirectional Feature Harmonization Decomposition) enforces bidirectionally coupled translation and uses feature-wise output gating to produce an explicit decomposition in the original measurement space. On synthetic data and real clinical assessment pairs it **achieves broader feasible harmonization coverage and better subset stability than the baselines**.

papers.title: Asymptotic Behavior of Transformers
papers.abstract: In this paper we study the behavior of transformer networks generating text over long periods of time. We show that even a three-token, single-layer attention-only transformer can fail to converge. We then study a rich class of transformers with arbitrary finite depth, layer normalization, MLPs, RoPE encodings, and an arbitrary mix of local and global layers. Every transformer in this class has a softmax temperature threshold above which its empirical cache distribution converges to a unique limit, independent of initial conditions. We show further that, while each transformer has a temperature threshold, the supremum of this set is infinite, so there is no global minimal temperature that forces all transformers to converge.
papers.summary: The question is what happens to the distribution of tokens a transformer generates as it runs for arbitrarily long. The authors first show that **even a three-token, single-layer attention-only transformer can fail to converge**. They then analyze a broad class of transformers with arbitrary finite depth, layer normalization, MLPs, `RoPE` position encodings, and any mix of local and global attention layers, proving that every member has a softmax temperature threshold above which its empirical cache distribution converges to a unique limit independent of initial conditions. Because the supremum of these thresholds across the class is infinite, no single minimal temperature forces all transformers to converge.

papers.title: Steering Vectors for Competing Ethical Frameworks Are Interchangeable: A Competing-Target Test for Activation Steering
papers.abstract: Activation steering adds a vector to a model's hidden states to control a named behaviour. A gain on that behaviour, however, does not show that the vector controls it directly: it may act through a component shared with neighbouring behaviours, which unsteered and random baselines cannot separate. We introduce the competing-target test: a vector is compared with the vector built the same way for a competing target, and an equivalence test states when their difference is below a useful margin. We apply it in open-weight models to vectors for Kantian deontology, which judges an act by the rule it follows, and act utilitarianism, which judges it by the welfare it produces. On held-out situations, prompting a framework raises its score and lowers the other's, whereas vectors for either framework move both scores alike, and none reaches the margin. The two vectors share most of their direction, a request to apply some framework; the same construction separates an optimistic from a pessimistic tone, whose vectors share much less. What a vector shares with its competitors therefore sets what it controls: steering a perspective can deliver a mixture, and measuring a disposition can measure its neighbours, unless tested against the competing target.
papers.summary: Activation steering adds a vector to a model's hidden states to control a named behaviour, but a gain on that behaviour does not prove the vector controls it directly, since it may act through a component shared with neighbouring behaviours that unsteered and random baselines cannot separate. The authors propose the competing-target test, which compares a vector against one built identically for a competing target and uses an equivalence test to decide when their difference falls below a useful margin. Applied in open-weight models to vectors for Kantian deontology and act utilitarianism, **prompting a framework raises its score and lowers the other's, whereas the steering vectors for either framework move both scores alike** and none reaches the margin, because the two vectors share most of their direction, essentially a request to apply some framework. The same construction separates an optimistic from a pessimistic tone, whose vectors share much less, so what a vector shares with its competitors determines what it actually controls.

papers.title: VLX-Go: Robust Embodied Tracking through Multi-Stage Learning and On-Policy Refinement
papers.abstract: Embodied visual tracking requires a robot to identify a designated target from visual observations and control its own motion to follow that target through an environment. Following an isolated person is a comparatively simple demonstration of embodied visual tracking, but following the intended person among distractors remains challenging. Existing methods exhibit a substantial drop in success from single-target to distractor tracking, motivating a focus on the shared spaces that person-following robots must navigate. We present \method{}, a vision--language waypoint policy built around the hypothesis that visual and language representations should be aligned before tracking-specific motion is learned. The policy combines complementary frozen visual encoders, multiscale temporal context, a transformer backbone, and a lightweight head for robot-centric waypoint prediction. Its training progresses through vision--language alignment, multimodal reasoning mid-training, and tracking specialization on 19,532 oracle episodes. Compared with 41.54\% distractor-tracking success for our earlier OmTrackVLA model, the complete multi-stage recipe achieves 55.80\%. We then explore on-policy refinement using filtered oracle labels for states visited by the policy. This preliminary study adds 2.42 percentage points of distractor-tracking success, reaching 58.22\%, while reducing collision rate by 1.99 pts. The final policy records the highest distractor- and ambiguous-tracking success rates among the compared methods. These results support staged multimodal learning as a promising direction for tracking among distractors and motivate further study of on-policy refinement for person following in shared spaces.
papers.summary: Embodied visual tracking requires a robot to identify a designated person from visual observations and control its own motion to follow them, and existing methods lose much of their success when distractor people are present in shared spaces. `VLX-Go` is a vision-language waypoint policy built on the hypothesis that visual and language representations should be aligned before tracking-specific motion is learned, combining complementary frozen visual encoders, multiscale temporal context, a transformer backbone, and a lightweight head for robot-centric waypoint prediction. Training proceeds through vision-language alignment, multimodal reasoning mid-training, and tracking specialization on 19,532 oracle episodes, and the full recipe **raises distractor-tracking success from 41.54% for the authors' earlier `OmTrackVLA` model to 55.80%**. A preliminary on-policy refinement step, which uses filtered oracle labels for states the policy actually visits, adds 2.42 points to reach 58.22% while cutting collision rate by 1.99 points, giving the highest distractor- and ambiguous-tracking success among the compared methods.

papers.title: Tail Competition Explains Scaling in Best-of-N Sampling for Verifiable Problems
papers.abstract: Best-of-N sampling is a simple inference-time scaling strategy for large language models, yet its behavior under incomplete reward models remains poorly understood. We study Best-of-N as a competition between the extreme reward tails of correct and incorrect responses. This view shows that success depends not only on the probability of sampling a correct response, but also on whether correct responses dominate incorrect ones in the upper tail. Using extreme value theory, we characterize three asymptotic regimes: correct-tail-dominant, incorrect-tail-dominant, and critical explaining both monotonic gains and reward-hacking-induced degradation. We further derive finite-sample scaling laws for representative reward distributions, showing that, under Gaussian rewards, incorrect responses with sufficiently large variance can dominate selection even when their mean reward is lower. Unlike oracle selection, convergence with an incomplete selector can be polynomial rather than exponential. Finally, we propose a lightweight tail-tension criterion to estimate when additional sampling may become harmful. Experiments on synthetic data and real reward model scores are consistent with the theoretically predicted regimes, scaling laws, and diagnostic behavior, suggesting that tail competition provides a unified lens on Best-of-N sampling for verifiable problems.
papers.summary: `Best-of-N` sampling is a simple inference-time scaling strategy for large language models, but how it behaves under an incomplete reward model is poorly understood. The authors model it as a competition between the extreme upper tails of reward scores for correct and incorrect responses, so success depends not just on the probability of sampling a correct answer but on whether correct answers dominate the upper tail. Using extreme value theory they identify three asymptotic regimes, correct-tail-dominant, incorrect-tail-dominant, and critical, which explain both monotonic gains and reward-hacking-induced degradation, and derive finite-sample scaling laws showing that **under Gaussian rewards, incorrect responses with large enough variance can win selection even when their mean reward is lower**, and that convergence under an incomplete selector can be polynomial rather than exponential. A lightweight tail-tension criterion estimates when further sampling may become harmful, and experiments on synthetic data and real reward model scores match the predicted regimes, scaling laws, and diagnostic behavior.

papers.title: Dynamic Graph World Modelling: Learning Future Dynamics from Temporal Context
papers.abstract: Dynamic graph learning models how entities and their relations evolve from historical observations to predict future graph states. Existing methods do not fully address dynamic graph world modelling, which requires learning transitions from temporal context to future latent graph states. This is difficult for three reasons: nodes and relations rely on different historical evidence, structural evolution is path-dependent, and future snapshots provide sparse and realization-specific targets. We propose Dynamic Graph World Modelling (DyG-WM), the first framework to jointly predict future node and relation representations from temporal context by answering three questions: what has evolved, how it evolved, and what will evolve next. To capture what has evolved, a historical node-relation context encoder summarizes node-neighborhood trajectories and pair-specific histories. To characterize how it evolved, a node-relation path-signature encoder captures ordered structural changes. To predict what will evolve next, a dual-level joint-embedding objective predicts target-snapshot node and relation representations without reconstructing the raw graph. Experiments on 12 link-prediction and two node-classification datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of DyG-WM across both tasks.
papers.summary: Dynamic graph learning models how entities and their relations evolve in order to predict future graph states, but existing methods do not fully address world modelling, meaning learning transitions from temporal context to future latent graph states, which is hard because nodes and relations rely on different historical evidence, structural evolution is path-dependent, and future snapshots give sparse, realization-specific targets. `DyG-WM` (Dynamic Graph World Modelling) jointly predicts future node and relation representations from temporal context through three components: a historical node-relation context encoder that summarizes node-neighborhood trajectories and pair-specific histories, a path-signature encoder that captures ordered structural changes, and a dual-level joint-embedding objective that predicts target-snapshot representations without reconstructing the raw graph. The authors describe it as the first framework to do this jointly and report **effectiveness across 12 link-prediction and two node-classification datasets**.

papers.title: Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning: The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory
papers.abstract: Multimodal models and agents have emerged to enable AI systems to learn from and interact with the real world more like humans by integrating information across multiple modalities. However, enabling multimodal agents to continually acquire useful information from complex, heterogeneous multimodal data remains a significant challenge as they move toward long-horizon tasks and lifelong settings. Addressing this challenge requires effective memory mechanisms that can maintain continuity across sessions, adapt to changing users and environments, and refine memory-management policies through accumulated experience. We introduce a two-axis analytical framework for multimodal agent memory structured around two key questions: how multimodal information is formed and represented (Axis I, Formation and Representation), and how its management adapts with accumulated experience (Axis II, Memory Management). Axis I, Formation and Representation, characterizes what information is retained and how it is encoded (e.g., modality-specific embeddings, textual and structured records, latent and parametric representations) to support subsequent reasoning and action. Axis II, Memory Management, distinguishes three tiers: T1 Static Memory reuses fixed memory; T2 Dynamic Memory updates memory through a stable policy; and T3 Self-Evolving Memory updates memory through an evolving policy. Based on this framework, we synthesize recurring design patterns and derive principles for balancing source fidelity with abstraction, maintaining temporal validity and provenance, grounding memory use in recoverable evidence, and evolving memory policies over time. Furthermore, we discuss the challenges and potential future directions for the memory mechanism of multimodal agents.
papers.summary: Multimodal agents that must continually gather useful information from heterogeneous data across long-horizon and lifelong settings need memory mechanisms that keep continuity across sessions, adapt to changing users and environments, and refine their own management policies through experience. This survey organizes the field along two axes: how multimodal information is formed and represented, covering modality-specific embeddings, textual and structured records, and latent or parametric representations, and how memory management adapts with experience, split into **three tiers of static memory, dynamic memory updated by a stable policy, and self-evolving memory updated by an evolving policy**. From this framework the authors distill recurring design patterns and principles for balancing source fidelity with abstraction, maintaining temporal validity and provenance, grounding memory use in recoverable evidence, and evolving memory policies over time, then close with open challenges and future directions.
papers.highlight_summary:
Multimodal agents operating over long horizons must retain perceptual experience from images, video, audio, GUIs, and 3D environments that, unlike dialogue text, cannot be losslessly flattened into a compact editable record, and must keep that memory valid as users and environments change. A two-axis lifecycle framework organizes the field around how experience is formed and represented (Axis I) and whether memory management stays fixed, updates under a stable policy, or evolves its own policy through feedback (Axis II).

- Axis I classifies memory by the representation actually consumed downstream, from source-preserving and modality-encoded forms such as `PixelRAG` screenshot tiles, `MovieChat` merged frame tokens, and `DynaMem` voxel maps, through textual and structured records such as `MIRIX` and `ConceptGraphs`, to latent or parametric state, with hybrids like `M3-Agent` linking compact abstractions back to recoverable source evidence.
- Axis II distinguishes three tiers: T1 Static Memory reuses fixed memory with no persistent change, T2 Dynamic Memory updates memory state under a stable policy by appending, revising, merging, invalidating, or forgetting entries, and T3 Self-Evolving Memory uses feedback to revise the policy that governs memory writing, maintenance, or retrieval itself.
- Across a corpus of **297 memory architectures and 82 benchmark records**, the authors find T2 dynamic updates prevalent, hybrid representations widespread, and **deployment-time memory-policy evolution (T3) scarce**, with embodied and video memory growing fastest since 2023 while audio/speech memory remains sparse.
- The recurring trade-off is fidelity versus abstraction: textualization creates a semantic bottleneck that discards visual, temporal, or acoustic detail not anticipated at write time, while learned encodings are non-invertible and tied to a compatible model interface, motivating design principles around recoverable evidence, temporal validity, and provenance.
- As a survey it reports no new empirical results, and its stated open problems include provenance-aware and recoverable memory, cross-representation consistency, self-improving management, bounded lifelong memory, governed forgetting, and lifecycle-aware evaluation.

papers.title: Beyond Corrected Actions: Training LLM Agents on Textual Critiques
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for multi-turn agentic tasks that require interactions with users and environments over extended sequences of actions. A common approach to improving LLM agents is to use more capable expert models to provide training supervision, either by behavior cloning the expert's trajectories or by using the expert to correct the actions in trajectories generated by the weaker student model. However, expert LLMs can provide richer supervision than actions alone: they can directly generate textual critique that explain why specific actions are incorrect. We study whether training on such feedback benefits LLM agents and propose Critique-Augmented Agentic Fine-Tuning (CAFT), a framework that elicits textual expert feedback on student-generated trajectories. For each incorrect action, the expert yields both a corrected action and a textual critique explaining the student's mistake--which we then use as the training target for fine-tuning. Across four student models from the Nemotron 3 and Gemma 4 families on the agentic domains $\tau^2$-Bench Airline+Retail and WebShop, adding critiques to action-level supervision improves performance by 8% on average over action-only distillation. Additionally, CAFT checkpoints can also provide a better warm start for reinforcement learning than expert-trajectory distillation. Our results demonstrate that textual critiques can strengthen supervision for multi-turn LLM agents.
papers.summary: Expert models are commonly used to supervise weaker large language model (LLM) agents by cloning their trajectories or correcting the student's actions, which discards the explanation of why an action was wrong. Critique-Augmented Agentic Fine-Tuning (`CAFT`) has an expert produce both a corrected action and a textual critique for each incorrect step in student-generated trajectories, and uses both as fine-tuning targets. Across four `Nemotron 3` and `Gemma 4` student models on `τ²-Bench` Airline and Retail and `WebShop`, **adding critiques improves performance by 8% on average over action-only distillation**, and `CAFT` checkpoints also give a better warm start for reinforcement learning than expert-trajectory distillation.

papers.title: The Impact of Detector Architecture, Model Scale, and Scene Density on Multi-Pedestrian Tracking
papers.abstract: Pedestrian tracking in video is important for applications such as surveillance and scene analysis, but it becomes more challenging in crowded scenarios with frequent occlusions and rapid motion. This paper analyzes how detector architecture, model scale, scene density, and inference regime affect the tracking of multiple pedestrians. We compare the YOLO11, RT-DETR, and YOLO26 detector families with the ByteTrack and BoT-SORT trackers on sequences from the MOT17, MOT20, and SOMPT22 benchmarks. For YOLO26, we also compare traditional overlap filtering via Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) with end-to-end inference. The RT-DETR family achieved the highest mean scores on the HOTA tracking quality metric across all three benchmarks with both trackers, with a more pronounced advantage on MOT20, albeit at a higher computational cost. On MOT17 and SOMPT22, YOLO26 variants, especially YOLO26-L with NMS, offered favorable combinations of quality and speed compared with RT-DETR. In the YOLO26 inference comparison, the end-to-end mode did not yield consistent tracking gains over the NMS-based regime. Taken together, these results provide a practical guide for selecting detectors and trackers for this task based on application priorities.
papers.summary: Tracking many pedestrians in crowded video is hard because of frequent occlusion and fast motion, and practitioners lack clear guidance on which detector and tracker to pair. The study compares the `YOLO11`, `RT-DETR`, and `YOLO26` detector families with the `ByteTrack` and `BoT-SORT` trackers on `MOT17`, `MOT20`, and `SOMPT22`, and for `YOLO26` also contrasts Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) filtering with end-to-end inference. **`RT-DETR` achieved the highest mean HOTA scores on all three benchmarks with both trackers**, most clearly on the dense `MOT20` sequences, but at higher compute cost. `YOLO26-L` with NMS offered a favorable quality-speed balance on `MOT17` and `SOMPT22`, and end-to-end inference gave no consistent tracking gains over NMS.

papers.title: Policy-Verified Self-Training: Learning Agent Compliance from Verifiable Policy Rewards
papers.abstract: Runtime policy verifiers can prevent agents from executing disallowed actions, but their decisions are typically used only for enforcement and discarded afterward. We ask whether these decisions can instead become verifiable policy rewards for training the agents they guard. We introduce Policy-Verified Self-Training (PVST), a post-training paradigm in which an agent generates its own interaction trajectories and an executable policy verifier, here a deterministic gate compiled from a written policy, evaluates whether each action complies. Compliant trajectories are reinforced, and violations become negatives for preference optimization; beyond the gate and the benchmark's task-success signal, PVST needs no stronger teacher model, no human preference labels and no attack-specific supervision, although rollouts are collected in the benchmark's attacked environment. On held-out AgentDojo tasks under prompt injection, policy-verified preference training of Qwen3-8B reduces violating trajectories from 37.2% to 10.3 $\pm$ 0.9% (three seeds) and successful attacks from 12.4% to 0.5% at equal or higher pooled task utility, although utility falls on travel, compared with 22.0% when negatives are selected by an attack oracle and 31.9 $\pm$ 0.9% with negatives that contain no violation. The learned behavior holds under an attack template never used in training (37.7% to 11.0%) and on a suite excluded from training (34.8% to 16.7%), and the retained verifier's intervention rate falls from 39.2% to 8.8% (seed 0). Our analysis identifies two conditions under which the verdict is most informative: success must not already imply compliance, and guarded actions must appear in both permitted and forbidden contexts.
papers.summary: Runtime policy verifiers block disallowed agent actions, but their verdicts are normally discarded after enforcement. Policy-Verified Self-Training (`PVST`) turns those verdicts into training signal: the agent generates its own trajectories, a deterministic gate compiled from a written policy judges each action, compliant trajectories are reinforced, and violations become negatives for preference optimization, with no stronger teacher, human labels, or attack-specific supervision. On held-out `AgentDojo` tasks under prompt injection, **training `Qwen3-8B` this way cuts violating trajectories from 37.2% to 10.3% and successful attacks from 12.4% to 0.5%** at equal or higher pooled task utility, and the effect holds on an unseen attack template and an excluded task suite. The verdict is most informative when task success does not already imply compliance and when guarded actions occur in both permitted and forbidden contexts.

papers.title: Evaluating Compressed Memory: Dependence, Utility, and Content Benefit
papers.abstract: Does a language model answer better because its compressed memory contains useful document information? Replacing memory vectors with zeros can lower a trained model's score without showing that it outperforms a model trained without memory. We combine zeroing with separately trained models that cannot access stored text or receive the same constant input for every document. Across nine systems, some models rely on memory yet perform worse than the trained alternative. For example, in experiments that predict states in generated stories, zeroing memory worsens a model's prediction loss, yet a model trained without memory achieves lower loss than the original model with intact memory. On TriviaQA, giving xRAG memory from another question's passage raises F1, which measures word overlap with accepted answers, from 19.38 without a document to 24.78. Its effect on how often outputs contain an accepted answer is statistically uncertain. The question's retrieved passage scores higher still (29.88 F1). Thus a gain over no document alone does not establish that the gain requires the question's passage. Evaluations must therefore specify the comparison model, absolute performance, and generation and scoring conditions.
papers.summary: Zeroing a language model's compressed memory vectors shows the model depends on them, but not that the memory helps relative to a model trained without it. The authors pair zeroing with separately trained control models that either cannot access stored text or receive the same constant input for every document, across nine systems. Some models rely on memory yet perform worse than the memory-free control: in predicting states in generated stories, zeroing memory worsens loss, yet a model trained without memory achieves lower loss than the original with intact memory, and on `TriviaQA`, **giving `xRAG` memory from a different question's passage still raises F1 from 19.38 to 24.78**, against 29.88 with the correct passage. The authors conclude that evaluations must state the comparison model, absolute performance, and generation and scoring conditions.

papers.title: One-Step Prediction Fidelity Is a Poor Proxy for Planning Performance in JEPA World Models
papers.abstract: Latent world models are routinely selected, checkpointed and ablated on one-step prediction loss, on the assumption that a model which predicts the next latent better is a better model. In model-based RL this assumption is known to be unreliable; we ask whether it also fails for latent world models, where the training target is the model's own embedding and the loss is not expressed in interpretable units. We introduce a frozen-decoder protocol reporting one-step error in physical units, decomposed into the part already present in the encoder's representation and the part the predictor adds. Applying it to a recent end-to-end JEPA world model across three continuous-control environments, we move the metric by fine-tuning and measure goal-conditioned planning on the same checkpoints, with three training seeds and paired planning seeds throughout. Within one environment, a per-epoch ladder shows the relationship saturating after a single epoch: the first epoch improves fidelity by 32% and planning by 4.4 pp, but across the fifteen checkpoints that follow -- a further 15% fidelity improvement, monotone in every training seed -- the correlation between one-step error and planning success is r = -0.010. This is not a task-ceiling artifact: stratifying by a model-independent measure of training-data support, planning in the lowest-support stratum starts at 80%, leaving ample headroom, and is nonetheless flat from epoch 1 onward. Across environments the exchange rate is equally unstable: a 93% fidelity reduction on TwoRoom yields -0.7 pp of planning, while a 40% reduction on PushT yields +4.9 pp [+1.1, +8.9]. All results replicate under a decoder-free measure, latent drift. We also show that a matched continued-training control absorbs the entire fidelity gain we had attributed to an auxiliary objective.
papers.summary: Latent world models are routinely selected and ablated by one-step prediction loss, on the assumption that better next-latent prediction means a better model. The authors introduce a frozen-decoder protocol that reports one-step error in physical units, split into the part already in the encoder's representation and the part the predictor adds, and apply it to an end-to-end `JEPA` world model across three continuous-control environments while measuring goal-conditioned planning on the same checkpoints.
