In a per-epoch ladder, the first epoch improves fidelity by 32% and planning by 4.4 points, but **across the following fifteen checkpoints the correlation between one-step error and planning success is r = -0.010**, and across environments a 93% fidelity reduction on `TwoRoom` yields no planning gain while a 40% reduction on `PushT` yields +4.9 points. A matched continued-training control also absorbs the entire fidelity gain previously attributed to an auxiliary objective.

papers.title: Robust Explanatory Analysis for Structured Optimization Networks (REASON) in Learning
papers.abstract: We seek a hierarchical resolution of residual error under a composite learning objective as a principled mechanism for identifying and exploiting additional information, particularly under distribution shift and perturbation. Inspired by the System 1/System 2 paradigm, we formulate this principle as a two-loop mechanism serving a common inference goal. A fast, System 1-like loop resolves the residual addressable by the available evidence; the remaining epistemic residual triggers a medium speed, System 2-like loop that actively acquires additional evidence and measures its informational value through residual reduction. Over nested solution spaces, the medium-loop optimum is provably no worse than the fast-loop optimum. Experiments show that the resulting two-loop model consistently improves upon the fast loop at approximately half the computation of the medium loop, including under unseen corruptions, and, when provided a cleaner observation, outperforms staged classifiers and learning-to-defer methods at equal computational cost.
papers.summary: The work frames hierarchical resolution of residual error under a composite learning objective as a principled way to identify and exploit extra information, especially under distribution shift and perturbation. Modeled on the System 1/System 2 distinction, a fast loop resolves whatever residual the available evidence can explain, and the remaining epistemic residual triggers a slower loop that actively acquires more evidence and scores its value by how much it reduces the residual, with the slower loop's optimum provably no worse than the fast loop's over nested solution spaces. Experiments show **the two-loop model consistently beats the fast loop alone at roughly half the computation of the slower loop**, including under unseen corruptions, and outperforms staged classifiers and learning-to-defer methods at equal cost when given a cleaner observation.

papers.title: Learning What to Keep: Transfer-Aware Personal Skill Learning from User Feedback
papers.abstract: User feedback enables LLMs to refine reusable personalized skills, but often mixes persistent preferences with request-specific corrections. Indiscriminately retaining both risks negative transfer, motivating selective retention at the level of individual requirements. We frame this challenge as selective transfer over atomic rules and propose SkillGrain, a framework for learning reusable personalized skills from user feedback. SkillGrain decomposes feedback into independently actionable rules, predicts their transferability, and retains only those suitable for future requests. To learn these decisions, we combine rubric-guided skill rewards with fine-grained credit assignment that separately evaluates rule content and retention decisions. We further jointly optimize skill induction and skill-conditioned generation through reinforcement learning, ensuring that learned skills support downstream personalization. We construct a benchmark spanning five personalized writing tasks to evaluate cross-request generalization. Experiments across three base models in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings show that SkillGrain achieves the best overall average performance among competing methods.
papers.summary: User feedback lets large language models refine reusable personalized skills, but it mixes lasting preferences with one-off corrections, and keeping both causes negative transfer to later requests. `SkillGrain` decomposes feedback into atomic, independently actionable rules, predicts each rule's transferability, and retains only those likely to apply in future, learning these decisions through rubric-guided skill rewards with separate credit assignment for rule content and retention choices. Skill induction and skill-conditioned generation are optimized jointly with reinforcement learning so that learned skills actually help downstream personalization. On a new benchmark of five personalized writing tasks, **`SkillGrain` achieves the best overall average performance among competing methods** across three base models in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings.

papers.title: RA$^2$: Retain-Anchored Attraction Preserves Forget-Adjacent Utility in LLM Unlearning
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) unlearning is often evaluated primarily by target suppression and clean retain utility. These metrics can miss a local failure mode: a model may perform well on standard retain prompts, yet degrade on benign reasoning when prompts lie near the forgotten domain. This phenomenon is termed forget-adjacent utility loss. A fundamental question is: where should forget representations go after they leave the removed behavior? Successful unlearning depends not only on whether forget-conditioned representations depart from the harmful computation, but also on the direction in which they are redirected afterward. We propose RA$^2$ (Retain-Anchored Attraction), a latent-space unlearning method that redirects forget-token states toward nearby retain-supported representations while preserving higher-layer behavior on retain data. On WMDP and MUSE, RA$^2$ yields higher forget-adjacent utility than strong unlearning baselines at similar broad-utility levels. These results show that the migration direction of forget representations materially affects benign behavior near the forget boundary. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZacLing/retain_anchored_attraction.
papers.summary: Unlearning in large language models (LLMs) is typically judged by target suppression and clean retain utility, which misses cases where benign reasoning degrades on prompts near the forgotten domain, termed forget-adjacent utility loss. The authors argue that where forget representations are redirected matters as much as whether they leave the harmful computation, and propose Retain-Anchored Attraction (`RA²`), a latent-space method that pulls forget-token states toward nearby retain-supported representations while preserving higher-layer behavior on retain data. On `WMDP` and `MUSE`, **`RA²` yields higher forget-adjacent utility than strong unlearning baselines at similar broad-utility levels**.

papers.title: The Sum of All Summaries: PROPALIGN for Graded Proposition Salience Evaluation
papers.abstract: Identification and ranking of salient propositions in documents is indirectly involved in many AI tasks, but few papers define proposition salience scores clearly, make diverse data available, or evaluate models directly on the task. This paper proposes PROPALIGN, a multiple-summary-based approach for propositional salience score estimation, and releases PROPALIGNBANK, an accompanying dataset for the method with 138K alignments of over 35K propositions. We compare several approaches to salient proposition extraction in English across a broad range of spoken and written genres, and demonstrate that naively asking models for judgments leads to inconsistencies. By contrast, graded, summary-based metrics are more stable. We further observe that while single models perform worse than humans, an ensemble of models incorporating linguistic features approaches manual annotation quality ceilings. In addition, analyses of the model outputs suggest insights into how models can extract salient information with and without the use of summaries.
papers.summary: Identifying and ranking the salient propositions in a document underlies many tasks, yet salience scores are rarely defined precisely, diverse data is scarce, and models are seldom evaluated on the task directly. `PROPALIGN` estimates graded proposition salience from alignment with multiple summaries, and the accompanying `PROPALIGNBANK` dataset provides 138K alignments over more than 35K propositions spanning spoken and written English genres. Directly asking models for salience judgments produces inconsistent results, whereas the summary-based graded metric is more stable. Single models fall short of human annotators, but **an ensemble of models with linguistic features approaches the manual annotation quality ceiling**.

papers.title: ELARSpeech: A 30K-Hour Dataset Across 675 Underrepresented Languages for Long-Tail Multilingual Speech Technologies
papers.abstract: Massively multilingual speech modeling has made remarkable progress in recent years, yet existing training resources and benchmarks still underrepresent much of the linguistic long tail. To address this gap, we introduce ELARSpeech, a large-scale multilingual speech resource comprising 30,202 hours of speech across 675 underrepresented languages, curated from the Endangered Languages Archive. Combining human-annotated and unlabeled recordings, the corpus spans diverse recording conditions, domains, and language families. Beyond corpus construction, our experiments show how ELARSpeech supports extending ASR and TTS capabilities to diverse underrepresented languages, with further benefits from pseudo-labeling unlabeled data. At the same time, our speech representation analysis reveals remaining limitations in transferring existing multilingual models to the linguistic long tail. Together, ELARSpeech provides both a resource and a testbed for extending multilingual speech technology further into the linguistic long tail. We publicly release the dataset, all trained ASR and TTS models, and the complete data construction pipeline to facilitate research on long-tail multilingual speech technologies.
papers.summary: Multilingual speech models have advanced quickly, but training data and benchmarks still leave out most of the linguistic long tail. `ELARSpeech` is a corpus of **30,202 hours of speech across 675 underrepresented languages**, curated from the Endangered Languages Archive and combining human-annotated and unlabeled recordings across diverse conditions, domains, and language families. Experiments show it supports extending automatic speech recognition (ASR) and text-to-speech (TTS) to these languages, with further gains from pseudo-labeling the unlabeled portion, while representation analysis shows existing multilingual models still transfer poorly to the long tail. The dataset, all trained ASR and TTS models, and the full construction pipeline are released publicly.

papers.title: Fully sequential Gaussian process regression for preference learning
papers.abstract: We study continuous global optimization problems in which the objective function cannot be directly evaluated; rather, we observe only which of two selected design points appears to perform better, subject to noise. Such comparisons complicate the use of Gaussian process regression because they yield non-Gaussian posteriors. We consider a fully sequential approximation, based on moment-matching, that yields a fast closed-form update of the metamodel's mean and covariance. We then propose DOVE, a fully sequential sampling policy that combines an information gain criterion with randomized sampling designed to control error accumulation. Under fairly standard regularity conditions, we prove convergence rates for both statistical error and expected simple regret that depend on kernel smoothness. To our knowledge, these are the first such rates for fully sequential approximate Bayesian inference in continuous global optimization.
papers.summary: In some continuous global optimization settings the objective cannot be evaluated directly, and only noisy pairwise comparisons between two design points are observed, which produce non-Gaussian posteriors that complicate Gaussian process regression. The authors use a fully sequential moment-matching approximation that gives a fast closed-form update of the surrogate's mean and covariance, and propose `DOVE`, a sampling policy that combines an information gain criterion with randomized sampling to control error accumulation. Under standard regularity conditions they prove **convergence rates for both statistical error and expected simple regret that depend on kernel smoothness**, described as the first such rates for fully sequential approximate Bayesian inference in continuous global optimization.

papers.title: Selective Next-Location Prediction with MetaModelSelect: A Lightweight Post-Hoc Confidence Metamodel
papers.abstract: Next-location prediction can support proactive mobile-network decisions, but acting on unreliable predictions can waste resources. We apply MetaModelSelect, a lightweight post-hoc confidence metamodel, to selective cellular next-location prediction. The mobility-specific model combines a learned embedding of the predicted location with the four largest softmax probabilities and Softmax Concentration. It learns whether a frozen recurrent neural network's top-1 prediction is correct, using only its outputs and without retraining the backbone. On path-balanced Changchun cellular mobility trajectories, we evaluate backbones trained with cross-entropy (CE) and self-adaptive training plus entropy minimization (SAT+EM), comparing against eight scalar confidence scores, two location-aware lookup methods, and a raw-logit multilayer perceptron. Relative to maximum softmax probability, MetaModelSelect achieves mean per-run reductions in area under the risk--coverage curve (AURC), excess AURC (E-AURC), and area under the generalized risk--coverage curve (AUGRC) of 2.6%, 4.2%, and 3.0% for CE, and 2.0%, 3.3%, and 1.9% for SAT+EM. It also achieves the lowest reported mean risk at every evaluated partial coverage. The results show that MetaModelSelect improves confidence ranking in this mobility setting while leaving the underlying location predictor unchanged.
papers.summary: Predicting a mobile user's next cell location can drive proactive network decisions, but acting on wrong predictions wastes resources, so the system needs to know when to abstain. `MetaModelSelect` is a lightweight post-hoc confidence model that learns whether a frozen recurrent predictor's top-1 output is correct, combining a learned embedding of the predicted location with the four largest softmax probabilities and a softmax concentration measure, without retraining the backbone. On path-balanced Changchun cellular trajectories with backbones trained by cross-entropy (CE) and by self-adaptive training plus entropy minimization (SAT+EM), it is compared against eight scalar confidence scores, two location-aware lookups, and a raw-logit multilayer perceptron. **Relative to maximum softmax probability it cuts the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC) by 2.6% for CE and 2.0% for SAT+EM**, and it achieves the lowest mean risk at every evaluated partial coverage.

papers.title: KoAGE: Do Large Language Models Know, Learn, and Coin Korean Neologisms?
papers.abstract: Korean neologisms arise through diverse mechanisms, a demanding test of language models beyond lexical memorization. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce NeoTrace, an automated, rerunnable framework that collects and dates neologisms across genres. Its 4,271 entries support KoAGE, a cutoff-aware benchmark with three acquisition and two generation tasks---the latter, to our knowledge, the first to compare model coinages with attested neologisms under their original materials and community context. Across 21 models, lexical recall diverges from contextual inference: in a five-model temporal analysis, models define only 13-30% of cutoff-year words, yet can infer meaning from one usage. However, structural understanding remains limited: even correct definitions barely improve formation analysis of pre-cutoff neologisms. Given word-building materials, single models often follow human formation mechanisms, whereas multi-agent coinage favors abbreviation and depends on interaction framing. KoAGE thus separates what models know, learn from use, and coin.
papers.summary: Korean neologisms form through many mechanisms, making them a test of language models that goes beyond memorized vocabulary. `NeoTrace` is an automated, rerunnable framework that collects and dates neologisms across genres, and its 4,271 entries back `KoAGE`, a cutoff-aware benchmark with three acquisition tasks and two generation tasks that compare model coinages with attested neologisms under the same source materials and community context. Across 21 models, lexical recall diverges from contextual inference: **models define only 13-30% of words from their cutoff year, yet can infer meaning from a single usage**, while even correct definitions barely improve analysis of how pre-cutoff words were formed. Given word-building materials, single models tend to follow human formation mechanisms, whereas multi-agent coinage favors abbreviation and depends on how the interaction is framed.

papers.title: Train to Stitch: Topology-Preserving Regularization for Interoperable Representations
papers.abstract: As large, powerful pre-trained models become more prevalent, there is growing interest in developing methods that allow different neural networks to be seamlessly combined with little or no direct communication between them. Take autoencoder-based data compression as an example: the ability to independently choose architectures and train encoder and decoder models, while still ensuring they work together, could fundamentally transform how such models are built, deployed, and updated. In this work, we introduce a novel approach that leverages topological regularization to align the latent spaces of two independently trained autoencoder models, entirely eliminating the need for coordination during training. We provide a conditional theoretical analysis showing how the structural agreement encouraged by our regularizer can translate into approximate geometric compatibility between independently learned representations. Reconstruction experiments validate this approach empirically, substantially narrowing the interoperability gap across multiple datasets.
papers.summary: As large pre-trained models proliferate, there is growing interest in letting independently built networks be combined with little or no coordination, such as training an autoencoder's encoder and decoder separately yet having them work together. The authors introduce a topological regularizer that aligns the latent spaces of two independently trained autoencoders with no communication during training, and give a conditional theoretical analysis of how the structural agreement it encourages translates into approximate geometric compatibility between the learned representations. Reconstruction experiments show that **the regularizer substantially narrows the interoperability gap across multiple datasets**.

papers.title: ActMOF: Mapping Reticular Synthesis through Active Learning
papers.abstract: Reticular chemistry allows metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) to be designed from their building units, yet their synthesis remains constrained by sparse experimental data, noisy crystallization outcomes, and the absence of benchmarks for comparing active-learning strategies. While data-driven approaches such as Bayesian optimization (BO) can improve synthesis success rates, selecting appropriate optimizers beforehand for mapping MOF crystallization landscapes remains largely empirical. Here we present ActMOF, an experiment-grounded benchmark for comparing search strategies in aluminum-carboxylate MOF synthesis. ActMOF is emulated from experimentally measured microwave syntheses with each encoded condition assigned a crystallinity index calculated based on diffraction peak intensity and full width at half-maximum. By benchmarking policies guided by Gaussian processes (GP), tree ensembles and large language models (LLM), ActMOF placed the GP family among the leading policies for active learning in sparse synthesis landscapes. It then demonstrated transferability by guiding the microwave synthesis of six reticularly related aluminum MOFs. All six campaigns gave crystalline products within a fixed budget of 12 experiments each, and established a reusable testbed for AI-driven MOF synthesis.
papers.summary: Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) can be designed from their building units, but their synthesis is limited by sparse experimental data, noisy crystallization outcomes, and the lack of benchmarks for comparing active-learning strategies. `ActMOF` is an experiment-grounded benchmark emulated from measured microwave syntheses of aluminum-carboxylate MOFs, assigning each encoded condition a crystallinity index derived from diffraction peak intensity and width, and it is used to compare search policies driven by Gaussian processes (GP), tree ensembles, and large language models (LLM). GP-based policies rank among the strongest for sparse synthesis landscapes, and in a transfer test **all six reticularly related aluminum MOFs were obtained as crystalline products within a budget of 12 experiments each**.

papers.title: Scaling LLM Inference via Parallelism: Throughput-Latency Trade-off
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) serving systems must balance latency and throughput while efficiently utilizing distributed GPU resources. This challenge arises because inference consists of two fundamentally different phases: prefill, which determines time-to-first-token (TTFT), and decode, which determines inter-token latency (ITL). The use of tensor parallelism (TP), pipeline parallelism (PP), and hybrid configurations exposes different trade-offs between these latency dimensions, making the optimal parallelism configuration highly dependent on workload characteristics, latency requirements, and context length. Moreover, despite the widespread adoption of distributed inference, there is still limited understanding of how parallelism configurations should be selected under varying workload conditions and service-level objectives (SLO). In this paper, we develop a systematic framework for characterizing LLM inference parallelism via throughput-latency trade-offs, SLO-aware serving, and long-context scalability. We introduce the notion of parallelism operating regions by constructing TTFT-ITL feasible sets and Pareto frontiers across different workload compositions, thereby revealing a systematic transition from TP-dominant to PP-dominant configurations as workloads become increasingly prefill-heavy. We further formulate SLO-aware parallelism selection using goodput, showing that stringent TTFT requirements favor PP-dominated configurations, whereas relaxed latency constraints progressively shift the optimality toward TP-dominated configurations with higher serving capacity. Finally, we demonstrate that increasing context length fundamentally changes the relative advantages of parallelism configurations, with PP-dominant configurations exhibiting more favorable scalability and SLO attainment in the long-context regime.
papers.summary: Serving large language models (LLMs) across multiple GPUs means balancing time-to-first-token (TTFT), set by the prefill phase, against inter-token latency (ITL), set by decode, and tensor parallelism (TP), pipeline parallelism (PP), and hybrids of the two trade these off differently depending on workload and context length. The authors build a framework that maps parallelism configurations onto TTFT-ITL feasible sets and Pareto frontiers across workload mixes, formulate service-level objective (SLO) aware selection using goodput, and study how context length changes the picture. They find **a systematic shift from TP-dominant to PP-dominant configurations as workloads become more prefill-heavy**, that strict TTFT targets favor PP while relaxed latency budgets favor higher-capacity TP setups, and that PP-dominant configurations scale and meet objectives more favorably at long context.

papers.title: Vision-Language Models Integrate Conflicting Evidence Like Biased Bayesian Observers
papers.abstract: Vision-language models must reconcile conflicting text and images. Prior work has characterized the resulting behavior in terms of modality biases--e.g., a "blind faith in text"--but why preferences vary across models, domains, and input conditions remains unclear. We develop a predictive account from a Bayesian perspective, positing that VLMs combine conditionally independent evidence from each modality with prior beliefs, subject to modality-specific biases. The resulting two-parameter cue combination model accurately predicts VLM preferences under unseen combinations of input degradation and transfers to new forms of unreliability without refitting. Separating evidence strength from integration bias explains how VLMs can follow text even while weighting visual evidence more heavily, reconciling reports of text and vision dominance under a single combination rule.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) must reconcile conflicting text and image inputs, and prior work has described the result as modality bias, such as excessive trust in text, without explaining why preferences shift across models, domains, and input conditions. The authors propose a Bayesian account in which VLMs combine conditionally independent evidence from each modality with prior beliefs, subject to modality-specific biases, yielding a two-parameter cue combination model. **The model accurately predicts VLM preferences under unseen combinations of input degradation and transfers to new forms of unreliability without refitting**, and separating evidence strength from integration bias explains how a model can follow text while still weighting visual evidence more heavily, reconciling earlier reports of text and vision dominance.

papers.title: ForkGRPO: Efficient Exploration and Fine-Grained Credit Assignment for Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet strengthening their reasoning through reinforcement learning (RL) remains an open challenge. Any-order generation can suffer from entropy degradation, which narrows the reasoning paths available for exploration. Recent work mitigates this issue by applying standard GRPO with left-to-right generation. However, independently generating every rollout from the input prompt can leave alternative continuations from intermediate states underexplored, while trajectory-level advantages assign uniform credit to all tokens without distinguishing the contributions of individual reasoning segments. We propose ForkGRPO, an RL framework that couples efficient exploration with fine-grained segment-level credit assignment. It samples multiple continuations from high-entropy intermediate states along a reference trajectory, prioritizing textual boundaries and reusing shared prefixes. The continuations provide complementary learning signals: within-state group-relative advantages guide which continuations to reinforce, while Monte Carlo state-value differences indicate which reasoning segments improve expected outcomes. Among the evaluated architecture-preserving RL methods, ForkGRPO achieves the best performance on three of four benchmarks, while improving over the directly comparable JustGRPO by up to 1.2 percentage points and using up to 27.8% fewer generated tokens. ForkGRPO-Fast further achieves a $2.49\times$ training wall-clock speedup with negligible accuracy loss.
papers.summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) are advancing quickly, but strengthening their reasoning with reinforcement learning (RL) is hard because any-order generation suffers entropy degradation that narrows exploration, and existing left-to-right `GRPO` variants regenerate every rollout from the prompt and assign one trajectory-level advantage to all tokens. `ForkGRPO` samples multiple continuations from high-entropy intermediate states along a reference trajectory, preferring textual boundaries and reusing shared prefixes, then uses within-state group-relative advantages to decide which continuations to reinforce and Monte Carlo state-value differences to credit individual reasoning segments. Among architecture-preserving RL methods it is best on three of four benchmarks, **beating the directly comparable `JustGRPO` by up to 1.2 percentage points while generating up to 27.8% fewer tokens**, and a `ForkGRPO-Fast` variant trains 2.49 times faster in wall-clock time with negligible accuracy loss.

papers.title: W-JEPA: Wavelet Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for Wearable Activity Recognition
papers.abstract: A major challenge in wearable device activity recognition is the heterogeneity across datasets in sensor placement, channel count, sampling rate and subjects. Moreover, the motion patterns that distinguish activities often appear as subtle, scale-specific variations within otherwise similar waveforms. As a result, raw signals are often ambiguous, and models trained on them tend to rely on cues specific to a particular sensor setup or participant, which limits both cross-dataset transfer and generalization to unseen participants. Addressing this requires representations that preserve such activity-relevant, scale-specific variation. We introduce W-JEPA, a self-supervised framework that exploits the multiscale structure of inertial motion and leverages a joint-embedding predictive architecture, by organizing windows into a fixed grid of wavelet tokens indexed by scale, sensor axis, and time. These wavelet tokens help expose activity-specific detail within broadly similar raw signals, and serve as the units of masked latent prediction. W-JEPA predicts masked token representations supplied by an exponential-moving-average (EMA) target encoder. Because recovering a masked token requires relating motion at one scale and axis to motion at other scales and axes, the model learns the cross-scale, cross-axis structure of human movement. Across six wearable activity benchmarks, W-JEPA outperforms state-of-the-art methods under random-window splits and remains the strongest when subjects are held out, improving average macro-F1 by 8.7 percentage points over the strongest published baseline. These results indicate that physically grounded multiscale tokenization, combined together with latent predictive learning, provides a promising foundation for transferable representations of heterogeneous wearable inertial data.
papers.summary: Activity recognition from wearable sensors suffers from heterogeneity in sensor placement, channel count, sampling rate, and subjects, and the motion cues that separate activities are often subtle, scale-specific variations in otherwise similar waveforms, so models trained on raw signals latch onto setup-specific or person-specific cues. `W-JEPA` is a self-supervised method that organizes each window into a fixed grid of wavelet tokens indexed by scale, sensor axis, and time, then trains a joint-embedding predictive architecture to predict masked token representations supplied by an exponential-moving-average (EMA) target encoder, forcing the model to learn cross-scale and cross-axis structure of movement. Across six wearable activity benchmarks it outperforms state-of-the-art methods under random-window splits and **improves average macro-F1 by 8.7 percentage points over the strongest published baseline when subjects are held out**.

papers.title: How Do LLMs Understand Legal Philosophy? Diagnosing Legal-Philosophical Reasoning in LLMs
papers.abstract: Legal reasoning is a fundamental capability for large language models (LLMs) to complete legal AI tasks such as legal judgment prediction. In legal practice, this reasoning is shaped by legal philosophy: a judge's view of the nature and sources of law guides how legal materials are interpreted and applied, so judges working from the same statutes and precedents can reach different judgments. Existing research has largely overlooked whether LLMs can understand legal philosophy and apply it in legal reasoning, an ability we call \textit{legal-philosophical reasoning}. To fill this gap, we introduce LePhilBench, a benchmark for evaluating the legal-philosophical reasoning of LLMs that comprises two benchmarking tasks and a dataset. The two tasks evaluate how well LLMs understand legal philosophy and how well they apply it in legal reasoning, respectively. The dataset is manually and meticulously constructed. Its test set contains 220 U.S. Supreme Court opinions. A law professor designed fourteen annotation questions on legal philosophy, and three law-trained annotators with formal training in jurisprudence answered all fourteen questions for every opinion, yielding 9,240 legal-philosophical labels. LePhilBench takes the first step toward exploring legal-philosophical reasoning in LLMs.
papers.summary: Legal reasoning by large language models (LLMs) is shaped in practice by legal philosophy, since a judge's view of the nature and sources of law determines how statutes and precedents are interpreted, yet whether models can understand and apply such philosophy has gone largely unexamined. `LePhilBench` evaluates this legal-philosophical reasoning with two tasks, one testing understanding of legal philosophy and one testing its application in legal reasoning, on a manually built dataset whose test set covers 220 United States Supreme Court opinions. A law professor designed fourteen annotation questions, and three annotators with formal training in jurisprudence answered all of them for every opinion, producing **9,240 legal-philosophical labels**.

papers.title: Comprehensive Comparisons of Reinforcement Learning Algorithms in Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive comparison of four representative reinforcement learning (RL) methods in autonomous vehicle (AV) decision-making, including: Fitted Value Iteration (FVI), Rollout Classification Policy Iteration (RCPI), Deep Q-Network (DQN), and a discrete-action adaptation of Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (D-DDPG). The four methods are applied to the same AV decision-making problem at an unsignalized intersection and are compared in terms of optimality and safety, training stability, and training and decision cost. RCPI is the closest to a reference solution and has the most stable training process. However, it is the least data-efficient. D-DDPG reaches the second-smallest gap to a reference solution with the highest data efficiency, but has the least training stability. DQN is the most stable model-free method but has the highest collision rate. FVI achieves a lower collision rate than DQN, but is less data-efficient and less stable. Based on these results, we provide suggestions for selecting a method according to whether a model is available, the budget for training, and whether stable training is required.
papers.summary: Choosing a reinforcement learning (RL) method for autonomous vehicle (AV) decision-making involves trade-offs that are rarely measured side by side. Four representative methods, `Fitted Value Iteration`, `Rollout Classification Policy Iteration` (RCPI), `Deep Q-Network` (DQN), and a discrete-action adaptation of `Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient` (D-DDPG), are trained on the same unsignalized-intersection task and compared on optimality and safety, training stability, and training and decision cost. **RCPI comes closest to a reference solution with the most stable training but is the least data-efficient**, while D-DDPG is the most data-efficient and the least stable, and DQN is the most stable model-free method but has the highest collision rate. The authors turn these results into guidance for picking a method based on whether a model is available, the training budget, and whether stable training is required.

papers.title: Learning to Select Features with Manifold Deep Unfolding PCA
papers.abstract: Unsupervised feature selection (UFS) is of great significance in image processing and pattern recognition. Nevertheless, existing model-based methods often rely on manually tuned hyperparameters, while deep learning-based methods generally require massive training data. To address these issues, this paper proposes an efficient manifold deep unfolding feature selection network (MDUFS-Net). Technically, we first incorporate the $\ell_{2,0}$-norm into the classic principal component analysis (PCA) framework, then unfold the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM)-based iterative algorithm into an end-to-end trainable network, thereby enabling automatic parameter learning. Moreover, a manifold optimization strategy is developed to improve the numerical robustness. On this basis, we further extend MDUFS-Net into an enhanced variant called MDUFS-Net+ by introducing the $\ell_{0}$-norm for more discriminative feature representations. Extensive experiments validate that our proposed MDUFS-Net and MDUFS-Net+ outperform state-of-the-art methods in the UFS task, with promising performance in clustering. Our code is available at https://github.com/xianchaoxiu/MDUFS.
papers.summary: Unsupervised feature selection (UFS) methods either depend on hand-tuned hyperparameters or, when deep learning is used, on large amounts of training data. `MDUFS-Net` adds an l2,0-norm constraint to classic principal component analysis (PCA) and unfolds the resulting alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) solver into an end-to-end trainable network, so the parameters are learned rather than tuned, with a manifold optimization strategy for numerical robustness. A variant called `MDUFS-Net+` swaps in an l0-norm for more discriminative features, and **both outperform state-of-the-art UFS methods** in experiments, with strong downstream clustering performance.

papers.title: Progress-Aware Distillation for Mitigating Stagnation in Small Language Model Agents
papers.abstract: While LLM-based agent systems have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in reasoning and solving complex real-world tasks, they also come with substantial token consumption and inference latency, limiting their practical deployment. To enhance the efficiency of agent systems, recent efforts have focused on transferring agentic capabilities from large-scale models to small language models (SLMs) via supervised fine-tuning-based distillation. Nevertheless, as interaction trajectories grow longer, involving extended reasoning-action chains and extensive environmental feedback, distilled student agents tend to experience progress stagnation: becoming trapped in unproductive loops characterized by persistent failed strategies and difficulty making meaningful progress. Our systematic analysis shows that this phenomenon consistently occurs across diverse SLMs and task domains. To address this issue, we propose Progress-Aware Distillation (ProD), which explicitly detects and penalizes stagnation in student-generated trajectories. ProD encodes the stagnation gap between student and teacher into an adaptive margin for dynamically penalizing possible stagnation. By iteratively applying this procedure, ProD enables student agents to progressively approximate teacher behavior. Extensive experiments involving 8 SLMs, ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters, on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrate that ProD substantially mitigates progress stagnation while enhancing both the success rates and task-completion efficiency of distilled SLM agents.
papers.summary: Distilling agentic capabilities from large language models into small language models (SLMs) via supervised fine-tuning works, but on long interaction trajectories the student agents tend to stall, looping over failed strategies without making progress, a pattern the authors document across many SLMs and task domains. `Progress-Aware Distillation` (`ProD`) detects stagnation in student-generated trajectories and penalizes it with an adaptive margin derived from the stagnation gap between student and teacher, applied iteratively so the student approximates teacher behavior over time. **Across 8 SLMs from 0.6B to 8B parameters, ProD substantially reduces stagnation** and raises both success rates and task-completion efficiency on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks.

papers.title: More Than Seeing: Vision as Scalable Anchors in Native Multimodal Pre-Training
papers.abstract: Native multimodal pre-training trains a single model from scratch on text and multimodal data, enabling it to understand both language and visual inputs. However, how visual signals shape scaling behavior and support capabilities beyond visual understanding remains unclear. We investigate this question through controlled visual-content ablations across model sizes and training budgets. Specifically, we replace image embeddings with content-free padding token embeddings. Retaining visual content improves text prediction on image-text examples without materially changing the lowest text-only loss at a given compute budget, the optimal balance of model size and training data, or aggregate language scores. The relative multimodal loss benefit grows approximately as a power law of compute. To test benefits beyond understanding images, we evaluate spatial reasoning from text descriptions alone. Both conditions improve with model and data scaling. During training of the largest model, visual gains are most sustained in localization, navigation, and symbolic planning, which involve maintaining object configurations or composing spatial updates; gains in spatial relations, geometry, and physical commonsense are less consistent. These findings identify visual content as a scalable anchor for multimodal learning, with benefits that extend beyond visual inputs while preserving aggregate language performance.
papers.summary: Native multimodal pre-training trains one model from scratch on text and image-text data, but it has been unclear how visual signals affect scaling and whether they help with anything beyond understanding images. The authors run controlled ablations across model sizes and compute budgets in which image embeddings are replaced with content-free padding embeddings. Keeping the visual content improves text prediction on image-text examples without changing the best text-only loss, the optimal model-size-to-data balance, or aggregate language scores, and **the relative multimodal loss benefit grows roughly as a power law of compute**. On text-only spatial reasoning, visual gains during training of the largest model are most sustained in localization, navigation, and symbolic planning, and less consistent in spatial relations, geometry, and physical commonsense.

papers.title: Large-Step Last-Iterate Convergence of Random-Reshuffling Stochastic Gradient Descent
papers.abstract: Random reshuffling stochastic gradient descent (RR-SGD) is widely used for finite-sum optimization in machine learning. For convex $L$-smooth components, recent work establishes convergence guarantees for an averaged iterate with component stepsizes as large as order $1/L$. However, the final iterate is a natural output in practice, and existing last-iterate guarantees in this setting require stepsizes that scale inversely with the number of components $n$. We establish an expected objective-gap bound for the last iterate of standard RR-SGD on unconstrained problems with a constant component stepsize satisfying $0<\eta\lesssim 1/(L(1 + \log(nK)))$, where $K$ is the number of epochs. By retaining the sampling bias at random comparison points, we remove the explicit $1/n$ factor from the stepsize restriction. Combined with existing small-step bounds, our result matches the corresponding averaged-iterate convergence rate up to logarithmic factors.
papers.summary: Random reshuffling stochastic gradient descent (RR-SGD) is standard for finite-sum optimization, but existing convergence guarantees for its last iterate, the output people actually use, require stepsizes that shrink inversely with the number of components n. The authors prove an expected objective-gap bound for the last iterate of standard RR-SGD on unconstrained convex L-smooth problems with a constant stepsize of roughly order 1 over L times 1 plus the log of nK, where K is the number of epochs. By keeping the sampling bias at random comparison points, the analysis **removes the explicit 1/n factor from the stepsize restriction**, and combined with existing small-step results it matches the averaged-iterate rate up to logarithmic factors.

papers.title: MIPS: Mitigating Mode Collapse in Reinforcement Learning for Large Outcome Spaces
papers.abstract: Expected-reward maximization in reinforcement learning concentrates probability mass on a few outcomes, even in tasks that require many distinct, high-quality solutions, a failure known as mode collapse. Inverse Probability Scaling (IPS) counters this in group-based policy gradients such as GRPO by dividing each reward by the outcome's probability, estimated from its frequency within the sampled group. When the outcome space is large relative to the group, outcomes rarely repeat and these estimates become uninformative. Since an outcome can be constructed along many trajectories, its probability is a sum over all of them, and computing it directly is intractable. We propose Marginal IPS (MIPS), which performs marginal evaluation by combining the sampled trajectory with a learned model of the trajectories that lead to each outcome. On Hypergrids, where the exact sampling distribution is computable, MIPS stays near the reward-distribution target as the outcome space grows relative to the rollout group, while frequency-based IPS degrades. In molecular synthesis and phylogenetic inference, MIPS sustains diverse, high-quality sampling where GRPO and frequency-based IPS collapse, showing that MIPS serves as a reliable solution to mode collapse in RL.
papers.summary: Maximizing expected reward in reinforcement learning tends to concentrate probability on a few outcomes, a failure called mode collapse that matters when a task needs many distinct high-quality solutions. `Inverse Probability Scaling` (IPS) counters this in group-based policy gradients like `GRPO` by dividing rewards by outcome probabilities estimated from frequency within the sampled group, but those estimates become useless when outcomes rarely repeat because the outcome space is large. `Marginal IPS` (`MIPS`) instead estimates an outcome's probability by combining the sampled trajectory with a learned model of all trajectories that lead to that outcome. On `Hypergrids`, where the exact sampling distribution is computable, **MIPS stays near the reward-distribution target as the outcome space grows while frequency-based IPS degrades**, and in molecular synthesis and phylogenetic inference it sustains diverse, high-quality sampling where GRPO and IPS collapse.

papers.title: ActICL: Post-Training for Agentic Multimodal In-Context Learning
papers.abstract: Multimodal in-context learning (ICL) is an important capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Its performance is closely tied to the demonstrations it uses, making demonstration retrieval a core problem for ICL. Common methods use fixed scoring methods to retrieve all the demonstrations at once, which may introduce redundancy and noise. Context-aware retrieval methods have emerged to address this problem by allowing incremental retrieval from a growing context. However, none of them lets the MLLM learn how to judge what new demonstrations it needs and then carry out progressive retrieval on its own. To this end, we introduce ActICL, which trains an MLLM agent to acquire and use an ICL context via tool-augmented reasoning. An ActICL agent analyzes its own information gaps during iterative reasoning and tool-use actions. Based on these gaps, it performs targeted retrieval to acquire a set of initial candidates. It can then use the existing context to further filter the candidates and refine the context, or it can iteratively perform a new retrieval. When the agent judges that the context is sufficient for the task, or when the resource limit is reached with the user request met, it sends the acquired context to an answering model, either the agent itself or another MLLM. We use a two-stage post-training procedure that jointly optimizes the agent's acquisition and answering. With an adaptive number of demonstrations, ActICL improves average performance by 11.6 percentage points over standard similarity-based retrieval across seven benchmarks and three MLLMs, and by 4.4 points compared to the strongest prior baseline. The contexts acquired by ActICL agents can also be used effectively by frontier models. When GPT-5.6-Sol performs 4-shot ICL, ActICL's contexts improve its performance by 3.5 points over standard retrieval, averaged over three benchmarks.
papers.summary: Multimodal in-context learning (ICL) in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) depends heavily on which demonstrations are retrieved, and existing methods either fetch everything at once with a fixed scoring rule or retrieve incrementally without letting the model decide what it needs. `ActICL` trains an MLLM agent to identify its own information gaps during iterative reasoning, perform targeted retrieval with tools, filter and refine the growing context, and hand the result to an answering model once it judges the context sufficient, using a two-stage post-training procedure that jointly optimizes acquisition and answering. With an adaptive number of demonstrations, **ActICL improves average performance by 11.6 percentage points over similarity-based retrieval** across seven benchmarks and three MLLMs, and by 4.4 points over the strongest prior baseline. The acquired contexts also transfer to frontier models, lifting `GPT-5.6-Sol` 4-shot ICL by 3.5 points over standard retrieval.

papers.title: What Does LALM Post-training Learn? Rethinking Audio Understanding and Reasoning Capabilities
papers.abstract: Post-training often improves the performance of large audio-language models on audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks. However, these improvements may reflect adaptation to specific question formats, such as multiple-choice questions, rather than genuine advances in audio understanding and reasoning capabilities. To investigate what LALMs actually learn from post-training, we conduct controlled experiments that disentangle improvements in audio understanding from adaptation to specific question formats. Across different models and post-training methods, we find that much of the reported improvement persists even without informative audio, but largely disappears when the question format changes. These findings suggest that post-training often teaches models to exploit task-specific textual cues and answer patterns rather than developing generalizable audio understanding and reasoning capabilities.
papers.summary: Post-training reliably raises large audio-language model (LALM) scores on audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks, but those gains may reflect adaptation to question formats such as multiple choice rather than better audio understanding. The authors run controlled experiments that separate the two, testing models with and without informative audio and under changed question formats, across several models and post-training methods. **Much of the reported improvement persists even without informative audio but largely disappears when the question format changes**, suggesting that post-training mostly teaches models to exploit textual cues and answer patterns rather than generalizable audio capabilities.

papers.title: AgriJev: Efficient Agricultural Candidate Scoring with Multi-Scale Adapted Models
papers.abstract: Agricultural systems make decisions over heterogeneous entity types, textual judgments, and knowledge-question options. Generating a textual answer adds decoding and extraction steps to decisions that ultimately require a candidate choice. We introduce AgriJev, a family of adapted Qwen3.5 models at 0.8B, 2B, 4B, and 9B. A shared interface conditions on agricultural text, a judgment question, and candidate definitions, returning scores and relative probabilities in one forward call. We prepare source-aware training records and frozen evaluations from existing agricultural resources, retaining original groups and annotation provenance. Comparisons include original Qwen3.5 models and matched agricultural SFT models, both evaluated through native answer generation. Across 17 external test views, AgriJev-9B reaches 75.44% mean accuracy, exceeding the original and SFT generators by 5.89 and 3.79 percentage points. It outperforms the original generator on 13 views and narrows the mean gap to hosted Jev 1.13.0. On a fixed A100 workload, its median scoring latency is approximately half that of same-scale answer generation. Task-dependent gains and failures characterize a practical choice among agricultural model weights and inference contracts.
authors: Xuechen Li (University of Minnesota Twin Cities)
papers.summary: Agricultural decision systems often need to choose among candidates, such as entity types, textual judgments, or knowledge-question options, yet generating a free-text answer adds decoding and extraction steps on top of that choice. `AgriJev` is a family of adapted `Qwen3.5` models at 0.8B, 2B, 4B, and 9B parameters with a shared interface that conditions on agricultural text, a judgment question, and candidate definitions, and returns scores and relative probabilities in a single forward pass. Trained on source-aware records built from existing agricultural resources and evaluated on frozen test sets, **`AgriJev-9B` reaches 75.44% mean accuracy across 17 external test views**, beating the original and supervised-fine-tuned generators by 5.89 and 3.79 points, with median scoring latency about half that of same-scale answer generation on an A100.

papers.title: State-Matched Sequence Conformal Prediction
papers.abstract: Sequential conformal prediction needs to decide which past errors should calibrate uncertainty for the current target. Recency and online error feedback are useful when recent observations remain relevant, but the recent past can be a poor reference when comparable states recur at nonadjacent times, with the recurrence pattern generally unknown. We propose State-Matched Sequence Conformal Prediction (SMSCP), which constructs an explicit one-sided local-linear state from pre-target information, uses state similarity to select a matched reference set of past calibration scores, and then applies the ordinary unweighted conformal order statistic. In contrast to existing approaches, SMSCP uses state similarity to identify calibration observations relevant to the target score quantile. This motivates a theoretical analysis of whether nearby states have comparable target score quantiles under temporal dependence. We establish control of the resulting conformal cutoff and characterize predictive information not captured by the chosen state. Simulations show that state matching is most effective when score-relevant states recur across nonadjacent times, while revealing settings in which its advantage weakens or reverses. Across solar irradiance and bike-demand benchmarks, SMSCP improves interval score over recency, weighted, adaptive, and HopCPT comparators, and achieves coverage closer to the nominal 0.90 level than ResCP on five of six benchmarks.
papers.summary: Sequential conformal prediction must decide which past errors should calibrate the uncertainty interval for the current target, and recency-based or online-feedback approaches fail when comparable conditions recur at nonadjacent times with an unknown pattern. `State-Matched Sequence Conformal Prediction` (`SMSCP`) builds an explicit one-sided local-linear state from pre-target information, selects a reference set of past calibration scores by state similarity, and then applies the ordinary unweighted conformal order statistic. The authors analyze when nearby states have comparable target score quantiles under temporal dependence, prove control of the resulting cutoff, and show in simulations that state matching helps most when score-relevant states recur nonadjacently and can weaken or reverse otherwise. On solar irradiance and bike-demand benchmarks, **SMSCP improves interval score over recency, weighted, adaptive, and `HopCPT` comparators** and lands closer to nominal 0.90 coverage than `ResCP` on five of six benchmarks.

papers.title: Digital Self-Interference Cancellation for In-Band Full-Duplex Systems Based on Transformer Neural Operators
papers.abstract: Digital-domain self-interference cancellation is essential in in-band full-duplex radios after passive suppression and analog cancellation. It is particularly challenging when the desired signal is strong relative to the residual self-interference. In this regime, conventional iterative digital cancellers update their coefficients from desired-signal-contaminated received samples and may suffer substantial performance degradation. This paper reformulates digital-domain self-interference cancellation as an operator-learning problem. The proposed framework learns the temporal evolution of the residual self-interference channel from historical observations and uses the learned operator together with the known local transmit signal to reconstruct the current residual self-interference. A Transformer neural operator is used to realize this framework. The resulting method is trained in a desired-signal-free setting and then applied in the presence of a desired signal. A continuity-based analysis characterizes the sensitivity of the learned operator to the resulting input perturbation. Numerical experiments in static and time-varying channels, including time-varying SIR conditions, demonstrate stable cancellation performance over a wide range of interference levels. At 30 dB SIR, the proposed method improves the cancellation performance by 5--15 dB over the considered conventional methods.
papers.summary: In-band full-duplex radios need digital self-interference cancellation after passive suppression and analog cancellation, and conventional iterative cancellers degrade badly when a strong desired signal contaminates the samples used to update their coefficients. The authors recast digital cancellation as an operator-learning problem: a Transformer neural operator learns the temporal evolution of the residual self-interference channel from past observations and reconstructs the current residual using the known local transmit signal, trained without a desired signal and deployed with one present. A continuity-based analysis bounds the learned operator's sensitivity to the resulting input perturbation, and simulations in static and time-varying channels show stable cancellation across interference levels, with **a 5 to 15 dB cancellation improvement over conventional methods at 30 dB signal-to-interference ratio**.

papers.title: Towards Efficient Simultaneous Inverse Text Normalization with Pretrained Text-to-Text Language Model and Read-Tag-Write Policy
papers.abstract: Streaming Inverse Text Normalization (ITN) is vital for converting spoken-form outputs from streaming Automatic Speech Recognition into formatted written text. Existing streaming ITN methods rely on hybrid systems combining neural tagging with expert-crafted finite-state transducer rules, limiting scalability across domains and languages. While end-to-end models offer superior scalability by learning directly from data, standard encoder-decoder architectures are inherently non-streaming due to global attention. In this paper, we propose an efficient streaming end-to-end ITN system, adapting a pretrained text-to-text model to leverage its robust linguistic knowledge. To enable streaming, we introduce architectural adaptations, a specialized training strategy, a Read-Tag-Write decoding policy, and inference optimizations. Experiments on Vietnamese datasets show accuracy comparable to non-streaming baselines, outperforming hybrid methods while satisfying real-time latency requirements.
papers.summary: Streaming inverse text normalization (ITN) turns spoken-form output from streaming automatic speech recognition into formatted written text, but current streaming systems combine neural tagging with hand-crafted finite-state transducer rules that scale poorly across domains and languages, while end-to-end encoder-decoder models are non-streaming because of global attention. The authors adapt a pretrained text-to-text language model for streaming ITN through architectural changes, a specialized training strategy, a `Read-Tag-Write` decoding policy, and inference optimizations. On Vietnamese datasets the system reaches **accuracy comparable to non-streaming baselines while meeting real-time latency requirements**, and outperforms the hybrid rule-based methods.

papers.title: Structure-Preserving Document-Level Data Augmentation via Discourse Parsing
papers.abstract: Data augmentation (DA) plays a vital role in improving model performance in low-resource or limited-supervision scenarios within Natural Language Processing (NLP). Existing DA methods, such as synonym replacement and back-translation, have demonstrated effectiveness on the word or sentence level; however, they frequently neglect discourse-level coherence and logical flow, which are essential for complex tasks dependent on inter-sentential relationships. In this paper, we propose a structure-preserving document-level data augmentation framework based on large language models (LLMs) and document-level discourse structure parsing. Our approach identifies rhetorical relations between sentence pairs and extracts key phrases, which are then replaced with semantically coherent but topically shifted content while preserving the original discourse structure. Experimental results on text summarization and question answering show that the proposed augmented data provides complementary supervision and improves combined-data training across the evaluated tasks. Comparisons with a standard RST parser and controlled ablations further support the proposed discourse representation.
papers.summary: Common data augmentation (DA) techniques for natural language processing (NLP), such as synonym replacement and back-translation, operate at the word or sentence level and ignore discourse-level coherence that tasks depending on inter-sentential relationships need. The proposed framework parses document-level discourse structure to identify rhetorical relations between sentence pairs, extracts key phrases, and uses large language models (LLMs) to replace them with coherent but topically shifted content while keeping the original discourse structure intact. On text summarization and question answering, **the augmented data provides complementary supervision that improves combined-data training**, and comparisons against a standard Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) parser plus ablations support the proposed discourse representation.

papers.title: What You Sign Is Not What You Run: The Verifiability Gap in Quantized LLM Supply Chains
papers.abstract: Model signing authenticates the full-precision weights W an LLM is released with, yet users run a quantized artifact Q whose producing transformation is not uniquely determined under current disclosure. We separate the non-environment inputs from the execution environment E and measure a quantity that, to our knowledge, has not been measured before: the Independent Verifiability Rate (IVR), the fraction of a popularity-sampled GGUF ecosystem that a third party can re-derive bit-for-bit. Across the 200 most-downloaded Hugging Face GGUF repositories (198 in scope), no artifact or model card records the build environment, so under a recorded-inputs protocol the IVR is 0/198. Yet the artifacts are not irreproducible. On four in-sample repositories that disclose their inputs, the card's information alone reproduces no Q4_K_M file, but two coordinates the card omits - the build's floating-point-contraction setting and, for hybrid models, the per-tensor quantization recipe - re-derive 7/8 target-quant files bit-for-bit on x86 (5/8 on arm64); the fp16 re-derives from the provider's checkpoint, but the calibration imatrix must be shipped and hash-bound, since recomputing it did not match. An older release additionally pins the instruction set and did not re-derive. Reproducing the divergence reported with llama.cpp PR #25353, we show that E is a necessary coordinate and that one compiler setting yields a unique output across the tested platforms at negligible quality cost (+0.06% perplexity). As a security characterization, benign floating-point non-determinism separates from uniformly placed nibble-flip tampering above a detection floor that grows with the environments a verifier must allow, but a targeted embedding edit evades the statistic, so the proposed protocol rests on exact re-derivation; adversarial-fp16 attacks lie outside it. We release the audit data and a re-runnable harness.
papers.summary: Model signing authenticates the full-precision weights a large language model ships with, but users actually run quantized files produced by a transformation that current disclosure practices leave underspecified. The authors define the Independent Verifiability Rate (IVR), the fraction of a popularity-sampled GGUF ecosystem a third party can rebuild bit-for-bit, and audit the 200 most-downloaded Hugging Face GGUF repositories. **None of the 198 in-scope repositories records its build environment, so the IVR under a recorded-inputs protocol is 0 of 198**, yet on four repositories that do disclose inputs, adding two omitted details, the floating-point-contraction compiler setting and the per-tensor quantization recipe, re-derives 7 of 8 `Q4_K_M` files exactly on x86, while the calibration imatrix must be shipped and hash-bound because recomputing it did not match. Reproducing a divergence reported in a `llama.cpp` pull request, they show the execution environment is a necessary coordinate, that one compiler setting gives platform-unique output at a 0.06% perplexity cost, and that while random nibble-flip tampering is statistically detectable, a targeted embedding edit evades the statistic, so verification must rest on exact re-derivation; audit data and a re-runnable harness are released.

papers.title: SKG: A Law-Induced Engine from Inference to Induction
papers.abstract:
This paper proposes the SKG (Symplectic-Kernel Gradient) reasoning engine for law-induced inference and induction. Laws are a priori; data provide instances. Inference is geometric evolution under law constraints. We organize symplectic geometry, GENERIC, kernel methods, RKHS, group-equivariant networks, and constrained mechanics into a unified, analyzable, implementable, verifiable framework. We propose the SKG octuple S = (M, g, omega, H, S, G, Delta, Pi), whose four components correspond to four levels of laws: conservation laws, constitutive relations, symmetry groups, and axiom systems.
  Main results: (1) Invariants enter metric construction via the Jacobian: g = J^T Sigma^-1 J + epsilon_G I. For constant cases, we establish inverse reconstruction theory: solvability rank condition (Thm 3.9), consistency criterion (Thm 3.11), and uniqueness theorem (Thm 3.14). (2) The kernel bandwidth matrix is uniquely determined by Fisher information and satisfies task-independence (Thm 3.19). (3) The metric reconstruction error decomposes into four terms (Thm 3.21), with squared condition number kappa(Sigma^*)^2 as the dominant amplification factor (Thm 3.22). (4) For state-dependent cases, we establish function-space reconstruction theory on matrix-valued RKHS (Thms 4.8, 4.9). (5) Three-layer projections handle axiom, symplectic-step, and conservation constraints. (6) The residual equation yields the observable formula, four-dimensional rank condition, and noise propagation, while g_qq is structurally unidentifiable. (7) Kernel parameterization yields the RKHS extrapolation bound (Thm 4.15) and strict OOD gain theorem in group directions (Thm 8.15). (8) The learning-decoupling theorem (Thm 9.1) proves the sole object of induction is the parameters of the task energy.
  Validation: 1D damped oscillator and 2D rotation-invariant system; 6 unit tests, 10 experiments (paired t-test, p < 0.01).
papers.summary: The `SKG` (Symplectic-Kernel Gradient) reasoning engine treats laws as a priori constraints and data as instances, framing inference as geometric evolution under those constraints. It organizes symplectic geometry, the GENERIC formalism, kernel methods, reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS), group-equivariant networks, and constrained mechanics into a single framework built on an octuple whose components encode conservation laws, constitutive relations, symmetry groups, and axiom systems. The main results are a set of theorems covering inverse metric reconstruction from invariants via the Jacobian, a Fisher-information-determined kernel bandwidth, a four-term error decomposition dominated by the squared condition number, function-space reconstruction on matrix-valued RKHS, an RKHS extrapolation bound, and a learning-decoupling theorem stating that **induction reduces solely to learning the parameters of the task energy**. Validation consists of a 1D damped oscillator and a 2D rotation-invariant system, with 6 unit tests and 10 experiments.

papers.title: CktHGVAE: A Symmetric Design/State Heterogeneous Graph Variational Autoencoder for Transistor-level Analog/Mixed-signal Circuit Design and Analysis
papers.abstract: We propose CktHGVAE, a heterogeneous graph variational autoencoder for transistor-level analog/mixedsignal CMOS circuits that takes not only design variables but also state variables as its inputs and outputs. With a single hyperparameter configuration without topology-specific tuning, comparison between model-generated and SPICE-simulated circuit operational states gives median R2 values above 0.9 for typical single-ended voltage amplifiers and the CMOS inverter, and 0.81-0.96 for differential amplifiers with larger datasets. Latent-space optimization in the PCA-reduced latent space with Bayesian optimization, evolutionary search, random search, and quasi-exhaustive search is demonstrated for a common-source voltage amplifier with NMOS input and resistive load, where the objective function is defined as a penalty for deviation from required circuit specifications. For each search strategy, 93.3 - 100% of all design candidates suggested by the model satisfy the required circuit specifications at the decoder output, and SPICE simulations verify that 90 - 100% of them indeed satisfy the requirements. The model pretrained on a batch of topologies can be transferred to unseen topologies without retraining at all, with zero-shot reconstruction median R2 values of 0.72-0.90 in three of four scenarios, including transfer from single-ended to differential topologies, although the transfer fidelity depends on the choice of pretraining topologies. Our demonstrations suggest that the proposed model can potentially serve as a basis for AMS CMOS circuit design automation.
papers.summary: `CktHGVAE` is a heterogeneous graph variational autoencoder for transistor-level analog and mixed-signal (AMS) CMOS circuits that takes both design variables and circuit state variables as inputs and outputs. With one hyperparameter configuration and no topology-specific tuning, its generated operating states match SPICE simulation with median R2 above 0.9 for typical single-ended voltage amplifiers and the CMOS inverter, and 0.81 to 0.96 for differential amplifiers. Optimizing in the PCA-reduced latent space with Bayesian optimization, evolutionary search, random search, and quasi-exhaustive search for a common-source amplifier, **93.3 to 100% of suggested designs meet the required specifications at the decoder output and SPICE confirms 90 to 100% of them**. A model pretrained on a batch of topologies transfers to unseen ones without retraining, with zero-shot reconstruction median R2 of 0.72 to 0.90 in three of four scenarios, though fidelity depends on which topologies were used for pretraining.

papers.title: One Block Ahead: Promoting Sampler State in Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Block-diffusion language models denoise a whole block of token positions in parallel so each forward pass can emit many tokens. However, blocks are still denoised in strict sequence, a cost that within-block acceleration leaves untouched. Here, we investigate decoding blocks concurrently and propose One Block Ahead (OBA), a training-free decoding algorithm that denoises the next block alongside the current one. We demonstrate that for uniform-state diffusion LMs, where a block's denoising progress is not visible in its intermediate tokens, concurrent decoding is advantageous if the next block's tokens are promoted together with the corresponding sampler state, including the self-conditioning signal and the denoising time. We also derive a break-even criterion that relates the benefit of OBA to the relative cost of a paired-block forward pass. On DiffusionGemma, a state-of-the-art diffusion LM, OBA increases the tokens per forward pass by 42.3% (from 15.64 to 22.25) and the single-request denoising throughput by 16.3%, averaged over ten benchmarks, with a small accuracy regression.
papers.summary: Block-diffusion language models denoise a whole block of token positions per forward pass, but blocks are still processed in strict sequence, a cost that within-block acceleration does not address. `One Block Ahead` (`OBA`) is a training-free decoding algorithm that denoises the next block alongside the current one; for uniform-state diffusion models, where a block's progress is not visible in its intermediate tokens, the authors show this works only if the next block's tokens are promoted together with their sampler state, including the self-conditioning signal and denoising time, and they derive a break-even criterion relating the benefit to the relative cost of a paired-block forward pass. On `DiffusionGemma`, **OBA raises tokens per forward pass by 42.3%, from 15.64 to 22.25**, and single-request denoising throughput by 16.3% averaged over ten benchmarks, with a small accuracy regression.

papers.title: High-Probability Regret Bounds for Feel-Good Thompson Sampling
papers.abstract: Feel-good Thompson sampling (FGTS) augments the posterior of vanilla Thompson sampling with an exploration term that favors reward functions with high predicted optimal values. This modification achieves minimax-optimal regret up to logarithmic factors in linear contextual bandits, but existing analyses of its two standard variants establish regret guarantees in expectation. In this paper, we derive the first high-probability regret bounds for both cumulative and current-step FGTS in contextual bandits with general realizable function approximation. Our bounds depend on the corresponding decoupling coefficients and the prior mass near the true reward function. In the $d$-dimensional linear setting, both variants satisfy $\mathrm{Regret}(T)=O\big(d\sqrt T\log(2T)+\sqrt T\log(1/\delta)\big)$ with probability at least $1-\delta$, where $T$ is the time horizon. This bound matches the dimension and horizon dependence of algorithms based on the upper confidence bounds, up to logarithmic factors. Relative to the expected-regret guarantees, the cost of controlling the regret with high probability is confined to additive terms with at most linear dependence on $\log(1/\delta)$. The proof ideas are partially developed by GPT-6 Astra under the authors' guidance.
papers.summary: Feel-good Thompson sampling (FGTS) adds an exploration term to the posterior of vanilla Thompson sampling that favors reward functions with high predicted optimal values, achieving near-minimax regret in linear contextual bandits, but prior analyses of its two standard variants only bound regret in expectation. The authors derive the first high-probability regret bounds for both cumulative and current-step FGTS in contextual bandits with general realizable function approximation, with bounds depending on the decoupling coefficients and the prior mass near the true reward function. In the d-dimensional linear setting both variants achieve **regret of order d times sqrt(T) times log(2T) plus sqrt(T) times log(1 over delta) with probability at least 1 minus delta**, matching the dimension and horizon dependence of upper-confidence-bound methods up to logarithmic factors, and the cost of the high-probability guarantee is confined to additive terms at most linear in log(1 over delta). The proof ideas were partially developed by `GPT-6 Astra` under the authors' guidance.

papers.title: HankelKANet: Lightweight Path Loss Estimation via Physics-Inspired Hankel Convolution
papers.abstract: Accurate path loss (PL) estimation is essential for wireless network planning and optimization. This paper proposes HankelKANet, a lightweight physics-inspired network for PL estimation that structurally embeds electromagnetic propagation characteristics into the neural architecture. Built on a single residual UNet backbone, the proposed model integrates urban layout features with a convolutional Kolmogorov-Arnold network(KAN). Specifically, the convolutional kernels are parameterized by the radial amplitudes of the zeroth- and first-order Hankel functions. This formulation acts as a physics-inspired nonlinear distance encoding, enabling the network to capture dominant attenuation characteristics directly without requiring additional physics-based loss terms. Experimental results demonstrate that HankelKANet achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and efficiency on both the simulated RadioMapSeer dataset and the real-world Huawei RSRPSet. Compared with the leading baseline, PEFNet, it reduces the parameter count by 78% and lowers the RMSE by 16.96% on the simulated data, while further exhibiting robust cross-dataset transferability and high data efficiency during target-domain adaptation. To interpret these empirical gains, we mathematically establish a parameter-conditional spatial gradient bound. Using discrete Dirichlet energy (DDE) and Jacobian sensitivity heatmaps, we empirically verify that this physical encoding intrinsically constrains the network's spatial derivatives. This structural smoothness effectively eliminates non-physical spatial ripples, preventing overfitting to simulator artifacts and serving as the fundamental driver for robust real world generalization.
papers.summary: Path loss (PL) estimation underpins wireless network planning, and `HankelKANet` is a lightweight network for it that embeds electromagnetic propagation characteristics directly into the architecture. Built on a single residual UNet backbone, it combines urban layout features with a convolutional Kolmogorov-Arnold network (KAN) whose kernels are parameterized by the radial amplitudes of zeroth- and first-order Hankel functions, giving a physics-inspired nonlinear distance encoding that captures dominant attenuation without extra physics-based loss terms.
