papers.summary: Neuro-symbolic models offer interpretable deliberate reasoning, but their symbolic backbones are hand-built and domain-specific, so one route to scaling them is aligning and merging existing symbolic systems, which first requires matching units across them. `SAE-IDF` encodes each symbol in its native context into a sparse code with a sparse autoencoder (SAE), reweights every dimension by its rarity in the manner of inverse document frequency, and matches across systems. On 12 tasks spanning 6 kinds of symbolic system it beats the same model's dense-embedding baseline on all tasks with `Gemma-2-9B` and all but one with `Llama-3.1-8B`, **by up to 45 points**, consistently across SAE layers and configurations, and because each sparse dimension carries a human-readable meaning, every match decomposes into named concepts.

papers.title: J-tau: A Fully Localized Japanese Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction
papers.abstract: We present J-tau, the first publicly available Japanese benchmark for evaluating tool-using LLM agents in interactive customer-support scenarios. While tau-bench is widely used to evaluate LLM agents, it is English-centric and cannot evaluate agents in other languages. Existing multilingual extensions offer no public Japanese version and rely primarily on machine translation, leaving locale-specific entities such as addresses and currencies inconsistent with the target region. To enable reliable evaluation in Japanese, we carefully localize tau-bench through machine translation, entity adaptation, and human review. During this process, we also uncover and fix two flaws in the original tau-bench: invalid tasks and a score aggregation error that inflates certain models' results. Experiments show that J-tau yields fewer evaluation errors than a naively machine-translated counterpart and that our fixes resolve both flaws.
papers.summary: `tau-bench`, the standard test for tool-using agents in customer-support dialogue, is English-centric, and existing multilingual extensions rely on machine translation with no public Japanese version, leaving locale-specific entities such as addresses and currencies inconsistent with the target region. `J-tau` localizes it through machine translation, entity adaptation, and human review, and along the way the authors found and fixed two flaws in the original: invalid tasks and **a score aggregation error that inflated certain models' results**. Experiments show the localized version yields fewer evaluation errors than a naively machine-translated counterpart and that both fixes hold.

papers.title: Synthetic reaction data from transformation rules for graph-to-sequence pretraining in biodegradation pathway prediction
papers.abstract: The scarcity of observed biodegradation reactions constrains the training of product and pathway predictors. We present enviGraph, a framework that generates and curates synthetic reaction data, uses these data to pretrain a graph-to-sequence predictor, and fine-tunes the predictor on observed environmental reactions for product and recursive pathway prediction. Applying inherited environmental transformation rules to structures from PubChem, NORMAN SusDat and EPA DSSTox, followed by curation, produces 776,851 canonical parent-product pairs for pretraining. We compare this dataset with three United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) reaction datasets: USPTO-50K, USPTO-MIT and USPTO-Stereo. We evaluate enviGraph and the sequence-based enviFormer using ten folds split by pathway on the EAWAG Biocatalysis/Biodegradation Database (BBD), regulatory pesticide biodegradation data (Soil) and activated-sludge biodegradation data (Sludge). For both predictors, synthetic pretraining gives the highest BBD mean precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) among the evaluated pretraining datasets for single-generation and multi-generation prediction. enviGraph achieves BBD single-generation PR-AUC of $0.202 \pm 0.050$ with synthetic pretraining, compared with $0.169 \pm 0.065$ for the retrospectively selected strongest USPTO condition, USPTO-Stereo (mean $\pm$ sample standard deviation across folds). Its exact BBD top-1 and top-5 accuracies with synthetic pretraining are 0.355 and 0.594. The strongest USPTO conditions give higher PR-AUC means than synthetic pretraining in most Soil and Sludge comparisons. enviGraph has higher Soil multi-generation PR-AUC means than enviFormer under each of the four main pretraining datasets, and with synthetic pretraining it also leads enviFormer on BBD single-generation PR-AUC and exact top-1 and top-5 accuracy.
papers.summary: Predicting how chemicals break down in the environment is limited by how few biodegradation reactions have been observed. `enviGraph` applies inherited environmental transformation rules to structures from `PubChem`, `NORMAN SusDat`, and `EPA DSSTox` to synthesize and curate 776,851 parent-product pairs, pretrains a graph-to-sequence predictor on them, and fine-tunes on observed reactions for single-generation and recursive pathway prediction. Against pretraining on three `USPTO` patent-reaction datasets, synthetic pretraining **gives the highest mean precision-recall area under the curve on the EAWAG biodegradation database, 0.202 versus 0.169 for the strongest USPTO condition**, with exact top-1 and top-5 accuracy of 0.355 and 0.594. The advantage does not transfer to the soil and activated-sludge datasets, where the best USPTO conditions usually come out ahead.

papers.title: Model What Matters: Decision-Guided Selective World Modeling for Language Agents
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning provides a direct mechanism for optimizing task objectives in large language model-driven agents, but task rewards are typically sparse trajectory-level signals that only evaluate task success, without directly supervising action-conditioned environment transitions, leaving the model with limited explicit understanding of action consequences and environment dynamics. Recent work introduces auxiliary supervision through policy and world modeling co-training, yet typically treats complete environmental observations uniformly as world modeling targets, overlooking the varying decision relevance of observation content. We propose DGS-WM (Decision-Guided Selective World Modeling), a decision-guided policy-world modeling co-training approach for language agents. DGS-WM employs a Decision-Guided Observation Selection component that filters observation units with decision value as world modeling targets based on their support for subsequent policy responses, and a Confidence-Adaptive Weighting component that adaptively adjusts supervision strength according to the model's prediction confidence on selected targets. Together, these components form a decision-aware auxiliary world modeling loss, jointly optimized with the RL loss on the same policy model. Across multiple benchmarks covering single-hop/multi-hop question answering and interactive web tasks, DGS-WM achieves consistent improvements under different model scales and RL algorithms, demonstrating more stable and effective performance compared to full-observation world modeling methods.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning for language agents usually supplies only a trajectory-level success reward, which says nothing about how individual actions change the environment. Co-training a world model alongside the policy helps, but existing versions ask the model to predict entire observations, treating every part as equally worth learning. `DGS-WM` keeps only the observation units that support the agent's next decision as world-modeling targets and scales supervision strength by the model's confidence on them, forming a decision-aware auxiliary loss optimized jointly with the RL objective on the same policy model. Across single-hop and multi-hop question answering and interactive web tasks, it **improves consistently over full-observation world modeling at different model scales and under different RL algorithms**.

papers.title: Selective Reasoning for Typed Decision Models: When to Start, Read, and Stop
papers.abstract: Typed decision models need an interface that can use additional reasoning while retaining candidate outputs. We train a shared candidate-answer reader on a frozen Qwen3.5-4B backbone to unify direct decisions with on-demand, interruptible reasoning. The reader returns distributions from empty and partial reasoning prefixes. A benefit gate starts reasoning, a natural-state trigger requests explicit reads, and an entropy rule accepts acquired answers and cancels generation. Measurements distinguish answer-query work, generated output, and pipeline time. Across 768 questions from ProofWriter, LogiQA 2.0, and ARC-Challenge, accuracy rises from 70.96% for direct reading to 84.38%. Relative to 512-token terminal reading, accuracy improves by 7.29 percentage points with 2.25% more mean output work. Relative to 1,024-token terminal reading, pipeline time falls by 46.30% with an accuracy difference of -1.17 points. Exact-prefix controls isolate the saving from interruption, while read-scheduling controls distinguish reduced observation work from shorter response time.
papers.summary: A decision model that can optionally think longer needs to decide when to start reasoning, when to read the partial chain, and when to stop. The authors train a candidate-answer reader on a frozen `Qwen3.5-4B` backbone that returns answer distributions from empty and partial reasoning prefixes, then gate the start of reasoning on expected benefit, trigger explicit reads from the model's state, and accept an answer by an entropy rule that cancels further generation. Over 768 questions from `ProofWriter`, `LogiQA 2.0`, and `ARC-Challenge`, accuracy **rises from 70.96% for direct reading to 84.38%**, beating 512-token terminal reading by 7.29 points for 2.25% more output work, and cutting pipeline time by 46.30% against 1,024-token reading at a cost of 1.17 points.

papers.title: On Global Joint Lower Bounds in Zeroth-Order Nonconvex Optimization
papers.abstract: Recent work has sought to transfer first-order nonconvex optimization guarantees to zeroth-order methods through gradient estimators, typically incurring a factor linear in $d$. \citet{kornowski2024} obtained an $\mathcal{O}(d\delta^{-1}\epsilon^{-3})$ oracle complexity for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization and asked whether its dependence on all three parameters is jointly optimal. Although the dimension dependence and the first-order dependence on $(\delta,\epsilon)$ are separately known to be unavoidable, a matching zeroth-order lower bound has remained open. We answer this question in the unrestricted full-space setting. For smooth stochastic nonconvex optimization, we establish a scalar-oracle lower bound of $\Omega\!\left(dL_0^2\min\{\Delta H,L_0^2\}/\epsilon^4\right)$ assuming a smooth, globally lower-bounded population objective and a second-moment bound on sample Lipschitz constants. A smooth reduction then yields a lower bound for Goldstein stationarity, proving the joint minimax optimality of the dependence on $(d,\delta,\epsilon)$ under explicit high-dimensional and small-accuracy conditions. Crucially, our results allow algorithms to query arbitrary points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, adaptively select sample-function labels, reuse the same sampled function at any number of locations, and output points without spatial restrictions. Thus, unlike lower bounds based on bounded query regions or fresh evaluation noise, our guarantees apply to a fully adaptive, reusable-sample scalar oracle. We also establish a separate noiseless exact-value lower bound against randomized algorithms, and hence also against deterministic methods. Our proof combines a globally defined sequential nonconvex construction with an exact Gaussian scalar channel, multistage random-field estimates, and an antithetic finite-sample realization that preserves information hardness under adaptive reuse.
papers.summary: Zeroth-order methods for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization inherit first-order guarantees at a cost linear in the dimension, and a recent complexity bound left open whether its joint dependence on dimension, smoothing radius, and accuracy is simultaneously optimal. Working in the unrestricted full-space setting, the authors prove a scalar-oracle lower bound for smooth stochastic nonconvex optimization and reduce it to Goldstein stationarity, **establishing joint minimax optimality in all three quantities** under explicit high-dimensional and small-accuracy conditions. The bound holds against a fully adaptive oracle that may query arbitrary points, choose sample-function labels adaptively, and reuse the same sampled function at any number of locations, unlike earlier bounds assuming bounded query regions or fresh evaluation noise, and a separate noiseless exact-value bound covers randomized and deterministic algorithms.

papers.title: HACHIMI-II: From Role-Play to Learner Behavior Modeling for Faithful Student Simulation
papers.abstract: Simulated students let researchers test tutoring systems and teaching strategies before real learners are available, but only if the simulation reproduces where a particular learner succeeds and fails. The common approach asks a large language model to role-play a student, but a role does not model what this learner knows or will do next, so the model's own competence fills the gap. Simulated students perform at a level set by the model, differ little from one another, and seldom make the real learners' errors. We model the learner's behavior and recast student simulation as third-person prediction of the learner's next action. HACHIMI-II builds a student model from the learner's history, infers the learner's state for the current item or tutor turn, and compiles it into a behavior harness that constrains the next action. On three item-response datasets, the Wasserstein-1 distance between simulated and real student ability is 2.4--8.4$\times$ smaller than that of the strongest baseline. On two dialogue datasets, HACHIMI-II reproduces real student errors with the same knowledge type, locus, and mechanism 1.8--5.1$\times$ more often than the strongest baseline, and ablations trace the gains mainly to the explicit learner state. Predicting the learner makes capable models usable as simulated students.
papers.summary: Simulated students help test tutoring systems only if they fail where a particular real learner fails, but the usual approach of asking a language model to role-play a student lets the model's own competence stand in for the learner's, producing near-identical simulants that rarely make authentic errors. `HACHIMI-II` recasts the task as third-person prediction of the learner's next action: it builds a student model from the learner's history, infers their state for the current item or tutor turn, and compiles that state into a behavior harness constraining what the simulant does next. On three item-response datasets the Wasserstein-1 distance between simulated and real student ability is **2.4 to 8.4 times smaller than for the strongest baseline**, and on two dialogue datasets it reproduces real errors with the same knowledge type, locus, and mechanism 1.8 to 5.1 times more often, with ablations crediting the explicit learner state.

papers.title: Measuring and Reducing Unusable Replies of LLM Agents
papers.abstract: People delegate multi-step work to LLM agents and read only the reply that the agent hands back. Current evaluation scores task completion and the faithfulness of reports, and it leaves open whether the requester can understand and use the reply. We call this property reply usability and measure it with a reader model that takes the requester's position and tests whether the reply can be interpreted from what the requester has seen, is in the requester's language and answers the request. Its agreement with the majority of five annotators lies within the range of the individual annotators. Across eight models from seven families, 54% of 480 replies fail, and the best model still fails on 30%. Failed replies mostly point to material the requester has not seen or use labels that the agent coined during its work. Stating explicit requirements for the reply reduces the failure rate from 0.52 to 0.43 together with errors and omissions, and a secondary model that rewrites the reply reduces it to 0.36, which human annotators confirm in a blind comparison. Reply usability can thus be scored alongside task success and improved with one appended message or one call to a secondary model.
papers.summary: Agent evaluation scores task completion and report faithfulness but not whether the person who delegated the work can understand and act on the reply they get back. The authors define reply usability and measure it with a reader model placed in the requester's position, checking that the reply is interpretable from what the requester has seen, in their language, and responsive to the request; its agreement with five annotators sits inside the annotators' own spread. Across eight models from seven families **54% of 480 replies fail, and the best model still fails 30% of the time**, mostly by pointing at material the requester never saw or using labels the agent coined during its work. Stating explicit requirements for the reply lowers the failure rate from 0.52 to 0.43, and a secondary model that rewrites the reply lowers it to 0.36, which human annotators confirm in blind comparison.

papers.title: MCAIR: Monitoring and Correcting Agent Unfaithfulness via Internal Representations
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in completing complex tasks through multi-step reasoning and tool interactions. However, recent studies have revealed that LLM-based agents can exhibit unfaithful behaviors, where their final reports fail to faithfully reflect their actual execution trajectories. Specifically, when agents fail to accomplish tasks through the intended sources or procedures, they may resort to alternative sources or strategies while failing to disclose such deviations, leading users to incorrectly believe that the tasks have been completed according to the original requirements. We refer to this specific form of agent unfaithfulness as Agent Completion Unfaithfulness. Detecting and mitigating agent completion unfaithfulness is critical yet remains largely unexplored. In this work, we propose MCAIR, a runtime monitoring and correction framework that leverages internal representations of LLM-based agents. MCAIR uses multi-step internal representations as inputs to train a risk-aware probe, enabling online detection of potential completion unfaithfulness during execution. Furthermore, MCAIR introduces a risk-guided correction loop that prompts agents to review their execution history and mitigate potential inconsistencies between their execution trajectories and final reports. Additionally, we construct ACUD, a dataset for Agent Completion Unfaithfulness detection that provides step-level execution traces, step-level internal representations, and consistency annotations for training and evaluating runtime detection probes. Experiments demonstrate that MCAIR outperforms LLM-as-a-judge baselines, generalizes across prompts and tasks, and effectively reduces agent completion unfaithfulness.
papers.summary: Agents sometimes finish a task by a route other than the one requested and then report success without disclosing the detour, a failure mode the authors call agent completion unfaithfulness. `MCAIR` trains a risk-aware probe on an agent's multi-step internal representations to flag it online, then runs a risk-guided correction loop prompting the agent to review its execution history and reconcile its report with what it actually did. To support this they build `ACUD`, a dataset with step-level execution traces, step-level internal representations, and consistency annotations. The probe **outperforms LLM-as-a-judge baselines and generalizes across prompts and tasks**, and the correction loop reduces unfaithful completions.

papers.title: Enhancing Latent World Models with Associative Memory
papers.abstract: World models trained via latent dynamics offer a scalable path for embodied planning, yet existing methods suffer from representational collapse, computational overhead, and limited long-horizon capability. We introduce a memory-enhanced latent world model that augments JEPA-style prediction with a content-addressable memory bank. Our approach learns high-level representations directly from observations, operating at multiple temporal scales within a shared latent space, and conditions predictions via adaptive layer normalization. To prevent collapse and ensure effective memory usage, we design two complementary losses that encourage slot diversity and balanced temporal utilization. Experiments on PushT, Tworoom, Reacher, and OGBCube demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance with a lightweight architecture, outperforming conventional latent world models on long-horizon planning tasks.
papers.summary: Latent world models offer a scalable route to embodied planning, but they suffer from representational collapse, heavy compute, and weak long-horizon performance. The authors augment `JEPA`-style prediction with a content-addressable memory bank that operates at multiple temporal scales within a shared latent space, condition predictions through adaptive layer normalization, and add two losses that encourage slot diversity and balanced use of memory over time. **On `PushT`, `Tworoom`, `Reacher`, and `OGBCube`, the lightweight model outperforms conventional latent world models on long-horizon planning tasks.**

papers.title: Beyond Distribution Matching: Selective Margin Preservation for Supervised Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) changes logit margins among non-target tokens at teacher-forced prefixes. Matching a local reference distribution keeps those probabilities and also penalizes margin expansions. We ask whether a soft auxiliary can preserve selected local non-target margin relations without freezing that distribution. We introduce \textbf{Selective Rank-Preserving SFT (SRP-SFT)}, a soft margin target: a hinge on reference-scaled lower bounds for pairs from the reference's top-$K$ non-target tokens, applied at fixed teacher-forced prefixes. The hinge stops once the requested bound is met. We derive the KL cost of violating a margin, characterize the feasible region and its conditional utility, and give a finite-step condition for reducing aggregate violations. In one-epoch experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base and UltraFeedback, this target raises MATH-500 and code-generation scores over CE and LP-SFT at all three training seeds. At seed 1234, MATH-500 pass@1 rises from 49.56\% to 54.56\% and the four-metric code mean rises from 65.91\% to 69.50\% relative to LP-SFT. Ranking controls, held-out cache diagnostics, sensitivity sweeps, and six additional backbones show where these score changes appear.
papers.summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) reshapes the logit margins among non-target tokens at teacher-forced prefixes, and matching a reference distribution preserves them only by also blocking useful margin expansion. Selective Rank-Preserving SFT (`SRP-SFT`) instead adds a soft hinge loss on reference-scaled lower bounds for token pairs drawn from the reference model's top-K non-target tokens, which switches off once the requested margin is met, and the authors derive the KL cost of a margin violation along with a finite-step condition for reducing aggregate violations. **In one-epoch runs on `Qwen3-4B-Base` with `UltraFeedback`, the target raises `MATH-500` pass@1 from 49.56% to 54.56% and the mean of four code metrics from 65.91% to 69.50% relative to `LP-SFT` at one seed**, with gains over cross-entropy and `LP-SFT` at all three seeds and diagnostics on six further backbones.

papers.title: Interlock: From Local Correctness to Task Completion in Long-Horizon Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model agents increasingly undertake long-horizon tasks in complex environments characterized by fragmented evidence, partially completed states, and dependencies across resources and artifacts. Existing agents may satisfy individual requirements while failing to maintain these relationships, producing locally correct but incomplete outcomes. These failures arise because task completion depends on relationships among environmental evidence, consequential decisions, and required effects. To address this completion gap, we propose Interlock, a framework for task synthesis that represents each task as a typed completion graph. Grounding edges connect public evidence to decisions, coupling hyperedges impose joint constraints across components, and realization edges connect decisions to all required downstream effects. Interlock compiles this graph into a resettable workspace, a public request, and an evaluation rubric. A source-coverage review checks whether the original requirements survive generation, while a public-input review checks whether the rubric is supported by the materials available to the solver. An agent-as-judge inspects execution artifacts and runs verification scripts, retaining trajectories judged to satisfy all mandatory requirements. To evaluate training utility, we fine-tune two Qwen3.6 backbones on their own accepted trajectories. Across the two backbones, training improves AutomationBench task pass rates by 4.00-4.50 percentage points, JobBench weighted scores by 3.20-6.64 points, and Harvey LAB criterion pass rates by 3.89-4.16 percentage points. These results demonstrate the training utility of the synthesized experience across external task environments.
papers.summary: Large language model agents on long-horizon tasks often satisfy individual requirements while missing the dependencies among evidence, decisions, and downstream artifacts, yielding locally correct but incomplete results. `Interlock` synthesizes training tasks as typed completion graphs, with grounding edges linking evidence to decisions, coupling hyperedges imposing joint constraints, and realization edges tying decisions to required effects, then compiles each graph into a resettable workspace, a public request, and a rubric that is checked by source-coverage and public-input reviews. An agent-as-judge retains trajectories that satisfy all mandatory requirements, and fine-tuning two `Qwen3.6` backbones on their own accepted trajectories **improves `AutomationBench` pass rates by 4.00 to 4.50 percentage points, `JobBench` weighted scores by 3.20 to 6.64 points, and `Harvey LAB` criterion pass rates by 3.89 to 4.16 points**.

papers.title: Function-Space Temporal Self-Distillation for Policy Optimization
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves reasoning in language models, but scalar outcomes provide coarse supervision over response trajectories. Self-distillation offers denser token-level guidance by comparing an unassisted policy with a feedback-informed self-teacher, yet the teacher evolves with the student, creating unstable targets and motivating additional regularization. We introduce Function-Space Policy Optimization (FSPO), a single-policy framework that combines current privileged adaptation with function-space temporal consolidation. FSPO stores sparse historical next-token distributions as fixed temporal targets, providing temporal separation without maintaining a persistent teacher model. It further introduces privileged disagreement correction to explicitly suppress locally overvalued actions, reliability-adaptive grounding that strengthens reference supervision when self-generated evidence repeatedly fails, and quality and coverage-aware temporal memory that retains verified behaviors and improves privileged demonstrations. Across reasoning and tool-use benchmarks, FSPO achieves the highest average accuracy under a 5-hour training budget, improving over the strongest baseline by approximately 4% points on average while reducing peak memory from about 70 GB to 56 GB on Olmo3-7B-Instruct.
papers.summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) gives only coarse scalar feedback over a whole response, and self-distillation from a feedback-informed self-teacher offers denser token-level signal but produces moving targets as the teacher co-evolves with the student. Function-Space Policy Optimization (`FSPO`) keeps a single policy and stores sparse historical next-token distributions as fixed temporal targets, adding privileged disagreement correction to suppress locally overvalued actions, reliability-adaptive grounding that leans on reference supervision when self-generated evidence repeatedly fails, and a quality- and coverage-aware temporal memory. **Under a 5-hour training budget on `Olmo3-7B-Instruct`, `FSPO` reaches the highest average accuracy across reasoning and tool-use benchmarks, about 4 percentage points above the strongest baseline, while cutting peak memory from roughly 70 GB to 56 GB.**

papers.title: Annealed L\'{e}vy Diffusion via Gaussian Surrogate Reverse Dynamics
papers.abstract: Gaussian diffusion models offer a practical framework for generative modeling. Denoising L\'{e}vy Probabilistic Models (DLPM) introduce heavy-tailed perturbations with a fixed tail index throughout denoising. We introduce Annealed L\'{e}vy Diffusion (ALD). ALD varies the stability index $\alpha(t)$ to combine heavy-tailed exploration with Gaussian refinement. Our marginal-first formulation represents stable noise as a scalar Gaussian scale mixture. This formulation enables standard Gaussian noise-prediction training with one additional scale input. We study two sampling processes. ALD-renoise estimates the clean sample and injects fresh marginal noise. ALD-posterior preserves dependence between successive states through an accumulated conditional variance and a Gaussian bridge update. Both samplers reuse the same trained predictor with different scalar inputs. We evaluate ALD on four 2D benchmarks and an imbalanced nine-mode mixture. We also examine training efficiency and the effects of prediction perturbations on clipped Holtsmark data. Additional experiments evaluate MNIST and CelebA64 generation and CIFAR-10LT augmentation. ALD preserves local geometry on the evaluated light-tailed and manifold-structured targets.
papers.summary: Denoising Lévy Probabilistic Models (`DLPM`) inject heavy-tailed noise with one fixed tail index throughout denoising, while Gaussian diffusion offers simpler training and practical refinement. Annealed Lévy Diffusion (`ALD`) varies the stability index over time to combine heavy-tailed exploration with Gaussian refinement, representing stable noise as a scalar Gaussian scale mixture so that an ordinary Gaussian noise-prediction network can be trained with a single extra scale input. Two samplers share that one predictor: `ALD-renoise` re-estimates the clean sample and injects fresh marginal noise, while `ALD-posterior` keeps dependence between successive states through an accumulated conditional variance and a Gaussian bridge update. **Across four 2D benchmarks, an imbalanced nine-mode mixture, clipped Holtsmark data, `MNIST`, `CelebA64`, and `CIFAR-10LT` augmentation, `ALD` preserves local geometry on light-tailed and manifold-structured targets.**

papers.title: Share the Symbol, Not the Vector: Training-Free Fact Communication Across Language Models
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems allow language models to solve tasks collaboratively by sharing complementary information. These systems typically communicate through text, while recent approaches also explore exchanging internal model states. However, sharing these states across architectures often requires learned translators or assumptions about model compatibility. We introduce SYNC (Symbol-Indexed Neural Communication), a word-indexed interface that connects heterogeneous models without fine-tuning or a learned translator. From descriptions only it can see, the sender selects words from a shared list and sends their indices for each object, without seeing the questions. The receiver writes the described facts into its hidden states using its own word directions, vectors fitted once from its activations. We test selective use by swapping one attribute between two objects and requiring correct answers about both changed and unchanged attributes before and after the swap, four answers in total. We choose an early write layer on four development receivers and then fix it. With three different senders and nine newer receivers from five families, four-answer success on new scenes reaches 72.0-98.3%, up to 96 percentage points above middle-layer writing, and the two largest receivers match plain text. A task-free probe predicted in advance which depths each new receiver can use (45 of 45 cases). Without retuning, messages listing every fact keep 89.6-100% success under new layouts, and sender messages reach 23.9-64.0% on a landmark task with multi-token symbols, below text but from 0% without a message. These results show that shared word indices and receiver-local directions can support selective fact use across model families without additional training.
papers.summary: Multi-agent language model systems usually exchange information as text, and attempts to share internal states across architectures typically need learned translators or compatibility assumptions. `SYNC` (Symbol-Indexed Neural Communication) has the sender, which sees only object descriptions and not the questions, pick words from a shared list and transmit their indices, while the receiver writes the described facts into its own hidden states at an early layer using word directions fitted once from its activations, with no fine-tuning anywhere. **With three senders and nine receivers from five model families, success on a four-answer attribute-swap test reaches 72.0 to 98.3% on new scenes, up to 96 percentage points above middle-layer writing, and the two largest receivers match plain text.** A task-free probe predicted usable depths for all 45 new receiver cases, messages listing every fact retain 89.6 to 100% success under new layouts, and a landmark task with multi-token symbols reaches 23.9 to 64.0%, below text but up from 0% with no message.

papers.title: ReGRA: Residual-Gradient Adaptation for Complementary Low-Rank Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning by learning low-rank weight updates. Increasing rank expands adaptation capacity, but does not guarantee that all learned directions improve downstream performance. In a diagnostic experiment with rank-16 LoRA, we show that retaining only the top singular components achieves the best performance, whereas adding further components degrades it. Motivated by this, we propose Residual-Gradient Adaptation (ReGRA), a two-stage method for making more effective use of a fixed rank budget. After the first stage, ReGRA estimates task gradients on a calibration set and removes their projections onto the two-sided subspace induced by the first-stage update. It then aggregates the residual-gradient directions to initialize a second-stage adapter without changing the first-stage update. An orthogonality regularizer encourages the two updates to capture complementary directions. Both updates can be merged into the pretrained weights, incurring no additional inference overhead. Across diverse benchmark sets, ReGRA achieves stronger performance than alternatives with the same total rank and even matches LoRA adapters with twice the rank. Ablation studies and further analysis support the contribution of its core design choices. Code is available at https://github.com/Fanyao-Li/ReGRA.
papers.summary: Raising the rank of low-rank adaptation (LoRA) expands capacity, but a diagnostic with rank-16 `LoRA` shows that keeping only the top singular components of the learned update performs best and adding the rest hurts. Residual-Gradient Adaptation (`ReGRA`) trains a first-stage adapter, estimates task gradients on a calibration set, removes their projections onto the two-sided subspace of the first-stage update, and uses the residual directions to initialize a second-stage adapter, with an orthogonality regularizer pushing the two updates toward complementary directions. Both updates merge into the pretrained weights with no inference overhead, and **across diverse benchmark sets `ReGRA` beats alternatives at the same total rank and matches `LoRA` adapters with twice the rank**.

papers.title: BANGLAPLAN: A Benchmark for Constraint-Based Planning and Decision-Making in Bangla
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly help users arrange appointments, plan journeys, and allocate limited resources. These tasks require models to satisfy constraints on time, cost, capacity, and order, or determine that no feasible solution exists. Bangla is the world's seventh most widely spoken language, and existing benchmarks cover many language and reasoning tasks. However, benchmarks for evaluating planning and decision-making in Bangla under explicit constraints remain lacking. We introduce BANGLAPLAN, a benchmark of 1,000 problems across ten task families grounded in everyday life and institutions in Bangladesh. It includes feasible and infeasible problems in four language registers: everyday, formal, colloquial, and Bangla--English mixed. Answers cover eight structured types, including schedules, routes, allocations, and ordered steps, in a common JSON format. We construct the benchmark through language-model-assisted drafting and independent human validation. We evaluate 11 open-weight and proprietary model configurations using exact match, separately reporting feasible-case accuracy, infeasibility detection, and format errors. We find a large performance gap: GPT-6.1 Sol achieves 98.7% accuracy and Qwen3.5-27B with thinking reaches 80.3%, while direct-answer configurations score at most 30.9%. Seven of eleven configurations perform below the always-``infeasible'' baseline. Our findings also suggest that harder problems primarily reduce plan-construction accuracy, while infeasibility detection remains more robust. BANGLAPLAN provides a reproducible basis for evaluating planning and decision-making in Bangla. BANGLAPLAN is available at: https://github.com/mrayhanulmasud/banglaplan.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly asked to schedule, route, and allocate under constraints on time, cost, capacity, and order, yet no benchmark tests this in Bangla, the seventh most widely spoken language. `BANGLAPLAN` contains 1,000 problems across ten task families rooted in everyday life and institutions in Bangladesh, spanning feasible and infeasible cases in everyday, formal, colloquial, and Bangla-English mixed registers, with eight structured answer types in a shared JSON format, drafted with model assistance and validated by humans. **Across 11 open-weight and proprietary configurations scored by exact match, `GPT-6.1 Sol` reaches 98.7% and `Qwen3.5-27B` with thinking 80.3%, while direct-answer configurations top out at 30.9% and seven of eleven fall below an always-infeasible baseline.** Harder problems mainly degrade plan construction, while infeasibility detection stays comparatively robust.

papers.title: RouteWeaver: Weaving Mode Selection and Execution into Unified LLM Routing
papers.abstract: LLM routing dynamically selects and coordinates heterogeneous language models across diverse tasks. However, existing approaches are largely built around a predefined execution paradigm, such as single-round, multi-round, or agentic routing, which fixes how model calls are organized and limits adaptation to different query needs. We propose RouteWeaver, a unified routing framework that integrates these routing modes within a single LLM policy, jointly learning which mode to use and how to select models within that mode. To jointly optimize mode selection and within-mode execution, we develop COMET-GRPO (COordinated Mode-Execution Training), which decouples the trajectory-level advantage into separate signals for mode selection and within-mode execution, enabling more targeted credit assignment to each decision level. We further introduce progressive exploration, which gradually shifts training from externally assigned modes to autonomous selection, so that the router first learns how to execute each mode before deciding when to use it. We evaluate RouteWeaver across mathematics, coding, knowledge, logical reasoning, and factual recall. RouteWeaver achieves an average accuracy of 61.4%, an 11.03% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, and outperforms all compared baselines in each of the five domains. Ablations show that both COMET-GRPO and progressive exploration are important for adaptive routing; without progressive exploration, the routing policy collapses entirely to single-round execution.
papers.summary: Existing LLM routers commit to one execution paradigm, such as single-round, multi-round, or agentic routing, which fixes how model calls are organized regardless of the query. `RouteWeaver` folds these modes into a single learned policy that decides both which mode to use and which models to call within it, trained with COordinated Mode-Execution Training (`COMET-GRPO`), which splits the trajectory-level advantage into separate credit signals for mode selection and within-mode execution, plus a progressive exploration schedule that moves from externally assigned modes to autonomous selection. **Across mathematics, coding, knowledge, logical reasoning, and factual recall, it averages 61.4% accuracy, an 11.03% relative gain over the strongest baseline, and leads in every domain.** Without progressive exploration the routing policy collapses entirely to single-round execution.

papers.title: Beyond State Capacity: Why Retrieval Breaks in Mamba
papers.abstract: Mamba models underperform Transformers on in-context retrieval. This gap is usually attributed to Mamba's fixed-size recurrent state, which loses information as the context grows. We challenge this assumption by focusing on query-first retrieval, a setup in which the query precedes the context and state capacity should not be the binding constraint. We show that even in this setting Mamba lags substantially behind Transformers, despite its selection mechanism, which was designed to distinguish relevant content from distractors. We then demonstrate that the Mamba selection gates have sufficient control over the state updates to influence the model output: intervening on specific gates alone can swing accuracy between extremes. However, as gates are input-dependent, they require the incoming token's representation to encode its relevance to the query. We therefore probe token representations across layers, and find that the relevance signal emerges only gradually with model depth, and that the gates begin to reflect it only several layers deeper. Crucially, we find that gates in retrieval-critical layers are not yet aligned with relevance. The selection mechanism is thus expressive enough to solve the task, but it commonly operates on a relevance signal that has not yet arrived. Mamba's retrieval bottleneck therefore extends beyond state capacity: even when capacity is sufficient, the delayed emergence of relevance information across depth often prevents successful retrieval.
papers.summary: The retrieval gap between `Mamba` and Transformers is usually blamed on `Mamba`'s fixed-size recurrent state, so the authors test query-first retrieval, where the query precedes the context and state capacity should not be the binding constraint. `Mamba` still lags substantially, even though intervening on individual selection gates can swing accuracy between extremes, which shows the gates have enough control over state updates to solve the task. Probing token representations across layers reveals that the query-relevance signal emerges only gradually with depth and that the gates reflect it only several layers later, so **gates in retrieval-critical layers are not yet aligned with relevance at the point where they are needed**. The bottleneck therefore extends beyond capacity to the delayed arrival of relevance information across depth.

papers.title: New Model, Old Habits: Behavior Transfer under Model Swapping in Multi-Session LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Multi-session agents can switch between LLMs to balance performance and inference cost. Such switches require transferring a history for continuity, yet their effects on the recipient remain underexplored. Through controlled experiments with multi-session tasks, we uncover behavior transfer: recipients tend to adopt reasoning and action patterns from the models that generated their histories. This effect is most evident with raw-history transfer but is substantially reduced by summarization. Based on these findings, we propose Direction- and Authorship-aware Summarization of History (DASH) that preserves stronger-model behavior while minimizing weak-to-strong transfer via summarization. Experiments with repeated swaps show that DASH outperforms raw-history transfer and naive summarization baselines. These results suggest that effective multi-model orchestration requires considering not only which model to use, but also which behavioral patterns to carry forward.
papers.summary: Multi-session agents that swap between LLMs to balance cost and quality must hand over a conversation history, and controlled experiments show the recipient model tends to adopt the reasoning and action patterns of whichever model wrote that history. **This behavior transfer is strongest with raw-history handoff and is substantially reduced by summarization.** Direction- and Authorship-aware Summarization of History (`DASH`) exploits this by summarizing so as to retain stronger-model behavior while minimizing weak-to-strong transfer, and under repeated swaps it outperforms both raw-history transfer and naive summarization baselines.

papers.title: Learning Individual Scientific Taste with Privileged Hindsight Distillation
papers.abstract: Scientific taste shapes which research directions researchers pursue, and it varies across individuals. Existing work evaluates research directions along multiple evaluation criteria or models scientific taste using community feedback signals such as citations and reviews, but neither directly captures how individuals translate assessments under the same criteria into different preferences. We model scientific taste as a researcher-specific mapping from criterion-level assessments in a shared, evidence-grounded evaluation space with proposal-visible evidence, to relative preferences. A population-level mapping learned from retrospective supervision provides a cold start when individual feedback is scarce. We introduce Privileged Hindsight Distillation (PHD), which uses later-emerging scientific evidence during training to improve proposal-time criterion assessment and the population mapping, while exposing only proposal-visible information at inference. We evaluate our approach primarily in quantum research, where structured public reviews are largely unavailable, and use pairwise proposal comparison as a direct interface for observing individual taste. With only 15 comparisons per researcher, our method captures sharply different tastes, including opposing preferences over the same research-direction pairs when they trade off across evaluation criteria. In an interactive study, personalized rankings also surface proposals associated with greater subsequent user engagement, connecting learned taste to downstream research exploration.
papers.summary: Which research directions a scientist pursues reflects individual taste, yet prior work either scores proposals on shared criteria or models taste from community signals like citations, neither of which captures how individuals turn the same assessments into different preferences. The authors model taste as a researcher-specific mapping from criterion-level assessments, grounded in proposal-visible evidence, to relative preferences, bootstrapped from a population-level mapping learned from retrospective supervision, and introduce Privileged Hindsight Distillation (`PHD`), which uses later-emerging evidence during training to sharpen proposal-time assessments while exposing only proposal-visible information at inference. **In quantum research, where public reviews are scarce, 15 pairwise comparisons per researcher suffice to recover sharply different and even opposing preferences over the same proposal pairs**, and an interactive study links the personalized rankings to greater subsequent user engagement.

papers.title: Articulation Upper Bounds for Language Models
papers.abstract: Language captures only a subset of the perceptions, intuitions and intents that form meaning between speakers. What, then, are the limits of language? We take steps towards measuring this in LLMs as follows: for a set of concepts, we measure how well each concept can be transmitted between two LLMs as their capabilities scale. This requires novel measurement tools: (1) optimal messages: we introduce a prompt optimization algorithm that beats existing algorithms by up to 14% on benchmarks and accurately estimates prompt upper bounds. (2) A transmission measure: the sender is asked to label text; the receiver then tries to recover the sender's prompt, and recovery is measured; we find this correlates strongly with human label error. With these measures, we use observational scaling laws to study how transmissibility of a concept, conveyed with optimal messages, increases as transmitter and receiver capacity grows: does it asymptote below or above a threshold? Measuring 1.2k concepts in eight domains, we find concepts that (a) can be fully articulated; these concepts usually depend on local patterns, e.g. "joke ends with surprise"; (b) might be articulated by future, stronger models; these rely on whole-text structural patterns, e.g. "story's worldbuilding coherence"; (c) concepts that face articulability limits; these concepts' meaning, we find, is tied to identity and social-group awareness, e.g. "comic voice". Interesting, these same concepts are not all challenging for humans: humans have moderate-to-high levels of agreement in 76% of concepts that LLMs struggle with; articulation limits, we find, are executor relative. Finally, we characterize the nature of improvement in each case: while recoverable concepts can be articulated through definitions and explanations, irrecoverable concepts cannot be transmitted, even with examples, and might require novel learning mechanisms.
papers.summary: Language conveys only part of what speakers mean, and the authors ask how far LLMs can push that limit by measuring how well concepts transmit from one model to another as capability scales. They build two tools: a prompt optimization algorithm that beats existing methods by up to 14% on benchmarks and estimates prompt upper bounds, and a transmission measure in which a sender labels text, a receiver tries to recover the sender's prompt, and recovery is scored, which correlates strongly with human label error. **Across 1.2k concepts in eight domains, observational scaling laws separate three groups: concepts that are fully articulable, which usually depend on local patterns like a joke ending in surprise; concepts stronger future models might articulate, which rely on whole-text structure such as worldbuilding coherence; and concepts facing hard limits, whose meaning is tied to identity and social-group awareness, such as comic voice.** Humans agree moderately to highly on 76% of the concepts LLMs struggle with, and the hardest concepts resist transmission even with examples, suggesting novel learning mechanisms would be needed.

papers.title: Recognizing Dialogue Ambiguity via Candidate Set Visual Grounding
papers.abstract: Interpreting an ambiguous utterance in real-world interactions often requires context beyond a single utterance. When the utterance refers to objects in a visual scene, it is necessary to maintain and update the set of plausible referents as context accumulates, without assuming that the available information identifies a unique object. However, prior work on interactive visual grounding, which localizes objects referred to by linguistic expressions, has focused on identifying a unique object once sufficient dialogue context becomes available. To address this gap, we propose Candidate Set Visual Grounding (CSVG), a task for estimating the set of objects consistent with the given dialogue context. We further introduce CandVG, a benchmark that evaluates how the candidate set changes across dialogue turns. Our evaluation of vision-language models shows that stronger visual grounding capability does not necessarily yield better CSVG performance. In particular, models have difficulty predicting the complete candidate set, owing to challenges in candidate generation and premature commitment to a small set of candidates in early turns. Nevertheless, we find that this limitation can be partially mitigated in the evaluated large-scale models using instructions designed for CSVG.
papers.summary: When an utterance refers to objects in a scene, interpreting it under ambiguity means maintaining a set of plausible referents as dialogue unfolds, but prior interactive visual grounding work assumes a unique target once enough context arrives. Candidate Set Visual Grounding (`CSVG`) instead asks a model to estimate the full set of objects consistent with the dialogue so far, and the `CandVG` benchmark tracks how that set should change across turns. **Evaluating vision-language models shows that stronger standard grounding does not translate into better candidate-set prediction**, with failures traced to weak candidate generation and premature commitment to a few candidates in early turns, though task-specific instructions partially mitigate this in the larger models.

papers.title: TIMERSI: Towards Self-Improved Agentic Deployment for Time-Series Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Time-series foundation models provide strong zero-shot forecast, but deployment for real- world applications still requires task-specific designs for model inputs and outputs. Direct inference can leave domain knowledge and re- curring forecast errors unaddressed, while tai- lored pipelines require substantial human ex- pertise and effort. We introduce TIMERSI, a self-improving agentic deployment system around frozen forecasting models. A cod- ing agent translates task descriptions into ex- ecutable pipeline changes. It tests each re- vision on historical forecasting windows and uses observed errors to guide subsequent re- visions. During deployment, an adaptive se- lector chooses among the resulting pipelines using completed forecasts under similar con- ditions. Across 198 tasks on TIME and FEV- bench, TIMERSI outperforms all submissions on six point and probabilistic forecasting met- rics. Controlled comparisons support the value of feedback-guided revision over non-iterative pipeline search. Further experiments verify the generalization with different coding agents and forecasting models.
papers.summary: Time-series foundation models forecast well zero-shot, but real deployments still need task-specific input and output handling, and hand-built pipelines demand expert effort while direct inference ignores domain knowledge and recurring errors. `TIMERSI` wraps a frozen forecaster in a self-improving loop: a coding agent translates the task description into executable pipeline changes, tests each revision on historical forecasting windows, and uses the observed errors to guide the next revision, while an adaptive selector picks among the resulting pipelines at deployment time based on completed forecasts under similar conditions. **Across 198 tasks on `TIME` and `FEV-bench`, it outperforms all submissions on six point and probabilistic forecasting metrics**, controlled comparisons favor feedback-guided revision over non-iterative pipeline search, and the gains hold across different coding agents and forecasting models.

papers.title: Mitigating Video Hallucinations via Attention-Guided Representation Perturbation
papers.abstract: Video large language models (Video LLMs) often generate responses unsupported by the input video. Contrastive decoding (CD) can mitigate these hallucinations, but its effectiveness depends on how the negative branch weakens visual evidence. Existing methods rely on predefined perturbations or masking guided by question reconstruction, offering limited control over the model's visual reliance during answer generation. We introduce Attention-guided Representation Perturbation for Contrastive Decoding (ARP-CD), a training-free framework for constructing contrastive negatives directly in representation space. ARP-CD uses the attention mass assigned to visual tokens at the answer-prediction position to guide bounded gradient updates of the language model's input visual hidden states. These updates reduce visual attention and produce a negative input, whose predictions are contrasted with those of the original branch throughout generation. Experiments across four Video LLMs and four benchmarks show that ARP-CD outperforms representative training-free baselines in most model--benchmark settings, reducing hallucinations while improving general video understanding. Further analyses show that attention-guided perturbation directions improve negative quality and that the resulting negatives provide effective contrastive references for correcting the original predictions.
papers.summary: Video large language models (Video LLMs) often describe things absent from the input video, and contrastive decoding (CD) helps only to the extent that its negative branch genuinely weakens visual evidence, which predefined perturbations or question-reconstruction masking control poorly. Attention-guided Representation Perturbation for Contrastive Decoding (`ARP-CD`) is training-free: it uses the attention mass that the answer-prediction position places on visual tokens to drive bounded gradient updates of the visual hidden states fed to the language model, lowering visual attention to form a negative input whose predictions are contrasted with the original branch throughout generation. **Across four Video LLMs and four benchmarks, `ARP-CD` beats representative training-free baselines in most model-benchmark settings, reducing hallucinations while also improving general video understanding.**

papers.title: What Happens to the Goal? Distinct Failures of Policy Alignment in Goal Misgeneralization
papers.abstract: Goal misgeneralization is a common failure mode in which an agent behaves competently out of distribution but does not pursue the intended goal. However, we still have a weak understanding of what happens to the intended goal in misgeneralizing agents. Across three Procgen environments and five robot tasks, we find three distinct forms of policy-goal misalignment: (1) functional target substitution, where behavior follows an alternative goal, (2) a policy shortcut, where behavior follows a learned action strategy, and (3) cue competition between intended and proxy goal cues. We distinguish these regimes by tracing where goal information remains available internally, how strongly it influences the policy, and what role it plays in action selection, and find that the goal is lost at different depths. Where the goal reaches the decision, as in cue competition, steering redirects the policy to the goal's location, raising intended-goal reach from 16.0% to 95.3%. Where it reaches the policy but not the decision, only new downstream wiring recovers goal reach, from 31.6% to 84.3% in the environment with the action shortcut. Where it is inert, neither works. Our results show that goal misgeneralization is not a single failure of goal representation, but distinct failures of policy alignment at different depths, tightly connected to which recovery works.
papers.summary: Goal misgeneralization, where an agent acts competently out of distribution but pursues the wrong goal, is poorly understood at the level of what happens to the intended goal inside the policy. Across three `Procgen` environments and five robot tasks, the authors trace where goal information remains available internally, how strongly it drives the policy, and what role it plays in action selection, and find three distinct regimes: functional target substitution, where behavior follows an alternative goal; a policy shortcut, where behavior follows a learned action strategy; and cue competition between intended and proxy cues. **Which recovery works depends on the regime: steering raises intended-goal reach from 16.0% to 95.3% under cue competition, only new downstream wiring recovers it, from 31.6% to 84.3%, when the goal reaches the policy but not the decision, and neither works when the goal is inert.**

papers.title: MakSafe: A Spatiotemporal Semantic Framework for Formal Specification and Compliance Checking of Road Vehicle Safety Rules
papers.abstract: Scenario-based validation is essential for automated road vehicles but cannot cover the full variability of openworld traffic. We present MakSafe, a formal spatiotemporal framework for specifying and checking road vehicle safety rules through semantic zones, action-based forecasting, and trace-tree reasoning, avoiding uniform time discretization. We formalize the road network, vehicle states, and occupancy zones, then build executable rules for front-vehicle identification and timeto-collision (TTC) verification. The evaluation combines a tracedependent case study with a scalability benchmark over traffic density (N ), horizon (H), and branch factor (B). MakSafe yields branch-specific verdicts, deriving safe and unsafe outcomes from the same initial scene, and re-evaluates a scenario after a control update. A single rule check stays well below a millisecond across the reported sweep, and longer horizons slow the TTC check.
papers.summary: Scenario-based validation cannot cover the open-world variability that automated road vehicles face. `MakSafe` is a formal spatiotemporal framework that specifies and checks road safety rules using semantic occupancy zones, action-based forecasting, and trace-tree reasoning rather than uniform time discretization, formalizing the road network and vehicle states and building executable rules for front-vehicle identification and time-to-collision (TTC) verification. **It yields branch-specific verdicts, deriving safe and unsafe outcomes from the same initial scene, and a single rule check stays well below a millisecond across a scalability sweep over traffic density, horizon, and branch factor**, though longer horizons slow the TTC check.

papers.title: ProtModernBERT: Compute-Efficient Protein Language Modeling
papers.abstract: Large protein language models provide a powerful framework for learning sequence-function relationships and guiding experimental design. However, architectural improvements are underexplored, especially in low-compute regimes of relevance for resource-constrained research laboratories. We show that the training cost for encoder-only transformer architectures can be reduced by leveraging modern architectural refinements, offering an encouraging performance / compute-efficiency trade-off. We introduce ProtModernBERT, a modernized BERT-style model pre-trained on amino acid sequences, and compare it with ProtBert, Amplify, and ESM2 across a set of supervised structural tasks -encompassing secondary structure prediction, disorder prediction, and subcellular localization- and ProteinGym's zero-shot functional benchmark. We find that ProtModernBERT matches or closely tracks the performance of Amplify-120M and ProtBert with up to 80-90\% reduction in pre-training FLOPs, and narrows the gap to ESM2 when controlling for pre-training. Our analysis using a cluster-based validation protocol for hyperparameter selection and randomly initialized models disentangles the contributions of architecture and data, showing that modern components provide stronger inductive biases that are more consequential than parameter count in low-compute regimes.
papers.summary: Large protein language models are expensive to pretrain, and architectural improvements have been underexplored in the low-compute regimes that matter for resource-constrained labs. `ProtModernBERT` applies modern encoder refinements to a BERT-style model pretrained on amino acid sequences and is compared with `ProtBert`, `Amplify`, and `ESM2` on secondary structure, disorder, and subcellular localization prediction as well as the zero-shot functional benchmark `ProteinGym`. **It matches or closely tracks `Amplify-120M` and `ProtBert` with up to an 80 to 90% reduction in pretraining FLOPs** and narrows the gap to `ESM2` when pretraining is controlled, and analysis with cluster-based validation and randomly initialized models indicates that modern architectural components matter more than parameter count at low compute.

papers.title: Does the Linguistic Register of Thinking Matter? Wenyan as a Compact Reasoning Register for Chinese LLMs
papers.abstract: Visible reasoning traces of Chinese reasoning-oriented LLMs are typically written in modern vernacular Chinese, which may be verbose under limited decoding budgets. We ask whether the linguistic register of reasoning can be used to improve efficiency. We propose Wenyan Thinking, which emits intermediate reasoning in Classical Chinese (wenyanwen) while retaining a short direct-answer output. Starting from modern-Chinese reasoning traces, we rewrite only the reasoning field into wenyan and fine-tune Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 on the rewritten supervision. To distinguish register shift from generic compression, we construct a compact modern-Chinese control using the same source data, teacher family, base model, and SFT recipe. Across budget-sensitive evaluations on MMLU-ProX-Lite-ZH, CEVAL, and AGIEval-CN, Wenyan Thinking substantially reduces reasoning length and missing-answer rates under constrained decoding. Compact rewriting explains much of the efficiency gain, while wenyan consistently outperforms the compact modern-Chinese control on the primary benchmark and remains competitive across the additional benchmarks. These results identify linguistic register as a practical design axis for efficient visible reasoning in Chinese LLMs.
papers.summary: Reasoning traces from Chinese reasoning-oriented LLMs are written in modern vernacular Chinese, which can be verbose when the decoding budget is tight. `Wenyan Thinking` rewrites only the reasoning field of existing traces into Classical Chinese (wenyanwen) while keeping a short direct answer, fine-tunes `Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507` on the result, and controls for generic compression with a compact modern-Chinese variant built from the same data, teacher family, base model, and recipe. **On `MMLU-ProX-Lite-ZH`, `CEVAL`, and `AGIEval-CN` under constrained decoding, it substantially shortens reasoning and lowers missing-answer rates, and while compact rewriting explains much of the gain, wenyan consistently beats the compact modern-Chinese control on the primary benchmark** and stays competitive on the others.

papers.title: Discriminative Score Function: Turning Pretrained Models into Functional Generative Priors
papers.abstract: Discriminative models are trained with task-specific objectives such as classification, detection, or representation learning, yet their practical utility depends on generalizing beyond the training task to unseen samples from the same domain. This suggests that a discriminative model may retain an implicit trace of the data manifold beyond its task labels. We ask whether this trace can be exposed as a generative signal without task-specific guidance. We introduce the Discriminative Score Function (DSF), which extracts an image-space generative field from the loss-gradient geometry of a pretrained discriminative model. DSF provides a training-free update rule that moves images toward model-consistent visual regions without retraining or task-specific targets. We apply DSF to diverse pretrained discriminative models, including ResNet classifiers, DETR detectors, and DINOv2 ViT encoders. DSF generates unconditional images from noise and supports conditional guidance, editing, inpainting, and explanation through the same field. DSF-generated samples also provide effective zero-shot quantization calibration when real images or labels are unavailable, preserving feature geometry better than data-free calibration baselines. These results show that discriminative training leaves a generative functional signal for synthesis and calibration. Project page: https://junhoo.me/dsf.
papers.summary: Discriminative models such as classifiers and detectors are trained for narrow tasks, yet they generalize to unseen samples from the same domain, which suggests they retain an implicit trace of the data manifold. The Discriminative Score Function (`DSF`) extracts an image-space generative field from the loss-gradient geometry of a pretrained discriminative model, giving a training-free update rule that pushes images toward model-consistent regions without retraining or task-specific targets. Applied to `ResNet` classifiers, `DETR` detectors, and `DINOv2` ViT encoders, the same field supports **unconditional image generation from noise** as well as conditional guidance, editing, inpainting, and explanation, and `DSF`-generated samples serve as zero-shot quantization calibration data that preserves feature geometry better than data-free baselines.

papers.title: Beyond Reachability: A Relation-Semantic Reasoning Framework for Biomedical Multi-hop QA
papers.abstract: Biomedical multi-hop reasoning over knowledge graphs requires identifying a semantically valid relation sequence that supports the answer. Existing methods can retrieve correct answers, yet often rank them poorly within a large pool of seemingly relevant candidates. Even when a correct answer is retrieved, its associated evidence and reasoning path may fail to support the relation composition required by the question. We term this disconnect between answer reachability and evidential validity the reachable-but-invalid problem. We present ReSemReason, which shares a question-induced distribution over typed, directed relation schemas between candidate discovery and evidence selection. Schema compatibility guides graph search; ReSemAttn then uses relation-conditioned key/value projections and an uncertainty-weighted path prior to attend to candidate-specific evidence. A separate absolute-support score complements normalized attention when all retrieved paths are weak. The reported experiments on BioHopR, PrimeKGQA, and MedReason show improvements in answer ranking and answer-set quality. Path-discrimination analyses examine the distinction between endpoint correctness and evidential support. We also specify matched controls for search, attention, and schema uncertainty.
papers.summary: Multi-hop question answering over biomedical knowledge graphs often retrieves the right answer but ranks it poorly, and the supporting evidence path may not match the relation composition the question demands, a gap the authors call the reachable-but-invalid problem. `ReSemReason` shares a question-induced distribution over typed, directed relation schemas between candidate discovery and evidence selection: schema compatibility steers graph search, while a `ReSemAttn` module uses relation-conditioned key/value projections and an uncertainty-weighted path prior to attend to candidate-specific evidence, backed by an absolute-support score for cases where every retrieved path is weak. Experiments on `BioHopR`, `PrimeKGQA`, and `MedReason` report **improved answer ranking and answer-set quality**, with path-discrimination analyses separating endpoint correctness from evidential support.

papers.title: Qwen-MT-Lumen at WMT2026: Instruction-Specialized Translation via Quality-Aware Training and On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: We present Lumen, The open-source model is available at, our submission to the WMT 2026 General Machine Translation Shared Task. We focus on instruction-specialized translation, where systems must produce accurate translations while satisfying fine-grained requirements on style, terminology, and structured output. Lumen follows a four-stage pipeline. First, continued pre-training and supervised fine-tuning jointly strengthen multilingual translation competence and the ability to follow translation-specific instructions, such as terminology, style, and format constraints. Second, we extend the originally offline M^{2}PO preference-optimization framework into an online preference-optimization stage: the current policy samples candidate translations, an LLM judge assigns continuous direct-assessment scores, and the resulting multi-pair preferences are used to update the model. Third, on-policy distillation transfers stronger translation-instruction-following behavior from a larger teacher model to the Qwen3-14B student, improving translation-instruction adherence while retaining a 14B primary translation backbone. Finally, structure-aware inference and postprocessing preserve required formats, while selective repair addresses clear structural or decoding failures before submission. We participate in 23 translation directions. Under an absolute 1--5 LLM-judge rubric that evaluates translation-instruction following and translation quality separately, Lumen reaches an overall mean score of 4.60. Despite using a 14B translation backbone, it achieves performance comparable to leading proprietary systems in both translation quality and translation-instruction following.
papers.summary: Instruction-specialized machine translation requires systems to translate accurately while honoring fine-grained constraints on terminology, style, and output structure. `Lumen`, a submission to the WMT 2026 General Machine Translation task, follows a four-stage pipeline: continued pre-training and supervised fine-tuning for multilingual translation and instruction following, an online extension of the `M2PO` preference-optimization framework in which an LLM judge scores sampled candidates to form multi-pair preferences, on-policy distillation from a larger teacher into a `Qwen3-14B` student, and structure-aware inference with selective repair of structural or decoding failures. Across 23 translation directions, the system reaches an **overall mean score of 4.60 on a 1-5 LLM-judge rubric** and is reported as comparable to leading proprietary systems in both translation quality and instruction adherence despite its 14B backbone.

papers.title: CAST: History-Adaptive Spectral Clipping for LLM Pretraining
papers.abstract: Soft spectral clipping (SSC) reduces gradient singular values, but its effect depends on the gradient scale and clipping threshold. We introduce CAST (Clipping with Adaptive Scales and Thresholds), a history-adaptive extension of SSC. AdamW's previous second moment sets row and column scales. An exponential moving average of the clipped output's estimated spectral norm sets each matrix's threshold. CAST restores the original coordinates before the AdamW update. We train a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 19.08B total parameters for 83.89B tokens. CAST achieves lower training and mean validation losses than nine gradient-processing baselines, with the fewest relative gradient spikes. It reaches the best baseline's final smoothed training loss in 7.2\% fewer steps.
papers.summary: Soft spectral clipping (SSC) shrinks the singular values of gradient matrices during training, but its effect depends on gradient scale and on the clipping threshold. Clipping with Adaptive Scales and Thresholds (`CAST`) makes both history-adaptive: `AdamW`'s previous second-moment estimate sets per-row and per-column scales, an exponential moving average of the clipped output's estimated spectral norm sets each matrix's threshold, and the original coordinates are restored before the `AdamW` update. Training a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 19.08B total parameters on 83.89B tokens, `CAST` achieves lower training and validation losses than nine gradient-processing baselines with the fewest relative gradient spikes, and **reaches the best baseline's final smoothed training loss in 7.2% fewer steps**.

papers.title: PRISMATIC : Prescription Risk Inspection System for Multi-Agent Treatment Interaction in Clinical Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Medical prescribing errors for multimorbid patients, who require complex drug regimens, are a major patient safety concern. These errors often stem from fragmented decision-making across medical specialties, a critical coordination failure that leads to adverse drug events and rehospitalizations. To address this coordination challenge, we introduce PRISMATIC, a multi-agent architecture where specialized agents, each representing a workflow role, collaboratively generate and refine treatment plans. Operating on a blackboard architecture, the system first structures patient information from clinical notes, then iteratively develops safe, rational, and interpretable drug regimens. The agents' collaboration is governed by two novel adaptive coordination mechanisms: (1) Dynamic Self-Updating Weight Adjustment (DSWA), a long-term mechanism that adjusts the influence weights of agents based on historical case outcomes, enabling the system to adapt and trust more reliable specialists over time. (2) Discrepancy Feedback Precise Calibration (DFPC), a short-term mechanism where agents provide iterative feedback to resolve disagreements and eliminate prescription conflicts for the current patient. Experiments on patient records from the MIMIC-IV database show that PRISMATIC significantly reduces drug conflicts, improves prescription coverage, and enhances treatment consistency compared to strong LLM baselines. Our work demonstrates that structuring clinical co-treatment as a multi-agent coordination problem offers a promising path toward safer and more coherent multidisease management.
papers.summary: Prescribing errors for multimorbid patients often arise from fragmented decision-making across medical specialties rather than from any single clinician's mistake. `PRISMATIC` recasts co-treatment as a multi-agent coordination problem: specialized LLM agents representing workflow roles share a blackboard, structure patient information from clinical notes, and iteratively refine a drug regimen under two coordination mechanisms, Dynamic Self-Updating Weight Adjustment (`DSWA`), which reweights agent influence based on historical case outcomes, and Discrepancy Feedback Precise Calibration (`DFPC`), which runs short-term feedback rounds to resolve disagreements on the current patient. On patient records from `MIMIC-IV`, the system is reported to **reduce drug conflicts, improve prescription coverage, and increase treatment consistency** relative to strong LLM baselines.

papers.title: Analyzing and Mitigating Poisoning Attacks on Flow-Based Intrusion Detection
papers.abstract: Although Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) are increasingly deployed in operational networks, their dependence on large-scale training data introduces a critical vulnerability to stealthy poisoning attacks.
