We demonstrate that latent backdoors can be successfully implanted in flow-based IDS models by poisoning as little as 0.001% of the training data, maintaining near-nominal performance on clean inputs while ensuring high attack success rates. To address this threat, we propose a diagnostic-first methodology that localizes trigger-relevant features through constrained perturbation analysis and detects poisoning-induced behavioral drift by comparison with a distilled baseline model. The proposed methodology further enables targeted mitigation via automated data sanitization or neuron pruning. Our findings expose the operational risks of near-undetectable backdoors and provide a scalable approach to analyzing, quantifying, and mitigating backdoor exposure in AI-based IDS.
papers.summary: Flow-based intrusion detection systems (IDSs) built on machine learning depend on large training sets, which exposes them to stealthy data poisoning. The authors show that a latent backdoor can be implanted by **poisoning as little as 0.001% of the training data**, keeping near-nominal accuracy on clean traffic while achieving high attack success rates. They then propose a diagnostic-first defense that localizes trigger-relevant features through constrained perturbation analysis, detects poisoning-induced behavioral drift by comparing against a distilled baseline model, and enables targeted mitigation through automated data sanitization or neuron pruning.

papers.title: Likelihood Is Not Authorship: Can We Reliably Measure Human Contribution in AI-Assisted Writing?
papers.abstract: AI-text detection generally asks whether a machine wrote a text. As AI becomes an increasingly integral and accepted part of writing, the more relevant question is no longer whether AI was used, but how much of the text reflects human contribution. A prominent line of work estimates this by measuring how predictive a person's prompt is of the final text. We show that this measure can be easily manipulated. We introduce SPECIFICITY PADDING that simply asks the model to copy a few random IDs from the prompt, and that alone makes a title-only request look more human than one that supplies the article's key ideas. A context-swap audit then holds each document fixed, and only shows or hides the IDs to the evaluator. The score of the unchanged text swings by a third to half of its scale, and it rises for every document we test, on news and scientific abstracts, across varied LLMs from 3.8B to 753B parameters. The same articles can average 85\% human or 15\% human depending only on which prompt is on record, and even with no prompt at all, the output-only variant rewards the random strings themselves. An exact identity, the credit ledger, explains why. The score is a surprisal-weighted average over the text, so rare strings that the context makes copyable collect the credit, whatever they mean. A two-point bound marks a deeper limit. If the prompt could have been machine-written, every transcript-only method must, in the worst case, miss by half the contribution at stake. Likelihood-based scores alone cannot reliably establish human contribution without evidence of what the person added and how the text was produced.
papers.summary: As AI-assisted writing becomes routine, the question shifts from whether a machine wrote a text to how much of it reflects human contribution, and one prominent approach estimates this by measuring how predictive a person's prompt is of the final text. The authors show the measure is easily gamed: a trick they call `SPECIFICITY PADDING`, which asks the model to copy a few random IDs from the prompt, makes a title-only request look more human than one that supplies the article's key ideas, and a context-swap audit that only shows or hides the IDs **swings the score of an unchanged document by a third to half of its scale** across news and scientific abstracts and models from 3.8B to 753B parameters. An exact identity they call the credit ledger explains why: the score is a surprisal-weighted average, so rare strings the context makes copyable collect the credit regardless of meaning, and a two-point bound shows any transcript-only method can miss by half the contribution at stake whenever the prompt itself could have been machine-written.

papers.title: Learning to Compute Is Not Learning to Retain or Reuse in Looped Transformers
papers.abstract: Looped transformers compute by applying one block repeatedly, so they can run for more loops than they were trained with. Recurrent reasoners are known to overthink: iterating past the trained depth can turn a correct answer into a wrong one. Such a late error can reflect failed computation, loss of retention, or a state that later computation cannot reuse. We separate these cases in in-context Mealy-machine execution, where a simulator supplies intermediate targets and exact counterfactuals for hidden-state interventions. Models trained to answer at loop 32 are fully correct there but keep only 22% of these answers at loop 64. Retention depends on what training asks for: supervising one randomly chosen position per example, instead of always the last, keeps 99.8%, and randomizing the number of training loops also helps; truncating gradients, as in progressive training against overthinking, does not. The computation itself is exact: position $k$ is computed at loop $k$, and swapping its loop-$k$ hidden vector for the one from another input redirects every later position to that input's exact continuation (237/237 pairs in each of ten models). Retention, however, is not reuse. Even in models that keep nearly all answers, holding each position $k$ fixed from loop $k$ drops accuracy to 4--6%, whereas holding it from loop $k+4$ is harmless. A released recurrent maze network trained to avoid overthinking behaves the same way. Learning to compute is thus not learning to retain, and avoiding overthinking does not make a state reusable when its answer first appears.
papers.summary: Looped transformers apply one block repeatedly and can run for more iterations than they were trained with, but such recurrent reasoners are known to overthink, turning correct answers wrong when iterated past the trained depth. Using in-context Mealy-machine execution, where a simulator supplies intermediate targets and exact counterfactuals for hidden-state interventions, the authors separate failed computation from lost retention and from states that later computation cannot reuse. Models trained to answer at loop 32 are fully correct there but **keep only 22% of those answers at loop 64**, whereas supervising one randomly chosen position per example keeps 99.8%, randomizing the training loop count also helps, and gradient truncation as used in progressive training does not. Hidden-state swaps confirm the computation itself is exact (237/237 pairs in each of ten models), yet freezing a position's state from the loop where its answer first appears drops accuracy to 4-6%, so a model that computes correctly may neither keep its answers nor leave them in a state later loops can reuse.

papers.title: When Does the Dependency Graph Help Code-to-Architecture Mapping?
papers.abstract:
Architectural technical debt arises when a system's implementation drifts from its inten ded modular decomposition, while the mapping between source files and architectural modu les is missing, incomplete, or costly to maintain manually. We formulate code-to-archite cture mapping as semi-supervised node classification over a directed multi-relational de pendency graph, with files as nodes, typed dependencies as edges, and lexical features d erived from code identifiers and directory layout. Starting from a small labeled sample,
  an iterative self-training procedure expands the mapping to the remaining files. We com pare a graph convolutional network (GCN), a graph attention network (GAT), and a graph-f ree multi-layer perceptron (MLP), using identical features and training procedures for t he learned models, against a Naive Bayes reference. Across 100 runs on ten open-source J ava and C/C++ systems, all three neural models outperform the reference on both F1 metri cs. GAT achieves the highest averages of system-level median macro and micro F1, at 83.5
  and 92.2, respectively, whereas MLP remains competitive or superior on several systems.
  On Chrome, the largest system with 18,343 files, GAT and GCN exceed MLP by 22 and 19 ma cro-F1 points, respectively, and have substantially fewer persistently misclassified fil es. Connectivity and homophily are associated with where neural message passing helps, w hile multi-relational aggregation outperforms a single merged edge type on every system for both GCN and GAT. A follow-up study finds that several model rankings depend on the training seed, qualifying smaller advantages without removing the large graph benefit ob served on Chrome.
papers.summary: Architectural technical debt accumulates when an implementation drifts from its intended modular decomposition, and the mapping from source files to architecture modules is often missing or costly to maintain by hand. The authors frame code-to-architecture mapping as semi-supervised node classification over a directed multi-relational dependency graph, with files as nodes, typed dependencies as edges, and lexical features from identifiers and directory layout, expanding a small labeled sample through iterative self-training. Across 100 runs on ten open-source Java and C/C++ systems, a graph convolutional network (`GCN`), a graph attention network (`GAT`), and a graph-free multi-layer perceptron (`MLP`) all beat a `Naive Bayes` reference, with `GAT` reaching median macro and micro F1 of 83.5 and 92.2, and **on Chrome's 18,343 files `GAT` and `GCN` exceed the `MLP` by 22 and 19 macro-F1 points**. Connectivity and homophily predict where message passing helps, multi-relational aggregation beats a single merged edge type on every system, and a follow-up study finds several model rankings depend on the training seed, which qualifies the smaller advantages without removing the large graph benefit on Chrome.

papers.title: From Global to Tail Convergence: Dynamics of $\alpha$-Stable Score-Based Generative Models
papers.abstract: Score-based generative models driven by $\alpha$-stable L{\'e}vy processes have been proposed as an alternative to Brownian diffusion models, with empirical evidence suggesting improved sampling and better modeling of heavy-tailed data. Yet theoretical guarantees for these models remain limited. We develop a non-asymptotic convergence analysis for scale-preserving $\alpha$-stable generative dynamics, covering both compactly supported and power-law targets. In p-Wasserstein distance, we quantify the effects of early stopping, initialization, score approximation, and time discretization, and show exponential decay of the initialization error. A comparison with Brownian dynamics reveals that global Wasserstein convergence alone does not fundamentally distinguish the two models: both initialization errors decay exponentially with the forward horizon on the common class of heavy-tailed targets. A sharp separation emerges instead in the tails. At any positive generation time, stable dynamics produces power-law tails with index $\alpha$, whereas Brownian dynamics remains light-tailed. For a target with tail index $\nu$, asymptotically correct extreme-quantile scaling is possible precisely when $\alpha$=$\nu$. These results identify tail-index matching as a principled mechanism behind the ability of stable generative models to capture extreme events.
papers.summary: Score-based generative models driven by alpha-stable Lévy processes have been proposed as a heavy-tailed alternative to Brownian diffusion, with empirical evidence of better sampling on heavy-tailed data but few theoretical guarantees. The authors develop a non-asymptotic convergence analysis for scale-preserving alpha-stable generative dynamics in p-Wasserstein distance, covering compactly supported and power-law targets and quantifying the effects of early stopping, initialization, score approximation, and time discretization, with the initialization error decaying exponentially. Comparing against Brownian dynamics shows that global Wasserstein convergence alone does not separate the two models; the difference lies in the tails, where stable dynamics produce power-law tails with index alpha at any positive generation time while Brownian dynamics stay light-tailed, and **asymptotically correct extreme-quantile scaling holds exactly when the stability index matches the target's tail index**.

papers.title: SNACK: A Sequential Notation Framework for Probabilistic Graph Generation
papers.abstract: We introduce SNACK, a string representation for probabilistic graph generation that enables sequence models to generate and model graphs with discrete node and edge features. SNACK linearizes graphs by encoding the nonzero entries of the lower-triangular adjacency matrix, establishing a bijective correspondence between valid sequences and ordered adjacency matrices. This design enables invalid logit masking to enforce structural constraints--such as chemical valence and ordering rules--guaranteeing 100% valid generated sequences. SNACK also enables principled string-based GFlowNet training by explicitly accounting for node-ordering symmetries. Across standard graph-generation tasks and molecular distribution-learning benchmarks, SNACK achieves competitive sample quality, while substantially improving the throughput of GFlowNet training relative to graph-based generation. Probing analyses further show that models trained on SNACK encode meaningful local and global graph structure despite receiving only sequential supervision. These results position SNACK as a practical framework for probabilistic graph generation with deep sequence models.
papers.summary: Generating graphs with discrete node and edge features using sequence models requires a string encoding that keeps structural constraints enforceable. `SNACK` linearizes a graph by encoding the nonzero entries of its lower-triangular adjacency matrix, giving a bijection between valid sequences and ordered adjacency matrices, so invalid-logit masking can enforce rules such as chemical valence and ordering and **guarantee 100% valid generated sequences**. The representation also accounts explicitly for node-ordering symmetries, which enables principled string-based `GFlowNet` training with substantially higher throughput than graph-based generation, while sample quality on standard graph-generation and molecular distribution-learning benchmarks remains competitive and probing shows the models encode local and global graph structure from sequential supervision alone.

papers.title: Learning Who Benefits Most: Multi-Treatment Causal Ranking for Population Health Stratification
papers.abstract:
Population health stratification frameworks, such as the Italian DM77, organize patients by clinical need and care pathways but offer limited guidance on which care changes to prioritize under constrained resources.
  We present PROMETHEUS (Proactive Resource Optimization through Multi-treatment Effect-based Targeting in Healthcare Environments Using Stratification), a framework that formulates population health stratification as a multi-treatment causal ranking problem. Its objective is to order eligible patient-treatment opportunities by expected incremental benefit rather than obtain perfectly calibrated individual treatment-effect estimates.
  Each clinically admissible care intensification is compared with maintaining the patient's current pathway. Treatments are learned jointly to produce a globally comparable ranking across patients and care profiles, within domains sharing a reference condition, outcome, follow-up horizon, and benefit scale. This separates clinical need, treatment benefit, and resource-constrained allocation.
  PROMETHEUS combines doubly robust causal signals with a Siamese neural ranking model and contrastive representation pretraining. The shared representation captures similarities across care transitions, supporting prioritization under capacity constraints.
  Synthetic experiments and semi-synthetic experiments using real administrative covariates from ASL Benevento evaluate ranking quality, allocation value, robustness, and failure modes. The results support the framework's ability to recover generated benefit orderings and prioritize care opportunities in the evaluated settings. PROMETHEUS provides a preclinical approach to actionable stratification; validation with observed treatment-outcome data is required before clinical use.
papers.summary: Population health stratification frameworks such as Italy's DM77 group patients by clinical need but give little guidance on which care changes to prioritize when resources are limited. `PROMETHEUS` (Proactive Resource Optimization through Multi-treatment Effect-based Targeting in Healthcare Environments Using Stratification) reformulates stratification as multi-treatment causal ranking: each clinically admissible care intensification is compared against maintaining the current pathway, and treatments are learned jointly so patient-treatment opportunities can be ordered by expected incremental benefit, combining doubly robust causal signals with a Siamese neural ranking model and contrastive representation pretraining. Synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments using administrative covariates from ASL Benevento **recover the generated benefit orderings and prioritize care opportunities under capacity constraints**, though the authors note validation on observed treatment-outcome data is required before any clinical use.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning via Advantage Guidance
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) holds the promise of learning a policy that can outperform what is shown in the data. However, in practice, such systems suffer from instability and hyperparameter sensitivity. In contrast, supervised learning provides a stable and scalable training objective, but is fundamentally limited by the quality of the demonstrated behavior. In this paper, we ask whether we can perform policy optimization with something as simple and stable as supervised learning but as performant as RL. Unfortunately, naively training the policy with supervised learning and conditioning on future rewards or advantages typically underperform dedicated RL methods. We introduce a new policy extraction method, Advantage Guidance, that retains the simple supervised learning structure with advantage conditioning while outperforming prior RL methods through effective conditional training and contrastive diffusion guidance during sampling. We show that Advantage Guidance can significantly improve a model's ability to respond to conditional advantage signals, and the contrastive guidance during sampling can use the learned advantage-conditioned policy to target the KL-regularized optimal policy. Empirically, we find that Advantage Guidance significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art RL methods on 26 long-horizon, sparse reward tasks across datasets with varying degrees of optimality.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) can learn policies that exceed the behavior in a dataset but is often unstable and hyperparameter-sensitive, while supervised learning is stable and scalable yet capped by demonstration quality, and naive supervised training conditioned on future returns or advantages typically underperforms dedicated RL. `Advantage Guidance` keeps the supervised, advantage-conditioned structure but adds conditional training that sharpens the policy's response to advantage signals and contrastive diffusion guidance at sampling time that steers the learned conditional policy toward the KL-regularized optimal policy. The method **outperforms prior state-of-the-art RL methods on 26 long-horizon, sparse-reward tasks** across datasets with varying degrees of optimality.

papers.title: More Methods, Better Agents? A Reality Check on Self-Distillation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Self-distillation in agentic reinforcement learning has produced a growing number of methods. However, existing evaluations often reuse published baseline scores under differing experimental conditions, provide few direct comparisons among contemporaneous methods, and give limited attention to training stability and computational cost. These limitations obscure the source of reported gains and the practical strengths and weaknesses of competing methods. Costly agent training further motivates a common basis for comparison. To address these gaps, we compare ten representative methods against GRPO on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, Search-QA, and WebShop across three model sizes. Our study comprises 132 training runs totaling 12,124.4 recorded H800 GPU-hours, with repeated evaluations over eight rollout seeds for the pretrained backbones and all eleven trained methods. Beyond final task performance, we examine training progress, stability, and measured computational cost. Our evaluation yields three key findings. First, gains over GRPO remain limited in scope, with no method consistently outperforming it across settings. Second, strong final performance can mask unstable training. Third, additional training cost does not consistently translate into better performance. We establish this benchmark to support fair, comprehensive comparison and guide future research toward reliable and cost-effective improvements in agent training. Project page: https://aim-uofa.github.io/Self-Distillation-AgentRL/
papers.summary: Self-distillation methods for agentic reinforcement learning have multiplied, but published comparisons often reuse baseline scores from differing conditions, rarely compare contemporaneous methods head to head, and say little about training stability or compute cost. The authors retrain ten representative methods alongside `GRPO` on `ALFWorld`, `ScienceWorld`, `Search-QA`, and `WebShop` across three model sizes, in 132 runs totaling 12,124.4 recorded H800 GPU-hours with evaluation over eight rollout seeds. They find that **no method consistently outperforms `GRPO` across settings**, that strong final scores can hide unstable training, and that extra training cost does not reliably buy better performance, and they establish the setup as a common benchmark for future comparisons.
papers.highlight_summary:
Self-distillation methods for agentic reinforcement learning have multiplied, but their reported gains are hard to trust because evaluations reuse published baseline numbers under mismatched conditions, rarely compare contemporaneous methods head to head, and ignore training stability and compute cost. The authors re-run everything under one protocol to find out which gains survive a fair comparison.

- The benchmark trains ten representative self-distillation methods plus a `GRPO` baseline on `ALFWorld`, `ScienceWorld`, `Search-QA`, and `WebShop` at three model sizes, totaling **132 training runs** and **12,124.4 recorded H800 GPU-hours**, with each pretrained backbone and each trained method evaluated over eight rollout seeds.
- **No method consistently outperforms `GRPO` across settings**, and the gains that do appear are limited in scope, so much of the reported progress does not hold up under matched conditions.
- Strong final task performance can mask unstable training, which the authors expose by tracking training progress and stability rather than reporting only end-of-run scores.
- Additional training cost does not consistently translate into better performance, so the more expensive methods are not reliably the better ones.
- The conclusions are bounded to these ten methods, four text-based environments, and three model sizes, and the abstract gives no per-method magnitudes or names for which methods proved unstable or expensive.

papers.title: JetSpec++: Foresight Parallel Drafting with Self Refinements
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding's effectiveness is governed by two quantities: the acceptance rate of drafted tokens and the cost of producing them. We show the two objectives can be co-optimized with algorithm-system co-design, and present JetSpec++, which retains a strong learned draft model while hiding its cost almost entirely. JetSpec++ combines three components: intra-block self refinement, which trains the draft model to iteratively correct its own parallel predictions within a block of tokens; inter-block foresight drafting, which begins the next block before the current one is verified; and pipelined drafting and verification, which overlaps the two stages so drafting's marginal wall-clock cost approaches zero. In comparison with state-of-the-art speculative decoding methods, JetSpec++ attains a wall-clock speedup of up to $7.45\times$ over autoregressive (AR) decoding and $1.54\times$ over DSpark, with up to 1,361 tokens per second for a single request on GB200, and an average acceptance length of 8.94 across seven benchmarks, while preserving the target model's output distribution. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/JetSpec.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up autoregressive generation in proportion to how many drafted tokens the target model accepts and how cheaply the drafts are produced, two quantities usually traded against each other. `JetSpec++` keeps a strong learned draft model but hides its cost through three pieces: intra-block self refinement, which trains the drafter to iteratively correct its own parallel predictions within a token block; inter-block foresight drafting, which starts the next block before the current one is verified; and pipelined drafting and verification that overlap the two stages so drafting's marginal wall-clock cost approaches zero. Across seven benchmarks it reaches an average acceptance length of 8.94 and **up to 7.45x wall-clock speedup over autoregressive decoding and 1.54x over `DSpark`**, hitting 1,361 tokens per second for a single request on a GB200 while preserving the target model's output distribution.

papers.title: StateCraft: Augmenting Video World Models with Abstract-State Reasoning
papers.abstract: Video world models aim to simulate complex environments with realistic appearance and dynamics. Maintaining consistency over long interactions requires tracking past actions and understanding how those actions affect the environment. Video world models can only generate partial observations of the entire world at a time. Remembering past observations alone may not be sufficient in every scenario, as they may no longer reflect the world after a sequence of actions. We introduce a paradigm that decouples a persistent, updatable abstract state from the visual state. The abstract state keeps track of the entities' changes as the world evolves, and is used to condition the visual state, which represents the current view. We propose StateCraft, a novel architecture that pairs a language model with a video diffusion model to evolve the dynamic world. We evaluate our approach on generative interfaces, which pose a substantial challenge because a single action may change parts of the state that are not currently visible. To support training and evaluation, we develop a data collection pipeline that produces informative, densely annotated trajectories at scale without human or agent supervision, together with a benchmark measuring generation quality, memory, and controllability. On this benchmark, our approach improves surpasses the state-of-the-art baselines. We demonstrate that StateCraft maintains high self-consistency and strong generation quality over long trajectories. Because the abstract state is explicit, it can be edited directly, and generation follows edits to states never observed in the data. Finally, a proof-of-concept 3D experiment, in which actions change the illumination of an unobserved room, shows that the paradigm can also be applied to spatial environments. Project page: https://insait-institute.github.io/StateCraft/.
papers.summary: Video world models must stay consistent over long interaction sequences, yet they only ever render a partial view, and remembering past frames is not enough when an action changes parts of the world that are currently off-screen. `StateCraft` decouples a persistent, editable abstract state from the visual state: a language model tracks how entities change as actions are applied, and that state conditions a video diffusion model that renders the current view. Evaluated on generative interfaces, where a single action can alter unseen state, with a new large-scale annotated trajectory pipeline and a benchmark covering generation quality, memory, and controllability, the approach **surpasses state-of-the-art baselines and maintains self-consistency over long trajectories**, follows direct edits to abstract states never seen in training, and extends in a proof-of-concept to a 3D room whose unobserved illumination changes with actions.

papers.title: Learning Perception to Action Rules through Reinforcement Learning for Theory-of-Mind Reasoning
papers.abstract: In Theory-of-Mind (ToM) reasoning, large language models may correctly infer the agent's mental state but fail to use that inference when predicting or judging the agent's subsequent actions. In this work, we investigate whether explicitly connecting perception, belief, and action with rules improves ToM reasoning. We generate concise \textit{if--then} rules that express relations between perception to action and use Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to train Qwen2.5 and Llama3 models across four ToM benchmarks. GRPO with rule generation outperforms prompting, supervised fine-tuning, and think reasoning. Moreover, rules generated by larger models ($\geq$3B) provide transferable knowledge that improves downstream performance of GPT-4o-mini. These findings suggest that explicit rules help models bridge the reasoning gap in ToM and support knowledge transfer across models.
papers.summary: Large language models can often infer an agent's mental state in Theory-of-Mind (ToM) tasks yet fail to use that inference when predicting or judging the agent's next action. The authors have models generate concise if-then rules linking perception, belief, and action, and train `Qwen2.5` and `Llama3` models with Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) to produce such rules across four ToM benchmarks. **Rule generation trained with `GRPO` outperforms prompting, supervised fine-tuning, and think-style reasoning**, and rules produced by models of 3B parameters or more transfer as knowledge that improves the downstream performance of `GPT-4o-mini`.

papers.title: Evolve Together, Fall into Place: How Social Scaffolding Shapes Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Recent work lets LLM agents evolve their own harness, up to the team itself. Yet in human groups, the same abilities achieve different outcomes under different social conditions. Borrowing the notion of scaffolding from developmental psychology, we investigate whether the social scaffolding of a self-evolving multi-agent system (MAS), namely its team composition and structure of interdependence (e.g., collaboration, conformity, or competition), shapes how the team evolves. We present AGORA (Agents Growing through Organization and Relational Arrangements), a framework that varies the two axes independently across three evolution mechanisms. Across web search, codebase understanding, and document QA, we find that (1) evolution alone rarely helps, while the right scaffolding surpasses a strong agent evolved alone by up to 25 points; (2) it does so by moving authority to the most capable member while the others step back; and (3) this member, having grown within the team, outperforms the same model alone. Designing a self-evolving MAS thus requires designing its social scaffolding, which shapes not only how its agents learn, but who gets to lead.
papers.summary: Recent systems let LLM agents evolve their own harness, up to the composition of the team itself, but in human groups the same abilities yield different outcomes under different social conditions. Borrowing the idea of scaffolding from developmental psychology, `AGORA` (Agents Growing through Organization and Relational Arrangements) independently varies the team composition and the interdependence structure of a self-evolving multi-agent system (MAS), such as collaboration, conformity, or competition, across three evolution mechanisms. On web search, codebase understanding, and document QA, evolution alone rarely helps, while the right scaffolding **beats a strong agent evolved alone by up to 25 points**, chiefly by shifting authority to the most capable member while the others step back, and that member, having grown within the team, outperforms the same model alone.

papers.title: Delta Tokenizer: Reference-Identical Tokenization of Session Deltas and Segment-Parallelism for Long Prompts on Multicore CPUs
papers.abstract:
An agent that drives an LLM sends the model the same conversation again and again, and each turn adds only a little text at the end. Inference engines reuse the KV cache of the shared prefix, so only the new tokens pass through the model. However, tokenization has no such shortcut. The CPU front end of the serving engine converts every request back into token IDs from its first character, which lengthens the time to first token (TTFT) and consumes CPU on every turn.
  We present Delta Tokenizer, a CPU tokenization front end that tokenizes only the delta between a request and the previous request of the same session. It retains the earlier token sequence, encodes again only the appended text and the short tail whose tokens the append could affect, and joins the two only at a position the tokenizer's splitting rules themselves cannot move, which keeps the result exact. For long requests with no state to reuse, it cuts the text where practical tokenizers already keep neighboring pieces independent, encodes the pieces on several cores at once, and concatenates the outputs into the reference encoding, exactly. A shared CPU pool schedules these chunks together with the short incremental updates, so an update runs between two chunks rather than behind an entire long job.
  The incremental path shortens the tokenization of a session turn by roughly 40x relative to the Hugging Face reference tokenizer, and on 16 cores the chunk-parallel path encodes a four-million-character request 8.2x faster than a serial encode and 1.6-2.1x faster than LoPT. Inside SGLang, Delta Tokenizer reduces the median TTFT through the chat interface by 59% at 100K tokens and brings the P99 TTFT of agent sessions down 9.5x under load and 23x when long requests tie up the front end. Every output we checked matches the reference, among them 41.8 billion documents encoded by its fast encoder.
papers.summary: Agents that drive an LLM resend nearly the same conversation every turn, and while serving engines reuse the KV cache for the shared prefix, the CPU tokenizer still re-encodes each request from its first character, inflating time to first token (TTFT). `Delta Tokenizer` keeps the previous turn's token sequence, re-encodes only the appended text plus the short tail it could affect, and splices at a boundary the tokenizer's own splitting rules cannot move, so the output is exact; for long stateless requests it splits text where practical tokenizers already treat neighboring pieces independently and encodes the chunks in parallel on a shared CPU pool that also schedules incremental updates between chunks. The incremental path is roughly 40x faster than the Hugging Face reference tokenizer on a session turn, 16-core chunk parallelism encodes a four-million-character request 8.2x faster than serial and 1.6-2.1x faster than `LoPT`, and inside `SGLang` it **cuts median TTFT by 59% at 100K tokens and P99 TTFT for agent sessions by 9.5x under load**, with every checked output matching the reference across 41.8 billion documents.

papers.title: Asymptotically Exact Negative Guidance of Diffusion Models via Positive-Unlabeled Learning
papers.abstract: Negative guidance of diffusion models generates samples that avoid an undesired condition, specified either by reference samples or by a conditional score alongside an unconditional model. Existing methods inject repulsive terms derived from local information at each sample, so the resulting sampler does not target an explicit density, and its bias cannot be systematically reduced by increasing computation. We instead present a negative-guidance method that samples from an explicit target density, which uniformly handles both reference-sample and score-based specifications and suppresses probability mass near the undesired condition with an avoidance strength that parametrizes the target density itself. Realizing this target requires estimating, at each diffusion timestep, how likely each sample is to belong to the undesired condition. We cast this estimation as a Positive-Unlabeled learning problem that admits lightweight online training along the diffusion trajectory, using condition samples as positives and diffusion particles as unlabeled data. Because the guided particles drift from the unconditional marginal, we further correct the residual mismatch via Sequential Monte Carlo, yielding a sampler that is asymptotically exact in the particle limit and that turns any existing negative-guidance method into its proposal kernel. Empirically, our method approaches the ground-truth target on Gaussian mixtures and Pareto-dominates existing methods on trade-offs between avoidance and generation quality, distributional bias, and diversity, including in an image-generation setting with a pretrained score network.
papers.summary: Negative guidance steers a diffusion model away from an undesired condition, specified by reference samples or by a conditional score, but existing methods inject local repulsive terms that do not target any explicit density, so their bias cannot be reduced by spending more compute. The proposed method instead defines an explicit target density whose avoidance strength is a parameter, handles both specification styles uniformly, and estimates at each timestep how likely each sample is to belong to the undesired condition by casting it as Positive-Unlabeled (PU) learning trained online along the trajectory, with condition samples as positives and diffusion particles as unlabeled data. A Sequential Monte Carlo correction removes the residual mismatch from particles drifting off the unconditional marginal, yielding a sampler that is **asymptotically exact in the particle limit** and can wrap any existing negative-guidance method as its proposal kernel; empirically it approaches the ground-truth target on Gaussian mixtures and Pareto-dominates prior methods on avoidance versus quality, bias, and diversity, including with a pretrained image score network.

papers.title: Efficient contextual partial monitoring with general function approximation
papers.abstract: We study finite stochastic partial monitoring (PM) games with side information, a paradigm of sequential learning with partial feedback. On each round $t \in [T]$, both player and environment observe a context and player chooses an action and environment simultaneously chooses an outcome. The player neither observes the outcome nor the loss; instead, they only observe a feedback symbol which is partially informative about the outcome. We utilize the Estimation-to-Decisions (E2D) meta-algorithm of Foster et al.(2021) to design E2D.PMSide, a computationally efficient framework for contextual partial monitoring, which uses an online regression oracle to efficiently estimate the outcome distributions based on historical (context, action, feedback symbol) tuples. Since the exploration rule given by the original E2D algorithm is intractable to compute, we propose two computationally efficient exploration rules that achieve optimal regret orders in $T$: in the globally observable setting, our exploration rule is based on $\epsilon$-greedy, while in the locally observable setting, our exploration rule uses inverse gap weighting (Foster & Rakhlin, 2020), which was previously only known to be effective in the bandit setting. We show that a variant of E2D.PMSide named OE2D.PMSide can be combined with offline regression oracles to give an efficient algorithm with optimal regret when the contexts are drawn independently from a fixed distribution. We evaluate our algorithm on a synthetic label-efficient prediction game and an LLM routing task, in which a learner decides from prompt, uncertainty, and internal state features whether to escalate a query from a weak model to a strong one. We show that our method has superior performance to prior approaches.
papers.summary: Partial monitoring (PM) games are sequential decision problems in which the learner never observes the outcome or its loss, only a feedback symbol that is partially informative about the outcome, and here every round also comes with a context visible to both player and environment. Building on the Estimation-to-Decisions (`E2D`) meta-algorithm, the authors design `E2D.PMSide`, which estimates outcome distributions with an online regression oracle over past (context, action, feedback) tuples and replaces the intractable exploration rule of the original E2D with two efficient ones: epsilon-greedy for globally observable games and inverse gap weighting for locally observable games, a rule previously known to work only for bandits. **Both exploration rules achieve optimal regret orders in the horizon T**, and a variant called `OE2D.PMSide` works with offline regression oracles when contexts are drawn independently from a fixed distribution. Experiments on a synthetic label-efficient prediction game and an LLM routing task, where the learner decides from prompt, uncertainty, and internal-state features whether to escalate a query from a weak model to a strong one, show the method outperforming prior approaches.

papers.title: ReproBAIT: Can coding agents build their own biological AI tools?
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly competent at leveraging scientific knowledge and existing computational tools to execute complex workflows. At present, little information exists on their ability to reconstruct tools when given limited descriptions of such tools. We introduce an evaluation titled ReproBAIT (Reproducing Biological AI Tools), which measures the ability of coding agents to design, implement, and train biological AI tools taken from published research across a range of information access conditions. The coding agent is securely sandboxed without internet access and receives training data, a fixed time and compute budget, and limited information about the tool to replicate. We then score the reproduced biological AI tool based on its performance (tool-specific metrics) on held-out data. We evaluated a set of biological AI tools of varying complexities: ProteinMPNN, an inverse protein folding tool, RFdiffusion3, an all-atom generative diffusion tool, and a closed-source molecular design tool. We institute a methodology to check for memorisation, as the open source tools are likely to be included in models' pretraining corpus. Across a range of leading closed- and open-source coding agents, we find substantial reproduction capability for some selected tools, though limited capability for a highly complex tool. We find moderate evidence consistent with memorisation, varying across coding agents. These results suggest that tool developers need to be increasingly cautious when releasing information about the tools publicly; re-creation of the tool based on such information could undermine a tool's commercial value or invalidate dual-use managed access strategies.
papers.summary: Coding agents can already run existing scientific tools, but little is known about whether they can rebuild such tools from limited descriptions. `ReproBAIT` (Reproducing Biological AI Tools) sandboxes a coding agent without internet access, gives it training data, a fixed time and compute budget, and partial information about a published tool, then scores the reconstruction on held-out data with tool-specific metrics; the targets are `ProteinMPNN` for inverse protein folding, `RFdiffusion3` for all-atom generative diffusion, and a closed-source molecular design tool, with a methodology for detecting memorisation since the open-source tools likely appear in pretraining corpora. **Leading closed- and open-source coding agents show substantial reproduction capability for some tools but limited capability on the most complex one**, and there is moderate evidence consistent with memorisation that varies by agent. The authors argue that publicly released tool descriptions could undermine commercial value or managed-access strategies for dual-use tools.

papers.title: Calibration and Risk-Budgeted Decisions with System One Models
papers.abstract: LLM workflows and agents rely on a set of binary decisions like allow/block an input, or discard/retain a retrieved document. When human deferral is unavailable, uncertain cases must still receive an action. We study System One decision scores in this setting by defaulting to a conservative fallback when uncertain, and controlling the false omission risk within the subset of inputs assigned the utility-maximizing action. Across six datasets covering moderation, safety, and reranking, we compare general System One models with task baselines and a local open-weights fine-tuned System One model. We show that naive baselines for threshold selection exceed the target risk in roughly half of settings with defined test risk, compared with 7.8\% for Learn Then Test (LTT), which leverages finite-sample statistical guarantees. Our results show why relying on a probability-like interface is insufficient for deployment decisions and how risk-budgeted selection trades useful action against observed error.
papers.summary: LLM workflows and agents make binary decisions such as allowing or blocking an input or retaining a retrieved document, and when no human is available to defer to, uncertain cases still need an action. The authors study System One (fast, non-deliberative) decision scores in this setting: inputs the model is unsure about receive a conservative fallback, and the false omission risk within the subset assigned the utility-maximizing action is controlled through threshold selection. Across six datasets covering moderation, safety, and reranking, they compare general-purpose System One models, task-specific baselines, and a locally fine-tuned open-weights model. **Naive threshold selection exceeded the target risk in roughly half of the settings with a defined test risk, versus 7.8% for `Learn Then Test` (LTT)**, which carries finite-sample statistical guarantees, illustrating why a probability-like score alone is insufficient for deployment decisions and how risk-budgeted selection trades useful action against observed error.

papers.title: VaryST: Generalizable Spatio-Temporal Forecasting Beyond the Closed-World Setting
papers.abstract: Spatio-temporal forecasting is fundamental to many real-world systems, yet deployment environments are inherently varying: temporal distributions may evolve, spatial domains may change, and observation availability may shift from training conditions. Existing models are often tightly coupled to their training environments through node-specific representations, predefined spatial support sets, and reliance on consistently available observations, limiting generalization to changing environments. To this end, we propose VaryST, a compact spatio-temporal forecasting model trained from scratch that achieves strong generalization by dynamically constructing predictive context from available long-term observations. To accommodate temporal changes, VaryST derives node representations from long-term histories, capturing current behavior in the context of longer-term patterns. To adapt to spatial changes, it dynamically selects functionally relevant support nodes beyond predefined neighborhoods and integrates their information with recent and long-term target states and global context. To handle varying observation availability, VaryST selectively masks historical patches on which the model relies most during training, encouraging it to exploit alternative temporal and spatial dependencies for accurate forecasting when key observations become unavailable. Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets against seventeen baselines show that VaryST achieves strong in-domain forecasting accuracy, substantially improves zero- and few-shot generalization under spatial and temporal changes, and remains robust to varying observation availability.
papers.summary: Spatio-temporal forecasting models are typically tied to their training environment through node-specific representations, fixed spatial support sets, and the assumption that observations are always available, which limits transfer when temporal distributions drift, spatial domains change, or sensors go missing. `VaryST` is a compact model trained from scratch that builds its predictive context dynamically: node representations are derived from long-term histories, functionally relevant support nodes are selected beyond predefined neighborhoods and combined with recent, long-term, and global context, and during training the historical patches the model relies on most are selectively masked so it learns to exploit alternative temporal and spatial dependencies. **Across six real-world datasets and seventeen baselines, it achieves strong in-domain accuracy while substantially improving zero- and few-shot generalization under spatial and temporal changes**, and it remains robust to varying observation availability.

papers.title: When Does Depth Help? Understanding Layerwise Inference in Tabular Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Transformer-based tabular foundation models (TFMs) achieve state-of-the-art performance on small to medium-sized tabular prediction tasks while processing diverse inputs through a shared stack of layers. Recent layerwise analyses identify strong predictive performance in early TFM representations and substantial overlap in computation across layers. However, early predictive accessibility alone does not establish whether later layers are dispensable for every input, and aggregate accuracy can obscure which inputs benefit from additional computation. We study all 24 in-context-learning layers of TabPFN-3 across 272 classification datasets, combining representation geometry, prediction trajectories, truncation, and structural interventions, while also examining related representation dynamics in four additional TFMs. We uncover a pronounced expansion-compression trajectory, with stronger late dimensional contraction associated with larger increases in class-prototype separation. A targeted analysis of early-stabilizing samples shows that substantial representational changes persist after predicted classes stabilize, while locally ambiguous queries obtain larger accuracy gains from shallow to late layers than well-separated queries. Repeating a single pretrained block or perturbing layer order reduces predictive performance on average, constraining simple post-hoc substitutions in the frozen model. These findings distinguish predictive accessibility, class stability, and the benefits of continuing computation, supporting an input-dependent assessment of depthwise redundancy in TFMs.
papers.summary: Transformer-based tabular foundation models (TFMs) are known to form strong predictions in early layers with heavy overlap in computation across layers, but that does not settle whether later layers are dispensable for every input. The authors analyze all 24 in-context-learning layers of `TabPFN-3` across 272 classification datasets using representation geometry, prediction trajectories, truncation, and structural interventions, with supporting analyses of representation dynamics in four other TFMs. They find a pronounced expansion-compression trajectory in which stronger late dimensional contraction accompanies larger gains in class-prototype separation, and **locally ambiguous queries gain substantially more accuracy from late layers than well-separated ones**, even though representations keep changing after predicted classes stabilize. Repeating a single pretrained block or perturbing layer order hurts performance on average, so depthwise redundancy should be judged per input rather than assumed globally.

papers.title: Model vs. User: Whose Values Prevail? Inference-Time Value Alignment in Multi-Turn Conversations
papers.abstract: Human values shape how we expect language models to behave. Dominant alignment approaches treat values as global objectives, although the appropriate value orientation is personal and contextual. Training-free alignment can steer models toward target values at inference time, yet has been largely evaluated in single-turn settings and with a single steering direction (e.g., toward safety). We evaluate four prompt- and activation-based steering methods in multi-turn conversations, where user and assistant models push toward the same or opposing, equally desirable values. We track alignment with a linear probe across three models and two value trade-offs. When assistant and user pull in opposite directions, the side matching the assistant's baseline bias often prevails, and effects that look successful early often fade or reverse after a few turns. Steering should therefore be evaluated over full conversations and in both directions of a value trade-off.
papers.summary: Training-free alignment methods can steer a language model toward target values at inference time, but they have mostly been tested in single-turn settings and in one direction, such as toward safety. The authors evaluate four prompt- and activation-based steering methods in multi-turn conversations where a user model and an assistant model push toward the same or opposing, equally desirable values, tracking alignment with a linear probe across three models and two value trade-offs. **When the two sides pull in opposite directions, the side matching the assistant's baseline bias usually prevails**, and steering effects that look successful early often fade or reverse after a few turns. The authors conclude that steering should be evaluated over full conversations and in both directions of a value trade-off.

papers.title: JointServe: Serving Multi-Model Agents on Memory-Constrained GPUs
papers.abstract: LLM agents are evolving from a single model calling tools to planners that orchestrate multiple expert models whose capabilities live in distinct weights. This shift breaks a hidden assumption of today's serving systems: that the working set of models fits in GPU memory. On the memory-constrained GPUs typical of private and edge deployments, naive whole-model swapping serializes weight transfer with computation and, without host-backed KV restoration, discards session state at a switch. We present JointServe, a serving system that treats weight shards and KV blocks as residency objects competing for one unified memory budget. JointServe exploits three structural properties of agent workloads (directed calls, gapped execution, and dual-state residency) to prepare models before they are called: an intent signal parsed from the caller's own output stream triggers prefetch during generation, partial k* residency reduces switching to incremental layers, and a preemptive transfer scheduler protects live-session KV with a guaranteed bandwidth share. A carve-out control step adjusts the weight/KV allocation as workload demands change. Evaluations show that JointServe reduces session completion time by 21.7% over the strongest whole-model swap baseline and stays usable in a crash regime where every whole-model swap baseline fails to finish (a 46-fold gap). On replayed SWE-bench, tau-bench, and OSWorld traces, it cuts session completion time by up to 49% and lifts SLO attainment from 2.8-24.5% to 76.8-100%.
papers.summary: As LLM agents shift from a single model calling tools to planners that orchestrate several expert models with distinct weights, the serving-system assumption that the working set fits in GPU memory breaks down; on the memory-constrained GPUs typical of private and edge deployments, naive whole-model swapping serializes weight transfer with computation and discards session KV state at every switch. `JointServe` treats weight shards and KV blocks as residency objects competing for one unified memory budget and exploits three properties of agent workloads (directed calls, gapped execution, and dual-state residency) to prepare models before they are called: an intent signal parsed from the caller's own output stream triggers prefetch during generation, partial residency reduces a switch to loading only incremental layers, and a preemptive transfer scheduler guarantees a bandwidth share for live-session KV. It reduces session completion time by 21.7% over the strongest whole-model-swap baseline and remains usable in a crash regime where every swap baseline fails to finish. On replayed `SWE-bench`, `tau-bench`, and `OSWorld` traces it **cuts session completion time by up to 49%** and lifts service-level objective (SLO) attainment from 2.8-24.5% to 76.8-100%.

papers.title: MAPLE: A Multi-Axis Parametric Knowledge Extraction Lens for LLM Evaluation
papers.abstract: LLMs absorb vast knowledge from training data, yet their inherently probabilistic nature offers no guarantee that this knowledge will surface in their outputs. To bridge this gap, Knowledge Extraction Enhancement (KEE) techniques such as activation steering, decoding adjustments, and prompting modify inference, potentially reinforcing existing predictions or surfacing less accessible answers. Yet their evaluations centered on aggregate accuracy, which obscures diverse effects by collapsing recovered failures and disrupted successes into a single score. We introduce MAPLE, a unified framework for characterizing how KEE techniques affect parametric knowledge extraction. Its diagnostic metrics disentangle these effects at the surface, probability, and beyond-sampling levels by measuring answer recovery and disruption, gold-token rank shifts on unrecovered failures, and recovery of answers missed by fixed-budget sampling. We evaluate six KEE techniques spanning decoding, activation steering, and prompting across three model families: OLMo2, Qwen2.5, and Llama3. Our analysis reveals distinct effects and trade-offs across techniques, highlighting the value of MAPLE for understanding and comparing KEE beyond aggregate accuracy.
papers.summary: Knowledge Extraction Enhancement (KEE) techniques such as activation steering, decoding adjustments, and prompting modify inference to surface knowledge a model holds but does not reliably output, yet they are usually judged on aggregate accuracy, which hides recovered failures and disrupted successes behind a single number. `MAPLE` is a diagnostic framework that separates these effects at three levels: answer recovery and disruption at the surface, gold-token rank shifts on failures that remain unrecovered, and recovery of answers missed by fixed-budget sampling. Applying it to six KEE techniques spanning decoding, steering, and prompting across `OLMo2`, `Qwen2.5`, and `Llama3`, **the authors find distinct effect profiles and trade-offs per technique that aggregate accuracy conceals**.

papers.title: CTIA-ODE: Continuous-Time Inter-Variable Attention for Long-Term Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Although multivariate time series forecasting has broad application prospects, effectively incorporating exogenous variables remains challenging. Prevailing discrete-time architectures often impose rigid temporal alignment across heterogeneous variables, which may limit their ability to capture continuously evolving external effects. To address this limitation, we introduce CTIA-ODE, a continuous-time forecasting framework centered on Continuous-Time Inter-Variable Attention (CTIA). Specifically, CTIA is embedded within an ordinary differential equation (ODE) solver, enabling the continuously evolving endogenous trajectory to dynamically query a static exogenous context along the integration path without requiring explicit temporal alignment. To improve the stability of the continuous latent dynamics, we further introduce a dual-stabilization strategy: architecturally, a Linear Residual Augmentation (LRA) module provides a macroscopic trend anchor, while an Outlier-Robust Hybrid Loss (ORHL) mitigates the influence of heavy-tailed anomalies during optimization. Extensive experiments across eight real-world datasets demonstrate that CTIA-ODE achieves state-of-the-art forecasting performance across diverse datasets and prediction horizons, while maintaining a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off with a compact memory footprint and low inference latency, particularly under long-horizon forecasting settings. Anonymous code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CTIA-ODE-15A6/.
papers.summary: Incorporating exogenous variables into multivariate time series forecasting is difficult because discrete-time architectures impose rigid temporal alignment across heterogeneous variables, which can miss continuously evolving external effects. `CTIA-ODE` embeds Continuous-Time Inter-Variable Attention (CTIA) inside an ordinary differential equation (ODE) solver so the evolving endogenous trajectory can query a static exogenous context along the integration path without explicit alignment, and it stabilizes the latent dynamics with a Linear Residual Augmentation (LRA) module that anchors the macroscopic trend and an Outlier-Robust Hybrid Loss (ORHL) that dampens heavy-tailed anomalies during optimization. **Across eight real-world datasets it reports state-of-the-art accuracy over diverse horizons**, with a compact memory footprint and low inference latency that are most favorable in long-horizon settings.

papers.title: Rent-Seeking Language Models: Reward Models Set the Prices, Frequent Audits Curb the Rent
papers.abstract: Reward model overoptimization in RLHF is usually described as reward hacking. We recast it as rent-seeking: the policy, a firm, earns reward from a regulator, the proxy reward model, that true quality does not back. The lens turns overoptimization into measurable quantities, namely rent, a capture index and deadweight loss, and into testable predictions from the economics of regulation. In a fixed, version-controlled testbed with three model families, accuracy-matched proxy reward models and two gold reward models, RL turns 41% to 66% of its proxy gain into rent while gold reward plateaus. Rent follows each regulator's prices. Neither proxy verifies facts, but one pays for confident specifics and the other for displays of diligence, so RL policies learn to fabricate details about nonexistent entities (97% to 100% of probes) or to deflect factual questions (67% to 98%). Kinship between policy and regulator adds a fixed premium of about 0.1 standard deviations but gives the policy no extra leverage under optimization. At a fixed expected fine, frequent mild audits beat rare severe ones, and random audits are as efficient per audit as targeted ones. Bringing the bunching estimator of tax economics to RL training, we also find a first sign that policies learn to stay just below a targeted audit's threshold.
papers.summary: Reward model overoptimization in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is usually called reward hacking; here it is recast as rent-seeking, with the policy as a firm extracting reward from a regulator, the proxy reward model, that true quality does not back. The framing yields measurable quantities (rent, a capture index, and deadweight loss) plus predictions borrowed from the economics of regulation, tested in a fixed, version-controlled testbed with three model families, accuracy-matched proxy reward models, and two gold reward models. **RL converts 41% to 66% of its proxy gain into rent while gold reward plateaus**, and the form the rent takes follows what each regulator pays for: one proxy rewards confident specifics, so policies fabricate details about nonexistent entities in 97% to 100% of probes, while the other rewards displays of diligence, so policies deflect factual questions 67% to 98% of the time. Kinship between policy and reward model adds a fixed premium of about 0.1 standard deviations without extra leverage under optimization, frequent mild audits beat rare severe ones at a fixed expected fine, and a bunching estimator borrowed from tax economics shows a first sign of policies learning to sit just below a targeted audit's threshold.

papers.title: EGCForest: Structured Agent Memory Organization for Enterprise Group Chats
papers.abstract: Enterprise group chats record project progress, decisions, task ownership, and other organizational information valuable to enterprise agents. Reliable retrieval is challenging because evidence spans interleaved threads, channels, and time, with meaning and authority conditioned on the speaker. Neither RAG's independent chunk retrieval nor memory systems' summary-based consolidation can reliably recover such distributed evidence. We present EGCForest, a novel multi-view hierarchical memory framework for enterprise group chats. EGCForest organizes an immutable message log into three complementary forests: a Channel forest for temporal workflows, an Actor forest for speaker-conditioned context, and an Artifact forest for deliverable lifecycles. Cross-view connections are enabled by a Placement Map and sparse structural bridges. Built on this memory backbone, EGCForest retrieves and assembles evidence by jointly leveraging message-level relevance, hierarchical context from forest summaries, and cross-view links, recovering distributed evidence. Experiments on three enterprise-chat benchmarks show that EGCForest consistently outperforms RAG and memory-system baselines, improving answer accuracy by up to 20.85 points over MemOS while supporting efficient online retrieval.
papers.summary: Enterprise group chats hold project progress, decisions, and task ownership, but the evidence is scattered across interleaved threads, channels, and time, and its meaning and authority depend on who said it, so neither chunk-level retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) nor summary-based memory consolidation recovers it reliably. `EGCForest` organizes an immutable message log into three complementary hierarchical forests, a Channel forest for temporal workflows, an Actor forest for speaker-conditioned context, and an Artifact forest for deliverable lifecycles, connected by a Placement Map and sparse structural bridges. Retrieval then combines message-level relevance, hierarchical context from forest summaries, and cross-view links to assemble distributed evidence. **On three enterprise-chat benchmarks it outperforms RAG and memory-system baselines, improving answer accuracy by up to 20.85 points over `MemOS`**, while keeping online retrieval efficient.

papers.title: Memory-Efficient Subspace Optimization with Residual Correction: From Momentum SGD to Muon
papers.abstract: Memory-efficient subspace optimization has emerged as a practical approach to reducing the memory cost of LLM training while preserving optimization performance. Previous algorithms typically rely on the leading singular subspace of stochastic gradients, yet the gradient noise may dominate the subspace in later training stages and can prevent convergence. To overcome this limitation, we adopt a residual correction framework, which maintains the optimizer states in the subspace and adds the orthogonal residual gradient to the parameter update. We first integrate this scheme into momentum SGD to develop SMRC, which attains an $O(T^{-1/4})$ convergence rate for a fixed orthonormal basis, matching that of full-space momentum SGD. Our analysis introduces a subspace virtual iterate to resolve the coupling between the momentum and the residual correction. Furthermore, we extend SMRC to a multi-stage variant which periodically recomputes bases to track the evolving dominant subspace and retains the same rate. Since each basis refresh breaks the consistency of the virtual iterates, we devise a boundary correction approach that aligns them across stages. Beyond momentum SGD, we incorporate our framework into Muon and propose PMRC, which applies the matrix sign to the projected momentum. Through a weighted momentum tracking analysis that accounts for the residual gradient, we establish an $O(T^{-1/4})$ convergence rate for PMRC, which matches the rate of full-space Muon. We also design a multi-stage PMRC with periodically refreshed bases, which maintains a convergence rate of the same order. Extensive experimental results confirm the effectiveness and efficiency of our algorithms.
papers.summary: Memory-efficient subspace optimizers reduce the optimizer-state memory of LLM training by working in the leading singular subspace of the stochastic gradient, but gradient noise can dominate that subspace late in training and stall convergence. The authors adopt a residual correction framework that keeps optimizer states in the subspace while adding the orthogonal residual gradient directly to the parameter update, first yielding `SMRC` for momentum stochastic gradient descent (SGD), where a subspace virtual iterate resolves the coupling between momentum and the residual, and then `PMRC` for `Muon`, which applies the matrix sign to the projected momentum. **Both attain an O(T^{-1/4}) convergence rate matching their full-space counterparts**, and multi-stage variants that periodically recompute the basis to track the evolving dominant subspace keep the same rate through a boundary correction that realigns virtual iterates across stages. Experiments are reported to confirm the effectiveness and efficiency of the algorithms.

papers.title: OpenTWBench (Open Taiwan Benchmark): Taiwan-Domain Knowledge Evaluation for Large Language Models, and How the Measurement Apparatus Shapes the Score
papers.abstract:
We present OpenTWBench, an open evaluation suite for Taiwan-domain knowledge in large language models, built around two benchmarks. tw-exam-bench contains 255,854 four-option questions across 148 academic subjects, from fifteen years of Taiwan's national examinations published as open data by the Ministry of Examination; answer keys agree across 31,312 duplicated question groups at 99.91%, with all 27 disagreements accounted for. A reviewed second pass withdrew 2,180 items whose stems depend on a figure the text does not carry; all scores use the remaining 253,674. tw-formosa-bench contains 1,696 difficulty-curated questions about everyday and contemporary Taiwan - the Taiwan that licensing examinations never ask about - generated from a community-curated corpus under a discipline in which no model writes a ground truth, and curated against a frozen seven-model pool so that the pool scored at the passing margin (46.9-74.6%, median ~54%); a leave-one-out experiment shows the selection preserves model ranking (near-zero bias). Within six weeks the frontier had cleared that band: of 108 models now on the public board, 22 score above its ceiling, the best 91.6%.
  We also document how much of a score comes from the apparatus rather than the model. On identical questions, switching answer extraction from pattern matching to an explicit \boxed{} answer moves accuracy from 20.8% to 93.9%; a single placeholder character in a system prompt moved one model from last (58.2%) to first (83.9%) on the same benchmark; doubling the thinking budget from 8k to 16k tokens bought 0.2% while shuffling which questions failed; and a three-judge validation panel proved to be one judge in disguise, two members approving 92-99% of everything shown. We release all datasets, per-item difficulty data, curation manifests and a leaderboard at https://opentwbench.ai
papers.summary: The suite pairs `tw-exam-bench`, 253,674 scored four-option questions across 148 subjects from fifteen years of Taiwan's national examinations, with `tw-formosa-bench`, 1,696 difficulty-curated questions about everyday and contemporary Taiwan generated from a community corpus with no model writing ground truth and selection calibrated against a frozen seven-model pool in a way that a leave-one-out experiment shows preserves model ranking. Within six weeks the frontier had cleared the curated band, with 22 of 108 models on the public board above its ceiling and the best at 91.6%. The authors also quantify how much of a score comes from the measurement apparatus rather than the model: **switching answer extraction from pattern matching to an explicit boxed-answer format moved accuracy from 20.8% to 93.9% on identical questions**, a single placeholder character in a system prompt moved one model from last (58.2%) to first (83.9%), doubling the thinking budget from 8k to 16k tokens bought 0.2% while shuffling which questions failed, and a three-judge validation panel proved to be one judge in disguise because two members approved 92-99% of everything shown. All datasets, per-item difficulty data, curation manifests, and a leaderboard are released.

papers.title: Energy Consumption Analysis of Discrete Diffusion and Autoregressive Language Models
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to scale, their energy consumption during inference has become a critical concern. While Autoregressive (AR) models are the industry standard, Diffusion Language Models (DLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative capable of parallel token generation. In this paper, we perform a comparative energy benchmark of diffusion models (LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B) against AR counterparts (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B). We analyze the trade-offs between model architecture, KV-cache optimization, and Joules-per-token efficiency. Our results show that at longer sequences (200--600 tokens), diffusion models achieve 2.5--2.7 J/token, approximately 2$\times$ more efficient than AR models with KV-cache (5.3--5.7 J/token). KV-cache provides substantial benefits for AR models at longer sequences (50--70\% energy reduction).
papers.summary: Inference energy is a growing cost as large language models scale, and diffusion language models (DLLMs), which generate tokens in parallel, are an alternative to the autoregressive (AR) standard. The authors run a comparative energy benchmark of the diffusion models `LLaDA-8B` and `Dream-7B` against the autoregressive `Llama-3.1-8B` and `Qwen-2.5-7B`, examining the trade-offs among architecture, KV-cache optimization, and joules per token. **At longer sequences of 200 to 600 tokens, the diffusion models use 2.5 to 2.7 J/token, roughly twice as efficient as AR models with KV-cache at 5.3 to 5.7 J/token**, while the KV-cache itself cuts AR energy by 50 to 70% at those lengths.

papers.title: Text-Informed Training Data Filtering for Enhanced Virtual Flow Meter Performance
papers.abstract: In sectors such as energy, aquaculture and chemical processing, the effectiveness of both mechanistic and data-driven models is frequently limited by poor-quality training data, which obscures underlying physical laws and degrades predictive accuracy. Such quality issues commonly manifest as anomalies in the dataset, ranging from sensor faults to process upsets and incorrect operator inputs. While traditional rule-based filtering can remove a subset of the anomalies, it is unable to leverage contextual information stored as unstructured text, such as engineer comments and operational logs that explain under what conditions the data was collected. We propose a text-informed data filtering method that leverages large language models (LLMs) to integrate unstructured operational data with tabular sensor data. The method consists of two steps: (1) contextual anomaly detection by reasoning over both data modalities, and (2) generation of a binary mask that is applied to filter the training dataset for model development. To investigate the potential benefit, a steady-state soft-sensor regression model, namely a virtual flow meter that estimates well flow rates, is used as the downstream evaluation target. Experiments on a synthetic oil and gas dataset show improved model performance compared to traditional rule-based filtering. Ablation studies show that textual operator comments can provide filtering-relevant signals beyond sensor data alone, with the multimodal approach reducing downstream MAPE from 7.1% to 5.4% relative to sensor-only filtering. This work demonstrates that integrating unstructured operational knowledge with sensor data through LLMs can improve data quality for industrial machine learning applications, offering a scalable alternative to manual data curation.
papers.summary: Mechanistic and data-driven models in energy, aquaculture, and chemical processing are often degraded by anomalous training data from sensor faults, process upsets, and incorrect operator inputs, and rule-based filters cannot use the context sitting in unstructured engineer comments and operational logs. The proposed method has a large language model reason jointly over text and tabular sensor data to detect contextual anomalies, then emits a binary mask that filters the training set before model development. Evaluated on a synthetic oil and gas dataset with a virtual flow meter, a steady-state soft-sensor regression model that estimates well flow rates, as the downstream target, it outperforms rule-based filtering, and **ablations show the multimodal approach reduces downstream mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) from 7.1% to 5.4% relative to sensor-only filtering**.

papers.title: On the Optimisation Landscape of Overparameterised Weighted MMD
papers.abstract: We study the optimisation landscape of the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) over weighted atomic measures. For the one-dimensional Gaussian kernel, we show that, for any compactly supported target distribution, sufficiently many particles ensure that every local minimum has arbitrarily small MMD. Moreover, any stationary point whose MMD remains bounded away from zero is unstable under an unweighted gradient flow over the particle locations. These results hold both when the weights are constrained to the simplex, and when they are unconstrained but optimised at each step. When the target is itself finitely supported, we further strengthen this result: beyond an explicit particle threshold, there are no spurious local minima, and every spurious stationary point is unstable. To our knowledge, these are the first finite-particle overparameterisation guarantees of their kind for weighted MMD optimisation.
papers.summary: The optimisation landscape of maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) over weighted atomic measures is analysed for the one-dimensional Gaussian kernel. For any compactly supported target distribution, **sufficiently many particles guarantee that every local minimum has arbitrarily small MMD**, and any stationary point whose MMD stays bounded away from zero is unstable under an unweighted gradient flow on particle locations; the results hold whether weights are constrained to the simplex or left unconstrained and optimised at each step.
