When the target is itself finitely supported the result sharpens: beyond an explicit particle threshold there are no spurious local minima at all, and every spurious stationary point is unstable. The authors state these are the first finite-particle overparameterisation guarantees of their kind for weighted MMD optimisation.

papers.title: Explorer-Zero: Improving Self-Play for Long-Horizon Tasks with Decomposable Verifiable Rewards
papers.abstract: Training LLM agents on long-horizon interactive tasks with reinforcement learning typically relies on human-annotated tasks and reliable verification, both expensive to construct for stateful environments. Self-play offers an alternative, but must generate achievable, compositional tasks and provide feedback beyond binary outcomes. We propose Explorer-Zero, a self-play framework that jointly generates tasks and fine-grained, verifiable rewards through environment interaction. A learned proposer explores the environment, constructs tasks, and records intermediate and final states as verification targets. These checkpoints reward partial completion, while alternating proposer--solver training adapts the generated curriculum. We show theoretically that subtask rewards reduce collapse among unsuccessful rollouts when they complete different numbers of subtasks. Without human-annotated training tasks, Explorer-Zero outperforms the evaluated self-play baselines across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and AppWorld; on AppWorld, our 30B agent reaches 59.67% task success, approaching 62.65% for RL on human-annotated tasks. Further analyses support task-relevant composition and benefits on complex tasks, while self-play initialization improves subsequent human-data RL across all three benchmarks.
papers.summary: Training LLM agents on long-horizon interactive tasks with reinforcement learning usually requires human-annotated tasks and reliable verification, both expensive for stateful environments, and self-play alternatives must generate achievable, compositional tasks with feedback richer than a binary outcome. `Explorer-Zero` has a learned proposer explore the environment, construct tasks, and record intermediate and final states as verification targets, so checkpoints reward partial completion; proposer and solver are trained alternately so the curriculum adapts, and a theoretical analysis shows subtask rewards reduce collapse among unsuccessful rollouts that complete different numbers of subtasks. Without any human-annotated training tasks it outperforms the evaluated self-play baselines on `ALFWorld`, `ScienceWorld`, and `AppWorld`, and **on `AppWorld` a 30B agent reaches 59.67% task success, close to the 62.65% of RL on human-annotated tasks**. Self-play initialization also improves subsequent RL on human data across all three benchmarks.

papers.title: SEA-HELM Audio: Evaluating Multilingual ASR-LLM Pipeline Performance Across SEA-HELM Subsets
papers.abstract: We introduce SEA-HELM Audio, a Southeast Asian (SEA) multilingual evaluation framework that extends the text-based SEA-HELM benchmark to assess performance degradation in cascaded automatic speech recognition and large language model (ASR-LLM) pipelines. Using synthesized speech, we compare speech-input and text-input performance across five languages (Chinese, English, Malay, Indonesian, and Tamil) on multiple-choice reasoning and instruction-following tasks. We evaluate open-weight and commercial ASR-LLM systems using identical verifiers and quantify the speech gap as the difference between text and speech accuracy. Results show substantial degradation, with accuracy drops of 9.00 to 18.50 percentage points for multiple-choice reasoning and 20.00 to 42.86 points for instruction following. Tamil exhibits the largest degradation, exceeding 40 percentage points. Our findings highlight the limitations of text-only benchmarks in predicting voice-agent reliability and demonstrate the value of SEA-HELM Audio for evaluating multilingual voice-agent systems.
papers.summary: Text-only benchmarks may overstate how reliably voice agents work, since cascaded automatic speech recognition and large language model (ASR-LLM) pipelines lose information at the transcription step. `SEA-HELM Audio` extends the Southeast Asian (SEA) `SEA-HELM` text benchmark with synthesized speech in Chinese, English, Malay, Indonesian, and Tamil, scoring open-weight and commercial ASR-LLM systems on multiple-choice reasoning and instruction-following tasks with identical verifiers and defining the speech gap as the difference between text and speech accuracy. **Accuracy drops by 9.00 to 18.50 percentage points on multiple-choice reasoning and 20.00 to 42.86 points on instruction following**, with Tamil degrading by more than 40 points.

papers.title: Rationale Distribution Distillation via Flow Matching for Distributional Continuous Latent Reasoning
papers.abstract: Sampling multiple chain-of-thought rationales from a language model can uncover correct solutions missed by a single attempt. However, these rationales are typically lengthy, making repeated autoregressive generation costly. Continuous latent reasoning offers a compact alternative, but point-valued methods condition repeated answer sampling on a single rationale, which can limit exploration of diverse paths and answer coverage. We thus propose rationale distribution distillation (RDD), training a conditional flow over fixed-length latent sequences by distilling from multiple textual reasoning paths. Furthermore, we expand the distillation targets through within-query mixup, interpolating between complete latent rationales for the same query. The flow nonautoregressively generates the entire latent sequence, and a frozen language model autoregressively decodes answers from sampled rationale contexts. Empirically, the resulting distributional reasoner achieves higher answer coverage than the evaluated point-valued latent reasoning baselines, particularly on advanced mathematical tasks.
papers.summary: Sampling several chain-of-thought rationales can surface correct answers a single attempt misses, but repeated autoregressive generation of long rationales is costly, and existing continuous latent reasoning methods condition every answer sample on one point-valued rationale, limiting the diversity of paths explored. Rationale distribution distillation (`RDD`) trains a conditional flow over fixed-length latent sequences by distilling from multiple textual reasoning paths, enlarging the distillation targets through within-query mixup that interpolates between complete latent rationales for the same query; the flow generates the whole latent sequence non-autoregressively and a frozen language model decodes answers from the sampled rationale context. **The resulting distributional reasoner achieves higher answer coverage than the point-valued latent reasoning baselines evaluated**, with the largest gains on advanced mathematical tasks.

papers.title: RCCM: Diagnosing Gains and Harms in Reasoning-Prompt Transfer
papers.abstract: A reasoning prompt can improve one deployment and degrade another. RCCM (Reasoning-Control Capability Mismatch) examines these reversals by pairing answers to the same questions with records of how generation ends. Across five open-weight deployments and nine strategies, aggregate accuracy hides substantial question-level gains and harms; a common-budget MATH500 evaluation examines transfer on a separate sample. On 60 additional questions, concise reasoning improves Phi's automatic answer matching at a 2,048-token cap across three collections, but sharply reduces Qwen's. Author-reviewed final-answer commitments give a smaller, statistically unresolved Phi gain. Reserving an answer stage also improves matching, with additional input and call costs. These results show why a prompt benefit must be interpreted alongside its execution and evaluation: matching a reference answer need not mean delivering it, and an apparent compression benefit may admit another explanation. RCCM records this evidence for reproducible transfer comparisons.
papers.summary: A reasoning prompt that helps one deployment can degrade another. Reasoning-Control Capability Mismatch (`RCCM`) examines such reversals by pairing answers to the same questions with records of how generation ends, across five open-weight deployments and nine strategies, with a common-budget `MATH500` evaluation of transfer on a separate sample. Aggregate accuracy hides substantial question-level gains and harms: **on 60 additional questions, concise reasoning improves `Phi`'s automatic answer matching at a 2,048-token cap across three collections but sharply reduces `Qwen`'s**, author-reviewed final-answer commitments give a smaller, statistically unresolved gain for `Phi`, and reserving a separate answer stage improves matching at additional input and call cost. The authors argue a prompt benefit must be interpreted alongside its execution and evaluation, since matching a reference answer need not mean delivering it, and an apparent compression benefit may admit another explanation.

papers.title: SPARS: A Stability-Plasticity-Aware Region Selection Framework for Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Continual learning aims to acquire new knowledge while retaining previously learned knowledge. However, updating shared parameters when learning new tasks often overwrites existing knowledge, causing catastrophic forgetting. Memory replay methods mitigate catastrophic forgetting but rely on previous samples, raising privacy, memory, and scalability concerns. On the other hand, parameter isolation-based methods preserve learned knowledge but may limit knowledge transfer, whereas regularization promotes adaptability but remains susceptible to interference between old and new tasks. To maintain the stability-plasticity trade-off, this paper proposes Stability-Plasticity-Aware Region Selection (SPARS), a replay-free hybrid framework combining global parameter isolation with localized parameter regularization. SPARS estimates parameter importance using either the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) or a novel Confidence Score (CS) estimator that leverages logit sensitivity and achieves comparable performance to FIM without requiring labelled data. Based on parameter importance, SPARS partitions parameters into three importance-aware regions namely, winning, neighboring, and non-important parameter regions. Each region receives a different adaptation strategy: selective freezing, soft regularization, or unrestricted learning based on its role in the stability-plasticity trade-off. To mitigate classifier bias in class-incremental learning, we employ Quadratic Discriminant Analysis to improve performance on previously learned classes .Experiments on CIFAR-10 and TinyImageNet demonstrate consistent improvement in average incremental accuracy over existing isolation- and regularization-based methods across task- and class-incremental learning. On TinyImageNet, SPARS achieves the best performance with 6% improvement for class-incremental learning while retaining over 60% of parameters for future tasks.
papers.summary: Continual learning systems overwrite old knowledge when they update shared parameters for new tasks, and replay-based fixes require storing past samples, which raises privacy and memory concerns. `SPARS` is a replay-free hybrid that scores parameter importance with either the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) or a new label-free Confidence Score estimator based on logit sensitivity, then splits parameters into winning, neighboring, and non-important regions that are respectively frozen, softly regularized, or left free to learn. Quadratic Discriminant Analysis is used to counter classifier bias in class-incremental learning. On `CIFAR-10` and `TinyImageNet` it beats existing isolation- and regularization-based methods, with **a 6% class-incremental gain on `TinyImageNet` while keeping over 60% of parameters free for future tasks**.

papers.title: Neural Wasserstein Splines: Representation-Invariant Second-Order Priors for Trajectory Inference
papers.abstract: Population dynamics are often observed only as unpaired snapshots, which leave the evolution between measurements underdetermined. Second-order regularization can constrain it, but a penalty on the accelerations of sampled particles is a prior on joint particle paths, and different particle representations of the same marginal curve can have different acceleration costs. We therefore introduce Neural Wasserstein Splines (NWSP), a sample-based method that learns a continuous population curve under a Wasserstein smoothness prior. A neural network maps latent variables to the control points of a cubic spline in time, so samples at any time come from the spline basis without numerical integration. We project the generator's velocity onto gradients of a finite dictionary of scalar potentials and differentiate this measure-dependent projection in time, obtaining a finite-dimensional surrogate for the intrinsic Wasserstein acceleration, trained jointly with distributional fit losses. For a fixed dictionary and ridge parameter, we prove that the population penalty depends only on the marginal curve and bound its sensitivity to moment-estimation errors. Learned potentials (NWSP-N) sharpen acceleration estimates. On various synthetic and single-cell benchmarks, NWSP is highly competitive with transport and flow-based methods, ranking in the top two in 11 of 16 settings. The penalty improves on an unregularized spline in 13 of 16 settings and, while competitive with a particle-acceleration penalty, adds provable representation invariance.
papers.summary: Trajectory inference from unpaired population snapshots, such as single-cell measurements taken at different times, is underdetermined, and the usual acceleration penalty on sampled particle paths depends on which particle representation is chosen for the same marginal curve. Neural Wasserstein Splines (`NWSP`) train a network that maps latent variables to the control points of a cubic spline in time, so samples at any time come straight from the spline basis without numerical integration, and regularize with a finite-dimensional surrogate for Wasserstein acceleration obtained by projecting the velocity onto gradients of a dictionary of scalar potentials. For a fixed dictionary and ridge parameter, the penalty is proven to depend only on the marginal curve, with bounded sensitivity to moment-estimation errors. Across synthetic and single-cell benchmarks, **`NWSP` ranks in the top two in 11 of 16 settings**, and the penalty improves on an unregularized spline in 13 of 16.

papers.title: Occupancy Modeling via Drifting: One-Step Generation Enables Direct Policy Extraction
papers.abstract: The growing interest in behavior foundation models, combined with recent advancements in generative modeling, has led to an appealing recipe for reinforcement learning from unlabeled data: pre-train a generative model to model occupancies, i.e., discounted state visitations, on reward-free trajectories, such that a policy can be easily extracted once a small reward-labeled dataset becomes available. We decompose this recipe along three axes: (i) the degree to which the multi-modal structure of occupancies must be captured, (ii) the class of generative model, and (iii) the method used for policy extraction. Along each axis, we consider existing choices, propose simpler alternatives, and validate each decision experimentally. This analysis culminates in a novel, streamlined method that leverages drifting, a modern one-step generative sampler, to model the occupancy. We show that this enables policy extraction via direct differentiation through the occupancy model, and bypasses the need for critic distillation. Overall, we observe that this nimble setup leads to improvements in performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.summary: Pre-training a generative model of occupancies, the discounted state visitation distributions along reward-free trajectories, lets a policy be extracted later from a small reward-labeled dataset, but the design space for this recipe is large. The analysis decomposes it along three axes: how much multi-modal structure the occupancy model must capture, which class of generative model to use, and how to extract the policy, testing simpler alternatives at each step. The resulting method uses drifting, a one-step generative sampler, to model occupancies, which allows **policy extraction by differentiating directly through the occupancy model** and removes the need for critic distillation. This streamlined setup improves performance on standard benchmarks.

papers.title: Frustratingly Easy Majority Voting Using Length Conditioning
papers.abstract: Majority Voting (MV) is a simple and widely used strategy which improves the reasoning accuracy of Large Language Models (LLMs) by allocating additional inference-time computation. Specifically, in MV multiple Chain-of-Thoughts (CoTs) are independently sampled and the most frequent final answer is selected. In this work, we propose Length-Conditioned Majority Voting (LCMV), a Test-Time Training approach which improves MV leveraging an empirical observation that has recently been established in several studies: longer CoTs tend to be associated with a lower probability of correctness. We formulate this inductive bias as a length-conditioned prior probability, which is modeled by a simple logistic function. Moreover, we adapt this prior at test time using only unlabeled testing data and without fine-tuning the LLM. Finally, the adapted prior is used to weight the vote of each sampled answer. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and reasoning benchmarks show that LCMV consistently improves over both standard MV and existing length-based and confidence-based aggregation strategies, while retaining the simplicity and model-agnostic nature of MV. Our code is available at: https://github.com/aimagelab/LCMV.
papers.summary: Majority voting (MV) improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by sampling several chain-of-thought (CoT) traces and selecting the most common final answer, but it treats every sample equally. Length-Conditioned Majority Voting (`LCMV`) exploits the established observation that longer CoTs are less likely to be correct, modeling this as a length-conditioned prior with a simple logistic function and adapting the prior at test time on unlabeled test data without fine-tuning the LLM. Each sampled answer's vote is then weighted by the adapted prior. Across multiple LLMs and reasoning benchmarks, **`LCMV` consistently beats standard MV as well as existing length- and confidence-based aggregation strategies** while staying model-agnostic.

papers.title: On the Limits of Representation-Based Test-Time Adaptation for Multimodal LLMs
papers.abstract: Vision-language models suffer significant accuracy drops under common corruptions. While test-time adaptation (TTA) successfully mitigates these shifts in CLIP-like contrastive models, its application to generative multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remains underexplored and uniquely challenging due to their sequential token generation. In this work, we demonstrate that representation-based TTA fails to recover performance in MLLMs. Our experiments reveal that even when violating standard TTA assumptions by leveraging target data offline, sample-blind feature alignment recovers only marginal accuracy. We attribute this failure to the nature of corruption shifts: unlike CLIP-like architectures, which benefit from a shared domain-shift direction within a single pooled classification embedding, MLLM visual token sequence shifts are nearly orthogonal and span the full embedding space.These findings bound what any sample-blind, position-shared correction at a single encoder site can achieve, establishing that representation-space interventions alone might be insufficient to ensure corruption robustness in MLLMs.
papers.summary: Vision-language models lose substantial accuracy under common image corruptions, and while test-time adaptation (TTA) recovers much of that loss in `CLIP`-style contrastive models, its use for generative multimodal large language models (MLLMs) is complicated by sequential token generation. Experiments show that representation-based TTA fails for MLLMs: **even with offline access to target data, sample-blind feature alignment recovers only marginal accuracy**. The explanation offered is that `CLIP`-like models benefit from a shared domain-shift direction in a single pooled embedding, whereas corruption shifts in an MLLM's visual token sequence are nearly orthogonal and span the full embedding space. This bounds what any sample-blind, position-shared correction at a single encoder site can achieve, suggesting representation-space interventions alone may not deliver corruption robustness for MLLMs.

papers.title: Few-Shot Adaptation for Anomalous Sound Detection at Low False-Positive Rate
papers.abstract: Reliable fault detection is crucial for industrial machinery in large-scale facilities, where unexpected failures can cause costly downtime and production interruptions. Although acoustic monitoring provides a scalable solution for machine condition monitoring, its deployment is often constrained by high false-positive rates. We propose a two-step approach to automatic anomalous sound detection: first, when only normal operating audio samples are available, a regularized unsupervised model is deployed; then, after the first machine fault, a few-shot adaptation strategy exploits the anomalous samples acquired during the fault to improve the system. This adaptation increases the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPR) from 23.0 to 64.0 and improves detection in the low false-positive-rate region, with the partial area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (pAUROC) increasing from 39.6 to 72.8. We also show that covariance regularization improves both prediction accuracy and training stability in the unsupervised model. These results provide a practical strategy for acoustic anomaly detection systems, enabling improved accuracy and reduced false alarms.
papers.summary: Acoustic monitoring is a scalable way to detect faults in industrial machinery, but high false-positive rates limit deployment. The proposed two-step approach first deploys a regularized unsupervised model trained only on normal operating audio, then, after the first real fault, applies a few-shot adaptation strategy that uses the anomalous samples captured during that fault. Adaptation **raises the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPR) from 23.0 to 64.0** and lifts the partial area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (pAUROC) in the low false-positive region from 39.6 to 72.8. Covariance regularization is also shown to improve both accuracy and training stability of the unsupervised model.

papers.title: Universal Sample-Based Embeddings of Higher-Order Objects
papers.abstract: Neural networks operate naturally on finite-dimensional vectors, yet many problems require reasoning about higher-order objects such as distributions, functions, and graphs. Such objects capture relationships within a ground set and rarely admit an explicit compact representation. Moreover, we typically want a compact representation not of a single higher-order object but of an entire family of such objects, including members unseen during training. While a few approaches exist for particular object types, none is designed to work across object types. We propose a unified framework that represents any higher-order object as a fixed-size embedding vector learned over a family of such objects. An encoder maps an object, seen only through a finite set of samples, to an embedding, and a domain-specific decoder supplies the training signal by modeling the object conditioned on that embedding. Since the encoder works only from samples, one architecture serves different object types. Because the decoder is a model already suited to single instances of the object type, the framework inherits that model's native operations and inductive biases. We instantiate the framework on distributions, functions, and graphs. In each case we show that a single trained model represents an entire family and generalizes to members unseen during training. Furthermore, we demonstrate the downstream utility of these embeddings: interpolating distributions in embedding space, solving differential equations in embedding space, and predicting unseen edges from a graph's embedding.
papers.summary: Neural networks work on fixed-size vectors, but distributions, functions, and graphs are higher-order objects that rarely have compact explicit representations, and existing approaches handle only one object type at a time. The proposed framework maps any such object, observed only through a finite set of samples, to a fixed-size embedding using a shared encoder, while a domain-specific decoder that models the object conditioned on the embedding provides the training signal and contributes its native inductive biases. Instantiated on distributions, functions, and graphs, **a single trained model represents an entire family of objects and generalizes to members unseen in training**. The embeddings support downstream uses such as interpolating distributions, solving differential equations in embedding space, and predicting unseen edges from a graph's embedding.

papers.title: Multimodal Medical Image Parsing with Task-Specific Low-Rank Adapters
papers.abstract: Adapting a single vision-language model to medical image parsing requires training choices that reflect the demands of each task. We study task-specific adaptation with Qwen3.5-9B for FLARE 2026 Task 3, covering six task families and seven imaging modalities. Our system couples a shared, frozen 4-bit backbone with LoRA adapters selected from the input question. We customize adapter ranks and prompts, rebalance rare classification targets, and supplement regression training with dermatology classification examples. On the fixed internal holdout, the task-specific adapters achieve a dataset-macro balanced accuracy of 0.7791 for classification, a dataset-macro micro-F1 of 0.6286 for multi-label classification, a counting mean absolute error (MAE) of 11.73, a dataset-macro detection F1 of 0.8914, a dataset-macro regression MAE of 9.78, and a report-generation CRIMSON score of 0.8204. On the organizer's 1,703-example hidden-validation set, the submitted system achieves 0.8496 classification balanced accuracy, 0.5338 sample-averaged multi-label F1, and 14.5950 regression MAE. The final 30.1 GB container averages 3.1 seconds per case, including model loading, and produces identical outputs across repeated verification runs. The benefits vary across tasks, supporting the use of task-specific adapter configurations and image budgets within a shared medical vision-language model. Code is available at https://github.com/TahaSabir0/FLARE26-Hexapus.
papers.summary: Adapting one vision-language model to many medical image parsing tasks requires per-task training choices. For `FLARE 2026` Task 3, spanning six task families and seven imaging modalities, the system keeps a frozen 4-bit `Qwen3.5-9B` backbone and routes each input question to a task-specific `LoRA` adapter, with customized adapter ranks and prompts, rebalanced rare classification targets, and dermatology classification examples added to regression training. On the organizer's 1,703-example hidden-validation set it reaches **0.8496 classification balanced accuracy**, 0.5338 sample-averaged multi-label F1, and 14.5950 regression mean absolute error (MAE). The 30.1 GB container averages 3.1 seconds per case including model loading and produces identical outputs across repeated runs.

papers.title: Beyond Benchmark Accuracy: A Diagnostic Test for LLM Chemical Prediction
papers.abstract: LLMs have achieved strong performance on chemical prediction benchmarks. However, existing evaluation methods typically provide target entity identity information directly, making it difficult to determine whether model predictions arise from transferable structure-property reasoning capabilities or rely on target-related contextual information or memory retrieval. We propose the Identity-Blinded Reasoning Diagnostic framework to evaluate chemical prediction models when target entity identity information is hidden. In this framework, the target is no longer directly defined by its entity identity, but instead by a known source entity and an explicit structural edit operation. This setting preserves the information required to determine the target while reducing the opportunity for models to access target identity cues. We evaluate this framework across six tasks spanning odor prediction, molecular property prediction, retrosynthesis, and reaction yield prediction. The results show that models generally achieve better prediction performance when source and target entity properties are consistent. Providing explicit source entity labels further strengthens this dependence. Moreover, while keeping the target entity, structural change, and ground-truth label unchanged, replacing only the source entity label causes some model predictions to systematically shift toward the substituted source labels. These results indicate that high benchmark accuracy in chemical prediction tasks does not necessarily imply that LLMs possess reliable structure-property reasoning capabilities. Our diagnostic framework provides a controlled evaluation approach for testing whether models can genuinely update predictions according to entity changes. The framework can be extended to other AI for Science tasks, particularly those where targets can be defined through transformations of known entities.
papers.summary: Strong large language model (LLM) scores on chemical prediction benchmarks may come from memorized target identities rather than structure-property reasoning, because standard evaluations hand the model the target entity directly. The Identity-Blinded Reasoning Diagnostic framework instead defines each target as a known source entity plus an explicit structural edit, preserving the information needed to answer while hiding identity cues. Across six tasks covering odor prediction, molecular property prediction, retrosynthesis, and reaction yield, models do better when source and target properties agree, explicit source labels strengthen this dependence, and **swapping only the source entity's label, with target, edit, and ground truth unchanged, systematically shifts some models' predictions toward the substituted label**. The framework is offered as a controlled test of whether models genuinely update predictions in response to entity changes, extensible to other AI for Science tasks.

papers.title: When Non-Adversarial Noise Hurts Learning: Benchmarking Skill Self-Evolution in Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model agents increasingly improve by distilling experience into reusable skills, but errors in that experience can persist in learned rules and affect later tasks. Existing evaluations largely examine clean learning or perturbations encountered after skills are frozen, leaving robustness during self-evolution insufficiently understood. We introduce RSE-Bench, to our knowledge the first benchmark for evaluating skill self-evolution under ordinary, non-adversarial noise. It spans four domains and six benchmarks, with controlled perturbations to instructions, environmental evidence, execution records, and outcome--record pairings that preserve the underlying tasks and native scoring rules. The protocol separates noise during learning from input-side noise at evaluation, testing frozen skill stores on held-out tasks. We also introduce \textsc{RSEClaw}, a method-agnostic framework supporting consistent noise injection and process diagnostics of actual exposure and skill updates. Across three methods and two backbones, noisy learning retains only $25.5\%$--$42.1\%$ of the aggregate gain achieved by clean self-evolution, depending on the noise type. Perturbations confined to execution records and outcome--record pairings cause average losses comparable to input-side noise, despite leaving the original executions and evaluations intact. Diagnostics further identify differences in candidate skill text that coexist with small changes in mean held-out performance.
papers.summary: Large language model agents increasingly distill their experience into reusable skills, but errors in that experience can become baked into learned rules and affect later tasks. `RSE-Bench` evaluates skill self-evolution under ordinary, non-adversarial noise across four domains and six benchmarks, with controlled perturbations to instructions, environmental evidence, execution records, and outcome-record pairings that leave the underlying tasks and scoring intact. The protocol separates noise during learning from input noise at evaluation by testing frozen skill stores on held-out tasks, and a companion framework, `RSEClaw`, provides method-agnostic noise injection plus diagnostics of actual exposure and skill updates. Across three methods and two backbones, **noisy learning retains only 25.5% to 42.1% of the aggregate gain from clean self-evolution**, and perturbing execution records or outcome-record pairings alone hurts about as much as input-side noise even though the original executions and evaluations are untouched.

papers.title: CARD: Closing the Teacher-Student Loop for Adversarial Robustness Distillation
papers.abstract: Adversarial robustness distillation typically treats a robust teacher as a fixed knowledge source and transfers robustness to a compact student in a one-way manner. This paradigm terminates teacher-student interaction once the student is distilled, thereby discarding potentially useful feedback from the distilled student. However, exploiting such feedback is nontrivial because indiscriminate weak-to-strong transfer may propagate student errors to the teacher. To address this issue, we propose Cyclic Adversarial Robustness Distillation (CARD), a closed-loop framework that turns the distilled student into a feedback source for refining the robust teacher and subsequently transfers the teacher gains back to the same student. CARD first performs strong-to-weak adversarial distillation and then uses reliability-enhanced student feedback to refine the robust teacher. The refinement combines inverse adversarial student feedback with teacher-student discrepancy maximization, after which the refined teacher is used to continue training the same student under the unchanged base distillation objective. We further establish a sample-level sufficient condition for reliable weak-to-strong feedback transfer and derive a distribution-level upper bound on the refined teacher's risk. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet-10 across multiple teacher-student architectures and base distillation methods show that CARD improves adversarial robustness in most evaluated settings while generally preserving clean accuracy. These results show that the distilled student can provide useful feedback to the teacher, enabling robustness transfer to proceed beyond the conventional one-way teacher-to-student paradigm.
papers.summary: Adversarial robustness distillation normally transfers robustness one way from a fixed robust teacher to a compact student, discarding any feedback the student could provide, and naive weak-to-strong transfer risks propagating student errors into the teacher. Cyclic Adversarial Robustness Distillation (`CARD`) first distills strong-to-weak, then refines the teacher with reliability-enhanced student feedback that combines inverse adversarial examples from the student with teacher-student discrepancy maximization, and finally continues training the same student from the refined teacher under the unchanged base objective. A sample-level sufficient condition for reliable weak-to-strong feedback and a distribution-level bound on the refined teacher's risk are also derived. On `CIFAR-10`, `CIFAR-100`, and `TinyImageNet-10` across several architectures and base distillation methods, **`CARD` improves adversarial robustness in most settings while generally preserving clean accuracy**.

papers.title: Not All Criteria Matter: Importance-Aware Criteria Weighting for Rubric-Based LLM Evaluation
papers.abstract: Rubric-based evaluation assesses the responses of large language models (LLMs) by aggregating the verification results of explicit criteria, yet not all criteria matter equally. However, existing methods commonly aggregate the verification results with uniform weighting, which assigns minor and overlapping criteria the same weight as essential ones and thus produces misleading evaluation scores. Although some methods prompt an LLM to directly assign weights, direct weighting requires a holistic judgment over all criteria that LLMs struggle to make reliably. To address these limitations, we propose Importance-Aware Criteria Weighting (ICW), which derives the weights of criteria from pairwise importance comparisons made by an LLM. Specifically, ICW transforms the holistic judgment over all criteria into a series of pairwise importance comparisons, checks and revises inconsistent comparisons, and derives the weights from the principal eigenvector of the comparison matrix. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ICW consistently outperforms uniform weighting and competitive weighting methods, and translates into better policy models in downstream reinforcement learning.
papers.summary: Rubric-based evaluation scores a large language model (LLM) response by verifying explicit criteria and aggregating the results, but uniform weighting gives minor or overlapping criteria the same influence as essential ones, and asking an LLM to assign weights directly demands a holistic judgment it makes unreliably. Importance-Aware Criteria Weighting (`ICW`) replaces that holistic judgment with a series of pairwise importance comparisons by an LLM, checks and revises inconsistent comparisons, and derives weights from the principal eigenvector of the comparison matrix. Experiments show **`ICW` consistently outperforms uniform weighting and competing weighting methods**, and the improved scores yield better policy models when used in downstream reinforcement learning.

papers.title: Beyond DFT electronic band structures via dual-space orbital learning
papers.abstract: Accurate electronic band structures are essential for predicting material properties, but high-fidelity calculations are computationally demanding. We introduce O-kRystal, a dual-space orbital-learning framework that uses a lower-cost Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) calculation as both an energy baseline and a source of structured orbital information. Combining PBE band energies with real- and reciprocal-space orbital matrices, O-kRystal predicts higher-level corrections for individual electronic states as a function of crystal momentum and spin. For states within 5 eV of the band-edge midpoint, it predicts Heyd-Scuseria-Ernzerhof (HSE06) band energies with a mean absolute error of $0.171 \pm 0.009$ eV across nearly 6,000 three-dimensional materials spanning insulating, metallic, magnetic, and nonmagnetic systems. On a separate benchmark of six strongly correlated materials, it reduces the corresponding PBE band-energy MAE by 68.7% and resolves orbital-dependent changes in the relative placement of transition-metal d and ligand p states. Despite training only at high-symmetry points, it maintains comparable accuracy at unseen points along band paths and reconstructs HSE06 densities of states from dense Brillouin-zone predictions. Finally, training O-kRystal on $G_0W_0$ quasiparticle energies for two-dimensional materials demonstrates its applicability across levels of theory and the potential of orbital learning for higher-fidelity, momentum-resolved electronic-structure prediction beyond density functional theory.
papers.summary: High-fidelity electronic band structures are expensive to compute, so `O-kRystal` learns to correct cheap Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) calculations toward higher levels of theory, using PBE band energies together with real- and reciprocal-space orbital matrices to predict per-state corrections as a function of crystal momentum and spin. For states within 5 eV of the band-edge midpoint, it predicts Heyd-Scuseria-Ernzerhof (`HSE06`) band energies with **a mean absolute error of 0.171 eV across nearly 6,000 three-dimensional materials** spanning insulating, metallic, magnetic, and nonmagnetic systems. On six strongly correlated materials it cuts the PBE band-energy error by 68.7% and resolves orbital-dependent shifts between transition-metal d and ligand p states, and it generalizes from high-symmetry training points to unseen points along band paths. Training on G0W0 quasiparticle energies for two-dimensional materials shows the approach transfers across levels of theory.

papers.title: MolHop: Scaffold-Hopping Molecular Design with Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Molecular design is often formulated as an optimization problem over existing molecular spaces. However, molecular optimization and the discovery of structurally distinct replacement molecules represent two fundamentally different search problems. LLM-based molecular design agents typically perform the former, conducting local refinement within the neighborhood of existing structures to improve target properties through structural modifications. In contrast, the latter requires exploration of a broader chemical space to discover molecules with entirely different scaffolds while preserving the functional characteristics of reference molecules. We propose MolHop, an agentic framework for cross-scaffold molecular discovery that enables models to navigate and edit within a pre-organized chemical space. MolHop organizes approximately 1.6 million molecular scaffolds from commercial molecules into a coarse-to-fine hierarchical action space. The agent selects new exploration regions through scaffold navigation actions and adjusts candidate properties through molecular editing. The framework maintains historical trajectory memory to support long-horizon search processes. On drug molecule and commercial compound tasks, connecting Grok-4.6 and DeepSeek-Flash-V4.1 to the MolHop framework substantially improves their cross-scaffold joint success rates. We develop MolHop-9B through agentic reinforcement learning, and MolHop-9B outperforms generative baselines including GPT-5.6-sol, Claude-5-Opus, and Gemini-3.1-Pro, while generating candidate molecules with larger scaffold differences from the reference molecules. These results demonstrate that effective molecular discovery beyond the traditional optimization paradigm requires structured chemical and action spaces, enabling agents to explore new structural regions rather than merely refine existing molecules.
papers.summary: Optimizing a molecule locally and finding a structurally different replacement with the same function are distinct search problems, and large language model (LLM) molecular design agents mostly do the former. `MolHop` organizes roughly 1.6 million scaffolds from commercial molecules into a coarse-to-fine hierarchical action space where an agent navigates to new scaffold regions, edits candidate molecules to tune properties, and keeps a trajectory memory for long-horizon search. Plugging `Grok-4.6` and `DeepSeek-Flash-V4.1` into the framework substantially raises cross-scaffold joint success rates on drug and commercial compound tasks, and a 9B model trained with agentic reinforcement learning, `MolHop-9B`, **outperforms generative baselines including `GPT-5.6-sol`, `Claude-5-Opus`, and `Gemini-3.1-Pro`** while producing candidates with larger scaffold differences from the reference molecules.

papers.title: Convergence Rates of Gaussian Process Thompson Sampling for Efficient Global Optimization
papers.abstract:
Efficient global optimization aims to identify a global optimum of an expensive black-box function within a limited evaluation budget $N$. We investigate the convergence rates of Gaussian process Thompson sampling (GP-TS) under noiseless observations, assuming a fixed objective function in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). For Mat'ern kernels with smoothness parameter $
u$ in dimension $d$, we establish a worst-case expected simple-regret upper bound of $O(N^{-
u/d}\sqrt{\log N})$ for both discrete GP-TS on sufficiently fine grids and its continuous counterpart. For the continuous implementation, we develop a nested-grid argument to control posterior sample paths over the entire domain. We further establish matching lower bounds of $\Omega(N^{-5/2}\sqrt{\log N})$ for both implementations under a fixed one-dimensional Mat'ern-$5/2$ kernel, demonstrating that the logarithmic penalty is intrinsic to standard GP-TS in this setting. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Gaussian Process Capped Thompson Sampling (GP-CTS), which caps posterior sample paths using a valid RKHS norm upper bound while preserving optimism. This modification successfully eliminates the logarithmic penalty and achieves the minimax-optimal rate $\Theta(N^{-
u/d})$ for both discrete and continuous implementations.
papers.summary: Efficient global optimization seeks the optimum of an expensive black-box function within a fixed evaluation budget N, and Gaussian process Thompson sampling (`GP-TS`) is a standard approach whose convergence rates are analyzed here under noiseless observations for a fixed objective in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). For Matérn kernels with smoothness ν in dimension d, both discrete GP-TS on sufficiently fine grids and continuous GP-TS achieve a worst-case expected simple-regret bound of order N^(-ν/d) times the square root of log N, with a nested-grid argument controlling posterior sample paths over the whole domain in the continuous case. A matching lower bound for a one-dimensional Matérn-5/2 kernel shows **the logarithmic penalty is intrinsic to standard GP-TS**. Gaussian Process Capped Thompson Sampling (`GP-CTS`), which caps posterior sample paths using a valid RKHS norm upper bound while preserving optimism, removes the penalty and attains the minimax-optimal rate of order N^(-ν/d).

papers.title: MemDuet: Learning Dual-Process Memory for Long-Context Reasoning
papers.abstract: Reasoning over infinitely long documents is becoming a reality with recurrent memory agents. However, increasing context length exacerbates the trade-off between reasoning performance and inference efficiency. Inspired by Kahneman's account of fast and slow thinking, we propose MemDuet, a dual-process memory framework that learns to coordinate a small language model for fast, parallel evidence selection from raw context chunks (System 1) with a large language model for memory-update verification and memory updates in document order (System 2). We train MemDuet in three stages: supervised fine-tuning of System 1 for evidence selection, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) of System 2 for verification and memory rewriting, and joint optimization of both policies to coordinate selection and updating for long-context reasoning. Experiments on diverse long-context reasoning benchmarks (RULER-HQA, LongBench v2, and 2WikiMultiHopQA) demonstrate a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off as context length grows. Averaged across evaluation settings on the three datasets, MemDuet achieves an end-to-end inference speedup of 9.74x and an output-token reduction of 73.91% relative to RL-MemAgent.
papers.summary: Recurrent memory agents can reason over arbitrarily long documents, but longer contexts worsen the trade-off between accuracy and inference cost. `MemDuet` pairs a small language model that selects evidence from raw context chunks quickly and in parallel (System 1) with a large language model that verifies and rewrites memory in document order (System 2), trained in three stages: supervised fine-tuning of the selector, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) of the verifier and memory updater, and joint optimization of both policies. On `RULER-HQA`, `LongBench v2`, and `2WikiMultiHopQA` the accuracy-efficiency trade-off improves as context grows, with **a 9.74x end-to-end inference speedup and 73.91% fewer output tokens relative to `RL-MemAgent`** averaged across evaluation settings.

papers.title: SAM3RL: Memory Control via Reinforcement Learning for Visual Object Tracking
papers.abstract: Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) is a foundation model for image and video segmentation that sets the state of the art in visual object tracking. Its tracker, inherited from SAM 2, stores information from past frames in a memory bank, managed by a simple First-In-First-Out rule, allowing temporal consistency in complex videos. Several recent methods improve SAM 2 with hand-crafted memory update rules, each targeting a specific failure mode, such as distractors, occlusions, or object motion. However, their gains transfer only partially to the stronger SAM 3 backbone. We instead present a more general, data-driven approach that frames memory control as a sequential decision-making task. SAM3RL is an extension of the SAM 3 tracker with a lightweight memory controller, trained by reinforcement learning, that decides which frames enter the memory bank in order to maximize tracking performance. SAM3RL sets a new state of the art on 10 of 12 tracking and video object segmentation benchmarks, outperforming all hand-crafted rules without any runtime overhead. The same approach applied to SAM 2 gives SAM2RL, which outperforms hand-crafted rules on 9 of the 12 benchmarks, showing the generality of our method across model generations.
papers.summary: `SAM 3`, the state-of-the-art foundation model for image and video segmentation, tracks objects with a memory bank managed by a simple first-in-first-out rule inherited from `SAM 2`, and the hand-crafted memory update rules designed to fix specific `SAM 2` failure modes transfer only partially to the stronger backbone. `SAM3RL` instead frames memory control as a sequential decision problem and adds a lightweight controller, trained with reinforcement learning, that decides which frames enter the memory bank to maximize tracking performance. It sets **a new state of the art on 10 of 12 tracking and video object segmentation benchmarks**, beating all hand-crafted rules with no runtime overhead, and the same recipe applied to `SAM 2` yields `SAM2RL`, which wins on 9 of the 12.

papers.title: To Reason but Not to Stop: Understanding and Recovering Pruned Large Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Weight pruning can degrade the accuracy of large reasoning models (LRMs), yet it remains unclear whether it damages reasoning itself. We find that much of this degradation stems from a failure to stop rather than to reason. As sparsity increases, pruned LRMs increasingly fail to terminate within the token budget, often after the correct answer has appeared in their reasoning, instead falling into repetitive loops, even though they still recognize where the dense model would stop. We further find that the hidden-state difference between terminating and looping continuations is consistent across pruned checkpoints, suggesting a shared direction associated with committing to an answer. Building on this, we propose Termination-Guided Activation Steering (TGAS), a training-free method that adds this direction to the residual stream at inference time. Across six LRMs, three pruning pipelines, and math and code benchmarks, TGAS improves termination and overall accuracy while reducing repetitive reasoning and generation length, showing that this failure is actionable.
papers.summary: Weight pruning hurts the accuracy of large reasoning models (LRMs), and the analysis finds the loss comes mostly from a failure to stop rather than a failure to reason: as sparsity rises, pruned models increasingly exhaust their token budget in repetitive loops, often after the correct answer has already appeared, even though they still recognize where the dense model would stop. The hidden-state difference between terminating and looping continuations is consistent across pruned checkpoints, pointing to a shared direction associated with committing to an answer. Termination-Guided Activation Steering (`TGAS`) adds this direction to the residual stream at inference time with no training. Across six LRMs, three pruning pipelines, and math and code benchmarks, **`TGAS` improves both termination and overall accuracy** while cutting repetitive reasoning and generation length.

papers.title: MorphingNet: Symbolic Regression Where the Network Is the Formula
papers.abstract: We introduce MorphingNet, a network for symbolic regression (SR) whose units change their function continuously. Instead of searching over expressions built from a fixed operator library, MorphingNet trains the form of each function as a parameter, so SR becomes one continuous optimization problem. Its units are either pole-free rational functions or complex exponential--logarithm functions, which move between exponentials, sinusoids, damped oscillations, power laws and logarithms as their parameters change. The network is a readable formula at every step of training, and no operator library is needed to train it; a structure-recovery step afterwards rewrites the trained formula into short elementary expressions. Training is dense linear algebra, so it is GPU-friendly and scales to large data. MorphingNet achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on SRBench, recovers most generating formulas on synthetic benchmarks, and on large data is up to two orders of magnitude faster than the strongest search method. By turning the search for a formula into the training of a network, MorphingNet offers a new paradigm for SR and for scientific discovery from data.
papers.summary: Symbolic regression (SR) usually searches over discrete expressions built from a fixed operator library. `MorphingNet` instead makes the functional form of each network unit a continuous trainable parameter: units are pole-free rational functions or complex exponential-logarithm functions that move among exponentials, sinusoids, damped oscillations, power laws, and logarithms, so the network is a readable formula at every training step and a post-hoc structure-recovery step rewrites it into short elementary expressions. Training reduces to dense linear algebra, making it GPU-friendly and scalable to large data. It reaches **state-of-the-art accuracy on `SRBench`**, recovers most generating formulas on synthetic benchmarks, and on large data is up to two orders of magnitude faster than the strongest search-based method.

papers.title: Does Machine Translation Retain Media Bias?
papers.abstract:
Within the most recent two decades, machine translation (MT) has been advanced from a research area to a mature, deployed technology for prose text and most language pairs. However, language has different dimensions of meaning, and the alluded progress has primarily been demonstrated for propositional meaning.
  In this small exploratory study, we investigate whether one type of affective meaning, namely different types of linguistically expressed media bias, are retained under automatic translation for two language pairs, English and German as the source languages, and Bulgarian as the target language. We evaluate four state-of-the-art translation methods to answer the question whether and to what degree a loss of non-neutral language (specifically, 27 types of media bias) can occur as a result of applying MT.
  Our empirical findings are consistent with the claim that MT does not fully retain existing news bias of its input source text, but also may add extra bias of its own. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first experimental study of MT media bias retention.
papers.summary: Machine translation (MT) is mature for propositional meaning, but whether it preserves affective dimensions of language such as media bias is largely untested. A small exploratory study checks whether 27 types of linguistically expressed media bias survive translation from English and German into Bulgarian across four state-of-the-art translation methods. The findings are consistent with **MT failing to fully retain the news bias of its source text while sometimes adding bias of its own**, and the authors describe it as the first experimental study of MT media bias retention.

papers.title: Learning Graph Energies for Finite-Time Generation
papers.abstract: Energy-based models can represent distributions over discrete structures such as molecular graphs, but an energy that is accurate at equilibrium need not yield accurate samples when the sampler stops after a fixed number of steps. We introduce finite-horizon energy learning, which adapts the acceptance energy of a Metropolis--Hastings sampler to the distribution it returns after a prescribed number of steps, with initialization, proposals, and annealing schedule held fixed. For graph generation, a frozen pretrained model supplies initialization and proposals, and a learned energy governs acceptance. A training-only discriminator scores completed samples, and coupled continuations of the accepted and rejected branches of a proposal give an acceptance-gradient estimator that is unbiased for a fixed discriminator under stated conditions, without equilibrated negative samples or differentiation through discrete states. Generation uses the learned energy in the original single-trajectory sampler, without discriminator evaluations or reranking. On twelve pairwise binary targets with exactly evaluated terminal laws, learned energies have lower median terminal total variation than the equilibrium-correct energy in every tested short-horizon setting, and than its numerically tuned scalar multiple in most settings. On MOSES, a learned two-coefficient combination of pretrained Graph Energy Matching (GEM) potentials lowers FCD by 3.7--10.5\% relative to scale-calibrated GEM at matched sampling steps, with validity gains at the shortest budget and a sub-point validity trade-off at higher budgets.
papers.summary: Energy-based models can represent distributions over discrete structures such as molecular graphs, but an energy that is correct at equilibrium need not produce good samples when a Metropolis-Hastings sampler is stopped after a fixed number of steps. The authors propose finite-horizon energy learning, which adapts the sampler's acceptance energy to the distribution it actually returns at a prescribed step budget, using a training-only discriminator on completed samples and coupled continuations of the accepted and rejected branches of each proposal to obtain an acceptance-gradient estimator that needs neither equilibrated negative samples nor differentiation through discrete states. For graph generation, a frozen pretrained model supplies initialization and proposals while the learned energy governs acceptance, and generation runs in the original single-trajectory sampler with no discriminator calls or reranking. On twelve binary targets with exactly computable terminal laws, learned energies beat the equilibrium-correct energy on median terminal total variation in every short-horizon setting, and on `MOSES` a learned two-coefficient combination of pretrained `Graph Energy Matching` (GEM) potentials **lowers `FCD` by 3.7 to 10.5% relative to scale-calibrated GEM** at matched sampling steps, with validity gains at the shortest budget.

papers.title: AtomSearch: Evidence-Grounded Tree Search for Agent Skill Optimization
papers.abstract: Agent skills adapt frozen models through editable external instructions. Revising several rules at once makes changes difficult to inspect, while judging each local edit only by its immediate score can discard useful intermediate states. We introduce AtomSearch, which keeps revision actions local while using subsequent skill states to guide search. Contrastive atomic editing links each primitive rule edit to failed and successful executions, a behavioral hypothesis, and an intended scope. Skill-State Tree Search (STS) evaluates short edit compositions and selectively retains them as executable states that can be revisited and extended. Outcome memory supplies later proposals with observed repair and regression statistics. We evaluate AtomSearch across four tasks and five target models. With deepseek-v4-flash, it exceeds SkillOpt on three of four tasks, including a 9.68-percentage-point gain on LiveMathematicianBench, and SkillOpt's final skills contain 2.3-19.7 times as many characters. In 67% of completed searches, the best validation state passes through an ancestor that was not highest-scoring at its depth. These results show how local rule edits can support the exploration of useful revision paths and yield compact skills, with additional offline evaluations used to explore alternative states.
papers.summary: Agent skills, editable external instruction files that adapt a frozen model, are hard to optimize because revising many rules at once makes changes difficult to inspect, while judging each local edit only by its immediate score can discard useful intermediate states. `AtomSearch` keeps every edit atomic, linking a single rule change to contrasting failed and successful executions, a behavioral hypothesis, and an intended scope, then uses Skill-State Tree Search (STS) to evaluate short compositions of edits and retain promising skill states that can later be revisited and extended, with an outcome memory feeding observed repair and regression statistics into subsequent proposals. Across four tasks and five target models, with `deepseek-v4-flash` it beats `SkillOpt` on three of four tasks, including **a 9.68-percentage-point gain on `LiveMathematicianBench`**, while `SkillOpt`'s final skills are 2.3 to 19.7 times longer, and in 67% of completed searches the best validation state descends from an ancestor that was not the top scorer at its depth.

papers.title: Choosing the Number of Attention Heads from Intrinsic Dimension: A Small-Scale Study
papers.abstract: The number of attention heads in a transformer is usually set by convention or grid search. We test a simple heuristic for setting it in advance: estimate the intrinsic dimension of token representations without labels, and use roughly that many heads. We estimate intrinsic dimension with a nested-dropout VAE trained on DistilBERT embeddings of WikiText-2, choosing the KL weight at the knee of the VAE's rate-distortion curve rather than by hand. This gives $k^*=9.2$ (95% CI [8.6, 9.8]). In a small 4-layer transformer trained from scratch, 10 heads and 32 heads are statistically equivalent on SST-2 and on MRPC (paired TOST over 10 seeds, $\pm1$ point margin), with 69% fewer attention parameters for the 10-head model. Training 10 heads from the start also slightly outperforms training 32 heads and pruning to 10 (0.6 points, $p=0.008$). The evidence is narrow: two classification tasks, one small architecture, no pretrained models, and no formal link between intrinsic dimension and head count. We present the result as a practical heuristic worth testing at larger scale, not as a general principle.
papers.summary: The number of attention heads in a transformer is usually fixed by convention or grid search, so this study tests whether the intrinsic dimension of token representations, estimated without labels, can set it in advance. A nested-dropout variational autoencoder trained on `DistilBERT` embeddings of `WikiText-2`, with the KL weight chosen at the knee of its rate-distortion curve rather than by hand, gives an intrinsic dimension estimate of about 9.2 with a 95% confidence interval of 8.6 to 9.8. In a 4-layer transformer trained from scratch, **10 heads and 32 heads are statistically equivalent on `SST-2` and `MRPC`** under a paired equivalence test over 10 seeds, with 69% fewer attention parameters for the 10-head model, and training with 10 heads from the start slightly beats training 32 heads and pruning to 10. The authors stress that the evidence is narrow, covering two classification tasks, one small architecture, no pretrained models, and no formal link between intrinsic dimension and head count, and present the result as a heuristic worth testing at larger scale.

papers.title: Safe-FCL: Continual Risk Awareness and Fine-Grained Safety Aggregation for Federated Continual Learning of LLMs
papers.abstract: Federated fine-tuning enables large language models (LLMs) to learn collaboratively from distributed client data, but malicious client updates can compromise global model safety. As federated tasks evolve, changing malicious update patterns challenge the ability of existing defenses to maintain reliable risk detection over time. To address this challenge, we propose Safe-FCL, a framework integrating continual risk awareness with fine-grained safety aggregation for federated continual learning of LLMs. Specifically, the Continual Risk Awareness (CRA) mechanism learns emerging risk patterns across sequential tasks and constrains detector updates using a protective subspace derived from historical features, mitigating forgetting of previously learned malicious patterns while adapting to new risks. To translate risk awareness into aggregation-level safety control, the Fine-Grained Safety Aggregation (FGSA) mechanism combines client-level risk assessments from CRA with module-level deviations from historical update behavior to adaptively regulate aggregation contributions, suppressing potentially malicious updates while minimizing unnecessary restrictions on benign updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Safe-FCL outperforms current SOTA methods, improving global-model Rule and MD-Judge scores in federated continual learning by 0.41% and 0.64%, respectively, while increasing average risk recognition accuracy by 2.01%.
papers.summary: Federated fine-tuning lets large language models (LLMs) learn from distributed client data, but malicious client updates can degrade the global model's safety, and as the sequence of federated tasks evolves the attack patterns change, which defeats static detectors. `Safe-FCL` pairs a Continual Risk Awareness (CRA) mechanism, which learns emerging risk patterns across sequential tasks while constraining detector updates to a protective subspace derived from historical features so earlier attack patterns are not forgotten, with Fine-Grained Safety Aggregation (FGSA), which combines CRA's client-level risk assessments with module-level deviations from historical update behavior to adaptively down-weight suspicious contributions without unduly restricting benign ones. In experiments it outperforms prior methods, with **average risk recognition accuracy up 2.01%** and global-model `Rule` and `MD-Judge` safety scores up 0.41% and 0.64%.

papers.title: LatentLoop: Scaling Looped MoE Models with Asymmetric Compute Allocation
papers.abstract: Looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models combine parameter reuse with sparse computation to improve performance under matched budgets. Prior work demonstrates that different loop visits can play different roles even when they share parameters. To probe the contributions of different loop visits, we learn separate residual coefficients in a model that applies a shared block twice, observing a smaller scale in the first visit. Fixed coefficient experiments show that reducing the first visit's scale preserves or improves performance, whereas the same reductions to the second hurt it. This asymmetry motivates us to explore asymmetric compute allocation. We propose \textbf{LatentLoop}, which compresses the first visit's sequence, retains full resolution in the second, and reallocates saved computation to increase the hidden size. We further learn how strongly the first visit updates the full sequence, and share MoE weights across visits while using separate attention parameters to accommodate their different sequence resolutions. Across 15 configurations spanning 1.3B--7B parameters, with the largest budget exceeding $10^{21}$ FLOPs, LatentLoop consistently lowers validation NLL. At a fitted NLL of 1.988, predicted compute savings are 19.0\% and 7.9\% relative to vanilla MoE and the looped baseline. It also improves average scores on nine benchmarks at all sizes in 0-shot and 5-shot settings. These results suggest asymmetric compute allocation is a promising direction for looped MoE models.
papers.summary: Looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models apply a shared block multiple times to combine parameter reuse with sparse computation, and prior work suggests the repeated visits play different roles despite sharing weights. By learning separate residual coefficients for a block applied twice, the authors find the first visit settles on a smaller scale, and fixed-coefficient experiments show that shrinking the first visit's contribution preserves or improves performance while the same reduction on the second visit hurts. `LatentLoop` exploits this asymmetry by compressing the sequence on the first visit, keeping full resolution on the second, and spending the saved compute on a larger hidden size, with MoE weights shared across visits but separate attention parameters to handle the different sequence resolutions. Across 15 configurations from 1.3B to 7B parameters, with the largest budget above 10^21 FLOPs, it consistently lowers validation NLL, with **predicted compute savings of 19.0% over vanilla MoE and 7.9% over the looped baseline** at a fitted NLL of 1.988, and it improves average scores on nine benchmarks at every size in both 0-shot and 5-shot settings.
papers.highlight_summary:
Looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models reuse a shared block of middle layers across two visits, but the two visits turn out not to be equal: a learnable residual coefficient on the first visit collapses to roughly 0.3 while the second stays near 1, and fixing the pair at (0.25, 1) beats (1, 1) at no cost. `LatentLoop` exploits this by deliberately starving the first visit of compute and spending the savings on model width, under budgets matched to within 1% on parameters, KV cache, and FLOPs following the `SMELT` recipe.

- The first visit runs on a sequence mean-pooled over adjacent token pairs (compression factor 2), its latent update is written back with learned per-channel, per-receiver-position coefficients that add only 2d parameters, and the two visits share MoE routers and experts while using separate attention blocks, paid for by dropping one stored expert per layer (76 to 75 at 3B).
- Across **15 matched configurations from 1.3B to 7B parameters**, with the largest budget above 10^21 FLOPs, validation NLL is lower than both `MoE Base` and `MoE Loop` at every endpoint, and fitted power-law frontiers predict **19.0% and 7.9% compute savings** respectively at an NLL of 1.988.
- In 3B/40B ablations the final design reaches **2.0199 NLL versus 2.0293 for `MoE Loop` and 2.0426 for `MoE Base`**; sequence compression beat halving residual width, halving expert width, or halving active experts, and a single learned writeback scalar recovers most of the gain (2.0210), with the learned coefficients settling well below one at about 0.20 and 0.16.
- On nine downstream benchmarks `LatentLoop` has the best average in all six size and shot settings, but margins over `MoE Loop` are modest at 0.73 to 1.18 points in 5-shot and only 0.17 to 0.67 points in 0-shot, from a single training seed.
- Only a two-visit loop with compression factor 2 is evaluated for the full method, the paper notes the mechanism behind the residual asymmetry is unexplained, and the roughly 2x ratio between consecutive coefficients seen with three and four visits is left to future work.

papers.title: SoK: Grading Open-Text Legal Answers, from Law School Exams to Trustworthy Rubric Judges
papers.abstract: Law students are examined through open-text answers: case solutions, essays and memos that apply the law to a set of facts. Such answers are expensive to grade, human graders disagree widely on them, and large language models (LLMs) now offer to grade them at scale, both in teaching and in the benchmarks that test legal AI. This paper systematizes how open-text legal answers can be evaluated. We derive eight desiderata from educational measurement and from the law that governs exams, among them validity, reliability, reasons, credit for defensible alternative solutions, robustness to gaming and human oversight. We then compare eight evaluation paradigms against them, from unstructured human grading to LLM judges with instance-specific rubrics and pairwise comparison. Three findings stand out. A rubric written for the task is the strongest lever for agreement between an LLM judge and human graders, but the reported figures answer different questions and rarely come with the human agreement they must be read against. The central validation gap lies where examination law is most demanding: defensible alternative solutions, follow-on errors, and the examiner's correction of model judgments. And rubric-centred grading is the most auditable family, because it makes the standard, its application and the final decision checkable. From this we derive the trustworthy rubric judge: an instance rubric that credits arguments and alternative paths,evidence checked in code, probes, repeated runs, calibration against independent human grades,logging, and an examiner who reads every script. We state what each safeguard rests on, what remains to be tested, and the uses the evidence supports today.
papers.summary: Open-text legal answers such as case solutions, essays, and memos are expensive to grade, human graders disagree widely on them, and large language models (LLMs) are now used to grade them both in teaching and in the benchmarks that test legal AI. This systematization derives eight desiderata from educational measurement and the law governing examinations, including validity, reliability, reasons, credit for defensible alternative solutions, robustness to gaming, and human oversight, and compares eight evaluation paradigms against them, from unstructured human grading to LLM judges with instance-specific rubrics and pairwise comparison. **A rubric written for the specific task is the strongest lever for agreement between an LLM judge and human graders**, but reported agreement figures answer different questions and rarely come with the human-human agreement they must be read against, and the central validation gap sits where examination law is most demanding: defensible alternative solutions, follow-on errors, and examiner correction of model judgments. The authors propose a trustworthy rubric judge design that combines an instance rubric crediting arguments and alternative paths, evidence checked in code, probes, repeated runs, calibration against independent human grades, logging, and an examiner who reads every script, and state what each safeguard rests on and what remains untested.

papers.title: Gray-Box Hallucination Detection in LLMs with Token Identities
papers.abstract:
Large language models often produce fluent but factually incorrect output. Gray-box detectors identify such hallucinations from the token-probability statistics emitted during generation, avoiding the need for white-box access to hidden states that frontier models do not provide. These detectors, however, typically rely only on probability-derived representations and ignore the identities of the candidate tokens. They can therefore observe how uncertain the model is, but not what it is uncertain about. Consequently, they cannot distinguish between a model that is torn between "big" and "small" and one that is torn between "big" and "huge" when the two pairs receive the same probability distribution.
  We introduce GURI (Gray-box Uncertainty Representations with Identity), a lightweight gray-box hallucination detector that combines candidate-token probabilities with per-token vector identifiers. This exposes which alternatives the model considered while preserving the accessibility and transferability of the gray-box setting. Across three open-weight models and three question-answering benchmarks, GURI increases mean test ROC-AUC from 72.09% to 79.09% over a probability-only baseline. On the closed-source GPT-4.1 model, mean ROC-AUC increases from 67.39% to 71.84%. Among the three open-weight models, GURI outperforms transferred probability-only baseline in 17 of 18 directed cross-model transfers without fine-tuning. For the three open-weight models, cross-dataset transfer between HotpotQA and TriviaQA with the model held fixed improves mean ROC-AUC over transferred LOS-Net by 3.76 points.
papers.summary: Gray-box hallucination detectors work from the token-probability statistics emitted during generation, avoiding the hidden-state access that closed frontier models do not expose, but they typically ignore which candidate tokens the probabilities belong to, so they can see how uncertain a model is without seeing what it is uncertain about. `GURI` (Gray-box Uncertainty Representations with Identity) is a lightweight detector that combines candidate-token probabilities with per-token vector identifiers, exposing which alternatives the model considered while keeping the accessibility and transferability of the gray-box setting. Across three open-weight models and three question-answering benchmarks it **raises mean test ROC-AUC from 72.09% to 79.09%** over a probability-only baseline, lifts the closed-source `GPT-4.1` from 67.39% to 71.84%, beats the transferred probability-only baseline in 17 of 18 directed cross-model transfers without fine-tuning, and improves cross-dataset transfer between `HotpotQA` and `TriviaQA` by 3.76 points over transferred `LOS-Net`.

papers.title: Empirical Boundaries of Reservoir Computing for Few-Shot Sequence Pattern Tasks
papers.abstract:
Efficient sequence modeling remains a fundamental challenge in machine learning. Despite the success of Transformers, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have recently re-emerged as efficient alternatives. Particularly, Echo State Networks (ESNs) offer a compelling framework of randomized RNNs that have been extensively studied for time-series forecasting and dynamical systems. This paper presents an empirical analysis of distributional, architectural, and optimization variants of ESNs evaluated on few-shot sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) pattern tasks. These synthetic tasks utilize discrete symbol sequences, characterized by delays, inactive phases, and triggered markers to isolate and evaluate memory and pattern recognition capabilities. The minimality of these tasks is crucial to understand the strengths and limitations of machine learning models. Furthermore, when the input signal utilizes a one-hot encoding, ESN dynamics are governed strictly by their weight distributions, offering an ideal lens through which to study reservoir computing.
  Our findings map the performance boundaries of ESNs relative to state-of-the-art (SOTA) models. We show that preserving a linear state regime is vital for memory tasks, such as pattern completion or simple copy. We propose a data-dependent modulation mechanism for nonlinear input injection into the reservoir (G-ESN). G-ESN functions as a statistical filter capable of solving tasks that conventional ESNs cannot (the adding problem and bracket matching).
