Finally, we extend the stochastic approximation framework to prove convergence rates of these two algorithms under the minimal assumptions used in the literature.
papers.summary: Q-learning with options, which are temporally extended and hierarchical actions, has lacked finite-sample guarantees in the average-reward formulation of reinforcement learning (RL) that covers continual tasks rather than discounted or episodic ones. The authors show that both inter-option and intra-option Bellman operators satisfy multi-step span contractions under unichain assumptions, propose synchronous estimators of these operators that yield two option Q-learning variants, and extend the stochastic approximation framework to bound their error. The result is **the first convergence rate on the order of 1 over the number of iterations, in mean square**, for average-reward option Q-learning, obtained under the minimal assumptions used in prior work.

papers.title: NeuroDETR: Multiscale Discrete Spatiotemporal Tokenization for Asynchronous EEG Event Detection
papers.abstract: Asynchronous EEG event detection supports practical brain-computer interfaces by identifying event classes and temporal boundaries directly from continuous recordings without predefined event boundaries at inference time. The primary challenge lies in extracting event-related patterns embedded in ongoing background activity. To address this, we propose \textbf{NeuroDETR}, a discrete spatiotemporal multiscale framework that combines structured tokenization with event-aware feature refinement. Multiscale temporal codebooks capture brief responses and sustained dynamics, while Spatial-Pyramid VQ hierarchically encodes spatial structure across EEG channels. These complementary representations form a compact event memory for jointly classifying events and estimating their onsets and offsets. Before tokenization, we apply FOCAL, an event-aware sparse attention module that uses predicted event presence to guide temporal feature refinement and spatial aggregation, emphasizing likely event periods while preserving context across the recording. Experiments on eight EEG datasets that span diverse paradigms demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. These findings provide a basis for the development of BCI systems that recognize meaningful neural activity during continuous interaction and monitoring.
papers.summary: Detecting events in continuous EEG recordings without predefined boundaries at inference time requires separating event-related patterns from ongoing background activity, a prerequisite for practical brain-computer interfaces (BCIs). `NeuroDETR` tokenizes signals with multiscale temporal codebooks that capture both brief responses and sustained dynamics, plus a Spatial-Pyramid vector quantization scheme that hierarchically encodes structure across channels, forming a compact event memory used to jointly classify events and estimate their onsets and offsets. An event-aware sparse attention module called `FOCAL` refines features before tokenization by emphasizing likely event periods while preserving context, and the authors report **state-of-the-art results on eight EEG datasets** spanning diverse paradigms.

papers.title: Lifted State Policy Optimization: Internalizing Self-Correction through Transition Geometry
papers.abstract: Preference optimization ranks final answers and trajectory RL maximizes aggregate returns, yet neither credits the local change that turns a flawed reasoning state into a better one. We introduce Lifted State Policy Optimization (LSPO), which establishes this finite, cost-adjusted transition as the primary unit of learning. Each textual answer is augmented with a learned continuous coordinate, forming a lifted state that an energy function evaluates and orders. A shaped reward drives energy descent net of edit and step costs, and an internalization loss absorbs selected low-energy answers into the direct generator. On Qwen3.5-27B, the resulting single-pass policy reaches 71.8% aggregate accuracy across mathematics, science, code, and logic benchmarks, matching test-time reflection at 71.9% with 28% lower latency and 25.8% fewer tokens. The pattern holds across dense and mixture-of-experts backbones, and matched controls confirm that transition credit and the lifted coordinate each contribute, as does answer internalization. Our code is available at https://github.com/Venomrko/lspo.
papers.summary: Preference optimization scores final answers and trajectory-level reinforcement learning maximizes total return, but neither gives credit to the specific local edit that moves a flawed reasoning state to a better one. Lifted State Policy Optimization (`LSPO`) makes that cost-adjusted transition the unit of learning: each textual answer is paired with a learned continuous coordinate, an energy function orders these lifted states, a shaped reward drives energy descent net of edit and step costs, and an internalization loss folds selected low-energy answers back into the direct generator. On `Qwen3.5-27B` the resulting single-pass policy reaches **71.8% aggregate accuracy across math, science, code, and logic benchmarks, matching test-time reflection at 71.9%**, with 28% lower latency and 25.8% fewer tokens, and matched controls show that transition credit, the lifted coordinate, and answer internalization each contribute.

papers.title: Beyond Expert Rankings: Contrast Calibration for Mixed-Precision MoE Quantization
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models activate only a few experts per token, yet all expert weights must be stored. Mixed-precision quantization reduces this storage cost by assigning higher bit-widths to sensitive experts and lower bit-widths to resilient ones, but expert rankings alone do not determine how strongly to weight their errors. To address this gap, we propose NatScale, a contrast-calibrated allocation framework for mixed-precision MoE quantization. It uses a model-specific power transformation to calibrate gradient-based expert weights to an information-theoretic contrast target while preserving rankings. We jointly evaluate each expert's gate, up and down configurations to estimate its output error. We then combine these errors and calibrated weights with an existing prior based on weight spectra, variance and precision decay to select configurations under a storage budget. Across three models, NatScale achieves the lowest native-to-quantized KL divergence and the highest top-token agreement in all nine settings against five allocation baselines. It also yields the lowest perplexity in seven settings. These findings highlight the importance of objective-aware precision allocation.
papers.summary: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models activate only a few experts per token but must store all of them, and mixed-precision quantization assigns bit-widths per expert based on sensitivity rankings that say nothing about how heavily each expert's error should be weighted. `NatScale` applies a model-specific power transformation that calibrates gradient-based expert weights to an information-theoretic contrast target while preserving the rankings, estimates each expert's output error by jointly evaluating its gate, up, and down projection configurations, and combines these with an existing prior based on weight spectra, variance, and precision decay to pick configurations under a storage budget. Against five allocation baselines on three models, it achieves **the lowest native-to-quantized KL divergence and highest top-token agreement in all nine settings**, plus the lowest perplexity in seven of them.

papers.title: Do AI Agents Gossip? Evaluative Talk in Human and AI-Agent Online Communities
papers.abstract: Gossip, defined as evaluative talk about absent third parties, is widely seen as a uniquely human social practice. This study examines whether comparable discourse emerges spontaneously in a community of autonomous AI agents. We compare Moltbook, a Reddit-style platform populated by AI agents, with PTT, a large human-operated bulletin board in Taiwan. To reduce differences attributable to communicative setting, we analyze two public, asynchronous forums using the same operational definition of gossip. Gossip occurs on Moltbook, but its prevalence is 2.6 to 6 times lower than on PTT, depending on the denominator used. On both platforms, gossip frequently targets locally prominent figures, tends to elicit agreement from the first respondent, and is rarely presented as unsupported rumor. The clearest difference concerns how subsequent responses develop. Among threads containing at least one codable reply, challenges occur in 65.1% of human threads but only 21.3% of agent threads. Moreover, following an early aligning response, consensus remains unchallenged in 83.6% of agent threads, compared with 44.7% of human threads. This thread-level contrast remains after controlling for thread depth and board composition and under recalibration against two human annotators. Estimates based on individual reply turns are less robust and are therefore reported as bounds. These findings suggest that AI-agent communities reproduce the informational dimension of gossip, while the extent to which gossip performs comparable relational functions remains unresolved.
papers.summary: Gossip, evaluative talk about absent third parties, is often considered uniquely human, so the authors test whether it arises spontaneously among autonomous AI agents by comparing `Moltbook`, a Reddit-style platform populated by agents, with `PTT`, a large human-run Taiwanese bulletin board, under a single operational definition and matched asynchronous forum settings. Gossip does occur on the agent platform but at 2.6 to 6 times lower prevalence depending on the denominator, and on both platforms it targets locally prominent figures, draws agreement from the first respondent, and is rarely framed as unsupported rumor. The sharpest divergence is in how threads develop: **challenges appear in 65.1% of human threads but only 21.3% of agent threads**, and after an early aligning reply, consensus stays unchallenged in 83.6% of agent threads versus 44.7% of human ones, a contrast that survives controls for thread depth and board composition.

papers.title: Fractional is Better: Learnable Derivative Orders in Neural Operator Learning
papers.abstract: Neural operators learn mappings between function spaces, enabling fast surrogate solutions to partial differential equations. Despite remarkable architectural diversity, these methods often share a common input representation: raw coordinate-value pairs $(x, u(x))$. We ask whether inputs aligned with PDE differential structure can improve learning. Through Picard iteration on mild solutions, we show that derivatives of the input appear explicitly in the solution operator, suggesting that providing derivative features should reduce the network's implicit differentiation burden. We prove this intuition: providing derivative features improves approximation bounds from $O(W^{-(s-m)/d})$ to $O(W^{-s/d})$, where $W$ is parameter count, $s$ is input regularity, $m$ is the PDE order, and $d$ is spatial dimension. Our central finding, however, is a surprise: the optimal derivative order $\beta^*$ is strictly less than the PDE order $m$. This gap arises from a bias-variance tradeoff in spectral space that we characterize in closed form. Learning $\beta$ from data achieves automatic spectral regularization. We introduce $\partial$-NO (del-NO), for derivative-augmented neural operators, an architecture-agnostic augmentation that provides learnable fractional derivative features to any neural operator backbone. Across benchmark problems and architectures, $\partial$-NO consistently improves prediction accuracy, with learned orders that reflect a representation of known physics modulated by noise and finite-sample constraints.
papers.summary: Neural operators that serve as fast surrogates for partial differential equation (PDE) solvers almost universally take raw coordinate-value pairs as input, prompting the question of whether inputs aligned with the PDE's differential structure help. Via Picard iteration on mild solutions, the authors show that input derivatives appear explicitly in the solution operator, and they prove that supplying derivative features tightens the approximation bound by removing the PDE order from the exponent on the parameter count. What the authors highlight as a surprise is that **the optimal derivative order is strictly less than the PDE order**, a consequence of a spectral bias-variance tradeoff they characterize in closed form, which motivates `del-NO`, an architecture-agnostic augmentation with learnable fractional derivative orders that consistently improves accuracy across benchmark problems and backbones.

papers.title: Lexical Persistence Without Semantic Entrenchment in AI Agent Communities
papers.abstract: AI agent communities sustain lexical persistence, popular terms spread, recur, and achieve broad adoption, but whether they also develop the temporal semantic structure characteristic of human linguistic communities remains open. We compare MoltBook (AI agent community, 8 weeks), PTT (Chinese human BBS, 19 years), and Reddit (English human forum, in matched 8-week windows) using Compass-Aligned Distributional Embeddings (CADE), measuring semantic drift (B1), neighborhood stability (B2), and lag-1 autocorrelation of per-word drift trajectories. Across the platforms, lag-1 autocorrelation forms a memory-horizon continuum. AI agents' result clusters at the low end, while human platforms show longer-range temporal dependence. MoltBook exhibits approximately 2$\times$ the B1 drift and 20-30% lower B2 stability than both human platforms. As a partial control for community age, r/vibecoding (founded 2025-02-08) shows significant ACF in its first 8 weeks ($0.082$, $p<.001$) and over 15 weeks ($0.220$, $p<.001$); MoltBook's ACF remains non-significant ($p = 0.41$), consistent with the gap not reducing to developmental stage alone. We interpret this pattern as evidence that lexical diffusion alone does not guarantee diachronic semantic consolidation. The findings are consistent with a contrast between communities whose semantic trajectories accumulate long-range interaction constraints and communities whose outputs are repeatedly regenerated from largely fixed pretrained distributions.
papers.summary: Communities of AI agents adopt and recirculate popular terms, but it is unclear whether their language develops the temporal semantic structure seen in human communities. Using Compass-Aligned Distributional Embeddings (`CADE`), the authors compare `MoltBook`, an eight-week AI agent community, against the human platforms `PTT` and `Reddit` on semantic drift, neighborhood stability, and lag-1 autocorrelation of per-word drift trajectories. MoltBook shows **roughly twice the semantic drift and 20 to 30% lower neighborhood stability than both human platforms**, and its autocorrelation is non-significant while a young human subreddit, r/vibecoding, already shows significant autocorrelation in its first eight weeks, which the authors read as evidence that the gap is not just community age but reflects agent output being regenerated from largely fixed pretrained distributions rather than accumulating long-range interaction constraints.

papers.title: Cascaded Retrieval with Cross-Modal Query Refinement for Efficient Visual Document Search
papers.abstract: Retrieving information from visually rich documents requires matching queries against pages that contain complex evidence in tables, figures, and layout-dependent structures. Current vision-language retrievers address this but incur query-time costs that grow with corpus size and are impractical to scale. We propose SCOUT, a cascaded two-track retrieval framework that separates retrieval performance from exhaustive search. The visual track first uses a lightweight parent retriever to filter the corpus to a compact candidate pool, then applies a stronger multi-vector reranker only to those candidates. In parallel, a semantic track retrieves over hierarchical page and document summaries generated offline to provide a signal complementary to visual matching. The outputs are fused through cross-modal query refinement, which uses semantic scores to adjust the visual query representation before final ranking. We evaluate SCOUT on 4 major benchmarks against 6 baselines and observe a significant query-time latency improvement up to 80.7x (28.8x on average) relative to the best baseline, while exceeding state-of-the-art retrieval performance by up to 7.8% NDCG across all benchmarks.
papers.summary: Retrieving pages from visually rich documents, where evidence sits in tables, figures, and layout, is handled well by vision-language retrievers whose query-time cost grows with corpus size. `SCOUT` splits the work into two tracks: a visual track in which a lightweight parent retriever narrows the corpus to a small candidate pool before a stronger multi-vector reranker scores only those candidates, and a semantic track that searches hierarchical page and document summaries generated offline. Semantic scores then adjust the visual query representation through cross-modal query refinement before final ranking, and on four benchmarks against six baselines the system cuts **query latency by up to 80.7x (28.8x on average) relative to the best baseline** while exceeding state-of-the-art NDCG by up to 7.8%.

papers.title: ReAl: Refine neural operators via aligning dynamical flow
papers.abstract: Neural partial differential equation (PDE) surrogates trained with mean squared error (MSE) can capture dominant dynamics but often lose high-frequency information and fine-scale structures. Generative models (e.g., Flow Matching) can capture the distribution of fine-scale details, yet stochastic errors may accumulate during autoregressive rollouts and compromise long-term stability. To address these limitations, we introduce Refine and Align(ReAl), a model-agnostic plug-in that augments pretrained PDE surrogates to improve the reconstruction of high-frequency structures associated with complex physical phenomena. In the refinement stage, a conditional flow-matching model learns the residual distribution around the deterministic base prediction, recovering missing fine-scale structures while retaining the dominant dynamics. In the alignment stage, to mitigate the generative discrepancies amplified in the autoregressive rollout, particularly in chaotic systems, we generate multiple trajectories from the same input and reinforce the refiner with trajectory-level rewards, thereby achieving long-horizon dynamical alignment. Experiments across diverse surrogate architectures and PDE tasks demonstrate that ReAl consistently improves high-frequency fidelity, forecasting accuracy, and long-horizon stability.
papers.summary: Neural surrogates for partial differential equations (PDEs) trained with mean squared error (MSE) capture dominant dynamics but lose high-frequency, fine-scale structure, while generative alternatives such as flow matching recover detail but accumulate stochastic error over autoregressive rollouts. Refine and Align (`ReAl`) is a model-agnostic plug-in with two stages: a conditional flow-matching refiner learns the residual distribution around the deterministic base prediction, and an alignment stage samples multiple rollouts from the same input and reinforces the refiner with trajectory-level rewards to curb drift in chaotic systems. Across surrogate architectures and PDE tasks, the authors report **consistent gains in high-frequency fidelity, forecasting accuracy, and long-horizon stability**.

papers.title: From Triage to Impact: A Multi-Hop Reasoning Benchmark for Explainable Persian Hate Speech
papers.abstract: Hate speech has become increasingly prevalent on social media, raising concerns about its detection, interpretation, and moderation. Persian, a relatively low-resource language, lacks sufficient annotated data and computational resources for fine-grained hate speech analysis. In this study, we introduce a fine-grained, multi-hop benchmark for explainable Persian hate speech analysis, covering content triage, target identification, hate tactic and moral foundation analysis, textual evidence extraction, harmful narrative inference, and severity assessment. By evaluating state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs), we find that performance generally declines as tasks require more fine-grained semantic and inferential reasoning. Proprietary models generally outperform open-weight models, while reasoning-oriented models show no consistent advantage. Incorporating intermediate reasoning steps substantially improves severity prediction compared with one-shot assessment. Our analysis further reveals that Incitement to Violence or Harm is most strongly associated with higher severity, while political-affiliation targets are particularly associated with subversion-based moral framing. Overall, this work provides insights into LLM-based hate speech analysis and supports more accountable moderation of Persian-language social media. The benchmark is publicly available at https://github.com/kalhorghazal/From-Triage-to-Impact.
papers.summary: Persian lacks annotated resources for fine-grained hate speech analysis, so the authors build a multi-hop benchmark spanning content triage, target identification, hate tactic and moral foundation analysis, textual evidence extraction, harmful narrative inference, and severity assessment. Evaluating state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs), they find performance declines as tasks demand finer semantic and inferential reasoning, proprietary models generally beat open-weight ones, and reasoning-oriented models show no consistent edge. **Adding intermediate reasoning steps substantially improves severity prediction over one-shot assessment**, and the analysis links incitement to violence with the highest severity and political-affiliation targets with subversion-based moral framing.

papers.title: Hypothesis Selection via Weighted Medians
papers.abstract: Given $n$ distributions (hypotheses) $\mathcal H=\{H_1,\ldots,H_n\}$ and samples from an unknown target distribution $P$, proper hypothesis selection seeks a distribution whose total variation distance to $P$ is close to the best achievable within the known distributions. We give an algorithm that, using $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(n/\delta))$ target samples, running in $O(n\varepsilon^{-2}\log(n/\delta))$ time, with probability at least $1-\delta$, returns $H_{\hat i}$ satisfying $d_\mathrm{TV}(P,H_{\hat i})\leq 3\min_{i\in[n]}d_\mathrm{TV}(P,H_i)+\varepsilon.$ The algorithm achieves the optimal approximation factor and sample complexity. The running time improves the dependence on the failure probability from polynomial to logarithmic in the state-of-the-art bound $\tilde{O}(n\varepsilon^{-2}\delta^{-1})$ of Aamand, Aliakbarpour, Chen, and Silwal (COLT 2026), thereby answering their Question~2.
papers.summary: Proper hypothesis selection asks, given n candidate distributions and samples from an unknown target, for a candidate whose total variation distance to the target is close to the best achievable among the candidates. The authors give an algorithm that uses a number of samples scaling as log(n over delta) divided by epsilon squared and returns a hypothesis within 3 times the optimal distance plus epsilon with probability at least 1 minus delta, matching the optimal approximation factor and sample complexity. Its running time, linear in n times the sample bound, **improves the dependence on the failure probability from polynomial to logarithmic**, resolving an open question posed by Aamand, Aliakbarpour, Chen, and Silwal at COLT 2026.

papers.title: FOLD: Position-Free Far Memory with Local Order for Long-Context Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM generation through lightweight drafting and parallel verification. It is particularly promising for long inputs, where KV-cache access costs can be amortized over multiple accepted tokens. Yet most drafters are trained on short sequences and degrade on long inputs, while long-context training is costly. Existing training-free approaches restrict the context window, rescale positions, or augment recent context with retrieved distant entries. Drafters, however, read target hidden states that already encode contextual and positional information, and their lightweight architecture makes full-history attention affordable. We propose FOLD, a training-free method that preserves exact local positions and treats all distant entries as far memory at a shared position. To counter attention dilution as the memory grows, we sharpen attention within it to emphasize relevant entries while separately controlling its total weight relative to the local window. Across six target-drafter pairs and diverse benchmarks of up to 256K tokens, FOLD predominantly delivers the highest speedup, with the best case more than doubling the speedup over autoregressive decoding, from 2.08$\times$ to 4.22$\times$.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding pairs a cheap drafter with parallel verification by the target model, which is especially attractive for long inputs where key-value cache access cost is amortized over accepted tokens, yet drafters trained on short sequences degrade on long contexts and retraining them is expensive. `FOLD` is a training-free fix that keeps exact positions for the local window and places all distant key-value entries into a far memory at a single shared position, exploiting the fact that drafters read target hidden states that already carry positional information and are cheap enough to attend over the full history. To counter attention dilution as the memory grows, it sharpens attention inside the memory while separately controlling its total weight relative to the local window, and across six target-drafter pairs on benchmarks up to 256K tokens it predominantly delivers the highest speedup, **in the best case raising the speedup over autoregressive decoding from 2.08x to 4.22x**.

papers.title: From Human Corrections to Learned Segmentations: A Critical Mathematical Review of Information, Learning, and Human Effort
papers.abstract: When does a human correction become useful learning, and what establishes better segmentation at matched human effort? This critical narrative review follows feedback through its selection, learner update, and evaluation. It compares active learning, machine teaching, interactive segmentation, and sequential predictive evaluation using a common mathematical account of target information, predictive error, response predictability, and human work. An exact Bayesian update converts evaluation-label information into expected log-loss improvement; an excess-risk decomposition explains what an approximate learner can lose. Conditional information decompositions separate the roles of selected locations, labels, and displayed context. Empirical comparisons show why response protocols, update mechanisms, and effort denominators matter, distinguishing current-mask refinement from reusable learning and simulated interaction from human evidence. We identify what logs can reveal, what requires independent evaluation, and what remains model-dependent. The resulting research priorities are to test what selection reveals, whether using it improves assimilation, and whether the resulting interaction policy benefits segmentation at matched effort. These are distinct claims: predicting a teacher's responses need not identify human intentions or establish better learning. No new acquisition algorithm or empirical superiority is claimed.
papers.summary: The review asks when a human correction becomes useful learning and what determines better segmentation at matched human effort, tracing feedback through selection, learner update, and evaluation. It compares active learning, machine teaching, interactive segmentation, and sequential predictive evaluation under a shared mathematical account of target information, predictive error, response predictability, and human work, including an exact Bayesian update that converts evaluation-label information into expected log-loss improvement and an excess-risk decomposition explaining what an approximate learner loses. The authors argue that response protocols, update mechanisms, and effort denominators change conclusions, distinguish refining a current mask from reusable learning and simulated interaction from human evidence, and stress that **predicting a teacher's responses need not identify human intentions or establish better learning**; no new algorithm or empirical superiority is claimed.

papers.title: Cortex: Consolidating Context into Parametric Memory
papers.abstract: Context can improve large language model performance, but these gains may be lost after context removal. Inspired by biological systems consolidation, we formulate Memory Consolidation (MC) as internalizing these gains while preserving non-target capabilities, connecting context-specified editing, skill learning, and behavioral steering under a common objective. We introduce a five-task-family testbed measuring consolidation and retention under single, batch, and sequential updates. We propose Cortex, which generates prospective queries to anticipate uses of context and distills context-conditioned outputs into mergeable low-rank or structural feed-forward network updates. Across 4B--120B dense and mixture-of-experts backbones, including both text-only and multimodal models, Cortex lies on the empirical consolidation--retention Pareto frontier in most evaluated settings. After 50 sequential factual edits on a 14B model, Cortex-Structural recovers 88.9% of the context-induced gain while retaining 99.8% of original non-target performance.
papers.summary: Context given to a large language model can lift its performance, but the gains vanish once the context is removed. The authors formulate Memory Consolidation (MC) as internalizing those gains while preserving unrelated capabilities, uniting context-specified editing, skill learning, and behavioral steering under one objective, and build a five-task-family testbed that measures consolidation and retention under single, batch, and sequential updates. `Cortex` generates prospective queries that anticipate how the context will be used and distills context-conditioned outputs into mergeable low-rank or structural feed-forward updates; across 4B to 120B dense and mixture-of-experts backbones it sits on the consolidation-retention Pareto frontier in most settings, and **after 50 sequential factual edits on a 14B model, the structural variant recovers 88.9% of the context-induced gain while retaining 99.8% of non-target performance**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Context-conditioned gains in large language models disappear once the context is withdrawn. The paper frames Memory Consolidation as internalizing those gains into parameters while preserving unrelated capabilities, unifying context-specified editing, skill learning, and behavioral steering under a single objective, and proposes `Cortex` to perform that consolidation.

- `Cortex` generates prospective queries that anticipate how the context would be used, then distills the model's context-conditioned outputs on those queries into mergeable low-rank or structural feed-forward updates.
- Evaluation uses a new testbed of **five task families** that measures both consolidation of the target gain and retention of non-target performance under single, batch, and sequential updates.
- Across dense and mixture-of-experts backbones from **4B to 120B** parameters, spanning text-only and multimodal models, `Cortex` lies on the empirical consolidation-retention Pareto frontier in most evaluated settings.
- After **50 sequential factual edits** on a 14B model, `Cortex-Structural` recovers **88.9%** of the context-induced gain while retaining **99.8%** of original non-target performance.
- The Pareto claim holds only in most settings rather than all, and the headline figure comes from one variant on one model size and one task type, so compute cost and behavior beyond 50 edits remain unreported.

papers.title: HRTF Upsampling and Personalization via Neural Operators
papers.abstract: Head-related transfer function (HRTF) spatial upsampling from sparse measurements is a fundamental challenge in personalized binaural audio. We formulate HRTF upsampling as an operator learning problem and introduce SPARO, a neural operator that maps sparse measurements at a set of spatial directions to the HRTF field, a continuous representation that can be queried at arbitrary positions. SPARO projects the measurements onto a learned set of spherical latent modes, processes the latent modes with Transformer blocks, and decodes the resulting representations at query directions. On SONICOM, using the LAP24 measurement configuration, SPARO attains the best log-spectral distortion (LSD) and interaural level difference (ILD) error at every sparsity level from 3 to 100 measurements (18% lower LSD and 43% lower ILD error than the strongest baseline at 100 measurements) while remaining competitive in interaural time difference (ITD) error. It reconstructs a dense HRTF 15 to 373 times faster than the leading neural-field method RANF. We further validate the approach on HUTUBS, demonstrating its effectiveness across HRTF datasets.
papers.summary: Personalized binaural audio depends on head-related transfer functions (HRTFs), which are costly to measure densely, so the task is to reconstruct the full spatial field from sparse measurements. `SPARO` treats this as operator learning: it projects measurements at a few directions onto a learned set of spherical latent modes, processes them with Transformer blocks, and decodes the field at arbitrary query directions. On `SONICOM` under the `LAP24` configuration it achieves the best log-spectral distortion (LSD) and interaural level difference (ILD) error at every sparsity level from 3 to 100 measurements, with **18% lower LSD and 43% lower ILD error than the strongest baseline at 100 measurements**, stays competitive in interaural time difference (ITD) error, reconstructs a dense HRTF 15 to 373 times faster than the neural-field method `RANF`, and generalizes to `HUTUBS`.

papers.title: Training Language Models to Fail Gracefully
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning makes language models better at solving tasks, but the same mechanism also rewards guessing. When success is the only way to earn reward, opting for a safe fallback is always worse than a long-shot attempt. When a wrong action can corrupt a database or ship broken code, that incentive can be costly. Therefore, we propose training models to fail gracefully: to preserve successful behavior whenever possible while learning to execute a safe fallback policy when acting would be unreliable. However, naively using policy gradients with intermediate reward for fallback behavior is brittle due to unfavorable optimization dynamics. We address this challenge with GracefulRL, which reshapes the optimization landscape to promote graceful failure. Importantly, this behavior emerges directly from outcome-level reward signals, without annotations specifying when to fall back or additional inference-time machinery such as a verifier. Across a range of tasks and scales, we train models that largely preserve their task-solving capability while selectively falling back when acting would be unreliable. More broadly, our results show that reinforcement learning can not only incentivize models to succeed, but also to reason about the limits of their capabilities and change course when they determine that success is out of reach.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with success-only rewards pushes language models toward long-shot guesses, since a safe fallback never earns anything, which becomes costly when a wrong action can corrupt a database or ship broken code. The authors propose training models to fail gracefully, keeping task-solving behavior where possible but executing a safe fallback when acting would be unreliable, and show that naively adding an intermediate reward for fallback under policy gradients is brittle because of unfavorable optimization dynamics. `GracefulRL` reshapes the optimization landscape so that graceful failure emerges **from outcome-level rewards alone, with no annotations of when to fall back and no inference-time verifier**, and across tasks and scales the trained models largely retain capability while selectively changing course when success is out of reach.

papers.title: Posterior Frequencies and the Cost of Not Fitting: A Correction to a Memorization Lower Bound
papers.abstract: Feldman's memorization lower bound assigns a frequency coefficient based on how often a point appears in the training sample. We give an exact three-point counterexample to its conditional and averaged forms, using independent fair labels and a permutation-equivariant learner. A sequence of sampling priors makes the ratio of the proposed penalty to actual excess risk grow exponentially, ruling out a universal positive constant-factor repair. The priors vary with sample size, the offending profiles become rare, and both quantities vanish. Retaining the original model, we obtain an exact replacement using full-sample posterior probabilities. Under exchangeability, these depend on multiplicity and the complete frequency profile. We characterize the largest multiplicity-only coefficients valid for unrestricted learners. The original coefficient has the posterior-mean form of Good's exact frequency formula and is an occupancy-weighted average of the corrected coefficients.
papers.summary: Feldman's lower bound on how much a learner must memorize assigns each training point a frequency coefficient based on how often it appears in the sample. The authors construct an exact three-point counterexample with independent fair labels and a permutation-equivariant learner that breaks both the conditional and averaged forms of the bound, and exhibit a sequence of sampling priors under which the ratio of the proposed penalty to true excess risk grows exponentially, **ruling out any universal constant-factor repair**. Keeping the original model, they derive an exact replacement using full-sample posterior probabilities, which under exchangeability depend on both multiplicity and the complete frequency profile, characterize the largest multiplicity-only coefficients valid for unrestricted learners, and show the original coefficient is an occupancy-weighted average of the corrected ones.

papers.title: Hyperspherical Contrastive Representations Unlock Planning and Exploration
papers.abstract: We develop a self-supervised reinforcement learning algorithm that learns to build towers of up to eight cubes from scratch, without prior data, rewards, demonstrations, or pretrained models. Our method, Contrastive Planning via Spherical Linear Interpolation (C-Slerp), uses contrastive representations as reusable building blocks and repeatedly composes them to infer a sequence of intermediate waypoints. Under our hyperspherical parameterization, the learned representations allow intermediate waypoints to be inferred in closed form through spherical linear interpolation, without training a separate high-level policy or performing graph search. Importantly, the representation geometry also tells us how to adjust the number of waypoints based on the difficulty of each goal-reaching problem. Experiments show that our method succeeds on long-horizon navigation and robotic manipulation tasks, including settings where strong baselines fail to achieve a single success. Ablations further show that using a fixed number of waypoints substantially degrades performance, highlighting the importance of adapting the plan to task difficulty.
papers.summary: Long-horizon goal reaching without rewards, demonstrations, prior data, or pretrained models is hard because the agent must discover its own intermediate subgoals. Contrastive Planning via Spherical Linear Interpolation (`C-Slerp`) learns contrastive representations constrained to a hypersphere and composes them so that waypoints between the current state and the goal can be computed in closed form by spherical linear interpolation, with no separate high-level policy or graph search, while the representation geometry also indicates how many waypoints a given goal needs. The method **learns to stack towers of up to eight cubes from scratch** and succeeds on long-horizon navigation and manipulation tasks where strong baselines record no successes at all, and ablations show that a fixed waypoint count substantially degrades performance.

papers.title: When Does Momentum Help in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards?
papers.abstract: Momentum is a classical tool for accelerating convex optimization and a standard component of modern large language model training. Yet recent empirical work has questioned the usefulness of first-moment momentum in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We study this question through a bandit formulation of RLVR with bias-corrected exponential moving average (EMA) momentum, where the EMA coefficient $\beta$ controls how quickly the weights on past gradients decay. When policy gradients are evaluated exactly, we prove that increasing $\beta$ within a range that prevents overshoot strictly accelerates optimization. When gradients are estimated from sampled responses, a positive expected gain can be obscured by sampling fluctuations. We show that as the learning rate $\eta$ decreases, the expected gain with fixed $\beta$ vanishes faster than these fluctuations, whereas increasing $\beta$ to keep $\eta/(1-\beta)$ within the safe regime preserves a nonvanishing gain that eventually dominates them. Bandit simulations quantitatively validate these predictions. RLVR experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base using SGD with EMA and AdamW support our principle of choosing larger coefficients in practical LLM post-training. On Qwen2.5-32B with AdamW, simply increasing $\beta_1$ improves mean validation accuracy by nearly $2$ percentage points over the conventional choice, demonstrating the principle's effectiveness at a larger model scale.
papers.summary: Momentum is standard in large language model training, yet recent empirical reports question whether first-moment momentum helps in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Using a bandit formulation with bias-corrected exponential moving average (EMA) momentum, the authors prove that with exact gradients a larger EMA coefficient strictly accelerates optimization within the range that avoids overshoot, and that with sampled gradients the expected gain from a fixed coefficient vanishes faster than sampling noise as the learning rate shrinks, whereas raising the coefficient to keep the ratio of learning rate to one minus the coefficient in the safe regime preserves a gain that eventually dominates. Bandit simulations and RLVR runs on `Qwen3-4B-Base` support choosing larger coefficients, and on `Qwen2.5-32B` with `AdamW`, **simply increasing the first-moment coefficient improves mean validation accuracy by nearly 2 percentage points** over the conventional setting.

papers.title: One Size Does Not Fit All: Curvature-Aware Adaptive Perturbation for SAM
papers.abstract: Poor generalisation in deep neural networks is frequently associated with convergence to sharp minima. Sharpness-Aware Minimisation (SAM) improves generalisation of deep neural networks by minimising a combination of the training loss and the local sharpness of the loss landscape, biasing convergence towards flat minima. However, SAM relies on a fixed perturbation radius $\rho$ that ignores local curvature, leading to inefficient behaviour: the perturbation may be too small to escape poor basins defined by sharp local minima, or too large to allow convergence to solutions with good loss-sharpness tradeoff. We reinterpret $\rho$ as the intensity of the perturbation signal and propose Curvature-Aware Adaptive Perturbation for SAM (CAP-SAM), a geometry-aware method that modulates the perturbation radius based on a sharpness ratio, enabling a more effective search for robust minima on the loss landscape. We prove that CAP-SAM preserves the same convergence rate as standard SAM in non-convex stochastic settings. Extensive experiments indicate that our approach consistently outperforms SAM and its most prominent variants across diverse network architectures on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet.
papers.summary: Sharpness-Aware Minimisation (`SAM`) biases training toward flat minima, but it uses a fixed perturbation radius rho that ignores local curvature, so the step can be too small to escape sharp basins or too large to settle into solutions with a good loss-sharpness tradeoff. `CAP-SAM` (Curvature-Aware Adaptive Perturbation for SAM) reinterprets the radius as a perturbation intensity and modulates it with a sharpness ratio measured during training. The authors prove the method keeps the same convergence rate as standard `SAM` in non-convex stochastic settings and report that **it consistently outperforms `SAM` and its most prominent variants across architectures on `CIFAR-10`, `CIFAR-100`, and `ImageNet`**.

papers.title: Tracking a Small Set of Experts in Online Convex Optimization
papers.abstract:
For the fundamental problem of prediction from expert advice, Freund asked whether one could compete with a comparator that switches $k$ times among only $m$ experts. For a discrete set of experts, this problem was resolved by Bousquet and Warmuth (2020), who gave an efficient algorithm with optimal regret matching the information-theoretic limit.
  We study the analogous problem in online convex optimization, where the action space is continuous. An inefficient algorithm can be derived by discretizing the action space and applying the Bousquet--Warmuth algorithm, giving regret of $\widetilde{O}(md+k)$, while the best known efficient algorithm for this problem has regret $\widetilde{O}(dk)$. We show that this computational inefficiency is inherent, establishing a separation between the information-theoretic and polynomial-time regret achievable for this problem. Specifically, under the hypergraphic planted-clique conjecture, we show that for every polynomial-time algorithm there exist instances for which it incurs at least $(k\sqrt d)^{1-o(1)}$ regret.
papers.summary: In prediction from expert advice, Freund asked whether a learner can compete with a comparator that switches k times among only m experts, and Bousquet and Warmuth settled the discrete case with an efficient algorithm matching the information-theoretic limit. The analogous problem in online convex optimization, where actions are continuous, admits an inefficient discretization-based algorithm with regret on the order of md plus k, while the best known efficient algorithm has regret on the order of dk. The authors show this gap is inherent: **under the hypergraphic planted-clique conjecture, every polynomial-time algorithm incurs regret of at least (k√d)^(1-o(1)) on some instances**, establishing a separation between information-theoretic and polynomial-time achievable regret.

papers.title: From Unreliable to Usable: Decomposing Failure Modes and Confidence Signals in LLM Entity Extraction - Evidence from Cyber Threat Intelligence
papers.abstract: Audits of large language model (LLM) extraction from full-length documents report severe unreliability, leaving two questions open: what the failures actually consist of, and whether confidence signals can turn unreliable output into usable output. We run a preregistered, fully frozen evaluation of two new-generation low-cost LLMs (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash) with a flagship-tier control (GPT-6.1-Sol) on a public corpus of 354 incident campaigns (315 unique reports, 630 model-report evaluations), scoring extraction quality against gold, confidence calibration, and robustness to single-sentence perturbations. Three findings emerge. (1) Unreliability persists across tiers: micro precision is 0.03-0.34 and verbalized calibration error (ECE) 0.53-0.94 across both splits; the gap does not close at the flagship tier. (2) The dominant failure is not hallucination: a full mention census plus a three-tier annotation of 360 sampled candidates (two independent LLM annotators from vendors outside the evaluated set, Cohen's kappa = 0.79 on the preregistered acceptance line, fully disclosed) back-projects to 65.6% background mentions and 19.9% gold-scope gaps, with only 1.2% unsupported candidates. (3) Confidence ranks but does not verify: zero-cost self-consistency-frequency tiering passes a preregistered top-30% precision-gain bar in all six test-split model-type cells (4/6 on train), the zero-cost text-frequency x SC frequency combination wins 3, ties 2, loses 1 across cells, yet relation-level counterfactuals on all 45 targets show that a single misattribution sentence flips high-confidence judgments in 95.6-100% of cases, and even a background sentence explicitly marked as unrelated still binds a fake vulnerability in up to 26.7% of them. We conclude with a deployment boundary: confidence tiering may set review priorities, never truth.
papers.summary: Audits of large language model (LLM) extraction from full-length documents report severe unreliability but leave open what the failures consist of and whether confidence signals can make the output usable. A preregistered, fully frozen evaluation runs two low-cost models (`DeepSeek-V4-Flash`, `GLM-5.3-Flash`) and a flagship control (`GPT-6.1-Sol`) over a public corpus of 354 cyber threat intelligence incident campaigns, scoring extraction against gold labels, confidence calibration, and robustness to single-sentence perturbations. Unreliability persists at every tier, with micro precision between 0.03 and 0.34, yet **a full mention census attributes 65.6% of flagged candidates to background mentions and 19.9% to gold-scope gaps, with only 1.2% unsupported**, so hallucination is not the dominant failure. Zero-cost self-consistency-frequency tiering passes a preregistered top-30% precision-gain bar in all six test-split cells, but a single misattribution sentence flips high-confidence judgments in nearly every case, leading the authors to a deployment boundary where confidence tiering may set review priorities but never establish truth.

papers.title: OrionMoE-v1.0: A Mixture-of-Experts Foundation Model for Tabular In-Context Learning
papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models enable in-context learning by predicting unseen observations from a labeled support table without task-specific parameter updates. Despite recent advances, most existing approaches rely on dense architectures that apply the same transformations across features and datasets. We introduce OrionMoE-Small, a compact tabular foundation model that combines distribution-aware representations with dataset-conditioned sparse mixture-of-experts computation. Built on a dual-axis Transformer architecture, OrionMoE-Small selectively activates experts along the feature axis, with routing decisions informed by both individual feature representations and the broader dataset context. This design enables adaptive allocation of computation across heterogeneous tabular problems while retaining a shared computational pathway across tasks. OrionMoE-Small is pretrained entirely on synthetic classification tasks generated from a structured causal prior and performs downstream prediction without gradient-based adaptation. Experiments across multiple tabular benchmarks demonstrate competitive performance against substantially larger foundation models, with particularly strong results on small-context and high-dimensional datasets. Further analysis reveals favorable relative performance under class imbalance and highlights the importance of feature composition.
papers.summary: Tabular foundation models predict unseen rows from a labeled support table without task-specific parameter updates, but most rely on dense architectures that apply the same transformations to every feature and dataset. `OrionMoE-Small` is a compact dual-axis Transformer that routes computation through a sparse mixture of experts along the feature axis, with routing conditioned on both individual feature representations and the broader dataset context, and it is pretrained entirely on synthetic classification tasks drawn from a structured causal prior. The authors report **competitive accuracy against substantially larger tabular foundation models, with the strongest relative results on small-context and high-dimensional datasets** and favorable behavior under class imbalance.

papers.title: Analyzing performance of Retrieval Augmented Generation models for Question Answering Tasks
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models have become almost a cornerstone of open-domain question answering tasks; in which the quality of answers generated in the process, greatly relies on the effectiveness of retrieval mechanisms. In the realm of LLM, the last two years have seen tremendous progress in RAG architectures, with many models reporting to have improved performance through various design innovations. The cultural question and answering systems of South Asia, in particular, present a specific challenge since the region is home to the vast number of languages and traditions, which are closely interrelated. Along with these deeply intertwined historical narratives increase the need for culturally grounded and context-aware interpretation. Despite major architectural advances in LLMs, claiming significant improvements, challenges remain when answering these region specific questions in native languages. In this study, we aim to extract high-performing factors to guide the development of optimized hybrid RAG systems. We further explore whether the integration of RAG changes performance differently for culturally grounded and non-cultural questions in a South Asian multilingual setup, and whether RAG produces a higher overall percentage of correct answers than contexted answering. We also examine how LLM performance changes when RAG methods are integrated into the question-answering pipeline in comparison with non-contexted and contexted answering and, evaluate whether the introduction of RAG benefits popular or non-popular culturally grounded questions more. Not only does our work evaluate the current methods but also carves a path for future designs of more accurate and efficient question-answering pipelines.
papers.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is now standard for open-domain question answering, but culturally grounded questions about South Asia, with its many interrelated languages and traditions, remain difficult for large language models even with retrieval. The study compares RAG-augmented pipelines against non-contexted and contexted answering in a multilingual South Asian setup, asking whether retrieval helps cultural and non-cultural questions differently, whether it raises the overall share of correct answers, and whether popular or obscure cultural questions benefit more. **The stated contribution is identifying the factors that drive performance** in order to guide the design of more accurate and efficient question-answering pipelines.

papers.title: Continual Learning for Reliable In-Sequence Molecular Communication
papers.abstract: This paper considers reliable in-sequence molecular communication, where bio-nanomachines exchange molecule-encoded information in a specified order, and investigates a new simulation-based method to incrementally evaluate communication protocols by gradually increasing the complexity of experimental settings. The proposed method, called Affine Memory Replay (AMR), builds a continual learning (CL) model to estimate communication performance between bio-nanomachines. AMR stores past simulation samples and synthesizes additional replay samples through interpolation and extrapolation between past samples. Through incremental performance estimation tasks, it replays both past and synthetic samples to regularize model updates, helping the model adapt to new experimental settings while retaining knowledge from earlier ones. Experimental results show that AMR significantly outperforms existing CL methods in maintaining overall estimation accuracy across sequentially learned estimation tasks. It effectively balances memory stability and learning plasticity under moderate training cost.
papers.summary: Bio-nanomachines that exchange molecule-encoded messages in a fixed order need reliable in-sequence molecular communication, and evaluating such protocols by simulation becomes costly as experimental settings grow more complex. Affine Memory Replay (`AMR`) builds a continual learning model that estimates communication performance incrementally across settings of increasing complexity, storing past simulation samples and synthesizing extra replay samples by interpolating and extrapolating between them to regularize each update. The authors report that **`AMR` significantly outperforms existing continual learning methods at maintaining estimation accuracy across sequentially learned tasks**, balancing memory stability against plasticity at moderate training cost.

papers.title: SwarmRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Evolving Scientific Agent Swarm
papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) in scientific research aims to improve agents' research capabilities through their own experimental experience. Scientific agent swarms can combine evidence and implementations from different research directions to guide their agents' subsequent experiments. However, poor experimental results can leave unclear whether to revise a hypothesis or its implementation, while overall program scores can hide components useful to other agents. To address these challenges, we introduce SwarmRSI, a framework that evolves scientific agent swarms for recursive self-improvement. We devise Feedback-Guided Swarm Mutation to refine hypotheses and their implementations using experimental feedback from other agents. We also propose Complementary Swarm Recombination to reuse retained hypotheses and complementary program components across agents, allowing partial results to support new research. Recursive Swarm Evolution integrates both mechanisms into a feedback loop, using new experimental evidence to guide subsequent research. Experiments on OpenProblems, NatureBench and MLE-Bench Lite demonstrate SwarmRSI's state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance. Further evaluations show that accumulated research experience improves performance on held-out tasks. Biologists also reproduce its programs for follow-up biological analyses.
papers.summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) for scientific agents aims to raise research capability through the agents' own experimental experience, but a poor result leaves it unclear whether to revise the hypothesis or its implementation, and whole-program scores hide components that other agents could reuse. `SwarmRSI` evolves a swarm of scientific agents using `Feedback-Guided Swarm Mutation`, which refines hypotheses and implementations with experimental feedback from other agents, and `Complementary Swarm Recombination`, which reuses retained hypotheses and complementary program components across agents, with `Recursive Swarm Evolution` closing the loop so new evidence steers subsequent experiments. The authors report **state-of-the-art results on `OpenProblems`, `NatureBench`, and `MLE-Bench Lite`**, show that accumulated experience improves performance on held-out tasks, and note that biologists reproduced its programs for follow-up analyses.
papers.highlight_summary:
Recursive self-improvement for scientific agent swarms stalls on two problems: a failed experiment does not reveal whether the hypothesis or its implementation was at fault, and a program with no overall gain can still hold a component another agent needs. `SwarmRSI` addresses both by evolving the research states agents inherit, recording hypotheses, programs, experimental evidence and unresolved needs in a shared graph so each experiment reshapes what later agents start from.

- Feedback-Guided Swarm Mutation uses other agents' results to choose between revising a hypothesis (H-mutation) or repairing its program (P-mutation), Complementary Swarm Recombination reuses retained hypotheses on other agents' program bases (rebase) and splices per-instance winning components from up to two donors (crossover), and a discounted-UCB controller decides whether the next step works on the hypothesis or program frontier.
- With `Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview` it reaches an `OpenProblems` average of **76.2** (74.2 with `DeepSeek-V4-Pro` versus 67.1 for `TusoAI`), a **44.4%** Match-SOTA rate on all 90 `NatureBench` tasks with either backbone (7.8 pp above `Arbor` and 16.7 pp above `AIDE` at the same backbone, both significant), and an **81.8%** Any-Medal rate on `MLE-Bench Lite`, which beats same-backbone evolution agents but not `Arbor` running on `GPT-5.5` at 86.4%.
- In one `DeepSeek-V4-Pro` seed about **77%** of final best `NatureBench` programs descend from a rebase, crossover or feedback-triggered update, later refinement rescues 35% of failed implementations (versus 12% for `AIDE` and 5% for `Arbor`), and ablations show removing P-mutation costs 13.3 pp Match-SOTA while removing H/P selection causes the largest drop in mean improvement.
- Inherited states also transfer across tasks, raising Match-SOTA on 12 held-out `NatureBench` tasks from 41.7% to 86.1% over a cold start, and biologists reproduced two evolved programs for follow-up analyses of intestinal enterocytes and splenic B-cell neighbourhoods.
- Most of the search budget still goes to dead ends, since 93.3% of 644 annotated failures were faithful interventions that simply produced no gain, Surpass-SOTA on `NatureBench` stays at 15.6%, the headline reuse statistic comes from a single seed, and significance testing covers only the `Arbor` and `AIDE` comparisons while the rest are descriptive.

papers.title: The Accuracy Well: Nonmonotone Accuracy Dynamics at Vanishing Initialization
papers.abstract: We study classification dynamics under small initialization and identify a pronounced non-monotone behavior of accuracy that we call the accuracy well: accuracy rises rapidly early in training, subsequently drops, and only much later recovers. We observe this phenomenon in deep linear networks, fully connected ReLU networks on MNIST, deep convolutional networks on CIFAR-10, and controlled synthetic tasks, across different losses and optimizers and in both training and test accuracy. We propose a three-stage explanation in terms of target-driven organization, a degeneracy bottleneck, and subsequent recruitment and recovery. We develop a rigorous theory of these dynamics for shallow and deep linear networks, showing in particular that high accuracy can emerge while the predictor and the change in loss remain asymptotically vanishing, before continued optimization causes accuracy to deteriorate. For a simple synthetic classification task, we prove an extreme instance in which accuracy asymptotically rises to 100%, collapses to 0, and later recovers permanently to 100%. Our results show that classification accuracy can reveal aspects of learning dynamics that are not captured by the training loss alone.
papers.summary: Under very small initialization, classification accuracy during training can rise quickly, fall, and only much later recover, a non-monotone pattern the authors call the accuracy well. They observe it in deep linear networks, fully connected ReLU networks on `MNIST`, convolutional networks on `CIFAR-10`, and controlled synthetic tasks, across losses and optimizers and in both training and test accuracy, and explain it in three stages: target-driven organization, a degeneracy bottleneck, and later recruitment and recovery. For shallow and deep linear networks they prove that **high accuracy can emerge while the predictor and the change in loss remain asymptotically vanishing**, before continued optimization degrades it, and for a simple synthetic task they prove accuracy rises to 100%, collapses to 0, and then recovers permanently. The results show that accuracy can expose learning dynamics the training loss alone does not capture.

papers.title: What Does Disagreement Mean? A Semantic Identifiability Frontier for Pairwise Preference Learning
papers.abstract: Pairwise comparison data are a standard supervision signal in preference learning, but disagreement in such data can reflect stable latent heterogeneity, ephemeral stochasticity, or non-binary responses hidden by a forced-choice interface. We study which of these semantic distinctions are identifiable from the feedback channel itself. We introduce a nonparametric latent semantic model with three querywise quantities: aggregate directional preference $\mu_q$, persistent disagreement $\tau_q$, and non-binary mass $\alpha_q$. Under the anonymous binary channel, we prove an exact semantic fiber theorem: $\mu_q$ is point-identified, whereas $(\tau_q, \alpha_q)$ vary over an explicit feasible region compatible with the same binary law. Same-annotator repeats identify $\tau_q$ through a covariance identity, abstention-enabled feedback identifies $\alpha_q$ directly, and together they point-identify the full semantic triple. We also derive finite-sample estimators, nonasymptotic concentration bounds, and semantics-aware action-recovery guarantees, and validate the theory on theorem-matched synthetic data.
papers.summary: Disagreement in pairwise comparison data can reflect stable differences between annotators, transient randomness, or non-binary responses that a forced-choice interface hides, and the authors ask which of these can be told apart from the feedback channel itself. They introduce a nonparametric latent semantic model with three per-query quantities: aggregate directional preference, persistent disagreement, and non-binary mass. **Under an anonymous binary channel only the aggregate preference is point-identified**, while the other two range over an explicit feasible region consistent with the same binary law; same-annotator repeats identify persistent disagreement through a covariance identity, abstention-enabled feedback identifies non-binary mass directly, and together they pin down the full triple. The paper also derives finite-sample estimators, nonasymptotic concentration bounds, and semantics-aware action-recovery guarantees, validated on synthetic data matched to the theorems.

papers.title: The COUNT: Counting N-grams Unlocks Scaling on Host Memory and Training-Free Adaptation
papers.abstract: The scaling relationship of compute and performance for language models (LMs) has been extensively studied; more recently, models are being designed to scale memory use, as well. In particular, adding embeddings for n-grams scales memory separately from compute use, because each pass only processes individual embedding rows, which are much smaller than the storage used for the whole embedding table. However, existing methods train embeddings from scratch, which needs expensive GPU memory for fast reading and writing. Meanwhile, the ordinary memory of the host system is cheap and underutilized by these training methods. To scale on host memory, we introduce COUNT (Counting Offline Unlocks N-gram Transformers), which builds n-gram embeddings without adding learned parameters by storing precomputed n-gram counts on host. We use the corpus frequencies to weight together the LM's own unembeddings of the next tokens most often following the current n-gram history. At a fixed compute budget, COUNT can be added as an additional input embedding for pretraining 1B-parameter LMs to improve validation loss as much as an LM with 57% more compute. If GPU memory is limited, using COUNT to let backbone parameters fill GPU memory gives better performance than splitting memory with additional learned n-gram embeddings. Beyond efficiency, COUNT allows switching in a different table of n-gram counts from a domain-specific corpus at inference time to adapt to a new task without any training.
papers.summary: Adding n-gram embeddings lets language models scale memory separately from compute, but existing methods train those embeddings from scratch in scarce GPU memory while cheap host memory sits idle. `COUNT` (Counting Offline Unlocks N-gram Transformers) builds n-gram embeddings with no new learned parameters by storing precomputed n-gram counts on the host and using corpus frequencies to weight together the model's own unembeddings of the tokens that most often follow the current history. At a fixed compute budget, **adding `COUNT` as an extra input embedding when pretraining 1B-parameter models improves validation loss as much as giving the model 57% more compute**, and when GPU memory is limited it beats splitting that memory with learned n-gram embeddings. Because the counts live outside the model, a count table from a domain-specific corpus can be swapped in at inference time to adapt to a new task without any training.

papers.title: Same Claim, Different Interpretations: How LLM Agents Resolve Ambiguity in Scientific Claims
papers.abstract: Co-scientists and agentic scientific claim verifiers are increasingly used to assess claims across the sciences. Natural-language scientific claims, written for human experts, are often underspecified and so admit several defensible interpretations. Such verifiers usually pick one, often tacitly, and benchmarks score their verdicts against expert labels without recording the expert's interpretation or the verifier's in a comparable form. This leads to disagreements with expert labels that cannot be traced to the evidence or the interpretation, and to compute spent on unchecked interpretations. We introduce Claim Cards to make such interpretations explicit in the reasoning itself. A Claim Card records a verifier's interpretation as nine fields before evidence gathering, each marked stated, inferred, or default. To test whether an agent's interpretation can change its verdict, we ran a GPT-5.4 agent five times on each of 60 expert-labeled materials-science and biomedical claims with a card, without one, and with one card frozen across runs (900 runs). Over 40% of card fields were not marked stated, and a card added about a tenth to a run's GPT-5.4 tokens and time without measurably changing agreement with expert labels. The agent's own interpretations varied between runs, although within a claim this variation did not measurably track the verdict. A deliberate change to one field of the frozen card, however, making the quantifier universal or the threshold for support stricter, changed the verdict on about a third of the claims, against about one in seven expected by chance (p < 0.001 for each edit). On 24 materials-science claims run with computational tools, the stricter threshold also changed what the agent asked those tools to compute. We therefore argue that verdicts should be reported with their interpretations and that benchmarks could publish the interpretation behind each label.
papers.summary: Agentic verifiers increasingly assess scientific claims, but natural-language claims written for experts are underspecified, so a verifier tacitly picks one interpretation and benchmarks score its verdict against expert labels without recording either side's reading. `Claim Cards` make the interpretation explicit as nine fields recorded before evidence gathering, each marked stated, inferred, or default. Running a `GPT-5.4` agent five times on each of 60 expert-labeled materials-science and biomedical claims with a card, without one, and with one card frozen across runs (900 runs in total), the authors find that over 40% of fields were not marked stated, that a card added about a tenth to tokens and time without measurably changing agreement with experts, but that **deliberately editing one field of the frozen card, making the quantifier universal or the support threshold stricter, changed the verdict on about a third of claims versus one in seven expected by chance**. They argue verdicts should be reported with their interpretations and that benchmarks could publish the interpretation behind each label.

papers.title: MolLean: A Process-Verifiable Language for Chemical Reasoning
papers.abstract: Chemical chain-of-thought can contain hallucinated structural and property claims. We thereby introduce MolLean, a process-verifiable language that grounds chemical reasoning in an explicit molecular state. A layered Lean-based kernel checks state transitions and assertions over molecular readouts, from primitive graph edits to compound transformations. Meanwhile, a typed witness protocol separates native structural checks from externally supplied measurements. We further introduce MolLean-MCP, a stateful tool interface that exposes these transitions, checks, and readouts during generation: the model receives feedback to decide its next action, and rejected actions leave the state unchanged. MolLean supports one-pass trace execution, whole-trace refinement, and interactive reasoning through MolLean-MCP. We evaluate these three modes with direct chain-of-thought on 8,800 matched examples across 12 tasks spanning molecular generation, editing, optimization, and reactions. With Qwen3.6-27B, whole-trace refinement outperforms direct chain-of-thought on all 12 tasks. MolLean-MCP complements whole-trace refinement with stepwise verification feedback, reaching better performance in reaction tasks. Together, these results highlight an executable foundation for chemical reasoning, in which explicit chemical commitments can be checked and revised rather than remaining solely in free-form explanations.
papers.summary: Chemical chain-of-thought can assert molecular structures and properties that do not hold. `MolLean` is a process-verifiable language that grounds reasoning in an explicit molecular state, with a layered Lean-based kernel that checks state transitions and assertions from primitive graph edits up to compound transformations, and a typed witness protocol that separates native structural checks from externally supplied measurements. `MolLean-MCP` exposes these transitions, checks, and readouts as a stateful tool interface during generation, so the model receives feedback before choosing its next action and rejected actions leave the state unchanged. Across 8,800 matched examples on 12 tasks spanning molecular generation, editing, optimization, and reactions, **whole-trace refinement with `Qwen3.6-27B` outperforms direct chain-of-thought on all 12 tasks**, and the interactive `MolLean-MCP` mode does best on reaction tasks.

papers.title: Equal CER, Unequal Damage: Severity-Weighted Character Error Rate for OCR
papers.abstract: Character Error Rate (CER), the standard metric for OCR and vision-language models (VLMs), charges a typo as much as a wrong name. We introduce semCER, which keeps CER's alignment and denominator and charges each grapheme edit a severity from an LLM judge, with no word segmentation. Normalized CER keeps the score of a whole transcription, where it tracks readers as well as semCER or better, and semCER breaks that score down into named edits. The charges track readers' ratings edit by edit in English, Vietnamese, and Chinese and put the edits readers rate most severe near the top of a sorted list. On pairs drawn where CER and semCER disagreed, readers side with semCER more often than with normalized CER in English and Chinese, and equally often in Vietnamese. Across 16 languages, the judge charges a wrong diacritic or tone mark almost nothing in Spanish but nearly a wrong letter's severity in Telugu. Where we can count real words, a general VLM's wrong letter forms one far above chance while a classical pipeline's stays near it. We release the 61 million judged edits, the aggregated reader ratings, and the distilled scorer at https://github.com/nguyenx2t/semcer.
papers.summary: Character Error Rate (CER), the standard metric for optical character recognition and vision-language models (VLMs), charges a harmless typo the same as a corrupted name. `semCER` keeps CER's alignment and denominator but weights each grapheme edit by a severity assigned by an LLM judge, with no word segmentation, so a transcription's score breaks down into named edits ranked by damage. **The per-edit charges track human readers' ratings edit by edit in English, Vietnamese, and Chinese**, and on pairs where CER and semCER disagree, readers side with semCER more often in English and Chinese and equally often in Vietnamese. Across 16 languages the judge charges a wrong diacritic or tone mark almost nothing in Spanish but nearly a full letter's severity in Telugu, and the authors release 61 million judged edits, the aggregated reader ratings, and a distilled scorer.

papers.title: Learning by Examples: Power Grid Steady State Analysis with a Tabular Foundation Model
papers.abstract: Foundation models have shown strong generalization across scientific domains, but their use in power systems remains largely task-specific. We investigate whether a pretrained tabular foundation model (TFM), TabPFN, can serve as a general-purpose neural solver for power grid steady-state analysis. We evaluate the TFM on three tasks: power flow (PF) prediction, N-k contingency screening (NCS), and voltage stability margin (VSM) prediction. We performed experiments on 118- and 2000-bus systems, comparing the TFM against task-specific neural baselines. Without retraining or fine-tuning, the TFM matches or outperforms the best task-specific model in several settings across the three tasks. For 118-bus PF prediction, a variant of the TFM achieves errors of $1\times 10^{-3}$ pu for voltage magnitudes and $0.30^\circ$ for voltage angles, outperforming all baselines. On unseen N-1 contingency and close-to-infeasible PF cases, the TFM is competitive with the DCPF approximation. For millions of unseen N-2 contingencies, the TFM achieves AUCs of 0.92 and 0.95 for branch and voltage violation screening, respectively. The TFM also attains accurate VSM prediction performance for the 2000-bus system with limited labelled data. The TFM attains strong results across the tested tasks despite pretraining without any power-system-specific dataset and requiring no fine-tuning step. These results offer a glimpse into the potential of pretrained TFMs as a neural solver for a range of power grid analysis tasks.
papers.summary: Foundation models generalize across scientific domains, but their use in power systems has stayed task-specific.
