The authors test whether a pretrained tabular foundation model (TFM), `TabPFN`, can serve as a general neural solver for steady-state grid analysis on three tasks, power flow (PF) prediction, N-k contingency screening (NCS), and voltage stability margin (VSM) prediction, over 118-bus and 2000-bus systems against task-specific neural baselines. **Without any retraining or fine-tuning, the TFM matches or outperforms the best task-specific model in several settings**, with a variant reaching voltage-magnitude errors of about 0.001 per unit on 118-bus power flow, AUCs of 0.92 and 0.95 for branch and voltage violation screening over millions of unseen N-2 contingencies, and accurate VSM predictions on the 2000-bus system with limited labels, despite pretraining on no power-system data at all.

papers.title: Selective Growing Q-Networks (SGQN): An Analysis of Adaptive Action Grids in Decoupled Q-Learning
papers.abstract: Value-based Q-learning for continuous control can discretise the action space, but the resolution of the discretisation trades early exploration against final precision. Growing Q-Networks (GQN) grow the resolution uniformly from coarse to fine. We introduce Selective Growing Q-Networks (SGQN), which keeps decoupled Q-learning and replaces uniform growth with an adaptive action grid: bins are added next to bins with high estimated Q-value, bins with low Q-value are pruned, and actions are chosen epsilon-greedily. On eight DeepMind Control Suite (DMControl) tasks with 2 to 12 action dimensions, SGQN has the highest mean final return among the compared methods on four, is within 1.1% of the best method on three more, and is 3.4% below Bang-Bang MPO on Walker Run, using on average 7.5 of 9 available bins per dimension. We then test whether the adaptive grid explains these results, and find that it does not. Growth activates every candidate bin and behaves like uniform growth, and removing pruning changes the return by at most 1.1%. Two other choices matter: starting from a coarse grid, since starting with all 9 bins produces collapsed seeds, and epsilon-greedy selection, since an annealed softmax lowers the return by 23% to 100%. SGQN is insensitive to its growth and pruning hyperparameters. It also differs from the GQN and DecQN baselines in other respects, notably one gradient update per environment step instead of one per eight, which we did not control for, so we do not attribute its advantage to a single component. We present SGQN as a competitive value-based method and as an analysis of which ingredients of a growing action grid matter.
papers.summary: Value-based Q-learning can handle continuous control by discretizing actions, but the grid resolution trades early exploration against final precision, and Growing Q-Networks (`GQN`) grow it uniformly from coarse to fine. Selective Growing Q-Networks (`SGQN`) keep decoupled Q-learning but add bins next to high-value bins, prune low-value bins, and select actions epsilon-greedily; on eight `DeepMind Control Suite` tasks it has the highest mean final return on four and is within 1.1% of the best method on three more. **The ablations show the adaptive grid does not explain these gains**: growth activates every candidate bin and behaves like uniform growth, removing pruning changes return by at most 1.1%, while starting from a coarse grid and using epsilon-greedy rather than annealed softmax selection matter a great deal. The authors also flag an uncontrolled difference in gradient updates per environment step relative to the baselines and so decline to attribute the advantage to any single component.

papers.title: ChronoCulture: Evaluating Cultural Awareness Across Time in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Cultural attitudes and social norms evolve over time, yet most cultural benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) treat culture as a static attribute of a country or region. We introduce ChronoCulture, a benchmark of 10,360 temporal pairs built from longitudinal survey data across 72 countries. Each pair contains the same survey question asked in the same country in an older and a newer year, with full population response distributions as ground truth. Across six LLMs, we find that models can often predict a country's attitudes at one point in time but do not reliably capture how those attitudes change. Their predictions for different years tend to stay close together, failing to capture much of the observed change. Specifying the intended year in the prompt also offers little overall improvement in alignment with survey responses. These findings suggest that models often present a largely static picture of cultural attitudes, highlighting the need to evaluate cultural awareness across time.
papers.summary: Cultural benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) usually treat a country's attitudes as static, even though norms shift over time. `ChronoCulture` pairs the same survey question asked in the same country in an older and a newer year, with full population response distributions as ground truth, yielding 10,360 temporal pairs from longitudinal surveys across 72 countries. Evaluating six LLMs, the authors find that models can often predict a country's attitudes at a single point in time but **their predictions for different years stay close together and miss much of the observed change**, and specifying the intended year in the prompt offers little overall improvement in alignment with survey responses.

papers.title: SafeAdapt-Poker: Counterfactual Risk Calibration for Budgeted Adaptation under Opponent Shift
papers.abstract: Opponent histories can mislead after behavioral shifts. SafeAdapt-Poker formulates budgeted adaptation under opponent shift as a dual-counterfactual sequential-control problem using only information available before each decision. At each decision the controller asks two distinct questions: what local downside a deviation from the frozen anchor would induce under matched legal continuations, and what future adaptation value would be lost by consuming part of the remaining deviation budget now. The first question is answered by a monotone strategic-risk model over deviation intensity; the second by a paired budget-state continuation model that prices current budget consumption. The controller selects among support-preserving candidate deviations by trading immediate adaptation value against these two quantities, a pathwise cumulative-KL ledger bounds total anchor-relative deviation, and a finite family of frozen controllers is screened on complete paired calibration sessions before held-out interaction. A finite-candidate perturbation bound shows that the allocation objective degrades continuously with continuation-value estimation error. Evaluation covers exact-game exploitation and safety, four opponent shifts, local-risk calibration, delayed-opportunity allocation, direct opportunity-value estimation, value-error robustness, factorial mechanism attribution, budget sensitivity, abstract-HUNL cross-play, and player/time-held-out public-history behavior. On exact Leduc the full controller attains a matched weak-pool gain of +0.0718 with a worst-opponent delta of -0.0126, raises delayed-opportunity capture from 0.6318 under myopic allocation to 0.7841 under the same session budget, and reaches +42.7 mbb/hand in abstract-HUNL cross-play; the retained public-history screen reports 0.5820 action accuracy and 0.9277 log loss versus 0.5039 and 0.9778 for a public prior.
papers.summary: Opponent histories can mislead once an opponent's behavior shifts. `SafeAdapt-Poker` frames budgeted adaptation under opponent shift as a dual-counterfactual sequential-control problem using only information available before each decision: a monotone strategic-risk model estimates the local downside of deviating from a frozen anchor strategy, and a paired budget-state continuation model prices how much future adaptation value is lost by spending deviation budget now. The controller chooses among support-preserving candidate deviations by trading immediate adaptation value against these two costs, a cumulative-KL ledger bounds total deviation from the anchor, and a perturbation bound shows the objective degrades continuously with continuation-value error. On exact `Leduc` poker the full controller **raises delayed-opportunity capture from 0.6318 under myopic allocation to 0.7841 at the same session budget** with a worst-opponent delta of only -0.0126, and it reaches +42.7 milli-big-blinds per hand in abstract heads-up no-limit (HUNL) cross-play.

papers.title: AdaRSI: On-Demand Recursive Self-Improvement for Embodied Agents
papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs) often fail midway through unseen long-horizon tasks. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a remedy, but embodied RSI methods either refine the harness around a frozen executor and so cannot add a missing motion, or train the executor on persistent failures without asking whether a failure lies in how the executor is called or in what it can do. We ask when a self-improving embodied system should change the weights of its executor, and propose AdaRSI, an on-demand RSI framework for embodied agents. A coding agent first improves its skills and harness, then attributes persistent failures by retrying failing sub-steps from saved states, and fine-tunes only the sub-steps that remain unreliable, with demonstrations it collects itself and experience carried over from earlier tasks. On all 50 target tasks of RoboCasa365, with GR00T N1.5 as the executor and no human demonstrations, AdaRSI improves the VLA on all three suites and raises its success on unseen composite tasks from 4.6% to 13.8%. Compared with fine-tuning every sub-step, it reaches slightly higher success while using only 28% of the GPU time and 22% of the self-collected demonstrations, and fine-tuning without a harness trains more yet gains far less.
papers.summary: Pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs) often fail partway through unseen long-horizon tasks, and existing embodied recursive self-improvement (RSI) methods either refine only the harness around a frozen executor, so they cannot add a missing motion, or fine-tune on every persistent failure without asking whether the fault lies in how the executor is called or in what it can do. `AdaRSI` has a coding agent first improve the skills and harness, then attribute persistent failures by retrying failing sub-steps from saved states, and fine-tune only the sub-steps that remain unreliable, using demonstrations it collects itself plus experience carried over from earlier tasks. On all 50 target tasks of `RoboCasa365` with `GR00T N1.5` as the executor and no human demonstrations, it improves the VLA on all three suites and **raises success on unseen composite tasks from 4.6% to 13.8%**, slightly exceeding fine-tuning every sub-step while using only 28% of the GPU time and 22% of the self-collected demonstrations.

papers.title: Lost in Translation: Why Lower Bias Scores Don't Mean Fairer Models
papers.abstract: Bias audits of multilingual language models usually compare a model's average stereotype score in English with its average in another language and read the difference as a difference in fairness. We ask how much of that difference is noise. Auditing ten open models in eight languages, we measure how far scores move when English test items are merely reworded, test every language shift item by item, and check that the test catches shifts we inject on purpose. In all 70 model-language pairs the stereotype score falls below its English level, and for Hindi, Korean and Swahili the drop clearly exceeds what rewording English produces; most of it comes from StereoSet items. Judging every translation, we find that imperfect ones drop more, but faithful translations alone drop nearly as much. Still, a lower average does not show that a model is fairer. An item's English score predicts its translated score far less well than its reworded score (correlation 0.23, 0.27 on faithful translations, vs. 0.48), while scores stay as far from neutral, models agree on translated items, and within Hindi or Spanish a translated item's score correlates with its own rewording at 0.84 and 0.82. The average cannot distinguish lower bias from a different pattern of item-level scores. We also document three common pipeline errors that silently erase bias signal, and release our code.
papers.summary: Multilingual bias audits usually compare a model's average stereotype score in English with its score in another language and read the gap as a fairness difference, and the authors ask how much of that gap is noise. Auditing ten open models in eight languages, they measure how far scores move when English items are merely reworded, test every language shift item by item, and confirm the test detects deliberately injected shifts. In all 70 model-language pairs the stereotype score falls below its English level, and for Hindi, Korean, and Swahili the drop clearly exceeds rewording noise, mostly from `StereoSet` items; yet **an item's English score predicts its translated score far worse than its reworded score (correlations of 0.23 to 0.27 versus 0.48)**, while scores stay as far from neutral and models agree on translated items, so the lower average reflects a different pattern of item-level scores rather than less bias. The paper also documents three common pipeline errors that silently erase bias signal and releases its code.

papers.title: Decoupled Marginal Sharpening for Training-Free Inference-Time Scaling
papers.abstract: We study how to improve LLM reasoning at inference time without updating model weights or using external reward models. Recent reward-free power-sampling methods define the sequence-level power target $\pi_\alpha(y\mid x)\propto p_0(y\mid x)^\alpha$, where $\alpha>1$, which increases the relative probability of completions that are already likely under the base model. Existing methods use Metropolis--Hastings or Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) to approximately sample from this target. However, two challenges arise at different levels. At the target level, full-sequence sharpening can concentrate probability on a few exact reasoning--answer trajectories, suppressing alternative paths that support the same answer. At the sampler level, finite-particle SMC can suffer from path collapse when resampling repeatedly duplicates a few high-weight prefixes. To address these challenges, we propose Decoupled Marginal Sharpening (DMS), which separately controls how strongly the model favors particular reasoning paths and how strongly it favors final answers after aggregating support across those paths. At the target level, DMS first samples from a sharpened reasoning distribution, then marginalizes the model's answer probabilities over the resulting weighted reasoning population and sharpens the induced answer marginal. Separate exponents allow mild reasoning sharpening to encourage exploration of diverse paths, followed by stronger answer-marginal sharpening to concentrate probability on answers with greater aggregate support across those paths. At the sampler level, we develop Fully Adapted Annealed SMC, which combines an annealed sequence of power targets with locally fully adapted proposals and predictive ancestor resampling. Experiments on MATH500, GPQA-Diamond, HumanEval, and AIME24/25 across three base models show that DMS achieves the highest mean pass@1 among the compared methods in all tasks.
papers.summary: Reward-free power sampling improves large language model reasoning at inference time by targeting the base distribution raised to a power alpha greater than 1, approximated with Metropolis-Hastings or Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC), but sharpening whole sequences can concentrate mass on a few exact reasoning-answer trajectories while suppressing alternative paths to the same answer, and finite-particle SMC can collapse onto a few duplicated prefixes. Decoupled Marginal Sharpening (`DMS`) separates the two levers: it samples from a mildly sharpened reasoning distribution to keep paths diverse, then marginalizes the model's answer probabilities over the weighted reasoning population and applies stronger sharpening to that answer marginal. A companion sampler, `Fully Adapted Annealed SMC`, anneals through a sequence of power targets with locally fully adapted proposals and predictive ancestor resampling. **Across `MATH500`, `GPQA-Diamond`, `HumanEval`, and `AIME24/25` on three base models, `DMS` reports the highest mean pass@1 among the compared methods on every task**.

papers.title: Average-Reward Policy Identification from a Single Continuing Trajectory
papers.abstract: In reinforcement learning, an agent must explore an unknown environment to learn how to make good decisions. Unlike methods that can freely sample any state--action pair, an agent learning from a single trajectory must spend additional time navigating between states. It is therefore natural to expect that learning from a single trajectory requires more experience. In this paper, we show that this additional cost is not always necessary. For average-reward reinforcement learning, we develop an algorithm that learns where to collect information while ensuring that the required samples can be obtained efficiently. We establish an upper bound on the number of interactions needed to identify a near-optimal policy. Furthermore, we prove a matching information theoretic lower bound, showing that, for a broad class of environments and at sufficiently high accuracy, learning from a single trajectory is no harder in the worst case than learning with unrestricted access to state action samples. Our results reveal that the additional complexity cost of navigation can be avoided by adapting information gathering requirements to how the environment provides information.
papers.summary: An agent learning from a single continuing trajectory must spend time traveling between states, so it is usually assumed to need more experience than one that can sample any state-action pair at will. For average-reward reinforcement learning, the authors design an algorithm that decides where information is needed while ensuring those samples can be collected efficiently along the trajectory, and they prove an upper bound on the number of interactions required to identify a near-optimal policy. **A matching information-theoretic lower bound shows that, for a broad class of environments at sufficiently high accuracy, single-trajectory learning is no harder in the worst case than learning with unrestricted sample access.** The navigation overhead can therefore be avoided by adapting information-gathering demands to how the environment reveals information.

papers.title: Hindsight-Privileged RLVR: Single-Rollout Token Credit Without Group Sampling
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains language models from checked task outcomes, but assigning a terminal reward to individual reasoning tokens or actions remains difficult. Group-relative methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) sample several attempts per prompt, but lose their reward-based learning signal when all attempts receive the same outcome. We propose Hindsight-Privileged RLVR (HP-RLVR), a single-rollout method that turns a completed trajectory's own future into token-level update weights. The generating policy snapshot scores each eligible token under its causal history and under a hindsight context containing the realized future and verifier feedback. A normalized Jensen--Shannon divergence between the two views weights the reward relative to a historical baseline, yielding bounded token credit for both successful and failed attempts, with no reference solution or learned critic. In paired Qwen3-8B runs over a shared $100$-step schedule, HP-RLVR trains $1.21\times$, $1.46\times$, and $2.30\times$ faster than GRPO on mathematics, code generation, and ALFWorld, using one eighth the rollouts per prompt. Accuracy is comparable overall, with HP-RLVR ahead on mathematics at all three sizes and GRPO ahead on code and ALFWorld. In ALFWorld, $43.2\%$ (4B) and $49.0\%$ (8B) of GRPO's gradient-norm records are zero, versus none for HP-RLVR.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains language models from checked outcomes, but group-relative methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) need several rollouts per prompt and lose their learning signal when every attempt earns the same outcome. Hindsight-Privileged RLVR (`HP-RLVR`) uses a single rollout: the generating policy snapshot scores each token under its normal causal history and under a hindsight context containing the realized future and verifier feedback, and a normalized Jensen-Shannon divergence between the two views becomes a bounded token-level weight on the reward, with no reference solution or learned critic. In paired `Qwen3-8B` runs over a shared 100-step schedule, **training ran 1.21x, 1.46x, and 2.30x faster than the group-relative baseline on mathematics, code generation, and ALFWorld while using one eighth the rollouts per prompt**, with comparable overall accuracy, ahead on math and behind on code and `ALFWorld`. On `ALFWorld`, 43.2% and 49.0% of `GRPO` gradient-norm records at 4B and 8B were zero, versus none for `HP-RLVR`.

papers.title: Graph-Enhanced Disease Trajectory Discovery and Temporal Endpoint Forecasting from Longitudinal Electronic Health Records
papers.abstract: Longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) can reveal disease-progression structure, while useful forecasting requires leakage-controlled discovery, censor-aware outcomes, and inspectable trajectory evidence. We developed a graph-enhanced framework in MIMIC-IV v3.1 that splits patients before graph construction, learns train-only consecutive-admission transitions, and freezes endpoint-specific branching-motif policies selected on validation data. The final catalog contained 99,527 motifs, and a time-aware Transformer retrieved at most 24 patient-compatible motifs per endpoint through endpoint-specific cross-attention. Across five training seeds, micro-AUPRC increased from 0.9330 to 0.9357, while event-time MAE decreased from 676.9 to 657.7 days (reduction 19.2 days; 95% paired patient-cluster bootstrap CI, 13.8-24.8). Timing effects were heterogeneous: MAE worsened for events within 730 days but improved by 58.9 days for events occurring after 730 days. In an exploratory internal temporal split, branch conditioning reduced conditional event-time MAE by 26.9 days (95% CI, 23.0-30.8) without evidence of better micro-AUPRC. Corrected survival evaluation over the supported 0-2,555-day interval did not establish macro C-index or integrated Brier score superiority over a matched history-only discrete-hazard model. A directed, degree-matched GNN repair substantially improved unseen-edge discovery, yet replacing GNN-derived scores within fixed motif identities did not improve downstream forecasting. These results position branching motifs as structured trajectory context whose main value is long-range timing support rather than uniformly stronger endpoint discrimination, survival prediction, or causal explanation.
papers.summary: Longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) encode disease-progression structure, but turning it into useful forecasts requires guarding against leakage, handling censored outcomes, and exposing inspectable trajectory evidence. Using `MIMIC-IV v3.1`, the authors split patients before graph construction, learn consecutive-admission transitions on training data only, freeze a catalog of 99,527 branching motifs selected on validation data, and let a time-aware Transformer retrieve up to 24 patient-compatible motifs per endpoint through cross-attention. **Motif conditioning lowered event-time mean absolute error from 676.9 to 657.7 days**, with the gain concentrated in events more than two years out, while micro-AUPRC barely moved and corrected survival metrics showed no advantage over a history-only discrete-hazard baseline. The authors conclude that branching motifs mainly provide long-range timing support rather than stronger endpoint discrimination or causal explanation.

papers.title: ReaDy: Recurrent States as Dynamic Context for Speculative Drafting in Hybrid Linear Attention Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting multiple tokens per step, yet feature-based drafters rely on target hidden features whose contextual emphasis may not align with the needs of subsequent draft positions. Hybrid linear attention (HLA) models maintain compact recurrent states that accumulate historical associations, offering an efficient source of complementary context for speculative drafting. We introduce ReaDy, the first speculative decoding method, to the best of our knowledge, to leverage HLA recurrent states for position-specific context retrieval during drafting. ReaDy equips each draft position with a learned query to retrieve supplementary context directly from the target's committed recurrent states. A lightweight state reader integrates this context into draft representations through residual updates, while low-rank state reads and fused operators keep additional computation and I/O overhead low. Building on DSpark's parallel backbone and sequential prediction head, ReaDy employs a lightweight two-stage adaptation strategy, with reader capacity, state sources, and residual placement examined through ablation studies. Across seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and dialogue, ReaDy achieves an average $3.16\times$ decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding with Qwen3.8-27B on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU. It outperforms DSpark on every benchmark, improving throughput by 7.97% and acceptance length by 8.50% on average. Our code is available at https://github.com/StartLuxLabs/ReaDy.
papers.summary: Feature-based speculative drafters reuse the target model's hidden features, whose contextual emphasis may not suit later draft positions. Hybrid linear attention (HLA) models keep compact recurrent states that accumulate historical associations, and `ReaDy` gives each draft position a learned query that retrieves supplementary context from the target's committed recurrent states, folding it into the draft representation through a lightweight state reader with low-rank reads and fused operators to limit compute and I/O overhead. Built on the parallel backbone and sequential prediction head of `DSpark` with a two-stage adaptation scheme, the method reaches **an average 3.16x decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding** with `Qwen3.8-27B` on a single NVIDIA B200 across seven math, code, and dialogue benchmarks. It beats `DSpark` on every benchmark, with 7.97% higher throughput and 8.50% longer acceptance length on average.

papers.title: VascuSR: Iterative Anatomy-Aware Diffusion for CT Super-Resolution
papers.abstract: Generative super-resolution (SR) can recover sharp detail in computed tomography (CT) images from severely downsampled observations, but the missing high-frequency content is not uniquely determined by the low-resolution input. Consequently, visually plausible reconstructions may contain anatomically unsupported vascular detail, such as missing, spurious, or incorrectly connected vessels. To overcome this challenge, we introduce VascuSR, an iterative anatomy-aware diffusion framework that combines image reconstruction with explicit 3D vascular guidance. First, to provide richer anatomical guidance, we use an explicit 3D vascular representation that captures structural information beyond individual slices. This representation also simplifies vascular refinement by allowing a lightweight 3D generative refiner to focus on vascular structure rather than complex CT appearance. Second, to guide slice-wise SR, a lightweight anatomy controller injects the refined structure into the diffusion decoder, while iterative feedback updates this guidance from each new SR volume. On re-annotated MSD Task08 and HVM datasets, VascuSR outperforms interpolation and learning-based SR baselines in segmentation accuracy (Dice and clDice) and 3D vascular structure (connectivity and mean centerline distance), while maintaining image quality comparable to its SR backbone. Compared with learning-based baselines, VascuSR reduces class-averaged connected-component counts by over 20% on both datasets and mean centerline distance by over 10% on MSD.
papers.summary: Generative super-resolution (SR) can sharpen heavily downsampled computed tomography (CT) scans, but because the missing high-frequency content is not determined by the input, plausible outputs can invent, drop, or misconnect blood vessels. `VascuSR` pairs slice-wise diffusion SR with an explicit 3D vascular representation: a lightweight 3D generative refiner cleans up vessel structure, an anatomy controller injects that structure into the diffusion decoder, and the loop iterates so each new SR volume updates the guidance. On re-annotated `MSD Task08` and `HVM` data it beats interpolation and learned SR baselines on Dice, clDice, connectivity, and mean centerline distance while matching its backbone's image quality, **cutting class-averaged connected-component counts by more than 20% on both datasets** and mean centerline distance by more than 10% on MSD.

papers.title: A Two-Level Clinical Novelty Prioritization Framework for Disease Trajectories Discovered from Longitudinal Electronic Health Records
papers.abstract: Graph-based analysis of electronic health records (EHRs) yields disease-trajectory catalogs, but structural support does not establish semantic novelty. We present a two-level framework to prioritize 99,527 branching motifs previously discovered by an upstream patient-disjoint, train-only MIMIC-IV v3.1 pipeline and frozen after validation-based catalog selection. The framework separates path-level and node-to-endpoint semantic sparsity from reliability-adjusted clinical priority. Three deterministic textualizations per motif or node-target pair were embedded with BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 and calibrated against 166,972 pre-2023 PubMed references using mean top-20 cosine distance. Positive recombination occurred in 8.63% of motifs and had negligible effect on global ranking, whereas specificity and support/GNN reliability terms changed clinical-priority ordering. Robustness analyses across neighbor counts, templates, encoders, generic-label taxonomies, score settings, PrimeKG, and corrected density-based RND showed that broad ordering was more stable than hard top-k membership. A semantic-dose analysis did not support a monotonic relation between score and forecasting benefit after endpoint and token-count adjustment (1.96 days per SD; 95% CI, -0.75 to 4.68). In the frozen catalog-q90 high-semantic subgroup, branch-enhanced forecasting reduced conditional event-time MAE by 20.1 days (95% CI, 13.3-27.0) and sMAPE by 2.37 percentage points (95% CI, 1.81-2.93), while discrimination and endpoint-ranking differences were inconclusive. Corrected RND showed low tail agreement with the primary score (Spearman rho = 0.430; q90 Jaccard = 0.125) despite a similar aggregate timing association. These findings support representation-aware, uncertainty-aware literature-relative prioritization of discovered trajectories rather than causal discovery or clinician-adjudicated novelty.
papers.summary: Graph mining of electronic health records (EHRs) can produce large disease-trajectory catalogs, but structural support alone does not show that a trajectory is semantically new. Starting from 99,527 branching motifs frozen by an upstream patient-disjoint `MIMIC-IV v3.1` pipeline, the framework separates path-level and node-to-endpoint semantic sparsity from a reliability-adjusted clinical priority, embedding three deterministic textualizations per motif with `bge-small-en-v1.5` and calibrating against 166,972 pre-2023 PubMed references by mean top-20 cosine distance. Broad orderings proved stable across neighbor counts, templates, encoders, taxonomies, and `PrimeKG`, whereas hard top-k membership did not, and a dose analysis found no monotonic relation between semantic score and forecasting benefit. **In the high-semantic q90 subgroup, branch-enhanced forecasting reduced conditional event-time error by 20.1 days (95% CI 13.3 to 27.0)**, which the authors frame as literature-relative prioritization rather than causal discovery or clinician-adjudicated novelty.

papers.title: Bayesian Learning to Select Fair Classifiers
papers.abstract: Evaluations of classifiers (AI or human or agents) often assume a batch setting in which every agent produces labels on every example in a test set, which can be expensive or impractical in many contexts. This motivates online policies that adaptively select agents to query as examples arrive and update policies as outcomes are observed. We study the problem of selecting, in an online stream, the agent that best balances (i) predictive performance and (ii) subgroup fairness of a sensitive attribute, and that allows for delayed observations of true class labels. We formulate this as a Bayesian multi-armed bandit problem using Thompson Sampling, explicitly balancing accuracy and fairness. We conduct empirical evaluations on real-world datasets spanning problems involving tabular classifiers, large language models, and human labelers, demonstrating substantial reductions in regret relative to baselines. Our theoretical contributions include guarantees on the performance of the selected agent that incorporate both the accuracy and fairness aspects of the problem.
papers.summary: Evaluating a pool of candidate labelers, whether tabular models, large language models, or humans, usually assumes each one labels every test example, which is costly when examples arrive as a stream and true labels show up late. The authors cast the choice of which agent to query as a Bayesian multi-armed bandit solved with `Thompson Sampling`, with an objective that trades predictive accuracy against subgroup fairness on a sensitive attribute and tolerates delayed label feedback. **Across real-world datasets spanning tabular classifiers, large language models, and human labelers, the policy substantially reduces regret relative to baselines**, and the paper adds theoretical guarantees on the selected agent that cover both accuracy and fairness.

papers.title: VASPO: Self-Distillation with Privileged Value Estimation
papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation provides dense supervision for reasoning models via a privileged self-teacher. However, this supervision reflects local token preferences rather than the expected return of an unguided student continuation. Recent methods combine this signal with GRPO. They use GRPO for update directions and the teacher for signal scaling. However, we demonstrate a more effective integration within PPO. Specifically, we identify complementary positional dynamics: privileged information enhances a critic's value-prediction accuracy toward the response's end, whereas self-teacher guidance is strong initially, drops mid-generation, and rebounds finally. These insights motivate Value-Augmented Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (VASPO), wherein a self-teacher and critic evaluate identical privileged information at student-generated prefixes. The critic computes token-level PPO advantages from predicted continuation returns, while the self-teacher modulates selected positive advantages via bounded probability ratios. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VASPO improves mean accuracy over PPO by 2.59 and 1.81 percentage points on Qwen3-4B and OLMo3-7B variants, respectively, and achieves the highest mean accuracy among evaluated methods on Knights and Knaves. Our code is available at https://github.com/cii030/VASPO.
papers.summary: On-policy self-distillation gives reasoning models dense token-level supervision from a privileged self-teacher, but that signal reflects local token preferences rather than the expected return of an unguided continuation, and recent methods attach it to `GRPO` only as a scaling term. The authors identify complementary positional dynamics: privileged information makes a critic's value predictions more accurate toward the end of a response, while self-teacher guidance is strong early, weak mid-generation, and strong again at the end. Value-Augmented Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (`VASPO`) therefore has a critic and a self-teacher evaluate identical privileged information at student-generated prefixes inside `PPO`, with the critic producing token-level advantages from predicted continuation returns and the teacher modulating selected positive advantages through bounded probability ratios. **Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, mean accuracy rises over PPO by 2.59 points on Qwen3-4B and 1.81 points on OLMo3-7B**, and the method posts the highest mean accuracy of those compared on `Knights and Knaves`.

papers.title: The Physics Is the Network: Fast, Training-Free Neural Emulation
papers.abstract: Neural emulation need not require learning a substitute for known physics. We investigate PolyNets that couple a continuous-time neural representation of polynomial dynamics with a simple recurrent network for discrete-time integration. When the governing coefficients are known, the resulting tensor graph requires no training and preserves the prescribed numerical scheme while enabling efficient hardware execution and parallel simulation. Using the one-dimensional Korteweg-de Vries equation, we compare PolyNet with CPU and GPU finite-difference Runge-Kutta solvers and three trained neural models: a state-map emulator, a physics-informed predictor, and a learned-tendency integrator. Analytical soliton solutions provide a reference for amplitude and phase errors across grid resolutions, 10^6 dispersively scaled time steps, ensembles of up to 10^4 trajectories, and varying initial amplitudes. PolyNet achieves accuracy comparable to the numerical solvers, including at amplitudes outside the learned models' training conditions. It combines this fidelity with high GPU throughput, approximately constant over the tested resolution range, and favorable ensemble scaling.
papers.summary: When a system's governing equations are known, a neural emulator does not need to learn a substitute for them. `PolyNet` couples a continuous-time neural representation of polynomial dynamics with a simple recurrent network that performs discrete-time integration, so with known coefficients the resulting tensor graph requires no training, preserves the prescribed numerical scheme, and runs efficiently on accelerators with parallel simulation. On the one-dimensional Korteweg-de Vries equation, it is compared with CPU and GPU finite-difference Runge-Kutta solvers and three trained neural models (a state-map emulator, a physics-informed predictor, and a learned-tendency integrator) across grid resolutions, a million time steps, and ensembles of up to ten thousand trajectories. **Its accuracy matches the numerical solvers, including at wave amplitudes outside the trained models' training conditions**, while GPU throughput stays roughly constant over the tested resolutions and scales favorably with ensemble size.

papers.title: ActiveEvidence: Decision-Focused Evidence Graphs with Verifiable Acquisition Gaps
papers.abstract: A multimodal agent must decide whether visual evidence is worth acquiring, which candidate or resolution to query, and when further interaction can no longer change its decision. We study this problem under a strict free-metadata/paid-observation boundary, stochastic vector costs, and a frozen execution trace, and treat it as decision-certifiable active evidence acquisition. A Counterfactual Evidence Interaction Graph (CEIG) represents unary evidence value, signed second-order interaction, and directed conditional harm while maintaining explicit score enclosures for unresolved interactions; a decision-weighted enclosure objective tightens the bounds that can change action identity. Gap-directed refinement evaluates only interactions that can displace the incumbent acquisition and stops once an $\epsilon$-decision certificate shows that unresolved terms cannot change the selected action beyond a declared tolerance. The certificate is model-relative: it verifies policy-consistent optimality under the pinned learned score, and semantic quality is measured separately through post-freeze labels. Paired continuation rollouts learn the downstream value of paid previews, an online operational cost filter is separated from independent finite-policy-family trajectory certification, and an acquisition monitor with an independently implemented verifier binds every certificate to the frozen trace. On 640 cases split into 384/128/128 training, validation, and test cases, the controller reaches task score 0.842, grounding F1 0.816, evidence recall 0.873, 1.74 accepted calls, 286.5K visual tokens, and 742ms p95 latency. Dense replay of issued certificates shows 0.992 action agreement and a 0.988 certificate rate while evaluating 19.6 instead of 191.4 expensive interaction terms per decision.
papers.summary: A multimodal agent that must pay to observe visual evidence has to decide whether acquiring it is worthwhile, which candidate or resolution to request, and when further interaction can no longer change its decision. Under a strict free-metadata, paid-observation boundary with stochastic vector costs and a frozen execution trace, a Counterfactual Evidence Interaction Graph (`CEIG`) tracks unary evidence value, signed second-order interactions, and directed conditional harm with explicit score enclosures, and gap-directed refinement evaluates only interactions that could displace the incumbent choice until an epsilon-decision certificate shows the unresolved terms cannot flip the action. The certificate is model-relative, verifying optimality under the pinned learned score, with semantic quality measured separately through post-freeze labels, and an independently implemented verifier binds every certificate to the frozen trace. On 640 cases split 384/128/128, the controller reaches task score 0.842 and grounding F1 0.816 with 1.74 accepted calls and 742 ms p95 latency, and **dense replay of issued certificates shows 0.992 action agreement while evaluating 19.6 instead of 191.4 expensive interaction terms per decision**.

papers.title: Generative Representation Learning for Scalable Latent Tokenization
papers.abstract: We introduce an approach for self-supervised representation learning designed to be used as a tokenizer for generative modeling. Our objective supervises a representation loss by factorizing the pointwise mutual information of the data, which we estimate by taking information differences between conditional predictions from a learned generative model. We justify our algorithm theoretically and empirically, demonstrating that our generative approach to representation learning avoids dimensional collapse and feature suppression in cases where commonly used methods like DINO and LeJEPA fail. Moreover, we show our representation learning technique is scalable; expending more compute leads to predictably better latent tokenization. For the first time, we perform a careful analysis of the combined flop efficiency of tokenizer and generative model and demonstrate that our approach is a compute-optimal improvement over direct diffusion for pixel-space generation, obtaining an FID-50K of 2.18 with JiT-L. Applied to ImageNet and the text-to-image dataset GPIC, we show tokenizer encoder scaling laws for diffusability, where extrapolating our approach achieves representations in 7x fewer FLOPs than DINOv2 on ImageNet and 8x fewer FLOPs than WebSSL on GPIC.
papers.summary: Self-supervised representation learners such as `DINO` and `LeJEPA` can suffer dimensional collapse or feature suppression, which matters when their outputs are meant to serve as tokenizers for generative models. The proposed objective supervises the representation by factorizing the pointwise mutual information of the data, estimated from information differences between conditional predictions of a learned generative model, and the authors show theoretically and empirically that this avoids those failure modes while improving predictably as compute grows. **A joint FLOP-efficiency analysis of tokenizer plus generator finds the approach compute-optimal relative to direct pixel-space diffusion, reaching an FID-50K of 2.18 with JiT-L.** Encoder scaling laws for diffusability on `ImageNet` and the text-to-image dataset `GPIC` extrapolate to matching `DINOv2` with 7x fewer FLOPs and `WebSSL` with 8x fewer.

papers.title: Revisiting Simple Baselines for Relational Deep Learning
papers.abstract: Relational deep learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning end-to-end predictive models over relational databases by representing them as temporal heterogeneous graphs. Recent advances based on graph neural networks and Transformers have achieved strong performance across diverse domains. However, the effectiveness of simpler relational baselines remains underexplored, making it difficult to assess how much architectural complexity is needed to achieve strong predictive performance. Motivated by the observation that predictive signals arise from target attributes, relational attributes, and historical labels, we revisit how effectively these signals can be exploited using simple propagation methods. We adapt fixed low-pass feature propagation to relational entity graphs and train an MLP for prediction. The resulting predictions are further refined using Correct-and-Smooth, a graph-based label propagation algorithm that incorporates historical labels over task-specific meta-graphs connecting target entities. Across classification and regression tasks on RelBench, an MLP trained on neighborhood-filtered features outperforms one using only target-entity features on most tasks and recovers a substantial portion of the performance of heterogeneous GNNs. Correct-and-Smooth provides further gains from historical labels, although applying it requires a separately constructed meta-graph because connections among target entities are not directly specified by the relational entity graph. Together, our studies revisit the effectiveness of established propagation methods as simple RDL baselines while identifying canonical meta-graph construction as a key challenge for effective label propagation.
papers.summary: Relational deep learning (RDL) treats a relational database as a temporal heterogeneous graph and trains graph neural networks (GNNs) or Transformers end to end, but how much of that architectural complexity is actually needed has been unclear. Reasoning that predictive signal comes from target attributes, relational attributes, and historical labels, the authors apply fixed low-pass feature propagation over the relational entity graph, train a multilayer perceptron on the smoothed features, and refine predictions with `Correct-and-Smooth`, a label-propagation method run over task-specific meta-graphs connecting target entities. **On RelBench classification and regression tasks, an MLP on neighborhood-filtered features beats a target-only MLP on most tasks and recovers a substantial portion of heterogeneous GNN performance**, with `Correct-and-Smooth` adding further gains from historical labels. Because the relational entity graph does not directly connect target entities, constructing a canonical meta-graph emerges as the key open challenge for label propagation in this setting.

papers.title: PrismaCoder: Pushing the Boundaries of Open Multimodal Code Intelligence through Decomposed Rubric Synthesis
papers.abstract: Multimodal code intelligence connects the symbolic world of programs with the visual world their execution creates. Interest in this capability is burgeoning, as models are increasingly asked to produce charts, webpages, animations, and semi-structured documents. Recently, proprietary models have pushed far ahead, producing interactive artifacts even from a text description or a screenshot alone. Yet their data and training remain closed, and open progress is held back by the quantity and quality of available data and by the pipelines and methods for producing it. Quality is the harder of the two, since a sample must be correct as a program, well built, and above all visually right once rendered. No existing signal covers all three. Execution often returns just a pass or fail, code similarity does not map to the visual output, and task-specific verifiers do not generalize. To push open progress further, we start from the data side with PrismaForge, a hierarchical data pipeline centered on a synthesized rubric that decomposes these factors into checkable criteria. The same rubric serves as both filter and reward: it curates the supervised corpus, then drives reinforcement learning on visual-coding tasks. Leveraging PrismaForge for data synthesis and filtering, we build PrismaCoder-2M, the most diverse open dataset for multimodal code intelligence and the largest to date. On the model side, we train PrismaCoder-9B and PrismaCoder-35B on this data and release both. They lead the open state of the art by a wide margin and rival leading proprietary systems. Our analyses further show that the proposed rubric-based pipeline improves multimodal coding performance across model backbones. We release our code and data at https://qiushisun.github.io/PrismaCoder-Home/.
papers.summary: Generating charts, webpages, animations, and semi-structured documents from text or screenshots has been dominated by closed proprietary models, with open progress limited by data quantity and especially quality, since a good sample must be a correct program, well built, and visually right once rendered, and no single signal checks all three. `PrismaForge` is a hierarchical data pipeline centered on a synthesized rubric that decomposes those factors into checkable criteria, used first to filter the supervised corpus and then as the reward for reinforcement learning on visual-coding tasks. The resulting `PrismaCoder-2M` is presented as the largest and most diverse open dataset for multimodal code intelligence, and `PrismaCoder-9B` and `PrismaCoder-35B` trained on it **lead the open state of the art by a wide margin and rival leading proprietary systems**, with analyses showing the rubric pipeline helps across model backbones. Code, data, and both models are released.

papers.title: Detection of Potato Plant Leaf Diseases using Convolutional Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Potato is an important food-security crop in Ethiopia, but its production is affected by foliar diseases, particularly early blight and late blight. This study develops a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) to classify potato leaves into three categories: healthy, early blight, and late blight. The proposed model was trained using 2,215 images from the PlantVillage dataset and evaluated on an independent field dataset containing 247 images collected from potato farms in Banja, Awi Zone, Ethiopia. On PlantVillage, the model achieved 99.04% training accuracy, 98.21% validation accuracy, and 98.66% test accuracy. On the field dataset, it achieved 90.28% accuracy. The study also compares the proposed CNN with VGG16 and MobileNetV2 in terms of classification performance and computational efficiency. The proposed model contains 446,787 trainable parameters, occupies approximately 1.70 MB, and requires an average of 5.58 seconds per training epoch in the reported experimental setup, compared with 9.96 seconds for VGG16 and 7.68 seconds for MobileNetV2. The results demonstrate the potential of a compact CNN for potato leaf disease classification and highlight the importance of independent field evaluation, where image conditions are more variable than in controlled benchmark datasets. The proposed approach may support preliminary disease identification for smallholder farmers in Ethiopia and similar agricultural settings.
papers.summary: Early blight and late blight threaten potato production in Ethiopia, motivating a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) that classifies leaf images as healthy, early blight, or late blight. The model has 446,787 parameters and a footprint of about 1.7 MB, was trained on 2,215 `PlantVillage` images, and was compared with `VGG16` and `MobileNetV2` on accuracy and per-epoch training time, where it trained fastest. It reached 98.66% test accuracy on `PlantVillage`, but **accuracy fell to 90.28% on an independent set of 247 field images from farms in Banja, Awi Zone**, underscoring the gap between curated benchmarks and variable field conditions.

papers.title: PerSo: Investigating Facets of LLMs' Social Intelligence in Real-World Persuasion Scenarios
papers.abstract: Understanding the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly important for applications involving human-AI interaction and multi-agent environments. Social intelligence comprises two aspects: cognitive intelligence, the ability to infer others' mental states, and behavioral intelligence, the ability to select appropriate social actions based on these inferences to achieve social goals. Persuasion provides a natural testbed in which both aspects are simultaneously at play, yet prior benchmarks typically evaluate them in isolation using synthetic scenarios. We introduce PerSo, a benchmark that evaluates both aspects on real-world persuasion dialogues from Reddit's ChangeMyView community, using an LLM-in-the-loop pipeline to construct the evaluation tasks, validated through human annotation. Our evaluation of diverse LLMs shows that performance generally scales with model size but varies across dimensions. The strongest LLM slightly surpasses the best observed human performance on the behavioral task, while the best human participant remains ahead on the cognitive task.
papers.summary: Social intelligence in large language models (LLMs) spans cognitive intelligence, inferring others' mental states, and behavioral intelligence, choosing actions that achieve social goals, yet existing benchmarks test them separately on synthetic scenarios. `PerSo` evaluates both facets on real persuasion dialogues from Reddit's ChangeMyView community, with tasks built by an LLM-in-the-loop pipeline and validated through human annotation. Across diverse models, performance generally scales with model size but varies by dimension: **the strongest LLM slightly surpasses the best observed human on the behavioral task, while the best human participant still leads on the cognitive task**.

papers.title: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting
papers.abstract:
Automated research with LLM agents has shown promising results in various domains. Through iterative refinement and scored verifiers, LLM agents are capable of discovering new ideas. There are different ways to scale automated research: let one agent iterate for longer, run several agents in parallel, or further let the parallel agents communicate and build on one another's candidates. However, we find that all three strategies eventually plateau as the agents accumulate history. Each agent becomes anchored to its own past attempts, making fewer and smaller edits. Beyond this point, additional budget brings little further improvement. In this paper, we show that the key to scaling discovery further is to forget. Periodically discarding the search state, including every agent's session and the candidate history, and restarting from the best candidate found so far, unblocks the search and pushes the same budget further.
  We implement forgetting in a team of agents with communication and evaluate it on four tasks spanning heuristic programming, kernel optimization and model training. The results show up to 15% improvement compared to parallel agents, and up to 39% compared to a single agent. Our results suggest that, for open-ended discovery, what an agent is allowed to remember matters as much as how much compute it is given.
papers.summary: LLM agents can discover new ideas by iterating against scored verifiers, but the usual ways to scale this, running one agent longer, running many in parallel, or letting parallel agents share candidates, all plateau as agents accumulate history and anchor on their own past attempts with fewer and smaller edits. The proposed remedy is to periodically forget: discard every agent's session and the entire candidate history, then restart from the best candidate found so far. Implemented in a communicating team of agents and tested on four tasks spanning heuristic programming, kernel optimization, and model training, **forgetting improves results by up to 15% over parallel agents and up to 39% over a single agent at the same budget**. The authors argue that what an agent is allowed to remember matters as much as how much compute it receives.

papers.title: Manac\'a-1B-Instruct-2: Reproducible Safety Alignment for a Native Brazilian-Portuguese LLM. Negative DPO Results, a Controlled Composition Scan, and a Silent Failure Mode of the LLM Judge
papers.abstract: Brazilian Portuguese remains underserved by open-source language models, and the few that are safety-aligned rarely document what did not work or validate comparisons with statistical significance. We present Manac\'a-1B-Instruct-2, the second-generation post-training alignment of Manac\'a-1B (1.72B parameters, trained from scratch for PT-BR), with an SFT corpus of 291,223 examples. We document three DPO attempts, all negative, including a case where the training reward margin reaches 1.0 while free generation does not change at all, and show that safety came from a dedicated safety-SFT (LLM-jp AnswerCarefully style), refined over three iterations until closing the safety-helpfulness frontier. A controlled scan of the fraction of general data in the safety-SFT mix (10% to 60%) reveals a non-monotonic over-refusal curve with a knee point at 40-50%. The final model is compared against four external PT-BR models on the same items, with Wilson confidence intervals and paired McNemar tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction: the lower bound of its safety interval (94.1%) lies above the upper bound of all four baselines. We also report a methodological finding for LLM-judge evaluation: on two of six safety items in MT-Bench-PT, the judge categorically refuses to assign a score regardless of the evaluated response, silently reducing the effective N of that category in every prior report of the project. We complement this with an n-gram decontamination check and a Chinchilla-anchored compute-budget table that attributes the gap in general capability to pre-training scale rather than alignment methodology. All code, raw data, logs, and scripts that produce every reported number are publicly released.
papers.summary: Brazilian Portuguese has few safety-aligned open language models, and those that exist rarely document failed attempts or test comparisons for statistical significance. `Manacá-1B-Instruct-2` is the second-generation alignment of a 1.72B-parameter model trained from scratch for the language, using a 291,223-example supervised fine-tuning (SFT) corpus. Three Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) attempts all failed, including one whose training reward margin reached 1.0 while free generation did not change at all, so safety came instead from an `AnswerCarefully`-style safety-SFT refined over three iterations, with a controlled scan showing over-refusal follows a non-monotonic curve with a knee at 40 to 50% general data. **Against four external PT-BR models with Wilson intervals and Holm-Bonferroni-corrected McNemar tests, the model's 94.1% safety lower bound exceeds every baseline's upper bound**, and the authors also report that the LLM judge on `MT-Bench-PT` categorically refuses to score two of six safety items, silently shrinking the effective sample in every prior report of the project.

papers.title: Recovering Reliable Supervision via Critique-Guided On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model on its own rollouts with token-level supervision from a teacher, assuming that the teacher can reach a correct answer from any prefix the student writes. We call this property the recoverability of the teacher and show it fails on incorrect rollouts: the teacher follows student errors, although it recognizes them. We propose CriticOPD, using error recognition to restore recoverability. The teacher critiques an incorrect rollout, allowing the student to rewrite its solution following the error. The resulting output, including the critique as privileged information, is scored by the teacher while the student uses the revision without the critique for training. On two Qwen3 students and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CriticOPD improves OPD, with the largest gains on competition problems.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts with token-level teacher supervision, implicitly assuming the teacher can reach a correct answer from any prefix the student writes. The authors show this recoverability fails on incorrect rollouts, where the teacher follows the student's errors even though it recognizes them. `CriticOPD` has the teacher critique the faulty rollout so the student can rewrite its solution from the error onward, and the teacher scores the revision with the critique as privileged information while the student trains on the revision alone. **On two Qwen3 students across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, the method improves over standard OPD, with the largest gains on competition problems.**
papers.highlight_summary:
On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts with the teacher's next-token distribution as target, which only corrects mistakes if the teacher can still reach the right answer from the student's prefix. The authors show this recoverability collapses after a student error even though the teacher still recognizes the error, and propose `CriticOPD`, where the teacher critiques a failed rollout, the student rewrites from its last mistake with the critique in context, and the teacher scores that rewrite with the critique as privileged information the student never sees at training or inference.

- Diagnosing a `Qwen3-1.7B` student against a `Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507` teacher on `DAPO-Math-17k`, teacher continuation accuracy on incorrect rollouts of teacher-solvable problems falls from **0.82 to 0.29** as the prefix grows, with up to **50%** of failed teacher continuations ending in the student's own wrong answer, yet the precision of the teacher's flagged errors stays at **73 to 81%** across all recoverability bins.
- For each incorrect rollout the teacher, given the reference answer, lists erroneous paragraphs with short fixes, the student keeps its prefix through the last flagged error and rewrites the remainder with the critique appended, and only that student-written suffix is trained with the critique-conditioned teacher distribution as target, which raises teacher recoverability on the rewrite from **0.14 to 0.67** at 75% of the continuation.
- On six math benchmarks `CriticOPD` lifts average accuracy over `OPD` from **50.08 to 54.65** for `Qwen3-1.7B` and from **34.80 to 38.86** for `Qwen3-0.6B`, with the largest gains on `AIME 2024`, `AIME 2025`, and `AMC 2023` at +6.01, +7.36, and +6.94 points, beating `FastOPD` and `RelayOPD` by 2.10 and 0.97 points on the larger student and reaching its selected checkpoint with **0.42 times** the total training compute of OPD despite one extra teacher and student generation per critiqued rollout.
- Ablations show the critique is the active ingredient, since removing it costs **5.90** points and drops below plain OPD while scoring the suffix without the critique costs 1.19, and the per-token advantage decomposes into the OPD advantage plus a pointwise-mutual-information reward under which a correcting continuation leads an error-continuing one by **1.47** per token versus 0.24 under OPD scoring.
- The method depends on reference answers to trigger and ground the critic, so it applies directly only to verifiable domains, and it was tested only on math with non-thinking `Qwen3` students plus a single-seed `OLMo-3` run, uses a critic whose flags are only 73 to 81% valid, trains with a biased surrogate gradient because the suffix is sampled with the critique but the student's log-probabilities are computed without it, and part of the gain arrives with longer responses alongside modest declines on code benchmarks.

papers.title: One Task, Many Interfaces: Simple Cross-Interface Consistency Training Improves LLM Agent Robustness
papers.abstract: Post-training binds the competence of an LLM agent to the interface it was trained on. Semantics-preserving perturbations of that interface, such as renaming an action or changing the notation, leave the underlying task unchanged yet make the agent worse at it. Scoring each sample independently means interface randomization only broadens this dependence from a single interface to the training interface distribution, so out-of-distribution perturbations still degrade the agent. We propose Cross-Interface Policy Regularization (CIPR), a self-supervised objective that replaces action names with uninformative identifiers and presents each training sample under two interfaces in which equivalent actions are identified by construction. CIPR penalizes the KL divergence between the action distributions induced under the two interfaces, so the policy behaves consistently across them. We evaluate CIPR in both supervised and reinforcement-learning post-training, where it improves robustness. On agentic function calling, held-out interface perturbations reduce the accuracy of a post-trained agent by nearly 25%, and CIPR recovers 10.5% while leaving accuracy on the unchanged interface intact.
papers.summary: Post-training binds an LLM agent's competence to the exact interface it saw, so semantics-preserving changes such as renaming an action or altering notation degrade performance even though the task is unchanged, and randomizing interfaces during training only widens that dependence to the training distribution. Cross-Interface Policy Regularization (`CIPR`) replaces action names with uninformative identifiers, presents each training sample under two interfaces whose equivalent actions are matched by construction, and penalizes the KL divergence between the resulting action distributions so the policy behaves consistently across them. Applied in both supervised and reinforcement-learning post-training, it improves robustness: **held-out interface perturbations cut a post-trained agent's function-calling accuracy by nearly 25%, and the regularizer recovers 10.5%** while leaving accuracy on the unchanged interface intact.

papers.title: Latent Compaction with Test-Time Training
papers.abstract: Long contexts enlarge key--value (KV) caches, increasing memory use and attention costs during generation. Compressing these caches must preserve information for unseen questions. We introduce **Latent Compaction**, which learns a compact document-specific cache through test-time training. We initialize cache entries using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity. Training first fits attention outputs and log-normalizers to those of the full cache, with reconstruction-selected entries held fixed. It then jointly optimizes the entire cache through end-to-end distillation from the full-cache model. Model weights remain frozen throughout, and training uses only generic prompts about the document, without access to downstream questions or answers. Experiments on RULER, LongBench, and Phonebook Lookup demonstrate substantial gains over budget-matched compression baselines. On a RULER, for example, our method achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32$\times$ compression, compared with 40.0% for KVZip+. The method also transfers across model scales and families, with retrieval gains on both Qwen3 and MiniCPM5. These results show that treating the KV cache as a neural network and optimizing it with test-time training can preserve retrieval accuracy under aggressive compression. The code is released at https://www.github.com/THUNLP/latent-compaction
papers.summary: Long contexts inflate key-value (KV) caches, raising memory use and attention cost during generation, and any compression must preserve information for questions not yet seen. `Latent Compaction` learns a compact document-specific cache through test-time training with frozen model weights: entries are initialized from reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity, first fitted to the full cache's attention outputs and log-normalizers with reconstruction-selected entries held fixed, then jointly optimized by end-to-end distillation using only generic prompts about the document. On `RULER` the method reaches **96.7% accuracy at 32x compression, versus 40.0% for the strongest budget-matched baseline**, `KVZip+`, with substantial gains on `LongBench` and `Phonebook Lookup` as well. Retrieval gains transfer across scales and families, including `Qwen3` and `MiniCPM5`.

papers.title: Learnable Hodge-Laplacian Driven Mixture of Experts for Steady-PDE Surrogates on Coarse Unstructured Meshes
papers.abstract: Current approaches for steady partial differential equations surrogate models on unstructured meshes apply a single mixing mechanism to the whole solution. This paper proposes an architecture that partitions the solution among vanilla transformer experts, each focused on a different spectral scale. The partition is built from a discrete Hodge Laplacian $L_0=\star_0^{-1} d_0^{\top}\star_1 d_0$, that serves as a fitting layer measuring high-frequency content. A gating mechanism takes the mesh as input and produces the per-vertex weights that recombine the expert outputs. AirFRANS is a steady Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) airfoil benchmark. We evaluate our approach in a reduced remeshed version of the benchmark with each unstructured mesh counting 9.6K faces and 4.9K vertices. We compare our approach with the Transolver on the same dataset and dataset slit. Our approach reduces relative $L_2$ error by 31\% and interior mean squared error by 47\%.
papers.summary: Surrogate models for steady partial differential equations on unstructured meshes usually apply a single mixing mechanism to the entire solution field, which struggles to capture smooth and sharp features at once. The proposed architecture splits the solution among several vanilla transformer experts, each assigned a different spectral scale, using a discrete Hodge Laplacian as a fitting layer that measures high-frequency content, while a gate that reads the mesh produces per-vertex weights to recombine the expert outputs. On a reduced, remeshed version of the `AirFRANS` Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) airfoil benchmark, with meshes of about 9.6K faces and 4.9K vertices, the method **reduces relative L2 error by 31% and interior mean squared error by 47%** compared with `Transolver` on the same data split.

papers.title: Continuum Attention
papers.abstract: We introduce Continuum Attention (CA), a causal Transformer attention operator that replaces discrete key and value lookup with integration over a continuous, piecewise linear memory curve. Each query induces an exponential relevance density along the curve. Integrating the density and interpolated values yields exact normalized attention from closed form exponential moments, including half token boundary contributions. The gradients follow analytically from moments of order at most two, enabling parallel GPU implementations while retaining quadratic sequence complexity and the standard Transformer decoder. Compared with ordinary softmax and focal attention, CA reduces mean validation negative log likelihood by 0.0200 and 0.0480 nats per byte, respectively, winning all paired comparisons. An additional disjoint validation slice yields a 0.0457 nats per byte advantage over the strongest selected softmax baseline, with a paired 95% confidence interval. These findings motivate continuous integration as a promising attention alternative while leaving larger scale generalization open.
papers.summary: Standard causal Transformer attention performs a discrete lookup over keys and values; `Continuum Attention` (CA) instead integrates over a continuous, piecewise linear memory curve along which each query induces an exponential relevance density. Because the density and interpolated values integrate in closed form from exponential moments of order at most two, attention and its gradients are computed exactly, run in parallel on GPUs, and keep the standard decoder structure and quadratic sequence complexity. In byte-level language modeling, CA **lowers mean validation negative log likelihood by 0.0200 nats per byte versus softmax attention** and by 0.0480 versus focal attention, winning every paired comparison, with a further 0.0457 nats per byte gain over the strongest softmax baseline on a disjoint validation slice; generalization to larger scales is left open.

papers.title: Price of Anarchy of First-Price Auctions in Agentic Markets
papers.abstract: An agentic market is a decentralized serving-time market where AI agents bid to claim each user prompt. An agent's bid is based on its expected value for the prompt, which is the expectation of the reward for its response minus its inference costs. First-price auctions (FPAs), in which the highest bidder pays its bid and receives the prompt, are a natural way to allocate prompts in such a market, since they are simple and transparent to run, and do not require central knowledge of private capabilities and costs. However, FPAs are not truthful: participants may bid less than their true value in the hope of a larger profit, and the prompt may then be allocated to someone other than the bidder who values it the most. This welfare loss is quantified by the $\textit{price-of-anarchy}$ (PoA). In this paper, we argue that agentic markets are likely to possess features that reduce the price-of-anarchy. The first is a $\textit{competitive floor}$, which occurs when multiple bidders usually value the prompt above some baseline share of the optimal welfare (e.g., because the best models are often distilled into cheaper alternatives, which perform similarly). We show that competition among them then limits the welfare loss, which can be driven to zero as the floor rises. The second feature is $\textit{near-independence}$ of values after conditioning on the prompt, which occurs when most of the predictable variation in the expected value is determined by the difficulty of the prompt. As the value distribution approaches conditional independence, we can derive an efficiency guarantee that approaches a factor of $1 - 1/e^2$ of the optimal welfare. Thus, both features give rise to welfare lower bounds that are significantly better than the well-known general case of $1 - 1/e$. We validate these results empirically using auctions with strategic bidders simulated on the EmbedLLM prompt routing dataset.
papers.summary: In an agentic market, AI agents bid at serving time to claim each user prompt, with bids based on expected reward minus inference cost, and first-price auctions (FPAs) are a simple allocation mechanism that is nevertheless not truthful, since bidders may shade below their true value. The work quantifies the resulting welfare loss through the price of anarchy (PoA) and argues that two features likely in such markets shrink it: a competitive floor, where several bidders value a prompt above a baseline share of optimal welfare because strong models are often distilled into cheaper near-equivalents, and near-independence of values once conditioned on prompt difficulty. Under a competitive floor the welfare loss can be driven to zero as the floor rises, and under conditional independence the **efficiency guarantee approaches 1 − 1/e² of optimal welfare**, both improving on the general-case bound of 1 − 1/e. Simulated auctions with strategic bidders on the `EmbedLLM` prompt routing dataset support the analysis.

papers.title: Your Transformer Is Secretly Elastic
papers.abstract: Scaling up transformers has produced models with broad capabilities, deployed across heterogeneous hardware and fluctuating workloads. Yet, model families offer only a few fixed sizes (e.g., S, B, L), forcing users to commit to a model based on hardware and latency constraints. This rigidity is often suboptimal under varying query loads. We introduce a retraining-free method that elastifies pre-trained transformers into a single model that adapts on-the-fly across a continuum of computational budgets. Our key contribution is a differentiable relaxation of the functional unit-ranking problem: unlike prior work, which optimizes a single importance weight per MLP block or attention head, we rank every individual MLP neuron and attention head jointly, on a common scale, by minimizing the model's loss under soft pruning across many sparsity targets, all at once. Across 27 vision and text transformer encoders ranging from 22M to 8B parameters, our method yields smooth degradation up to 60% sparsity and outperforms one-shot baselines under deep pruning. For example, pruning DINOv3 ViT-H+/16 to 50% sparsity removes 427M parameters while reducing ImageNet-1k linear-probing accuracy by only 0.8%, without the need for weight correction or retraining. At 60% sparsity, a pruned AugReg ViT-B/16 model achieves up to $1.80\times$ higher throughput and $1.26\times$ lower single-query latency on an A100 GPU. Elastic models are produced in minutes, with construction time scaling sub-linearly with parameter count.
papers.summary: Model families ship in a few fixed sizes, forcing users to commit to one size even as hardware and query loads vary. The method elastifies a pre-trained transformer into a single model that can run at any point along a continuum of compute budgets without retraining, by solving a differentiable relaxation of the unit-ranking problem that scores every MLP neuron and attention head jointly on a common scale, minimizing loss under soft pruning across many sparsity targets at once. Across 27 vision and text transformer encoders from 22M to 8B parameters, accuracy degrades smoothly up to 60% sparsity and beats one-shot pruning baselines; pruning `DINOv3 ViT-H+/16` to 50% sparsity **removes 427M parameters while costing only 0.8% linear-probing accuracy** on `ImageNet-1k`, with no weight correction or retraining. At 60% sparsity a pruned `AugReg ViT-B/16` reaches up to 1.80x higher throughput and 1.26x lower single-query latency on an A100 GPU, and elastic models are built in minutes with construction time scaling sub-linearly in parameter count.

papers.title: Co-Evolving Acting and Forecasting for Language Agents
papers.abstract:
Training language agents is bottlenecked by the high cost of long-horizon rollouts, yet standard agentic reinforcement learning (RL) learns only from a terminal scalar reward, leaving the supervision in intermediate steps largely unused. Prior work exploits this supervision through value targets that estimate per-step success probabilities or observation targets that fit environment response.
